_childDocuments_.review: So I think it's only fair that I revisit this since I have since put in another 90 hours since my first review (and I think I'm addicted). I must admit I judged too soon and I have left my original review up for reference. If you want the short answer, yes I think it's worth the purchase but read on for why.My original problem turned out to be my own failures. The game is not easy, in fact I would say it suffers from a classic pitfall in this type of game: the learning cliff. But that said I wouldn't change it, because I hate games that hold your hand too much. In fact in retrospect this game does a great job to hold your hand just enough to not be annoying on additional playthroughs yet still let you fail by your own stupidity.Designing a production line is frustrating, complicated, and yet amazingly rewarding process. (prepare to ask "where did the last 4 hours go"?). Unlocking new toys is fun as hell! Realizing you unlocked something amazing and can't build it until you go find a bunch of new stuff is super annoying (in that I get to go search for stuff and die trying way), but wait there's more!Being chased by scary ass giant freaking spiders will probably induce nightmares (there's an arachnophobe mode which changes the sprites, thanks devs but I like my adrenaline injections)! You will learn the sounds of some mobs and reflexively jump to avoid their attack. Oh and even though it doesn't kill stuff there is no end to the fun of running over above mentioned mobs with your dune buggy thing. Yes I have parked the vehicle on top of them to keep them from attacking me, this is a viable tactic.Ultimately I would say buy the game if you have $25 to spend (at time of writing) and love these types of crafting exploring games. But do be aware that there are bugs, some of them can be fun, others annoying. However I haven't seen a truly game breaking bug yet, so for early access at this price point it's a great game so far.P.S. If you're like me and struggling, go find the wiki and an online map to help you out. It may feel a bit like cheating but even on my second play through I am finding the wiki very helpful!Original Review:Honestly I wanted to love this game. And on a level I do love it, which is why it pains me to say no right now. Ultimately I love this type of builder game, I loved Factorio for example, however I hated resource depletion in that game. I had thought maybe this game turned it into 3d and ditched that, which it did. BUT, the problem is power generation. There are no other depletion mechanics but after a short period I found myself constantly maintaining power generators. I want to love this game, and on a level I do, but I also want this game to be more of a sandbox than it is. It is for this reason that I at this moment I can't so solidly "yes buy it". I do hope given the early access status that the game will catch up.

_childDocuments_.review: As a pioneer for FICSIT Inc, I have logged 167 hours of work as of the time of writing this. _childDocuments_.review: It's hard to begin to tell, what makes this game so great. One aspect is, that it doesn't try to be a factorio-3D. There are commonalities but it is a really different gameplay with its own focus. Besides the countless options to build up and link your industries already implemented in the game, the world is designed lovingly and full of secret places to uncover. _childDocuments_.review: I absolutely love this game! i'm at almost 60 hours of game play, it's insane how the pacing in this game is perfect. Grinding to reach an objective doesn't feel like grinding. Especially when you think about the research aspect of this game, the elevator, building your new toys. I keep making fun new discoveries late in the game about stuff I could have been using the entire time!! I'm at the point of the game where I'm drawing different resources from different biomes on the map and finally going all out and creating my organized base to create a fully automated production line. And that my friends is pretty satisfactory.

_childDocuments_.review: The pinnacle of base builder crafting games, hands down. It's not a voxel miner, mind you, so if you're after that aspect maybe try Astroneer. But if turning "one workbench where you hammer out iron parts" into "a sprawling factory that extracts various ores and liquids and churns out quantum computers" is the kind of thing you look for in a crafting base builder, you'll have a good time with Satisfactory. The exploration aspect is also excellent, with a huge world that seems insurmountably large at first, but that you'll gradually reach the far corners of with the vehicles you unlock. You'll even be able to automate entire outposts' and bases' logistics with trains and drones.Speaking of which, Satisfactory has been an example of Early Access done right. The devs are clear about their intentions for each update, and provide general but reliable release windows. If you don't want to wait for new content, they have an experimental branch to beta test with. So far, they've already met and exceeded the original scope of the game, so I wouldn't be bothered if they took it out of Early Access, but, I guess they will once they feel like it's finished. I'm sure they'll continue to improve it after the last EA update though.

_childDocuments_.review: As always when writing a review, I read what people are saying in the negatives and I do have to agree with a lot of what I'm seeing. However, this game is in early access and the devs are constantly updating it and adding new features. In fact, a lot of the reviews I read from 2020-2022 aren't all that relevant now.Now, if, like me, you're coming into this from something like Factorio or Dyson Sphere Program - well, you'll either be pleasantly surprised, or majorly put off. Rather than being a full-on factory-building and automation game, this is more like a semi-open-world sandbox builder. I could probably make a case that this game is more akin to Minecraft with tech mods, than it is Factorio. That's not to say that Satisfactory and Factorio don't share a lot of similarities, because they do - for obvious reasons, but, at least for me, the flow of gameplay is very different. Firstly, Satisfactory has a single large map, that is pre-built - which does mean that once you've explored the map a few times in Satisfactory, you know where everything is - however there is far more to discover here and the scenery and layout are far more interesting than anything you'll get in something like Factorio. You aren't just looking for your next resource vein to go and dump 45 mining rigs and 400 smelters on, you're looking for crashed pods to loot of their precious hard-drives, alien slugs to farm to turn into overclocking devices and interesting vistas.Secondly, which possibly should have been firstly, this game is first-person and 3D, not a top-down overview where your player avatar is nothing more than an extension of your mouse cursor. Exploring and building feel so much more immersive with this setup and it also has the added bonus of allowing the player to see the world for what is actually is - and here it is beautifully done, with different biomes and terrain types.Thirdly, which will be another big point from people coming from games like Factorio, is that combat here is mostly up to the player. You aren't playing a tower-defence simulator in the later stages of play - this is something that the devs have said they will not be implementing. Some wild animals will attack you if you get too close, but they will not come and destroy your factory or try to ruin your life. For me, these are all pros of Satisfactory, rather than cons, so here are some of the cons of this game:If you are playing solo, getting through some of the phases will take you absolutely ages, as, unlike Factorio, there is no copy-paste blueprint function for your production-lines. There are blueprints in this game, but they require unlocking a specific technology that might take you a good couple of hours (if not quite a few) to unlock and then they need to be manually built first in a specific building, before you can then use them elsewhere.Now, I don't think Factorio's implementation would work here, but I would say that this feature certainly needs work in Satisfactory.Furthermore, as this game is 3D, the environment can be far harder to work with and build in than Factorio, which is mostly flat. Here, destroying terrain is not as simple as a right-click to mine it away, you need specific tech and items, some of which are not available for quite a while on a new play session. Some smaller rocks do get destroyed with the use of the chainsaw, but I expect this is more a glitch/exploit and likely to be patched out. On top of having uneven terrain with obstacles, there is the 3rd dimension of verticality here. You can either make do with what you have, or replace the gorgeous terrain with gaudy foundation platforms. Or, do what a lot of players seemingly do, which is create a giant platform over the terrain and build on that instead. Going back to the first point, the way research and progression is done is this game could use some work. Some of the recipes are ridiculously expensive, while others are locked behind the "M.A.M" in what feels like a "oh shoot, we wanted that in phase 2, but forgot it, so let's dump it in this separate research facility". Furthermore, some objects that should just be there from the get-go, such as lights for your factory, or walkways and modular walls are locked behind a resource sink that requires a metric ton of input, before you can purchase those items from an in-game shop. This is a game about building my own factory, but I can't even have lights or sheet-metal walkways before I dump mid/end-game level materials/items into a sink? This review is already too long, so I'll finish up by saying that those are the pros and cons of this game for me. It's still in development and the devs are active and receptive to feedback (there's a specific bug reporting website), so what I dislike now, might be fixed/changed in the next big update (I know some are for U8). I'll certainly recommend this game.P.S: I didn't mention bugs because it's early access. Personally, I experienced 2 hard-crashes in almost 50 hours of play, but barely anything game-breaking - just a fair amount of physics and engine jank.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like to build, if you like to plan, if you like to take out your calculator to perfect your ratios and make your factory more efficient, if you like to find ways to manage your space and make your factory aesthetically pleasing then this game is for you. _childDocuments_.review: new review: they fixed all the stuff below. It sill have some other issues but, way more playable and would recommend :Dold review: So for context, me and 2 friends started going for a run in multiplayer (no mods) before the 1.0 release and we hosted a server on a powerful server. The game has a lot of memory issues (CPU and GPU related). for a 13900k and 4080 should not have issues of this many crashes. We could count at least 20+ crashes with different errors every day. We checked the game files and found no problems. There are also a lot of errors on the server side and crashes all the time. List of problems:Keyboard input stops working sometimes forcing you to disconnect and reconnect to fix it.Blueprint missing pieces and even unconnectable belts when placing (console errors)Blueprints that cannot be connected (e.g. a long train track, conveyor line, hypertube line)Hypertube causing crashesTrains and trucks causing rubberbanding (client and server have really good internet connection and performance, so this is NOT a hardware or basic software issue. )-Train stations are not recognized by the game, forcing you to disassemble and reassemble them.Game crashes on some map areasGame crashes on random occasions, player loses all inventory, inventory chest/body is under the map (unreachable), hotbar also gets reset because now a new player instance is created, so you have to reset the hotbar only to crash again 5-10 minutes later to lose everything again.Conveyors and pipelines not connecting as they shouldAs a fellow software developer, I understand that there will always be problems. But stopping bug fixes for over 8 months is insane. I love this game and have played it for over 1500 hours. These issues should be considered critical. So we all take a break and hope that all the issues are fixed in 1.0. You guys have lost about 8+ players from my friend group in the last 3 months. I hope to revisit the game and give it another try. Coffee Stains, if you need any server files to analyze problems, contact me.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is really beautiful and I wanted to love it...but ended up refunding the game. Dismantle mode in this game is visually triggering for me.  There is a red pulsating frame that I can only tolerate for a second at a time.  It seems dismantle mode is rarely used in this game, so it might have been tolerable for me overall, but a still red overlay would have been preferable as a warning for me personally.The first person user interface gave me a bit of motion sickness and was visually uncomfortable.  The giant mechanical hand was really uncomfortable on my eyes.  I think it would have been less of an impact if I could have adjusted the hand size so that it was a lot smaller.  I tried playing with field of view settings and adjusted the vsync but the game was still visually uncomfortable for me personally.  The option of a third person view probably would have made all the difference for me as far as this goes.Getting to the craft table and the hub created a sensation like walking into a wall.  A third person view would have been much more comfortable visually, or alternatively a setting that would allow a more compact view so as to not have the walking into a wall sensation.I didn't find the user interface friendly or intuitive.  I found the scanner frustrating.  It was slow to scan and I couldn't tell whether it was scanning for iron or copper.  I kept trying to set it to copper, but kept finding iron.  Eventually I found copper but still wasn't sure whether I'd somehow managed to fluke setting the scanner to copper or whether picking the copper setting caused it to scan for both copper and iron and that by chance I picked a copper node to head towards or whether I just ran over a copper node by chance.I found placing stuff visually uncomfortable and random.  Whatever I was trying to place completely blocked my field of vision so where-ever it landed was totally random for me.  I had no sense that I would ever be able to arrange or align elements of my factory later in the game.  I couldn't work out how to get my first portable miner to work.   I placed it on an iron node but it didn't seem to be doing anything.  I couldn't find any way to interact with it other than picking it up and putting it down.  I had a friend beside me who raves about this game so I asked him how I get it to work.  Even though he raves about how good this game is, he couldn't get it to work either.  Also, the first person view made placing the portable miner really uncomfortable for me - like standing with my nose up against a wall trying to place it.I would definitely have another go at this game if a third person view was implemented.  I think that would make the user interface a lot less clunky and mostly resolve my issues as far as the visual discomfort I feel playing this game.  Which in turn would have me be more relaxed about dealing with other elements that I found un-intuitive - like understanding how the scanner and portable miner works.

_childDocuments_.review: Summary: Get Factorio if you want to build a factory.  Get Satisfactory if you want to explore.Pros:- Good graphics and world design.- Loading times are great considering the sheer amount of stuff I've built.- Good performance most of the time (the belt-placement-hologram has some kind of serious performance issue in extremely complex bases).- Exploration is fun and there are a lot of different biomes.Cons:- The alignment grid is too small, causing you to mis-click too often.- You can't continuously lay down belts, pipes or train tracks and you have to constantly backtrack when reaching the "too long" indicator.- Things don't snap or align themselves in several situations where you'd expect them to which requires cumbersome workarounds.- It takes too long to move around your factory and you need to be physically present to do almost everything (including controlling trains).- Until mid-game, it's extremely cumbersome and time-consuming to build anything vertically.- Trains are incredibly annoying to use for all but the most trivial things.- Blueprints are too small to be useful.  It's basically impossible to use them to speed up train station and track construction.- Blueprints don't automatically connect belts/pipes/power to neighboring entities like they do in Factorio.  This means even if you have blueprints, a lot of your time is still spent connecting them.- There are six tiers of conveyor belts and upgrading them periodically will waste WAY too much of your time.  In Factorio, you would just have bots do this for you.  In Satisfactory, you have to do them all by hand.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is still in early access as I write this, and is currently fairly fun. There are quite a few items that have been removed, leaving redundant resources behind with no purpose that I assume will also be removed at some point in the future. Currently, there are multiple products for you to manufacture that have no purpose other than to further your objectives. There are also alien artifacts that the game demands you collect that have zero purpose, as of writing this. I hope that the developers have plans to rectify this in the future, too. But the game has some great mechanics to it! You can play music on an 80's boombox to jam out while you build, and even damage enemies with it. There are plenty of QOL items that you can earn to make your builds all the more unique and special to you. You can even mod the game already, somewhat. There are multiple areas of the map where you can start out, each with their own pros and cons. There are terrifying creatures, but great weapons. The rifle has a satisfying weight and fire to it. You should go into this game knowing that the goal isn't to reach your milestones and objectives as quickly as possible, however. You should take your time to build up each factory with care and love. Because, while the milestones and objectives can be completed rather quickly and easily, you will then be left with little-to-nothing left to do with yourself once you do. Unless you're seriously motivated by the game's mechanics to move on to further areas and rebuild fresh factories to connect back to your HUB, you'll have nothing at all to motivate you forward. The best advice that I can give you is to be slow and patient with objectives, while focusing on building your factories and leaving plenty of real estate for future machines that need to connect with them.

_childDocuments_.review: Automation games are games that in the past, I wouidn't have given a second thought to. It's simple enough to grasp the mechanics yet quite challenging, and as the name suggests, extremely satisfying to set up factories of ever increasing complexity. An absolute recommend for anyone who enjoys this kind of game.

_childDocuments_.review: You land on a vast, sprawling planet, with very little but your wits and a taser about you. You forage for leaves, twigs, and bits of metal. You turn this metal into a machine, powering it with the leaves. You then need another machine to make parts for the next machine, parts which you need to generate power, so you can stop picking up leaves. You then need more machines to make parts for the other machines you need to make, so you can upgrade your power even more. You build a large elevator, you paint it, and everything else, pink. You then realise you built all the other machines in the slightly wrong place, and now need to pull them down and rebuild them so you can more efficiently make parts for even more new machines. You go for a walk. You find new materials, meaning you can make even newer parts, but - you need more machines. But now your other machines need moving again, so you can be even more efficient. You start seeing conveyor belts in your dreams. You have suddenly spent 60 hours repeating all of the above. But you don't care. You need more machines. Repeat.

_childDocuments_.review: If you have played and enjoyed Factorio then this is the next logical progression from that game. A fully rendered 3D world, just the one map but loads of challenges gameplay-wise. There's the obvious challenging start to all these type of games but that is thankfully short and in the early game you are very much goal driven to improve things for yourself as you try to tame the planet you find yourself on and carve out a bit of the industrialisation you need, not just to survive and upgrade but to appease the people at Ficsit who want results in the form of uploads of the things you have made to give to them in return for unlocking technologies to make more complex items and push you to explore the planet even more.When it comes down to it this game offers a player a huge amount of depth and reward for their time, which keeps the game fresh. I tend to play in bouts now on my original world where things in some areas are chaotically laid out and although I have the best intentions to redesign the messy initial production and mining layout I just find a new unexploited area and build anew and keep the chaos as a reminder to myself of how not to do things.From a gameplay perspective you can play an number of ways but having some sort of plan is best. Enclosing your manufacturing works well as it keeps the dangerous creatures away when you're doing your thing with your production and resources. Getting transport networks up and running rather than endlessly long conveyors or pipes is a good move and there are plenty of great guides and videos and some excellently involved setups that you can try and emulate from the online community. I have spent most of my game time as a solo player but I think this game excels in the multi player. When playing mutiplayer I find working on a large scale project with friends is always a great way to have fun and while away some time with a great looking and hopefully functioning factory at the end of things.There's plenty of scope in this game, the customisation is excellent, the humour is there too and its a challenge that gives you a sense of real achievement when you get that little manufacturing problem sorted out or you come up with a smart way to do something. There is a bit of something for everyone and the technological advances are meaningful and stepped in a logical way but it does get complex in later stages and if you have a messy start setup then you will make the later stages of making the more complex components more difficult than it needs to be but that's part of the fun and challenge of this game.All in all I would recommend this game. Its still early access as I write this (Jan 2023) but its been around for a while now and is very much a polished experience. I have had many hours of play out of this game and I can say that my experience of playing has much better than Satisfactory. Buy it, play it and enjoy it, you won't be disappointed.

I do recommend a good computer with lots of memory and dedicated video memory, my computer has 16gb main and 8 vram with a Geforce GTX 2060 and I'm able to run the game on high and ultra graphic settings.No Con's except that starting over means starting from the very beginning of the tech tree and creatures can kill you very fast.  It would be nice to have a quick tutorial that explained each machine, otherwise YouTube has all the answers.Update: October 2022... Okay, I've restarted the game maybe 4 times in all since my first start with the game.  My new factory complex which contains 4 building, 3 of which are up to 3 levels each, is now in its third revamp and since update 5 and 6 I have now torn down alot and rebuilt using the new building parts.  As for my WORLD train system, well, that's in its 6th rebuild and I'm still working on it as of this update.  Oh, I now have 3 nuclear power plants (plus 2 more currently turned off) currently putting out nearly 14 million MW.  Still highly recommend the game and YES I'm still losing sleep.  Cheers !!

Seriously, when people say game are like crack, that's how I feel about this game. The game feeds you new systems at a pace where just as you have gotten to understand one production line, they give you something to do with it. That cycle repeats, and your factory grows. You'll be building production facilities all over the alien planet, and there is something so satisfying and relaxing about it. Honestly, now that I've hit Tier 7/8, I'll *likely* build a few new facilities with the new technology unlocked, then take a break to see where the updates take the game. It's kind of staggering how well made the game is, and yet they expect it to be "complete" in 2022. Cannot wait to play more as updates roll in. 100% heartily recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: 1.0 is out so I'm updating my review. A lot has been improved in this factory building game. I started a new game and the progression feels a lot better now. There are new options to keep your conveyers straight which helps a lot, and it's (mostly) a joy to build in this game, except when you accidentally build a blueprint 1 inch over from where you intended and have to erase it all.The graphics are still great, the world is beautiful and the music and sounds work perfectly. Getting the boombox later in the game makes for some serious jams. Sadly on my PC I have to turn the graphics settings to low if my base gets too hairy, but that gets the framerate back to playable in the most spaghetti base of situations.Multiplayer is improved a lot and I've had a blast co-op building. It is still a bit glitchy at times when building conveyers -- sometimes they just appear completely empty after you finalize the connections, and I've noticed even single player is oddly glitchy sometimes where connected conveyers are just not working until you delete and rebuild them. The only other negative is the devs did not improve combat at all from early access, they just added even more annoying enemies, and you are forced into situations where you have to fight something at literally every interesting discovery. Combat in the early game is a lot of "what hit me", "why am I dying", "how did that enemy randomly appear 300 feet in the air on a sky bridge I built to avoid enemies", "why am I flying 10000 feet off a cliff" and "this sucks". Later you get a machine gun with homing ammo and a hover pack so combat becomes "hold button down while sort of aiming at a target".  I'm little annoyed they didn't do anything to improve this aspect of the game. If you could keep the chievos on and turn the combat off, the it would be a lot better.All-in-all it's still a great game and a true early access success story the devs can be proud of the long road to get here. Hopefully the remaining glitches get ironed out soon!

_childDocuments_.review: This game can be addicting. It has an excellent game loop and progression. Everything is up to the player. The game doesn't dictate how you do things. Satisfactory is well suited for a lot of different players and play styles. You can build clip-infested spaghetti messes built for progression optimization, or jaw-dropping thousand hour masterpieces of aesthetic design. You can do anything in between.Do you like the brutal efficiency of a mega-factory with only using belts? Do you like the idea of modular factories with easily-expandable train lines. Do you just really love trains? Do you like to make fun of self-driving trucks getting confused? What about spending time getting perfect curves? It's your world.I enjoy playing this game just building and planning. There are many calculators available to help you. It is more fun to start the game without using them. As you figure out the game, you may enjoy restarting using all your learnings make more optimized factories. If you want to really get into large modular factories with trains/trucks/drones as logistic between factories you may enjoy Satisfactory Logistics or Satisfactory Factories depending on how you like to build your factory calculators.While this game can appeal to anyone, I think Satisfactory specializes in the player that likes sandbox building games without base defense, but like the progression. Resource nodes are infinite, so you can plan and expand without having existing factories go obsolete from resource exhaustion. Spending time building can be both for aesthetics and function. As you progress, an item production rate of 10/min could take thousands of machines. By then, you'll be a pro at planning. I like using blueprints - designing reusable and modular blueprints that interlock like a puzzle. I spend more time creating blueprints than actually building out a factory. I find it fun to iterate on these blueprints.I recommend a few mods if you enjoy building and want to do it more efficiently. Infinite Nudge: vertical nudging and more increment options. A save file does not depend on this mod and it works on non-modded servers. It is much faster to build with this mod. If you really like blueprints, Progressive Blueprints increase blueprints to up to a 8x8 foundation footprint. If you build a blueprint designer on a save file, that save file will need the mod, but you can create a blueprint on one savefile and import to another game. I do this on a "creative" savefile and import the blueprint to a dedicated server without the mod. I wish the mod supported 12x12 like it did pre-1.0 for those late game factories. I like all-in-one modular blueprints that can scale so that I can break a complete factory into fractional pieces. An example is my mid-game oil blueprints - 6x6x6 tileable with a power production block, plastic block, rubber block, and petroleum coke block. These can be stacked horizontal or vertically. As the game progresses, I can no longer fit entire production chains into a single blueprint block and planning interconnecting block blueprints gets more interesting.
_childDocuments_.name: Satisfactory

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, one of the most fun builder games I've played in a long time. The world; although not seed generated, is lush and the biomes are varied. In its current state, the game has only a few enemy types, but there are also a few friendlies along the way. You start small and progress in chunks. It's definitely for those who love logistical flow and planning. That might sound boring to some, but it's something that honestly isn't. Frustrating at times, yes; boring, never. There's a few bugs here and there, but as of writing this, it's still in early access. Would I recommend this? Definitely.  - Good graphical design - Music matches the game style - Simple UI and UX that is pretty intuitive - Many things to do, planning and exploring included - Alternative recipes to most items leading to more construction ideas - Tutorial is well thought out. - Good for those who enjoy a little bit of methodology and planning - A few bugs that get in the way from time to time** - Not good for those who want to go around blasting everything in sight... at least to begin with - More to come..?
_childDocuments_.name: Satisfactory

_childDocuments_.review: It's a factory building game like Factorio. In contrast to Factorio this game has a fully realized 3D world and this is a problem. The main game loop revolves around building various factory elements and the 3D world makes it difficult and tiresome to build those. In the 2D world of Factorio the act of lining up the buildings or removing swaths of constuction elements is easy and here it's a chore. You will spend some time designing your factory and a lot of time trying to align a conveyor belt against a constructor or something like that. The 3D nature of the world and FPS aspect of the game make it very unpleasant experience.

_childDocuments_.review: The opening cinematic is STUNNINGLY gorgeous. The game itself is nice graphically, but not nearly as nice as the opening. The worlds seem reasonably sized but they are honestly bland. Very little incentive to explore. The game play is just boring. It's just grinding materials until you can automate the grinding. Then grabbing things from one machine and moving it to another. Your goals are to send these items away via a terminal and your incentive to do so is the ability to make new items to send away. It's just grinding with extra steps and no real goal.

_childDocuments_.review: I concur with the majority of opinions:  THIS GAME IS FUN.   You gather/craft materials you need until you are able to begin automating the process.  The majority of materials have a production chain that you set up.  In addition to this you have a research tree to help you progress and make life easier.  There are aggressive alien lifeforms that will attack you, making exploration a challenge and not just passive wandering.  The coop is fun as well...I have a separate coop-only map as it is a much different experience having help.  This is one of those games where you look at the clock thinking an hour has gone by and it is actually 2-3 hours that have passed.  I can't wait to see where this game goes with future updates!

_childDocuments_.review: This game finally scratched the Sim City itch that I have been trying to ignore for over a decade. And even if you are new to builders, they do a great job of easing you into the grind with this one. I just completed 1.0 at 800 hours on this save, I had completed Early Access as well. I took my time and was able to avoid burnout, I used a simple scaled approach with emphasis on excess as too much planning ahead can lead to problems. _childDocuments_.review: Don't buy if you only meet the minimum specs for this game, they havent been updated in a very long time. We use UE5 now, and if the game isnt on your C drive you may have some issues. I own a 2060 and the game can't hold 60 on minimum settings if i wanna play at my own resolution. Also theres no option to downpatch without doing the lengthy depot download process manually, which many people may not know how. Not only can many people no longer play the game they paid for, but the devs also don't offer a solution to those in that situation. A build that caps at Update 7, or just a branch available per major release update would be highly appreciated by many people.Besides that though, the game itself is fun, especially if youre a nerd for logistics, and its pretty cool experimenting with different factory configurations to find out if a goal is even possible. Maybe it's not for everyone, but it doesn't make it any less fun to me.Again, you probably want like a 30xx card at the least if you want 1440p 60+fps on higher than minimum settings.

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent infrastructure building game that has it all; explore an exotic, hand-crafted map of nearly 50 square kilometers (which feels much bigger!), extract and exploit it's resources to extend ever-bigger, ever more complex and ever more satisfying factories, export items per space elevator, explode the local flora and fauna and grind your way to satisfaction!Great customization, great community, great dev team, I can't extol this game enough! _childDocuments_.review: It is good solo.  I'm sure it would be really good co-op, but I can't ever get any of my friends interested enough to give it a go.   I've never made it past the oil phase because tbh, it becomes almost too much work to manage solo at that point, and I generally lose interest and go do something else only to return to the game a few months later and try again.  I like it, but I don't love it.  The "combat" is dumb and should be taken out of the game altogether. It adds nothing and is actually just annoying as mobs guard some of the resources.  You can now turn the combat off in the settings which is nice.  I also think that it would have been more interesting to procedurally generate the environments.  The maps clearly have a formula that should be followed and on your 10th play through of the map, it gets kind of old.

_childDocuments_.review: Not yet on par with Factorio but it is already very, very good in its current state. The one thing I really miss is an end game challenge that builds up. Factorio does this very well with the constant threat of indigenous critters, which becomes a real challenge if you set the parameters yourself. I would like to have that choice in Satisfactory as well. For now all you are faced with is expanding your production to the next level. There is no threat whatshowever and you can potentially go through the whole game without ever expanding your factory much. The only restricting force is time. On the other hand, it is a far more beautiful game with the maps being a handcrafted piece of art. I would like to have a procedually generated choice, but I see why the devs went with the handcrafted world(s). The 3rd plane opens up so much more possibilities and fun expansions.   Exploration is as well superior to Factorio and I love the challenge in that.Keep up the good work Coffe Stain Studios!PS: I waited a full year to get it on Steam. It was the worst wait ever for a game I really wanted and I was tempted to just  re-open my Epic account to get this one game, but I managed to hold back. I closed my account on Epic 2 years ago because of horrible service, constant account hacks and absolute unethical business practices. Do not support scumbacks like Epic!

_childDocuments_.review: Wow...and I mean wow, that escalated fast!!! Here I was completely happy playing Valheim and obsessing over that. So many hours just gone and loving it. Then, I am just bored looking through the store and I notice this game called Satisfactory. I read some reviews, which are awesome, and then I think, why not. I download it and start to play having no idea what is about to happen. After 15 minutes, I am hooked and I mean HOOKED AF! I love this game more than AIR. If God said, would you like some oxygen to live or this game, I would take the game...100% Valheim is now on the back-burner and I can't believe I just said that. I love that game but this game is another level of fun. First off, this game is gorgeous. The graphics are truly awesome. The colors and textures are second to none. It reminds me a little of Avatar with the bright colors and gorgeous plants and wildlife. Second, the game play is just  a good way. It is a first person game that has a little bit of everything. Exploring, combating the alien animals on the planet and they are just awesome looking. It is a open world, you can go anywhere your heart desires. You have to survive, craft, and then gather to craft more and then the next thing you know, you are starting to get cramps and your back hurts because 23 hours have gone by and you have barely scratched the surface of this truly amazing game. When I am not playing, I am thinking about playing and I am googling tips and tricks and there is just SO much to this game. They did a truly amazing job with this. I have never done crack, but I have a feeling the addiction is pretty similar to this. I am warning you now, if you have a good life, a boy or girlfriend that loves you, or a job that you need to keep, you may want to stay away from this. If you have no life and nothing to do for the next 2,652 hours of your life, you are in for a treat. My only regret is that I didn't have this game when the pandemic started and I was trapped at home. Now when I am working, all I am thinking about is playing this game and more ideas of how I can streamline my compound. I give this game a 10/10. If I had one complaint, and this is a very small tiny tiny one, I wish they would get the tutorial a little better. There is so much I learned watching you tube videos that the game never teaches you. There is a great tutorial but they don't show you a lot of the stuff you can do. Other than that, this game is perfect. Great job team that built this. You have earned your paycheck and I will continue to watch for more of what you guys do! Thank you!
_childDocuments_.name: Satisfactory

_childDocuments_.review: I came for building and exploring, and was not disappointed! I had no idea how much I loved factories, and I can't get enough. I'm doing algebra for fun.350 hours in and I want to build the perfect worldwide rail system. I've studied other's megaprints and blueprints, and I am absolutely in this game.There's already been an update since I started a couple months ago that solved some issues I was having as a player, so that's good. _childDocuments_.review: As an engineer in real life who works on construction in factories it's no wonder I would love to continue my work at home (at least here I can drink on the job). This game hits every one of my OCD tendencies to never stop improving my world and factories. It gives just enough exploration and enemies to keep it interesting while also keeping you on your toes to continue to build and improve. Hands down has been one of my most played games and can't wait for 1.0 release!

_childDocuments_.review: Satisfactory is grand so far. It's open, large in all the right ways, and plays well despite being early access. Great graphics for this type of game so be wary of extra large builds and framerate drops on higher settings, but it's to be expected when you have a mega factory automated on your screen.My experience so far has been similar to a 3D idle game. Gather, build, automate. Get new, more efficient stuff. Plan. Gather, rebuild, automate.Once you get everything running smoothly and eliminate some spaghetti conveyors, it's just so....satisfactory.

_childDocuments_.review: While I'm far from finishing it, and I just restarted because it went full release, this game is amazing. _childDocuments_.review: Absolutely wonderful mix between Factorio and Subnautica, with incredible fun to be had between friends as well as solo. Factorio does a wonderful job of doling out tools when you need them (giving you drones when it becomes too tedious to build by hand, etc.) and Satisfactory could do a better job of smoothing out the higher tiers. Factorio has you dealing with units of items in terms of belts, but this game has much more various needs, so it would benefit from a way to read how many items per second are being produced on a belt at a single time. Another great change to keep the player thinking at the higher level would be to add drones or something similar (understandably way more difficult in 3d space). Overall I really enjoyed my time with it but I think it overstays its welcome in the later phases, probably as a result of the staggered release early access, rather than people playtesting the entire game as a single experience.

I haven't played the multiplayer for this game yet but I have every reason to believe that it is super fun with friends.

_childDocuments_.review: Satisfactory is a brilliant Early Access game by Coffee Stain Studios. The objective is to build a factory on an alien planet and make it as efficient as possible. The game ropes you in with a fairly straight forward tutorial and keeps things easy at the start, getting progressively more micro-managing and new as you continue to reach milestones and objectives. I did think to myself "Why would I want to have a game where I just make a factory and create resources?", but before I knew it, I was playing the game consistently for a while because it had me hooked. You manage power, train lines, drones, conveyor belts, it never seems to end. It has a calm feel to it, enemies don't come and ruin your factory, they just lurk about in the exploration areas and you can create weapons to defend yourself against them when you are adventuring across the huge map that is available to you. There's many different ways to build, its entirely up to you as long as you have the resources. The community behind the game is great and seeing other peoples builds gives you inspiration and it pushes creativity out of everyone. I rate Coffee Stain Studios very well for their developer updates and community interaction and can confidently say that this game is worth buying at full price even with the Early Access title attached to it. On top of all this, the game looks graphically pleasing and finds the gap where it isn't too demanding but looks good. I've played a few times with friends too and it helps to get the factories off the floor when you start a new world. The game is a gem and should be in all Steam libraries.With my current factory, I'm near an end game point, and it's definitely dragging due to the fact I have less to focus on. The new update does help end game factories and builders by giving that new content itch, but it could do with some more to it when you're at that point. Apart from that, the game is a no brainer.

_childDocuments_.review: Satisfactory is a first-person open-world factory building game with a dash of exploration and combat. Pioneering for FICSIT Incorporated means charting and exploiting an alien planet, battling alien lifeforms, creating multi-story factories, entering conveyor belt heaven, automating vehicles, and researching new technologies.

name: Victoria 3
detailed_description: Get your Grand Edition today! Get the full experience of Victoria 3 with the Grand Edition, which includes the base game as well as the expansion pass, including : Melodies for the Masses Music Pack Dawn of Wonder Art Pack Voice of the People Immersion Pack Colossus of the South Region Pack Sphere of Influence Expansion The Expansion Pass Bonus: The American Building Pack Get your Expansion Pass today! About the Game SHAPE A GRAND TOMORROW Paradox Development Studio invites you to build your ideal society in the tumult of the exciting and transformative 19th century. Balance the competing interests in your society and earn your place in the sun in Victoria 3, one of the most anticipated games in Paradox’s history. THE ULTIMATE SOCIETY SIMULATOR Lead dozens of world nations from 1836-1936. Agrarian or Industrial, Traditional or Radical, Peaceful or Expansionist... the choice is yours. Detailed population groups with their own economic needs and political desires. Reform your government and constitution to take advantage of new social innovations, or preserve the stability of your nation by holding fast to tradition in the face of revolutionaries. Research transformative new technology or ideas to improve your national situation. DEEP ECONOMIC SYSTEM Expand your industry to take advantage of lucrative goods, taxing the profits to improve national prosperity. Import cheap raw materials to cover your basic needs while finding new markets for your finished goods. Secure vital goods to fuel your advanced economy and control the fate of empires. Balance employing available labor force with the needs for new types of workers. PLAY ON A GRAND STAGE Use your diplomatic wiles to weave a tangled global web of pacts, relations, alliances, and rivalries to secure your diplomatic position on the world stage. Employ threats, military prowess and bluffs to persuade enemies to back down in conflicts. Increase your economic and military strength at the expense of rivals. Accumulate prestige and the respect of your rivals as you build an industrial giant at home or an empire abroad.

It follows on from the success of CK3's well-fleshed-out initial version. It's a way more economy-and-business focused and kind of feels like a business simulator. I'M IN!

_childDocuments_.review: I cant recommend this game in its current state. It is supposed to be an "economic society simulator"BUT the whole thing is just porely explained and comunicated. The user interface is just so opace, you need to scram through so many layers to find basic info. Industry, Economy and Society/Internal politics are not fleshed out. I mean, there is a detailed system, but it has "a solution". If you want to get rich and have happy and prosperous people and immigration, you go liberal democracy. Every game. Adittionally, every country plays the same except some arbitrary different numbers for wood/arable land/mines you can build. Internal politics are the same between Ottoman Empire or Prussia or Russia or France, except some different starting numbers for the IGs. All the different political styles play the same. And if someone comes and says "you can do so much cool things, liberalise Russia, nazify USA,..." I ask you: Do you do those things because they are incentivised or bring you any gain or do you do them just for the movie in your head? Dont get me wrong, if you can play out your political fantasy with this barebones and very limited simulation, good for you. But I want a little more cause and consequence, pros and cons, "depth" for my one.

_childDocuments_.review: I played Victoria 3 just a little bit when Paradox did their "free weekend" thing. Starting of with the positives, I really liked the graphics and overall art style. The game implements a lot of fun ideas, my favourite being government/population management, someone clearly put a lot of work into these things. But there is just so much wrong in this game, at least when I last played it. The economy system that is so iconic in Victoria series is just painfull, management of that ♥♥♥♥ is simply not fun. Not to mention that UI is terrible, it's hard to find what you need, and the game doesn't help you one bit. It's not a learning curve, it's a learning cliff. These things bring me to another issue. For some reason, some things in this game fell undeveloped, when others feel overwhelming. While politics and economy can be fun ( but are a pain in the ass to navigate ), then diplomacy and warfare are beyond simplistic and bare bones. The overall balance of gameplay elements is just awfull. And as summary, I must say something that concerns me deeply; the game is still kinda fresh, and it is already cursed with Paradox's greedy DLC practices. And it's going to get a lot worse. Seeing the overall quality of the game and the rising price, it's just not worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: I was hoping for more of a civilization type game. Got a political and economic game instead. War is very obfuscated. Methods for expansion seem to favor conquering over any other political mechanism. The time limit (100 years) also encourages the faster outcome of war to other methods. No direct control over wartime forces - basically protect the front or attack the front, thats it. No strategies to out maneuver your opponent, its purely mathematical in outcome. Some concepts are difficult to master, and the requirement to balance means you cant hyper-focus on one aspect of your country (e.g. industrial ramp-up) because are constantly catering to the demands of this group or that to keep from going into succession/revolt.Graphics are decent, but sounds are all pretty much like background noises and ambiance.Love Paradox and their dedication to their games, but this one just isnt for me.

_childDocuments_.review: While the game is not perfect, it is very entertaining and accomplishes what I expected from the release. The only major aspects left that I feel still need refinement before I can begin to consider this a perfect installment is the combat system (fronts move wildly and dramatically in unpredictable ways sometimes, such as during failed naval invasions), and naval combat can have a more direct influence on the game. _childDocuments_.review: I Pre-ordered this game knowing it would have flaws, because i believe in the evolution of this product, because Paradox has shown that they will make their games better and better as years go by. As it stands, a few weeks after release this game looks unpolished, has a few problems, but these i believe can and will be addressed in Patches, specifically performance in the later stages of the game. I bought this game as a vote of confidence in Paradox, but if I see that the content coming to the game in it's evolutions is not on par with my expectations as a consumer, I will not buy them and I will not invest in this product anymore, but for now, after 100 hours, I like it a lot.This game is exactly what I wanted when I envisioned the sequel of Victoria 2. A political and economic simulator of the 19th century, right in the middle of the industrial revolution. From the tensions of geopolitics through diplomatic plays, to social upheaval represented in the pops, how interesting and bang-on the internal politics are (minus a few rare weird scenarios where the landowner and trade unions form a government lol). This game so far, in spite of it's flaws it's delivering, but it needs to grow, it needs to become not just good, but it needs to be great. I expect this game to become what HOI4 is now, that is to say their best most well developed and content-filled game.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a casual. I do not want to spend 200, and really not even 20 or 2 hours stuck stumbling about menus trying to understand a video game. I just want to sit and play and get it as I go. Sufficed to say HOI4 is beyond comprehension to me. But while HOI4 feels incomprehensible but logical even when I don't understand what is happening (always), Vic3 feels (especially warfare and diplomacy-wise) like it's incomprehensible and random. Which sucks. Cheating in HOI4 will still make you lose because you likely have fundamental problems that make you lose that simply adding moar units won't fix, but cheating in Vic3 will make you still lose because you can't control your armies, and they will do nothing. I cheated myself half the world and my armies would simply not fight, there was no way to know why, or how to make them fight.If you buy this - downgrade to 1.1.2 via the Beta menu, this lets you play the game as what it is - a fun econ sim where you pick options from a screen based on bigger green numbers or strategize to have numbers go bigger later as an abstraction of import and export orders in the 19th century and watch the impacts of laws, institutional investments and policy changes on your economy and standards of living of the population. Now that game - I loved and enjoyed and would happily do another playthrough of - start to finish (I had no technical issues personally).It's filled with cute little details like miniatures of trains and railroads and buildings bustling with life as you undertake the industrial revolution and urbanization by increasing production. Just avoid warfare at all costs and don't bother with diplomacy or anything serious colony-wise (just build the Suez if you're playing a great power and leave it at that) and you will have fun!What I would not play, nevermind pay for is the current version that is like an Imperator: Rome-esque never-ending civil war ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of overly-animated flashing graphics for children or people with the dopamine systems of children, historical member berries with a combat system that moon phases have as much control over as the player does yet the player is needlessly forced into in a perfectly decent econ sim game.

_childDocuments_.review: I love a paradox grand strategy game. I’ve played most and must have sunk somewhere beyond a thousand hours into them because they’ve always triggered that part of my brain that refuses to be beaten by puzzles. Stellaris is good for new players as it’s relatively less complex and the blinky lights help push through that initially intimidating difficulty curve; Crusader Kings provides a more role-playing experience; Hearts of Iron is great for people weirdly obsessed with Warhammer and Victoria is for people sexually aroused by accounting.Victoria is a great big real time board game set during the industrial revolution that focuses on economic dominance and government and it really is as dreary as that description. It’s all about supply lines, production methods, resource availability and pacifying the population to balance the budget. I wouldn’t blame you for skipping over this one entirely but allow me to explain why it’s sucked up so much of my time.A large part of my enjoyment of Crusader Kings came from trying to master its complexities. It took me like fifteen attempts and then suddenly the enjoyment dropped off. I’d mastered it. It was too easy to dominate the world and I found myself cracking open the modding tools to chase that feeling. After 200 hours into Victoria I’m still getting my ass handed to me. It’s the sort of game that requires careful micro-management and where the slightest mistake will send you spiralling into debt and failure.Let me try and explain the core mechanics (bear with). You take control of a pre-industrial nation and attempt to force your rivals into submission with your sheer economic power. You do this by researching new productive ways of producing your goods to sell, boosting your income and allowing you to dominate the other nations either militarily or diplomatically. For instance, iron is an important resource for a developing nation and you have plenty to extract. That iron could be sold for profit but to extract it you require tools. A shortage of tools would drive up their price making the extraction of iron unprofitable and causing your economy to tank. You could import tools from a foreign nation but that takes up your bureaucratic resources and increasing those are incredibly expensive. Later you could use engines to extract greater amounts of iron but you’d require engines and coal, produced or imported.If your eyes are glazing over reading that last paragraph that is entirely understandable. It’s a complex and delicate web of production where the slightest change could bring the whole thing toppling down. It requires careful micro-management to make sure each building uses the resources available to it to maximise its production.This is the era when the nations of Europe was colonising Africa of course and that brings a whole bunch of new problems. Some nations can be conquered, while others have no government to force into submission and can only be gradually colonised. Doing so gives you access to new resources to feed into your factories but are a drain on your funds, adds another province to manage and might piss off some very powerful neighbours.The game does feature a very token combat system for conquering territory but the emphasis is on providing the equipment they need to keep going. There’s no equipment customisation or freedom to plan your strategy like you might get in Hearts of Iron, it’s just this army attacks that province. It always just comes down to who brought the biggest stick, which is a shame because it could be much deeper. It shouldn’t be difficult to transplant some of Heart of Iron’s mechanics.This game is Paradox’s final boss. The one to play if you’ve mastered the others and want a real challenge. It’s like juggling twelve spinning plates and I’d recommend it only if you’re mad. And apparently I am because I’ve sunk 200 hours into this game and it absolutely won’t beat me.

_childDocuments_.review: This will be my 3rd edit. I will sum up the game from 1.0 to 1.3.Game released as a disaster. Constant crashes, AI failing to manage a country or causing any challenge, performance issues and MP stability.1.2 patch fixed a lot of things and I felt that only problems left were AI and MP stability.Then came the 1.3 patch. Which destroyed 1.2.Main problems;- AI can't manage economy- AI can't manage revolutions- AI is easly fooled while having war- Multiplayer hotjoin breaks down- Multiplayer desync issues can't be handled without a rehost, which takes tremendous amount of time.- Lack of content for major countries- Performance issues ( I have RTX 3070, Intel i7 10700K and 32 gb ram and I still can't manage to get more than 30 FPS)- Warfare is senseless. It's just numbers against numbers.- Technology seems unbalanced- No depth in economy- Minor QoL issuesI should explain more.The logic behind a great economy is Tax more > Construct more > Gain more tax(through production and wages). QoL issues are the easiest. There is no hold and drag to constructions or technologies. Having technologies added to queue was nice. But we should be changing the order.Warfare is dull because you have no interaction at all. You only put generals on the fronts. You can't change generals theatres. You can't somehow train generals or soldiers to be more efficient. However, you can research technology for difference. Which is also dull. No cavalary types, no ammunition types, no bayonet techs... Production methods for army are meaningless. You can research 3rd and 4th production methods in late game but there is nothing for early game. And those researches are too close to each other, you end up not using some of them. Peformance is a disaster due to population getting divided constantly by their culture, religion and class. Check out the performance mods, they are all using increased assimilation and conversion.Multiplayer is such a huge disappointment to me. I have played other Paradox titles for years. I still can't understand how it doesn't work. The best MP tech was in HOI 4. You could resync in-game and have hotjoin without problem. After 6 years, in Vic3, you can't seem to hotjoin without breaking the game or make a resync. This doesn't feel like a progress to me. For core players, it makes a lot of difference.Lack of content is a bummer but I can't say it's the main problem.I want to love this game. I do play this game. I loved Vic2. But the problems for the core game itself is too much. The progress of fixing those, ends up breaking other things. Which frustrates me even more. Use testers, use open beta as you did in 1.2. Let people help the process.1.2 was a success because warfare system was a failure. The new changes in law-change process is succesful too. But as 1.3 introduced, AI failed to manage economy. Which was fixed in 1.2. Devs can successfuly change things but other things ends up broken. My initial comment was that "there is a long way to go for this game". I still stand by it. I am sad to see this game trying to hold on to life.People tend to confused by the gameplay hours. I have played 2000+ hours of HOI4 just to see it got destroyed by some dlc. And let's be honest to each other, there are no games like these in the market. Not graphic wise or QoL wise.TL,DR;I can see Paradox is simplifying the games for new players. I am not against that. But DLC's and mechanics are getting simplified too. I want more complexity. More to discover. More to micro manage and a good performance while doing those. Also, for God's sake please fix the multiplayer.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is extremely fragile in terms of stability — crashes regularly. Also, the gameplay is extremely unstable. [Note that in the original game a revolt was not a "game over" thing — you just continued as the new government; now it's an immediate game over.] Victoria 3 has the makings of a great game, eventually. _childDocuments_.review: I have some mixed feelings about the title, and while folks talk about how future DLC or updates may fix common complaints, I gotta review the game as it stands at time of review.Excellent Economic Simulation, might not appeal to all and may be a turn off for some, but its the core of the game and it is well handled. Only real complaint for the economic gameplay is that having a separate menu for just the buy/sell orders of your nation (rather than your market) could be extremely useful for subject nations who risk market isolation or want to go for independence down the line. Honestly, the core of the game when it comes to econ and politics and how they work together is very good.But diplomacy and warfare are so God awful so as to completely ruin much of my enjoyment of the game. Its not the war that is the problem, I honestly like not having to order armies around, and I think a stronger emphasis on diplomacy over player skill in warfare is a good choice. But, the diplomacy and diplomatic plays in the game as is cannot carry the weight that necessitates. Whether or not the AI is willing to join a play can feel arbitrary, often joining wars against the player regardless of good relations with the player or bad relations with the AI. Loading a save often results in a diplomatic play going completely differently, demonstrating just how arbitrary the underlying system is.Some degree of randomness and variance is of course necessary, however arbitrariness is the enemy of fun in a strategy game. If a random dice roll at the start of a diplomatic play has more of an outcome on a war than any economic, military, or diplomatic choices the player made, then the heart of strategy, making decisions and watching them bear fruit in future, is completely undercut, and the player can only ask why they wasted their time.Great economic simulator. Failed product as a strategy game. Will still play, cannot recommend

_childDocuments_.review: The war gameplay in this game is the most unfun experience I've ever had in a 4X game. It is quite obvious that it was a feature brought to term by an overzealous game designer who insisted that it would just work. In an effort to reduce the micro of maneuvering multiple armies across thousands of provinces, you must instead play whack-a-mole with thousands of fronts opening up, where your enemy can relocate a hundred battalions halfway across the globe in 30 days, behind enemy lines, bypassing your armies, and then reinforcing a tiny province that they have no other access to. Couple this with an unintuitive and uninformative UI and you will need to keep a bottle of asprin next to you any time you want to go to war with anyone that has more than 6 states. Napoleon wasn't thwarted by the winter in Russia, he was thwarted by the 30 fronts he opened.Couple this with the most idiotic AI I've ever seen in a Paradox game (I backed a Greek uprising in Egypt and Greece itself sided with Egypt) and you're looking at the second Imperator: Rome launch.I look forward to coming back in a year when a couple of DLCs and an apologetic team lead have finally turned this into something more than Factorio Nation Simulator.

_childDocuments_.review: I have sunk a lot more time into this game than I should've, and I'm going to continue sinking time into this game in the future. I'm going to start this review with the positives, and then go over the negatives. This game has a fun economics system. The recent update, "Spheres of Influence," has added some VERY good features to the game. Foreign investment has to be one of the biggest game changes, and one of the best, in this games history. This allows you to build resources and other buildings inside of foreign countries to exploit the resources the AI won't. This is especially useful for your puppets. A couple updates ago, (I don't remember which), they added the private sector. The private sector builds buildings automatically, based off of the materials and resources that are demanded in your economy. These features are awesome, and definitely make the game 100% better. Now, the war system. Victoria 2 had a decent war system, but to me it wasn't made well. Victoria 3, barely has anything resembling a war system. The developers have tried changing the war system, but it STILL has the same bugs and problems it has had since the release of the game. While war isn't the direct focus of the game, I believe that war should play a much bigger role. Most wars in history were about economics. The American civil war, the Opium Wars, etc. The economic system in this game isn't exactly realistic. The rich actually spend their money, which is fine, but I don't think it resembles real life economics. Companies don't play as big of a role as I think they should. Companies only provide a building boost to 1-3 types of buildings, which is extremely useful, but I think they should do more. Politics play a bigger role in this game than the war system does. When it comes to laws, the goal for most players is to liberalize your country. The game does give you the option to do other stuff, like absolute monarchies, command economies, technocracies, and communism, playing those types of nations don't make a huge change to your gameplay. Like most Paradox titles, late game is very repetitive, and you get to a point where you're too powerful to stop. In CK3, they added plagues to the game, which help throw you off balance in the mid-late game. Plagues kill of strong characters, kill your economy, and overall add a big challenge for you. Victoria 3 lacks any sort of challenges like that. There's no economic crashes, no depression, no inflation, nothing. Ultimately, Paradox is going to keep updating the game, avoiding important features such as war, politics, and other features that I listed above. Paradox is also going to keep releasing countless DLC, and lock every good feature they release behind paywalls. I hope whoever reads this find this review helpful!

_childDocuments_.review: I'm really on edge here on how to give this review, because the game has great potential and tickles the itch of grand strategy as only paradox titles can do. However, it was released in a completely broken form. Tons of bugs, empty world, unplayable for the later half of the game. (My specs fulfill the recommended system requirements) If this wasn't a game, but any kind of other consumer good, the publisher would be sued into the ground for fraud. Communication has been dishonest: What is being hailed as a massive FREE update barely manages to fix the worst of the issues the game has and puts it into Early Access territory from a technical demo. When I read forums on the game, most players seem to suffer from Stockholm Syndrome: They want to hype up the game to increase player numbers that so the developers continue to support it (any by that I mean fix).So what are the major issues still around after 1.2?- Diplomacy and Warfare are still unpredictable. Allies will crash out of wars even when winning, and this might delete vital fronts. - Once you fix your country there's nothing to do. WIth the new update you might be able to see the end screen, but for the last 30 years there is no game-play outside of just conquering everything.Minor Issues:- There is little flavor to the countries, outside of early-goals, they mostly feel the same to play.- The economy is fairly unbalanced, with the most vital industry being Arts  Academies. While the game can be fun, it is not worth the price at the moment, and personally I feel ripped off by the false advertisement, so I will leave a negative review for now, but closely watch the development progress. Depending on how the free updates go  I will amend my rating. As a last point, I truly don't understand why this wasn't released in Early Access. Paradox Fanboys will buy it anyway (myself included), but it would have been much more honest to say "Hey, this isn't finished yet, but you can have a taste."

_childDocuments_.review: I have given this game so many chances and I desperately want to enjoy it and love it but I seriously cannot overstate how frustrating and downright bad this game is. The choices you make are so depressingly insignificant and it is almost impossible to actually control or do anything you want to do in this game due to how it is designed. It takes decades upon decades in game and hours upon hours to actually try and achieve one thing. Want to declare a war of independence as the Dominion of Canada, have fun spending hours trying to increase you ever falling liberty desire while Great Britain continues to buy out your entire GDP without really being able to do anything to stop it. Paradox has ruined its potential by catering to the select few players that enjoy the mind-numbing extreme detail of a game like this and alienated casual gamer's who don't have the time or the interest to learn volumes of historical economic policy in order to succeed in this game. As an avid player of CK3 I have always enjoyed that I needed very little knowledge going in to any given game and that I was able to enjoy my run through without feeling like the game was playing me. Everything in Victoria 3 just feels formulated to be gate-kept as much as possible, the tutorial is no help, and it feels as though everything was specifically designed to make you angry.Its unclear who or what you are actually in control of in this game, is it the government? I can't tell, because it all seems to operate independently from you and so many decisions are locked behind prerequisites that wouldn't really make much sense f you were actually the person or entity in charge of the country.I just can't express how disappointing and unfulfilling this game is, I had such high hopes and I have tried so hard to learn it and to enjoy it but is just one thing after another.
