_childDocuments_.review: I am very sad to say that the game not the great in my opinion.The gameplay loop is unbearably dull. You just end up building wood, and iron to support your spiralling construction industry.In fact you almost control every building you can think of. In Vicky 2 you would influence you economy but such as economies are, there is inertia and you cannot directly control everything. You could make the argument for it in an authoritarian command economy but it just not a good economic sim. It feel more like you are in a city builder with nice road layout at the end of it.Interest Groups are also a pain and are arbitrary in switching political positions. For example, I was playing in a nation that had a large trade union pop and the leader supported a certain thing (can't remember the exact position they took) when he was replaced as leader the new leader was the antithesis of him and I got large amounts of discontent as people were now not happy. The problem is it is idiotic to say that as soon as the leader of an interest group flips ever single pop who is in the focus group flips. It should be proportional. Really buggered my nation and caused a revolution. Skill issue I guess.When it comes to Diplomacy it is mediocre at best. You don't really feel like you are having a tangible diplomatic play and if you do it results in war where the frontline where the war system that despite its rework is completely idiotic at best and Enrique de Trastamara at worst.I get what Paradox were going for but man trusting the AI to manage a war front is like trusting your kids to the Child Catcher for the weekend.The game has a long way to go and honestly I wouldn't pick it up even on sale. Getting into Vicky 2 with the HMP mod would be a better choice and more value for money.If you want an economic sim the fun trickles down slower than Reganomic wealth. Give it a miss.
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: My current game I'm playing as two Sicilies and I've had a blast. I don't tend to enjoy battles so I'm made my little nation one of the great powers. My economy was massive, got up to 3rd highest GDP. Standard of living is pretty great and I have a decent military that I don't use. Feeling great and powerful, everyone seems to be mindful of me even if they're not afraid. I'm getting two big for my britches though. A war starts out in the 1870's, no big deal cause no one is dragging me in. I have immigrants coming in and this is helpful because I don't have enough laborers and this has slowed my economic might. Well, for some reason my income of over 100k is dropping into the negative 10k-20k. Not a big deal, I have plenty in reserves. My standard of living is dropping, not drastic but it's dropping. My taxing is starting to take a hit though. I look and my trade routes almost entirely stopped working (I assume from the war that broke out into an entire European conflict.) I've thrown in emergency relief in all my territories.I'm still playing this so I don't know if I'll bounce back or if I just stumbled into governmental collapse. I'm not even entirely certain what to do if my current measures don't work but it's been an amazing second run on the game. I recommend the game  with one caution. The end/mid game slows down terribly. By that, I don't mean game play but there's just so much going on my computer just can't handle it (Seventh gen i5 with 16 gigs of Ram.) This might be the main consideration on if you want to play it or not.
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: The amount of negative reviews would have you believe its a poor game. Its really not. In-Game tabs could be organized cleaner, but other than that no real issues. Its new and complex so it will come with a high learning curve. Quite enjoyable once you master it, especially if you're into economic sims
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: Base game was questionable on release, and updates have just made it worse - from a broken vic2 simulator to a do-nothing simulator, diplomacy still 100% useless, major powers are inactive on the global stage, and the whole world simply feels dead. If you want to play this game watch a youtube video of someone speed-running a nation; that will be just as if not more interactive than you actually playing the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: I keep going back and forth about how to rate this game, but I've settled on not recommending it. The main issue with the game is the lack of player agency - too many things feel like they happen to the player without their input. While it's true that this game has a complex and engaging economy sim, often your economy will take a hit for no apparent reason, and it's left to the player to track down where the losses are coming from through the complex and byzantine system of menuing. The political system of passing laws is equally unsatisfying, and it can often feel like your playthrough is screwing you over because of repeated dice rolls keeping your country in the stone age. The sheer lack of flavor and detail makes the majority of nations feel very similar to play, and I've seen many bugs in my near-100 hours in the game. And this isn't even mentioning how the entire war system feels unfair, unresponsive, and obtuse.When I play this game, it's fun for the first few hours of every playthrough. Setting up your economy, passing basic laws, etc. But about the two- or three-hour mark I run into too many of the above issues, and it breaks the immersion.
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: Industrialization and politics are big strengths of the game as of launch. Diplomacy and war are weaker but can definitely be built upon. The game also needs a lot more country-specific flavor, as of right now the main things that differentiates countries is their allocation of different POPs and resources. Overall it's a good experience that I'm sure will improve with future updates.
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: Victoria 3 commits the cardinal sin of video games, being boring.  You can overlook when games have half baked mechanics, frustrating moments, or terrible ui; all of which Victoria 3 has in spades.  But to do that the core of the game needs to be good and this game frankly isn't.I really wanted to like it but after taking an extended break and then trying again I just had to admit that Victoria 3 is a deeply flawed game that isn't even fun to play.And to top it all off, performance seems to get worse with every patch.
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: A very good bad game.There's nothing to do in it, all the flavor is locked behind DLC, the mechanics are buggy and uninspired, and features that should've been in the game from launch aren't here almost 2 years later.Massive let down. The game is mindless fun because you can just powerscale as anyone and be OP that way.
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: Played it for free on a weekend. On one hand I feel as though I'm being given too much control over my economy, and constantly have to build lumber mills and iron mines in a vain attempt to relieve a deficit that capitalist's building and trade unions create. New goods don't feel new, just another burden on your iron and lumber industries. On the political side of things it really seems as though there is no progression. Groups either like or dislike you based on what you do and there's no ability to compromise, flavour is shallow. Got an event for Bismarck. The two options do basically nothing. There is a consistent false sense of progress throughout the game. Victoria 2 is more easy to read and do stuff in, and I don't have to use this weak-ass construction queue to build units. This just feels like watered-down Anno 1800 and Making history, except you can't actually relieve your good's deficits or make any real progress. Not fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: The AI in this game still remains not just bad but non-existent.The absurd lack of mechanics, flavor, complexity and pretty much everything that makes a game are somewhat filled by mods (of course this doesn't justify the state of the game you buy). However nothing saves you from the inability of the AI to play the game, it will never industrialize, never fill its basic needs, never compete, never do anything at all. Even the AI mod which is a must if you value your time isn't enough, despite being a huge improvement over vanilla. Also when you need so many mods to not even make the game playable you might as well code your own game.Which would be preferable given the optimisation, if they even have any, is so bad that despite nothing happening it remains so painfully slow.They haven't addressed something so fundamental for so long it's obvious they don't care.Instead they'll keep releasing simplistic DLCs and rework the UI while pretending the game is functional.
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: As a huge fan of Vic 2 i was super excited for this game, and having put nearly 10 hours into i have found nothing but disapointment. There is no reason to keep playing once you've formed your nation. Wars are boring and besides seeing a meaningless number go up, its hard to justify continued play. In Vic two you looked forwards and built towards the next war, in this there is no next war. There is no reason to build up, there is no reason to play, there is no fun to be had here.

_childDocuments_.review: Having played two full playthroughs and several observe games, I can reflect that the game in the current state is not recommendable for a buy at the given price.A more realistic price would have been 40 at most, as it gives a very nice framework to build upon. However, I cannot endorse the concept of NOT CARRYING OVER nice mechanics from Victoria 2. How can you possible downgrade a game I have no idea.Obviously, the map is beautiful and seems to run very well, but the content is very unbalanced (from my playthroughs and observe games). Seems the AI is super bad. Before buying, ssit on the fence for a month or two, wait for the community to deliver on patching the game balance with mods and giving more content wiht mods too. That is why, unfortunately, I cannot recommend the game in current state at the current price!
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: Review written after finishing a full start-finish run as Belgium, under the Learn to Play rulesetThe core of the game is incredibly solid. They nailed it, although some information is a bit hard to find. There is very little flavor though. A few events here and there, but the game was mostly just interacting with the systems directly. War is so much better now. No more micromanagement, and it's usually pretty clear what's happening. I'd like a few more options, but overall great.Social reforms are too easy right now. Maybe it's different on higher difficulty, but I never got major penalties for pushing reforms through. And I was generating so much bureaucracy that I could trivially have all institutions maxed. Overall, vic3 is a great game. It is lacking in some areas, but the core is strong and feels fun to interact with. An easy B or B+ right now, but once some good content mods or expansions come out it will easily be A+. Unlike some other paradox games, it doesn't feel like I'm waiting for them to fix a broken foundation, but the house isn't fully built yet.There is definitely enough content to maintain interest for 2-3 full playthroughs, which is a good deal
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: Okay, i am here on free weekend, just to check what this game is about.And i can see this is one of that classic hard core strategy.So you have to be very smart and much more have lot of free time.Because here you must go via lot of tables, data and etc.So spend so much time on analyses, decision and then you can become great leader and lead your contry or people to victory and write your name in history.I CAN RECOMMEND THIS GAME TO MY FRIEND BUT NOT MY GRANDMA.
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: I'm enchanted by this game's countries' political and economical mechanics. I think they did a wonderful job representing to some degree their real-life complexity in a fun and engaging experience. I do feel a bit confused about diplomacy and how wars are played out. I love how a war on the other side of the world can cripple your economy but I would love to have more detailed info on how the battles are being resolved. I still think this game is awesome even if they don't touch anything more about it. I'm excited to see what they will do with it.
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: Overall - very fun game. Positives:+ Watching GDP, standard of living, prestige etc go up is satisfying.+ The different resources each country has make it a fairly fun challenge+ Choosing to go to war is an important, costly decision - but it has actual benefits in adding new resources and pops to your county. Negatives:- Warfare is passable in my opinion, but there are the problems you'd expect with ai - e.g. your generals going and doing silly attacks, leaving capitals undefended and the like.- Once you get to a really strong point, the economy is just about hammering the 'build' button almost without planning. I look forward to playing this a lot more.
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: Really boring game, you're pretty much just focusing on economy, everything else is made really bad. You can't expand much, you have to wait two decades or more between each war, it gets superslow in just 2 decades, and then continues to crash.Every aspect related  to war is terrible. Most of the time you have a much larger more advanced army, for a long period of time it makes battles in which you are in such inferiority that the war stalls for so long. If you want to play a small nation and expand, good luck. It's almost impossible. You literally have huge nations jumping in and annihilate you.You spend almost the whole game looking at numbers. Complexity is good, but not when it's all you're doing.Unless you're an economic or politic fanatic, most probably you bought this game to play nations and expand (through war). Since through diplomacy it's impossible, and all the war related development is so bad that makes it not fun (and in my opinion unplayable), what's this game really about?For example, if you play in europe and make a war, let's say you're france vs belgium, 400 armed units versus 20, you literally spend tens of minutes waiting to breach, continuing to fight battles the computer decides for you in which only 6 of your units are fighting 20.Once you win the war, annexing 2-3 territories put you almost in pariah state, which means that you have to wait decades before making another war without causing all big nations to go against you.So what is the point of this game? Build buildings, make laws and wait for your life to pass?I'm extremely disappointed, Paradox used to make great games, this one only has a beautiful map and nice complexity, but it's totally unplayable and for a historic simulation totally misses the main thing that people want to do: make a nation great through expansion.Unless you play Russia or the US, you can't expand pretty much at all. And obviously after you played those two you wouldn't continue playing the same.And even if you play those two, the game will get so painfully slow in such a short play time (i have a super gaming computer that doesn't have one single issue with any other game) and it then crashes often. Last but not least, i can't even get a refund because of how slow it is, it took me longer than expected to really understand the game and see there's no way around all its problems. I tried to go deep in any function to see if it was me, but obviously that took time, and now i'm stuck with a game i won't ever use again, and i paid 60$ for nothing.Well done Paradox.
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: Luxury goods are a money machine. In a game centered around the economy, the ability to practically print money defeats the fun and challenge of balancing your nation's economy.If you are considering purchasing Vicky 3, just wait until Paradox releases the inevitable post game patches (or the modders fix the game for them) before spending the money on a half baked game.
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: Breath of fresh air from the dense and (to me) impenetrable mechanics of Victoria 2. I always wanted to enjoy Vicky 2 but couldn't make it past the initial hurdle. I don't have that many hours in this game yet, so there are still many, many things I don't understand, but it has been a while since I've been so engrossed in seeing a little line keep going up. This game has so much potential and I am so excited for the future. I'd highly recommend checking out Quill18's Canada Lets Play or the Two Sicillies Stream!
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly as this game stands now its a disaster. The economy is interesting but needs some work in certain areas. My main source of complaint is the war system. Its bad...like really bad. I think the whole point of this system was so we as the player wouldn't have to micro the fronts thus leaving us more time to focus on diplomacy and the economy. This has in my opinion spectacularly backfired because as the base game stands there's nothing super interesting you can do with diplomacy that should take up a large portion of your time. The economy though has potential as it stands is really just a "clicking simulator". Build buildings where you can, look at market demand/supply, pray to the economy gods that "green line go up", and repeat. Once you play a couple of games you really just find yourself doing it unconsciously and since you're progressively getting quicker at it-guess what? You have a lot of time on your hands to do nothing. Then there's the military....honestly this system stresses me out a lot more than victoria 2 ever did. I won't say victoria 2's war system was good...it wasn't the micro was a huge hassle, but with this game you never know where you stand militarily. I genuinely after 43 hours have no idea how the combat works. I've had experiences where I've lost even though I had better offense/defense and more troops and experiences where I've won in situations where I 100% shouldn't have (I would like to emphasis that all these battles took place on plains terrain so neither side should receive any hidden bonuses for that). I have also seen frontline battles where I outnumber the enemy 120 x 30 start battles with my troops having 9 units and the enemy having around 18 or more so clearly either the rng gods have not blessed me this day or a lot of my generals need to be executed immediately. I've started a habit of launching Ck3 before each war and sacrificing orphans to please satanic gods so they will grant me victory because that's a better explanation to me on why I win/lose battles compared to whatever's really going on in the background. Naval invasions are a nightmare since the frontline invasion mechanic can't seem to handle the basic idea of "I need to guard my port". Watch as your army engages with an enemy army and another enemy army swiftly walks into your port from another frontline because "frontlines for whatever reason can't fight more than one battle at a time and therefore your occupied army can't do anything. Watch as your army magically teleports back home even thought their entry naval port was taken. How do they do it you might reasonable ask? Couldn't tell you I've learned not to question the pdx gods and their dlc powers. Not to mention frontline warfare in the 1840s and 50s makes no sense historically but I digress. All in all the current state of victoria 3 leaves a lot to be desired. Paradox experimented and at least looking at the current reviews on the game came up short.
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: im going to play a lot more of this game, but i have major gripes i would like to get off my chest. the UI is very cluttered and disorganized, the old vic2 interface you could see every trade good and its values on one tiny screen, every political change, every general, vic3, however, involves a lot of scrolling and much of this information has been spread around. the vic2 map modes were clearer and gave more info than these here. everything is big like its meant for a mobile game, the character portraits and map are too cartoony for a game that is not really for kids.lots of things have been improved, especially trade and diplomacy, i like what they did to colonialism with decentralized states. i like state edicts out of a mana pool instead of state focuses. i dont mind the warfare as much as i thought i might, vic2 combat wasnt great either, but it is definitely lacking here, battles involve staring at numbers going down. it does free up the rules for a non-province based system that feels unique in the paradox lineup.the performance is significantly improved, but i have had multiple crashes. the biggest issue is a huge lack of flavor, same as CK3 had on launch. they clearly want to hock overpriced DLCs slowly over time. CK3 is much better now so i might change my review with some updates.i went into this game blind to the hype and was mostly disappointed, that said paradox has had no problem in the past completely overhauling their games to cater to criticism, so i am hopeful they address the gameplay problems. the UI problems will likely not get fixed and that really sucks, all of their new games have been using this god-awful font that started with stellaris.  it works in a sci-fi or ww2 game, but here and in ck3 it is very out of place, and they will never change it to something more sensible. all in all i had a lot more fun with imperator rome, and that's my bar for a mediocre paradox gameEDIT: i didnt realize at first just how much 21st century politics has seeped into this game. there are events, art,  and mechanics that push a very western liberal view of the world that just wasnt present in vic2.  it doesnt belong in a historical simulation game, and whitewashes much of the past that im interested in.EDIT 2: 250+ more hours and the game is still such a disappointment, they fixed maybe one or two issues with it, im a masochist for playingEDIT 3: then new warfare changes have actually made the game worse if you can believe itEDIT 4: new DLC is out and not only have they not added very much content, or any warfare fixes, the new thing, the political law rework, made the problems worse then ever
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: I start as tsar of russia and I want to build up economy and industrialize. I quickly realize my laws is what holding me back - the capitalists don't pay me any taxes, I have to build factories out of my own pocket, I have no schools and my universities are run by clergymen. So I open the politics tab and try to reform. I then realize I can't pass any laws - even though I'm literally an absolute monarch and autocrat. The government is dominated by gentry and clergy and an attempt to abolish serfdom leads to a civil war. I am annexed, gg.I try again and this time I'm taking it slowly - introducing intelligentsia into the government and building up their political clout. I start dicussions for introducing private schools, and I get a glorious 4.9% chance every two years for this law to be passed... and then I get random event that my intelligentsia is corrupt, giving me a 15% success chance debuff and basically leaving people of russia with no chance of ever getting a school. Then I realize it's already 1870 and I still haven't accomplished anything.In CK3, if I want to change succession laws and my vassals oppose - I got tons of options. I can bribe them, I can befriend them, I can devour them. Here I find myself staring at the screen for hours praying for a beneficial random event.
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: Dont get me wrong, the game runs pretty good even for my dinosaur of a computer, but it does have some issues:Gameplay:>country's economy can be caught in an essentially endless debt loop, however there could be better ways to specify how to go about this>I do enjoy the representation of the decentralized nations in africa, kazakhstan and the americas.. only downside being you cant play as one. Try to centralize/unite the region would be fun, this could be used to some extent to create custom nations to a degree.>the war system.... ok moving on.>Diplomatic plays are a good feature in my opinion and do add a good bit of immersion compared to instant war.. we are not talking about the war system..>Colonization of africa takes far too long to do, and by the time you reach the technology to prevent the malaria debuff to colonizing, the europeans would have already shown up and began amassing on your borderlands>Technology research is good but It does seem almost impossible to get pass a certain range before technology takes too long to be viable, and the methods to getting faster research as minor nations tend to end up placing you back into the bermuda triangle that is debt.Overall tho, the game is pretty good, yet it does need a bit more time in the oven; and not a light breeze from a hair-dryer.
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: I played Victoria 3 at launch, then put it aside because I found it boring. I returned to the game during the holidays and I found that in the meantime, successive patches and rebalancing had turned it into a fun game - with plenty of rough edges and room for improvement.At its core, Victoria 3 is an economic and political simulation. Your country's political and social make-up directly influences its economic performance and vice versa. By this point in the game's development, I find the ways in which the two systems interact fun, interesting, and believable. Other systems don't work so well, with the controversial new warfare mechanics and diplomacy merely serviceable at this stage. Victoria 3 is also short on country-specific flavor. Still, game's improved a lot in the last year or so, and the company seems committed to continued development.
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: I was excited for Victoria 3 when it was first announced and bought it day 1. This was a mistake and the most recent DLC only confirmed it. The foundation for the economic game play is there but as it stands it's barebones and repetitive. Internal Politics are okay but don't have that much depth. Warfare is overly simplistic and boring on land and the naval game lacks feedback, is frustrating and is annoying more than anything else. Diplomacy is terrible the AI makes decisions seemingly at random and there are far too few diplomatic interactions. Flavor is lacking after the early game just about every country feels the same and the earliest hope any of these issues will be fixed is March of 2024 if the game even makes it that far which I am unsure of.

_childDocuments_.review: Victoria II is probably my favourite game of all times.While Victoria 3 has it's flaws, it's still a great baseline, and if you can overlook flaws that can easily be fixed by PDX over the next few weeks I think it's worth its money already. _childDocuments_.review: The game is fun, graphics are nice and the warfare mechanics are quite novel and refreshing. However, there's one major flaw which is that every country feels almost identical.The most anticipated and highly complex economy system in Victoria 3 would be rendered meaningless if the play-style is nearly the same no matter which country you chose. Not to mention that the diplomacy and colonisation mechanics in this brand new 2022 game is a joke. I have like only one available interaction with my vassals and colonies.I might as well go back playing EU4. And where is the espionage system？
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: Do not currently recommend. Better release than Imperator: Rome, but that's not saying much.Issues:- UI wastes lots of space- UI has too many menus with things not where you'd expect- Less complex than even HoI4 (Already felt like I have free reign in game to do what I want after 4 hours of play time, which is insane for a grand strategy game)- Any depth to warfare has been removed, you just hire the general you prefer, mobilize, then send them to the front and watch the ai fight itself- Core gameplay loop is dull, there isn't really any thinking to be done. You just build a new building that will make you money, create an export trade route (with mana), and if a good gets too expensive create an import trade route. That is essentially 80~90% of what you do in this game, and no thought is required- Despite being advertised as an economic simulator, goods are created from thin air if there isn't enough supply- Every nation plays as if it was socialist/communist, no matter what government type/laws you have. There is no free market, you (the dictator) control all trade and building in your nation- Laws are poorly balanced, I haven't messed with them as much but from what I've seen some laws are objectively better than any other option, some to an insane degree. Multiculturalism being the biggest one, all cultures being accepted. The alternatives are nowhere close to as good, mostly just giving slightly more (mostly useless) mana- Almost no unique flavor for different nations. I've played Cape Colony, Sweden, and some African nation, and they all played identically with no flavor at all. Only difference was starting techs.I will say that the new tutorial system is great and I hope they do similar for all future games. The tooltip system is good as well.Despite all the issues I have with it, I think with updates (hopefully no core mechanics/fixes behind dlc...) and mods, this game could be decent. I don't condone them releasing a barebones game, howeverUPDATE:While there is some fun to be had, there are way too many ways the game is frustrating. My last few games I've had a group of states revolt, and then their revolt has a revolt. When I beat the original revolt, the sub revolt becomes an independent country with no way of easily reclaiming them. This has happened more than once, and just kills any desire to continue playing. Most games the AI doesn't develop resources properly at all, which always results in countries just sucking out my resources. War is way too easy once you understand it, can easily win any war in most situations, though tedious. It is almost impossible to get AI to ally you. Another issue is that every time you gain or regain a state you basically have to reset all your production methods to the correct setting. There is no way to save these settings. Mid to late game you likely have a vast amount of states, and potentially every kind of building, and are potentially constantly at war. This means you are constantly clicking dozens of production methods back to what they should be. This is insanely tedious, when you gain a state it should just get your default settings.I could keep going, but the point is even if you like the current state of the game, there are way too many quality of life issues that make it way too frustrating to play.
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: Complete buggy mess. Unplayable. Frequent crashes. If you ignore the majority of bugs your play through is rendered unplayable by the constant civil wars, split off glitches, and weird war mechanics.Paradox clearly does not respect their customers and thinks it is okay to charge 49.99 for what should be considered an alpha version of the game. The first two dlc should be free for the players who payed this price. How did this make it into beta and then full release? Their patches released thus far are focusing on pissing on the small insignificant bugs rather than the dumpster fires that make the game unplayable.Paradox, focus on fixing the constant Civil wars, civil war split offs, combat system , combat bugs, front split offs and idling generals when fronts split, make navy controllable in an effective sense, make naval invasions easier to do, the debuffs are insane, give the player an effective way to suppress rebels.Everything else is irrelevant to being able to play the game and can be fixed later.

_childDocuments_.review: As much as I love Paradox, I'm sorry to say this game should have been released with more music in the in-game soundtrack. As released, the soundtrack is quite repetitive. I expect this game will grow in depth in the coming months/years, which I feel is probably why the game has such mixed reviews. I'll reserve comment on the other aspects of the game for a later date, if I ever care to update this review.

_childDocuments_.review: Against all odds this became my favorite paradox title. What always continues to impress me is the remarkable overwhelming depth this game offers - I think the entire playerbase, myself included, came in trying to play like other paradox titles and were somewhat disappointed at first. The learning curve is steep, and war has enormous and frustrating consequences for the unprepared. Where this game truly excels is the manipulation of the background simulation - beyond just transforming the political realities of your nation, you can shape the world around you through trade, politics, and diplomacy. No other game will give me the high of making the united states my dominion playing as Luxembourg, after I manipulated the power of the south with my exports to make the north succeed from the south, leaving them weak and the scraps of their expansion up for grabs. Nothing can top paying close attention to the UK to see when it's empire has stretched it too thin, and shredding their empire to pieces as an Ethiopian principality because they can't reinforce its troops in Kenya. Sometimes I'm in the mood to wreak some peaceful havoc as the Danish, watching Prussia collapse because I convinced a city state to join my market and splitt a great power in two. There's so many opportunities, and maybe the greatest weakness of this game is the lack of flavor for small fledgling nations - and the communities fear of trying out the few that do. I really do believe this is the most underrated paradox title out there, I pray the company continues to invest more into this game, and the community gives it a second chance. This game pushes the limits of how much it's players are willing to improve there skills - those willing to suffer through the learning curve will find a hidden gem unlike anything else out there.

_childDocuments_.review: Victoria 3 is the long-awaited sequel to Victoria 2, a 12 year old cult classic. Although it was a buggy, janky, fundamentally broken mess, the economy of Victoria 2 was unique among games. It featured a closed loop economy, where every good bought or pound spent by one entity is a good produced or a pound earned by a different entity. The entire thing operated and changed by itself. You could not control it, only influence it. It had many bugs and design flaws, but it was a truly unique economic system for a videogame. The surrounding systems like diplomacy and war were simple and lazy, in the old Paradox style, but just functional enough.In comes Victoria 3. Looking at it as a sequel to Victoria 2, it disappoints in most ways. The unique economic system is gone, and the economy more closely resembles Anno. Your goal is to grow your economy using your construction sector, and your main activity is fixing the economic impacts of the last thing you did. Supply, demand, and prices change instantly. Nothing in your country happens without your input, and you have absolute control over every production building in your country. Making new buildings and changing how they operate is your primary gameplay loop, making you feel more like a middle manager than a country. While balancing production methods in every backyard moonshine-still is fun once as a small country, it devolves into tedious micromanagement quickly when playing anything larger than Liechtenstein.The only thing that happens without your input is other countries setting up trade routes, but this is mostly just infuriating. Because everything is in short supply and the AI is incompetent at growing their own economy, these trade routes mostly just steal your resources and rarely if ever sell you anything of substance. Protecting particular goods could have been an interesting gameplay mechanic, but it isn’t. You can’t stop a good from being exported. You can only embargo entire countries. So trade boils down to you trying to steal resources you’re short on, the AI doing the same, and you embargoing the AI if it starts stealing too many of yours. Devolving into isolationism becomes an appealing prospect, if only to remove the micromanagement and instability.Speaking of the AI: In typical Paradox fashion, it's terrible. As a result, singleplayer is a bland, sterile experience. You are playing in a sandbox with other kids, but the other kids are just balloons with faces drawn on them. It would be nice to believe that the AI will get better with some patches, but this is unlikely given the reputation of Paradox and Victoria 3’s game director. The AI nations in Victoria 3 are slow to grow, constantly in turmoil due to mismanagement, and regularly destroy themselves over the tiniest diplomatic disputes.Those diplomatic disputes are probably the one aspect where Victoria 3 actually has some interesting innovation. Most hostile interactions are no longer just a button, but executed through a ‘Diplomatic play’ mechanic involving all major powers with an interest in the region. Diplomatic plays are a neat concept, but they are sadly underdeveloped, and let down further by the bad AI. There is no real distinction between a small colonial engagement and major war in Europe. Both become plays potentially involving every country with an interest committing their entire army. It’s impossible to ensure a nation’s neutrality beforehand. If you plan to simply befriend the other powers, or convince them to stay out once it’s started, good luck. Friendly nations will turn on you in a heartbeat during a play, and major AI powers will join a diplomatic play for the most insane reasons. The US will fight to the death to defend Danish Holstein in exchange for an IOU. China will sacrifice millions to keep an Indonesian province out of Dutch hands because they were promised war reparations. The East India Company will happily fight a war against its overlord over some border dispute between Indian nations, before magically returning to being an obedient dominion once the war ends.This entire experience is wrapped up in a UI more hostile to the end-user than a suicide vest. Tooltips can be helpful, but the endless recursion of tooltips on your tooltips on your tooltips, ad infinitum, invokes an Escherian feeling of endlessness that makes you feel more lost than before you started. This wouldn’t be as bad if these tooltips did not contain important information that can’t be found elsewhere. The game will only tell you the most important information at a glance, such as the number of radicals in your country, but make it impossibly difficult to find out exactly who is radical and what caused it.Critics have said the game looks like a mobile game, and while this is unfair to the gameplay, the UI does lean heavily towards modern mobile-friendly UI trends. Lists and tables are frowned upon, while grid layouts are preferred whenever possible. The amount of information allowed on the screen at any one point is extremely limited, forcing you to constantly swap between windows. Multiple lists simply can’t be sorted at all, and no list ever takes up more than a third of your screen width. A full screen table with all the information you could want is anathema. Buttons are large, and the UI scaling is very high by default, unless you have a widescreen monitor, in which case it defaults to unreadably tiny. The game defaults to tree maps instead of pie charts, suggesting that the UI designer had some very strong personal convictions about design without necessarily having the understanding of visual data comprehension to back them up.I have yet to mention the political system, because it hardly matters. Unless you are trying to change a particular law that’s affecting your gameplay, like isolationism, it’s possible to forget it exists entirely. The interest groups controlling your government do nothing to stop you from changing the economy and eroding their power, so the power of interest groups is just a result of what buildings you build rather than an interesting mechanic.Ultimately, the game is an exercise in making a line go up for the sake of the line going up. Every country plays exactly the same, and there is no real payoff at the end. Warfare could theoretically provide something to work towards, but the war system is so barebones, clunky, and dysfunctional that warfare is more frustrating than fun. There is no micromanagement of units, as that system has been replaced with automatic AI fronts, but fronts split, merge, and disappear so much that the micromanagement is somehow just as annoying. Since the fighting happens automatically, wars are heavily affected by arcane mechanics behind the scene that the player can’t see or interact with, such as the number of troops that participate in a battle, or the direction a general advances. The reward for dealing with this system is often lackluster, since wargoals are decided during the diplomatic play phase and cannot be altered during the war.Victoria 3 isn’t a terrible game per say. It is simply mediocre as a game, and bad as a Victoria sequel. If it had been an early-access indie game for 30 dollars under a different name, it would have been received very well, with praise for some of its innovative ideas and its potential. As a released full-price sequel to a cult classic developed by a major studio, it is disappointing. The arguments about its potential ring hollow in the context of a studio known for selling buggy, half-baked products that had potential but failed to deliver.If you are looking for a complex economic simulator, this isn’t it. If you are looking for a game focused on diplomacy and war, this also isn’t it. If you are looking for a cute Anno-style economy game that you can play with friends so you can bicker over who ate all the tools in the market, this is actually alright, though buggy and overpriced.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Better in every way but that doesn’t make it perfect.Victoria 3 is a worthy success improving on nearly all parts of the previous game. It is worth noting that better doesn’t necessarily mean that it is perfect. The ai is still incapable. But less so than in Vicky 2. The market and immigration can still function irrational. But are a massive improvement over the systems in Vicky 2. Smaller nations can still lack flavor. But by the gods is it better than Vicky 2.Combat is probably the most divisive change. And I feel that it is a good example of how the game is received by the community. On the one hand you have people pointing out that it lacks strategy and is a massive abstraction. Basically, they think it sucks. On the other hand, you have people pointing out that combat in Vicky 2 also sucks and we loved that game despite of the combat mechanics. So just like the rest of the game. It is good but it’s not perfect and your enjoyment will depend on if you can look past some of its flaws. I was able to love Vicky 2 even though I had to use cheats to have fun in smaller countries. Even though I had to modify game files to make immigration make more sense.  If you were in the same camp you will love this game. If you expected something perfect or close to it you will be disappointed

_childDocuments_.review: Good game overall. Time will make it better with rolling updates and DLC. Least favorite part of the game is "Declaring Interests" as it really limits who you can interact with on the map. If you want to change interests, you risk losing trade routes or relations with people in the previous interest area you declared, so you'll likely have to do work on your current trade routes before switching interests to make sure the switch is seamless. Only way to declare more interests at a time would be to increase your prestige. Also, the 'Events' in game are sorta lack luster compared to other paradox titles and really feels like this component is missing. Looking at Crusader Kings 3 version of interacting via diplomacy, it's just far superior as it's just based on distance (i.e. you rule Spain, you can't perform any diplomatic actions on someone holding territory only in India unless you conquer your way there). Obviously this system wouldn't work in Victoria 3 since you've sailed around the world at this point, but having one area of 'Declared Interest' feels really bad as you'll likely use it to work towards a trade partner.

_childDocuments_.review: Review of 1.8 (23/11/24):...And turning it back to negative.Unplayable. Crashes my GPU when I try to run at 5x speed.Review of 1.7 (10/10/24):Finally going to turn that thumb to positive. Many systems work, have depth and have better feedback. Economic system is pretty good and the main content of the game. Combat and AI diplomacy has improved over the last few major patches to where the amount of glaring bugs are fixed, but still frustrating at times. The game also chugs in the late game (1900-1936) with revolts and colonies creating huge amounts of conflict and nations like the UK creating 200 1 man armies and fleets that are nearly constantly mobilised to combat them.Review of 1.6:Pretty much the same as v1.5 with some clean up of bugs encountered. AI still is pretty dumb in most economical and diplomatic decision making, which makes the SP game not fun to play. Review of 1.5:v1.5 is probably where the game should have been at releases. That being said...The whole game is a giant patch and you are the QA for it. It's become ridiculous. It's been a buggy/broken mess from day one and while numerous patches have improved things, I can't justify recommending the game to someone. My most recent run included:-Armies and fleets with 0 units created for no reason and with no way to disband-Upgrade mechanic doesn't upgrade units (15 line infantry > 0+3 line infantry, 12 skirmisher). Stays the entire game-Unable to adjust barracks buildings to different unit types (eg. infantry to artillery)-Armies sometimes moving off frontlines for no reason (back to HQ and to other fronts)-No path to fronts that are adjacent to my territories making wars impossible to win-Naval invasions. Pfffft.. I don't even know where to begin-Fleets getting put into permanent limbo when in port of captured province-Unable to upgrade fleet variants so you end up destroying and rebuilding to modernise a fleet, increasing radicals in the process-Peace deals not firing with accepted demands and 100% war score-Constant radical increases due to opposing IG demands, bolstered by agitators Overall review:My biggest gripe is that the game is a waiting game, running the game at 5x speed to try and get to something happening. Other Paradox strategy games always have mechanics for you to play with OR you can 5x speed in quieter times; its the player's choice. When you are interacting with the game, many of the mechanics are either extremely micro heavy (UI, economy) or frustrating to interact with (UI, diplomacy and warfare).Generally interacting with the AI is a bad time. Diplomacy is the worst with great powers letting other great powers do whatever, but will break treaties whenever the player does ANYTHING.

There simply isn't enough differentiation between the factions to make it feel like you are playing a different country when doing another playthrough. This is perhaps not helped by the fact that there are no major historical events (such as in Hearts of Iron) that are nation-specific. I know they released a DLC for France just recently that does just that, but this is only one country and is overpriced as such. I also believe that the war system needs further enhancement to align it more with what we have in other Paradox games. Overall, I've had a lot of fun playing this game thus far and would recommend it to any strategy gamer enthusiasts out there.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: I've played Victoria 2 for well over 500 hours, and the sequel fails to have any of the charm of the original. Do not recommend at the moment, although it's certainly getting expansions in the future that'll make it better.After playing two full campaigns as GB and Japan (and a smattering of abandoned runs) in Victoria 3, I've come out of it with very mixed impressions about the game in general. The core gameplay is decently fun, in the model of Victoria 2: build factories, industrialise your nation, and generally watch the GDP line go up. The political system with interest groups (essentially different factions in government) is interesting, and the different goods represented in the game are a welcome change. However, the main issue I have with the game is the lack of replayability and lack of player action in the running of the nation. In Victoria 2, after the initial setup, there were a few things you generally did in every campaign: set your budgets, research tech, declare wars, do your sphere of influence, build/expand factories, and set your national foci. In Victoria 3 you do much of the same, except the satisfaction of doing so is completely gone: sliders for budget are removed, replaced with static tax levels, the varied techs of V2 are slimmed down, spheres and national focuses are gone, and (most importantly) building/expanding buildings has no immediate effect that you can look at and get feedback from. Oftentimes I found myself just spamming factories for goods that were expensive, but the UI didn't really give me any data on how that was impacting the price of the good. Another issue that's mainly QoL is that every time you research a new production method in Victoria 3, as well, you have to do a billion annoying and monotonous clicks to switch the method in every single one of your buildings, and this happens way too often: for instance, when I research fertilisers, I have to manually go into every single type of farm (rye, wheat, rice, etc) and do two clicks: one to select the production method, and one to select the new one. This may sound like a meaningless gripe, but the amount of things that you have to click for no reason in this game is way too large. The law system sounds interesting, and is interesting, but the different laws aren't really different enough to drive me to debate whether one is better than the other. This is an issue that Victoria 2 had as well, where laws are just progressively better, but considering how this is a sequel and much was made of the political aspect of the game, I expected something more nuanced. The way that you enact laws is absolutely awful as well, it's an RNG system reminiscent of Europa Universalis sieges, with ticks taking forever and it being a simple dice roll if something gets passed or not. I tried to pass a law for wage subsidies for like a decade and a half with a 25% chance just because I got bad luck, and I could do very little about it except shrug and try again. There's basically no flavour differences between nations as well. Japan actually has a lot of different events and such (using the Journal system, of which my thoughts are generally positive), but really, every country feels the same when you get down to actually playing the core loop of the game. When I played as the UK, there was basically nothing I could do that really showed how preeminent I was as a power. The events are all generic and shared across every nation, and aside from "Confederating Canada/Australia", the journal entries were the exact same as any other nations I played. Nothing interesting about it.And to keep it brief, the war system is an absolute unmitigated disaster. Each front can only have *one* battle at a time, making long fronts such as in China or the USA absolute slogs. The general system is intuitive but annoying, requiring lots of boring clicks every time you declare a war to throw them into battle. The amount of troops set to a front has basically no bearing on how many troops actually go into the battle: I had 2 million soldiers fighting in Russia against a similar amount of Russo-French soldiers, and every single battle that happens only has 8k or so engaged, with the front moving a miniscule amount every time I win or lose. In that war, I had 1.5 million dead and wounded, where 50,000 were from battles and the rest were all attrition due to the ridiculous lack of battles (especially big ones). This is absolutely outrageous: I know disease, starvation, etc were massive killers in the 18th and 19th centuries, but that proportion is just wrong.All in all, I did enjoy the game for the little time I played it. Was it worth the price? In my opinion, absolutely not, and I don't see myself playing it for more than 50 hours or so until there's a big change in the game. The fact Paradox will surely make me pay £30 per DLC or more pushes me even further away from trying it out in future updates, especially since I'm certain it'll be 3 or 4 DLCs until the game is better, and many of the new features will probably just be random mechanics taped onto a base game that just isn't that good (cf. CK3 Royal Court).Save your money and buy Victoria 2 with all expansions. The game is janky, buggy, unintuitive, but it's something that Victoria 3 is not: consistent fun.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm really enjoying Victoria 3. Playing as Chile which is one of the starting options, I find it fascinating to play at a slow pace and watch as the towns and railroads appear on the map. There is a lot to learn, but I find the game very addictive. A lot of Vic 2 players seem to dislike the fact this is not, in fact Vic 2 but I hadn't played Vic 2 for years. Doubtless some of the concerns raised by the people leaving negative reviews will be dealt with over time anyway. I see the point about RNG, events etc. but really you build your nation in a way that stacks the odds to give the best chance for the RNG to fire off the things you are aiming for. For example I learnt early on in my several playthroughs that gaining a customs union with the UK means all your commodities are dirt cheap and you can grow your industries far more that way. Another interesting thing is that you actually WANT native uprisings in the areas you are colonising so you can simply invade the poor natives and take all their land in one go. For the greater good of course.Anyway, all in all a great fun game if you want a leisurely few hours watching your nation grow (micromanaging every 5-10 minutes, of course). If you want a wargame or map-painter, then you may not enjoy it so much due to the abstraction of some of those systems. Still - recommended already and it will surely get better too.

_childDocuments_.review: For the TLDR: The game is Mediocre at best and I feel like paradox really dropped the balls with many of the design choices of this game. Theres a lot that I'm willing to forgive the game for such as the controversial war system that many are harking on right now and the AI being bad in general as thats some things that can be expected. but What can't be excused is the complete barebones nature of the game, Every country in this game has the exact same loop for the most part, the exact same gameplay. with barely little flavor. There is some if you look for it but there is no universal Historical events or things that impact the world, a lot of big no brainer countries that you expect people to try have very little content, the majors have some unique stuff but not enough for example the USA has maybe three events that just happen and you have to deal with, the first is the indian removal acts and then the very easily avoided civil war that you just pass a law to ban slavery for, and then prohibition. With a handful of decisions as well. Thats it.  Most nations aren't that lucky. Ottomans have a crisis at the start that resolves pretty early. Japan from the bit I had played seems to not really have anything other than the decision to overthrow the shogunate and all you need for that is to not have an interest group in the government. Sorry the TLDR ended up being a little long, but for a more detailed reason why please read on. Here are my list of Grievances:1.The Politics screen is pretty lackluster with the ability to just completely ignore elections and keep the party in control with seemingly no downside other than "Legitimacy" which ties into time to enact laws, with lower legitimacy taking longer to pass. Parties that the population votes for don't get added automatically to the government based on voter share or something similar. You can pick and choose however you want really as long as you don't care about law passage time.  It's just completely lackluster. Barely serviceable as a base game experience. 2. The Economy is very much a departure from Victoria 2 and that is not a good thing. Vicky 2 had its problems but the Economy fascinated me, with so many different ways to manage your country, all of this has been reduced in Vicky 3 to what is in the most basic terms possible, a "Command Economy" with private Investments. What I mean by this is that you the player. I.E. The "spirit" of the nation has complete control over what your little pops employ themselves into, what gets built and where. This is probably my biggest dislike of the game. It is hilariously tedious to click through and provide the goods needed and by late game it seems to take up a majority of my time checking the market and building like 20+ of whatever good is needed by the pops. There is no international trade like in Vicky 2 either you have to manually establish those trade routes for every good you need and even then there is a level cap that I for one cannot really figure out, some trade routes seem to just increase the amount of goods available from that nation with no rhyme or reason. I much prefer the Vicky 2 system of trade. The Population should be able to grow and expand factories as it pleases, and fail at those endeavors as much as succeed with government intervention when necessary. 3. The War system needs to be ironed out. Now I'm not one of those band-waggoning the new war system being ass. I think that the concept is very interesting but definitely poorly executed. I do understand the idea of Vicky being more of an economic sim than another paradox war sim, but there needs to be some input from the player other than what we have right now. You can have 500 battalions on a front to the enemies 100 and still have the AI auto gen you engagements where the enemy outnumbers you 3 to 1 for seemingly no reason other than the luck of the draw. You can win wars you should in theory lose and Lose wars you should have no way of losing just by the way the game handles the front for you which is kind of dumb imo.4. The Politics that I have already described to some extent, but to add on to it, All government types and laws feel fundamentally the same, The Economic laws as far as I can tell only really determine what you can subsidize and what your investment pool if you have one is used for with the most extreme command economy meaning you subsidize everything. Its kind of weird how most laws give you a new government institution but it seems like you don't really have to pay for it in any way, i.e. a dedicated police force doesn't cost money it costs bureaucracy, which while fundamentally might be the same thing since you have to spend money to build government centers, is kind of a weird choice, and same goes for most of the expenses other than The category for the pension laws which do cost money.  Sorry that wen't back into the economy for a little bit but it is all tied in the end. One of the biggest interesting things for me with the politics is the Interest groups and you being limited to picking three at the most usually for how many are in your government. Because in a democratic system if they garnored enough votes would they not have senators or MP's or whatever for that party? especially if we are looking at the US system where in Vicky 3 Every interest group is getting millions of votes, there seems to be no way that they don't get their own little stake in the government. All in all if I do get any feedback from this I expect it will be the same things I've heard for every other paradox game. "This game *Just* got released you can't expect a paradox game to be good on release"  or "Just wait for the DLC" or  "wait for mods" or something like that. But Don't you see how that is a completely unacceptable way of thinking? Why do we have to wait for the game to be fixed on a $50 dollar title from a studio with decades of experience and be okay with it? Are you really so beaten that YOU are okay with it? if it was any other studio many of you would refuse to purchase from them ever again. Its ridiculous the amount of hoops of logic I hear from fanboys of Paradox and don't get me wrong I'm one too I love paradox but I'm sick and tired of giving them excuses for the mediocre ♥♥♥♥ they shovel down our mouths every few months and we as a community are just supposed to take it because no matter what when that next DLC or expansion or game whatever comes out, people are going to buy it, ♥♥♥♥ I'm probably going to but all I'm saying is the Criticism is totally valid and you know it too. Thanks for reading my little tangent. Have a good day.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR; At the time of writing this I currently have 2,444.5 hours played in Europa Universalis 4 and 1,134.1 hours in Crusader Kings 2. This is in all likelihood the last Paradox game that I will ever buy, as this game's release state and the release state of CK3 have turned me off of the company in it's entirety for several reasons. In both EU4 and CK2, I learned to expect less from the release state of Paradox games than how their marketing is portraying their games, but CK3 and now V3 are so far below my already low expectations for content that I can no longer support a company that releases unfinished games.1. Neither V3 or CK3 released with any content of note that made countries play differently from one another. In V3 there are journal entries for the US and the Ottoman Empire that affect the direction that you play the country. France? Prussia? Austria? Great Britain, in a game named after Queen Victoria? Nope. You play them all the same, and the ONLY journal entry that you get in all of them is a laughably dumb journal entry where a character in your country is a serial killer that causes "widespread panic" that gives debuffs to your country that you can safely ignore until the RNG roll you have little control over decides it's time for Abraham Lincoln to be caught red-handed after killing his 20th victim. There are an unacceptably small number of events in the game in my opinion, and next to no flavor events.The developers have defended this absence of content by stating that their goal was for each nation to develop and play differently based on the differences in starting positions and did not want to "railroad" the player; however, given the fact that they as the developers can make the journal entries ignorable by making them not give penalties to nations if they are ignored or unmet this excuse rings hollow in my ears. Taking the example of CK3, and taking the plenitude of mechanical problems that need fixing in V3's current state that CK3 did not have, I expect the earliest we will see any mechanics or flavor of note to be added to V3 2 years after release at the earliest, as the DLC that did so for CK3 was released about 1.5 years after that game's release.2. There are two very glaring mechanical problems that severely affect this game in a negative way. I personally find the trade system to be acceptable if annoying in it's current iteration. But the lacking AI and war system are completely unacceptable for not only the caliber of game that V3 was marketed as, but also what I expected from Paradox given what I experienced in EU4 and CK2.The AI is nonsensically bad. In vanilla V3, you can start as any nation in the game and become the highest GDP, largest military in the game by 1870s-1880s at the LATEST. There are plenty of examples available if you search for such things, one such that I am aware of is a player starting as Laos, a landlocked unrecognized nation in southeast asia that starts with a single state, who didn't expand by a single province for the entirety of the game and became the country with the highest GDP and largest military. The AI does not exist in vanilla, and given that this game is based entirely around singleplayer vs AI, to me this makes the game not exist. This is not to mention that larger countries are willing to lose tens of millions of their citizens to attrition defending the interests of *random unrecognized nation in Africa* so that when you try to play as a smaller country to give yourself a challenge, you just get blocked by a major power like France who loses 10 million men to attrition and contracts their GDP by 40% just to stop you from making a single diplomatic play for no discernible reason. This means you have to play with a mod, Anbeeld's Revision of AI, to even have an enjoyable experience playing this game. Paradox should consider contacting Anbeeld and negotiating to pay him ~20k euro just so they can copy and paste his mod into the base game files. That is how bad Vanilla AI is.The new war system is both laughably bad in its current iteration and laughably easy to fix, and it would have been fixed by a modder in a week or less if Paradox was willing to be embarrassed by having a random, singular modder in their community fix such a core mechanic in V3 in such a short amount of time. They must have decided they weren't willing to be embarrassed though, as that is the only reason I can think of for why MAX_NUM_BATTLES_PER_FRONT = 1 isn't in the modifiable DEFINES file for the game. In vanilla V3 you can only have one battle per front, and battles take approximately the same time from beginning to finish no matter what stage of the game you are in or what version of military building production method(line infantry, skirmish infantry, etc.) you are using. This makes warfare an incredibly tedious and boring affair, particularly in the late game as one thing that Paradox did is they made it so that the more advanced military building production method you are using the less provinces you take when you win a battle. Modders currently have the ability to change the time for a battle to start, the amount of provinces you take when you win a battle, the stats of the various military productions methods, and the amount of regiments that are in the front that participate in any given battle; however, as it is currently not possible to change the maximum number of battles per front it's generally not worthwhile assigning more than 100 regiments to a front. Modders are currently hamstrung from totally fixing the warfare system and so are forced to put out band-aid mods using what they can change to make it more bearable in its current state. How bad the current warfare system is, is compounded by the nonsensical AI as the AI rarely has the capacity to upgrade their military building production methods to a better form of infantry. So in the later stages of Vanilla V3 you are generally fighting against Line Infantry from the 1830s with Tanks and Airplanes, so Paradox fixed this by making it so that if one side of a battle is using a better military production method, then the other side gets to bring more regiments into the battle. So you get to watch as your tanks and planes slowly lose morale due to base morale loss (morale loss being the only reason you lose a battle) while they slaughter tens of thousands of line infantry per week.3. The UI was marketed as being streamlined and easy to follow, but is the most clumsy UI that I have yet to experience in a Paradox game. They replaced 30+ map modes with 5 Lenses, so instead of the 2 step process of 1. Find map mode 2. Click or hover on province to see information, you now have to go through an indeterminate step process of 1. Find lense that probably, MAYBE pertains to the information you seek, 2. Click or hover on province, 3. Hover over part of description that pops up that sounds like what you're looking for, 4. Repeat 3 for each nested description until you get to what you were looking for. Some information like Population Needs/Wants are a 6 step process to find, to the point that describing that information as hidden is apt. But don't worry, there are UI mods that you can download to fix the UI!!! ....... Notice how the modding community is fixing or trying to fix all the problems the game has? I very much believe that Paradox has become incredibly lazy in their game development, all the while telling themselves that they are "focusing on the core mechanics of the game" because each of their games has such an active modding community that any problem can and probably will be fixed by the modding community. No content or flavor? Don't worry there will be content or flavor mods for people that want it. ♥♥♥♥ AI? Don't worry there will be AI mods for people that want it. This might not be an openly stated opinion in their offices, but given the release states of their 2 latest titles, I can only assume this to be the case.

_childDocuments_.review: 1.3 released. The game is pretty good by now. There has been significant quality of life increases, new content and some flavor added to a few countries (France mostly). Diplomacy and war are barebones but internal politics and the economy are pretty good. I haven't noticed any game breaking bugs either. The game is prone to crashing and can run pretty slow on a decent computer, but I expect these things to be ironed out in the near future. Some things I have a problem with:Many nations are in need of more flavor and internal economic systems need more differences (Ex: a market economy and a command economy control pretty similarly), usual paradox DLC policy, immigration never happens the way it did historically, being super liberal is too OP and doesn't cause major stability issues, American Civil War sucks, too many radicals, not enough player control over war, diplomacy too simple. Paradox has already begun to tackle most of these things and they will probably be improved on substantially by 1.4 or 1.5. There's also no foreign investment though that has been guaranteed to be coming according to DLC pages on steam published today.Here are some things I do like:Internal politics (made much better 1.3 and Voice of the People)Economy (The gameplay loop of importing and building stuff based on demand + researching and upgrading building and then watching GDP soar is pretty satisfying and relaxing)Factions/Interests groups - They are simple to understand yet add more dynamics to politics. Supporting them and weakening groups through the passage of laws, suppressing and agitators and then trying to go for the law you really want while trying to avoid a revolt is pretty cool and a substantial challenge. Interest/Political groups have been theorized to be based off of Marxist ideas of class warfare and it actually seems pretty historically accurate and realistic. Game looks great and UI is nice Technology tree is well developed along with all the different types of laws and production methodsPopulation, cultural/ethnic and economical graphs are fun too look at and seem pretty accurate to 1836Game lasts a good amount of timeJournal entries are pretty good for the major nationsI would reccomend this game, especially if you are into graphs, statistics, The Victorian Era or stuff like that.

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of recent Paradox games have been criticized for being "bare bones" and some of them feel warranted, this game is not one of them. The economic simulator they've created for this game is light-years ahead of any other game I've ever played and puts all other paradox games to shame. The political aspect defiantly needs refinement but the structure is there it isn't missing. The diplomatic aspect again similarly needs refinement but the structure is there. The only part of this game that needs a lot of work, and the reason I believe so many people have disliked the game, is the  warfare. Frankly, this game needed a good few more months to cook in the studio because warfare is a total after thought. You can tell the team put all their effort into the economy and any spare time went to diplomacy and politics and the warfare just didn't have enough time to be fleshed out.
