_childDocuments_.review: EDITED REVIEW, INITIAL REVIEW BELOW:I had initially given this game a positive review, but after spending more time with it and taking a much closer look at how the economy and trade actually works in the game, I actually can't believe how unrealistic and broken almost every aspect of the game is at the moment. Politics, government, and events are a complete mess. The diplomatic play system simply adds such a random element to foreign affairs that everything becomes a gamble rather than a strategy. It's not too bad in the early game, but by the time you get to mid game, almost every major power will have an interest in the entire globe, which results in incredibly stupid diplomatic choices by the AI. I've had the equivalent of WWI kick off multiple times as early as the 1850s over things as stupid as me trying to annex an African tribe. Politics is even more nonsensical, with sudden and massive swings in the balance of power between conservatives and liberals with seemingly no rhyme or reason. Some of this is for stupid but explainable reasons (an extremely charismatic leader taking over for a marginalized group and getting them to reverse course on an issue, okay fine), but other times it makes so little sense that I must assume it's a bug. Some events have such strict conditions for the AI that they're effectively impossible because of the AI's cheats (e.g. Alaska Purchase). The AI is completely incapable of handling revolutions so Europe is an endless series of civil wars. It's incredibly easy at the US to avoid the Civil War entirely, in the 3 games I played as them I was simply able to ban slavery and elicit nothing more than some discontent from the Democrats.The combat system is even worse than I originally thought at first. The front line system is bad enough, but managing your generals and admirals is an even bigger nightmare. Once promoted, you cannot demote a general, you can only fire him (which incurs penalties). I don't get any say in how many units a general is commanding, they simply have an upper command limit and troops are automatically distributed among generals. Which means you have to be very careful who you promote and when, because it means there's very little strategic flexibility in your wars. If you have the entirety of your army under the control of a field marshal, but a relatively small navy, you will not be able to send that field marshal with only a small number of troops to launch a naval invasion of an undeveloped nation without incurring the enormous penalties that come with not having enough ships to support them. Your only option is to train more troops and put them under the command of a brigadier general. Why can I not have a say in where troops are actually used?The trade in this game is so broken I don't think I can even go into detail without this turning into a lecture on trade theory, but it is not realistic. The long and short of it is that Victoria 3 gives you a ridiculous amount of control over things that countries historically did not have control over, but virtually no control over things they had absolute power over. Producing more things for your economy is almost an exercise in futility because it will immediately be scooped up by foreign powers with no way to stop it unless you're completely isolationist, e.g., you built a bunch of new grain farms to feed your starving population but France immediately swooped in and grabbed every bushel of grain and threw it on their ships without you being able to do anything to stop them. Insane. Your control over your puppets is virtually non-existent. Puppeting a country simply gives you a flat percentage of their income, you have no say over their laws unless you want to potentially go to war with the rest of the world over how you govern your territories (you also cannot peacefully annex a subject that is loyal to you, you have to hate each other and create a diplomatic incident that hopefully doesn't descend into a World War). You cannot invest in foreign nations like you could in Victoria 2, which was a huge game mechanic both in the game and in real life. You can't even invest in your colonial nations, which is a massive problem because the AI is so incompetent when it comes to building things it will run them into the ground. I could go on for hours but it's clear to me now this game isn't even close to being complete. They took Victoria 2, beat the **** out of it, and then put on some foundation and blush to cover up the bruises.ORIGINAL REVIEWIt's hard to recommend this right now because of the amount of problems with it, but ultimately I feel the current Steam score is unfair to the game. I went into this as a die-hard Victoria II fan, with several thousand hours in the game both on and off my Steam account. In many ways, similar to how Paradox handled Crusader Kings III, this game is quite a few steps forward. But in other areas they have taken too many steps back.For starters, they really did a great job with fleshing out the economy simulation in the game. Victoria II was notoriously difficult to understand, with your economy suddenly crashing with little to no understanding of why it was happening. Victoria III does a much better job of explaining where exactly money is coming from and going to. However, a big red flag for me is that every economy plays the exact same. For some reason, whether you're an agrarian nation or a laissez-faire society or a command economy, it plays the same. You pick and choose what gets built, how it produces goods, etc. The only difference between vastly different economic systems is what you're allowed to subsidize or not. Besides being incredibly unrealistic, it's annoying. I don't like having to constantly babysit my buildings, the aristocrats and capitalists who own them should be expanding their factories or changing their production methods when the economy suits (assuming it's a free market economy), the King/President/Whatever should not be the one telling you it's okay to add another assembly line to your ludicrously profitable steel mill.This leads into my next major issue with the game. I feel perhaps the devs made building management this tedious to hide how little other content is in the game at the moment. The biggest example of this is the warfare. I understand they wanted to focus more on the economy for Victoria III, which makes sense, but at the moment the warfare system is completely devoid of any fun and is often very vague and difficult to understand. Armies will win or lose seemingly at random, with neither numbers or technology making much of a difference. The front line feature, supposedly introduced to make managing wars simpler, does the exact opposite; it doesn't take very long for a single front line to break into a bunch of scattered front lines with armies and generals that are difficult to keep track of and even more difficult to get them to do anything. I actually like the new system for diplomacy leading up to war in theory, but in practice that is just as broken. At times it seems impossible to do anything because the AI is so asinine with their decisions on who to support in diplomatic plays. In my most recent game, Great Britain sat back and did nothing while the Ottomans overran all of North Africa, but decided to mobilize 200 battalions and get involved in Belgium's war with an undeveloped African tribe in the Congo.There's a few other features that are broken/annoying at the moment, like revolutions (and the AI's inability to handle them), but these are my main issues. Still, with that said, we all know Paradox's business model. Love it or hate it, Paradox releases a game and then spends the next few years building on it with patches/DLC. With the exception of a few games they truly abandoned after rough releases (Imperator...), they're pretty good about this. So I'm sure after 3-4 years and $400 worth of DLC this will be a masterpiece to rival EUIV.

_childDocuments_.review: So many people don't understand Victoria 3. It's an ECONOMY SIMULATOR so PREPARE to micromanage your industries. If you want an indepth war simulator, look elsewhere.Otherwise, I've enjoyed this game quite a bit, there are a few crashes but I think the CK3 launch was rougher tbh in the crash department. I've gotten to the early 1900s and don't really have too many performance issues and I'm playing CANADA with like 40 Million population (lots of mass migration) and 3rd largest GDP so there are tons of micropop groups that have moved in that would theoretically slow down the simulation (it has, but there are worse games for slowdown imho). I also got into trying colonization but I got in late and missed out on being able to grow rubber so my electronics industry is really hampered by rubber prices in the British Market. I've done really well with trying to spend, expand industries, and trying to be first-to-market for emerging industries (made serious $$$ with Power Plants for example). I imagine there are tons of unique fun starts, but considering that Hudson Bay Company is this enjoyable to I really think this is a good game, and I honestly don't know if I like Victoria 3 more than CK3. (Though this is coming from a person that couldn't get into EU4 and has no interest in HOI4; Plays a lot of RimWorld and Cities:Skylines, so I have different tastes than the average Paradox strategy gamer).People are complaining about performance and stability, I'm on Arch Linux btw and there are some crashes but as I said CK3 at launch was far worse for me for crashes when compared to Vicky 3, and 99% of the time it crashes AFTER an autosave so you don't really miss that much if it crashes once every 3 hours after autosaving. I use a 3900X and an RX 6600, if your computer is struggling you probably have a potato CPU (Zen 2 isn't really that new anymore) and should upgrade to something like the 5800X3D. As for warfare, I like the hands off style especially since this is NOT EU4 or HOI4. However, sometimes setting up who's side your on and war goals can be easy to screw up when initiating the diplomatic play for your war.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't often make reviews on game, but this one needs a review from me. To put it bluntly no replayability, no flavor, future DLC expansion to make it passable, interesting premise but severely lacking military system, and everything is micro intensive with the economy. This is the basic thoughts on this game for many people but i just wanted to mostly reiterate it. I feel this game has potential but removing all aspects of micro from everything else and throwing it into the economy just felt obsessive. Victoria 3 had so many paths it could have gone down, i just wish that it had had more time. I spent money on this game solely out of respect to Vic 2 even though i knew it was gonna be unfinished. I feel like all this game needs is for paradox to give it the respect it deserves. They called this one of the most anticipated games in paradox history but it feels like this got worse treatment than Imperator Rome did, and they did an amazing job fixing a lot of the problems (don't worry i still know there are plenty left) when they chose to dump it entirely. Victoria 3 did not have to be this massive endeavor to create a game where you throw everything but the start time out from the much loved previous title. That is what has put it in this precarious position. My final point for this is simply put, if they had not called this Victoria 3 and just let this plan be for something else then it might have been received better. Don't try to make something but only take the name from it to call attention to it. This isn't much different than what call of duty did with Black Ops 3, where there was nothing from the previous titles to connect it but there wasn't much wrong with it if it had a different title. I love a lot of paradox games and i have made many friends online from it but sometimes companies need a wake up call to how they do things, i hope they learn from their mistakes here and fix this game. Maybe it will change with time and i can remove this review with happiness behind it, but at its current state i cannot with good intention leave a positive review. This just felt like a cash grab using Victoria 2 to do it. That is its main drawback and it has upset the community greatly, multiplayer and single-player alike. I doubt paradox will ever read this but i do hope for them to remake this through updates to fix things and listen to the community. This is just not victoria 3 plus the many problems that others talk about.

_childDocuments_.review: Do not buy this.It is indefensibly bad.They made war something you are a passenger to, and made the entire affair RNG.You can now get fully annexed because the RNG put 2 units against 20. How many do you have? 40. How many does the enemy have? Just 20. But you ceased to exist because the dice determined only 2 units were allowed to fight.Cool.People said, the minute they announced these gimmicks; "Do not put these in the game. This is not wanted. This will only make it worse."They went ahead with the gimmicks anyways. And wowee, they are just as bad as everyone knew and said they would be.They literally took the crisis system from Victoria II, repainted it, called it "diplomatic plays," and made it mandatory for EVERY WARGOAL. This has, in effect, made the entire game unplayable for all but the Great Powers. Every. Single. War. Goes through "diplomatic plays" where the AI (and you, but in effect only the AI gets any actual utility from this system,) gets to go through a list of countries and try to convince them to support it in this crisis.This means that even if you are some random tribe in Africa trying to reunify your tribal kingdom that just split up, you have to deal with the AI bribing France to come support it, just to take one nation back.Every war. Every attempt to do anything other than accept that expanding, or in any way growing, is agonizing, unfun, and miserable. I have never hated something more. I have no idea who on the staff thought every single act of diplomacy needed to follow the Victoria 2 crisis mechanics. Those mechanics were extremely mixed and a lot of people hated them, but at least they weren't THE DEFAULT.Alliances? They exist. But "diplomatic plays" literally makes me wonder why they even exist. They're so insignificant and pointless when every single war has the potential to randomly decide to be WW1 in 1840 because Persia wanted to slap Afghanistan with a herring and France, Britain, and Austria decided to support Afghanistan.I don't know, I just don't... I mean I just am so disappointed. This is so bad, I've tried to explain it but I doubt I even got it across how frustrating, arbitrary, and bad it is in practice.There's so much more wrong but I just don't care anymore. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------It's gotten even worse since launch and the only thing they've meaningfully fixed of the complaints is they made navies not a strictly abstract concept lmao

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR : It's an early access that doesn't tell its name. Victoria 3 is not a bad game. It is, however, like 90% of the games released those days, a rushed and unfinished game. It will be good at some point, maybe after a year of patch and QoL improvements. I don't regret buying it because I really enjoyed the time I spent on it so far and that I believe this will be, in the long run, a must have (hence the "positive review" because steam don’t allow neutral reviews) and I do believe hardcore Paradox/Vic2 players that don't want to buy it now because of its current state, should check it now and then to see how it improved over time.So yeah, Vicky 3 is out and it is... an okay game. I mean, it doesn't compare well with other Paradox games like EU4 or HoI4 or Vic2 but it can stand on its own as a "correct game". But, astutes gamers of Paradox games will be disappointed. Not because it's a bad game, but because it's a rushed and unfinished game. It's an early access that doesn't tell its name. Which it should be. Those games are so complex, with expectations so large and so precise on what the game should look like, should contain, studios like Paradox should release those games as early access to have this instant feedback of what is working and what’s not. I mean, Kerbal Space Program 2 is doing it and they are right to do so, because they want to nail the base game as stable as possible so the rest is working as intended and Paradox should do the same for their next game.Yes there are bugs and crashes and this, I think, is to be expected for any new game as no QA department is capable of testing a game as extensively as the entire population. So I won't talk about it here, also because I assume this will be the first thing to be fixed (at least the crashes, Paradox usually act on crashes). Edit : The late game is particularly unstable, as I had something like a crash every 25 minutes in the last 3h of gameplay. And some bug are, if not game breaking, annoying nonetheless.What about the rest, well, you can resume the whole game with the same phrase : "it's a good idea, but it feels incomplete, not pushed far enough".Let's take the war system for example (that everybody's piling on).I like, even love, the idea. I really do. As the Vicky games is more an economic and social simulator, representing a moment of transition in history when leaders of nations stopped riding along their armies, it makes sense that it's not your charge to move units individually but command your generals to "do something" on selected fronts. But, as a rushed system, it is painful to read and to understand. I also don't like the way HQ and regiments are managed (or more micromanaged); units are acting like buildings and since the building management is too convoluted, it's not good. As an improvement, and if we want to keep the front system as currently designed, I would have done the creation of regiments and units close to Vicky 2 (fixed or templated types applied on X units created) but with assignation to generals in the same way HoI4 works, to finally use those general on the fronts selected (and make the fronts more readable).Or let's mention buildings and political systems. And no I won't talk about the "build building to meet demand" mechanic because it's not a faulty mechanic in itself, it's how supply and demand work. Now, I won't pretend I was fully capable of understanding how Vicky2 worked. But I liked in this game that, depending on your economical system (liberalism, socialism, communism, etc...) you had a certain level of control over the economy, and usually the economy would be in the hands of the IA (i.e. private market). And that you could create industries abroad when needed. This feels (and is) completely absent in the game. And it's cruelly missing.Also, the political system is as simple as the one in Vicky 2. I like the different interest groups creating political parties and stuff, but as a new game, I was hoping for a little more "umpf" to it, like seeing parliamentary groups (when you have a parliament), government toppled by opposition in time of crisis, a bigger impact of GDP on political results, the power to call general election, and so on. Vicky 2 was lacking, in my opinion, in the political life department, I want more in Vicky 3.And finally, the "geopolitical" part of the game is, like the war, not properly working. I get what they tried to do, basically taking the "crisis" feature of Vicky 2 and building the whole diplomatic part of Vicky 3 upon it, but it is not working. And placing the revolutions/revolts as part of this system was not really a good idea, because there are no more small revolts anymore, and where there is one, it turns it into an international crisis but it shouldn't be. Also, have a level of engagement for a country in a crisis. Like "I won't help you but I'll send weapons/money/volunteers", it works really well on HoI4 and an inspired version could work here.So there you have it. The bottom line is : I don’t regret buying it so I won't have to buy it later and I did enjoy the 22+ hours I spent so far on it and so, I have to post this as a positive review but it still needs work. A lot, a lot of work. And I kinda trust Paradox to do the work. Succeeding at it would be a whole other task, but they have proven they are capable of reworking complex and deep systems in their games, sometimes replacing flawed systems of another flawed one, but a lot of time nailing the problem and making the game a lot better (and we’re talking systems here, not balance).And yes, I’ll review it again in a few months if there are changes and, hopefully, improvements.

_childDocuments_.review: I've found Victoria 3 to be really enjoyable. It has a different core gameplay loop than Vicky 2 so it is understandable that some people are upset about it. Some pros and cons I've experienced:Pros:- Good modelling of opportunity cost (if you choose to do action A you won't have the resources to do action B)- Migration system is fixed from Vicky 2. In Vicky 2 pops were hard coded to want to go to North America (read America) and it didn't matter if life was great in a European country beside them- You now actively develop base resources. This makes many countries more interesting to play and you can focus on those strengths to build wealth for your pops- National Markets force you to choose between producing a broad range of goods or specialising to produce goods more efficiently and trading. Many people are complaining that they just produce whatever is most expensive in their market and rinse and repeat. That's an inefficient way to play. Every country has pros and cons and exploiting those might take additional thought. For example, when starting as one of the Canadas the most expensive good in the British Market is groceries, but building a food industry is a bad idea. Why? Because it costs 450 construction to build and takes more infrastructure. In the same time you can build 3 logging camps, employing more people and using less infrastructure per job. The AI appears to just build the most expensive good. Are people smarter than the AI? Maybe.- The cap on economic growth from Vicky 2 is removed. In Vicky 2 you could only have 8 factories per state and if all of them are expanding you are at the limit of growth. Fast growth needed more states which needed warfare which is why people talk about warfare so much when comparing the two. In Victoria 3 truly exponential growth is possible and is very satisfying when it does.Cons:- I'm open to the new warfare system but it is too opaque to be interesting. Why did my troops lose a battle against a weaker foe? Why did my General choose to use 10 troops instead of 15? How important is 45 defence vs 50 defence? Nobody knows.- It is hard to find stuff in the menus. Undoubtedly I'll get better at finding info but some stuff is hard to find. For example, seeing how many convoys you have to trade with when being a junior in a market. Right now the only way I've found is setting up a new trade route which is annoying. I should be able to open the market tab and boom, you have this many convoys.Altogether a good game that I've really enjoyed so far. Will update the review if things change.

_childDocuments_.review: After over 1000 hours I believe I can make a somewhat informed opinion. Firstly, the things it does well it does really well, the things it does badly it does really badly. In whole, Vic 3 is perfect for aspiring statisticians and lovers of economic and political management. There is very little to no railroading on the direction you choose to play, do you want to become an autocratic U.S? You can! Do you want to become the largest exporter of fruit in the world? You can! Unfortunately, what most of the negatives aspects of the game consist of are in the awful and frankly boring combat system. There is NO micromanaging of troops, the player has control over 3 areas of the military; quantity, weapon production, and tech. Battles are handled through a front-line system that is automatically assigned during war, each battle will have a random number generated determining any buffs or debuffs for combat stats. The same is true for naval combat as vessels are assigned to specific sea nodes spread through the ocean to block enemy ports. In short, Vic 3 is superior to its competitors in terms of economic management and its evident that this is where the development team mostly focused on. On the contrast, the military feels like a complete afterthought.

_childDocuments_.review: This game feels unfinished. There are a lot of good ideas in this game but are either poorly implemented or too complex to be enjoyable to the casual player. The wars are fun at a glance but lack the depth needed to make it engaging, also the process of declaring wars can be kinda ♥♥♥♥♥, an example would be a dominion being swayed against its overlord.Also, playing anything lesser than a minor power is incredibly boring and the process of becoming a minor power is very tedious and time consuming, thus creating a less enjoyable experience.Finally, there are numerous errors with the culture map, and religion has no overall bearing on your countries overall trajectory. While yes the religious are represented with a political party it is usually only one religion being represented.Can this game get better with updates and future DLC? Yes it can get better. But it should of launched in a better state.TL:DR; Do not buy this game.

_childDocuments_.review: The game feels very empty, it'll throw annoyances your way but not give you many solutions, almost like it doesn't know what to do with you and kinda doesnt really want you there.Basically the game is missing a core gameplay element. In CK3 and EU4 you can take action in the moment and feel involved in the world while also managing a slower paced long term development of your land. This game is missing the first part.The war system in the game is simple but its not as awful as a lot of other reviews make it seem but it is weird just how simple it is, now I'm not a massive fan of how HOI4 does things but youd expect more from the company that managed to design something like that.As for the actual management of your chosen country, everything moves at a GLACIALLY slow pace. It can take so long for a law to come even close to a chance at succeeding and then twice as long for it to even get enacted that I forget I was even trying to pass it in the first place. Same goes for turmoil (basically resistance to invaders in captured provences). It doesnt really stop you from doing anything except it slows everything in that province down but OH MY GOD it just never goes away and the icon just sits there taunting you! And other than choosing what to build there isnt really much else to do. Like I said before its a bit empty. A lot of the things you can do in the game have a passive effect as they are supposed to but its almost to passive.The Standard of Living (SoL) mechanic is similar in that its just more annoying to try and deal with than anything else. Even if you have a handle on it, the amount of Loyalists or Radicals you have in your country will sometimes just randomly jump up and down because their needs arent being met but thats it, thats all you get. Nothing you do seems to have much of an effect even in the long run and I mean in that youll basically have the same ratio through pretty much the entire game and the game isn't really forth coming with explanations as to why things are happening just tool tips that give you the definition of the terms used.These things would probably actually add a lot of depth and texture to the game if they weren't the only things this game has to offer. I would say don't spend your money on this game unless it receives a significant gameplay update with more engaging features.   The map is pretty though. Which is nice I suppose.

_childDocuments_.review: The good:-By far the best game Paradox has released so far when it comes to potential. Lots of historical inaccuracies like culture, faction ideologies/preferred laws, etc.-Most mechanics need a lot of refinement such as the logistics, ideological revolutions and combat.Also stupid AI as usual, but that's a certified classic for Paradox.All in all, worth it at launch and there is A LOT of room for improvement. It really has the potential to be an incredible game with enough updates, DLCs and mods.

_childDocuments_.review: I had been looking forward to Paradox Interactive's new economic strategy sim, Victoria III, and I have not been disappointed. I tried playing its predecessor (Vicky 2) with the House Divided and Heart of Darkness expansions, but while the setting elements highlighted by those were strong draws and several game concepts really provoked me to think about interesting decisions, I ultimately found the older game to be too much of a simulator and too little of a game. I am happy to say that in my experience with Victoria 3, the player feedback loop is very well established and there will always be something interesting to manage either in your nation's economy or its international affairs.The first major noticeable improvement is that the economy is always player-driven. Buildings are the main organizing elements for your workforce, since they employ pops, take in inputs, and produce outputs. Most buildings are built by the player regardless of what economic law one chooses, but Subsistence Farms and Subsistence Orchards allow peasants to use a small amount of Arable Land and produce a small amount of many different basic resources. Your usual goal throughout the game will be to employee these peasants in more specialized labor by building either Agriculture Buildings, which employ pops to farm arable land, or Extraction Industries, which employ pops to exploit natural resource deposits. And of course, you have Production Buildings you can construct to turn raw resources into processed resources. Balancing the raw resource production with the development of processing methods that use up those resources is one of your main goals in managing your economy.One decision I think deserves special attention is that the developers have introduced an Objective whenever you first start a new game. This Objective can be just to Learn to Play the game, which suggests several ideal nations with which you can play a tutorial with a loose set of optional missions to teach basic concepts of the game. Other objectives create a set of missions for you to focus on with certain playable nations: you can opt for Economic Dominance, Military Supremacy, or an Egalitarian Society, and the game will suggest several nations to play with that Objective. You will have a set of journal entries depending on the objective you chose that will teach you different approaches to playing the game.In addition to the other objectives, there is also a Sandbox mode that will be familiar to fans of previous Paradox games, in which you can play as any "organized nation" in the world. This includes a variety of nations in every region, but excludes those who territories can be colonized by other nations. Disorganized nations can still but useful as international relations however, as they can launch a Diplomatic Play (a type of negotiation that can lead to war) in order to seize territory from any nation that is colonizing their land. This can potentially make disorganized nations into very interesting allies for the rival of the colonizing power in that region.The other compelling loop of the game, besides managing resources on the market, is to reform your government. Depending on what interest groups and coalitions are in power, you will be able to enact laws that have support within your government depending on the total support that exists from politically active pops and interest groups throughout your nation. Eventually you may be forced to outlaw child labor and give voting rights to more and more people simply because the popular demand for such laws becomes so high that they would be easy to pass and cause unrest if they are resisted.I should mention that events like the Opium War between Britain and China and the American Civil War are represented in the game, much like in the expansions to Vicky II, and they are already included in the sequel at the time of release. While there is now 1860s start date like V2: A House Divided, the Legacy Slavery system of the USA in 1836 virtually ensures a semi-realistic civil war unless the player exploits certain game mechanics, like the ability to release the nation of New Africa from the United States at any time with no real cost. However, current update plans from Paradox Interactive are to more fully prevent circumvention of this event, leading to a historically plausible outcome in the United States more often than not.Managing the development of production and railroads provides a very interesting throughline to playing Victoria III. As far as I have seen, complaints have been centered around the simplified and abstracted war system. I have personally experienced some frustration with the movement of generals from one front to another, mainly because if a general is redirected en-route by the closing of his target front, his existing travel time is seemingly not taken into account when determining his new route. But other than certain hiccups like these, I vastly prefer the warfare system of Victoria III to the Risk-based army management of Victoria II and other Paradox games. The use of the front system of Heart of Iron IV and the elimination by abstraction of individual army units on map provinces has been a highly effective way to streamline and automate military conflicts while allowing the player to continue focusing on the main gameplay loop: managing the economy.

_childDocuments_.review: Like a lot of paradox fans, I blindly jumped on the hype train since the anouncement of the game. I knew Paradox had a reputation of releasing lackluster, unfinished and buggy dlc's and games, but yet again I chose to ignore it and pre ordered. Its suffices to say I hope I won't do so again. Let's start with the economic system which the developers made out to be the cornerstone of the game. It mostly is clicking on your market screen and clicking on your construction screen to meet your people's demands. This is literally all you have to do since resources your country doesn't produce can be very easily required through colonizing East Africa or spamming gov administration buildings, getting more bureacracy and opening infinite amounts of trade routes. barely any flavour mechanics or events are tied to this, so it seems like you're doing the same economic strategy over and over again for majow powers. Minor nations do feel a little bit different because though. Also leaving or joing a customs union/market of a bigegr country can potentially tank your GDP, because your buildings and resources are according to the previous market.It is impossible for me to feel immersed into the diplomacy because of the horrible AI. I had a game in which The USA tried to liberate Finland for some reason while being attacked by the UK. They ended spiralling downwards because of the treaty ports and war reparations they had to cede. Its also baffles me that there are very little consequences for breaking an obligation. I offered France an obligation to back me in a diplomatic play which I won. They asked me to join their customs union after this which I refused. You should think that France wouldn't forget this slight for years to come, but they accepted my obligation in a different play 3 years later.Politics feels like your trying to please some braindead robots. Within ten years you can completely turn the tide of your nation towards liberalism and democracy and conservative interest groups are not doing anything about it at all. There should be events of people getting very angry and rebellious when you steer away from the status quo, but it's just not happening.The military system is liked by some, but completely misses the mark for me. I get that they took a different approach to Vicky 2's system which was suboptimal. However, this war system feels like your only staring at your screen and watching it happen. You only get to build barracks, supplies and decide how advanced your army is going to be and press the attack or defend button. Navy feels just the same.Despite all this the game can be a bit fun for a while, but usually I get bored of playing a nation after 30 years and end up playing another nation hoping it feels different. It doesn'tDon't reward Paradox for releasing a lackluster game which feels like an early acces game. Can't wait for 10 DLC's and the modding community to make this game fun.

_childDocuments_.review: Victoria 3 is fun if only in comparison to other Paradox car crash releases. Put up against games like Stellaris or Imperator when they came out, it's much better. But as it currently stands, rather than being a deep and interesting game, it's a game that gives the illusion of depth by throwing so many systems at you that you get initially confused. The idea of "Not knowing what you're doing" is a classic Paradox game meme, and that confusion is often a substitute for making something genuinely deep and interesting. The reality is that these systems are mostly something you can ignore and are redundant. I have never lost a revolutionary war - so you can mostly ignore interest groups. The AI never approaches me with hostility - so diplomacy is irrelevant. Conscription and trade makes developing your military infrastructure and arms industries mostly irrelevant. You can go through the entire game ignoring research and just selecting the next one whenever your current one is done. There is supposed to be a system around it based on Innovation and Education (i.e. Research speed and Technology spread from other countries) but you don't need it.The primary limitation you have to consider, and only partially, is natural resources. For example, if I am playing as Ireland, I have no coal. Coal is the centre of industrial development - you NEED coal. So, of course, I traded for it. And kept trading for it. In fact I traded for so much of it that it used up all my trade capacity. So I had to build more ports. And then more. And then I had to use more advanced shipping technology to increase my number of convoys. This was the only mechanic that required thinking - balancing your trade routes. Which imports or exports were the most important?Other than that, the economy in this game is mostly brainless and thought up by some first year econ student who thinks they understand economics rather than someone who actually does. I have a Masters in Economics, and the way that Paradox hyped up the economic simulation was something that intrigued me. And it's clearly where they put a huge amount of their effort - and failed. It's utterly bizarre that you cannot stockpile goods, or that you cannot directly feed resource inputs into other industries (If my wood production and my furniture production is Government Owned, I should be able to tell my wood cutters to hand over the wood to my furniture makers for free). The biggest crime of the economic system and the fundamental problem is that the entire system is geared towards trying to force you to balance your goods upon an arbitrarily determined "base price" at which you will find equilibrium. Sure, you can operate at cheaper or lesser than the base price, but not by TOO much. The idea of world or even market price averages doesn't come into this, and at the end of the day my Government Owned wood cutters would rather export than to provide wood to my other Government Owned industries at a cheap price. There's no reason why I shouldn't be able to control exports and imports of certain goods - if you want to restrict trade then your only way to go is Isolationism, which bans all trade completely.The devs know that the game's economy is brainless, because it's so easy to make money that they had to create sinks for it in the form of Construction and tediously designed Bureaucracy. In order to gather taxes, you generally need Government Offices. These Government Offices also give you Bureaucracy, through which you can create trade routes and manage Institutions. In order to deal with bureaucratic shortfalls, you have to build these buildings, and the workers here must be paid. And you will have to build A LOT of these. And to build them in a timely manner, you will need to develop your Construction sector. And these are the two areas you will spend most of your money, and most of your book balancing is going to be focused around these two buildings. The one thing here for which I will give Paradox some kudos is that you can use wages for government workers as a form of economic stimulus - people with more money will buy more stuff. Where this completely falls short, as do taxes and tariffs, is that these things are not on a slider. I cannot decide that I'd rather pay my government employees 5% more or less, or 13%, or 93% - no, there are 5 fixed wage rates. Outside of the economic stimulus aspect of wages, the only other impact of adjusting them is IG approval.Taxes could have been interesting but the taxation system is poorly explained and it is in no way configurable. You have 5 different taxation types, decided by Law, and that's it. You can tax higher or lower within the bounds of those laws, but nothing else. I cannot decide to tax a particular type of industry or even a particular POP strata more or less - the rates are completely fixed. Additional taxes in the form of Consumption taxes can be added, but these taxes require Authority which means that unless you're a dictatorship or monarchy you wont be able to add more than one or two types of Consumption tax. What a bizarre system. Taxation is something that should be decided by your bureaucratic capacity, not your system of government with arbitrary "Authority Points" assigned to it.The political system of this game is internally inconsistent and self-contradictory, and it feels like you have no influence upon it outside of trying to economically boost certain POP types over others (i.e. build more factories = less peasants and more labourers = relevant interest groups weakened or strengthened. Similarly, more soldiers = stronger Armed Forces interest group and so on). The Government is stupid, there's no reason I should be able to appoint my government in a democracy. I have Universal Suffrage and a Council Republic, in no world should I be able to have a one party government where the party got 6% of the votes and the opposition is composed of 94% of the electorate. This kind of government control should be reserved for monarchies and autocracies. Interest groups themselves have internal inconsistency - you can have an IG that is both in favour of universal suffrage and strongly opposed to any kind of democratic system of government, or who are marked by the game as "Egalitarian" but who are still against women's rights (in fact the only people who are pro-women's rights are IG leaders with the Feminist ideology, which means that as far as the game is concerned Feminism is incompatible with a whole range of other policies such as having a Command Economy!). Furthermore, Bolstering and Suppressing and IG seems to do fundamentally nothing and is a waste of Authority.There's no getting around the fact that Interest Groups are a badly implemented idea and it was pretty obvious from the day they were announced that that would be the case. They would have been better off sticking to political parties a la Vicky 2 and then iterating upon the design to make them more dynamic (i.e. emergent political parties as opposed to the rigid ones in Vicky 2 and the IG-driven nonsense in Vicky 3).As for the war system, it's actually OK in concept, just lazy in implementation. If they were going to abstract it out to get rid of the needlessly tedious micromanaging of Vicky 2 (a decision I agree with) then they had a ready-made system in HOI4. Instead I go to war and IF I have a land border, the entire war is reduced down to dice rolls weighted by my technology, military PMs and my generals. I have no agency other than saying "Advance" or "Defend". Want to conduct multiple simultaneous attacks along a front? Good luck with that buddy, in this game we decide where and when the battle is done via dice roll, and if the game decides 4 units of your 30 stack are going to fight their 20 stack in some useless corner of the front then that's what's going to happen.The only reason I'm still playing this game is because I was gullible enough to buy it in the first place.

_childDocuments_.review: Victoria 3: Faustian Bargains.I have a rule with games, especially ones locked under the divine tutelage of Paradox Interactive. "Give it half a year and then bite". Nothing personal to popular games, I've just learned after the last decade of bad initial releases. Half a year gives a game time to burn through the initial shilling, fix some of the issues and ideally be in a functional state. Vic 3 was the same thing. I saw it on release, saw the videos on it and was hesitant, and so I decided to bide my time. Wait for it to go as cheap as possible and then see how it operates. Got lucky and managed to get it for a whole 15 bucks and man.I hate how I like it and I hate the issues WITH it as well.Victoria 3's root problem is the fact it's a perfect sequel on paper. This game knows the root issues that made people love and hate Victoria 2. Everyone loved industry and the economy system, while hating warfare and the AI. So it made overall improvements to everything and is now rife with what I will only describe as "Paradox Bargaining" as a result. Every single marked part of this game is an improvement on the original, and to an extent that it ends up neutering the game in some aspects. Your economy management is now upgraded with the ability to micro each industry's upgrades, and the improved tech system that allows you to just pre-plan out what tech you research is SO nice. It beats the constant red light/green light of Vic 2 or HoI's tech system, and it means no more searching for each port you need to upgrade. You have one menu. It's then kneecapped by the market system, which keeps certain nations tied to their own markets. On one hand, no more flooding the markets and causing an international stock market crash, but you also will now have to deal with the fact you can't really economically cause problems. The Army system makes sense on paper, no more accidentally nuking your economy with 934 dragoons nor having to micro every soldier. You have a front lines mechanic and the ability to just set a point and watch your men commit crimes against humanity prior to the Geneva Convention existing. Which is fine. The issue is the barracks system, tying individual armies to barracks you have to build. Sure it means you have to make sure you can afford an army, but it doesn't stop the AI from farting out 9 gorillion conscripts suddenly. Let alone the random modifiers that make naval invasions a gamble half of the time. Speaking of which.I whinged about Victoria 2's AI, calling it a trigger happy monster that didn't know how to manage itself while also barreling across the map causing problems. Clearly they knew that as well, but they overcooked it. Vic 3's AI is a dumbed down menace to fun, somehow barely managing their nations and yet still at the last second clinching any power play you try to make. It's been an absolute delight to watch in some aspects, seeing France go through Napoleon's and Louis's like a revolving door of monarchs but it's a constant problem in the game. Things just do not happen without you either kickstarting it or in some way inducing it. I've seen America's still not annexing Texas by 1890 or the Qing still being alive and not filled with opium. I think we can ratchet it up at least a smidge, although knowing Paradox, they'll overcook THAT as well.And no I will not be mentioning the DLC's, I didn't buy them. It's the real reason I didn't buy in until now because I know the first few DLC's for a Paradox game are basically tinsel before they actually nut up and give us something good. Vic 3's a good framework of a game, which is classically Paradox but don't fully uninstall Vic 2 yet. This game still has a lot of flab that they're going to iron out over time, the question being how much of that ironing out is going to have a price tag attached to it? Time will tell. Until then, I'm going back to beating up Paraguay.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a simplified and gutted of complexity shadow of Victoria 2. PDX seems to target mobile and console players with the design, and game philosophy follows that lead. Whole gameplay basically focuses on few dumbed down mechanics - following the need of the market and clicking and scrolling and clicking and scrolling trough  and through badly design graphs. You could basically automate that with two if macros. Perhaps they will add more systems that the predecessor already had at launch. They'll add them as DLC, and that's something I'd even buy if I believed that they wouldn't continue on the path of console-like repetitive clicking of oversized buttons. This game needs complexity to make it click, you need to be able to see more in tables and stats, engage more with internal politics based on pops needs, not on RNG. As a player I want to get involed in multi-angled dyplomatic struggles that I can read more about, not offensively simplistic "mana" system with "obligation" as only currency and no insight why other countires want what they want. Not to be overly critical - a few shortcuts can be forgiven, like the war system (although an expansion towards hoi 4 would be great). However, it's the economics and demographics that stand at the center of the game, and these are really disappointing in their current state.

_childDocuments_.review: 12/11/22The war system really needs to be more clear. The idea is not bad, but it needs so many fixes. Hopefully in the next 6 month is completely fixed. I will just wait for any big update. It was fun!30/10/22So after playing for several more hours, this game has potential. It's like playing "Modern Times". You have to tweak and make the engine works. It's fun, but for example if you upgrade your Urban Center to become a Market Squares, you can't go back and stop using glass. In my opinion their should be a degradation system. If you already made the upgrade after a while if you are not supporting let says 50% of the needs to maintain that building, it goes backward and again it will take some time to get back there. Not just pushing a button, this kind of upgrade take time. This way the player does not need to go back and forward always just to fix the economy.Then there is the UI, the game is not complex, it's the UI. Tool tips are not there to be helpful you have to go from one tool tip to another to get important info.This is the one thing that I REALLY don't like about this game: the lack of mystery behind developing, colonizing, inventing. This could be implemented for all the countries: how? first, your market and the markets that you have more relationships, and diplomacy you know better how they work. But let say you are from Europe and you go to Africa, why would you ALREADY know the borders of the UNKNOWN, It will be MUCH better not see borders and you will need to send EXPLORERS, DIPLOMATS, TRANSLATORS etc to understand the other countries! All of this can be done with the CHARACTERS, not with the pops! The same can be done if you are from Africa and you want to understand the European market. The game just give ALL the mystery away. Really a shame.The same goes with technology, it just feels underwhelming discovering things. It will be nice that there was MARKETWIDE or WORLDWIDE a pool of knowledge. They are making a technology revolution not just unlocking buffs. Why the technology spread arrives to you? This can be fixed so easily with w the convoys, taking into account, your neighbour etc etc  More events please!And at last newspaper, Will not be better to know what great powers that has an interest in your region or they have influence all over the world to receive this kind of news?? For example, when Victoria becomes the Queen and you are in India, you get that notice. It's SO underwhelming how we get all the info. Like wars, death of important characters. etc Just show it big as an event. Or more importantly all the monthly reports! I want to know what's happening BIG AND CLEAR! Having all the news down below, it's so missable.Does this game has a promising future? Yes, after fixing all the problems. Please make the mystery more interesting. I prefer to DISCOVER the mysteries of the world than just unlock them.26/10/22This game is quite interesting, it's ambitious, it's in the most interesting era that I know. The map is lovely. I think It has a bright future.The things that needs:* The UI needs to be more organized, the map should be easy to change and select what you are looking at, the goods should have a proper tab, it would be nice to be able to arrange the list of pops by different characteristics, tooltips are really good but they become uncomfortable if there are used to show important info, I wish the migration system to be more clear like Imperator etc* Flavor packs, it's interesting to chose different places, because it changes the conditions but apart from that nothing else.* War: it's not bad, it's just that's so confusing what's the AI is doing or how are they planing their attack. I prefer this system mostly because this is a game that you have to pay attention to other things but at least it would be nice to have the power to influence war in another way, or at least interact somehow.It's a cool game, I'm going to keep playing it but I'm not engaged like any of the other Paradox's game that I played. but Honestly, I came late to the party to most of them and they got so many juicy expansions and flavor packs. Except for CK3 which was fantastic from the get go.At last, as always if you are a new player, watch videos, read and relax. It's complex, it does feel complex, but It's manageable.Have fun!

_childDocuments_.review: Overall a good base for what is to come. Specific things that are missing that should be adjusted:It's nigh impossible to conquer colonies in the endgame. There is no "dismantle empire" CB like in vic2.Infamy for states is ridiculously high. Nobody should care if a random state in Africa is conquered from an insignificant power, but it inflicts 17-35 infamy.It's possible to fall into a welfare trap with institutions, where minimum wage is 100% and welfare is 100%, which causes everybody to quit their job. This is unintuitive.There are simply not enough of certain resources available, limiting growth absolutely. I own the entirety of the middle east and cannot supply my army with oil or rubber. Either make it easier to have split production types in nations or make it more viable to set an entire army to tanks.Only being able to have one diplomatic play is incredibly annoying. Why do OPMs count as a full diplo play in this case? Make it so that play time is dynamic on country size or something similar.The politics are still obtuse. You can have an entire country of loyalists and have the country completely flip-flop in one election.Secessions are confusing and ill defined. They start randomly and are nigh-impossible to slow down or stop. Especially confusing after you annex a state and then it starts to rebel. They just lost a war, they shouldn't be able to fight yet.There are plenty more, but these are what stand out after a full campaign. It'll be interesting to see what things they can adjust, as some of these feel baked into the game intrinsically. Maybe HPM2 can overhaul some of these, but the designs of the plays worry me. Overall, it is still enjoyable and hopefully fixable. 7/10

_childDocuments_.review: So far, this game is terribly flawed. Other people who are smarter than me have pointed them out better than I could, like the war system, the AI etc. etc.But what I find myself longing for, is the incredible realism Vic2 had. Sure some things were limited to make the game playable, but most of it is really realistic. If you wanted to expand a factory you either used the resources you had on hand or bought it from the market, if you wanted to defund your military in order to enhance your nation, you could do that, if you wanted to build buildings slower (but not less in numbers), you could do that, if you wanted to make the rich richer so that they can build your economy with you, you could do that. If you understand what I mean, it's that Vic3 has none of those aspects. Instead of realistic ways you can shape your nation, you have tiers for your taxes, tiers for your military and tiers for your building. Instead of it being your money and your funding how quickly you build up your economy, it's a number that goes up by building things, a limit instead of a slider. If you see, that you cannot afford all of those buildings to be finished so quickly, be it oyur taxes are already maxed out or your naton is too unstable, you can either pause it completely, or reduce the funding, where your buildings will take longer to complete and you can only build less buildings. This of course is not everything I dislike about the game, but it is what nags me the most. Overall this game will suffer the fate as other Paradox titles do, we will wait for a few months, get a DLC that improves something and then we wait for another. We repeat this until we've spent over 200 bucks on a singular game, just to make it playable, only because Paradox has a monopoly on grand strategy map games.

_childDocuments_.review: So , I've got some 4-thousand-hours in Paradox Games.CK3 was an okay-ish release, but mechanically the Game lacked any depth.Victoria3 follows the CK3 model. Unifinished release, mechanics cut down, actual depth is only imagined - you only *think* the game is deep, because the UI obfuscates alot of Info or hides many things away somewhere. You could, I suspect, spend the entire Game just sitting in the Construct Buildings Menu and click Green Building, and you'd be pretty much fine.You also need to *IMPORT* alot of stuff. Do not let yourself be misled when clicking onto trade menu, whenit tells you "goods with significant demand for import" - it lies to you. You look at your overall balance. Small Blue Number? You good fam. Gold Number? You Gucci. Big Blue Number? -> Just click *every* import for said good you can find. Don't worry about red or green number when importing stuff from somewhere - just click everything.Most frustrating is Warfare ... and Diplomatic Plays in a way. Sometimes it's not clear what you can do. Why do I have an Obligation on Britain, and I also have an Alliance with them, but I cannot have them Back me in a Diplomatic Play? Nobody knows.Why do the smaller German States readily confederate as a general rule of thumb, when you improve relations, start bankrolling and maybe invite them to defensive pact (which makes sense, and is all you can do) ; but some states ( Brunswick in my first game , Bavaria in the second ) will sit forever in your market, will have +255 and +155 opinion mods towards you, you will have an Alliance even, you will have Obligations (and infrequently while bankrolling, I forgive the Obligations, but it doesnt boost opinion further) .... I have spent 8 hours looking at German Unification, and have not gained any deeper insight as to what else I could do to confederate.But you can. With Patience, and you can Form germany, Peacefully.Aint a thing.Remains: Warfare. The Game is *very bad* at teaching you stuff.Build 10 Dockyards, get an Admiral with 10 Man-o-Wars (or later the Ironclads) ; and you will be able to succesfully launch naval invasions. Else, don't bother.Warfare: Don't overbuild Military stuff. Mostly it just costs money.During the Diplo play leading up to war, purchase *every* small arms, munitions and cannons trade you have available. You'll be Gucci.Build Foodstuffs, Ryefarms and Wheatfarms (neither produce Rye or Wheat exclusively, but also Wine and such) ; and import all the stuff your lower Strata consume, just always import it, and your radicalism will never get out of hand.In Hoi4 it took me 600 hours before i felt I had a mastery of the game.In Imperator Rome it took me some 150 hoursin CK3 it took me 50 hoursin Vic3 it took me 4 hours to have reached the depth of the actual game mechanics.But while Imperator, Hoi and CK hold some replay value, because it is *fun* to play smaller nations and try to outmaneuver the AI on the battlefield when in a much weaker position, Vic3 doesn't hold this. You cannot win a War against a significantly bigger Foe, generally, because the way Diplomacy and Bankrolling work, you will never get as many alliances as them or anything, and since there is no micro management in moving your armies at all, you can only ever blob by tackling near-peer-enemies.Honestly, Vic3 is Aesthetically very pleasing.But a polished Turd remains a Turd.Paradox, somewhere along the Way, lost some good Game Designers I feel.

_childDocuments_.review: At this current point I cannot recommend this game to another person in good faith, I will, and want to, change this review if some of my problems are addressed. There is the foundation of a good game in here, but the same was true about I:R and now that is dead and gone, so who knows. Let's talk about the good, the meh, and the ugly. The Good--The game is beautiful. It looks fantastic, and the ambient sounds bring a lot of life to the map, it's just fantastic looking from the map to the events, to the UI. With one notable exception below.-Economics. The core of the game is well handled with plenty of options to manage. This is where the majority of your time will be spent, upgrading and changing, and it's a simple and rewarding game play loop.-Diplomatic Plays. This is a nice addition to this game. It needs some work, but the diplomacy is great with the expanded options. Unfortunately, tied very closely to the terrible warfare system. This does however feel like it could become one of the star features of Vic 3.  The Meh--Soundtrack. I have come to expect some rather rousing soundtracks from Paradox titles, and though this soundtrack isn't bad, it does seem to be mostly just actual classical pieces from the era, where as in other Paradox titles they have put an effort into composing music that fits the era, in this they have just grabbed music from the era and put it into the game, or close enough that makes no difference. It feels like I am playing one of those 100 card games on disk from the 1990s, just lacking in my opinion. -The MapIt may look beautiful, but you will spend most of your time in menus. Unlike other Paradox games the map part of this one is quite optional. It is easier to deal with your economy from the menu, warfare is automated, and politics has it's own screen too. The only time you will need to click on the map is for Diplomatic plays, and that is a shame because as said, the map is beautiful. -The 3d Models. There are some real issues with them (Looking at you naked Japanese heir, and that child of my ruler who had stubble and looked like he was 45 at birth). The generals also look more like they are getting ready to fight sim style in a dust cloud rather than a decisive battle...which kind of makes sense considering the outcomes you get in the war system. The 3d models kind of work in CK3, but here? They feel out of place, and I don't enjoy them. Game would have been better without it, a HoI4 portrait system would have been better, and more fitting for the period. -Lack of Flavour. This is one I expect any DLC released will focus on. But as it is now, there really is very little difference in playing as any nation. You can get the same outcomes in the same way as any nation. And yes, the goods and crops I produce may change based on location, but that isn't enough. I have played a decent portion of a game as Japan, Mexico, and Belgium, and I cannot say I played the game any differently despite the massive cultural, and geographical differences these nations have, yet I received the same outcomes, namely: economy line goes up. -Politics. I think it is tied to a known bug, but some parts of Politics are more or less useless, or at the least, optional. I kind of just ignored it after a while and suffered no real issues, only changing things around to pass laws.The Ugly--The warfare systemIt does not work as intended or as a viable substitute for the traditional Paradox war formula. It just doesn't. Allowing the AI to completely control your forces is horrible, and the system has no depth and just does not work as the developer hoped or described, ending with some very odd and often frustrating outcomes, choices, and unexciting, stale, unrewarding game...watching, I can't call it game play since there is no human input in any meaningful way. I was willing to try out this new system, war has never been well handled in Paradox games, honestly, stack zerging cap points does not make you the next Alexander, but it is terrible, and if any problem in this game needs fixing it is this. Requires a total redo in my opinion and until this central system is fixed I cannot recommend this game to current Paradox players or new players given that the devs wanted there to be alternatives to war available, but those alternatives are either missing or lacking themselves. Also the AI cannot see the difference between a colonial scuffle with natives, and a great conflict like WW1. It will send its entire military to fight to destruction over a tribe that no longer exists and for wargoals that are no longer valid. Terrible, terrible system with zero redeaming features.-The UI. It looks pretty, sure, but it is a mess. There are buttons every where. Buttons that lead to buttons that are inside of buttons. These nested tooltips often have vital information but getting to it is a chore. I'm sure it will be cleaned up over time, but currently it can be a real hassle finding things. This game is super rough. I would need warfare to be completely overhauled before I could recommend. They fixed something that was not broke. The rest I expect will be addressed over time. I just really hope they don't give up on this game like they did with I:R. But, like with all the new Paradox games, this one will take a few years to get to it's golden age. I really would wait to pick it up if you are on the fence.

_childDocuments_.review: I am absolutely blown away by this game. It is truly impressive and easily one of the best economy simulators I have ever played. What makes this game stand out is its incredible attention to detail in simulating the intricacies of a complex economy. From supply and demand, to trade, to the impact of government policies on the market - everything is modeled with an astonishing level of accuracy.What's more, the game's economy is deeply intertwined with its political system, creating a truly immersive and believable world. The decisions you make as a player not only impact your own financial success, but can also shape the fate of entire nations.But what really sets this game apart is its sense of realism. Unlike many other games in the genre, it doesn't rely on simplistic models or oversimplified mechanics to make things easy for the player. Instead, it challenges you to truly understand the underlying systems at play and make smart, strategic decisions that will lead to success.Overall, I cannot recommend this game highly enough. Whether you're a fan of economics, politics, or just looking for a truly engaging and immersive gaming experience, this is a game you simply have to play.

_childDocuments_.review: Probably the most bare bones and shameful release Paradox has dared to deuce onto the market. Blatantly incompetent and cheating AI aside, this game has all of the depth and immersion of syrup spoon.To pick out the worst aspect, that's most definitely The war system.Want to conquer the world? Bum-rush the artillery and bolt rifle tree and slap the war button like a chimpanzee because that is literally all there is. I stopped checking my opponents strength 40 years in and just conquered whoever I wanted because HOI this is not. 1+2=3 which is more than their 2 so you win. That's it. There is no secret, you have better tech/numbers you win. There is NO way to counter a technologically superior enemy. The mid-game is also somehow even worse than Stellaris. You'll be spending the vast majority of your time at maximum speed staring at bars moving up and resolving the same 3 events every 8 minutes. I tried to wander from my computer to do something else and found out the game doesn't even pause when one of those pops up so you HAVE to sit there bleery eye'd and dazed waiting for that hit of sweet, sweet dopamine of one bar filling and being replaced with the next. Nothing else to say here, avoid and if you were unlucky enough to trust them to make a reasonable grand strategy game, may Steam bless you with a refund.Back to CK & EU for me.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll change this review if my impressions change, but it's not looking too hot.The command the player has over the economy makes the game feel more like a city builder or playing EU4 tall as opposed to wrestling with a global economy, the warfare system has severe issues, and the diplomatic AI is bipolar, but my biggest problem that is being brought up less, and is probably never going to change, is the UI.I honestly want to know what kind of heavy doobies the UI team was smoking when they designed this abomination of an interface. There is no excuse for Victoria 2, a game which is mocked by outsiders for being an unreadable pie chart simulator, to have a more readable interface and legible map, with more crucial information close at hand. It takes the worst tendencies of CK3's UI (large buttons, lists that don't scale well), and adds new issues of its own (aesthetics are strongly favored over functionality, summaries of important information are not compact, the lens modes honestly feel like they shouldn't exist, no really for god's sake, why do we need lens modes).I'm once again finding myself rolling my eyes at the gRapHIcal iMpRoveMenTs. I don't play games in this series (or catalog, for that matter), for the visuals. I don't care that you perfectly animated a horse drawing a buggy, or that the pops have cute little 3D models that look much worse than stylized 2D art would likely look, or about water reflections or high resolution mountains. This obsession with visual polish bleeds over into the UI, which is so heavily stylized in places as to be painful to look at for extended periods. The veneer of *style* does little to hide the fact that most panels look like a choleric coal miner projectile vomited buttons of various sizes all over the screen. Commands that are in the same subject area and should be close together instead too often require you to go back and forth between the relevant lens mode and another summary panel to get feedback on changes. On large countries you'll be doing this A LOT with trade in particular. The whole thing just feels slick and fake, a lot of the art for buildings reminds me of a mobile game, and the game is stuttering quite a bit for me on a 2080ti, so I'm sure it's not brilliant for people on worse setups. The "feel" just isn't there. Victoria 2, which this game will be obsessively compared to until the end of time, feels chunky and utilitarian. When you get to grips with it, though, everything is a few clicks away, often in a small window. In Victoria 3, some menus unnecessarily take up the entire screen (the tech tree and laws are the biggest offenders here), while in other cases, like the trade routes map mode, you have to scroll through fifty different goods in a tiny panel crammed at the bottom of the screen. Information screens often feature text with five to six different combinations of colors, underlining, font size, and gradients, which is not only hard to parse, but fittingly evokes a circus clown motif.Maybe I just need more time with this interface or something. Maybe I'll get to that point where everything feels close at hand in V3. I am going to give it a fair chance. My first impression now that I have my hands on it, though, is that I hate it. And before someone tells me that I'm a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ idiot and that the UI progress was in Dev Diary #263 or something, just know that I don't actually give a ♥♥♥♥! I don't follow dev diaries! I simply don't have the time. If they don't want people to complain, maybe they shouldn't make it suck so bad!EDIT: I'd also like to add that the art for buildings and trade goods is some of the shoddiest art I've ever seen in a PDX game. They all have garish colors, are not easy to read at a glance, and generally look like they were pulled straight out of a mobile game (complete with rounded edges and drop shadows). Some of them, like furniture factories, look like Dali paintings. On the other hand, many icons are way too small and lack sufficient detail. Good luck recognizing general traits at a glance! You can't convince me that the art for trench rat trait isn't a shield with Gorbachev's birthmark on it. Compare this to V2, which had simple, consistent pixel art. The technical and financial limitations placed on development actually contributed to a more cohesive and readable end product.

_childDocuments_.review: Yesterday I played as Japan. Defensive pact with Russia. Civil war pops, the revolt is hilariously outgunned, Russia only sends one stack of 8 to help. Civil war lost. This time, same story. Defensive pact with Russia, Korea, Austria, and Spain. Spain won't join, Russia sends a stack of 8, Austria sends a stack of 16, Korea just doesn't send anyone at all, and landowners who are only at 30% support magically have 80% of our armed forces and plow through us. Civil wars are currently unwinnable and frankly after the direction Stellaris, EU4, and every other paradox product has taken, I'm considering just not supporting them as a company going forward. It isn't even a matter of bugfixing and balancing following a new patch, because they don't fix long-standing issues regardless of the game. Several years of a Stellaris bug which just makes your ships stop attacking for no reason is what I have to look forward to in this game in the future as well. Most people complain about the price of supporting them, with outrageous DLC prices, but to me it's not the DLC prices that are the problem, it's the amount of development time spent on trying to sell their products and the lack of time on basic quality control that's driven me away. Paradox has adopted the sales strategy of taking a big obnoxious flashing sign that looks like what's underneath it must be really fun, and then pointing it directly at a latrine. The more you understand how these games work on a technical level the more you should hate them.

_childDocuments_.review: Warfare: Ever play Hearts of Iron 4 and try to use battle plans so you can focus on other things, only to have the AI make some awful decisions on where to deploy/redeploy divisions, push ineffective or inconsequential areas?... Vicky 3 is that, but way worse... There are no sprites for you to directly control on the map to override the decision or bail out the AI, and your ability to edit and customize orders are virtually non-existent (you can defend, or attack). This used to be mitigated slightly by the ability to teleport your units to fronts, but they "fixed" that. Rating - Absolutely god-awful.Economy: The economy is actually super fun, but late game gets difficult because the production chains for advanced industrial economies is just too difficult for the AI; the AI is generally good at early resource development and production of early input goods (machine tools, etc), but it struggles to balance its economy as input chains become more complex. The AI is also very myopic on its existing economy-- if a resource or input good isn't needed in its own current input chain, it will not develop or produce that good/resource, even if producing something unused by its own economy exclusively for export would be profitable. The prototypical example is oil -- oil is limited to very specific regions and it's only consumed in late game economies. The AI simply will not develop it until it begins to use it, which will happen significantly later than the Player. Consequently, even on "peaceful" eco-focused games, I find myself eventually having to snipe Venezuelan, Texan, or west Asian oil field just so I can support a late game society.Rating: Great, but limited by the AI's ability to keep up with the complexity. Diplomacy and Internal Politics:I can keep this part short -- diplomacy and politics feel good albeit somewhat lackluster -- but this is common for Paradox games on release. Fortunately, these two areas in particular are ones that Paradox is particularly adept at filling out via DLC updates (however you feel about the DLC model aside).On release these areas felt a bit like Stellaris -- a bit hollow, but a good structure to build on. I know we'll get more here in time. Conclusion: I am confident that a lot about this game will get better with DLC and updates. Diplomacy and politics in Paradox games always get more rich and diverse over time, and I'm sure there will be regular updates that make tweaks to AI economy management that will make it increasingly effective. However, I simply cannot recommend this game to anyone based on the warfare mechanics alone. In every Paradox game there is a point where you have to pause and dive in to figure out "why am I performing so poorly at war"; in these games there is always something to tweak (combat width, unit quality, terrain, generals, etc). Eventually, you understand enough to make good decisions and perform competently. In Victoria 3, there is still some degree of that, but once you've composed your army/navy, you can only assign the most basic orders (attack, defend, naval invade), and then you hand the rest of things over to the AI. This tends to go uniformly awful -- the AI is terrible about assigning units to fronts, prioritizing targets, or pushing through favorable terrain -- but unlike EVERY other Paradox 4X grand strategy game, you have virtually no ability to override the AI awful decision-making. On the other hand, maybe Paradox wanted to give players an authentic 1800s experience -- sending the boys off to war in a triumphant mood and eagerly awaiting news of victory at the front, only to have constant reports trickle back of ineffective generals ordering suicidal charges, marching across terrible terrain to seize inconsequential targets, or halting an offensive within sight of an enemies' capital to march off to another front instead.

_childDocuments_.review: This is perhaps one of the best economy simulations I've ever seen.
