Also, despite what others say the diplomatic play mechanic is a brilliant addition. Perhaps the AI is a bit too friendly to one another at times, and so it would be nice to have more options to break up the friendly attitudes between countries in order to get diplomacy done.It is a flawed gem, but a gem regardless. And, as has been announced, PDX plans to modify/overhaul a few aspects of the game in the near future, and so many of the problems may be reduced/fixed. At the end of the day, I feel like the $50 was well-spent, and I'll enjoy many, many more hours in this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I gave a real shot, but there's just so little to do in this game.  Who knew that the Industrial Revolution and 19th century could be so boring?Victoria 3 is a strategy simulation of the macro-level effects of the world from 1836 to 1936. The core gameplay loop is choosing buildings to build in your country while an economic simulation plays out in the background--it's simultaneously micro-intensive and unrewarding. You can change some parameters with an internal politics feature. While it's functional, it's hard to see what the immediate impact of a change will be, and I found it to more frustrating than rewarding. Worse, the world is totally static. Across two playthroughs, the AI did very, very little, and the world looked pretty much the same at the beginning as it did at the end. Compare all this to another Paradox game, Crusader Kings 3, where the player is constantly engaged with tough decisions and evolving challenges. By contrast, Victoria 3 was a dull, passive experience. I recommend passing on it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is unfortunately a shoddy sequel to Victoria 2.In aesthetic it seems overly optimistic. The victorian era was an era of grim machinery. The wake of industrialisation and colonisation reshaping the lives of millions, both for the better but most often for the worse. The era ended with the first world war, a human tragedy beyond measure. The aesthetic this game provides, that of wholesome social change doesn't feel right.The mechanics regarding industrialisation and economy are shallow. You have a shortage of (x) resource and so you build the production buildings of (x) resource. This is the whole game loop. I reached a GDP of 350 million as France in 1888. A GDP higher than that of the British Empire in 1900. I did this with no effort, or thinking on my part. I didn't even colonise. Logically my economy should have become deadlocked due to lack of resources, but it wasn't. It feels like Anno 1800 on a map. If industrialisation is supposed to be the main focus of the game, then the game has failed. In Victoria 2 you industrialise to gain access to more resources and improve your industrial score. A secondary reason is to gain access to military goods, and fuel a large army efficiently, so you can fight for more resources and continue industrialising. A natural loop that feeds into itself.  Here there is no point to warfare, either for fun, or for industrialisation potential. In addition, the warfare as implemented is practically non-existent. Three buttons, and your generals will throw troops into battle against impossible odds, causing you to lose despite massive advantage. There is no strategy here. I had hoped the political system would be better, but it too is shallow. Elections mean nothing, even in a Republic. Never once had a revolt, even while pissing off as many interest groups as I could. This in contrast to Victoria 2, where rebels will burn your entire country down to the ground over the right to vote. The UI is terrible. Victoria 2 is rough, and shows its age, however its systems are timeless. I wanted to like this game, but I don't. I hope it can get reworked soon. Almost all the systems of the game need to be improved upon.

_childDocuments_.review: There appears to be an in dept system on how combat results are calculated, but the game does not communicate it in any way. _childDocuments_.review: Note: Having played this only recently, I missed the first year of typical Paradox  content updates filling the game out.It's in a decent place. It truly gets into the complexities of economics, focusing on supply & demand, supply chains, competitive wages, and availability of goods, all of which generates an environment for the social conflicts of class warfare, human rights, and politics -- very few of which other similar games exist (such as Tropico). It really is special for this, even if it's imperfect, missing a few key elements of economics, in addition to its social classes and politics systems needing to be deeper to truly capture the dynamic industrial and political era it's set in and move the game beyond largely just chasing numbers. More flavor to its regions or even specific countries would also greatly benefit it to avoid being too similar across games like it currently is and which HOI4 also suffered. But with these key developments, I don't think they necessarily need to do deeper into other areas that are currently shallow and generate the most complaints like diplomacy, warfare, and colonization, although surely future DLCs will.Its new model of trying season passes which always contain the same number and type of DLCs (new mechanics; regional flavor; cosmetic) is interesting and we'll see if they can keep up with it as well as keep them equal when they've now forced themselves into a particular publishing model.While it doesn't have the flair (or music!) of Tropico, it does have a more rounded package and will likely continue to grow into a strong title. However, it won't ever be for everyone. I recommend it if you're into the economic side of things or you can get it for cheap.

_childDocuments_.review: This is probably the most frustrating Paradox release to date; it's a really deep simulation with a shallow game wrapped around it. It's a game full of contradictions; it simplified the war system to focus on the economy, and yet they managed to replicate the tedium of previous province-style tactical battles with an simple idle-clicker building system. They wanted us to have sandbox experiences, yet we have only 40-50 technologies and quite limited or linear choices in building. They wanted to offer us greater control or interaction with populations, but forgot to add an actual features or incentives to do so. There is a war-goal/diplomacy/escalation system, which often just turns into 'grab a province every 5 years', and most games are 'done' within the first 20 years.Mostly, the game feels only 'deep' by virtue of having the single worst UI of any title to date and a potentially broken or non-functional AI. The UI prime case study of wasting screen-space, hiding critical information, and making crucial systems entirely opaque - requiring the top UI mods to fix the game. The AI will stagnate entirely and most of the post-1880 period devolves into you putting the game on fast-forward to wait for buildings to finish so that you can just balance your domestic economy - this also requires the top AI-fix mod.I tried to really like the game, but after a few different nation runs, I felt like I was sleep-walking into #1 GDP by just doing the exact same thing each time with little challenge or reason. It boggles my mind how I've had significantly more engaging and challenging economy-based experiences in HOI3-4, Stellaris, CK3 and EU-series.   It has a lot of promise, but currently it wholly deserves the 63% rating. I'd wait and see if they can deepen the game, or if it goes the way of Imperator.

_childDocuments_.review: This game scratches every gaming itch I have. I had been watching it since the messy release and waiting for an opportunity to arrive where it was in a state where I felt I would enjoy the hell out of it. I've always enjoyed pretty much all of the Paradox suite of games, but I'd say this one has very quickly become my favorite. I love the simulation this game delivers, and the alt-history silliness that can happen. I've made an ultra-capitalistic Presidential Republic Spain, a militarist Sokoto Caliphate, and most recently I had a blast with Japan achieving the Meiji Restoration achievement.Normally, I hate randomly generated systems in games with almost no exceptions, however, V3 has somehow achieved a way to make it feel fair. The events that are purely bad don't linger for too long, or they are there to present a reasonable challenge. The difficulty varies all over, and I wholeheartedly appreciate it. The challenging starts that I've tried genuinely feel fun, for example: Egypt is a race against time to build up military to defend against an eventual Ottoman attack, and I'm not good enough yet to figure out how to do it without ruining my run. I actually enjoy playing all the way through to the end when in EU4 I've only ever done that once. The soundtrack is absolutely without a doubt my favorite soundtrack in all of the Paradox suite of games. I have had a lot of fun so far, and I think that especially if the development keeps going in the direction it has been I will continue to have more fun. I definitely feel good recommending this game.

_childDocuments_.review: My opinion changed with time. After staying up ungodly hours playing this game I can comfortably say I enjoy GDP number go up simulator. Does the game have much depth? Not really. Is the warfare system fun? Not really, the AI controls too much and makes silly decisions that have lost me wars I should have easily won. Is the AI smart? No, it's just very stubborn and doesn't make a lot of sense. Are the Diplo-plays interesting? Sometimes, often times they're just weird/frustrating. Does the game need a lot of love and improvement? Yes, in nearly all aspects. Do I recommend Vic3? If you like seeing numbers go up and staying within a building screen for 90% of the game, YES! Otherwise, you might want to wait for a nice sale or for the game to have some serious updates. *************************************************************************************OLD REVIEW (Did Not Recommend):I'm hoping my opinion will change with time, but based on my first few hours of gameplay Victoria 3 is simply not very fun, in depth, or rewarding. It took me a while to get into Victoria 2, so I'm holding out hope that I'm missing some key game feature that transforms my experience. That being said, everything I've done in the game up until this point has felt hollow. I click buttons and see no game impact. I send generals to the frontlines and see them win and lose with me observing in silence, feeling powerless to effect the outcome in any meaningful way. The game is soulless, it lacks the flair and depth of past titles and other Paradox products that I have become so invested in over the years. The AI's head is empty and unfortunately it controls half of what my nation does.

_childDocuments_.review: Victoria 3 - A Complex and Engaging Grand Strategy GamePros:Deep Historical Simulation: Victoria 3 offers a detailed historical simulation, spanning the period from 1836 to 1936. The game accurately portrays the events, policies, and social and technological advancements of that era, allowing players to experience history in an immersive way.Strategic Complexity: With a wide range of aspects to manage, from economy and politics to international relations and militarism, Victoria 3 provides a rich strategic experience. Players must balance economic development, diplomacy, technological research, and military strategies to achieve their goals.Customization and Personalization: The game offers a high level of customization and personalization, allowing players to define their own goals and strategies. The ability to choose different nations, governments, policies, and ideologies adds depth and variety to the gameplay experience.Emergent Narrative: Victoria 3 is known for its ability to generate complex and captivating narratives. Player actions and historical events intertwine, creating unique stories and memorable moments in each campaign.Community and Ongoing Support: The game has an active and dedicated community, providing opportunities for interaction and sharing experiences. Additionally, Paradox Interactive, the developer of the game, is known for providing support and regular updates to enhance the gameplay experience.Cons:Steep Learning Curve: Victoria 3 is a complex game with a steep learning curve. The amount of systems and mechanics can be overwhelming for new players, requiring time and effort to fully understand them.Prolonged Gameplay Time: Due to its long-term gameplay nature, campaigns in Victoria 3 can be extensive and time-consuming. This can be a hurdle for players who prefer shorter and more focused gaming sessions.Dense Interface: The game's interface may appear dense and cluttered, especially for less experienced players. Navigating menus and information panels can be confusing at first, requiring familiarity and patience.Demanding Hardware Requirements: Victoria 3 is a resource-intensive game, which may limit its accessibility for players with less powerful computers.Challenging AI: The game's AI can be highly challenging and aggressive, which can be frustrating for some players. Dealing with competent AI opponents can make campaigns more intense and complex.Overall, Victoria 3 is a complex and engaging grand strategy game that will appeal to genre fans. With its deep historical simulation, complex strategy, and emergent narrative, it offers a rich and challenging experience. However, its steep learning curve and lengthy gameplay times may be obstacles for less experienced players or those with limited available time.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fairly decent game that IMO is utterly ruined by the terrible AI and absolutely awful War system.  The AI is extremely placid and loves backing down from conflict.  As Russia, I grabbed Persia and Afghanistan without fighting a single battle - even though they had support of their neighbors!With regards to War: In theory, I like the idea of a streamlined 'Front' system where you don't have to keep marching dudes around obscure regions.  In practice, the system plays out exactly the same as before - it's just a glorified Whack-a-Mole, except the armies teleport around and you have very, very little control over who goes where.  An enemy ally has 2 divisions attacking your distant border?  Too bad!  You have no choice but to spread out your divisions evenly, so you're forced to assign about 30 divisions to take care of them.  The "flow" of war becomes utterly incomprehensible when there's more than 2 nations involved.  All you're doing when fighting a war is constantly re-assigning generals to empty fronts that the AI decided to sneakily open up.  If you don't pay close attention and micro-manage the war, you're going to get your ass handed to you because the general AI is basically nonexistent.In practice, this is exactly like the Whack-a-Mole system in previous games, except you have frustratingly little control over your units.  The economic part of the game is pretty fun, but what's the point if diplomacy is nonexistent and the game utterly falls apart the moment a war breaks out?

_childDocuments_.review: Update:- Combat is still terrible. The latest patch made it more complicated, you now have to balance the ratio of infantry, artillery, and cavalry. I will be winning wars only to have my generals stand down and my fronts overrun while my units now wander the map, since they now have to path to a front. I felt the game had hit a pretty good sweet spot before the latest combat patch.My original thoughts still stand.Here are the things I like about this game:- economy building, really like how the game forces you to balance the inputs and outputs of production- diplomacy, its pretty straight forward. Sometimes the AI turns against you for no apparent reason, but in general its easy to play nice or not with your neighbors- politics. I like how laws have to supported by the government and even then goes through a process to get enacted.- Missions vs Sandbox. The design lets you play the game how you wantDislike- Combat: Even after 200 hours I still cannot wrap my head around how to successfully wage war. I have no sense on how my troops are doing, where my generals are fighting, or where they will fight next. - Revolution: With the latest update my country continually falls into civil war. Despite my best efforts of managing the economy, growing peoples wealth and standard of living, the behind the scenes conflict of agitators vs government eventually forces me into civil wars. _childDocuments_.review: Victoria 3 ends just when the gameplay loop starts to feel satisfyingI stopped playing major powers for the most part because I realized the gameplay loop and decisions were the exact same for pretty much every country, you just start further or farther ahead on the path than others based on what country to choose. This lead me to start playing small countries but I ran into a problem and realization that makes me not want to play the game altogether.I feel like 90% of the game is waiting for the gameplay to become satisfying. This problem becomes so much worse for smaller nations. From the start of the game to about 1900 you are just sitting there waiting for things to happen. I'm waiting for technology to make my economy more efficient. I'm waiting for laws to pass to reform whatever backwater ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ I'm playing. I'm waiting for the small chance that a neighbor gets tied up in a war and I can hopefully take a couple of provinces, but even THEN I'm just sitting there waiting for my army to capture provinces, I'm not doing anything.Just when I reform my country into something I'm proud of and want to lead into the future the game only has 10-20 years left. These last few years feel pointless to me. In hoi4 I can use those last few years and everything I have built up to to wage war and conquer an enemy. In eu4 you can do the same thing. In CK3 I can see how powerful my empire and vassals have become and see how my family tree has changed the course of history. In Victoria, I can use those last few years to.... build more power plants??Another problem I have is that when the game ends I don't feel like I've really accomplished anything. In the other games I have mentioned towards the end of the game I can feel how most decisions and choices I have made lead me to that point. I get satisfaction because I have made so many different and unique choices and I can see how they paid off. In victoria 3 I have waited 90% of the game for buildings to finish and I've made maybe a total of 5-10 decisions that actually affected my experience. I honestly think that I could turn almost any nation into an economic powerhouse without even worrying about laws too much even though some laws are just so clearly better than others that there is no point in choosing them.Sure, I've taken Greece or whatever nation and made them a top 10 power through my economy, but when the game ends I can't shake the feeling of "so what?". There is no payoff and the game ends too quickly without a vic3 to hoi4 conversion mod for any sort of late-game payoff feeling to exist.DO NOT BUY THIS GAME. It is sorely unfinished and lacking any flavor. Every single game you will feel like you're doing the same thing. You're waiting. In ever single game. You're just waiting.

_childDocuments_.review: I have less than 54 hours on this now: I may have more to say later.1. My BackgroundI have been playing Paradox games for the past twenty years, alongside other games from other studios within the genre, e.g., Total War, Secret Government, Civilization, etc.I have close to 15 thousand hours on Paradox products amassed in my life because this studio consistently develops games that make me think.Games from Paradox are different and that is why I like them.2. Victoria 3Verdict: This game is amazing!This game is for you if:- You want a challenge- You like many things connected to other many things, e.g., the price of wheat affecting your ability to make supplies for your army- You like painting the map your nation's color using other methods than simply building an army and marching it all over the map, although you can do that in this game also, (see Spiffs videos).This game is not for you if:- You want to turn your mind off- You are impatient- You want to see your large army physically marching all over the map- You don't want to worry about economics and politics because it gets in the way of your army leadership.3. The Future of this GameThere are things about this game that I am learning about now which I do not like. But as I learn how to play this game, that list is getting smaller. There are things that I will probably learn about and still not like, but it's too early to know that now.Right now, I encourage you to be open to this like you were to anything new from Paradox that you loved. Adjust your expectations to what the studio is trying to do.This quite possibly is the best game they have every created.

_childDocuments_.review: The short of it is it's a flawed but good grand strategy game that provides a sandbox with plenty of depth to have fun in.I got into paradox in this generation of their games starting with eu4, ck2 then 3, hoi4, and now this one. I never played the previous Victoria game so I can't rightly judge this against it and instead will be comparing it to other offerings by paradox and the few competitors they have.First let's look at the worst part about the game, combat. Its ♥♥♥♥♥♥, like actually braindead sometimes as you have to leave the large part of it to chance but with the type of game this is it almost fits. With Victoria, focusing mainly on economics you really don't want war. It costs a lot and people hate it so it's really a last resort as is with plenty of diplomatic workarounds to circumvent it, and where you can't avoid you can focus on preparation and guarantee your victory before it even starts. Basically I think the taking war out of your hands was entirely intentional as to prevent you from focusing entirely on military aims. It's a direction I am mixed on but have come to look past.Now everything else. It's perfect.The indepth politics system is just complex enough to understand and influence with the rigidity to make it not to easy to steamroll.The economy is fleshed out and with the addition of dlc like sphere of influence really makes it feel like you're having a global influence. The pop system is one of the best things to come to the series and works with the other two systems to provide a clear reason not to be an autocratic tyrant(sometimes)

_childDocuments_.review: The game's core, economics, is a fun and well polished game mechanic. It offers a lot of replayability. That being said, the game in these early days suffers from bugs and balancing problems. All while at the same time the AI is doing crazy ♥♥♥♥ like the US puppeting Portugal or Spain sending 120 battalions to protect Finland from being annexed by their overlord. All around lots of weird nonsensical plays by the AI. The combat is a joke. I don't even mind that they went with the super simplified war front thing. What I mind is that there is almost no way for the player to affect how a war is going, its terribly balanced and generally just leaves you feeling frustrated as you wait for the RNG to swing your way. And you know its not like they saved the development time fleshing out diplomacy instead. Managing your country's laws and government is fun and overall works fine as it is, but the system feels like its a shadow of what they wanted to do. The UI has a lot of problems. Especially when it comes to understanding your pops and radicals/loyalists. Also explaining where money comes from and where its going. Especially so if you don't have experience from other Paradox games. There are no speadsheets and the mapmodes are bad. There is very little flavour to the different countries and very little historical immersion. Overall I think the game is like the steam reviews say, mixed, for me its leaning to the positive side.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is being balanced for Europe and America, but no one else. Every new patch makes playing anyone other than major powers painful.You start with next to nothing. You can't build quickly because you need more construction sectors. You cant afford to buy the building materials because you either dont have enough wood or iron and they need hundreds of units of material to get the construction sectors to work quickly. You cant even build a single military unit because barracks need to be built by sectors and when you do you run out of qualified workers because you have no schools and if you do you need way more.If you dont have iron or a wood deposit, its already game over and some countries dont have these and are forced to build western style structures. No, there are no substitutes like clay, adobe, or stone.You build 2-3 things and immediately run out of infrastructure while employing less than 1/100th of a state, which needs an expensive port or tech for trains you likely dont have and cant afford even if you did because you need motors which need steel and coal. You are locked out until you get more tech or more money that you most likely dont have for something as simple as a grain farm to feed your people.To fund your constructions sectors without going bankrupt immediately, you need resource extraction with better tech. To get tech you need universities and most likely you start with none. You spend tons of money and a long time to build one that gives you 3 research points while paying thousands of workers because its government run. You need way more because the game expects you to be a major power already to even compete.These universities need paper, which is also another thing you need to build and takes way too long to get going. By the time you get the basics down to START the actual game with a functioning economy, its 1880-1890 and the game is already mostly over since it ends in 1936 and you spent this entire time at MAX SPEED to start the actual game.You can trade for stuff, unless you start as a nation with landowners in power who ban trade. Politics is ruled by who has money, and every farm you build makes them powerful. You cant get rid of them until you build factories you either dont have the tech to or cant afford to build or feed with materials.All while hoping a major nation doesn't decide to annex you, colonize you, or anything while the game actively tries to stop you from PLAYING THE GAME until you do a bunch of prepwork to use any of the mechanics. when you do meet that point, its MORE WAITING to reach parity to even have a chance of defending yourself or getting parity because warfare has no cap anymore. Its a pure numbers and quality game, and if you dont have both then dont bother because your T1 unit always loses to a T2 and if you have a T2 you cant replace them against a nation with more population and a looser conscript law.Its like a mobile game now where you need to wait to even BEGIN to play the game. previous patches werent like this. You could build quickly and get a lot done but paradox has decided to make hard nations even harder and turn Victoria 3 into a glorified mobile game with timers if you wander outside Europe or America.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Extremely enjoyable game in my opinion, but your mileage may wary. For some it might be best to wait until a few patches are done and a major DLC is out.I really, really enjoy the game. Building your economy, which is the main focus of the game is extremely enjoyable and there are multiple feedback loops that you need to juggle, and the economy keeps getting more complex as you go along the techs as it should. Balancing a starting economy is easy compared to one where you need to keep up fertilizer production to get your raw materials for your factories that can then produce the intermediary goods for another industry.Also the political simulation is excellent, although could use some tweaking as it is currently a bit too easy to pass law reforms that would in reality be dead on arrival based on political clout. But I've had a lot of fun trying to chip away at the power of the aristocracy to get the intelligentsia and industrialists into power to complete the Meiji reformation, but now I need to start undermining the industrialists to get even more sensible set of laws in place regarding for example child labour etc.I've not run into any major bugs myself, but there are certainly issues. The current version of trade routes is functioning weirdly, but as you can just import back anything someone exports from you, you can try to ignore the system in the end. Hopefully there is a patch incoming for that pretty soon.But all in all, I've enjoyed myself a lot, some of the best experiences I've had in gaming for years, but there are some rough edges. Might not be everyone's cup of tea.

_childDocuments_.review: While Victoria II is a fun game, it also has many issues that I and many other players thought would get fixed in Victoria III. That did not happen as Paradox decided to take a new route, a disastrous one.The most prominent controversy has to do with warfare. Hearts of Iron IV's frontline system would be better. It allows players to make choices. Do I want to massively micro this front? Do I want to put units on a frontline and play hands-off? Do I want to play strategically and have multiple frontlines on one front? Victoria III instead simplifies things far too much. Paradox expects you to play tall and focus on managing your economy.What bugged me the most was how Paradox released Victoria III with features missing that were previously in Victoria II. It does not make sense not to include them, as Victoria II had so few DLCs. I admit, Paradox did release some of those features months after the game's release; however, I believe they only did so because the game was either rushed or Paradox intended to include them in DLCs, but after the amount of hate they were getting, they did not want another Imperator Rome.TLDR: This game sucks, and I would rather play Imperator Rome.

_childDocuments_.review: This game excels at what it intends to be: a social, political, and economic simulator. You guide your nation through the Industrial Revolution into the beginning of the 20th century, adapting the production methods, laws, and political institutions as the years go by. Warfare is secondary (and most of the negative reviews fail to understand this).If you do go to war, you better make sure your economy can sustain your wars before diving into them. While games like HOI4 have a button to switch to war economy, in V3 you really feel the focus of the economy completely shifting to feed the war machine.I've played 2 full campaigns so far, a few months apart. Both were great, though at some points you do feel like maybe it would be better for you to not touch anything and just watch the days pass and your country develop. Finding ways to make the game a bit more interesting with in-campaign events and such could be a potential improvement, to make sure you always have something to do. Diplomacy is another area that could use some work (please let me suggest my own war goals when joining a conflict to something that is actually relevant).

If you are concerned about some of the yet-to-be-done fine tuning, you can easily mod it, or wait a month for the developers to incorporate it in patches themselves.EDIT for patch 1.2: The recent updates have DRAMATICALLY improved the overall polish of the game to the point it is entirely playable smoothly without mods. (Some great improvements include the vic2-style private industry doing autonomous construction from their investment pool, overall military changes, oil and arable land locations, just to name a few). Notes for the upcoming 1.3 and 1.4 patches show that they don't intend to stop improving it even further.

_childDocuments_.review: + The map is beautiful to look at, and it changes over time.+ The soundtrack is amazing.+ Many of the underlying economic systems seem deep and interconnected.+ The flags aren't pre-made pictures, but are composed of colours and elements defined by scripts, which has allowed Paradox to make a canton system for colony flags. It's minor, but it's very cool! + There are some funny events.+ The built-in map editor allows for very easy terrain editing.- There are many bugs, and ironing them out is likely going to take a year or two. As an example, I gave up on one Austria game after a war I started against Prussia resulted in Prussia surrendering but a tiny landlocked German principality remained in the war. With no allies or enemies between me and them, I was locked into an eternal war, unable to demobilise my troops, doomed to decades of bankruptcy.- The tech tree is quite shallow and boring.- The Interest Groups don't respond to events or change much over time. They're a step up from EU4's Estates, but barely.- The historical events of the time don't really matter. Nationalism, liberalism and socialism aren't dangerous forces putting monarchies at risk of revolution. The competing dynasties (Bourbons and Bonapartes, Isabelistas and Carlists, the Meiji Restoration) don't threaten to seize power (if they even make an appearance). - This lack of responsiveness makes the game quite easy. You can take the "backwards" Qing Empire and conquer the world if you like, no one inside the country offers any reason to stop, and your enemies aboard are totally incompetent. - The map editor itself has bugs and oversights which make it hard to do certain things which other Paradox map editors excelled at, like political borders.

_childDocuments_.review: Do I enjoy this game? Yes. Will say that right out the gate. Never played Victoria 2, so nothing to really compare this to besides Stellaris and Crusader Kings 3. Will say right away that this has a monster of a steep learning curve, but if I wasn't enjoying myself I wouldn't have scaled that learning curve to make the Ottoman Empire the most powerful nation in the world over the course of 100 years - after failing many times within only 20 years while I figured out how the game works.I can't recommend this game because it just isn't ready for prime time. It could be in a month or three, but it isn't yet. Certain nation-wide bonuses don't seem to do anything, several event chains don't apply bonuses or maluses correctly, some pretty embarrassing typos come out of the woodwork to say hlelo, there's baffling geography decisions like  the entire front system is an orgiastic mess that teleports your generals around to places you would never want them to be, and most egregious to me: I'm pretty sure the entire loyalist vs radical system is fundamentally busted, making any campaign from beginning to end near unplayable.To elaborate, if there are radicals present, whenever you would otherwise gain a loyalist you instead make a radical into a normal citizen. Solid idea! But events that create loyalists in the first place are so rare that I'm convinced they're bugged in such a way they don't fire at all. As such there are plenty of ways to  radicals but very few opportunities to  them, so by the end of a campaign every province in the entire globe will be swarming with radicals. By the time January 1st, 1936 rolls around it's like The Tragedy from Danganronpa, with a full fifth of the human population wreaking death and destruction worldwide! All that's missing is the Monokuma masks!This game desperately needs the love that Stellaris has been getting, with weekly status reports from the devs, quarterly overhauls to existing systems, and the occasional expansion pack that broadens the game's breadth and depth. I deeply, sincerely hope it gets just that.
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: Half-decent, but half-baked.Politics are surface level and easily exploitable; interest groups are stagnant and don't evolve over time to meet changing circumstances and social movements. Laws can be enacted far too quickly (Slavery Banned ---> Multicultural US in the 1830s, or multicultural Germany by 1845 are both possible!). Interest groups, in general, rarely present a credible threat to enacting your agenda, and can easily be appeased by enacting laws in a certain order. Using the Suppress or Bolster authority actions often isn't even needed to marginalize a group completely. There's few downsides to heavily supporting/favoring groups like the Intelligentisa and Industrialists, and powerful bonuses are given for doing so. Lack of historical flavor. Several pivotal historical moments are absent, including the Mexican-American war, revolutions of 1848, etc. Failure to balance 'lack of railroading' with 'including actual historical content' by Paradox.Warfare is atrocious. Popups on the map during war are loud and noisy. Generals teleport around fronts arbitrarily, and fronts themselves appear and disappear for mysterious reasons. Wars involve huge amounts of RNG. Attrition numbers are monstrous; expect to lose literally tens of thousands of men in minor wars with few casualties in battle unless you have extremely advanced hospitals. A HOI4-like system with front management and commands that can be given at a high level would make sense. Current system is not engaging, lacks meaningful opportunities for player input and skill expression, and is a major part of the game anyway despite being so poorly implemented. Diplomatic behavior by the AI is strange and comes off as arbitrary (German minors viewing a 0 infamy Prussia with 'caution' at high relations, and refusing to defensive pact them - Which would alleviate the problem of 'this country may attack me'). Diplomatic plays and maneuvers are interesting in theory, but irritating in implementation. The ability to 'back down' as the defender and obtain a 5-year truce in return for giving up a single province, in a game that lasts only 100 years, is a serious problem. There's no way as an attacker to truly force a war against somebody. As an example in this system, Mexico could just give the United States a single province for every single diplomatic play demand, delaying America's conquest of the west despite being economically and militarily inferior by 40+ years simply utilizing the truce timer. Multiplayer becomes exponentially unstable with high numbers of players.Trade is tedious and micro-heavy. There are no stockpiles.Generic events are, for the most part, flavorful and well-made. There are some events which are far too punishing (For example, an event in Africa that gives tons of infamy).Infamy penalties do nothing to address or punish puppet spam.Economic management is probably one of the game's strong points, but fails to introduce compelling gameplay for different types of societies; the answer is always 'industrialize as fast as possible with tons of construction', maybe after fixing your country's intrinsic issues (Such as Austria or Qing's poor tax capacity). Tooltips and information given are inaccurate and do not properly account for all inputs and externalities. Buildings that the game insists will be 'unprofitable' if built are often some of the most profitable. Pops are overly detailed, such that migration and changing of culture late-game will cause crashes and extreme lag on many machines. The requirement to simulate the political and economic behavior of Catholic Mongolian English-Speaking Pops who work as a laborer in factories in New York does not add any particular value to the experience, but does result in catastrophic performance problems. While pop simulation is necessary, there needs to be a more pragmatic solution here. The AI has literally no clue what it is doing, and will absolutely fail to use its country to the fullest potential. France and even Austria involved themselves in a war to defend Mexico for no apparent gain. The AI will not structure its economy well, exploit goods with high market demand, etc. Puppets and Dominions are often a bad idea because the player cannot invest in them. Failures of AI makes peaceful playstyles less possible due to critical shortages of goods, forcing the player to conquer in order to fuel their economy instead of just trading. This causes engagement with the war system, which is currently horrible - See above. Tech tree feels a little short. Deceptively small due to knowledge spread.Minimum wage is straight up a trap and will destroy even the most developed of economies, leading to economic stagnation and mass unemployment. Game presents itself as a society simulator and for the most part does this well, but liberalizing is usually the right call for your society, but paradoxically removes a crucial gameplay tool you have to direct your nation (Authority), meaning less engagement and more automation. There's ultimately little incentive or disincentive to liberalizing as quick as possible; choosing to remain conservative will absolutely destroy your country in the long-run, and while this is accurate, the game doesn't do enough to force you to stay on these non-ideal systems. It's always a LARP-decision moreso than something that is mechanically enforced. That is to say - Choosing to stay agrarian is moreso a deliberate choice you'd make, rather than something the game tries to constrain you to due to the limitations of your country and the demographics within. Art direction and music are delightful, echoing the spirit of the era with beautiful illustrations and engaging tunes. Sound design in events is great, painting a picture with audio. The art direction and music are easily the best part of Victoria 3. Overall, Victoria 3 is a 6/10, perhaps a 5. Paradox has created a surface-level game that is somewhat engaging in what it does correctly, and absolutely horrible in what it doesn't. While the game is fun, the depth and system competency required to engage me over a long period of time just isn't present. Perfect title for people that just want to do quirky things with their country, like turning the USA into a monarchy by 1844 or something, but not a good title for strategically minded gamers who are looking for a challenge and engaging gameplay. Cannot recommend for people like me in good faith.

_childDocuments_.review: I think this is a big improvement over Victoria 2.  I think that the industrialization and management of buildings is more tangible and interactive.  I think that the "diplomatic play" feature is a really novel and much more sophisticated concept than the old "justify war->attack". And while warfare isn't completely fleshed out, I appreciate the change from trying to micromanage individual regiments (which was a huge pain in late game Vic 2).  Note that, although I like those features I mentioned above, I see room for improvement. E.G. Buildings come with a auto-upgrade function (if enabled), but the conditions for auto-upgrading are not manageable by the player (for instance I would love to say "yes expand but only if the building is above X% profitability").  It also appears that diplomacy is not constrained by any sort of range or is, at least, ahistorical at times. I've seen the US be interested in Indian subcontinent in the 1860's, which doesn't make much sense given the politics of the time.IN SUMMARY: If you're really on the fence about it, wait, give it a few months to a year and see what patches/DLC comes out.  I think that this game has enormous potential to become just as immersive and detailed as HOI4 or EU4, provided it gets the same attention from Paradox in the coming years.In relation to that final note, I know we all moan about the business model of base game and then procession of DLC's. I myself am on the fence about it.  Yes it would be nice to have a as in depth as EU4 ready at launch, I don't know if it is possible in the industry today.  Certainly if it were, would Paradox be the only company trying to fill this market segment? I really don't know.

_childDocuments_.review: The strategy gamer in me wants to tell you to look past all the crashes, all the bugs, the absolutely dreadful and arbitrary warfare mechanics, the totally railroaded cultural development mechanics, the random and poorly explained questlines that can completely ruin your game as the USA, the lack of a search feature or knowledge page for research. That part of me wants to tell you "It's a good 1800s economics and geopolitics simulator and that's what it should be".Unfortunately there is another part of me that has a sense of justice and a sense of right and wrong. There is a part of me that cares about abstract concepts like design and utility, and believes criticism is only helpful to others when it is objective. That part of me joined the "Victora 3 sucks" party, along with the software developer in me that knows when i have been given a late alpha build presented as a finished product, and the part of me that is sick and tired of screaming at the game for crashing when I do something as basic as "click the colonization option" and make a 6 hour save file unusable. Just like in Victoria 3's actually really good (if poorly explained) government system, I can't make those two sides of myself that love and hate this game work together. I have to kick the part of me that likes this game and wants it to be good out in order to write this review.Yes there are a lot of things in this game that work great. Yes there will be 4 expansions in 2 years over the course of which you will be paying extra money to make this game functional and fully featured (♥♥♥♥ that!). Yes I have played more than 50 hours. Yes, for a lot of this time I am having fun, especially when I'm playing Japan; a well-balanced country that's just begging to become an economic powerhouse and start slapping around european "majors". But, I just can't recommend this game to people who aren't passionate about this genre.The tutorial system that they have been hyping up is completely useless because it is mixed in with actual game mechanics that progress your story, politics, and economy; it's very hard to tell which of these are guidelines and which demand attention in order for you to do important things. The economics simulation is actually the least complicated thing about the game, it works decently and is engaging. The warfare is a mind numbing mess of micro, classic paradox "cat herding" that's even worse than HOI4 because at least in that game _sometimes_ units stay where you ask them to go.One last thing before I wrap up; the people online, ie. youtubers like iSorrowProductions and pontificators on le reddit, saying that they would rather play Factorio... They're entitled to their opinion (especially iSP who does this for a living basically), but I think that their criticism is not aimed well. Map games like this are there to help you construct a narrative around what you are doing. I just don't really enjoy straight up economics/production simulators like Factorio, and I should be able to enjoy this game (and I somewhat do). I really did enjoy beefing up Japan into a world power and then losing it all late in the game over a bad political gamble. That part works great, and is what shines in _all_ paradox games and separates them from games like dyson sphere simulator, factorio, etc. where it's just you and an economy waiting to happen. When those people criticize and lament this game in that way, it hurts both genres of games because it doesn't really address what's wrong with this game. Those games can't be what this game is, and vice versa, even if this game was perfect. What's wrong with this game is; it's crashy, the developers made poor choices with the tutorial system, the combat makes no sense and needs way too much micro for what it is, there are only 4 sound tracks in the game and you're forced to listen to "glory to the queen" while you fight a revolution to replace her, nonwhite people wear nothing but traditional clothes all the way through 1936 no matter how advanced your society is, etc etc etc. What's wrong with this game isn't that it's not Factorio, or hell it isn't even that it's not HoI4, Steallaris, or CK3, or even Vic2. What's wrong with this game is that it's a bad Vic3. That's it. Anyway, I preordered this game and it's a sunk cost, so i'm getting what enjoyment out of it that I can. But if you're on the fence and looking at reviews to help you make a decision on this game, I would say please don't buy it. Wait 2 years for the game to become playable and refined, and be sure to never pay full price. The developers who worked on it are nice, hard working nerds with metal band t-shirts, but their bosses and VPs and Execs and shareholders need to be punished for releasing this mess and the only way we can do that is through the market. How fitting!

_childDocuments_.review: After playing the game as Germany, USA and Russia it's clear that the game needed more time in development.The game has a lot of potential - but it's either going to take mods or DLC to make it replayable. I'll list a couple of the larger issues.1) The AI is pretty bad at managing their nations and fighting wars. This is readily apparent in how Prussia has a hard time forming Germany and the USA more often than not can't beat Mexico in wars and form their traditional borders in North America. Its just deflating not seeing the AI be able to do the things that are easily done by a player - and are easily done in Victoria 2 most of the time. There is nothing wrong with their being ahistoric outcomes - but that shouldn't be most games - in V3 it is most games.On top of that - the American Civil War when it launches can include non-slave states - so the bordergore in this game is horrendous and seemingly random due to the way civil wars currently work.2) The second reason is that the way the game operates currently is you spend 80% of your time figuring out what economic buildings to build, balancing your budget with construction needs and prioritizing construction of buildings of in demand goods in your market. The diplomatic game is pretty devoid of choice and same goes with warfare, there are limited options with both of those sides of the game so you end up spending your entire time completing economic building chains and researching technologies to improve those same buildings. It's interesting to learn - but once you've played a few games it isn't entertaining.Overall - game needs more time - can definitely be good with mods or more DLC but its clear to say the game needed more time.

_childDocuments_.review: Victoria 3 has had a hard time of it, but after biding my time, getting it for 50% off, and waiting for 1.5 to hit, I can say the following:Absolutely marvelous. Easily my favorite Paradox Sim next to Europa, and I look eagerly to Paradox supporting the title because the potential on this one is immense. But don't let potential distract you, let me hit you with the now -- why does 4000+ hours EU IV man recommend Vicky 3? 1) The systems nail the time frame and theme. I study political philosophy, history, and economics. When economic theory and systems are well-modeled in your video game, I take note. As a philosopher, I'm also charmed that you can upgrade your philosophy departments. 2) Might just me, but I love development in EU IV. Victoria 3 is like if you made development the entire game. It's fantastic. For me, it takes alot of the best parts of each of the modern Paradox Sim titles (Stellaris, EU IV, CK3, HOI IV) and does a great job of implementing them for the period. 3) People have b!@($d about the military and diplomacy in the game, but I want to tell you that I am absolutely jaw-droppingly amazed at how well they pulled it off for the time period. Start with military This is the period of the modern, industrial wars: the Crimean War, the U.S Civil War, and WWI. It's also the time of the sharp quick war: The Franco-Austrian, the Franco-Prussian. But it was also the time for just peace: consider that from 1871 to WWI, the great powers fought a total of 0 wars. This is an unheard of period of peace and prosperity. To that end, it gets thing done well. The quick, sharp wars were primarily a matter of diplomatic power and the power of reform and technology on an isolated opponent (good job Bismarck). You can totally do that, if you're clever. Otherwise, wars devolve into basically an industrial calculus -- JUST LIKE THE ACTUAL WARS OF THE TIME. Without the mobility of WWII, industrial war is just on a scale such that the larger engine wins. The fact that you have quite limited ability to control your troops in the field is, I think, a perfect encapsulation of this. Gameplay wise, I much prefer letting my armies fight for me. If I want to micro divisions, I can play Ultimate General, or Unity of Command -- you know, a war game. A game about fighting a war.4) This is the best diplomacy system I have ever seen. It nails how diplomacy worked during this time period, and the idea of diplomatic plays is so obvious that I wish it was in EU IV. It still needs some work -- countries do silly things, there's no open borders ??? to allow movement ?????. 5) I want to praise the UI design. Truly, truly, truly intuitive. I mean, for a game where you're mostly looking at graphs WOW. Also the detail of the world is splendid as well. Very glad they went with few-states over many-states approach when it comes to management.

Now, these developpers have the absolute gall to release features that should have been in the game in a functional state at release, in a DLC priced at 30 US dollars. _childDocuments_.review: Victoria 2 was a broken, yet brilliant game. I, as many others, waited for a fixed version of Victoria 2 for many, many years. I couldn't believe it when I heard Victoria 3 was in development. I waited for a while to get it; I was busy, but once I started playing, I couldn't believe it. The guys that created this "game" most likely never played Victoria 2, or if they did, they never loved it or at least understood it.Firstly, why was Victoria 2 great? Because it really successfully emulated the geopolitics of that imperialistic age. It was really natural and logical that countries at that time were urbanizing and industrializing. If they wanted to have a chance to resist the other imperialistic powers, they had to become big boys themselves, big industrial powers, they needed to industrialize. But to industrialize and satisfy modern needs for new consumer goods and colonial items, countries needed resources (and overseas territories that produced those colonial goods, to make sure your industry is not starved). Most advanced and industrialized countries were in Europe, where they lacked the needed amount of resources to keep the industry going and the insatiable thirst for colonial goods among the population. If there were not enough products to satisfy the needs of the population, they would become radicals, nationalists, communists, anarchists, fascists, etc. and cause lots of trouble, maybe even destroying the country. On the other hand, many European powers had subjugated nations that would develop nationalism and demand independence, provoking crises that led to conflicts between the great powers. So to resist being dismantled, any country had to grow strong economically, expand, and keep the population happy. For example, people needed tea, but only China and India had highly productive tea provinces, and in fact, China, as a backward country at the time, had small productivity, so that left Great Britain as the owner of a few massive tea production provinces in India. The other countries have to buy most of it from GB, but generally, that supply is shared by the big dogs, who also fight over it and have the first pick. To produce fabric, you need dye, which has a few high-production provinces in India, also owned by GB. To produce very profitable and demanded luxury clothing, you need silk. Again, the highest production province for silk outside China is India, owned by GB. Then there's tropical wood, etc. So you see how the conflicts are born; unless you are GB or on good terms with GB, you'll lack resources, so you must somehow get them. You are forced to do something about it, and everything, including diplomacy, industry, and tech, serves this purpose. The AI is also playing this game, trying to secure its needed resources and a place under the sun. Later, the scramble for Africa will start to get the hands on some of the much-needed resources and cannon fodder; for some countries, the only way to get some is to get some lands in Africa. The warfare is also very, very enjoyable. Actually, in V2, unlike EU4, you have the money to do stuff, like build the economy, infrastructure, armies, and navy. So this game has a lot of gameplay in it; players can do a lot of stuff in it. But the economy was broken; that was the very frustrating flaw of V2. But that needed some tuning, plus adding some more goods. Actually, the great geographical discoveries were made in search of spices, but spices are missing all together; sugar, furs, etc, that were just as important are also missing. Anyway, you needed cotton to sustain the fabric and clothing industry. You searched for an owner of a cotton province, not just any one, but one with a high enough population to make it, and either try to do something diplomatically (sphere it) or used brute force to secure that resource. Also, to have a competitive industry on the world's market, there were a lot of things to be done apart from securing abundant and cheap resources.And all this is just scratching the surface of V2.Now, what do we have in "V3"? Nothing like that. As a minor power, you can build one thing at a time, then wait for 1,5 years to be finished while staring at the screen, then realize roads are not enough; you need railways. Wait the other two years if you have railway technology. In the meantime, the other provinces are screaming as they have no economy going and no infrastructure, so the "gameplay" is just waiting forever to build your economy. Unless you are a greater power, which makes things slightly faster, like building two at once, but in a way larger empire. Wait, wait, and wait. Winning some wars against bigger powers, like in V2, is useless because you'll get other underdeveloped provinces that need to wait in line since your country has not yet discovered that it can build more than one thing at once. Building more construction sectors has a negligible positive impact and usually makes the country go bankrupt (same for administrative buildings). With full gold reserves, it's incredible how fast you can go in the red, meaning interests will also add up, making it even harder or impossible to get over. For one moment it's swimming in gold and bankrolling other countries, then in a year or two bleeding huge amounts of money and going bankrupt. Then the value of provinces means little now; there are no special provinces with high productivity colonial goods or minerals like coal, iron, sulfur etc to drool over and dream about and plan their conquest. You can (in theory) get only one cotton province and expand its plantation; it's not like you can develop more than two provinces or something at a time. Warfare? Streamlined? What a joke! It was streamlined in V2, you had the armies with 'hunt rebels' activated, and that was it, and the big wars were the best part of the game. Now that the rebellions are as annoying as possible, before they erupt, they ruin your country anyway with those trolling events. The few wars I waged were carefully chosen and quickly won; I don't even know how, apart from just having more troops. The most ridiculous thing ever is recruiting units, then having to stare at the screen waiting for barracks to be built for those units, even at max speed. Then there is any change in the composition of the army, and those barracks are gone and have to be rebuilt. In all my life of playing, I never saw anything so ridiculous. Some government building that took two years to build is making me bankrupt. I cannot fire its employees or set its occupancy level, but just press minus so that all the waiting for it to be built is wasted in an instant, later waiting for another year or so to be rebuilt. It must be a new generation of game developers, the kind that never played any games, so they have no clue what a game is supposed to be. I think the first thing asked from the guy in charge of Victoria 3 should have been, "How many hundreds of hours of Victoria 2 have you played?" Obviously, he had none. I think I will leave this world before something worthy as a successor to Victoria 2 appears. And some guys here are saying this game will be fixed in several years with patches and addons. Nothing's going to happen; there's no fixing this.PS: The interface is also terrible; if I want to check the provinces that have railways built, I have to click on them and scroll to the bottom of each of them. There's probably another way, but I couldn't be bothered to discover where it was hidden. The only positive things I can say about this game are its graphics (actually unnecessary, Victoria 2 is looking fine enough) and the idea of GDP and GDP/capita, but that doesn't make the game anything more of a game, let alone a good game.

_childDocuments_.review: Like a lemon, lime and bitters, with a heavy emphasis on the bitters. There's a lot of cool things going on but there's alot of not so cool things happening too. If you were a big fan of victoria 2, it's going to be a let down.-The GoodThe economic management element to the game is actually on point, trade between markets, make resources, make factories, all what you would expect, but maybe a little too much, to the point where the whole game becomes you sitting in the buildings tab.The game looks nice, if you care about that.-The BadThe game crashes fairly frequently and as per typical of these games as you go on becomes slower and slower. the last 30 years will feel like the first 50 in my experience.There is a lack of historical agency to guide the world along, I understand the sandbox direction, but I don't understand removing some of the best historical events to happen within the time period that people would have been interested in, for example there's no guaranteed american civil war and for some people that alone could be a game killer.Nations feel the same, most countries feel the same, they don't have nation specific events or focuses to trigger interesting nation specific bonuses and stories.Politics right out sucks, for a game that is focused so heavily on being a geo-political simulator how about some actual connections between nations., It dosent feel like there's any politicking to be done when the only way to get nations to make basic trade deals with you is to just give them a ♥♥♥♥ load of money until they like you. The system feels shallow, and while i don't miss political spheres from victoria 2, this system feels as shallow as the dog wash tub.A Lack of upward mobility for smaller nations, Keep in mind it depends on what your goals are, but if you wanted to go from a <100 ranked nation to a >5 nation your options are limited. Albeit if you're playing a nation with some goldmines, you have options like South Africa or Australia, but if you don't have that natural resource wealth you're almost 100% stuck and ♥♥♥♥♥♥ like a step-sister in a washing machine.-The UglyThe war systems while not as bad as some seem to exaggerate are still horrendous and hands-off, there will be times where you just have no agency within the system, nothing to do but sit and race war exhaustion because there's no direct land route to your foe and they refuse to naval invade you.The tutorial is straight up nasty, giving poor economic advice and leading players astray. If all you did was export a good to a market that was in need of that good and upgrade only that one building, you will do better then advice the tutorial gives you. (make tools, clothes or groceries and join someone elses market if you're small and not in one already)

_childDocuments_.review: I'm enjoying the game so far but the amount of crashes, bugs, and other issues I've run into coupled with the lackluster war and diplomacy system make this game disappointing in terms of being a sequel to Vicky2. War: As a whole every feature is brought to the most basic rudimenitary level it could be. Generals can teleport randomly after cleaning up small pockets from Africa to Europe in seconds but then need to take 60 days to get back to the front you want them on. Navies and Troops don't truly deplete and there isn't a concrete way to check on enemy nations tech so you pretty much have to go in blind and hope your troops are better. Now granted that isn't even a problem as the AI other than France and GB barely even try to industrialize or upgrade certain sectors of their econemy. Fronts can only have one active battle at a time. Despite being Germany  invading Russia and having a front from Ukraine to Estonia you can only advace in one space at a time. Aditionally Puppets/Co-Billigerants on both sides all get there own fronts. So if you only have one beefey general as 80K death stack you can only attack one target even if both nations are neighboring. Limited ability to add wargoals severly limits any feeling of winning a war. You can gain total domination over France and be limited to War Reps if you forgot to add anything during the Diplomatic Play. PDX should definitly consider Wargoals mid war or being able to add after a war at increased Infamy or unused 'warpoints' or whatever it's called. Infamy is actually just a number since having a decent army of 300 troops can destroy any AI Nation alone. In Vicky 2 I constantly managed Infamy to stay under 25. I had a stable smaller state since I have never been a god at it. Vicky 3 thinking is out the window. 1000 infamy constantly as any embargos recieved don't matter since your econemy will always be ♥♥♥♥♥♥. Either you go into Isolation and bankrupt or constantly have Minus 5k-10k missing Wood, Iron, Sulpher, etc because some nation is importing half your market for no reason. Diplomacy: While there are many options to interact with other nations few actually feel fleshed out. Certain ones like aksing/offering a nation protecterate status will almost never happen. Of course this doesn't stop the Ai from asking tiny African minors they don't border with -1000 malus to become one. Unforutnatly I can't use 'people skills' with the AI to actually get and maintain any allies so there isn't really a point to maintaining relations with anyone but your subjects. Diplomatic plays feel hallow and frankly uninteresting. While yes they can be a little more accurate in terms of how wars start they can severly limit your success. There is no way to bribe or convince nations to leave the play, you cannot change or remove wargoals so once you've made a choice that's it. Misclicked once on some Siberian state you don't want? ♥♥♥♥ you, 30 infamy. General Complaints: Markets are a buggy mess that consistently crash late game. Turmoil is laughable as there is no clear indication on how to fix it. Many modifiers don't have popups on why they exist such as insufficient landing support. A moddifer that can reduce naval invasions up to 99% from my experince. (BTW the fix is obvious that being a bigger fleet, but for someone new to the game it was infuriating not knowing what to do.) BTW the answer was in a Reddit thread, not the offical wiki is laughable at best but that's besides the point. I'm not sure if intentional or not but Civil War states like the Confederacy can't be justified against at all even after they've offically obtained independece. I wanted to get an American treaty port but unfortunatly the Confederacy is uniquie and thus I just have to leave it alone. Occasionally leaders become 'busy' permanatly locking their use entirely until they die as there is no way currently to retire them since they're busy. Theres so much more I could say but the most important is that this game needs so much more work. I'm obviously going to keep playing as I enjoy aspects of it. This review is to prevent anyone not on Paradox copium from buying this unfinised, unpolished, and frankly barebones game. It's a dissapointment compared to what their promises and vision for the game led us to believe. I can only hope that many new features and changes are locked behind DLC's but I already know they will. Paradox please for the love of christ fix this piece of ♥♥♥♥ so I can watch green line go up.

_childDocuments_.review: I personally enjoy this game, but I cannot give it a positive review. In short this game feels incredibly unfinished and low pop multiplayer is miserable. The economy system of this game seems solid although simplistic and nearly the same for every country. It has a very similar loop that rarely differs between nations: build iron, coal, and/or wood; build tools, always more tools; find silk, opium, and sugar; build luxury items. The nation you choose has nearly no effect on how the game plays. The above economic loop is nearly universal. Location also is not nearly as important as any other grand strategy games, the loop of England, France, and US intervening in squabbles between minor or insignificant powers anywhere in the world grows old quickly. The war system......Multiplayer is what makes or breaks a game for me. I have 1000+ hours of multiplayer on HOI4 and EU4 and it has been the main drive of replayability for me, in this regard VIC3 has fallen short. Large player count multiplayer lobbies are fairly fun, but are very unstable. They are getting more stable as updates are rolled out, but in some lobbies containing players with less than perfect internet you will likely spend as much time paused or rehosting as playing the game. Smaller player lobbies in the 2-5 player counts are fairly stable, but are simply not fun. The AIs in multiplayer ruin the experience, forcing players to choose only major nations or spend the entire game barely scraping by, fending them off. And frankly there are not enough players to pick up casual games, requiring a group of dedicated players to assemble a lobby.In summary, the game is very simple, the economy is simple and fairly easy to manage, the game has little variability and low amounts of replayability, the war system is terrible, and the multiplayer is not at a state that I believe will maintain a sizable player base as related games have.

_childDocuments_.review: After playing for just over 11 hours and starting to really get into the game, I can definitely recommend this game, although it's not without its flaws. The Good: The economic system is fantastic and absolutely addictive to play, think Factorio but in grand strategy. It's very satisfying, and although it can take a moment to click, once you start to get the hang of it you learn it very quickly after that. It's easy to lose track of time perfecting your production lines, I'll admit I've spent more time than I meant to playing this game because of how engrossed I was. The war system is also something which I find to be a positive. I've always felt that Paradox' grand strategy games have suffered from being map-painters, so the fact that Victoria 3 moves the focus from war and territorial expansion to diplomacy and economics is greatly appreciated, and Victoria 3 is much better for it. Diplomacy is also quite good in my opinion, although its one of the weaker positives. It generally feels pretty good to use and the diplomatic plays system is great, although overall diplomacy is a bit barren and could use a bit of work. The political system is also very good. Everything in it feels good and responsive, and I love how many factors can go into the clout of interest groups, and how tailoring your economy a certain way can boost certain interest groups and weaken others. Overall most of the systems in the game are very fun to play with.The Bad: The UI definitely needs streamlining. Often I find myself having to navigate through multiple menus or tooltips to find the information I need, and the trade lens in particular sucks to use. Not a huge problem but one that needs to be dealt with regardless. One thing that a lot of people have pointed out as a problem is the fact that there just isn't much flavor for really any country. Although having a sandbox is nice, allowing players to follow historical paths if they want is very important for any grand strategy game. I do think the lack of flavor is blown out of proportion as a problem, the game is still very fun despite the limited flavor. My last and biggest gripe with Victoria 3 is that it hits a wall around the 1870s, and performance quickly grinds to a halt. While the systems are fun to play with, that doesn't matter when it takes several seconds to get through a week on speed 5. I have a decent pc and ended up killing my Brazil run in the 1890s because of how slow it got. Others have also reported performance decreases even on high end pcs.Conclusion: Victoria 3 has an amazing foundation, and already stands near the top of all Paradox games. I expect it will shape up to be Paradox' best game, and I'm enjoying it right now. Everything I like about it are strong foundational things, and everything I dislike about it are fixable. Shifting focus away from map-painting may be alienating to traditional pdx players, but unless you need that kind of gameplay to have fun I would recommend Victoria 3.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a narrow "No" for now. I'm a huge Paradox fan; especially Crusader Kings 2 and 3, and Stellaris. That said, I think there's a ton of room with future DLC to improve upon.Society simulation. I enjoyed starting as a traditional monarchy and watching/pushing the country to develop into a democracy. It's fun to balance the various interest groups that didn't want that to happen.Economy simulation, to a point. You can set a tax policy, turn your society into a libertarian or communist utopia (or dystopia?). That said, you're always effectively a command economy, as the player decides what industries get built and what they build.Warfare! I’m a massive fan of what they’ve done with combat. Combat has, in my opinion, always been the least interesting part of Paradox games for me. I enjoy characters, societies, and diplomacy. In Vic 3, war is pretty simple: Assign a general to a front, and he’ll do his own thing. That said, I wish the map made it more obvious where generals actually are.User interface. This is weird to put on a review, but bear with me: The game is very complex, but every single term is labeled, usually with an interactive tooltip that updates dynamically. As a creator of software, I’m just in absolute awe at the level of polish that went into this UI. It explains itself in a way that almost no other games do. Bravo.Economic micromanagement. As I said above,  despite being a libertarian utopia, I had to set  trade routes, and decide on what industries get built and even what they produce and how they produce it! This is unrealistic and tedious. I’d have preferred if the game gave other levers for government incentivizing certain industries; like perhaps tax breaks or grants.Characters. In the real world during this period, great personalities dominated society. Lincoln, Marx, Simón Bolivar, John Stewart Mill, Victoria herself, and many others changed the world in ways that are felt even today. But in the game, these characters have no voice. I’d have preferred a system more like Crusader Kings 3: Put characters front and center! Let us talk with them, let them yell at us, or like us, or .For me, there’s just sort of a lack of things to do. In Stellaris, there are planets to run, wars to fight, crises to conquer. In CK3, there’s marriages to arrange, plots to plan, castles to build. In Vic 3, most of the moment to moment gameplay is managing buildings. It’s just not enough for me.With DLC and a few more content patches, and ideally a big shift towards characters, I think Vic 3 could be fantastic. For now, though, it’s likely not worth your time. Unless you make UIs for a living, in which case, boot it up and take notes.

_childDocuments_.review: This is not yet a Victoria game, rather a colourful package waiting to be filled with DLC to (hopefully) become a successor to Vic 2. If you are looking for an economic sim, be aware that economics in this game model something akin to the NSDP´s or CCCP´s ( or any of the other manifestations of communism and  socialism) system of dictating the marketplace.  Moreover, their are obvious instances of the current far-left / woke ideology forcing itself into the game, with the expected result of being a detriment to the game. This won´t age well. While it can indeed be fun to pick and choose what industries are made etc, the more realistically representation of free market economics l found in Vic 2 is no where to be seen. Instead, it has been replaced by HOIV ´s buld system. For this reason alone, this game in its current state is a confused mix and has little if any resemblance to the Victorian age. But alas, the list goes on from there. All the meaningful control, complexity and variety between cultures and game play are missing. I think the review by The ArchCast  gives an honest commentary on many of the other  current shortcomings.                       So, sadly this is another example of Paradox creating yet another empty shell to later be filled by actual game mechanics. Well, at least we can HOPE that they eventually create some meaningful game play. On the positive side, it looks nice, which it needs to so that in 5-10 years when the game is fixed, it will not look to terribly outdated.
