_childDocuments_.review: The game still has some problems that make it simply not fun to play for longer than a bit at a time every other patch. I have some hope this is eventually going to be solved by the devs and I am going to eventually change my review when it happens. Then again we are closing in on DLC #3. The game has been out for almost two years and some problems like frontlines or naval invasions continue to be a source of frustration although in different shapes and sizes every other patch. I won´t lie, I have had a lot of fun, too. Most of that can be attributed to my initial enthusiasm when V3 came out and to a great extent to some awesome friends I did play the game with largely in spite of all the issues like irrational AI, frontline bugs or out-of-synchs or relobbying-issues. I would love to play this game in a stable multiplayer lobby for once, but you simply can´t play a few hours and return to it on another free evening more than two times in 50% of the cases.In single player I have enjoyed industrializing some countries or reforming them, but there is only that many times I enjoy simply going through the building loops. Which is fine. I like this part of the game somewhat. More militarily focused campaigns are not fun to me yet. Too many bad experiences with frontlines, naval invasions or erratic AIs. Might get used to it and you can reload every time it happens, but that sure is killing the fun for me at least.Political reforms on the other hand often feel arbitrary especially in more traditional countries. Sure you can work on your odds, but at any point when passing reforms everything can turn against you for no other reason than being unlucky. There is no actual political progress or developement while passing laws. Percentage chances change, dice are rolled, but what was a 40% chance a minute ago being explained in debate-events can all turn around to failing completely. Those events don´t mean anthing but a change in chance. They are in detail not connected to parties or peoples stances. Sometimes they boost parties or politicians, but you never really interact with them as in offering them something for fixed support that is going to remain for the duration of the reform process. One debate-event I get opposition support and the next one somehow that is lost due to something that doesn´t make any sense in relation to the overall process and the previous events positive change. What could I have done? I guess nothing really and that makes it rather frustrating.All in all I have played the game a good bit and I am not mad at the money I have spend vs the fun I have gotten out of it. But I can imagine the overall experience being a lot better, if it wasn´t for the issues one could detect and solve. I could see past the frustrating gameplay aspects in the last paragraph, if that was the only issue. Thanks for reading.

_childDocuments_.review: A very marginal recommendation. The core simulation around pops and the economy is very strong and ties into the political system well. Unfortunately, there are many QOL issues that impede the overall experience.Diplomacy is non-existent. There is no point to establishing puppets or dominions as their market contribution and tributary payments are virtually null. Directly developing the resources owned by them is the superior option and in that case, puppets serve only as an intermediary to an 'annex vassal' diplomatic play. The AI will escalate diplomatic plays nonsensically, and so deciding to annex Sulu as the Netherlands will see Qing involvement who will happily sacrifice millions to keep you at bay. Prussia is constantly at war with France as it carries out unification to secure German borders, and if you dare try to take land in Africa where France and Britain will have interests declared owing to their colonies, they too will fight you to the death for it.Warfare is frustrating at best. Quantity of troops has no relevance to your ability to defend or push - you can hold off armies many times your size with superior (i.e. higher quality) troops as battles are often conducted on equal numerical footing. Fronts are advanced one battle at a time with very little ground taken until you unlock later military techs. These later military techs require rubber and oil which the AI will not develop and allow you to trade for, thus leaving it to you to expand to secure these resources. Do not expect to be able to enable hospitals for your soldiers as you will not have access to opium.Colonisation is poorly balanced. There is absolutely no cost involved in establishing a colony and therefore no reason not to establish a colony wherever you can declare an interest. As a result, Russia will always colonise Hokkaido in Japan as well as much of the pacific, the French will snake their way throughout Africa, the British will be unable to colonise much of the Africa interior themselves thus relying on their puppets to do it (which they won't), and the US never manages to secure its current borders (instead opting to snake partway into Canada and to keep a Mexican enclave and Indian territories puppet).As a QOL example for warfare, you will attempt to conduct a naval invasion only to find out that your troop number must match the ship number or otherwise suffer a significant malus to your offensive capabilities. This is not indicated anywhere in the tutorial or in the tooltips. For the economy, infrastructure levels are not declared when building ports and railroads (needed to expand market access). Expanding your economy will see you constantly building whichever goods are in shortage, which to be quite honest could be broken down into an automated algorithm perhaps with presets. To play optimally, you only want to adjust employment methods (thus decreasing labourer employment and freeing pops for higher wage jobs) lategame which is a frustrating affair.The pops are satisfying to engage with and interact with. Your improvements to the economy will see their wealth increase and so will their influence on your politics. The creation of your industry will lead to the overthrow of the traditional land-owning class and as your factories increase in employment and specialisation, your trade unionists will begin to appear. Thus, by being targeted in your construction, you can influence the laws of your nation without risking revolution or severe radicalism. The biggest change to your politics will come with the advent of public trading which will double the number of capitalists in your economy and thus spell the end of your aristocrats.The political system is acceptable. Taking a long time to pass laws is very much due to a lack of legitimacy and political strength and so not the best criticism. If you look after your nation well enough, it is very possible to maintain an autocracy until the end date. I feel that there needs to be more nuance to the laws as as described by other reviewers, the 'meta' strategy is to adopt multiculturalism with universal suffrage - while I appreciate the complexities involved in endorsing such things as 'national supremacy' there should be an appreciable reason to retain the law other than for an authority boost.Finally, as mentioned, the map is beautiful and will reflect many of the economic changes you implement as you construct your Victorian empire.Overall, the game is promising and parts of it work well such that you can spend a reasonable number of hours watching 'line go up'. Unfortunately, the economic loop falls apart from a lack of automation and the other features that you might wish to explore will leave you feeling deeply unfulfilled, almost to the point that you feel like the only nation actually exerting any influence upon the world. By your third or fourth game, a sense of deja vu will set in and the complexities you once battled with will no longer keep you entertained.I appreciate the ambition of the devs and the scope of the work that they have undertaken, and I'm certain a lot of bugs will be resolved and features added upon the game to make it more engaging. The simple truth is that no amount of paid QA can compete with the testing undertaken by millions of different players on a game with a complexity such as this, and so I look forward to seeing what the game has to offer in a year's time once many of its kinks have been ironed out.

_childDocuments_.review: As of writing this the base game costs £42 off sale, with a 50% sale. Putting it bluntly this game isn't worth twenty pounds let alone forty, playing on the free weekend the game was enjoyable but felt lacking. The economical side of things were fine, but the military was both underwhelming & awkward. Armies are either stationed at a strategic HQ, these covering vast areas lacking more specific placement, or a front line. If for example your army is invading a state and beats the opposing army to the point all the land has been occupied the front line is removed and your army is automatically sent to either another front line if available or the HQ it was stationed at prior to being deployed. This leads to very annoying micro management in wars with multiple theatres, and doesn't lead to a peace settlement immediately if there are no other front lines which is a waste of time.The AI is also disappointing, they often only want bizarre states for offers, such as Britain asking for Eastern Andalusia from Spain. Having the AI join your wars is generally pointless unless they border the state your going to war with, and joining the AI in a war is often disappointing as the game has no way of forcing you to help the ally you've pledged to unless you share a border with the enemy. As such you can be given all of Canada & Australia for just offering support to Britain invade a state that has no army.The decisions are underdeveloped, the decisions I saw were form Canada/Australia, and explore the Nile/♥♥♥♥♥/Congo rivers and explore the American interior. Forming Canada/Australia is just the same as form-able nations in Hoi4 except it's a puppet rather than your own state. The explore decisions are basically the same, in fact the three river ones were as far as I was aware the exact same as each other. You pay a relatively sizable chunk of money every week whilst the expedition is on going and get occasional random events that you pick from two options that either add or subtract from a progress and a peril bar, or delay which just means a bit more time before the next random event. Fill the peril bar the expedition fails and you receive a small penalty to prestige, fill the progress bar you receive a small bonus to prestige. One event allows you to pay more money to avoid a chance of gaining some peril. Successful expeditions don't aid colonization of the respective areas, they aren't aided by any laws or technologies or relations with the natives of the explored areas.

_childDocuments_.review: Victoria 3 is a fun and engaging Grand Strategy game.  It's strongest element is the economic simulation, which blows most other strategy games out of the water, and the "Just one more..." aspect is super strong here as you adjust and balance your economy throughout the entire campaign.The Diplomatic Play system feels like a solid improvement over Victoria II's crisis system, allowing much more engagement by nations below Great Power ranking, I look forward to seeing where this goes.The War System is currently the weakest element, but a lot of this has to do with a few key weaknesses rather than the system itself.  First, there are a number of bugs and mishaps, such as an army closing a front and returning home, rather than moving to the nearest front (but not always).  Some of the aspects of the system are unclear, as to why you lose or win some battles, especially when the Offense and Defense rolls don't match the way the battle goes.  Ultimately, I still enjoy the system and the deprioritization of war as a focus.At time of this review, there are some frustrating bugs, for example permanent revolter states, but the key parts of the game work well.  Watching your GDP number go up, and seeing the impacts of your decisions and reforms play out in your society is thoroughly satisfying.As someone who has worked on mod teams for EU4, HOI4 and Stellaris, I am eager to see the possibilities for mods in Victoria 3.  The systems as they are lend themselves heavily to Cold War and later scenarios in a way that other Paradox Titles don't quite nail.Victoria 3 is a great foundation for a Paradox Game.  Long-term fans of the developer know that the game receive extensive support after release, so I know the game will continue to develop and expand with critiques of the playerbase in mind.

I am in the mid-game of the tutorial, yet, I can't wait to start a new campaign. Replayability appears to on par with (release) Stellaris and EU4, therefore thumps up and an early 11/10!-Fuel

_childDocuments_.review: I'm changing my recommendation to "No" more out of protest. Depending on how much you enjoy trying to find and tweak every lever, Vic3 certainly has a lot of content to keep some people engaged.However, after 2 years on the open market. The fact that Warfare is such an utterly abyssal system leaves much to be desired. Despite some good improvements in other systems. Leaving IMO a core system broken for so long in the state that it's in is inexcusable.1. The system itself is extremely poorly executed, I get the abstraction concept that is attempted to be executed However the actual manipulation of warfare with it's teleporting armies, nonsensical front line management, the Infantry/Arty/Cavalry units, conscription mechanic, management of individual armies, assignment/traits of generals. Is all very poorly done and not up to my customer view PDX standard of offering meaningful choices and levers.In a nut shell the systems and levers in place are a PIA to manage through a terrible UX. Examples include the assignment of armies to frontline, managing armies via the barracks in specific states and the subsequent moving units across the front as states are captured. For example there are some fronts in Russia, where if you attack from one direction and move the frontline. The amount of time it takes your units to transfer to the new front (even with transportation options) is longer than the teleported defenders to appear at the new front, attack the front four times and send your armies back to where they were.2. Of the systems/mechanics provided, beyond the terrible UX of interacting. The choices/content/design available leaves much to be desired. Leading to many choices that provide no meaningful choices.Examples, generals are randomized as are their traits, without any skill levels/difference between the general besides their ideology and combat traits.Another example, the Infantry/Artillery/Cavalry units offer no meaningful choices. Somehow artillery is not useful on defense and is an offensive unit, infantry is a defensive unit, and cavalry is lackluster in both offense/defense but if you have enough it speeds up the amount of land you occupy per successful attack. And yet, the base capture rate per state is 25% and you don't often field enough cavalry to increase occupation from 25%->33% so it still requires 4 attacks to occupy a state. Just examples of nonsensical decisions and mechanics.The designate strategic objective mechanic doesn't work half the time as expected. And even if you try to create sensible armies, 100% infantry on defense only, 50/50 infantry/arty for attacking armies. When you attack armies attack, they seem to pull a random ratio of units available to the entire front. like 2 infantry/38 arty or 35 infantry/5arty, even if you have several 20/20 infantry/arty armies.3. Even after the terrible UX and options available. The actual goal posts, what constitutes victory/defeat itself is atrocious. The math that calculates whether an AI is ready to accept peace/continue fights/war exhaustion is all over the place. Most war goals cannot be pressed if the war goal is not captured (i.e the math makes the AI say NO, keep fighting). The war goal target for different war goals rarely makes any sense.Examples: Great Britain declares war on you (Japan) in 1840s because you say no to their demand for investment rights. Because of the naval penalty, and you're defending an island. You slaughter 2 million British troops on the beaches or 5 year period. GB Govt doesn't bat an eye, the fact they've lost 2 million troops invading you means absolutely nothing. Nor does the fact they've spent millions of pounds on mobilized goods for the war over a 5 year period to try to attack you on the other side of the world. Neither of two variables have any impact on the AIs determination to continue the war or not. To clarify, losing that many troops does make their war support go down...to zero. But war support of zero does not mean much, war support needs to be in the negative territory to affect any real outcomes.The simplest war goal to ask for, or defaulted on defense is War Reparations. War Reparation however requires you to occupy a single INCORPORATED state. In the 1840s the only territory directly incorporated by GB is the british isles. So it doesn't matter if GB has lost 2 million men, spent millions of pounds on this campaign, and have gotten every single unincorporated outpost of the British empire not held by a vassal occupied for over a decade. The AI will never back down. because their warscore cannot tick below zero. And since all other mentioned variables (causalities, money spent, unincorporated territory occupied) do not factor into the final decision of yay/nay. The war continues.My absolute preference would be a proper warefare system that allows for role-playing, fun, meaningful give/take decisions. Something that actually resembles strategy.But if this is not the direction that PDX wants to take and is instead adamant on an abstract system. Then provide an actual abstract system. Completely do away with all the frontlines/units/bloat and just have an abstract ticker regarding war between two nations.Either way, commitment to a systems, what we have right now is an incomplete, ill-thought, broken mess that makes me want to completely disengage from all warfare. And not for the reasons of warfare is dangerous/expensive/unpredictable, but instead because its full of junk, bugs, exploits, poor-decisions.

_childDocuments_.review: New review after playing patch 1.5:Victoria 3, the latest addition to Paradox Interactive's repertoire, brings a distinctive approach to the grand strategy genre but falls short in several crucial aspects. While it can provide enjoyment for a period, I find myself on the fence, leaning towards a tentative "maybe" if that were an option.Firstly, the game places an overwhelming emphasis on the construction sector, often overshadowing other vital elements. While economic intricacies are expected, the game's heavy focus on construction tends to dominate the overall experience.Additionally, the economic development in Victoria 3 appears to move at a slower pace on its own, demanding players to engage in meticulous micromanagement. Unlike other economy simulations, where economic systems can naturally evolve, Victoria 3 leans more heavily towards requiring direct player intervention. This particular aspect may not appeal to everyone, resembling a gameplay style more akin to a cookie clicker game.One noticeable drawback is the comparatively limited role-playing (RP) aspect when measured against Paradox's other successful titles like CK3, HoI4, and EU4. The depth of personal and political narratives that players can weave falls short, leaving enthusiasts of intricate RP experiences wanting more.Summing up, Victoria 3 brings forth innovative concepts, yet its emphasis on the construction sector, sluggish economic development, and insufficient RP depth render it a mixed experience. While these issues could potentially be addressed and resolved in the years to come, the uncertainty of the waiting period leaves me undecided about whether I'm willing to wait.

_childDocuments_.review: If you have no idea what to do, just think of this game as a global Factorio. Make base buildings profitable, start more advanced buildings/production techniques, make the original ones cheap (by spamming them or joining a big market) to make the advanced ones MORE profitable, repeat. Now for the review:The good:- Very addictive once you get the hang of it. There's always something to fix or optimise with the added fun of global strategy on top- What makes it more challenging than Factorio is that you are not the only guy around. Other countries are industrialising too and you have to keep an eye out for their demands or potential monopolies, although the separate markets ensure that you can play in your own backyard if you so desire- Very different challenges depending on where you start- Fun social engineering aspect. You can do anything from socialist utopia to slave holding ethno-state- Manages to look the same as most paradox games while playing radically different, even from its own predecessorThe bad:- AI is still somewhat awkard, sometimes going for odd places and not focussing historical ones- The learning curve is rather steep and the feedback isn't great. Tutorial campaigns are a must, but with practice it becomes more intuitive and more gameplay options open up- The timeframe is somewhat limited, sadly. Can't really go rags to riches with everyone, the same way you can in EU4 or Ck3The ugly:- Seems to be poorly optimised. At least on my system i'm getting heavy stuttering in lategame, like with Stellaris at launch- Occasional CTDs even, probably for the same reasonAll in all it's great fun even at this state, if you're willing to put up with the frustrating learning curve and technical hickups. It's definitely unlike any other game out there rn

_childDocuments_.review: Perhaps the single worst combat system in any strategy game. Vicky 3 completely forgoes player agency by removing all tangible game pieces or "units" from the board which have been a staple of the genre since its inception, and instead opts for a system of double chance. The first being the chance that your general staff will actually comply with your desires and the second being the outcome of the battles themselves which have become so whitewashed since the previous title that Risk appears more appetizing. The player will quickly find themselves frustrated by the lack of separation between diplomacy and war making the lackluster combat often unavoidable which is then further undermined by the flippant decision making of the game's diplomatic AI. Suspiciously, Ironman mode permits save scumming which at least on the surface level would appear to be an acknowledgement of this poor system on behalf of the developer.While the current and previous patches for the game have attempted to apply a small adhesive bandage to the issue, it is a far cry from what fans have become accustomed to in previous and parallel titles. I have little doubt that Paradox will address this issue in time in the form of yet another paid patch for the bargain price of $29.99.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the better Paradox games at release. Systems are mostly good. Needs some patches for refinement and quality of life. If you generally like Paradox games for the nation building, you might enjoy Victoria 3. If you are hesitant, wait for the inevitable first DLC, and get it on sale. If you play Paradox games to micro armies, you probably already know Victoria 3 gutted army micro, virtually removing it as a mechanic. It is 60% a supply chain simulator-strategy game, with the normal diplomacy, politics, and things from other Paradox titles thrown in. The diplomatic play system in particular is very promising and injects a lot of opportunity for fun/interesting moments. Most mechanics are approached from the macro side of things, with control being loose in politics and war. You try to enrich your nation, and satisfy the needs of your population, as expected from a Victoria game. Pretty big departure from Victoria 2 in the way its approached. The player input into the economy is much more central and fleshed out. You can actually develop resources beyond just building railroads in your provinces, and 90% of the economic chain is in your hands. Additionally your politics are a little deeper than Victoria 2, with interest parties being more dynamically modeled, and having a wider set of laws and effects you can try to achieve in the world of government and policy.The Bad:A lot of the dislike for Victoria 3 comes from jankiness or oddities like random small nations with gold mines becoming the wealthiest and most advanced nations on Earth over night. It also has issues with information density, and UI/UX design. Of course the highlight and contentious matter is the macro-only war system, where players who enjoy the micro control of stacks not getting that itch scratched at all in Victoria 3. If thats what you like, it simply isn't here. Personally I always found unit micro to be an occasionally enjoyable facet of Paradox games that more often than not was a headache. I usually prefer the nation building aspect of their games, and as such have a more favorable opinion of Vicky 3. I can understand the disappointment among those who mourn the loss of Micro, but I don't share the feeling. To be sure, I also have some gripes with the war system. Why can't I manually split fronts, or set the actual number of troops a general controls? Why can there only be one battle at a time? Why can't a front be attacked from both sides at the same time, with different areas being pushed both ways simultaneously? If all of this was addressed, it would be near perfect to me. I never enjoyed the stack management game play much to begin with, so if this current system was made better, I would prefer it to any other Paradox game.The game also, at the time of this writing, could use a lot of flavor. And the flavor that is there needs fixing. Most nations only get one or two unique bits of flavor. The US gets the ability to fix its northern border with Canada, and claim Mexico's northern states. Yet the systems are flawed. For example; the bits of the American-Canadian border north of the fixed line that America can (And the AI almost always does) colonize are NOT traded to Canada when the US gets its land south of the new line. Rather ugly and annoying to look at. And Mexico, lacking a good mobilization law and military buildings, is so scared of the US that they often just back down every single diplomatic play the US makes to actually get their states, forcing both the AI and player USA's to suffer through multiple plays and truces for what should be one or two wars. Slavery is barely even an issue in the US, with it often just being abolished without the chance for a Civil War. Flavor in other nations is likewise lacking, or broken, at time of release. We expect it to be addressed in the near future.Puppet management is poor, and subject nations are a headache. You can't build in your puppets, or command them to colonize, or transfer them land, or use their war goals, or pursue wars on their behalf. That second point is more annoying when you know that Australia cannot be federated if Britain colonizes the last part of Australia itself, and the Australian AI often just doesn't do it. Yet another bit of annoying/lacking flavor.The Good:For the issues with UI and mechanics that the game has, its systems are still fun. Its only days old but I have over 50 hours in it. I expect to put in a lot more. Hopefully it's gaps and flaws get addressed. For what it is, I enjoy it. I like the game play loop of advancing economically and politically and having to balance the economy, I enjoy the buildup to conflicts and the positioning game of diplomacy and colonization, and I enjoy when the green line goes up. The building game, trying to balance your resources and pop needs, trying to acquire more resources, and cope with changing economic needs as time advances, is very addicting. You can become invested, and want to see all of your goods prices go into the blue, or panic when everything shoots up to +75% price after a major economic shift. Organizing and planning ahead economically is fun, and the AI is more competent at it than one would expect. Still, they can rarely challenge a player, as is standard for these games.The politics and interest system are decent. I like how reactive they are, not just being a pre-determined support % for every nation that barely moves over the course of the game. You can really see and feel the different needs and wants of a political body. It feels hard to shake the Isolationism of Japan, and difficult to resist liberalization in Western nations, as it should be.The plays system is great. It introduces the ability but escalate and de-escalate conflicts in both multiplayer and singleplayer in an actual game mechanic. The way you can add goals and bribe other nations to your side with said goals is fun. I wish though you could do some kind of mid-war play, where you could change the nature of the war, by again, escalating or de-escalating. WW1 didn't begin as a fight to the death, but it certainly became that. In most Paradox games, every war is a full on slugging match, and I would like to see a day when Victoria 3 can represent limited wars, wars that change in nature, and wars that begin or end unexpectedly. HOI4 has border conflicts, and EU4 has Condot, but those systems are anemic and rare.The actual visuals are pretty nice. I enjoy the map, and like its depiction. Additionally, the game is somewhat RAM heavy compared to other Paradox titles, but otherwise performs wonderfully. It can lag in the later years of the game, not unlike HOI4, but still performs quite well, and runs lightly. All things considered its pretty stable and smooth in singleplayer. Multiplayer yet to be determined, the word out is that its pretty unstable as the game goes on. Will have to wait and see if this is fixed.As you can see from the things I like, I do enjoy the mechanics. I just wish they were broader/deeper, with quality of life changes. Still, my rating is based on the game as-is, and I recommend caution if you are already weary of buying the game.6/7 out of 10, closer to a 7 than a 6. If the AI made better Diplomatic Play decisions, flavor was added, and some mechanics were deepened, it would be a 9/10.

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend this game only if you like economy management. There is a severe lack of flavor between each nation, war is pretty terrible, information can sometimes be really hard to find, diplomacy is wonky, and the AI seems poorly optimized.Now, I've had an absolute blast playing it and I can see the potential this game has with future updates.  So I will recommend it and hope either modders or Paradox finish the game.Let's talk about my biggest issues.Flavor: Nation specific flavor events are nowhere to be seen. Next to nothing concerning the unification of Germany and Italy. Transforming from the Shogunate of Japan to the Empire of Japan was as simple as changing some laws. I've yet to see a Russia implode and the Soviet Union rise. In general, events are related to your political parties and not your nation. Therefore, you will have nearly the same experience playing Japan as you would Great Britain or Prussia.War: I'll give an example. Quite often, fronts will become split in wars as your generals will pick a direction to push. Sometimes, they can push in opposite directions. Let's say one goes east and the other goes west. The east general can finish sieging down the eastern half of the country and immediately decide it's time to teleport home. Or, if I'm lucky, he will instead join the western front (also by teleporting there). However, if I am unlucky, I now have to send him back from his base to the front and wait the 30/60/90 days to do so.Naval invasions are busted by the way. You should absolutely abuse them because the AI cannot handle multiple front wars and war can take an ungodly long time to push even before trench warfare is unlocked.Information: Why are my people radicals? Why is it so hard to find that? Why do my shopkeepers/laborers/etc in most of my country have a standard of living of 20-30 but my average is 12? Stop hiding the information behind multiple tooltips. Stop hiding information in general. Give me a ledger. No, seriously, GIVE ME A LEDGER.Diplomacy: I need poor relations to declare war on someone. Fair. I need poor relations and potentially war to annex my subject? Annoying but whatever. Why did I have to go on reddit to even find out if I could annex my subjects? Why was that option just gone until I lowered relations enough? I still don't know why other options don't show up sometimes. For some reason, I just can't join someones customs union and I have no idea why. I guess what I'm saying is, STOP HIDING INFORMATION FROM THE PLAYERAI: Oh my god, sometimes they can be so clever and I doubt it is intentional. The thing is, they suck at preparing for late game. If you want oil, electronics, rubber, opium, sugar, etc, you better get it yourself. Colonization is a requirement late game. If you didn't colonize, you better be ready to fight a great power or a major to get yourself some colonies. The AI is terrible at late game industrialization. However, they can be really good at importing/exporting goods to/from your country and crashing/raising the price of certain goods in your country. I really wish I could limit that better when my trading policy is Mercantilism or whatever. You can't trade embargo your allies.One last thing, the AI very much hates players. You can make them a little more lenient in diplomatic plays with the game settings, but I'm specifically referring to alliances, custom unions, trade agreements, etc. I can have basically max relations, 0 infamy, mass trading, the largest army in the world, the largest economy in the world, and the only nations that want to ally me are countries like Brunei and maybe Persia if I'm lucky. God forbid you try and get Austria or another Great Power to ally you. Even when you succeed, they WILL break it the moment you get the tiniest amount of infamy.So if you loved Victoria 2, this game isn't for you. If you loved EU4, this game isn't for you. But if you want a Victorian Era economy simulator, yeah, I recommend this.

_childDocuments_.review: I got this for free from someone who already had the game but had a spare key from a humble pack. I'm glad I got it for free because I would be mighty pissed off if I had paid £40 for it. I've played a lot of Parodox titles. Too much in fact. Over 1000 hours in EU4 and more then 800 in HOI4 and a few 100 in this game predecessor VIC 2 as well as some in Stelaris. I have tried to like this game. I have tried so hard to try and figure out how to enjoy it, playing majors and minors across the map with different play-styles. But it is just too still and stiff and limited in its mechanics to warrant the upfront cost let alone the extra payments for its DLC. It does not flow in a way my brain can get behind and I believe its core issue lies in how its core base is modelled around the building of economies.Another review here summed it up great The Core game-play loop is about being able to build construction centres. You build buildings to make goods that make you money so you can build more construction centres to make more buildings. You then have to build each unit a building so you can then use these units to go do whatever you want to do militarily with the ultimate goal of presumable either getting more money (to build more CC's) or to conquer territory to get goods which might then get you more CC's. And this is where you run into what is for me the main stand-out issue.War ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Sucks. It's so bad. In a period defined by colonial conquest and the limited wars of the concert of Europe before the large sprawling total wars of the early 20th Century, this game does not give you enough control over your forces to allow you to effectively do these wars in any satisfying way. The brother's war for example was in reality a quick affair where as trying to execute it here results in the 30 Years War Part 2. Where you have battles that happen without your control that you win or lose without your input. Is this perhaps accurate to being a head of state and having to leave it to the hands of your general? Sure. But for a game like this? Where its predecessor and its other parallel titles allow you more direct control over how you fight? No, I don't believe it's a good system. Not to mention Naval combat makes little sense and can not even act as a blocker for crossing tiles (e.g. islands that have a land connection that would be impossible to reach without naval supremacy like Sicily and Italy) removing another layer of strategic action from the player.I could rant about the social reform aspect, or the lack of inter-connectivity between your actions and results, or the lack of flavour events to flesh out the world but this review is already too long for something most people wont even read and most of my feelings can be summed up by the boring core game play and the madding war system.If you want a decent economic sim I would recommend you play ANNO 1800 instead, where the limited military system works less as a pillar but more as a functional extra (needing production chains to build the units while being limited to building cap and time required). It has a much more simplified to non-existence social reform aspect but I would argue that this game does a terrible job at implementing that as well. Will this game ever be good? Maybe. Right now I can not recommend it in its current form unless something major changes.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Trade has the biggest performance impact on the game, and this hasn't been fixed for years. Please fix this.-----This is a good game but something I would like to see them fix is the trade system. Trade, market dominance, and employee productivity are the driving factors of your nation's growth in power and prestige in this game - and increasing standards of living through profit margins and funding public programs is crucial for maintaining political stability and high taxes for further growth. Naturally, your nation is not going to have all the natural resources available to it needed for such growth, so trade is a natural alternative in the absence of the possibility for military intervention.The problem with trade, however, is that A.I nations will not always trade with you if your products are cheaper - and this itself wouldn't be an issue if the player was easily capable of setting up trade routes themselves.This is the catch: Player-led trade routes have the largest impact on game performance than any other aspect of the game, bar-none. It's 1935, my game hasn't slowed down a single bit from the start. I set up trade routes to hit the much coveted $2billion gdp as China - what do I get? An FPS drop from 60fps to 4fps. So long as the trade screen is open, the game is a slideshow. Even when it's closed, at best you might hit 10fps.I see people complain all the time about culture groups slowing the game, but the biggest culprit is hands down ALWAYS trade. Devs, PLEASE fix this core aspect of the game. It's literally a game about economics, TRADE shouldn't be broken like this.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has generated a surprising amount of controversy, so while I normally don't bother with reviewing games, I think it's worth sharing my thoughts here given the focus on it and the difficult nature of evaluating this game, which I would say overall is a flawed but still enjoyable game.For context, I am a huge fan of Victoria 2 and have played many hours of it outside of Steam in addition to what is listed on my Steam account. In that context, I do disagree with a couple of the decisions made in the development of Victoria 3, but that being said, the fundamental mechanics of this game in terms of economics, politics, and diplomacy are for the most part strong, even if the game is also flawed. As I see it, there are 4 main gameplay pillars to this game which are varying in their level of polish and engagement for the player: This is the strongest point of the game. The switch to market-based economies from the unrealistic (for the era) global economy of Vic2 is a big step forward and creates more interesting decision making regarding resource and goods production. If you don't have the potential to extract certain resources in your land and you aren't in a customs union with someone who does produce that resource, you are going to need to trade for it (which is limited by your bureacratic capacity so not an unlimited option), or go about securing land that produces that resource, either via war or diplomacy. There is an argument that some resources are too common relative to history, which can make the game a bit too easy for huge nations, but for small and medium-sized nations the struggle to procure the resources you need to build your industry is real and engaging. And TBF in Vic2 if you had enough prestige you could just access goods from the global market anyways, so big nations are always easier in this sort of game if you know what you're doing.The consumer and industrial good production chains are also far more complex than in Vic2, and provide a constant need to think about how to balance and expand your industries to supply your market with needed goods. For example, in Vic2 if I wanted steel I would build a steel mill which consumed coal and iron from RGOs that I couldn't really interact with. In Vic3 if I want steel I have to build a steel mill which consumes tools, coal, and iron, which to produce everything efficiently requires a tooling workshop, iron mine, coal mine, chemical plant (for explosives in the mines), sulfur mine (for the chemical plant), logging camp (for wood for tools), railroads (for transportation of goods to improve efficiency), motor industries (so the railroads have trains), etc. It's much more in depth and requires more thinking on the part of the player to set up a successful economy since so many industries are co-dependent on each other in some way. I can see an argument that it should still be possible for capitalists to build industries themselves, it would certainly make things a little easier in the late game. That said, I don't think the player should ever be locked out of building factories like in Vic2 laissez-faire as it is a key gameplay mechanic that should have player agency. The interest group system is at a baseline the most interactive internal politics gameplay mechanic Paradox has created. Pops organize into IGs based on their needs, profession, strata, beliefs, etc. and those IGs pressure or support you as you try to implement or remove laws and policies. Depending on the social and economic structure of your nation, an IG that only represents 2% of the population might hold 30% of the power, as is not uncommon with landowners in the early game in many nations. The issue that remains here is balance. The actual mechanics are solid, but powerful IGs as it stands are not dangerous enough. Powerful and angry IGs need to be much more willing to revolt, right now they are too willing to stand by as they lose laws and policies they like. Even happy powerful IGs should occasionally come to you with demands if they think they can force the issue. But these are balance tweaks that can be made and the mechanics themselves work well. Diplomatic plays are a great idea and are just the evolution of Vic2's crisis system. It feels accurate to the era that powers can choose to jump in alongside a smaller nation if it serves their larger geopolitical interests even if they don't have an official alliance or pact. However, there are balance issues at play here, where it seems like currently major powers are a little too eager to jump in to help minor nations, particularly in the early game. This should probably be looked at and toned down a bit so that huge wars aren't breaking out over minor colonial conquests. Similarly, it would be nice if minor colonial conquests across the globe were treated a bit differently in the system compared to a nation trying to conquer a minor that borders a major power.I also like the ability to diplomatically influence nations into your customs union, joining them with your market. However, it does feel like there needs to be a way to "defend" your customs union diplomatically, as it stands you just have to hope that if you maintain good enough relations with them that they won't agree to join another major's customs union. This is undeniably the weak point of the game and where a lot of the complaints come from. For one thing, warfare is buggy, I've had generals unassign themselves from fronts randomly and other bugs that make war unnecessarily frustrating.Fundamentally though, this is the one area of the game where I think the mechanics need an overhaul as opposed to just tweaking and balance. I understand the move away from army micro as it did not represent early 20th century warfare well, but the new system lacks player agency as the fronts are all auto-generated and the player cannot direct their generals much beyond basic attack, defend, and stand by commands. What I would suggest is more of a "HoI4 light" system where the player can draw their own fronts if they wish and can direct attacks along specific approaches (battle planning essentially), manually garrison areas, create fall back lines to defend, etc. I don't think the return of army stack micro is truly necessary, but a better frontline system with more player agency is needed.The final thought I would note is that there is a valid complaint regarding lack of historical flavor for many nations. That said, I've always felt that mods were primarily what added flavor for Vic2, so it isn't that surprising. And nations do feel different to play already if they have different resource potentials, interest group power dynamics, and laws. With tweaks to how impactful powerful interest groups are, they would feel even more different. But I would certainly welcome more historical flavor myself.If you played Vic2 or other strategy games primarily for the economic components and internal politics, I would recommend Vic3. If you are more focused on war, I wouldn't recommend it for you at this time. Fundamentally it's a game with a solid economic, political, and diplomatic base that needs some tweaking to resolve its flaws, plus a larger overhaul of warfare.

_childDocuments_.review: Temporarily swapping this to Not Recommended as the November 2024 update has (for now) introduced some rather aggravating bugs, gameplay issues, and user interface difficulties. It feels like it's undone a lot of the great progress the game has made since its rough launch. Hopefully things will be fixed promptly.--------This game is essentially an economy simulator, focused especially on growing your economy through construction, research, and expansion. The game had a rough start, but with the 1.5 update (November 2023) a lot of the more substantial issues have been resolved & the game finally looks to be on a positive path to the point that I've changed my Not Recommended to Recommended.That said, there's still a lot of work it needs, and my review is more "Recommended if you're really interested, but it still needs work". Some of the things I hope the design team takes on in the coming months: - Fixing bugs (including a few substantial ones) - Improve the user interface with quality of life improvements, hotkeys, shortcuts (especially the outliner, army management, everything involving navies, and setting default building types for each use) - Improve the economic modeling (or give better user feedback) as an economy can swing between death spiral & mega-powerhouse every other week - Improve AI for other nations (which to be fair feels adequate... just not great) - Add a resource availability check to Auto-Build - Either make individual characters & agitators more meaningful or trash the system entirely; it requires so much micromanaging to keep up with, but also feels like an almost totally ignorable system - Refine resource availabilities & especially more regional modifiers. And I probably shouldn't be able to develop my early 20th century economies to the point that they can use every drop of the oil in the world & still not have enough. - More laws, tech, and ways to customize your builds & empire - Fill out more nations with tailored events & other unique things.

_childDocuments_.review: The game has potential but I would not recommend it at this stage.So far it's a nice economic simulation with a fairly realistic portrayal of supply and demand. Unlike most, I do not mind the unusual war mechanics either. However, diplomacy feels very odd. Most powers are very happy to get involved in any wars all over the world, which leads to huge conflicts, which seems somewhat ahistorical for the 19th century. My biggest objection however is that the game feels somehow "empty". There are very few events that often repeat themselves and there are very few national differences. I've played as Prussia/Germany, Sicily/Italy, Persia and the US and they all played very similar. Unification of Germany or Italy was ridicously and ahistorally easy. Also, the characterstics of your rulers and political leaders are pretty much inconsequential. In my games there was also never really the danger of revolution, which made politics a bit boring (tbf though this could be because I never played into the 1900s).I am sure they will fix this with DLCs in the future, but I don't have the patience and mind to wait for that. The best thing that could happen to this game is that it gets the same treatment as Imperator: Rome, which became a really good game after several years and updates. But again, I don't think I have that much patience with Paradox.

_childDocuments_.review: No idea why this game is getting so much hate. Is it perfect? No. Is any game release? Definitely not.This game is a fantastic update of the kund of genre-bending complexity that Paradox is known for. It has a steep learning curve but it's core loops of "national gardening" are fun and unique in the grand strategy genre.In general the game could use more content/events/journal goals, which I expect the dlc's will address along with the modding community. Some people dislike the war system; to be honest, I get the war system, I enjoy it, and war was something I found tedious and boring in Vic 2 and hoi4's endgame division unit spam destroys game performance. The front system is a great abstraction of this that is immersive and computationally cheaper. To people who want a economy-building wargame; hoi4 is probably on sale and a lot more detailed in that regard. Vic3 is not a wargame (you hire generals but the specifics of battle are managed by them) and was never intended to be and I prefer that. The war system UI and front system could use some polishing, the splitting front mechanics are a little janky. The chill nation-gardening of Vic3 is-at its core- a mechanically brilliant platform on which to immersively build a nation from an economic, political, and cultural perspective. The supply chains are very satisfying to setup, similar to Factorio.Overall, 9/10. If you read the dev diaries, this is what was promised and it's an excellent game and will likely be one of the best of it's genre given time to develop and fill out with mods and dlc content.I recommend the tutorials to everybody, beginners and experienced folks alike.

_childDocuments_.review: I only just started to play this game, I am by no means a paradox veteran, although I did play 680 hours of HoI 4, but only really few hours on the other titles like EU IV, CK 3 and Stellaris (I did try my hand once on Vic2 and a few times on HoI 3). I've spent 2 - 3 years playing only Hearts of Iron 4, cause it's the only game I had a grasp on - but just recently I finally decided to spread my time on the rest of the titles.Paradox from the new testament seems to be a lot more consumer friendly in terms of expanding the game without releasing mandatory and predatory DLC (Finally!). CK 2 and EU 4 (+Hoi4 and Stellaris, to a lesser degree) are their worst examples, where yearly they would release a DLC fleshing out both cosmetically and mechanicaly a different portion of the game (economy, war, politcs, etc) giving the game more depth, difficulty and unfortunately, almost mandatory (cause they would balance the game around the DLC, not owning it gives you a tougher time than before the release). But it seems like they have been trying to release important mechanics for free, while charging for flavour, events and enhancements, making the community a lot more united - and I'm all in for it.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm updating my review as I feel that the game is now different enough from the state it was released in that it deserves a new review.I'd give this game a tentative recommendation*, with the asterisk being try the base game before buying any of the DLC. If you do decide to buy the DLC, it's worth waiting for it to go on special first, as the DLC pricing (particularly for Sphere of Influence) is pretty egregious for what you actually get out of it. To put it in perspective, Sphere of Influence is priced at $42.95 AUD when the base game is $69.95 AUD, which is roughly 60% of the price of the base game. At the end of the day it's up to you if you think the DLC would be worth it, and I'm just glad that I got it for free as part of the season pass.This game has good bones for mods, and with the Steam Workshop you can craft this game into something that you can enjoy for nearly a thousand hours. I'll be honest and say that only approximately 400 hours of my playtime is in the base game, if that, and the rest of my playtime is with various mods such as Divergences or AD 1648, and I look forward to seeing what the Anbennar team can do with the game.I'm just asking, nay begging, the team to properly play test the updates before they come out. While Paradox is fast at releasing hot-fixes for bugs, it honestly feels a bit like they're leaving in easily noticeable bugs that can quickly be fixed so it looks like they're listening to the community. Either that or the devs are so overworked that they can't give the game the proper polish it deserves during the initial development time, and can only work on bug fixes after the DLC has been released.I'll finish this off with a quick list of pros and cons.Pros:You can develop your economy and laws however you want within the frame that the game gives you. Want a Lassez-Faire economy with a strong public health insurance policy? Sure. Want a Communist Dictatorship with a Peasant Army? Why not. Want to release Jan Mayen and turn an Arctic Island into the best place to live in the world? Go for it.You can play out several alternative history scenarios. This is great if you're one of the lost causers think that the American Civil War was about 'State's Rights' (to own slaves). It's also great if you're one of the people that think that the USA post-Civil War was too lenient on the South and should have instead focused on lifting up the then-freed slaves as equal citizens.It scratches an itch to develop your country and watch your GDP and Standard of Living go up.If you have issues with any part of the game then 9 time out of 10 you'll be able to find a mod that fixes it for you.Cons:There are objectively good ways, or meta ways, to play. There are states that are objectively the best to build certain industries in, and it's worth going for these states in each play through because they're that good. There are starting moves, such as puppeting Mexico as the USA, that set you up so well for the rest of the game that if you don't do them it will take a lot more time and effort to reach the same level. 'But you should just roleplay' - I don't find handicapping myself in games for the sake of 'roleplaying' to be fun. If you choose to actively hinder yourself for the sake of roleplaying, you're probably better off watching a youtuber play the game.The warfare and battles system is a mess, and it will probably keep being a mess until the DLC that addresses warfare is inevitably released.You can't join in or swap sides during the course of a war. To point to Italy as an example in WW1 - they declared neutrality in 1914 when the war first broke out, then joined the war in 1915 almost a year after war started, so there's historical precedence during this time period to let you do the same.There's a steep learning curve for newcomers to the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Lately, apart from HOI4, paradox has been kinda slow, even unpolished with the other 4X titles.I never played Vicky 2, but I had high hopes for this game and kept up with all the dev diaries.The promise of Victoria 3 was a deep economic and diplomatic game with some wars and rp on the side.Sadly, it only partially delivers on the economics front and absolutely blunders on all of the others.It doesn't feel like a 4X game very much and I'd rather compare it to some resource management heavy city builders.And that part is actually very fun and addicting for me, even if it doesn't really accomplish the feeling they were going for."Diplomatic plays" and "non-micromanaged frontlines" in wars have potential but are absolutely terrible currently. Unreasonable amount of rng, unclarity when it comes to mechanics and lack of control even when you do understand what's happening in them.I'm 100% convinced that the choice to give achievement in non-ironman mode was made because they knew the wars are nearly unplayable and it's unreasonable to ask you to go with it.The amount of country/region specific events is laughable, it has to be the worst one from paradox yet.Internal politics is mostly just waiting for 10-20% chance rolls to pass laws.Other reviews mention the upcoming DLCs and fixes but I'm worried that's not coming.Imperator had mixed reception like this, and it's just abandoned now.CK3 was good, but not a money maker like HOI4 is and therefore has gotten 1 real DLC and couple minor ones in 2 years.Sadly, I think Victoria 3 is now about as good as it's going to get.But still.. there just isn't much competition in the genre, and especially with the setting and gimmicks Victoria 3 has, and playing without warring is actually viable.And while others might disagree, I think Vicky 3 has the best looking 3d map so far.All in all, if you like games with "grain number go up - i build mill - pop happiness go up - i build workshop" -type gameplay and are willing to put up with or avoid cancer war mechanics, maybe get it at 50% off.I'll probably keep playing it on and off but for now especially for the price:2/5.

_childDocuments_.review: Buggy. Streotype IGs and no historic research for individual countries. Things can and should sandbox as time goes on, but things go completely off the rails within <4 years. USA shows awful application of a generic template: people are all speedruning banning slavery pre 1840 and there are no consequences when it should cause an early civil war or a crisis of some sort. Generic template means coalition governments in the usa are easy when Jackson literally pioneered the spoils system that currently defines the US political system / cabinent. Andrew Jackson can't get re-elected, gets replaced with Calhoun who Jackson actively fought against in the nullifaction crisis - it should at least be Martin Van Buren or James K Polk. Slavers arent their own IG, so many northern states join the csa if you do try force get a civil war - everyone remembers how mass and ny are even remotely plausible bastions of the csa. Diplomacy is awful - being able to surrender the primary war goal for a truce should still require the other side to accept - if I want to escalate for the whole Mexican Cession, I can't - i can take 1 "state" and then wait an entire truce to take another. Because of the horrible set up, this really means the half of texas is a truce, and the tiny southern mexcian bit of Colorado is an entire truce - i dont even get a whole state.  Europe and Ottomans isn't much better. Egypt taking istanbul, northern greece, or izmir (e.g. Thessaly or Macedonia) instead of anything contiguous. Instead of Kars or the balkans, it goes for some random exclave?France has a bonapartist party, but there is no way to make Napoleon III the emperor.If you don't want it railroaded, there should be optional decisions or events or flavor. You get a frontline with a general and set them to either attack or defend, nothing else. You want to hold the mountainline and let the AI grind against it while cycling your other troops? You cant manage your troops, sort out reinforcements or even cycle them, you have to pray and hope the Ai just holds for you. Well good for you, except you didnt add any wargoals at the beginning (because you didnt think you'd actually win) so have fun getting nothing out of that war. _childDocuments_.review: Having put some hours into the game, I think it’s time to give my input. I want to like the game. Underneath everything there’s the bones of a genuinely unique and potentially enjoyable experience. Improvements have been made, work has clearly been put in, the ideas of interesting and the concept is appealing.But, as it stands, the game is more frustrating than it’s worth. There has always been some degree of save-scumming or restarts to Paradox games, but Victoria 3 seems to have taken it to a completely new level. You can do everything right, and still get screwed over because of unpredictable AI or bug at the wrong time. Your armies unable to find their way to the battlefield for no reason, or your alliances or pacts frequently broken by a sudden change of heart on part of the AI (which you hope you catch from the small box in the corner of your screen containing dozens of messages, as the game neglects to tell you otherwise or even give you an indication of why). The randomisation of some game aspects could be fun, but there’s no real reward to sticking with a less than optimal start as a result. Why struggle with a moderate landlord leader when you know a quick restart could easily land you a jingoist, or even a democrat?  Why struggle trying to build a customs union when you know a quick restart could make all those nations love you, if you act quickly enough.Diplomacy itself, something that should be a cornerstone given the period, is lacklustre. The AI doesn’t seem to follow any real logic, as previously friendly nations suddenly turn hostile in a single diplomatic play or suddenly find you to be threatening despite having no issue a minute or so earlier. Hundreds of thousands frequently die in minor disputes as powers send everything they have to fight over a minor German nation revolt.In short, Victoria 3 suffers from some fairly standard Paradox problems. It is, for all intents and purposes, underdeveloped. It currently lacks that distinct “thing” that makes the struggle worth it, to make you feel like you accomplished something. To say nothing of the late game, as you notice a significant drop off in speed during the last third that makes sticking to any game where you might have accomplished something to be a chore.My advice? Check back after an expansion or two. Victoria 3 still has a long way to go.

_childDocuments_.review: Victoria 3 is the long-awaited sequel to Victoria 2, a 12 year old cult classic. Although it was a buggy, janky, fundamentally broken mess, the economy of Victoria 2 was unique among games. It featured a closed loop economy, where every good bought or pound spent by one entity is a good produced or a pound earned by a different entity. The entire thing operated and changed by itself. You could not control it, only influence it. It had many bugs and design flaws, but it was a truly unique economic system for a videogame. The surrounding systems like diplomacy and war were simple and lazy, in the old Paradox style, but just functional enough.In comes Victoria 3. Looking at it as a sequel to Victoria 2, it disappoints in most ways. The unique economic system is gone, and the economy more closely resembles Anno. Your goal is to grow your economy using your construction sector, and your main activity is fixing the economic impacts of the last thing you did. Supply, demand, and prices change instantly. Nothing in your country happens without your input, and you have absolute control over every production building in your country. Making new buildings and changing how they operate is your primary gameplay loop, making you feel more like a middle manager than a country. While balancing production methods in every backyard moonshine-still is fun once as a small country, it devolves into tedious micromanagement quickly when playing anything larger than Liechtenstein.The only thing that happens without your input is other countries setting up trade routes, but this is mostly just infuriating. Because everything is in short supply and the AI is incompetent at growing their own economy, these trade routes mostly just steal your resources and rarely if ever sell you anything of substance. Protecting particular goods could have been an interesting gameplay mechanic, but it isn’t. You can’t stop a good from being exported. You can only embargo entire countries. So trade boils down to you trying to steal resources you’re short on, the AI doing the same, and you embargoing the AI if it starts stealing too many of yours. Devolving into isolationism becomes an appealing prospect, if only to remove the micromanagement and instability.Speaking of the AI: In typical Paradox fashion, it's terrible. As a result, singleplayer is a bland, sterile experience. You are playing in a sandbox with other kids, but the other kids are just balloons with faces drawn on them. It would be nice to believe that the AI will get better with some patches, but this is unlikely given the reputation of Paradox and Victoria 3’s game director. The AI nations in Victoria 3 are slow to grow, constantly in turmoil due to mismanagement, and regularly destroy themselves over the tiniest diplomatic disputes.Those diplomatic disputes are probably the one aspect where Victoria 3 actually has some interesting innovation. Most hostile interactions are no longer just a button, but executed through a ‘Diplomatic play’ mechanic involving all major powers with an interest in the region. Diplomatic plays are a neat concept, but they are sadly underdeveloped, and let down further by the bad AI. There is no real distinction between a small colonial engagement and major war in Europe. Both become plays potentially involving every country with an interest committing their entire army. It’s impossible to ensure a nation’s neutrality beforehand. If you plan to simply befriend the other powers, or convince them to stay out once it’s started, good luck. Friendly nations will turn on you in a heartbeat during a play, and major AI powers will join a diplomatic play for the most insane reasons. The US will fight to the death to defend Danish Holstein in exchange for an IOU. China will sacrifice millions to keep an Indonesian province out of Dutch hands because they were promised war reparations. The East India Company will happily fight a war against its overlord over some border dispute between Indian nations, before magically returning to being an obedient dominion once the war ends.This entire experience is wrapped up in a UI more hostile to the end-user than a suicide vest. Tooltips can be helpful, but the endless recursion of tooltips on your tooltips on your tooltips, ad infinitum, invokes an Escherian feeling of endlessness that makes you feel more lost than before you started. This wouldn’t be as bad if these tooltips did not contain important information that can’t be found elsewhere. The game will only tell you the most important information at a glance, such as the number of radicals in your country, but make it impossibly difficult to find out exactly who is radical and what caused it.Critics have said the game looks like a mobile game, and while this is unfair to the gameplay, the UI does lean heavily towards modern mobile-friendly UI trends. Lists and tables are frowned upon, while grid layouts are preferred whenever possible. The amount of information allowed on the screen at any one point is extremely limited, forcing you to constantly swap between windows. Multiple lists simply can’t be sorted at all, and no list ever takes up more than a third of your screen width. A full screen table with all the information you could want is anathema. Buttons are large, and the UI scaling is very high by default, unless you have a widescreen monitor, in which case it defaults to unreadably tiny. The game defaults to tree maps instead of pie charts, suggesting that the UI designer had some very strong personal convictions about design without necessarily having the understanding of visual data comprehension to back them up.I have yet to mention the political system, because it hardly matters. Unless you are trying to change a particular law that’s affecting your gameplay, like isolationism, it’s possible to forget it exists entirely. The interest groups controlling your government do nothing to stop you from changing the economy and eroding their power, so the power of interest groups is just a result of what buildings you build rather than an interesting mechanic.Ultimately, the game is an exercise in making a line go up for the sake of the line going up. Every country plays exactly the same, and there is no real payoff at the end. Warfare could theoretically provide something to work towards, but the war system is so barebones, clunky, and dysfunctional that warfare is more frustrating than fun. There is no micromanagement of units, as that system has been replaced with automatic AI fronts, but fronts split, merge, and disappear so much that the micromanagement is somehow just as annoying. Since the fighting happens automatically, wars are heavily affected by arcane mechanics behind the scene that the player can’t see or interact with, such as the number of troops that participate in a battle, or the direction a general advances. The reward for dealing with this system is often lackluster, since wargoals are decided during the diplomatic play phase and cannot be altered during the war.Victoria 3 isn’t a terrible game per se. It is simply mediocre as a game, and bad as a Victoria sequel. If it had been an early-access indie game for 30 euros with a different name, it would have been received very well, with praise for some of its innovative ideas and its potential. As a released full-price sequel to a cult classic developed by a major studio, it is disappointing. The arguments about its potential ring hollow in the context of a studio known for selling buggy, half-baked products that had potential but failed to deliver.If you are looking for a complex economic simulator, this isn’t it. If you are looking for a game focused on diplomacy and war, this also isn’t it. If you are looking for a cute Anno-style economy game that you can play with friends so you can bicker over who ate all the tools in the market, this is actually alright, though buggy and overpriced.

But its way way worse in Vicky 3. In fact, its non existent. This isn't a game about conquest, but war is a reality when it comes to grand strategy. They have completely removed player agency from war and now its just a frustrating game of watching the RNG dice rolls because you can't do anything.This is the ego/ stubbornness issue I was referring to. Paradox fans have been telling the devs to fix this but they refuse because their fragile egos can't accept that they are wrong. 3. They keep adding things no one asked for instead of fixing core issues. Who asked for agitators?? Who asked for local prices?? I am not saying these are bad features but these are things you add later once the core game is fixed. 4. AI is a real concern. AI has never been that good in Paradox games but its especially bad here. AI can't do anything right.5.  Plenty of other things that need fixing. Resource allocation is also very unfair with Asia, Africa, South America getting way less than what they actually have. _childDocuments_.review: Make no mistake I was looking forward to this game. I love the series. I love the genre. But Paradox here done really ♥♥♥♥♥♥ UP. I hope the Devs fix this crap before it ends up like Imperator Rome or March of the eagles.So starting off:-The game crashes. A LOT. Paradox games usually require you to play for a minimum of 2 hours and the game crashes about every hour.-The game is too expensive for the currently implemented features. The only meaningful features of the game are economy and trading. I'll get to the features later.-MANY features that we have come to enjoy from grand strategy series such as a diplomacy and warfare are COMPLETELY shoved into the trash can and pushed over to the zoo corner with the abacus monkeys to develop.-Diplomacy. Gone are the spheres of influence, most nations won't accept your proposals because the "base reluctance" is MINUS 100 which is ridiculous even for a trade agreement! Heck, sometimes allies won't even join your wars, obligations mean nothing in this game and what's worse the subject nation management is atrocious, yeah I'm talking to you all EU4 players that love subject interactions, there's none here for you.-Warfare. Warfare is completely automated and bought over by Elon Musk and sent to Mars. Litteraly can't even phrase this any better. The generals are 90% of the time retarded and get encircled, admirals never seem to be able to naval invade for players and are also unable to protect YOU from naval invasions, but hey bro, we need 100 ironclads so better pay up. By far warfare is the most guttered aspect of this game. No occupation laws, no micromanagement, just giving the AI guns to fight your wars which is the dumbest idea ever.-Economy. Economy management is probably one of the better aspects of the game, allowing you to tax different goods in order to control prices, as well as enact economic reforms through the politics menu for pensions etc. Overall good work here.-Trading. Trading is mediocre at best. The AI buys off most of your stock so you end up with an order book of MINUS two THOUSAND of cloth so prices get insanely high. Build more clothes factories..? Nope. Russian AI will buy off ALL of your clothes anyway! And what the hell is up with this bug where I get notifications that my ports need extra convoys for trade routes while having over two thousand convoys available? Seriously. Did nobody backtest this before release?-Politics. Politics is probably the last part this game shines, allowing you to interact with different classes within your country, enacting religious and discrimination laws as well as pensions with different buffs or debuffs, overall good work here, would have been much nicer if you could change primary culture or religion like EU4.-Population mechanic. Don't even get me started on this one. People within your market will flock to whichever province you have available jobs for, I'm speaking to you. Yue culture in Wales. Yeah you. And don't get me started on how it's impossible to assimilate people from their homelands completely, I get it, you don't want cultures to go extict, then add a debuff for assimilation, don't disable it completely Jeez...-Conclusion. Essentially this game offers nothing to expand or improve upon other titles, it doesn't offer the combat of HOI4, it doesn't include the diplomacy of EU4, and it barely simulates the economy of the previous Victoria title. Paradox has only itself to compete here on this genre of games and they know it by pushing out unfinished games one after another. I really loved you Paradox. I used to play your games since I was 12. I was really amazed on how you were the only ones who could feed me this niche gaming experience I was longing for. And now you're starting to become just another company that cuts corners in order to generate more profit. I remember the loading screens "This game is dedicated to our fans". You used to have passion for your games, and you've disappointed us all.
