_childDocuments_.review: In 2020, I promised my good friend I would play this game from start to finish with him when it came out.This game in its current state, if you attempt to play from 1836 to 1936, is literally completely unplayable. I have played games as most of the major nations (Prussia/North Germany/Germany, Russia, United States, Ottoman Empire) as well as some minor states (Chile, Cape Colony, Egypt, Persia, Belgium, Sweden/Scandinavia) to get a detailed look.The game feels more like an engine than an actual game. I think it has a lot of promise and could be a good or great game in like 5 years much like how eu4 was terrible in 2013, but I started playing in 2018 and so never had to deal with it. This game right now is terrible. Paradox shipping this product out is a war crime. The multiplayer experience is especially bad. I played several multiplayer games that ultimatley culminated with a full runthrough from 1836-1917 with myself as Egypt and my friend as Persia. The game started out fine and even fun and challenging, but by the mid game was starting to show signs of how unpolished the game was, and by 1900 was becoming increasingly unplayable until reality itself no longer made sense and the game was running so slow, made so little sense and was so boring and stupid that we were forced to stop in 1917 despite wanting to continue.We were playing casually and were not attempting to break the game at all. Additionally, we haven't been playing for a thousand hours, only since the game came out, which isn't very long.Some things went wrong such as -The American Civil War makes zero sense and is often never resolved (this happens in most games)-You can build multiple suez canals, panama canals, skyscrapers (I built 30 suez canals and became #1 great power solely off the prestige, and built 50 skyscrapers to absolutely destroy trade) we found this out by accident, the AI also built 20 skyscrapers-the AI is so awful it should just be called A (other reviews explain this)-Kathiri (random arab state) had 67 standard of living for like ten years-I puppeted france, the UK and the ottoman empire and they all just backed down-infamy is literally a non-issue-countries randomly declaring bankruptcy because the "A" cannot properly manage an economy-britian deletes their entire army, navy and ports (???)-the CANADIAN BORDER OH MY GOD-colonization conflict events triggering continuously causing -10 prestige hits over and over again and you can't stop it-markets become impossible to control late game (and it's not fun either)-the war system is so garbage it makes no sense and you have no control over it (again other reviews explain this better but it feels like a mostly random system in any battle where your forces are comparable that you can only barely influence and its extremly shallow, it is genuinely the worst system i have ever seen, i hate front lines) -THERE IS NO UNEMPLOYMENT MAP MODE WHY (this causes the game to become a tedious nightmare (much like vic 2))-everything is hidden behind stupid tooltipsoverall this game is absolutely atrocious, but I still had fun mostly because the concept is so interesting, the barebones are there and it could be a good system and it was funny to destroy the world like an ISP video, but i do not find it enjoyable and it is certainly not historical.if you want to play, just buy it, play it, hate it and come back in 5 years.if you know how to play vic 2, just play vic 2. at least vic 3 is relativley easy to learn compared to other paradox games (partly because its so shallow and is more like a game engine than a playable, shippable product)otherwise i'll just stick to eu4.at least the dynamic flags are cool.
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: They did it. They actually did it.For almost a decade, we wanted the dream of Victoria: a comprehensive economic, political, and sociological simulator of the century of expansionist capitalism. Bugs aside, this *works*. I played a game as Cuba, under the wing of Spain's market. I grew a massive industrial base, importing raw materials and transforming them into luxury goods and engineering wonders. I grew rich. I declared my independence and won a war against Spain. Then I realized: no Spanish market, no raw materials. My GDP and standard of living plummeted as I scrambled to invade third world countries for their cheap inputs. This is How Economics Works (I mean, in a simplified way). It's a wonder to watch a game simulate the needs of billions of people at scale. It's light on historical content, which is a bummer. But the mechanics are there. Bugs will be ironed out. The UI will be cleaned up.They actually did it.
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: This game is good. It's not wonderful, but it's also not bad.While a lot of the hate at launch about some of the mechanics had some backing, now it's irrelevant.The economy is a lot of fun. The resources are plentiful, but still need extraction, so there is actually competition for that. In addition, resources like dye and rubber can be hard to come by and incentivize colonization and conflict. I wish there was a way to push for investors to build certain buildings, but despite that, the economy is easily the best part of the game.The political system could use some work. While I like the way the interest groups are done, they need to be more dynamic and change with the times. In addition, while the policies available are decent, having more variety for some of them could be fun. However, I understand how difficult it is to add dynamic features in these sorts of games.The last big part in Vic 3 is diplomacy. This just needs more. The stuff already included is good and is implemented well, but there needs to be more options. The Power Blocs helped a bit with this, but I shouldn't be having to fight off dozens of my subject's revolts in a single year, especially since being at war stops you from starting other diplomatic plays. In addition, the navy could use a rework. The AI will just send out tiny groups of ships to disrupt so much of your trade, and they are able to just run away from my bigger stack of ships way too easily. The actually army stuff is actually nice, as the improvements since launch have made the AI controlling the armies smarter.Overall, I'd give this game a low 8, and it could easily be a 9 in another year if the devs keep up this pace of work
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: The game feels designed to be played in a very specific way, for a specific experience, with set parameters. For some, this is enough. For most, especially fans of true sandbox and what Vic2 and older paradox games were, this is not enough. The game has guide rails everywhere, limitations, and pre-set settings to ensure you don't stray too far from an "intended" experience. So sad, so unlike what a simulator is. This isn't a simulation, it's an arcade. I gave it a 50 hour play-through so far, and that's the best I can come up with; an Arcade gaming experience from this. Update to Review: The game is still feeling like a busy-work arcade simulator. However, it's nice to see they're still trying to work on it. It would have been nice to have "sold" a finished product to begin with...I'm also still waiting on a true Vic3. That's a personal note only.
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: Victoria III lacks lots of features Victoria II had. The military part requires absolutely no strategic skill. There are no political crisis, seccessions or there like - the Ottoman and Austrian Empires just continue to exist without any problems. Therefore, if you've played three games, you've basically seen it all.
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: Is this it? Won a 1v1 independence war as Moldova against the Ottomans plus war reparations plus Dobrogea by clicking 3 buttons and waiting. I'll do yet more waiting for 5 DLC. Constant crashes, corrupted save files, broken civil wars, broken AI production, broken USA both manifest destiny and civil war, annoying diplomacy mechanics (Want to press all your claims? Too bad if your opponent is afraid of you and they give up Mexican Utah; now you have to wait on a 5 year truce you can't break, then rinse and repeat). Can't build in your subjects. Can't do foreign investments. Whole economy loop consists of switching between three menus to check what's needed (because multiple windows on a desktop application is so 1995), then waiting, then rinse and repeat. Armies teleport across the world by themselves, then take 2 months to get back where you want them to just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ sit. Absolutely no flavour to the countries and everyone plays the same. African countries are on par or more prosperous and educated than some European ones. Speed of technology development is ridiculous across the board. Politics railroads you into this 2022 multiculti progressive utopia with no downsides whether you're playing Vietnam or Switzerland. Elections are meaningless. Pop cultures are empty shells that are there just for additional pie charts and marketing. Performance ♥♥♥♥♥ the bed after 1900 on a high end machine. No supply lines, decisive battles, encirclements. I've never seen a battle (which takes weeks) go over 10'000 casualties, even with machine guns and mustard gas against 70 battalions of pitchforks. War exhaustion is nonsensical (I can just sit there on an island, with no mobilized troops, no convoys sunk, no casualties whatsoever, no nothing changed, and I can still get shafted). Assigning a general to an expedition can put 100 battalions out of service for years. More repetitive memey events meant to end up on reddit as "isn't this game so funny le lol XD" than meaningful ones. It looks nice and has some unique mechanics I guess. I put an additional 65 hours after my initial negative review like a battered wife after waiting for so many years. It's a massive disappointment riding on pure marketing and the expectation of DLC and free labour from mods. ♥♥♥♥ this.
_childDocuments_.name: Victoria 3

_childDocuments_.review: Haven't played in a couple months...decided it was a long enough break for the many issues in this game to be fixed and as I enter my first war as america I cannot assign any army to a front as it says "no path available"....even though our lands/states are right next to each others in the continental US. Needless to say it is still a trash game

name: Ancestors: The Humankind Odyssey
detailed_description: Ancestors: The Humankind Odyssey is a third-person open world survival game where you Explore, Expand, and Evolve to advance your clan to the next generation in this exhilarating new adventure from Panache Digital Games. Embark on the most incredible odyssey known to humankind: human evolution. Spanning from 10 million to 2 million years ago, begin your journey, before us, in Neogene period Africa. Explore a beautiful yet ruthless world, from swinging through tree branches in the jungle to stalking prey across the golden savannah grasslands. Decide what attributes to learn and hone in order to pass down knowledge to future generations, from crafting tools to enhancing evasive tactics against predators. Just like real life, make sure to eat, drink, and sleep to stay alive and have the energy to face any danger that may come your way. Grow your clan and find strength in numbers as you progress through critical evolutionary stages of human evolution. Your choices will write your clan’s story and determine if you can survive your evolution. Explore Ruthless Africa Explore the never-before-experienced world of Neogene Africa starting 10 million years ago at the dawn of humankind. From the tops of tree canopies overlooking lush jungles to the golden grasslands of the savannah, traverse a beautiful yet unforgiving landscape. For every breath-taking view, beware of the weather, predators, and other dangers that threaten your survival. Expand Your Territory and Grow Your Clan Increase your chances of survival by uniting new members of your species and giving birth to future generations. Control different clan members, form bonds to create families, and work together to intimidate predators during expeditions. Conquer fear as you explore unknown locations in order to expand your territory. Evolve Through Multiple Generations See the physical and intellectual evolution of the first hominids as you explore, learn, and survive. Spanning from 10 million to 2 million years ago, play as one of the first hominids and evolve over the course of millions of years during key stages in human evolution. Make crucial discoveries and hone physical abilities that will be passed down to future generations such as Ardipithecus ramidus and Australopithecus. Choose How You Survive Evolution was not written in stone. Your decisions shape how you will overcome obstacles, increase your species, and what knowledge will pass on to future generations. Focus on specific attributes or choose a more balanced approach to survival. Your clan’s ability to survive will be directly impacted by your choices, making each player’s experience unique.

_childDocuments_.review: This game isn't bad and tells a compelling story about the evolution of humankind. It focuses around learning how to use your environment and managing your tribe, which is a decent aspect of the game that forces the player to care about the members of your family. That being said, it would be easier to manage with real people to play with. An open-world game that has you collaborate with others of your kind should have a multiplayer feature, since humans are in fact social beings. This would allow for players to discover the game and its many hidden mechanics together rather than alone with a bunch of lowkey useless AIs. But, overall a good game. Would recommend to anyone who prefers a singleplayer open-world survival experience

I had to learn the controls by just pressing random buttons on my keyboard and searching google (which wasn't at all help full) But other than the fact that I can barely play the game I'd say its pretty good. Wouldn't recommend for pc users though

_childDocuments_.review: Fun little open-world survival game. I went in blind and only searched up things when I was utterly stumped once or twice, which was quite fun. But it was a bit hard in some cases, especially with the QTEs I really didn't get how to do the various versions for a long time, and my poor apes got hurt so often, lol. The in-game guides are hazy at best, but I suppose that was part of the difficulty "figure it out naturally" vibe the developers were going for. The gameplay loop became a little rote and boring by the second to last/last evolution because I had explored everything, so I was mostly just grinding out neurons just to change generations and evolve. One gripe I had used the Intelligence search so much that Scent (food was too plentiful to need to search this way) and Hearing (with a good eye and ear, it's easy to spot predators from far away) became almost useless, but that may be because I played on the easiest difficulty. A little sad that it ends so abruptly instead of letting me play infinitely as the last evolution (instead re-loading me to before I evolved), but it's understandable. Overall, a good 4/5 stars from me. Got 50+ hours out of me and I regret nothingmonke
_childDocuments_.name: Ancestors: The Humankind Odyssey

_childDocuments_.review: I really really wanted to like this game, and I kind of do. Unfortunately it feels unfinished with limited a core gameplay loop, clunky mechanics, and a desire to hide all this behind an unforgiving, and unrewarding, progression system. Ancestors looks great and exploring the primitive jungle and the other various environments is definitely one of its strongest features. Swinging through the canopy and leaping across ravines as an angry ape with a sharp stick is one of the main reasons why I was interested in this game and oh boy does it deliver in this regard. The controls are a bit lack luster, especially if you happen to be using a mouse and keyboard, I frequently found myself jumping in the wrong direction or not at all resulting in a missed grab and a whole days delay as I patched up my hominid. However I still found the movement system to be fairly robust and one of the games stronger features.My main issue with this game is the lack of diversity in progression. Generally speaking you have to perform specific actions a certain number of times to strengthen the neuronal connections before spending neural energy to unlock the next locus. This presents a fairly significant grind, especially when your neurons are reset between generations or evolutions but is especially tedious when you consider the limited mechanics presented in your options. Every bit of crafting, called “altering”, in the game is composed of holding the correct two items in your hands and holing down a button until you receive a prompt. There are a few interesting options but this system is creatively limited by the sheer lack of recipes in the game. Most recipes are strictly linear. There is one type of of wood in the game, a dead branch, which can be turned into a stick and then sharpened. That’s it. The deepest recipe in the game with the exception of opening a coconut. This contributes to a general lack of progression. Within a half hour you can sharpen a stick and have the best “weapon” in the game no matter your current evolution. Access to food and other resources is similarly shallow. You might need a simple tool like a stem to get honey or termites but other than that there isn't much in the way of innovation or creativity here. The game tries very hard to hide this behind obfuscated mechanics and no instruction or tutorial but as a result the game just feels even more shallow. There just aren’t that many options for interaction so trying in vain to find what specific set of objects in which hand will result in the desired outcome just ends up undercutting whatever sense of achievement or discovery the devs were going for. Additionally clunky fear and path-finding mechanics mean trying to organize an expedition with a troop of your fellow hominids is more an exercise in frustration than cooperation.The concept is definitely here and they have strong bones to make an interesting and comprehensive game, but this isn't early access so what we have is what we get and unfortunately it just isn't worth the money. If you have a thing for beautiful handcrafted environments and vertical game play then you can definitely get some mileage out of this but if you are looking for a genuine survival experience you’d be better served somewhere else.

_childDocuments_.review: [1h]Starting out[/h1]So this will be a guide, and as you can figure out, it will be some what of a spoiler, so you are forewarned!Starting out can be confusing. The first thing you'd want to do is increase your motor skills, which can be done by picking up various items and examining them, which also levels up your sense. The starting point will be different for different people, specifically me, I was attacked by a large tiger-ancestor, and due to me waiting for the load, I was not able to do the dodge rolls.Surviving through sleeping, eating, and drinking water all allow for you to build up your neural pathways, because it refines your abilities. Among basic needs, you also may need to stay warm, and no wet. Its pretty easy, our ancestors have fur unlike us, which protects them from the mild cases, however if you become severely cold kath, a medicinal plant found in the world, allows for upkeep in warmth, and some for protection against getting wounded, it does not cure being wounded!From fall, to getting hit. Wounds happen, to cure them fairly annoying and easy. First, you lose health from your wounds, so its suggested not to wait on it, or switch to a clanmate who isn't wounded, and get the medicine through them. Its best to climb to a high place so you can search through the trees, and you'll find fibers in the trees, which your ancestors use to bind up their wounds. You should carry them to your home for your hurt clansmate to seal their wound, and hell it could help in the future, so stock up! The game is something of a survival rpg, in my opinion. You level your individuals by most successfully carrying your baby generation as you complete various tasks. You pick up an item, and sniff it, baby gives you neurons to use for leveling. You eat, drink, or scream at your family, your little chimping baby cradled against you has learned something, and grants you more leveling essence. Now when you finally do get this neuron capacity to level up a certain task, you find a sleeping spot, which you can make, unless your starting point already has one set up. The level screen is called evolution. In this screen you can choose to level, go to the next generation, or the whole damn species ladder. The more individual level is what we want to start with. Leveling the motor skills will allow for the most success.This is largely the backbone of the game, which you can actually use a bone as a weapon. I killed my first warthog ancestor and started using its tusk to bash other animals' heads in. It is exciting! Though we need to start at the beginning, which until you level your motor skill, you wont be able to do. Your most easiest to craft item is sharpened sticks, rocks broken down to make certain tools, beds, walls, and messing with coconuts when you find em. : First you must locate these gathering locations, go in and open your intelligence sensory. You'll focus on a dead tree, which tells you a quick tooltip about the focus. You then approach that focus, and analyze it. This begins the crafting process. You can now pluck dead tree sticks off of a dead tree. from there when you activate the motor function, switch the stick to the other hand and can start interaction with it. I find it easiest to strip the stick without a rock, but you can strip dead sticks with rocks and your bare hand. After that you gain a regular stick. This point you need a rock, which will sharpen the stick. You can choose this as a weapon, gathering tool, and the such.Rocks are useful, especially the basalt. They all have their own practicality. Basalt, changes how quickly you sharpen a stick or item. Granite Grinders allow for medicinal items to be made. The rocks can also be used to defend yourself.So the construction system is truly lackluster. You may become disappointed quite easily late game when you want to have some mighty fortress of sticks, or something. Anyhow, Its pretty simple to make a construction. You place enough of the same item into a stack, and when you place enough the construct tooltip comes up for available options. Now, if I remember right, the original amounts for these constructions are as followed:  = 4 Cycads bushes  = 4 dead tree stick, that has not been turned into a regular stick. So when you make a decent bed and area you want to live at, you will have the option to make that area your settlement. Take your clan to the new settlement by using the unlocked communication neuron, and then to get them to stop following you, end the exploration, which is found at the sleeping spot you newly made. This will make your clan settle at the new location.So you made a settlement and find it boring to see your clan standing around. Well, time to introduce the bonding system, real easy to grasp, no motor skill needed. You begin by grooming a chosen member of the opposite sex, and after that you become bonded to that clanmate. You can groom others of the same sex, but it doesn't really offer much towards the grand scheme of things. I guess you make a friend from it. When you obtain your mate, go back to your sleeping spot and do the action to call for your mate, and pregnant them, or become pregnant. Then after a cut scene you will have a giving birth option with no respectable time span. You can choose to immediately give birth, the time frame will skip the months ahead, and time passes as well. After sometime the scenes become repetitive. I would recommend skipping them, or watch em if you really enjoy the whole scenery. I got tired of the cut scenes of the discoveries of new areas.So I mentioned new areas, so lets hit up that beckon of joy. You of course have the starting area. Though you can expand past that, of course. These areas function as their own ecosystem. There will be birds, snakes, hogs, felines, and the such trying to kill you! So be ready for that when you come across a new place. Each of these places give you the action to face your fear, which is what happens when you turn and scream at the evil trying to stalk and kill you. Facing your fear expands your home space, which allows you to make the settlements.So after two days of dodging and get mad. I didn't understand how the combat worked at all. I had to actually watch a video on it. You can choose to avoid, dodge, or counter attack your predators. Boy once you get it down though, its fun as hell beat the creatures that made you so annoyed. I chased down a huge snake till my man knock the brains out. In the beginning though, what can you do against any of those things, avoiding. Its a powerful strategy. You can actually make these creatures fight themselves! I led a panther into a snake, and watched the thing kill it in two strokes. Made me feel like a giddy ol' master mind. So you're probably wondering, how do I counter attack and dodge. Real easy, depending on your gaming set up. The computer has visual and a musical que on when you do your action. So when a predator tries to attack you, you have about two seconds to react. You hold down the action button, and then choose which way you want to react. Depending on where you react towards, you will dodge, or counter attack. If you react any way, but towards the attacking party you dodge. When you react towards your predator, you counter attack. To put this into perspective though, I have a software that slows my game down to half-time, and I perfectly hit the que for the counter attack priming visual and musical que. I still became wounded. Its chance related, which can be in your favor the more you develop it, in the neural pathing leveling system.That is all I can think of right now, but if I can find anything else I'll be sure to add it.

Though the gameplay is limited and repetitive because evolving means repeating for generations but if you understand the mechanic of the game it's not really hard. You can even get 100% achievements in one playthrough (there're only 13 of them).Combat system is really easy and doesn't has much flavors but has several approaches. _childDocuments_.review: This game is great for people that have the patience to die and grind before getting good. The concept is great as well as the execution, people just fail to understand that because they get mad when they die and think that  grinding is too boring, but thats what the game was made to be like, so don't complain and say, "there's too much grinding", if you think so, just don't get the game. And dying is a part that is your fault, you can just stay in your settlement and have fun there if you want, You do not have to explore and try to evolve, it can be more fun, but it can be dangerous and frustrating. So a short version of that rant is, if you aren't patient and don't like grinding, don't get the game, but if you can get through that it is one of the best games ever in my opinion. Sorry about that huge rant about chimp game.

_childDocuments_.review: The behavior that you exhibited was ape-like, the ape jumped out.This game unlocks the primitive little goblin instincts from the deep recesses of your brain in the most pleasant of ways. Some of the monkey moments I've had so far, in order:- Accidental lesbianism. Ended up losing most of my clan and was trying to repopulate, couldn't get my mate pregnant. Finally paused and saw on the menu that the ape I was controlling was also female. Love that for them.- Said "Oh my god, did you steal my stick?" aloud at a fellow clan member, genuinely felt rising anger, then found my stick on the ground nearby. Realised I needed to take a break.- Spent a lot of time collecting rocks and putting them in piles.- The rush of power once you successfully start countering predators and shedding serious blood is The Human ExperienceTo those who think the games mechanics ruin it or get in the way, I'd simply say... it's okay to not like a game. I think this kind of gameplay and control scheme tickles a very specific part of the brain that some people adore and some people don't get at all. I think that the controls (using a PS4 controller) are perfect for the intention. Once you learn it, it's second nature. That's why you can turn the interface off. Imo, if it still feels janky you haven't learnt it. I'd also like to say that a game not rewarding you for playing your own way is not the same thing as a game punishing you for doing so. There is definitely a chain of events the game wants you to follow, but you can do your own thing. Take your time. Get attached to your hominid (and hurt about it later), explore, fail, start over. You can have fun and not make progress, and not making progress isn't a game having a vendetta out against your playstyle. ((((But rushing / misunderstanding game mechanics is not a playstyle.))))ps. My first playthrough of this game was not on Steam, but it sure wasn't on Epic either. Glad to have somewhere to finally support the game. Down with this new trend of games being paid off and held for ransom, I have enough game launchers on my PC.
_childDocuments_.name: Ancestors: The Humankind Odyssey

_childDocuments_.review: I tried...I just don't see the appeal or the fun in this game. It's just tedious and boring. And I wanted to like it. I thought the idea of progressing a pre-human "civilization" through time might be fun. And it could be if the game either had a tangible narrative or wouldn't be so obtuse with its gameplay elements. As it stands I'm simply too dumb to even find my way back to my settlement. One would think that even these apes were able to communicate with one another (as the game even states), so why is it that there's not a single of my clan mates answering my calls? The recognize and memorize feature is also extremely user unfriendly. Let's not even speak of combat (or dodging at least). The rest of my complaints could only come from reviews I've read and watched, so they're not valid here, as they're not my personal story.But damn...when you make a game...you should make it fun, no matter the subject. Europa Universalis, Crusader Kings or Mudrunner or Euro Truck Sim are great examples of games that are "different" without an actual narrative, but still fun. This game, however, just throws you right into the mix and expects you to..."do" stuff. Even Dark Souls has a better tutorial. It feels overwhelming and, frankly, just boring. Sorry.

_childDocuments_.review: Ancestors: The Humankind Odyssey is a game about 10 million years evolution of humans where you'd start with discovering basic interactions and exploration. It's an interesting and unique concept with lots of cool features and ideas. Then you'd be able to kill a sabertooth tiger with a stick and chop him with a meteorite stone at some point. Cool stuff. It's a great game if you're into crafting/survival and trial and error gameplay doesn't scare you. However, there's 2 major gameplay issues that could be more or less obvious depending on your playstyle and luck. Freedom of what to do and where to go is an illusion here. I had to abandon my 6 hours playthrough because I became  the last monkey in the jungle and new ones didn't spawn (I've checked almost the whole map). This was reported a year ago (one year beta-test wasn't enough) as I've checked forums and many people had this issue but it happened. When I encountered the same problem for a second time then I decided to only follow "the orders" (there's something like a super weird quest order tab but only to some point). So I don't really believe that any playthrough here will be unique.Even if you'd be lucky enough to not end up in a situation when you'd have to abandon your 6 hours save - you'd still experience a lot of annoying/frustrating mechanics with clunky controls. I'm not talking about things that are here for immersion, only about poor adaptation to mouse + keyboard and non-intuitive mechanics. There's nothing challenging in this game. I've never had this feeling during 70 hours in Death Stranding on max difficulty while I was constantly annoyed in Ancestors and wasn't able to get used to some things even after 10 hours in the game. All in all, Ancestors: The Humankind Odyssey is a fun and unique game - I'm mostly enjoying it so far. At the same time this game may heavily disappoint you if you're not ready to google what to do in a certain situation and if you're not ready to follow in-game instructions to a certain point, because as a "sandbox" experience it doesn't work too well while "trial and error" method may end up in a completely lost progression. This is a first game where I had to backup saves and it's definitely not adding up any fun. 8/10 for the game itself and 3/10 for poorly implemented mechanics.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're looking for a conventional game with combat and experience points and a static hero or party, this is not that. Instead, this is a much deeper and more meaningful experience, a journey that spans generations.As your homonid clan learns and evolves, you'll be quite pleased with how even the simplest change in your abilities, such as holding an item in each hand, can dramatically alter the flow of the game and your clan's survival. The rocks you once used to bash in the skulls of snakes can be made into tools for improving food and medicine, or sharpening sticks as weapons. Your advancements in language will allow you to give commands to the whole tribe, allowing you to stockpile resources or treat individual wounds.The game is, by design, not going to hold your hand. It's up to you to learn how to navigate the jungle with all its dangers and resources. You WILL lose clan members, at least a few from falling accidents as you avoid the forest floor jumping between trees. You'll also learn the value of safety in numbers and ingenuity.And after a few discoveries, you'll appreciate what it means to be human, with all of our intelligence and complexity.

_childDocuments_.review: Let's start by saying that Ancestors: The Humankind Odyssey really, really doesn't try to be likeable when you launch it for the first time. As the devs say in the intro, they won't help you much, and it's quite likely that your first few hours of playing are gonna be... tedious. Heck, the tutorial section is absolutely (and probably willingly) confusing, and the controls aren't really easy to understand at first.But the magic of it all is that, in this very case, it all makes absolute sense thematically. You're here to explore, try new things, learn and, ultimately, die after passing on your knowledge to your child. If you manage to get past the initial confusion, you'll find yourself in a weird mix or roguelite/survival/exploration game, where you play as a small tribe of monkeys (or, more precisely, homininians), who are weak, scared of the unknown, and pretty much at the bottom of the food chain.Pretty much everything you do will make your monkeys improve. First by unlocking new neurons (ie. skills) in a pretty huge skill tree. For example, crafting a lot of tools will unlock a neuron to make crafting easier and faster. To activate this neuron, you'll need neuronal energy (ie. XP), which is gathered by carrying children on your back while you do stuff.Long story short: you'll quickly learn ways to make survival a bit easier, and to handle the various threats nature will throw at you. By exploring and just playing the game, you'll unlock evolution feats, which in turns will let you advance time, and replace your monkeys with other (more capable and more recent) subspecies of homoninae. The game, which include various biomes, ends when you make the jump to the Ho-mo (gg Steam for censoring this word...) genus.I personnally enjoyed every bit of Ancestors, which is filled with interesting things to discover and explore, in a trully amazing and beautiful world. And I think the game did a great job of linking its theme and its gameplay. I hope there's a sequel in the work.That being said, the game was sometimes a bit repetitive, as it goes through many gameplay loops that aren't necessarily interesting (but can be automated later on, as you unlock more neurons). For example, you gotta reproduce everytime you jump to a new generation, and that can take up to a few minutes. You gotta craft always the same stuff before you start an expedition, etc. You gotta feed your monkeys because they sometimes won't do it by themselves...I also think the difficulty balance was a bit odd. The game can be quite daunting early on, but the difficulty quickly drops. It's part of the theme, I know, but the fact that you can learn how to craft the best weapon really early on doesn't help. Once you've found it, you immediately find yourself at the top of the food chain and only ever get really threatened when you overextend or play recklessly.

_childDocuments_.review: I review most games based on one criterion in particular and the rest is secondary.  That criterion is control.  This game fails in this aspect, ruining access to any and all cool parts that might be beyond.  You play as an ape, at least to start.  Have you ever seen an ape move through familiar territory?  They are parkour masters.  They move from swinging on a branch to hopping across a log to another branch like living water.  Animals are extremely kinesthetic.  The apes in this move like uncomfortable people in gorilla suits.  They fly past obvious holds and plummet to the forest floor, somehow surviving anyway.  I suspect the devs looked at the cost and effort of making a good control/movement system and said, 'Nah, just turn down fall damage.'  The quicktime events are just as dumb in this as they are in everything else (excluding rhythm games) so I won't get into how pointless and lazy they are.When the controls are this bad it ruins the experience of anything else the game might have to offer, so unless you particularly enjoy the sensation of hitting buttons and just hoping it goes well, find something else to play.  Even if you do enjoy that, there are better games, really.

_childDocuments_.review: I was waiting so long for this to be released on PC and it is finally here. Where do I start?Positives:This game is truly a good game, it's hard but really fun and you can just immerse yourself in the dangerous world our ancestors lived in and truly feel to some extent the harshness and dangers of what it was like. You start off as prey and work your way to the top being the apex predator just like our ancestors. You discover new technologies, mutations, neurological improvements along the way until your walking upright and dominating the landscapes of Africa. The game doesn't give you much guidance which truly immerses you in the mind of a developing Hominid; if you do however get stuck you can always refer to trusty old google unlike our Hominid ancestors. The graphics are nice and the landscapes are beautiful with varying biomes, terrains with benefits/negatives for each one. The game takes a lot of time to finish and complete all the achievements, I spent about 60 hrs for my playthrough and you really feel a sense of accomplishment on finishing each one. I truly hope they make a 2nd game exploring into the next stages of our evolution. It does truly well to make sure the game is very factually correct to the best it can and makes a lot of effort in making it realistic to that period of time.Negatives:To delve into the negatives this game, which it has unfortunately, I'd start off by saying some of the mechanics for fighting and dodging are a bit confusing at first and it took me a while to figure it out even with a guide. That may be my own incompetence though. Since it doesn't give you much guidance you could also consider it a negative if you're one of those people who requires babysitting throughout an entire game. Something that bothered me to some extent was that a lot of the tools, medicine, weapons and food are all very repetitive and a bit lackluster once you discover everything, it just gets repetitive seeing the same gathering spots for various objects and when you do find something new it is basically the same. The food variation is also kinda pointless as most food doesn't really give any outlying benefit to other food other than maybe quenching your hunger better, would've been cool to see meat give benefits to your brain power like it was in our development or fruits which quench thirst. The game does run on a kinda linear system and I'm not sure how much re-playability there is for it as of yet since every playthrough from now on will be about the same just way easier.However to end on a good note, I really hope they continue this saga and continue the humankind odyssey all the way to our recent ancestors. Thanks to all the guys at the development team, this was a great break from the world into our past!

_childDocuments_.review: Play the game... and find out the real monkey is YOU!A good game is not defined by graphics, sound, innovation or even story. What makes a game great, is how it makes you feel. The immersion. When the game becomes you, when you become part of the game.This game does exactly that.You start out as a confused monkey, who barely knows how to move around or how to grab something. By trying over and over again, experimenting with different materials and styles, you learn. And just like the in-game monkey learns, you the player learn. You learn how to quickly find a weapon, be it a stick, a rock, or a bone. You learn to always carry a weapon. You learn to eat & drink in time, when & where to sleep safely. You learn to identify a coconut tree, whose fruits can satisfy both thirst and hunger and can heal an upset stomach. You start wielding power over not just one ape, but an entire clan. The secrets of generation switching or an entire evolution unfold. That feeling when you can make what once was mystery then work for you in the way you want it - that is the feeling a video game should give you. And ancestors does.The game does a great job not holding your hand too much, and letting you explore, discover and learn, while still avoiding you get stuck or bored. It's forgiving enough to allow mistakes, while being brutal enough to keep you on your toes and let you realise that the danger is real. One killed monkey does not mean the end, but when you're at your last monkey, you'll quickly learn to sleep in trees or use your sense of smell and hearing before jumping into the unknown - which will turn out to be a crocodile. As you get further in the game, the threats get more varied, but you'll also conquer more. The feeling when that panther who's been stalking and killing your clan for ages finally ends up dead on the ground after a brutal battle - that's amazing. That is why we play. And that is why you should play this game! And offcourse, your monkey will not just kill the panther. It'll also bang its fists on the dead head of the fallen foe, go totally bananas in the victory rush as all clan members join in the wild screaming and chanting... and then you find a rock, buther the corpse, and eat the meat. Woops, not carnivorous yet? No worries, your upset stomach now means your offspring will be... one day.Does the game have downsides? Off course. It's a game about evolution, so you'll spend quite some time managing your traits and passing generations. And that means ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ other monkeys. A lot of them. And everybody knows: doing the same thing too often can feel repetitive - even ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Oh well. You learn a quickie is good enough to generate a baby monkey and you'll be enjoying the new traits fast enough to reap the benefits. After a while, you unlock a trait that auto-couples and auto-reproduces, and the grind lessens. Soon, you will dominate the world.

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, yes, I absolutely recommend this game. It's hard to put into words what this game actually is, but it's really nothing like other conventional games out there. I guess I'll just address some of the possible negatives about the game.1: The first obvious thing is the tutorial. The game tells you what you need to do, but not how to do it. I actually really like this. In this game, you are NOT a human. You don't know what is what in this world, and you are learning at the same pace as your tribe. I recommend you go in completely blind, and learn slowly what "hit rock with other rock do," but if you don't I understand. :P2: The game is pretty repetitive. Unfortunately, for the game the devs were going for, that was kind of unavoidable. The gameplay loop revolves around learning a new skill, and maybe you can pass it on the the babies in your clan, or you will have to relearn the skill. There are 3 stages, the first is your personal skills, the second is next generations skills, which allows you to make some skills permanent, and the third evolves your species as a whole.3: Controls for me are kinda weird, using a controller like the game recommends works pretty well, but some things can be mapped weird, for example, the button for run (Hold A) is the same for jump (Release A while moving). So you have to release the A button while moving to jump, this can make climbing high up dangerous as you can easily fall to your death.4: Some of the "Quicktime" events are hard to understand. They all have an audio cue and a visual effect, but I've notice that the visual effect is less important than the audio clues. For a while I could not figure out how to counter attack, even though the tip for it was that same as the dodge's tip. Turns out you have to wait for that audio cue, and then you can attack.Overall the game is great, and these issues are very minor. The exploration is fun, and making connecting neurons is my heroin at this point.TL;DR- Kinda grindy/repetitive. Overall great. 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: A great concept. The game is immersive, and there is much to discover. There is a real sense of accomplishment and progress when you get your specie to evolve. Group behaviour improves in interesting ways, and automation through immitation works more or less. Movement is fluid. Play this if you like to explore a well crafted world and discover how you can interact with it. You will need to be curious, and be prepared to miss some important elements of the game at first as it gives very minimal instructions.The goal of the game is to advance through time to evolve, and this happens by doing feats, like discovering new places, doging attacks and many other things. Every time you validate your progress, the game makes you start fresh with a new clan, that inherits your previous clan neurons and mutations. You are also expected to reproduce, and pass one or two generations per clan to "lock" newly acquired skills.As this is a "humanity ancestors simulator", there is some repetitive actions to do, like drink, eat, sleep, make tools, reproduce (maybe the most repetitive and less interesting action), prepare camps, and so on. There are evolutions that reduce how much time it takes, but it won't go away. I actually find it not that taxing on the game time, while creating enough pressure so that you have to organize your expeditions a bit. As long as you actally . Indeed, I lost a lot of time grinding on my 5-7 first hours because of this. This time could have been reduced a lot, and my enjoyment multiplied if I followed instructions. But I am not this kind of Hominid, it would seem.I would advise to play with the UI on at first, and maybe de-activate it later, to learn the many contextual actions and the idea behind the control scheme.  and read carefully, so you can enjoy really playing with each generation, and advance at a good pace.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is incredibly immersive. It has very good survival mechanics, which are not too complicated but still require your attention and time. There's hunger, thirst, sanity and rest/sleep. Time is also a thing in this game, the days are long but they don't last forever, and you don't want to be caught by night in the middle of your adventure. There's always threat waiting for you, and although fighting is very simplified, this game's immersion gives you real, unpleasant feeling of danger when you leave your enclave. Jumping from one tree to another feels very joyful and when you get the hang of it you can move through the forest really fast. On the bad part controls can feel clumsy and it's not possible to customize gampead controls so you have to get used to it. I have not seen the endgame yet, but overall it's a very good game, I gladly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: I honestly don't understand why this game doesn't have more positive reviews. Sure it has some minor bugs and some things that could have been implemented better like the mimic function but the game is solid. Also this game is mostly a survival game so if you have certain expectations then you may be disappointed. I would say that most of the time it's a very relaxing game except when it's not. You get attacked by a predator and it's literally a run for your life. Also you don't get to attack directly, it's always a counterattack so don't expect going hunting with your tribe buddies, you can however have them defend themselves.Beautiful scenery, a huge map and rewarding gameplay as long as you don't go straight to Google to ask where to go or how to achieve something. The game rewards you for trying things and exploring, looking stuff up on the internet will definitely spoil the game. The world is big and beautiful making exploring and finding new locations and landmarks a lot of fun. The exploration is not only limited to the map but you also have to explore new ways of finding food, healing/curing yourself, making tools, surviving attacks, etc. even finding new tribe members so there is a lot of experimenting. It may be a little frustrating when you start the game because you have no skills so everything takes what would seem too much time or too many hits to make something, everything you eat makes you sick, etc. but as you acquire new skills it will get better. You can survive at first with the basic stuff and as long as you are curious you should have no problem finding all this other stuff on your own little by little, give the game a chance!The skill upgrade tree is a little tricky at first but you really don't need to pay too much attention to it in the beginning, you will figure out later how to maximize your upgrade points. You start out very weak and slow but you will gain skills that make you move or climb faster or jump further and it will become easier so again give the game a chance!Now for some things I think they could have improved. As I mentioned above, the mimic function. I wish there were less steps in between ordering your followers to mimic an action, it's a little convoluted. Also one of the more annoying bugs was when I was trying to have someone mimic an action and getting whatever they had in their hand stuck and not able to make them drop it. The only workaround I could find was to switch over to control that ape, drop what he was holding then switch back otherwise it would not eat or sleep and if it was hurt eventually die. That is the only bug I remember because it was annoying when it happened but it was rare but honestly this is a very minor issue in a very well made game.I hope they make a new one with UE5 it would look sick and I would buy it in a heartbeat.TL;DRGame is beautiful and fun to explore just don't look stuff up in the wiki, it will spoil it. Game starts slow but it picks up quickly just give it a chance.

_childDocuments_.review: I really, really, wanted to like this game. I think that it has a fantastic and original premise, I also think that most of the gameplay mechanics are fine as they are. I loved the fact that there was very little hand holding in comparison to other games and I liked having to use my brain to figure things out. I genuinely believed that this game would become a fast favorite. It hasn’t. Here is the issue. A game about adaptation and evolution should have gameplay that adapts and evolves. This game doesn’t do that. I was excited by the gameplay initially, but after several hours of repeatedly clicking on boxes while an unending onslaught of tigers, snakes, and warthogs attacked me, it wore pretty thin. I was disappointed in my desire that the game would eventually allow me to actually defend myself without a gimmicky quick-time event. The other big issue is the neuronal energy system. Why is does it take several hours to fill the energy bar every single time? It takes so long that actually filling it became the the ONLY thing I was doing.Don’t buy this game unless you’re a masochist or you’re trying to find a reason to stop playing video games for a while. This is the only game that has ever made me rage quit.

_childDocuments_.review: In a nutshell: A game with great potential, but wasted by an approach that is what you'd expect from indie games. To start with, the tutorial is useless. Great, but nothing tells you how to make it, or what you need to make it. You need to keep a balanced diet! How? No indicators. Sleeping is important! Yeah but how much should I sleep?! I found myself going back and forth to websites explaining how things worked in order to play the game. That should not ever happen in a good title! Controls on PC are also pretty poor - some actions seem to require you to lift your mouse button, just to re-press it microseconds later. Microseconds, because otherwise you need to start over. All actions also require you to keep the button pressed for a while, very bothersome. Some actions seem to require you to keep pressing the buttons too. Again, not explained ad all.All in all, a very frustrating game.

_childDocuments_.review: Whoa... This was different in a way I wasn't expecting.The actual game play is just okay, with it feeling a little fiddly when I first started. Also it gives the option of no HUD when starting a game, I tried this but I personally found it less immersive, so I quickly turned the HUD back on. Once you get used to the controls and moving through the canopies, oh man, what a thrill!Where this game really shines is in the level design and character progression. You can tell there is no procedural generation here, with each "level" encouraging you to develop and evolve to deal with new challenges in a way accurate to our current understanding of human history.  The progression feels good, especially if you're not worried about maximizing gains quickly. If you'd like to power level, I'd suggest reading a guide as the game is rather coy about the mechanics.I also would like to call out the enemy AI. I love that the enemies are not overly aggressive like you'd find in other games. You hit a predator in the face with a rock, and you can bet (until the next generation) that they'll think twice when you yell at them, haha! (As a general pacifist in games, and a vegetarian in real life, I've never felt like it was my duty to eat other animals as much as in this game. Take that antelope!)I played relatively slowly, and it took me about 65 hours to hit credits. (My play time is higher, because I wanted to check out survival mode. Pretty much the same, but still a good time!)

_childDocuments_.review: Wow. That's about the best I can do to describe how TERRIBLE this game is. This is a full release game at $40 full price that plays like a version 0.1 game better priced at $4. Right away it plays like it's just the initial Early Access release where the devs are still trying to get the basic functions implemented.During the so called "tutorial" I had the same functions presented to me with the left mouse button to trigger the first time, then the next time it told me to do the same thing it was the right mouse button. The "senses" controls seem to randomly pick whether you start in the sense of smell or hearing. Then there are the functions like grooming and sleep, which you have to press and hold a certain button for. It shows a circle that fills in as you hold like a timer would. What the game says nothing about, is that even after this "timer" completes and goes away you are still expected to HOLD THE BUTTON. Overall, the controls seem like the devs were trying to cram too much into too few buttons and never tested the way they implemented the controls.Have you played a survival crafting game before? Then forget everything you know about crafting and building in games. I know this is meant to be about ancient apes, but the crafting/building system is absolutely terrible. There's no directions to do anything other than "build." First you are told to build a bed. No information about what to gather for it or how to build it. You just start grabbing leaves and pile them in a spot on the ground. Then once you have a certain amount, it let's you "craft" a bed. That basically means you just beat it with your hands but not just anywhere. You have to make sure you hit a certain spot for it to work except there is nothing to indicate where that spot is.Overall, this is probably hands down the worst survival crafting game I've ever come across. It plays like the devs have never played a survival crafting game before, or even other games before considering how bad the controls are. This is a $40 game that even 20 minutes into it is already repetitive and lacking direction. For comparison, ARK: Survival Evolved original game is $30. So you can have a much better, fuller gaming experience and save $10 at the same time.Don't just not buy this game. Run far away from it.

_childDocuments_.review: A truly unique and captivating experience that will hold your attention tightly till the end and then stay strong in your memories thereafter. With a growing interest in survival games and a very long-standing interest in human evolution, the concept of this game grabbed me from the start and continued to keep a hold of me. I'd spend time outside it, carefully planning my next play session's expedition, keeping in mind what I'd learned along the way to make it smoother and safer for my ape-people. Now almost 150 hours in and doing regular skirmishes into the final biome, I don't want the experience to end! I've stopped playing as much to try and keep this unique and compelling experience going as long as I can. Now all me and my fellow devoted Ancestors fans can hope for is news of a sequel. We need to continue the path to ♥♥♥♥ sapiens and beyond into the stone age!

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game but despite it being recommended for controller use there are some controls that just make this game hard to handle.  I wanted to keep my HUD up but some controller controls change that.  Having to go into my settings to fix that because it doesn't make it easy to fix is also annoying.The concept is kind of cool, but after a certain point it just feels over clunky and not quite the sort of game you'd want to play if you like colony survival sims.  I've put 20+ hours into this game, and realize every time I play it just how clunky the game can be.  There are some instances where trying to dodge creatures becomes annoying as heck, or trying to just groom.  There's no real clear concise way of getting things to work.  If you hold a button for too long you break things you don't necessarily want to break.  You mess up grooming if you don't have an idea of how it's supposed to work (and tank a grooming session that way).  All in all, the concept is great but the the game itself is very clunky and overwhelming.That said, it's not a bad game, but it's definitely not a game I can say that's enjoyable unless you have way too much time on your hands and you've got literally nothing better to do.

_childDocuments_.review: This game DOES NOT hold your hand!It can be a bit slow starting out but holy Christ is it a gem once you start to get your ♥♥♥♥ figured out! I normally hate survival/crafting type games but this one is done really well. You basically get tossed into the jungle afraid and alone and have to find your tribe and get yourself situated in such a way that you can survive properly in the wild. This game truly portrays the struggle to survive as a wild beast. Sometimes you are a predator and sometimes you are prey and you have to think and act fast to avoid being eaten by a jungle cat or a python. In other situations maybe you kill the Saber Cat or the python, it's up to you. To gain experience and expand your neural network to learn new cognitive functions, you must use your 5 senses. Gain xp with these:Visualize your surroundings.Hear what's around you.Smell whats around you.Attack new beasts to gain new understanding (which is like gaining xp)Lure beasts to get attacked by other beasts for a similar outcome.    For example the rock python can kill off 5 other beasts and vice versa. This gives lineage experience. Fruit in the world could be ripe or it could be rotten. You need to visualize or smell it to determine if it is good to eat. The area you start in is quite vast but if you move on to farther areas you will truly see how vast the world is. I have traveled so far from my settlement that I couldn't even fathom the idea of trying to make it back there again and it seems like I can go that far many more times over. The world is gigantic! There are a few animals in the jungle when you start out, but there are many more to be discovered as you venture onward.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the only games, possibly the first, that I have ever requested a refund for on steam. The controls are pretty terrible on keyboard and mouse. The game says it's best played on controller, but that doesn't really justify the awful controls if you are going to release it on PC. The tutorial is just awful. Most games you can figure out what you are doing pretty easily even without the tutorial, but this game is supposed to be about experimenting and discovery, but they do a really poor job telling you how to get started. I chose the immersive start (Full tutorial, minimal HUD) and didn't even realize I had a HUD at all because the game doesn't tell you how to bring it up (it's one of the arrow keys). Maybe that's just me, but there are a lot of unexplained mechanics that are essential to the game.The game has a lot of points of interests when you go into the intelligence mode, but you have to be perfectly still to view them and you can't highlight ones behind you. Once you discover something, lets say a plant for example, you will unlock some features and information about the plant. The problem is that all the other plants of that type don't become discovered as a POI in intelligence mode. They remain a gray square until you focus in on it. I would have to compare it to scanning something in No Man's Sky, but instead of scanning the plant once you have to scan every single plant on the planet.Lastly I have to talk about the climbing/jumping mechanics. Imagine every time you've played Assassins Creed and your character didn't go the way you wanted him to or he jumped and didn't grab onto anything causing you to fall to your death. Now imagine that x10 in the jungle. What really makes it bad is as you watch all the branches fly by that you're not grabbing you realize that when you hit the ground your clan will lose another valuable member to poor game mechanics. Then you get to stare into the eyes of your lifeless corpse while the game autosaves.Overall I think this game could have a lot of potential and it's an interesting concept, but the execution of it is very poor and not worth the $20 I spent let alone $40 at full price.

_childDocuments_.review: I had this game wish listed for a long time because I thought the idea and concept behind it were interesting. I actually had forgotten about it until the recent seasonal sale and I grabbed it for roughly 15 bucks and I am so glad that I did because I knew I wish listed this game for a reason. This game is definitely not for the faint of heart or might not be what you expect - which was my case, but in a great way. Long Story Short = This game is about our early ancestors roughly 10 million years ago before we evolved into ♥♥♥♥ sapiens, the game is about not only surviving in the wild but thriving and evolving which is definitely harder said than done. This game is very unforgiving in certain terms, they let you know from the beginning that they wont offer much help and you have to figure it out, which to some gamers would be extremely frustrating and that's why this game isn't for everyone. But for me its a lot of fun to figure things out and actually use your brain to determine how to survive in the wild. Long Story Long (potential spoilers) = Even though the game is very unforgiving in some regards it is forgiving in other ways, mistakes WILL happen, but you'll learn from them. You probably will die or come close but you'll learn from it. it wont be end game as you are not just "one character" but you are the tribe in itself. you can switch to any member(to play) and through evolution unlock more possibilities. the game focuses very hard on a slower pace play style to focus on learning about different food sources & food types, learning the surroundings as well as inspecting and figuring out how to change or alter your surroundings or resources with tools and other resources. you'll have to take care of your clan and its members, which is done semi-automatically. heal injuries, make sure the clan is eating and getting water etc. you might think you'd need to switch to every member and eat/drink etc that's not true that's just tedious and boring. if you are playing as a member and are in the settlement, whether others are following you or not, if you start drinking or eating the tribe generally starts drinking and eating too. however injuries and other ailments like poisoning etc will require a more manual approach, you'll need to get specific items to the injured tribe member and either use it on yourself as the injured member or give the item to them and hope they use it on themselves which doesn't seem to work 100% of the time i believe its because when or what in their hands when you give it to them etc. or what they are in the middle of doing.If you like survival/crafting/settlement management/thinking outside the box/tree climbing/jumping/hardcore parkour/evolving/exploring/discovering/learning and aren't afraid to brave the wild.. this game might be for you.

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of reviews complain about the lack of hand holding and tutorial quality but I bought the game anyways. And then I returned it. After three hours of gameplay that was honestly not fun at all but mostly frustrating. And it wasn't the lack of tutorial or missing support but the fact that so many things in this game are so tedious and unnecessarily slow and infuriating. Some examples:While in "intelligence" mode, which means that time seems to stop and you can look around to discover new things, dozens of unknown squares show up. Once you focus on one the item behind it is revealed. But it takes a few seconds for each square, and there must be several hundred of them just in the starting jungle.Climbing and moving on trees is incredibly slow and tedious. There really isn't a good parkour system like in Mirror's edge or AC. For example, once on a branch, you can't turn around (or I didn't figure out how), which means that if you want to go back you have to walk backwards. Also, jumping to other trees is difficult, so I relied on walking on the ground more, but there are other dangers there...Days are so short that you barely have time to explore between eating, drinking, and sleeping. You get the feeling that as soon as you leave your home turf it's already time to get back.The list goes on and on. The graphics aren't that amazing either. Not bad, but not outstanding either.I'm very disappointed. This would have been exactly my thing, but the grindy, frustrating mess this game is, I really tried, but I can't. It's too bad.

Release A button... while not moving the control stick- jump? Release A button... while moving the control stick- pick up an item? Release A button while near it. Hope you didn't also want to jump.- catch vines while jumping? Hold the A button.- jump off of those vines? release the A button. Hope you didn't want to go down, or just hang there, or climb.the rest of the face buttons are mapped to various vision modes, and could very easily have been a selector instead, considering the fact that there's never any urgency to use them because you can't use them while moving...Definitely not worth the asking price, and up to you whether it's worth a deep discount (for me it's still a no).

_childDocuments_.review: Good presentation (graphics, sound, music), and a big world to explore.  However, the mechanics really let it down, and very quickly become incredibly tedious.  (And that's once you understand them, which the game does nothing to help with.)Firstly, this isn't a game where you just control a single monkey and go off exploring on your own.  You're managing a whole tribe, and you need to develop their skills and help them evolve.  You do this via unlocking nodes using "neuronal energy" (i.e. XP) on the "neuronal tree" (i.e. a skill tree).There's a huge problem with this system: Eventually, you'll need to pass a generation.  When you do, you only get to "lock in" a handful of skills.  Everything else will be wiped out, and you'll have to spend XP on them again.Eventually, yes, you can lock in everything and finally stop losing skills every time you gen-up.   But it's needless grind that seems to exist solely to pad the game's length.  (Plus, advancing a generation is tedious: You need to pair up all your monkeys again, make them mate and have kids, etc.  This takes about 5-10 minutes or so, and it's just needless busy work.)Each kid has a chance of having a helpful mutation, and once you're satisfied with the mutations in your tribe, you can "evolve".  This is like a super-generation-up.  These mutations become a permanent part of your skill tree, and any feats you've completed — like "discover {location}", or "dodge an attack from a giant warthog two times", or "apply the healing properties of honey two times", etc — advance you by a certain number of years, typically 20,000 to 40,000.  (You need to have completed at least one of these to evolve.)At first, it's easy to evolve.  Everything you do is new!  But late in the game, I ran out of locations to explore and had done all the spontaneous feats I was going to do.  I had to start treating it like a tedious achievement checklist, and doing things I would never have done otherwise.  (Dodge a warthog?  Why?  I've killed dozens of them for their meat already.)There's a ton of other problems, too.  Early on, before you've learned weapons or how to intimidate as a group, your only realistic option is to stick to the trees, away from the dangerous predators on the ground.  But the jumping system is  — no preview of where you'll land, and the game uses the same button for both "jump" and "grab onto surface", meaning you'll probably just end up immediately letting go again.  Be ready for tons of "broken bone" injuries, and learn what plants heal them.Speaking of which, the game pretty much  a controller — I tried KB+M and it was awful — and even then, the button overloading is .  I know that console games in general have this problem, but this takes it to a whole new level.  The same button is used for• sprinting• swimming• jumping• grabbing onto something while falling• standing up• laying down• sleeping• picking things up• taking things from other people• trading your item for theirs• butchering• constructing stuff• probably several other things I've forgottenMeanwhile, there's a whole button pretty much just dedicated to smelling things, and two whole triggers dedicated to adjusting your "mood".  It's the most bonkers control scheme I've ever seen, and there were probably hundreds of times where I did the wrong thing as a direct result of this awful system.But, back to the game.  One key part of the game is leading your tribe around the map, either to change settlements (which you will do a lot, there's rarely any reason to stay in a location very long) or just so you can keep an eye on them / intimidate animals better.You can also have your tribe do things, like sharpen sticks to turn them into spears, or grind herbs to turn them into medication — pretty useful if you want to arm your entire tribe , treat wounds, or apply preventive medication.  You do this via a mimickry system, which involves doing an action and then pressing a button that makes them mimic what you just did.To understand why, you need to understand the equally awful inventory system.  You only have two hands, and you always do things with your right hand, while your left one is used for holding things while you "alter" them.Let's say one of your monkeys is injured.  You've got a grinder in your hand, so you could grind them some medicine to help.  You see the plant you need on the ground.  What do you have to do?• You'll need  your hands.  If the grinder is in your left hand, move it to your right hand by pressing L1 (swap hands).• Drop the grinder by pressing R1.• Press A to pick up the herb.  (Don't hold A or you'll automatically start eating it.)• Press L1 to move it to your left hand.• Hold L1 to enter alter mode.• Hold R1 to begin altering it.  (Don't start holding R1 before L1, or you'll throw it away as far as you can.)• Let go  you hear the audio cue, or you'll destroy it.  (Can't hear the cue?  That's your problem, go play another game.)• Go find your grinder and pick it up by pressing A.• Hold L1 to enter alter mode.• Hold R1 to begin grinding it.• Let go when you hear the audio cue.Congrats, you've got medicine.  Now you need to give it to the injured monkey, which means juggling  inventory, too.  (Are you having fun yet?)Now imagine if you want to have your entire tribe do this, so you can "mass vaccinate" everyone against injuries.  You're looking at doing all of the steps above  pressing "mimic me" between every step  making sure there's enough grinders that everyone can do it  making sure there's enough plants that everyone has one.  And all the while, your food and water and sleep timers are all counting down, and you're at risk of being attacked by predators.A lot of the game's systems would be great in a single-monkey exploration game, but utterly fall down when you try to apply them on a tribal scale.  Even with something simple like "grab a dead tree branch and strip it with your bare hands to make a basic stick weapon", I would find some of them carrying an un-stripped branch, and some of them carrying nothing at all.  And there's a bunch of activities that can't be mimicked at all, like fishing, or fetching coconuts from trees.  It's unreliable and frustrating as all hell.  Oh, and did I mention that , and they need to eat and drink ?Ultimately, it's simply not worth trying to get your monkeys to mimic anything complex.  They never evolve to the point that they understand how to do these things efficiently.  If you really want to arm your entire tribe, you're better off making a pile of weapons yourself and then telling them to pick those up.  (And don't forget to have your tribe put their weapons in a pile before you gen-up or evolve, because the game  taking your stuff away from you whenever possible.)All in all, of the 50 regrettable hours I spent playing this game, about 5 of them were spent coming to grips with the horribly explained mechanics (the tutorials are ), 10 were spent actually having some fun exploring, and the remaining 35 were just me hate-playing the game to completion because I'm stubborn like that.  (And because I wanted to see if it ever addressed my problems with the game, which it didn't.)  The ending actually came as a surprise — I thought I had 2 million years left to go, but it's just "NOPE you're done roll credits".  But it was a very welcome surprise, and I wish it had come much sooner.
