_childDocuments_.review: This game has so much potential.  However, it is falling flat on me.  15 hours of play and it is already tedious.  There is so little discovery.  I also love learning to play, but the game controls are just too finicky.  I broke down and watched some walkthrough videos, only to see that they all have the same ridiculous troubles that I did just getting the UI to work right.  Why won't that question mark go away?  No idea.  Just doesn't.  Picking up items is frustrating at best.  I don't want to spend my game time trying to nudge the mouse just a tiny bit to pick up the right thing.  Since "run" is holding down the "jump" button, every run ends in a jump.  Aiming at trees is hit-or-miss (again, 15 hours of play... still missing 1 in 5 jumps that I think I'm aiming the same way.)  I assume there just isn't a lot of content, so they tried to drag out every bit of content to last as log as possible.  I play survival games all the time (Forrest, Grounded, SubNautica, Raft, etc.)  The premise of this one is so good.  Even the tiny bit of crafting is novel and fun.  The sensory investigation of the world (look, listen, and smell) is brilliant.  So is the brain development "tech tree".  But fighting is horrible.  The clan is nearly useless.    And I feel like I've already exhausted the interesting content, and it says I'm 10% through the first section.  If I don't get new tools, convenience features, etc., this is just going to be a grind the rest of the way... off to watch a walk-through summary instead.Would someone please clone this concept and do it better?

_childDocuments_.review: This game seems really cool in concept. Play through the early stages of what became mankind and live in the dangerous world we evolved from. Pros: the graphics, controls, and sound are all pretty good. There are some minor targeting issues when it comes to cursor placement but I'll chock that up to it being intended to play with controller. When you get a real good combo of swinging vine to vine and you're hurling through the trees it definitely is fun.Cons:There is no real gameplay. There's 4 minutes of content played over and over and over. You inspect this thing, bash it with a rock, get evolution points. Next generation, rinse and repeat. And if something goes wrong you better start all over cuz it death spirals hard. If the game had more variety to it I would excuse its difficulty but there's nothing to warrant the grind, there's no reward for your efforts.

_childDocuments_.review: I have mixed feelings about this game.It is really a unique experience to play as our ancestors. I am a biologist so I can relate to.Visual are great, mechanics are interesting, quite refreshing experience.The game doesn't hold your hands and tell you what to do. In the beginning it's a bit confusing but hell, such is life. You really feel like a species struggling to survive.But life finds a way, it's great when you trying to learn better to survive and have evolved better traits for survival.Some mechanics are a little bit annoying. For example if you want to max out evolution traits, you actually want to NOT DO THINGS to speed up evolution. Very unintuitive and and works against you. You basically have to literally kill your apes to get the pentalties so you don't leap too far in years, so you have more time to evolve traits.At a later point it become very grindy and repetitive. I have to use cheat engine to speed up the game play and eventually I used a trainer. It feels to me the dev has bloated the mid to late game to increase the play hour. But it's just too much. If it could keep to the same pace when starting the game, it will be great.In summary, it's a unique experience. Early game is great. Just until a certain point, don't try to grind. You are not rewarded for too many traits anyway. The end game and ending is a bit of a lackluster. Still recommend to try the game out.(I got the game from a bundle)

_childDocuments_.review: Ancestors: The Humankind Odyssey is a very interesting new approach on exploration, a small part survival and of course evolution of mankind from it's ape-like ancestors. You start as a youngling on the back of your mother, then all of a suddon comes a giant bird out of the air, attacks and kill your mother while you get lost in the dense and unkown jungle. You can walk, you have your senses to search the unknown, but you also feel fear. In fact in this simulation you can see 'fear' by shadows of sharp predator teeth shine out of the dark unkown. So you can try to reach your nest or hide in a hideout and wait for other members of your clan to find you. It is an open world experience and the center of your world is your clan and it's progress. You learn with every new item you encounter, with every tool you learn, with every item you may explore to craft with different tools. You use your natural senses to explore and your two hands to carry and craft. Eating, drinking, sleeping are the only things you have to care of on a regular frequency, but it isn't overwhelming, so you have plenty of playtime for the real core of the game, exploring and learning. In fact there is no real path, nevertheless the goal to become human is fixed. It is up to you, how to path to that goal. Every decission you make can be a step forward or just survival. The graphics are nice and suit that simulation quite well. In parts it reminds a bit on Subnautica, but with a more basic and natural biome, while you don't swim, but climb and jump to reach the interesting places. Advancing is related to your learning process by neurons you could reveal and which you combine with the children of your clan to give them forth to the next generation. A very cute and interesting way that represents how our ancestors may have struggled through the eons of time until they became human. It is (sadly) only singleplayer, but a lot of fun doing things learning-by-doing instead of following a given route. You have to learn every single step...like one quite basic early step is to learn to hand over things from one hand into the other, but also other things like you could poke a processed palm stick in a bee nest to gain new food - honey. It is a journey, a journey of learning and exploring how to do things, to learn for itself and to gain a very new perspective on how humans or in this case to-become-humans might learn. A very neat and interesting new game idea and hopefully there will be other games that take up this very unique gaming experience. Recommended? Yes, if you like open-world and life simulations, if you like to learn how animals or children might prosper in an unkown but very interesting surrounding. The parts of survival are mild and also crafting isn't the core, it is exploring that is the main attraction and the pure fun to climb and jump around in a dense jungle until you find new things to explore. Rumors tell, later you'll get into the savanna with threats like lions, elephants or water buffalo, but I am still only exploring the very start of this great journey. Linux is supported with Steam's Proton support and the game runs like native. If you could grab it on a sale, you can't do wrong. Have fun!

_childDocuments_.review: First impressions - beautiful graphics, loads of promise.But the tutorial is TERRIBLE. Make a bed. How? Google it. Pile up 5 leaves. So I do that. Nothing happens. No cue. Google it again. Stand on the leaves. Still doesn't work. Turns out you can't do this when you are a baby, which is what I've been since the start of the game and at no point has it either said that babies can't craft, or told me that I can actually swap to another character to get this done.  So I Google it (again). Swap characters. Get the bed. Now I have to make a couple How? Google it again. Groom a member of the opposite gender. Try that. They just shake me off constantly. Google it YET AGAIN. Apparently there should be some kind of "snipping" sound cue when you release B. No such sound cue. Either I'm deaf or it's bugged.I shouldn't have to be Googling every single thing I have to do in the first hour of a game. I get they are trying to be immersive here, but I set it on first-time player mode. I'm not an idiot. I've played tons of these types of games before, and most of them give you at least an idea of how to craft and interact other than "Make a couple".I get that this game is pretty new on Steam but my understanding is that it's been out on consoles for a while so they really should have sorted this out by now. I don't expect to be spoon fed, but at least some idea of how to achieve these nebulous goals without having to be constantly searching on the Internet for the wise words of those who have gone before and sworn at the screen going "Yes, I get what I have to do, but how?!"If they made the tutorial actually tutor you, this might be a fun game. Right now it's just frustrating. I shall persevere but it's not fun yet.I'm of a vintage where we had new games and didn't have the Internet to look stuff up all the time. Games had to be designed to teach you everything you needed to know to play them. These days they just get lazy and assume everyone is just going to watch a YouTube walkthrough instead.../edit To sum up - if you want a game to be immersive, making it so that people have to look on forums and walkthroughs every five minutes is not the way to achieve that./edit. Persevered. Turns out to groom you don’t just hold down B. You hold down B BEYOND the circle filling up. I can’t explain better than that. The mini game is not intuitive at all. Again, I get that they are trying to be immersive. The whole “being a monkey” part needs to be just up to you. But the interaction between you and the game needs to be either intuitive or explained. Monkeys don’t need to be taught how long to press a button to pick a flea off a friend; they just see the flea and pick it off. We need to be able to see how to control, and this is very, very lacking. It just feels like they’ve used “we want it to be immersive, no help” as an excuse to not bother writing a decent controls tutorial.It does look really promising and if I could give it a 50/50 review I would. It’s just that the first few hours of this game are a hot mess and it’s jarring. I want to explore the mind of my ancestors, not breaking immersion all the time to find out why pressing the button it’s telling me to press isn’t working and then finding out it’s because I’m a baby and, I’ll say again, the game started with me as a baby and has made no attempt to tell me I don’t have to be a baby and in fact shouldn’t be a baby for this, the very first task.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay... I tried.I won't say I tried everything. I barely scratched the surface. But I tried.To be honest, I like this game. It is intelligent and quite beautiful. But it suffers from flaws that makes it difficult to recommend, at least in the actual state.I find the camera very, very disturbing. Too close to the character. I understand there is probably a reason for this : it makes it more intimate, more close to the subjectivity of your character, without being a first person camera. But you lack situational awareness, and you have to fight with the camera just to gather some fruits. more than that : the angle of view is very narrow, it's like trying to shoot a movie with a long focal lens. It moves a lot and it isn't very precise, you spend your time being too much on the left, then on the right, then on the left again.This makes us talking about playability : The jumps when on trees should be automatically directed to an other branch or not jump at all. I don't have the ability to jump from trees to trees. I don't know what  kind of branches I can grasp or not, and since the camera is very clumsy, I really don't see where I am going. So there should be a mechanism that allows your characters to do those things with her own senses. Trees are dangerous, so maybe in a "hurry" mode you can jump freely and pray you find something to grab (and even then this would... (well actually it is already) be a nightmare since again, you don't see where you jump, you have to turn your camera so you can't go fast like a real tree animal would do...), but the default way should be from a safe place to an other safe place.Communications with other members of the herd/tribe is quite difficult to understand too. Actually, most of the interface is difficult. It is a mode style interface, but instead of having a key/button to leave a mode, you have to move to do it. So you spend generally a lot of time trying to understand/remember how to leave a mode, then you hit the button for an other mode, then you come back to the original mode you where in and then at last you understand that all you have to do is to move, you do it and you lost a lot of time just for that.Transitioning to time. The day is measured in hours. That's strange. I would have used sunrise, midday, midnight and other things like that, it would have been more intuitive and less destructive considering the immersive feeling this tries to give you.Time runs very fast too. Eating, drinking and sleeping is supposed to give you a durable satisfaction feeling, but you can't stop thinking about this watch showing time, every minutes going every seconds, and that you now have to hunt/gather and explore again. Most survival games does that, it gives a very "arcade" feeling, bringing you intensity and pushing you to think fast, while in real live, you spend a certain amount of time moving, gathering and hunting (which is an intense phase) and then resting, exploring and socialise for the species that are adapted to it. (a calm phase). Here, the calm phase is reduced to it's minimum.At last, I have a big problem with the introduction. Credits, videos, time-consuming presentation, you can't play directly, you have to watch all those names which are of course important (the team who made this game deserve recognition) but when you just want to play a game, that's an enthusiasm breaker.I would love to recommend this game. Especially since it's base on scientific method, it tries to respect what we know of those eras and our species, and it is very clever, intelligent, intuitive (except those exceptions I developed before) and deserves recognition.It is an important game in the gaming sphere. But it needs a lot of ameliorations before being considered a "good" game. I clearly recommend this game to anyone who is passionate by science, anthropology, palaeontology and biology.  This is a must for them.But as a video game, it needs a lot of work to make it better/more intuitive/more adapted to different styles of gaming (pressuring people to move fast and hunt and gather and move and hunt and start over without any rest isn't for everyone...) I have some suggestions, of course, because constructive criticism is easy but is worthless without trying to fix the problems : 1 : Put your credits to the end. I insist. Really. When you finish the game, the reward is the credits. It works in movies, in video games, it will work here. You have a "credits" button on the menu. It's great, it's enough. Or you could if you wish make the credits roll on the side while on the main menu, that's some name exposition here !2 : Allow skipping the video at the beginning. We get it. To eat ot to be eaten. "Skip". Allow it. It works. Everywhere else it works. It will work for you.3 : Allow a change of the clock's speed. Yeah, I know "gameplay". But you already have different difficulty levels. So just let people explore at their own rhythm, everyone isn't a hard core gamer able to run through thing with a focused mind for 2 hours. It is tiresome for a lot of us. A choice is better than no choice at all. Allow us.4 : allow to have a "safe" button for jumping. For instance, while keeping the jumping button on, the character will jump from branches to branches without hurting herself, direct the jump to the nearest possibility, or will stop if no options are available. And, if someone wants to test the limits and have fun, he/she will simply have to tap on the jump button once and the character will jump regardless of if there is a safe possibility or not, and everyone is happy. Please note that this is inspired from other videogames that found a good way to explore while jumping without making it impossible because of camera and lack of 3D perception and situational awareness.5 : camera should be more adapted to what we want to see. I don't have a specific suggestion here, most of this would be solve by point 6.6 : Allow a change of angle of view of the camera by the player. Either in the options or with a key or a combination of a button. Don't mix up camera distance from the subject and angle of view. One widen the angle, the other keeps the angle narrows but push the subject further away without solving anything. (the opposite is true : if you have a wide angle of view and people complains about it, pulling the subject nearer to the camera will only make things weirder...) You have a very interesting, very important game in this community of gamers, geeks and scientists. It is mainly well executed and only lacks those small things to make it better. I really suggest you do it, you give the option to people to tune it a bit to their own tastes and abilities, so this game is more universally recognised and allows players with different profiles to play it without having to sacrifice too much the difficulty. (when you have more time, you take it, it is still a menace in the long run, it just allows you to have more fun with the features that the game gives you and there are plenty ! Same for cameras !)Take care, this isn't a negative review, it is a "so so". I can't put a thumb up because a lot of people I know may take it as a great game without flaws and I can't honestly say this is it. But this isn't a bad game, it needs tweeks but it isn't bad at all. It is a great game that I can't play for now because it doesn't allows me to do so without being overstressed by time, clumsiness and lack of accessibility features.Still, congratulations. This is one of a kind.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely awesome concept of a game. I'm in the midst of a playthrough several million years in, and I'm having a total blast.Starting out and knowing nothing and just trying stuff out is really cool. Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn't, and I really see the vision of learning to "become more human". The progression of going from a tree climbing and vine swinging wild animal into the gradual changes that make us humans is really ambitious. Any time I've done a "new thing" I get a huge rewarding feeling - especially killing something for the first time, the kill animation and my ape brothers getting hype made ME hype.I really haven't ever seen a game quite like this before, and it's scratched so many itches from my enjoyment of science and history that I never would have thought I'd see in a video game. If you also find yourself reading up on evolution in general, or what makes us "us", then I recommend this game with my whole chest.

_childDocuments_.review: Since there is not a "Meh" (average) vote option I currently am down-voting it (this could change)It's an interesting concept that is hampered by two VERY annoying an clunky mechanics/featuresThe 1st is the control interface.......O M G, this has to be the 3rd or 4th worst CI I have ever had the misfortune to contend with.  It's rather clunky and delayed.  Actions often present the feeling of lag even when they are actually responsive.   Crisp is not a term one will ever use about the CI as is.  It works poorly with both controllers and mouse/kb. This is compounded by the next barrier to success the game has...The UI.It uses a contextual interface what you are standing near, holding, or interacting with has a lot to do with what you can cannot do.  This is not helped by the same key/button being responsible for vastly different actions based purely on environmental context.  (somewhat understandable with a controller set-up, largely heresy with mouse/KB).  This can be annoying if your innate  understanding of tool use does not match the developers.  As an example; a beehive reqs a certain type of stick while in the real world...not so much.  One may or may not be as effiecient  (or safe) but it'll get er done.  Much like using a screwdriver as a lever, chisel, back-scratcher, or nose picker(care in deploying this technique is advised).  This would be fine if it was more intuitive regarding developer intent/perspective, and if the CI didn't lag behind.  As is it just contributes to annoyance and frustration not challenge or fun.  Also at issue the prompts are somewhat subtle audio and visual cues.  Individuals with certain disabilities (hearing loss, colorblindness ect) will likely struggle.  These are not impossible "features" to improve, only time will tell if they are.Those are the two main gripes I have with one additional minor gripe(also fixable)  If/when you master frustration with the CI & UI and get as comfortable with them as you can, you encounter the next problem.  Content tedium....there is an incredible amount of mindless repetition in advancing your tribe.  This gets worse as the game progresses (not due to added repetition, but due to lowered challenge)  As ones tribe advances, the environment, AI, and biomes become less challenging without becoming less tedious.   Early game everything feels big and dangerous; mid/late game it's boring.

_childDocuments_.review: A longtime interest in anthropology and having recently read Yuval Harari's  prompted my eager purchase of this when I noticed it on sale. I'm not disappointed; it's been an incredible imaginative vehicle against the informational backdrop of that book. My takeaway: whether you're a kid who grew up on a stack of s or you're just a hard-nosed open-world-survival-craft buff, this one's for you. On sale.  game mechanics, from genetics to teaching offspring, are thoughtfully and uniquely developed. The world is immersive, the risks are believable, and the evolutionary tree is an excellent motivator. I'm really blown away by the nutritional food system and the nuanced depiction of "unknown danger." And while I understand from other reviews that the narrative development (not that there really is one) can be slow and ultimately becomes open-ended, I've thoroughly enjoyed the experience so far. I don't need another .  In fact, I'm kind of looking forward to going nowhere with this. After all, it's nonfiction, and the ultimate conclusion of this human species drama is... exactly what I'm doing in this present moment.One critical note: Since the controls can be a little sticky and there's such a learning curve to survival, do yourself a favor: keep the tutorials with full HUD at the game's start.

_childDocuments_.review: To open, I imagine this game is "Australia simulator", where everything wants to kill you. It's not hard to survive, really. However everything wants you dead, and perhaps as a nice snack. The trees are safer but not totally(i won't spoil THAT WTF moment).I love the concept and I even love the majority of the gameplay, it's a unique idea in a field of redundant shooters, platformers, etc. HOWEVER where the concept falls flat is the controls, they're not absolutely horrible but I can't count the number of times my monke has failed to grab  a branch and goes falling to the forest floor, even better when there's a predator below waiting to "wtf pwn me" with a rodeo backflip attack.Literally got eaten by a croc that somehow managed to lunge halfway up my tree from behind itself. While this hasn't been typical I think with a bit more care and attention to detail this could have been a revolutionary game that would have influenced future game concepts and development. The game otherwise runs well, without any major bugs yet. IMO the one thing that brings this game down to being frustrating to deal with isn't the difficulty or lack of hand holding. It's absolutely the controls and dodge mechanics. If they would fix those issues and improve them I would give this game a solid 10/10 for being an innovative and unique MUST PLAY. However the controls mar an otherwise wonderful experience. Which in my opinion still leaves it at a 7-8/10. If the Devs ever improve the controls and tree jumping mechanics on mouse and keyboard, I'll update the review to reflect as such.In conclusion, if you're willing to deal with a few issues with poor controls and the game looks interesting to you as a concept, and the game is on sale. You probably won't regret your purchase but there are times you'll curse the terrible control mechanics and it will cost you a clan members life because of it far too often.

_childDocuments_.review: BLUF: Don't even bother. UI is bad, controls are clunky, game is not intuitive, graphics are dated.So many issues with this game that I have no idea where to start. I guess I'll just start with when you first start up the game.1. When you open the game for the first time it automatically assumes you're using a game controller, even if you've never had a controller within 50 yards of your computer, let alone installed.  You then have to reset everything before you even get past the start menu. Not a good omen.2. So, now you've sorted out the basic UI, you go to start your first game, and then have to wait a good 10-15 minutes through the unskippable opening credits. And i'm not talking about an even slightly interesting cut scene to get you into the mood of the game. No! it's a black screen with elevator music, with the names listed of everyone who delivered pizza to the developers while they made the game.  You know you're almost going to be able to play the game when the pretentious claim that it's a true story comes on the screen.3. Now that you've rolled your eyes into the back of your head, you might as well keep them there for a little bit longer.  The next cut scene highlights the finest graphics from 1995 as you watch a comically large eagle effortlessly lift two apes hundreds of meters into the air at once.  Didn't I just say this is based on a true story? oh well.4. Now you're finally into the game and able to control a character.  Your first job is to control a lost infant ape as you walk him 20 yards to hide under a log. But that's complicated by your screen going on a bad mushroom trip as  it bombards you with cartoonish lion's teeth all over the screen.5. Now that your baby ape is hidden, you take control of an adult who has to go rescue the baby. Despite what you'd think would be an urgent situation, you're going to spend at least one in-game day walking around the start point, figuring out how to pick up a rock.  Now that you've picked up the rock, you need to inspect it.  Upon inspection, you find out that it is, indeed, a rock.6. Now that you've made that scientific breakthrough, you proceed out of the starting area to find you have to climb and swing your way through the trees. You quickly discover that the controls are as awkward and clumsy as a 12 year old on their first date. As you climb trees, you'll get hung up on invisible obstacles, try to swing to branches you'll teleport through, and fall hundreds of feet to end up completely fine unless it's not a specific place the game's designers decided you  shouldn't, then you're dead.7. Controls are atrocious.  The developers decided that you only need four buttons for everything.  Climbing in trees? well hold space to jump to another branch. Grabbing the next branch? then hold the space bar also. What's that? you wanted to grab that branch? too bad, you were already holding the space bar.  You want to inspect that item the game prompts you to? Too bad, you just yelled out, alerting any predators in the area to your location. The game will give you an on screen list of things you can do with an item then randomly do a different action that's also tied to that key.

_childDocuments_.review: Simultaneously the most basic yet complex survival game out there. Some parts you will probably wind up having to look up, but most of the time the solution/path forward is pretty simple. Once you understand that you have very limited tools to work with and you get a feel for the neuron/evolution system, it isn't so difficult to survive as it is to explore. You start out in the corner of the jungle, in a safe oasis atop a high plateau, but within a generation you will find yourself needing to venture out further into the unknown (a mechanic I'll talk about in a minute). You see, instead of new recipes or pieces of tech to unlock, you are attempting to broaden the intelligence of your clan, from a tiny group of ancient primates afraid of fresh water and berries, cowering in high places and caves to a (relatively) modern gang of bipedal apes hunting gazelle and scaring off water buffalo in the Savannah. In order to do this, you need to investigate and discover your surroundings. You get "neuronal energy" for every time you identify something, discover a new location, inspect your food before eating it, create or use a tool, cure a stomach ache by drinking water, walk through shallow water etc etc. ( basically everything) with at least one baby monkey around. You then are awarded "mutations" or "matured" neurons, which basically means you've done the activity enough to the point where you're able to do something more advanced but related. Like the more you fight, the faster fight/flight neurons mature, and the more likely you'll be to land a killing blow, not drop things while dodging, giving a better chance your clan will successfully counterattack or dodge without getting hurt (provided they have the proper tools), etc. You then spend your neuronal energy to unlock these traits and incorporate them into your genome, provided you can secure them there with "reinforcement points" which you get from having kids and finding meteorites. Once a gene is reinforced, every member of the clan will permanently have that trait/ability unlocked, but if you switch generations or evolve without reinforcing a gene, you will have to re-unlock (but not relearn) that trait/ability. If you can't tell by now, there's a lot I like about this whole system, and once you get past the learning curve, there is a lot to like. Some caveats though; exploring unknown territory is unnecessarily complicated. You have to "rationalize" your surroundings and then follow a bright light to a special area where you can "conquer your fear." But many times the bright light isn't visible; either it doesn't trigger or it's being obscured by the terrain or landscape, so even though you've already rationalized that there's no danger present, you still have to fumble around in the (imposed and extra disorienting) dark until you happen upon the correct area. Also, you and your clan are ridiculously needy when it comes to food, water, and sleep. I know its silly to say in a survival game, but I wish they were a little more lenient about these. You really do have to eat and drink 3 about 3 times a day and get 8 hours of sleep or else your monkeys will NOT be happy. the screen effects for being low on any of these are really annoying and inconsistent, as i've had many instances where the guy ate, drank, slept 8 hours, woke up, ate a whole coconut after drinking all the water in it, and then he still complains he's hungry/thirsty/tired via those screen cues. So much so that I don't even pay attention to them (besides the fact that they're frustrating), I just look at how much energy I've got and base my daily habits off that.A few other things are a little wonky, but overall I would highly recommend this game to survival enthusiasts. Really hoping for a sequel where we get to use fire and work our way up to more modern times!

_childDocuments_.review: Yes, this is "return to monke", the game. And that is totally fine by me. I've sunk a bit more time into the game now than I had initially, so I'll have more to add about its flaws... It starts fast of learning, slow of movement.  It works its way up to fast of movement, slow of learning. Still a bit too slow on both counts though.Trying to progress some of the neurons is troublesome as the devs are REALLY cagey about information.  They arrogantly present their cagey crap as a feature, but it is just annoying.  I'd rather a detailed walkthrough than all this "we're not going to tell you anything" bullsh!t. The controls are janky as hell but I've mostly got used to them.  Having got used to them doesn't make them any less janky though.  My fingers are in quite a bit of pain from playing this game every day for the last week or so.   Seriously, the controls are THE worst thing about this game.  They could have been so much better.   Like setting Left and Right to toggle the moods instead of having them activated while holding the shoulder triggers, which could have been dedicated to running or something (not only because holding A to run is a huge pain, but to free up the running from the jumping, as they should NOT be together). I even wrote a movement guide precisely because the controls are so janky and the devs so cagey with info. I figure some people might benefit from what it took me many hours to figure out on my own and wished I'd known from the start.Also there are some areas of the game that are dangerous for the wrong reasons... i.e. poorly programmed game mechanics rather than actual features.  Losing my monkes because the game  them  rather than next to me, causing them to be ambushed by a certain venomous cave predator where I couldn't even reach them, is NOT my idea of good game design.That said, despite the various flaws, I am technically still enjoying this game.That is to say I'm mostly enjoying monkeying out all over the place and being a silly sod because I have a juvenile sense of humour. I also like murdering various animals and leaving their corpses all over the place just because it feels good to be the top predator. This game, while ostensibly serious, is actually very silly in all the best chest-beating, screeching, monkey magic ways.  Also lots of pretty vistas.  The game world is very pretty, assuming you're not viewing it through the annoying motion blur or temperature-triggered vignettes.

_childDocuments_.review: Extremely frustrating and grindy, with some of the buggiest climbing mechanics I've ever seen.I keep coming back to this game hoping that somehow after giving it another chance it'll be fun, but it hasn't turned out that way so far.  You progress your hominids by repeating basic chores while carrying a child, and you lock in skill points by completing a generation.  Afterwards, you get to do it all again, because all of the skills you unlocked last generation have been reset.  High levels of RNG with the mutation system gating off skills until you "mature" a child with a particular mutation, and unless something seriously changes in the platforming late-game I really can't see this being a fun game to play long term.  Your character moves at a snail's pace, they let go randomly while climbing, and one fall is all it takes to kill an ape.  Hope that child you were carrying didn't have an important mutation, because they're dead now too.  Apes have a wierd sense of parinoia that I can't figure out and will randomly act like they're being stalked by a predator when there's no threat to be found, which is a major pain since they'll run back to base if they're afraid for too long.While the idea is interesting the assembled game is one of the most frustrating to play survival craft games I've experienced.  I probably won't be giving it another chance.

_childDocuments_.review: The game and it's concept are BEAUTIFUL and I just LOVE it. BUT. The implementation of the game mechanics is unfairly clumsy and I would've enjoyed this SO MUCH MORE if the experience was overall more polished.Anyway, just so I'm clear with my thumbs up, I really recommend this game to anyone that likes original, intriguing and immersive experiences and/or liked Desilets's Assassins Creeds far more than any others that came after them. Why? Because they where genuinely thought out out of passion and both artistic and intellectual ambition.SoI get why there is a lack of guidance for the player. I love the focus and I found the game really really enjoyable. Is ment to be immersive (as I understand) and it has been for me so far. The concept of the game itself I believe it is superb.NowThe AI of the NPCs is very clumsy and I personally found the control of the main character not as realiable as I think it should be, concerning the situations and dangers you are brought into... which they are, more often than not, too complex for the solutions to them that the game offers.As I understand, the game is supposed to be realistic. You know: a monkey in the jungle, among saber tooth tigers, pythons and crocodiles...!? That is dangerous. The game is trying to transmit that tension. That's why it is hard on the player. But a lot of the times I have felt ENRAGED, because the control you have over the monkey is very limited when you are being attacked and NPCs behave even worse in these situations. It feels like when Altair wouldn't jump in the direction you where pointing to. Ahh... those're some memories.There was one situation, after the first evolution process was done, I was in a new settlement and I had to guide some monkeys that where lost in the jungle. And then two tigers come. Is not just that the NPCs couldn't deffend themselves; they wouldn't even try to get away!! They would be eternaly struggling with the tiger until I came along.As far as I'm concerned, Desilets (main creative mind behind the game) tries to get away from mechanics that feel "gamey", like combat mechanics or maps full of icons and such. I wholeheartedly respect that, I love that focus of creating a "virtual experience" rather than "another" videogame. But I think, in this particular case, the character should have a bit more control options. I don't know. If you have a stone, you should be able to hit the beast, right? Or have more control on escaping or helping others.And yes, it is ment to be an "experience", but STILL, there ARE "gamey" features in Ancestors. You are supposed to find your own way, but in the same time, the game is giving you quests to accomplish. Some things don't work well either in this regard. Between "you're on your own" and "this is your mission" focuses, there are colissions.An exampleI found some monkeys and convinced them to join the clan before the quest that pushed me to "meet a stranger" for the "first" time was given to me. The game would not recognise that I already did that, so I'd have to find more strangers... but there where no more strangers nearby. So I started to explore further and further and further... like REEEALLY far (still didn't find any) until there was no more adults left in the clan (... because they where killed mercilessly by merciless beasts).Also, I don't get how the little ones grow up. Should I just play for years until they do? Because if I decide to evolve I just start with a completely different clan.So, anyway.That's a lot of complaining here, complaining that I still think is a bit justified BUT I still recommend the game to anyone that wants something different and likes immersive experiences......................................................................NEW NOTES / EDITED: I discovered how to counterattack. I found the mechanic very difficult to figure out at first... but now that I know, the game becomes much more rewarding. I still think the main problems are NPC's AI and clumsy playability... but man, overall, I really enjoyed the game......................................................................There are more situations where the game works than the ones that don't. I think that this game is actualy very interesting, very rewarding when it works and inspiring really. Making a game like this is risky and I very much respect the ambition of the developing team. In fact, this is the kind of game I like, really. I'm so f@#!g tired of the Triple A industry.The concept of ANCESTORS, The Humankind Odyssey and what I believe it is aiming for, WORK. It's original and ambitious and I LOVE that there are veteran developers making this kind of games. They just need to polish the idea. I'm eagerly looking forward for the next game.

_childDocuments_.review: -Visuals do a great job of conveying a lush, unknown jungle just waiting for you to explore and play around in it-Sounds and music are both great-The typical survival game elements of managing hunger, thirst and energy aren't taken too seriously, thus you're much more free to explore-The mechanic of using your animal instincts are adapted in a fun and immersive manner-There are multiple aspects of gameplay to enjoy and/or tweak around with-Controls can act a bit wonky from time to time-As it often happens with these games, it's easy to get lost not only in where to go to proceed, but the game also doesn't do the greatest of jobs explaining the mechanics (evolution, fear of the unknown, terror etc.)I think the key here is to not view Ancestors as a hardcore survival title, but rather as a journey or and exploration experience, as I actually believe it is meant to be viewed !For further info and a look at gameplay, please feel welcomed to check my thoughts in this video: .

_childDocuments_.review: Go back! I want to be Monke! This game defines this idea. If you're not ready to be a clueless ape fighting for your survival in a Jungle for 3 hours then you're not ready for this game. That being said, this game performs that function extremely well. You scavenge, climb, and fight your way through ancient Africa as a common ancestor. It does give tutorials for some things, but for the most part you're on your own to bang rocks together and lead your ape troop how you see fit. The one thing that I would add to this game that we probably won't see due to the construction of the game is a multiplayer setup. I would love to see an option to play co-op and play side by side with your friends. This would make certain aspects of the game easier, such as hunting. The ape AI is pretty lack luster and despite them having the ability to attack the enemy after certain evolutions, they rarely do. Having a friend would make this easier despite the fact that it's not too hard if you plan correctly. Still nothing would be beat being be able to do monkey stuff with a friend.

_childDocuments_.review: It's basically unplayable. There's a tutorial, but it consists of multiple popups explaining high level topics that are unrelated to your current task. Also, there is a weird design choice where you press escape to bring up the menu, but you can't press escape to back out of the menus; you must use the mouse to click on the "exit" options.Your first objective is to help a child find a place to hide. The location of the hiding place is indicated by a nondescript white square. This is the one time that the tutorial was helpful. Never would have known to head to the white square.Your next task is to control an adult to find and then calm the child who you just hid. Getting there is easy enough, although the jumping and climbing mechanics are awkward. However, calming requires you to call, wait for the child to respond, then time your next call correctly or you'll lose progress. There is no timing indicator. You have to guess.Once calmed, the child climbs onto your back. Returning to your living area is easier than climbing down was.Next you get an objective to build a sleep(sic) spot. After receiving the objective you get about 6 popups explaining how longevity and energy work. That's nice, but I need to know how to build a "sleep" spot.After you Google "ancestry humankind odyssey how to build a sleep spot" you are given the objective "form a couple". I can't remember if the tutorial explains that this involves grooming or if I had to Google that, too. What you will have to Google is an explanation of the grooming mechanic. This is another timing based mini-game with no context clues about the appropriate time to release the mouse button. Oh, you don't even have indicator that you're supposed to hold down the mouse button; I spent several minute before going to Google just clicking and wondering what was supposed to be happening.You final objective is to request a refund. Fortunately Steam's refund process is intuitive and you won't need a tutorial or Google.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is revolutionary in many ways. What a bold move to produce such a title in modern times!It really looks and plays fresh. Concept is phenomenal, and it's execution, being far from ideal, still provides a truly rewarding and engaging experience. At least when you play for the first time.It's like an Animal Planet/BBC Earth documentary, but interactive and not that chilled out, because you have to be cautious and constantly on the watch for omnipresent threats.I absolutely love this game, BUT it is only because I decided to play against the rules. I did a lot of manual save file backups to avoid the torment of repeatedly losing and starting from scratch, because of some stupid mistake, strange design decisions or a bug.Game does not communicate it's rules clearly enough, sometimes you do something that should work, basing on your experience, but for some reason it doesn't. It also cheats, breaking it's own rules, for instance spawning enemies from thin air in an area they shouldn't be able to reach.Because of that, if I played it as it was designed to be played, so no manual save/load, I would most likely rage quit forever after second or third fatal accident I couldn't foresee and prepare for. I am not that much into replaying dozens of hours of any game, and this one in particular, as it can become very repetetive if you already know it's secrets.Do yourself a favor and try my approach as well, it allows to really enjoy this gem, otherwise - it's only for very determined breed of gamers.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is phenomenal.  If you find prehistory / paleontology interesting and want to try a game where you explore a representation of what the world may have been like a few million years ago, this is by far the best example I've seen at actually doing it.  It's incredibly immersive, putting you in control of an early hominid in a gorgeous but dangerous world, giving you next to no guidance with threats everywhere.  You have to learn how to use anything & everything to survive; it's one of the few exploration-focused games that manages to make simple things like coming across a new type of fruit interesting because you have to figure out what to do with it - you might need to get a rock to break it open, or if you aren't familiar with how its color changes at different stages of its ripeness then you might get food poisoning by eating a rotten one.  And almost everything you do gives you progression - walking, using tools, healing injuries, dodging attacks, hearing predators, smelling food (yes, really), etc., all of them can unlock that next ability that then branches out to more potential abilities.  It's incredibly addicting just trying to figure out what the next ability unlock requires (as the game doesn't completely spell it out to you, instead giving hints that often make you wondering if you just need to do the action a few more times or if you're totally off track).I can't recommend this game enough if you have any interest in ancient life, enjoy exploration games, or just want to try something totally new and difficult to compare to almost any other game I've ever played.  It perfectly combines a very unique progression system with an exploration style that focuses on the minute details of figuring out how to use simple objects found throughout the world instead of relying solely on spectacle, and that gives it a truly distinct feel (though don't worry, there's still plenty of spectacle too, mostly from reaching new environments & finding new wildlife - there's nothing quite like journeying from the safety of the jungle trees to the open savannah and coming across a Miocene Elephant for the first time).

_childDocuments_.review: ***might contain spoilers to the game mechanics***Unique game that throws you into the “shoes” of individuals in our ancestral lineage. The game mostly revolves around a small tribe of individuals and you get to play as one of them in a lone wolf type of gameplay, or as the leader of the tribe, leading the group to scavenge, hunt and explore. The game is a survival based game and similar to our ancestors, you are an easy pray, but as you gain experience, a neuronal energy, your character develops and learns new skills, even how to counter predators. In order to speed the development, you can carry up to two infants with you to gain more of the neuronal energy.Unlike other games, where your playable character is permanently improved, here everything gets lost, unless you pass the generation and eventually evolve. In order to evolve your species efficiently, you need to gather mutations and fyi you can load up 3 adults with 6 infants, when you mutate your offsprings.Additionally, the developers really did their job when going through anthropological facts. In this regard, the game gives you an introductory information about human evolution. Unfortunately, they get many things wrong and it is important to note some examples, such as the Australopithecus species is not our ancestor, rather a dead end branch in our ancestral tree. Another downside is that evolution is not linear and does not jump from species to species. On the other hand, the mechanics regarding omnivorous behaviour and bipedalism are well implemented and, as it was with our ancesters, greatly improve humans “game”.I bought at the discount for about 10 euro. It was one of the best games I have ever played. I enjoyed it even more, because it reminded me a lot from what I have studied in my majors. If there are any DLCs going forward, I am definitely in. Great job, developers!

_childDocuments_.review: Every now and then there's a rare occurrence that pops up of Art imitating Life rather than the reverse, and unfortunately that's all that I can see contained within the immersive setting that is Ancestors: the Humankind Odyssey. The gameplay is ungodly annoying and frustrating at the best of times, such that your attempts at seamlessly traversing through the forest will always be cut short of whether or not you can make a jump or climb on a surface. The social aspect epitomizes these constraints beyond what words can manage, as you're constantly using inputs to determine what items are in what hand, if you're giving, dropping, or tossing an object (all mapped to the same button), and whether or not an interaction particular is long-press, pressed once, or mashed. It feels the whole point of the control system was to reinvent the wheel with bells and whistles attached.The sleep, eat, and drink system is counter intuitive as it conveys the means of similarity to any other simulation game or even survival games, which wouldn't be a bad thing if the game was just more transparent with your needs rather than just surprising you with hunger and thirst notifications. The game itself starts up in right in the middle of the Neogene at 10 Ma, starting you off with primates never given explicit detail, though the in-game system does refer to them as hominids (not hominins) which would make them ancestral by 3 million years of either Graecopithecus or Sahelanthropus just depending on what the fluid definition of hominin currently is. All in all the game is far closer to Life of Black TIger than it is Green Hell.

_childDocuments_.review: As much as it might seem fun to buy this "for the memes" and to "return to monke" - do not bother.Devs very cheekily tell you that they will not help you much at the start of the game and they mean it.Even with what this game considers "most help" setting of tutorial, it expects you to beat your head against their clunky controls to figure out how to even play it.To give an example - at the very start the game gives you an objective to construct a sleeping spot.Except it does not bother to explain that you can not, in fact, build as a child (that it starts you as) and that you can switch between your tribe members.Then, it tells you to go and find some location that I assume is for another camp and I honestly have no idea where it even is, or how do I even begin going in the right direction.It is one thing to give the player the tools to play the game, and then expect the player to figure out the content, but it is completely another expect the player to figure out the tools at his disposal, too.There also seems to be no reason to explore or really to do anything.Your starter camp seems to have an infinite amount of food, water, and is secluded enough where there are no predators.As the game does not bother explaining itself you have absolutely no idea what can you even do, or why would you bother taking the time to learn.After looking at the external tutorials the repetitive claim I heard is that the game is grindy and tedious.So not only is it hard to get into, there is no "payout", neither.It also seems to like to revert your progress to make you "rediscover" your abilities that you lost between generations - "because that's how evolution works, right?"Save yourself the time and the money.If this game seems appealing - go watch someone play it on youtube or something and invest only if after that it still seems like fun.

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent, very insightful game, stifled by an unimaginative endgame.Ancestors is not a game about humans; it is a game about the many species that, over 10 million years, would eventually evolve into humans. I feel like I should make this clear. You are not gonna make fire, or a cave painting, or learn how to talk. You will, however, slowly evolve from a scared, clueless ape into a master of your surroundings. The way the game models this is by growing neurons - doing new activities will grow new neurons, which will, in turn, unlock more new activities. It is ingenious game design: as you learn the game, your apes will also get smarter and gain abilities to help you make the most use of your newfound learning.The world does a great job feeling BIG. It is an awe-inspiring feeling to leap through the branches of enormous trees. It is divided in biomes, and I really like the way the game handles progressing between them up to a certain point. You start off in the Jungle, where you can easily escape predators by just climbing a tree, but there's little variety in food sources and traversal is difficult; predators also get an advantage in that it's easier for them to hide here. You'll then proceed to the Great Lake, a wide valley with more flat terrain and more types of animals - including otters which you can hunt, helping your species acclimate to eating meat. After that, it's on to the Savanna, which will present a huge new variety of plant and animal life. Encountering new things helps your species evolve. There is a sort of achievement system that controls the limits of what you can do - whenever you do something new, you will gain an "evolution feat". Each evolution feat gives you fuel for when you decide to do an "evolutionary leap" and advance millions of years.The problems come with the last two biomes, the Canyon and the Ocean (really just a beach, since swimming kills your energy). They are, for lack of a better phrase, utterly devoid of interesting content. They have barely any new fauna, being simply chock-full of the same tigers and snakes you've been fleeing from since the Jungle. They have barely any landmarks. They have barely any food and water sources. There is simply no incentive for you to move your clan into them, unlike the previous biomes. Even the game's main objective line ends when you get to the beach. And the only way to progress from this point is to achievement hunt: the chore of hitting each of the three kinds of tiger with each of the tree kinds of stone, finding each landmark and each item, witnessing each predator kill each prey, etc..If the devs ever release an update to the late stages, I'm sure to come back!

_childDocuments_.review: Warning: this review sounds much more negative than it is. I love that game, but see lots of missed opportunities - hoping for a part 2The only thing I really don't like about this game are the controlls (with controller) - they are wonky at best and get frustrating quickly (who puts jump and sprint on the same button?! why?! and as if that's not annoying enough, the same button is to - partially - interact with the world... standing on a stick and trying to jump?! - no ... sprinting up a tree while escaping a predator?! you better not let go of that A button, or you uncontrollably jump down again). Also the UI is a bit weird - you shouldn't have to guess if you're hungry, thirsty, tired or anything else - those things should be apparent - you feel them in real life and never get unconsious suddenly because you forget to fulfill one of them for days, becasue you didn't know why your vision gets blurry. Then move along ^^It's a slow game and that's good. I love roaming around and exploring the environment - I just wish there were more things to discover - maybe I'm simply not far enough into the game (40h), but it feels like I have everything uncovered that there is. (and I really don't want to look it up - I want to find stuff myself) Tools for example - there's pretty much only Obsidian and Granite - out of which you can make a ... this fits the evolutionary timeframe the game is set in, but I still wish there was more - maybe a second part of the game that focusses more on (stone) technology and the possibilities they unlock in the world and less on trying not to die of dehydration would be in order. _childDocuments_.review: One of the most striking aspects of the game is its emphasis on exploration and learning. Instead of traditional objectives, you're encouraged to experiment and discover your surroundings. I loved how this approach made me feel connected to the environment, whether it was foraging for food, learning to use tools, or avoiding predators. The sense of accomplishment from mastering these skills was incredibly rewarding.The visuals are stunning, capturing the beauty and danger of the prehistoric world. I found myself often stopping just to take in the scenery. However, I did encounter some frustrating moments with the controls and navigation, which felt a bit clunky at times. This can be challenging, especially when you’re trying to escape danger or interact with the environment.The game also does an excellent job of highlighting the importance of community and lineage. As you progress, you can pass on knowledge and skills to future generations, which adds a meaningful layer to the gameplay. This aspect resonated with me, reflecting the real-world importance of family and learning.Cons: Clunky Controls: The controls can feel awkward and unresponsive at times, making navigation and interactions frustrating, especially in high-pressure situations.Slow Pacing: The game's emphasis on exploration and gradual evolution can lead to slow pacing, which may not appeal to players looking for more action-oriented gameplay.Limited Guidance: While the lack of hand-holding can enhance the experience, it may also leave some players feeling lost or unsure of their objectives, leading to moments of confusion.Permadeath Mechanics: The permadeath system can be punishing, as losing a character means losing progress and learned skills. This might discourage some players from taking risks or fully engaging with the game.Repetitive Gameplay: Some players may find that the core gameplay loop becomes repetitive over time, as the tasks and challenges can feel similar across different playthroughs.Technical Issues: There have been reports of bugs and performance issues, which can detract from the overall experience.Pros:Unique Concept: The game offers a fresh take on survival and exploration by focusing on early human evolution, providing a distinctive gaming experience.Immersive Environment: The stunning visuals and richly detailed prehistoric world create an immersive atmosphere that draws players in and makes exploration feel rewarding.Emphasis on Exploration: Players are encouraged to experiment and discover their surroundings without traditional objectives, promoting a sense of curiosity and adventure.Skill Progression: The ability to pass on knowledge and skills to future generations adds depth and strategy, enhancing the game's longevity.Realistic Survival Mechanics: The game incorporates survival elements that challenge players to gather food, avoid predators, and learn new skills, creating a sense of accomplishment.Community Building: The importance of lineage and community in gameplay fosters a deeper connection to the characters and their development.Diverse Gameplay Styles: Players can choose how to approach challenges, whether through stealth, exploration, or strategic planning, catering to different play styles.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm torn on this game because there's some really good stuff here. I think the idea of a crafting/survival game following our early hominid ancestors is really cool. I enjoyed exploring and finding new environments, and I actually did, for the most part, enjoy struggling to understand the different environmental interactions, the controls, etc. without much guidance from the developers. However, once you get through that struggle, the threats of the game become trivial, and there's nothing to do except grind. Unlocking new abilities requires repetition, so to learn to digest new foods you have to find them and eat them, to get better at dodging and fighting you have to dodge and fight, etc. That's cool except there are no real goals in the game except to develop the species, so instead of doing interesting things and developing your skills incidentally, you end up chasing snakes around to trigger the fight mechanics or eating your 500th mushroom in the hope it opens up your next set of unlocks. There is map exploration and there is satisfaction and enjoyment to be had by moving about the environment, climbing up cliff faces and jumping from tree to tree (once you figure out how to do this without dying), and discovering new landmarks, but even that gets stale after a while once predators are no longer a concern and there's nothing to do except from move from point A to point B while occasionally stabbing yet another machairodus that hasn't figured out it's no longer the most dangerous species on the planet. I think it's probably still worthwhile as a chill game to play every now and again if you like the general flow and vibe of the game, but for me it ran out of steam once the initial struggle is overcome.
_childDocuments_.name: Ancestors: The Humankind Odyssey

_childDocuments_.review: The game is actually a lot of fun.  In short, you run around, as our ape ancestors, trying to "invent" and "discover" the various things that made us the way that we are -- be it walking on two legs, using sticks and other tools for defence and offence, or whatever else -- in a _very_ unguided way. It's up to you to figure out what to do with something that you see or find -- how to make it useful -- and the game does very little to help you in this regard on purpose, though if you turn up the HUD, that can give you a good sense in many cases. Honestly, I love the way that the game works and find it incredibly fun, but I will say that if you feel frustrated or lost, there are a lot of resources online that can help you figure out how to, for example, get a mate and produce offspring or whatever else you want or need to know. I like that it's fairly unguided because I like "discovering" that I need this or that to do something or that putting a bunch of these things in a pile lets me build "fences" and things like that, though I'm sure that some will find that either daunting or perhaps simply lost.

_childDocuments_.review: **Review of the Game Ancestors: The Humankind Odyssey****Rating: 7/10****Introduction***Ancestors: The Humankind Odyssey* is an ambitious and unique project from Panache Digital Games, led by Patrice Désilets, one of the creators of the Assassin’s Creed series. The game invites players to travel back in time and experience the evolution of humanity, starting with our distant ancestors who lived around 10 million years ago. It’s a captivating experiment that aims to recreate the process of survival and evolution of our early predecessors.**Gameplay**The core gameplay revolves around managing a small clan of primates that gradually evolves and adapts to the surrounding world. The game begins in the forests of Africa, where players must explore the environment, find food, avoid predators, and secure safe places to sleep. With each generation, your clan becomes more advanced, acquiring new skills and adapting to the environment.One of the main features of the gameplay is the lack of clear instructions and hints. The game throws you into a wild world and forces you to figure out the mechanics on your own, which adds to the authenticity of the evolutionary process. However, this aspect might deter less patient players, as the game can sometimes feel overwhelmingly difficult and confusing.**Graphics and Sound**The visual aspect of *Ancestors: The Humankind Odyssey* is impressive. The developers have created a detailed and beautiful world, where the African jungles come to life thanks to high-quality textures, dynamic lighting, and realistic character animations. The sound is also well-executed: the environment is filled with the sounds of wildlife, helping you fully immerse yourself in the game’s atmosphere.**Pros**- **Unique Concept:** The game offers an original take on the process of evolution, which has no analogs in the gaming industry.- **Freedom of Exploration:** Players can choose their own path of development, experimenting with different approaches to survival and evolution.- **Atmosphere:** The graphics and sound create a deep immersion into the world of the wild.**Cons**- **High Difficulty:** The game provides almost no guidance, which can make it challenging for less experienced players.- **Repetitiveness:** Despite the richness of the mechanics, the gameplay can become monotonous and repetitive over time.- **Limited Interactions:** Interactions with the environment and other creatures sometimes feel limited and not always realistic.**Conclusion***Ancestors: The Humankind Odyssey* is a bold and original game that offers a unique experience in the survival and evolution genre. It’s designed for those who are ready to face challenges and patiently explore the mechanics to uncover all its secrets. However, the game is not without its flaws, such as high difficulty and a certain degree of monotony. If you’re looking for something unusual and are up for a challenge, *Ancestors* could be an exciting adventure for you, but don’t expect an easy and intuitive gameplay experience.

_childDocuments_.review: I honestly love this game. It's a combo of "Breath of the Wild" and "Upgrade Complete!" (Yes, the ancient ArmorGames one) You start off as a wimpy borderline useless ape that can only scare off snakes and moves like a sloth on a caffeine binge. You quickly start to develop new skills by doing certain things, such as discovering resources nearby with your senses and practicing standing up. You use "experience" you gain from doing various activities to unlock and activate your new skills as you unlock them. When you change generations, letting your babies mature, adults age, and elders pass on, you can lock in 1-12 of those skills permanently depending on how many babies you have (max 6) and how many of them were exposed to meteorite radiation (+1 per baby). Any skills you haven't locked in will remain unlocked, but you will have to reactivate them during the next generation. Babies also have a 50% chance to be born with a genetic mutation, and can be forcibly given one by exposing them to meteorite radiation. When you activate a generation leap after those babies have grown into adults and elders they'll be unlocked and locked in automatically for you.You quickly grow from a lame, slow, jankily moving ape that has to stay in the trees to avoid predators to an apex predator that can sprint along the ground without needing to worry about predators, because to you the predators you learned to fear in previous generations are now your prey. The seemingly endless, maze like jungle you started off in becomes a small corner of a massive hand crafted map you get to explore at your leisure, full of gorgeous scenery and resources you can experiment with and collect into a treasure trove.The game has a lot of negative reviews which I really haven't experienced the issues of myself. Here's my tips on how to get the most out of it.1: Use a controller. The game starts with an unskippable loading screen that states you should use one. If you don't have one, maybe just add it to your wishlist and forget about it til you can get one. It won't measure up without one.2: The movement starts off pretty bad. IMO, this isn't a game design flaw, it's a feature that helps make future evolutions that enhance your movement abilities all the more satisfying.3: The controls tend to be heavily context specific. For example, A is run and releasing A while you're moving is jump. It's never bothered me, but you should pay attention to the fact that you have control over these differences if you control the context of the input, even if they're admittedly not your traditional control setup.4: The community building/interaction with your clan is largely overstated, but it also gets better as you evolve further. For the most part you can ignore your clan mates completely, they'll teleport to you when you get too far from them as long as they're set to follow you. They're at their worst around other animals, even when you've unlocked the ability for them to dodge and attack automatically. Your best bet is to travel small or fast and use intimidation rather than engage when you've got more than 1 or 2 followers.5: The first 200-300 meters of your starting oasis downriver are perfectly safe. It's only once you're entered the swampy area that the sabre tooth tigers will spawn on you if you're travelling on the ground. They're terrifying at the start, but if you attack them or intimidate them they'll disappear for a while, and if you manage to kill them they won't spawn again in a wide area until you pass generations. Meaning you can clear a path if you take it slow, killing any threats you come across. It's slow, but safe.6: Your current settlement prevents sabre tooth tigers from spawning, and it can be abused to move safely if you feel the need to. It also means you don't have to worry about clan members if they're at your settlement. I HIGHLY recommend only placing your permanent settlement at one of the many discoverable oasis's, specifically centered where the white flowers are growing in circles. It guarantees your borders won't overlap with regular animals' territory and just generally optimizes the AI to work in a non-suicidal manner.7: After a generational leap, your settlement is moved randomly to a nearby oasis. If you feel you're not ready to deal with the new area and the threats that come with it, just travel back upstream and you'll reach your first oasis, and you can re-settle there without consequence.8: Clan members that aren't following you cannot be attacked if they're outside YOUR render distance, and will not die of starvation/dehydration/sleep deprivation, even if they're outside your settlement. Which means you can travel without worry!7: As long as you're near clan members when they're attacked, they won't be killed immediately, including yourself if you fail a dodge. Just approach the attacking animal with a weapon to wound it and make it run off, or use intimidation to make it run off. If you travel with at least 1 other ape, the only thing you have to worry about is a deadly fall.8: The only thing clan members can die from other than being left alone after a direct animal attack is if you leave them bleeding, which you can see at any time in the bottom right corner of the UI. If an ape is bleeding then there will be a dot with a flashing red background. Bleeding doesn't heal on it's own, so you'll have to treat it yourself, either by switching to them or handing them medicine.9: There is a "secret" fast travel method to return to your settlement instantly. Simply allow yourself to reach the hysteria stage of fear by hanging out near enemies such as in a tree above them or by sitting in an undiscovered zone for too long. Your dopamine meter will run out and turn red, then you'll be teleported back home with the message that you freaked out and ran home. *I admittedly do not know if this has a chance to result in death, I've only ever been teleported home safely.There's so much you can do and far more than 40 hours of gameplay available. It starts off as a slow burn that quickly ramps up with your evolution speed, and I highly recommend it to anyone who's curious about it. After just 2 generational leaps I went from a crawling sloth to a bipedal sprinting spear hunter ready to kill anything in my path, from snake to tiger to elephant. A few leaps later and nothing beat the feeling of discovering what lay beyond the desert.

_childDocuments_.review: Im not what you would call the most experienced gamer(up until the past year + where Ive gotten heavy into gaming.) You would think with that said, someone like me would have a terrible time playing a game with little to no instruction, but thats the beauty (AND THE POINT) of it. The player experience very much mimics the chimp/clan experience of having to go with trial and error and hope for the best. For me, each new thing I learned to do was very rewarding as it took the time and effort of learning what works and what doesnt just through literal experimentation. I admit this can be frustrating at times just not knowing what to do, but again, its kinda the point so I didnt let it bug me too much and the determination of wanting to figure out how to use the next new resource I came across forced me to figure it out on my own. This definitely isnt a game for everyone, but contradictory to that is that it actually COULD be a game for everyone from long time gamers, to someone relatively new like myself. I could see an older crowd or younger crowd being interrsted in it for different reasons, and it a small way...it could also be seen as an educational tool in the right aspect. I could see this being a VERY COOL class project in middle school or something. The survival game aspect of collecting and hoarding goods is def there, albeit on a smaller scale of something like say ARK or valheim without a way to carry hundreds of items and craft storage boxes etc. I could definitely see myself playing through this a few times to try and improve with the things I learn and master from each previous playthrough.
_childDocuments_.name: Ancestors: The Humankind Odyssey

_childDocuments_.review: This game needs an expansion that pushes further into the human evolution. Hopefully it inspires another game in the future. Buy that game. Maybe get this one on a 90% sale.

_childDocuments_.review: After getting all of the achievements for this game/beating the game I feel like I’m in a position to give this game a good review for multiple reasons (potential spoilers). Pros----The game map is absolutely massive, so much to explore.The game has amazing graphics. at points if felt taken aback by a certain view I got from a high cliff. truly amazingThe evolution system is great! Having to train a certain skill before you evolve it makes the game more grindy but a lot more fun. I would probably have less hours than I have now if I could just level up what ever skill I wanted when I wanted. The game allows you to forge your own path. The game tells you it wont help you, funny enough it doesn't. when you discover how to do things (like make a spear or crack a coconut) You can’t help but feeling like you accomplished something. My only criticism about this is that the player should be told that you need to pass a generation to keep mutations (I’m pretty sure in some menus it was there, but early on I didn’t understand why I was loosing them)Cons----Although this game is one of the best, I’ve played there are drawbacks.After the midgame, tasks become tedious, you already know what to do so you don’t get the same feeling of accomplishment as easily (I only got this when I killed a new animal or saved my ape from the grips of death) When you get near the endgame you literally run out of things to do. I backtracked from the ocean to the starting oasis to find unexplored locations so I can finally beat the game. but there was no sense of accomplishment there, it was annoying. There is 0 replayability with this game. once you have beat it and got all of the achievements starting a new clan wont feel the same. you might start by making a spear (like I did) . which most of us didn't learn until the first or second evolution leap, in my case I didn’t know how to do an evolution leap, so I discovered a good portion of the jungle before making one lmaoooo. All and all this game is amazing. but can get boring rather quick.
