_childDocuments_.review: One of the best co-op shooters ever made, and I wish I could find anything else like it. While Deep Rock Galactic borrows elements from Left4Dead, Team Fortress 2, Minecraft, and other games, it is greater than the sum of its parts and none of those others really capture the same magic of this game.The addictive gameplay loop involves 1-4 players playing four unique classes across 8 different mission types in procedurally-generated, fully destructible worlds, beautifully realized in Unreal Engine with shockingly good performance. Since each map and biome feels different, every mission feels like its own little puzzle. One map might entail a search for minerals in cramped and claustrophobic sand tunnels, whereas another involves setting up pipelines is a vast and overwhelming glacial cave; each provides its own challenges to overcome for all classes. For me, the appeal of the game at this point is two-fold: (1) there's always something to do; whether it's shooting alien bugs, reviving a teammate, completing an objective, or doing all of them at the same time and (2) incrementally learning to do all of these things better and better; min-maxing builds for different mission types, making subtle improvements to strategy, and controlling the chaos to consistently overcome higher and higher hazard levels.For anyone looking to take the game too seriously, I recommend checking out YouTubers like AxisKronos, LazyMaybe, FourLeafGaming, waste, and USteppin, to name just a few. They have links for useful discord channels on their YouTube profiles. For an encyclopedic tips & tricks guide, I highly recommend googling DRG Tips & Tricks by CupNoodles27 on Github. I also recommend getting into mods (google mod.io drg) sooner than later since the developer has done an amazing job of incorporating them into the game. I would recommend starting off with Verified mods since these were approved by the developer for normal gameplay and don't impact other players. There are a ton of awesome quality of life mods that greatly improve the experience like Showable Legs, Brighter Objects, Steeve Better Visibility, and Pickaxe Bonk! SFX, to name a few of the most important.And don't forget that, legally speaking, rocking is more legal than stoning -- godspeed miners!

_childDocuments_.review: + stylish character and world design, with fully customizable dwarfs and breathtaking levels+ excellent gunplay with satisfying combat action, great technical performance+ efficient soundtrack with horror and scifi atmosphere+ lots of weapons, armor, hats, weapon skins and 4 types of facial hair+ No cash shop or real money tokens, ingame currency only+ free new gameplay content since release, dlcs are optional cosmetics+ optional missions for extra loot and experience, addiotonal challenges+ bar area with minigame, beer recipes, jukebox and dancefloor+ intimidating enemies that act in packs or ambushes, featureing Tyranid-like boss creatures- very time intense, grindheavy, game has addictive properties- no test drive option for guns or upgrades, some overpriced or borderline redundant- robot npcs have annoying movement patterns- End game unlocks are almost entirely luck based- Hazard 3 and 4 need difficulty tweaking- no crafting or player trading- unpolished low budget voice acting that gives limbo of the lost vibes, gets repeatative- no streaming material, boring to watch for uninitiatedI can say with little doubt that Deep Rock Galactic is currently one of the best inexpensive FPS game that you can currently purchase on steam. its the best shooter game ive played in well over five years and can be enjoyed just as much alone as with friends. _childDocuments_.review: After playing Season 5 for a bit, I'd say my review has gone from negative to mixed. The new overclocks that they have added were a breath of fresh air, some of them are very gimmicky which is awesome, it allows for some new playstyles and adds more interesting ways to play a class. Genuinely very good part of the season.I also liked the fact that the season wasn't really themed around anything, having evil stuff happening on Hoxxes every year felt a bit comical. The new enemies are alright, Stalker has his place and has his moments, the aoe spitballer type enemy sounds cool but so far he feels a bit weak, Scalebramble is ok but I kinda don't get understand the point of his existence, like is he meant to be a little time waster to look out for when entering a new cave (similiar to cave leeches)??This season felt more like an update we used to get which is fine by me. I still think it's funny they're called seasons though. However, I'm still mixed because of the way overclock system works. I had friends who dropped the game when they realized they'd have to come back weekly to play to get cool new upgrades for their guns, they couldn't progress at the pace they wanted. And even back when I was on the grind myself, I wasn't a big fan of it too at times. Getting matrix cores upon promotions was a step in the right direction, it was something I wished for a long time. Tho I still think something needs to be done about this system. And in conclusion, if you're reading this thinking whether you should get the game or not, I do think it's worth the money. Just keep in mind that you'll have to play weekly to get to the cool part of the gun modifications faster. Old review that I wrote when Season 4 released (I think, i forgor tbh) below:I only recommend getting this game for modding, as they actually make the game good.Think of interesting overclock idea, maybe like a grenade launcher that shoots smoke grenades that give enemies in radius a debuff at the cost of not having any splash damage. Now think of a boring overclock, like less damage but more ammo. The most boring one is the one that actually makes it into the game.Seasons don't change gameplay in any way and it's mostly just a event, new coat of paint in the lobby, new cosmetic slop drop and a comically low effort dlc.Basically, devs make the most blandest decisions possible (kinda like Mojang lol) and don't really experiment with gameplay ideas. Bring the GSG boys from 2019 back - the ones that made silly balance and game design decisions BUT AT LEAST they were trying new things, not making the same thing over and over but slightly different.

_childDocuments_.review: Yes, I do recommend this game.This game feels like an amalgamation (did I spell that right?) of all the games I really wanted to enjoy. It feels like the developers have really sat down and looked at popular games and asked themselves "what makes these games fun?"I think what grabs me with this game is how they have made a vanity shop without money involved. You get the same progression, but it's actually FUN to play it. I don't have to constantly open my wallet, but instead I ponder how to maximize profits. It keeps me in the game and is a genuine escape from my day-to-day life at the moment.Gameplay is pretty straight forward, and I doubt you'll have much issue getting into the game quickly. A great tutorial exists in the game which is repeatable. I enjoy the art style even though it was a bit jarring to get to grips with the way the dwarves look. The caves you explore are varied, and there is enough enemy types to keep you on your toes. All in all this game has a lot going for it.The main pull of the game for me is the community. This game HEAVILY promotes teamwork. It makes people pull together and you will find a very patient community that just enjoys playing the game. Add on that the communication system in the game (VOIP and basic emotes) is enough to make a team communicate well, even without words. If you dwarf sais something, everyone around you hears it. That means "out of ammo" is broadcasted so everyone knows.I love this game. It's great.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're looking for a fun co-op shooter to play with your friends, look no further. Explore dark caves, mow down waves of unfeeling insectoid killing machines, and mine valuable minerals to pay off your bar tab!I've always enjoyed playing first-person-shooters, especially in multiplayer with my friends. I used to play a lot of Team Fortress 2, CSGO, Titanfall 2, and Rainbow Six Siege, but after awhile I got burned out of playing with and against strangers who could sometimes be jerks or cheaters. I still wanted to be able to play with my friends, but I just couldn't enjoy playing online anymore.Fortunately, I received this game as a gift a few months ago and I have been playing it frequently ever since. Blasting the bugs is satisfying and there's enough variety in the weapons and class features between the dwarves that I can change things up and keep it feeling fresh even after playing for 250+ hours. The developers are also legit, providing free content updates to the game and including a battle-pass style bonus unlock system that is . _childDocuments_.review: I haven't written a review in awhile, but this game deserves one. Do you like exploration? this game has randomly generated biomes, and I've yet to be disappointed by the unique threats and environments they've created. Despite how stylized the graphics may look, the game is gorgeous in it's own way.Do you like cooperative team based survival games, like Left for Dead? This game is perfect. Every class has its own quirks that help you control the battlefield via exploration or combat. "Does that mean I'm gonna be hardstuck playing a class I don't like with my group of friends?" Sure as ♥♥♥♥ doesn't. You can all run the same class and have slightly different builds to make up for the minor setbacks, but you'll have a bit of a leg up in the classes specialty. "But what if I don't have friends to play with?" Cool, the matchmaking works just fine and the community is rather wholesome and welcoming. Or if you'd rather play by yourself to learn the ropes for a little bit, you can have a little drone help you explore, mine, and fight hordes of never ending bugs.On top of all of that, the devs are remarkably passionate and transparent, and have an amazing track record thusfar. The entry price for the game itself is remarkably cheap for how much content is in the game. Especially considering every single DLC content that they've added has been purely cosmetic. This is one of the very few games I've ever bought cosmetic DLCs for, if not the only one, PURELY to support the developers. This is a game that's hard to really review and give you an idea of what it is when you're unsure if it's for you. If you've made it this far you're on the fence and looking for that definitive "Yes" or "No" review. Just glance at the ratio of positive to negative reviews, and that should be your answer.And don't forget, ROCK AND STONE!

_childDocuments_.review: DRG is easily in the Top 10 co-op experiences in all of gaming history.I actually bounced off the game earlier on because I was a little too turned off by the initial visuals, and I didn't really understand some of the depth that is built into the core gameplay loop. A little later on, I got back into the game when it had some extra polish and was seeing it's first big boom in popularity. I was kinda angry with myself that I had such a bad read on it the first time around.It's a total package. Visuals aren't excellent in terms of fidelity or anything, but they are so well-designed and coherent in presentation of the world that only really petty gamers would take issue with them. Bright, vibrant colors. Interesting designs. Strangely believable equipment and environments for a game about dwarven miners in space. Excellent use of lighting (both to guide the player, and at the same is it's own gameplay element). And level design that, while procedural, often manages to be artistic in it's structure.The sound is incredibly underrated in DRG. From the soundtrack being a list of solid tracks one after another, to the really expertly deployed audio queues about enemies and the environment, to great voice acting, and of course awesome sounding weapons and tools. Any veteran dwarf knows the sound of BET-C, an exploder about to detonate, or that impressively gross burping sound of a Glyphid Menace.And of course there's the meat of the gameplay. I can't and shouldn't really go into the whole game here. There's a surprising amount of depth with the progression system, upgrades, and overclocks that would take up too much space and ruin a lot of the fun of discovery and trials with all the new toys you can get. There are a variety of mission types, with more being added in new seasons, four different classes (but each with a handful of different playstyles based on loadouts), a dozen or more enemy types, and several different biomes each with their own unique characteristics that affect the gameplay of every mission. No two missions are the same, but they all still follow broad themes. Teamwork is required for the higher Hazard levels, but at the lower ones DRG can be pretty casual and relaxing. Even if you're bad at shooters - you can just get a gun that automatically targets things for you, or (my preference) take the nuclear option because accuracy doesn't matter when your firepower is measured in Sieverts!This is one of the few games that I can confidently say is for just about everyone. And it's continued success and growth only suggests a very bright future moving forward. DRG has real staying power. Join today and dig for victory!

The developers put so much effort into realizing their hyper focused vision - you are a dwarf working for a galactic mining corporation on a deadly planet. Everything is built around this including the hub world.The DEV team is continuing to update this gem. There is no pay to win, but a few DLC packs have amazing cosmetic additions. I have purchased a few because I feel like I owe it to the makers of this game to continue to support their work.Music is great, cave generator will make you say "whaaaaaaattt" a least once a session, wide range of difficulty if you want to pickaxe and chill or go full tight butthole for an hour straight (looking at you Elite Deep Dive).The only room for opportunity here is a lackluster perk and promotion system. There are lots of reasons to pump hours into this game, but the end game is less rewarding after you have promoted your characters and gotten most of the good overclock upgrades. Keep doing what you are doing devs, and start to look into the end-game a little as you build out your roadmap.Rock and Stone.9/10

_childDocuments_.review: There was a time--probably a decade ago--where my friends and I would play video games all weekend. This is why Deep Rock Galactic is perfect.The format allows us to play 3-4 hours a week without committing ourselves to a grand campaign. We can catch up while still blasting away some aliens. _childDocuments_.review: Updating this review as of 1.0 release:Dwarfs, Digging, Destroying local flora and fauna in a area that is procedural generated.. whats not to love!?The game is simple but fun..Deploy, complete objectives(find x of y resource etc), extract, profit.Progression is via levels that unlock cosmetics and upgrades for your equipment.You purchase these items via credits and special resources you collect when doing missions.You can further upgrade your weapons with 'Overclocks' that rebalance the weapon they are applied to with buff/debuffs.The game scales from 1-4 players well so even if you only want to run in a group of 2 or 3 this is possible.For the solo players you get to command an AI hovering drone that can dig, fight and collect.There is lots to unlock now like cosmetics, perks(character perks), and overclocks(weapon perks)!New biomes, missions and mission modifiers(no shields, more gold, exploding critters)For end-game there is Deep-Dives which put you into a 3 mission chain where your resources from mission 1 carry on through the dive with rewards for completing each level of the dive.And for those that might only play now and then, there is also weekly missions to complete that give you resources and or items.All in all, it is a solid and enjoyable game if you are into 4 player coop/gathering games.Personally I really enjoy the game and would say it is well worth its price if you enjoy coop shooters.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game.  Going on mining expeditions with my friends has been one of the most fun things I've done in a while.  The tense, action-packed, and even the frustrating and hilarious moments during each mission have made every single play session worth it.. we've had stories to tell to the people who couldn't be there, and funny references to old missions to bring up and laugh about.For those of you who don't have online friends who would play this, you can always jump in with some random people on servers, and there's even a built-in voice chat function for communicating with those people.  Even if you don't have a headset, you can use the pointer tool for some basic communication.. so really, just play this game in multiplayer if possible, I don't think it'd be as fun solo, even though that's an option.Just when we were thinking that the game might have a little too much repetitiveness, we found out that there are more game modes.. in addition to mining and egg-collection missions that are availible early on, you'll eventually be able to get access to hunting and point extraction missions, which play fairly differently.  The enemy variety COULD be a little better, but it's fine as-is.. and maybe more enemies will be added during the Early Access period anyway, we'll just have to see.The 4 distinct classes work well together in almost any configuration.  Though it's probably best to have a mix of different classes in a team, it's perfectly playable if everyone wants to play the same class, really.  More engineers means more turrets and placable platforms.. more gunners means more ziplines and more firepower.. The sky is the limit, and you'll find yourself having a unique type of fun and challenges with any configuration.I love playing Gunner, because I love ziplining around the levels.. especially during escape sequences, when seconds matter toward getting back to the dropship in time, and large gaps may need to be crossed, however, I can't tell you how many times we've had our butts saved by my friend playing Driller who simply tunnelled us to victory.  We like to laugh at our Scout, who tends to die a lot from fall damage, but is good at finding where we need to go next.. and our Engineer, whose turrets have gotten us out of plenty of sticky, hectic enemy swarms.The feeling of cooperation in this game is hard to match... and like I said before, you'll certainly have some awesome stories you'll be able to tell from your expeditions down into this games varied types of cave systems and mission types will.This is Early Access done correctly.  The game is already fun, already stable, already great.. and it can only get better from here on.  I look forward to seeing what the updates bring.  If you're thinking about this, Definitely get it!

_childDocuments_.review: This game, and its developers, are incredible; a true diamond in the rough. DRG blends fun missions, excellent level design, and teamwork-rewarding game design into one true masterpiece. There are gameplay elements for almost anyone—dozens of things to mine, hundreds of items to unlock, and countless waves of diverse enemies to blast through.On top of this, the dev team is one of the greatest I've ever encountered in my entire life of gaming. They deliver constant, high quality updates that have yet to disappoint, and listen closely to community feedback and are not afraid to make changes because of it. Also, aside from a supporter upgrade (which does nothing but give you a gold skin and supports the devs), there are absolutely zero micro transactions.If you don't have any friends to play with (like myself 90% of the time), this game is still great for the solo player. With the help of a personal drone, every single class can solo any mission on their own, and it even provides some extra fun trying to think of unconventional ways to reach far-off items or traverse enormous caves.Finally, this game has one of the best communities I've ever been a part of. In my 100+ hours of playtime (most of which is online with strangers), I have yet to encounter any toxicity. Seriously, this game is possibly the only place on the internet where everyone is nice and friendly. People are friendly and courteous to you as soon as you join their lobby, and (unless they are newbies themselves) are quick to cooperate with you in game. If it weren't for this amazing community, I wouldn't have  the amount of playtime as I do. This is one of my favorite games of the past few years, and is quickly becoming one of my favorites of all time. This game, the dev team, and the community are all top notch, and are without a question worth your support and the many hours you will inevitably sink into it.

_childDocuments_.review: Deep Rock Galactic* and the 500 Lives I Saved: A Journey from Pixels to RealityThere are moments in life when a game transcends entertainment and becomes something more profound—something that shapes your actions and changes your perspective. For me, that game was *Deep Rock Galactic*. It’s not just a co-op, sci-fi, mining, and combat game; it’s where I learned the value of teamwork, sacrifice, and the kind of grit that extends beyond the digital universe. Little did I know that playing this game would eventually lead me to saving the lives of 500 homeless people. I know, it sounds insane, but let me explain.It all started innocently enough. A few friends and I were looking for something to do together, something cooperative and fun. After a couple of rounds of various games, we stumbled across *Deep Rock Galactic*—a game where you play as a team of dwarves sent into deep, alien caves to mine valuable resources. There’s a catch, though: the caves are crawling with dangerous creatures, and the mission is dangerous from the moment you step inside. But what really drew me in was the camaraderie—four dwarves, working together, each with different skills, facing impossible odds in the pursuit of profit.At first, it was all fun. The game was an exhilarating mix of combat, resource gathering, and working as a team to stay alive. There were moments of chaos, moments of triumph, and moments of failure. As a team, we’d get overwhelmed by alien swarms or buried in the depths of the cave, our way out blocked by shifting terrain. We learned quickly that *Deep Rock Galactic* wasn’t about playing solo—it was about relying on your teammates, each dwarf’s skills complementing the others’. Without communication and trust, the whole mission would fail. But as I spent more time playing the game, something unexpected started to happen. It wasn’t the game mechanics or the addictive loop of mining and shooting that started to stick with me—it was the *feeling* of teamwork and purpose. Each mission in *Deep Rock Galactic* was about making it to the extraction point alive, ensuring that everyone had what they needed to survive, and that no dwarf was left behind. It was about sacrifice—doing whatever it took to protect your crew, even if it meant putting yourself in danger.I didn’t know it at the time, but this mindset would change everything for me.One weekend, while playing with my friends, I found myself reflecting on what I was really doing with my life. I’d been in a rut for a while—working long hours at a desk job that drained me, living in a city that felt increasingly detached and impersonal. I had no real sense of purpose outside of work and gaming. It wasn’t until I found myself in one of those high-pressure *Deep Rock Galactic* missions, where the whole team was about to fail, that I had this strange moment of clarity. I was working with my team to fight off hordes of enemies and trying to clear a path to the extraction point, and in that moment, it hit me: **If we could band together to survive in this game, why couldn’t we do something similar in real life? Why couldn’t we come together to help people in need?**The thought stayed with me for days, gnawing at my conscience. I was sitting comfortably at home, playing with my friends, while others in the world—people struggling with homelessness—had no such luxury. They were stuck in real-life caves, in a sense—trapped in situations that felt impossible to escape. It was a stark realization: **I had a chance to make a difference, to be part of something bigger than just my own comfort.**I couldn’t shake it. The idea of rescue, the idea of *saving* people from their own alien-like cave, took root in my mind. And like any good mission in *Deep Rock Galactic*, it needed a plan. I began researching local shelters, talking to people involved in homelessness outreach, and trying to figure out how I could take action. I wanted to be a part of the solution, not just a bystander in the face of such overwhelming need. I began to understand that helping people wasn’t just about writing a check or volunteering on occasion—it was about building a system of support, about pulling people out of the metaphorical caves and providing them with the tools and resources they needed to survive, thrive, and ultimately escape their situation.Soon, I was in contact with several local non-profits. At first, I helped organize fundraisers and drive supplies. But as I got more involved, I realized that my work wasn’t just about giving material resources—it was about creating lasting change, about restoring dignity and hope. I wanted to offer more than just handouts; I wanted to help build a community where homeless people could get the help they needed, whether it was shelter, mental health services, job training, or simply a hand to pull them out of the depths they were trapped in.The more time I spent helping, the more I realized how much the analogy to *Deep Rock Galactic* applied. Homelessness, in many ways, was a game where survival was the ultimate goal, and each person needed a team to survive. A team of people who were willing to fight alongside them, no matter how dark or dangerous the environment. And like the dwarves in the game, I began to see that no one should be left behind.I decided to make it my personal mission to rescue 500 people from homelessness in my city. It wasn’t easy. There were countless setbacks—shelters full to capacity, bureaucracy that slowed progress, and the harsh reality of how deep the problem went. But each small success kept me going, kept me motivated. I spent hours organizing events, building partnerships with local businesses to create job opportunities, and advocating for policies that would provide more affordable housing. I poured everything I had into it. The same teamwork and resolve that I had learned from playing *Deep Rock Galactic* became my guiding principles. **Rescue wasn’t just about completing a mission. It was about lifting others up, making sure no one got left behind, and working together to break through barriers.**Eventually, I reached my goal: 500 people helped off the streets and into safe environments where they could start rebuilding their lives. These weren’t just numbers to me—they were lives saved, families reunited, individuals who had been lost in the system now given the chance for a future. It felt like we had fought our way through the worst of the alien infested caves, and now we had our hands on the precious resources they so desperately needed to survive.In the end, *Deep Rock Galactic* wasn’t just a game I played for fun—it was a catalyst that inspired me to take action, to use the values of teamwork, sacrifice, and perseverance to make a tangible impact in the world. The feeling of pulling together, rescuing my fellow dwarves from danger, eventually turned into the motivation to rescue real people, helping them out of the caves of homelessness and into a better future. If anything, I learned that games can teach us more than we think—especially when we realize that sometimes, the most important missions aren’t the ones we complete on the screen. Sometimes, the real mission is saving lives. And sometimes, it all starts with a game that teaches you to fight for those who can’t fight for themselves.

They are each very fun to play. Some people like to main one class, but I more or less play them all equally.The game combines the teamwork of classic co-op games with the fully procedurally generated and destructable environment of Minecraft. _childDocuments_.review: I CAN'T FEEL MY BEARD! HELP!It's very much like Left4Dead was when it first came out. You team up with friends (if you have any, you bearded blunderbuss) and wade through wave after wave of enemies. It's not easy. The objectives are fun and the caves range from too easy to ridiculously difficult to traverse. When you find a team of players who know their spelunking, you can pull off some seriously rough missions; that feeling of having left behind some skin after a harrowing escape is what I play this game for!The dev team is exceptional! For an Early Access game, I expected some wonkiness and bugs. There was phenomenal wonkiness and there were tons of bugs - thousands, even, but that's what I paid for. I have so many bugs I bought a flak cannon to get rid of them. This game is super fun when you have friends in Discord, all organizing and getting the job done as best you can.There is plenty of replay value, since you have quite a large improvement system and tons of different ways to set up your character. There are a fair number of different mission types, a fair spread of different bug types (there could always be more!) and more weapons than your dwarf can carry on a single mission. Bouncy plasma ftw.I highly recommend this game if you enjoyed TF2 or L4D. Some asymmetrical multiplayer could make this even more intense (like L4D2 was) but the devs have a pretty well planned roadmap. Can't wait to see what they have for the next year or two!

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent show in the team shooter genre with a unique take being that your purpose is to explore for minerals to mine for while also hunting monsterous bugs of various type.  Each mission type feels like a unique experience and it is easy to stay engaged through the multitude of mission/map combinations.  The downtime, upgrade, and cosmetics system are extremely well developed too.  As much as you can play for fun, there are plenty of upgrades cosmetic rewards to fight for as well to inspire those who enjoy rewards for their time invested.  All told, this game can easily keep you engaged be you a solo player or someone looking for a team multiplayer shooter.

_childDocuments_.review: A fun game that's worth your time and money. Though it can feel a bit grindy at times, because there's a ton of stuff to unlock, you can play for a long time without feeling any need to worry about those things. There's a wide variety of missions to play so you'll get plenty of game play in without feeling bored.The game also supports a wide range of play styles. You can choose from a few different difficulty levels, which is great for days when you want to relax and mine some goodies, or days where you want a challenge. For those who want a big challenge, there's a fifth difficulty level that you can unlock after completing some missions. You can also unlock deep-dive missions for more game play.I've also found the community to be very non-toxic. It's easy to jump in with a group of players and have a good time. It's also possible to solo all missions if that's how you'd rather play.

_childDocuments_.review: I have spent over 650 hours in the caves since my first review of Deep Rock Galactic (which I have left below)The game has gone from strength to strength. Expanded in every direction. It is now, more than ever before, filled to the brim with content, re-playability and endless, endless amounts of fun. Each game is a fresh experience, each tricky situation a new puzzle to unravel, each new player that you meet a potential friend.This game has done more for me in a tricky period in my life (a tricky period in everybody's lives, really) than any news report or real world action could ever hope to achieve. It is a remarkable, unique piece of work that has, in short, altered my life.I cannot recommend this game enough. Dare I say, or even whisper it in such esteemed company, but it is my favourite game of all time.Rock and Stone!- - - - -Imagine it; you're a space Dwarf and you're on a mining mission. You're so deep underground that there's not a ray of natural light. Everything that you can see, all the beautiful caverns and ravines, are illuminated by equipment that's flickering and humming as if it's all held together with sticky tape. There's giant bugs everywhere, but you've got your colleagues and a host of big guns. There's treasure to be gotten and you'll be damned if you're going to let it go un-dug.This game is like the job that you've never known you've wanted; presented to you without possibility of dismemberment or digestion-by-giant-bug. After choosing one of four very cool and different classes, you undertake a task and delve into a a randomly generated cave. You dig, blast and laugh to your heart's content. You level up by gathering xp and resources, and spend these on upgraded gear and new beard-styles. Simple, effective and amazing fun.Everything is presented in a wonderful polygonal style - where you need to go, what you need to dig and what you need to shoot are all displayed to you very clearly. You'll feel and work like a pro and look fantastic doing it.The soundtrack is almost a masterwork and will get your heart pumping at times and set out a magnificent atmosphere at others.There isn't much else to say here apart from this: Deep Rock Galactic is one of my favourite games of the last decade. Recommended with highest (and deepest) honours.Rock n' stone!

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the best games ever created. I love every aspect of this game and quite frankly there's no other co-op shooter that even comes close. You seriously can't get a more fun, unique experience.  Drink yourself stupid, hop in your orbital drop pod, mine incredible riches from a deadly world, and kill thousands of alien monstrosities while you're at it. Then, once you've collected a kingdom's ransom worth of gold and jewels, return to the satellite and drink yourself stupid again. That is the life of a dwarf.There's a ton of super fun weapons and the overclocks which are the "Endgame progression" of the game are all fantastic. I have only found about half a dozen overclocks that are "unfun" or "Boring," because most of the overclocks are nothing if not fun tweaks to your existing weapons. Sometimes an overclock straight up changes the weapon into a brand new one, like the Icicle Spear for the Frost Launcher, or the Neurotoxin Payload for the Thunderhad Auto-Cannon, or the new Goo Bomber Special for the Toxic Sludge Cannon.There's so many fun little details that really flesh out the game. You finish the escort mission, and the head of the Drill Dozer pops off and you can bring it back to the drop pod. It doesn't give you any resources or anything special for doing it. So why? Because No Dwarf Gets Left Behind, and you'll be damned if you leave Doretta down there with the bugs. You can tip your bartender with a few credits. This doesn't actually do anything for you because 1. you won't get a discount because it's a tip, not some sort of secret payment and 2. the bartender is a ROBOT. He can't actually BUY things. But you do it anyway, because Lloyd is the best damn bartender in the system and your beer is delicious. There's a jukebox to dance to, a soccer minigame to play with others, a barrel-kicking minigame, and so much more and it's all just in the game, not technically contributing to the core gameplay loop in any way but it's so damn fun. They could very easily have just automated all the screens between missions, from the buffs, to the cosmetics, to the mission selection, to the armory, to the smithing. But the developers chose to give you an entire playground of a space rig to hang out in, drinking beer and dancing badly to crappy music because it's FUN.This game is all about FUN. Play it. ROCK AND STONE!

_childDocuments_.review: This is the sort of game that makes me cry out for it to do more, but in a good way.  It's so polished I constantly forget it's early access, and it has the best destructible terrain and accompanying movement physics I've seen in any game, period.  When I'm using the game's amazing digging and terraforming mechanics, I'm constantly wishing for the DRG team to add more persistence to this game, or use their engine for a persistent world game.  Oh, how I'd love to settle down, make a home in one of these caves and really make it my own...  Nonetheless, as is, this is already a killer fun game.  It manages to be tightly paced and exciting, and with terraforming tools so streamlined that modifying the cave to your needs doesn't feel cumbersome even though you know it's ephemeral, and a variety of fun-to-use weapons with pretty effects.  This game doesn't use its digging as a crutch, and would be a super fun and well-paced bug shooter even if it didn't have such an amazing terrain engine.  But it does, and it opens up a whole extra world of possibilities for fun tactics and cheese, but clever and versatile enough enemies that none of your cheap tricks work as a silver bullet.

_childDocuments_.review: Deep Rock Galactic is a game that truly rocks! This game is an absolute blast to play and is definitely one of the most entertaining games I have played in a long time. I am not a big fan of shooters, but this game has won me over with its exciting gameplay and hilarious humor.From the moment you start the game, you are immediately immersed in a world of dwarven miners who have been tasked with exploring and mining the depths of an alien planet. The game's graphics are stunning, and the attention to detail is impressive. The environments are beautifully rendered, and the creatures you encounter are terrifyingly realistic.What really sets Deep Rock Galactic apart from other games is its sense of humor. The dwarves are a hilarious bunch, and their banter and interactions with each other are always entertaining. The game also has a unique and quirky soundtrack that perfectly complements the game's style and tone.The gameplay is incredibly engaging and addictive. You and your team of dwarves must work together to explore the planet, gather resources, and fight off waves of alien creatures. Each mission is unique and offers its own set of challenges and obstacles to overcome.One of the best things about this game is the sense of progression. As you play, you earn experience points that allow you to unlock new weapons, gear, and upgrades for your dwarves. This adds a sense of accomplishment and satisfaction to the gameplay, and encourages you to keep playing and exploring.In conclusion, Deep Rock Galactic is an absolute gem of a game. It's funny, entertaining, and offers hours of engaging gameplay. If you're looking for a game that is both challenging and hilarious, then this is the game for you. So grab your pickaxe, put on your mining helmet, and get ready for an adventure that's out of this world!

_childDocuments_.review: Deep Rock Galactic is a game I can only describe as an original. It takes ideas laid out by its predecessors and refines them into pure, precious minerals. To be devoured by Loot Bugs. In ten years, I believe people will look back on this game fondly. It's a classic in the making.Procedurally generated voxel caves are the big feature of this game. You will never play the same stage twice, and I personally guarantee that (Except in cases of Deep Dives, which are purposely static seeds.)The degree of unique terrain generation Deep Rock Galactic has is absolutely staggering. It creates unique gameplay every single time you step foot off of the drill pod.The story is simple. You're a space-mining dwarf. Your mining company, Deep Rock Galactic, employs you to enter the treacherous caves of Hoxxes IV. The planet is full of irritating little (and all other sizes of) bugs that want to kill you. Others are harmless, some are even helpful. Regardless, it is also full of valuable minerals and resources that the company would gladly throw you into a pit for. You, a dwarf, however, are really hard to kill. This helps as the entire planet is attempting to do so.There are four classes: Driller, Scout, Engineer, and Gunner. Each of them does about what their names suggest. All classes have alternate choices for each of their main weapons that you can unlock down the road as you rank up. Each class has an assortment of different gadgets to assist their teammates. Every class has one piece of equipment in common: Your pickaxe.The Gunner is the heavy. Pick this guy if your weapon of choice is heavy, requires time to rev up, and shoots really ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ fast. Gunner's sidearm is handgun that kicks and does a ton of precision damage. Gunner also has a zipline that helps you traverse chasms, in addition to a nifty shield generator that creates a bubble to keep you safe.The Scout is the lightweight. If something is hard to reach, you send the Scout. Despite being armed with Lightweight weaponry, he is nothing short of lethal. This class' damage is nothing to sneeze at. With a carbine as your primary, you can spray to your heart's content. Secondary consists of a double-barreled shotgun, with the traversal tool being a grappling hook and last but not least, a Flare Gun with extremely bright (but non-regenerative) flares that can keep an entire cavern well-lit.The Driller is the go-to excavator. Armed with a flamethrower and a powerful set of drills, they can create paths to anywhere in the map if necessary. Secondary is a pistol, but despite being just a handgun it can punch well above its weight. Lastly, an explosive satchel charge for when excavation starts to feel too dull or boring the traditional way.The Engineer is, as his name would suggest, the one with all the neat gadgets. An automatic shotgun, and a grenade launcher are the arsenal for this one, with a Sentry turret (can be upgraded to allow for two to be placed at once) that needs refilling as it mows down legions of disgusting bugs. Their tertiary is a platform gun, which does exactly as one would expect: creates platforms where you shoot it.Each of these classes brings their own distinct, meaningful flavor to the roster. Together, anything can be accomplished. The game takes its time introducing you to each new mission type and mechanic, and it can be a bit of a slog at first. However, the breadth and variety of each of the mission types will likely always keep you from getting bored. You can simply do mining expeditions, all the way to setting up a complex underground oil rig with pumps to defend.There are eleven different locales in the game (at the time of writing) that are all crafted with great care, precision and love from the developers. They all have different types of minerals and resources that can be farmed and are used to craft different items at the workbenches placed around your home base.For those of you with personalization desires, each of your classes can be outfitted with all kinds of neat hairstyles, hats, facial features like beards and mustaches, and paintjobs for your gear and weapons. Here at Deep Rock, we take pride in the variance of our workforce.For anyone seeking a more involved challenge, end-game experiences like Deep Dives and Elite Deep Dives are the crowning achievement of a miner's career. Each week a randomly generated new seed is put into the Deep Dive terminal, allowing you to play it for a change at high-tier cosmetics and gear overclocks that alter your arsenal. These are not for the faint of heart, and can sometimes range into hours-long sessions at a time. Be prepared before you step foot into the depths of Hoxxes.New content is coming all the time, and by the time you end up reading this review, new features will likely be on the way or implemented. With all that said, Deep Rock Galactic thanks you for listening to this introductory guideline to your mining adventures. Take good care of your pickaxe, look after your crew, and always remember: Rock and Stone.

_childDocuments_.review: A great game that is consistently being updated by the developers. I've played close to 20 hours of the game, with friends, and find it to be a great multiplayer experience. The main basis of the game is that you, and three other dwarven space miners, go on missions to collect various minerals from planets that are infested by alien-bugs. Pretty much Starship Troopers, if your mission was to mine instead of wiping out the alien-bug race. You, and your crew, will traverse the underground of the planets you visit, collecting minerals, fixing machines, and fighting back the bug menace until you can escape back to your ship. The game is really meant to be a multiplayer game, so if you're looking for a singleplayer experience, look elsewhere. The game itself can be very challenging at times, depending on the difficulty you set for missions, as well as the experience of your crew. A great game with various mechanics that work, and the gameplay is pretty smooth for what it is. As for graphics, think a slightly updated version of Minecraft, without the pixels, but it certainly works for this game.If you're looking for a great multiplayer game, that you can put more and more hours into, and that the developers are updating regularly, then look no further.....plus if you like the movie Starship Troopers that couldn't hurt either.Overall, I'd say its 4/5 stars, especially for the price.

_childDocuments_.review: I only dislike this game because of how quickly it becomes repetitive for gameplay sustinence- and of course I only poured just over 6 hours into it, but I genuinely didn't feel much when it came to my finalized thoughts at that point. I can understand why it's highly Overwhelmingly Positive, because it appeals to that niche of mindless fun. Even as I type this and fully am aware that I kindof played myself for getting into something I wasn't *quite* sure I'd like, I thought it would be my cup of tea since I love games with seemingly endless grind like Destiny. But hey, friends gotta peer pressure one way or another. I don't discourage playing this game, because you quite clearly are either on the bandwagon of love or you're not, and that bandwagon is pretty giant, so most people must love this game. I more or less just might be a rare instance where the gameplay didn't click because of peer pressure, or because it didn't feel similar enough to other games, and I may never be entirely sure what it was. By all means, buy this game if you deep down know that you'll be wanting to grind endlessly for hours upon hours upon hours, essentially being led by how minimal the game's complexity is. Plenty of games in my past have done that exact same thing, just differently, and can be psychologically tailored without the developer knowing or not. So I can fully understand why the game is Overwhelmingly Positive, I'm more or less just an outlier for the crowd.

_childDocuments_.review: Breakpoints matter. Appropriate difficulty settings. Mission-based objectives. A war against topology: Skill-based, role-based FPS combat, with exploration, terraforming, and light platforming. Active development team is creating more content.You are a miner. You come equipped with thousands of rounds of ammunition, devastating explosives, on-demand infinite defense, and Dwarven sensibility.On topology: Your enemies are not bound by gravity! The innumerable Glyphid chase you across walls and ceilings, but are equipped only with their jaws. While they don't need light to see, they also can't jump - you can take advantage of their mode of locomotion by jumping across small gaps.On terraforming: each role has a mobility ability. The Scout can grapple to any surface (and has a lighting tool); everyone else changes the shape of the world. The Driller drills away material, while the Engineer adds platforms. The Gunner fires ziplines, enabling fellow dwarves to ascend cliffs and cross chasms.The procedurally generated level terrain leads to variety, skill-testing moments, and novel terraforming opportunities.Difficulty (hazard level) ramps well: engaging and rewarding play for new and experienced players. Hazard 5 is still very hard, to me.This may be the best action game I've ever played. A lot like Vermintide 2; has some elements in common with Payday 2. Be most of all advised that the veneer of Minecraft-y terraforming doesn't really get across why most people would want to play this.Rock and stone.

_childDocuments_.review: All the buzz around this game isn't just for show, Deep Rock Galactic really is *that* good. The game itself has a good deal of things to do, 4 classes with unique roles and a hefty arsenal of weapons, a bunch of biomes and mission types and modifiers. Gameplay is fun and polished overall, with new stuff coming out at a decent pace. There are two glowing points for this game:1. The monetization system. You buy the game once, thats all you need. All seasonal content is fully free, and accessible at any point after its release (you can switch seasons at will!). Only thing you can buy afterwards is cosmetic but even then, fully optional and free cosmetic options are more than enough to have good (or stupid) looking dwarves.2. Community and culture. There's just something about it. People are very often helpful and welcoming to new players (lovingly referred to greenbeards). Any given lobby is likely to have chill players just looking to disintegrate some bugs. There's also a lot of fun community in-jokes like pinging one specific mushroom repeatedly and driller always managing to blow up the scout. This game is perfect if you, like me, have approximately 3 other very close friends to do stuff with. Less than that? Singleplayer is perfectly fine too (and so is finding random lobbies). More than that? This game and its developers are very cool with modding, so you could probably find a way to increase playercount. Probably, don't 100% me on that. I highly recommend DRG, full stop. Rock and Stone!

_childDocuments_.review: Deep Rock Galactic (DRG) isn’t just my Labor of Love Award nomination for the Steam Awards 2024. It’s also my 2022 Game of the Year, beating out some tough competition from Total War: WARHAMMER III & Judgment that year.My first experience with DRG was in January 2022. I had just about had it with the huge disappointment that was Halo Infinite, which has been uninstalled since early February and I am unsure if/when I will give it another chance. One day, I saw an old Halo acquaintance playing this co-op shooter with space dwarves. I was intrigued by the brief research I did and the nostalgia it brought back for me for Awesomenauts, another light-hearted, futuristic outer space game which I no longer play due to more or less being abandoned by its developers. So, I decided to give DRG a go at the full $30 price. Well, after 230+ hours over the past 10 months, I gotta say DRG is hands down one of the best-designed games I have ever played, PERIOD. Firstly, the four classes: Engineer, who can deploy sentries & shoot out platforms; Gunner, who can drop shield generators & launch ziplines; Scout, who can fire flares & traverse with a grappling hook; and Driller, who can blow ♥♥♥♥ up with satchel charges & has power drills to rapidly dig. I have only played a little on the hardest difficulties, but from my experience all four classes are very well balanced and any combination of the four generally works well. At the time of review, each class has 3 primary weapons, 3 secondary weapons, & 4 grenade variants. While this might seem paltry, each primary & secondary weapon has 5 tiers of upgrades to unlock with 2-3 choices to decide between in each tier. Additionally, each weapon has 5+ Overclock mods to earn/craft to further enhance it, such as converting the bullets into electro minelets after making contact with terrain. These are balanced by a tradeoff in weapon boost & penalty (the ones that give the smallest boost have no penalty at all). On top of that, the two tools for the two functionalities I mentioned earlier for each class each have 3-4 tiers of upgrades with 1-3 choices each, the standard pickaxe all classes have has 2 tiers of upgrades with 1 & 3 choices in each of those, and each class has its own armor rig with 4 tiers of upgrades with 1-3 choices in each, with the 1 choice in the 3rd tier being unique to the class. Plus, each class can equip up to three passive perks from a common 13+ pool and up to two active perks from a common 9+ pool. Up to 6 loadouts per class can be saved and switched between before standard missions & Deep Dives. Engineer was and still is my go-to class, but it didn’t take long before I enjoyed the other three classes almost just as much. Whether I am optimizing my sentry placement, getting shield generators down in time to save the team from full wipes, grappling all over caves like that one spider superhero, or reliving the good old days a decade ago now of C4 + Fast Hands on Black Ops II, DRG’s classes are a joy to play as.Secondly, the various missions and the procedural/random cave generation for them. Starting with mission types, there is the standard Mining Expedition, Egg Hunt, On-Site Refining, Salvage Operation, Point Extraction, Escort Duty, Elimination, and Industrial Sabotage. Each of these are unique, fun, & engaging while retaining that satisfying general gameplay loop of killing space bugs and digging up those precious minerals & loot as the aforementioned classes. Each mission also has a randomly selected secondary objective that can optionally be completed as well to “[secure] yourself a nice bonus” as “that guy in Mission Control [with the] cushy job” providing the team intel & “other” communications during missions & at the Space Rig hub puts it. Furthermore, occasionally a mission may have special, varied random event(s) occur which can be “completed” to earn additional minerals and/or loot. Additionally, each mission may have positive Anomalies and/or negative Warnings modifiers which make them even more varied. Regarding the procedural cave generation, DRG easily has THE BEST random level generation in a video game I have ever seen. Standard missions, which rotate the biomes which they’re available in every 30 real-life minutes, are procedurally generated each time they’re launched. While one might see some small similarities in cave systems after dozens if not hundreds of missions, the generation is so good that each mission almost always feels new/fresh. Here are a couple screenshots of a really cool, huge cave I encountered a few hundred missions in:  . Deep Dives, which are three missions back-to-back with an MMO dungeon/raid-like feel, are similar in this regard. While these are pre-seeded, every week they are swapped out with new randomly generated ones to help keep things fresh. All of this plus the 10+ diverse, atmospheric biomes, Dense Biozone & Azure Weald being my favorites, result in a consistently satisfying and rewarding gameplay experience that I don’t see getting old for years to come.Thirdly, character & weapon cosmetic customization, updates, & DLC practices. DRG boasts numerous customization options from beards to headwear to weapon frameworks to pickaxe frontblades and So Much More!. Like with class loadouts, up to 6 character customizations for each class and 6 pickaxe customizations for each class can be saved and swapped between while on the Space Rig. The game is regularly updated, usually every week, with bug fixes and/or changes addressing player feedback. There are seasonal events throughout the year where the Space Rig & even the cave systems have fitting decor and completing each part of the seasonal assignment will grant additional minerals and/or themed cosmetics. As a quick side note, an assignment is a set of standard missions which can be selected to gain additional rewards. Other than the seasonal assignment, Weekly Priority Assignment, & Weekly Core Hunt, these have no time limit, and one can still queue any standard mission or Deep Dive they want while it’s active. Continuing, last November, Ghost Ship Games (GSG) introduced Season content updates which have so far been released semi-annually. In addition to new content like weapons, grenades, & mission types/events, these updates include a free 100-tier battle pass (Performance Pass) which is progressed by simply playing the game and completing simple challenges that don’t encourage bad player habits. Plus, a free Cosmetic Tree which includes even more cosmetics & minerals unlocked by season points (Scrip) which are earned by progressing the Performance Pass as well as completing those aforementioned season challenges, which up to three are active at a time, regenerate at a rate of one per 21 hours, and one can be swapped out daily. If you are unable to complete a Performance Pass before the Season ends, which likely will be the case as they’re LONG having grinded both Seasons 1 & 2 to completion, all the cosmetics get added to the loot pool of those aforementioned random mission events so next to no FOMO. DRG’s only paid DLC are totally separate cosmetic packs which are really to support GSG to help them continue supporting the game with updates & free content. This imo is a fantastic business model which is also followed by my Labor of Love 2022 runner-up, Holdfast: Nations At War developed by Anvil Game Studios, and I make sure to purchase these when I can to support both developers and their consumer-friendly business practices.All in all, Deep Rock Galactic is an absolute gem and another deliverer of hope in the gaming industry. Just keep in mind, “If you don't Rock and Stone, you ain't comin' home!” :D

_childDocuments_.review: Deep Rock Galactic is a co-op shooter where you mine minerals and shoot bugs.The concept is simple, drop in, complete the objectives, get out. But the combination of classes, weapons, different objectives, fully destructible environment and procedurally generated levels make it fun for many hours. Most of the time you are on the move, exploring the caves, mining ores and kiting bugs, except for some defense objectives.There's a lot of customization to find a playstyle you like with many weapon builds, overclocks (gun mods), perks. With the weapon builds and overclocks you can have bullets that ricochet from enemies, specializing your weapon for primary shooting or charged shots, elemental effects and even shotgun jumping. You can only choose up to 3 passive and 2 active perks that allow you do things like return melee damage, insta revives, shield boosting and the best of all, taming an enemy bug that you can pet!The best combo in the game is the engineer's platform with the scout's grapple to get to any place out of reach. The driller can create a makeshift bunker by drilling the wall or use his drills to directly reach the drop pod. And the gunner has zip lines to help carry teammates and big ores.The main lobby features a Barrel Hoop mini game where you kick barrels into a moving hoop, lots of beer that have plenty of fun effects and some that give buffs during a mission and a jukebox with a dance floor. After you experience the main content of the game, you can level up to get prestige, get dwarf and pickaxe customization, complete the weekly deep dives and get overclocks. Overclocks are sadly dropped randomly, with some choice on machine events, so it might take a while to get an overclock you like.Compared to similar co-op games, DRG provides content updates for free, while paid DLCs are only for soundtracks and cosmetics. It also has an amazing feeling when you join other lobbies, salute with your "Rock and Stone" and get saluted back!For achievement hunters:There are some challenging ones that are easier in co-op and some that require 4 players in the same lobby. You have to complete 100 solo mission and the biggest grind is getting all 4 dwarfs to Gold promotion.

_childDocuments_.review: Rock and Stone.Deep Rock Galactic is surprisingly good for a game in Early Acess. Stable, Performing well and geniunly fun its great to see Early Acess produce quality once in a while. TL;DR on bottom for those who dont like giant walls of text.FEATURES:1. The planet Hoxxes and its many wonders - the game is set on Hoxxes, a planet so deadly you could fit it into Warhammer 40k, imagining youre a squat.  The Caves - your main play area, bristling with ores, crevaces, deadly murder bugs and general unpleasantries. The main thing about levels in DRG (Deep Rock Galactic) is what EVERYTHING (even y o u) is Voxel. You could literally dig your own (albeit empty) caverns if your wish so. Caves feature Length and Difficulty settings. Length determines the complexity, from a simple tunnel zigzaging deeper, to giant (and thats not an exaggeration) caverns, full of native wildlife and ore. Difficulty not only affects how hardy the Nasties of Hoxxes are, but also their numbers. Hordes will most likely deplete your ammunition very quickly on higher difficulty, forcing you to employ strategy and teamplay to survive.  Biomes - for a planet which is completely barren on surface, Hoxxes caves are magnificent. The game features multiple biomes, each nothing like the other, from dry sand pits to literaly fungus jungles. Coupled with random generation, no mission is alike. A prime example is my experience in Fungus Bogs: during mission one, the caves were full of poison mushrooms, giving the slushy hellscape its name, however during mission 2, instead of ample fungus supplies, i found myself in a middle of an Alien nest, with eggs scattered everywhere (which can be destroyed to release the nasties inside) and finally, on third mission sticky, slowing goop was randomly pooling around, making progress difficult. Each Biome has different things for it, giving you an unique experience in each, well worth to see. The Glyphid - your main adversary. Nasty lil ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, Glyphid come in in all shapes and sizes, from tiny nibblers to giant, poison spewing Praetorians. Glyphids, like everything else, are voxel which is a good thing, since you can literally tear their shells apart, making combat quite brutal (as you literally turn that one warrior into a pile of meat). Glyphid themselves are also tricky, while the AI does get silly sometimes, theyre still capable of feats such as sneaking (im looking at you, exploder) or just overwhelming you in sheer numbers, while some species have their unique behavior.  Native Wildlife - while as of now theres not much, alongside Glyphids theres plenty of flora and several fauna you can see in your adventures, most passive with a few either agressive, or defensive. Despite how scarce fauna is, it makes the biomes alive, immersing you in the idea that hoxxes is a truly alien world. Despite just being there, fauna and flora can be useful, platforms, light and so on.  Temperature - newest addition to the game, now you can freeze your dwarven arse if youre not careful in Glacial Strata. Lucky for you, there are ways to keep yourself warm, as long as you dont stick your face in those ice vents.2. The Stout Lads (aka you.) The Classes - DRG features 4 distinct classes, each with their own tools and weaponry. 1) Gunner is the fighter of your team, sporting a nifty minigun to mow down the enemy (just dont let it overheat) alongside a powerful magnum, explosive satchel (essentially C4) and a zipline for Utility.2) Scout is the lightbulb of your party, with his flares allowing you to see whats happening, without tossing your glowstics every 5 seconds while assisting with his full auto rifle and double barrel shotgun. Uses grapling hook to get to places.3) Engineer can be considered your line of defence, his sentry guns packing quite a punch, considering theres 2 of them. Engineer also has a semi auto shotgun and a grenade launcher. Platform gun (literally creates platforms) is the ulitily.4) Driller the hardworking digboy of the crew. Digger allows you to pass into dirt-blocked areas of the caves without it taking ages to dig out (or wasting C4) while providing AoE damage with his flamethrower with a pistol for single targets. Drills serve as Utility. The Upgrades - in DRG, your equipment (even flares) have upgrades to them, damage and ammunition size for weapons, and recharge rates/special bonuses for armor. flares increase brightness and duration while pickaxe give meele damage. Cosmetics - conquer the depths in style. DRG allows you to change the following on your dwarf:1) Armor (includes both body and variety of helmets)2) Skin color3) Mustaches4) Beards5) Hair  Cosmetics are bought with credits and resources you earn through gameplay, no lootboxes.Perks -  DRG features a perk system, from move/carry speed, to jump damage reduction to more resource yields. Perk points are aquired by completing milestones (such as complete X missions in biome B or do secondary objective of type A X times) which give from 2 to 5 perk points. Perks are split into tiers, with the next tier generally consisting of upgrades for previous tier. 3. Gamemodes - Shooting'n'Looting 101 DRG features several gamemodes:1) the Standart Mining operation: you must venture underground to collect X (depends on cave length) amount of morkite. While you dont have to gather anything else, it would be silly to ignore all this gold scattered about. in Addition to Morkite, you have a secondary objective which, while not required to complete the mission, provides with a healthy credit bonus.2) Egg hunt: Collect Alien Eggs hidden throughout the cavern, their location visible on the map and defined by an Organic growth to get the egg itself.3) Point Extraction: youre dropped off in a large chamber, with a mining rig which serves as your main holdout. your mission is to dig out chunks of Aquarq hidden within the walls, and deliver them to the mining rig all while fending off an endless onslaught of Glyphids, eager to chew you up. upon mission finish, you must holdout until the drop pod arrives.4) Elimination: The boss fights of DRG. Your goal is to eliminate Glyphid Dreadnaughts, monstrous boss type enemy with multiple healthbars and attacks. VERY hard to solo and requires quite a bit of team effort to bring the Monsters down.5) Salvage operation: Your objective is to repair several mini M.U.L.Es and then repair the broken Drop Pod, which you will use to escape.  Mutators - added in update 15, Mutators spice up the game even more. Mutators are split in 2 categories, Warnings and Anomalies. Warnings - negative mutators which increase hazard bonus. currently the game has 4:1) Exploder Infestation: Bugs ko kaboom. And theres a LOT of them. +30% hazard pay.2) Shield Disruption: your shields are always down.  +30% hazard pay.3) Mactera Plague: LOTS of flying bugs. +20% hazard pay.4) Cave Leech Clusters: remember half life barnacles? Same thing except more horrifying. +15% hazard pay. Anomalies - postive or neutral mutators which DO NOT increase hazard bonus. currently the game has 7:1) Gold rush: M O R E gold.2) Mineral Mania: Crafting materials (NOT morkite or secondary) spawn in larger amounts.3) Double exp: self explanatory.4) Low Gravity: ditto.5) Critical Weakness: enemy weakspots deal even more damage.6) Golden Bugs: every glyphid killed gives you gold.7) Rich Atmosphere: move faster, have helium voice and spring while carrying heavy rocks. This sums up the game. i hope.TL;DR Game is good and well polished for an EA titles. Devs are transparent about development. Best enjoyed with friends.

The game is very well optimized already, with beautiful graphics and stellar netcode. Only a couple of times did I have any connection issues but I'm pretty sure that was on my end. Controls are tight and gameplay doesn't get stale due to procedurally generated caves and caverns, and you're always worried about when the next swarm is going to stear your squad apart.I think going class based was a great choice, since the game is PvE and focuses a lot on cooperation. You'll quickly find yourself asking your teammates to deploy one of their classes' special tools to help you get to hard to reach minerals. During a bad swarm you'll pray that you have an Engineer to put down automated sentries. _childDocuments_.review: Supports up to 4-player online co-op, but the difficulty scales to keep the game balanced as intended. When playing solo, you're accompanied with a support drone so that you don't miss out on the benefits of working in a team.In addition to automatic difficulty scaling, players can select their own difficulty level for the mission. Each mission is also designed in such a way that some are inherently harder than others, while others can be a casual breeze.Strong replayability because of the diverse mission types, mission modifiers, sub-activities, and playable classes. Small game size because the biomes/caves are procedurally generated. Various progression systems that extend out for some time, but the main progression loops are kept close to the player.The four classes function in distinctly different ways that are still fun and useful, and can be built to play into either more generalized or more niche roles depending on your playstyle.Mission loops are designed well enough that most aspects of the missions are fun to do and come back to.Music and audio design is great. The dialogue is a solid "hot potato" out of 10. Graphics are great, and the art style is consistent throughout the game and its cosmetic DLCs.

_childDocuments_.review: Co-op first-person shooters haven’t had a big impact these days. Left 4 Dead and Left 4 Dead 2 put this style of game on the map by creating exceptional gameplay. Vermintide and Vermintide 2 took it in a somewhat different direction adding character persistence and a little more variety to the combat. Deep Rock Galactic builds on this further by giving you more objectives than simply going from A to B, and the additional mechanics add great depth to this subterranean adventure.Abbreviated Review: The premise of how exactly these Space Dwarves came to be on an orbiting station around a planet full of underground resources to mine isn’t explored in the introduction to Deep Rock Galactic. I suppose it’s not particularly important since it’s easy to surmise that it’s just what they do. What’s left is a scenario where your first task is picking one of the Dwarves and getting acquainted with their loadout.The choice of the Driller, Engineer, Gunner, or Scout is usually a pretty easy one to make once you’re familiarized with them. They have very clearly defined roles. While in every role you’ll be mining resources and collecting items, they each come together to contribute. It’s possible to have duplicate Dwarves in a team (if the host allows it), and you can be successful, but the missing skill set will be noticeable.The Driller can use his hand drills to quickly create a path between caves and tunnels. The Gunner can shoot zip lines everyone can use to cross gaps and go up and down sheer rock faces easily. Engineers have a platform gun that places mountable platforms on any surface that can be incredibly useful. Then the Scout, while not the most effective class, has the powerful flare gun to create a long-lasting light in the darkness of the depths.Resources you collect can be used for upgrading their weapons and gadgets independently as well as accessing the massive collection of cosmetics. These unlock with levels gained by the player as well as each Dwarf as you play them. Special minerals mined and cash collected for completing missions are required for all of these purchases.One thing that makes Deep Rock Galactic unique is that the vast majority of the light in the game is generated by the players. There are some bioluminescent flora and fauna as well as some glowing crystals and heated rocks, but never enough to navigate. Each character has a headlamp that provides the bare minimum of a spotlight, but the flares are a requirement in being able to see.The recharging stockpile of four flares lets you bring light to a small bubble of your surrounding area with what is a fantastic lighting system. The Unreal engine, of course, can take partial responsibility for this, but they’ve done great things with it. The flares recharge slowly enough that, if moving quickly or alone, you will soon be in darkness. This happens quite a bit in the chaos of each mission if you’re not careful, and it’s a great addition.Being lost in the dark with minimal light knowing that you could easily plunge over a hidden cliff face or wander into a bunch of angry alien bugs is a thrilling, yet terrifying, experience. Making use of the Scout’s flares in wide-open caverns where your light may not reach far becomes very important. Extended battle sections such as boss fights often have your flares burning out mid-fight leaving you clamoring to get them in places to help you see. It adds substance to an otherwise relatively simple combat system.The procedural caves of Deep Rock Galactic are filled with minerals and materials to unearth. They’re also home to plenty of hostile plants and creatures. The spider-like monsters are the most common and the majority of them can be killed with the variety of weapons the Dwarves use. Some, however, require a little more finesse to dispatch.The tougher aliens usually have glowing weak points on which you can focus your fire. You’d think this would make them easy, but they’re often on their back – which is facing away if they’re charging at you. This means team play is even important for fighting. It also makes fighting in the dark more dangerous as some enemies are invisible while others are only partially glowing. Sometimes shooting everything you’ve got in the general direction is the best choice.Boss fights and especially large aliens can make for really challenging encounters. If you split off to mine some resources by yourself, these guys can ruin your day. Even smaller weaker enemies can swarm the unprepared, but an armored monstrosity cornering you will leave you incapacitated and hoping your team can get to you. This situation can happen even while playing as a team though, as some enemies can grab you can drag you off to far reaches of the map.Deep Rock Galactic can be played solo, but it’s certainly not the intended experience. Since you can be so easily overwhelmed, you’re given a flying robotic companion with the ability to blast enemies with machine guns and rockets, revive you, and mine minerals high on cave walls for you. It seems useful, but the AI is mediocre at best and the experience is slow and painful by comparison. The game is meant for co-op play and is best experienced that way.There’s something magical about the combination of combat, resource objectives, and navigating/manipulating the dark tunnels. The procedural construction makes some very natural looking cave designs and the way you can carve through them makes them wonderful to explore. Even with how somewhat repetitious the objectives can be, the diversity in the map design and enemy encounters makes every mission feel unique.I do hope that the future brings more of everything to the table. More enemies, more mission types, more biomes, maybe even more Dwarf classes. I also wouldn’t mind seeing the Scout get an additional tool to make him more useful. Given that the only thing critical I can think of for this game is that I want more of what is there, I hope I am conveying how much I enjoy it. With the 26 hours I’ve put in it so far, I feel like I’ve only just gotten started. I look forward to diving in more in the future and seeing how high some peoples’ levels are in the game, I’m not the only one with that sentiment.

_childDocuments_.review: Possibly the best co-op shooter I've ever played, so far free from live service ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. This game doesn't try to monetize my time and rewards me for playing. I can enjoy playing it solo, with pubs, and with my friends. So far I haven't had any issues with the community, with all of the randoms I've played with typically being very friendly.
