_childDocuments_.review: This game is going to be my game of the year, and no I did not forget about games like "Cyberpunk 2077". I want to explain all of you why, and why this game is definetly worth its money  (I played the demo since release, so I have a bit more playtime then it displays on the main game.)"art of rally" is a arcade rally game, which uses some interesting graphics design and camera. The game currently has over 40 cars and 15 tracks, all of them are heavily based on real cars/locations. The games biggest selling point, at least in my opinion, would be the overall feeling of the game. As Kotaku said, "art of rally turns driving into meditation". The graphics stlye is unrivaled, and the photo mode can make some crazy pictures. The OST, the graphics, the sounds, the controls, the general driving feel - everything works together perfectly for this masterpiece of a game. You just plug in your controller, boot the game, and drive for hours on hours, which brings us to the next topic:The game itself has some assists like ABS and stability-control, but they are configurable from 100% down to 0% for purists. You can obviously switch between automatic or manual shifting, and if you choose manual then you even have to use the clutch in certain cars. The story can be challenging, at least you will have to get used to some tracks before you will master the art of rallying there. But of course you can also compete agains your friends:Currently, every track has its own worldwide leaderboard for you to compete in. But there are also daily and weekly challanges, so you have something new to master every day.The game currently has over 40 cars, which you unlock as you progress through the story (yes, there even is a story.) All of the cars are very very heavily inspired by realy world (rally) cars, for example you can drive a BMW 2002 Turbo, a BMW M1, a Ford Escord 1600, a Porsche 959 rally, a Lancia Delta, Lancia Stratos, I could go on like this forever. Basically there will be at least 2 or 3 cars everyone will like.The tracks are based of real tracks aswell, at least for the country / general location. There are tracks in Japan, Africa, Sweden, Poland, Marocco, even the german "Panzerplatte" - more then enough. There also is a freeroam map with some collectibles.Obviously, this game is an arcade game that was designed around using a controller. The game has mouse and keyboard support, but is definetly best enjoyed with a controller.This game was designed almost entirely by one dev (@funselektor on twitter.) "art of rally" is an incredible game, even for a 30 man dev team. But if you think about the fact that one guy did almost all of this by himself in over 5 years, it is even more impressive., and is a must have for every singe rally fan out there. The complete vibe and package you get with this game is incredible, I can guarantee that I will spend way too much time with this game. There is so much variety, daily challanges to compete in, leaderboards to climb, tracks to master and photos to shoot. If this review or any of the trailers made you interested in the game but you are still unsure, try the free demo in the steam store. Its free and 800mb, so why not?See you on the leaderboards, and watch out for the trees.I dont write that many steam reviews, and english is not my native language, so please ignore any spelling mistakes :)

_childDocuments_.review: Art of Rally is the easiest way to get that rally/drifting flow-state high with just a controller. Don't be fooled by the cartoony appearance; the feel of driving in the game has been tuned to perfection. Without introducing a ton of unnecessary complexity, the cars have the right weight and momentum, and the tires do the right things on each of the surfaces and conditions. If you've played Dirt Rally 2.0, you'll feel right at home. Content-wise, the campaign is long and varied and lets you work your way up through all of the car classes. I'm perfectly fine with the number of locations and courses given the diversity of car models and the fact that a stage never feels the same twice. Free roam is a nice touch, and the collectibles just ensure that you see every part of the beautifully designed locations.The visuals in this game are a triumph. Every frame feels like it could be a desktop wallpaper, with just the right amount of detail and visual flourishes. It's really very beautiful, although max settings on some stages were surprisingly demanding for my old RTX 2080 Super.Great game to blast through some rally stages while listening to music.

_childDocuments_.review: Art of Rally is an indie racing game that follows the history of rallying from its early days through its peak with the banned Group B cars and then the aftermath in the 1990s. The game is unlicensed, but all the cars are close recreations of legendary (and forgotten) real-life rally cars, even recreating the liveries in which they had their greatest success. The way they get around the licensing is with the simplified art style and by giving them all fake names.I was really into watching rallying when I was young, and have played many rally games over the years, so this stylish indie effort has been on my wishlist since it came out.  ---{ Graphics and Art Direction }---☐I want to live in this world☑Beautiful☐Functional☐BadI adore the art style, and I think it will age much better than a lot of "realistic" rally games. Despite the style, there is some modern rendering going on here, with beautiful volumetric light and real-time shadows. The thing keeping this from the top rung is that it has some surprising performance issues, with stutters and fps drops. I wasn't able to find a low-impact way to mitigate stutters, so had to turn down graphics, and below the highest settings there are some issues: ugly jagged shadows and lots of distracting LOD pop-in. ---{ Gameplay }---☐Hall of fame☑Keeps me coming back for more☐Fun enough for a few hours☐Watch paint dry instead The most important thing in a rally game is how the cars handle. From the art style you might think this is an arcade game, but in fact the driving model is surprisingly deep and more akin to a simulation rally game. Cars all handle realistically based on the characteristics of their real life counterparts. Hit a jump at the wrong angle and you feel like there's some real suspension modelling going on here.The main difference between this and a normal rally game is the camera. A normal rally game you're either sat in the cockpit or with a close trailing camera. Because you're travelling at very high speed, and most corners are unsighted, rallying (in real life and in games) relies on a co-driver who is calling out corners a few beats ahead of your arrival at them. In this case, the game pulls back to a very high drone camera angle, giving you full advanced sight of the corners to come. This allows the game to forego the co-driver, which does allow it to be played muted unlike normal rally games.The downside to the camera angle is that you're further removed from the action, and so you lose out on the visceral feeling of nailing a few difficult corners back to back, which is the usual dopamine rush from rally games.One small note is the default settings amplify counter-steer inputs, which because of the way most cars behave makes your life more difficult for no reason, so I suggest changing that setting immediately. ---{ Story / Writing / Lore }---☐Deserves a Pulitzer☐Wouldn’t be out of place on a bookshelf☐Nothing special☐Written by teenagers☑No Story No story, but the game is clearly a labour of love, and makes an effort to front the lore of rallying. Part of this is in the little descriptions of each vehicle and their place in the history of the sport, part of it is in the vehicle selection itself.This article explains a bit how the game engages with rallying history: ---{ Music and Audio }---☐Earned a permanent spot in my playlist☐Enjoyable☑I didn’t notice it☐Mute immediatelyMusic is simple techno / synth. Works well enough but nothing special. There are subtle sound effects for locking brakes and spooling turbos, and cars do sound like their real-life counterparts, but nothing worth writing home about on the audio front.  ---{ Difficulty }---☐Walking simulator☐You can technically die, but you probably won’t☐Easy to learn / Hard to master☑Hard to learn / Hard to master☐Dark SoulsRallying is the most difficult motorsport, and rally sim games have a reputation of being the Dark Souls of racing games. This game shares the difficulty of navigating a realistic handling vehicle down narrow forest roads at much too high speed. There is difficulty settings for your opponents, but as rallying is a time trial, the only thing it affects is where you place on a leaderboard. As with all rallying games, the real challenge isn't your competition but personal: keeping your vehicle on the road and nailing each stage. This game seems to recognize that, and in what I think is a stroke of genius, there doesn't seem to be any progression (other than a single achievement) tied to beating your opposition - the only goal is to finish, and as you move up through the categories it becomes harder and harder to get the cars through the stages. Rewards are tied only to using as few 'restarts' as possible.However, it's a little easier than something like Dirt Rally for a few reasons: the camera angle and lack of co-driver means you don't have to split your attention between your eyes and ears; one of the things lost in the simplification is immediate roadside hazards like ditches, so it's much more forgiving of going slightly off-track; and the default damage model is way too forgiving (I suggest bumping the damage model up to the highest setting for something approaching the normal setting in other rally games. ---{ System Requirements }---☐Could run on a Samsung smart fridge☑Modern console or decent PC☐Ask NASA if they have a spare computerAs I mentioned, there are some surprising performance issues.  ---{ Length }---☐<10 hours☑10-25 hours☐25-100 hours☐Hundreds of hours, if you wantProbably 20 hours to 100%, which I will likely do. ---{ Value }---☐Buy it twice☑Worth full price☐If it's on sale☐Not recommendedOverall an 8.5/10 for me. Good value at its normal price of C$29.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a huge fan of rallying and I also liked Absolute Drift very much, so  was pretty much a must-have from the day it was announced. It has a great selection of cars, pretty varied stages and events as well as a great stylized look. I also like how it's focused on classic rally including Group S which never came to be due to the events in 1985's and especially 1986's rally seasons — do not expect to see the latest WRCs here! The dynamic crowds sometimes standing in the middle of the road further help to give this game a 1980's vibe since crowd control was pretty much unknown in south western Europe back then... The beautiful soundtrack furthers this impression, sometimes you feel like you're part of one of marvdogger's YT rally compilations. And that is pretty darn cool!The FISA groups assigned to some of the older cars in-game are kinda off — which is a problem for enthusiasts only, I suppose. Same could be said about technical data in many cases being on the fantasy side. But why even the very late Group A cars portrayed in the game lack a sixth gear... I don't know. And even supercharged cars at times feel like there's some lag present. Then again, this is no simulation by any means. The absence of pacenotes fits this more casual style and does surprisingly little harm, though there are turns which will run in an unpredictable way or simply appear out of nowhere during fast night stages. I was wondering whether this problem would worsen when advancing through the classes, but it didn't. Partly because even a 205 T16 does not feel like a cannonball on wheels in this game. For which, at least to some degree, the point of view is responsible, I guess.Loading times are (very) short and the game runs pretty much flawlessly. I used to get micro freezes every now and then (appear to be fixed with the latest update) and it only crashed on me once during freeroam with no progress lost.Originally, there were two things I was not overly fond of. One was the unpredictable behavior of cars after jumps. While it's still not perfect, it has gotten much better and is not really worth mentioning anymore. You have to get used to it at first, but that's about it.So there is one thing left, and that's the auto reset when leaving the track. It's far too aggressive in my opinion and disrupting the experience. Give me a (hefty) time penalty, but let me return to the track on my own, please.This on its own can absolutely not spoil the fun though, so  is definitely recommended!Addition: You have to give the dev HUGE credit for releasing content which would be a DLC elsewhere as free updates for the game, so that's a big PLUS which definitely strengthens my "Thumbs up" rating!

_childDocuments_.review: Are you looking for a different experience in racing games? A big fan of Rally/Rally games? Then you've come at the right place, art of rally offers a great experience, something not quite the same as other offerings at this time in the Rally genre (like DiRT Rally, WRC, or DiRT 5, etc.).You probably already noticed the cartoon-ish artstyle, and are thinking it's a casual game, right? Well, you're wrong. The artstyle is one thing, but it handles like a proper Rally game, with a different perspective than what you'd find in DiRT Rally for example, as you don't have access to pace notes. You won't need them anyway, as your POV is very high above your car, like a very far Chase cam.If you're looking for a racing sim, this is not it, there's no cockpit camera for once, but it sure offers it's own set of challenges, as you can set the camera higher and see more of the road ahead, but in turn can make it harder to see in more detail what's immediately in front of you, the elevation changes, your car's attitude, etc. Conversely, you can get it closer to your car, and in turn lose some of the ability to see the next few corners. The placement of trees and hills will make it less straightforward in just looking ahead, hiding part of the corner, or even how tight it can get, so it keeps the unique challenge that is rallying.At this time I've only played 5 hours, but I can definitely say that it's definitely a game to at least try for yourself, it's fun, it's beautiful (yeah, it's not a realistic artstyle, but it can definitely strike you with some beautiful sceneries as you slide around multiple countries), it's got a career mode where it'll take you from the late 60s to the mid 90s, completing seasons through every year, with cars corresponding to each era, and each season is randomly generated using different stages, so you can repeat a season and get totally different countries and/or stages. There's no licenced cars, but their replacements are equally unique, with matching caracteristics and feeling to their inspirations, which is something else to take note and practice with.It's a game that has more than meets the eye, and has a soul that you can feel, unlike some games being released these days from companies that should be doing better.

_childDocuments_.review: This was the racing game I didn't realize I wanted. A pure rally racer with controls somewhere between arcade and simulator, with a clean and pleasing aesthetic and a sountrack to match.The feel of the cars is definitely not arcade, requiring more judicious use of the gas and brakes for proper weight transfer. At the same time, this isn't a simulator in that most mistakes can be saved with proper throttle control or light braking. Sliding your car through a turn feels great when executed correctly. These controls are definitely easy to learn but tough to master.There is a career mode that takes you through the six car types available, ranging from the classics of the 60's, to the Group B monsters of the 80's, and finally at the (way more powerful than reality) 90's with Group A. Time attack is the closest you'll get to multiplayer, since it keeps records of both your friend's times and times from around the world. There's also some more sandbox-y elements with the inclusion of a custom rally maker (pick the stages, no actually stage maker) and a free roam mode. The free roam has an item hunt so you explore the extent of each map.Aesthetic-wise, though the graphics are of a solid color, low-poly variety, it works very well. The stages have great ambiance, and the lighting effects are the icing on the cake. Adding to this is the soundtrack, which is 51 tracks of synthwave/retrowave goodness that'll make you don a pair of Wayfarers and wish you owned a Ferrari Testarossa.You can achieve some high speeds in this game, yet overall this is actually a somewhat relaxing experience, but is still great fun. If you want something that controls with more depth than your standard arcade fare, but without the serious nature of a simulator, this is your ticket.

_childDocuments_.review: I love everything about this game, the setting, the music, the art style. Everything except the gameplay.A shoddy physics engine that rolls the dice on whether your car drives normally or flips end over end, and a barebones career mode with none of the otherwise expected racing game features. There's no ghost cars, there's no previous attempt timer, there's no track map, there's really nothing besides driving from point A to point B and hoping to god that you qualify at the end of the attempt. The worst part is some of the maps take almost ten minutes to complete, so if you make a mistake and need to start over you're going to have to spend another ten minutes completing the track. On top of this because the timer is so rudimentary you have no way to know if you're making good time until the very end of the attempt.The game is so interested in it's own aesthetic that it forgets it's supposed to be a video game.

_childDocuments_.review: HOW is this priced at $36AUD with no appreciable sales when it's so bad?! What were you thinking? At time of writing, Dirt Rally 2 is less than 1/4 the price of this game, with all its DLC. That game has way more cars, more stages, more disciplines, more choice, better handling, better visuals, the works. React with jester awards all you like but you can't argue with the fact that this game is a rip-off.The game runs TERRIBLY. Easily the worst optimisation I've seen in memory. The camera angles make seeing subtle elevation changes impossible, but you are required to do this - this makes every single stage just trial and error to deal with the bad camera system the game forces on you. To compound this issue, the game's shading seems deliberately designed to HIDE elevation changes. It's genuinely like the developers have not played this title even once, because these issues are so easily fixed and ruin the game so badly. The game is RAILROADED and barebones as all hell. Very little to no reason for a player to do anything other than have their hand held. There are no choices, there is no strategy, there is no complexity. The handling model feels good at first, but as you learn how it responds, you quickly find it is far, far less detailed or realistic than it seems, with auto-countersteer and auto-recovery forced on with no way to disable. This is presumably due to the developer's determination to stick with the terrible camera angles at all costs (the dev even has snarky forum posts about this; they have contempt for players who don't love the camera). Menu transitions are at least 4x as long as they should be. This is a meme game with AAA pricing, and whoever was silly enough to overestimate its worth to that degree is insane, stupid or both. 2/10

_childDocuments_.review: Art of rally is a top down view racing game exclusively focusing on rally discipline in point-to-point special stages. What sets this game apart from others in the genre is it’s stylistic visuals and a handling model that is satisfying to learn.I have played only with the Switch Pro controller so far. The handling feels distinctive, and while playing I feel to be in complete control  of the steering. The game can be played with a keyboard, however. Something about the handling mechanics and the camera perspective evokes the feeling of playing around with matchbox cars and the like from my childhood, it is a very enjoyable and playful experience!The game features dozens of familiar looking rally cars from different decades beginning from the 60’s, along with six locations in Finland, Japan, Germany, Norway, Italy and Kenya.The career mode puts you through randomized sets of special stages with different car classes of each time period. In addition, time trials, custom events and community events are available. The gameplay is simple, and fun. The focus is on the experience of racing itself at is what makes it so enjoyable.The designs of the environments and cars are top-notch, and the visual aesthetics mesh well together. The game is also coupled with a soundtrack that fits the aesthetic to a tee.The game runs well enough on my laptop, I do not have complaints regarding optimization. For the price of the game I have received tens of hours of enjoyment already and look for more as I am learning to master all the car classes and environments. And in addition to that, the developers have added in the ability to mod your own liveries for the cars in image editing programs. The possibilities are limitless. Combine this with the robust screen capture mode and you can have countless of hours of fun hunting for perfect photo opportunities capturing your sleekest drifts or highest jumps.

_childDocuments_.review: Art of Rally is an absolute gem of a game that has revved up my love for racing in ways I never thought possible. What truly sets this game apart is its mesmerizing music that transforms each race into a symphony of speed and sound.From the moment you hit the accelerator, you're greeted by a soundtrack that feels tailor-made for every twist and turn. The music seamlessly weaves into the gameplay, creating an immersive experience that's both thrilling and euphoric. As a racing enthusiast, I've played my fair share of games, but Art of Rally takes the cake with its unique blend of visual artistry and audio magic. The tracks pulse with life, and the music acts as the heartbeat that keeps you in tune with the road. It's a symphony of engines and melodies that work together in perfect harmony.Whether you're a seasoned racer or a newbie to the genre, Art of Rally is a must-play for anyone who craves an adrenaline rush accompanied by a killer soundtrack. It's a driving experience that goes beyond the finish line, creating a lasting memory of racing to the rhythm. _childDocuments_.review: Preface this by saying that I would actually recommend this game, but that I "don't recommend it" purely so that this may get more visibility from purchasers who may find this specific issue to be particularly annoying. My original review was different than this one, I have updated it to reflect my impressions as I've played more and as some issues I brought up have been addressed. The main issue (the one causing the negative review) has been "solved" per say but the "solution" was less of a solution and more of a bandaid "this is the best we can do for now" so I'm keeping the review negative until a more appropriate "fully fledged" solution is added. Which it does look like the devs are working on :) .The Issue:Since my original review, the dev's confirmed that AI times were based on leaderboard times like I hypothesized. They also "reset" the AI times to a pre-release state. Originally here was a longwinded story. Since the issue is semi-resolved and this review was long. I will shorten it for you. Basically, the AI times (all of them) are based on human leaderboard times. Thus when the leaderboards were not kept "clean" of hacked/glitched runs, the AI (on master difficulty, maybe others) would go faster on stages than a car would be physically capable of doing, because their times were based on hacked/glitched runs that were also faster than physically possible. We aren't talking seconds, I mean whole minutes faster.  Meaning the AI were literally unbeatable. The example stage I gave was a 7mi stage where the AI set a 3min stage time, I set a 4:28, and the leaderboard leader set a 1min stage time. Here's the avg speeds:1min leaderboard time: 420mph avgAI 3min time: 140mph avgMy time: 93mph avgThis was in Gr.4 cars. 140mph avg isn't physically possible for cars in that class. At all. So my new findings are as follows:With the reset of AI times, AI on master do not set unrealistic stage times. I've done about 50 stages without a single dodgy AI time. HOWEVER, I also now pretty much slaughter them on every stage. I am not sure if this is the AI being worse, or me being better. I now consistently set top 100 leaderboard times on every stage, with most stages in the top 30. Much better than the top 500 times I was consistently setting before. But I'm also pretty sure the AI are slower than before, but I'm not sure by how much. I'm going to leave this info here and let you decide if you think it's me or the AI. Personally, I am unsure, but I'm leaning towards the AI being worse than they should be. Beyond this issue:At the time of my original review I had only driven Gr.4 cars. Since then I've driven up to group b. The RWD cars of Gr.4-2 are all very fun to drive and each vehicle handles uniquely. They don't handle in a "realistic" manner, most of the cars are able to hold slides much much easier than they should. If you're looking for realism here, you may dislike this. I like it quite a lot. RWD cars of Gr.4-2 are all dodgy over jumps, they do some odd bouncing on landing. It seems that jamming the brakes over a jump always has a better outcome than flat out, even if you have the runoff for it. Purely b/c the cars don't take hard landings well. It would be cool to be able to go flat out over a jump without fear of instant death, but I've been able to adjust my style to accommodate the cars. The one FWD car in Gr.4 (the meanie) is still weird to me, handles like a weird oversteery FWD car, not intuitive I find. It is also the only FWD car in the game afaik, so I'm sure not a lot of work was put into how it handles compared to RWD and AWD. The AWD Gr.B cars I have driven are quite a different beast and I'm still learning them, they seem to understeer a ridiculous amount. The Gr.B RWD cars just drive like more powerful Gr.2 cars, which is an easier transition. Graphics and art style are mostly very good looking and seem to run well at 4k60hz on my 1080ti. I would hope so. In my original review I noted that Pop-in of grass/shrubs seems to be the biggest issue, even with the draw distance set to max. Since adding more playtime, this issue seems to be less visible on pretty much every map, except japan. Down the mountain portions of Japan have some very obnoxious pop-in. Other maps do have pop-in but they are much less noticeable, you have to look for them to see them. Original review also bashed Norway for looking a bit barren, and in truth it still does, but I've grown to enjoy the barren nature. You may still dislike it, so I'm still mentioning it. But something about the barren landscape has grown on me to like it a lot more than I originally did. Original review also had some issues with crowds. 1) Was that crowds seemed to move in funny ways that seemed unnatural while I was driving Gr.4 cars. I chalked this up to Gr.4 cars probably being too slow. The "unnaturalness" is still prevalent, but is much much less noticeable in faster cars. Since I've also gotten faster, Gr.4 cars have also had a reduction in "unnatural" crowd behavior. So it wasn't the cars that were too slow, it was just the driver. So with that in mind, if you are not a fast driver, you may also notice the crowds behaving in odd ways when you are driving the lower tier cars. 2) was that dark colored crowd members looked like bollards and I kept thinking I was gonna crash into them. I have since realized there are no solid bollards in the game to worry about, so the dark colored crowd members no longer ruin my rythym. New things:Car sounds are not the best for some cars, the "wedge" (stratos) for example sounds terrible. Lots of the inline 4 cars don't sound good either, some turbo cars you can't even hear the turbo. Some cars do sound pretty good though, like the cozzie sr5 (sierra rs500) it has a majestic turbo sound that I am deeply in love with. Orange temporary fences, the ones that are like cheap and thin plastic. That easily come down in real life? Yeah those are solid as concrete walls. Kind of annoying, I can get used to it sure, but it might piss some people off. Night stages in this game are beautiful, the lighting is just amazing. But speaking of lighting, devs please turn on the headlights in all fog stages. Sometimes I get into a fog stage with the headlights off and can't see anything. Theres also tons of little annoying things here and there that I hate with a passion, but they are part of the games charm and SHOULD NOT be edited in any way. See tombstone barrier things in germany and all of finland. Things that kill your car super easy and make the game way more challenging. So I hate them, but like I  would sorely miss the added challenge they pose. Also the "das uberwhip" (M1 Procar) seems to damage it's engine much much easier than other cars in its class. Not sure if thats intentional, but it's caught on fire more than once for me, while in any other cars throughout the whole game I've barely damaged engines at all. As usual I'll update this review as I play more and as the devs change things. Feel free to leave comments asking questions or otherwise and I'll try to answer them best I can.

_childDocuments_.review: I am not someone who knows a lot about rally or racing. The only experience that I have with racing games is playing some of the earlier Need For Speed games ~15 years ago. However, I came across a video of art of rally on YouTube, and thought it looked gorgeous and might be interesting to try out. And wow, what an adventure it has been.The game (I will only be reviewing the career mode) is divided into 6 "worlds" or "groups", which each have 5 rally races, consisting of 2-5 tracks, within them. Each group has a certain specification of car, and the farther you get into the game, the more powerful the vehicles are. The earlier groups have shorter rallies, and as you progress, the rallies get longer, with multiple stages. The graphics and aesthetics of the entire game is absolutely stunning, as seen from the screenshots. There are a wide variety of tracks that you get to race down, with varied landscapes, from frozen lakes, to rocky forests.Playing with the controller is a sublime experience as the rumble and vibrations really help to get across what's happening in game. As you drift, the controller vibrates in accordance with your drift, and as you straighten out, your engine roars, but the controller becomes steady, matching your experience on the track. In a piece of beautiful design, unlocking a rally only requires you to have completed all the previous rallies. There is no need to win. This means that the entire game is just a long series of experiments to see how the cars work, and what is the best way to move all that power through the long and winding tracks.Being an absolute newbie to the genre, this experimentation was liberating for me. In the first world, Group 2, I struggled to control the vehicles. I searched a bunch on YouTube, but there were no guides for this game available. So I ended up watching a lot of real world rally content, as well as content for other rally games like Dirt 3, and I learnt that the "Meanie", with its front-wheel drive should be a lot easier to control, and I finished up the first group driving just that one car.Entering the second world, Group 3, however, I saw that there was no front-wheel drive available, so I was forced to actually learn how to handle the hefty backsides of the vehicles, sliding all over with a mind of their own. I realised that once the car is drifting, pressing the accelerator will tend to prolong the drift. This is useful in the early stages of a drift, if you have realised that you started off too early. However, this also means that if you are sliding uncontrollably, trying to straighten your vehicle on a straight, it's best to just lay off the throttle and allow the car to settle down. Slowly I learnt to understand the cars behaviour and got an instinct for nailing the throttle at the exact moment that the car has regained grip, and that was exhilarating.I found myself doing fairly well on the "Normal" difficulty, so I thought I would up it to "Skilled". The races became more challenging, and I found that I seemed to have a very wide range of performances depending on the surface. I struggled to perform on tarmac, and I dominated in rainy conditions. Again, I went back to watch some real world rally content, and saw my mistake. I had been treating all road conditions as equal, and was just drifting through all corners to my hearts content. I learnt that on high-grip surfaces like tarmac, it is better to spend as little time as possible drifting, as you be a lot faster by braking late and accelerating out of corners. On snow and rainy conditions, acceleration was much slower, so drifting was useful to maintain speed through corners.Progressing further, I decided that I wanted to try out manual gear transmission, just to see what it would be like. So I started off Group 4 by shifting the difficulty down to Novice, and checking the controls to see how to shift up and down. It took a while to get adjusted to, but soon it was even more fun. I slowly learned that shifting a gear up in the middle of a drift just because you engine is over-revving is not a good move, because once the drift ends, you will be a lot slower, and will need to be on the lower gear. I found that it is better to be on the lower gear and quickly shift up, rather that being in the higher gear and slowly gaining revs. However, I also saw that if stuck in a higher gear, it was better to swallow that loss than to shift down and shift back up, as it tended to be slower overall. It seemed that shifting into a higher gear near the end of a drift, can end the drift and get you accelerating out of the corner (however I am not entirely certain that this is the case, as it just might be that I have figure out the exact moment that a drift ends, and just happen to shift gears at that instant). The game got a lot more involved, and a whole lot more fun.Moving to Group B, I was back at Skilled difficulty, but now with manual transmission. The rallies were getting longer, and multi stage rallies were becoming more common. Now that decision to unlock progress based on completion rather than wins started to shine through and allow for some truly memorable moments. I was on the last track of a rally, and in second place behind one of the Finn AIs. I was around a minute and 13 seconds behind, with the Swede in 3rd being more than 2 minutes behind me. With the last stage being a 2.6 mile tarmac course, it was unlikely that I would be able to gain that much time. So I just blundered my way around the course, confident that I would keep my second place regardless of the result. I ended up finishing the race in 6th, but to my surprise, was leading the rally. Turns out that the Finn in first had hit a house on the race, and ended up 4 minutes behind the winner. I would never have been able to experience that rush of joy and relief if I had been forced to restart the whole rally for the sake of winning to unlock progress.Group S was when it all started to gel. I suddenly learnt the power that is available in first gear. The pure boost that you get coming out of a corner was almost palpable through the screen. I learn to take hairpins on 2nd gear, and then shift back down to first, as I straightened the car out of the turn. I felt the thrill of gunning down a straight on 5th gear, having absolutely no idea where the next turn would be, and absolutely fearful in the knowledge that there was a 20% chance I would not be able to slow down in time, and would probably throw myself off of a Scandinavian mountainside into the sunset. I found myself perfectly shifting gears as I slid sideways over the snowy track in the middle of a frozen lake, inches away from the edge of the road, which would be a slippery slide into oblivion (commonly experienced as a forced reset and a 5 second penalty).I cursed those pillars along the sides of the German freeways, which instantly kill all your momentum. I prayed that as I slid off the Japanese downhill slaloms, a tree would manifest itself, and perfectly kill my momentum, and leave my car facing in the correct direction. I finally learned to quickly recover from a spin-out, by shifting all the way down into reverse, gathering a little momentum, and start the rotation to face forward, while quickly shifting into second and maintaining all that momentum with a perfect J spin.I am currently in the middle of Group A, the final group. But the more I play, the more I realise that though I am almost done with the career mode, I am not close to finishing the game. I am probable going to go back through, and play on the highest difficulty, and try to win all the rallies. Maybe move to time attack mode, and memorise a few tracks and perform better on them. Maybe return for the daily and weekly challenges as well.This game has been an incredible experience for me. From learning about racing and all its intricacies, to to soaking in the Sardninan sunsets. I would give art of rally 5 stars.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is stunningly beautiful. Simple, yet visually appealing. Calming, even. Each map has their own beauty, and each stage has their own beauty. The cars themselves look beautiful and cute at the same time.Don't let the simple visual art fool you; this arcade rally game has quite a high skill ceiling. You can't just come in and quickly drift around the track like no one's business. This game requires skills and patience to learn the intricacies of how the car behaves on the track.To make it more difficult, each car is extremely different from one another; you cannot translate what you learned from one car to another car. On the positive note, because there are a huge variety of cars to choose from, you can easily find one that suits your style the most. A low powered FWD, a handbrake friendly RWD or a powerful AWD... All are there and ready for you to master!To make matters even MORE difficult, the weather affects everything. The same track on dry can be completely different when it is wet; you had to take different lines, different braking zones, different throttle inputs, etc. And they're the exact same track, just with different weathers!A few of the achievements can be quite grindy, which sucked a bit of the fun out the game. One of the achievements forced you to use a single car for a LONG time to get the achievement. If you suck with the car, you are not having a good time.The only biggest "problem" (it's more of a personal problem really) to this game is the camera angle. It's not a "third person" view like you get from typical racing games; it is more a top-down view. This camera angle is needed and a must because the maps have tall hills and blind corners that you can never see if you're in 3rd person view. So it's taking quite a long time to get used to. If you REALLY want that 3rd person view, it is recommended to download the Camera Mod from NexusMod. It requires a little bit of fiddling but it is possible.And I'd say I HIGHLY recommend the Camera Mod. Because your camera angle is now different, the art now has a different kind of beauty to them. Because your camera is now closer, everything feels more intimate, feels a little bit more closer to heart. Granted, the details are not great because they're not meant to view up close, and you can get the low angle views in Photo Mode, but they have a certain type of beauty you can never get without the Camera Mod.This game is truly amazingly put together, tons of fun to play, a gorgeous piece of moving art and a beautiful love letter to the golden era of Rally. It really is the Art Of Rally.

_childDocuments_.review: Art of rally plays in an alternate universe where the legendary "Group B" never ended the greed for more horsepower and lighter cars in the rally sport. Due to multiple accidents in the Group B series including multiple deaths (of spectators and drivers) the series had to get canceled. Cars going 0-60 mp/h in less than 3 seconds on gravel that could keep up with F1 cars of the era might've been a bit too much to pilot on narrow technical roads, even for the best drivers. However, in this game the series continued and the planned "Group S" is a reality, with actual prototype cars that were in development before the series got canceled.Despite it's innocent look and low-poly art style, this game is still to be taken seriously. The physics are incredibly well optimized for controller gameplay and dare I say - realistic. All the real life rally techniques can be applied in this game: clutch kicking, scandinavian flicks, weight transfers, anything you can think of, can be done in this game and the best thing about it, it gains you time. Heck, the developers visited rally schools and it shows in the physics. It's obviously not a simulation, but this is as good as it gets for a game that isn't meant to be driven with a wheel and pedals.Due to the game playing in an alternate universe, you won't find any licensed cars. However, this is actually a brilliant way to bypass licensing fees. All the cars seen in the game are basically real life cars as they exist, but with a slight change in the name, as you would imagine, since it is an alternate universe after all. Regardless of that, the vehicle descriptions are hilarious and filled with references. Any enthusiast that knows the cars and the history of rallying is going to love it, especially since all the iconic cars are featured. On top of it, every car has very distinctive handling, mimicking their real life counterparts.Unfortunately this is where the game falls a bit short. You can't change the car setups, solely the paint. You can unlock new paints by finishing stages and most of them are also references to the real world counterparts, but that's about it. Not a big deal for me since I don't fiddle all that much with setups, but still worth mentioning.Why would I talk about the music in a racing game, when all you want to hear is the car sounds? Simple answer: the music is absolutely brilliant. Synthwave isn't necessarily a genre I was familiar with, but after completing the game I fell in love with it. It just adds so much value to the whole experience. Driving a stage with synthwave blasting, hitting the apex of every corner, the vibrant colors - it just sends you into a trance-like state and I loved every bit about it.All in all, this game is an actual masterpiece filled with humorous references, amazing music and of course - brilliant gameplay. The more you love cars, the history of them and the stories motorsport produced, the more you are going to love this game. This is more than just a game, it's a work of art - The art of rally - an homage to the sport as a whole. A must play for every rally enthusiast.

_childDocuments_.review: I definitely recommend this fun and somewhat casual rally game.  I don't consider myself a sim-racer but I have been playing game series like Forza, Dirt, Burnout and Flatout for years.  This game lies somewhere in-between arcade and sim with a less-than-serious aesthetic but surprisingly engaging driving.  The handling reminds me of the original Flatout in that it is not a full simulation yet demands reasonable driving input.  Be careful or you will crash, unlike something like Burnout where you just apply full left or right and scrape the wall.  A lot of people compare art of rally to Dirt Rally, but I feel that Dirt Rally is much more of a simulator than this game is.  The biggest downside to art of rally is the high camera angle which makes judging elevation changes or crests kind of hard.Anyway, if you wish the '80s and Group B never ended than buy this game!

_childDocuments_.review: is a fun rally-inspired game with plenty of cars to unlock among a variety of tracks. The game features year by year career mode, free roam, and also has online daily and weekly events. The artwork is amazing, it's in low-poly but looks absolutely beautiful. For people who enjoy rally-style racing games, this is a pretty good addition to your library. For people who don't enjoy racing, you can still have fun running around in free-roam mode, but you will need to complete some career events to unlock new cars. This game is made by the same developers as  and I think the physics is pretty similar. It does take a while to get used to, with the stability assist probably more troublesome to have on than off. After playing around for a while, I saw benefit of it when I was being lazy. But when I actually tried to steer, the stability assist was really messing with me. So ultimately I turned it off.This game only offers top-down camera view from several perspectives, so for people who enjoy games like  for the head-cam, this won't be available.In free-roam mode, you will be able to explore all of the landscapes/roads available in the game otherwise, without any worries about making the best times. Instead, you will be just driving around collecting cassette tapes (to unlock new audio tracks) or looking a few pre-set views. In addition, gather the letters r-a-l-l-y to unlock the subsequent free-roam stage.There are several difficulty levels to pick from, so you don't have to race against hardcore AI who can zip around every corner with perfect precision. There is an easy mode even below novice mode, for people who just want to win every race with no pressure at all. In addition, you can turn off damage to the vehicles, so tumbling off a cliff means that you will only get a 5 second penalty on your time as the car is being recovered.You can also try out daily and weekly challenges set for the game.I played with a controller and tried it on a keyboard as well. I prefer the controller.It's lo-poly artwork with a really bright color palette, a lot of the scenery looks like watercolors so it's enjoyable to just look around as you are playing through the game. There's probably a large group of people who wishlist the game for its general appearances alone.The music is really fun to listen to, the vibes are really great for this game. The sound effects are mostly fine, some of the car engines sound a bit funny, but it could just be me.This game is good for people who like the artwork or who enjoy rally-style games. If you like both, then even better.Base price of $24.99 is a little high, but then again it's a game you can get countless hours of fun from, so I suppose it's okay.1. I would love to have a few more camera options that are closer to the ground, a better forward looking chase-cam would be fine, even if I cannot have an in-car head-cam. Even the lowest POV angle is higher than I would like.2. The pre-set sights in free-roam mode is only available one time. Once you collect it, you cannot go look at it again. The car displayed in the scene is what you are driving at the time, it would be nice to be able to go back and re-access it later.3. Better fine-tuning control options would be nice.I am not a good person to tell you whether or not  is a  rally game, because I am terrible at such games. But I can tell you that it's fun and pretty to look at. As mentioned above, the physics took a while to get used to and I find it more realistic with the stability assist off, so use that at your own risk.With all of the different ways to play the game, the different cars available, and its core as a time-attack race against-yourself kind of game, you can be playing this for many hours and still be having fun, so I think the price is reasonable.Score: 8.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: You come to in a carpark in Finland. Given the glare, the hangover is implied. Your in-game father, a giant, low-poly golden Buddha statue, phases up through the ground, gives you a short history of the noble and eponymous art of rally, warns you about trees and then, just like your real father, ♥♥♥♥♥ off until you've made him proud.You promptly floor the accelerator, wildly overestimate your skill level and chuff yourself into a ditch. Neither of your fathers are proud.But you try again, regardless. The road ahead of you winds, bucks and narrows, outraged that you'd dare try to traverse it - or at least, travel it without the proper respect. You're thrown off. Glumly, you read the fun slogan on the bottom of your car as it sinks into the Sicilian ocean.You try again. Funselektor makes trying again easy. The music swells and pulses, four hours' worth of bounding synthwave that begs patience, calm and focus as it weaves and spins; like Gandalf on rollerskates. Like a real life Gandalf on rollerskates, it is irresistible and you follow it, and try again.You book it into a fir tree. You try again.You misjudge a jump and cartwheel past impassive cows. You shame them and yourself. You try again.You entirely underestimate the stopping power of a hay bale and lose valuable seconds doing a 13-point turn. You grit your teeth, and try again.On a rainy night somewhere in the Japanese hills, you perfectly drift an 80s Volvo around a hairpin. You are aroused for longer than four hours and need to phone your doctor.You learn to fear Germany and the precision its landscape demands, but love its automotive children.You learn to take your eyes from the car below you, positioned, as you are, as a phantasmal observer high above yourself - out-of-vehicular-body experience entire - and watch instead that distant horizon, reading it like an augur. You might be moving in the present, braking and sliding around the current corner, but your mind is two turns ahead, six seconds; you are racing the future.At a certain point, you will realise that you've been reacting to the pitch of your car's engine, listening as it instructs you when to lift off the accelerator, so that you can clip the apex of the corner and still be facing the right way to floor it into the next. There will come a time when you fight not to make up seconds, but shave off milliseconds. art of rally is a language, and you have become fluent.You come to in a Finnish carpark, blinking owlishly at your screen. The HUD tells you that you've just finished a stage, but you're not entirely sure which one; the wave of the music, the rhythm of accelerate-brake-turn, the hypnotism of that ever-moving horizon has lulled you and you forgot you were racing. You weren't even really thinking. The leaderboard puts your time in the top 5% of drivers. That is the art of rally.Somewhere at least one of your fathers is proud, probably.

_childDocuments_.review: Art of Rally is a fantastic racing game that offers a unique and engaging experience. The isometric perspective provides a refreshing take on traditional racing games, and the gameplay is both challenging and satisfying. The physics engine is incredibly well-tuned, and the cars feel great to drive, with each one providing a distinct and satisfying handling experience.As someone who loved Dirt Rally (2015), I found Art of Rally to be a great successor in many ways, with a similar level of difficulty and a focus on skill-based driving. The variety of tracks and environments is impressive, and each one presents its own challenges and opportunities to hone your driving skills.While the graphics may not be hyper-realistic, the stylized art style is a perfect fit for the game's overall aesthetic and adds to its charm. Overall, Art of Rally is an amazing game that offers a truly unique and enjoyable racing experience.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a masterpiece. Yes, it may be a top down arcade game, something that could make sim fans look elsewhere, but its physic engine really puts many sims to shame (for me, it's the second best rally game after the great old Richard Burns Rally). Once you get the hang of the driving model, you will be hooked forever, AoR really is a work of love, and it shows it every moment you play. The only downside for me is that wheels are not officially supported, so they can work or not, but it's not a great problem in the end. It's a game meant to be played with a gamepad, but it's surprisingly good with a keyboard too. It has more than 50 cars (plus some "extras"), ranging from group 2 to group A, and 8 rallies (Finland, Sardinia, Japan, Norway, Germany, Kenya, Indonesia and, with the dlc, Australia), for a total of 84 (96 with the Australia dlc) stages, considering normal and reverse versions (complete with daylight, night, fog, rainy/snowy conditions). Graphics speaks for themselves: Its wonderful, minimalistic art style is simply beautiful to look at, it's like looking at a childhood dream come true, with little cars running in amazing dioramas. It has beautiful replays and an A-M-A-Z-I-N-G photo mode to make every virtual photographer happy, especially now that you can create and/or import custom made liveries. It also has an amazing soundtrack. If you love cars, rally, or simply a game that you can easily pick up and play for a few minutes (but remember, this is one of those games where you say "just five minutes more" and then you look at the clock and hours have passed :) ) there's really no reason for not buying Art Of Rally. Do it. You won't be disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm around 5 hours into art of rally at the time of writing this review - a point at which it appears I'm around 50% of my way through career and the core of what this game has to offer, having seen enough to feel qualified to offer my opinion.First off, let's clarify what type of game this is: art of rally is an indie game designed to showpiece everything cool about the history of rallying... borrowing from the 90's isometric viewpoint of successful 90s classics, amalgamating with the art style of games such as Abzu and Journey - vibrant, distinct but minimal scenery, and a modern synthwave soundtrack plays seamlessly between rallies and menus. It's stylish for sure... but don't go in expecting Micro Machines. There's a depth to the handling model that puts it somewhere between Forza Horizon and Dirt Rally in terms of handling, with a selection of driving aids for those less confident.It celebrates the history of rally, from the classics such as the esky and the meanie (Escort and Mini), through to Group B, and finally the cozzie, fujin (Impreza) and liftback (Celica) from the 90s. Most of the cars feel different, with the heavier cars such as the turbo brick having substantial weight to them, whilst the 4r6 drives with reckless abandon. There's a definite level of nuance here that you'd not necessarily expect from the screenshots.The sound effects are adequate for what the game offers - tyre squeals and engine noises are distinct but unremarkable. I get the impression the developer may have been torn on how much effort to put into the sound effects, given the stunning soundtrack by Tatreal with his 80's inspired synthwave is a real highlight. It's a must-listen for those who enjoy the likes of the Midnight, or those who adored the much acclaimed sounds of Drive.Visually, the game looks stunning. I can't speak much for performance on lower end PCs, I have it locked at max settings 100fps (9900k/2080Ti) and there's only a handful of visual options, but draw distances are as far as the eye can see and the game sacrifices polygon count for style - delivering a striking visual experience that varies dramatically across the 5 countries you visit. With 40+ vehicles, a free play mode, integrated time trial / leaderboards, there's plenty to offer for those driven to master the game, and it's an absolute joy to play along the way.Thoroughly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Almost gave up early but glad I didn't. First starting out, it felt like the controls were wooden and stiff, the cars were unresponsive, and the camera angles were always messing me up. I couldn't control the cars, kept crashing into things, and generally wasn't having any fun.Having stuck with it a bit longer, I came to realize that the game is closer to a sim than an arcade racer and the physics model is heavily focused on vehicle weight transfer. After that, the rest fell into place.Hints:- Control problems? You're probably using too much throttle and not slowing down enough for turns. The physics engine punishes you for constantly flooring it and rewards you for easing into the throttle and using part throttle in a lot of situations. - The brakes are exceptionally strong on all cars on all surfaces. Use them!- You don't need to Fujiwara Takumi every single turn.- Understeering in a slow corner? Lift off the throttle entirely to get the weight back over the front tires.- The game punishes you for crashing. Even the lightest collision almost always results in a 180 spin. Avoiding offs in the first place is the best strategy. - Loss of control and pendulum-ing all over the place? The camera lags behind the car's movements, and amplifies the situation. Lifting off the gas prevents the pendulum effect.- There are no pace notes and sometimes you can't see the hairpin or decreasing radius turn coming up ahead. Discretion is the better part of valor.- Hate the rainy stages? They're the perfect place to practice your throttle control and tons of fun once you get it down.Things I like:- Charming aesthetic- Nice variation in levels and cars- Music selection- Once you get a hang of the physics model and start putting it all together, it becomes super rewarding to chain together an entire stage of perfect corners. Stick with it!Nitpicks:- Camera lag / sometimes you can't see what's coming up ahead- Occasional performance problems / FPS drops- Cuts are allowed but sometimes the game questionably resets your car when you're only a few feet off the road

_childDocuments_.review: A really fun little game, that's easy to learn but truly difficult to master. While the cars fly as if they were in low-gravity when catching airtime, the driving physics are surprisingly great and much better than some AAA games out there (cough cough Cyberpunk). Each car has a unique feel and handles completely differently from the rest, the scenery is downright gorgeous, and you can find yourself completely lost in the game for hours! I recommend this to any and all auto racing enthusiasts who want a small lightweight indie style alternative to Dirt that they can play in class or at the office. The one thing I would really love to see added in the future would be some sort of split-screen co-op mode so I could compete against my friends in races.

_childDocuments_.review: Art of Rally is a minimalist, conceptually simple game where you go throught the different ages of rally. It projects a very ZEN aura and along with the soundtrack poses a perfect relaxing game. At least in concept.If I could I would give this game a neutral rating. It is not a bad game. It runs just fine even on lower end PCs. However the gameplay is very flawed. For a game that presents itself as a casual, relaxing game, the controls of the cars are very fiddly, even inconsistent. This is made worse by the fact that you cannot turn of automatic compensation and oversteering, which often results in cars zig-zagging out of the track without you having any reasonable say on it. Not only that, the grip of the car onto the road changes from track to track with no discernible logic. Sometimes I have better control on snow than I do on gravel or even asphalt.It feels like you're driving on ice cream, is what I am saying, regardless of conditions.Do not get me wrong, I like the game. But it is very frustrating, very inconsistent and does not deliver the experience it advertises. I am sure I will get derided a lot for saying this, but it does not feel like driving skill (not mastery of mechanics, driving) has anything to do with how well you do in the game and for these reasons I cannot give it a positive review, even though it runs well.

_childDocuments_.review: I originally wrote this in April 2023 but didn't upload it. I wasn't sure how to approach this game from the perspective of a reviewer because it's so bloody perfect, and a lot of these sorts of games I class as "unreviewable". As an example of what I mean, other games that would fall into that category are arcade classics that are still talked about and played over 40 years later such as Pac-Man or Space Invaders, or games with ridiculous amounts of memetic discussion surrounding them like Half-Life or the original Doom. Like, how the hell can words do enough justice for this level of quality and discussion? To be honest, a better review is simply a gameplay video. A picture can say a thousand words.---I haven't had this much fun in a driving game for a long time. It's incredibly hard to put my Deck down, like it was made for it or something. It's relaxing yet satisfying once you get into the flow state, and more forgiving than the developer's drift title. 10/10 soundtrack too. They didn't put "art" in the title for nothing either - this is one of those games that can be used to convince philistines that videogames are an art form.It takes a couple of hours to start driving well, especially as you're forced to drive crapboxes at the beginning, but that means that once you unlock the real rally cars you'll truly appreciate it and know how to use them properly. It's game blue-balling done right, in that it teases you until you desperately want access to a proper car and then oooh it feels so damn good.I guess it's a simcade, but it differs from other simcades in that the elements that are usually arcadey are simulation-like here, so it won't have you setting up your vehicles but you better know a bit about how cars behave. You just go straight into it. My only non-technical critique is that a view from the front of your car would be nice. Regardless, it is a beautiful game, and the minimalist menus bring that beauty to the forefront. You get into this sort of meditative state once you get good, and it feels incredible. Turn off the crowds not only for a performance boost but, imo, better atmosphere.Now for the bad part, and probably the most important: The Linux version seems to perform a lot better than Windows. On Windows the game has very little optimisation. Running a dual boot system with Manjaro, in one OS I can max the game out at 1440p 120fps, while on the Windows it struggles on medium (which are Deck settings at a higher resolution) to maintain a consistent framerate. In some ways it's amusing to me that *Linux* is the preferred OS for this game!!!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is peaceful and meditative, while also somehow evoking rage quits :) If you're a fan of racers with other cars on the track, then probably won't enjoy this game. The challenges with those games come from having to drive fast and conquer the course, with cars behind you, pressuring you. This game is not like that. It is much more a "cross country runner" type of game: the race is against yourself. How well can you drive fast and conquer the course, driving entirely by yourself?If you played Absolute Drift, then you are already familiar with Art of Rally's style (and you're probably aware of how sneaky difficult Funselektor games can be). There's fun to be had with this game. It's not exactly a true-to-life sim, but it's also not arcade. It's sim-adjacent, which makes it challenging and rewarding. You'll need to finesse your way to success.I have an absurd number of games in my Steam library, but right now, I find myself coming back to Art of Rally, struggling to admit my budding addiction... (And it has a photo mode, which make replaying your races arguably as fun as, if not more fun than, actually driving the races).As with Absolute Drift, the environments are minimalistic (though, Art of Rally is much more scenic than Absolute Drift; but it retains a similar low-poly aesthetic). The music is zen. The color palette is relaxing. The game is good.  You'll need a controller though - gamepad at least (I play with a PS4 controller).I'll admit I'm biased :) I received the game for free -- I was a beta tester, and I learned that my beta key enabled me to receive the release for free. But also, I know the lead developer. Dune is awesome, and I tried to pay for the game anyway; he wouldn't let me. I am not bragging here; my point is that Funselektor is an awesome indie team, they put a lot of love into their titles, and they are also actually good peoples.In conclusion: Art of Rally is totally worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: There's a lovely moment when, after many hours of banging into fences and failing to brake properly, you achieve a perfect drift around a corner into a crowd of onlookers. _childDocuments_.name: art of rally

_childDocuments_.review: The game is a jewel! art of rally is a very nice game. What makes the difference is the gameplay itself. Like an old style racing game, this requires you to practice. You'll need to play with brake and accelerator, the physical engine seems realistic and satisfying. The speed sensation is really there when you pass 100mph. It's challenging and it really makes you want to get better, if you like the whole driving subject.The ambientation is fine. Cars are graphically essential but precise, there are many of them but the engine sounds are different too and "defining". This is surely a good thing, when you recognise things that are well represented (specially if you are a rally fan).Tracks are nice, not really "a lot" but a good number on which you can spend many time and for all tastes.Career mode is a bit "raw". You get to make rallies but there's just one "season" per group of cars. You do that mostly to unlock all cars. Once you did that, you go on time trials and try to beat worldwide opponents and that is ok, but i feel that with a better career mode (like really a "career" with progression through the years, teams, car improvements and stuff) this would be an outstanding game. I recommend the game, but it could be greater with more content. I wouldn't mind paying something more for other content like a better career or more complex online events (like worldwide rallies). Apart from this i can't see any other problem in the game.
_childDocuments_.name: art of rally

_childDocuments_.review: Simple Graphics, Beautiful music and awesome physics. Not the most realistic, but with stability assist turn off, you can comfortably slide your car around. The first few hours can be tough as you learn the cars and the roads but if you are a fan of rally it is most certainly worth it. I would also like to mention while there is no FFB this game DOES fully support a wheel (much to my surprise as I had bumped it while playing). Overall 100% worth the 25$ asking price, even more so if you can get it on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: art of rally

_childDocuments_.review: Driving physics feel really awkward. The brakes are too strong, it is hard to take corners smoothly and holding slides is difficult because the car just doesn't seem to handle like a rallycar at all. I've played several rallygames like Richard Burns Rally and loads of CMR and Dirt titles. The horrible steering doesn't help either. It feels inconsistent when sliding and is way too direct when you want to make slight adjustments on the straights. _childDocuments_.review: Great gameplay, simple yet challenging, big learning curve.The game is entirely focused on a great gameplay, realistic driving feelings and a minimalistic art direction.Photo mode, daily events, free mode, time attack: extremely complete game for just 20 bucks.Relieve the golden age of Rallying, with cleverly made stages to remind you of the real world, and ingenious names for your favorite rally cars.However, sound design could use some work in my opinion, especially engine sounds, but at this point we're just nitpicking.Bonus point: The game receives regular updates !

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so good I love it so much. The physics are very simcadey, with very challenging driving that you can truly master. _childDocuments_.review: halfway through the career and I'm struggling to recommend this game. Overall, it plays like a basic unity engine indie game.I had continuous issues with the camera angle, viewing objects/height, no textures, and handling settings.1) I only found one usable viewing angle - the one that showed the most track ahead. There is no navigator or mini map or heads-up display. So you need to see whats coming ahead, but the game views are mostly blind top down views.2) All the viewing angles hide different obstacles/objects. Grass height is the same as small objects which makes them tricky to see. A lot of stages in the early game had hidden fence posts, rocks or stumps that couldnt be seen until too late. It also makes it hard to see elevation. Cars are floaty when airborne which makes it twice as difficult when you weren't sure if there was a crest ahead.3) A lot of the visibility issues are to do with the lack of textures. Grass has the same texture/colour as flat ground. Driving surfaces all look and sound the same with no dust being kicked up (unlike in the screenshots).4) Always playing around with the control settings and could never find a good setup. All cars brake WAY too well in a straight line even with ABS set to low. Then they're on ice skates when engaging a high speed slide. I could not get used to the counter steering no matter what I set the percentage to. It feels like I'm the only entrant in a multi-year career. The game occasionally shows you flags and names of the opponents (meaningless), but what is wrong with stage rankings and a small visual to show opponents cars and livery? There isnt even a podium, just a number of your place. It's all very disengaging and confirms that the game is very much style-focused.5hrs in, I'm not having fun or impressed with the visuals anymore. It tries to strike a tricky balance between arcade and sim-lite but isnt fun or interesting enough to be either.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the only racing game that's ever put me into a "flow state" similar to Tetris.  In tune with the car, drifting serenely through obviously pretty environments.  I appreciate the campaign mode has no requirements to be a god at the game, anybody can progress and unlock everything it has to offer.  There's no penalty if you have a bad season, unless its the sort of thing you take personally.I also appreciate the story is short, surreal, and most importantly,   If I play one more driving game where I constantly get hassled by an insufferable personality about my internet popularity I might swear the genre off for good.My one gripe is with fade in with certain areas.  Japan is particularly bad.  The plants and shadows are instantly generated (or LOD increased) before your eyes - other areas the draw distance is both much further and the fade in more gradual, making it less noticeable.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great little game. It has just enough difficulty to seem impossible at first, but with a bit of patience and a controller one can master the art of rally.I'm far from good, but I have gotten far more fun out of the game than any of the racing games since my teens.Once I finished with the carreer I had a few moments where I just couldn't fathom how I did some of the really fast and technical parts without any mistakes at top speed. Just did it without thinking. Had I thought I would have failed. It made me all giddy with tension. This is very rare in a game.A few hints:- Staying on the road is usually more important than speed. Since road helps you to change both speed and direction of the car faster. Learn the game by staying on the road.- Play through the carreer mode even if frustrating. No need to re-do as the amount of driving will teach you a lot once you conclude with 1995. You can always return and re-do whole seasons once you get grasp of drifts and how breaking will affect the steering and all the tiny micro-skills that exist out there. Trust your brain to learn a lot of it. Experiment.Read the lore; it's fun.- Play with the accellerator by pushing it repeatedly when taking turns. It will help your brain find the balance spot of control.- Try to find cars which have better sideways-grip. Those stabilise better.- Plan ahead. You can't handle some turns by improvising on the go.

_childDocuments_.review: Therapeutic gaming at its best.If you're the kind of person that loves rally, or finds himself smiling when seeing old clips of turbocharged behemoths racing through the forest, then this game is absolutely for you. If you're an appreciator of stylized polygonal art, then this game is for you. Even the music in this game is incredible, with Tatreal producing a soundtrack worthy of driving to during your morning commute.No game that I have played has brought as much simple, pure joy as this one. Whether I have 10 minutes, or a couple of hours to dedicate to playing it during a session, I always close 'Art of Rally' with a smile on my face, and usually with a new wallpaper or two (since the game is very photogenic).The learning curve is real, but absolutely doable. The stage design manages to be challenging without feeling deliberately vindictive. The cars all behave differently, and you'll earn great joy as you learn to handle vehicles that strike your fancy.I would happily purchase new AoR course DLCs in perpetuity given the quality present in this game.I never would have thought that a game like this would crack my all-time top 5, but AoR is safely in that group.

The first time you pick it up you will be sliding off the road, overcooking it and thinking it is impossible .... give it a couple of hours and you will be sliding through the corners and dancing through the stages.The graphical style is refreshing and the camera angle works really well.  The Career ensures you get used to the speed and handling characteristics of the cars as you unlock more modern eras.Handling has and arcade simulation feel and feathering brakes and accelerator through the corner rewards you with accurate feedback. _childDocuments_.review: As someone who's 100%'d Absolute Drift and has played every Codemasters (and RBR) rally game - This game is okay.What works? It carries Absolute Drift's simplistic art style and beats - leading to a game that you can just veg out and slide around the roads in Free Roam collecting all the collectibles.What doesn't work? Firstly, no pace notes. Don't know if I should hit the hill at full throttle because I have no idea if there's a corner coming up. To pile on the lack of pace notes, there's no feedback from your car. The difference between a perfect slide through a corner and bogging down and spinning out seems to be somewhat random. You can almost never tell if a corner is going to let you cut (again, no notes) or reset you for a 5 second penalty. Then, there's no checkpoints. No way to tell if you're +10 seconds off pace or crushing the competition - so you might have a perfectly clean run only to find out you could've shaved +16 seconds off... on Normal mode!It's still satisfying to play and when you have a perfect slide and come in first? Amazing but the game feels like it's setting you up for failure and also limiting your restarts. I'd be fine with the limited restarts in career if I at least had pace notes and splits. As it stands, you've got to commit 4+ minutes just to find out you apparently could've been MUCH faster and then have to decide if you want to waste another 4 minutes and one of your limited restarts or potentially waste another 4 stages as now you've got to replay the whole season because you couldn't manage to make up that 16 second deficiency.

_childDocuments_.review: A great, relaxing rally game. There is a decent selection of cars, each with different handling, liverlies, and engine audio. There's a nice career mode following rally history which will unlock more cars as you complete races. The graphics are splendid with a nice minimal aesthetic, however the lighting and colors of the different locations are fantastic. I definitely recommend for a chill racer, its one of the rare indies where you can feel all the developers passion being dumped into the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I wasn’t expecting this, given what I enjoy most about rally titles, like Codemasters’ outstanding Dirt Rally and Dirt Rally 2.0I was sceptical with the overhead pulled back view, but I honestly found it to be fun. Giving it a different challenge to what I've always been used to. Sure, there are other camera angles, each with their own pros and cons.The colourful and vibrant effects on each different rally is stunning, I do like the Cherry Blossoms of Rally Japan especially. A vast array of WRC cars through the years makes it easy to drive cars you don't often see anymore. An easy pick up and play game to kill time. Do recommend, even if you're a more hardcore rally fan like myself

All the cars handle differently adding more depth to the driving, as well a different road surfaces and weather effects.Overall a casual, fun game that presents enough challenge to be engaging, but not too much that it's frustrating to learn and play.
