_childDocuments_.review: Pretty much everything about this game is great. _childDocuments_.review: I played the whole thing with default settings with arrow keys and had a blast. Found out later you can adjust the camera and controller can be more fun. _childDocuments_.review: This game is amazing.The physics are close to real life, yet the game doesn't take itself overly seriously.The driving experience is about as far from "arcade style" as you can get. There are some modest adjustable driver assists in the settings, but in general the game will not help you to smooth out your inputs. To stay on the road and go fast, you have to think about weight transfer, tire slip, timing, and positioning - just like in real life. Surface changes, elevation changes, and sudden dips/ crests, will upset the car's balance and it's up to you to manage all of that. FWD, RWD, AWD, front/ mid/ rear engine all matters in this game for how a car behaves and rotates.The graphics and illustration style are fun and minimalistic. The music is great, too. It's clear that a lot of care and attention went into making this game.The game has great replayability if you are someone who enjoys driving IRL. Since the driving in this game is genuinely challenging, there is always something to improve on and it's very rewarding to find more speed and more control.I have no real gripes with the game. It would be nice to have some sort of navigation or codriver voice to let you know what turns are coming. The overhead view is good enough most of the time, but the night courses and blind corners increase the chances that you're either going to go off the road or slow down too much for corners. But I don't see a way to add this to the game and still retain that casual minimalism that I like so much, so I give it a pass on this issue.Overall I would recommend this game to any driving enthusiast.
_childDocuments_.name: art of rally

_childDocuments_.review: I want to love this game, I really do. The soundtrack is incredible, the graphics are smooth and fun, the car designs and sounds are great, but the physics just makes no sense to me. The car has like 100% grip, until it doesn't, and then just slides wildly out of control. Throttle control in slides is almost nonexistent. If you are on the gas in a corner without grip, you slide straight sideways off the road. Coming out of corners or when regaining control after a slide, the car pendulums back and forth without staying straight. Your car reacts wildly to camber and elevation changes on the road, but most of the time you can't even see those changes because of the graphics and camera angles. Its like halfway between an arcade game and a realistic driving sim and just never feels right. It is fun for a while but eventually the frustration of your car never doing what you want it too kinda ruins it. Group B was especially hard to manage which unfortunately are the cars you most look forward too.

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful visuals and easy to grasp controls; whether want to just turn and brake with automatic transmission or prefer a more sim experience by using manual, and there's a metric ton of unlockables.  Forgiving difficulty and lots of gameplay customization with a galloping, nocturnal retrowave soundtrack...I think I've died and gone to heaven.
_childDocuments_.name: art of rally

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an amazing simulator style rally game. It is endlessly replay-able and highly rewarding and challenging. The developers continue to add cars and stages, although I defiantly race the F40 clone in every track. The team nails the handling properties and road phyisics. To be fair, compared to a game like Assetto Corsa, this experience is a bit easier and less punishing. Notably, when running far off track the game will respawn you back where you left with a relative time penalty. There is no customization besides the livery schemes, but the selection of cars is epic and historically relevant despite the car designs being unlicensed. Great for kids and adults, not highly demanding hardware requirements, online time trails. I would like to be able to race head to head, but besides that minor gripe this game is the complete package rally sim. Ok, one more gripe: how about some pace notes, WRC style?

_childDocuments_.review: Art of Rally is a colorful window into a bygone era of unhinged, unfettered competition. It’s a satisfying, mechanically complex racing game that hooks you into the mindset of “just one more race.” It’s also a tribute to rally history, and the developers clearly let their knowledge and interest of the sport’s past influence the game’s every facet.It’s minimalistic in the best way— you, your iconic car of choice, and challenging roads. An exceptional synthwave soundtrack aids in achieving the perfect flow state when you’re chaining corners together at high speed. If you’re on the fence, I’ll try to convey why I think the small team at Funselektor has earned your money with Art of Rally—and importantly, why this game deserves your time.This aspect is deeper than you might expect. It’s not a full simulation—but the handling model is no slouch either. Weight transfer is key, as well as speed conservation and grip limit. Utilizing real knowledge of car behavior and racing techniques will help you place first. There’s options for vehicle damage—the strictest of which will incentivize you to learn every corner and pick your driving lines thoughtfully. Certain cars you will naturally mesh with. You’ll wonder if you can push those cars further. In fact, at some point in your quest for speed you might actually find yourself wrestling with the controls. You may feel like they’re holding you back in some way, you may get frustrated. I personally had to adjust some game settings in order to fully bend certain cars to my will. There’s no vehicle-specific tuning options, which I think was the right choice. But there  meaningful adjustments you can make, to change the responsiveness of the cars.Consider changing the deadzones/steering sensitivity if needed. Some players claim the handling is outright bad. That’s an unfair assessment. The game requires you to understand it. The different driving surfaces demand your attention. Changes in terrain elevation are to be respected, as are puddles in the rain. Each car feels distinct. Each  feels distinct, and you’ll need to adapt to the changes that come with higher horsepower and the advent of AWD. It’s  rewarding and satisfying to master a car in Art of Rally.There’s a wide selection (62) of vehicles to choose from. Each car is lovingly modeled, with several livery options. They are based on real rally cars with a few easter egg vehicles thrown in the mix as well. They all have written descriptions, which are a blend of humorous and fact-filled.I’ve spent most of my time in career mode. It begins with the early days of Group 2 in the late 60s, and culminates in the era of Group A—which ultimately became the basis for modern rallying. However, the horsepower of Group A in-game is much higher than in reality. I’m ok with this for the sake of gameplay progression, and it results in these cars feeling like the pinnacle of what you can drive within the game.At the center is the mythical Group B. Car manufacturers and racing teams spared no expense in creating some of the most insane machines that were constantly pushing the boundaries of what was possible for vehicular development, within the confines of extremely loose regulatory restrictions. During this time in history, drivers contended with many obstacles. They had to tackle dangerous roads at near-inhuman speeds. They had to race the clock, and set competitive times against their peers to make their mark on the rallying world. And, they were also navigating through crowds of spectators—hordes of motorsport fans and photographers encroaching on their path for a chance to see the action up close. A perfect recipe for some of the most memorable moments in motorsport history, and an era that—despite its extraordinary danger and eventual loss of life—is looked upon fondly by rally enthusiasts and former Group B drivers alike. Art of Rally gets this era spot-on. As soon as you get into those cars, the feeling of pushing the limit of your vehicle is heightened. The stages you’ve been learning in the previous classes now seem more daunting, and you begin to morph your driving style to suit the new capabilities of your car. Taking things further, the game allows you to set foot into the realm of Group S. It’s often forgotten in other rally games, as it never saw the light of competition after Group B was canceled. But, the vehicles slated to compete in Group S are some of the most interesting and unshackled 4-wheeled machines ever developed. It's great to see them!You'll race across 7 countries in the base game. Each is varied, and feels handcrafted and engaging to explore—and they’re inspired by real-world rallying locations. They strike a balance between technical challenge and high-speed segments, with their own intricacies to learn. There’s 42 unique stages in the base game, and they can be driven in reverse which adds more variety. Elevation changes and multiple driving surfaces will keep you on your toes. Weather/time of day variation keeps the stages feeling fresh. The cars sound great, and have fairly distinctive engine notes. Details include turbo flutter, gearbox whine, exhaust crackles, and the thunderous staccato of anti-lag. Subtle ambient noises, such as the cheer of the massive crowds or the sound of gravel hitting the underside of the car add to the atmosphere. The game’s soundtrack is  and extra songs can be unlocked via free roam collectibles. The soundscape as a whole works wonderfully in pulling you into the world, making you feel like the hero driver at the starting line we all wish to be.The graphics are simple, but there’s robust detail and endearing care taken in the art design. The lighting and shadows at sunset are stunning. The stylistic choices of the game work really well, from the charming yet accurate appearance of each car model to the cube-like spectators which congregate along the roadside. There’s a full-fledged photo and replay mode which I’ve spent a lot of time in. Your screenshots will be displayed on the 5 polaroids in the main menu, which is a nice touch. I wish there were even  of those polaroids to show off my ever-growing album.Racing games are often misunderstood. Sometimes they get categorized with the likes of football or basketball games—but they aren’t like those. You don’t control a team of athletes. And in rally racing, you are alone on a stage with no other cars to consider overtaking. You aren’t looking at other competitors and trying to outwit or outmaneuver them directly. Instead, your fight is through the intermediary of the track. It’s driver versus road, and the one ally you have in that fight is a monstrous machine which isn’t interested in behaving. You must tame it, convince it. Become one with it. The best racing games allow you to feel a fraction of what it’s like to really be behind the wheel. They emulate what it is to extend yourself into the car, acting as if it is a part of you—and masterfully controlling it to the limits of human comprehension, all the while you’re gripped by the creeping sensation that it could all be lost at any second. That is what makes all motorsport compelling. And in my opinion, despite its simplistic looks, Art of Rally manages to capture that in an authentic and rare way.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is good however there's a couple of questions you need to ask yourself before purchasing it.1. Are you prepared to get good at it?This game is no arcade racer and can be very frustrating if you just go in thinking lets throw this car around and get from A to B asap. I quickly found a certain degree of feather was required on the brake and accelerator.2. Are you ok driving on your own with no other cars to be seen and no real feeling you're in a race?Yeah i know that's what rallying is but it can be sobering experience driving without any visible stimulus.I liked the game hence the recommendation however i didn't love it and at times found it a bit boring also the graphics for this game get a lot of praise and yes at times it can look very pretty however a wet foggy night in Kenya is like a mud party in a sewage plant.The graphic style though is pleasing and the sound was decent and driving through the different era's of rallying was fun just be prepared to put the time into mastering the techniques you will need to win.The one big thing i hated in this game was gravestones at the side of the road......anyone who has played this will know what i mean ;)In summary - Good game but tricky to master.

_childDocuments_.review: Whoever made Farschweiler and other German stages with those tombstones, I hope you get whatever you deserve... Don't get me wrong, they would have been awesome if this game was designed to be played with a wheel. Alas, it was not and so they're simply not fun. But the game is SO GOOD that it compensates. Seriously, it's really good. Graphics are beautiful and dripping with style. Stages are designed well (except Germany). Handling is riding a fine line between realism and arcade, but close enough to realism that simulation fans like myself who normally can't stand arcade racing games can still have a good time. Cars jump a lot even after the update, but it fits the style. I think it would be weird if they didn't jump that much. The differences between cars of the same era aren't huge, mostly it's about the wheelbase and body length, but it's enough to give it color. And the car names and descriptions are a riot. I'm truly in love with this game, despite the few flaws it has. It's one of the games in my PC that I don't think I'll ever delete, because it's the perfect game to play when you have 30 minutes to kill. If you're a sim fan or an arcade fan, doesn't matter, if you like racing games, I'll bet my left testis that you'll like this game.*And don't come at me with that "Those stones are there in real rally stages" ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. This is a game, you ignore things to make it more fun. In real life, you have only one single chance to do a stage right. But nobody complains that this game gives you multiple chances. It's so that it's more fun. Farschweiler stones should have been ignored, or other stages without stones should have been chosen. But don't get me wrong, I wouldn't be complaining so much if I didn't love this game as much as I did. It's all out of love and passion :)

_childDocuments_.review: Art of Rally is a loveletter to Retro Rally games. Isometric racing with A hybrid simulator and arcade physics system makes difficult mountain roads feel incredibly satisfying and cinematic while you're challenging your car and yourself to chain your drifts together and get the fastest times. The Graphics are simple yet iconic, low-poly cars that look like toys are found to each have a different deep handling. Clear cute models of recognizable cars from your favorite eras are in place with names that reference the cars culture. With 4WD FWD RWD as well as front mid and rear engine cars the choice in car makes each map very re-playable trying to get gold in every career group and better times in the time trials. As you progress you unlock cars from further generations of rally, starting with group 2 in the late 60s ending with group A in the 90s, the unlocked cars are noticeably faster and harder to control but allow for faster times and better drifts. This is a racing game through and though, designed for DIRT fans who want a Sandbox made of beautiful polygons, smooth drifting and little square people standing in the middle of the road. Buttery Drifts I've killed so many pedestrians in Group B9/10 Beautiful Polygons

_childDocuments_.review: As an avid rally gamer this game is deceptively brilliant.It may look lo-fi with the simple polygon non-textured graphics and sound arcade-y with that pulsating synth-wave music throughout, yet under this exterior is one of the best car physics simulation I've come across in any rally game (yes, I've played many over the years).You may think "yeah but why would I play this when I have [insert rally game] which also has awesome handling, an in-car view and proper realistic graphics?" the answer would be:- the soundtrack is great- the courses are fun with a bit of challenge to themand most importantly (for me at least):- the handling with a controller is the best I've come acrossOf course it's not just a case of downloading the game and it handles great out of the box, there are fine-tuning options for the controller settings, and I would recommend playing around with these to get across the handling.Overall this is an excellent simulation of rally beneath a very arcade-looking veneer, and the devs have continued to add new locations and cars since the release - I have definitely got my moneys worth.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm playing with a keyboard, so controllers may be different, but this is ridiculously difficult to navigate. Let's imagine you're approaching a long, shallow corner. You're in a rally car, you want to drift around it, right? So you turn in, ease the accelerator and... continue moving in a straight line and slide off the track. Well okay, maybe you were too fast that time, let's try braking a bit. Approach the corner, turn in, tap the brakes and... immediately jerk to a halt. So what are you meant to do here? Well your guess is as good as mine because I still haven't figured it out. The floor has no grip. The brakes are way too strong. Dare to even breathe against a wall and you'd best strap in because your car is about to perform its best teacups impression. If you go over a jump you'll think you're going to spaaaaaace... because a big metal car weighs as much as bag of feathers apparently. I know this an arcade rally game, and realism often takes a back seat with these, but this is so far from believable it's near unplayable. The game wants you to drive around in a semi-realistic manner, but gives you physics that simply don't work together. If there's no grip, I want to brake. If my brakes are too strong, I want to use them as little as possible. Combine the two and you're forced to drive around at a snail's pace to get around corners. Quite how I'm meant to get through this quickly is beyond me.

_childDocuments_.review: It's remarkable the amount of realism they were able to cram into this adorable looking indie race title.Cars all handle differently, learning to drive each one to its limits requires time and patience. The physics are fantastic. The atmosphere and sounds just absolutely nail the feel of rally. Everything from the crowd nearly being run over, to the blow off valve and afterfire from the Audi Quattro S1's exhaust, it's all here.The difficulty is much higher than you would expect, especially if you're competing in the top 1% of players, where every thousandth of a second counts. The skill ceiling is just mind blowing.Some use this as a relaxing, care free title. But I'm not one of those people.
_childDocuments_.name: art of rally

_childDocuments_.review: A driving game that can be at times relaxing or at times intense. Here you drive from a top down kind of view with there being plenty of different things to do. Different modes from a career mode where you explore the various large mapped area in search of collecting photo views and other items. The maps are quite big so it can take some time to find everything within, and at times circling yourself and meeting where you have before. You can also race among the many stages that there are and take part in time attacks where you go on a leaderboard to compete amongst your friends as well as other steam members who play the game. Customizations can be made when playing as well from setting the climate and weather of the area you play in to the class of your car. Physics is also a key component of the game, where going too fast and not managing your acceleration greatly impacts your course and can drive you other off the path. The game is nice to play when you just want to do some chill free roaming or replaying the maps and trying to best your time to beat others and be the best.
_childDocuments_.name: art of rally

_childDocuments_.review: I was impressed at the depth of this game. I was expecting a very simple driving model, but within a few minutes of playing I realized that the driving model is deep enough to give the player a lot of the key components of rally driving. Weight transfer is modelled, allowing you to tuck the nose in by lifting of the gas, or if more rotation is required, stabbing the brakes. Weight transfer also allows for the scandinavian flick. The e-brake is modelled, for when weight transfer isn't enough and more low speed rotation is required. The clutch is modelled, which allows for clutch-kicking to get the rear out, similar to using the e-brake but when you want to gain speed/radius instead of decrease.I was not expecting to get much enjoyment out of the game since I'm accustomed to the realism of rally sims, and also real life rallycross. But they've got just enough of the core driving tools to make it interesting.My only complaint so far is that some of the engine sounds are terrible. In a game trying to distill rallying to just a few core pillars, with sound being one of them, it sticks out like a sore thumb. Cars with very unique engine sounds like 911s and Imprezas have very generic 4-cylinder-like sounds in this game and it kind of takes me out of the experience.TL;DR:Pros: More realistic driving model than expected, with tools such as weight transfer, e-brake, clutch kicking allowing you to sort of drive the car like you would want to in an actual rally sim.Cons: Engine sounds on some cars with very unique engine sounds in real life, instead have very generic sounds in game that take you out of the experience.Summary: Really fun and complex enough for someone that's used to rally sims or real life rallycross/stage rally.

_childDocuments_.review: If you want a quick review before I go in detail: - Price is fair- Handling feels very satisfying, semi-realistic- Great music, suitable selection of cars and tracks- No story, multiplayer activities (daily and weekly too)- Devs are cool and release updates and DLCs for free (Consider buying OST)- Good graphics, but surprisingly intensive on GPUAnd now, for actual review I suppose:Going as fast as possible, passing by spectators that don't care about their safety at all, Eurobeat blasting in the radio - that's art of rally, at least according to the devs, but honestly, I dig their vision. Yeah, the game has its own Eurobeat (it slaps btw) and generally good selection of music to let you feel the flow better.Cars, colorful and diverse - they resemble real world ones, not only by looks, but also by the anecdotal behavior (Cause I haven't driven 'em irl, besides RBR and DiRT Rally games, what you hear about the cars IS reflected somewhat in AoR) which makes every one of them feel like a unique driving experience, lengthening your fun time in game.There's also fair share of just random vehicles to use, like a lorry that has very noticable weight to it, or VW Pickle bus with way too much power for it's own sake.For tracks - paired with the incredibly cute and atmospheric graphics of the game, they are vastly diverse and provide the expected feeling you'd see in other rally games or in your TV. Among like *maybe* 10 countries in the game, you have different stages with their reversed patterns too, longer or shorter ones. These are also affected by weather, you can encounter rain which makes things very slidey, or night where if you have a frontal crash... things do get a lil' teeny weeny bit harder (yeah, broken lights make seeing harder, who would've thought)The driving - Delightful on a gamepad, satisfyingly difficult but not resistant to be bridled. From my own experience, it required a bit of tweaking in the settings like adjusting camera FoV or the countersteer speed to get it to my liking, but after that I haven't had many issues controlling the car in a way I want. I feel like fair warning would be that the faster the cars and speeds get, the less confidence you usually have.Cars behave in a semi realistic way which for people that just want an escape and relax while playing a car related game - it is perfect. BUT! BUT BUT BUT - I've seen people have fun and learn thing or two about car control while playing THIS very game too.For everything else - Game looks really good, it has its own artstyle, but is suprisingly resource heavy, at least for the GPU. DX12 version seems to be unstable for me and shows graphical bugs after a while, DX11 is fine. Sadly you can't just save replays, you can always record them though. There is some multiplayer to play, competing against other people in daily and weekly challenges, or just trying to break world records in specific settings. I played without any assists and in maximum damage possible, although it's very inconsistent as you can be fine after striking a tree with a roof of your car or have terminal damage after trading paint with a guardrail. *Damage system is really frustrating at times*Game gud, worth price, dribing fun.

_childDocuments_.review: A competent racing game, just not a very good  game. The irony is thick.Pros:+ Physics. The cars are weighty and different enough from each other based on rally class; they are a joy to maneuver over the many terrain types+ Graphics. The neon pastel colours fit the minimalist aesthetics of the UI / cars / terrain perfectly+ The sense of progression. Unlocking cars and new liveries while advancing from one rally class to the next is satisfying+ The cars. Most of the iconic rally cars from the '70s up to the '90s are in the game, easily recognizable (although with silly names and cringe descriptions that subtract from the immersion)+ The music. There is a variety of styles that suit the arcade-y nature of the game well+ Custom car liveriesCons:- No keys rebinding. This, along with the next two points, is absolutely inexcusable in this day and age- No pace notes, either as audible or visual indicators. In a rally game. Let that sink in- The dev obstinately refuses to allow for custom car and driver names, invoking the ROI (!) and the mess it would make on the online leaderboards. Quickly and easily debunked by the next forum reply:Shows that not everyone falls to the dev's egregious gaslighting attempt. He said numerous times that people come to the game with various expectations, and it's on them to adapt to the game's 'vision', therefore everything should be taken as-is and accepted unconditionally. To that I say that maybe it is him the one who is confused by what he wanted the game to be vs. what rally racing actually is. When you call your game 'the art of rally', people come with the clear expectation to play a rally game, not the dev's own vision of what rallying is, or should be- Inconsistent physics. Employing real-world rally techniques will not get the fastest times (despite the presence of  in the game's name and even having the  achievement hinting to this effect). Instead, touring-car type cornering is the way to go, as advised by one forum user:- Inconsistent physics. Side-swiping the guardrails will turn the car 180 degrees. On purpose, just to fxck with you, courtesy of the dev- Inconsistent rules in regards to corner-cutting. On some you need just touch the grass to be auto-resetted while on others cars are allowed to pass through unpunished. This, in turn, leads to the next point- Uncurated online leaderboards. Instead of promoting fair-play racing - in the spirit of rally-racing which the dev claims he tries to emulate - people are encouraged (through non-intervention) to find how much they can cut corners without penalty. As a result, the leaderboards are populated at the top only by 'cheaters' and no-lifers- No multiplayer of any kind. No online servers, hot-seat or split screen, nothing. Daily / weekly challenges are no substitute for head-to-head rally racing- Weak, buzzing, unconvincing engine sounds, particularly the Mazdas' rotary ones which verge on the unbearable- The camera. Only external cameras are allowed during gameplay. No optional hood or bumper views, let alone car interiors and view- Extremely short stages that average 6-8 Kms / 2-3 mins, with the longest being about 13 Kms / 4 minutes long. Again, not very rally-like (hillclimbing would be a more appropriate description but I don't think the dev loses any sleep over such trivialities)- While on the subject of rally stages - the dev has a strange way of choosing new countries to be added to the game. Indonesia and Australia (outrageously priced for what it offers) are in, but no Monaco's Monte Carlo, France (Tour de Corse), Greece (Acropolis Rally) or Great Britain (RAC Rally) to name but a few

_childDocuments_.review: When was the last time you played a racing game? For me, it had been years. When I stumbled across art of rally, I decided to give it a try because it seemed to focus on mechanics over graphics and user experience before realism. In practice, this gave the developers the excuse to make assets that look aesthetically pleasing without aspiring to look like real life. It also allowed them to fine tune each car for the perfect (at least compared with other racing games) mix of respect for its real life counterpart and arcade-y motion.As you may have gathered already, I have an appreciation for this game that allows me to sing high praises, but there are a few points of criticism I hold as of the date of posting this review. Firstly, it would be nice to select a "ghost" to race against outside of one's own runs in order to better understand the mechanics. Second, any tutorial present cannot prepare one for the vastly different styles of driving required between cars--providing a tutorial for driving different cars might be a welcome addition.Overall, the game is a pleasure to play. There are no DLCs as a barrier to driving cars, only a simple unlock system. This is a no-frills racing experience that takes the best parts of racing games and leaves the rest out.

_childDocuments_.review: Funselektor's take on rally is a charming low-poly visual feast that delivers a competent sim-cade experience. The game masterfully captures the delicate dance of counter-steering, weight transfer, braking, and throttle control - all in a cutesy package. RWD is appropriately skittish but agile through the corners; FWD providing a more stable alternative. 4WD is predictably monstrous but require finesse negotiating narrow turns. Road surface, elevation changes, and weather are factors that actually affect how you'd attack a stage - adding a welcome layer of depth to this racer. Overall, a passionate love letter to the age of the supercar. Highly recommended for anyone looking for a racing game that has style and challenge in equal measure.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't play many driving games, but I really enjoyed Absolute Drift a couple of years ago and despite rallying being the least interesting racing to me after F1, I decided to give this game a try. In brief: this is a driving game anyone can pick up if you are happy to spend a little time getting used to it, and I think that time investment is well worth it.The driving itself feels crisp and consistent, so much so that after a while you find yourself making instinctive changes to your speed/angle in the approach to a corner, without having a good explanation as to why, but when those instinctive changes are right and you slide through the corner perfectly...there's few experiences like it.You can play this a bit like Absolute Drift, where you explore the open areas and find collectibles/do challenges, or you can do what I did and absolutely laser through the career mode after you do your first race. There's something incredibly compelling about knocking out just one or two more stages, gambling with your restarts to try and get a better placement, trying out a new car and struggling with its nuances. I like the game a lot because it rarely makes you repeat stuff, you usually only repeat if _you_ want to do better. Really messing up a stage isn't that uncommon, but this is not a game where you make one or two mistakes and have to retry to proceed. It's not so much that it is forgiving, as that pretty much every driver is going to have screwups and slow stages across a rally. So if you come 5th in a stage, and you don't feel confident in a rerun, just let the cards fall where they may and you could have a huge time advantage after another stage or two. Get used to using the 'back to road' rescue button though, just because sometimes you'll waste far more than the 5-second penalty getting yourself back.*If you are struggling early on:* Try more cars! I found the initial group a bit of a struggle to get to grips with, possibly just because getting used to the control system, but I probably stuck to one of them for too long. I was afraid of failing badly in season mode with an unfamiliar car and being 'stuck' but you can always just try again. Worst case, quit the season and try another if it's feeling bad after two races. Or if you're better at preparing than me, try the car in single races instead of in a season!The music bears mentioning all on its own for being truly great, a serious contributor to the relaxed feeling I have when proceeding through a stage that isn't going terribly. Tatreal did an unreal job and I went directly to Bandcamp to buy the OST.Thank you Funselektor and especially thank you for the continued updates, I hopped on pretty late (only a couple of months ago) and there is a TON to see and do.

_childDocuments_.review: When one of my friends posted this game in the group chat on discord, I was very curious. After checking the steam page, popping in on the broadcast, and watching some of the store videos, I was hooked. It's not often that you come across something that draws you in like this.I. Love. Rally. I freaking love it. So I decided to give this game a shot, and I am  satisfied.This game appears to be arcade but that's it's trick. Every car and course will be different and new. You don't run out of track. You'll learn how to handle and master both course and car after a while. And while the maps are gorgeous; you'll be spending most of your time keeping your eyes on the road ahead. Check out the replay function and catch your best moments, which is also a great tool for studying your driving. There's a lot to explore starting off, and I don't want to spoil too much!Third person view from the eagle-eye perspective is alright, but not great. Something closer to a chase cam might be something for the future which would make the game probably feel immersive like other rally games. However for someone starting out, this view will help to teach them how to predict turns and calculate their slides.There's plenty I haven't explored yet, and I'm sure plenty is to come in future in the form of new courses, vehicles, and game modes. If you've got the money to spend and  enjoy the thrill of rally driving, this game is worth picking up!

_childDocuments_.review: Art of Rally is a racing game that explores rally's golden era with an unabashed fervor and tasteful minimalist (but not too much) graphical design. The game has such a passion for the sport and driving in general, that it resonates through the whole experience. Is there a plot? Not in a traditional sense. Every stage is a story, from popping your tire when you decided to cut on a hairpin or nailing that upcoming corner after hitting an incline flatout. A narrative isn't necessary, because the experience communicates to you what the era of driving is like, as you see the vehicle grow immensely in power, adapt all-wheel drivetrains, and feel in your own hands the exponential speed the technology was growing as you struggle to keep up with the extra power as many drivers at the time did, as it was at the end of the Group B era of fast but dangerous experimental race cars. It's perspective might not be standard, but is welcome in malaise of similar looking racing games, especially so since you will not be hearing from a co-driver. The cars are all here and you'll recognize them not just by how they look, but how they drive too, each feeling sublime in the hand but distinct as well. Evidently, the developers passion didn't end at just making the game itself as they continue to release updates since the games release. This is fantastic, especially considering the games relatively niche status. Don't let a $25 price tag scare you, it's completely worth asking price. It's the Alfa Romeo of racing games: not many people are going to own it, but it is nonetheless a treat for those who do and an absolute gem that bleeds passion. If Forza Horizon gets you down with shoddy online racing, if Need for Speed is too cheesy, if Assetto Corsa is too involved, if Wreckfest is too lacking in sportsmanship, and if Gran Turismo is too on Playstation, Art of Rally will be here to pick up the pieces, tell you everything is alright, and to focus on the one thing that matters: the drive. What beautiful drive it is.

_childDocuments_.review: A quite decent game with a great concept is undercut by invisible walls, poor attention to detail and a somewhat strange handling model leaving it somewhere in between a relaxing "zen like" tribute to the greatest form of motorsport and a rage inducing nightmare with frustrating map design, invisible walls and a lack of the finer details that would have made this game the love letter to Group B and rally fans it claims to be.  This game features a wide variety of rally cars from all different eras from the 1960s through to the 1990s as well as a parallel universe class known as "Group S" which is the developers interpretation of where rally development would have gone if Group B was not discontinued. Really this is one of the games main strong suits as it most certainly has a wider variety of cars than you would first expect (including my favourite the Ferrari 288 GTO EVO which never actually got to race as it was developed right as Group B ended). However a few let downs were the engine note of each car being far, far too similar and a few famous liveries being left out of the options, although these can mostly be overlooked.Another main selling point of this game is its somewhat unique low poly / cartoony artstyle this in my opinion works quite well with the semi arcadelike feeling that this game was going for with its more striped back approach. Overall I like it quite a bit (especially how the different time of day impacts the look of each stage) however some of the stages / maps have textures clipping into each other and other details which undercut what is otherwise a really appealing clean artstyle. The worst part is the new Indonesia maps don't have this problem which tells me that it is absolutely fixable and it is just a product of the devs not putting the effort in to get the game polished on release almost making the game feel a bit rushed when it should be leaning more in the labour of love direction, considering how this game is supposed to be a tribute to Group B and all.  Another positive of this game is the inclusion of different modes which can suit different play styles / moods and can add variety to the gameplay they are as follows:In this gamemode you play linearly through the history of rally starting in the 60s and working your way through chronologically until you reach Group A rally (Group S is slotted in between Group B and Group A and it is required that you play through Group S before reaching Group A). The career mode is broken up into the years each class of rally took place in (eg. Group B in the 80s and Group A in the 90s) you play through each year completing multiple rallies competing not only in each stage but each rally and also for the overall championship for the year. Throughout the career mode you will unlock cars and (if you have at least one restart remaining at the end of the year) bonus liveries which add a small sense of progression on top of the fact that you are progressing forwards in the history of rally after completing each year. this is my favourite game mode purely because it adds a sense of competition through the AI and it is such a satisfying feeling progressing into a new era of rally as the cars feel completely distinct across classes.This game mode has you compete against the clock in the car/stage/conditions of your choice nothing more nothing less. You can try to work your way up the leader board or just improve upon your own times using either the world record ghost or the ghost of your fastest time.Freeroam allows you to freely travel across a map (eg. Finland, Japan, Sardinia etc.) collecting the letters R, A, L, L, Y, to progress to the next map as well as collecting points of interest (which are spots where you can get a scenic view of your car against a backdrop of the map) and cassettes which unlock different songs for the soundtrack. All of these elements are hidden across the map encouraging you to drive around and explore, this gamemode is pretty good to unwind to as there is no real pressure to preform and you can just drive your favourite car as you wish through each map.For example there are a lot of invisible walls right next to the road on all stages, this means that for some tight corners for example cutting the corner close to the road is absolutely fine but for other corners you'll clip into an invisible wall which will send you tumbling through the sky ruining your stage and breaking any immersion / flow state you may have been in. This isn't only an issue when it comes to corner cutting however sometimes if you find yourself drifting slightly off of the marked road / track you will come head first into an invisible wall which will not only take away all of your momentum but if playing with damage turned on will ruin your car. I must stress that these invisible walls are  the road in a lot of areas and are in no way consistent making some stages feel like a game of random chance instead of a test of skill. What I will say however is this seems like it may not be as bad in the new stages added in the Indonesia update or at least it doesn't feel that way.As much as this is personal preference for me the handling in this game exists in a sort of 'no mans land' between being completely arcade like and being semi realistic almost as if the devs weren't sure in which direction they wanted to go and instead went straight down the middle. It definitely could be worse though and it is something you just get used to after a little bit of playtime, however I still sometimes find myself surprised when a car behaves unexpectedly relative to the road surface (tarmac, snow, gravel etc.) which can sometimes feel a little counter intuitive the main one that sticks out is the lack of grip on tarmac for example. As much as I want to love this game it is the smaller details and the frustrating at times gameplay that let it down for me, for any die-hard Group B / Rally fans I would still recommend picking up this game on sale as there are definitely a few details (especially the cars) that I'm sure you'd enjoy to see in a game like this. If you are just looking at this game for an arcade like rally experience I am sure there are better options out there that are worth looking at as it would be a bit harder to overlook the more frustrating elements of this game.
_childDocuments_.name: art of rally

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing since around 1.10 and the game has only gotten better and better the more I play. The achievements and car unlocks are fun and challenging, and flow well with the main campaign. This is my first ever racing game and I found myself having fun through every stage of progression, from learning how to maintain a drift, to mastering trail-braking, it's rewarding every step of the way. Only at 200+ hours am I running out of things to do in game, but (at the time of writing) luckily the Kenya Update is soon around the corner. I joined the Funselektor Discord soon after purchase, and the community has been incredible. From beginning tips, optimal setting adjustments, and sharing custom liveries, the community surrounding this game has helped tremendously. I seriously can't recommend this game enough, 10/10 experience all the way through.
_childDocuments_.name: art of rally

_childDocuments_.review: What a beautiful game. A great reminiscence to the time when rally games didn't have cutting edge graphics and hundreds of licensed cars - but were actually tons of fun.Add an almost meditative experience here, as Art of Rally's race tracks and sound tracks melt into a flow that manages to both push your adrenaline and calm you down at the same time. Definitely a recommendation.
_childDocuments_.name: art of rally

_childDocuments_.review: Requires a controller / wheel to make it actually enjoyable to play. A wider range of camera angles would be appreciated, although a larger monitor / tv helps with the distance. The game is pretty demanding of system requirements for what it is. A decent computer is required to fully appreciate the work that was put in building this low-poly piece of entertainment.
_childDocuments_.name: art of rally

_childDocuments_.review: Beautifully executed game - the music, the controls, the scenery, the progression, etc. It's a perfect racing game. Being able to play this game on the highest graphics settings is fairly important though. The shadows and colourful environments are rich with and beautiful.I've been playing rally and F1 games since the PlayStation 1 era. This game stands out as a unique but flawless experience. Just buy it. You won't regret it.
_childDocuments_.name: art of rally

_childDocuments_.review: SAMIR YOU ARE BREAKING THE CAR: The Game.Okay but to give a more genuine summary, this game took me by surprise. The art style and camera perspective initially felt kind of odd to me, but art of rally quickly won my heart through it's simple yet engaging mechanics and how the cars handle, the graphical style makes for a much more unique experience than the same old photorealism-type beat, the cars all feel at least somewhat unique and the way progression works as a sort of "rally through the years" journey is very charming. It's fun to go through the various stages improving your times and upping the challenge with various AI and damage settings, the free-roam mode is good for learning the mechanics in a safe space, and I've taken way too many photos using the game's photo mode and there are plenty more I want to take the more I play.Oh yeah, you can drive a Daihatsu Midget, for that reason alone you should buy this.

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful racing game. _childDocuments_.review: All in all: This game is a masterpiece!This game has so much potential and so many hours of pure fun. The game design is brilliant. The sounds are awesome. Progession happens by increasing your overall driving skill  meaning if you don't win you won't advance in the season and get new unlocks. It's very fun and every car has it's unique feel when driving it. EDIT: With the recent updates the game got very polished and all the small details got fixed. _childDocuments_.name: art of rally

_childDocuments_.review: Fun little rally game, semi-realistic handling and great driving experience, however there are plenty of smaller issues that are downgrading this title to no-recommendo zone.-Obnoxious texture pop-inAs stated by many before, the texture pop-in is really bad even when draw distance is set to max, and with such a super minimalistic game, it is really annoying especially in the forest stages.-After race UIYou finish one season/year and you have to click like 6 times to get back to the group menu and everytime you do this, you hear this annoying children cheering soundbank sound, only to receive a really, really ugly "bonus" livery. Great to see banter in the cars descriptions, but what about weight, its distribution or some other stats?-LiveriesThank god for the 3rd party liveries as those in-game are just scuffed, like some other parts of the game. There was so much potential to make the original ones at least somewhat nice and minimalistic looking, but they are really ugly. Not to mention those "bonus" liveries, which are essentially just copypasted patterns and look like trash with zero thought about how it looks in a car.-RoadsLiterally same width of the track in each and every stage. Maybe I am nitpicking, but it is adding to the monotonous and later boring gameplay. One more negative point about roads is the scuffed corner cutting system - sometimes you can cut corners like Nasser, sometimes the game will recover you straight away when you barely touch the corner. Why, why, why is this somehow at least consistent?-OptimisationThis point was said in so many more reviews, for such a minimalistic game, it is quite demanding and does not run well, fps drops are quite common.-Lack of varietyAfter few hours of playing, the game feels monotonous as each track looks similar and the only thing changing are the colors and some assets around the track. Once you get to the best rally part of group B, the game is already boring and massively repetitive  due to this issue. The career is also just bloated, doing the same maps again and again and again and by the time you get to better, faster cars, the tracks just feel boring and you come to recognition that the career mode could be much shorter and the experience would be so much better. Even Ignition from 1997 had so much more variety and career mode felt less scuffed and bloated.-PriceNowhere near the quality for 20,99 euros. For 10? Maybe.
_childDocuments_.name: art of rally

_childDocuments_.review: Hit 10 spectators and a giraffe in a single accident with the E1S2 in Kenia, would flat out again.Pros:* A decent top down Rally game! There aren't that many, so that's very cool.* Good selection of cars and tracks (minus the very first ones in career mode)* Good use of 3rd dimension in the tracks, lots of up and down, hills, etc.* Camera position is very good: not too close, and can be tweaked in the menu.* All the game modes you expect (career, custom rally, time trial) plus an open world-like free roam mode!Cons:* The handling of the cars is terrible imo. The delay in input, the lumbering controls and the slow-mo-like sliding made me feel like the car I am driving weighted 3 tons. It's not as bad as in Absolute Drift, the previous game of the developer, but it's still quite bad. The more you turn on the 'stability control' assist setting in the menu, the worse it gets, but even at 0%, it's bad. Driving in the rain is a pain.* The simple graphics are okay but I am not a big fan of the kitschy lighting.* The road surface never seems to change within tracks, and the roads keep the same width all the time. Some of the early tracks are very boring.* The game seems rather badly optimized. Not always, but on some occasions, I experienced very low frame rate and stuttering (!) on my very powerful system. Had to restart the game then. It was always on the Finland summer location and happened both in open world mode and in during a career event.Two tipps:* Make sure to have a look at the assist settings in the menu, I hated this game before I found them and turned them off.* Don't judge the game by the early tracks, driven with the early cars. It gets better.As a huge rally fan, I expected a bit too much after seeing the review score on Steam. Still I am very grateful they made a top-down rally game! Overall 7/10.
_childDocuments_.name: art of rally

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing since the closed alpha and I have to say that the ammount of dedication put from the developers, from listening to the community, fixing bugs and glitches, adding new things, changing old things, is just astonishing. art of rally succeds on giving an amazing driving experience through arcady physics. Drifting around, jumping, counter-stering is just so much fun in what is a fantastic love letter to old and classic eras of of rally. A huge selection of cars is available, from the 1960's to the Group A and even the prototypes of Group S. There's quite a fez game modes, including a randomized career mode, time trials, single stage, custom rally, free roam, daily stages.There's a lot of details in here, from spectators watching in the middle of the road to the tents and camping spots of those that stayed for more than a day watching legendary cars like subarus, bmws, audi quattros, etc blistering trough asphalt, dirt and snow.art of rally, is what should be expected from more AAA titles, wich is the ability to make a proper homage to what rally is about.
_childDocuments_.name: art of rally

_childDocuments_.review: Race in the golden era of rally. Drive iconic cars from the 60s to Group B on challenging stages through stylized environments inspired by real worldwide locations. Will you master the art of rally?

name: TUNIC
detailed_description: Full Controller Support TUNIC on PC is best experienced with a gamepad or controller. About the Game Explore a land filled with lost legends, ancient powers, and ferocious monsters in TUNIC, an isometric action game about a small fox on a big adventure. Stranded in a ruined land, and armed with only your own curiosity, you will confront colossal beasts, collect strange and powerful items, and unravel long-lost secrets. BECOME A LEGEND Stories say that a great treasure is hidden somewhere in this land. Perhaps it lies beyond the golden door? Or somewhere deep beneath the earth? Some tales tell of a palace high above the clouds, and of ancient beings with incredible power. What will you find? REBUILD A SACRED BOOK During your travels, you’ll reconstruct the game’s Instruction Manual. Page by page, you’ll reveal maps, tips, special techniques, and the deepest of secrets. If you find every last one, maybe something good will happen... BE COURAGEOUS, LITTLE ONE! Dive into varied, technical combat. Dodge, block, parry, and strike! Learn how to conquer a wide cast of monsters, big and small — and discover useful new items to help you on your way. Explore a hostile and intricately-connected world of shady forests, sprawling ruins, and labyrinthine catacombs Fight mighty bosses deep beneath the earth, high above the clouds, and in places stranger still Collect the missing manual pages, bursting with hints and original full-color illustrations Discover hidden treasures to help you on your way Unearth secret relics, secret techniques, secret puzzles, and… listen, there’s a lot of secrets! Featuring sound design by Power Up Audio And an original soundtrack by Lifeformed (Terence Lee and Janice Kwan) Keep your wits about you and be brave, little fox!

_childDocuments_.review: Instantly one of my all-time favorites! It's an unforgettable adventure and an experience I wish I could have for the first time again...This game throws you into a world that you will have to discover on your own. You will be able to explore it, to firgure out what you are  and to have a nostalgia orgasm if you ever played old action adventure games. I enjoyed the challenge of figuring out the manual and the whole meta-game aspect of it. It's based on old gaming experiences, yet it feels very unique in a modern game. I also enjoyed the difficulty curve, moderately clumsy, yet intentional combat, plenty of exploration and secrets (oh, there's so much wall-hugging!) hidden in plain sight, and the deep and mysterious lore with some major plot-twists along the way. All of that is just wonderfully implemented, nailed down to the details and feels like a labour of love from a very professional and passionate indie game studio.My only gripe with it was that the final boss is way too hard. I spent a lot of time on it, and it felt like a big achievement to beat it, but it was just a bit overpowered in my opinion. Luckily, there is a flexible assist mode in the settings, so anyone can enjoy the game without getting stuck on the combat.

_childDocuments_.review: Not a relaxing game, a bit awkward, and not exactly as shown in the marketing material. Fans of course would probably disagree with me, but wanting to play this game casually just isn't going to happen. And it's just not deep enough, not exciting enough, not interesting enough to want to invest time into making it fun. I just get a really empty, blah feeling when playing Tunic. I really want to like this game after seeing everything on the store page, but I just can't enjoy it. That's almost a first for me. It's not that the game is bad, it's just the approach is awkward and intentionally confusing. I'd rather it be clever to make me think, but no, it's just awkward to make me bang my head against a brick wall until something happens. Again, this is a first for me: a really blah feeling. And I loved the Zelda series, Neutopia series, and many other adventure action games like this. Am I getting old, or is this just boring?Oh, and the game is damn short. Really short. And unfulfilling. So unfulfilling that you will be pissed when you reach the end. Utterly POed at the developer.

_childDocuments_.review: TUNIC is my nominee for Game of the Year (The Steam Awards), and even though I played only one other game that I felt more affection for this year (Psychonauts 2), as a 2022 game TUNIC is a definite no.1 spot for me.Funny thing is, I couldn't (read: mostly just didn't want to) even finish the game legit.. the Garden Knight bit frustrated me, and I'm not that into "souls-like" approach of boss fights, not because they're hard, but mostly they're just tedium that get in the way of exploration and puzzle solving, which for a game like Tunic are the only aspects I want to deal with honestly. Somewhere before the second major boss I got stuck pretty hard trying to figure stuff out, so I resulted to using guides and a trainer to speed through it to the end - somewhat annoyed with combat, but loving the world, I still decided to see everything for a 100% completion.This is a shallow review, and I'm not gonna parrot what probably thousands have said better already, but TUNIC deserves a spot in most of these Steam Awards categories - it is a Labor of Love just by the fact of how much effort went into making every little detail of its world ; it is visually very appealing (stylistically similar to 'Link's Awakening' remake), with an amazing soothing soundtrack, making it a great choice to sit back and relax (for the exploration bits) on Steam Deck ; it has the same complexity in what at first seems like a simple exploration game (much like 'FEZ' or 'The Witness') having that "oh, wow" effect once you start figuring out just how deep this rabbit hole really goes, and since these types of puzzle games aren't too common, to me that feels innovative still ; and lastly I'd say this is 'the best game I suck at' - being at the top of all of these categories mentioned, making this a pretty easy choice for a Game of the Year in my opinion.P.S. That in-game manual is just the coolest thing ever. Very well done!

_childDocuments_.review: On first glance, Tunic looks like an indie derivative of every classic action/adventure hit of the past few years. Souls-type combat with clear inspiration from the Zelda franchise is a pretty obvious pull, but while these are fair comparisons initially, Tunic makes a name for itself by instead codeswitching its functions and becoming more akin to a exploration-based cryptogram. You are dropped into Tunic with little more than your preconceived notions of an adventure game. As a cute, tiny fox, you are led forward through a colorful and dangerous isometric overworld to steadily pick up a stick, then a sword, and later some magic items to aid on your quest. What quest? You...don't really know. Most of the text in the game is written in an unreadable set of runes and symbols, from signs to dialogue, as well as the game's own instruction manual, given to you page by page within the game itself. It is this manual that champions Tunic's foundational excellence, as players are tasked with using the game's own untranslated text to deduce context clues and controls to figure out how the game even works. It sounds tedious, but the process of finally understanding what an item does or that a button had a hidden function from the start is a gameplay loop unlike anything I've ever played. The game's best surprises come from this unending source of discovery, a testiment to its expertly designed pages and knowledge of its players' playstyles. Tunic adopts the intense, risk-based combat popularized by the Souls franchise. Even the simplest enemies start deadly, and flagrant use of dodge rolls and wild weapon swings will send you back to the checkpoint. As a person who doesn't play FromSoft titles often, I found the combat just the right amount of challenging and the repetition through sections after dying was always the perfect length. Death isn't as punishing here, only losing a little money, which you can reclaim if you can return to where you were last defeated. There was only one later section which felt unfair given the circumstances but it is over quickly. If jumping into this game sounds intimidating, Tunic has also added accessibility options to mitigate the difficulty, from no stamina loss, to not dying ever. It ensures anyone who wants to see the game through can all still have a great time. The world of Tunic is fascinating; unraveling bits and pieces from the manual and your actions throughout the story reveal a very different tale than I was expecting. Secrets and treasure lurk around every possible corner, so players with a watchful eye will have their hands full scouring the world for shortcuts and items scattered across the overworld. While sometimes it felt a little too cumbersome to get where I wanted to go, Tunic usually has a nice balance of interconnecting its areas to never make any one section a linear death trap. Boss fights are similarly versatile, open to multiple attack options, while still keeping you on the edge of your seat. Saying exactly why Tunic is one of the best games this year and perhaps in a long while would be spoiling and disservicing the game's best moments. Needless to say, there is so much crammed into this title that it is worth every penny and I think many types of people will find something to love about it. It's a love letter to game fans, and a homage to gaming discourse, but it transcends even that sentiment and becomes a genuinely brilliant work of puzzles, narrative, and hidden figures to craft something I've never quite had the honor of playing.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll just keep it brief as possible: I liked a lot of the game, but overall grew to dislike other sections of the game more as it went on.The world looks great, sounds great and everything amongst those lines is solid. Early exploration is really fun too. At first I even enjoyed the combat. Plenty of fun mystery to go around too, just generally a really great vibe.But then there's the bosses and the lategame. The former I liked one of, the rest I genuinly despised and simply turned godmode on for. A part of it is me being bad at the game, yes, but the combat also failed to grab me and was generally just boring, also doesn't help that I'm not a huge fan of "souls-like" stuff. The lategame is cool initially and when seeing how all of it clicks together it seems really cool, but I was already tired of just running around the map at that stage to the point where I gave up.Maybe get it on a sale/in a bundle.

_childDocuments_.review: Here's my old review: "It's not what I expected, wanted, or enjoyed. It's a very difficult game, combining both souls like and puzzle elements. The puzzles would be more fun if actually required thinking. Instead most of the puzzles involve just going back to places you've been before to see if something has changed now that you have another item. The secret treasures are more interesting to hunt than every other puzzle in the game.The soundtrack is drab, and has no dynamic development. Combine this with the absence of dialogue and lack of readable writing means that your ears start to bleed after a while. It's just so boring. Ultimately, you get to the end and you're left asking 'What's the point and why should I care" even if you get the true ending.The enemies respawn every time you save, so there is literally no reprieve. And like every game that wants to make things harder without putting effort into new concepts there are often hordes of monsters to fight. Nothing more exciting than fighting six of the same enemy at the same time."I played another 15 hours. the puzzles are... very rough. But there's also a lot of exploration and different solutions to the puzzles. It does require a bit of problem solving. And that's okay. Just needed to be a bit more patient.The soundtrack... really isn't that bad. it can be repetitive, but it doesn't even come close to some of the games I grew up with (looking at you RoTMG). Actually some of the sound effects are really fun, like weapon sounds, distortions, and various noises. It's really not bad at all.The enemy respawn can be frustrating - the trick then becomes the player becoming confident enough to handle the small groups of enemies and getting to a point where you don't need to respawn every 15 minutes. It takes practice - just like most souls like.

_childDocuments_.review: The Progression and how it made me actually freak out IRL with how amazingly put together this game was says something, its fun and cute, the manual aspect is unique and adorable, the visuals are fantastic and breathe taking, and the puzzles you need to do are simple but the puzzles not required really make you think and feel amazing after you get them. the combat is fun! like a combination of the good ol fashioned Zelda mixed with Dark souls yet the accessibility menu in the setting making it for people who aren't so good at combat to also be able to play and enjoy! honestly its my favorite game and I have enjoyed every second of playing this wonderful game, if I had to choose my problems then playing it on a keyboard is not ideal (for me personally) and there are a couple glitches, like a glitch where the shield will stop being able to be held up while targeting, but that's the only one that comes up to mind because of how much this games plus's take over my brain. simply astounding

_childDocuments_.review: So I will say that I have mixed feelings about this game. I enjoy the exploration, combat and puzzle solving.Spoiler warningWhat I didn't enjoy was the second part of the game outside of the dungeons. I though the in game puzzles were very cool. I wasn't really sold on the booklet thing at first, but some parts of it seemed pretty cool, like the learning new mechanics that you always had was really fun at first. The spell casting/ritual thing with the directions was ok once I figured it out.The golden path stuff was garbage. I really feel they wanted a literal 100 input secret and that is not fun even knowing what should go in. If you are just trying to figure it out, it is super easy to think your approach is wrong just based on a single bad input. Its also not worth it.The fights at the end of the second part have a huge difficulty spike especially if you have not figured out how to get your stuff back.I felt like the first half of the game was one of the best iso games I'd ever played. The second was like some weird player mod where all they cared about was stupid hard puzzles and a couple of crazy hard fights.So how do you rate that? Fantastic 5 for the first half and a 2 in the second for a 7/10? Seems like that doesn't do justice to the fantastic parts of the game brought down by a bad ending.So if you want to play this I recommend that you know this is no casual zelda clone. It will take thought and play skill and up to a point rewards that very much. But there are things that are going to be beyond many players unless you are willing to put in the time and effort. The thing is the extra completionist effort doesn't seem to be worth it compared to the base game they seem to abandon at the end, which totally is worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: TUNIC is a cute, absurdly charming souls-like. It doesn't try to be a difficult game in every way like the souls games, but it will have you stressing out a bit pretty often. I feel a little bad calling it a souls-like, because it tries hard to be it's own thing, and honestly, it really is. It's a similar idea to souls, but in a cuter, friendlier package.A lot of your time will be spent exploring, but it's never dull, because there are always enemies to fight or secrets/handy shortcuts to find. I went into this thinking it was more of an ARPG because my sleep-deprived brain wasn't paying enough attention to the details and all that, so when I realized what it is, I was pretty surprised, but very pleasantly. I had no idea what I had gotten myself into, and I've loved games like the souls series for a long time, but sort of fell away from them after I switched to PC. I bought them all on steam, but I haven't played them much, and this game makes me want to jump back into this genre of games and play through them, starting with this one.The gameplay is incredibly smooth, the music is very nice and enjoyable, the atmosphere is great, the art style is very pleasant, and graphically it's gorgeous. The lighting is fantastic and really brings the whole visual package together. It's easier to pick up than others in this genre, you don't lose stamina as you attack, and you can continue to attack just fine without any stamina. The stamina penalties that you really need to pay attention to come in the form of less stability, which makes it easier to be knocked back/down by attacks, and taking extra damage when you're past a certain threshold or have none at all. The story is told through the gameplay and little things, and the way it's all done makes the game feel like a form of art.I'm going to be honest, when I bought this game, i didn't pay too much attention to it, I only bought it because I needed steam points and figured I should get a game that I might play later on so it wouldn't be a waste of money. I don't regret playing it when I should have been working (I work from home atm), and I don't regret buying it. Few games have managed to captivate me as quickly as TUNIC has, and for that alone, I can easily recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll preface that this game won't be for everyone. Do you like dying 27 times to a boss till you finally figure out the fight after cussing at the screen and yet still smiling because it's rewarding? Do you like cute foxes?If your answer was yes to all of the above, then this game is for you. Very well done graphics with an enchanting soundtrack. The game's charm, difficulty, and level of "just figure it out" is balanced to perfection.This will be a timeless classic.

_childDocuments_.review: Tunic is an ingenious mesh of well-proven inspirations and new ideas. The game is often as much of a tricky puzzle game as it is an enjoyable and familiar-looking action RPG. Tunic undeniably lifts the base of its presentation, top-down camera, tough-yet-fair sword-and-shield combat, and clever interconnected level design from iconic sources (i.e. Link's Awakening and Dark Souls), but the game adds a layer of ‘knowledge-progression’ that’s hidden within a nostalgic, half-translated in-game strategy guide.In a gripping perspective-expanding process akin to the joy of solving Outer Wilds, from the start, you essentially already have everything you need to go anywhere (or at least do some serious sequence breaking before key items get in the way), but you don’t yet know enough about this new land to harness your own potential. Here, knowledge from the game’s scattered manual has the same door-opening/problem-solving power as keys or ‘super missiles’ might. While you go about the intended adventuring route, so many shortcuts and interactions lay just out of reach, merely hiding in plain sight.The value Tunic places on information is quite refreshing. As your tools and stats progress, so does your understanding of the world. You have no idea what subtle details could become relevant later, which bestows this unknown depth and mystery to the whole experience. When new pages of lovely art and inconclusive imagery are revealed to you, deciphering them makes you feel like a real detective. I also love the dramatic irony of knowing that nothing was stopping you from your goals besides a trick that seemed obvious in retrospect.This  concept works so well. That guidebook/exploration dynamic makes for some unforgettable moments. But it’s also worth briefly complimenting how Tunic’s other components elevate the game into something much greater than the sum of its sources. The story is told indirectly and silently. It brings further intrigue into this seemingly friendly animal world. The music, while an initially unexpected tone, evokes waves of synthy nostalgia. Tunic’s soundtrack could’ve been a lot more predictable and I think Lifeformed and Janice Kwan found a great way to add to Tunic’s unique identity. Combat isn’t a major thrill, but it has good moment-to-moment pacing. While parrying is a little slugging, it’s far from necessary to succeed. Most bosses require ample mastery to overcome without having to pull out any hairs.And if it ended there, I wouldn’t be hesitant to rank Tunic among its like-minded masterpieces.Sadly, the game ends on a pretty painful note. I was so into the first two-thirds of this game. Tunic is still certainly worth experiencing for those first ten-ish hours, so don't let my need to discuss my discontent with the final act stain your impressions of the truly brilliant parts. Seeing as fun as Tunic’s learning process was, perhaps it’s fitting that an end to that growth would entail a decline in my interest in it.
