_childDocuments_.review: This is a beautiful game :)I originally purchased it because it looked absolutely gorgeous, and I was not disappointed in that regard. It has such a beautifully stylized, highly detailed, handcrafted world for you to explore. Basically every 10 square feet of this place has something important going on with it. It's not particularly big, but the stark lack of dead space here makes it feels like a continent.But OH BOY it is so much more.Basically everything that you need to know in order to play the game is kept a secret from you in the beginning. There is an in-game manual, but its are pages scattered throughout the world, and you need to collect them in order to get any sense of what you're doing (otherwise, it's trial and error). I'm a person who loves making secret codes and conlangs in their free time, and finding the first few pages of the manual lit that part of my brain up like a fireworks show. While there are parts of it you can get from context, more than half the thing is written in a secret language you have to solve. Remember how I said every 10 square feet of this game has something important going on in it? Well, this game actually has another name, "Secret Legend", and given how many secrets there are in this game, it fits very well. While this game has been appropriately labelled a Zelda-Souls-like, it is first and foremost a game about learning secrets. There are collectible upgrades and special abilities you can access, but secrets serve as your primary means of progression. I was afraid that this would hurt the game's replayability, but here's the funny thing: IT DOESN'T. While there is a New Game+ option that makes things a bit tougher, restarting the game from scratch with a totally new save is a completely different experience, since the secrets you have learned from completing it still apply: while in-game you are as weak as you were when you first started out, you can use your old knowledge to completely overthrow the order of progression.It is a wild experience, and I would highly recommend it to anyone who loves a mystery. A few things you should know, though (and keep in mind, this is a person who likes solving puzzles): 1. If you get any pleasure from puzzle-solving, PLEASE STAY AWAY FROM INTERNET GUIDES AS MUCH AS YOU CAN. While there are a rare few who respect the player's intelligence by tastefully dropping hints, most resources you find on the Internet just give you the answer, sometimes spoiling more than you'd have liked to know. There were a few times I had to look something up (one of the late game secrets required me to know a game mechanic I should have learned in the early game),  But if you really like the thrill of solving a puzzle yourself, read the manual closely. Try different tactics and perspectives. Heck, if it's still pretty early in the game, save it for later. It might be frustrating in the moment, but once you solve it, you'll be glad you did.2. While there are some opportunities to softlock yourself, there are even more ways to get physically stuck that aren't actually softlocks, i.e. getting temporarily stuck on a ledge or cheesing your way into an area before knowing how to get out. There are a few game mechanics that are particularly tricky on this; they've been fined-tuned to greatly reduce the likelihood, but it can still happen. Usually, getting stuck is just a matter of finagling your way out, but it you do softlock, you can just reload the save to escape them.3. Keep an open mind going in. I went into this thinking this was going to be an ordinary adventure, but I was completely caught off guard by its sheer complexity, in more ways than one. I don't want to spoil the surprise, but all I'll say is this: This is a beautiful game, so be ready for anything.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: Right away the world is appealing and feels as real as a diorama. The music starts calm but inviting. It always sets the tone perfectly as you progress, and is just good to listen to. It isn't long before you also realize that a good deal of the features in the environment are going to be meaningful and not just there to look good. Even later in the game, things you simply walked by earlier take on significance.Tunic gives you nothing for free, not in a sadistic way, but rather in a way that respects your intelligence and rewards you for getting better at playing. You're quickly introduced to an intriguing coded language, and even the instruction manual is largely written in it, and the manual is discovered in-game page by page. There is enough English though that you're not completely left in the dark.Speaking of the manual, it does an amazing job of throwing back to the days when games had printed manuals. As always with Tunic though, it does that in a purposeful, functional way that's not just for nostalgia. It particularly conjured up two unique aspects of that time. One is simply that feeling you got when you borrowed a friend's game or got a used copy that came with a manual which already had cryptic notes in it, and learned a bit more about secrets in the game than were printed. The other is when all you had was the manual to scour for anything that might give you an edge or a secret you didn't realize. I strongly urge not Googling things for this game; using the manual is usually useful, and cryptic enough that it's not obvious, and rewarding when you figure something new out. It adds another dimension of fun to the experience and is not a tedious thing to use.As the enemies get a little tougher you begin to realize this game isn't going to be as cutesy or easy as you worried maybe it might be. Combat becomes more than just button mashing, but not so complicated that you need to achieve elite, arcade fighting game-level mastery. When the game becomes difficult, you often will discover you might be missing something that could make it easier, whether that's some item or power-up, a clue about a weakness, or just something about an enemy's attack pattern you can exploit. Of course if you want it to be harder, you can go without these things.The story of the world becomes apparent as you go around, delivery almost entirely via inference from the surrounding world, with a little support from the manual. It actually is fairly dark at times, in spite of walking around as a little fox.After you discover a few secrets, you'll start to realize the game is absolutely stuffed with them in almost every way you can engage with it. Some potentially sequence-breaking routes are hiding in plain sight in spots, but you only find them by progressing through in sequence. These were always a delightful surprise to discover.For me, all of the above describes a near-perfect game. The attention to detail is so thoughtfully astounding, the environment and music is beautiful, the world and story is full of intrigue and mystery, the puzzles and game play are challenging but not impossible, and there is zero hand-holding through all of it. Definitely a must-play for people into these kinds of games.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game that will make you realise how great some people are at the art of making games. It's a really great experience. Beautiful worlds, controls great, the music is the perfect enabler of the perfect atmosphere for this game... it's a 10/10 kind of game, imo. It's not without a blemish, some of the navigation hinges entirely on the fact it's an isometric view and not a first person view, and the rare enemy attacks have some questionable hitboxes or windups, but that's extremely minor in comparison and you should not let this discourage you even the slightest amount from playing this absolutely excellent game. I think everyone would do well to experience this game. There are a couple of tough bosses toward the end, that you may need to use the 'deal extra damage when on low health' card and stun crystal thing to deplete their health more quickly - like, this shouldn't be the first game you ever play (as beautifully as they nail the joy of exploration and atmosphere in this world) (i mean it would be a great first game to play if not for the fact the latter bosses would destroy you) - but if you've played games for a while, you love the medium, then this game is for you. It is an exceptional, outstanding video game.

_childDocuments_.review: Tunic is a wonderful top-down action-adventure game that draws heavily from the Zelda series and somewhat from the Soulsborne series. While a good deal of your time will be spent in combat and there are (relatively) tough bosses to beat, the main draw of the game is the puzzle-filled exploration. You are given hints, but never outright directions on where to go and what to do.The gameplay is smooth and responsive, the art style is amazing and the music creates the perfect atmosphere of action and mystery.Do yourself a favour and get this game. Do yourself an even bigger favour and don't look at a walkthrough!
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: I wish I could recommend this game, but the more I play the more it becomes an absolute slog to get anything out of it. It has a lot going for it with the art style, premise and design of the world. Sadly terrible design choices in how the combat system works lets the whole thing down. They've basically tried to put in a dark souls like combat system into a GBA Zelda game, and while Death's Door did something similiar and nailed it, here everything is just a bit off. Check points are spaced too far apart, enemies deal too much damage, are damage sponges, and generally have attack patterns that just repeatedly hammer you beyond what dodging can mitigate. Meanwhile your actions are incredibly slow and generally have a massive delay between input and outcome, meaning the best strategy is to run out of combat and then spin around to attack again. The game forces you to use controller and the lock on system has a tendency to lock on to a random target rather than something right in-front of you while locking your motion as you sort through targets. Using a menu doesn't pause the game, which makes trying to do anything in the menus during combat a death sentence. It's just tiring to do anything with the combat system when it shouldn't be, to the extent that you're better off just running through enemies until you hit a boss.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is amazing!I wasn't expecting such a deep game in every aspect, I was expecting a Zelda with a fox as the protagonist.But this is not the case!This is a real souls like with a crazy storyline and level design.Maybe a bit overpriced for an indie (I've got the platinum in like 20 hours) but definitely fantastic!

_childDocuments_.review: Played the game with a friend on his account. - Disregard the low playtimeAt first the game seemed a bit slow, however it all made sense after collecting the first few items and pages. The way the book is used to describe the mechanics, puzzles, etc. is something I haven't seen before! The game managed to introduce mechanics in a intuitive and fun way without you feeling overwhelmed with information. The large world was fun to explore and the many secrets scattered all over the world made me view the world in a different way every time we passed by the same spot. The structure of the world allowed us to defeat the bosses in our own order thus allowing us to create our own unique adventure (even though the book suggests an order). The story itself is also quite special! I don't won't to spoil anything as I think you should experience it yourself ;). If I had to draw similarities to anything else I think the game resembles the feeling of the tv show "Gravity falls", it is eerie and mysterious yet feels like home. The world is yours to explore, decipher and understand. Some of the puzzles were quite difficult and we had to backtrack quite a few times to find the correct solutions, however most of the truly difficult puzzles are optional except . All I can say is that almost nothing in this game is random, everything serves a purpose!Likely the  game I have ever played. It is one of the few games where I was truly sad when the game ended!

_childDocuments_.review: A beautifully crafted old Zelda like experience. Grafics are simple, yet cute, and beautiful.The whole thing about the game "being in another language" with just tid bits of info on conversations or in the manual (I'll get there soon) makes you work your brain out with all the clues left around, clues that mind you, sometimes don't click right away, but when they do? Man you will feel a bit smarter and proud.The game manual is an amazing idea, from the maps, to the puzzles, the guides, the pointing in the right direction, and so on and so forth. You'll get some people complaining "oh you gotta become a master code breaker to understand this!", and that's when you entirely miss the point. You don't have to, and you are not expected to either. Every piece of info is properly conveyed through the translated segments, and the imagery. You just gotta be willing to allow the game to NOT hand hold you.In another aspect, this "game in an entire different language" made me feel EXACTLY how Zelda: Link's Awakening DX made me feel when I was 12 and my grandma got me the game, but it was in japanese. So I had to guess, struggle, and figure out what to do with what little information I could get my hands onto (by now you might have guessed that internet was not yet widely used at that time)Overall? You HAVE to play this game, and I'll encourage you to go blind and not resort to a youtube video, or a walkthrough when (or if) you get stuck. Enjoy the ingame manual.

_childDocuments_.review: I went into this game thinking it was a Zelda clone, which might have made this game okay. But when the puzzle aspect of the game was revealed, I thought its easily one of the best and most immersive puzzle games I've seen. Its hard to describe without giving away spoilers (And this game HAS to be played without spoilers), but basically even after hours of exploring and mastering the basic Zelda-like mechanics, the game will eventually reveal to the player already implemented mechanics many hours into your gameplay and its so mind-blowing how well these are revealed to you. A lot of the game is hidden but available to the player from the get go but these slow reveals is what truly makes this game fun and immersive. These discoveries really hits you as a player who's already explored a good chunk of the world and realize that there's more areas to discover and more puzzles to solve.I'm writing this review after seeing the Steam Awards nominations and I'm actually surprised that this wasn't even nominated for "Most Innovative Gameplay" as it truly is that: Having a component of the game be the player's tutorial, guide, lore-book and a puzzle itself is a really creative way of merging story-telling and gameplay. What an experience this game was and I look forward to what the developers have in store for their future games.If you love puzzle games, I highly recommend this.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: TUNIC is a game that at first glance wears its inspiration on its sleeve, but is far more than just a Zelda clone.  The visual style is immediately endearing, made up of rounded shapes and "soft voxels" in a way that is friendly and inviting, much like its cute, foxy protagonist.  Almost as though it was a game specifically made for younger players.  The more you play, however, the more you start getting a sense of a darker tone simmering beneath the surface, of something mysterious and disquieting teasing at the edges of the calming facade.Along with a unique mechanic of finding the oldschool-style game manual of the game you're playing while you're playing the game, TUNIC abounds with little secrets and cryptic plot elements that it doesn't do a lot to explain, quite on purpose.  Similar in style to Zelda, you gradually collect a small assortment of equipment and special items you can use to backtrack and progress farther and farther through areas, solving puzzles and finding hidden things.  The bosses you face--and even some of the silent NPC's--are intimidating and gigantic compared to your little fox.  (The merchant, notably, made me panic and think I was facing some horrific enemy the first time I found them.)  As you travel through segmented zones and encounter environmental details, you'll find some of which feeling at odd angles to the rest of the landscape, as though a corruption of it, and finding out more about what they are and what they mean is as inscrutable as the rest of the game.There is definitely a difficulty element to the game, so one might compare it to a Souls-like, but the aesthetics and style of TUNIC makes it an experience that you might enjoy even if you're not a fan of those types of games.  A superb indie recommendation.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: Before getting into the review, I'll say the game has an "Infinite Stamina" mode and "No Fail" mode which is just invincibility if you just want to enjoy the exploration without the challenge from the combat. I played with these modes off but, of course, you should enjoy the game how you want to.Tunic is a top-down Zelda style game with some Dark Souls elements that has a big emphasis on exploration and acquired knowledge through that exploration and inferring what things do.In additional to the exploration elements, the game also has challenging bosses that can be approached a few different ways since there is no one progression sequence in the game and is open-ended shy for a few ability-gated parts that give it a bit of a Metroidvania flavor at times. I wouldn't define it as a Metroidvania but there are hints of that flavoring. I would say the strongest focus and feel is Zelda and Soulslike with probably more Zelda than Souls and a lot of the normal combat can be addressed more with a mind toward Zelda's top-down combat rather than just relying heavily on the dodge roll i-frames. You will want those dodge rolls for the bosses, though. And reflecting a bit more on the bosses, there's also at least a little hint of Gungeon in there, too.It's an amazing game that has an interesting visual style and a lot going for it in the gameplay and design departments. Also the soundtrack is great if you're down for a chill electronic vibe and, if not, mute it and play whatever music you like! :D

_childDocuments_.review: All the frustrating parts of Hyper Light Drifter, except even more punishingly difficult combat. Exploration mostly consists of finding routes that are not visible because of the isometric camera angle, and feel cheap more than they are interesting. Hoping to avoid combat, as that was the most frustrating part, I turned on No Fail so I could explore but then I became softlocked behind a boss that was equally invincible, requiring me to turn off No Fail.At that point I realized I could appreciate neither the combat nor the exploration, and I stopped.

_childDocuments_.review: The sort of game that comes along once in a generation and absolutely engrosses you completely. I felt like a kid on summer break sitting in my Dad's house playing the Original Legend of Zelda, furiously scribbling down notes and making maps to help keep track of the world's mysteries. Start to finish I wanted nothing more than to delve deep into the world and uncover all of the hidden lore and collectibles, the rare sort of game that tests your wits, reflexes, and resolve.  I say with no exageration that this is one of the best video games I have ever played, and you would be doing yourself a disservice not trying it.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: TUNIC is basically what Fez would be like if it was inspired deeply by Zelda games instead of platformers, and also really liked Dark Souls.The game has simple but gorgeous graphics and introduction that doesn't match the work you'll be doing, either keen puzzle-solving or sometimes punishing combat with a Souls twist on Zelda (saves restore HP/MP and also all enemies, dodges consume limited stamina and attacking prevents it from recharging, and there are a ton of paths forward that you unlock either by dropping down ropes and ladders or learning secret routes so you can skip the enemies next time through).The best conceit of the game is that the manual exists in-game, unlocked by finding pages in-game. The pages are not discovered in-order. As a result, the game keeps game mechanics a mystery until you're finally rewarded with them and can go back and retrieve chests and access new areas. The same manual also provides the lore and story for the game. It's a gorgeous affair that looks exactly like what an original Zelda manual would look like if Link was a cute little fox. The manual gives plenty of hints for the many hidden secrets as well as outright telling you many of the things you'll need to figure out through the game, even if most of the text in it is what I like to call Fox Glyphs.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely stunning game, the art style, to the composition of music, to the puzzles, to the boss fights, TUNIC is very expressive, even without knowing any of the language. I appreciate every bit of detail that went into the Instruction Manual in the game as well, its above and beyond the idea of creativity of how to keep people engaged with a game, and the option of the no fail mode/no stamina restrictions is very nice for people that want the cute part of the game without the hardpart of the boss fight/harder enemies. Because on the surface level it might NOT look like its difficult, but the game will surely surprise you especially in NG+
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: I really thought I'd like the game. I'm a big fan of adventure games. It's very cute, and the graphics style obviously tugs at various sources of nostalgia.But I just got bored. Maybe partly due to the seemingly random levels of difficulty, but, mostly just the emptiness of the game in general. Hours in and it feels like you're just doing chores. The most interesting aspect of the game is the cryptic nature of its own presentation, but, that got really old really fast. There are fundamental gameplay elements that are hidden in this mess of fake language symbols and progressive disclosure of the game manual. That's annoying.Reality is that there are thousands of these kind of nostalgic adventure games and I've had a lot better connection with other games. Tunic is cute and clearly there's some uniqueness, but the gimmicks quickly change from interesting to irritating. What's left is a fairly bog standard Zelda-alike without the benefit of Nintendo's amazing level design skills.So bottom line is, I was just bored and after months of not playing I haven't had even the slightest motivation to try again. The only reason I even remembered to review it is because I wanted to uninstall it and get it off my list of installed games. The total lack of hesitation to do so struck me and made me feel it was worth doing a review.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: I don't recommend this game, but that doesn't mean I think it is bad. The first half of the game is incredible. The combat is fun, the bosses are tough, and the music/visuals are great. Where I think the game loses steam is in the last half. To keep this spoiler free, I don't think the game does enough to encourage the use of the D-pad. It's a feature almost exclusively used for secrets and not really for anything in the normal gameplay loop. The most obvious use of the D-pad is for opening doors, but it was easy for me to think that opening doors was the only use for the D-pad. I'm sure someone could say "skill issue" or whatever, but a game like The Witness does a better job of forcing me into situations where I have to think about using everything available to me. If you aren't actively looking to try to find secrets, the D-pad is rarely used and you'll finish the game wondering if that was everything, which is really a shame because the developers did an amazing job with the secrets in the game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game filled with wonderful ideas.I just wish they were executed better.Overall I would say this game is less than the sum of its parts. There's not much I can say without spoilers, so I'll just say that this game tries to have exploration like a Zelda game, combat like a Souls game, and complex puzzles. In my opinion this game almost succeeds at having good combat, but is otherwise not worth your time or money. Spoilers Ahead:Tunic is a game that wants to be 3 games at once:- An isometric souls-like- An exploration heavy action-adventure game.- A complex observation-based puzzle gameIf any (or all) of these seem appealing to you, I have bad news, Tunic doesn't really do any of them particularly well.Let's break them down in order of appearance.Tunic the exploration game:This is Tunic's gameplay roughly 20% of the time.Tunic's approach to exploration consists of the same trick played over and over again: you can't see something because it's blocked by objects in the foreground. That's it, you explore to find chests, these chests can contain currency, consumable items, upgrades, or other items, but they're basically all hidden the the same manner.Prepare yourself for the exciting gameplay of moving your character into places you can't see, and praying that a button prompt appears to inform you that there's something there (usually consumable items, sometimes upgrades, and on rare occasions: the critical path.)The game is also surprisingly narrow in where it will allow you to explore. Access to specific items limits your access to most areas until relatively late, making your journey through Tunic a mostly linear one.The size of the world relative to your movement speed also makes backtracking take forever. Exploration is about wandering and discovering things you didn't expect, Tunic's world never really surprised me, it just sort of annoyed and bored me a bit, so I can't recommend Tunic as an exploration game.Tunic the Souls-like:This is Tunic's gameplay roughly 50% of the time.Tunic's core combat system isn't bad, you have movement, melee attacks, ranged/magic attacks, a dodge roll, and a lock-on. None of these things are particularly problematic, however the roll and lock-on both have notable issues that become more annoying as the game's difficulty increases.The roll:- Its distance is too long. (using it to dodge attacks almost always puts you too far away from most enemies to effectively counter or otherwise benefit from having dodged the attack.)- Its unreliable. (from my testing, it appears that some attacks from specific enemies ignore the roll's iframes, I'm not sure if this is a bug or not, but either way it was still very annoying to deal with.)The lock-on:- Bad target prioritization. (the lock-on almost always seems to target the enemy furthest from the player instead of the closest, this makes the lock-on a massive liability in situations where you need to deal with multiple enemies fast.)- Causes camera problems. (In some arenas and particularly in boss fights, the lock-on will rotate the camera around the stage to keep the player and enemies in frame, this results in the camera almost constantly spinning around during some fights. This adds significant difficulty due to all player inputs being relative to the camera (eg. dodging the wrong way because the camera turned as your were pressing the dodge button).)These issues aren't deal breakers, but they aren't really good enough for me to be confident recommending Tunic as a souls-like. (as a brief aside, if you want a game that does these exact things but better, play Death's Door)Tunic the puzzle game:This is Tunic's gameplay for roughly the last 30% of the game.This is, in my opinion, where the source of Tunic's problems stem from.There is, in essence only 2 kinds of puzzles in Tunic:- Deciphering the manual.- The manual:Easily the better of the game's 2 types of puzzles.The manual is a collectible in the game, you gather its pages and can learn new tricks about how to play the game and get hints on how to progress by deciphering its contents. Of course, I hope you enjoy cryptography, because it's all written in an admittedly pretty complex symbol substitution cipher. I personally enjoyed this part, but I'm not sure I'd really call it a "puzzle" in the same way that a game like Portal has "puzzles", I'd say it's really more of an activity/worksheet you're going to have to do if you want to finish the game. (almost all tooltips are also written in this language, so if you're just playing casually but you want to know what any of your upgrades do, you'll also need to decipher the symbols.)(If you want a game that's just this, but an actual game, play Chants of Sennaar.)Now, I'm not going to say these aren't puzzles, I'd say they are, but I'd also say they're far more tedious and repetitive than fun, so no, I cannot recommend Tunic as a puzzle game.Overall, I did not enjoy my time with Tunic, and it's higher-than-average price for a game of its size makes it impossible for me to recommend. If you read this and still want to buy it, you do you, but maybe at least wait until it's on sale?

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible game for my tastes! Usually a casual gamer who only makes time for stuff like the Legend of Zelda and Portal type games. It feels as though someone put the Link's Awakening remake in a blender with a lite version of Dark Souls to make something very special and all its own. This is action adventure RPG at it's finest. An isometric exploration game wrapped in mystery. Only vague hints of what's to come are given as you try to piece together the story, mechanics, and advance. Don't let the chlll vibes and beautiful cell shading fool you though... the combat can be *very* challenging. Only about six hours in and the enemy variety is deep. I really have to pay attention to attack patterns, resource management, and crowd control to survive a lot of situations. Though difficult, combat and mechanics feel balanced and fair. There are some situations I've stepped back from to level up to make it a bit easier, but "get gud" or get smart really do be the answer to conquering a lot of hard spots, it seems.10/10, do recommend. Buckle up!
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: In an odd way, this game has the best tutorial in any game. Tunic shows you everything you need to know little by little in collectible pages of an instruction booklet. If you're nostalgic for the days when you would go to a store, buy a game, and spend the car ride back furiously reading through the included booklet, you will love this.As you collect pages, you learn about the story, items, moves and abilities you didn't even know you had from the beginning. It also builds your map of the world. "Ugh" I thought when I saw the pages of the map, "there isn't going to be a player marker on this is there?" Thankfully they do show you where you on the map. Every page is a treasure trove of information. References to different pages and small hand-drawn notes will have you scouring every pixel for secrets and hints.Apart from the instruction book mechanic (which I absolutely love) the art and music are both fantastic. The combat feels tight and is challenging. There are parts where you might feel a little overwhelmed but overall I felt it was fair.This game really shines in its exploration and puzzles. Finding shortcuts, deciphering the mystery of the world and of course the way it all ties it together with the instruction book quickly made this a favorite game of mine. If you like classic Zelda games, souls-like combat, and a bit of metroidvania I would highly recommend this.

_childDocuments_.review: Whilst I can see why people like this game, given my own experience of the game so far, I can't help but feel that 92% positive almost seems like those 9/10 or 10/10 reviews often seen from games journalists. So far, I'm a 4 bosses in and there's not much I can think of that lends to an overall positive experience. To me it seems like a lot of people just like that this game is going back to how old games used to do things. Lots of reviews detail why they think the game is great, so I'm going to go through my gripes with the game. This is really one of those games where I feel like it deserves something in-between a positive and a negative review. If I were to put a number to it, it would probably be something like a 7/10 (on an actual scale out of 10, not a the games journalist scale which only uses the top third). I'd only recommend it if you're looking for this specific kind of game or you can take the gamble when it's on sale for a lower price than it is currently (30% off, £17.49). Jump to the last paragraph for a TLDR.The exploration isn't particularly fun. Nothing that other games haven't already done but with some overdone aspects. Lots of things are hidden from view of the camera, so you just end up sticking to walls all the time to find all the hidden alleys and rooms. Having to do this everywhere isn't particularly fun and dulls down most "aha" moments due to the many things that are hidden this way. To me, this kinda of exploration isn't all that fun. It's exploration turned into busywork, especially when a lot of the rewards for doing it are just money and the occasional consumable. The mystique and intrigue that Zelda dungeons create is quite absent from this game and the bosses don't really do anything to balance that out.The puzzle element is mysteriously absent from this game, despite being tagged as so, unless the dev's idea of a puzzle is trawling through an area just to flip a switch. This game is as much a puzzle game as dark souls is if you consider opening doors from the other side or knocking down a ladder is a puzzle element. I haven't played through the whole game, so maybe all the actual puzzles are later, which is a failing of a game aiming to be and is lauded as a puzzle game.Of the bosses I've encountered, only 1 really felt all that well designed with the others having major issues with the camera that make focusing or moving accurately far more difficult than it should be. Imagine trying to beat a group of enemies whilst your camera is spinning just so it can keep the boss on the same place in view. You have no control of the camera throughout the game and it's just for the cinematic aesthetic and  hiding things out of sight. I'd also recommend turning off depth of field for at least the boss fights. The effect is way overdone and often leaved the boss and the environment blurry unless you're up in its face.The combat overall doesn't feel particularly great. It's relatively basic and of a similar vein to that of Zelda but they've tried to make it more challenging. Personally, I don't find it all that interesting or challenging after you get to grips with the general feel. There's not anything fundamentally flawed about it, just nothing that makes it something I actively want to do more of. Most encounters practically can be attempted the same way with a handful of enemies needing something other than your sword and shield to initiate. I've enjoyed a number of Zelda games, but so far, this game has too much of an emphasis on combat without making it interesting. The game forces you to do things different very infrequently. It's only when you get to boss fights do you actually have to use your brain in a meaningful way. Where in many other games, the encounters you have leading up to a boss will teach you things that are useful when facing the boss. In this game, every boss (of the ones I've faced) have been completely blind and will be the first time you actually need to use core mechanics. To me, this means a significant portion of the real challenge in the boss fights is in learning the mechanics in the middle of a boss fight (or relearning them because you haven't had to use them in a long time). This only creates needless frustration and means the devs could make simpler bosses with the illusion of difficulty.The game takes an old school approach to tutorials in this game, relying on a manual to communicate mechanics, objectives and the like, but the manual is built into the game and you have to collect the pages as you play. The execution of this is mostly well done. You get more pages as you explore. It's one of the few actually meaningful rewards you get for exploring outside of upgrades and equipment. That's not to say it's flawless. At the start of the game, you're given very little direction, aside from a few pages in the manual. This manual is mostly written using pictures and a cryptic unreadable language with the occasional interpretable thing or english word. There's a lot of guesswork that goes into understanding what the manual is going on about and on a number of occasions, I only understood the actual point until I had already done the thing, practically making portions of the manual redundant.The game is also specifically advertises its soundtrack as a point to buy the game. I love a good soundtrack. A good soundtrack can be the cherry on top in a truly awesome game or can save an average game from too many bad reviews. Hollow Knight, Vermintide 1 and 2, Link's Awakening, and Octopath Traveler are a few games that come to mind with great soundtracks. This game's soundtrack is a bit of a let down without even considering those prior mentioned games. It's just okay. It's a bit of background music. It doesn't do all that much to set and maintain the atmosphere. It is truly just an accessory to accompany the rest of the game. It is not a soundtrack that is worth my money.All of this is to say that in my experience, there isn't much to cry home about. It relies on an old school way of designing games which is absent from modern game design and that alone seems to be one of the major features that people love about the game. I think it has plenty of flaws and is far from a perfect game, but people are willing to overlook that because of the different design philosophy used in this game. There's very little hand holding. All the gameplay is reliant on exploration and using your brain when you're stuck. With all that said, I am mostly enjoying the game. It's not amazing but I am entertained and I don't feel like I'm wasting my time most of the time. If what I've said above doesn't sound all that bad to you and you want an exploration/combat game with very little hand holding and some occasional difficulty, then it's probably the game for you. I'd still recommend waiting for a sale though (larger than the 30% at the time of this review).

_childDocuments_.review: Yet another game where I wish I could put a "mixed" review and not outright good or bad.Tunic is an interesting spin on Zelda games that is ultimately let down by its combat. It's beautiful, has interesting puzzles and a cool story concept. Unfortunately, the 2nd half of the game has a huge difficulty spike with enemies that spend the combat dodging just out of reach while the camera just spends all the fight rotating constantly messing up your movements.I had great fun up till said halfpoint after which it just felt like a chore to get it done.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: This game oozes charm from every pore. The game is deceptively simple, and as it progresses you discover some rather shocking depth. I GREATLY appreciate the way the game is laid out, where you make inferences based on clues to continue, and you have a little guidebook that you assemble as the game goes on, giving you insight on how the game works and how some items work, without actually telling you outright. You have to experiment, try new things (or cheat and look it up online) and it really brings be back to the old game boy days when I didn't have access to guides or the internet.You may see some other people leaving mixed or negative reviews because of the guidebook. Do  listen to them! The modern gaming industry has spoiled them with big text dumps or some NPC explaining every little thing you need to beat the game. Please, take some time, figure it out on your own and experience the dopamine hit you get when you succeed. I highly recommend this game to anyone who is looking for a good adventure, and especially to those who are fans of souls-like games and older Zelda games. Secrets galore await you here. Fantastic soundtrack and sound design as well!
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: If you don't like Souls-likes, don't bother.  I thought this would be a fun adventure game, but it's just awful.  Everything is tumble-dodge, tumble-dodge, whoops!  You started your attack two frames late, so now you're going to eat an unavoidable attack that kills you instantly if you're not at full health.  Also, real cute, providing NO INFORMATION WHATSOEVER on what the items you collect do.  Way to make me waste them trying to figure it out, because the developer would rather write everything in this made up language instead of providing a real description.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: A must buy & play game. Amazing music and Graphics not to mention the beautiful style of the 3d world itself.Tunic also provides a decent challenge while you explore its world which keeps the game from getting repetitive. The Digital Manual is such a cool Idea for a game like this and is oddly my favourite part about the whole experience. (I would recommend only picking this game up if you have a Pc/Xbox controller as Duelsense wont work.)
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: Everything about Tunic really hooked me, the otherworldly yet aptly fitting music , the adorable little fox fellows, the shockingly brutal enemy encounters, the intricate and elaborate puzzles (I now have a sudden appreciation for line puzzles, they're actually not that bad!), and how can I forget that gorgeous and vibrant isometric world! I often found myself just stopping in my tracks just to absorb my surroundings and combined with those ethereal tones, makes for truly awe-inspiring experience. (kinda wished there was like a sit down button just for those moments).  I don't normally write reviews, but my whole experience with Tunic was really special to me. Despite a lack of voice acting and mysterious indecipherable text littered throughout every corner, Tunic truly moved me... everything landed just right for me, it made me feel like a starry-eyed kid again, especially with those little hand drawn notes scattered throughout the old-school instruction manual. This is a game I've always kept at the back of my mind when it was first revealed all those years ago, and now its finally out and to put it simply, the wait was indeed worth it. I'm glad I made the decision prior to invest in a high end gaming laptop to play such brilliant gems like Tunic. Thank you to all the wonderful people who worked their hardest to contribute to this game.Also as a brief side note, I would pay absolutely ungodly amounts of money for any Tunic merch, especially that instruction manual (hint hint) :)
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: An absolutely incredible experience to play through.What starts off as a charming, early Zelda-like evolves into so much more, offering the challenging combat and complex puzzles found in soulslike games and Fez respectively, all set in a beautiful and charming world stylized after hallmarks of NES/SNES gaming. The hardest part of the game, though, was deciding when to stop playing, as every second had me entirely hooked into exploring the world or overcoming obstacles.Tunic constantly teases the player with hints and vague imagery in every inch of its being, often making me reconsider my entire thought process many times over in many of the later () puzzles, and it's still unbelievable to me how much every aspect of the game ties into something grander. I'd highly recommend coming into the game as blind as possible as the sense of wonder it brings is truly something to be treasured.Tunic is one of the few games I could tell from the start that it would become one of my favorites, and by the end I'm completely head over heels in love with it. ♡
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: Real review, old review below. Wow, just wow. This game is amazing. There is a learning curve though. So you play as a fox who has to solve puzzles, and piece together what's going on. You as a player have to do that as well, as nothing is explained, and mechanics are very nuanced. I'm still learning what to do, and I think I'll be doing that the whole game, there are that many tricks up the game's sleeve. I'm having a ton of fun just exploring, and thinking to myself, now, how would I get THERE? When I run into a secret, I'm like 'Oh, Wow, this is cool, did not expect it'. The graphics are one of the best things about the game, they are vividly realized, and there are tons of extras, like where there are water reflections on the walls. The gameplay is very solid, but sometimes I'm feeling like there's something crucial, but it's just out of my reach. Also, there is a lot of thinking outside the box. Piecing together the manual is cool, but trying to figure out how to reach certain pages can be head scratching at best, and head banging on desk at worst. At the moment, I'm clueless about what to do next, and am just a titch frustrated. Alll in all, though, this is a great game, and it's very pick-up-and-play, which is a total bonus. Old review -> I have a very soft spot in my heart for foxes. This game, ticks off so many boxes. Enough rhyming, time for a 'First Impressions' review. The full one will come later. This game is a fairly basic (but that's not a bad thing) TLOZ-like, with a cute spunky fox as the hero. The developer/s of this obviously put a lot of heart and soul into making Tunic. I fell in love the moment I got into the game. Also a plus is all the  accessibility options for those who need them. _childDocuments_.review: This is a game where you do not need any guide, walkthrough, or anything to play. _childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game, something I haven't ever really seen tried before, and it succeeds on all accounts.The design of the earliest console games (NES, yes I know there's older) is basically alien to the modern gaming ecosystem and doesn't really exist anymore. Remakes and rereleases of old games which clean up the gameplay make it less and less likely for people to be remotely familiar with the oldest tropes, but Tunic sets out to remedy that. This game recreates the experience of playing a game in a language you don't really know and whose mechanics are never explained in-game anyway, with nothing but guess-and-check to guide you through and relying on others to fill in the gaps. It's impossible to replicate exactly, of course; many of the most distinct aspects of these early games (secrets scattered around a map haphazardly, dumbass useless NPCs, legitimately inscrutable gameplay mechanics) were due to time constraints or incompetence or both. Here, since they all have intention behind them, they're much gentler; secrets are hard, but deliberate, and there's no major quality of life issues with the gameplay. The NPCs are hilariously useless (and don't type in English), but if you translate them a few of them are actually useful and don't just sit around saying "GO TO THE NEXT ROOM" or whatever. The combat is probably the furthest away from older design out of anything in the game, and feels mostly modern though I think it works very well. The game shines in its design philosophy; the vast majority of progress in the game rewards you with knowledge, and not tangible checkpoints. When you reach a new area, you find out that there was a ladder to the beginning all along; when you pass a crucial point you find out how to use overworld objects that were available and functional for the entire game. It's not items, but knowledge, that shapes your journey, and if you have the knowledge from the get-go you can travel all over the place in any order you like for the most part.Gamers of yesteryear were quite fond of speculating about esoteric sequences of button-presses and their real or imagined impact on gameplay. It's obviously been quite popular to actually put these obscure secrets into games for more than a decade now (after all, most game devs grew up when it was popular). Tunic follows a similar philosophy, and while the idea behind the holy cross puzzles isn't new it's very well-executed, much better than most other games that attempt it. Very few of the puzzles are overly obscure and even then the game gives you ample hints.It's interesting looking at reviews for this, since it seems like the intent of the game flew right over most players' heads at mach five. You know the industry is just straight up ♥♥♥♥♥♥ when the only frame of reference most players have is Dark Souls, but I guess the likelihood of most modern players having touched any of the games this is based off of is pretty low. I'm honestly not even sure most players of this game have played Fez, which goes a long way to explain the general attitude towards it. It's a shame, but for the game's intended audience, it doesn't get much better than this. 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: What I expected: Miniature Legend of Zelda with a cute little fox and a fun find-the-pages-of-the-manual gimmick. Should be a chill experience. WHY IS IT FULL OF PURPLE‽" Post-game review update: Part of what makes this game so good is that it drip-feeds you information about itself, and you as the player have to puzzle it out yourself. As such I can't say much in a review, but if you liked post-game FEZ, where in you discover a fundamentally new way to interact with the game world to solve puzzles, you'll love late-/post-game TUNIC. This game was just about perfect for me. Cute world, fun music, surprising and clever hidden mechanics, and fun language puzzles. It's one of the few games that I expect to 100%, and one of the few that I'll interact with outside of the game for a long time. (The runes are super fun!)TUNIC is easily going into my list of favorite games. (Combat tips for people starting out: Bombs are your friends. Also the shield is nice, but practice dodging.)

_childDocuments_.review: Although calling "Tunic" an in-depth metroidvania from an isometric perspective is correct, it doesn't properly convey what an adventure this game was.More than just beating bosses to unlock gameplay mechanics, "Tunic" also unlocks gameplay mechanics by awarding players with pages of a manual — one that's written almost entirely in a fictitious language accompanied by colourful symbols and illustrations. It is then up to you, the player, to give your best guess in interpreting the pages because these pages hold the secrets to abilities you've had ever since the beginning — you simply hadn't known yet.In a literal sense, knowledge is power.More than collecting items that add abilities to your arsenal, more than testing your technical skill with the controls, "Tunic" is a game where your curiosity in exploration and intuition in cryptic data are rewarded with power. More so than most metroidvanias, knowledge makes you more powerful.That feeling of acquiring knowledge gives a potent shot of exhilaration surpassed only by another knowledge-based game I've played — The Outer Wilds.I strongly recommend playing Tunic.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun zelda-esque game with some inspiration from Dark Souls. They use a bonfire system, there's a lot of boss fights, and the combat is focused on slower but high-damage enemies. I liked the puzzles, and the minimal dialogue. Oh and the in-game manual is great, make sure you pay attention to it. There's a good 6-8 hours of fun before you hit a stats reset which really breaks the game. Clearly this was done to pad for time, suddenly you you face enemies that 2 shots you, on top of which each hit permanently reduces your health, so you'll be stuck at 1 hp until the next bonfire. To escape this section you have to handle a multi-fight battle arena (almost like a boss-rush), with reduced stats this is extremely annoying and not any fun. A very strange and poor design decision, I actually thought I was playing a DLC meant for hardcore players by accident, however this is on purpose. Granting a lot of people won't see this section of the game since it's pretty far in, but my overall opinion of this game was certainly diminished by this part. My recommendation is very tentative, clearly most people give up on the game after a few hours due to the difficulty, and I'm sure a lot more give in when they hit that mid-game reset, so if you fully understand that and think the first 6-8 hours are worth it then I'd say pick this game up.Played on Deck with no problems.

_childDocuments_.review: Tunic is the most thought provoking and engaging game I have played in a long time. Initially it presents as a solid (but beautifully stylised) third person adventure with your normal attack/dodge/block core mechanics but slowly reveals itself to be much more.The game starts without stifling you with a mandatory hand-holding tutorial segment - instead mechanics and the main quest are explained through interaction with the world and collecting mysterious manual pages for the player to interpret. This may sound daunting but worked seamlessly in practice. I never stalled on where to go and game progression was rewarding because it was entirely driven by the player's desire to explore.Progression through the game comes in the form of upgrading your character, picking up new equipment and techniques and consequently being able to access new areas with new enemies. Normal enemies are typically only challenging in groups but the game operates off a system of checkpoint shrines so it is really a game of how many encounters you can endure while exploring. Game bosses were distinct, challenging, and were satisfyingly spectacular.The game truly shines however on the depths of its puzzles and the evidently large amount of care the devs have put into them. The more you as a player are willing to invest to decode the manual and solve the various puzzles without looking at guides the more you will appreciate the game - I highly recommend playing with pens and paper handy.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the best game in my Steam library. It's the best gaming experience I've had in literally over 20 years. My top experiences being mostly in the 90s - Zelda: Link's Awakening, Zelda: Ocarina of Time, and Final Fantasy VII. The game's aesthetics are simple yet gorgeous; the music/sound-effects are stellar. S-tier indie studio game that is better than most AAA titles. Is it perfect? No, it has flaws for sure. But it was a pleasure to play through and was a fun challenge. Highly, highly recommend this.The gameplay is a mix between a chill, low-key Zelda-like dungeon puzzler and a hell-hole, get-yo-ass beat souls-like boss grind. To be frank, the difficultly of the combat can be a bit frustrating at times - that is my major complaint. But I don't really play souls-like games and this level of pain and difficulty will be enjoyed by many. The only reason I got past some of the boss fights was because I figured out a strategy to abuse some gaps in the AI...Rather, I vibed with the more Zelda-like exploration, puzzler, and dungeon crawler aspects of the game. I did find the cryptic, figure-it-out-yourself design quite fun and refreshing. Flipping through the manual and putting the pieces of the puzzle together of where I had to go, when I had to go, what items I needed, etc. Very satisfying. I highly recommend you do NOT use a guide for your first play through - at all. Good luck!

_childDocuments_.review: The best Zelda game ever made.The whole world is a puzzle, and not merely a straightforward wysiwyg logic rooms like Zelda dungeons. You have the whole solution to the puzzle already, but you have to decipher it piece by piece to complete it. Unfortunately, there is no cryptography involved. The language is IPA symbols of English existing in a custom glyph set.Also the combat sucks, but not as bad as Zelda combat (both before and after BotW). Enemy hit points and whatnot, however, acts as more of a skill check rather than as a difficulty feature. Hopefully the devs can address this and make the combat more enjoyable as the roll mechanic is cool and all, but there are no active defensive mechanics, and this one passive mechanic is, as one would expect, clumsy and awkward-feeling in execution. When making swings, you expect at least some sort of stun mechanic, but that's only if you do enough damage to a given enemy, and due to the tendency to sort of spam and inability to dodge during attacks, you just get hit which is absolutely trash combat that deserves zero praise whatsoever (there's no skill in waiting for things to happen so I can do what I must, even on the order of milliseconds). This reduces the skill gap check to a monotonous "trudgingly survive" (in certain instances) until you can level up your stats enough to the point where it doesn't matter anymore. Terrible UX. Fix your stupid combat, and definitely don't pretend to fix it and then call it fixed either, or I will fight to the death for a refund for what would be nothing less than an inexcusable compromise no different than contemporary Nintendo!

_childDocuments_.review: Tunic is perhaps the most memorable singleplayer game I've ever played. Come for the top-down action blending Zelda games and Dark Souls, stay for the amazing scene-setting and puzzles.As you may have heard, part of this game's challenge is the fact that the manual is presented  and is rendered mostly in a fictional language. This is a major part of what gives the game its unique flair, but it also means that this is a game that requires some measure of patience. In addition to being the most memorable singleplayer game I've completed, Tunic is also the one that had me staring blankly at my ceiling for the longest time. On dozens of occasions I was very, very tempted to just look up solutions to puzzles or guides on what to do next after running in circles -- and in the end I eventually did look at a couple hints just to make sure I wasn't gaslighting myself on a couple of the more elaborate puzzles.If you have the patience to handle the arcane process of learning a game without having any guides, Tunic is sure to be a treat for you. I've never played a game that gave me such a visceral feeling of solving a mystery before.

_childDocuments_.review: My friends keep asking me for my opinion on this game because a common friend of ours has given a "negative" review on this game.So I have to right their error.(Please do not take this serious, people are entitled to their opinion it's just what led me to this review.)Simple Tl:dr, so far the best game I've played in 2022.Now to the actual Review:Tunic's an interesting "Zelda-like" looking exploration heavy action adventure.So despite that, it is not a Zelda game. It resembles Dark Souls more than it resembles a Zelda game.secondly, this game does not hold your hand. It will very much make you figure everything out, make you use your brain and all at some point Information will become a better loot than any weapon, item or whatever the hell you can find.But sadly talking about the puzzles themselves would probably ruin the experience.So let's just keep it simple with a pros and cons list:Pros:-Decent Combat, something you'd somewhat expect from a Soulslike, rolling, getting a few hits in and stuff like that.-Puzzles range from "kind of genius" to literally exploiting the general "gaming" instinct people will have built up.-The Isometric camera and the game's utilization of it is great.-Every single loot item in this game actually feels worthwhile-Good visuals. This game's usage of lighting is kind of stellar.Cons:-The Story, the ending kinda didn't do it for me.-The Target Lock-On, you will probably die once to the wrong thing being targeted.-The Repetition in the second half.Sadly I will not elaborate on my final gripe as that would spoil...... some things but a simple explanation would be.The way to access 100 % completion in this game has something that repeats quite a bunch.They tried a few ways to mix it up but it's just so many that repetition was bound to happen.And one where I am not sure if I should call it a pro OR a con:-The shift from the first half to the second half.I personally loved it, can I see it upsetting people, absolutely.And that's my review, sorry about the bad formatting, just needed to finally stop people from asking me about my opinion on this.This game's great, I don't give scores but i'd give it a recommendation, definitely not perfect but ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ great and my favourite game of this year so far.

_childDocuments_.review: Tunic is inspiring! Pure art. The entire game not only looks good, plays well, it also shows the entire way how much love was put into it. A testament for the kind of experience I look for in a video game and I was more than glad to find this little cute fox gem!

_childDocuments_.review: An incredible game that leaves you with goosebumps at each new discovery. Secrets upon secrets upon secrets, means that almost nothing can be said about this game without spoiling it. In an extremely broad sense, fans of Fez's layered puzzles, and Hyper Light Drifter's atmosphere and combat will love this game. The only thing that ever had me putting this game down for a night, a week even at times, was the difficulty spikes at some bosses or other pivotal moments. In those moments it really matters to take it slow, learn the fight, don't try to face-tank through an encounter. And ho wow is it worth it to stick it out past those difficulty spikes, for the environmental storytelling this game gives you is second to none. Most text is in a secret runic language, so story and lore is given to you via the sometimes even jaw-dropping environments you traverse, and the creatures you encounter. This game is absolutely my game of the year. I'll be thinking about it for a very, very long time. Bravo to the developers.

_childDocuments_.review: It deconstructs the game and lays it wide open on your table, for you to put your own soul in it.It also testifies to video games as "wonder machines". All games try to create wonder to the best of their resources (even  don’t laugh!), but  seems to be more focused on the process than the output, more interested in the "clockwork" behind the magic, the “machinery” that makes the god appear rather than the god himself (shifting the emphasis in the traditional  device). It even has the mechanics and the meta-narration for it. Your main mission will be to piece together and figure out the manual that describes the game, which is also a game guide, a cheat book and your most important resource for puzzle solving. All that because  is essentially a puzzle game, masquerading as a top-down souls-like metroidvania only so that it can push the puzzles into the meta layer of its narrative, hiding them in plan sight, as it were. And they are wonderful, brilliant puzzles! So great they totally overshadow the action mechanics the game relies on in its early stages, to the point that it almost makes them irrelevant by the end game (you can choose a greatly reduced difficulty for enemy encounters and boss fights  if you want to concentrate on the puzzles). And the game will want you concentrated on those. That’s not to say its action mechanics are less accomplished, of course, but the gradual shift from action to puzzles as the game progresses is obvious and a great example of versatile and meaningful game design, that I’ve not seen many games able to attempt so successfully. Therefore, if you want to play it as a slick souls-like metroidvania in a colourful Zelda-like setting, you can totally tackle it like one of those, but its truest nature is closer to the ascetic self-awareness of  and the game manual it has you put together while playing is hands down the most self-referential statement ever made by a video game.LATER EDIT:  is basically two very different games, conjoined at the hip and wrapped in the same fox-shaped package. The greatest thing to ever come out of an identity crisis!

_childDocuments_.review: A nearly flawless adventure game that goes far deeper than you might expect. Tunic is a masterclass in air-tight game design, with a particularly keen sense for how and when to influence the player. It manages to nail down a particular kind of old-school childlike wonder that I didn't think a modern title could really faithfully emulate. If you're a fan of exploring and secret hunting, and you enjoy the look of the combat and aesthetic, I cannot recommend this game enough.I recommend playing Tunic completely blind, from start to finish, with no guides. It's tough, in a lot of ways, but it's extremely gratifying to unravel the game's web of secrets as the developers intended.If you're well and truly stuck on something to the point of giving up, the "Spoiler Safe Guide to Tunic" on the Steam guides page is a great way of giving yourself a nudge in the right direction. I needed this a couple times - though frankly, every time I looked at it, I felt pretty dumb afterwards.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish there was a star or scale from 1 to 10 for this, instead of yes or no.  I'd give this game a 6 out of 10.To be blunt, I enjoyed the first half of the game.  Pretty good action adventure, with responsive combat and different combinations which result in higher damage.  Parry, dodge, and stun can all be done, though requires practice to perfect.  The 2.5 design means hidden paths and what not, because that's always apart of a game with a fix camera.  Item combinations and things like that improve your combat and transverse potential.  The instruction manual provides hints, and requires you to pay attention and zoom in on each page to identify things.  An easy to understand combo, for those who like to live dangerously, is the berserk, critical damage, and critical defense combination, where your health is in critical levels at all times, so you deal more damage from the berserk and critical damage buffs, and the critical defense boosts your shield strength (I think).The second half, the line puzzles, I loath.  I don't mind puzzle games, in fact my library has the entire "The Room" series barring the VR game, and other puzzle games.  However, line puzzles, where you have to input a lengthy series of inputs with little feedback of where you went wrong, makes it frustrating.  Hence, I ended up looking up the solutions to most if not all of the puzzles.  The more complex ones requires good old fashion screenshots, and arrangement of images to solve.  Feels punishing to those who have only one monitor as the amount of screen space necessary to solve these things efficiently increases in proportion  the more complex puzzles.Hence, multiple endings, which requires you to know how to solve those puzzles to obtain.  The basic "bad" ending happens if you simply go through the game without doing any of the puzzles.  About the only thing I failed to find, is the ability to translate the language, and instead either intuit or looked up the meaning.I did enjoy the game, and its music.  Just not all of it, and cannot recommend something that has a bit of a niche audience to everyone.

_childDocuments_.review: Tunic is almost an interesting game within a game riddle that could've succeeded immensely, but I think the pacing undersells that part of the game, in the sense that it leaves most of the interesting parts of the gimmick lingering at the end, probably to lure the majority of the players in first with actual action/adventure gameplay.I still enjoyed it, and would recommend. But I'm not sure from personal experience if they nailed it. The lack of intuitive map traversal and possible backtracking/retracking tedium does have an old school feel to it, but it probably isn't fit for purpose in this day and age. Would've much preferred a warp "between checkpoint" mechanic than the actual hub system in place so I could feel like I was actively solving the overall puzzle than wasting most of my time wondering around aimlessly.

_childDocuments_.review: An incredible port of a timeless classicI was a little worried at first when I heard that Secret Legend was getting an updated rerelease (now called Tunic for some reason) but all of those concerns were unfounded. The dev went to great lengths to make sure that this version is as close to the original as possible, including using the original, non-localized language in a lot of places. It's alright if you're not a native-speaker though, the game's pretty intuitive and you can figure out what you need to do if you pay close attention!There are two clever nods that I want to point out, too: First, when viewing the in-game instruction manual (really clever usage of the scans from the OG booklet that came with the game!) you can use the right stick to get a peek at the game screen behind it, and they revert to the original graphics. Secondly, they even recreated the "phantom save file" bug, using the same inputs as the old cartridge.In short, if you never got to play the first release of Secret Legend (and considering it never released outside of its developing country, most people didn't) this version is a treat.

_childDocuments_.review: Curator page : TUNIC is an action-adventure game inspired by Zelda and FEZ.You play as a fox who wakes up on a ruined island, with no context and nothing else to do but to explore.You'll quickly find the bare minimum to fight the enemies wandering around, and a few pages of what appears to be the game manual : this manual is the core of TUNIC.The twist is that it is ciphered, written in a language you can't understand. Some words are still readable though, and the game revolves around that : making you guess and guiding you with your senses of observation and deduction. Nothing is directly told to you : everything, whether it is a minor or major thing, is in the manual and you'll have to study it.It has a strong nostalgic vibe, game manuals are not a thing anymore and anyone who grew up with them probably miss them too. I always read them before playing a new game, and I remember I had to put tape on my Super Mario Sunshine and Sonic Adventure 2 manuals due to reading them too much...The world of TUNIC is extremely well crafted, exploring it is very pleasant (the game is beautiful, cute and has a nice soundtrack) and very rewarding, there are TONS of secrets hidden everywhere. Once you get that this is this type of game, you'll start searching any corner you can find... and sure you'll probably get a lot of treasures.But what makes the level design of TUNIC so good and truly genius is not only the secrets you'll find. It's all the things hidden in plain sight that you'll still miss. The game doesn't even try to misdirect you, they are just so cleverly hidden that you won't see or find them.TUNIC has two major sides:- The first one is the adventure, the main game. It strongly reminds of Zelda, but harder. And I'm not just talking about the bosses, common enemies are also threats and some areas can be (very) challenging. The combat is punishing if you just brainlessly rush into the enemies. If you take your time and properly dodge/parry, you won't have much trouble going through the game except for an area near the end. You even have some consumables you can use if you really struggle.The bosses are still the highlights of course, being fun, varied, very strong and usually forcing you to use different items depending on which one you face.- The second one is the FEZ-like side that you'll discover near the end. Full of clever puzzles, including mind-blowing ones that you'll remember for a long time. Some people can find that part too difficult but it's not, it just requires patience and, as always, a thorough study of the holy manual.I unfortunately can't go into details without spoiling anything but if you like puzzles, it's heaven.At this point you probably wonder why I didn't talk about the story at all. Well, like anything else in the game, the story is also cryptic.You'll guess a few things and probably end up understanding what you're doing on the island. But the real story, the context of the game, is locked behind the ciphered language. And you're not supposed to decipher it, at least not until the very end of the game... and you probably won't anyway because it's absurdly hard.That's the only little sad thing I can say about the game, I would've loved more hints about that to really try to decipher myself.Anyway TUNIC is a masterpiece, in case it wasn't clear.And we need more games like that. Games crafted with a lot of love and time put into it. Games that don't hold your hand and recognize players are not devoid of brain. _childDocuments_.review: So the first 5-7 hours or so were fantastic for sure. Atmosphere is great, combat is not bad ("not bad" being the best it'll ever get ) and you figure out game mechanics through clever use of finding manual pages and part of the game is puzzling out how things work. All of this, when it works comes together well and feels great.However when it fails it fails also really hard and all the fun goes out the window pretty fast. There's multiple ways the game can do that. One is to simply be stuck on not figuring out where to go. Thankfully this didn't happen a lot to me and usually I could find my way to looking over the "map" again and deciding that "there is probably something here, so let's check that section out again". But generally almost all access points are hidden by the perspective of the camera. Be that hidden ladders or corridors or whatnot. I get the throwback to older games where some secrets where hidden that way, but it's way, wayyy overdone here by being basically the default way of going from section to section at times. This also makes it more annoying to remember which way you needed to go when going through an area later.Another really bad aspect is the combat. At first it's not too bad, since both you and the enemies seem equally clunky. But in the second half of the game enemies are mostly a keep away AI that runs away from you and then attacks from long range. And for some enemies it takes you longer to swing and hit with your weapon after they just attacked you than it takes the enemies to run away from you again. Some also get invulnerability frames just after their attack so you're guaranteed not able to hit them. Basically, most basic enemies become a huge pain in the ass while adding nothing interesting to combat.Similar for bosses. except bosses have the extra problem that for some the camera moves too fast (as it's always on the boss) so aside from that one boss where during a specific sequence all it does is circle around you (and thus move the camera, which made me dizzy as heck after a while) you often get problems of the boss attacking while moving fast that leads to not quite seeing what's going on or inputs not working, or blocking not working cause your character turns too fast (or not fast enough, idk). which means sometimes you block sometimes you don't which is also quite frustrating. Aside from the same keep away/i-frame stuff on top, which just drags out the already not so fun battles too much.Then the secret puzzles. I'd say I can see how some people can get really into those. And good for you, I hope you had a lot of fun with hose, but unless you enjoy staring at cryptic messages and just trying stuff out a lot and never getting clear feedback it's seems a bit too much trial and error. I even had it happened that I actually correctly figured out what to do, but then it didn't work anyway, so I assumed I needed maybe a certain item first, but as it turns out I did everything correctly already, it just didn't work as intended (for whatever reason), so that kinda sucked big time. Some puzzles/clues are incredibly vague at times and some seemingly require you to translate that whole fake language to even get the clues. So if you enjoy that kinda stuff, that's probably a plus, but I just thought the game had its head up wayy too far it's own arse at that point tbh.

_childDocuments_.review: Tunic is a cute game that initially appears as a standard rpg where you go around the world finding treasure, getting stronger, and killing bosses. The art style is simple yet experssive and the music is soft and atmospheric. While the combat targetting can be finicky against multiple enemies, it works.What sets the game apart is how you learn mechanics and get hints: by literally collecting pages of the game's manual.Even if you don't care for the hidden secrets, Tunic still has the basic outline of a story through the manual pages you do collect and even provides a twist, all without any dialog and with most text in a made up runic language. However, going for all the collectables is where the game really shines.Poring through the manual and understanding certain parts of it literally changes how you view the environment and the world's design. The isometric view and world design is cleverly used to hide secrets; you will miss something the first time around, no matter how thorough you think you were. Rereading manual pages to realize how to get to something you missed or understanding the initially random scribbles within the manual itself is very satisfying. However, not understanding or missing something can lead to you wandering around for a long time not knowing what to do. This is something that applies to the game whether you are going for 100% completion or not, but is a lot more noticeable while searching for every last secret.Tunic is a game best experienced as blind as you can. Only look up hints or guides as a last resort. The only exceptions I'd say are worth it are the two achievements that will be missed during a vanilla blind playthrough as it requires having the pages for two specific items, translating their descriptions, and inferring the meaning. By the time you have the resources to do so, you will have most likely already failed the conditions to get them. In addition, the items in particular don't really have a reason to be explicitly translated as you've probably inferred the descriptions while using them, meaning you'll be going out of your way to translate them.
