_childDocuments_.review: I hate to mention Dark Souls right at the start (it's the Dark Souls of Zelda-likes etc.), but it clearly had an influence on the design philosophy of Tunic. Bonfires that heal you and re-spawn enemies, currency that is lost upon death and can be retrieved, stamina management in combat, relatively challenging gameplay, you get the idea. If you're looking for a contemporary comparison it put me in mind of 2017's Hob, 2018's BELOW and last years Death's Door, three similar action adventure games that also have mysterious worlds with minimal exposition. You'll probably be reminded of various entries in the Zelda series too while the frequently obscure puzzle aspects might bring to mind games like The Witness, La Mulana and legendary non-game developer Phil Fish's classic, Fez. Then there's the secrets, lots of games have secrets, Tunic is basically defined by them. It's literally bursting with hidden stuff to find and some of the more tricky finds might have you running for a walk-through. It all comes together very nicely and the singular, cohesive vision that can come with a very small development team is one of the games highlights. In summary, if you're easily frustrated or dislike games with little overt hand holding this might not be for you but if you enjoy challenging, mysterious adventures that respect your intelligence, give Tunic a go. Oh, and those user manuals pieces you find throughout the game...use them!

_childDocuments_.review: Really enjoyable and worth the wait. The game is being frequently described as a "souls-like Link to the Past" which I feel is unfair. While there are very immediate and central connections to LttP, I wouldn't describe souls-like as very apt. There is a death mechanic, a parry, and an upgrade system, but the vibe isn't at all like dark souls and outside of the parry, the other two similarities don't feel all that similar either. The difficulty isn't nearly as high or feel as punishing. I'd describe as slightly more difficult than casual. This game is very responsive, intuitive and holds a incredible amount of character. I had been following this game's development for maybe 6 or 7 years and in that span of time there have been a huge amount of games modeled on the link to the past format. I was worried that my experience would suffer from the market's oversaturation, but this game does an exceptional job of keeping you engaged and interested. The primary storytelling and mechanics-explaining vehicle is based on an in-game instruction manual that you pick up pieces of bit-by-bit and I love everything about it. There is so much attention to detail, a plethora of subtle/enticing hints, and puzzles that are legitimately difficult and frustrating that feel genuinely rewarding.This is probably the best game in the genre that I've played since Hyper Light Drifter. I'd suggest playing blind and really keeping yourself from looking up solutions when you are stuck. There are loads of 'ah-ha' moments that I wouldn't want you to spoil for yourself.

_childDocuments_.review: TUNIC is a game that felt like it promised to be my game, and then said "I lied!" 10 hours later.What everyone recommends is that you go into TUNIC blind and free of walkthroughs, which I agree with, but from what you can see from trailers and the steam page is that it's a bit of a 2D Zelda clone with a manual that you can't read and secrets everywhere. That's good! I used to love those games and felt like this sort of exploration of old games' level design was a very fun idea.And the game exectutes this fairly well! The manual pages are fun to find and the secrets can be wonderful to figure out yourself, some many hours after you already had the opportunity to do something with them. A lot of people mention how this makes it so getting lost is way too easy, and yes, it is, but I think that is to be expected if you want the ideal experience with this game. ♥♥♥♥, go play the first Zelda on the NES, are you not lost?The problem is something else entirely. Because exploration and cryptic puzzles simply isn't enough to make this game entertaining (debatable), TUNIC has a lot of combat too. A sword and a shield, magic items, a dodge roll, and every type of enemy attacking you that you can think of. You heal through flask-like items, and using checkpoints makes enemies respawn. Sound familiar?Unfortunately, TUNIC's combat is an intrusive mess, a complete "♥♥♥♥ you" to the player with very easy to understand but mechanically unfair fights. Every enemy encounter is potentially fatal, and they're all okay at best and "immediately closing the application" at worst. Out of, what, 5 or 6 boss fights I did, only 1 was all that interesting. ♥♥♥♥, at some point they even give you It is upsetting to me how much a game so unashamed of showing its influences can also feel so afraid of having simple zelda-like combat. This game should not have been a soulslike. Its hostility towards the player can make some sense thematically, but is so frustrating that I've tried three times to give this game another chance and failed. I got to one of the parts people consider to be "when the game gets good" but at that point my patience had wore down so much that I couldn't bear to keep going.If you want to get this anyway but consider my opinion on this worth a listen, just... Don't be afraid to just use the invincibility. The fact that it's an option right there from the moment you start means something.I just wish TUNIC was a game about exploring areas and solving puzzles. It isn't.EDIT: since this review, as of July 2024 I restarted the game with invincibility and infinite stamina on and finished it, got all the secrets, etc. It was... Fine. I had fun, I really enjoyed the puzzles, I did not think they were that wiki heavy I only got stuck in a couple of them, but the couple that I did get stuck on kind of ruined the rest? The solution of puzzles and finding of secrets in TUNIC can be so inconsistent sometimes that it makes the puzzles you did figure out on your own seem lesser. And my opinions on the combat have not changed. There is no excuse. It just sucks. Now with the perspective of having finished the whole game, I don't think the combat in TUNIC complements the design or the themes of the game at all. Overall, I did enjoy my time, but with so many caveats that I don't know if I want to recommend it to anyone. I love some of the more fun puzzles and love that they even thought of them, but the game's quality is just too inconsistent to ever call this a masterpiece. I wish they could just retry.

_childDocuments_.review: Tunic is absolutely fantastic. It is the 2D Zelda Soulslike game people have been begging for for years. _childDocuments_.review: This game feels so tailor-made for me so I just have to write a gushing review for it! It's a combination of incredibly smart game design which relies on minimal hand-holding and rewards your curiosity; puzzles that give you that 'AHA!' moment and unlock a whole new way of looking at the world once they click; isometric action combat that feels just challenging enough to keep you on your toes but never making you feel like the task is impossible and you aren't going to progress further; beautiful art direction and compelling world-building through visual storytelling and last but not least, a cute af protagonist. If you are like me and all of that sounds exactly up your alley, then I highly recommend TUNIC! Very quickly into the game, TUNIC teaches you to be observant. You will not be able to progress unless you are curious and are looking for visual clues at all times. The most unique mechanic that TUNIC has is a game manual which can be accessed at any time and contains everything you will need to beat the game and solve even its hardest puzzles. It's very much inspired by actual retro game manuals and the aesthetic of it is *chef's kiss*. The twist is that the manual pages are written in a foreign language with only some english sprinkled around to guide you. You are also able to find only certain pages at a time so you are forced to solve as much as possible with as little as you have. You aren't always sure if you already have the information to engage with what you're finding so that fuels your curiosity even more. One of the smartest parts of TUNIC's design is how both your discoveries in the world and your reading of the manual pages is teaching you to be observant. You will always be rewarded for using your eyes in this game. As you progress the game will also reveal hidden paths & ladders that have been there all along, you just didn't know it but you  seen had you been looking closer. You will find little scribbles on maps in the manual, only to discover secret chests/paths/etc. in the world. It's an extremely smart loop of both secrets in the manual and smart level design that just constantly fuels your sense of wonder, curiosity and gives you a dopamine rush every time you figure out any of its secrets. I never found myself stuck or lost simply by keeping an eye out.Fair bit of advice though, go in as blind as possible (don't even watch the trailer/video on steam as it gives a fair bit away that would otherwise feel more rewarding to discover on your own). I went in knowing very little about the game except that it was a game all about discovery, had a cool retro game manual mechanic and that apparently had one big compelling puzzle (which I'll circle back to), that's about it! This is the type of game where you are doing yourself a huge disservice if you spoil yourself so my biggest advice is:  All I'll say is if you're stuck/lost: "When in doubtie, game manual-ie outie". The game is very smart in the sense that at all times you are given everything you need to progress further, the manual pages are very selectively given to you at certain times to give you all the knowledge you need (). And knowledge really is the biggest "power" you will be given. I was always so excited to receive a new page of the manual and analyze it as much as possible with my current knowledge of the game. Also worth knowing is that you do not need to decipher the manual language to beat the game with the good ending. You also do not need to understand every puzzle/scribbly note in the manual to beat it either. I completed some post-game/side puzzles that I got through using the hints in the manual (that do indeed make you feel like a genius), but there is tons in there just for the pure love of hard af puzzles. There is a whole rabbit hole of secret puzzles and insanity that the community has unearthed online that is worth looking into only  you finish the game. But safe to say, you only need to understand  of the manual puzzles/hints to finish the game and that is always connected to a repeating phrase/word, a whole page spread, etc. The game manual is very clear as to what's important and much more subtle about the extra fun notes/small hints to bonus puzzles. The game also has some awesome boss fights that have the difficulty fine tuned to challenge you but never make you despair and stop playing. I will say though, some of the boss hit boxes could be finicky and your attacks don't always hit despite not being physically possible to get closer to the boss/weak point. Leading up to each of the boss encounters there is so much visual storytelling and world building as you go from zone to zone, each weirder than the last. I was constantly at awe and curious about why this world is the way it is. There are few moments of "revelations" as well that are purely visual/environment storytelling that had me asking so many questions and made me very invested in the lore of the world. As a huge sucker for cryptic visually driven storytelling that doesn't give you all the answers but forces you to theorize, this game scratched just the right itch!Lastly, I want to talk about the "last" puzzle and the ending, but do not spoil yourself if you haven't figured it out yet as it's by far the most satisfying part of the game to figure out on your own.  I will say though, the puzzles/ world secrets in this game definitely lean towards the visual pattern-breaking observation kind of thinking and if that is not how your brain works this game's puzzle hints may not make a whole lot of sense to you. My brain clicks with that type of thinking and puzzle solving very well so it was all immensely satisfying throughout the game!TL;DR Amazing game, fantastic world, joyous game manual, smart puzzles that make brain go brrr, brb going to buy the fox plushie now

The very basics of what to do and where to go are locked behind a language youre not expected to be able to read (i was playing in english. the language i couldn't read was an in game language) and overall the game is derivative. im sure it would be fun if i could tell what was actually happening but as stated even actions such as what im assuming are "would you like to pick up this manual page" and "something something well?" are unreadable. All this game did was make me wish i was playing deaths door again. this game is not worth the price.EDIT:someone kept insisting i needed to keep playing after because "it gets better" and i did. i still do not recommend  it unless you have a second moniter that has a PDF of the in game booklet. theres too many things that are locked behind the booklet pages in that you could do them at any time but you wont know to do them until you get the booklet page that tells you that you could have.  this, obviously, leads to backtracking to places that had those pillar things if you can even remember where they were whenever you encounter them. so i really gotta say that my earlier review didnt even scratch the surface of how ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ this game is. i dont give two ♥♥♥♥♥ if its how it was designed, it just means it designed poorly. _childDocuments_.review: After gaining all achievements, I can say that I really liked this game, to the point that I think it's one of the best games "for me" that I've played in recent years. I found game design elements in it that I already enjoyed in FEZ and The Witness, but handled even better here.All the environmental puzzles and discovery aspects I found extremely satisfying, but there are a couple of points I'd like to address.Of the 36 achievements I managed to get 32 by myself and without any guidance or solution. This to me is extraordinary, since the game has many "metatextual/environmental puzzles" that in other games are generally done in a worse way or that depend more on moon logic. Things that in other games would have me searching on google in no time, here kept me in-game. Tunic is exceptional in giving you "everything you need".Of the other 4 achievements, instead:- One took me almost 3 "empty" hours because I knew "where it was", but a very stupid detail and a red herring (cryptic reference to understand which one I'm referring to: alarmed birds) distracted me.- I found one too "demanding", in the sense that it is the only one that requires understanding of the language that Tunic uses. I reached half of what was needed, but for the last part I looked online for the translation (cryptic reference to understand which one I'm referring to: wet letters).- One I found just free hate on the player. It's something that is extremely missable in the first playthrough, and asked me for an ad-hoc new game just to do it (cryptic reference to understand which one I mean: pew pew).- One is feasible as long as you play "conservative" (cryptic reference to understand which one I'm referring to: piggy bank). The problem I have with this achievement is that I already play conservative in these games by default, but the game at one point pushes you not to, to the point that another achievement is achieved by partially "letting go". It pissed me off that I had to recover it in the ad-hoc run for the previous achievement since I was "almost there" in the main run but reached a point where it wasn't achievable anymore.These last two achievements go so much against what (in my opinion) is the spirit of Tunic, that it would have been a better game without them.Apart from these small negative points imho, as I said above this has been an amazing experience. Without making too many spoilers, the yellow page has been one of the most satisfying videogame things in recent years. The click in my brain when I realized what I had to do was cathartic, I felt invested with otherworldly knowledge.TL;DR: I consider this game an amazing experience.

But the game offers you an option to turn on "no fail" which means you will not die in battle. This way you can focus on exploring the world and figuring out the puzzles. _childDocuments_.review: It's been quite some time since I've found a difficult game I enjoyed since Hollow Knight/Spelunky/Katana Zero/Celeste. I'm not very fond of soulslike games but this is a nice "introductory" course I'd say LOL. Although soulslike and a little difficult, it's truly not as bad as other soulslike games I've tried. The game presents a challenge but still enjoyable; and it's filled with little puzzles. The animation, music and graphics are very pretty, mechanics are great and although I have no idea what the story is even about, 2 hours in and I'm already completely hooked. _childDocuments_.review: Take the presentation and basic mechanics of top down zelda with the modern sheen of something like death's door, mix it with the mechanics and hardcore philosophy of dark souls, blend it all in pure metrovania fluid with a pinch of the language puzzles and look of Fez.  Marinate all this in pure nostalgia, all the way to the look of the NES in game manual, which is also a cypher for the game, and you have one of the most challenging, wonderful, work of video game passion of recent years.  Bravo, guys.  Bravo.

_childDocuments_.review: AMAZING GAME! Highly recommend to anyone looking for a sense of wonder and exploration. Finding the pages of the manual and having most of the in-game text be in a different language really makes it feel so damn good when you are able to figure out what's going on. I love that the game doesn't hold your hand and tutorializes as you play naturally, instead of having a giant tutorial dump in the front. I feel like I can't say much beyond that without spoiling the game in some way. Good zelda/soulslike combo. Will go down with Death's Door as the best adventure games to come out in the 2020s, at least to me.

_childDocuments_.review: Having the manual for the game scattered around the world to be found and pieced together in order to learn new mechanics  or different ways to solve puzzles or look at the world was incredibly fun. It was a serious throwback to the original Legend of Zelda and how its manual was crucial to learning how to play and solve puzzles in the game. But in Tunic its like your discovering old sacred text that also reveals more about the story and world itself.The combat and puzzles are far from easy, but that makes them that much more rewarding when overcoming them.The art style, atmosphere, and music are great. I felt the progression and exploration were well balanced and never bored me. Tunic overall is an incredibly well put together and polished game.If you like puzzle games like legend of zelda or really difficult combat games like hollow knight I would highly recommend Tunic.

_childDocuments_.review: Very cool game, it was about what I expected it to be. I had a few issues with it but I'll start with the pros first.Pros:Exploration is really cool. My favorite thing about this game by far is how the game introduces the mechanics to you... or rather you introduce them to yourself. Finding a new page of instructions is like finding money on the floor. You can't help but wonder what new possibilities are in store.This is more of a loor heavy rather than story heavy game. One of those games like hollow knight where you could beat the entire game and still have no idea what's going on. I think it gives it a nice charmThe game does not hold your hand unless you want it to be held. For the main story at the very least, you can easily complete it without help or guides, and every time you discover something for yourself, it feels really good.ConsIt feels like combat was sacrificed a little bit to fit the art style. It feels clunky and the 2.5D aspects of the game makes it difficult with the way the camera will move in a boss fight. Attack tells are pretty lacking, and blocking just doesn't work unless you're a second earlyThis may be personal, but I did not like the stamina mechanic much at all. I understand that many souls likes have some sort of poise bar that drops so you can't block everything, but this bar also takes away your ability to dodge, sprint, and evade too. I think personally this game would benefit to have dodge rolling and sprinting separate from block stamina.End game exploration for me was really boring really fast. Some of the puzzles in the game are really satisfying and really fun, and I can't think of much if any puzzles that were just down right bad. But by the end of the game even before I finished the main story I found myself just wanting to watch guides or shortcuts to get it over with. Once everything had been explored, I wasn't intrigued enough to keep finding all of the in depth secrets on my own.Basically, I really did enjoy the game. I do highly recommend it. Really fun exploration, decent combat, good story. For those who are wondering about the difficulty of puzzles, main story stuff is easy. If you're like me and you want to 100% the game, don't get discouraged if you can't do it all by yourself. It's a lot like FEZ, in the sense that the community worked together until all of the peaces were in place. I doubt anyone could find the solutions to every puzzle by themselves without at least a little bit of help. I would recommend looking up hints first and then look up answers as a last resort, unless you just want the achievements with the least amount of effort.One more tip for my 100% people out there: look up missable achievements before playing.

_childDocuments_.review: Don't let the clearly Zelda inspired aesthetics of this game fool you. It's less a cutesy Zelda clone and more a puzzle game. The game doesn't tell you anything. There are no tutorials, instead you are tasked with finding pages of the physical game manual in game. The manual becomes your guide as there are puzzles and mechanics that you will not figure out without it. The manual itself is a puzzle because most of it is written in an alphabet that is unique to the game. When you read signs or talk to characters in game, they use the special rune alphabet. So this game wants you to be in dark and the fun is all about figuring it out. The combat is brutal and simplistic but you can turn dying off in the accessibility options if you just want to focus on the puzzles.It's very clear the creators of this game played the japanese version of Zelda as a kid and also had the japanese manual. Very much feels like a love letter to that specific experience. Playing a game that's not written in your language.Big nostalgia vibes for instruction manuals. Some really were like that.

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't expect to enjoy this game. I'm not a fan of isometric games, nor do I like the general artstyle of the game. On top of that, I've currently got a bit of Soulslike fatigue. So, I didn't expect to enjoy a game that looks like a mesh together of Legend of Zelda and Dark Souls. Time and time again Tunic would be recommended by someone I respect. I'd consider it, then decide against it. But something about the overwhelmingly positive reviews eventually swayed me to get it. And I don't regret my decision one bit.The exploration in this game is fantastic. The game is in part a metroidvania - with traversal abilities you can unlock that allow you to explore the world. The game is also "metroidbrainia", with abilities you can do from the start, you just don't know how. The world is nicely interconnected with many satisfying shortcuts you can unlock along the way.The game drip feeds you pages of a manual, but unlike pretty much every manual in existence, this one doesn't bore me to death. In fact, it's fantastic! Most of it is encoded in a strange different language, with only key bits of information in English or told via images. The game slowly lets you in on little tips and tricks, but you don't NEED the manual, you can figure these abilities out on your own (and when that happens it is very satisfying).I mentioned earlier that the artstyle was not my favourite. Despite this, the animations, colour scheme, and the sound design are masterfully put together. The environments are far more varied than I would have expected. While I loved the atmosphere of the rustic forest temple-y areas, there were more impressive areas later into the game.The progression in abilities feels great. I love it when games make loot that feels valuable and most loot either contributes directly to a valuable upgrade, gives you an upgrade, or rewards you with information. The combat was good. The final boss was fantastic. The bosses in the runup ranged from decent to great. I had a little trouble with the lock-on system, but all of this could have been mitigated if I'd used the arrow keys to switch lock on targets. Even despite my Soulslike fatigue I still enjoyed the combat. You don't need to solve any  puzzles to get an ending, but if you want to get the  ending there are a lot to solve. The final puzzle required for the good ending is incredible. There are hints hidden right under your nose throughout the game; when you figure out the solution, it feels absolutely amazing. One downside, however, is when executing the puzzle solution, it is very easy to make a tiny error interpreting parts of it - which then unfolds into an unfortunately frustrating experience diagnosing the small error you made. At the end of the day though, I am still very satisfied with my experience figuring it out. This game had me hooked. From ringing the bells to now (having just completed the good ending) I had a burning desire to uncover the secrets around every corner; it takes masterful game design to create that feeling. I was able to recapture similar feelings in this game as when solving puzzles in Outer Wilds. I highly recommend playing this, and I highly recommend playing it blind.

_childDocuments_.review: Like most games in the last 10 years, Tunic is an amalgamation of previous games. It's part Zelda, part Dark Souls, part Fez, etc. Funny enough the shining star in Tunic for me is it's game manual. I don't want to spoil much but just know if you're ever stuck or frustrated the game manual you collect in game leaves bread crumbs in a new and unique way.The game has the usual award winning pros: combat is satisfying, music is great, beautiful visuals, etc. But that game manual made me grin ear to ear multiple times throughout the game. Boss fights were hard but never punishing, puzzles and dungeons had personality and rewarded curiosity.The only con which surprised me is is the lack of a cast of characters.

Acts as a tutorial/menu/map/waypoints/etc. Finding sheets along the way to push you in the right direction/fill in some blanks is really cool. _childDocuments_.review: 2 hours in and I'm definitely happy with my purchase. Everyone is making Zelda comparisons and they're not wrong. It's absolutely Zelda inspired but by no means a clone. One of my first games on NES was The Legend of Zelda everything in Tunic from the feel of the game to the manual pieces you pick up is giving me little flashes of nostalgia. It's also kind of souls-ish because if you die, you respawn at the last fire and can make your way back to your death spot but the only thing recovered is money and there's money everywhere. Playing Tunic feels like being bored on a lazy Sunday afternoon and your big brother is away so you go digging thru his games. You find a weird one from Japan with a cute fox holding a sword and a tattered manual with notes and scribbles on it. Nothing makes sense but as you play, questions get answered just as more questions get presented. I really appreciate how Tunic just tosses you into the game. No grand, sprawling intro. No explanation. No translating of the language even. I love the feeling of going back to the limited manual pages, pouring over every inch to find just the tiniest scrap of a hint of a clue. Then when you find a new one, delving back in to see what new info/art is shown. Support this developer. This is a good one.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr at the end.The game is fun at first, the art style is beautiful, the combat is weighty and fun, but the obtuse level design with poorly hidden pathways that you would never be able to find without a guide, as well as the way the game refuses to tell you any information about any of the items (because 99% of the text is in a fun made up language that you cannot decipher) gets old very quickly and starts to take a tax on your enjoyment on the game. When you can't reach a new area and are stuck because you need an item that is hidden behind an impossible to find cavern it's not fun. When the game fails to let you know that "praying" is a thing that lets you interact with the world in new ways, so you spend hours wondering how many items you're missing since you can't interact with the big metal pillars or the shiny golden platforms. There is no prompt, too. There is no hint, no tips, nothing. The devs just magically expect you to find out that by holding *Lock on + Dodge* you can pray and therefore power the statues (which i did not do because i encountered about 10 of those pillars before finding out -in a guide- that you can actually power them) and use the teleport platforms (because I only found out after looking up a different guide on where to go that teleporting exists, but don't worry, it's not fun either, since there is no way to know where you will be teleporting since all you see is blocks of light). Also, did you know you can run in the game? Because I sure as hell didn't. You have to hold the interact button to run. As well as finding out there's a grappling hook hidden away behind 4 or so caverns.Is that not enough to discourage you? Oh, well in that case the game also has special magical cards you can equip. I obtained about 6 of them. I have no idea what they do after trying every single one of them, healing, dying, fighting, they seem to have no apparent effect on gameplay. As well as the cool upgrades you can spend gold on! There are about 4 of them. Only one of them is useful, which is the one that makes you have a bit more HP, so you can get stunlocked for even longer.The combat is also not fun. It's like the worst aspects of a Kirby game combined with the worst aspects of a Souls game. Some enemies have tells so you can dodge or parry. Most enemies don't. Most enemies simply charge randomly with no way to counterattack or parry (See: large dogs, crows, frogs, large frogs, mages, etc).I wanted to love the game, but it feels like there is no learning curve as the game doesn't give you the tools to improve, it just drops you into the world without letting you know that those tools even exist, and when you get them, gives you no way to find out what they do.tl;dr: the first 30 minutes you'll think "oh man I can't wait for the game to lead me in any way to have fun" until you realize that the game will do nothing to help you have fun with it, and just trips over itself due to its lack of explanation so you know what anything does. Don't buy it.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: I don't think I've ever played a game quite like Tunic. On the surface one can pick obvious inspirations from the gameplay, perspective, and aesthetic, namely Dark Souls and Zelda. One can go throughout the entire game with this mindset and beat it, but in truth there's an entirely different beast lurking underneath, and it's there from the moment you start the game. Going into this game blind is the best thing you can do, because once you realize what's going on underneath the 'Zelda/Dark Souls' hybrid all the people and publications are going on about, it feels amazing. If you grew up in the era of games before the internet was widespread and game manuals were actually a thing, this game will rekindle that magic. I won't spoil the ending of this game, but I will say it resonated with me a lot, and I think it has a lot to say, despite no actual words (aside from the in-universe language) being spoken. And as icing on this delicious cake, the presentation is astounding. Superb visuals, music, and atmosphere make this an amazing package, and definitely one of my top favorite games of all time.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: Tunic is one of the most enjoyable gaming experiences I've had in a while, and it is definitely the most special game I've seen so far. The thing that made it so special was the huge sense of discovery that you feel throughout the entire thing. From the start of the game you are given little to no (written or spoken) information about the world you are in, how to play, and what anything does. As you explore and make your way through the world, you find pages of an instruction manual that gives you information, but still is mostly in a constructed language. It is such an unconventional but really engaging way to tell a story and to introduce gameplay mechanics. Even up until the end, you will find things out that completely blow your mind and recontextualize earlier moments. It's hard to convey to someone who hasn't played it just how brilliant this design is. The combat of the game is also really engaging.Another thing that really draws you in is the super charming artistic and audio/music direction. The graphics are really beautiful and the game runs perfectly (like seriously I didn't encounter a single bug or performance hitch), and the vibe and artstyle are something special.I seriously recommend this to anybody who enjoys video games. 10/10.

But either way, I had fun and ultimately it's well worth the $30 I paid for it.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a tough game to review because there's very good parts of the game and some rather unpolished and clunky parts. First the good: The first half of the game is great. There's a real wonder in exploring the world, given only fragments of the game manual, which are mostly not in English. The graphics are simplistic, but work well with the nostalgic game play. The early levels are dense with secret areas and the enemies are engaging, requiring you take full advantage of your move-set. I'm going to dwell a bit on the bad aspects of the game, because there's more to talk about, but you will easily have a good 10-15 hours of enjoyable game to play, which is why I'm giving it a thumbs up. There are a few bugs in the game (i.e. places you can get stuck) and the controls are occasionally a bit laggy (I had to rebind two attacks to the same key to get one combo attack to work consistently on PC), but overall it's very polished.The bad: Too much of this game is a pastiche of other games. Take away the creative manual idea (which is a great idea, mind you) and you will be left with a rehashing of the ideas of other developers. The Zelda influence is obvious, but it doesn't end there.This game steals far too many of the mechanics of the dark souls series. This went beyond being an homage to just plagiarism. Flasks, bonfires, dodge-rolls and a from software stamina bar all make an appearance. The bosses hew to the dark souls style closely. The difficulty is not that high (about like Elden ring, but way shorter and you can't just level yourself up to victory). Only 1-2 bosses will either require you to learn their move set or cheese them. The fights don't quite have the tedium of your typical dark souls boss, where you are forced to wait until just the right moment after a combo before you can attack, but do expect a few to have decent health pools, esp. if you aren't keeping your levels up.But beyond the obvious souls borrowing, you'll find bits of the hollow knight plot line lifted for the default ending with a slight science fiction wrapping and even a dramatic reveal that would be a more dramatic if it wasn't a copy of a shot from The Matrix. Everyone's a battery? Really? This surprise twist was laughably bad.In general, the story is the typical self-serious collection of cliches found in your modern indy games. To the extent that it exists, is told in snippets (as is the default these days) and hinted at through the manual. The basic ending (aka the bad ending) is profoundly unsatisfying. The "best" ending is not much better, though. (Does a crappy ending also count as a dark souls ripoff?) The best thing about this game is its cutesy beginning, but like many games in this genre, the developer's felt the need to make the game turn moody and it doesn't really work.How you feel about these "references"/copying of other games is a matter of taste, but I can mostly look past it to just enjoy the game. However, the last ~1/3 of the game is much weaker than start. The areas become more linear and the items you find are mostly worthless as you seem to stop getting the items you need to level up after a while. You do get one final power-up, but it's so over-the-top it more or less breaks the fun of exploration that was the center of the first part of the game. If you are feeling energetic, you can try to get the good ending, but the final puzzles are tedious and much less clever than the developers must have thought. (One also involves destroying a wall, which has was never possible throughout the rest of the game, as far as I know.) You will find yourself doing variations of the same puzzle over and over. It's not great. My advice is to skip this nonsense and just take the basic ending.With all that said, though, it's an indy game with a small team of developers and the cost isn't that high. You will probably enjoy the opening, from other reviews, it seems most people aren't as bothered by the way it lifts mechanics from other games as I was.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: The central mechanic of discovering bits and pieces of the rulebook and figuring out how to even play the game is delightful. The art-style is immensely cute and has a very pleasant stylized feel to it. The puzzles are delightful, although I personally found the combat less fun. There are a fair amount of weapons to use, but I ended sticking with just a few through the whole playthrough. It was slightly too difficult for me (very bad at video games) and I wish there were a few more options to adjust the difficulty of the game in the settings. One area in particular (the mountains) was a complete slog for me, and I ended up having to turn on invincibility a few times. Anyone who plays a significant amount of video games will likely find it much easier than I did. Still recommend wholeheartedly.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: I played through all the way up until the end, and that's where I stopped. The game play is  fantastic, the main quest is super fun! HOWEVER, the "good" ending requires, frankly, WAY too much work, so I would recommend playing through the game, doing the "bad" ending, and then looking up the good ending.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: I have to be cryptic explaining this game, but it's definitely worth it. Play this blind!Classic Legend of Zelda with really light Souls-like elements.A lot of 'meta'-like elements similar to Fez. Lots of secrets and hidden items that rewards an observant eye.Earning the Sword felt good, earning the Shield felt good. The souls combat makes combat more tactical and makes to really methodical in how you approach fighting bosses. The way you uncover information about the world seeds objectives and goals, but the game isn't wholly linear. The game will definitely lead to some interesting sequence breaking opportunities for experienced players.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: It was pretty fun. I really loved exploring the world and learning what was going on through the collectible pages of the manual. It made me feel like a kid again exploring a world where I would continually look at the manual and learn more and more about the game as I go through it. I found the a-ha moments where you find a secret or where something clicks to be the bread and butter of the game.For negatives, I didn't like some of the gameplay choices. For example, having the camera rotate during boss fights was incredibly annoying, especially since for the rest of the game the camera is essentially fixed. It made it annoying to move at times. The parry mechanic is way too slow but I guess the reward of a successful parry is worth it. It felt like I spent quite a bit of time just running around the map trying to figure out what to do which I didn't enjoy at all (if you don't have a sharp memory or if you play in small bursts over a long period of time this game will be hard to remember what you should be doing). As a quality of life recommendation, I would love it if the manual marks if some places are completed or if you found a eecollectible. The manual itself has the check boxes already implemented so it wouldn't be a huge next step, considering you can't really print out the manual.Overall, I found it pretty fun and worth my money.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: First, I want to say that for the intended audience, I imagine this game is a dream come true. In many ways, this feels like a modern "old-school" metroidvania/Zelda-like.  However, for the casual gamer or non-puzzle enjoyers, I'd strongly advise you avoid or wait for a sale. Level and map design is very old-school and personally was annoying to deal with. Art direction was fantastic but combat could definitely be improved on. Maybe Tunic 2 could be the game for me, but this one really didnt sit with me.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the best games I have played in a long time. It captures the overall experience of playing a game like Legend of Zelda Majora's Mask. Despite being very cute in appearance, combat is very punishing, and there are puzzles and secrets in almost every chamber.Another game that qualifies as more of an experience than an actual video game.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: I don't write reviews often. This game as a big fan of Zelda like action RPG games and Dark Souls esk Combat, is one of the best games I have played in a long time. The more time you put into the game, the more you get out. Plenty of secrets and for those who have played ... you know the mind blowing one haha. I am eager to see more from this developer, the game design, mechanics, soundtrack, animation and overall feel of the game is very nostalgic. The only thing i would like to see changed is some more challenge in the New Game + side.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: Tunic is an absolutely phenomenal experience. The many many secrets and simple but fun combat make Tunic shine. I had a blast working out how to read runes, use the Holy Cross and follow the Golden Path. Try to avoid getting too many spoilers, since the fun comes largely from solving the puzzles. If there's one caveat, it's that the game is not super-long and won't have great replayability (since you can only figure out a secret once), but the hours I spent were great.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: Hands down one of my favorite games of all time. Gotta agree with a lot of other reviews in that it definitely isn't for everyone, but I enjoyed this game enough to go back and play through it a second time to finish off the last few achievements I needed. I absolutely would recommend playing this game if you're a fan of top-down Zelda and souls-likes then definitely give this game a try!
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful callback to the classic Zelda games and one of the most rewarding puzzle games I've played in a long time. Very much a game where you have to think outside of the box, even when clues are plentiful. Tons of secrets to uncover, fun and challenging combat, fantastic soundtrack, great sense of mystery. An amazing experience all-around.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DRThe Good: Absolutely brilliant level design, really good aesthetics, gameplay is simple but tightThe Bad: The lock-on becomes more of a hinderance the moment you face more than 3 enemies, some of the puzzles are... unfairly obtuseThe ?????: FurryThe minimalist and clean aesthetic of Tunic might make you think that is a simple and straight forward game, but, much like the plethora of clerverly designed and hidden pathaways that dismantle the assumed linearity of this adventure, that is just a trick that the game uses to settle you in before bashing you in the head with challange after challange, forcing you to learn, plan ahead, and be crafty if you want to survive long enough to attain your goals. The metanarrative of a hint sistem being the very own game manual - wich must we pieced together from withing the game itself - its the perfect way the game has to tech you it's secrets without being too on the nose about it; they are giving you the answers, you only have to understand it.The game is not without drawbacks, the fights can move from challenging to overly frustrating quite easily, and if you are facing off against more than one enemy, the lock-on might as well be an opponent more. Tunic is filled with secrets, very clever secrets, sometime too clever perhaps, that rather requiring you to think outside the box, they rather ask you to stand a few blocks away, making certain things more of a headache to obtain.All in all, I certainly recomend this game, without a doubt one of the best indie releases of 2022.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: Wouldn't recommend looking up guides and walkthroughs unless you are absolutely at your wits' end. The main game puzzles are sometimes real headscratchers but it was worth it to figure out the answers on my own. The visuals are simple yet charming and the combat is average. What stands out the most is the instruction manual and how it connects to absolutely everything in the game. Great stuff.

_childDocuments_.review: Tunic is an enchanting and adorable Zelda-like adventure that draws inspiration from both classic action-adventures and the challenging mechanics of souls-likes. From its whimsical aesthetics to its evocative soundtrack by Lifeformed, known for their unforgettable work on Dustforce, every aspect of the game radiates charm and showcases the developer's immense care and passion.The combat, while challenging at times, maintains a beautifully balanced difficulty curve, with only minor issues appearing in the New Game+ mode. In this mode, more dynamic and interesting difficulty scaling would have enhanced the experience. However, these minor flaws do little to detract from the overall enjoyment of the game.Even if traditional Zelda games aren't to your taste, Tunic is still worth a try. The game offers a rich 15-20 hour experience, including all optional challenges and achievements. It is a cohesive experience where the whole truly exceeds the sum of its already fantastic parts.The only real downside is the bittersweet feeling when you reach the end, wishing the adventure could continue for several more hours. I wish I could re-experience the magic that this game has to offer anew.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful top-down RPG with a stunning visual style and amazing soundtrack. Comes with a great sense of exploration as you try and decipher where to go/ what to do next. The game play itself can be challenging, but is still very enjoyable. I 100% recommend this if you enjoy top-down RPGs, interesting games, or just want to see a fox in a tunic.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: At the beginning I enjoyed playing a fun little zelda-like that reminded me of Hyperlight Drifter.By the time I finished I had a notebook full of diagrams and translations, and I felt like I was playing The Witness' endgame.10/10 would have my genre expectations thrown profoundly on their head.Also the combat is not as bad as people say, but there are accessibility options to make it easier if you want to focus on the puzzles.

_childDocuments_.review: Such a fun game! Just an adorable platformer at face value but it has a deceptively monstrous underbelly of story and game play that made me never want to turn it off. _childDocuments_.review: I tried to like this game, but I just can't. The rolling feels like ♥♥♥♥, the combat is boring compared to other dark souls games, everything is in a made up language making it very hard to tell what the actual ♥♥♥♥ you need to do, enemies are impossible to run away from and with rolling being absolutely ♥♥♥♥ I barely have the motivation to even fight people. _childDocuments_.review: This game is something else.Tunic has learned from and built upon it's predecessors. It's hard to say Tunic is "inspired" by Zelda or Dark Souls, because at this point those games are just a part of its DNA. Really, Tunic was created from the lessons learned by games like Hyper Light Drifter and Death's Door.Tunic is best experienced blind, it shares a quality with Outer Wilds, where learning the game is part of the experience. With that in mind, a rundown of what to expect is: The start of the game is *very* Souls-like, with a slow transition to a more Zelda feel as you progress. Then puzzles start to become more crucial, and the game feels very much like Fez.Tunic is an easy recommendation. It's clever, beautiful, and fun to play. It's a celebration of games and the people who play them.

_childDocuments_.review: I loved it and it clicked on me something I haven't feel for a videogame in such a long time.I literally spent hours deciphering the mystic glyph language and translating the booklet pages and, man, it was so much fun. The game is cryptic and yes, sometimes is too cryptic and even more, sometimes the game trolls you. But it's ok, the amount of Aha! moments this game gave me because of it worth it a 100%.Although the first hour is hard. You have no powers, no equipment, everything is trying to kill you... but afterwards, is such a joyful ride.I can't recommend it enough.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: TUNIC's blend of Souls-like combat, FEZ-like puzzles, Zelda-like overworld, and beautiful art style, music and sound design has quickly catapulted it into becoming .From a semi-forced isometric world view, you play as a young fox cub as they stumble around in a world that has fallen from grace, and left worse for wear. What strikes you first time you play it is that the text on signs, the HUD and even the in-game manual is written in a mysterious, indecipherable alphabet, and you have to rely on your own instincts, logical reasoning and curiosity to figure out what most of the things mean. The game does no hand holding. It throws you into the world and goes "You're on your own now!" And that is something you don't see much these days. There's a lot of hand holding in modern games, and TUNIC bucks that trend, which is something I appreciate very much. The game trusts the player to be smart, attentive and inquisitive, and explore every nook and cranny of the world to find all the things hidden just around the corner, out of sight.Depending on how quickly you pick up on the things the game gives you, the  to complete the game can take anywhere between 10 and 30 hours. There's also the case of getting a  ending, which takes up the majority of the time in the second half of the game. And that extra time is well spent for getting the true ending, I will go ahead and say that much.In terms of , it runs excellent on both my PC AND my Steam Deck. Crisp 60 FPS on my Deck with zero dips in framerate and plenty of battery life.So yeah, an absolutely rock solid recommendation from me.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: This might be the saddest Negative review I have ever had to give. This game is fantastic on so many levels. The games visuals are absolutely fantastic. The music is extremely relaxing and nice. There are a lot of clever gimmicks and map design that are a ton of fun to explore. And just the amount of surprises and genuine adventure feel is incredible.My main disappointment with the game comes from 3 problems:- Combat can feel extremely simplistic until the game decides to throw massive HP pools and enemy counts at you, at that point it starts feeling awkward and clunky. Those moments really showcase just how incomplete the combat can be, and some enemy designs as a result feel infuriating to fight against.- Do you want to experience what it is like to go on vacation to a foreign country without barely any guidance at all? Yes? Then this is the game for you. A lot of the game is told in some weird in game language, and the game developers put a ton of trust in the player to find their way through it all. Most of the time this actually works out and its a ton of fun, but like 33 % of my playtime was just spent running around trying to figure out what was the next place I had to go. Not only that but there are so many items that I still have no clue what they do. Those moments are super boring and it feels like a major interesting part of the game is just forever locked behind the gimmick of everything being unreadable.- My last main complaint is related to the ending, some late game spoilers: In the end Tunic is not what I looked for. Its not the 2D Zelda like that I was expecting, and the central gameplay kept pulling me in just to disappoint me right afterwards. It IS a fantastic game, and I think many people will find enjoyment in it, but I also think many players will come out the other side with a sour after taste. It is the type of game where I wish I could give it a neutral review because I absolutely don't believe it deserves a negative review, I just wouldn't actively recommend it either. I think if you go into it expecting a bumpy ride you will find an absolutely adorable, unique and very fun experience. Its just an experience that didn't manage to completely grab me.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those that's close to my GOTY, but I think doesn't quite make it. It's a beautiful game, carefully crafted, with nods to nostalgia a-plenty, but some of the delivery falls a little short to me. Just enough to keep it from being a shoe in.There's been so much good said about it, I feel it's almost a little pointless to expand upon that too much, but I don't want to ignore the positives: The game is gorgeous. The world rewards poking around and acting on the thought "I wonder if I can do that" because often, you can. It constantly finds new ways to expand bit by bit. The story it tells through almost no text is not unique certainly but it's compelling and surprising enough at times. And, maybe most impressively, despite drawing heavily from Zelda and Dark Souls, it manages to feel almost completely new and novel.The negatives are real though, too. There are a BILLION secrets, I'm not sure what percentage of the content is actually secret in some way but it's not insignificant, and a number of the secrets are exceedingly obtuse. Some straight up could not be solved until the most recent patch if you had certain hearing issues (or played with sound low, or had bad speakers, or or or). Some secrets are solved in totally different ways which don't always lead you to figuring out the next ones intuitively.On top of all that, exploring is fun but the game gets in the way of itself there quite often. There is fast travel, but the layout of the levels makes it less useful than I'd like. There are also VERY few "shortcuts" you can unlock to save time backtracking later. You have to backtrack for secrets, and anything you missed, but upgrades / chests that were gated behind an ability or power are pretty rare so it makes the game feel more linear at times than it could have been. And on top of that enemies never stop being dangerous, you can run past most of them but if you're exploring you might want to linger in areas and the combat isn't the games' strongest point - it's functional, but I'd hesitate to call it fun enough to stand on its' own through repetition (I wouldn't play a rogue-like with this combat, for example). I see that in the latest patch the added a new difficulty for combat which maybe makes it less cumbersome if you can turn it down later in the game (not something I normally do in my games, as normally you get strong enough to just bop enemies down trivially).Overall it's an excellent game - it just needed to give you a tiny bit more to work with to flow better and feel better and that would have made all the difference. I played it pretty close to release and it does look like recent patches addressed some of the accessibility issues (i.e., reasons I would not have recommended PLAYING the game to some friends) at least, which is great. Despite being a game I'll remember for some time to come, I have no real interest in replaying it for now.

_childDocuments_.review: I have mixed feelings about this game. On the one hand, many things such as the levels, the graphics, the instruction booklet, the enemies, (most of) the puzzles, the music & sound design, and especially the cute fox had the utmost care and craftsmanship put in them, and I enjoyed them all immensely, to the point where I have earned all the achievements, solved all the puzzles, and found all the secret items. Walking around through the world, solving puzzles, trying to figure out What It All Means, was a great time. On the other hand, holy mommy fox the combat is GARBAGE. Almost all the equipment cards have no obvious effect and you have to look them up online, the sword range is absolutely tiny compared to the melee range of every boss, there were multiple instances where I took damage during the alleged "i-frames" of the dodge roll (including one time where a bullet killed me while dodging and the game's death slomo really rubbed it in), there are only two (2) ranged attacks which both fluctuate wildly in damage dealt throughout the game (if there is a rule I could never discern it), for some reason the devs thought it would be a great idea if the normally-static camera spent every boss fight spinning in circles around the arena making lining up shots basically impossible, and the awful, TERRIBLE parry. Oh my god the parry is a nightmare. It pisses me off so much. So in the game you get a shield, right? You can see it in the game image, it's mapped to R2 (the right analog trigger on an Xbox controller), and holding R2 makes the cute fox block. If you have played a video game before, you're probably thinking "oh wow now I can probably parry things with this bad boy." And you'd be right! It even has a slomo animation when successful and stuns some enemies."Sweet! Do I parry by pressing R2 when attacked?" No. "Okay, so obviously I parry by releasing R2 when attacked." ALSO NO!"What the hell!? How do I parry then??" Well, it's surprisingly simple. You have to press AND release R2. But you have to do it fast enough that the game decides to parry and not block (which is about half a second, maybe less), which means parrying is inconsistent if you're too slow. And since this is on an ANALOG trigger (there is no input remapping for controller), there's no physical feedback of where "pressed" is, which makes reacting to "pressed" fast enough to "release" in time even harder. And there's a large windup to the parry animation, so you have to do the parry well before the incoming attack actually hits you (there is equipment which grows your parry window, but it still lags the input). And the parry doesn't actually protect you from incoming attacks for its entire duration (!!!); when facing e.g. enemies which fire volleys of projectiles, the parry animation will stop parrying, and there is another second or two of uncancellable recovery animation in which you are completely unprotected and can get hit by the next projectile volley (not great for damage mitigation!!!)....But other than that, Mrs. Lincoln, how was the play? None of this is mentioned in the game by the way. In fact, the existence of the parry is only obliquely mentioned, which is incredibly annoying because the parry is basically the only way to deal with the second-to-last boss in melee (this boss was the most frustrating to me in my first playthrough and almost certainly has attacks which damage through dodge roll "i-frames" and blocking). If anyone reading this is an aspiring game developer, please for the love of what little is good and holy, do not do anything even remotely similar to this in any game. Just do parry on button press like a sane person.So overall, it's a game that's amazing in every way, except the actual game, which makes it hard to decide how to rate it. I have decided to give this a thumbs up because of cute fox, highest-venerated of all tiebreakers.

_childDocuments_.review: I so badly want to like this game. The concept is cool and the mystery is fun, but the gameplay just isn't fun or memorable. I gave it a sincere shot, all the way to the final boss' second phase just to realize I've lost all interest. It's cheap and indie so try it if you want but I can't recommend it in good faith. Try Hyper Light Drifter if you like the vibe.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: On the surface, this game looks like a well-executed, cutesy take on a Zelda-like action adventure game, and it definitely does have that aspect, and does it well, so if that's all you're looking for, then great, you'll find it in TUNIC! But if you also like the idea of uncovering the secrets of a deep, mysterious world using clues that you slowly put together, then this game has A LOT more to offer you.Without getting too much into spoiler territory, TUNIC has several levels of puzzles/secrets to discover, and the great thing is that it's completely up to you, the player, how far you dig. For less puzzle-savvy players like myself, there's a major mystery that was *just* challenging enough for me to solve with a nice payoff, but for  secret-seekers that like more difficult/esoteric puzzles like the kind you find in Noita, then you're in for a treat.TL;DR: If you like action adventure games like Zelda, you'll like this game. If you like mystery/puzzle games like Outer Wilds or the Witness, then you'll also like this game.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best experiences I have ever played.Impeccable level design, puzzle design, and simple but to the point combat. I am not usually a person to sing a game's praises (if anything I usually talk about the things I don't like in a game), but this game blew me away so much so that I felt compelled to leave my first (and probably last) review on a game ever.For anyone on the fence about this game: Yes I know, it looks childish initially and the start is a bit slow since you don't yet have much in the way of equipment, but if you push through that early part it becomes an incredible experience with interesting locations to visit, puzzles to solve, treasure to loot, and bosses to fight. If you are into these things, I can't recommend it enough.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: This is probably the best game of all time.Comparing this masterpiece to Zelda or Dark Souls is a compliment to both Zelda and Dark Souls.And this is coming from someone who really likes tloz mm, I'd say the main difference is this game doesn't insult your intelligence.In Zelda you reach a dungeon, solve some easy puzzles that are mainly there so the game is longer and you can justify spending money on it, and get your item, beat a boss that sort of thing.But in tunic there aren't any silly puzzles to solve (maybe some of the fairy ones), it's just that everything else has a secret that you can solve.The whole game uses a writing system that's similar to runes. You can decipher it, it's not too hard, but it's going to take pen and paper and some deduction skills. Every page of the manual you get is filled with secrets, so is every area in the game. Many things are things you could do from the very start of the game, and that makes it all the more funOn top of that the manual is so pretty, you'll spend a fair amount of time just gazing at it in awe

_childDocuments_.review: I originally played this game on Microsoft Game Pass and finished it.  It is an amazing puzzle game that quietly hints you in the right directions while still leaving lots of things to be discovered. Its amazing use of the in game manual you slowly unlock is genius. I would say the only things that were slightly a downer was the very late game puzzles become a little repetitive, and I personalty with translating the in game language was a bit easier, but I would still argue that it adds to the charm of the game. Please get it and RTFM.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is one of the best games I've EVER played in a very long time. It was a refreshing take on players using their brain, both for combat and intuitive purposes that most of all made you actually care to move the story forward. I can't stress enough the frustrations I've had on finding a game that hit so many things right, between the music, the playstyle, the atmosphere, and the outright charm this game has. I could be considered a grumpy person, but this game felt extremely magical to the point where I felt like I was one of those characters from a Pixar film that goes from hard to approach to beaming with sunshine. The level of detail in this game is amazing, the sense of wonderment that I thought was long gone from games because of my age (and even discussed with a few friends not too long ago how when you grow up, games just aren't that magical to you anymore) well, I was wrong! I honestly wish I could wipe the memory of playing this game from my brain, just so I could experience it all over again.That's how I'd describe this game. When you finish it, you'll want more, you'll want to find the end, but when you do, you'll wish there was no end to it. It's witty, it's charming, it's beautiful. I'd give this game an actual 10 out of 10. I didn't even mention the music, one of the most beautiful soundtracks I've ever heard that made me buy it just so I could fully support whoever I could who composed it, and I usually don't care enough to do something like that. Leave here knowing you will truly fall in love with this game if you like a real sense of adventure, you'll WANT to help this fox get through his journey, and that is an accomplishment I find very rare in games, just period, even from years ago.I want to mention something, that this game had me thinking, like, REALLY thinking, both for combat and puzzle solving, and I enjoyed every moment of it. I played this only like a few days or so after it dropped, but I wanted to be absolutely sure I solved every single thing about this game before fully reviewing it. I have to say, even after practically unlocking everything, I'm at my wits end at the very last, LAST secret of the game, so much so that I knew that it was above my scope and I decided to write this review. One day, one day I'll get back to it, try to figure it out, but as frustrated as I am with it, I enjoy it, I'm happy about the level of detail this game puts for you the player to enjoy, and the masterful dedication they put into having you come up with figuring this out. I had no clue how much I enjoyed a genre like this and this is a community I want to be a part of. I want to find more people who enjoy things like this, to befriend them because the energy this game gives off, I can only imagine that the players that figured these kinds of things out are some intuitive people who enjoy adventure!

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game! Fills a old-school Zelda vibe while also being unique to itself with its own gimmicks, the fighting is pretty average, but honestly when it comes to these types of games as long as the fighting isn't bad the adventure carries the load. The environments are varied + fun to discover, but the main feature to this game is finding and deciphering the instruction manual. Very unique element to hide gameplay elements behind discovering pages of the manual, and as you progress the pages get filled out giving you key valuable information that hits you with a feeling of "wait I can do WHAT now?!". Definitely play this game blind without looking anything up about this game, because this is 100% the type of game where if something gets spoiled it'll most likely ruin the experience to a degree. Game is good for about 10 to 15 hours from start to finish (mileage may vary depending on how good you are with puzzles), but this game is absolutely worth the price of admission.

_childDocuments_.review: While charming, TUNIC suffers from being too repetitive. The first 2 hours? Well, it started to go downhillEverything started to look more as a copy of other zones, and while I do really appreciate the way the game drops small hints about what's going on and what's happening as you explore, it wasn't nearly enough to justify the monotonous and extremely dull combat loop. Almost to add insult to injury, the game is EXTREMLY linear, which makes the previously mentioned dull combat loop more and more noticable every minute you play. I've a been playing for almost 7 hours, and it's just been getting less and less fun. It's gotten to a point where I only feel the need to play as a means to justify this very overpriced purchase. Of course, this is all very negative and I do want to shine a light to some pretty good points that stuck with me. The music is really good, even with it just looping until you switch to an area with a different track. Also, the gamebook menachic is very original and charming, something that I now wish would be implemented to a bunch of other games as a sort of challenge mode. But sadly, none of this really matters, as the game utlimatly fails at being the most important thing:FUN.

_childDocuments_.review: TUNIC has to be hands-down one of my favorite games ever created. Easily 10/10, one of the best games I've played all year. * Stunning, clean, incredibly well executed isometric 3D art style* Interesting, subdued story that gets deeper and more complex the further you play* Unique, compelling, and rewarding mechanics in the form of the ingame manual and (maybe spoilers) the golden path* Tight, responsive, consistent combat and movement, with enough depth to be interesting and engaging, but nowhere near overwhelming in its complexity* Varied and challenging but not frustrating encounters* Lovely music* Fantastic world building and level design* Chock full of secrets: secret areas, secret mechanics, secret puzzles, and secret shortcutsIf you enjoy classic 2D Zelda, FEZ, FromSoft games, and games that use knowledge as progression (Outer Wilds, Antichamber, The Witness, Return of the Obra Dinn), you'll absolutely love TUNIC. This game has all the best parts from all of those games, and still manages to be greater than their sum.The unique mechanic of TUNIC is the game's manual. The manual itself is a point of game progression, wherein you collect its pages scattered throughout the world in order to reconstruct the knowledge hidden within. Only trouble is, the manual is 70% written in a foreign language you can't understand, with only a few scattered words and phrases legible. You'll use inference and deduction to glean as much information as possible from each manual page you find in order to progress in the game. The game delivers moments of revelation again and again when you find that one page which completes the puzzle in your mind you've been poring over for hours, or reveals a hidden mechanic that had been hiding right under your nose the entire time.All the while acquiring manual pages and discovering the game's hidden mechanics and secrets they reveal, you're also playing a classic Legend of Zelda style open world game about clearing dungeons, collecting their loot, and improving your arsenal with a variety of tools and items, magical and otherwise. The combat is top notch as well, and every encounter with even basic enemies is engaging and never gets monotonous. That's not even mentioning the variety of fantastic boss encounters, offering both dramatic scale, challenge, and satisfaction from beating them. The Librarian and Siege Engine are two of my favorites.Even upon beating the game, if you choose to go back and try to locate all the remaining manual pages (which you definitely should), be ready to break out a pen & paper or your image editing software of choice, as the secrets and puzzles only ramp up in complexity from here. I finished with a veritable collage of all the solving I had to do for many of the puzzles required to follow the golden path.While the intended progression path is well established, the game is incredibly open ended, and can be potentially beaten in any order the player desires with the right knowledge beforehand, much like dark souls.My only critisism with this game is that in some areas, the orthographic camera of the level geometry clashes visually with the perspective camera view of the background, causing some visual inconsistency and a slightly uncomfortable notion of space-warping. It's particularly apparent in a specific late game area, the rooted ziggurat. Other than that, I can't really think of anything else. The game is just that perfect.If you even moderately enjoy any of the games I've referenced thus far, you will not be let down with TUNIC. It delivers in every conceivable way with confidence and unrivaled finesse. Everyone should play this game at least once in their life if they have the opportunity.

_childDocuments_.review: 7.5/10Tunic is a cute and impressive game. On the surface, it is a Zelda-like third person action adventure game with a few puzzle-elements sprinked in. If you dive deeper, it is a game FILLED with secrets around every corner with puzzles that make you scratch your head so much your hair falls off. I want to applaude the developers for their impressive design of puzzles and secrets, but with that said there is a lot of BS and/or quality of life-stuff that I believe is necessary in order to make completing this game the way it wants to be completed possible without a guide.In Tunic you play as a little fox, dressed in a green tunic. You wake up on a beach with no clue what to do. By exploring you come across a few pages of a manual, the manual to the game that you are playing. Throughout the game these pages are scattered about and you HAVE to collect each and every one of the pages in order to understand what to do, how to solve puzzles and how to interact with certain game-mechanics. On the surface this is super cute and fun! Certain things can be worked out beforehand but there is just so much that clicks when collecting certain pages and filling in the blanks. Again, on a deeper level, you need to study these pages like they were art in order to figure out how they relate to certain late-game hard puzzles. Others might disagree, but I found a lot of the puzzles and their solutions to be rather BS and extremely unintuitive as to their solution. My main gripe is that I only get feedback to my actions if I do them RIGHT. If I do something wrong, nothing at all happens. It would have been the same as if I had not done anything. So there is very little to do if I believe that I have a solution and get it wrong, as I do not know if I am in the wrong place, doing the wrong thing or is just misinterpreting things completely. This completely ruins certain puzzles where the solution is so long that I do not know exactly where in my proposed solution I am wrong.Back to the game you travel through dungeons, fight monsters and pick up power-ups that help you on your quest. The combat is simple but the controls are awful. The input-lag and the angles in which the character swings its sword and the hitboxes of certain attacks of enemies work terribly together and in many of the boss-battles it gets extremely frustrating. I compare the combat here to Death's Door, a game with phenomenal controls and combat that is just as simple and just as flashy as I believe is necessary in this game. I know it could have been better, and I am sad that it is not.Getting through the game takes around 12 hours, with lots of beautiful scenery and music and good enemy variety. The story is alright and is completely serviceable for this type of game. The character-designs are stunning and the gloss that everything has is very appealing.Again I have to stress how impressive the world-design is and how cleverly certain secrets are hidden. You both feel really smart and properly rewarded when you find the tons of hidden treasures spread throughout the land.+ Beautiful designed game with lovely characters, environments and sounds+ Impressive world-design with a lot of focus on puzzles and secrets- Poor feedback on how the player fails to complete certain puzzles- Sub-par and frustrating controls leads to lackluster combatAll in all, I still recommend this game. If you truly want to deep-dive and complete everything, be prepared to take tons of notes, discuss with friends and try not to look up too much online. It feels more rewarding that way. A really interesting experience!
