_childDocuments_.review: I've been waiting for this game since it was shown at Pax 2016 under the name Secret Legend, and the wait was definitely worth it. The game is tough. It's a lot more challenging than the graphics let on in both its combat and puzzles. It's freeing to not be told where to go, what to do, or why you are doing anything. By not being told anything you are adventuring on your own terms, and a lot of the game can be done out of order, with a few exceptions that I won't cover so I don't ruin anything. There is no intro, no explanation, and no guide when you start. Everything needs to be figured out on your own. This game does not hold your hand. The reward comes from figuring it out on your own, if you look up any tutorials the magic will be instantly ruined. The combat is made up of simple dodges, blocks, and attacks but besides the first few enemies you can't just hack and slash your way through the game. Combat at times requires incredible precision.  Bosses are tricky and you won't beat them first try. The puzzles are amazing, and boy are they complex. I don't want to go into detail as to not ruin any puzzles, but the developers used every asset of the game to their advantage. Everything in this game serves a purpose, no matter how small.Writing a review for this game is incredibly difficult as the best way to experience it is to go in blind. The less you know the better. If the going gets tough take a break, think about the challenge and try again. I can't stress how important it is to experience this game without the help of an online guide. Seriously don't look anything up! It's more rewarding knowing that you solved the puzzle, without assistance. Tunic is an amazing game. I had a blast playing it, and hope that it gets the recognition that it deserves. If you are Mr. Shouldice, or any of the rest of the amazing development team reading this I just wanna say that Tunic totally was worth the wait and was an amazing experience from start to finish! I'm looking forward to finding those last few hidden secrets I know I missed!

_childDocuments_.review: A charming zelda-like that really captures the classical fantasy adventure RPG while also serving as a masterclass example of knowledge based unlocks with its secrets upon secrets.It's actually tough to talk about the game without spoiling things so all I can really do is comment on how excellently designed it is, providing new twists on old tropes and managing to completely change your perspective on things at several points. The method used is nostalgic and it ends up re-creating experiences that older gamers will appreciate.The art and music are beautiful and really encapsulate the retro feel without actually being retro. The only things I complain about are boss fights having massive difficulty spikes and the souls-like combat feels very out of place.Overall a creative, wholesome, and clever game that takes you on a surprising journey with a lot of unexpected turns.

_childDocuments_.review: Remarkable game. Only complaints are the macabre elements as well as incomplete lore. I understand why they chose to use macabre elements (can't be too similar to a Zelda game otherwise you're not original, trying to channel some Dark Souls vibes) and I can see a case for leaving some of the lore unknown. I've just run into other stories where incomplete lore never gets explained in future works and that leaves a very unsatisfying taste in my mouth (as I value the story element highly). Those aside, I would absolutely recommend it.I don't think the puzzle complexity is suitable for young kids. Bring a pen and paper.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately, a beautiful game with some seemingly rich lore marred by its extreme difficulty and pacing issues.  I was not expecting such bulls*** combat from this game.Good: * The art style & graphics are great * Music is great * The store/lore is goodBad: * If you don't pay attention to the "manual" you collect then you may miss crucial game mechanics. * Lots of wandering and trying to figure out where to go * Unmoveable camera is used to obscure paths you need to find * Very difficult.  I liked Hollow Knight but this is harder and the main character just feels slow during later boss fights. * I did not like the stamina system as I feel it contributed to the overall slowdown of combat and punishes you for blocking and dodging.Ugly: * Enemies gang up on you, will notify other nearby enemies, and they will all chase you forever * There are limited ranged weapons so most combat is a slog as you chip away at their health, dash back, wait for an opening, and repeat * There is a "no damage" mode, so the developers acknowledge the BS difficulty, but you still get knocked around if you get hit so it's still a slog trying to get through an area.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: I said "yes", but the more accurate answer to the question "would I recommend this" is "maybe".The game is clearly inspired by the old top-down Zeldas, and I got heavy gameplay and nostalgia vibes on my playthrough. This is probably evident at face-value and almost every review you read will parrot as much. That said, there is one thing you should be aware of that brought this 9/10 back down to a 6/10 is the overabundance of secrets. At first it was refreshing. Too many games nowadays have secrets, but in my subjective opinion the game goes too far. Many tools have no instruction or tutorial to teach you, and even a surprising number of core gameplay mechanics are completely hidden. I was more than three-fourths through my playthrough before I figured out some basic actions.I would still recommend the game to those who can appreciate the classic 2D Zeldas, but I would suggest allowing me to provide several 'spoilers' so a beginner doesn't get lost, stuck, or accidentally make the game unintentionally difficult for themselves out of ignorance.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a specific target audience. That target audience is people who grew up playing NES Legend of Zelda in Japanese who only spoke/read English. They could not understand the words but made sense of things through pictures and context and got through the game anyways. They enjoyed tough battles and hidden secrets, either by stumbling upon them or scouring the game for clues. They liked to reconstruct the story of the game purely from the in-game and game manual imagery.I am not that target audience. I love The Legend of Zelda dearly, but I love it for the story and character dialogue and other text I can read, and for the approachable combat which can be challenging but not too hard aside from major/endgame bosses. In TUNIC after a while I turned the difficulty down to "easy" and eventually to "no dying" mode. After finishing TUNIC I looked up what the story was, because I knew other people would have translated the writings, but I didn't experience much story until then.TUNIC is visually beautiful and I really wanted to like it because it's my favorite genre of game, but it just didn't have the things that make me love the genre.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: This game is flat out awesome. Fun and entertaining for someone who just wants to play a chill, aesthetically pleasing adventure game. And for those who would like to dig deeper, it offers intense, head scratching puzzles that are completely satisfying to figure out. As an older gamer, this scratched an itch I've had for a long time. Super fun, super rewarding, and honestly one of the craziest, most original puzzle game experiences I've ever had. Can't recommend enough.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: This game was a truly beautiful experience, many of us have a similar memory of playing an adventure/RPG in another language and having to scribble a whole notebook while looking for clues on magazines. The square soundwaves of its soundtrack and the gorgeous illustrations within the manual just sold me on this, and the rest is a whole lot of icing on the cake. Wish I could grasp again the sense of wonder this game brings when you play it blind.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: While I did enjoy Tunic, I personally wish it was more Zelda and less Dark Souls.  I got legitimately frustrated with this game's difficulty a number of times, particularly when fighting bosses.  I felt like I either needed to use consumables (Which felt cheesy and trivialized the fights) or die over and over again to find their patterns.  Other than that, the game had some good subtle secrets or things you'd learn about as you go along that were pretty cool to discover.  I also really liked the endgame  ability!  I did feel the game overstayed its welcome for me, but for people that are really into figuring out deep puzzles/secrets, I could see how that would have landed for them.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely amazing game! I love the art style and the game plays so good. An excellent blend of classic 2d Zelda with a mix of souls like combat and exploration. Please do not let the souls like comparison draw you away from this game. If you love A Link to The Past or other 2d action adventure games, you will love this game. Its a bit short, but honestly I think the time is actually very comparable to other games of this nature. There are a ton of really fun and clever puzzles and secrets to discover. There are so many times I thought I found everything in an area only to be brought to a shortcut that would have saved me minutes if I searched a little harder earlier. Its cool things like that and how the game handles the progression of certain abilities that makes this a truly great game. If you are on the fence, please go all in, you will not regret it.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: Wonderful game. Often the reward for exploration is knowledge, whether it's of a shortcut that was there all along, or of a mechanic you could have always used. Makes you crave replaying the game knowing what you know now at every step of the adventure. Captures a "weird imported game" feeling that I haven't felt since playing the games it clearly holds dear. I do have some performance problems, even after fiddling with the graphics options, on a computer that can run Very High Quality Games, but the game is literally so good that I chose to ignore a sluggish framerate in certain maps.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: If you love mysteries, cryptography, guessing games, being confused, good art, and top-down combat, you'll like this game a lot.I like the art and the combat, but as it turns out, I can't stand the rest.  This isn't a game for everyone- it's a game for a certain kind of person- which is how games ought to be designed.  I am just not that person.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: Tunic revolves around exploration, problem-solving, and combat. In this sense Tunic is reminiscent of the first Zelda game. However, Tunic is far more difficult than anything you might find in Zelda, especially in terms of combat. Particularly annoying enemies that appear in the later part of the game did hurt my enjoyment of this game. Fortunately, there are a couple accessibility options if combat seems too difficult and you'd simply like to progress. Despite that, Tunic is one of the best games I have played, if not the best, when it comes to a sense of discovery and adventure. Much of the game will be spent exploring, finding hidden paths and rooms, or deciphering the game's manual, which which is written in a strange language. Tunic never spells anything out for you. The story itself seems to be a puzzle to solve with what little you are shown.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: If you're bad at soulslike games play this. I had this game on game pass for a bit. I loved the game so much that I decided to buy it. The game is a lot like a soulslike game. And it's a perfect way to get someone younger into the swing of the kind of controls they'd be seeing in something more intense like Elden Ring. (I will note that Elden Ring is the only Soulslike I've completed and even so I did it following guides the whole way) Checkpoints that refresh monsters. Potion based healing, stamina based combat, and mana based magic. Heck it's even got a dodge roll. But i would say this and Hyper Light Drifter are closer than a soulslike. The game is shrouded in mystery and has a beautiful soundtrack to accompany it as well. The more I play it, the more it starts to climb the ladder for favorite game of all time. Visually it looks stunning. Clearly taking some inspiration from the Link's Awakening remake. TL;DR Game is like dark souls for kids. Got a beautiful soundtrack and I can't read anything like in Hyper Light Drifter. 10/10 Definitely playing again and again.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: This sucker punched me in nostalgia so hard I don't care if this review is biased. Nothing has captured that feeling of being a kid playing Legend of Zelda and not being able to read and just trying to figure things out from a worn out instruction manual, and notes from your parents that also were trying to figure stuff out.The game is gorgeous and adorable and atmospheric, and I've started playing the OST on loop.The combat is alright, but the real star here is exploration and puzzle solving, which I am here for.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: The instruction booklet aspect of this game is by FAR the most interesting and unique part of it so far. It has a beautiful way of showing you what to look out for, without holding your hand and explicitly stating what each and every thing does. Every bit of information it reveals just prods your imagination and leaves you with more questions than you had, and keeps you engaged and exploring. The combat is simple in concept but really challenges you to manage your space and stamina, and the fact that you can still attack and somewhat dodge even when your stamina is gone, risking only more damage and being knocked off your feet, is a good way to encourage players to sometimes take riskier fights even when they're at a disadvantage in the moment. The art style and music are exceptional as well, and figuring out what everything does on my own has been massively rewarding so far. I'm having a great time with this game, and I'm looking forward to playing it more.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: While not my normal genre (Souls-like), there's a lot to love about Tunic. Visually, the simple style lends itself very well and doesn't detract from the big scenes or intense moments. The music is fantastic. I really enjoyed the meta of the game manual and although I haven't just yet, I look forward to reading translations of the text and getting the full story. Because I don't play Souls-likes very much there was a learning curve for me, personally; and there were a few times where I had to put the game down because of frustration. Nbd, I expected it as I'm not the most skilled at this style of combat. I will say that the end-game puzzle content was not my cup of tea. I *did* it, but (without spoiling anything) the ending for sharing wisdom did admittedly annoy me. I like a lot of puzzles but... not these types of puzzles. They detracted from the overall experience of the game for me. That said, I'm not saying they're not inherently bad, just that they weren't for me.Overall I greatly enjoyed the story told and would recommend the game to most people.

_childDocuments_.review: First game i have played in some time where I went through and 100% it. its very good. simple yet fun, its a great puzzler and has some dark souls feelings. you will die alot. but its not bad. after you finish a fight that kicked your butt it feels rewarding. its a cutesie looking game but its replayability is fantastic. after first completion you unlock New Game + with harder enemies and more challenges. give it a shot! you wont be disappointed
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: Tunic is an amazing Zelda-Souls like puzzle game with a bit of everything in it.Its a breath of fresh air when a game doesn't force a boring tutorial in your face and then proceeds to spoon feed you exactly what to do and how to get to your destination.But then the question comes up "Where do i go?" "What is my goal??". The instruction manual pages, they brilliantly show you your goals and helpfull tips. Most of the text but not all in the manual is in some gibberish rune language that you have NO IDEA how to read, but adds to the mystery of the story if you are into that :)Its a hard YES if you like to be off your leash and find out stuffs on your own.

_childDocuments_.review: First of: I am not a furry. I swear, I am not identifying as this fox character....However, if i  consider myself a furry.. ....and even if I  identifying as the fox... ....this masterpiece would  be an absolute !The game looks cute and childish, but do not let that deceive you - stumbling into the 'Dark Tomb' for the first time without the lantern is  and the lore of the game is kinda messed up! If I was a furry I would probably also tell you that the game strikes a perfect balance between open-world and preplanned experience, where the map usually opens up in digestible steps, but you can also always choose to do things in your own order and the game will make sure to make you feel it when you are entering territory where you really are not supposed to be (yet). The world contains close to no filler space, so exploring felt really rewarding. There comes the point where the sudden realization kicks in that everything,  in this game world is , and that every little thing has purpose. The game wants you to decrypt a whole fantasy language and if you want to 100% understand the game, it even wants you to translate a whole book. I didn't really care for the fox character, since I'm not a furry, but as you can guess from the trailer, the game also looks gorgeous, some landsights even stunning! There is not a huge quantity of bosses (sadly), but the boss fights are really fun (e.g. you fight a gigantic golem that shoots a fat beam from it's face; no one can hate that) and they are pretty different from one another! If you want to solve the final puzzle, you will have to do some Sherlock Holmes type ♥♥♥♥ and really, really ..My final verdict is:It was perfect.  Everything....Down to the last minute details.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed this game so much I can now read its language, which says a lot since I previously played FEZ and while I enjoyed that game I basically tapped out on all the puzzles that require understanding its language. So when I started playing Tunic, I planned to stop once the game expected me to be able to read its language. However, Tunic never forces you to learn its language, and in fact there are maybe 2-3 extremely optional end game puzzles that use it, so you never feel forced to learn it unlike in FEZ. Every puzzle needed to get the good ending is solved with knowledge that the game wants you to have, although you will have to have a keen eye to notice it. On top of that, if you do decide to learn the Tunic's written language, it feels far more rewarding then in games like FEZ, because its not just "I replaced the letter A with this squiggly line", and it looks really pretty too.

_childDocuments_.review: This is pure gaming right here, folks. It's similar to Outer Wilds in how the game operates on a knowledge-based system. The boss battles were okay, but the exploration and puzzles... I simply can't tell how fantastic they are without revealing too much. Avoid detailed reviews and spoilers, and you will experience the greatest unique adventure.11/10, can't wait for Alzheimer's to kick in so I can replay the game again.

_childDocuments_.review: The combat of Darksouls meets the exploration of Zelda with no actual puzzles.The combat is dodge roll attacks, attack with your slap-range sword, and spam attack until it dies.Bosses will be constantly moving, so you're trying to reach the boss more often than actually attacking.Alongside that, endgame enemies reduce your max health whenever you get hit by them, and the only way to regain that lost hp is by resting at the game's version of a bonfire.You run around and explore. You can TWO tools good for unlocking new areas to explore in, one mid-game, the other late game.I only played through the main game, no super secret ending or anything of the sort.I saw zero puzzles I can think of. you kill enemies, flip switches, and proceed.Any puzzles would be from figuring out what the hell the guidebook means, translating text, and The art is great, the music is great, the story would be great for someone who actually wanted to translate whatever the ♥♥♥♥ is being said/written. The gameplay has much to be desired. I suggest anyone wanting to experience the gameplay anyway, to enable "no fail mode" after

_childDocuments_.review: Truly a masterclass of gaming, taking the novelty and dungeon crawling of SNES era games like ALTTP and Super Metroid and merging it with the obscure, unique-feeling experiences and deadly encounters of a Souls-like makes for an incredible game. It perfectly paces itself with knowledge provided by the handbook, making you wonder what else there is to learn. The first playthrough will be full of experiences subequent playthroughs won't have because a huge element is the discovery. Each mechanic of the game, the maps, Nintendo power-esque tips, the guidebook has it all. I recommend this game to just about anyone, especially those who grew up in the SNES era

_childDocuments_.review: Tunic is such a great game, It has an amazing art style and soundtrack as well as good gameplay mechanics. It seems a bit expensive at first but it's really long so that makes up for it. I've currently played for 11 hours and I'm pretty sure I haven't even gotten close to beating it. It is definitely very immersive and it is best to play it without looking up any guides or videos on it. Spoilers really break the emersion so I won't put any in this but I will say there is a very cool mechanic where the game tells  you how to play slowly throughout it and you have this instruction manual and you find pages to it as you play which give you hints. About 90% of the game is written in a made up language which is also pretty cool. Overall 10/10 great game

_childDocuments_.review: For something that is eeeeereferred to as a Zelda / Dark Souls fusion doesn't come close to describing the charm that this game has.While it does capture the original essence of Zelda 1 with its open world and lack of dialogue, it's puzzles are easier to glean and the hints that they give in the collected pages of the manual are more intuitive. It even does a very amazing job at telling a story without using exposition, dialogue, or spoon-feeding everything to the player.However, some of the late game puzzles are too opaque even if you know the method of how to solve them.It's certainly more simple than a Dark Souls Difficulty, because the enemies won't break logic just to straight up cheat-kill you, but that isn't to say the game isn't without challenge. Although, it seems like sometimes you'll still take damage even during the invulnerable frames of the tumble leading to some really cheap deaths.Overall, I really loved this game, and I'm going back in for second and third playthroughs, and grabbing all those achievements!

_childDocuments_.review: Only 5 hours in, but i'm gonna write a review anyway. I thought I got this game for like 5 dollars, but I got it for 25.97. I was thinking the whole time "what a steal!" I am not unhappy with paying as much as I did for this game. I will beat this game. The game rewards exploration with hidden chests, hidden shops, and hidden areas. Very often i'm just looking for the way forward or a hidden chest and then I stumble upon something rewarding like a shortcut, loot, a new map that I didn't suspect was nearby, etc; it's all good stuff. Combat is easy, you've got your 1, 2, 3 combo, you've got a shield, bombs, pots, and other utilities that are easy to use. The music blends in with the scenery and is easy on the ears. There are various enemy types from slime likes, knights, skeletons, angry birds, and so so.There is no dialogue and the story is up to interpretation. You develop an understanding as you progress and retrieve pages of information that are still not completely spelled out. It's very fun to feel that there is a mystery to be unraveled when it comes to what's happening in the game and "what the heck does this do!?"There is no difficulty setting just like a souls like. It's challenging enough for me. You can swim past some of the fights, other fights mess ya up. I like that variation in difficulty with enemy types just as much as I like the variety of enemy types. I like them good nuff!I like them colors! So vibrant! The look of the game, so simple and eye grabbing! Much wow!Alright cons if any:There's the targeting system which is simple at first. You just hold shift to lock on to enemies. I have not found a convenient way to switch between enemies when there are many of them and so I could be swinging or blocking in the wrong direction and obviously that leaves me vulnerable. I have had another problem with that while traversing the map with a tool for crossing gaps. You have to lock on to points that allow you to traverse gaps. There's an area that spawns enemies on top of the point you need to traverse to. What this does is it causes you to pull in the enemy and in this situation I was on an island of sorts, a minecraft block wide, and as I pulled the enemy they fell below my attack range, dodging my attack. There were two others who proceeded to blast me while I had little space to dodge around on. I was a sitting duck because I could not easily traverse like I wanted. I found that using the directional keys allows me to change my target, but it feels inconvenient to use when you have to use semicolon for blocking along with j, k, and l for attacking and such and so I cannot simply defend myself while switching targets.There is a mechanic in the game, that I'm not sure if I should speak on in detail about so I won't, which you need to know in order to progress in the game. I had not seen an indication for its use in the player book in game. I was stuck in multiple areas and spent time roaming around the large map looking for things that I had missed until I eventually just played around with some things and accidentally found the way to progress. This is me saying that the element of mystery can lead you to become lost or confused. I suggest that if anyone with low patience becomes stuck you should google it.Again, I've only played 5 hours. My feelings on the game may change later, but as for right now I'd say get it if you're looking for a challenging yet relaxing experience. Or maybe it's challenging at times and relaxing at other times. It's up to the player, I reckon.Beaten it at 28 hours. Final notes. The game has so much mystery because you're constantly trying to interpret characters on paper that you cannot understand, which is the intention. I learned about the end game secret mechanic, started doing the secret dance and what not, and the whole time I was so confused. Does it want me to input this or that? Oh, it wanted something else for this one. I felt like some details were missing, which is usually intentional, but I had no idea how to go about doing some other things that I found for the find all the secrets challenge. It has kept me up 'til 5 in the morning. I punched in so many key combos, obviously first doing the ones I was supposed to do, and nothing would work so I just went and had my 35 attempts at killing the boss and got the sad ending. Sad ending didn't make me feel great, but it was still a great game. Maan, that sucks...

_childDocuments_.review: I'm sure there's nothing I can say about this adorable, engaging puzzle adventure that a hundred people haven't said before, but yeah - I loved it!! Don't be fooled by its squishy cute appearance; this game is hard and asks a lot of you in both combat and puzzles. I bounced off it twice before I really got stuck in, but then it was all I could think about for weeks. It's game where I definitely recommend keeping a notebook next to you - and this kind of engagement isn't for everybody but if you enjoy that kind of intense puzzle gameplay and 'knowledge based progression' ('wait, I could have been doing that the whole time if I'd just known how??') you'll probably have a lot of rewarding fun like I did! All of that is wrapped up in a genius premise and a lot of loving nostalgia for classic games.I looked up a couple of puzzle hints when I got too stuck to be having fun anymore, but even that honestly didn't diminish the enjoyment much since there is a great online community who can help you get a start on puzzles without spoiling everything.Check it out if you're looking for something to really get your teeth into!!

_childDocuments_.review: Summery: Review contains mild spoilers. TUNIC, as some folks in the reviews have said, is a Zelda-Like mixed with Souls combat mechanic game. The game itself is very good and has some very satisfying moments. Especially the adventure and exploration aspects. It’s so much fun to run around and hack and slash stuff on the main area. Our little hero is just too adorable and makes this experience so much fun. The plot unravels like an onion at times and is fluid as it intermixes with the fun of exploration. The pros: Like I said in my summery, the games’ plot intermixes with the discovery and exploration aspects of the game so well. Even the somewhat obscure stuff, like the Golden Path, becomes easy to understand with a little work. The environments and places you will go are also very well designed and rather beautiful. Even some of the more… bleak… areas have a unique charm to them. The overall atmosphere a 10/10 for me. The sound and music design is phenomenal. I like games that reward the player for their curiosity and exploration, and this game delivers in a big way. The cons: The overall difficulty curve really ramps up to a 12 from a solid 8 in the final act. It’s such a climb in difficulty its rather jarring. Specifically, a certain environmental effect you first encounter late in the game, which you have no defense for until later. One of the final boss fights is such a stark difficulty ramp is so stark and jarring it’s borderline impossible. I spent over a week re-playing that fight trying different strategies and things until I managed to win. If they had just nerfed one of his attacks, he’d still be really hard! Overall: I love this game. It’s difficult at times, but very fun and rewarding and aesthetically pleasing other times. 8/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Giving this a recommendation with the caveat that this game may be polarizing. For a quick descriptor: it is essentially a mini  Souls-like that is trying to emulate the sense of discovery from old school adventure games (both for better and for worse).The usual Dark Souls structure is there: picking up your currency where you died last, melee combat with an emphasis on patience (mind you, it is much less difficult than most souls-likes), environments that loop between each other to create an elaborate world map, etc. This is all presented through a cute, minimalist art style with an isometric camera and an atmosphere that emphasizes tranquility and isolation, and the controls are all simple and streamlined. It's a strong loop that is extremely playable.But here's the warning: This game takes a lot of pride in how little it tells you, occasionally to a fault. Throughout the game, you collect pages of "the manual" (it is literally designed to look like an instruction booklet from a GBA game), and even that is primarily written in a cipher that is not intended to be readable. In fact, every time you pick up an item (including consumables), it's name and description are written in that same code. This encourages experimentation, but it also means the early portion of the game can feel extremely opaque. On top of that, remember the isometric fixed camera? Well, the game has a lot of its exploration hiding around blind corners and through hidden passages that don't do much too hint at their presence. Finding hidden secrets around corners felt less like "Ah ha!" moments of discovery, and more disheartening as I felt like the game had trained me to just rub against every surface and cliff side I could see.The game is a masterclass in subtle tutorial design, as the early portions of the game do an impressive job at guiding you to figure out the fundamentals on your own before handing you the instructions. However, it means that the game is built to force you to just "try things", and does not care to give the player context to know how much wiggle room they have. It took about 3 hours before I felt like the game clicked, and I could comfortably appreciate the game's rules. The sense of discovery and experimentation is a wonderful throwback to old school games, but can feel incredibly jarring for a modern release, even for someone like me who's been gaming for about 25 years.TL;DR - Mini Dark Souls that tries to emulate the vagueness of old school games to encourage experimentation and exploration. It's well designed enough to help you figure it out, but the learning process can feel overly unclear at times. A well crafted adventure that may be a bit too proud of it's willingness to spit in the face of modern conventions.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall: A Many games, especially in the indie scene, play to nostalgia. They attempt to evoke the style and feeling of games the developers enjoyed growing up and seek modernize established genres to mixed effect. Tunic evokes nostalgia and discovery in a time laden with instant gratification and day-one walkthroughs.  The world resembles the NES Legend of Zelda right down to the green tunic. The resemblance is well understood and the game wants to play into that nostalgia so the game feels familiar. What makes the game unique is how central mechanics are obscured almost completely. Over the course of the game, you will find pages from the instruction manual to the game which help explain key mechanics, maps for areas, and give general guidance. The extra twist comes from most of the game being written in a fictional language meaning deciphering the pages becomes a meta-puzzle to help solve in-world obstacles. It feels like experiencing the joy of video games again for the first time. The, admittedly decipherable, language helps divorce the player from the meta knowledge of games and puts them in the mindset of not fully understanding the references but learning them as you go.  When I was in middle school, I was playing through the original Legend of Zelda on my parents’ old NES. My dad also had a strategy guide where he wrote notes into the margins and, as I played, I made more notes of my own. Seeing the manuals in Tunic feel like putting together those pieces left behind in the guide book and adding to them myself. I even had to grab pen and paper to help make sense of some of the later puzzles. Special praise needs to be given to the developers who expertly dole out information. They constantly showing little pieces at a time, a hidden pathway, an unspoken mechanic, a secret item. It creates so many situations where I feel incredibly clever for figuring out a solution and then seeing how the developers hid all the clues right before my eyes and I simply couldn’t see them without a bit more context. The game simply makes the puzzles just feel like uncovering an adventure. Surprising, charming, and memorable. The game is a masterpiece of puzzle design and should be studied. The world feels deep and meaningful and evolves with the player, not because the landscape has changed much, but because you have changed. The player slowly learns the language of the game and begins to see just how much it has to offer. It is a damn shame it kept crashing on me (though it does save every screen transition).

_childDocuments_.review: The gimmick of this game is that you know nothing about it at the start (so don't look it up!), except the movement controls. You're missing almost all the pages of your game manual and it's in an alien language. But you're controlling a cute fox who's ready for an adventure, so you go on one anyway and decide you'll learn as you go.This game is phenomenal - I had so many jaw-drop moments as I discovered something new, and it goes through so many different genres! Can't recommend highly enough. Also if you loved Outer Wilds, you'll love this game for sure.

_childDocuments_.review: I love Zelda, soulslikes, and metroidvanias but this game just didn't do it for me.  It's not terrible, and it's close to being good, but overall I just found it annoying.  Everybody compares it to Zelda and while the visuals and themes are very Zelda-ish there aren't actually any puzzles to solve to progress.  It's very much a souls game level design where you run from checkpoint to checkpoint.  The only puzzles are these weird Dpad input combos that you don't even know about until the end of the game.  Some of them are clever but some are really annoying.That would be fine if it really leaned into the soulslike elements but the combat just isn't good enough to carry the game.  A lot of bosses/enemies are super annoying as they constantly jump back.  Funnily enough you can use that against them and get them up against the wall and just wail on them as they keep trying to jump back.  Combat lacks the finesse and tuning of souls games and the strategy and puzzle element of Zelda games.  Exploration was very meh as well.  90% of the secrets are just things hidden by the camera perspective or darkness.  So you run along the edge of the wall until you fumble through a passage or the interact button appears.  It became very tedious running into every wall obscured by the camera to see if there was anything behind it.These kinds of games don't really need a story or clear directions so the gibberish dialogue isn't a big deal but my god at least tell us what stuff does.  You can figure out what most of the items do easily enough but the cards are often just stat buffs or conditional stat buffs that you usually won't notice.  The gibberish/picture book manual is hit or miss.  I like the overall concept but they took it too far.  It also makes picking the game back up very difficult.  You gotta keep this one fresh in your mind because there is no indication of where you have been or where to go next.  A lot of the shortcuts are obscured by the camera so unless you remember where they're at it will take forever to navigate the world as you gotta run into every obscured area again looking for things hidden by the camera again.

Couldn't imagine how the game would feel if you spoiled anything by looking it up,  so play BLIND and have fun :)

_childDocuments_.review: Mix Zelda with the cryptic puzzles of Fez and a drop of Dark Souls and you get Tunic.Tunic is a perfect example of not necessarily doing anything incredibly out of the box, but refining the basics and essence of what makes these type of games fun, it really brings out that feeling of wonder, mystery, and intrigue the first time you booted up your first Zelda game as a little kid. _childDocuments_.review: Like the game itself, its manual is beautifully nostalgic and delightfully informative, albeit in often unexpected ways. It's also written in a constructed language and scatted throughout the world. The puzzles in Tunic are a challenging, unique blend of Zelda and The Witness. Despite the 2D nature of the game, the combat mechanics are deeply reminiscent of Dark Souls I, requiring careful stamina management, timing, and spacing. Highly recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: It's rare to find a game that has so much heart put into it. Tunic is a game that offers so much and shows so little. And by the end, you will be amazed how clever the puzzles, tight the combat and truthful to old video games!Is it hard? Yes! Is it manageable? Also Yes!Try not to look up solutions and avoid as much spoilers as you can.Tunic rewards the player by exploring, and offers the best that boot the Zelda and Darksouls games made of.I don't care if this game didn't win on the Game Awards (I should have). But for me, this is the true game of the year.JUST PLAY IT!

The game is really well designed and will makes you scrutinize the manual in search of some hints on how to use an items or some hidden secrets and feels rewarding when you figure it out. _childDocuments_.review: An unusual souls-like, with a lot of really clever design choices. The story is really interesting, despite being tragic. Audio and visual work is top notch, and the feel of exploration is, dare I say, on par with the Outer Wilds.If i had to find anything to complain about, it's the combat. There are some really frustrating aspects of it, but once you get used to them, it all becomes second nature to you.Strongly recommended overall
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: Tunic is a gem of a game that turned out to be much deeper, captivating, and challenging that I initially thought.The game is full of creative ideas, secrets, cryptic mysteries that all come together at the end if you choose to attempt to solve them. The craziest part of it, is that all of those puzzles are entirely optional, and should you choose not to look into the puzzles, the game is still very solid and worth the time.The use of a map with missing pages, written in an unreadable language is used cleverly and thoroughly during the whole game, you'll often get rewarded for paying close attention to what's in it, especially for puzzles !The music, story, graphics are a joy to experience.Easily one of the best games that I've played in a very long time, can't recommend it enough

_childDocuments_.review: Tunic is a challenging but ultimately delightful game. Much like Hollow Knight, it's a labor of love from a small dev team. And much like Hollow Knight combined classic Metroidvania gameplay with charming graphics and Soulslike elements to create a work of art, Tunic does the same with a Zelda-like format. But make no mistake, this is no mere Zelda clone. Gameplay is tight, bosses are tough but not impossible, and most of the puzzles and secrets are fair. Like most Soulslike games, one has to figure out the story and what happened to the world, and boy are there moments where your mouth will drop open. I enjoyed Tunic immensely and cannot recommend it highly enough.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is good. It's astonishingly good. It dropped my jaw a few times. There are a lot of different games that this game is like, but better. However, it is important to know a very select few things going in.1. This game is sparingly, occasionally, rather mechanically difficult. These instances are few and far between, so even if they aren't to your liking, they're still well worth putting up with.2. This game is highly, intensely cognitive. The developers did a very good job making sure that the necessary information to puzzles are always available somewhere accessible (which would be the manual), and ensuring that the information would also involve where to look. However, they did this with the understanding that the player will, by their own accord, keep track of where they've been, what they've done, and where they intend to go. All players should plan to keep a notes system outside of the game. They should also use it.3. This game's progression will depend on accepted gaming standards for things such as control systems, level design, and equipment. This is so that the developers can plainly state as little as possible about the game, no exceptions. It will be the player's job to intuit that "A" on the controller will trigger a dodge roll, and other such things.You must be prepared to be given nothing. You must be prepared to earn your every iota of meaning. You must be prepared to find things insurmountable, and be prepared to simply give up for the moment.If you are prepared, this game will without a doubt be the best game you've played in months. If you are not, then take heart; this game will still be here when you are.

_childDocuments_.review: Get your pen and paper ready for this one. You won't need it yet, but you'll be glad you put in the effort when you start getting to that point~That's not to say that the main course on offer here requires that you pour your blood, sweat and tears into understanding every nook and cranny, unlocking cryptic secrets and learning this game's language. There's a lot that you can enjoy more casually, and I very much recommend looking up as little as possible as you go. The mystery adds incredible layers to this game which feel great to discover at your own pace.There's a lot I love about this game. And a lot I still don't understand, even though I've completed its secrets and am putting it down for now. It's a pretty wild ride.

I highly recommend this gem to any person who is only remotely interested in adventure, puzzles or mysteries and of course... cute foxes.

_childDocuments_.review: I really liked Tunic. Its not the flashiest of games, but it knows what its doing and does it well. Its also very obvious where its inspirations lie, with old Zelda games being the most obvious - some of the illustrations in the ingame manual are very, very akin to those of the first Zelda games. _childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed my time with this game and highly recommend it. This is one of those games where the less you know about it before going into to play it, the better off you'll be. I think the best way to pitch it to someone in that spirit is: the devs want you to (re)experience the joy of discovering a game like the Legend of Zelda: Link's Awakening in the time before the internet, where all you had was the hints, a cryptic manual, and whatever friends you were playing with. If you aren't interested in that mystery and exploration (not just of the game space, but of trying to figure out how the game works), then you may not enjoy the game as much. I strongly suggest, however, that you just give the game a try. Get as far as you can without looking up the answers on the internet. Pay close attention to the help the game gives you, there's more there than you think. Ask a friend for hint before going straight to a walk through. There aren't enough games that strike a nice balance between not holding your hand but also giving you enough to figure it out, and Tunic deserves your time (and your attention without help) for striking that balance pretty well.

_childDocuments_.review: Tunic is a charming, concise little action RPG that captures the nostalgia of unboxing and playing Zelda 1 for the first time, translated to a modern audience. It borrows elements from ARPGs and puzzle platformers since that era (notably the Dark Souls franchise and Fez) to translate the challenge, mystery, and discovery to a modern audience, while evoking nostalgia for an earlier time through its art style and simplified gameplay.The game itself is not terribly long, but what's there is highly enjoyable and does not overstay its welcome. The combat draws from more modern Souls games while remaining faithful to its Zelda inspiration, allowing for multiple strategies and playstyles to prevail in each encounter. Its secrets and puzzles remain challenging without requiring more than details the game provides and pen and paper to solve (something that Fez notably stumbled with). And the game is very accessible to players with colorblindness, motion sickness, and who prefer to tune the combat to meet their needs. The soundtrack (by the same folks who did Dustforce) is an absolute banger, and hits all the right notes throughout the game.My only complaint with the game is that it's a bit small for the $30 price tag, especially when some of the discovery and mystery does not remain in subsequent playthroughs. That will assuredly improve over time, as DLC, randomizers, and new tricks get added to the game by the developers and community. The experience is also very high quality and respectful to the player's time, something that more padded out 100-hour experiences do not provide. But unless you need this very particular style of nostalgia right now or simply want to support the developers, it may be worth waiting for a sale compared to other options in the ARPG space.Overall though, what's here is very high quality, and when you do pick it up you're sure to have a wonderful adventure. Just don't forget your sword. It's dangerous to go alone. Take this.

_childDocuments_.review: The only games I remember from E3 2018 are Cyberpunk 2077 and Tunic, and this very much lived up to my expectations. Having to gradually find the game manual in order to learn how to play the game is a very interesting mechanic, one that scratches my itch for games like Outer Wilds and other knowledge-based-progression games. A good chunk of the game is fairly linear (even if it feels like you can go wherever you want), so there's rarely a feeling of being lost. There's nuggets of information that will drag you along, and context clues that will make you think and discover solutions on your own.Some of the late game puzzles are very creative, and would only really work in a game like this, and includes one of my favorite puzzles in gaming. That being said, if you're not keen on the idea of these more difficult puzzles, you can beat the game without doing any of the big-brain puzzles

_childDocuments_.review: To summarize my experience, I would say "I had a good time, but..."So let's discuss the good times.The map was good. It's a little cramped, and feels a bit discordant with the location of the fast travel points, but overall it has a good design. It's biggest weakness is the fact that most of the secrets are just passages that you can't see because you can't turn the camera.The music is great and the art speaks for itself.The real star of the show is the in-game user manual. You collect pages as you play, and those pages are integral to the game itself. For example, the world map is not some button you press to bring up its own menu, it's pages 27 and 28. There are also pages for the dungeons, and if you take the time to read them, not only do they reveal the layout, but also many of the secrets. Even further, the art within the manual is executed expertly, giving it the appearance of a late 90's strategy guide or an old Dungeons and Dragons module. It's honestly brilliant and I loved scanning through the pages looking for hints and clues. There are genuine layers to this portion of the game and how it interacts with the game proper, and I loved it.But here is where things go sideways. Here is the "but...".You may have noticed that this is a negative review. If I enjoyed the game as much as I did, why is this a big red thumbs down? Well, the question is not, did I enjoy it? The question is, would I recommend it?And the answer to would I recommend it, is no.Simply put, the combat ruins the entire experience. I even turned the combat down to "reduced" and it was still wildly over-tuned. Most of this game plays and feels like a "hit the red spot three times to win" type of game, but it's actually more of a "this boss has three phases, arena-wide AOEs, hyper mobility and attacks that must be memorized, and you die in two hits" kind of game. Every time I had to fight a boss, I just wanted it to be over so that I could go back to the parts that are actually fun.Like all the rest of the game, the combat should be based on knowledge checks. There should have been secret solutions to trivialize the boss fights based on information scrounged from the world. Every enemy should be weak to certain weapons and items. That type of combat would have been perfectly in tune with the themes of the game. But no, no such solutions exist. I even double-checked a few internet guides to make sure I wasn't misunderstanding something (especially since the in-game manual is written in a secret language and I had not yet learned how to translate it).The thing is, I don't hate hard boss fight games. I just think it was the wrong choice for this game. Tunic needed to spend more time trying to be Tunic and less time trying to be Dark Souls.I really miss the days when every single indie dev wasn't trying to ride FromSoft's ♥♥♥♥.

_childDocuments_.review: As a Christian I am deeply bothered by this game and consider it sacrilegious. At first it was incredibly fun to play, great mechanics, plot, and the idea of the manual, animation, enemies, challenge. All top notch, UNTIL you delve into the the mythology. This doesn't come up until about 1/2 way through the game, spoilers ahead. You sacrifice at pagan altars by giving offerings and coin to up your magic points, health, stamina, etc. You meditate at pagan altars and pray to transport to different locations. What pushed me over to not playing though is you find out that previous large foxes are spirits that have been crucified on the holy cross, yes those exact words in the manual. Those fox spirits are imprisoned against their will in obelisks throughout the game that you have to activate and you can hear them cry out mechanically as it were. You actually have to fight one at one point. The sacrifice of this large fox animal by the main character who appears benevolent because they are trapped but is actually evil is the focus of worship in the mythology. You see this crucifixion in the cathedral, yes a real cathedral with candles, pews, and an altar. The worship of this sacrificial creature or the consummation of its sacrifice, the chalice, as the manuals says, leads to forgetfulness of all beings. The smaller creatures that worship are forgetful zombies in the cathedral. As the main character, you are one of many "hero" reincarnations. Your role is to either take the place of the main villain whose imprisonment is an eternal beacon to subsequent reincarnations of you calling to you to take their place (so you become evil and perpetuate a death cycle) OR you convert the villain to be good by sharing the complete manual/knowledge with them. The villain then comes to it senses as it were. If I had known what I was signing up for my son and I would not have purchased or played to begin with. Seems cutesy and fun, then takes a dark turn. Disturbing.

_childDocuments_.review: You know it's a good puzzle game when you need a pen and paper. Tunic is one of the best, if not the best,  puzzle games I've played since Fez. The Legend of Zelda homage pulls you in and you stay for the incredibly challenging puzzles and decryption. My buddy and I spent several hours looking up information on linguistics and writing down different ciphers. I LOVE this game and more importantly, I respect this game. The music is 10/10. _childDocuments_.review: Tunic appears to be a zeldalike (if that's a thing) but is actually more its own thing than you might suspect looking at screenshots or footage. It PLAYS like a 2D Zelda (in two-thirds perspective) but the game itself has much more to it than that. Without giving too much away, Tunic treads some of the same MOMENT OF DISCOVERY feels that Outer Wilds, The Witness, and other modern puzzleboxes evoke but possesses its own way of giving the player access to those moments.In short, Tunic is unique despite appearing samey, and hits some notes that nothing else really has. Definitely worth checking out if you like Zelda, of course, but even more so if you like new ideas about how games can explore exploration, drop moments of discovery, and integrate the player as a part of the game rather than just as an executor of a predetermined course of actions.

_childDocuments_.review: It's got some fun gameplay, if you like sniffing out secrets and figuring things out.  *Do not spoil yourself for this game*.  Figuring out all of the many, many secrets and hidden pieces of information *is* the core gameplay.  If you find yourself stuck, then try reading the manual again... as much as you have of it.  It really does help.It's beautiful, and the music is quite nice.Most profoundly, though, this game does the thing it does with incredible elegance.  It is a constant process of discovery, and that discovery is done so *elegantly*.  You're just constantly discovering things and figuring out how they work by experiencing them in the world or figuring out what the relevant sections of the manual mean.  It shows both a great deal of love and a tremendous amount of skill in a thing that I don't even have the right words to describe.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't particularly know what I can say about TUNIC that doesn't feel like an inherent spoiler of some sort. What I will say is simply this. It is by no means a perfect game, I do think there are some parts that I was a little irked by during my 100% completion but those moments are vastly and almost entirely overshadowed by the sheer joy and satisfaction I felt unravelling the game's many mysteries. 2022 has started off very strong for me with the games I've played and TUNIC is no exception. _childDocuments_.review: Graphics: nice looking low poly 3D graphics. 7.8 out of 10Music: good songs. 8 out of 10Story: interesting story. 7.5 out of 10Gameplay: the main part of the game and what really matters to me. The gameplay combines elements of souls-like games with exploration and puzzles like those from the Zelda games.The controls are fine but I didn't like having parry locked to 'double tap block'(RT) which made me parry a few times during battles without wanting to do it. There should be a way to remap that but apparently there isn't.A better control scheme would be: RB to parry, LB to drink potion, Select to open inventory and RS or LS(press) to open the manual/maps.Another problem I had is that the lock-on system seems really fond of choosing the worst possible target for the situation, requiring a lot of manual adjusting to it which makes some battles kinda clunky.Having that said, everything else works great. Dodging and attacking is cool; using magic is fine as well (although they're really simple). Not using stamina to attack is possibly my favorite thing about the combat.Exploration uses some metroidvania mechanics which are cool. It also has a lot of visual puzzles, finding secret paths and so on. Some of them are cool, others not so much. Some puzzles are way too cryptic, and unless you have a lot of time and patience, getting 100% is almost impossible without using a guide.Difficulty is on the easier side for a "souls" game, but it does have it's difficulty spikes.Final score: 7.8 out of 10

_childDocuments_.review: 2D soulslike with a Zelda skin. At first I thought it was a Zelda-style game with soulslike elements, but it's quite the other way around. It revolves around a stabbing-blocking-dodging combat system with health potions that refill only at rest points. You also lose some of your money and have to go get it back from where you died after respawning at aforementioned rest points. Combat gets brutally hard sometimes, but usually it's very manageable. Overall, it's a fantastic game. Beautiful art, beautiful music, beautiful story told entirely through world building and finding pages of the game's manual, as very little is actually written out for you in English. The items are cool, the dungeons are cool, the enemies are cool (and extremely frustrating sometimes). Throws a myriad of mechanics at you from souls games and Zelda games that fans of either or both will recognize immediately, but it blends them together in a very clever way and absolutely holds its own identity. This one is definitely worth a grab for anyone that likes action-adventure games or indie games in general. Fantastic work from the devs. 8.7/10

_childDocuments_.review: Tunic is a great game that reminds me of older games, like zelda 1, where the game doesn't tell you much and you have to figure it out yourself. The game does help and guide you, so it's not as obtuse as zelda 1, but even most of the text in the game is unreadable so you have to interpret what the game is saying instead of being told. For the gameplay Tunic flows well with its movement and combat, the level design is expertly designed and you can see a lot of thought was put into it. It's shocking to me just how many secrets are in this game, your desire to explore is always rewarded with something, and I most likely missed at least half of the secrets.

_childDocuments_.review: Tunic is SO good!!It feels like an old-school classic adventure game with an outstanding level of detail in every puzzle.The art, the music, the sense of wonder and mystery you can feel throughout the entire game is fantastic.It says many things without saying anything. _childDocuments_.review: An isometric Ocarina of Time blemished by unforgiving souls-like combat in the late game. There are some interesting elements at play here that combine to make this a wonderful experience: a puzzle box map riddled with secrets, a story that unfolds itself to the player through pages of game manual found throughout the world, and light combat with all the gadgets you'd expect in a Zelda adventure. However, the game is held back from perfection by the combat which starts off relaxed - offering a slight, but surmountable challenge - only to wallop the player with a brutal mid-game difficulty spike that feels unnecessary and out of place given the Zelda model the game is so heavily drawing from. Luckily, there is a "god mode" toggle in the settings menu for those who prefer to focus on adventure and puzzle solving.

_childDocuments_.review: Highly recommended got to be one of the best games from 2022 and deserves way more recognition for what it's achieved. Great blend of old LTTP/OOT Zelda world design and progression mixed with Dark Souls style world building of being able to show so much just through the environment and the beings within it.My biggest piece of advice to fully enjoying this game would be instead of going to Google or whatever grab a piece of paper (or in my case many pieces) and a pen and even use your phone camera, note down important things, things that seem out of place and look over details in the world and the "manual" many times. This game has some incredible puzzles, all of which can be done by paying attention to what the game is telling you. Don't be deceived by the different language you only need that for one achievement, ("Vintage" which I do recommend you look up to solve unless you like transcribing languages) the rest is solved through normal means and has some of the most rewarding solutions I've had.

_childDocuments_.review: I need to emphasize that this game is not based around combat, it's not meant to be, combat is a part of the recipe but the primary game that is here is solving riddles as direct as they are and as vague as they can be. Every single one can be solved thinking about it long enough and looking close enough. You don't need to decipher the language either so don't worry about that unless you really want to but the prize isn't worth it in my opinion. It's polished to a T and I can't point to anything as being a problem other than the combat which I loved but I've also heard can be difficult for some. Soundtrack, art, layout, puzzles/riddles, bosses, characters(sortof), enemy variety, tools and locations. Everything is taken above and beyond. Please keep in mind however that of course this game is primarily a puzzle game, with the puzzled being the game itself. If that sounds a little interesting you will love this but if you think it might just be more annoying than anything I don't think you would have the patience to get to the bigger mysteries, rewards and secrets the game has for you.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is amazing! I wasn't sure what to expect going in, maybe an easy puzzle game. Instead of easy, I got a beautiful, difficult, and rewarding game. I couldn't stop playing it, and would've pulled all nighters for it if I wasn't busy. I could only think of this game at work and school. Definitely worth the 30 dollars imo

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing game. It is essentially an isometric soulslike with cool metroidvania elements and exploration. _childDocuments_.review: I just finished this game up less than an hour ago (got both endings) and it's pretty awesome. Really enjoyable the whole way through, as it gives you the opportunity to piece together what's going on as you go. Wish I could elaborate more, but I feel like spoiling any part of this game would defeat the purpose a bit, as a majority of the fun comes from what you discover. It's clearly meant to emulate what it was like to play the original NES Zelda game, but it definitely has it's own unique take that you really don't have to be a Zelda fan to appreciate. The difficulty level is up there, but I wouldn't let that stop you as the game options offer a wide array of accessibility features that let you adjust that difficulty to your own needs and preferences. You can even set it to no-fail mode if the combat is a little much, and it'll still keep you engaged with literally some of the most creative think-outside-the-box type puzzles I've seen in a game. 10/10 would recommend

_childDocuments_.review: This game is absolutely worth your time. On the surface it looks like a cute Zelda clone. There's an incredible puzzle nature to the gameplay that will leave you with a table full of hastily written notes. There's an in game source of information that hits the nostalgia for NES carts in an artful and deeply clever way. There's a level of clever and intentional game design to everything in this game. What seems trivial at first spirals into layers of interesting gameplay. If you liked Outer Wilds this has some aspects of that idea.

_childDocuments_.review: Recommended. A memorably pretty, strange and mysterious experience, obviously inspired by the original "Legend of Zelda" while having greater free-roaming. Best to go in without spoilers, but you may eventually find that certain things are so obscure you might break down and consult a guide. Resist the temptation for a while. _childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: What an amazing game. I thought Deaths Door was a great Zelda like but it doesn't even compare to Tunic! It's got a Zelda like theme and world progression with no hard barriers along with souls like boss difficulty. What more could you ask for? If you want a more casual play through there's even modifiers for that! Every bad review I've seen looks like its just written by someone who is just bad at video games. Any old Zelda game or Metroidvania is 1000x more difficult in terms of figuring out what to do next. I think people are just so used to having new games hold their hand the whole way. This game does not. But gives you clues that make you have to actually think. Its incredibly rewarding. Re-visiting the pages of the guidbook you've found to find the answer that you need is the coolest thing ever!
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: Want to go on an adventure? How about exploring a seemingly traditional and gamey world just to discover that there's much more underneath the surface. Don't be fooled by the cover: while clearly being presented as an action-adventure title, the core of the experience is much closer to a puzzle game. Not just because of the puzzles themselves, but because the player is asked to understand rules, uncover truths, figure out how the world works realizing that most of what the player sees actually hides a secret. This is done beautifully with close to no written text, just by virtue of observation and experimentation, with the aid of a "game manual" that ties in a whole new meta dimension into the game. The game manual itself is a brilliant addition that's extremely well executed, managing to drive the player to the next discovery without robbing him of the challenge and joy of actually grasping it.On top of it all, the presentation is top notch featuring one of the best soundtrack in years and great direction at every turn.Tunic is without a doubt a masterpiece: it provides a unique, engaging experience with fresh ideas, both well thought out and well executed, balancing freedom of exploration with a tight and exciting sense of progression. I'd also like to talk about how great, thoughtful and meaningful the story and inspiration behind the game are, and how great of a message it conveys, but that's something I'll have to discover on your own.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: Man, I was so looking forward to playing this game, but I was quite disappointed in the ned. Maybe I didn't do my homework first, but it had been described to me as, and the previews made it look like, a Zelda clone. But it really isn't. The basics are there, you have a sword, a shield, and a green tunic, but that's about it.On it's own, the game is pretty challenging... until you get to the bosses. The bosses are incredibly difficult. I found myself spending more time trying to beat the bosses then playing the game. Yes, there's some of the "git gud" mentality to them, but even after learning their attacks and how to dodge them, it still mostly came down to luck. For example, most games with difficult bosses, once you learn their patterns, you can beat them pretty reliably. In Tunic, you can beat a boss one try, and not even get a single attack the next. Not only that, but the boss battles are incredibly boring.The other thing that I disliked was the game instructions. Without giving away spoilers, there are no game instructions at the beginning. As you start to go through the game, you start getting some of those instructions, but at that point you don't need them. It was pretty interesting how the instructions tied into the puzzles though...And speaking of puzzles, the one part I really loved about the game is the puzzles. They were very difficult, and I love that. The problem is, they are not advertised to you at all. I didn't even know I was looking for puzzles until I was looking up help on beating a boss. Then I had to slog my way back through the game looking for all of them.All in all, it was a cute game, but I found the bosses too much of a pain, and there wasn't enough other stuff to keep the game fun.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic open world exploration game with tons of secrets, loads of mystery, beautiful scenery, and amazing music. (I highly recommend buying the bundle with the soundtrack, I would've if I'd known how entrancing the soundtrack was. I had to come back and but the OST separately because it's just that good.) _childDocuments_.review: Way too much is left completely unexplained, you'll be walking right passed things you can already interact with thinking you need a new item or something.Many enemies leave JUST enough of an opening to get a single hit in, the dodge-roll is pretty much useless since it doesn't cancel your attack animation, forcing you to rush down enemies before they can act or outright avoid them, unless you like spending an ungodly amount of time whittling down every enemy in the area.A lot of enemies appear in large numbers before you have the item to deal with them reliably, I'm only at the part after getting the shield and now every enemy in the way seems to have one as well, so I need the grappling hook to take their shields but I don't even know when I'll be getting that.

_childDocuments_.review: tldr: Tunic is an amazing top-down action puzzle game with fun boss fights, satisfying puzzles, exciting exploration, and a fantastic soundtrack. Starts kinda dull but then just keeps getting better until it's become one of the most memorable games you've ever played.Tunic is a surprisingly pricey game considering the store page makes it look like just another cutesy top down indie game. But my god, is this game worth it. I'll start by immediately addressing that this game starts off really dull. The best part of this game is navigating the world and its mysteries, and frankly the start of the game just didn't have enough going on to peak my interest. The world was still simple and very few gripping questions had really been raised. However, this is short lived, as the game quickly opens up by introducing new areas, new goals, and new questions that all serve to keep you invested.The combat of this game is its other weakest point as it's just not that much to it. The combat is very standard top down dodge roll melee combat with the only real mix up here being the different magic weapons you get. On top of this, one of the most basic parts of this combat, the 3 part sword combo that you will basically be doing for the whole game, just doesn't feel very good. In particular, the third attack of the chain just did not consistently work for me, whether in combat or out of it.The boss fights are a bit of an outlier though, as unlike the moment to moment combat, they are actually really fun, and a couple were even quite tough. Bosses had fun move sets to learn, great sound design, and some amazing music tracks that made them truly memorable.Basically everything else in this game is amazing, starting with the absolute best part, the puzzles and the navigation. I don't usually think of these two things as the same, but in Tunic they absolutely are. Navigating the world is the puzzle, and its largely flawless. Using the perspective to hide secrets is genius, and it's extremely satisfying to turn those hidden corners and walk a ways behind a wall to then see yourself appear in some area you thought was unreachable. The way this game likes to give shortcuts by simply showing you that there was a hidden path that could have gotten you there all along is hilariously unique and surprising. This does bring up the only problem I have with this area of the game however. Finding shortcuts that were always there but were hidden form view is fun, but if you take a break from the game you will come back having forgotten where most of these shortcuts were, meaning you may as well not have them as they are not marked on the map. This does make Tunic one of the few games i'd actually suggest people binge rather than playing little bits of over time.There are other puzzles of course that have nothing to do with navigating and they are just as good... sort of. Many of the "puzzles" in this game don't particularly feel like puzzles as you are often given the answer quite directly. This is hardly a problem though because while they may not feel like puzzles, it still feels amazing to finally find out what all the different curiosities in the world are actually for. There is one puzzle though that stands out as king among'st the rest. While I obviously won't spoil, I will say the puzzle is optional but is without a doubt the most hyped up puzzle I have ever solved and my anticipation for solving it still brings me joy thinking about it now. Solving it has become one of my greatest video game memories not because it was hard, but because it was just so much fun. Perfect.Similarly, the world is not all navigation as well. Tunic has a very cartoon art style, but it's cute, and is very often used in tandem with some amazing lighting to create really gorgeous scenes. The variety of locations in this game is really good as well. The variety keeps things fresh, and ensures your eyes stay glued to the scene.The soundtrack in this game is incredible. It's chill vibes rival those of even Minecraft's soundtrack and that doesn't even give credit to the boss themes which all do a grand job of amplifying their respective fights. It's all just so good.Lastly I'll mention the games story which is alright... I guess. For me, the story was largely irrelevant, and I think the game itself tends to feel that way as well. There is a story, and it's got some cool ideas, but the details are so vague as to be non existent for the common player. Fortunately, the story never needs to be a motivator for you to do things, discovering all the secrets strewn about the world does that plenty well.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: Let's start with the positive.  Neat atmosphere, and the way the game manual sorta steers you forward and reveals mechanics over time is a neat concept.  I just wish there was a way in game to translate it without needing to do the cryptography yourself.Now the negatives.  You move at a pounderous pace, but the game will throw enemies that move faster than you and entire hordes of them.  Your only defensive options rely on a tiny stamina bar, but you are punished double for over using stamina by taking extra damage when you run out.  On top of that, many threats will damage your maximum health until you go to a check point.

_childDocuments_.review: Abhorrent combat gameplay. I can't wrap my head around how terrible it feels to play tunic: roll, that Cutie Mc Fox starts with, sword that is shorter than gnome's ♥♥♥♥, paraplegic parry animations, MFing lock-on system in the isometric perspective and throwables that are affected by the physics engine - all feel like an absolute garbage to use. Music is bland. Visuals are simple, but unpleasant to look at, mostly because of the washed up color palette that clashes with eye-gouging visual effects and lighting. Manual, the main gimmick of tunic, is 50% window dressing for standard metroidvania power up progression, 50% FEZ puzzles.The only saving grace of the game is the competent level design. And, if you're into the stuff like that, maybe, the fictional language cypher(which is somewhat deeper than 1 fictional symbol == 1 English alphabet letter).If you want a competent 'what a twist!' game, where the twist actually affects gameplay, I wholeheartedly recommend The Messenger or Inscryption as much as I want to discourage you from playing Tunic. Hell, even the aforementioned FEZ I might consider to be a better game than this souls-like normiecore slop.Edit: Tunic is better than the Witness, though, don't you dare to play the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Witness!!!
