_childDocuments_.review: Edit 2: Months later and I'm still thinking about this game. Really standing the test of timeEdit: Have now finished Tunic, what an excellent game. And I'm just scratching the surface with the puzzles too because there are alternate endings, secrets within secrets, and more. Not sure if I have the time to keep digging, but I want to.Original: Have you ever looked at a puzzle game and though hmm, needs more Dark Souls? Well this game might be for you because it is most definitely for me. If you can go in cold please do, because the joy of discovery here is amazing. I'm 6 hours in, feels like im about halfway through the game, but i wanted to get this review out there for people who are on the fence.Without trying to spoil I'll try to explain what makes this game so good. This game is first and foremost a puzzle adventure game. You don't know whats going on, instructions and signs are in an unknown language, an you have to piece together everything through contextual clues. The world might seem locked away behind abilities like a metroidvania, but you actually have hidden abilities and skills you can do right from the start that unlock parts of the world. It will be interesting to see if / how speedrunners try to exploit these techniques.This adventure puzzle style would be fun on its own but then you have the combat, which is not much more than sword, shield, dodge roll, magic, grapple hook and items, but the enemies design is tough making you truly master the mechanics to beat each boss. Very much like dark souls, but probably closer to Death's Door. It is difficult, so I'm not sure I would recommend it for pure puzzle game fans, but definitely recommend to anyone who loves Souls games and especially the hidden lore aspects of Souls games.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: Almost everything about this game is great, except for the combat. It isn't overly difficult; it's just exceptionally poorly designed. It's clear that no thought was given to whether or not encounters would be fun. It's so bad that the devs actually implemented god-mode options in the game's menu. If your combat is so poorly designed that you felt the need to implement that, why didn't you just fix the combat instead? The mind boggles.The level design, sound design, story, lore, and aesthetic in this game are all fantastic; if I were one of the people who worked on those aspects of the game I'd be pretty sad that the combat designers effectively ruined the overall experience.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: Very good puzzle game. Cute and beautiful art design. One major flaw is the combat and bosses though. They have a level of mobility and range that that player simply does not, and the stamina system discourages rapid movement/rolling to compete with them. General combat against normal enemies is fine, the main problem is just that the bosses keep dashing away but your main form of damage is a very short range slash. Fortunately the game has accessibility settings that you can turn on/off at leisure, so you can easily sidestep the problem if you wish. If you like old school Zelda, Dark Souls, or Fez, you will probably enjoy this game greatly.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: A genuinely unique and incredibly creative game, I would recommend you to go in as blind as possible but your reading this so Ill try to keep it simple. it draws heavy inspiration from the classic top down Zelda games but then really steps it up a notch with its puzzles. One thing people go on about and for good reason is the instruction manual this game has. It's mostly in a made up language and really gives the experience of getting an second hand copy of a game that you can't read so your pouring through images and trying to piece together bits to figure things out, which it really leans into and utilises the fact its not a real manual and is digital while also having perfect looking hand scribbled notes in it.It's hard to talk about what makes the game so special without spoiling the experience, I can however say that so much in this game is hidden in plain sight, a very big part of the game is expanding the players knowledge and regularly challenging what you know. You will run through the early game and think you know everything maybe you found a few secrets, blew up a wall that was neat half way in you will have several realisations about the game and by the end your third eye will be open.The combat is somewhat challenging but honestly after a certain point it felt tedious to me, luckily there is a no fail combat option which normally I wouldn't recommend but I think using it doesn't detract from the main vision/experience of the game so in this instance I would wholeheartedly recommend using it when you feel you've had enough combat, I would recommend to turn it off for the boss fights they all have very quick ways to return to them.All in all, if your looking for a unique game that will stick with you for a long time that is in the vein of The Witness or Fez this game has you covered.

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely worth the money. The sense of exploration and wonder was incredible. Will say that outside help both helped immensely and also took away a bit from the experience. _childDocuments_.review: I've been really uninterested in trying new games as of late, but with the cute nature and charm I saw in the previews on steam, I decided to try it out. I was not disappointed. This game had me playing for hours before I took a break each time. Every monster has an appealing design while still holding a respectable tone despite being cartoony.           This game is in every sense a "zelda game." However it feels more punchy and fast paced while still holding onto those key elements of game play by having all those fancy gadgets you get along the way. What I admire about this game is the story. Everything is not a handheld "this is what happened" story telling. You practically piece it all together by finding fragments of an adorable game manual that tells you little hints at just the right time as you progress the game while the world itself tells you what happened. Something that the dark souls series (as this game does adopt mechanics and gets the silly "souls like" tag) did not really do "Here's an item that barely explains anything."          I'm learning what's going on AS I explore each new location, and the next location shows me why the last location is in the condition that it was. i'm around 10 hours in and what I think is the last boss might not even be that. I'm enthralled with this game, and if you're into exploration with a bit of challenge you would be too.      My only real pet peeve about this game though is the perspective i'm sad to say. There's no way to change your camera angle (playing it you can understand why) and it only changes in specific areas as you're walking. With the lighting in certain areas it also makes it hard to determine what's accessible or even where you are exactly.   Overall, however, even with this game not being beaten yet, I can see me playing this game again in the future when I do beat it.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this or at least be neutral, but this should be stated. This game Tunic has some really archaic secrets that even if you look them up on a guide are as tedious as pulling out your own teeth with a wrench.Tunic for the most part does a lot right: the adventure feels like classic Zelda, you find a stick, and then a sword, and a shield, and things around you slowly open up with each new item. The sword is stronger than the stick and can cut through trees once barring your path. The shield protects you from strong enemy attacks and projectiles. You gain a mana bar once you find your first magic item. And the bombs become very helpful the more you use them up.For a lot of freedom this gives you, it is also hard to find out exactly where you need to go next. You'll likely be stumbling upon secrets that are obvious in hindsight, but since the manual papers you find use a symbol language more often than English words, it wouldn't be much of a surprise if you look past them until later. Hindsight and all that. It feels like you've uncovered a new gimmick when you do, but it takes a bit of reading comprehension that is lost because, again, the text isn't fully translated. It's like trying to read a foreign language dictionary and trying to guess which words are right based on what you already know. Better to just ignore that and avoid making yourself look like a fool, you know?But what ultimately ruined this for me were the really hard to get secrets. There are a few doors and chests that can be opened or revealed inputting a whole series of buttons either on your directional keypad or controller d-pad. Up, left, right, down, in a series of inputs very fast. You have no prompt or indicator when or how to do just, just so long as you stand in front of the door as you do it. Some door commands are simple, like six inputs. But others, and practically all the chests too, require upwards to ten commands at once.One such secret to open the door in the mountains requires you to look through your manual pages and figure out which directional symbols to draw/input. It was tedious for me to just look those all over back and forth, so I just looked up the solution online... and STILL struggled to get it right. Can you imagine anyone else trying to do this the long way, as shown in the breadcrumb secrets, and still somehow get it wrong because of timing or not realizing they drew the wrong symbol or pressed the wrong button?! There's even a checklist for getting "fairies" in this game but that requires even more head-scratching logic on inputting codes. I gave up at this point because either I'm not sure if the codes were right at all, or if I wasn't pressing them fast enough, or even if I wasn't in the right place to push them. Worse is that they're tied to the second (true) ending so you're likely only going to get stuck with one ending depending on how clever you are finding obscure secrets, much less solving them RIGHT.This doesn't feel rewarding or exciting at all. It feels tedious and frustrating. It's one thing to have hard fights that subtly encourage you to get better with timing or using your items (either bomb throwing or upgrade offerings). It's another thing to have hard puzzles that barely have any sense to them. One you can learn how to do, but you'd have to be smart to figure out the other.

_childDocuments_.review: When you're looking at the screenshots on the storefront, Tunic looks like a cute and friendly Zelda clone. When you start playing Tunic, you begin to get the impression that it's actually a fairly punishing Dark Souls clone. And then, once you get into Tunic's late game, it just turns into something else entirely. It's hard to properly review Tunic without wading into spoiler territory, but what I can tell you is that there's people on both sides of the fence who either love or hate Tunic for the exact same reasons. If you ask me, I think it's worth playing if you have the right mindset.I'll start by saying that Tunic is designed to be played blindly, and you'll ruin the experience the moment you look up any sort of guide whatsoever. There's no tutorial or even any real sense of direction at first, with the game even going as far as to force you to find pages of the manual on your own. Some people drop Tunic within the first few minutes because  and that's perfectly fine because Tunic is made for people that actually enjoy it when a game assumes that they're an intelligent human being. Figuring things out by trial and error is, at least for me, refreshing and rewarding. I like it TO A POINT, a point which Tunic admittedly does reach towards the end of the game, but it's still good overall. I was able to at least beat the game without the use of a guide, but I DID have to go back and use a guide to Nature of the gameplay aside, Tunic has a lot of other things going for it. The colorful and minimalistic graphics get the job done, and the soundtrack is phenomenal. Tunic is certainly unique, and even though it draws inspiration heavily from Zelda and Dark Souls, it's able to use those elements as a springboard to become its own thing rather than being a simple clone. If you're okay with being frustrated by design, Tunic is an ultimately rewarding experience even if it has the occasional brief misstep along the way. I say it's worth a look if ya want something fresh!
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: A really lovely experience, incredibly evocative of being a young and barely literate child finding wonderment in every aspect of your first adventure game. I've rarely felt as constantly delighted, surprised, and confused. The visuals are both adorable and beautiful, especially the Instruction Manual artwork, which filled me with an immense nostalgia. It doesn't over stay its welcome, possibly even being slightly lean on main gameplay content. Personally I found the game somewhat challenging both in terms of problem solving and combat. There were a couple puzzles that relied heavily on the fixed camera perspective, and took an inordinate amount of time to merely notice a mostly obscured or unimportant looking background object, as opposed to the majority of puzzles that felt satisfying and fair. The audio design of the game is extremely effective in supporting the mood and mechanics, however there was a lack of memorable melodies.If you think the game sounds like fun, you'll probably love it. I certainly did.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: Atrocious combat completely spoils what is otherwise a gorgeous and actually quite interesting exploration-based puzzler, but even the puzzling elements are made needlessly obtuse by the game's refusal to actually tell you what the things in your inventory are. It puts forward Dark Souls-style 'what if you lost all your money/XP when you die' combat as a key design element, but then doesn't actually let you directly buy stat improvements with it, instead hiding those behind a double-confirm where you can only upgrade if you've found a corresponding coupon to a given stat. Imagine if Legend of Zelda made you spend 200 rupees every time you want another heart container, but also you still have to find the heart container. Combining that with stamina-based rolling and blocking(assuming you even can block; the game actively hides the shield behind several challenges to actually get) and a healing system so obviously inspired by Estus Flasks that it may as well have just called them that results in a player progression that doesn't just feel wonky, it feels actively bent. Boss design feels overly-punitive, with combos that punish you for failing to avoid the first hit by making it impossible to dodge any others, and the gating of upgrades means you can't even grind past a challenging foe. Your own attacks feel unresponsive, difficult to properly range, and there's shockingly little variety to the point the only way the game can make non-boss enemies challenging is throwing big clots of them at you.There's some genuinely good ideas in here, like the main collectible being pages of an actual game manual that give you additional context on the world and mechanics. But it's tied down and ultimately dragged-under by an unnecessary overfocus on combat that isn't rewarding to play and isn't satisfying to beat. It wants to be Zelda Fez Souls, but in trying to serve multiple masters, it ends up serving none of them very well at all.

_childDocuments_.review: Good mix of puzzles and action, also has accessibility settings for those who don't like the action. Feels fulfilling to complete the game and get the "good" ending! _childDocuments_.review: GOTY 2022. This is easily it for me. I was enthralled by this game start to finish and beyond as I continue to aim to solve its many extra mysteries and puzzles. _childDocuments_.review: A great game. If you fondly recall memories of internet-less age, playing oldschool action adventure games, learning tricks and secrets by reading signs, recognising few words, and analysing pictures within an enclosed intruction book of foreign language, (or you wish to experience such 'thrills'), then Tunic is a game for you. I'm all for "get gud", but the character is simply too slow for what it's put up against, and some of the hitboxes are so insanely huge that they can't be blocked or dodged. They are an unnecessary and frankly unfair difficulty spike in what is otherwise a very charming and rewarding journey. _childDocuments_.review: Very beautiful but very inconsistent.You can fight the same enemy doing the same patterns and get different results. Sometimes you parry and they're stunned. Sometimes you parry but it's ignored and their attack still reaches you. Sometimes you dash through the enemy and can backstab, other times your dash is blocked by that enemy's knee, other times you dash in their back but their attack gets instantly redirected to you anyway so their sprite gets flipped 180° before the end of your dash. Sometimes enemies are stunned from just a basic attack for no reason. Some enemies can dash backwards + lunge forward and hit during a single attack animation of the player. It doesn't happen frequently but when it does you have no way to dodge it. Movement is extremely clunky with the teleport dash because frequently there's only 1 tile to teleport to and it's not in one of the 8 targetable directions. Most of the game is searching for 1-tile gaps, hidden paths to chests , which is ok when we see a chest and look for a path, but it becomes ridiculous when the chest is hidden and the path is hardly noticeable so we have no clue there even exists something to search for, AND hidden paths to progessing the story, which is ridiculous especially for the west hero grave where the game tries its best to convince you that there is no way to go west anymore at that moment. Some walls have to be bombed but there's no visual hint about it. Frequently the access to a later zone is denied (even though it wouldn't be a big deal to allow the player to access it early) but instead of making it clear and blocking the player early the game lets you wander in and bump your head into every wall until you finally give up and try another zone. Some musics are way too close to zelda musics. The lore is very messy, going in all directions. There's an infinite production of power supplies going on but actually just a few dozens are needed to power the entire island. It's trying to bring a very industrial explanation to the global divine atmosphere of magic in the game. Wood objects like planks and ladders disappear during nights and reappear during days. Several items are barely useful and not relevant to the story, obtained at moments that feel very random.

_childDocuments_.review: To play and 100% this game blind was an incredible treasure. Discovering just how much the game offered and learning things as I went on kept me completely hooked. I loved all of the exploration, especially with its very frequent rewards for curiosity. I yearn for the next time I feel as much satisfaction in discovery as I did here. It’s not often a game doesn’t spoon feed you everything you need to know, but rather lets you deduce most things yourself. Whether it’s through the found pages of the most interesting instruction booklet I’ve ever seen, or simply trying things out, I love it. Puzzling out all the puzzles and decrypting the game’s unique language to understand Tunic in its entirety was immensely fun and satisfying. Although all of that was optional, I wanted far beyond the bare minimum. I wanted to experience everything the game provided.With everything alongside the amazing soundtrack I’ve listened to countless times both inside and outside the game (it’s actually how I found Tunic in the first place), every moment is made that much better. Now I can listen to it with personal memories and emotions attached as well.In short, I really enjoyed all this game had to offer. Some real effort went into making it, and I gave the effort it wanted right back to it. 10/10.Read the manual. Use what you’ve learned. Persevere. Get a notebook. <3

_childDocuments_.review: Tunic is one of those games that it's almost impossible to talk about in any depth without spoiling at least something. I shall attempt to be vague... but I can't write a review without talking about the game. If you absolutely, positively, 100% want to avoid ALL spoilers for 'Tunic'... then what are you doing reading reviews of it anyway?! It's good! Go play it!But that said, the fact that there is so much to it that it's difficult to discuss completely spoiler-free is a strength of 'Tunic', I think. There are so many layers and secrets and secrets within secrets to this game that even saying that is, technically, a spoiler because finding that out doesn't come until you're a fair way into the experience. Yes, the "Puzzle" tag is on this one for a very good reason."Oh, it's a Legend of Zelda homage. Of COURSE it has puzzles." I can hear the hypothetical snarky reader say. So I want to make this clear: LoZ games are action adventure games with puzzles. Tunic is the reverse - a hard-as-nails puzzle game with an action-adventure surface level. And yes, 'Tunic'  be played most of the way through on that surface level but a LOT of the experience would be missed.This, however, is Tunic's greatest weakness. Anyone who looks at this an expects a straight-up LoZ-style metroidvania will probably be disappointed by it, or frustrated by the difficulty of the brain teasers. Because let's be honest, as  an off-bran LoZ game this is pretty light. Combat doesn't have a load of depth, traversal doesn't feel that great, and very few of the items actually allow you to access more of the world.Indeed most of the really good traversal options are instead hidden behind player knowledge which is earned over the course of the game. This puts an interesting twist on the usual mechanic of "find thing > open path". Here you learn things, you as a player, and that knowledge opens things up for you. It's extremely clever at the expense of possibly ruining replays.I'm very glad I played this game even if I did have to look up some guides by the end. It's absolutely worth the asking price, and I hope that you buy it and enjoy it as much as I have.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fantastic, I loved the mystery/intrigue of the world and was hooked until I completed it. Honestly one of the better, more compelling games I've played in recent years. And definitely amongst the most clever and creative.(++) Awesome world filled with many, many secrets. It's an absolute joy to discover stuff, and was an even greater joy to see all the layers I missed after I completed it. No real tutorial, and it works great (mostly)(=) A lot of the gameplay is typical zelda/metroidvania stuff. _childDocuments_.review: It's like an old school Legend of Zelda game (NES, A Link to the Past, Link's Awakening), but with Souls-like dodge, revive and flask mechanics. Combat can be challenging, but difficulty is adjustable for an easier experience. The real meat of the game comes in its willingness to let the player figure everything out for themselves. There are dozens of secrets for you to figure out on your own, with little to no guidance directly given to you (unless you know where to look, that is). And, best of all, the game is a joy to look at. Cute. Adorable even.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: People often compare it to The Legend of Zelda (particularly Link's Awakening, Link to the Past, etc.), combined with the combat difficulty of Dark Souls, and Fez-like puzzles; but while all that is true, it must be emphasised that the game has oodles of unique spins, features, and charms all of its own.Rarely have I played a game as enrapturing as this one. The wanderlust the game instils in you is addictive, the combat is challenging but highly, highly rewarding; the puzzles are tough, but make you feel like Sherlock Holmes when you finally do solve them.It's best played with an XBox controller, and going in as blind as possible. It's very easy to be spoiled on the game! There's secrets and hidden things everywhere, all over the place.The care and attention to detail in this game is astounding, and is truly a tour de force from the sole developer behind it. As someone who's been waiting for the game for all seven years of its development—someone who signed up for the mailing list back when it was still called "Secret Legend," someone who played the demo of TUNIC all the way back at TwitchCon 2017—I can say that the wait was worth it.The soundtrack is fantastic, the art is beautiful, the gameplay is refined.Side note: if you're a Vtuber, this is an excellent game to use dynamic Vtube lighting on! The beautiful lighting of various areas lends itself very well to that effect.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: Really good game, like a mix of old school Zelda, Dark Souls and Hyper Light Drifter.It doesn't explain anything to you (except kind of, with an ingame instruction booklet), you'll have to figure things out for yourself. The feeling of exploration and discovery is one of the main points of the game, so don't spoil yourself by looking things up in a wiki or reading too much about the game before playing it.The amazing instruction booklet mechanic alone makes the game worth playing, but it's hard to explain without spoiling too much.The combat is simple but satisfying, it's easy to die if you're not careful and there's challenging bossfights.If you like the old 2D Zelda games, souls-like combat, exploration and figuring things out, you will love this.

_childDocuments_.review: When this game was first announced, I remember seeing that it was made by a guy in Halifax (the city I'm from) and I got really excited. The aesthetics really stood out back then and I wanted to throw some support to Andrew and his game. Throughout the years preceding the release, I forgot about the game, but I got into game development myself. I worked in a local game studio and heard about this guy through a bunch of random pipelines of my life. He was still at it.I never met Andrew but I couldn't believe he was still getting funding. I ran into his roommate one time at a bar and he said he was working day and night to bring this thing to life. My coworkers knew him, and I have a friend who is friends with his wife and my god, he was just putting his all into this.By the time the game was getting close to release, Death's Door came out right before it. I remember thinking to myself how I really was itching for a top down action RPG. I wanted to wait for TUNIC but Death's Door just looked so charming so I bit the bullet.It was fine.I left that game thinking, "maybe I just don't like the genre anymore?", It all felt so done already.After years and years of waiting for TUNIC, I just lost all hope. This game was so over-hyped in my life throughout the years of murmurs on the streets and console generations that went by. After Death's Door, I just didn't care anymore.I bought the game around release to support the scene but I let it sit...and boy was that a bad idea.This game is everything.The amount of times my jaw went to the floor. It is charming. It is inventive. It is a passion project where you can feel the amount of time that has gone into it. This is one of the best games I've ever played.You've heard it before, but the way TUNIC hides its secrets is just something that makes me happy.It is a puzzle game, inside a puzzle game, inside another puzzle game. I don't suggest this game if you're not interested in sitting there with a pen and paper sometimes, but that ♥♥♥♥ is for me.So thank you, Drew. Thank you so so much
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: Whilst overall I enjoyed my time with the game, and intend to keep playing after credits, I have two complaints.Firstly the language. I like the aesthetic of a game being in a fictional language. However this only really works if the language is meaningless and is only there for aesthetics. If interesting or useful information is being conveyed in a fake language then taking the time to diagram it out is just annoying. I think an improvement would be for the language to slowly translate over the course of the game. Keeping the aesthetic but also eventually actually giving the mechanic. If I need to put the game down and go looking on the internet for a translation, risking finding spoilers, then that's somewhat of a failing in my eyes. Secondly, my most significant gripe with the game. The parry. (yes, there's a parry). For the most part it's unneeded throughout the game. However for the final fight it feels like a very important tool. Frankly it doesn't really function well. It has a wind-up time and it's time of effect is far too short (even with the buff). It's too difficult to trigger, sharing a button with block. The animation can't be cancelled, so you're left vulnerable whilst it's winding-up. IMO, a parry should be a move you trigger the moment there is a signal of an incoming attack or at the moment an attack hits. More often than not I would get hit because the parry was still winding-up as the attack hit me. Or I would trigger the parry the moment an attack was telegraphed and the parry would be over by the time the attack landed. This is far too wordy now, but I could go on, fuelled by my frustration.Everything else about the game I really liked. The manual pages idea was excellent. The music and visuals are great. Exploration was wonderful, and is often rewarded. There are a ton of puzzles and mysteries that I feel I've hardly scratched the surface of. I'm looking forward to continuing to play until I solve everything or the game wears thin.TL:DR? It's excellent. Really good. But, useful info hidden behind fake language kinda annoying and the parry mechanic is terrible.(played most of this offline on my Steam Deck so recorded hours might be wrong)

_childDocuments_.review: Fun, cute game for about 70% of the game, up until you reach the point where you need to gather the last key item (LoZ style, three-count) in order to progress to the last leg of the game. Most of the game is pretty forgiving, with enemies *either* being annoying to fight overall and rarely coming in groups, or being trivial, but often coming in groups, sometimes with the more annoying mobs mixed in to teach you target priority and how to use your kit.The bit that ruins literally the rest of the game up to that point for me is when they decide to suddenly and jarringly pit you against swarths of strong, lithe, and agile enemies, or enemies that two-shot you (with several upgrades to your defense) with frequent, wide-range attacks and no stagger opportunities. That all could be forgiven if the boss guarding the third key item wasn't literally the worst designed boss in the game. Frequent, wide-sweeping attacks with extremely long active frames that make most of even your most perfectly timed dodges pretty much pointless, and only leaving opening for maybe one attack (which with fifth level attacks do maybe the tiniest bit to his huge healthbar), and he basically two shots you with any little thing he does. The gameplay skill requirement skyrockets out of nowhere, starting from baby steps, to okay, gotta be a little competent, to *be a god or you dont get to experience the story.* ♥♥♥♥ design. ♥♥♥♥ boss. Can't even progress the story because just trying to fight this thing is more infuriating than its worth. If you like souls-like games, there are better to play, and if you like story, dont bother, this game won't let you experience it without taking what patience you have with it.
_childDocuments_.name: TUNIC

_childDocuments_.review: Tunic is a fantastic and innovative Metroidbrainia.  I instantly fell in love with my first 10 hours in the game.  I've never seen anything like the way it incorporates the tutorial into the very fabric of the game, it makes exploring this world and story as deeply rewarding as any game I've ever played.  The layers of secrets and puzzles are woven together in a sublime way.That said, the ending, and the drip feed of lore really hold this game back.  There is a really unique and deeply intriguing story here, but even biggest geeks in the online community only seem to have a sketchy idea of what exactly is going on.  Just like Animal Well this game needs the full weight of a passionate community to puzzle out all of it's secrets.  However, here even after the community has had a few years to ponder... we still only have a sketch of what the game is saying with it's story, and that took some heroic work by the community.  Furthermore, this is a game about exploration and discovery, and you need a deep mystery to really make that discovery meaningful, and the Dev's made a fantastic mystery here.  However, after the work that the community has done to puzzle out the story, it feels bad that there is only enough detail for a sketch of the overarching story line. My only other criticism is are the difficulty spikes.  The game starts out difficult then after you get a few power-ups becomes very easy aside from two boss fights.  Both of which are legit difficult.  I don't mind a hard boss, especially in a game that is trying to be baby's first Souls-Like.  Here it just felt encounters fell only on one extreme or the other.  I clearly have a couple nitpicks, but Tunic is truly a wonderful game, and I would highly recommend it to anyone looking to relive a 2D Zelda like experience.  The exploration, graphics style, and game play are second to none.  It has inspired a deeply loyal fan base for a reason.  Just don't let that community set your bar of expectations too high, i.e. that this is a perfect game.  I fully bought into the hype train before playing this one, and it mostly lived up to that impossible expectation.  I just wish I had went in cold and been surprised by how fantastic this game was even with a few minor flaws.  Thank you to the Dev's for making something so familiar and so unique at the same time, and thank you for creating a mystery that is clearly sticking in the mind of this player.  I had to care a lot for the game to be puzzling it out this intensely.

_childDocuments_.review: I went into this game thinking it was a generic, cute, top down, indie game. Some souls-like elements, some hack and slash, with a unique in game manual gimmick. _childDocuments_.review: Tunic has great potential - like the casual Zelda games - but it doesn't strike the right balance between punishment & reward.It should've been non-stop fun & intrigue to keep you engaged for hours. The presentation is great, there's plenty of mystery and they've packed in lots of great ideas. It has a universal appeal and should appeal to a wide range of players, right?Unfortunately, though, too many of the game's mechanics are too punitive, too miserly, and too finicky to actually be fun.Examples: the relentless berserker bosses, or the non-replenishing consumables, or the special moves that require such precise timing that you might never be able to use them.If you can overlook all that and persist through to the ending, you might find that kinda cheap & insulting, too. It seems to be inviting a replay, but I can't see any reason to bother, when it already stopped being fun.So ultimately, I don't think Tunic is something I'd recommend to anyone I know, except as an example of how to undermine your own hard work and fall short of greatness.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr - Quite fun, do recommend, but the overall difficulty pacing, puzzle-aspect, and the combat satisfaction could be worked on. Overall, I enjoyed it, but I also have a lot to say about it.I feel like the game has an incredible potential, with its unique concept and mesmerizing graphics - however, what was built on top of that was a little underwhelming.First off, difficulty: I felt like most of the games difficulty was heavily biased towards the bosses, as I rarely died throughout the whole game, except for dying like 50 times on the bosses. Most of the game was idle route finding, while the bosses were sudden hardcore mode. This made a large portion of my experience feel rather dull, with the exception of boss parts being stressful. If the developers make a sequel, I'll love to see a more balanced gameplay. On the notion of bosses, the game gives you multiple times to use as you progress through their world. However, for bosses (where most of the difficulty is at = where you'll actually need items) there's rarely any time to switch between the items, so you end up using - and needing - only 2 types of items (excluding sword) throughout the whole game. It was disappointing to see so many types of unique items, only to never be really used.As for the idle parts, while this game overall is a puzzle-based metroidvania, most of the puzzles...well...weren't actually "puzzles." It was closer to guess-the-right-path using obscure hints and observations. There wasn't much of the "Eureka" moment / satisfaction that you usually get when  you solve good puzzles. It's more like "gah, I finally found the right path." I feel like a large portion of this is due to the nature of the game. The game tries to be mysterious, with your only guide booklet written in an unknown language. However, they overdid a little bit - rather than the healthy type of mysterious, the average player receives "I have no idea what's going on." The whole identity of the game, the booklet, does not provide much further useful information other than obscure hints on where to go and what does what. Although kind of useful, it doesn't feel that much more special than a bad map/guidebook. Or that might be because I'm stupid. I don't know.Finally, combat: while not bad, the combat was not as satisfying as I expected in the beginning. A fun combat (at least for me) is one where you narrowly dodge, hit, block some, get some good hits, immediately dodge again - you get my point. But for some reason, the game coded it so that the enemy backs off and dodges your attack almost immediately after it attacks, such that even if you successfully dodged an attack, rather you'll get hits off it or not is almost random. I feel like the attack pattern and difficulty is balanced enough where that "moving back" is not really necessary, but it moving back and you missing a large portion of your attacks really made the experience less satisfying. You also can't really interrupt your attacks with rolls, which makes you have to play wayyy more patient that usual. This part can't necessarily be considered bad, but at least it made in less satisfying for me. Yet, I can assure you that I definitely recommend playing game. While I pointed out various flaws, they are rather minor ones, and are closer to "If this company makes a new game, I'd like these to be considered." I did enjoy playing this world, and overall it was pretty good. If they make a new game, I'll definitely try it out - which is why I'm writing such a long review anyways.

_childDocuments_.review: Tunic deceived me.  I expected a cute isometric dungeon game like The Legend of Zelda: Link's Awakening and instead I was met with a cute isometric dungeon game like The Legend of Zelda: Link's Awakening with the difficulty of Dark Souls.  This game will test both your puzzle solving skills as well as your combat skills.  It will do this while playing a beautiful soundtrack with lots of stunning visuals and the most amazing hand-drawn in-game instruction manual that you have to piece together.  I will reiterate that this game is difficult on multiple levels.  If you want a true challenge, you could spend a lot of time with this game trying to uncover all of its secrets.  I will say that at times, the lock-on targeting can be a bit frustrating.  My other major complaint is that the game doesn't always lead you to an unlock directly so it is entirely possible to leave an area without knowing that you missed a key item or hit a switch.  Things are not always immediately obvious that you need to interact with them which is both some of the charm of the game, but also an added frustration at times if you don't feel like retracing your steps a bunch.  Overall, I really enjoyed Tunic and appreciated the risks that they took.

_childDocuments_.review: Tunic is SO GOOD.  I played Tunic in a frenzy.  During the few days it took me to finish the game, I played no other games, and booted up the game in every minute of my spare time.  This is not how I normally consume games, but there is something special about Tunic.  Tunic, on its face, is a three quarters view action adventure, with simple but beautiful and colorful graphics and a little fox hero.  The game wears its three biggest influences proudly on its sleeve.  Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past, Dark Souls, and Fez.  Imagine A Link to the Past but with 20 years of quality of life improvements, and a number of Souls-like systems grafted on to make things a little more challenging and interesting.  There are hidden paths everywhere, many of them using the barely controllable camera as cover.  The combat is excellent, you have a strong dodge roll with invincibility frames, a sword, and a variety of special items that use magic.  The combat is not quite as challenging as something like Dark Souls, but it is certainly no walk in the park either, especially some of the bosses.  The engine is fantastic, everything is colorful and the artstyle is consistent and interesting, the animation and controls are smooth as butter.  If the game was just this, it would get a strong score from me, as it is so well done, and the moment to moment gameplay is very enjoyable.  But there is more to Tunic.  There is an alphabet/language that has been created for the game.  All of the dialog and signage in the game uses it.  As you progress, you find pages of Tunics instruction booklet.  These do everything from providing information on the basic controls of the game to showing you maps of various areas, and more.  Unfortunately, the book is in foriegn language as well.  Yet between pictures/screenshots, various random english words, and logic, you can piece together a bunch of information.  As you explore both the game and the booklet more, you begin to notice more and more secrets within both of them.  At one point you will discover a secret that will lead to a cascade of other secrets and information.  It astonished me because it had all been right in front of my face the entire time.  As you go deeper and deeper into the game, your focus pulls back in a way that every time you revisit a screen, you might as well be in an entirely new area.  I have never played a game that pulled this trick off so well.  Another thing that I found astonishing about Tunic is its “puzzle balance”.  Never have I played a game that contained so many absolutely devious puzzles, some of which I just had to sit and consider for a bit, or turn over and over in my mind while I was not playing, but that were absolutely solvable.  I completed the vast majority of the game, and there were four things I looked up.   A puzzle that I couldn’t get at all and I’m glad I did, I still don’t fully get it.  Bad puzzle, in my opinion. A puzzle that I solved in my mind, but didn’t think I was right and was too lazy to go back and try it.  I was annoyed at myself after, and it was a good puzzle.A puzzle that I missed because I played a lot of the game with the sound turned pretty low due to my personal life, it was a good puzzle too.A puzzle that I figured out, but was going to require so much time and effort I needed to make sure I was correct before I committed.  Thats it.  I only had to look up four things in a game brimming with secrets and puzzles.  Just amazing balance work by the developers.Tunic should not, and can not, be missed.  It is an extraordinary game that impressed me more and more as I got deeper and deeper into it.  It is the middle of April and I can say with confidence that Tunic is one of the best games that will be released this year, and will be remembered as an all time classic.10/10

_childDocuments_.review: ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. I don't think I've ever been this pleasantly surprised by a game before in my life. The obvious reverence this game has for old-school 2d Zelda games is what initially caught my attention, but Tunic manages to surpass pretty much all of its inspirations in terms of sheer satisfying gameplay.The combat is simple, but in a well-balanced way that makes for a fair bit of challenge. I especially like the defensive options in blocking and rolling, since they both have distinct advantages and disadvantages. There's a variety of cool powers and items that you get over the game that have uses in both combat and exploration, and I always like when a game goes the extra mile to have mechanics serve more than one purpose. The way you upgrade your character is also really cool, and really incentivizes you to explore every last nook and cranny of the world. And the world is fantastic too, really distinct areas with that all carry a different type of serenity, which is a mood this game delivers on in spades while still being decently challenging. And a lot of that challenge lies in the bosses, of which there aren't many but they're all incredible. The second and fourth bosses (i think you might be able to do them out of order) especially stuck out to me, and all of them have that "climactic showdown" energy that you'd expect to see in some of Dark Souls' best bosses. A lot of people will compare this game to Dark Souls, but I think the big aspect that it carries over from that series is its most important one: making you respect your enemies' attacks.The true crowning jewel of this game, however, is the puzzle. Not puzzles with an "s", but a singular one. There aren't really any traditional dungeon puzzles like you'd expect to see in Zelda, but the entire game is structured like a huge puzzle, with several "a-ha" moments to find along the way. At the beginning, there really isn't much communicated to you about how the game works, and you slowly begin to piece it together by finding pieces of the game's instruction manual, of all things. This isn't your average instruction manual though, it's written in some sort of fake fantasy language and everything seems to be laid out as cryptically as possible. But finding a huge new piece of this book is immensely satisfying, whether that be a stylized map of the area you're in or a mechanic that you could have been using the whole time but just didn't know about. It doesn't feel like the game is withholding information from you, it just feels like uncovering more about the game is meant to unravel the world and its systems similar to finding items in a Metroidvania.All in all, this is the best game I've played in quite a while, and I'd highly encourage you to play it if even one of the aspects I've mentioned in this review appeals to you. This is for sure my Game of the Year for 2022, unless I somehow get totally blindsided over the next few months by something even more incredible.

name: Phantom Brigade
detailed_description: PRESS QUOTES 'Phantom Brigade is a tremendous f***ing video game' - Waypoint 'Wonderfully clever' - Rock Paper Shotgun 'I cannot overstate how cool this is' - Kotaku 'A triple-A experience ... made by an indie game studio' - VentureBeat About the Game Phantom Brigade is a hybrid real-time and turn-based tactical RPG, focusing on in-depth customization and player-driven stories. As the last surviving squad of mech pilots, you must capture enemy equipment and facilities to level the playing field. Outnumbered and out-gunned, lead the Phantom Brigade through a desperate campaign to retake their war-torn homeland. KEY FEATURES: Cinematic spin on the turn-based genre – Predict enemy movements, orchestrate precisely timed countermeasures, and hit “execute” to watch the physics-based action unfold in real time. An exquisite arsenal – Railguns, beam weapons, missiles, energy swords, and more! Rain destruction down upon your homeland’s invaders with weaponry salvaged from each enemy mech you defeat. Strategy – Make high-level tactical decisions on the world map, manage your mobile base, and decide how to apply your limited resources. Tactical combat – Take command of your squad in varied missions ranging from sabotage of enemy equipment and convoy ambushes to liberation battles and challenging outpost onslaughts. Customization – Featuring a rich customization system, Phantom Brigade enables you to fine-tune the performance of your mechs, install a wide selection of equipment, and access a wealth of cosmetic options. Prepare your squad for any challenge - in style. Highly moddable – Phantom Brigade has been designed from the ground up to be highly player moddable. Mix things up by playing the game with a community mod enabled, or try your hand at creating your own modded masterpiece! Destructible environments – It's not a proper game about giant mechs without destructible buildings! Phantom Brigade allows every square meter of each battle map to be destroyed. Shatter your enemy’s cover and collapse buildings on top of them!
