_childDocuments_.name: Phantom Brigade

_childDocuments_.review: Just because I don't recommend this game it does not mean that my experience with it was poor, I absolutely adore the combat system (arguably the main selling point) and the art style/aesthetic suits it perfectly. The sound design is on point and the UI, well, that could do with some work, but for the most part it's fine.My reason for not recommending this game is simply because I feel like it lacks features, hopefully something that future updates can add. For instance, no pilot experience/skills? this baffled me, maybe I'm too used to Battletech, but I was astounded to find out this didn't exist.The mech customisation does feel a bit shallow, after 6 or 7 hours I realised that most of the parts are just the same, but with different stats, granted there may be some more unique options later on, but that brings me to my next point: the game is repetitive. I'd like to think that I'm experienced with strategy games, so throughout my play time I never actually lost a pilot or mech, meaning that I ran with the same squad for every encounter. Maybe I should have took the initiative and changed my loadouts every so often, but honestly, I feel like if the game just gave me multiple convoys and multiple squads I wouldn't have felt so fatigued after only 14 hours. Again, this may be something that comes up further into the campaign, but if that is the case it should happen sooner in my opinion.And speaking of the campaign... the story is lackluster, which is fair enough, I never really play tactical games for their story, but simply going from battle to battle on the campaign map when the only thing in-between is watching the numbers on your mechs go up and down when you change something, it just gets stale.I've been pretty hard on the game so far, so time to talk about what I like. As I've already said, I love the combat system, the timeline system feels so fresh and innovative, and watching back the rounds at full speed is extremely satisfying (if only there was an option to watch the full fight back!) All the weapons are a joy to use, other than melee weapons which I could never seem to figure out to be honest. I've seen complaints about missiles, but I never had a problem with them, you can see the trajectory they are going to take, so you can plan accordingly and get to cover, I will admit you can't see their speed, so dashing to avoid them feels like complete guesswork.I'm getting bored of typing now so to summariseGood:Combat systemWeapon varietySoundArt styleBad:Mech customisationBoring pilotsNarrativeOverworld gameplayStale after so longI really, really wanted to recommend this game, but when I sat down and thought about it, I just can't. I would say if money isn't a problem for you and you like the look of the Timeline system, buy it and have fun for 10-20 hours. But if you're craving a more fleshed out experience, just wait for some updates.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: wishlist it and come back in a year.Phantom Brigade is a tactical mecha game that follows in the footsteps of Battletech and XCOM: you command a squadron of "walkers" as they fight an occupying army, battle by battle. The distinguishing conceit is the ability to preview enemy actions and then to plan your actions in response. The internal narrative for how this works is sparse: you have a "prototype" which does some predictive magic and spits out the preview you use for planning. I like to headcanon that you, the player, are the prototype: rather than imagine the brigade's commander issuing specific individual commands to each mech, second by second, the mysterious prototype simply says, "Go here. Kill this," and then the pilots faithfully do. No one knows how the machine really works because the machine is *you*.The trouble is that this conceit, while aided by a sprawling customization system and strategic overworld elements, is the game's only notable feature. The story is so sparse that your foe does not even have a name, nor the country you're liberating. Complex balance changes and critical bugfixes are still landing monthly; the UI suffers from numerous oversights that make optimizing your mech loadouts especially tedious. Crashes are common and performance is awful. Brace Yourself Games has a real gem on their hands with this game, but it needs a lot of polish to live up to its own shining heart.As of this writing, the game is essentially in open beta. With some time and considerable love, Phantom Brigade could be something truly rare and wonderful.

_childDocuments_.review: As a huge strategy gamer who enjoys mech games I really like this game but for the sake of transparency I have to give it a thumbs down for now.  As of writing this I'm 35 hours in.  I'll be comparing this game against similar games like Battletech, XCOM 1/2 and Into the Breach; which I have over 300 hours in across those.The good I will say first: the game has a very cool design and feel to it.  The mechs look slick and the variety of parts and weapons is awesome for creating unique machines.  I love that.  The battle field explosions and and special effects are pretty awesome.  Even the wonky melee system makes strikes look cool to watch. Seeing an enemy mech's legs get taken out or an arm blown off is always satisfying.  Battletech is a perfect example of doing all those things very well and Phantom Brigade has the ability to be a strong contender if they didn't fall short in many areas which leads to...My 4 criticisms.1. The outstanding issue is that the game play loop is exactly the same every battle, from the first tutorial mission to the last one you play, it's exactly the same with little to no variance.  Basically watch what units of yours the enemies are going after, plan to run your units away or shoot back, hit play and repeat.  This creates a "cat and mouse" type situation with your units and theirs all the time.  Once I figured out how to move the mechs around, got the hang of timing dodges and managing heat, that was basically the end of it and the game became boring.  If you have the Home Guard you can basically have them soak the hits and keep your pilots safe.  I can carry the game with 4 pilots pretty well now without breaking a sweat.  Adjusting the difficulty levers currently doesn't really make the game more fun, it tends to make my battles longer than necessary which is not enjoyable.2. You have all the time in the world to contest the regions.  Yeah if you lose a bit too much in a region you have to start over again but you don't really get punished because you can just come back.  If the region gets too "hot to handle" you just have to leave and let the enemy forces die down before coming back.  The enemy doesn't really push back once you have captured a region.3. Progression is not that rewarding right now.  Pilots don't have an upgrade system to watch them grow and I don't feel like I'm attached to any of them because their stories are pretty shallow if not non-existent.  Even if they go through a "random world event" and get punished they just lose a bit of health which I can heal up at any time.And there isn't really any incentive to upgrade the Mobile Base speed or additional items because see #2.  Expanding the mech bay to hold 4 mechs is probably the most impactful upgrade in the game and everything else is just fluff imo.4. The lack of a defined enemy and fleshed out story lines doesn't help me get attached.Suggestions to make the game better.---To fix issue #1, devs can do two things to battles: A) add more objectives with appropriate punishments and/or B) add in some sense of unknown or a random surprise which demands a player response.  A) Into the Breach and XCOM do this very well because the enemies are attacking not just your mechs but your objectives as well.  Having the enemy attack civilian buildings, civilians or deny you from key objectives raises the stakes and makes the mission a bit more challenging because you now have to balance priorities and make sacrifices.Examples of good mission variants: King of the Hill, Defend an Objective, Destroy Specific Buildings / Targets, Steal the Research, Assassin Missions, Attack and Defend, etc.  -- These are probably very easy to program in to the existing game because the assets are already there and the developers just need to add new "object flags" and adjust some numbers around unit/building health.Escort Missions and Carry the Payload are harder to pull off but can be very rewarding when designed correctly.  Lol I mean if the Convoy Missions had the enemy realizing they were losing and they started destroying the resources I'm trying to steal I'd be freaking out at the enemy for denying me Supplies and Equipment.  ("If I can't have it then you can't either!")B) Add randomness through unforeseen events.  In XCOM and Battletech, we don't know who the enemy is going to hit and shoot at so we have to plan around that.  Sometimes new enemies drop in and we have to deal with new problems now.  That creates fear and excitement.To fix #2, Set a Time Limit on the Story Line or on the Regions.  In XCOM, the game forces you to take objectives and upgrade as fast as possible because the AI has their own objectives and they are upgrading too.  You are forced into a race and if you lose too much then you get penalized with less resources eventually leading to the AI slowly strangling you into submission.  The fear of losing and punishments that XCOM 1/2 deal out make those games legends in the community; people actually respect the AI because it's mean.-- Side note: if PB had an Iron Mode, with a permanent game loss for losing all pilots or mechs then I would probably take my fights more seriously.To fix #3, add a Pilot experience system and have their skills scale with the type of mech and weapons they use.  As an example: if a Pilot is using Heavy mechs with Assault Rifles then give them Perks or Active / Passive abilities which are rewarded for surviving in that mech.  On the flip side you can add Penalties or Quirks for near death scenarios or watching team mates die.  XCOM and Darkest Dungeon are excellent at this.The Mobile Base upgrades need a reason to pursue them.  If I know the enemy is scaling their tech to find me faster or chase me down faster AND I have a Time Limit to complete objectives, then yeah I'm going to start prioritizing my base upgrades.To fix #4, just give the enemy a name and their true objective for "why they captured" the country.  The story is too shallow and the characters are not memorable in the least.  The Phantom Brigade fights against some ambiguous enemy that stole the land from the government.  Ok but "Who are the enemy?", "Why did they do that?",  "What is the ultimate goal of the enemy?" and "Why should I fight them?"  Outside of a 2 minute tutorial video about people being sad they are being subjugated I don't get many reasons after that to keep going.  In other games I know the name of the enemy, I know their purpose for why they do what they do and I know why I need to make it my mission to win against them.  In XCOM 2 I'm fighting aliens whose goal is to subjugate humanity to assist in advancing their evolution.  Into the Breach, giant bugs are breeding underground and destroying humans to take over the surface.  In Battletech's story line I'm assisting Kamea Arano during the Succession Wars to take back her kingdom which was stolen from her by her uncle and I need to free the planets while fending off other noble families vying for power.In those examples I'm consistently put into missions where if I don't accomplish that mission or beat that Story Line then something bad very happens.  Buildings get destroyed, lives are lost, kingdoms ruined, or in XCOM's case people get kidnapped for human experimentation.  Each mission is a reminder as to why the overall Story matters and calls out to us to take action so that we can mitigate damages, develop wins and create our own stories that are worth sharing to friends or online forums.Because Phantom Brigade hasn't fleshed out the background story of the enemy forces, why they do what they do and why you should care, the game overall lacks a soul that we as players can connect with.I love mech strategy games and this is great for me through the designs, battle field system, over world, wide variety of weapons and mech customization.  Overall an amazing game with lots of love put into it but it needs more work to realize it's potential.

_childDocuments_.review: Caught this on sale and was pleasantly surprised. I'm a mech-guy and easy to please with tactics games, so this was a gimme. It plays somewhere between chess and Adobe Premiere Pro. Phantom Brigade is not without flaws, it definitely under delivers on some fronts.Pros:-Physics based combat feels so good- The timeline-based system is well done- Solid variety of weapons and armor to use- Mechs are gorgeousCons:- Under cooked story- No pilot progression- UI needs improvement- Weapon balance is all over the place- You can't track projectiles- You don't get to choose where your mechs deploy on the battlefield- Figuring out how melee works is a pain (tutorial on this is non-existent)- Gameplay loop gets a bit stale with many hoursObviously there's some room for improvement but the core game is really great.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to like this game but it is very hard to recommend in its current state.First the gameplay, it is fresh, unique and fun, but it makes no attempt to try and change things up on you. In case you do not know, you can see every move that your opponent will do. It would be cool to have an enemy type that can scramble or even feed false information to you because the game gets extremely easy and really the only way they make it "harder" is by swarming you with hordes of enemy. Certain weapons are also pretty overpowered and really skew you to a certain playstyle and weapon types (missiles) as there really no counter play or countermeasure to them like chaff/flares or active protection systems. The campaign and story, there is no story really. You're rebels against your generic, oppressive regime with no name, no backstory, no real reason besides they really like killing civilians. There are random events, but they have no weight to the choices and really just feel like they implemented it to check off the "meaningful choices" box off. The mech design, the design of the mechs are great if you like the Japanese-style of mech designs. Though the designs of the mechs can seem pretty samey and no mech designs really pop in mind as an "iconic" one like ones you see in BattleTech or Gundam.The UI, this is such a pain point for the game. It gives such little information and is so confusing at times. Wish the game would give alerts to when my mechs are reaching critical damage and could better convey the damage received/dealt and the types of damage.This game definitely needs a lot of work and in its current state feels like a beta still. The story needs to be better fleshed out and the gameplay loop needs to be revamped to not feel so repetitive. The weapons definitely need an overhaul and rebalancing since missiles rule the meta currently and there's no reason to use mechs of a higher weight class as they usually get into the fight way too late with their extremely slow speed. The game is fun, but it is very short lived.

_childDocuments_.review: I read a lot of negative reviews when I first wishlisted this game and got turned off. Got it on sale when it updated to 1.3. I don't think it deserves as many negatives as it got. I'm really enjoying myself.UPDATE TO REVIEW 6/12/24: The game play cycle is a little dull after a while. Once you've seen a few fights, you've seen them all. The bosses only have slight variations. I think the game could really benefit from procedural generation on maps. Also, the time mechanic covers up a somewhat nonsensical AI. Enemy attacks seem almost RNG even if it doesn't make logical sense. BUT. I'd still recommend this game on sale, absolutely. It's fun but it needs some more updates. Personally, I want a level of difficulty where the enemy escort elite grinds my skull into the pavement instead of doing a silly monologue moments before I cut through several blocks of apartments, via laser cannon, to vaporize him. I want variation on bosses. Give me an ace pilot boss. I want melee enemy mechs. I want AI that makes logical moves. I want my time hacks to get interrupted more. I want more weapons and higher rarities. I want the enemy faction to invade me. I want the home guard to win some fights on their own. I want to be able to destroy civilian housing and instead of losing a mission, they just hate me. How can you give me a laser cannon and then tell me not to cut through a city block with it? It's impossible and I wouldn't want it to be possible because it's cool as hell. TL/DR: Still worth buying on sale but the gameplay loop is a little stale and needs more updates. I'm still enjoying myself.

_childDocuments_.review: Phantom Brigade is a good game and I recommend it. Everything is executed well, with no obvious flaws. I'm playing on Linux and I encountered no bugs while playing the game whatsoever. It just runs out of the box. Phantom Brigade presents an interesting twist on the TBT genre. The prediction mechanism makes things much more, well, predictable. One of the mainstays of TBT games is that you need to figure out what the opponent might be doing and devise a move that minimizes losses and advances your strategy. In Phantom Brigade this is exceedingly easy. You KNOW what's going to happen in the next few seconds, so you can plan accordingly. Therefore you can almost always plot an optimal path and firing solution for your units. Thus the fun shifts from divining the possible moves of the opponent to running countless simulations to find the best alternative. It's fun but there are very few surprises.What about the rest? You are on a campaign of freeing your home country from, so far, faceless minions. Your mobile base, a small dot on the map, moves around as you free region after region. You move around the landscape, chosing to engage enemy troops or attack bases. Your allies, the Home Defense Force, are fighting, too, and sometimes you join them in battle. There are liitle to no strategic challenges on this level. Sometimes enemy units chase you and you have to decide where to give battle, mainly to control how much enemy reinforcement can arrive. There are only a few special weapons that need ammo, so the only thing you have to look out for is your armor, which is easy because of the prediction mechanic. You get random missions (make sure to open the task item, so that you can see which symbol on the map corresponds to the mission) and events, not unlike the Battletech game by Harebrained. After battle you salvage parts or manufacture new ones in your mobile HQ to equip your mechs with them. There is a simple resource management component, which, after 20 h, hasn't made any difference so far. Pilots do not have skills or a career or anything. They are just another component of your mechs that can fail and has a special damage category aimed at it. This is supposed to change with an upcoming update.The graphics style is nice and clean, maybe a little too clean for a warzone, the animations are fine. The mechs are more like armored soldiers and less like tanks on legs. Even heavy frames look lithe. The sound FX are well-done and the score is, when I noticed it, some classical-inspired music. I would have liked something with a bit more punch to up the excitement but hey, I have a large collection of records. So, good game, but I'm laying off this game for now and wait for the pilot careers update to give it a new swirl.
_childDocuments_.name: Phantom Brigade

_childDocuments_.review: There is a good game in here somewhere but sadly for me the enjoyment passes quickly.Core concept, mechanics and presentation are excellent. Gameplay is general solid, there is a wide variety of weapons and mech customisation. Boss fights are a nice change of pace and do not overstay their welcome.Edit: There are 3 ways of getting Mech parts and weapons. Salvaged from downed enemies and allies, mission rewards or crafted from blueprints. Salvaging and mission rewards are fine but the crafting is awful, blueprints are rare and getting the one you want is even rarer. There is also no way to upgrade the equipment you already have leading to a boring, random loot treadmill made worse because game difficulty  seems to be tied to your average gear score meaning there is no way to get ahead of the curve. Mission design is a mixed bag, there is a good variety of maps and objectives, some are more fun than others. Difficulty is also a mixed bag, as the game uses some form of procedural generation in determining your opposition, this can result in a game where you are overwhelmed on your first turn because every enemy spawned right in front of you or a cake walk where they trickle in and die easily, neither outcome is interesting. As far as I can tell you can't choose your unit placement when starting a mission, so the first turn usually involves trying to get units into place without crashing, another needless frustration.World building, story and characters are non-existent, once the treadmill gets boring there is nothing to keep me invested. There does not need to be some epic tale of the tragedy of war, a small story involving the people of each region would have sufficed to keep me interested.
_childDocuments_.name: Phantom Brigade

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: The game starts out fun enough, having an interesting design and mechanics that almost seems like a blend between XCOM and Into the Breach. But the interest it garners starts to wane as the game suffers from a laundry list of issues that grew increasingly frustrating until it started to outweigh the fun. In it's current state, I cannot recommend others play it.---I went into this game with a positive mindset as I was looking forward to this game's release since I saw the trailer for it during E3 some years ago, and was excited to see the notification once it released on Steam. Not really much of a story on the campaign startup, just "Bad guys attacked, and now the good guys are gonna save the day", as much of a reason as any in many strategy games so I don't really hold the lack of depth against it.I play through the tutorial style beginning battles and everything seems pretty good at first since anything I notice or run into that doesn't seem right or doesn't make sense I just write off thinking "Oh, well the game probably hasn't explained this yet or there's probably some nuance there I'll learn later." But then after I've liberated my first province the tutorial is pretty much over, and as I play through a few more battles and liberate a province or two the questions or issues I'm having are stacking up.Like how am I supposed to tell when a missile salvo is going to land on one of my units so I know when to make them dash out of the way? The game tells me how long it'll take one of my missiles to reach the enemy, but apparently if an enemy does it I either just have to guess when to dash or devote a unit's entire turn to running and dashing like a madman to avoid taking a face full of missiles.Why are all my shots missing, or why am I doing a pittance worth of damage? The game will give you a number when selecting a target to attack that ranges from 1-100, with 100 being the "Optimal Range" for a weapons attack. Turns out this really only means that your shots will deal full damage...if they hit...accuracy is apparently up to the will of god who's busy looking the other way. I watched my sniper spend two turns shooting one stationary unit at optimal range, with an upgrade to reduce scatter which is apparently the only thing you can do to affect accuracy, and got to witness the 8th wonder of the world as 14 of the 15 shots just wizzed by the head of the mech equivalent for the broadside of a barn. Or how about watching my shotgun unit deal only 25% of the expected damage when standing directly behind an enemy unit at optimal range. The hell is the point of the optimal range if half the bullets are just gonna sail past either side of the enemy? You wanna try and stand closer so more bullets hit? I'm sorry but we'll have to significantly reduce the damage of your shots since you're no longer at "optimal range". What do you mean that defeats the purpose of a shotgun?Why can't I see damage values on replay? I plan out a turn, hit execute and watch mine and the enemies actions unfold. When a unit takes damage you'll see values pop up above them when it occurs, and you'll typically use that to figure out how deadly an enemy unit might be or how effective one of yours is (cue useless shotgun unit replay). But there's a lot happening, I cant' watch everyone at once, so I'll just hit "Replay" to watch the turn play out again. Except, now the damage numbers are gone...?????...like how is such an obvious issue not addressed? Also for some genius reason you can't even watch a replay of your winning turn. The game just immediately take you to a victory screen so hope you didn't miss anything cool or important in that last turn.I thought it'd be cool if when replacing parts on my mechs I could have a side by side comparison of stats so I can tell which parts I prefer, but I guess I never considered how fun it might be if the UI were excruciatingly difficult to parse. Wanna see how this upgrade will affect your gun? Guess you'll just have to equip it, then unequip your gun, then find said gun in the inventory and compare what you see to what you remember to see if you like it or not.There's an upgrade tree and I'm not sure why. There are about three of four upgrades that mean anything, and then the entire rest of the tree just looks like pointless filler. Wanna spend half your supplies and 15 rare components you don't have yet to increase your scanning range by 5% when moving in stealth mode in the overworld? Like 95% of the upgrades have nothing to do with the actual core gameplay and are so boring/pointless it feels like they were put in there as filler rather than for any actual reason.There's swords and axes, so I thought it might be cool to make a melee unit. Didn't take long to change my mind after learning melee weapons are basically still in their early access phase. You get this red attack zone you can place down when attacking with it, obviously with the intention being that anything in the red will get hit, except the part the game doesn't show you is where your mech pilot puts on a blindfold right before any melee attack and pretends everything except the enemy is a pinata.There's so much more and I could go on, but the short of it is that the game is plagued with so many issues that range from gameplay bugs to poor UI choices. Some of these issues are so evidently clear it's baffling how on earth they made it into the release version. Perhaps in the future some of these issues might be addressed in a patch, but as it stands right now this game feels like an undercooked Early Access title and I cannot recommend others play it in it's current state.
_childDocuments_.name: Phantom Brigade

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those cases where I wish one could give "mixed" review, but as I had plenty good times and it entertained me enough to push through the campaign, upvote it is. Phantom Brigade has very solid and enjoyable core gameplay, but falls short on promise due shallowness and lack of variation on almost every area.The core idea is combat, where you plan actions of your squad five seconds into future, while seeing prediction of enemy actions. After planning the timeline you watch actions unfold, with mechs exploding, missiles flying and buildings crumbling. The good stuff. Between fights there's customization, where you can build and customize every part of your mechs. Then there's also the map metagame, where you move with your base from province to province picking fights until you are ready to take on the capital. All good so far, you can see the good stuff in the trailer too so no point explaining more.Then the problems: Maybe biggest issue with the combat is the AI, which at least feels like every unit every turn randomly picks a target, tries to move to shooting range and shoots. Even if the target is behind a mountain and there's better options right next. Every AI on it's own, no teamplay. No sense of self-preservation nor idea of cover, rush on the open. This most of the time reduces the combat into moving the target lottery winners into cover and taking easy shots with rest of your squad. Rinse and repeat every turn until done.Other problem with the core gameplay is lack of mission variety. It's only elimination. While there techincally is capture target missions, the map design practically always forces you to go for elimination anyways, as standing the required two turns on target middle of the map on open is suicide. And it doesn't make difference anyways, you get parts and scrap from the destroyed enemies too.Then the metagame. It tries to be something akin xcom2 i guess, with the moving base thing. Ecxept there's complete lack of meaningful choices. When you win a province it is yours. If you fail to win province, no biggie, regroup and try again. The enemy never makes a move, and their numbers are based on your progress, so there's no time pressure outside the single province you are currently attacking (which you can keep retrying anyways). It also does not matter which provinces you take or ignore, all the same.Customization? It's fun for the first few provinces, until you realize you have seen it all and it's just same parts with bigger number for the rest of the game. No new weapons, no more interesting subsystem choices. Just small number increases. And even if you are stat minmaxing fan, that too becomes a chore because the ui lacks compare window. And the part levels don't help either, as parts have perk(s) that can make five levels worse version of same part better, but you won't see that other than hovering on the parts one by one. Graphics also lack variety. It's all same continential europe thing with same hills, trees and grass. Small town, factory, enemy base or highway. On final mission a city.Story? There's not much of that. In beginning, red team attacked your country. Now you want to take it back. In the end people are happy that red team has been removed. Who were they? Who are you? Why the war? No one knows. Or cares. There wouldn't really be difference if it started from first mission, as you would get that the red units are enemies anyways.There's the biggest issues, few smaller things here and there. Bugs weren't an issue for me, so that's a plus. As a conclusion I would say get it on decent sale. Doesn't quite live to the expectations of the full price tag.
_childDocuments_.name: Phantom Brigade

_childDocuments_.review: So far - Really enjoying it! Campaign map is maybe 7x the size than I was expecting, which is good or bad depending on what you want out of this.Very refreshing take on the "tactics-style" turn based genre.  You may feel like an genius on some of the stuff you pull off in this game.  Even after the 12+ hours I'm still flipping through replays of turns to see things in better angles.Some clear feature omissions leave i from being the most solid of recommends:* No gear compare on the loot screens* Lots of UI clutter and some tooltips that sometimes need more tooltips* Very redundant "random battles" on the worldmap.I'd also LOVE an optional full replay of the WHOLE battle after a fight.
_childDocuments_.name: Phantom Brigade

_childDocuments_.review: I don't usually review games but I wanted to explain where this game is at in early access, from what I see 20 hours in, the mechanics are there, the game runs well and its very good.  What it lacks aside from its core content (traveling the map, engaging in fights) is other things you can do, the crafting system is awesome but fairly shallow, random world events are cool but i haven't been very impacted by them yet, and aside from attacking a convoy you don't typically have many objectives besides kill.  ( for the developer ) I would take some more pages from games like xcom for fleshing out what else to do as the player, missions would be a lot more interesting with some variation in the objectives.  I would also make events in the world that create special, very difficult missions with very elite units that can give you good\unique gear for your units.  And lastly is the invaders could do with maybe some more explanation as you explore the world. overall the game is good mechanically and the content that is there is fantastic, I just want more of it.
_childDocuments_.name: Phantom Brigade

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to start by saying that I like the game. But it needs a bit more variance in combat and mech refits.The 5-second turns and prediction mechanics is a lot of fun and the combat is cool as hell. Mech modifications are a bit limited though. Once you find a build that you like, you are usually just adding more powerful parts of the same type to your mech over and over again. There are different types of weapons that differ in heat, range, damage, etc, but again once you find something that works you stick to it. Missions are almost all the same, the combat map differs of course but it essentially boils down to "destroy every enemy on the map". This game lacks variety in missions and after a while, it gets a bit tired & repetitive. The final mission offered some relief from the basic formula but in the end, it ended with all enemy mechs destroyed. The objective is to liberate provinces, but there are too many of them, and the game is too long for its lack of mission variance. Some things I would like to see: Combat replay. Missile impact time. More mission variance. Shorter campaign and voice audio for deeper immersiveness.
_childDocuments_.name: Phantom Brigade

_childDocuments_.review: This is an enjoyable mech squad based tactics game with a refreshing combat system which takes a while to get used to. You move your mobile base around on a campaign map trying to liberate provinces by attacking bases, patrols and convoys while trying to keep your mechs repaired and your pilots alive. There are base upgrades and a workshop to build items. The battles are fought on a time line that works in 5 second phases, the battles load quickly and are over quite fast so there is a lot of tactics action to be crammed into whatever time you have.Some tips for new players, don't try to command your mechs on the tactical map, focus on the timeline on the bottom left, scrolling left and right on this shows the actions of the next 5 second phase, only use the tactical map to select targets and move locations after clicking plugging the action into the timeline. Pay attention to your heat as there is no warning that your actions may overheat your mech. Scrap items when you have acquired a nice supply of loot, and upgrade your base fast to get the additional mech bays and also try to recruit pilots whenever you can.Some downsides are your pilots don't progress in any way, it would be better if you gained perks or some kind of progression based on missions, kills or events that occur throughout the campaign. The maps are all kind of similar, after liberating a number of provinces the biomes and maps don't differ at all. All the missions feel and play the same way, example is a convoy attack you can move to the capture point, but it is easier just to kill all enemies, which is how all missions have been for me. It would be better to have objectives that require you to diversify your tactics and use different mech builds, if pilot progression was a thing this could be combined to make a much deeper aspect when choosing what to deploy. The graphical style suits the genre and setting well, and the mobile base, upgrades, workshop, world map travel and random events add another nice management layer to the game. As mentioned by other reviewers it would be good if there was an option to watch the whole battle after a mission is complete, perhaps in a cinematic way where you can scroll or change cameras, as the time line control creates some tense moments but it is hard to pay attention to everything in the short 5 second bursts of action.A refreshing tactics game that is worth a play, there is potential for the developers to add quite a lot to this game to make it even better.
_childDocuments_.name: Phantom Brigade

_childDocuments_.review: This is turn based Armored Core and it looks amazing to boot. If you want to live out your favourite Gundam anime having a bunch of mechs in a truck driving around behind enemy lines, then yes this game will fill that niche.When other reviews talk about the story and pilots being shallow it's because there is literally no substance. I don't mean the dialogue is bad, or the end was rushed, or there isn't much character development... I mean there is nothing. You play the tutorial and then you have one objective and one alone. Retake the capital city. Upon doing so you complete the game. There is literally NO story whatsoever.There are lots of random events throughout the game if you choose not to storm the capital on day one. These events don't contribute to plot-related storytelling. The random events have an interesting knock on effect. For example you celebrate the liberation of a town which locks you in place for a set amount of time during which enemies might find you. Sometimes you may receive a gift such as an unmarked box which could be anything from a bomb to a crate of booze. You can put either in storage and use them in later random events use the booze for Pilot's birthday or better morale after liberating a town. The bomb can be used to bypass battles or donated to the local militia.Pilots have no impact on gameplay. You can edit them any way you want like XCOM, however they don't come with randomized stats or backstories except for the first pilots who are losely related to the story. I believe these are on the development road map and will have an impact on the game at a later date.The game is hellbent on this idea of "trade-offs". And it's more off than trade. The other reviews are not joking when they say there's "upgrades" they'll never touch. You can avoid this issue by installing some mods that rebalance the research tree.I'm happy to see the developers listening directly to mod authors and players through their Discord server. The quality of life changes coming through are a god send and the devs are constantly improving modding tools.In terms of programming, the game is exceedingly stable for what it offers. The premise is you have a new technology that allows you to see 5 seconds into the future. During that 5 seconds you can move the slider back and forth previewing everything going on in real-time with no lag or stutter. If you've ever tried to make a game with time manipulation you'll come to realize it is an absolute ***** to make.The long and short is this game is Marmite. You either love it or you hate it... But it is mecha Marmite!! And I love Mecha!
_childDocuments_.name: Phantom Brigade

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of games like Battletech (And its videogame adaptations Mechwarrior & BATTLETECH.), I was actually really looking forward to Phantom Brigade. I don't think I've seen a game which uses a timeline feature for organizing actions like this before, at least not in this genre, so I was curious to see how that would play out. Add destructible environments and a mechbay to tweak your mechs to your liking on top of that, and you have a very intriguing idea for a game.Loading into the tutorial, I noticed two things:1.) The tutorial leaves something to be desired. You are told only the basics to help you get started, but concepts such as "Crashing", "Concussion", and lots of other things (Such as the destructibility of the environment!) are left unexplained. The game starts at a breakneck pace, and I think that a little bit more time could be given to the player to learn these systems in a controlled environment, or give players pop-ups explaining mechanics as they happen to you, or a glossary. Maybe it's explained later in the game after the first mission, but it's all fine, I can figure this out as I go.2.) The performance of the game is dubious. I'm running the game on a fairly high-end rig, not the best on the market, but pretty powerful:RTX 3080 GPU.AMD Ryzen 7 5800x CPU.16GB of RAM.Installed on a decent SSD.Despite this, I can't seem to push my framerate above 70-80 FPS in the tutorial mission, no matter what graphics settings I use (V-Sync is off, framerate cap is set to 240.). I've tried lowering the resolution to 1280x720p, changing AA settings, AO settings, putting the game in windowed mode, but it's as if the game has preordained that "No, you get exactly 73 FPS in the tutorial mission or less. Final offer.". At one point my framerate dipped as low as 20-30 during a turn when you get attacked in the town, which is pretty grim.I've tried every fix that's listed by the devs in the forums, as well as tweaks that aren't listed. I've looked into my GPU and CPU settings, downloaded drivers, messed around with the config files, just to see if I can find what's causing this bottleneck, but nothing. It's to the point where most of my """playtime""" is actually spent benchmarking the tutorial mission instead of playing the game.Looking in the Steam Discussions threads, it seems that there are other players that are having the same problems as me. There is no good reason for why performance should be this mediocre. The game's graphics are all in all fairly simple; no ray-tracing shenanigans here. If the tutorial mission has performance like this, I can only shudder at the thought of the game having a major conniption fit once you throw in even more enemies, more missiles, more buildings in later missions.As it stands, while I would love to play more and to give the game's mechanics an honest evaluation, the performance problems are a deal-breaker. I will keep an eye on it in the short-term, but unless there's a week one patch that fixes this, I will regrettably have to refund this, which is a real shame since it looks like a ton of fun.

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game. I really do.I recommend this game. I really do.I understand the developers' statement that it is literally impossible for them to add in a feature that shows a replay of the entire events of the mission after the fact. I strongly recommend that they look to Ace Combat for inspiration - I don't need a 1 to 1 detailed movie recap of everything, though that is nice, I just want to be able to see any kind of representation at all - even a very basic one - of the events of the fight. That's all. Because it feels nice, and fights last long enough having that reminder would be very nice.As-is, I think this game could stand to still get some more content updates. I would happily pay for expansions onto this - more mechs, making pilots more important (give me a real reason to care enough to have them eject in a bad situation, let me build a story around them individually!), and the aforementioned replay system (seriously - 2D icons over a wireframe map. Trust me, it'll be worth it.)I really do love the unique mechanics at play here, the time-system for combat with the predictive stuff - god it feels amazing. They clearly put enormous effort into designing it and it shows. This game is made with a ton of love.You may be hearing all this and wondering: why do you have so few hours played, if you love the game so much?Because, for reasons I cannot explain, every time I've loaded it up I've played one mission, gone "That was fantastic!", and then immediately tried (again) to hunt down a copy of Front Mission 3.Unironically, not a joke, I cannot explain this compulsion. It's made playing the game difficult to stick to.
_childDocuments_.name: Phantom Brigade

_childDocuments_.review: It has a fair share of smaller indie jank- most notably now, after patches, melee targeting is basically an arcane ritual that may or may not work. After 24 hours of playtime at time of writing I still do not totally understand how to consistently land melee weapons.Additionally, I do feel like I wound up seeing a lot of what the game had fairly quickly. Initially you're finding new mech frame types, new weapons, better and better parts, etc, and it's very exciting. Later on your main progression is finding workshop blueprints to make specific parts on demand, however eventually you end up with high-level versions of all the parts you want and you end up kind of settling into a specific niche. This is a shame, as the early game you really are taking whatever you can get and forced to adapt to odder strategies based on availability. While it feels great to eventually become really powerful after this, I wish it lasted a bit less.I think the game would have been better if it was a bit shorter and more of a sort of rougelike structure, one that forced you to use whatever you had and also could stretch out its content, however what is here now is pretty fun still. I'm not sure I'll actually finish clearing the entire country before I get bored, but I don't regret any time spent on it. Ultimately it's pretty fun, if a bit easy, and the main gimmick of the game with the timeline + prediction stuff is really enjoyable to mess around with.
_childDocuments_.name: Phantom Brigade

_childDocuments_.review: The game itself is amazing and fun, if flawed.I really enjoy the visual style, and getting to see the mechs in action never really gets old. The cinematic style of combat is beautiful. (Though I do agree there really should be an end of battle show you can watch to see the entire thing play out from start to finish) That being said, it needs a lot of help in the strategic department.When playing, I feel very few strategic decisions are required. I never feel like I have to make a hard decision. On one hand this does make decisions easy, on the other it gets incredibly easy to exploit. Relatively early on I had a setup that was effectively unstoppable, and I can reliably end every single engagement in 2 or 3 turns max, making reinforcements a joke. I.e. why even bother offering me the option to hold a point for 2 turns to get the resources when I can just blow up every enemy on the map in those two turns without risking my mech to damage? Or why have the entire enemy army focus one singular mech for the whole match? That just makes it easy for me to play keep-away with the one mech while the other three stand and free fire.I will say, comparing it to XCOM or Battletech is somewhat unfair as they are their own unique games and do play slightly differently. However, both those games made tactical decisions meaningful and important. If you chose one action, you were sacrificing something else (for better or for worse). I would often agonize over the possible choices I would have to make, often times sacrificing something significant for the long game. PB lacks those meaningful sacrifices. Sure they're there, but the impact isn't nearly enough to offset their benefit. (I understand a lot of people like not having to make those heavy decisions, but I am personally of the opinion that an amazing strategic game is one that requires you to do so)Despite being flawed, the game is fun right now, but give it a few significant patches, balance passes, maybe even a mod or two, and we're talking home-run.
_childDocuments_.name: Phantom Brigade

_childDocuments_.review: The predictive gimmick that makes the game standout (and it *is* fun) makes the player far too powerful. I've never played an easier tactics/strategy game. It's like playing a game with handicap mode on. It truly feels as though it should be a consumable that we manufacture and apply during the strategy layer of the game to be used as a costly/temporary benefit... I wonder and I am eager to see how the game might play out if I didn't get to see what my enemy was planning every turn so that I could avoid 90% of the incoming damage while guaranteeing nearly 90% output.After finding numerous flaws in the strategy layer of the game (roughly 90% of it imo), the game reeks of being a prototype. All of the sidequests I encountered provided 0 benefit to me, while only taking time and sometimes asking me to backtrack (which is akin to watching a loading bar, or buffer), but there's also infinite time so it's 0 benefit, 0 cost, nothing. Everything that's liberated does virtually nothing, despite initially appearing as useful strategic points (battery/armor regen, manufacture bonus). There's nothing to be found through exploration. All but a few of the upgrades (and there's a lot), provide no tangible benefit to the mobile base or my progress. I can "stun" enemies with smoke, I can jam them with ECM, etc... but I can also just easily outrun them with 1 of the first upgrades "Overdrive" or hide using "Stealth" making most of these upgrades counter-intuitive and borderline pointless given that their costs are insanely high if you're playing on anything but generous settings for salvage. It's easier for me to just ignore most of what's on offer on the "strategy" side of the game, while just bee-lining it from one mission to the other. I'm at the point where something from Slay the Spire would be preferred for how lame this ended up being.The only real fun to be had is maybe in the first few hours or so, while still getting familiar with the game and being under-geared/understaffed. It looks like there's going to be a lot ahead... but then hours later I have 4 mechs outfitted with tuned gear, and it's easy to realise that nothing's ever going to change except I'll gain a level, and so will the enemy to match me. I'll be replacing gear with similar or the same pieces that are just higher level, and it seemingly scales infinitely. The enemies are always a few levels higher, while proving to be an actual challenge somewhat against an under-geared squad of 2-3 mechs, that 4th mech  + tuned gear suddenly trivialised them.I got most settings set to difficult other than HP/DMG because it's not my idea of fun balance to create bullet sponges vs paper and will likely just pigeon-hole me into even less options to enjoy myself with. I decided to try and go for the "Liberate all Provinces" achievement as being my first objective, but it's becoming so tedious that I doubt I'll complete it. There are some real stand-out good things here though as I've spent as much time playing as I did ogling the Replay camera or fiddling with paint schemes. It's fun to set up an action sequence and watch it play out, and it's AMAZING fun the things that can be done (like shield charging through lighter enemies, knocking them over) but there's next to no challenge and since the game's not encouraging me to use different tools/strategies for every encounter (nor to prepare with contingencies of any kind), it always ends up being the same action sequence over and over again on slightly different looking maps after a little while. That's where it begins to stagnate and all of it's flaws start boiling to the surface. The only things that really threw me off was encountering Railguns for the first time.So... Fun, but feels more like an Early-Early Access game that needs *a lot* of work to be recommended. What IS recommended is that if these devs don't want to expand on this, that other devs out there take some of these ideas and find ways to meaningfully include them in future games of the genre, because there is something here with looking at.
_childDocuments_.name: Phantom Brigade

_childDocuments_.review: The core of this game is incredible. The little time gimmick is fun and provides a nice tactical element that I really do love. The art is fun and really feels good to re-watch some of the clips of battle as you go through your turns. Soundtrack is an absolute BEAST and I found myself just sitting there listening to the opening screen for a long time. After about 15-20 hours of game-play I started to get a little bored. The fun mech customization gets boring once you get to about threat level 7-10. You're just grinding for mats to try and get a different item with SLIGHTLY better stats. You also can't deploy more than 4 units. Kinda wish there was a way to unlock something that allowed you to deploy more units, or a couple tanks like what you get during the homeguard missions. The "plot" is as deep as Slay the Spires plot. You just run around the over-world waiting for random stuff to pop-up forcing you to make decisions, but it feels like they mean nothing. I would never recommend this game for it's full $30... not even 50%. I'm still voting a Yes on this because if you can find this for $10, grab it and you'll have a solid 20 hours of fun blowing up mechs, and then re-watching the bullets shred through your enemies.

_childDocuments_.review: Play the demoIt lets you play the first whole continent the timeline system makes turn based strategy interesting in how much you can control it but when you get into 2 vs 1 encounters it's as simple as hide the one that is getting shot at and shot with the other. In the missions with lots of enemies it gets very chaotic. Try to use cover to block the shots at the time they will get shot. Enemies tend to tunnel until something dies. Don't underestimate the sniper I believe called the Midway it's hard carried me in the hardest mission I played.

_childDocuments_.review: The "Just one more turn" but then it's 3 hours later feel is real but it's "Just one more fight".How long has it been since we had a truly fun mecha game? Well Phantom Brigade is certainly one and I'm glad I no longer have to wait for it and wonder if I'll actually enjoy the game.The playstyle is something only a handful games has tried on. Deciding actions 5 seconds ahead and watch it play out can have some very enjoyable and awesome moments cinematically happen before you.It has the XCOM world map feel of constant threats. Battles can be breezes but suddenly something went wrong during the planning and now it's a scrap, you lost one pilot and you have no resources to recruit a new one and must deal with the next fight one pilot short and possibly with damaged units as the enemies outnumbers you frequently.There's plenty of weapon variety and guns themselves comes in varied versions. Even if a mech loses one arm it can still use the weapon in the other. And if you're truly running out, you can always ram into enemies (Heavier classed mechs benefits ramming into lighter classed ones).Fights can get truly brutal, and greedy players will suffer losing pilots trying to make them fight to the very inch of their life instead of ejecting them.I wish there was more varied color combinations. Like we have 8 different "black-red-gray" combinations but not a single that's yellow and blue?I haven't seen much of the game yet. Only the tutorial zone and the next one. I dont know if the experience gets worse down the line but if it does I'll make sure to change my review.I'm excited to see more what Phantom Brigade will be down as I continue playing. And with the devs designing the game to be moddable from the start, I'm excited to see what the community makes down the line if I ever get my fill of the base game

_childDocuments_.review: im loving it. a great evolution and original spin on the xcom form factor that i like much more than the original. any small inperfections or issues other reviewers have been greifing about is a non issue considering how much fun you will have for 30 bucks.im already hypes af for the next game in this series and i´ve just started playing this one. it´s a gem.

_childDocuments_.review: Just picked up Phantom Brigade and as someone that loves Mechwarrior and Battletech it definitely isn't that.  What it is, is a strange hybrid of X-com with a different turn based battle style with JRPG mechs and the most forgetable campaign story arch ever made.  That being said is it worth playing?  Absolutely.  The game has some of the best looking map overlays I've ever used.  The timeline mode for fighting is very fresh as well. You can see my full thoughts here:
_childDocuments_.name: Phantom Brigade

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to recommend this game but can't quite do it.If you are a fan of tactical battles and mech customization, this will probably be a decent experience, particularly if you get it on sale, but there are just too many quality of life issues to fully enjoy the game.The battle system is very engaging but a number of important important pieces of information like damage and hit status in replay and missile destination/timing information aren't available. Navigating the customization system is unwieldy and lacking a compare feature, which is a must have feature in any build focused game.EDIT: Update 1.2 has largely addressed the above point.The AI is sub-par, often firing into hillsides rather than firing at a target right next to them. The campaign map has procedurally generated encounters which reuse the same maps, leading to many battles that feel repetitive as the AI runs into your guns the same way, every time.If BYG makes a sequel with QoL/UI improvements and replaces the generic open world battle map system with a more crafted campaign experience with setpiece battles, it would be a must have for me. As it stands for me now, Phantom Brigade feels like a mechanical experiment rather than a game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is super cool mech game, something very similar to what I've been wishing to have for years. There are two gripes I have with the game. First is the fact you can't have extremely precise maneuvers with regards to time (let me manually enter  in the amount of time a mech should be waiting!!!!). The second is that there's no post-battle real time viewer a la doorkickers. If they added those two things this would be an incredible game.

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting game with cool visuals, but not enough content to be worth the purchase. Even after 30 hours of persisting through to higher levels, I had seen about all the game had to offer after 5 hours or so. The tutorial has a few different kinds of mission, but all those objectives aren't ever seen again outside the intro missions. EVERY encounter simply has you kill 5-15 tanks/mechs on one of about a dozen maps.On the topic of difficulty, there's really no downside to losing a mech or a crew member, since they are so easy to replace, and crew don't level up or gain new traits that make them an asset. New recruits are identical to veterans. I want to like this game, but it's an unfinished product, and not really worth your money in this state.

_childDocuments_.review: It's not a bad game, it's just the same thing EVERY mission. The core mechanics are fun. The loot system isn't too bad but it could do with some more customization. _childDocuments_.name: Phantom Brigade

_childDocuments_.review: Although they are very different games, it reminds me a lot of "Into the Breach." I personally love this game. Its combat system is unique and in depth, while still being intuitive and easy to learn. It has a huge amount of customization, and I find  great joy in min-maxing each of my 4 robots. There are ridiculous amounts of weapons and armor types, and I find myself constantly changing weapons as I steal them from my enemies. Even though you can see into the future, the game is still challenging, especially when fighting patrols with higher combat power. The salvage system seems balanced, in that if I perform better I will receive more loot. Right now there are a few minor glitches and bugs, but other than melee weapons being very finicky, it is in great order and I would suggest it to anyone who loves mechs, addicting progression systems, and combat puzzles.
_childDocuments_.name: Phantom Brigade

_childDocuments_.review: Ahhh, this one could have been something special. Could have been the one that brought balance to the force and finally give us some front mission goodness dressed in tasty looking combat system. But alas, it's just a mirage.The game will trick you (it certainly tricked me to play it for almost 20 hours) into thinking it has more to offer than it really has. Nice intro cut-scene, voice-overs in the tutorial sections, mission structure the works, and then...just one of the most bland sandbox territory conquest I've ever seen.The  robots are good looking I guess (at least some models) but they offer pathetically little in terms of customization, essentially trying to find balance between heat generation, armor and speed suitable for that role, which is essentially simplified into literally what weapon you're wielding. Guys, the idea was already there, you could have just taken it for ♥♥♥♥ sake. Either go hard points like battle tech or allow shoulder carried missiles, shields etc that front mission sported. Why the ♥♥♥♥ would you miss opportunity to allow pilots to gain experience? To have skills. For ♥♥♥♥ sake front mission did 3 decades ago.It's so ridiculous it's not part of the package as the game begs for it. there's more things to be said, unpolished UI, inconsistent AI etc etc, but in all honesty not worth going into too much detail.The bottom line is simple, this one needed A LOT of more work, and I mean A LOT. But it could have been the one.maybe it still can if they provide some crazy level of DLC goodness, or at least modding support. But I doubt it. I feel the way prologue is designed is purposefully misleading and a little bit scummy. To developers, I cannot believe you blew something that had this much potential. Hire some people who can actually put some meat on this thing and go back to work.

_childDocuments_.review: The game was mostly ok, solid 7/10 in gameplay. Showed lots of promise. Story? None to speak of, but hey, with updates and eventual dlc it should have been fixed. Silence. no updates. No bug fixes. No real announcements. The devs got your money and got out. _childDocuments_.review: The base tactical game is solid and it's a really cool spin-off for the tactical RPGs, but lacks polish, balance, performance optimization and most importantly meaningful strategic progression. After some time you see all the game has to offer and you're going through the same motion over and over again, it gets repetitive really quickly, as the strategic mode doesn't evolve or provide any interesting context from one fight to the next. Needless to say the campaign has not replayability.The coolest part of the combat - the melee weapons are extremely limited in diversity and janky to play, it's a coin toss between missing the enemy, colliding with the enemy, which could stun your mech or doing a one shot kill of one or several opponents.The base upgrade tree is extremely boring - most of it is increase speed by 15%, increase visibility range by 15%, increase energy by 10... No pilot progression or XP. The mechs are completely customizable, which however means that there's zero identity to them. Creativity comes from limitations, if there are no limitations to how a mech could be built such as different classes of mechs they loose meaning. I don't care, if I loose a mech, it's just a bundle of parts that I can easily put on another frame. Given the history of the devs and how slow they're releasing content I don't see them fixing even a fraction of all the issues in the game. I guess they're too busy figuring out their pronounces. I can't really recommend the game at this price point.

_childDocuments_.review: One of my favorite games of the year so far. This has been on my radar for the last 5 years as a massive mech fan, and although development looked rough for a while, they took a ton of player feedback and the game has launched in an incredible state. Little to no bugs, incredibly high quality animations, a nice soundtrack, and event text bursting with emotion, Phantom Brigade's only flaw is its almost non-existent story, which only serves as a basic rationale for why you're playing the game. But you're a mech fan. You know what you're here for.The game's super innovative turn-based/real-time time rewind gameplay system is one of the coolest takes on turn based games I've ever played, and it makes you feel like you're creating your own Pacific Rim action scene in every turn. Couple with a customization system that is a cross between Armored Core and Battletech, and you have an incredibly robust mech experience. In a time where mech games are few and far between more than ever, Phantom Brigade stands tall as one of hallmarks of how fresh the genre can still be even after all these years.
_childDocuments_.name: Phantom Brigade

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not all that far in, but in the few hours I have played the game has been very promising.At its core, Phantom Brigade is a mech combat game pitting you against AI controlled mechs. It has an overworld map with enemy patrols and sectors you can move around to liberate, while replenishing your forces and upgrading your units (as well as you main mobile base). Mechs are customizeable and can be upgraded with parts you salvage from your battles to fulfill various roles, and parts themselves can have a wide variety of effects and upgrades applied to them to keep builds unique. The meat of the game is in the combat aspect, and I find it quite enjoyable. You effectively play in five second rounds, with you and the AI moving simultaneously. However - the important part of this is that you can see what your enemies are planning to do in that time, and this allows you to effectively read the future and micromanage your units for maximum efficiency. You can see when an enemy with a missile launcher is going to fire, so plan a move to have your unit being targeted dash behind a tall building right before they hit. You can see when an enemy will come around a corner and into range, so plan to hit them with your sniper rifle right as they do. This leads to some really tense moments and really good gameplay, and while you are frequently outnumbered and outgunned you always have a chance due to this system.Mechs can be damaged in combat, limiting their effectiveness, such as losing their arms/weapons or being slowed to a limp by leg damage. This applies to both the enemy and to your own mechs, and while you cannot target specific parts of enemy units you can still utilize their weaknesses in a strategic manner. For example - enemies are weak to impact attacks from behind, shields can only be held up for so long in one go, and you can circle around to the weak side of enemies to get extra damage on them.In 7.7 hours, I have done the little tutorial area, and fought quite a few battles in the zone after that but am nowhere near conquering it. The game has about 20 or so more zones at least after this one, and I have managed to build up four mech units (you only start with two) by this point. I have a sniper with an augmented rifle and close quarters precision SMG if needed, who can jump into position to hide. I have a marksman unit with a burst shotgun secondary attack for enemies that get too close, with its very high mobility allowing it that option. I have a unit with a burst shotgun primary and a shield that dashes in and out of close quarters combat, usually running down pesky enemy snipers. I have a missile launcher extremely heavy mech that can provide constant firepower upon the enemies, with a heavy shield that can be utilized if it ever is in danger.All in all, I recommend it if you are into this kind of game. It is very well presented and has a very good core gameplay loop.Edit: After a few more hours, my review still stands. However, I will say that this game does have a few minor annoyance. The UI can sometimes be a bit rough to navigate - it lacks granular controls for certain things like telling your mechs to "Wait," so you sometimes will need to fiddle with things to get what you want. The writing sometimes comes across as a bit amateurish, but the game is clearly crafted with love. I also lament the fact that there doesn't seem to be much in the way of progression for your pilots - they have traits and such but they don't see to actually develop in any way, and this is a huge missed opportunity I hope they improve upon in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: Specifically due to the unique concept, I give it a thumbs up. The main highlight of the game, synchronous tactical battles, looks very fresh and intriguing. It appears quite spectacular and dynamic, considering each turn lasts for only 5 seconds. It's a pity that the developers didn't include a feature to review the entire successful battle. Nevertheless, observing the battles here is quite interesting!However, during the cleanup of the third location, I realized how much grinding here. Out of 5 hours of gameplay, about 1.5 hours are retries. There are a bit too many attributes, which makes the game's balance somewhat fragile, requiring careful study of each characteristic. After each battle, you acquire new items and start everything anew. Also, I couldn't quite get used to the controls; even though the editor seems simple, what you intend to do doesn't always get realized immediately, which adds frustration to the experience.Apparently, I wasn't in the right mood to play it.I don't regret purchasing and trying it. Perhaps I'll return here in a year. But I would like to see more projects like this.
_childDocuments_.name: Phantom Brigade

_childDocuments_.review: Aight, lets start with the bad first:- Weapon balance is wonky, you will find weapons that are fantastic (missile launchers) and weapons that suck (canons). They will dominate your choices for mech design and make some AI encounters feel terrible.- Melee is... to call it a learning curve isn't accurate, it's a cliff. Suddenly it works and you feel like a god.- While I ran into the last map about 30 hours in, 90% of them I had seen and replayed endlessly by hour 20.- Some spawns can feel unfair, imo this is balanced by the fact some spawns are downright unfair to the AI.- There's not really any curveballs in combat, no differences from hour 5 to hour 45 of combat.the TL;DR here is if any of these issues look like deal breakers, its probably not for you. This game relies on the "15 seconds of fun" concept far more than most and if that 15 seconds is not fun for you at hour 2 it won't be any more fun at hour 20 or hour 45.That said, for the love of god it grabbed me. That 15 seconds had me enraptured for all 51 hours of my first play-through, one that cleared the map and did basically everything you could do in the game on the standard difficulty. Hence why I still recommend it, if you enjoy every time you get into combat even if it seems repetitive on the surface this game will grab you and you will have an absolute blast.Said combat is challenging at first, but once you understand the gimmick and start to learn to use cover and attack intervals to your advantage you'll begin walking your way through enemies. Discovering good squad design is key, knowing which mechs pair well together and what sets you up to absolutely dominate the AI regardless of the engagement. The loop of raiding, getting more supplies, slowly upgrading your mechs, trying out new parts, and going at it again is fantastic. I was jumping from province to province excitedly looking forward to the next fight wondering what I could get at the end of it.The music is good. I won't say its amazing, you're going to be listening to the same tracks a lot but they're all really fitting for when they play and act as wonderful indicators of how you're doing in combat, but thats not the only thing you'll encounter in the overworld.If you want a game that fleshes out a world with the tiny things, this is it. I won't speak much on them so as to not spoil them but the little events you have a chance of running into add a flavor to the game that I genuinely don't recall running into anywhere else. It's refreshing, but also helps enrapture you in the world, making the nation and its people something you care about despite rarely actually interacting with them.As I said before, if the bad is a deal breaker, then thats understandable. The game isn't perfect by any means. But if by chance you do want to give it a shot, you have the chance to find gold here. (I know I did)
_childDocuments_.name: Phantom Brigade

_childDocuments_.review: Phantom BrigadeA fun, but slightly shallow turn-based tactics, mech-combat game with a pre-planning style combat system.Also, what's up with games set in an occupied Sweden-like nation that's been taken over by high-tech machines? Swear this is the third game I've played that's like this.The game has you follow a resistance group of mech-piloting Swedes hell-bent on taking their home back from The Evil Swedes (or something, fifteen hours in and I still don't really have any idea 'who' the invaders are). You'll slowly push into occupied territory, fighting enemy patrols and raiding enemy patrols and bases while you slowly liberate your home back using your prototype tech and the local resistance Home Guard, who're actively fighting alongside you (though don't actually make any progress unless you step in and save their ass every single time they get into a fight).Gameplay boils down to two 'loops'. The metagame/overworld map, where you control your little squad of mechs around, using the radar to discover new targets and patrols, with some minor crafting and decent mech-customization, along with a few little bits of gameplay elements. Then, when you engage an enemy patrol or base, you'll swap into the actual turn-based combat mode, in which you will pre-plan five-second intervals of your actions. Movement, firing, taking cover, boosting, blocking, etc, while also being shown the enemy's next five seconds of movement, letting you pick the best angles or pre-fire certain angles, or force enemies to friendly-fire themselves by knowing which of them are targetting which of your mechs, or where they'll be walking, and so on. It's a neat system, if a little cumbersome to get used to at the beginning. It's really, really grown on me. I've thoroughly enjoyed the system, since it lets me do some cinematic, perfectly-timed coordinated moves that'd be ♥♥♥♥ you'd see on a high-budget mecha anime or movie.Now, where the game is a little 'shallow' in my opinion, is in regards to it's progression systems and customization. The painting is alright. Could certainly be improved, but it's serviceable. There is no pilot progression. I've been deploying the same four pilots for fifteen hours, and I've yet to see them 'upgrade' or skill-up, or otherwise improve. Despite the game saying to the contrary, as far as I can tell- there's basically no real pain in losing a pilot beyond purely sentimental "Oh, well, I've had him for sooo long", along with the cost of buying a new pilot. Mech customization is the biggest pain, though. You have three tiers of parts: Light, medium, and heavy. Along with three rarities: Common, uncommon, rare. Both legs are considered one part, each arm is its own part, and the torso is its own part. That's a total of four parts. Then, you can pick between a primary, and secondary weapon, such as a shotgun primary, and a missile rack secondary. Or a machine gun primary, and a mini-shotgun secondary, and so on. The weapon selection is actually pretty decent, but... That's all you get... Unless you're using Uncommon or Rare parts, which allow you to add additional little bonus parts ONTO each part. For example, a rare leg lets you choose whether you use heavy armor, light armor, completely strip out some of its armor, or some other thing. Torso pieces let you choose which generator and thruster to use- but the differences aren't very noticeable, especially on torsos that don't naturally have good heat management. Most of these mods/attachments mostly have a benefit or downside of 5-20%, and don't really radically change how a weapon can be used. And most of them are kinda ♥♥♥♥.While all the mech customization is important- what has the largest affect on gameplay is weight, and weapon choice. Weight affects speed (Which, obviously, lets you move more or less per turn depending on how high or low it is). Weapon choice affects how often you're able to attack, at what ranges, with how much accuracy, and how much damage you inflict. Some weapons are better than others, for sure. The game definitely needs a decent bit of balancing done to it. Assault rifles are hilariously weak. Shotguns are middlingly alright. Sniper rifles kick ass, but rely on other friendly mechs to draw aggro, as sniper rifles have a minimum effective range- meaning if anything is within it, your rifle suffers a massive accuracy penalty, forcing you to use your secondary, or reposition. Machine guns are very powerful- provided you're willing to tank, or nothing's targetting you. For a rather long burst, you get a fairly heat-efficient attack that deals plenty of damage. The various missile launchers are pretty alright, especially since they're one of the few weapons (early game, atleast), that don't require direct LoS to fire. The various melee weapons... Are heavily map-dependent, but generally on the weaker side. The ones I've found take the primary slot, and kinda require you to play a light-armor mech in order to close the distance quickly enough to start dealing damage soon enough to be worthwhile, especially since many missions have timers before reinforcements can potentially arrive. Generally, the mix of weapons I've seen so far are pretty interesting and varied.Also, one thing that sucks, but isn't gamebreaking, is that there's no real 'replay' mode. You can replay the five seconds of the turn you just finished- but you can't replay the entire mission in real-time, which sucks. It's not going to kill the game for me, but it'd certainly be nice to review an entire mission in real time. Whether to see where you could've improved- or just for the sake of spectacle- since the game DOES look good.Despite my complaints- the game is still solid fun even at release. If given a round of updates, content additions, and rebalancing, I can definitely see it becoming one of the better tactics games we've had in a long while.
