_childDocuments_.review: This is a fun, little game that was inspired by FiM, and is a cute, humorous title. The music is well-done, and the fighting animations are clean.That's where my praise ends. Despite over a year of development, there is still no new story since last year, no new characters, and the DLC is comprised of skins and a soundtrack. Shanty was released well over a year ago, and I popped back on after noticing the game had a 1GB update. "New story!" I told myself, hoping that there would be SOMETHING different, something improved. It's the exact same game as a year ago, and I'm getting to the point of dropping the project altogether due to a lack of updates on story. Improvements are fine and dandy, but neglecting the game as a whole to focus solely on 'improvements' is not a good idea. As it is, I don't even notice any of the 'improvements' that have apparently been added over the year. I supported this team all the way back when they were trying to make their MLP fighting game, one of the first to play the demo. This game's story is a diamond in the rough, but seeing it sit on a shelf and collect dust is just depressing.Great concept, the dev team seems to have grown bored with it though. I recommend this to anyone who doesn't mind their story being stopped mid-way and don't mind a small cast of characters (seven, to be exact) to play as. For the average fighting game enthusiast, I would have to give this a hard pass for a recommendation as it is.EDIT: Frankly, I'll probably wind up changing this to a recommend once the story is done and the cast expands a bit. A whole year with no changes is a tad frustrating, regardless.

_childDocuments_.review: As an almost total newcomer to fighting games, I can't recommend this game enough just from the quality of its tutorial alone.I've always been curious about fighters and have bounced off more than a few of them, and never really understood any of the terminology or mechanics, but TFH taught me so much, and most importantly how to put it into practice as well. Beyond just the basics on combos, juggles, how to control your character etc, advanced concepts like hitstun, blockstun, negative edge, frame advantage, push blocks, armor, techs, cancels, resets, what '-2 On Block' means and so on are all explained in real, practical terms, with visual and playable examples that teach you how to actually use that information. In just a short time with the game, I've gone from knowing nothing about fighters to what feels like a really solid set of information, and in a way I don't think I could have gotten from just a guide, and definitely not from just bashing my head against CPU matches.It even encompasses character specific tutorials for each member of the cast, how to get the most out of training modes or understanding frame data, with the icing on the cake of being wrapped in a charming and approachable format. It feels strange having so much praise for a tutorial, but it was the most effective and thorough one I've seen in any game, ever.In my experience, as a newcomer to the genre you won't be immediately ready to jump right into online,CPU matches, or the story mode. This game does require patience and a willingness to learn, but I found it more than earned it, and the learning experience itself has been really compelling. It's a great feeling putting what I've learnt into practice against friends in online matches after going through its tutorial systems, and actually even being able to win matches faster than I ever thought I was going to during my time with the game.Netcode is absolute perfection, I'm an Australian playing with friends mostly in America, and I've never had such a smooth experience in any game with them, even at pings of over 200. Part of why I never played fighters was struggling with a lack of local community for them both on and offline, and the online experience being ruined by the quality of netcode across higher pings, but this game was such a pleasant surprise in that regard. I've seen GGPO praised a lot, but it has never been more apparent to me how much it earns it.As for the actual game itself, I'm so completely charmed by it, both aesthetically and mechanically. The world is unique and compelling, and I'm a huge fan of the character design and art style. Gameplay feels fluid and intuitive, the characters have a great combination of some universal inputs for basics like launchers or anti air, but beyond that could not be more different to each other. Even with a small cast size, it feels offset by just how varied and unique each character feels to play. Likewise, there is only a small set of stages, but each one has dynamic musical themes for each character, blending their own theme with the stage theme, and every matchup of characters has unique back and forth dialogue at the start of the fight. In general, the game gets a lot out of what seems like a little, and the level of polish on each element of it is incredible. The online lobby system stands out as wonderfully executed.I've never written a review on Steam before, but I really want people to give this game a chance, especially if you are new to fighters like me. It doesn't feel like a simplified version of the genre, but instead puts in the work to teach you how to play it for real. I don't want to see the developers work on this game overlooked, because I really think its doing something special. Also hey, it's only fifteen bucks.

_childDocuments_.review: I feel like I've played enough to give this game a fair review:This game is basically a non oficial My Little Poney Fighting Game (it was an Oficial MLP FG at some point but Hasbro chickened out). Just to be clear, I'm not really into this My Little Poney /Furry/Anthro/Whatever coummunity(nor do I have a problem with people are into that kind of thing), but I can appreciate a Damn Good Fighting Game when I play one, and fortunately, this is the case here. Also I think the concept of cute Ponies fighting each other is hilarious, in a good way.Them's Fightin' Herds is a 4 button 1 v 1 Fighting Game with 6 characters Total, I know, not a very impressive number, but each character is so Unique that I feel you are trading Quantity for Quality.  Their animations are all unique and full of personality, also the music kicks ass most of the time (there's one or two and not a big fan of, but most of them are pretty good). You'll probably find one or two characters that'll suit your playstyle, Personally I really enjoy playing Paprika for eg: The crazy Alpaca with a lot of gimmicks, random moves  and a fighting style that kills your opponents by Smothering them with love, literally, she doesn't want to hurt anyone, she just loves too hard... The Netcode is pretty Good, it uses GGPO Rollback and you can find quality matches with people from arround the globe. Trust me, I'm from SA and I'm finding good games with people in the NA and EU. The community for this game is not big, but I feel It's not going to die anytime soon, I've bough this game when it first launched in Early Access and I've been able to always find people to play with, and now that the game hit 1.0, I feel like it's more populated than ever.The game uses a lobby system thats really interisting, dare I say, the best lobby system in the whole industry (Learn from this game ArcSys!). You basically have different scenarios where you can walk, participate in community events (salty Mines), customize your character(and there's a lot of customization to your Lobby Avatar), and of course fight people, you can also train the lobby and the best thing, you can do all of that while Matchmaking (You basically can enter the matchmaking in almost any mode in the game, online and offline), meaning it's a lobby that never limits you.If you are a casual, this game tutorial got you covered, it's pretty good, one of the best I've played so far . It teaches you everything about the game system's and also fighting game in general, even Frame Advantage, Hit and Hurtboxes. If you are new to fighting games, I feel like it's worth a buy just for the tutorial, you'll learn a lot of fundamentals that applies in basically every other 2D fighting game.The Story is kinda of a Hit and a miss. I feel like the idea is in the right place, it's really unorthodox  compared to other fighting games story (and that's great, because I think most of them suck), you control an avatar just like the lobby system and you can explore through sections of the main adventure, basically advancing the story whenever you fight a boss. You can find secrets, explore secret areas and there's minigames that are really cool because they test your movements skills, it's almost like a Drill, or a mini tutorial in Super Jumps and Hops.The miss is the spikes in difficulty, some of the bosses are really unfair, even on casual difficultiy (wich you'll probably will have to play to win some fights ). If you are casual , I think you'll have fun in this game until you hit a Boss, then, I can see a lot of people dropping the game because it's not really casual friendly, it's not even beginner/ intermediate friendly. You'll have to get good if you want to beat the Bosses. One cool thing about the bosses is that they are really unique, they added different phases to them testing different skills of the player. (the biggest problem is that they always seem to recover Health when transitioning to another phase, meaning you basically have 1 health bar to defeat a boss that sometimes you'll have 3 healths bars, or 1 health bar to defeat 9 minions + the boss, that where the game is really unfair to you)There's one last thing I want to warn you about this game, it just hit 1.0 and got out of Early Access, but the Story is not complete (each character will get a chapter and currently there's only one chapter out), the Level 3 supers (the most flashy moves in the game) are not out yet, and the last character (a goat) is still development. The Goat I understand, but I would not really consider this game out of Early Access if those other features are not out yet. Will the developers deliver them? Most Likely, since the first day of EA they've always been very communicative, and they are still talking with the community through Discord, Steam Forums and Reddit. I trusted them a year ago, and I trust them now. But Since it's out of Early Access, this means technically they don't have to obligation to deliver this things. I believe they got out of EA for populate the lobbys or make a console port (with crossplay I hope) since you there was not really many people playing online back then and you can't release an Early Access game to consoles. But yeah, keep this in mind, Until Know the devs earned my trust and I really believe this will come out, but you never know, I'd say the chance of we not getting the rest of the content is less than 10% tho, the people behind this game are good people who are known in the community and have a reputation to maintain.Pros:Fun and Unique CharactersBeautiful GraphicsGood SoundtrackGreat TutorialBest Lobby system in the industryReally good Online (GGPO Rollback)Creative Story ModeCons:Story Mode difficulty is unfair, possibly the hardest story mode I've ever faced in a fighting game (casuals beware)No level 3 supers yetOnly One  chapter in Story mode is outI believe this game should've not leave Early Access yet.Story mode might be patched, if that happens I'll edit this review.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to start off by saying that I am not a brony and I really dont care for the idea of playing as an animal like a llama or a cow or a deer. However, as a fighting game player, I have been really enjoying this game and I certinally recommend it for those of you who disagree with the reasons I gave, or if you like fighting games, specifically skullgirls (you'll fit right in as it runs on the same engine.)This is a satusfying fighting game that offers a lot to learn for fighting game fans, and plenty for more casual players even at its current early access state. That being said, the target mode is pretty useless and just some kind of speedrun mode. If that is what you're into, godbless, but I dont find any value in it. The training mode has a helpful combo trial mode that can teach you the basics of combos for each characters and what you should think about landing in a match. as far as online, there are basic lobbies, but the highlight of online is the pixle lobby. If you dont find yourself privvy with the fighting game crowd, you'll really enjoy walking around here and chatting with other players and discussing strats or going into the salt caves, a pretty entertaining mode that could use some more fleshing out, but is still very interesting.Currently this game is in early access. It is missing animations, sounds, and has some balance issues. However, it is very much a playable and enjoyable game. Even now, i can recommend this game for nearly anybody. That being said, you may not get the most enjoyment out of the game if you are unwilling to learn even a bit of fighting game basics. Plenty of fun ways to play with friends, but expect killers online and ready yourself.This is a fun, enjoyable game that if even if the subject matter and history this game bothers you, if you can swallow your pride and give this game a fair chance, I think there is plenty to enjoy. Give it a chance before you judge it.Update: Recently there was a new mode added in the salt mines that is one of the most creative and interesting features in a fighting game i have seen in a long time. It truly gives you a new way to play the game. Players race to get the most salt from mining it from rocks and beating opponents. At the end of the round, the player with the most salt becomes the Bear, a super over powered boss character and has to hunt the other players down in the mine. It is a ton of fun. try it out.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is more astonishing than you may believe at first glance.Aside from the beautiful art style of the always astounding Lauren Faust, the play is extremely smooth, each character generally offers something different, and the game is genuinely trying to be a great fighting game.I'd like to first build on the art style. It's your typical Lauren Faust art, simplistic yet detailed, smooth yet much depth, forward yet much care put into them. The backgrounds follow what most 2D games attempt to do, make a 3D or layered background: that means the backgrounds have depth to them that help wrap the player into the game.Next to mention is the gameplay. Everything flows very well, as a person who plays many fighting games I can happily say this game nails it. I personally tend to struggle with arena sizes and height of characters (generally how high they jump or how far the screen goes up) which is a constant down fall in fighters that either tug the screen so one player is out of the screen, or the arena is too big and i'm left helpless against some spammer with no approach... Hugo mains lyf. This game mirrors Skullgirls, the game it's built off of engine wise, with a decently sized arena and abilities that use said space pretty well, I myself taking Pom under my wing and letting me float around as I need.Which leads me to characters. The only concern I have going into this game is the ability for characters to abuse range, long or mid range, I often struggle against people who have the fast, instant range bolts or massive area mid attacks when playing with friends, though to answer that most characters lacking in that department have answers. Paprika does... whatever Paprika does, some good range mixed with tossing stuff. Pom (my spirit animal no doubt) has a float that juuuust tops off some projectiles, as well as her evasive dash that can either set you up or bait depending on the light or heavy varients you use. The designs are brilliant and unique, and stick to quirks that I personally find just adorable to no ends. Silly llama, southern belle cow with an attitude, shy sheep, angry warmonger dragon, it's all so great for design.As a fighting game, this game isn't hard, and it isn't easy, it's a solid inbetween. _childDocuments_.review: There was a time I could say I highly recommend this game as a fantastic, fun 2D fighter with unique character designs, great music, and great mechanics. That time is no longer. And it has nothing to do with Mane6's development team, they're very talented people and did their best to make a great game. They succeeded, in a sense, but seem to have made a deal with the devil in the process. That devil is Modus Games, now rebranded as Maximum Entertainment, a publisher that handles indies like this.The long story short is Mane6 signed on with Modus to be their publisher. It worked for a time, and the game and community along with it flourished. However, it was announced a few months ago that after the final two characters (Nidra and Baihe) were released, major development would cease. Twelve of the fifteen members of the Mane6 staff were fired unceremoniously by Modus Games, and it was announced that the much-anticipated story mode chapters due to be released in the future would no longer be coming. Nor would any more characters, nor any major balance patches, nor anything other than maybe some minor fixes here and there if we were lucky. Soon after, Modus Games fired two more of the developers, stripping Mane6's original team of fifteen down to just one.Maybe these problems could've been overcome. But just a couple of days ago, patch version 6.0, which releases the final two characters I mentioned, was released. Baihe in particular, conceived as a zoner character, was given some of the most oppressive tools of any character in the game at any and all ranges, a thoroughly overpowered character, but more than that, she was broken. I don't mean "broken" in the "OP" sense, I mean "broken" in the "doesn't work" sense. She had easy-to-execute throw loops that could easily lead into effortless infinite combos. A single mistake is a round loss on the spot. And even worse, Baihe shipped with game-breaking crashes and bugs to boot. Inputting the right buttons with this character could (and would) cause bugs that broke the game or just made it crash entirely. It's a nightmare, and community organizers for tournaments are already debating whether to ban the character entirely or roll back to the previous patch version in the future. Even in those cases, Baihe's still totally playable online in casual matches, available for anyone to completely ruin the experience of other players.And then it gets worse. The game doesn't work on consoles anymore if you've got a digital release (which you almost certainly do), and I hear it doesn't work on Steam Deck either. As in, you actually just can't play it. It doesn't work.Even this could be overcome, perhaps, with a lot of community effort.. But now, at the time of writing, Mane6's own website seems to have been purged from the internet. It cannot be accessed, and therefore the art books, patch notes, and forum posts from the community are erased from time. Probably forever.Modus Games/Maximum Entertainment saw a game that wasn't turning the profits they wanted, and regardless of how good it was or how much the fanbase appreciated it, how loyal its grassroots fandom was, they didn't see enough dollar signs. They cut development, liquidated damn near the entire staff, released a game-destroying patch, and expunged a bastion of the community that cataloged the game's history. And then they rebranded from Modus Games to Maximum Entertainment to dodge the deserved backlash, duck the anger from the community they screwed over so thoroughly.I can't recommend this game at $20. I'm not sure I could recommend it at $5. Even if it were free, in its current state, I might tell you not to waste your time anymore. I legitimately don't know how much longer this game has left, and my guess is "not very."You'll hear people say that Them's Fightin' Herds died. It didn't.TFH didn't die.It was murdered.P.S. The upcoming Avatar: The Last Airbender fighting game is being published by Maximum Entertainment. Food for thought.EDIT: Mane6's website is back up as of Feb 27, but large parts of it are still gone and parts of it still don't work, like the News section. As far as I'm concerned this isn't really any better.

_childDocuments_.review: This is my first ever fighting game and I'm happy to say that I'm hooked.TL;DR - Excellent tutorial, great for new fighting game players.For a new player like me, it was kind of build into the back of my mind that fighting games were difficult and deep. However, playing it really taught me that I can't just keep mashing through everything. I started off with the story on the easiest difficulty. It was plenty easy to fight through the basic enemies on the map. Couple that with the generous health drops and I was cruising through. That is, until I hit the first boss. I had no idea what I was doing, so after the movement section, I finally was able to throw hooves at the lad. Then he hit me with some attacks and I realized something: I had no idea how to block. Or combo. Or... anything mechanical. Needless to say, I lost quickly.This is where the tutorial came into play. I wish every game had a tutorial like this. Not only did it explain the basic movements, it also led right into tutorials centered around each character. Since I started as Arizona in the story, I stuck with her. At the time of writing this review, I've played 3 hours. I think the story only took up a half an hour of that. While progressing through, I could see myself getting better. I started unable to build a combo. I ended able to......sometimes build a combo. I think the tutorial taught me 4 or 5 combos directly, but I was able to figure out some more along the way. Coupled with the game teaching advanced mechanics and systems, I was finally able to feel halfway competent with one character.I'm excited to keep playing. Don't let the aesthetic put you off, this is a solid game that I can see myself playing for a long time.

_childDocuments_.review: I was not meant to like this game. I've dabbled into more than my share of fighters but, on a mechanical level, I will always be held back by poor execution skills, a reason why I tend to stay away from combo-heavy brawlers. Cute critters isn't what I'm usually seeking in my games and, moreover, I'm certainly no MLP enthusiast (sorry Ms. Faust). Yet...What Mane6 managed to do here is absolutely bluffing. Those guys get what it takes to make a good fighting game.Built on the same engine than Skullgirls, the animations are slick, the combo system competent with universal safeguards implemented to prevent being chained to death without any opportunity to reset. The duels are tense and with its implementation of the GGPO rollback netcode, the game runs pretty smoothly online even with 100+ ping.Those things are to be expected in a modern fighter but Fighting Herds goes far beyond the basics by offering some excellent tutorials, certainly amongst the best on the market; very didactic they don’t shy away from more advanced notions like hitboxes and frame data, things that are central to the genre but usually hidden from the public eye. Even better, very complete training options allow the player to lab extensively. All in all very good things that make for a very accessible and beginner-friendly fighter.All of this would already be great but the game totally took me by surprise with a rather ambitious story mode at the crossroads of an early 16-bit era RPG (lite) and a fighting game, not unlike what we’ve seen in recent years with the Smash Bros series.So yeah, those devs made me a believer. There’s one big downside that prevents the game from reaching true greatness though : the core roster is very, very, small by today’s standard, with only six playable characters (seven very soon!). That’s even smaller than the original Street Fighter 2! Really not enough when most games in the genre won’t launch under 12 characters. Hopefully this will be addressed with future updates.

_childDocuments_.review: Them's Fighting Herds is everything you'd ever want from a fighting game. It's still in it's infancy and doesn't have a huge community, but it's a shining star to look out for and deserves more attention than it gets. MECHANICS -- TFH is mechanically like any other fighting game, but is extremely easy to pick up. The inputs for special moves are the perfect amount of complexity, and there aren't any strings you'd have to shove in to your brain to actually play the character. Each character's unique moveset fit comfortably on one sheet, with the very basics like basic attacks, blocking, and recovery being simple and universal. This games design revolves around keeping it simple, and profits heavily. Training mode is advanced, with lots of controls. It allows people to make their own playstyle and combos with every character, and even get some basic training. The tutorials are helpful, and you'd know how to play pretty well in about 30 minutes.GRAPHICS --They're not the most beautiful looking or most realistic, but they aren't supposed to be! It's a game about a bunch of hoofed animals having a fight. The cartoony style helps with simplicity, and the unusal character models help with making this game stand out!STORY --Let's face it, story mode in most fighting games suck! They offer no way to teach players about any mechanics, and is basically just a very specific arcade mode run to act as a buffer. TFH fixed that! While it's only got one chapter at the moment (game's still young) it offers you with the right amount of challenge and rewards you for exploring, and even teaches you important tech! You'll have a very basic mastery of Arizona after completing story mode, and I think that's a great thing that fighting games should do more of. ONLINE --two words, rollback netcode. Online plays great, even in 200 ping! SCORE -- 8.3/10 - needs a lot more flesh and bones content wise, but it's a great start!!

_childDocuments_.review: A great game that is being regularly updated by a dev team that really cares to make the best possible game and a very lively, passionate community of players who are FAR better than I am at the game. Netcode is great bar very occasional hiccups. I adore the character designs and the animations. The contextual taunts at the beginning of matches are a wonderful touch. Online lobbies are easy to navigate, though I usually play the Pixel Lobbies. Not a big fan of dressing up my character, but that's there for the sort of people who love TF2-style cosmetic items out of fights. Salt Mines, Story Mode, as well as the Tutorials and Training Mode are a great way to sharpen your skills offline. For new players, I'd recommend the Tutorials to learn the basics fast, as Story Mode is still pretty lean on the instructional side of things and kind of assumes you know basic combos. Apart from Story Mode, the rest can be accessed from the Pixel Lobbies while online, so you can practice while you wait for matches.TFH is an all around excellent title that will get even better in the future. One warning: I play with a 360 controller and I would warn that it is NOT an ideal input device for Them's Fightin' Herds. Proper arcade stick is the best option or perhaps a dedicated fighting game controller like a Hori Fighting Commander. You REALLY need to reliably differentiate between cardinal directions and angles as all of the attacks and blocks rely on those specific inputs. The 360 pad will give unintended inputs for days unless you take exceptional care and that WILL cause frustration aplenty and lost fights.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're a fan of fighting games, you should give Them's Fightin' Herds a chance.Whatever its origins, it's a fun, balanced, mechanically deep 2D fighter - and if you don't believe me, just search Twitch VODs for all the pro players who woke up to this game when it got an EVO slot and suddenly love it now.Features include:* A roster where every character plays very differently, and every character has stuff that makes you go "is this allowed??", and yet no character clearly outclasses any other.* Combo system that limits combo length and damage, incentivizes on-the-fly routing, and keeps both players thinking.* Top notch training mode, including dummy playback, built-in and downloadable combo trials, hitboxes, frame data...* Unusually comprehensive tutorial that comes in 3 parts: the basics (including move explanations for all characters), an intermediate section to tackle once you've played a while, and an expert section that gets into stuff most fighting games force you to go to a Wiki to learn.* Runs on a toaster; my 2012 Thinkpad with integrated graphics gets 60fps at 1080p.* Best-in-class GGPO rollback netcode. As long as both players have a wired connection, you can play intercontinentally and still feel like you're local.* HD 60fps 2D animation straight out of Saturday morning cartoons.* A story mode that's equal parts fighting game, long-form tutorial, and RPG - a far cry from the "cutscene, fight, repeat" story modes of Guilty Gear and its ilk.* A soundtrack that adapts to gameplay - character themes get interwoven into stage music depending on who has the momentum in the match.* Works bug-free in Proton if you enable it, as far as I can tell.* Technically zero ponies, as the only equine playable character is a full-size unicorn. :)Caveats:- Story Mode only recently got its initial release, and was designed by advanced fighting gamers, so it's still got a rocky learning curve for casual folks. If you're new to fighting games, it might be best to wait for this to get smoothed out.- There are only six playable characters, and there are unlikely to ever be more than ten. I'd argue that a small roster makes for a more balanced game, but if you don't like any of the options you've got, there's not much recourse but to wait for DLC (a seventh character is confirmed, with more hopefully on the way after).- Online lobbies have voicechat; if you don't like that, you need to disable it in the menu (turn "Voice Chat Volume" to 0%).- The training mode menu is huge enough that it's kind of hard to find your way around it.- Tianhuo's voice actor mispronounces the Chinese move names. :(

_childDocuments_.review: So far, I've only played the single player story mode (because with fighting games, I'm always too scared for PvP) so I'm gonna write about that.The story and the gameplay of the storymode itself are incredible, and not what I expected from a fighting game. The main bulk of the game has you running around as a sprite in a world that you can actually interact with a lot of the environment, and each NPC usually has at least one line of dialogue if you talk to them.The game mechanic that took me most by surprise though; there are platforming segments. The controls are a little clunky because ultimately, it IS a fighting game, but it does work quite well.The battle scenes change the style to a 2D, hand-drawn artstyle and play out like a normal fighting game (with it's own mechanics though, obviously). It's a four button system, you have light, medium and strong attack and a magic button which I personally really like.There's a great training mode built in to help you learn all the combos.And lastly, I want to give props to the artists for making the animals actually look like animals and avoiding giving the females weird proportions to let us know they're females. For real, I love the designs of all the characters, and the style as a whole is great.

Also, while the combos are Blazblue-like, they´re not as hard as some combos from those games, everything made better with a long but well explained tutorial to learn not only the game´s unique traits but understanding general terms of the fighting genre.Also, as an artist, I must say that this game´s art is very well executed, character design helps differenciate each character, and there are some interesting resources such as dynamic lighting in 2D sprites, that has been used in other games such as Skullgirls, but it doesn´t mean it´s worse because it has been done before.To sum up, it´s a nice game to try if you want to try unique characters with great 2D art without the difficulty of Skullgirls or Blazblue. _childDocuments_.review: I've come all the way from the early 2010's, back then when the build for "Fighting is Friendship" was still on it's first public builds for anyone to download, it was incomplete, but a progress that everyone at the time was giving as much support as possible. After a few years, and the game looking more polished and out of the character select screen basically just having Skullgirls's select character screen for a bmg background, I had not exactly played the game from some time. Later on heard that devs of this project tried to convince Hasbro into borrowing the trade mark of My Little Pony (oh boy do I feel old as ♥♥♥♥  )to get this game on console and/or Steam but with more improvements or a whole re-making with much more help of a bigger dev group. They declined, that was the end of it for my knowledge until recently. I noticed that bronies then had this many off topic characters, not oc's that belonged to personally someone, like they don't do on masses already, but I did not think much of it, there was just too much clop, derpibooru and the average daily dose of cringe by communities. Then I noticed this game, here, already on the Store and approved by Greenlight (if that's still a thing), took it for a ride. The gameplay is fine, mechanics  do connect, few nerfs to what the main game use to be nearly a decade ago. "Arizona" is basically MLP's Applejack; rope kicks and all concept of ; but more balanced and dynamic. The game years back was as much of a project as Skullgirls was, ironically enough, the team that too over the Skullgirls dev group apparantly helped making this game too. To know that the main project got rejected, and the devs of this decided to make a literal concept of an OC and make their own version that deos not involve MLP directly, but at least with many references and a decent amount of egg-easters from said series or other things. An retro explorable world in 8-bit style like certain flash game for social hang-outs that the bronies have-had for some time now, but kinda interactive. It's one hell of a plataformer, there's glorified but very punishing tutorials about cache area to reach a new space and progress, still plenty of plataforming and forcing you to do inputs properly, one mistake and you pretty start over without exceptions... Unless you jumped into spiked roof, but when falling literally 1 pixel from the corner of the area you were trying to get in saved you and didn't have to do it again all the way from the back. It has a good teaching gimmic unlike other fighting games, it has the option to be a plataformer not exactly like the Super Smash Brothers franchise that while does have loading screen tips and advice that matter it's really give you a proper learning tutorial besides a movie/menu-start mp4 video of the basics and nothing more, bound to learnt he hard way by playing online or see youtube videos all around by montages or actual informative videos. But the plataforming in which you fighter is by itself or not in a real fighting match while able too move freely but limited to reach a goal/space to progress with obstacles in the way, it's pretty nice way to make the player able to adapt to not just get into a fight straight up after cutscenes of sketchy background like your average arcade fighting game.The physics are fair, the hitboxes trigger properly, no matter how much testing, there's no phantom hitboxes or fake confirms neither by lag online or offline, it's programming is fairly executed, everything works like it's supposed to, which is gladly the most comforting thing you could get from a fighting game that forces so much limits or the pulling the same input twice and that second time never triggers (SSB Ultimate when grabbing twice in place without getting off the floor, the grab just won't happen, it applies to every character there, on several traditional fighting games this also happens), although the inputs are farily tight despite how simple the controllers are as well, it nearly feels like Skullgirls in terms that you can make your own combos and set ups, it is technically a arcade like playstyle.Making fighting game to actually function properly it's.. simply comforting.The soundtrack is diverse, a little country there, a little bit edgy there, some spiritual unexpected heavy ♥♥♥♥ there that'll make you want to download the OST off a webtsite or the bgms off a youtube playlist, it's finesse.The story is driving by fantasy like legends, it gives the antic vibe or people/character from fables and story books not exactly meant for everyone nor children, yet it remains safe to observe. Panels, like a pages swipping to the sides, nicely done.I could say more, but I'm really bad at giving details, this is just how I see this game. But it's fair to say it IS an actually well made fighting game, with or without the concept of mostly quadruplet beings for fighting characters, it's undeniably good.The menu welcomes you with an edge of "well, welcome to the brawl" imagery. A simple menu, with updates on a corner, DLC even incoming, the bgm is cool and relaxing. You'll have a blast, it's just the people on ther other end that might be ragequiting or get angry, like any fighting game powered by communication.Anything besides that. Good, just very good. With it's history and all to get were it is now. A little underrated though, it could have more players.Also a big issue would be that:- The campaign is fairly... too short and could have more potential and interaction.- While the 6 only playable characters and incoming 7th one in development for DLC are all diverse in terms of play style, unique strategies, and make it noticeable that the game doesn't need to be all 100% melee in order to win by how these characters are different from each other and can't just try to mash out at all. Again.. the issue would be there's just 6 and to be only 7 characters in this polished game.- Is not a bad thing, and it connects with the story mode mostly, but like in some games and this one, it has shown that some bystander characters are in a way forced to join the fight/plot or be there for no reason just  (cough cough every DLC/guest character ever and Smash character), but besides the spoty, and trying my best to not give away spoilers, the few characters could not just another champions like themselves, but maybe villians, and not talking about the NPCs enemy CPUs in the story mode, but make the enemy have some  besides mindless mass produced repetitive enemies in different quantities.Not necessarily suggesting to create an entire set of characters with a full set of personalities, but an enemy with a variety of options to not feel like you're dealing with the same patterns over and over, althought that gimmic does work well in this game as it forces the player to learn and plataform their way through and not single minded do the same thing over and over, it's a huge tide of both all together.

_childDocuments_.review: So what is Them's Fightin' Herds?Well, Them's Fightin' Herds is a 2D fighting game about quadrupedal animals hitting the snot out of eachother either offline with/without friends or online against strangers.First thing immediately seen from the visual design of the game is the main menu, and it gives off a great first impression for the game, from the simple but clean visuals of the menu to the amazing main theme of the game.After firing up the game's Practice Mode and getting greeted with the character select screen showing all 6 characters of the game and demonstrating the dynamic music system a bit.After checking out all the different characters i decided to go with the adorable alpaca named Paprika whose dialogue consists entirely out of different squeaks and funny noises.The spritework inside of the game is quite smooth and looks pleasing to the eye, the hitsparks and hit noises give enough feedback to feel good about hitting a poor wobbling lamb in the face with a potted plant. Visually the game has little to complain aboutNo fighting game review is complete without talking about the meat-n-bones of the game, the gameplay itself.Them's Fightin' Herds plays like a pretty traditional Anime fighter like BlazBlue or Under Night In-Birth, With 4 attack buttons, A (X on xbox) for light, B (Y on xbox) for Medium, C (B on xbox) for Heavy and D (A on xbox) for MagicPressing these buttons does different attacks.The game provides you with a practice mode and a command list for each of the characters for you to learn their various moves.The game is very combo focused and every character has a universal launcher move (3+C) that can be used to propel opponents into the air for even longer combos, so far it sort of feels like Skullgirls crossed with BlazBlue. The footsies are a bit awkward though with the characters having four legs.The game's online is quite interesting, The online is focused around Pixel Lobbies, which work sorta like the lobbies from Guilty Gear, allowing you to customize your tiny avatar and challenge other people to matches. The game's netcode uses GGPO and it has been pretty great so far with little to no lag during online play.Them's Fightin' Herds has a unique dynamic music system that depends on what characters are fighting currently, what stage they're on and who is currently winning. The soundtrack has some amazing music such as Paprika vs. Oleander on Woodlands or Arizona vs. Arizona on Sunset Prairie.Overall, Them's Fightin' Herds is an amazing fighting game made by passionate developers, It looks good and plays well, featuring some amazing music to boot. The tutorial of the game is one of the best i've seen in a long time in fighting games too! With the game's low price, there is no reason not to pick this up if you enjoy fighting games.9/10

_childDocuments_.review: I don't normally like Fighting Games, but Them's Fightin' Herds is so creative, endearing, and fun that it's on my top ten favorite games list of all time. Many people will write this game off because it's a "furry game" or whatever, but the characters are all really unique and charming. Once you get rid of your internalized fear of furries because of societal norms, you'll see that the characters are super awesome and were written really well. Though even if you ignore all that, this game is functionally better then most fighting games because it *actually explains how to play the game.* Games like Marvel Versus Capcom or even Dragonball Fighterz have really boring tutorials that bore the player and don't teach effectively. Marvel Versus Capcom in particular doesn't even explain that "B" doesn't mean the same "B" that's on your controller. Fighting Games expect you to already know all of this. However TFH does the exact opposite. Oleander leads the tutorial with her fourth wall breaking jokes, you can skip parts you already know or can't quite complete yet, and it's accompanied by the games amazing soundtrack. Well the whole game has that soundtrack but you know what I mean.Currently the game does suffer from a lack of characters though. A season pass has been announced where we will be getting four new characters, but there still should be more by now since it's been almost like 2 years since the game came out. Additionally, there aren't many players right now as well, though when this game comes to consoles with crossplay soon, that problem will be solved immediately. I know a toonn of friends on Discord who want to play but don't have PC's.And lastly the community is just super duper wholesome especially for a fighting game. And don't worry about people being weird, all the bronies and furries on the game are really nice and awesome.

_childDocuments_.review: The game strikes an excellent balance between the mechanical simplicity of games like Street Fighter and the deeper systems of games like Blazblue. It isn't as overwhelming as Guilty Gear or even Blazblue for beginners, and is an excellent entry-level fighting game while maintaining enough depth to satisfy more dedicated fighting game players. The game's aesthetic and overall structure is cohesive and satisfying, and the characters are portrayed and animated beautifully.At such a modest price point, especially for Skullgirls owners, I would recommend Them's Fightin' Herds anyone with even a slight interest in fighting games. The promise of more content and characters even after the full release is icing on the cake.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall: 3/5 Okay under the circumstancesA game that will never be finished and was never professional.The primary reason not to buy TFH is because its production has been canceled and all further proceeds will go to the publisher Modus instead of the individual developers. I picked it up for ulterior motives and am not likely to play it indepth. I am not in any rush to provide more money to either party.The other reason is that nobody plays it.The game was cancelled as the ultimate consequence of its unhealthy development, leading to reliance on third-party support such as Modus. Like many other Kickstarter projects, it is too ambitious of a title for its means, due to underestimating the budget needed, inefficient planning, and unknown other demands on the developers' time and energy (i.e. "we got jobs and families".) Because of all of this, it isn't an especially contentful or particularly polished fighting game compared to other modern offers. There are nine characters that work right and two that at time of writing do not. The character select screen looks depressing due to the massive amount of empty space, which could be mitigated just by larger icons but would ideally contain the other half of the character cast, a pipe dream which is no longer on the table.I've seen other players say TFH is most similar to Blazblue. I've never played Blazblue. The most similar game I'm familiar with is Skullgirls, whose engine was licensed to produce TFH, and which is based on Darkstalkers (which I played.) The primary inheritance of this is the combo system, which generally goes "up the ladder" of weaks to mediums to strongs to specials to supers with a few special cases. TFH gradually nerfs combos the longer they go on.TFH cannot make up its mind what image it wants to present, partially because it is held back by its fundamentally derivative origins.Much like Freedom Planet and Sonic, TFH is terrified of openly admitting its powerful and blatant creative influences from My Little Pony: Friendship is Magic and the fandom thereof, especially as it was in 2013. This is likely in part due to Hasbro's C&D against Fighting is Magic, which makes any perception of TFH as derivative in any way a dangerous concept.The initial six characters, whose redesigns are provided by initial FiM showrunner Lauren Faust, are directly based upon the main six characters of Fighting is Magic. As these characters were in different states of completion their gameplay similarities are stronger for some than others - e.g. Arizona plays almost identically to Applejack, while Velvet plays only vaguely like Rarity.Their personalities, however, are consistently derivative and recognizable to the pony fandom with one exception, and these personalities are extrapolated to form the civilizations of the game world. Oleander is a prim snob like Twilight in early seasons while collectively every other unicorn is Celestia seemingly ignoring Twilight's concerns, Velvet is Rarity if she thought being Swedish was in and every single deer is Rarity if she never realized what a PoS she is, Arizona is Rainbow Dash pretending to be Applejack and the biggest difference is her parents are around, Paprika is Pinkie under Poison Joke (while all other alpacas have no personality), and Pom is Fluttershy in constant "I guess I have to do something" mode while all other sheep are Fluttershy outside of that mode. Tianhuo is the exception: maybe if Rainbow Dash ever grew up she'd be more like Tianhuo, who is a bit showboaty but is very mature and responsible. The longma nation is typical wuxia fantasy stuff - not Rainbow Dash-y stuff.The voice acting varies dramatically in quality. Tara Strong with a goofy country accent gives Arizona easily the best vocal performance of the first seven characters, Paprika does not actually talk and just makes weird noises. The other five are quite frankly terrible, and out of them only Oleander remembers what her accent is (horrendously British.) Now, Velvet is supposed to be faking her accent, but she sounds bad regardless. Chris Sabat performs a fantastic booming superhero voice for Stronghoof and the other DLC characters are just kind of tolerable.The story mode is the most visible casualty as it was going to have a chapter each for at least the initial six characters but will never be finished beyond Ch. 1 (Arizona). The writing of story mode portrays the initial six with much heavier accents than the voice acting does except for Oleander who is English so her text is just English, Paprika who does not talk and whose text is wingdings, and Arizona who is properly accented in both. Shanty does not appear in Arizona's chapter to take a crack at Jamaican, which is unfortunate as that accent is endearingly incomprehensible both spoken and written.Reine City, home of the Rarity-deer, is hornier than Bangkok and loaded with unsubtle sexual references on just about every street corner. It's bizarre, and in context of its known pony influences and its preoccupation with shipping, a bit cloppy and uncomfortable.Online play features a Pixel Lobby with a Salt Mines PvE mode that is good for learning the basics of playing the game or developing a new character. Story Mode and the Pixel Lobby feature collectible cosmetics whose descriptions are absolutely all referential humor that further damages the game's dignity.All in all, the game is okay, but it never seized a hold in the fighting game market, no longer has a chance to, and was never going to escape its image as a My Little Pony fangame in any event.

_childDocuments_.review: It has the potential to become a fantastic fighting game if it's given the right support.Them's fightin' herds is a 2D fighter that works with a four button scheme. There are only six fighters so far, move sets & inputs aren't complicated to perform as one would think. And to make it better, the movesets themselves are as simplistic as UMVC3. despite the fact there's not a 2v2 or 3v3 mode, that makes picking one of these characters to main even easier as opposed to being forced to pick 3 members, then an assist move for each.Right now the arcade mode, target mode, and practice mode are the only things you can do locally, but then there's online. Is the netcode for online good? YES. I most framerate drop I ever experiecned was maybe 2-3 frames during online fight. To give you some perspective, Street fighter 5...it has moments it drops 7+ frames making awkward skips in the battle to catch up. So for the most of the game, you'll be playing in lobbies online.The lobbies themselves are these cute pixel area's to walk around in. As far as finsing items or cosmetics, i have no clue. haven't spent enough time out there. But its more entertaining than looking at a menu screen to say the least.Since the game is only a day old, running into other people is always there. And until the game progresses enough and the community surrounding it grows, there won't be many them's fightin herds tourney's or locals of any kind.Its clear that competition is in mind from the devs. there is just yet to be enough time for things to be worked into the game. If your so worried, keep in mind, its an indie game in early access. it'll get there someday.The game is in early access as in, WOW you can be reminded of that easily with some drops in framerate, the occasional crash, or lip syncing not working.For the most part, the only bugs I encountered were those, and with one I hope is only a visual hit box not aapearing in training mode. It also supports the use of fight sticks, which came at some surprise. I expected it to require me to go into a menu and switch controllers and remap the controls along with dealing input lag, but no. I put it in, click. and its good.For those who want to take it seriously, just play online for awhile and lets work to build a community around this game. Thats the healthiest thing for any fighter.until the game gets fleshed out some more, to later be a full release, I give Them's fightin herds7/10

For now only the first chapter is available but the other chapters will be added to the game later for free so personally i don't mind. Normanly the story mode in fighting games is mostly nothing special and kind of lazy. Luckily i can't say the same thing about this game. The story mode in this game is amazing: the story is great, you can move freely around the map, the characters are fun and have good dialog, the music is amazing, there are jump and run section here and there, the pixelart is beautiful and it has a lot of attention to detail and is in general a really fun and charming experience. The online mode is really good too, because you don't just get connected to a player and fight, you get a little overworld where you can walk around with other players and challenge them to fight. You also can buy cosmetics with the ingame currency salt. To get salt you can go to the salt mines with other players and collect salt, fight enemies and find chests with cosmtics in it. There is also the function that a chest with a lot of salt will drop and two players can fight for it, wich is a cool idea. As a whole the online mode is a lot of fun and i really like that the online mode is more then just fight with other Players. The only negative stuff i could think of is there are only 7 characters to play, but each character is so well thought, its not that big of a problem, and there will also be 4 characters added to the game with the season pass. The other thing that catched my eye was that there was not a lot of people in the online lobbys. I mean most of the time there will be enough players to play with, but mostly there is one lobby full and the rest empty, but hopefully the issue will be fixed when the game lauches on consoles with crossplay. In conclusion this game is a hidden gem, it has fun combat, it is beginner friendly, its well animated, the music slaps and it has a lot of attention detail. You can really tell that the devs put there hearts and souls into this game. I would recommend this game to everyone, especially for people who never played a fighting game. I know the whole pony aspect is a little meh, but if you look through that you will find a game who has a lot of charm and soul. So please give this game a try.

_childDocuments_.review: TFH is a gem among the many online-focused arcade-mode-only fighting games in today’s market and it’s admirably fulfilling for a casual who has tried and failed to get excited about participating in this genre.Each character in the game’s smaller, more precise roster is immediately distinguishable and comes equipped with their own distinct moveset, mechanics, personality, and catchy music. Seven doesn’t sound like a lot of characters, but to someone who constantly feels like a complete fighting game noob, it’s a perfect number. After all, it’s overwhelming to be expected to eventually understand the mechanics of 26, 45, or 89 opponents or even pick a main from an oversized cast that’s all instantly available to you.Even with all the fighting games that I’ve sampled, this was my first four-button fighter and I instantly found this layout to be more appealing than the traditional six-button one. It’s a massive relief to have less options to constantly consider as well as a single logical hierarchy of attacks. It also requires less right-hand movement on a fightstick, further reducing the unnecessary mental strain and physical fatigue that comes with playing with two additional buttons.There’s a universal character sheet that describes the basics that every character shares. So, once you know the straightforward fundamentals, you can pick up any character and not be completely stranded. It just goes to show that depth and fun can be achieved without forcing the player to wrap their head around the exact location of every finger on whatever button-covered device they’re using.TFH’s story mode is exactly what this genre needs and I desperately wish other games would adopt this standard. Rather than simply being a mix of cutscenes and default AI matches, story mode pits you against ‘shadow creatures’ that all act differently in predictable ways. Each one is there to teach and reinforce important concepts. Unlike scripted tutorials that tell you to block, grab, or anti-air on queue, these enemies punish and reward specific behavior in a free-form context. Since lost health carries over between fights and healing isn’t too common, it’s in your best interests to slow down and think carefully about the AI’s strengths and weaknesses. It’s more akin to genuine practice and scaffolding than the dull memorization that’s employed in the lab. After just a few hours of the story mode, I actually felt like I understood how TFH works. By the end, I may have not mastered performing any eccentric combos, but I felt as if I knew how to react to various common moves and how to position myself against different enemies. That’s why it’s all the more disappointing that I couldn’t find any human players to test my newfound confidence against.I’ve never been as motivated to lonesomely play a 2D fighter, but I can't seem to find any online matches. Thank goodness you can play other modes while you queue for casual matchmaking because I’ve spent hours doing so and have never found a single human opponent. Unless I go as far as to join the discord and  communicate with strangers, it looks like all I've got left to do is get destroyed by the vicious high-level AI or maybe grind out the combo tutorials. TFH may shortly end up on the shelf since the few internet strangers I know would be unlikely to look past the game’s premise and visuals (that I adore by the way). Regardless, I'll most definitely be back when the next chapter of the story mode is released!

_childDocuments_.review: There's a variety of reasons I can say that it's a great game, but at the moment there's a lot of weird issues that shouldn't be happening.The game was set to release in full the same day it came out in early access, and 2 days before the release date they announced the game would be releasing without story mode. While fine, there's a few issues with this. It seems the build up at the moment, is one that must be quite a while back in development. There are multiple things that are definitely not release quality other than story mode missing. Many characters have fill-in animations, much of the UI feels odd, and even intro animations in battles are wonky and unfinished.However, if you really don't care about these problems, and trust the developer to patch these issues, as they claim they will do soon, then the game itself is great and solid for the most part.The game plays as some kind of weird amalgamation of Guilty gear and Blazblue, with a hint of skullgirls feel. The game has a Light, medium, heavy, and a Magic/Gimmick button. Each character has a 'magic' bar in addition to their super meter, somewhat similar to the V-System in Street Fighter V. Every character gains magic in different ways, some over time, others by confirming certain moves.Pros!+The 6 characters feel varied, and feel unique to each other in their playstyles.+The movement and combo flow is extremely fluid and feels great and intuitive once you get practice in. +Match-ups seem, at least at face value, mostly evenly matched, and it seems like no character has anything more than a 6-4 matchup on another.+The game's training mode, as it is Skullgirl's heavenly Z-Engine, is amazingly robust and has plenty to work with for practice.+Pixel Lobby system s'alright, and there is a private lobby system as well.+I haven't played the Salt Mines mode yet in the Pixel Lobbies, but from what I've seen and heard it's decently fun+The music in the game alone is great, but the dynamic music system adds to an already great soundtrack. It swells and calms down at appropriate moments, and seems to decently follow the pace of the match. Mostly.+The animations look and feel great on many of the characters and their attacks, and have a lot of personality to them.+The character designs are 'unique' and have a nice artstyle to accompany them.Edit: The first patch has gone out and fixed some of these issues, I've marked them with a @, and moved them lower.Cons!         -Intros and Victories are so horribly bugged and painful, it kinda deflates a victory. Many of the intros will only have 1 character talking, their mouths flapping at random after they finish their line, while the other is silent but mouthing words. Then, an odd pause later the fight countdown will start. Same with victories.     -There is no where NEAR enough lines for characters and their intros/victories. It seems like most have maybe 2 or 3, and some of them will cut themselves off, like Arizona's victory. She has only 3 victory lines, which are all terribly out of sync with her talking, and one of them completely stops at the last line. "Kickin', Stompin', and Ki-" gets real old, real fast.     -While in theory this would be a good and simple game to have beginners in the fighting game genre start with, there is absolutely no tutorial of any kind for even basic game mechanics. Even the combo trials for the game are hidden inside of training, in the training options.     @-Hot damn that AI is a piece of ♥♥♥♥.It's understandable that AI in fighting games are always gonna be BS. atleast in some way, this game takes it back to the Mortal Kombat 3 era of enemies being absolute brickwalls with perfect punish strings. It doesn't help the AI isn't even set to Normal by default, it's set to Competent (Hard, essentially) @The AI is now set to normal by default, and it seems to not be so godly at defense and combos. They still occasionally do insane combos after a punish, but fighting a zoner AI won't make you want to bite through your own jaw.     @-Damage numbers feel incredibly wonky. As Arizona, a standard bread and butter (Gatling>Launcher>Special>Level1Super) does an okay amount of damage, but heavies from other characters seem to do as much as the simple combos I've figured out so far. It's possible this is on me, but it does feel unfair that a single projectile from Velvet does as much as a standard gatling gun combo. @After playing a bit more, I think I figured out what my problem was, I was fighting a mirror match in practice, and Arizona has a bit more health than others, so after optimizing my combos a bit and trying them on other characters with lower health, it looks like they're mostly fine.      @-The art assets on a few stages and characters are absolutely ABYSSMAL. Arizona, on her front fore leg facing the camera on any color that has a splotch, shows that it's almost barely attached to her skin. This is especially bad since her default design has this issue, and colors with monotone colors look better than the default. Some parts of the background stages, specifically the characters, are pixelated to hell and back. @Arizona still has that odd floating splotch, but I can't seem to find any background characters like I saw before the patch with horrible pixels on them.If you're looking for a good fighting game, and you're not stopped by a lack of polish and even essential features, this game will do great as a budget title.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall Impression: 4.0 out of 5. Them’s Fightin' Herds is an inspired, unique, and solid fighter that seems to be aimed at veterans of the genre. While the overall game is a solid buy, it is an unevenly polished product. If you love 2D fighters such as Killer Instinct, BlazBlue, or the more modern Guilty Gears, do not let the cartoon characters and few, but glaring, flaws of the game make you pass this by.Pros: Wonderful, funny, and extensive tutorial.Fast, smooth fighting system that allows for a lot of tactical flexibility.Parts of the story mode are clever, funny, and provide interesting insights into the world the characters inhabit.The small cast of characters have a surprising range to them when it comes to fighting dynamics.  Almost bug free as a whole and solid online fighting match making.Cons: Overpowered AI opponents.Cheap, unfair, and frustrating story mode bosses that the team has had to nerf once already due to even seasoned fighting game players calling foul.The platforming sections in the story mode are not needed, irritating, and poorly designed.Two of the characters allow for some nigh impregnable defensive tactics that can be exploited by human and computer players alike. (Velvet being the queen offender, followed very closely, at times, by Pom.)Overall Impressions:This game is a blast to play with others so long as they do not abuse character exploits. The AI ramps up from 'this is quite easy' to 'knock you flat before you know what hit you' fast, as you change difficulty levels. New players to the genre may want to stay to the lower levels to avoid frustration.While the game has a detailed tutorial for the games fighting system and aspects of each character, unless you put the game on its easier modes, the computer has a tendency to use wipe the floor with you in no time.The story mode is a mixed bag. The bosses are not fun, frustrating, and grind your progress to a halt. The platforming sections are ill designed and seemed to be aimed at being a painful chore that extend the playtime for players rather than adding anything to the game. The humor, world building, and light puzzle aspects of the story mode just make up for the flaws, as long as you have it on easy mode, so the whole story mode experience is neutral. I find this tragic since part of the reason, from what I understand, the game was delayed was due to the team getting the story mode into a working state. The fact that the story mode is incomplete does nothing but rub salt into the wound.Conclusion: If you are looking for a good fighter, Them’s Fightin’ Herds is a good choice so long as you stick with the fighting aspects of it and do not expect too much, if anything much, out of the story mode.  A concern of mine for the game’s longevity: While the Mane 6 team is very responsive to player feedback overall, a couple of complaints about difficulty have been met with ‘get good’ responses. As someone who has beaten Furi, Ninja Gaiden II, the original Xcom, and Ghosts ‘n Goblins, among other 'hard' games, I believe I have enough experience to back my decision to add my voice to those who suggest the game’s AI needs a little tweaking. A small, but telling, issue that I had with the tutorial’s AI is that while training you to launch your foe and follow up with an air combo that the window to do so is almost too small for a couple of the characters. For a tool that is aimed at beginners, it requires too much precision. The platforming sections of the story mode have also garnered a ‘we made it as part of a planned tutorial system that wasn’t implemented’ response that indicates the team knows there are problems, but have done little to fix them. Please, Mane 6, go back to your gaming roots (which are showing), and aim at making things fun for newbies while allowing competitive and hardcore players their options to get the snot beaten out of them as they would like. It is clear you have the talent to do so.

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent graphics. Fun, interesting characters. AI that cheats like a motherbucker.Don't let the cute graphics, childish characters and dead easy early bosses fool you, this is the Dark Souls of fighting games. When you first fight a champion, even on easy mode, this fact get hammered in *hard*. You are thrown into the deep end almost straight away. The game teaches you nothing of the controls, at least nothing of worth. If you don't spend two to three hours in training mode, have every combo memorised, the characters mastered and already have a decent win streak in multiplayer, youwillnotbeatsolomode.This is not a game to have fun with. This is not a game for even decent level fighting game players. This is for hardcore masochists who want to be punished. Do not buy this game for your kids thinking it is an introduction to fighting games. Do not buy this game because you have some misplaced nostalgia for My Little Pony. Buy this game because you hate yourself.Or better yet, just don't buy this game.Edit: Don't get me wrong, I'm going to keep butting my head against this brickwall of a game. But the game doesn't present itself as being this stupidly hard, nothing about it indicates that it should ever be this hard. I hate games like Dark Souls that punish you for just starting to play. That are nothing but god awful slogs until you get lucky and beat a boss, only to die repeatedly against the next one, without any sort feeling of accomplishment, just the ever building dread that the next fight will be an order of magnitude harder.Yeah, fighting games are kind of like that, but never before to this extent. Bosses don't just challenge you, they cheese like a bad player who discovered an exploit and they exploit *hard*. The AI doesn't key read, because they don't need to, their prediction algorithms are down right *precognitive*.If all of that doesn't dissuade you from buying this, well... there are easier ways to commit scuicide than giving yourself a heart attack out of sheer frustration. But hey, all the power to you.I know I'm building up to one...

_childDocuments_.review: If you can look past the visual theme and want a good fighting game, pick this up. I had little to no interest prior to it's release but I owned Skullgirls(which grants you a discount) so I figured,  for 11 bucks it's worth checking out. My mind was almost instantly changed to loving what this game has to offer from a gameplay and feature standpoint. - Character variety rivaling that of Guilty Gear and Blazblue. Puppet characters, zoners, hyper aggressive rushdown with fly mechanics, grapplers, you name it. Somehow with just 6 characters the game managed to have more variety and creativity than that of Marvel or Dragonball.- More training mode features than any AAA fighter out there. Most notably the ability to save and share combos through files that can be then added to your own game with ease and shown on the screen for you to do. - Better netcode than most fighters out there(GGPO). Gives you actual ping stats, not just ambiguous bars. GGPO then allows you to also set a delay to better accomate bad connections to make it much more seemless than most fighting games.- A lobby system that surpasses that of every other game out there, this ♥♥♥♥ has it's own single player elements woven into the 2d lobby you can run around in. Treasure chests will even appear in this lobby and you can challenge a person trying to open it to see who gets it. The lobbies also feature voice chat and highly accurate ping bars. Which could be toxic and bad for the game, but there is a mute feature and so far nobody has been toxic on the mic to eachother.- Gameplay is smooth and  intuitive. Combos and moves flow nicely and have enough freedom for higher level players to come up with crazy ways to combo without hurting beginners.

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game, but, as many others have stated, you will HAVE to turn the difficulty down on the bots unless you are VERY familiar with similar fighting games and are able to exactly press (NEVER spam) controller buttons, or play very well with a keyboard (for some reason I can press the buttons on the controller (wired XBox 360) and get a 50/50 response after a couple hits (unless you are VERY careful about exactly when you press the buttons, it seems to act as if there's a delay of about 100ms after most button presses, which can *easily* wreck your combos if you spam) but this issue is not present with keyboard, from my brief combo testing). The art aesthetic is the main draw (for me, anyways), and the combat system allows for skill and growth to most definitely be major factors. However, unless you can fairly capably beat Normal difficulty or better, you really should stay away from online fights; you will be destroyed. A lot. This game has definitely drawn its number of skilled players, and it makes most fights against them very one-sided. This wouldn't be much of a problem, except that they reward winners with salt, while losers get nothing, and you need salt to get cosmetic items from the salt mines, which you *also* can't even enter without salt. At least *most* of the players are sportsmanlike, but the ones that you come closest to beating (who also lose to everyone else) will more than likely spam-taunt you and abuse your/your character's weaknesses to the point of rage.Furthermore, I seem to be finding glitches that crash my game or make me spazz out pretty bad online (no crashes, glitches, or jerkiness offline, from my experience), which, combined with my lack of proper experience with 2D combo-based fighters such as this, inclines me to avoid online in its entirety for the time being. The single-player currently just consists of Training and Arcade at the moment, and they're adding a Story Mode, which I will be very glad for, as well as at least one more character, so, while I recommend this game to both fighter fans and fans of the artstyle, I think I'll be only occassionally playing this game until the Story Mode is in (Arcade gets fairly stale after about 10-20 times, and being beaten to a pulp too fast to even see where to improve or getting tilted doesn't strike my fancy, either). Of course, if you have friends that will also play this game with you, that definitely would change the whole online experience, so be sure to take that into account, as well. TL;DR: It's a great game, but most average players will have to start off slow and really hone their skills to get the most out of this game before they add Story Mode, unless they have friends who enjoy both fighters and Lauren Faust's artstyle.

_childDocuments_.review: This game's best unique feature is probably it's lobby system. The lobby system hasn't been done like this in any other game, as far as I'm aware. You're sent to what looks like a sprite style game mode where you can walk around on a small town map. You can interact with, and fight other players you find here. Treasure chests sometimes appear, and you can pick them up. During the 10 second window after you start interacting with the chest, another player can challenge you for the chest's contents. You can gain currency called Salt, which you can use to buy hats and other customizations for your lobby character. The shop is located in the town map your character walks around on.The best thing about the lobby is the "Salt Mines" lobby game. It's sort of like a PvE dungeon exploration salt collecting game that gradually adds more elements of horror as time goes on. Players in the mine try to explore and mine salt, while avoiding or fighting cpu predators in the game. The predators get more difficult as time passes. At the final stage of the salt mine mode, the player who has gathered the most salt becomes a predator character with a ton of health that scales to the number of players, and gets to hunt down all the players currently in the mine. Meanwhile, the players have to navigate their way through almost-complete darkness in the mines. This turns the last stage of the Salt Mines into a surprisingly good asymmetrical horror game. At the end of the round, everyone gets a certain amount of salt, which can be used to buy cosmetics for use in the lobby. If you get knocked out before the end stage, then you can spend salt to re-enter the mine.While the cast of characters isn't the biggest here, each character is radically different from each other. They all have unique mechanics. Even the way characters build up their magic gauge for special attacks is different from character to character. Arizona needs to use her lasso to grab an opposing character in order to get magic charges, while Oleander needs to sit and study her book in order to gain magic, and there are other characters that just passively gain magic over time. What makes it slightly easier to learn the characters is that each character has a small number of universal inputs, like a simple combo string, that the player can learn to add on to.

_childDocuments_.review: I’d like to preface this by saying I’m not new to 2D fighting games I’ve played quite a few. I can see this game has good potential but It’s not quite there yet. The CPU difficulty is punishing and combos don’t feel like they have good flow or are very intuitive. Trying to perform the special combos for each character is Ok, but performing the general combos is hard and only works when landing on opponents. So far I’ve only played on “Greenhorn” Difficulty but still the CPU can perform combo chains like it were nothing locking your fighter in an inescapable chain that will drain half of your health. This is the second difficulty what I would assume would be good for new players with other fighting game experience. I haven’t played enough to know all the combos, I can get about one maybe two before my opponent gets knocked out of reach and my combo dies. I get the feeling from the game that I should just spend hours in practise mode memorizing combos before moving on to even thinking about fighting a CPU. When this happens  I start asking myself, “Is it worth doing this?” or “Do I feel my hard work will be rewarded?” Right now that answer is No. Why would I do this if there's other games that make performing a combo easier to understand and more satisfying.Tl;dr Game has difficulty issues and pulling off combos isn’t fun or satisfying can’t recommend “Them’s Fightin Herds” maybe come back after a few updates.
