_childDocuments_.review: Outer Worlds is unique - visually impressive and with a interesting hook of corporations with all shackles loosened, you think that the first few hours are just an introduction. The enemy encounters will get better, the story will evolve into a more complex overarching narrative that leaves you with the same questions that you get from Fallout New Vegas or KOTOR 2, two of Obsidian's masterpieces.Nope. The story is really simplistic, and can be summed up in three words "Corporations are bad." These three words were apparently enough for the writers at Obsidian to think that it can carry the entire story, and that the nuances inherent to Fallout New Vegas and KOTOR 2 are irrelevant. The fun thing about both of those games, is that you can have a spirited discussion on the merits of each faction in New Vegas (yes, even the Legion) or a more in-depth look at what the universe of Star Wars would be like without the Force or Jedi and Sith. There's a discussion that is bloomed out of those scenarios. But that does not happen in Outer Worlds. Those same discussions cannot happen because each Corporation is portrayed as overbearingly evil, with a stranglehold on the lives of each person living under them. It's nearly impossible to make a genuine argument in favor of what I would consider the "Bad" ending to the game because the entire story is beating you over the head with "Corporations are bad."Gameplay-wise, this is not very fun either. There's almost no challenge to be had on "Normal", and harder difficulties simply bump enemy health and damage, though Supernova does introduce survival (tedium) mechanics to help balance things out. The introduction of skills like Persuade affecting moment-to-moment combat, as you cannot avoid fighting forever, is a neat idea. But the enemies already are nowhere near approaching a threat, so the benefit of those skills is largely irrelevant. Voice acting and story of the characters are good, but because the overarching theme of the entire game and each character in it is "Corporations are bad," the characters themselves are not revolutionary and simply fit into neat little boxes. Anarchic corporation hating freedom fighter. Perky mechanic. Wayward Priest. You think of it, it's in here. It's well voice-acted, but because the characters are just boxed into who they are at a surface level, the nuance of characters like Atton Rand, Boone, Veronica, Visas Marr and others from Obsidian's classic game library are not here.Visually, the game is very impressive. Nothing quite looks like Outer Worlds, and I think that's going to keep it in people's minds for a long time to come. I think that this art-style, in a much better game, would be appreciated and I am hoping that's what Outer Worlds 2 will be. In Summary: Outer Worlds is pretty, and its first hour is very excellent. Past the shiny veneer, and some of its neat ideas, the game completely falls apart. There's no challenge here. The story is simple, and requires little thought from the player. Characters, while being a highlight, are cardboard cutouts compared to prior games under Obsidian. It's also criminally short. I did a lot of side-content and other activities, and I ended up with 11.1 hours at the time I hit credits. (Note: I have not started either DLC yet)I deeply, deeply regret spending $40+ for this game and its DLCs. I would strongly advise getting the base game for no more than $5, maybe $10 for the complete package. What a disappointment from the RPG-kings of Obsidian.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR All in all...  a mediocre game.  But It's tries.  I would be interested to see what they do in a few years with this universe, because it has some wonderful ideas.  And it's a lot of work to make a big title.  So, hats off to the effort.  But it needs a huge clean up.  What to say...  After almost 90 hours playing on Hard difficulty, I've uninstalled the game (rage quit).  I've quit the game twice before because it was essentially boring, but I wanted to at least see where the story would end. Sort of. In the last mission, the developers decided to turned it into an arcade game, without arcade mechanics.  Brutal.  First off, this is not Fallout 3, NV, 4, etc.  Not even Fallout "light".  It's sort of open world, but not really.  The first part of the game makes you want to reminisce about "Firefly", a space cowboy odyssey, but it get's boring quickly.  You get your own space ship!  And I can fly around!  Nope, locations are locked behind the main quest line.  And the ship doesn't actually fly, just a moving blip across a screen.  The ship interior has some character, but limited storage containers, that can't be moved.  It's hard to make it feel like it's your own. If you have a workbench, why not a container or a series of containers right next to it to keep things organized?  Nope.  Probably the biggest complaint... interaction with the world involves lot's of dialogue, while not badly acted, they're long, repetitive, and essentially meaningless, with no way to fast forward. Regardless of your choices your intent is skilled blocked.  Either you have the dialogue skills, or you don't.  Side quests are generally unsatisfying, but necessary to level up. The perk tree is rather bland, and uninspired.  And no matter what you do, or how you play, if you don't level up your dialogue skills, you essentially have to resolve everything with a gun.  The shooting mechanics are dated.  Why is it that every Bethesda or Obsidian game has an absolutely terrible menu system?  To make it worse, they have multiple types of items that do exactly the same thing (or nearly) but have different names and can't be properly organized.  Weapons fall into familiar categories, better one's are really only levelled (mk I vs mk II, etc.)  Unique one's can't be modified, so they're actually weaker than normal ones at the same level, and a huge waste of "bits".  Most of the companions are kind of a mess, and have rather boring associated quests.  Parvati is a stand out in this regard, rather cute, but even that get's tedious.  The rest, rather meh.  Enemies, biomes, are essentially repeated, planet to planet.  Very poppy, very cluttered, and pretty boring. So while you think you're flying somewhere new, you're not really.  And on hard difficulty, they become bullet sponges.  So, while the developers want you to think a stealth build is viable, it's really not.  The weapons aren't really available for one shot kills (maybe on Normal difficulty?), levelling them to appropriate damage levels is extremely costly, and the implementation of Tactical Time Dilation (a twist of Fallout VATS) is very limited.  Essentially, after a few long rage shots (that only kill half the time) the TDD runs out and the enemy will swarm in.  Whip out a shotgun or a heavy machine gun to proceed.  So much for being a stealth sniper.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a veteran gamer and rarely if ever give feedback on games ( let my wallet do the talking) but figured I would this time in case it helps someone.What I liked: * the game runs very smoothly and I had no crashes or freezes at all* loading screens were over so fast they were a non-issue even though they were frequent* soundtrack/ score was excellent* voice acting was decent to very good* story was solid and explored from enough angles to maintain intrigue and contextWhat I feel could be improved:* the art style, color pallette and graphical choices combine to make many enemies difficult to see and hard to track in combat esp considering how fast they can move/ rush* the crafting/ modding system/ drop tables seemed only loosely connected to the story and even character level. Final mission of the main story and I was still seeing low level drops? Not able to mod an awesome new gun as it was 12 levels higher than my character? Seemed I got almost no mods or upgrades early and mid game then got a deluge in the last few levels when I didnt need them. Also- Mods have weight? in a game this short? *sighInventory management and carry weight are gaming staples I get it but in a game focussed more on story/ rpg it was dissapointing to see so many 'skills' and 'perks' affecting these areas* the character 'skill' tree didnt feel all that impactful as most of the time you were either way over or under levelled for an area yet you still managed to progress thru it* follower 'abilities' felt awkward to use (why cant they just do them during a fight) and did so little damage I ended up not using them as they simply disorientated me during a fight.* followers sories and character development felt a little weak and....formulaic* cinematic cutscenes were super rare and could have been used a little more imo* Overall it felt like the games many systems were designed to complement a much longer game/ main story. Just when my skills and perks and followers were starting to make a difference- the game was overOverallI feel the story, immersion and game in general  suffered due to the following:* The sprinkling of man bashing /shaming/ women better narrative ( of COURSE every badass in the galaxy is a black chick)  *sigh* The subtle undercurrent of 'white man bad/evil'. As a white man who is neither bad nor evil I choose to find this offensive. *sighThis is far from the only game I've played recently that suffers from these issues and it doesn't enthuse me for the future of the industry. Buy it on sale

_childDocuments_.review: The Outer Worlds:~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ The colony spaceship known as The Hope disappeared 70 years ago somewhere in the Halcyon System. All the occupants are now slightly stiff, shall we say (an understatement if you have been frozen for that long). A wanted scientist, named Phineas Welles, has found his way to The Hope, and you guessed it, you are the lucky one who he selected and woke up!  Like a baby in nappies, you have no idea what’s going on until you open your eyes, when you see and hear Welles rumbling about saving the colony, and within a few seconds you are sent to one of the planets within the Halcyon system via an escape pod to . . . . oh, for goodness sake, you just woke up; you have absolutely no idea what you going to do in The Outer Worlds!The Outer Worlds is a first person/action/RPG game developed by Obsidian Entertainment and published by Private Division on the 25th October 2019 on the Epic platform. The game is also available on Xbox One and PS4 while the Nintendo Switch version will be release sometimes in 2020. The Outer Worlds is now live on Steam on the 24th of October 2020!Before starting this review, I would like to mention that I was privileged as part of the E3 2019 Media frenzy to sit down in an exclusive 20-minute preview presentation of this game with The Obsidian Entertainment developers, and I must say, I was extremely impressed by what I saw at that time. I wondered if the released version would be as good as I had remembered in June this year!  Let me tell you, it is an absolutely cracker of a game!  As you launch the game, a fabulous cut-scene will appear which will show Phineas Welles docking onto the “Hope”, and from there you’ll start customising your character. When this is done, a new cut-scene will occur which will lay the story out in more detail, including who your contact is, on your way down to the first planet. Unfortunately, your contact was squashed upon your landing and he will be your first kill of the game! From here, quests will appear, and you’ll be on your way to an excellent game. Quests are divided into a few categories (Main, Side, Task and Companion) and you can choose whatever you want to do first, but if you are like me, you might want to complete most of the side quests and tasks before following the main story. This will allow you to gain more experience points and therefore level up your characters faster, improving your skill trees and giving you better odds both in fights and in dialogues. As you progress into the game, you’ll meet other characters, and if you choose, some of them will join your party. As you explore these planets and find settlements, you’ll be able to fast travel to each of the known locations from your map screen, as long as your party is not engaged in any sort of fighting. But before that occurs, you’ll need to find them, which in turn will lead you to explore these areas and engage in fights against cool creatures and bandits. Each winning confrontation will give your party extra experience points which will help you to level up faster in return. Each time your character levels up, you’ll receive 10 points which you can distribute between 7 skills set (each skill set has 2 to 3 options). Each even level up (2,4,6 etc) you’ll receive an extra point which you can only use to add a perk to your character.  So far, in my 30 hours of playing (which includes all side missions available to me), I visited three planets, two spaceships, and the scientist, Phineas Welles’ asteroid hideout, and I must say that I am absolutely blown away with how each of these places looks and the way the atmosphere is portrayed. It’s just brilliant! As you explore each of these locations, you’ll find stacks of items to collect in bins, fridges, cupboard, shells, corpses, stashes and many other places. Unfortunately, you are limited to how much weight your character can carry.  One way to rectify this is to find suit modification upgrades which will allow your character to carry more weight. There are also modifications for weapons. These modifications can be implemented at any benchworks you find within the game. One thing you need to be aware of is the wear and tear of your weapons and armour. You need to make sure you collect weapons and armour parts as much as you can and use them for repairs. If for some reason you are running low on any of these parts, you can break a weapon or a piece of armour for parts. You can also buy parts at merchants or at vendor machines, which are scattered all around the place. The combat phases are superb! At first, you’ll be fighting alone, which will be tricky as you will have an average weapon. Then, as new characters join your party, you’ll be able to select two of them each time you dock into a location. When in battle, these two characters will automatically engage in fights with you. However, each of these characters has a special move which you can activate at any given time during a battle. These moves are spectacular and will take time to recharge, so use them wisely. These types of games are quite hard to pull off, in my opinion, as they appeal to audiences of people who like RPG and first-person shooters. It is a big juggling act to make sure to appeal to RPG gamers with a good story and dialogs, as well as offering great battle scenes for first person shooter fans like myself. This game offers a great balance for both styles of gamer.  Visuals are stunning and each location you visit has its own feel and atmosphere, which is just amazing, and makes you want to explore and find out more about the story. I really like the voice acting, which is top notch (I did expect this), and the soundtrack and sound effects are fabulous too. Personally, I didn’t encounter any major issues during my 30 hours of gameplay so far, which is always a bonus.  I originally received an Epic key upon the game release back in 2019 and I was kindly offered a Steam key as well.Positives:~~~~~~~ +	Stunning visuals+	Great story, dialogues and interesting characters+	Stacks of items to collect, buy or sell+	Great selection of weapons, armour and upgrades+	Stunning monsters and cool enemies+	Good skill and perk treesNegatives:~~~~~~~~  -	Originally this game was an Epic exclusive  Visually stunning and totally entertaining from the start, this game is truly something out of this world!9/10Key provided by the developer/publisher for review purposes. Any opinions expressed are entirely my own!

_childDocuments_.review: It's New Vegas lite. About half as much content (maybe less) but with the same level of world building and attention to detail.Combat feels nice enough, better than NV's in almost every regard (that's not saying much) but I don't play these type of games for combat.I'm genuinely baffled that this game is only "Very Positive". I can only imagine it's the same reason I always find myself in the other side of the reviews of games I legitimately like. I do not create expectations from video games, and I'm always surprised. This game is not New Vegas though shares a lot of similarities with it, it's not Skyrim, it's not Oblivion, and it's not Fallout 3.I play these games for two feelings: "how will my build affect the story/quests" and "will the game allow me to think outside the box or just follow the quest marker". I am happy to say that both answers were satisfactory for me. More often than not, my build shines in a particular aspect which trivializes a certain part of the quest, or gives me more insight, whereas thinking outside the box has rewarded me with secret optional objectives (I can't attest that there were not any quest markers for the secret optional objectives, just that I managed to get to them without getting to a point where the game told me I could do something else)I will reiterate, it is *not* a Bethesda RPG, most of those make heavy emphasis on the sandbox-y mechanics, Outer Worlds does not have many sandbox mechanics, I would argue it has very little of them, and I don't think the game should suffer because of that. It's more HUB based than open world, but IMO there's basically no distinction. I would argue people are so accustomed to the sandbox mechanics that they expect every open world RPG to have them, when in reality, that style is a Bethesda RPG staple. This is speculation of course, I have no idea how other people think, I just find it really weird when they say things like "shallow" and "small", I feel those characteristics do not define this game appropriately.

_childDocuments_.review: Had a fantastic time with The Outer Worlds and will get the DLCs soon. The story was nothing super special, but all the different (well written!) characters made it so fun to go and explore the galaxy. LOVED Ashley Burch as Parvati! The artstyle and everything was cool, it all had a futuristic retro vibe and I guess this is where you can tell that there's some Fallout in there somewhere! :D As someone who has devoured Isaac Asimov novels and always dreamed of travelling the entire galaxy in like a week, this game made me incredibly happy, because some of the locations are just so gorgeous (like the Groundbreaker). unfortunately, the character animations were a bit off sometimes, especially in dialogues where you get to see them up close. And the lighting in those dialogue-scenes was off most of the time.What was REALLY strange was that the game pushed the Time Dilation mechanic to no end, but you could play the game without using it ONCE, making the time dilation itself and all the advertisement thereof somewhat... irrelevant. A little more weapon vareity would have been great as well, I really missed things like grenades or having mines that you could place yourself. What I really liked was the fact that this is an open world RPG that doesn't take years to finish, but it also never felt too rushed for me.So yeah- even though it's not perfect, it's fun, and I'd totally recommend it. :)

_childDocuments_.review: A compact yet epic story about the fate of you and a community in a far away space colony.It's really refreshing to play a game in the open word RPG/adventure genre that is not plagued with what now seems to be the industry standard "features": oversized map stuffed with pointless side chores, slow and non-impactful main story, and artificially bloated playtime filled with endless grinding. No, the Outer Worlds is a light-weight, on-the-spot RPG title that  open world (in the form of planet hopping instead of one big map) but doesn't have you constantly run around and get distracted with exclamation marks all over the map. It tells a cogent and engaging story (about a troubled colony in the Halcyon system) in which your choices make real differences and will determine the fate of the people in the colony. Moral dilemma, politics, branching narratives, you'll have plenty of those in this game. The game also has a very nice retro sci-fi aesthetics that is a bit similar to that in Fallout but in my opinion better done. The colour palette of the wilds look a bit like No Man's Sky but again, a much nicer version of that I think.Now, where this game falls short for me is the combat. I think the developer is a bit confused as to what the combat is supposed to be. It's mostly fps but the dev seems to want to add a bit of action and stealth in it which just doesn't work very well. I tried a bit of a stealth action in the beginning, but then you realise it's pointless so you just end up gun blazing everything. The "ability" system (especially your companion's ability) is also pretty useless...This is a solid game that we desperately need in this genre no doubt, but I still think it feels more like a 39 or maybe 49 dollar mid-tier offering. Full price is stretching it a little bit, but I'd still recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting game.Instead of the RPG that one would expect from Obsidian, The Outer Worlds has more in common with Borderlands 1/2 and  Fallout 4, but with a bit of KoTOR II mixed in.All the 'planets' one can visit consist of small hubs linked by a relatively small outside section, which is (IIRC) reminiscent of KoTOR II. But the gameplay is very much in the style of Fallout 4 or Borderlands.It basically plays like a FPS with bullet-time and your companions have 'special moves' with a cooldown.The graphics are fine, nothing amazing but they're good and have a strange sort of pop-art esthetic.Same goes for the audio, the effects are fine and although there is not a lot of music none of it is grating or bad.The voice acting is well done and all the dialogue is fully voiced.And there is an option to scale the UI font size, something that is fairly rare and thus a very welcome feature.I personally found the writing in the game to be above average.There were some genuinely funny bits in both the storylines and the dialogue and different combinations of companions have different conversations among themselves. These even take into account the companion quests you've completed.And several times I encountered situations where I'd done certain things before a quest requested them of me and the dialogue included lines that mentioned this, so they did a good job in trying to account for as much as possible in the quest dialogue.All in all, I think this is a good game.And I would recommend it, although obviously not to people looking for a hardcore RPG experience.
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty enjoyable from a game-play perspective. Guns are what you'd expect and while there are weapons that are much better than others (I found any melee weapon that isn't the scythe just isn't worth the loadout slot), you can mess with em and change their stats and damage type to try new things. Doesn't feel like anything too ambitious, but enjoyable nonetheless. My only real issue with the game is that the companions you pick up don't give you much of a reason to get invested. To be fair I only picked up a few and finished their stories, but across the whole game there weren't any characters that I could attach myself to or even care about for more than a mission at a time. Dialogue was fine, albeit lacking. Wish I could have had more interesting and meaningful conversations with my companions as the game progressed, but maybe I just missed things and could go back and find more. All in all, the game is perfectly average. Not outstanding by any means and a couple UI things bothered me (not being able to compare a weapon in a vendor to one you have equipped was frustrating), but an enjoyable playthrough nonetheless. If you're looking for something pleasant and not too difficult to pick up and comprehend, I'd pick it up at a discount.

_childDocuments_.review: The Outer Worlds made a big splash on release. Even with the whole Epic exclusivity kerfuffle. A cRPG created by icons such as Tim Cain and Leonard Boyarsky and developed by genre regulars Obsidian, would turn a few eyes. I certainly was intrigued. Obsidian having an axe to grind with Bethesda over their treatment regarding New Vegas, certainly added an extra dimension to this story, with Obsidian trying to present this game as a New Vegas "spiritual-successor" of sorts. The next thing to make an impression was how quickly the game disappeared from public discourse. After a couple of months of everyone ranting and raving about this game... silence. Now, well after the game made its way to Steam, the time came for me to experience it and see what the noise was all about.Let's begin with the basics, some story. The Outer Worlds takes place a few centuries from now, near the middle of the 3rd millennium. Humanity, spearheaded by powerful corporations has begun colonising the stars. Great ships, carrying skilled labour in hibernation, are regularly sent out to provide the necessary manpower for the various fledgling colonies. One such colony, situated 10 long years away from Earth, is Halcyon. One such skilled worker, making this long 10 year journey, is you. The parallels with the modern "private" space race and the rise of the megacorp are pretty obvious. Naturally, your trip goes wrong and after a long long time in hibernation you are awakened by a renegade scientist and introduced to a colony that is not quite the paradise that was promised. Halcyon is instead a civilization of the space-western/cyberpunk disposition, ruled by decadent megacorps and seemingly in terminal decline.Capitalism is a primary thematic focus and the game takes an extremely critical view of it. It incessantly parodies corporate practices, makes a complete mockery of advertisement, constantly pokes fun at the endless greed permeating business and so on. The irony of a product with that message being sold for money, relying on advertisement, even going Epic exclusive, was not lost on me. But I digress. The problem is not the message. The problem is that the game takes the mockery too far and forgets that it needs to be serious for a moment too. How are the corpos presented as a credible threat when they are all degenerate buffoons? How are they a faction one would even want to join when they are laughably irredeemable? The game supposedly offers you the option to join them, but why would you? What could possibly narratively compel you to?Playing through the game the question that kept coming back to my mind is how could this social structure possibly last this long. Indoctrination and oppression can only take you so far. The stick can only take you so far. You need some carrot too. You see, by presenting everything as one big joke the game misses the point of why capitalism is all around us. That's because, for many people, it works. Or at least works enough. Both the narrative and the message would have been better served if the game dealt with it slightly more seriously. If it afforded it some gravitas here and there. If the corporations were actually presented as slightly less incompetent. There is so much darkness to satirize in capitalism, but even that darkness isn't enough to ground things when everything is treated as an opportunity for yet another flippant take-that.Moving on, the game's presentation is great. Beautiful graphics, nice music and acting. Some pretty decent gunplay and an interesting, if eventually uneven character leveling system round the experience. The game is quite fun to play and yes the humour is often top-notch. I was constantly smirking at one joke or another. This great presentation would explain I believe the initial enthusiasm over the game. On the flip-side the game went by fast. It is pretty short for its genre and after the initial enthusiasm wears off the issues described earlier come to the fore. The game is vacuous, the plot unmemorable, there is no staying power. Even the NPCs are forgettable, with the exception perhaps of Parvati. The sole exception would be possibly the initial area of the game, Edgewater, there things do have some nuance. But that quickly disappears by the time you reach Monarch. This, I expect, would explain why the discourse over this game went subsequently silent. There isn't much to talk about.I am rather disappointed by the Outer Worlds. Not because it's a bad game, in fact it's a rather decent game. I'm disappointed because it's not a great game and from the likes of Tim Cain and Leonard Boyarsky, from the purported spiritual successor to New Vegas, I expected nothing less. The game falls decisively short of the hype it generated and I doubt it will be remembered much. Nevertheless, if people simply want to have a fun romp and a few superficial laughs at the ills of capitalism without expecting anything deep, then sure this is a great way to waste a few dozen hours. I do recommend it. Afterall, to quote one of the game's companies, you tried the best, now try the rest.
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed The Outer Worlds. I'm about to do a second playthrough to examine some details I missed the first time. Your enjoyment of The Outer Worlds is going to depend on what you want from a game. If you enjoyed the Fallout: New Vegas feel of many characters and paths as options, you may like this. Although the "open world" sandbox feel is not ideal; the quests and sidequests are faily no-nonsense. Once you've cleaned out an area it stays cleared out, and there is no appeal or reason to revisit locations. I'm hoping there's more expansion in a sequel. I mean you can visit half a dozen planets-- give me something else to do there!I enjoyed the plots and situations. I enjoyed the nuanced options to resolve the issues, and I liked the balance of violent space opera options and actual diplomacy and bridge building. I get bored with "kill everybody with this color of helmet yay you win the world!" and this allows you to listen to what the different factions want and actually effect change. It's easy to play in a mode of "everything sucks so I'm going to just make a mess." But it also gives you options to help people and fix things and try a little harder.You get half a dozen companions, who all have values and conflicts and motivations. Being able to change which two you bring with you into different situations is a great strategic action mechanic, but it's even more fun when you bring specific characters into diplomatic environments. Some will scold you or mess things up, some will provide you excellent bonues and dialogue options. And I loved bringing the first companion, who you meet stuck on a backwater station on a backwater world, and letting her explore luxurious new surroundings and exotic places. Seeing the game with her eyes adds a lot of flavor. Still working my way through the dlc but it's encouraging so far. Please make more dlc or a sequel! I love this world!
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: It's not the best choice, it's spacers choice.Obsidian straight up beat bethesda in their own sport. As many can feel this is New Vegas in space and The outer worlds really have that Firefly sci-fi western feel. The difference from NV is that shooting stuff actually feels good and overall the gameplay loop is more refined version of NV.Ups- mostly bug free- story branching choices (both main and side quests that will mix your final outcome)- you can play in party or solo (companions interact with each other and sometimes they insert themselves into dialogues)- both dlcs add some solid hours to the game with interesting self contained storiesDowns- weird use of invisible walls (mostly in edgewater)- color palette used might take a while to get used toSo the conclussion is pretty simple, if you like this kind of games buy it and play it.

_childDocuments_.review: SPOILER FREEAlso sorry for length, tldr at the endPreface:After watching the trailer for this game before it even came out I was lightly intrigued. It looked pretty cool, but at the same time something about it didn't really draw me in. That, coupled with the fact it wasn't released on Steam until recently, led me to forgo getting it at the time.HOWEVER, I decided to pick it up on a whim while it was 50% off, and I must say, that while the game certainly has its share of flaws, I would happily have paid the full 60 bucks for this game knowing what I do now. I literally just finished it, and I have to say the feeling is that I just wish there was more content that I would happily throw my money at. There is such a wealth of excellent world building and story here to continue, either in Halcyon or another colony, or somewhere else (wink.)The Review:Before I start just wanted to say, the only things "wrong" with the game are some of the mechanics, in that some combat mechanics could be improved, as well as enemy ai. In my opinion the game is perfectly fun as it is.Pros:-EXCELLENT Writing:     This goes not only for the main story, but for at least 90% of the side quests as well. Everything was well crafted and compelling, really sucking you in to their particular stories. Most of the time I even wanted to dig more into it, going into computers and reading correspondence to figure out more of what was happening, or had happened in a particular area or for a certain quest.-Dynamic World and Story     -The majority of quests allow for decisions, and these decisions can often affect the world and story in different ways.-Character Development     -This could go under writing, but I thought it deserved its own section, as the characters, both the companions you can get and many other npcs are phenomenally written, and feel more realistic than many other AAA rpgs. They go through a lot of growth as characters, and of course your decisions can change the outcome.-The Visuals     -This is something you just need to play and see. Hopefully you have a rig that can let you see how great the whole game looks. There is so much attention to detail in its design. So many colors and great designs.-The Humor     -As others have said, this game has a great sense of humor. I literally laughed out loud at least a dozen times. Wink.-World Building     -As I said in the preface, the world building for this game felt immense, and honestly more compelling and better written than the Fallout games in my opinion.-Combat     -Many complain about the combat, and while elements of it could certainly be improved, I found it fun and engaging for the most part every time. There are also a lot of options, and you could build your character in a number of ways. Even a potential pacifist build.Cons:-While 90% or more of the quests were fantastic, some could use improvement.-Enemy ai and detection.     -You kill somebody's pal that is no more than 30 yards away from him on the other side of building, and he doesn't hear the yelling or the gunfire.-That there isn't more     -It went by pretty quick and, and I took my sweet time on it, exploring most every nook and cranny I could find. Because of that, I felt like the game could have been improved if things had been slowed down and expanded.Conclusion:This game is a steal if it's on sale, and worth it in my opinion even if it's not. If you like games like Fallout and Skyrim you will probably like this game. It has a completely different energy and atmosphere when compared to those two, but in a lot of ways it is similar. I would love to see a game in this universe made in the same scope as those, with a larger world, longer quests, and more of everything great this game does already.tldr: Buy the game so they will hopefully make another and I can write another way to long review.

_childDocuments_.review: I basically murdered the whole solar system but made a good choice in the end so I was somehow redeemed and seen as a savior/legend.For a game that pushes the whole faction-reputation mixed with moral choice and consequence thing, there are little to no downsides to just turning whole towns and major planets into graveyards.. and that kinda sucks. So many strange dialogue options that don't line up with how your character is playing/what they've done.I did have a lot of fun just running around and soaking the atmosphere in. Great environment design, well optimized game, pretty fun weapons and skills to take...but it isnt enough to recommend this game to me. especially if you're looking for a decent RPG where choices matter.

_childDocuments_.review: HOLY ♥♥♥♥, JUST ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ BUY IT ALREADY OK!The charm and writing of witty remarks makes dialogue choices so fun. Very reminiscent of the original Fallout games (sort of developed by a branch of the original studio so it makes sense). More so optimistic and pessimistic dialogue responses rather than the modern day Bethesda YES, (INSERT BAD SARCASM), MAYBE, NO bs they give you. The freedom they give you in choice making feels almost unlimited. Can't side with 2 opposing factions, well kill one (it could open a completely new path) or kill both! The writers seem to pin-point almost every option you can consider. That said, if you do decide to be a blood thirsty maniac your choices will be narrowed down and you will likely miss a lot of side quest content. There's multiple endings depending on the main factions you side with and how you want to play out the important decisions in the narrative.The Gameplay feels fine-tuned down to a knot with multiple damage types for different enemies. Got practically every weapon type you can want if you find it. Early game can be a bit difficult, but once you get to the second planet loot for gear, improve your ♥♥♥♥ and you'll be fine. Really liked the slow-mo function in gameplay, feels like a better adapted version of VATS.Although the scope of the maps feels limited. I know, I know... I'm not asking for 16 TIMES THE DETAIL. Only a few more interactive places with a bigger map, which I'm sure they can improve on with the coming sequel this new gen. God I honestly don't know if I will ever find an RPG like this that will fill the void it leaves in my gamer blood.  10/10 - Some guy with an opinion.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, the story was unsatisfying, it definitely feels like unfinished. I mean you literally have no romance option with your companions, and their missions and characters are somewhat forced. The first companion is lesbian. Why? Don't get me wrong I have no problem with diverse characters, but the very first one and only decent romance option? Make her at least 2nd or 3rd, so that I can experience a decent dialog with my companions... Definitely cannot go near Fallout New Vegas, the gameplay is dull after a time later, definitely no good selection of weapons as well to see in a game. Also the time slowing power does not look like a power, it feels more like a patch. I guess the characters are made too fast and with this they kinda fixed it.Pros: No crash, decent first person shooting game, somewhat complete endingCons: It makes you continue to play it expecting a lot, but it never delivers..

_childDocuments_.review: After a very thorough Playthrough including the DLC's I have to say there are some interesting ideas but some absolutely terrible ones too plus bugs that remain still,  including the whole draw your weapon every time you talk to someone problem that is still not fixed after all this time. _childDocuments_.review: A very solid AA experience that was harmed by expectations of a AAA experience. The marketing did nothing to help that problem. It's pretty short, but I bought it on sale and with the expectations that it was a AA game. 30ish hours and I finished the vanilla and both DLCs with a heavy dose of the side quests (and unlokcing a little over 50% achievements). Not really a game I can get lost in and revisit year after year like New Vegas, but I thoroughly enjoyed it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: This game would need a "meh" review button.It is not horrible, but it just got.... boring.In the beginning I had high hopes. It looked like Fallout New Vegas in the Borderland Universe.But after a few hours it felt like a Walmart version of it. Like Fallout 3 in Mass Effect Andromeda.Pro:- The writing is mostly good, and quite fun at times- The worldbuilding is fun (although nearly a carbon copy from Borderlands)- You can play as non combat focus character and do fineCon:- The combat system is tedious. Enemies are bullet sponges. You are a bullet sponge. At least ranged combat is boring (I havent tried melee). I dont know how, but the combat in Fallout New Vegas felt more fun and refreshing, and that is 10 years older- The world itself feels empty. It is less open world than Fallout, and still manages to feel less rewarding to explore.- A lot of the worlbuilding is : "Read this e-mail conversation" - The mainstory was relatively boring.- A lot of side quests are: Go to building A), press button B) bring Mcguffin C)Final Score : Fallout 3/New Vegas
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: This game comes so close to what I had hoped Obsidian could make,but it falls so short just at the end of the raceThe Good:Combat is fairly engaging,allowing you to use different styles to fight,Guns are weighty and feel good,but the melee was never really there for meThe world is decently sizedThe characters are well voiced and feel like they somewhat impact your character.The little nods to other games and franchises are nice to see,and often funny.----The Meh:While the overall world is decently sized,it feels oddly empty,interiors are often copy-pasted (Though this may be a design choice based on the games story-line)The characters,while good,don't make me feel like they TRULY matter for the game,it never feels like you are missing something without them.For the size of the world,there simply is not enough variety in items (Armor/Weapons),It ends up being the same skin with different stats,and it feels useless.Again,while the world is big,the playable areas are very small,you often feel confined in your freedom.There isn't much depth to the story itself,it feels very surface-level with how it's given to you,I wish there was more to discover,especially with the issues regarding Earth.----Conclusion:This game was a good attempt at Obsidian to regain it's fallout glory,but sadly it falls just short of greatness. It is yet another game stacked with awards that no-one talks about because it simply isn't memorable,you can see this in the lackluster modding community( A fallout staple at this point). It is a shame because the recipe is here, On the surface it is a great game,with a great story,But that's the problem, It is only surface deep. There isn't the deep engaging story that fallout has,none of the wild shenanigans,deeply memorable characters,or an actual feel of belonging that fallout provides. You could spend years playing a fallout title and still find new and engaging content,yet in this game you could find most of the material within a few months of regular play.I still give this game a recommendation because it IS fun to play,it just isn't memorable enough for me to fall back on. I expected greatness,and what i got was another acceptable game with a stack of awards from its release.

_childDocuments_.review: Pro's: The writing is absolutely superb; story line decisions are satisfying; nice atmosphere in general. This game is focused on the different decisions you can make in conversations with NPC's. If that part of RPG games generally interests you, I can recommend this game. Cons: The game is very easy and I recommend to play on hard-mode or higher. The quests are repetitive and have no puzzling or challenging element to them. The game is short and feels a bit unfinished. If you like open world games where you can explore and hone your character's skills and items to perfection, I do not recommend this game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: The most engaging and enjoyable game I have played in a long time. The dialog and voice acting is engaging and I don't think I skipped a single bit of it. Combat is a lot of fun and gives plenty of tactical options without being complicated or overly technical. And the range of options at your disposal for solving quests and progressing the story is impressive.
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: An enjoyable, if brief game compared to other games in the RPG genre.  The 29 hours shown is having beat the game on Normal while completing most of the side quests by playing the main character as a morally flexible mercenary, freelancer, rogue, bounty hunter type.  This game was developed by the folks who participated in developing Fallout: New Vegas, and you can tell because it appears to use the same general engine and playing mechanics.  That said, this is it's own game for sure and not "Fallout in Space" at all.  The sci-fi story goes in the direction of the dystopian "worlds literally run by corporations".  The writers appeared to go for a "Borderlands" kind of story vibe, but deliberately more serious...but only slightly so.  This results in multiple awkward moments where the characters try for sarcasm and Borderlands-like humor, but fail in the delivery.  The gameplay reminds me extensively of the Fallout 3 onwards series, for both better and worse.  The game's brevity is concerning.  I can tell the developers built a solid game foundation that could easily last longer than 30 hours.  It almost seems like they artificially cut the game length to make room for the DLC?  Either way, this game was a solid, "high 80s percent / low 90s percent" type experience, and my schedule was packed, so in this case the 30 hours worked well for me.
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: The first hour of gameplay is nothing but dialogue options. You can tell that is literally all Obsidian spent any time working on. I did enjoy the multiple different types of Charisma checks, but there was SO much dialogue. The characters that I saw were very shallow and forgettable, I couldn't give a single care about any of them. Playing a charismatic character means literally nothing if I can't give a damn about any character, and that includes my own character.Then when I decided I was going to just murder hobo it up and ignore charisma checks, I figured out they expect you to output multiple types of damage to overcome resistances, or combat just isn't going to be fun for you. Pumping ammo into level 1 droids isn't fun when they do 1 damage each.Refunded after an hour. I had seen enough.
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: Waited a long time for a Fallout4 successor. This one is sublime with nice storytelling (realistic voices) and a lot of humor. Played all DLC too, they are worth the time and money. There are (nexus) mods to improve some areas. The ending is the best I've come across with detailed explanations. Thumbs up for this LOL/Labour of Love!
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: Overall: Barely thumbs up. This is a B+ or A- title, not a AAA.Pros:	- You've probably played this type of game before. It gives a retro feel to a game that is retro styled.	- Setting will appeal to Firefly fans.	- Most companions felt like they had personality, even if they were fairly standard tropes.	- A couple of companion quests were strong, but most were not or were just "go here, go there".	- A few nice pops of story here and there.	- Graphics aren't the finest, but style and aesthetic worked for me. Will be very familiar to Fallout 3+ fans.	- Not a lot of bugs relative to other games. Granted, the title has been out a while on other channels, but even early players commented on that in other forums.Cons:	- Including the first expansion, only took 37 hours to play through. Credits lasted longer than many subquests.	- Flashbacks to Knights of the Old Republic 2. Some parts of the game felt like they were just ended quickly. At least they were generally fully wrapped up.	- Plays like a game circa 2005.	- Until you pick up Parvati or get to the Botanical Gardens, the starting area is pretty dull.	- Barely qualifies as open world. "Broken bridge" games where you have to unlock more areas should be ancient history.	- Too many bits of story were too cliche.	- If story was stronger, weak combat would be excusable. As it is, it feels more like a distraction.	- Some companions' quests were really short. One was just a couple of trips to towns.	- Like so many similar games with weapon customization, special weapons just don't seem like they're anything special.	- No grenades. Some NPCs really deserved the grenade reverse pickpocket trick. Hortense Ingalsbee leads my list.	- Final quest ends the game. It does warn you, but when the next expansion comes out (slated for next year), you need to pick up a prior save or play through again. Not sure:	- The overall tone of the game is pastiche, satire, and parody. Some elements are VERY dark, especially in the Project Gorgon expansion and some of the penultimate decisions. Sometimes, it means the elements play well together, other times it misses.	- The Sublight Salvage faction alone could have been a whole game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: This game is superbly fun with interesting combat, customization and a relatively intriguing story line. The only problem I have with the game is the "delivery boy syndrome" where I just do favors for characters and run back and forth between planet to planet. This isn't as bad as one would think, it doesn't take away  too much from the overall experience of the game's fun.
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game about brilliant but greedy corporations who deliver sub-standard products because of incompetent management and impossible deadlines, made by a brilliant but greedy corporation notorious for delivering sub-standard products because of incompetent management and impossible deadlines.That isn't actually a joke. The first DLC - Peril on Gorgon - is an intense ultra-violent meditation on how a confluence of bad management, impossible deadlines and total lack of concern for the lives of employees/customers can come together to produce a disaster so much bigger than the sum of its parts. I seriously think the writer was working out some game development trauma writing it.The Outer Worlds is the semi-competent first draft of an RPG shooter which copied Fallout 3's homework and set it in space. It has zero polish: the game - nearly four years after release - is still rife with bugs and built on a foundation of objectively terrible design decisions.If you really liked Fallout 3 and have enough brain damage to not notice how poorly-made it is, you will like Outer Worlds. If you didn't and/or don't, then your fun will probably barely outpace your frustration until you complete exactly one playthrough, then uninstall this moderately-radioactive dumpster fire and never touch it again. Note that I said Fallout 3, not New Vegas - which is a much better game than Outer Worlds on every level.Before I get into details, here is a :None of my complaints about this game have anything to do with difficulty. This game was not difficult. I did not have any difficulty beating this game on Hard. I didn't even get the achievement for using the healing inhaler a lot, because I rarely needed to. If you think this is a hard game, then you're bad at videogames. Don't project your stupidity and lack of gaming skill onto me because I criticize the bad game you like.The dialogue is fairly good at times and the voice acting is more than competent. It's not Shakespeare, but it's a step-up from Fallout 3. Again, not nearly as good as New Vegas.Thematically, Outer Worlds is fairly shallow. Expect several dozen different variations of "CORPORATIONS ARE BAD". But occasionally the game poses serious moral questions that are actually intriguing.The worst part of the writing by far is the corporate slogans and jingles and over-the-top goofy "comedy". Your mileage may vary, but I find the Fallout 3 style of blunt-force satire repeatedly slammed into your face undermines the emotional impact - the whole game is basically a joke.This game is NOT a gritty first-person shooter.  My first experience with combat on Hard mode was walking up to a marauder and watching him tank HALF A DOZEN pistol shots to his unarmored face before dropping. Until you mega-upgrade all your gear and invest enough points in your shooting skills, expect combat to be bullet-sponge hell. Again, the combat isn't actually DIFFICULT - it's just tedious.Science weapons are special unique items that scale in effectiveness based on your Science skill, and are useless unless you invest maximum skill points into Science, at which point they become absurdly OP. I tried and failed to find any use for them until the late-game, at which point I re-specced to 150 Science and found that the Mind Control Ray turned the hardest and tankiest enemies in the game into chunky salsa so fast that they barely had a chance to hurt their teammates before dying.Even for a dyed-in-the-wool obsessive RPG nerd, the amount of micro in gear management is INSANELY STUPID AND TEDIOUS. It appears that one half-competent designer outlined a somewhat-interesting level-based gear progression system and another less competent designer who didn't like the idea proceeded to ruin it by implementing it very poorly.Gear is leveled from 1-99, but - with one exception - the maximum you'll get is 41. It appears that the original idea was that you could take starting items and continually invest in them with money so that they keep pace even to the end-game, with a continuing cap of +5 above current level. That would have been a really cool way to help players become emotionally invested in their gear and preserve unique weapons, but somebody in the dev team apparently didn't like that, so the cost of "tinkering" increases at an absurd exponential rate.To put this in perspective: purchasing the absolute best non-unique armor in the game cost me 570 bits. Upgrading my favorite pistol from level 28 to level 41, even with the Science skill bonus that reduces tinkering cost by 90%, cost about 50,000 bits.This was presumably to force the player to buy higher-level gear... which is usually just lazy re-skins of weapons you already had with a number tacked on the end - like "Plasma Rifle 3.0".Babysitting weapons and damage types like a fussy schoolmarm got a lot easier when I realized that no enemy in the game is highly resistant to both Plasma and Shock damage, which both scale in damage with more Science Skill. So - if you're maxing out Science - you can safely ignore the much more expensive N-Ray and Acid weapons.Towards the end-game, I was continually struggling with the weight limit. Then I realized that I was carrying roughly 100 lbs of healing items because I'd used so few of them throughout the game (again to neuroatypicals: THE GAME IS NOT HARD).Both DLC are meaty and fairly well-written, but - like the rest of the game - are implemented like hot anus on toast.The first DLC - Peril on Gorgon - becomes available at the END of Act 2 of the game and is recommended level 25. The second DLC - Murder on Eridanos - is available at the START of Act 2 and is recommended level 30. Read that again and roll your eyes with me.By the time you start Peril on Gorgon, you will probably already have beaten Murder on Eridanos and reached the level cap and have the best gear in the game (unfortunately for the fashion-conscious gamer, this gear will mostly be pink). That means all gear/XP in POG is worthless and any combat is extremely easy. The DLC's increased the annoyingly-low level cap from 30 to 36, but also unlocked an additional 50 points of progression for each skill... while only giving you only 60 extra points to work with. Does this sound like all upside to you? Au contraire, mon frere. In addition to raising level caps and skill caps, they also  to compensate. Several dozen skill checks randomly strewn throughout the game have been increased from 150 for REASONS.Near the end of the game, I did a full respec and made different buff outfits for Unlock, Hack and Persuasion buffs, then painstakingly curated my skill points so I could reach exactly 150 in each of these with any of the four companion-skill-bonus combinations of Parvati/Felix and Max/SAM (meaning two entire NPC's were completely worthless to me). The precious minutes of my life that I wasted doing this will never return to me and I will never forgive Obsidian for that.I'm not a big UI guy, so I'll just make it simple: the interface is clunky garbage and the gear stats shown are clearly rife with bugs. Expect armor/damage ratings for a given item to halve or quintuple depending on which of multiple menus you look at it from.I have played practically all of the western CRPG's ever made, and Outer Worlds is one of the rare few that I sincerely regret playing. Whatever magic Obsidian might have had with KOTOR 2 and New Vegas is gone. Face it: they are never going to release a complete game that lives up to their potential. It's just not in their nature.

_childDocuments_.review: I had a pretty good time murdering half of the capitalists pig dogs on Halcyon, but I can't in good conscience recommend this game, especially at anything resembling full price. The main story is extremely short, for one. I'll preface this by saying that I don't have a lot of patience for meaningless fetch quests and I also have never liked travelling with companions in games, so I only completed a few side missions on my way to completing the game. I also murdered a couple of key characters because I either didn't want to do meaningless fetch quests for them or just didn't like the lone dimensions of their invariably one-dimensional personalities; honestly, would you rather do a fetch quest while an irritating character you just met sobers up, or would you rather shoot her in the face and get on with the story? At any rate, I ended up completing the game in 8-9 hours. Howlongtobeat has 12.5 hours for the main story, so I suppose you could call it like 6 hours of substance and 6 hours of filler. For a $60 game by the studio behind Fallout New Vegas, that's extremely disappointing.The story itself was decent enough, length aside. The main critique I have on that front is how forgettable almost every single character in the game is. In a week's time I'll probably remember Phineas but I can't see myself remembering anyone else.The guns are fun, but there's not much variety there. Weapon balance is also a mess; light ammo weapons are basically useless, heavy weapons are underpowered, and high base damage weapons are extremely strong because of how many armored enemies there are. Mods are really useless compared to tinkering the heck out of the guns you find to raise the base damage. There's such an obscene amount of ammunition lying around that you're never in danger of running through it, even if you only use one weapon type the whole game. The armor and weapon degradation mechanic was just an annoyance and added nothing to the game. Most of the perks were centered around companions or time dilation, neither of which I used, and none of the rest are particularly interesting; I never made it to Tier 3 perks, but Tiers 1 & 2 were just basic stat buffs. To add insult to injury, the game would periodically offer me debuffs in exchange for perk points, but there's absolutely no reason to accept because of how bad most of the perks are.True to form for an Unreal Engine game, this game also performed terribly, especially in the first area of the game and in Byzantium. I have the recommended GPU for the game (GTX 1060 6GB) and a CPU substantially above the minimum (i5-6500) and performance was inconsistent at best at 1080p / 60Hz and minimum settings. Some areas, especially smaller indoor ones, held 60 FPS great. Others were extremely choppy.This game feels like an once-ambitious project with a solid foundation that ended up with a severe lack of content due to pressure to meet deadlines that just weren't realistic given the original scope. That's painfully apparent from how much better the first area is than the rest of the game. It's a shame really. A few more years in the oven and it might have been a pretty cool game. As is, you might get some fun out of murdering all of the characters who look at you funny, as I did, but it just isn't a good game. Shame Phineas was behind bulletproof glass. It would have been fun to murder him too to see how the game would react :(

_childDocuments_.review: So, this game is very good.Obsidian, the company behind The Outer Worlds and Fallout: New Vegas (My favorite game ever) really knocked it out of the park here. The story and characters are brilliantly written, with an awesome mix of horrifying oppression from powerful companies and very dark humor found in the cracks of the corporate reign. The combat is awesome, with weapons feeling powerful and having some great noises to back them up. The mod system does leave a lot to be desired, as the mods you find in the first hour of the game will remain the same, from level 1 to 30, which makes the progression feel a lot less impacting. My main criticisms of this game are as follows:1. Progression and leveling kind of sucks. The perks are not interesting, and usually just finding stronger guns is a better idea than actually leveling.2. Armor kind of sucks. The fallout games have always done a good job with encouraging certain builds to avoid heavy power armor, as they decrease things like agility, which sneak and sniping builds need to be successful. In this game, there isn't really any reason to pick a light armor build over a heavy armor build, as the only thing heavy armor affects is a very, VERY slight reduction to stealth, which isn't even an important stat in this game. This problem gets worse in the endgame, as the high level heavy armor no longer has de-buffs.3. Weapon leveling is boring. Since this game takes a much more looter-shooter-y approach to gameplay, the game needs certain weapons, such as the assault rifle (One of the best weapons in the game) to level up with the player as they progress. At a certain point in the story, the player will start to collect 'Mark II' weapons, which are literally the exact same weapons as the early game ones, but better in every possible way. This really ruins the fun of the early game, as you hit a point after only like 5 hours where you just don't find any new weapon types, but only find better versions of what you already have. 4. Ammo balancing is not good. In the early game, you will pick up powerful guns such as the AR or Plasma rifles, which do much more damage than the starter pistol. The balance for this is that the starter pistol uses light ammo, which is everywhere, but heavy and energy ammo is much more rare. This instantly goes away after the first few missions, as I had more heavy ammo than light at the end, making it a walk through the park as I plowed through literally hundreds of the most armored and well armed enemies in the game in the final mission. The whole weapon leveling thing really comes into the limelight here as well, as I beat the final boss, yes, the FINAL BOSS IN THE GAME with the same assault rifle that I had found off of the fist raider I fought (The first enemy in the game) but the mark II version. Just an estimate to how long this fight took? UNDER TEN SECONDS. The gun balancing makes the game's challenge a joke. I wish there were a difficulty thing other than supernova (Because it makes companions die permanently) that made the game actually challenging, as to really immerse yourself in the game, you want to have two of the brilliantly written and acted characters at your side. With the challenge of the game being this low without removing the main source of enjoyment I got out of the game, It really ruined the tone of the game, as when I entered the final mission where you are storming a heavily guarded compound after everyone you have talked to in the game telling you that you will be murdered brutally when you enter, I cleared the base in under ten minutes. This really makes the player feel like Halcyon is less of an 'Outer World' and more of a cake walk.All in all though, this game is really fun. I love it. I can't help but complain about some stuff like that and the ending, which isn't a huge deal, but when it just feels sub-par in a game will amazing writing, it just doesn't sit right with me. Although New Vegas has better progression and balancing, the games are very evenly matched in writing and atmosphere. This game really made me feel like a kid watching Star Trek with my dad for the first time again, the neon 60's-style spacepunk artstyle, the humor of the characters and writing, the design of the monsters, the background storytelling in the abandoned labs, the choices you make on all of the planets you visit. This game may not be perfect, and it isn't quite as good as New Vegas, but I will remember this game for a long time, and it is undoubtedly in my top five favorite games of all time. If this game goes on sale and you haven't played it, do it. Play it. My run took about 18 hours, and I really liked almost all of it. Give it a shot.8.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: I've seen a lot of folks comparing this game to Fallout New Vegas and if that is truly case, then I would say this game is far better than NV. In my opinion, NV had real potential but the company put out a flawed product that was riddled with bugs and difficult to play because of that. To the best of my knowledge, the company did not try and patch their problems and if they did it was a half-arsed attempt. Based on that, I was reluctant to play another game by this company. I took a chance with this one and was glad to see whomever was in charge on the NV project apparently had been let go because this game was galaxies better than NV (if you're the type to compare this game to NV). Game play, graphics and overall control mechanics are top notch and worked well! The story line (for me) was intriguing, engaging and adventurous. Companion NPCs were good but in my opinion could've been a bit more fleshed out but overall are interesting and bring color and humor to the story / quest. The overall length of play for the stand alone game for me was perfect... not too long but long enough to enjoy and develop a good plot with twists, turns and mystery. In other words, my character found himself understanding both sides and at times a bit conflicted on the best course of action for the overall good. Fortunately for the hero character I played, it came down to the attitude and overall intention of the other NPCs as to the direction my character chose. Combat portion was good and did not seem to go on and on for ever. However, I did play on a bit of a lower level so as to really let the story be the focus. Therefore, I cannot comment too much on the combat on higher difficulty levels. For me and my "in your face, gung-ho" play style, I thorough enjoyed what combat my character was involved in and how smoothly it was to conduct fire / move maneuvers. There's abundant loot and gear rewards from the combat and simply laying around. Again, this aspect may be a bit more scarce on higher difficulty levels. From what I've read, the game only takes about  27 hours or so to beat. I tend to go slow and look for all the loot and rewards I can find and try to explore as much as I can. So please don't let the number of hours I played mislead you. I play slowly and enjoy going over every nook and cranny the world had to offer. All in all, I'd give the game 8.5 out of 10. I will play again in the future and would recommend giving it a try at least for one play through. Peace and cheers!

_childDocuments_.review: Some pretty average reviews on this one....People comparing to Fallout, or Borderlands....While i can understand the comparisons, I think this game is great blend of the two.  For all the reasons I hated Fallout (hacky, weak story line, unnecessarily open world, clunky combat system and constant game ending bugs) and the reasons I didn't like borderlands (terrible story line, missions/quests that had no importance) this game i felt like got it right.  Also keep in mind I do like BL and FO, but if everyone is comparing to these two, I think Outer Worlds is hands down the best.  First, its a fully fledged game, and I encountered ZERO bugs...ZERO! I cant think of the last time I could even say that about a game.  That is no small feat. especially in this day of rapid development.  Took me 30 hours for my first run through, and I did every mission.  I will definitely play again to see the alternate outcomes, and check out the DLC.Graphics are great, sound/audio was great.  The story was fantastic. lots of sub plots that actually were intertwined into the main story and weren't pointless.  Your main companions also showed some character development as well.  The combat was satisfying, especially after modifying weapons and tinkering.  The ability to equip your companions and change their tactical approach was nice.  I found that special abilities confusing at first but they were useful.  The different weapon classes were good, and and offered variety.  I enjoyed that this is not a full on open world game. It gave enough space to explore and find hidden spaces, and i didn't have to walk for 10 minutes or ride a clunky vehicle to get where i was going.  Also the fast travel was fine IMHO. I hate it when games make you walk or travel endlessly.  I found this a good blend; yes you will still have to manually go places, but it takes maybe 2 minutes where in other games it can take you 10 min or more. I was able to stay immersed into the story and wasn't distracted by unnecessary long hauls on random terrain. Also i enjoyed that enemies just didn't randomly respawn.  I feel like if you go into a town, and murder everyone, they should stay dead....seems simple. If you like a good story in a FPS with some RPG aspects, this is it.  My only gripe would be that they do try to blend in some comedy here and there, but it never really hits and I found it unnecessary.  Its not a genre defining game, and its not going to start some new benchmark in gaming.  It IS a well thought out, and entertaining game.  8.5/10.

However there was some things which I thought it could do better, such as having more guns as well as adapting a little bit more on the story to widen it more. As with the story of the game, it is great however it is based solely around two main areas. _childDocuments_.review: If this was a $20 game, I'd say hell yeah, pick it up. It's a solid rpg shooter, but it doesn't really break any ground, or go the extra mile. I've put 4 hours into it, and I'm just not having $60 worth of fun. The story so far is predictable, acting and animation is okay but not great, and the setting, though visually not bad, feels like it's been done to death lately (i.e. over-the-top dystopian dark humor. Okay, I get it already. Megacorporations are evil.). I've loved Borderlands and the Fallout series, and this borrows from both of those, but it doesn't do anything that makes it worth $60, especially since it's a short game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Outer Worlds

_childDocuments_.review: I think people give this game a bad rap because of the way it was marketed. This game is not another Fallout game. In fact, it's not really even a Bethesda game at all. It's an Action-RPG with an emphasis on the RPG. It is good for what it is - which is a game where you can pick a role and do a bit of roleplaying in space.That said, it certainly has its flaws. I think the weapons and gear are almost laughably boring. All armor is just "Light Armor Mk.1" or "Light Armor Mk. 2." That definitely doesn't get players excited about improving their armor. If I know the next best armor I'm going to get is just the same armor I have now but with a higher number attached, I'm much less eager to find it.I also think the combat needs work. It's difficult to explain, but it doesn't feel good. It feels floaty and somewhat like you're shooting at toys rather than people.I still think this game is good, and I'm eager to see how the next game comes out.

_childDocuments_.review: 7/10Very disappointing  to be honest. Half of this game is good and interesting and the other half was boring and unfinished. Here are my bullet points:* The combat are boring and cheap * The story line was boring and stupid, I didn't even bother to read half of the game's story because  it sucked* The gun sounds were actually really good, they had impact and eco* The melee combat was seriously bad* The main story came up out of no-where. I was semi-enjoying the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ plot and then the game ended* Graphic were decent, game had it's own style but the style was basally garbage* Voice overs were not very good* Their attempt at making a star ship game with multiple planets and landings was decent, but overall failed.* This game was basically Fallout in space, but it failed to be unique and interesting at every turn.I disliked this game at almost every point that it tried to be Fallout in Space completely. But the game itself turned out to be decent and somewhat enjoyable from beginning to end. While it did that, it failed everything from beginning to end.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't understand how people can claim that this game is 30+ hours long. Finished it in 16.6 hours and that's with doing all the side quests and expansion Peril on Gorgon.It's a nice little game but long it is not. Choices of armor and weapons are rather lackluster as a lot of them are just reskins of the same 3-4 armor sets. while weapons are rather lackluster with no weird quirks. Also melee is unfortunately really boring and useless as you get spotted real easily and then you have to charge up to your enemies while the blast you with everything they got.Another gripe is that the maps are not big at all and if you really wanted to you could finish the main quest in under 4 hours.  Not saying this is necessarily bad but after playing it you will most likely walk away feeling it lacked something.Not gonna put a rating but if you want a short RPG that will amuse you for a little while I'd say yeah go ahead and try it.But if you are expecting some kind of long epic tale you will be disappointed.Either case it's an obsidian game so its solid and plays like a fallout knockoff.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR Unsubtle in its storytelling, a bit overzealous in its reuse of assets and mechanics, and weighed down by NPCs with much less emotional resonance than they needed, but well voice acted, and beautifully textured, The Outer Worlds qualifies as a competently made RPG, just a forgettable, cartoonish one.  It wants to be Firefly the RPG, but it didn't put the work in.ConsAsset recycling: An almost palpable fog of cut corners shrouds the game from nearly the beginning, with many, many, MANY reused assets, both in setting and items, some of which can be justified by the dystopian world building, but many of which strain what can be forgiven.  There are too few armor and gun archetypes, and your equipment upgrade cycle quickly degenerates into swapping in the next identical looking version without even an attempt at lampshading.  There are only 3 tiers of each weapon.  Many of the locations look similar because with the exception of the Groundbreaker and the Bzantium they are all using the same assets.    Exploration is somewhat damaged due to annoying invisible walls and poor/unforgiving jump physics.  With just three exceptions each, all the companions had the same options for the skill trees.Cartoonish storytelling: At the overview level, the story is solid.  You are a colonist recently thawed by a rebel scientist from an abandoned colony ship that time forgot.  You must make your place in a dystopian world while trying to figure out how to save the rest of your frozen fellows.  The problems come with the villains, the corporations of Halcyon.  They aren't just cold, ruthless, and cruel, they are positively cartoonishly evil often for little to no gain.  The Board of Halcyon's policies make Andrew Ryan (Bioshock) or Vault-tech (Fallout) both seem well adjusted by comparison!  I'm not a fan of Randian ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ philosophy, but the game lays it on so thick i simply could not take it seriously.  Weakly characterized Companions: This is admittedly subjective, but none of the companions caught my interest or made a firm impression as to who they were.  The only one I had any attachment to was Pavarti, your very first companion, and only because you spend the longest with her and her similarity to the must deeper and better portrayed Kaylee (Firefly), except as an asexual lesbian.  The rest of the cast had all the flair and depth of a mud puddle.  A few of the supporting cast at the various locations were memorable such as most of the faction leaders, but fewer of the niche NPCs left an impression than your average Fallout game.  ProsGraphics: It's damn pretty in a lot of places, especially when you get away from the massively overused shipping container home clusters that pass as cities.  Lava flows, rivers, tall grass of various shades, gorgeous character models, and well designed monsters all impressed me.  The sfx are a bit overbearing and distracting at times, but almost everything looks good.Voice Acting: Is pretty consistently good, much better than what I expect for this sort of game.  The script might not give them much to work with, but the delivery was usually well above average.Nothing fails utterly: Despite how many complaints I had, none of them were crippling.  At worst they were a little sour, more often just a bit eye rolling or uninteresting.  Even at it's worst, The Outer Worlds never lost my interest, and I logged a respectable number of hours on it.  I came away thinking the game needed more polish in a lot of places, a lot more... everything, especially as the game winds down, and some tweaks, but it was fundamentally a sound experience.  Not an instant classic to launch a few franchise or a game you will want to replay many times, but a competent if slightly underwhelming effort.  I wanted it to be more, but I'll settle for this.
