_childDocuments_.review: It's fun but it's feeling like its kind of lacking in a way. If you're looking for a super story based game this game isn't it. There's really no connections with the characters or the ooblets and it's not as engaging as I had expected it to be. I feel as though it's more based on mainly collecting and farming and kind of accessorizing your character and your ooblets. The map starts out super small and it threw me off and also the fact that farming is what you rely on the most but it's difficult to make a good earning in the game. There needs to be more ways to earn money rather than having to sell things or do quests that still require you to collect crops or materials. The ways you can collect materials is also very limited as you run out of wood and rocks eventually and have no other way to obtain them as far as I can see from the amount of time I've played other than buying them. The drawing and ooblets are fun and the dancing is interesting but it's always the same thing and it slowly starts to be less engaging since it starts to feel more like a grind instead of having any strategic way of winning. I wouldn't say I hated the game completely but It was lacking more than it was entertaining and I would not say it would be worth the money.

_childDocuments_.review: I was expecting to like this game, but not as much as I did. It came at just the right time, I've been going through a rough time and I just needed something cute and simple to take my mind off things. Ooblets scratched that itch.The game is a cute mix of farming, creature collecting, daily quests, friendship building, and dance battles.Farming can end up being fully automated so long as you provide seeds once you have enough ooblets and ooblet houses, so you can move on and explore.I enjoyed all the different islands you go to. They change it up too so it's not always just dance battles you need to do to accomplish thing (though I think I liked the dance battles the most).Eventually you can even open your own shop and sell your items to the townsfolk. I never really ran out of things to do as the game progressed, if anything I always wished I had more energy and time in the day so I could do more. Which isn't a bad thing at all.I'm glad I started playing during the Hallowe'en event. There were lots of cool spooky items to get for my house and with all the leftover candy I was able to recycle to make lots of bait for fishing which helped a lot with supplies I needed towards the end of the game.Oh and I really like their take on shinies (gleamies) in this game. If they spawn, you'll know. There's shooting starts and fireworks around the town so you can't miss them, you just need to look around a bit. So while it's still down to change that they'll spawn any given day it's not down to chance per encounter.Anyway this game has a lot to love. I've already gotten all the achievements but haven't finished the main story yet. I'm at the very end though, and I'm glad I played this game.There isn't much commitment needed either, you can play as much or as little as you like without feeling the pressure to get to the next save or the next big thing like in other games. It's just good casual fun for as long as you want or need.Pick up Ooblets and have a splenda time ;)Update: Wow after all these hours on the game I only just got the joke that is Outgrids name >_<

_childDocuments_.review: I might return to this review for revisions as I continue the game, but I feel like I need to express my thoughts on this game as is. This is going to completely disregard the entire EGS fiasco.Ooblets is a casual farm-sim, creature collector, deck building game. The game-play cycle revolves around you challenging ooblets to dance battles, which are basically simplified versions of typical card-battle games like hearthstone. Winning a battle nets you a seed that you can take to your farm to grow a new Ooblet. That's the core game play. I think the largest issue the game faces is how unbelievably slow the beginning of the game is. You're going to find yourself spending all of your money on seeds for your farm, and making back just enough to buy more seeds and maybe something else, if you're lucky. Everything you grow has some sort of in-game use, which typically is to feed to an ooblet to challenge them to a dance battle. You NEED the resources you grow in order to get more Ooblets or open new things in town, but, these plants are also supposed to be one of your main sources of income, either from the mission board or just selling them directly. It is a slog to get everything in Badgetown open, or expanding to new areas. The sense of progression is minimal, and it makes the game feel a lot more like busy work rather than a fun game. This game takes heavy inspiration from other life-sims like Stardew Valley and Animal Crossing. It doesn't try to hide that fact. it borrows many of its core elements from those games. However, those elements are watered down from their source material. There's a day/night system, but there isn't a season system or any sort of change in day-to-day life. You grow the same crops all the time, with the same ooblets, and any events are tied to the real-world calendar rather than an in-game one. Instead, the change in the daily-life comes through a level-up system, where new crops and ooblets appear as you gain XP. Leveling up is a slow process, meaning you're stuck with the same old same old for extended periods of time. It causes the game to feel very stagnate, rather than a living changing world like other life-sims. Characters. The characters in ooblets are completely unremarkable. Remember-able and unique NPCs are one of the foundational elements of a life-sim, and the characters in Ooblets are all too similar. There's a lack in dialogue variation, so many of the NPCs talk in the same way, and don't have much remarkable about their personalities. Even when doing introductions, I found myself unable to remember who it was I had just talked to. Many of these NPCs sort of just wander aimlessly around all day, lacking any sort of schedule aside from those who are also shopkeepers. With Badgetown also being very small, you'll wind up seeing them walking in circles or stuck on the geometry somewhere. The Ooblets themselves are the same. The player character is also a bit strange, as the character creator is barebones. Your character also has a voice, with the game already having quite a lot of dialogue for the player character, often breaking the immersion of you being a resident of this town. The game's art style is... okay. The biggest hindrance to it is that it's sort of generic. Everything looks so similar to one another, especially in regards to locations. I found myself trying to find a specific building in Badgetown, and going in 2-3 wrong ones every time. Ooblets themselves also look very same-y. There's not much interesting happening with the vast majority of them aside from trying to look cute and marketable. They all have the exact same animations that look like they were pulled from the unity store. Many of them are just an animal or a plant with silly eyes. The NPCs also have this issue with sharing too many animations. That and the game's programming often doesn't account for the outfits, environment, or anything the characters can hold, so these animations clip right through. The style of animation doesn't match the art style, really emphasizing  the "store-bought" feeling behind charcater movements. Especially when dance battles happen, which is what you're going to see the most of.The elephant in the room is the game's writing. I mean the literal writing in the game. It tries so hard to be weird and quirky that it comes off as forced. None of the characters speak in a natural way, instead, talking like 2012 tumblr posts. The slang and abrupt attempts at humor just feel so commercial. There's no thought behind it. No attempt to craft an interesting world or even a fun story. it's just bland. I don't know how an indie studio managed to make all of their dialogue feel like a corporate attempt at being quirky. It makes me feel cynical, but it's just not cute or charming. The excessive use of vowels and baby-talk feels like they're trying to replicate Adventure Time slang but didn't understand how to. Others may feel differently, but seeing "Ok cool." at the top of the screen any time i pick up something new just makes me feel upset. It's bad.

Farming is a thing you do so you can make recipes to unlock new ooblets; it works well, but it's a background system. _childDocuments_.review: Firstly, I'm being very critical of this game, and you may enjoy this game despite the things I find lacking about it.This game mixes the excitement of creature-collecting and creature-battling a la Pokemon with the coziness of a farming sim, and honestly, it works. The game is very charming. Each day I always find myself excited about what new ooblet I may be able to recruit into my ever-growing menagerie, and I get particularly excited when a shiny ooblet shows up in town.To recruit an ooblet, you must win a dance battle against it so it gives you a seed of its kind. To challenge an ooblet to a dance battle, you must give it a certain set of materials. Some ooblets ask for forage, others ask for crops, and others ask for crafted foods.This is where the negatives begin to pile up.See, for ooblets that ask for forage, you probably already have them on hand as long as you're not neglecting to pick up stuff while walking around town. But for the other two, it causes a dilemma. In a normal farming sim, the primary (if not the Only) purpose of crops is to make money, this makes sense. On occasion, you may need to keep a few crops on hand for quests or gifts, but still you want to sell the majority of your crops to earn money for the next batch of seeds or upgrades. Not the case in Ooblets, because now crops are equally important for money AND for recruiting new ooblets, which creates the two-pronged problem of wanting to hoard crops "in case i need it" and being constantly low on money because you're not selling your crops. It's even worse when the ooblet is asking for cooked foods. Many cooked foods require at least two steps to make (for example, Quib Tart for recruiting Unnyhunny requires you to process Sweetiebeetie into Froobtose, then Cook that that with Quibs to make the tart), while others are even more complicated (for example, Soggy Bread requires you to first process Sweetiebeetie and Muz into Froobtose and Muz Flour, then Unlock Bread Sammy recipe in the wishing well, cook that, then Unlock Soggy Bread recipe in the wishing well, and finally use the bread sammy to cook the soggy bread.)This, combined with how there's no clear linear way to progress in the game, makes it very overwhelming in my opinion. I'm always stuck trying to decide what I should be growing in my limited farm space, and what to do with whatever I grow from it. Do I sell it so I  can buy stuff? Do I keep it to recruit ooblets? Do I keep it for the 500 other quests that tend to just randomly require these crops? Am I suddenly developing a self-destructive hoarding habit? (the answer to that last one is yes)Anyway, cute game. Very overwhelming. 15 hours was enough for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Ooblets is a very special game to me. Special in the fact that after a 1 year wait to get it on steam, Glumberland is still hard at work making a fantastic game even better. Is it good though? Well this is a tough question to answer but the reason is with all the fun activities, where do I start with?I guess at its base it's a farming sim, the meat of the fruit and veggies is that you will be planting and watering a lot, kinda like other farming sims such as Stardew. The twist is that the second biggest aspect of your new farm life is that you must dance battle other plant/animal/robot monster things to get seeds to grow your own allies to get in even more dance battles! Shake it Followbabies!Other notable aspects are doing tasks for the mayor to help develop Badgetown, the town you live in, and progress the game's story line. Travelling to lots of different locations. Talking to people all over the world and giving gifts to help develop friendships. Raising crops to sell and cook into tasty dishes. Daily dance tournaments that give exclusive rewards. And my favourite task of all, tracking down beautiful colourful "gleamys" (they are effectively shiny pokémon folks) and really taking to the dance floor with tracers and sparkles as I dance the night away! There's also fishing that has no mini game! You just put bait on the line, cast it away and you're always guaranteed to get something, wow!If I haven't sold you on the ridiculous zany fun that is Ooblets by now, perhaps this is not the game for you. It is kinda a niché music card battler farming sim dance battle extravaganza. But if any of this sounds like it would appeal to you, I would heavily encourage you pick it up today and start your new life with your new Ooblet friends! <3

_childDocuments_.review: I will be honest. I read a lot about this game. It is highly suggested on different forums when looking for something cozy. I was expecting a great game.But... I was really disappointed. IN THE BEGINNING.This game at first, for the first several hours, was super confusing. I had no idea what to do. There's barely any handholding. I don't like when games treat you like an inefficient toddler but I also don't like it when they leave you alone to figure EVERYTHING out. But if I had to pick the lesser of 2 evils, I'd choose the former.This game at first is confusing af. I had to keep googling how to do things. I didn't understand how anything worked. The game gives you less than the basics when you start.However, now that I am 20+ hours in, everything is so much better. Don't get me wrong, I still have to look up certain recipes and how to do things but the game is SO much fun. And it IS relaxing. You can do everything at your own pace. Yes, there is a clock but nothing is constrained by time restrictions.This game is highly addictive in the farming Sim category. You need to grow various amounts of crops in order to make money. Some of these crops need to be further broken down into ingredients to use to battle ooblets in hopes to get a seed. This seed, once planted and cared for, will grow another ooblet and further grow your little army.I haven't played many card based battle games but once you get the flow of this, it's highly addictive and cute.I really recommend this game to anyone who is looking for a fun farming sim that allows you to take it easy. Be patient (more than me!!), explore, and enjoy.

_childDocuments_.review: I've put in a few hours and can say that I genuinely love the game! It has its own appeal to farm sim and creature collector fans, and I can see that it takes inspiration from a few other games. I was not aware of any community drama until after I got it so I don't care to comment on it tbh.The progress is much slower than Stardew Valley. In fact, it's just slow in general. The main campaign tasks are tied to your level, so you can actually complete them at a lower level and then only have side quest options. However, I never felt like I had nothing to do since I would spend my downtime foraging, micro-managing my farm, fishing, crafting, cooking, and decorating/accessorizing. Hot take, but I feel like Ooblets does the farming part better than SV. It's easier to gain momentum when harvesting/planting, and the crops are actually useful for completing the main campaign. They are also much easier to profit from, as you can process them into food with ease or you can use the Plenny export shack to earn massive profits for set amounts of crops. The creature part is very unique! The dance battles are executed via deck battles like Slay the Spire. When you win, you get an Ooblet seed which then can grow into a new friend! Your Ooblets follow you around like in Heartgold/Soulsilver, but you can also leave a few at the farm to help you take care of your crops. One of the cons is that the game doesn't let you talk with your following Ooblets or let you feed them treats, which I would've liked to see. There is an incentive to collect many different types to allow for synergy with your chosen dance troupe; some Ooblet dance moves work best with others. The game does allow for adventuring to other areas to collect new crops and Ooblets. The game also lets you put accessories on all your Ooblets! :DAll in all, I really do recommend it if you're interested!

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent experience of videogaming. Ooblets scratches a lot of itches at once. It's a little bit monster collector, a little bit farming sim, a little bit town life, but it's not too deep in any area. Although there are some ways the game could be fleshed out in perhaps a sequel or big content expansion (I'll get into a few ideas about this later), overall I think the balance is actually just right for me.I have a lot of games that ask a lot of me and I also have some games which are relaxing but in some ways ask *too little* of me. It's tough to find a game that hits a sweet spot between too much and too little sometimes. Ooblets is, for me, in an ideal point where there's just enough to engage with to keep me motivated but not so much that I ever feel overwhelmed or like I just need to slog through a bunch of grinding etc.The style and theme are unique and quirky in a way I overall liked. I'm not saying every joke lands or anything but such is the nature of comedy. Overall I liked the light-hearted interactions with townsfolk as a contrast from too many games which try to do Grand Storytelling when sometimes I just wanna buy a new jacket and didn't actually need to get a whole lore dump about how the shopkeeper was sad a lot as a kid.At just over 40 hours I've completed the main storyline and I'm now I'm mostly winding down and collecting gleamy ooblets, perfecting my farm, etc. I'm not sure if I'll get a ton more out of the game but I wouldn't be surprised if I play for at least 10 more hours and that's a pretty good value overall.There are a few areas I'd like to see fleshed out. Vacation spots are a little underwhelming. Having the Dance Barn as my only reliable source for battles with other trainers at the end of the game is a little disappointing it would be cool to maybe have Dance Barn type locations in other places like Nullwhere and Port Forward that maybe hold events less often but would give you another excuse to travel. Lastly, without major spoilers, the endgame feels like it could use some kind of epilogue focused on tearing out some unnecessary facilities and doing restoration perhaps.None of these criticisms are major detractors though and the game still stands up as a fantastic experience. My best hope is for an Ooblets 2 where I can dance battle my friends as so many of my buddies are playing this game and we all talk team composition/strategy and how we we wish we could battle each other!

_childDocuments_.review: I've put several hundred hours into this game on another platform before it came to Steam, and I look forward to playing it more here as well.Ooblets is a very cute and charming game with memorable characters and silly dialogue. There are lots of adorable creatures to befriend and collect, as well as a farm, home, and shop for you to expand, improve, and decorate however you want. You can travel to different regions of the world, each with their own unique setting and theme. There are also seasonal events that inject some fresh and exciting activities that will keep you coming back every few months, even if you haven't played in a while.Ooblets appeals to casual players and dedicated spreadsheet optimization folks alike. You can play at your own pace, and there are no consequences for doing anything "too slowly."This game is one that you can play for hours on end, but it is also easy to pick up and put down if you only have brief windows of time -- making it an excellent game to play on the go if you happen to have a Steam Deck.The community surrounding this game has been very friendly, positive, and rewarding to be a part of. The devs have been releasing free content updates several times per year since the game launched, and there are even more new features on the way.I have found it to be worth every penny at full price, and if you can get this game on sale, I consider it a no-brainer.Lastly, Nuppo is the best boy; may you all receive the blessing of many Nuppo spawns!

_childDocuments_.review: Quick Note: I have played Ooblets previously (many, many hours), and this is my sincere review of my love for this game. I hope this helps new players make a decision. I am also a casual player and enjoy many cozy titles.Dailyo!!Ooblets is a fun, cute, silly game that is charming and a real joy to play. I love this game with my whole being and I still regularly play often!It is one of the few indie titles that joins two of my favorite genres: monster taming and farm sims.It has all the wonderful qualities of a farm sim: farming, friendships, customization, home customization, cooking and some crafting.Ooblets has put a fun twist on battling. Instead of the usual battles we're used to in monster tamers, our Ooblet critters enjoy Dance Battles in the form of turn-based card battles and aren't afraid to show off their slick moves. This makes battling a bit less competitive, more casual and fun which I think proves a wonderful introduction to folks who haven't played monster tamers before. (And also means the battles tracks are so DAMN good)The dialogues between your townsfolk are silly and funny; it makes engaging with them feel rewarding and so much fun that I think cozy gamers will really appreciate. The story is also a fun ride and Ooblets holiday events are seriously the best events I've ever experienced in a cozy game.I have so much to say, but there is so much packed into Ooblets that I would rather not share so that new players can experience this game blind and truly enjoy what this game offers!The Devs put SO MUCH love into this game and I am so happy to see how Ooblets is doing today.Thank you so much to the Devs for making Ooblets happen and continuously giving us more content. I'll happily follow and support you in any future project(s) you pursu!. And with that, I wish everyone a grand journey in the land of Oob, where you heard fabled tales of oddity, creativity, and Ooblets!

_childDocuments_.review: OoOoooblets is a good game, I was playing Pikmin4 and this game at the same time, both games were 100% contented with my squirrel symptoms, I am a sucker for collecting stuff, but quite tired after 40 hours collecting the same thing from Ooblets (like mushrooms, shells, fruits, petals).On the one hand, collecting basic stuff was monotonous, on the other hand collecting creatures, seeds, and plants was AMAZING! they're unique and creative! My favorite ooblets were Gloopy Long Legs and Legsy! Farming was the most relaxed part of this game as well, with delightful art style and BGM, harvesting and making some food, not a cow but a plant can make milk is a very inspirational design. Dance battle gameplay was playable, it reminded me the time when I played Hearthstone. NPC from Pantsbear Hill called Shenaghy was gorgeous but speaking somewhat acrid, very suitable with her look.Even though I had lots of fun  Ooblets,  it still had some distinct problems, if people hadn't played any farming and collecting games like Animal Crossing,  Stardew Valley, Pokemon, Hearthstone they might confused at the beginning of the game. Personally I feel like had such problems:1) I didn't know furniture store could make a 5x5 watering machine and something else, making stuff on a workbench is a common design in this type of game, so I spent a huge time and energy watering my plants before I found this information.2) I was still stuck after playing 40 hours and didn't know what to do at the time, firstly I thought I triggered a BUG or something I couldn't start the final balloOn mission, after 2day in the game when I finished all the side missions, I realized it didn't have any final balloon mission  the final place was on the map already! I was like damn! what!?3) The wishing well had no description about what would go on if you upgraded the item which caused I didn't know the Plenny order could make money quickly if I upgraded it to the 4 level. During a 2 vs 2 match, I encountered opponents who stun-locked me until the battle's end, I could do nothing but wait. Some cards made me feel uncomfortable using them.It's hard to make upper desserts to earn money, basically the seeds were expensive and took loOong time to grow, and I spent most of them for ooblets demands (TAT), so most of the time I was a poor poor guy in this game looking for money and picked up litter.Yeah, but flaws do not detract from overall excellence, I like the vibe of it and give it 7/10. _childDocuments_.review: Things I love about ooblets:1.  SO many lil guys.  A game for lil guy fans.  And you can dress them up. And they can drive vehicles.  What's not to like? 2.  The game is very forgiving about time. There's no incentive to play daily, but at your own pace!  (Other than holiday events I guess.)  So if you're away for a few days due to life it'll open right where you save.  Plus, you can save in the middle of the day too!3.  No weirdly hard fishing mini game compared to the rest of the gameplay.4.  Fairly fleshed out NPCS, despite the amount of characters.  And no friendship decay (that I've spotted).  5.  Still getting updates!  Things that annoy me a bit about ooblets:1.  You can't really customize the deck that you build, but rather the ooblets that you choose are the way you customize your deck.  As someone who is a fan of deck based games this is something I had to get over.2.  The dance battles can be repetitive. 3.  Sometimes the changes of nouns (ei, caroot instead of carrot) can be funny, but some can feel childlike in like, a bad way. 4.  A game like this would 100% be a great place for modders (lots of customization options, low poly models), but mods aren't supported.  If you like casual silly games with card 'combat', lots of fetch quests, and collecting creatures, this is a game you might want to check out.  I've been listening to an audiobook while playing and it's been a great time.

_childDocuments_.review: Very cute game with better mechanics and fleshed out features than a lot of quick produced cozy games... however it's super buggy and the last two areas are... a mess. Doesn't help that it's an annoying 3 minute trek up a mountain each time to see if the bug fixed. Skates seem like a wonderful thing to discover until you realize the headaches both the movement and camera give you. The camera is great for overworld of the base town but it is so sloppy it's borderline unplayable in the Pantsabear hill. If you want a cute creature collector with unique game mechanics and a fun farm  piloted by little dudes it's worth it (just don't level up your coop past 2 or you'll never see your crops! lol) but beware that the endgame quests are less than fun fetch types and you may not even be working towards anything since the last quest is locked out. _childDocuments_.review: Without the fiasco.Game is very bland. Graphic wise, it's very bland and everything shares almost if not all the same animations. Physics is very weird and off putting. Everything just clips together, like clothing, tools, ect.Heck, even the chest slots is off, like someone just did a badly paste the slots into the less common (or 26 slots chest)Ooblets are cute I guess, but that's it. there's not much variations to it.While game is inspired by SoS(HM)/SDV/Pokemon, it barely touches the water or to into detail of what defines the genre.I love farming games and grew up with SoS(HM)/RF/Pokemon/Sims. And it's safe to say that Ooblets has none of the features, or any features that make it stand out or unique on its own.Farming is barebones, no seasons, no levels, same crops all the way. Also how farming grid is, it's also very clunky and not fun to farm.Ooblets/Pokemon-- none, there's no stats and the only thing is the earning exp for level and maybe moves (cards) level up, and I guess you can dress them up a bit.And Ooblets spawn per map is limited per day, they don't respawn until the next day.There's no days or seasons, or seasonal events (not real life events). Dance battles is very repetitive and it's pretty much the same animations over and over. and the cards are RNG. They definitely should change the description of the game, as claiming you can "train" ooblets is a false advertisement.One of the main thing that irks me, the crappy "baby" or terrible adventure time wannabe talk. And that's in the whole.game. there's not one remotely "normal" npc in game without the childish, overuse language.There's a difference in making a unique NPC with their own unique slang/catchphrase vs making every npc sounds outlandishly and ridiculously childish. Also the game treats the player the same way, when you pick up new items/level up/rewards/ect. The naming of items are definitely babystyle also.The game fails to blend in the sillyness, when they make the player have a set personality already. which also makes the set-player-response seemed like the player is the only sane one while the rest seems like they never graduated from kindergarten.All the areas aside from Badgetown, are extremely lackluster and empty. If the area is lucky, the NPC gets houses (that you can't enter). There's no reason to return back to them unless you want to get ooblets or ooblet. No special NPC or townsfolk that you can build relationship with. It's hilarious how some npcs said the area is a town, such as nullwhere or pantsahill, when there's really nothing there. There's definitely no "townies" there as the plot claimed to be.For the end plot, it's laughable how the game magically gets 100 votes when there's barely ANY living npcs.Maps aren't fleshed out and not even half finish.Townies NPC- no special feature or personality, they're very flat, no special events for friendship. You can college some bland stickers for friendship level I guess. Would not recommend.If I wanted to collect 'pokemons' type, there's re;legends or sunhaven. As much as I have a love-hate feelings towards those two, they're a tons better than ooblets.

_childDocuments_.review: Ooblets arrives a little late to the realm of life-style farming sims and given that there are so many out there to compete for your time what is unique about Ooblets?While the core remains the operating and improvement of your farm the name and main draw of the game is the Ooblets themselves. You'll collect the many ooblets wandering about by beating them in a dance battle. This is done with a card based battle system, you draw cards from your dance deck and play them to get an effect. The ooblets in your crew add their unique moves to your deck and that about it. The battle system is honestly bare bones and bad, I get that the uncomplicated system is supposed to lead to a more relaxing game but the lack features just made things frustrating. Mostly this comes down to being unable to customise your dance deck, for example alot of ooblets can add status effects that can cripple you deck, stacking a debuff that prevents your score cards from scoring or stunning an ooblet. There are counter cards tied to certain ooblets but without the ability to short your deck of useless cards you can get stuck sitting on your hands waiting to draw the card you need, especially with larger battles and more ooblets. You could stack your crew with the same ooblet but then you draw alot of support cards that do nothing when you need score cards. The only saving grace is that battles are short and easy. The AI won't play its best cards or will play a buff after a move that would that buff thus wasting it. It is rare to actually lose a battle and given how hopeless the AI is those loses will be at the hand of bad luck more than anything else.So the dance battles are a little plain, but what about the collecting of the ooblets themsleves? Well to start you'll need to join a ooblet club. Its the first choice you'll make and it doesn't really matter, you'll choose yourt starter ooblet and then nothing. The clubs have a function in that latter on they sell costumes for your ooblets as well as unique special card to add to your deck. But you have access to all clubs anyway, gaining no benefit from your membership. and the unique cards suffer from the non customizable deck thing, half the time you dont draw them when you need them and the other half they take up a slot in your hand and stop you from doing anything. But beyond that collecting the ooblets is pretty fun, you need to collect an item to offer them as a gift before battling them but theres a good range and as you unlock new ones which want rarer items there will be plenty of common ones around to collect while you find the stuff you need, especially as there are 3 variants (cosmetically) of each to collect add to your team. It all starts off well until you hit the cap. Theres a starting limit on how many oobs you can have and it gets tedious increasing that limit especially as you do it one ooblet at a time with resources that are constantly in demand for farm upgrades, quests and everything else.And here comes the rest, the farming progress is painfully slow, you barely make enough selling you crops to buy more seeds, you need the crops to make the items to catch ooblets. You scan the ooblets for cash, but you've hit the limit and you need to build houses for them. Things will get better eventually but that start curve is painful it takes too long to get to the point where you can start easing the busy work with things like sprinklers and once that hurdle is over the game gives you a shop to run, which is also painfully slow and tedious until you get upgrades to have it tick along at the level it should of started at (enjoy watching 6 NPCs wander around for 3 mins without buying anything while you get to do nothing).And to top it off the characters in town are as bland and basic as can be, Theres nothing here to hook you in getting you to care about the people in town, the only thing to seperate the main towns folk from the generic nobodies wandering about is the fact they have a little entry in the players guide book. I've finished tyhe game and I couldn't tell you their names, half of them you only talk to if you need their shop services, I had no reason to go into the barber or cafe for instance.The sad fact is that if I had to sum up the game in one word it would be tedious. Its not a bad game but it doesn't offer much beyond the cute creatures to collect. I want to like the game and I did have some good times but not enough to recommend, if you're looking for something in the same ballpark try Moonstone island.
_childDocuments_.name: Ooblets

_childDocuments_.review: I played like 20 more hours of this after I stopped enjoying it, damn completionism. Bad: The game just feels shallow and tedious in all of its mechanics - combat feels like a chore, there's no complexity to it, only strategizing you can do is pick which ooblets join the fight, but the winning strategy is just going all damage, and the debuffs you can do don't feel like they affect the AI opponent at all (if there's more than one ooblet in the fight, stunning one or two almost never matters). The musical aspect feels underexplored. Running a shop is extremely tedious, super slow, with NPCs taking ages to decide on something.Good: The aesthetics and the vibes of the game are absolutely amazing, There's somewhat of a story that drives you to progess with a simplistic anti-capitalist message in there too, which is cute. Ooblets helping you farm is a cool take at farm automation. If you don't care about completing the game, play for under an hour per session, and don't think about the combat too much,  this could be an enjoyable experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Really repetitive and bland to be honest which is insanely disappointing. Been waiting for this game for years and while I can tell the devs put a lot of work and heart into the game there's just really not a lot of meet to it. From what I understood in the marketing, it was supposed to be equal parts: Stardew Valley: farming and meeting interesting characters and getting involved in their stories. And another equal part Pokemon: meeting and collecting monsters, mastering the battle system (dancing) and that these two halves would make a holistically unique game.It's in fact just less involved Stardew. There's a bad battle mechanic you do sometimes.There's also monsters, I guess. Cool.The vibe gets grating and obnoxious after a while. Very wannabe adventure time and regular show with the made up vernacular and low self esteem teen comedy. I don't know maybe I'm just too old to gel with it. The NPCs are all bland and boring, with barely any ways to interact with them. The farming is weirdly really hard to make money with? It feels like no matter what you're doing you're barely making end's meet. Like dude come on I have to collect resources to battle monsters? And it doesn't tell me how to get the item I need to battle the monsters? There's no way to track what monsters need what food from the ooblet manual in the pause menu? There are plenty of other people, including club leaders that are basically gym leaders, but I can't battle any of them? I can't see what teams they make and strategies there are and learn about their personalities through battling? You couldn't put tool tips to explain the mechanics or what they mean? I can't even edit my deck, it's just a collection of really terrible base cards and whatever I get through leveling? Come on.I was looking for something that would let me pick and choose what I wanted to do so I could have fun with the game that I bought. Not a time-locked chore sim.One of the regular things that you do in the game is mash A to collect a pile of cans to feed into a machine that takes MINUTES to make bait so you can watch the same animation and get junk from the ocean. Almost every thing you do throughout the day is pretty much exactly that. They're not fun and engaging, but they're things you HAVE to do to progress. They're not suggestions, they're not "things you can do if you're out of things to do/need ideas on what to do today." They're required to get any sort of economy going. It's disappointing, tedious, and, at times, annoying. Sorry, Glumberland. I wish you luck on your next game. Like I said you guys are clearly passionate and had a vision and I respect that. Maybe with some polish this could be a really special game for the right kind of people. But I don't think I'll ever be that kind of person. I'm all set with this one.

A unique mix of farming, creature collection, card (dance) battles and exploring. The NPCs are adorable and quirky and there is a good portion of humor in this game. _childDocuments_.review: Edit after 11 hours: I still recommend the game, but I must say that the silly writing is really becoming tedious.  The struggle for resources early on was a true pain and my love for the game has dwindled a bit.  It's still a mostly pleasant experience, but not as endearing as it was at first.  The creature collection aspect is the most fun, but, again, collecting the resources to challenge the creatures can be frustrating.  The dance battles are the most disappointing part for me, as there is no real "deck building" to this game.  You are given random cards based on the level/species of your Ooblets.  I've yet to have a challenging battle.  Hopefully that will change the further I progress.  Thus far, frankly, every thing but resource gathering has been too easy (I've unlocked the third location), with friendship progressing so routinely, battles always being won, and no challenge to quests other than the grinding of farming for resources to use and sell.   Original review after one hour:  I don't usually review after such a short time, but I am absolutely in love with this charming game.  The graphics are lovely, the play is so pleasant, and though the silly language is, well, silly, the atmosphere is still pleasingly cozy.  One of the best features is that holiday/events can be turned off in the settings.  I'll definitely update this if I change my mind or if I make new discoveries that need to be highlighted, but for now, it's a keeper for me.

_childDocuments_.review: This review is all about the controversy (sorry in advance for hijacking the review system to do this). Please skip this if you can enjoy the game solely w/o looking at "the story behind the curtain." I'm really glad for you. In fact, a part of me wanna  the drama and just enjoy the game too!And if you decide to continue, maybe you might wanna read the official statement from the developer in "We did the thing" [1] and "Regarding what’s been happening" [2] first, to avoid my bias.TL;DR: it's the classic question: "can we support the art but not the artist?", which, in this case the artist's behavior quite outweighs the art.---The controversy took place in 2019 when Ooblets signed a time-exclusive deal with Epic, and the dev announce it in a "tongue-in-cheek" tone [1]. While you can communicate a non-serious and/or positive update (e.g., holiday patch) with a relax/joke tone, communicating bad news is already dangerous in itself. The least you can do is make it formal (and that's not even guaranteed you'll avoid the backlash). So why still going on with the troll-baiting style, which almost ensure a disaster?Ideally, that announcement should be short, to the point, empathizing, apologizing, and reassuring. Something like "Due to our financial status, we decided to take Epic's deal, resulting in a one-year time-exclusive on Epic Store. We will be happy to see your support on Epic Store when the game is out. However, we do understand that some players are unable to switch stores; thus, we apologize for this inconvenience. Rest assured that our intention is to publish the game on every storefront, and we will make that happen as soon as possible."I'm aware that paraphrasing the statement won't make the backlash vanished (since there are  of Epic haters). But at least, keeping it short means there'll be less chance to upset/offend someone with miscellaneous out-of-topic chitchatting, like suggesting people vent out the anger on the climate change instead.For me, I'm not ok with [1] in the part the dev assume everyone play Fortnite. Well, here I am, someone who never plays Fortnite because of motion sickness. So I'm really wonder why the dev make such strong claim over a diverse group of people (especially when Ooblets has non-overlap target group with Fortnite...) Nonetheless, I saw the whole announcement as a bad-taste joke which I can tolerate. And, honestly, if I were in their position, I'd take the deal too.I also understand that [1] meant to be communication only with their supporters. What I don't understand is why it's a public post? Especially when the dev seems fully aware that the statement will definitely upset the public: "Okay, so we did the thing! The thing people get angry about. But maybe don't get angry about it?" [3].Of course, after the announcement, the dev got backlash. I'm not surprised. What surprised me was that the dev themselves choose to participate in this flame war. Well, I'm aware many screenshots are fake (like the Holocaust or the Malaysian's dad). But would those fake screenshots look  and spread fast like fire if the dev choose their words wisely (or just stayed silent)? Not to mention that the real replies from the dev, although taken out of context, are still terrible way to talk to another , regardless of being their customer or not.And I'm also aware that, on the other end, there are people who send rape/death threats, which I condemn too. I condemn them to a greater degree than the poorly communication from the developer. Basically, no one should be sending/receiving such threat.I know the frustration being on the receiving end --- been there too. We are human beings with emotions and biases. We get angry when someone crosses the line, insulting us. That prompts us to fight back, luring us to think that we have all the rights to return the violence, right?But you can't fight fire with fire, especially when you are the one in the spotlight. You have everything to lose. Your reputation. Your customers. Everything. And what will the public anonymous lose? None. So why engage in this fight?Well, I believe that the dev already learned it the hard way, as seen in the aftermath write-up [2].However, there's an important point that's been overlooked in [2]: when you decide to fight in the public, you risk making collateral damages to bystanders, risk turning strangers into enemies.And the damage has been done.The least the dev can do is release an official apology. But no, [2] is just recap on what happened. Say thanks to their supporters. Never a sorry. (Go ahead if you gonna call it an apology. There's a huge gap between "It was a stupid miscalculation on my part." and "I say means thing to people, sorry." --- especially when the first one was followed by "I recognize that none of this post equates to an apology in any way that a lot of the mob is trying to obtain, and that's by design. While some of what I've said was definitely bad for PR, I stand behind it.")Sigh...This world is not black and white. Not everyone outside of your circle is going to be your enemy. There are people who are not taking side too. There are even people who never heard your game before. And when these people decide to learn more about the game, will they gonna hear about the cute-relaxing gameplay, or the louadspeaking drama which turning them away.The game has been out for a while, even surpassing the Winter Sale phase. The reviews almost land on the "Overwhelmingly Positive" zone. But the total number of reviews was not yet exceed 1k! Compared to other indies in the same spectrum, I'd say Ooblets could achieve a number of reviews (and sales figures) larger than this by a magnitude or two. (To get into perspective: Stardew Valley has 500k reviews, Hades 200k, Celeste 70k.) And that's is a missed opportunity, which I strongly doubt that the game would be more successful if it resolved the controversy better. (See No Man's Sky for how to comeback from the controversy. And IIRC, Hades was once Epic time-exclusive too, but still loved by players .)We are human after all. We made mistakes out of our stupidities. Everyone does that at some points in their life. Of course, no one should be punished forever, but it takes effort to ensure this kind of mistake won't happen again (or at least won't happen easily). While an apology won't help resolve every kind of mistake, saying a sincere sorry is a sign that  realize we are a part of the problem, and we're willing to fix it. (Besides, saying sorry literally costs nothing, except, maybe, one's ego.)I guess people won't forgive the developer easily when they don't even bother considering saying sorry?(Last but not least, it's seems like the dev already achieved the "magnet" aspect they sought for, only that it didn't quite attract customers to Epic Store [5], but attracted the same kind of people to their community instead. Either the haters who're gonna attack the game forever, or the overprotective followers who're gonna defend their dev . Especially Tim Sweeney, who fans the flame, instead of helping resolve the conflict [4]. All of them share the same qualities of being impulsive, unapologetic, overconfident, and trolling. Maybe this is the classic "you reap what you sow" & "birds of a feather flock together", huh?)Sorry for a lengthy post, which has nothing to do with the game at all. And thanks for a great case study on how  to do a PR.---[1]: We did the thing, [2]: Regarding what’s been happening, [3]: Ooblets's tweet, [4]: Tim Sweeney's tweet, [5]: The Verge's news,

_childDocuments_.review: It's a very well made casual farming/life sim and the weirdest one I've ever played. It's also a creature collector and I enjoy that aspect as well. It's also a card battler with good mechanics, even though nobody gets hurt in the dance-offs. I bought this game having fairly low expectations and have been pleasantly surprised. It's fun and it's strange. However, Ooblets has no replay value. Events are tied to real time instead of an in-game calendar which completely ruins the immersion because things like snow just happen randomly. There is a main quest line and by the time I finished it I had 100% achievements, a practically unbeatable team of Ooblets, all of the farm/house upgrades, all of the recipes and items from the stores and wishing well that are worth having, and more money than I would ever need. There are multiple areas you unlock during the quest line but all of them have way less to do than the main town and very little reason to visit them once you've completed the main quest there. I'm glad I bought Ooblets at a 40% discount because I don't think it's worth full price since the heavy hitters of the farm/life sim genre have far more to offer and some of the best are cheaper. Still, if you can pick it up on a good sale, Ooblets is a uniquely weird experience and it's worth a play through.

Just play the cards and win.On the non-dancing side of things I've found myself blasting through dialogue as fast as possible because nobody has anything interesting to say to me and nobody requires anything either. Every quest is a very simple collectathon, and leveling up relationship with other people is just a matter of speaking to them. Unfortunately, the characters all speak in a sort of pseudo-baby-speech that makes actually reading their dialogue cute at first and then infuriating later. On the whole I think it's cute and cozy, I like the simple satisfaction of collecting the ooblets and dancing to procure more of them, but the lack of complexity in this game leaves me wanting for so much more. In the end I'll probably tire of it and return to Stardew, and I'm sure other farming / life sim enjoyers have similar gripes about the total lack of emotional investment in this sickly-sweet world that is never playing itself straight with you.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm giving Ooblets a negative review, although I do believe that it's probably a great game for a different kind of person. If I had a 'meh' option, I'd pick that instead. I've played about 12 hours and haven't enjoyed the last 5 or so, if I think about it. The gameplay isn't linear, which is fine, but in being non-linear it quickly starts to feel like an overwhelming mess of things to do, which mostly get in the way of the other things you have to do. The farming element is painfully slow, even with upgrades (and the upgrades are their own battle to obtain, given the game has little direction, so you might spend X, Y, Z and put yourself behind without knowing), which makes obtaining certain Ooblets (read: anyone who requires farmed or crafted items to engage) obnoxious. Some days are entirely wasted with the energy system, and naps/snacks don't restore nearly enough to improve the way losing a day feels. Additionally, the humour/writing of the game got obnoxious after a few hours. Feels like a bunch of teens who really like Jim Carrey wrote it- everything is trying to be cutesy, whacky nonsense, but I personally didn't find that charming. Others probably would. Prices don't always match the demand of certain items or crops, there's too much back-and-forth, and the interesting things, like house size upgrades and crafting, are just too expensive to engage you in working towards them.It's not a bad game, but it feels unbalanced, and is relying too heavily on the "woahhh, whacky!!" element, which is present in e-ver-y-thing. I'll probably slog through to 100% it for my account, but I'm not charmed by the experience, and won't be trying to build relationships or improve my farm/character beyond what is required.It's fine, I guess, but it's not for me, and I feel it misses the mark. 5/10.

Oh, and if you win your dance battle, the creature will pop out a seed of itself and give it to you as a gift.I mean, as a concept, it's strange, but it works, so whatever.The dance battles are really just turn-based card battles, and the ooblets are dancing away as you have your card battle. _childDocuments_.review: I really want to like this game and, with some fine tuning, I think it has a lot of potential. The concept is fun and the design/style is adorable but, as it is, the game gets pretty boring, tedious, and repetitive after the first few in-game days. To get resources to proceed with the story, you have to either wait until the items randomly spawn around the very small map, or grow them over the course of several days. You can't sleep through the days easily as the game has "nap" options anytime you try to sleep that's not nighttime. Picking up anything takes energy, meaning you have to be super picky about what you spend your energy on. Earning money takes forever as you have to either complete item orders (which the items take several days to grow) or you have to sell crops (which take several days to grow). I enjoy the dance battles for the most part, but it can be difficult to enter them as you have to have specific items (which take several days to grow--unless it's a recipe, which the ingredients for take several days to grow) and the ooblets disappear at the end of the day and are replaced the next day with different ones, so you have to already have those items ready ahead of time, which is difficult as inventory and storage space are both limited, especially in the beginning.I think if the devs would go in and better balance the game through things like making more/easier ways to earn money and making there be starter crops that grow a lot quicker, they'd have something strong. The idea is fun and what i saw of the story is promising, but the game is so unbalanced and tedious that I couldn't stick with it.

_childDocuments_.review: Most important points: yes, you can pet the Ooblets, AND dress them up in funny accessories, AND put them in little cars.Ooblets is a pretty good game so far. It's also funny to me because it's the second time in a week I've picked up a "Pokemon clone" game that... is not a Pokemon clone.If I had to compare Ooblets to an existing game, I would actually go with Animal Crossing: New Horizons. NH, specifically due to how the game starts. Both games have a sleepy kind of pacing that's trying to remind the player that you don't have to grind every minute of every day. As far as I can tell, days of the week in this game exist mainly to plan out Dance Barn tournaments. Nothing is on a timer. You  get everything done in one day and honestly, once I managed to internalize that, I started having a much better experience.Ooblets does have 'mons that you can raise and battle, and recolor+sparkly versions (catch-em-all does pay off, literally, but it's not on a crunch). Until you open the Dance Barn, you might end up going a day or two with no 'battles' at all. The battle system is simple in a good way, and the individual strength of your Ooblets is less crucial than strategy skills. Knowing what your opponent can do and how to counter it can help, but nothing feels insurmountable even when I lose.One thing I find super neat is the way challenging wild Ooblets work - you need to pay a toll, and each Ooblet type has a different price. The price is the same across varients, however - so if you've gotten some Frubtose, you might find yourself waiting to see if tomorrow will have an Unusual or even Gleamy Clickyclaws available. Each game day starts with a report of what Ooblets are available and where, and you can check your bestiary at any time outside of battle to see what each one needs (provided you've encountered them before). This lets the player strategize if you aren't at the point where whatever resource is easy to get, yet.The game has some mechanical jankiness at times, especially oversight (ie trying to check that Ooblet report or see what Hankerbot told you), but overall the game lacks urgency, so if even failing doesn't sting like it might in a game where that has more major drawbacks. The farming system is pretty interesting, and there's friendships, quests, and a wilderness area to develop. You can dress up your character and get new hair and new hair colors (not sure if it's possible to change name or skin tone fwiw). You can 3D print figurines of Ooblets you've found. The fishing minigame is painless and always pays out to some extent. Overall, it's a very enjoyable experience to just pop in for an in-game day or two. Plus, you can save anywhere, not just by sleeping.One thing to note is the game is relentlessly whimsical, in the way that will either drive you up the wall or renovate your entire vocabulary (or both). If that's not your thing, this may not be the game for you.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: I'd say it's definitely worth a look if you like slower-paced and more cutesy style games, which I do! :DMy thoughts: It has a strangely slow intro and it can be a little hard to know exactly what is going on and what you need to do. The music is top notch and the ambient sounds are also great.+ There seems to be a nice variety of areas and other quests/characters to meet.Negatives:- The way each character talks might grate on some folks' nerves.- It doesn't seem to run at anything higher than 60 FPS which on my main PC, is a little annoying as it can, and does, cause stuttering.Overall thoughts: This game is really neat! _childDocuments_.review: I wish I could give a neutral review. Ooblets is a charming game with great visuals -- unfortunately most of everything else about it is...alright. Outside of combat, the gameplay boils down to collecting items (whether by growing it or foraging it) and turning them in. That's it, that's the gameplay. Other features in the game such as fishing and townie relationships feel like their presence is an obligation more than something with any depth or passion behind it.It's very clear this was made on a small budget and I think in some ways it's impressive what they pulled off, but in others I think it really made me yearn for something with more depth. The combat is mindlessly easy. I only lost 2 fights in my first 10 hours. Just spam hype cards at the beginning of combat, then point cards. That's all you need to know to win 95% of encounters for the game. And another thing, as a lot of other reviewers mention, requiring 3 X resources in your inventory in order to fight/collect new Ooblets in the wild is lame and is clearly a way to shoe-horn in the crafting/farming system you are already constantly doing to progress in the game.I don't mean to sound overly negative about the game, it's charming and some people will really dig what it is. But it hurts all the more because I feel like this was close to being a great game instead of an okay fetching-items-to-progress-the-story-simulator. I'd soft recommend it at $15-$20 because it's still fun, but nothing to write home about and not *that* much variety of content for $30.
_childDocuments_.name: Ooblets

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game. I have played it for 83.1 hours and have all 27 achievements. It's graphically pretty.Having your Ooblets be able to get driver's licenses and drive around in vehicles at max level is absolutely adorable, and watching the occasional wild Ooblet slamming into things in a tiny car is great.I have laughed several times at the NPC dialogue and references, so the humor is generally to my liking, and I do find the game cute in the silly way it names objects. I don't particularly care for the instances of toilet humor in the game. There are several things that are referred to as "tooting," plants named after farts, and the Ooblets audibly fart out seeds, which I find kind of gross and not relaxing.There are several things in-game that are not explained which you have to use a search engine to try and find answers to. These include: What do Ooblet levels do? What do your own personal levels do? Are Gleamy Ooblets better stat-wise than other rarities? I still haven't been able to find an answer to the second and third ones.This game lacks depth compared to similar farming/RP-type games because your relationships with the NPCs remain very surface level, and it feels like you're just repetitively grinding small talk with the NPCs in the town on a daily basis. You don't really establish a bond with and a sense of pride at improving the town like you do in Stardew Valley. The end of the game comes quite confusingly and I found it somewhat unsatisfying. I saw no reason to play anymore after the last quest. The game did not offer any more achievements or goals to pursue, so getting more currency or collecting more rare Ooblets was pointless.If there were some more features added onto the game it could feel less grindy:I wish there was an option to establish a deeper relationship with the NPCs, something that would allow you to choose someone to move onto your farm with you. I always enjoy the option to romance in these types of games, or to have a roommate. It feels a bit lonely all by myself with my trail of Ooblets on my farm.There are some quality of life improvements that would make this game friendlier towards people who have progressed further. We should be able to move buildings on the farm without stripping them of their Ooblets, which leads to a micromanaging disaster, especially if you don't have space for them to be stored. You can't sort/filter your Ooblets by what building they are assigned to, or even in alphabetical order. I have 112+ Ooblets now and it's really, really annoying to try and find them when I am swapping them between myself and my farm. Being able to name your chests would help, as well as being able to split stacks of items. Farm buildings should show what and how many seeds are stored without having to go through a cutscene to look into each of them.I wish fishing was more than just spending a long time getting bait and pressing a fish button and receiving one dispensed piece of randomized loot. If there was a mini-game option that gave greater rewards, that would provide more allure.I wish your Ooblets' costumes didn't go invisible when they were assigned to farm buildings, and their designs weren't hidden underneath straw hats.I wish there was more variety in music and dances. Hearing and watching the same thing over and over again in dance battles gets repetitive.I wish that your character's eyebrows would match your hair color as you change it. They just stay a clashing color all the time.I did run into a few bugs as a PC user with a keyboard and mouse. There are some parts of the game that don't support WASD movement, and some parts that are buggy, like the 3D printer which won't allow you to scroll down with the keyboard. Often a middle card in dance battles cannot be selected with the keyboard and you have to use the mouse to select it. Somehow I ended up frozen to a computer screen in the game and had to force quit the game to reload it.I recommend the game, as it does a good job of keeping you playing despite being somewhat grindy and repetitive.

I'm here for them!Solid 8/10.I had to take points off for the visuals.  It's near to impossible to see anything when it's snowing or raining and as someone who wears glasses? I moved my save files over to steam recently.This is a delightfully cozy creature collector; The world feels so adorable and quirky with lovable characters and appealing designs. The main story is fun to go through and doesn't take very long, and has a nice anti-capitalist message that I appreciate. It's a great cozy game, and great if you want to just turn your brain off and not think too hard.The battle system is very simple, but structured in a very nice way. It doesn't have too much depth to it, which could be either a positive or negative, depending on what you're looking for. The barn dances mix things up a little bit in difficulty, but most of the time, you'll find yourself just clicking the same cards without any regard to what the opponent is doing.The story is good, and I definitely got pulled into it a bit near the ending, but it too lacks a bit of depth.

_childDocuments_.review: Ooblets is a cute farming game with dance battles. The game is similar to Stardew Valley without the cave exploration. It has a story but most of it is told right at the end and it doesn't really engage the other characters much. The clubs also don't seem to have a lot of utility. As a farming and home decorating game it's very very cute and fun to make money and buy furniture and clothes for yourself and your little Ooblets. The game sports a collection feature in the catching and growing of the ooblets and a management feature as the ooblets take over chores on the farm. All in all it's a super cute game.
_childDocuments_.name: Ooblets

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fun and cute. You collect Ooblets through the means of dance battles. Family friendly game and great if you like games where you collect things, farming, item management, and decoration. It's such a vibrant, colourful game and I love the art style. I got this around Halloween and the town was kitted out in Halloween decorations so it seems like the devs put a lot of time and effort into seasonal updates.You might not enjoy this game as much, however, if you like story rich games. Asides from quests and the basic premise of the game, there's not much story at all.  NPCs are a bit flat too. This was definitely a downside for me unfortunately and I got a bit bored after a while. However, if these things don't bother you, and you're more interested in collecting and exploring then you will most likely enjoy this game. It's one I will definitely go back to in time, and overall had a lot of fun playing.
_childDocuments_.name: Ooblets

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent, super cute, relaxing game!I remember adding this game to my Follow list when it was first announced. I waited years to play it, and it has MORE than exceeded my expectations!It's so cute! A great way to de-stress after a long day at work and a terrible commute.It's like Pokemon combined with Stardew Valley, and the adorable low-poly graphics of Donut County. Now add in the number of collectables from Katamari Damacy. There you have it!
_childDocuments_.name: Ooblets

_childDocuments_.review: cute little game, but i do feel like there could be more. maybe I just have high expectations after playing similar games, but I feel like there cold be improvement in some aspects, such as character customization and more furniture/decor... but i did become oddly obsessed with this game when it first released, so it is a very cute and fun game
_childDocuments_.name: Ooblets

_childDocuments_.review: I've really been enjoying this game. It has cute and simple aesthetics and calming music. The cute ooblets are fun to collect, and there are so many. I've played for 8 hours so far and have done a lot, but there's so much more to explore. It's so sweet and peaceful. I look forward to buying new outfits and picking new hair color then browsing the furniture store. It's what life should be fr.
_childDocuments_.name: Ooblets

_childDocuments_.review: This is soooooo much better than other big names in farming sim this year!!To begin with, it is truly relaxing and the mechanics are perfect.I have tried other popular names like Coral Island and in most of these games I couldn't really relax because I'd never find ways to make proper amount of money and the controls of farming, like selecting the right square to water would be very tedious. I couldn't get past my frustration with those games.With this game, I never even got frustrated. The fact that there is a separate farming mode in Ooblets makes it so much easier to control. There's a variety of tasks you can do if you want to make money in some other way as well! The game is humorous in ways you wouldn't expect and the ooblets are the cutest. I also really enjoy where the updates are heading, such as the addition of Ooblet Vehicles. It's sooo fun to see a random ooblet drifting somewhere you don't expect sometimes.This game allows me to have fun without having to be a hardcore player.Other games with the "relaxing" tag need to learn something from Ooblets. If I wanted to grind, I'd play Dark Souls.On an ending note, the music is bomb.
_childDocuments_.name: Ooblets

_childDocuments_.review: Collect all the ooblets!Pro: I didn't feel like I needed a wiki to look up recipes and how to unlock stuffCon: I wanted it to be a low-stress game, but I got too focused on getting every new ooblets every day, especially rare onesReally enjoyed everything about this game until the level where you have to beat arcade games. I played ~50 hours on Switch, but pretty much gave up on that.
_childDocuments_.name: Ooblets

_childDocuments_.review: I.Love.This.Game.AND IT STILL GETS UPDATES.I bought it originally on Epic Games and i have over 170h in that alone already. Its funny, its silly, its so much fun to chill with. Its not time bound or stressy. You can just do your thing. Your own house, your own farm, your own shop, decorate, customize, little outfits for your creatures, collecting... It has it all. I adore it and i am happy i got it and play it even still on Steam as well. To be fair, i never thought i'd like it as much as i did. Recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Ooblets

_childDocuments_.review: So far, it's my favorite game out of all cozy farming games. Especially quality of life features like saving whenever you want to or precise controls when working on your farm really sold this game for me.Its systems are a bit more approachable compared to titles like Stardew Valley in a way that it makes mistakes much more forgiving. Still, that doesn't mean there isn't enough complexity and variety. There's always something to do that will keep me engaged. At first, I felt like the dance battles lacked in difficulty and I quickly became bored with them. However, the more you progress, they can become somewhat challenging. The different kinds of Ooblets with their variety in attacks really help to keep the battles fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Ooblets

_childDocuments_.review: This game is stellar is you love animal crossing, stardew valley, harvest moon, pokemon etc. It's the perfect amount of grind with a fun card game system involving silly humor and dance parties. It's got replayability out the wazoo and it's a super cute and fun experience.The only "problems" I'd say that I'd have with it is that it doesn't (hopefully yet) have modding capabilities. I've noticed a few bugs but It's mostly simple things that won't totally kill your game. Such as heads randomly shrinking on characters and if your wearing rollerskates you tend to get thrown behind furniture in your home.In the end though easily at LEAST 9/10 do recommend! :D
_childDocuments_.name: Ooblets

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really cute and derpy game with a mixture of farming, simple and easy dance battles with cards, and more! The sound effects are also worth noting because I've never heard anything like them in any game. Would def recommend this to someone who needs a simple game to play once in a while. It isn't demanding at all and easy to understand what you must do.
_childDocuments_.name: Ooblets

_childDocuments_.review: If you're looking for a game to relax with, you can't do better than Ooblets. Played best with a meditative attitude, Ooblets is a gentle farming sim with quicky characters and a really fun vibe. If you're looking for a super in-depth game with lots of deep characters and relationship building, this isn't the game for you - but if you're looking for something light to relax with after a hard day, I can't recommend Ooblets highly enough.
