_childDocuments_.review: It's been over 6 years since I played the original Freedom Planet, and since then, I've been waiting for what seemed like forever for Freedom Planet 2. Now, here we are. I've beaten the game for the first time, and I have to say, the wait was worth it--and then some.Freedom Planet 2 is something that I like in a sequel: one that is bigger and better than what came before it. The game took everything from the first game--from gameplay, to story, to bosses, to outright spectacle--and gave them a massive upgrade that is welcome to see.The world of Avalice is expanded upon with a brand new country. A fourth playable character joins the three from the first game. The story is bigger as it is darker. Nearly everyone from the first game returns, alongside some new faces. New revelations shake up what we know about our favorite characters, and set up what's to come in the franchise's future. There is a LOT that I enjoy about this game.As for who I began the game with, I chose Carol as my first character. She was my favorite character in the first game, due to her tomboyish charm, hilarious personality, adorable appearance, cool ride, and the fact that she's a cat (I am admittedly a cat person myself). And yep--Freedom Planet 2 made me love her even more. Her comedic charm is put on full display during her story, and the ending of Avian Museum reminded me why I love her in the first place.That being said, the fact that I played as Carol first instead of Lilac may not have been the intended path, in hindsight. Some story elements were clearly meant to be shown if you were playing as Lilac as your first character; because of that, some twists either don't have that wham to it or just come out of left-field unless you were playing as Lilac. Of course, this could be chalked up to my love for Carol; if I played as Lilac first, then these hidden plot points could have that same gravitas they were meant to have.But even with that in mind, it was still worth it playing as Carol and enjoying her hilarious antics. And as of this writing, I am indeed playing as Lilac, meaning that I'll see the plot twists the way they were meant to be shown soon enough.Regardless, Freedom Planet 2 is a game that makes the eight years of waiting worth it. And I want to tell GalaxyTrail, and in particular Sabrina DiDuro, something. You stated your intentions to make Freedom Planet a franchise with the release of this game. And I think--I hope--I bet you've succeeded. As long as people want to see the further adventures of Lilac and her friends, the Freedom Planet series should never end.I encourage you to create countless more games in this wonderful series, each one even bigger than the last in all facets. And it make take years for the next game to come out (I hope not), but remember: we've waited 8 years for Freedom Planet 2 (6 for me), so we're used to it.Which is to say, here's to Freedom Planet 3. Here's to more adventures in Avalice and beyond. Here's to the future of this incredible series: Freedom Planet!Weh.

_childDocuments_.review: In some ways, this game is better than the first; in others, it's honestly not as good.A lot of what I enjoyed about the first game is brought back here. The story takes place 3 years later and focuses on a new threat named Merga, the last of the Water Dragons who wants to destroy Avalice and wipe out the Earth Dragons. It's a much deeper story, one that focuses on political intrigue and social prejudices throughout the 3 Kingdoms of Avalice and its many species. There's also more backstory given to the characters, such as Lilac being the other remaining Water Dragon, and her origins with the Red Scarves. Carol has a sister, Corazon, who's working with Merga, and her main conflict is convincing Cory to defeat Merga instead. Milla's backstory is further elaborated, revealing who and where her parents are, but I won't give it away here. Neera Li joins Team Lilac, and is shown to have a hard time trusting people as she's constantly being betrayed; she has a black-and-white view of the world, calling everyone either an ally or an enemy; her loyalty to Shang Tu is sometimes taken to the extreme; but over the course of the game, Lilac and Milla help her to open up and have faith in their group. And, of course, the writing once again balances out with plenty of charming character interactions, which is the main source of comedy again.However, this game's plot falls into the same trap as the first game: some of the cutscenes still go on WAY too long and slow the pacing down; the only way they're sped up here is that dialogue plays out automatically, moving from one line to the next, unlike the first game where you had to keep pushing one button after every textbox. There are also instances where the game diverges from the main plot, and has the player go through 3 episodes in any order they want; the episodes have their own subplots that do connect to the main plot, but still make it go on longer than necessary.Otherwise, it's a great continuation of the plot that fleshes out Avalice and sets the stakes for the next game.I should also bring attention to the presentation. The pixel art is more detailed and expressive than the first game, leading to a wider range of emotions and more fluent movements from each character. The environments have a bigger color scheme, which makes many of the stages look gorgeous! And they take it a step further by making some objects 3D polygonal models that are well integrated into the 2D setting.The audio is a slight downgrade, but only slightly. The music has a few REALLY good tracks, but it's not as memorable or energized as the first game. The voice actors are just slightly less convincing than they were in the first game, and the sound mixing has the same issue, where the music can sometimes be louder than the dialogue; but they still give good performances that sell the characters pretty well.As for the gameplay, there's a LOT of improvement.Lilac can use her double jump without draining her blue meter and go straight into a dragon boost without waiting for the meter to fill back up. THANK YOU. She's easily the fastest character in the game, at the cost of having weaker attacks than the rest of the characters, something I found more noticeable during boss fights.Carol still has her motorbike which can ride up walls, but she also has the Jump Disc, a projectile to throw at enemies and even magnetize to them for a few seconds, dealing more damage; the Disc also lets her teleport, making it easier to jump across large gaps or travel up to high ledges.Milla's shield can now block almost anything; in fact, it can bounce most projectiles back at enemies, causing them to take damage, which is useful defense AND offense. She can also summon her big green gelatin blocks a lot faster, which she can either fire as a laser, like before, or she can shoot out tiny green bullets until the cube is depleted. And of course, she still has her floating ability, which is still fun to use.Neera is the powerhouse character, who can freeze enemies for a short time, and use her "Focus" ability to make her attacks faster and stronger. If you feel she moves too slow, you can speed her up by mashing the attack button, which forms an ice trail underneath her to slide across the ground like she's ice skating; this can make her sometimes move faster than Lilac!But beyond individual differences, each character has basic moves and abilities that they all share.They can all perform basic melee attacks, which vary in damage, status effects, and targeting based on which direction you tilt the control stick. As for defenses, the items in this game act similar to the elemental shields from Sonic 3 & Knuckles; letting you breath underwater, protecting you from fire or electricity, magnetizing collectibles towards you, or just providing basic protection like the shields from Sonic 1 and 2. And each character has a guard maneuver, which blocks enemy attacks and prevents you from taking too much damage, which is essential for the boss fights. Speaking of which, the bosses all have visible health bars, which also determines when the player reaches the next phase of the fight.And, I should mention that, as a game inspired by 2D Sonic, the high-speed platforming is expanded. If Freedom Planet was a combination of Sonic Advance 1 and 2, Freedom Planet 2 is closer to Sonic Advance 2; once again, acceleration goes from zero to sixty, and they've introduced boost rings and grind rails, both of which keep your character ZOOMING across terrain. It's still the best thing about the gameplay!But then there are the downsides of the gameplay; for one thing, the main campaign is TWICE as long as the first and ends up overstaying its welcome again. In fact, some stages here go on for 20 to 30 minutes at a time! Never mind Sonic, that's way too long for ANY 2D platformer. I've already mentioned the episodic structure that makes the campaign go on longer, but there's also exploration in between stages. The world maps are one thing, and they mark your next destination with red exclamation points; but then they have you going through HUBWORLDS in a 2D game! You have to go talk to certain characters in this or that building to watch the next cutscene, you have side missions to complete by talking to townsfolk, and there's NPC's in each area, some of whom offer their own perspectives on the events of the main plot. It's not terrible, but it still comes off as padding.Finally, on top of all this, Freedom Planet 2 has a true ending that you unlock by finding 13 time capsules! You do this by finding one in a HUBWORLD (the top of the tall building in the beach area), and then the other 12 are rewarded to you for completing Battlesphere Challenges. To give this game SOME credit, they made it super easy to find and collect these time capsules, just like collecting Chaos Emeralds in a Sonic game. It's better than other games where you go FAR out of your way to complete cryptic nonsense you'd only know about by using a guide. Here, it's just a small diversion that adds a little more time to your playthrough and involves the same content as regular stages. In that regard, the game is fair, but it still adds more extra steps to a campaign that's already bloated with content. I only went after the true ending with Lilac, because I just wanted to finish the game with the other characters and move on. I will say that the true ending has one more stage, and a cool final boss that gets me excited for Team Lilac's next adventure!Freedom Planet 2 makes improvements to the first game, and it's still a fun 2D platformer that took me for a WILD ride. Whether you're a Sonic fan, or you've played the first Freedom Planet, or both in my case, you owe it to yourself to play this game. But make sure you have enough free time and enough patience, because it's also a much heftier time sink, and you may be worn out by the end.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best 2D platformers around, honestly.At its core, it's a lot like Sonic, but with tighter movement and quick, satisfying combat, both melee and ranged.Stages are a great blend of Sonic-like rollercoaster sections with fast paced platforming and combat, and take place across a huge variety of environments, all fleshed out with fantastic pixel art and catchy music. To top it off, there's a massive amount of bosses, many of which are considerably challenging, and are quite satisfying to beat.As a sequel to FP1, it improves almost everything. It adds a world map, with towns and shops to buy items that can either ease the difficulty or make it much harder, if you want to chase those perfect scores. There's even arena challenges on top of all the regular levels, and a museum, for viewing the fantastic boss models you've faced along the way. It really built up the world as a whole and it feels like they went the extra mile.It's pretty great. Definitely pick this one up if you want some retro style platforming fun.

_childDocuments_.review: What is Freedom Planet 2?Freedom Planet 2 is the sequel to Freedom Planet 1, and tried to take steps to differentiate itself from being game in the similar style to Sonic the Hedgehog, which it'll naturally be compared to. As a 2D, pixel art, side scrolling platformer. Freedom Planet 2 was released on September 13th, 2022 across Windows, Linux, Switch, Playstation, and Xbox. With the Dev and Publisher being GalaxyTrail. It's quite the substantial development since Freedom Planet 1, which was largely a single person accomplishment growing into a fairly size-able indie team. Especially since the first game was a Kickstarter Project and the sequel was entirely funded by that success. -=-=- Art -=-=-The Art, and Character Design has taken a significant change of pace due to the inclusion of Tyson Tan, who did fan art of the various characters after the first game and was brought on to design the characters for the sequel. As a result, the design of the game has taken a notable change from the previous game's design limitations.Lilac has had a huge overhaul in terms of her design, while the rest of the cast has remained largely the same. With some small changes here and there to accentuate their various quirks. -=-=-Gameplay-=-=-Gameplay and Story is broken into a four character narrative with points where the story breaks off and the characters perform individual tasks related to their individual goals while beginning and ending at the same point. Each Character does play differently enough from each other, but I felt like Lilac, whose the series protagonist (and the frontliner, in Purple) at times feels like this game was designed around the other characters rather than her. Lilac (Purple Dragon) is defined as a "Speed" character, Carol (Green Cat) a "Brawler", Milla (A Dog that I keep thinking is a Rabbit) as an "Explorer" and Neera (Panda) with "Power."Each Character has their own quirks, Lilac is quite mobile, Carol is designed more around the combat changes since the first game, Milla is geared towards exploring environments, and Neera is a hybrid of the three with her own unique quirks. Freedom Planet 2 has a much stronger emphasis on combat this time round, and I don't know how I feel about it. Each boss encounter involves breaking through a bosses defenses before hitting the boss again to remove a hit point. I NEVER figured out how to use the Guard  or Parry mechanic. There is nothing that explains how that works beyond a bit of tutorial text (without demonstration.) This makes boss fights potentially drag on quite a bit. As you get used to the nature of how the fight goes, and then you have to make sure to capitalize on opportunities as they come.I didn't mind it, but I can see where people can get frustrated by it. So be aware. Beyond that, there was at least three bosses of note that felt like unnecessary difficulty spikes. As a change from the first game, there's a continue mechanic that involves spending the crystal currency you pick up during a given level to revive yourself either on the spot (with significantly less health) or at a check point for full health. I'd rather respawn at the point where I died then replay through a cutscene (even if you can skip it) to restart a fight. This felt like a feature that wasn't really thought out. Most levels consist of moving right, with the occasional left segment while trying to get to checkpoints. The levels are large and varied with some unique element to break them up. I found some of the ideas behind these levels to be rather enjoyable and they broke up what I expected from a 2D sidescroller. The levels can stretch into being rather long. These are not short 5 minute romps. Some can get upwards to 10-12 minutes from my experience. While they are rather large, I didn't have too many instances where I didn't know where to go or what to do. There is equipment this time round and it took a bit for me to get used to it. There are various potions that you can buy from Milla during the game that allot a small bonus to your game-play, such as increasing run speed, jump height, damage, defense, etc. They don't really explain how this mechanic works, so I had to figure out that you need to go to the bottle icon, then move over to the particular potion I wanted to add, then press "up" to add it to the bottle. This feels like an oversight.There are also equipment you can find in chests, but these are rather well hidden. So I can't really comment on them as I found one that made the aforementioned Defense/Parry Mechanic worthless and nothing else. I beat the game as Lilac and started two alternative runs as Milla and Neera. Both of whom start out with the same starting mission and have the same cutscenes, but from different perspectives: which is a nice touch. There are moments where Carol and Milla leave the team, so I'm interested to see if those come with wholly unique levels. -=-=-Story-=-=-There are two modes available, the intended "Adventure" mode which includes moving around an isometric map and checking in on non-combat and zones.There is also a Classic Mode which skips the plot and goes from area to area with the non-combat areas linked together into one large (growing) shop to make various purchases. You do not need to have played the First Game to enjoy the sequel. As I didn't. I had watched a play-through of the First Game, but hadn't had the opportunity to pick it up. You will miss out on some context, some jokes, and references to the first game, but I don't feel it's totally necessary. Following from the Steam Page: The story consists of Merga, a Water Dragon freeing herself from a prison and her ambitions for the world at large. With the four aforementioned heroines getting wrapped up in trying to stop her from her goals. Freedom Planet 2 expands on the world around the three Kingdoms from the first game and continues from where it left off.I can't really talk about the story without spoiling it, and I enjoyed my time with it. I didn't feel my time was wasted. -=-=-Final Thoughts-=-=-I completed the game, as Lilac, at about 8 hours and started two separate runs as Milla and Neera. While there was initial interest in continuing to see how the other characters go through the plot, I don't know if I'll actually play through the game (at least right now anyway) with the others. If you're looking for a 2D Sidescroller that is evocative of (2D) Sonic, while trying to become it's own thing: then I'd recommend Freedom Planet 2. There's some growing pains, but the sequel builds on the original and is one of those cases where the second game IS better than the original.

_childDocuments_.review: If you played the first, you'll almost certainly love this. If you haven't, I still think you'll love this.The original was a brilliant throwback to Sonic and Gunstar Heroes, and this neatly distills the formula into an even better experience. The characters are all charming and play very unique and distinct from each other, so playing the game from one to another feels like an entirely different experience. The storyline is simple but entertaining, and if you don't care about that, there's a Classic Mode that just gives you the gameplay. It even has a few branching paths and a "secret" ending you can get under certain conditions. And for FP1 fans, you'll be happy to know the story pacing is much better here: you'll never be stuck in cutscenes for  long before it's back to gameplay.On a technical level, the levels are technically brilliant. (Eh? Ehhhh? Oh never mind...) They're huge with numerous pathways, and taking the time to explore can yield some nice bonuses, though nothing is stopping you from trying to speed through them. They're also a visual treat with excellent pixel art and gorgeous backgrounds. And just about every single one has some unique gimmick or mechanic that shows up just for that level and then may never come back again... no surprise to fans of FP1, which similarly featured unique one-and-done level mechanics: a testament to the love and dedication that went into the game at a fundamental level. And of course, each level is capped off with a highly unique boss battle.It also helps that the controls are responsive and very easy to get the hang of, so if you're getting in trouble, it's not because the game is cheap, it's because you screwed up.A big change to the game is the new Items and Potions that let you customize and modify your experience. Some of them can make the game easier, while others are designed to make it much harder. More health, more lives, more speed? Not a problem. You'd rather play the game as a one-hit KO? Also not a problem!In terms of criticism, I don't have much, but here goes:-The music is still great, but I don't think it has quite as many earworms as FP1. None of it is ever annoying or uninspired, but I don't find myself humming it quite like I did the first game. And that's the meanest thing I can say about an OST that is still stellar.-The game is also significantly harder than FP1, which might be a plus for some folks. Admittedly, that's partly because the game really expects you to get good and use the new Guard mechanic and the Items and Potions, but, on the other hand, those aspects aren't taught as well as they could be either, even in the optional tutorial.Those minor gripes aside, this game is well worth your time and money. If you're a fan of retro throwbacks or just excellent gameplay in general, I highly recommend this one. Hopefully we get a Freedom Planet 3 within the next decade!
_childDocuments_.name: Freedom Planet 2

_childDocuments_.review: The first Freedom Planet was a game that held a very special place in my heart, not only for being a solid Sonic-esqe action platformer, but also for being incredibly inspiring to me as it initially started life as a Sonic fan project and it starred characters that I remember from browsing DeviantArt in the mid 2000s, since I have my own passion project I have had in the works that started out as a fan project.And now after waiting almost 7 years, listening to the Alpha OST religiously, seeing awesome fan art and watching the community grow, Freedom Planet 2 is finally here. And it's bigger and better than before!The gameplay is greatly expanded upon with the characters feeling a lot more versatile thanks to some new moves such as Lilac's Boost Breaker, Carol's Jump Disc and Milla's Cube Blaster. And the new playable character, Neera can be very satisfying once you get the hang of her powerhouse-like playstyle. The addition of a dodge button, the various hub worlds, the ability to revive yourself at the cost of a stock Smash-Bros style and ways to customise your play experience with the Potions, Brave Stones and various other difficulty options are very welcome.And the stages are still as fun, creative and action packed as ever, with big shout outs to Airship Sigwada, Globe Opera and Tidal Gate to name a few.One of my only real gripes with the first game as fun the story was, there were things that the game either forget to tell about or weren't properly explained such as the character's backstories. Not only does this game "mostly" address them, but greatly expands on the lore and world-building with it's more in-depth story and characters. There are a lot of fun and heartfelt moments along with some interesting themes,  twists and stuff left open for a potential sequel.The visuals, character designs and sprite work for this game are genuinely gorgeous and are some of best I have seen for a game of this type. And the music absolutely slaps!It has been quite the journey to see the evolution of this series from it's humble beginnings to now. After waiting a long time for this game, it didn't disappoint! I had a blast with this treasure of a game that deserves to be up there with the other indie greats such as Shovel Knight & Shantae!

_childDocuments_.review: I don't have a beefy PC, so 2D indie games are my main guilty pleasure, especially 2D side scrolling platformers. Freedom Planet 1 happens to be the first game I remember buying on Steam within launch week, and I had fun exploring the levels, listening to the soundtracks, trying out the different characters.Fast forward to 2022 and we now have Freedom Planet 2, and the developers definitely have much more work invested here. More levels (more than double the size of the first game), more soundtracks, a longer storyline, more characters, more pixels! The stages also all have something setting themselves apart from each other, each stage has its own theme / gimmick. They even threw in extra stuff like the museum and battlesphere which are decent additions.This 2nd game seems to have taken at least 8 years to release, and that's already with some ideas scaled back or left out, so that they could release what we have today. The plus side is, the devs are quick to try and fix/patch most bugs.If a 3rd game is planned, count me in as one of those excited for it. Freedom Planet was originally inspired by Sonic the Hedgehog games, but I think I had more fun with just FP1 + FP2, compared to playing Sonic(s) 1,2 CD, 3 and Mania combined.

_childDocuments_.review: After 7 years of development, GalaxyTrail released the sequel to Freedom Planet, a Sonic fangame turned full-fledged indie with cues from Sonic, Treasure, Mega Man, and more. The first game was already stellar, but with the hype that built up over the game's development cycle, the new eager fans (myself included) who got caught up in the wave from the console ports of the first game, and a highly passionate team with high ambitions, how did this sequel fare? I'll cut to the chase: it did Picking up three years after the end of the previous game, although Brevon's been long gone since his invasion of Avalice, a lasting peace has been difficult, what with a recent string of mysterious attacks. As such, Lilac, Carol, and Milla, our heroines, are summoned by the Royal Magister of Shang Tu to help investigate the matter and figure out what exactly is going on, with Lieutenant Neera Li accompanying them on their mission. What starts out as some seemingly disconnected incidents, however, lead back to a phantom from Avalice's past, one who has spent the past three years plotting her revenge...Summary aside, this game's story is absolutely stellar, helped by there being an actual writing team this time. The main cast's gotten older and wiser, the new characters, heroic and antagonistic alike, are incredibly written, making their arcs and character dynamics very compelling, and had me appreciate those I already did  even more than before. What also helps is the strong VA work by everybody on the cast, be it the returning faces such as Dawn M. Bennett (Lilac), Edwyn Tiong (The Magister), and Alejandro Saab (Zao), or the new additions to the cast, such as Christopher Sabat (Askal), Morgan Berry (Merga), and Lindsay Jones (Corazon). Even better, the voice acting quality is consistent by virtue of Christopher Sabat allowing the cast to record in his studio, Okratron 5000. I admit, my earlier summary of the story is only scratching the surface, but given how it's so impactful in its writing and handles really well heavy subjects in its back half,I do hope you forgive me for not elaborating much more on that matter. Trust me, it's well worth it.On the gameplay side, the returning playable cast feel amazing in motion, having picked up new tools that extend their already solid moveset (Lilac's Boost Breaker and Blink Dash), address their old moveset's key shortcomings (Carol's new melee options, Jump Disc, and bike reworks), or both (Milla's revamped Phantom Cube gameplay and her new melee attacks). Neera, an NPC and boss turned playable, also feels quite solid in motion, being lacking in a solid airgame but compensating with a strong combat-oriented movepool that can melt bosses when used right. This great feel, supplanted with the incredibly versatile new guard technique, works in tandem amazing well with the stage design, covering all kinds of fun challenges, from the pipe networks in Sherlin Park to the amusement park feel that is Zaoland. The strong stage design is complimented with some incredible bosses that are tough, but all manageable and satisfying to defeat, even if some of them, during endgame especially, ask players to have a strong understanding of all their tools to overcome them.The sound design is as strong as ever, with the stage themes covering all kinds of great moods that match their stages, the map themes suiting the overall feel of their areas, and the new hub areas having great songs to accompany their more downtime-oriented design. Leila Wilson (otherwise known as Woofle) and Falk Au Yeong have created some incredible compositions that help make the game incredibly memorable.Visually...it's sprite art. Need I say any more? The art shift away from the chibi style to a more proportioned design, beyond acting as a great look at how the cast's matured, also manages to make them look just as adorable as they were before, or even moreso  with all the great animation that game has to compliment its sprites. On top of that, the various locations, stages, maps, and hubs alike, are incredibly beautiful and make them an even bigger joy to run through. Just be mindful of some latergame stages, the shaders they use for their 3D elements isn't exactly the nicest on older systems, although it's nothing unplayable.Overall, this game is an indie masterpiece that has had so much love put into it, I could go on and on about what I enjoyed,  I wholeheartedly recommend this game to fans of the first game, Treasure fans, Sonic fans, or just anyone in general looking for a really good indie platformer.Verdict: Worth your time!Final remarks: Seriously, please play this game, I adore it so much~

_childDocuments_.review: Just like the first game, this is a criminally overlooked modern classic that blows the series that inspired it out of the water. Freedom Planet might have started out as a love letter to Sonic, but it improves on and surpasses it in almost every way. The tight gameplay, the flow of the levels, the incredible bosses, the lovely art, and the 10/10 soundtrack easily make this one of my games of the year. If there's any part of you that likes 2D action games, you owe it to yourself to play this.By and large Freedom Planet 2 is very reminiscent of the first game, though you don't have to have played FP1 to enjoy it. It's a bigger, slicker, tighter, and better paced experience than the original, hitting all of the same highs while offering more than twice as much game this time around. The gameplay has seen numerous small improvements like the addition of one or two extra moves for each character, along with a parry button that really helps take some of the boss fights to the next level. It's amazing to maintain your speed and momentum mid-fight by parrying your way through an attack rather than having to slow down and carefully dodge.The storytelling, as well, is probably the most notably improved area compared to the prequel. The FP games are bubbly and enthusiastic, but they do read like Sonic fanfiction at times. This is part of their charm for me, but regardless of whether the cheesy blend of silly humour and high drama works for you, it's delivered in a far more digestible manner this time around. FP1 suffered from trying to cram a world full of political factions, side characters, and interplanetary war into a linear action game, with cutscenes sometimes just as long as the levels they followed. FP2 carries all of this over, but with more stages and hub areas full of optional dialogue to dilute the cutscenes, resulting in much better pacing overall. The script also feels tighter, with the humour hitting the mark more often and the world building feeling natural rather than bloated.The addition of a fourth playable character and a bunch of optional challenges also helps to flesh out the playtime. If you want hours and hours of Freedom Planet, this game has it for you. This does lead into my one criticism of the game, though; while I'd say the overall quality of the experience is easily on par with FP1, it feels a bit more stretched. I found the gimmicky stages to be more conspicuous in FP2, and some of them felt like misfires. While it does modulate the pacing to intersperse fast actiony levels with slower puzzley and exploration-based ones, the action stages are universally better suited to the game's mechanics. I found the dedicated boss stages a lot more enjoyable than the ones that had me backtracking in multiple directions or hunting down keys to progress. I wouldn't have minded if the game had fewer, but more tightly designed levels.I could gush for a long time about how awesome some of the boss fights are, how many bangers the soundtrack has, or how the game pulls off a finale that's both similar and different enough from FP1 to stand toe-to-toe with it, but it's easier to just say that this game is incredible. Galaxy Trail have succeeded in putting out a fantastic sequel to Freedom Planet that I hope garners all the recognition it deserves some day. They've taken this subgenre and made it their own.

_childDocuments_.review: Freedom planet 2 is an incredible experience and is easily a must buy if you enjoyed the first game. Everything has been improved and expanded upon: from the absolutely gorgeous pixel art, to the infectiously catchy soundtrack and the overall much better pacing. The background lore for lilac, the squad and Avalice as a whole has also been expanded upon, presented very nicely through a well written narrative that actually features quite a sympathetic antagonist. On the gameplay side of things, each character handles well and can take advantage of weaving their way through the multiple pathways of each stage in their own unique fashion. Some characters are better suited fr specific purposes however: Lilac is great for speed and would generally be considered the easy mode, whereas Neera is a boss killer whom lacks mobility in comparison to the other heroins. Speaking of bosses, they're all a treat to fight, having well telegraphed attack patterns and make good use of the games' new dodge mechanic, but some less experienced players may have trouble with the insane speeds of later ones. To compensate for players of all skill levels, the settings menu has a plethora of accessibility options including free revives, auto guarding, reducing the cost of continues and increasing the sensitivity of the screen zoom out, among others. In addition to these options, if they weren't enough the game itself includes a shop system, accessed from vendors in hubs. As a side note these hubs all have their own atmosphere and incredibly charming NPCs that add to the feeling of this world being alive. Most of them have unique dialogue linking to different story events, some dialogue being character specific. Anyways, the shop system acts as a way for players to spend their currency rewarded by exploring stages on a multitude of items that either assist players, or hinder them in exchange for a higher rank and crystal bonus at the end of stages. If you want to be an absolute powerhouse then you can equip yourself with a full attack potion if you really want to, but if you want to go for those elusive rainbow S ranks, try using on hit KO and get through a stage without being damaged at all. Thankfully the ranking system has no in game effects outside of achievements and a higher bonus, so going after high ranks isn't necessary if it's not comfortable. Freedom planet 2 takes you on a tour of Avalice, with stunning visuals, amazing level design, a banging soundtrack, endearing characters, a smooth difficulty curve and bosses with so much spectacle. it's one of the most fun and well crafted experiences I've had in a video game and if you couldn't already tell, I love it to death. Wonderful 2D platformer, would highly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: The short summary: 11/10Much like its predecessor, Freedom Planet 2 is a side-scrolling, platforming adventure along the same vein as classic Sonic the Hedgehog games.  But Freedom Planet 2 has improved upon the original in almost every way, having grown from its Sonic-inspired roots into something more distinctive and unique.  Freedom Planet 2 feels much more fleshed out with a lot more story, which is just what I was craving most from the original; I wanted to learn more about these characters and this universe, and Freedom Planet 2 scratched that itch; though having played through all four characters' campaigns with the "true ending," questions around the history of Avalice remain,  which I hope to see answered in future Freedom Planet games, DLC, or other media.  Even if you haven't played the original (which you absolutely should), Freedom Planet 2 is well worth a playthrough.  The full review:Much like the original Freedom Planet, this is a side-scrolling platformer featuring four playable heroines, each one with their own style and characteristics.  Your first play through will be in Adventure Mode, which in my opinion is the best way to experience the game, because one thing FP2 does way better than the original is story.Cutscenes and dialogue flow better than they did in the original, with quality voice acting and funny moments throughout.  Many of these scenes are the same regardless of which character you play, but some are exclusive to each character, so to get the full story you'll have to play through as all four characters, but in my opinion that is just part of the fun!Gameplay is pretty simialr to FP1, except now we have more fine-tuned controls and returning characters have had their move-sets reworked. The biggest feature is the introduction of Guarding, allowing you to completely evade damage if well timed.  Traversing levels and battling bosses feels much more fluid and is super satisfying. The art style has been greatly improved upon from the FP1 style, and the levels themselves sport unique themes and charm, complete with amazing background music, much like the levels of FP1 did.  While FP2 dropped the collectible Cards of FP1, there are still secrets to be found within the levels, primarily Vinyls to unlock music and a few Brave Stones.Speaking of which, Brave Stones and Potions are a new feature added to enhance the gameplay.  Throughout your adventure you will collect Gems and Orbs, both of which can be exchanged into Gold Gems. Gold Gems are rarely found within levels too.  You can mix and match Potions to give yourself different buffs, such as increasing attack damage or making your attacks heal you a little bit.  Brave Stones can also offer buffs, but many act as difficulty multipliers, and you are rewarded with extra Gems for completing levels with detrimental Brave Stones equipped. I love this system because it allows players to tailor the difficultly to their liking, and gives them options if they find themselves struggling at a particular area.Additionally, if you're the completionist type, there's a Gallery in Adventure Mode that you can donate resources to in order to complete exhibits.  They're neat to look at, but in my opinion the main treat here is that you get access to a special gallery upon completing all the exhibits.  This special gallery shows off some behind-the-scenes stuff from the development of FP2, including early concept art and scrapped assets, so if you're into that kind of stuff, completing the Gallery is a worthwhile endeavor!As a final point, I've noticed some comments about issues playing the game (crashes, softlocks, etc.) so if you experienced problems before, I'd recommend giving the game another try.  The Developers have already released several updates to fix bugs and even add a few new features; it's obvious to me that this game was a labor of love for them and that they want this to be the best experience it can be after all this time since FP1. :)All in all, I've thoroughly enjoyed my time with Freedom Planet 2.  At the time of my writing this, I've completed all four characters' stories in Adventure Mode and unlocked all but two secret achievements.  I love the characters, I love the gameplay, I love the game world, and I don't plan to stop playing until I've done everything this game has to offer!

_childDocuments_.review: Freedom planet 2 exceeds the first game in every aspect. From charterer control, adjustments, level design, art and everything else. (But maybe except the story) The four different playable characters you play as have their own unique set of powers that vastly different from one another. Depending on who you play as, it may change the way you play the stage and how you interact with foes and bosses along the way. It creates great replay value and experimentation in each play-trough you do. From Lilac ability to speed trough the stage, or Milla's exploration and ranged kit. (My personal favorite is the newcomer, Neera. With her double jump and power moves, you can defeat foes and move around quickly if you know the stage well.)The stages in this game are wonderful design from art, to level layout. Each level having their own set of gimmicks as well to keep the pacing consistently fresh every time. Whenever it's climbing up an tower needed power throughout or a gauntlet of challenge rooms of tricks. The levels in this game are awesome! This also applies to the hub worlds throughout the game. Each having their own neat details and lore of that part of the world. You can also buy items from these hub worlds to help you out in the main adventure if things get tough.The story of this game is the only thing I kinda don't like about it. Compared to the first game, it doesn't have the same impact, from story beats, to the characters , it's watered down. It still has it's moments in the middle and all, but most of the time it remains flat and never evolves the new heights. ( If that made sense) Though I do very like the additions of the new side characters and the expanded world building. They are fun, cool to the world, and bounce of the main ones very well. If you want to see more of the same characters you like in the first one, you will probably like the story just okay. Overall, if you are looking for a platformer with plenty of  speed and awesome level design, and or liked the first game, this one is for you in my opinion. It has beautiful art design, music that suits the mood of each moment, and plenty of replay value as well. Outside the main game and unique playable characters, there's also a side challenge gauntlet mode that I have not played yet, but will get to. This game is well made and has plenty of love poured into it and it shows.  :)

Absolutely stunningly done. And when you unlock her secret level? Thats where the bonus marks come in. You Will NOT Regret It!  ALL FOUR Stories, while much more related to each other than FP1, Do a fantastic job expanding on each character; Poor Neela has a hell of a hard go but at the end earns her place.  Each of the four Story arcs had me stunned.Graphics - 10/10  They pulled off stuff with the medium that no way in hell even a Saturn could do. The love and lavish they poured into this is very clear. Perfection!Audio - 8.5/10 For the most part, the music is glorious.  Sound effects are clear, VA is Dead On. Level tracks are GORGEOUS!  My only real complaint is the boss battle tracks - some are remixes, but most with maybe two exceptions - thankfully the final bosses - tend to fall rather flat, IMHO. The boss battle tracks could of hit harder; but thats subjective. The explosions also need a bass boost, but again, extremely minor.Gameplay - 8.5/10 NOW THAT IVE DONE ALL FOUR ARCS - Lilac's combat capabilities are only slightly improved over the original. At times, it doesnt feel improved at all. I even went and did a boss rush back to back vs FP1, and while her charge attack DOES charge faster, it still feels damn slow, especially for someone thats supposed to be fast. If you are a dedicated old school Rocket Knight Adventures fan, Lilac is still going to be frustrating to play, but a bit of a slight improvement from FP1.   Carol's attack, once you master it? MUCH better than it initially seems. A step up.  Milla? ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ she got buffed!  Neela? She IS the hardest to get the hang of, but once you do, she's a solid fighter; and im pretty sure they buffed her guarding. Im certain it wasnt working in the previous patch; now it works just as well as the rest of the crew.ALL IN ALL? ABSOLUTELY WORTH EVERY PENNY.  Quite frankly My complaints are more subjective, most certainly not game breaking.  Most people wont notice the issues with Lilac, and all the gals gameplay is master-able. Hopefully, after the team rests for a bit, they go for a Trilogy.  They did drop the hints that a trilogy is on the table. GO FOR IT GALAXY QUEST! This game is worth DOUBLE what they are charging for it! Im dead serious; I virtually never say something like this, but this time? They absolutely EARNED it. BRAVO! This game is a MASTERPIECE!  Not only is it a Masterpiece? IT absolutely SHATTERS all expectations.

_childDocuments_.review: Ok I'm gonna start with one sentence:Freedom Planet 2 is the best game I've played this year and I could easily give it a 10/10Could end the review with that, but if you're thinking I'm joking or something or you're not convinced, well sit down, relax and let me explain why this game is so important to me:INTRODUCTION:Let's start with this: there is just no compareson with the first Freedom Planet, yes it's still a good game, but the sequel just overshadowed it completly in every feature. I need to remind you that the firts game was after all a solid Sonic fan game that gained his own identity and you can't deny that. This formula of taking inspirations from bigger franchises or creating spiritual sucsessors of our favourite games when the original creators are not willing to, as been used now more than ever to preserve good game design and artistic freedom and (when done well) can create true masterpieces and fix the hissues of the original proprietys.What FP2 did was cleaning up the dust from it's firts game and rebuild a totally new and original experience, detatching itself from the Sonic series wile still mantaining what made the game so good in the first place and did so much more.GAMEPLAY:The gameplay is fast, clean and fun! Every stage has it's own mechanics and all the 4 playable characters can provide new game experiences and the replay value is at his core!First thing they did was cleaning up the annoying parts of the firts game. The movement for Lilac for example feels much more fun, now the spin attack does not cost power so you can use it in combo with the charge attack and the collectibles are no longer like... 10 per level?! But just 1 or 2, because the devs understand that in a game where you need to go fast, the SLOW exploration can feel lame at some point. But don't get me wrong you still have a lot to collect in other fun ways.The first game was linear, a simple experience, this game have an overworld map, towns, NPCs, minigames, challenge modes and FINALLY a ranching sistem so you can have fun getting rank S for every stage in game. There are also items to equip, but I rarely use them cuz they take a way a bit of the final reward, but you can equip an hourglass to race against time and hearn extra cash for finishing the level before the timer runs out, super fun to play.STORY:Will be short to avoid spoilers, the first game got an average story that tryed to get cool at the end, but was nothing more than... the power of friendship against evil alien dude, that was good for a game like that, but the sequel got REAL!!You got world bulding, drama, relationships, betrayal, fun shenes, very sad shenes and jsut something that will make you feel so fulfilled at the end of it, plus a secret ending if you can get it (it's worth it).ART:Yeah the art in the first game was good, but a bit silly and I wasn't really convinced about any character that wasn't Lilac or Carol and yeah was still too similar to Sonic...This game owever changed the art completly and it's one of the amin reason why it feels so original. Every character EVEN THE NPC are fully animated and every stage filled with detail. Really nailed it this tme!MUSIC:The music is just great, not much to say about it, not an expert in music, but it fit the stages very well soooo yeah!DUBBING:Now the cherry on the top, the first game was already dubbed and that was impressive for an indie game like that, but with this? GOD! It is so well done! Every characters they played at was perfectly delivered expecially Lilac, Merga and Cordelia.I can say in some shenes I was at the edge of crying for that and you guys get all my respect for it.IN CONCLUSION:FP2 is how you make a good sequel, and I mean sequel! Not like we call it XXXXX 2 and then is a prequel or some kind of AU or whatever, I mean sequel sequel and all game devs big and small should take example. Can't wait for FP3, IF there's gonna be one (I hope so).wait... I should add some cons as well or people will think I'm just being a fanboy... OKCONS:That mech stage was trash why did you guys think that was a good idea!

_childDocuments_.review: Like its predecessor, it's hard not to be awestruck by the sheer passion and ambition of Freedom Planet 2, which introduces a bevy of smart, thoughtful additions and improvements to the core combat and platforming across a healthy variety of stages and situations.  That said, much of the first game's signature consistency, intensity, and precision feels somewhat lost in the exchange, with levels and bosses sometimes falling flat, and the otherwise superb pixel artwork appearing somewhat mangled by the dynamic camera.There's also the questionable decision to lock the story-free Classic mode away, but thankfully the writing, voice work, tone, and overall pacing have been significantly improved from the original (and you can still skip any and all cutscenes if you prefer).  More problematic is the non-linear progression of levels, which results in a scattershot difficulty curve that squanders one of the core strengths of Freedom Planet.  Conversely, improvements to Carol and Milla's movesets, as well as the addition of newcomer Nerra, ensure each campaign is as much a delight to traverse as Lilac's. Despite a lukewarm opening act, Freedom Planet 2 at last provides a definitively superior experience over the first game, although which one you'll prefer likely comes down to what drew you to the series in the first place.  If it was the Sonic-like traversal and platforming, as well as the callous difficulty curve, then you'll probably gravitate back to the original.  If it was the Gunstar Heroes-esque combat, stage variety, and cathartic boss fights, then the sequel achieves the fullest aspirations of that gameplay loop.  Whatever the case, Freedom Planet 2 is an absolutely superb, polished, unique, elbows-out platformer that shouldn't be missed.
_childDocuments_.name: Freedom Planet 2

_childDocuments_.review: It's a trite comment at this point, but this is another case for "Steam should have a mixed recommendation option instead of just 'yes' and 'no'."First of all, it's impossible not to be impressed by the amount of real content in this game. The game could feasibly take someone 10 hours to finish on a first playthrough and I expect most will be over 8 hours at least. For an indie 2D platformer with a breakneck pace that's a lot of level. The level design is more ambitious than the first game with long, complex, multi-route levels. There are many gimmicks and almost all levels have a good sense of individual identity both visually and in terms of gameplay.This scope is impressive but it's clear that the developers had ambitions beyond reason, leading to both a lengthy development period and a really hit-and-miss quality to the levels and boss fights. Some levels, like the Ancestral Forge and Nalao Lake, are really bad, but there are also some great stages— Lightning Tower is my favourite, mixing in some very light puzzle elements with hazards that are activated as you turn on power, and generally a more calculated level design with a good sense of progress as you climb.Sadly, most of the levels are at least a little chaotic, as there are enemies and stage hazards that seem unavoidable given the speed of the game. In one stage, there is a crushing block hazard that drops so fast that you actually can't avoid it if you're stood still, which you may be if you boosted forward and bopped off the wall where it comes down. Enemies are almost entirely not worth dealing with, as many of them have untelegraphed attacks and a tonne of HP, but you will still take plenty of damage from enemies that attack as you run past. The added guard mechanic seems useless but thankfully wasn't required for Lilac, whose dash has about a billion i-frames and does good damage.In general, the difference between FP1 and 2 is that the former feels more restrained, with level design that guides you forward, whereas FP2 regularly makes it difficult to tell which way you're meant to be going. And unlike FP1, the core gameplay isn't quite as engaging, since besides some good platforming and gimmicks you're mostly just ignoring the enemies and taking random hits. It lacks that sense of connection. Doesn't help that when you do attack an enemy, there is no feeling of impact (unlike the player character who gets stunned by hits). The effect of this is that the game is quite exhausting to play at times and it took me a while to finish.And those bad boss fights... man. The fights against really large bosses are usually fine, mid-sized bosses are mixed and the player-character-sized bosses are almost all complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Why? Well, smaller foes are typically either off-screen, or close enough to instantly cause harm to you. Also, many of their attacks turn their bodies into instant hurtboxes, and often aren't well telegraphed. Some are less bad than others, but the absolute worst is , who does half-screen jumps into ground-slams, and spends half his time surrounded by little projectiles. Also a dashing punch that comes from offscreen that you have to anticipate every time he stops slamming, because there is no other cue.The writing for the first game was much maligned and if anything this sequel doubles down, but I can't bring myself to hate it. I love that the furry freaks behind these games put their all into making their fantasy about anthropomorphic cats & dogs, colonialism and historical revisionism come to life... sincerely, it's kind of wholesome. In terms of quality it's like some kid's TV show. Whatever. The lowest point is probably Captain Kalaw. He seems as if the writer played the Ratchet and Clank remake and though Captain Klark was sooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooo frickin funny. To be fair, that only jumps out to me because the writing is otherwise much less bad than that game. I also saw a reviewer compare it to YIIK which seems like a wildly unfair assessment. This is fine for small kids but also tedious to sit through for us because we are adults and we like to consume dense things rather than liquid slurry.I know that this review comes across as negative, and that's largely because I can't help but compare it negatively to the previous game. It's really not all that bad though, just hit-and-miss. Some levels are fun and suffer less from the general design issues. There were points where I'd sit down to play the game, go through two 8-minute levels and be completely checked out afterwards. Other times I'd get hooked on a really good level or set of levels and find myself playing for a good while.For a quick summary, if FP1 is an 8.5/10 than FP2 is like... a 6.5 or 7.

_childDocuments_.review: Freedom Planet 1 was a good homage to Sonic games, with more than enough to set itself apart from its inspirational source. With its 16-bit styled graphics but refined controls, the game handled well and presented a high difficulty challenge, even on Normal mode. It had a good, compelling story, interesting world-building, fluid controls, excellent soundtrack and decent characters all around (albeit not perfect in this regard). What's most impressive about this game was that it was a passion project, made by a few fans from their homes, and still turned out as well as it did.Freedom Planet 2, which came out a full seven years later, proves that this new world of Avalice (the planet that Freedom Planet's series takes place on) can pull its weight, and then some. Everything that was present in Freedom Planet 1 has been taken and elevated to a new standard of quality:- The combat and controls are polished to a sliver sheen, with each character now having even more setting them apart than its predecessor allowed. Special mention goes to the new Guard feature, which allows you to precisely defend against and defeat tougher, more powerful opponents than what came in the previous game. This game does not pull its punches: you WILL learn how to fight, and fight well. Good thing this game's combat flows like a river of pure water and is a joy to figure out.- The level layouts show the series' homage to Sonic the most, being multi-layered and easily speedrunnable for those that have mastered the quick, responsive controls.- True to the generational shift, Freedom Planet 2 now emulates the 32-bit style found on the old Playstation systems, but still shows a serious upgrade to Galaxy Trail's budget and skills as developers and presents a wonderful charm to the world it depicts.- With Freedom Planet 1 laying the groundwork for its world-building, this game can now take the runway and fly high, telling compelling stories while digging deep into the world's lore--shaking up a few things along the way.- The next most notable upgrade comes from the characterizations and voice acting: everyone has improved from their record-from-home days with a bona-fide voice recording studio, courtesy of one Christopher Sabat (and yes, he too voices a prominent character in the game; bonus!). The characters truly have a chance to grow into their own as the story explores each of their backstories and personalities more.- Somehow, the soundtrack is even better than its predecessors' was. As of writing this, there is no immediate means to purchase it; this review waits (im)patiently for its release, so he can buy it post-haste.Overall, this game is absolutely solid and is a must-play for any Sonic fans, or any platformer fans out there. (And I recommend playing the first game so you can get a good idea of what to expect.) The seven-year wait was more than worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Before I begin, a foreword is necessary. The furry/sonic fandom is strange and terrifying. Wariness of any title featuring anthropomorphic animals doing sidescrolling is wisdom.With that out of the way, the game is fantastic. After playing the original Freedom Planet this was at the top of my wishlist, and the game hasn’t disappointed in the least. Gameplay is top notch and each of the four characters is worthy of a full playthrough. The game also does a good job of balancing the tone for the kind of game it is. The game goes from funny/derpy moments most of the time to discussing genocide, but somehow manages to stick the landing. The story was consistently fun, and the serious bits felt dramatic/heartfelt. A lot of it doesn’t quite make sense if you examine it critically, but if you don’t think too hard on it and you’ll have a fun time. A few other game highlights, some already mentioned above:• Really nice sprite work with a lot of love to characterization. Unnecessary touches like special animations when your characters talk to smaller animals abound• Great music throughout. In other reviews you will see people note boss themes hit harder in the first game (and I agree), but the music is still awesome. If Magma Starscape doesn’t get your blood pumping, you might be clinically dead• Good challenge baseline with options for both those seeking mastery and those who are bad at videogames• One of the characters is voice acted by the guy who does PiccoloIt is just a really fun game and worthy of the “Overwhelming Positive” status you will see once it hits 500 reviews.On the downside, your steam recommendations will have suggestions like Fur Affinity 4: Beasts in Heat for a while after you buy this. Ignore those suggestions for a few days and eventually your queue will go back to normal. Probably. Hopefully.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: Finished all characters and achievements. Gotta say that once you kinda know the layout of the levels and bosses, it gets a little better. But for a newcomer it's still confusing. Milla is obviously (again) the best original character, however it didn't save this game from my negative review :) Altough - maybe take it on discount?As quite a fan of the first game, I was sort of looking forward to this one. While the game does deliver somewhat of an experience not different from the first game, it's overall less effective for various reasons.First game featured small handful of levels with interesting biomes where each boss felt unique and thought through (some more than others, but still). This one offers you a s**tload of levels and about 40 bosses, where majority of them feel like a joke. Most of them only have three attacks and their animation is very static, it's clear devs love did not quite pour into these sprites. Same can be said about levels - they, unfortunately, follow same formula of the first game, which was already annoying, but they went bigger with this one, levels are larger and collectibles harder to find. There are also 40 of them, which makes biome specificity easier to overlook. They did have some interesting ideas, sure, but I found most of them annoying anyway and thats mostly due to inability to have the game zoomed out permanently, or at least, when you pick up speed. Its always just a blunt background and bunch of platforms. During the entire game not a one moment would come when I would think "damn, now the background really blends well with the foreground". It always seems like the background is there just so there isn't pitch black or something.Introducing hub mechanics to game was totally unneccesary and cities where you would buy items as well as items themselves samewise. I literally finished half of the game using no items, because I didn't know it was there (i knew there were potions, but I was saving them for when they will be needed - turns out they act as items, you can use them indefinitelly once you buy them - who knew...?).Photomode - wow, I mean... WOW. It must be first sidescrolling game where I've seen this feature. Saddest thing is that there is a visible amount of time that went into developing this... why? Why? It's not like this is a Horizon or God of War. The game doesn't look very good really, why would you put such thing in there?Ok so now that I estabilished what game did wrong, lets talk about the good part. Animations of main characters. I liked how they expanded upon sprites for all main characters and also I appretiated slightly more detailed models with introduced shadows and such. New guard blocking system was definitelly a missing feature in the first game, so nice job here. Bosses also look less like gunstar heroes/sonic bosses, but they paid heavy price for having detailed but overall static models.I have yet to finish game for other characters apart from Lilac, for which I unlocked everything that was unlockable in terms of collectibles and achievements including par times challenges and S rank in every level. I might change my mind, but right now - 7 years long work of a group of people seem like a lot for a result like this. Even if it was made by a single person over this span of time, I would still consider it a poor result. Other than that, fine addition to first game, except the first game was just better in terms of mechanics and redundant complexicity.

_childDocuments_.review: I waited 7 years for this sequel and it has been everything I've wanted and more!  -The movement is immaculate, it flows insanely well, using most movement options allows you to glide and slide, keeping the momentum you've earned, redirecting and adding to it-The level design has a beautiful, seemless flow, and they've solved the frustrations of 2d sonic games by making the game based on health rather than the danger being falling in frustrating random pits.  -The combat system allows for creative combinations of moves depending on the situation, and all of them keep your movement flowing and feeling natural.  The combat feels built into the game, rather than tacked on, and works well with the boss section after every stage-The art is BEAUTIFUL, the whole game looks amazing and I feel kind of bad for speeding through it when there's so much detail everywhere.  The game gives sections of time to just look at the world and appreciate it though, I love it-The story has gone further with themes and writing than the first game, and its really engaging and interesting to see where they go with it.  I haven't finished all of the stories yet, but though the story goes through the same flow it seems, each character has differing dialogues and situations explored in their story, and it seems you explore the whole story by playing all of themI can tell this game will be a long-term favorite of mine, it really encapsulates a lot about what I love about games

_childDocuments_.review: Freedom Planet 2 is a turbo version of Freedom Planet 1, with almost all parts of it being tuned up to be even better than the first one.While in the first game you would choose between Lilac and Carol (with Milla being a bonus character unlocked later on), here you have the option of the first three character plus Neera, one of the antagonists turned hero in this one.Not only that but the moveset for all characters were overhauled and added to, giving you way more tools to glide, fight and explore the stages, both at your own pace and on breakneck speedrunning speeds.The game plays really fluid and i had no problems at all on that department, the game does ask focus of the player and don't hold your hand at all in any way, if you don't up your own game, you gonna have trouble, even more so on bosses where they can very well drain your entire life bar in seconds if you don't focus.There are some hiccups here and there but they in no way get in front of the fun so i would give it a 9/10.Stage wise the game has more or less 30 stages i think, it's not a giant game, but it gives you enough content to deal with to not feel short, and that is not adding in the the campaigns of all 4 characters, since they all play different enough that you will have different problems to solve with each one. While i just finished the game i really want to get on the other characters to play through all the stages again from their perspectives, 10/10.Music is a blast just like the first one, even more so in some places, it's as close to perfection as i think a human made work can be, props to the musicians and sound design guys, they did one hell of a job here! 10/10!graphics are also amazing, everything is conveyed really well and danger is really easy to spot. Though the danger sign for projectiles outside of the screen does feel like a place holder and breaks alway from the game overall aesthetic, hope they fix that. 8/10.Now, story... that's where i think this game kinda fails, HARD.first, from a gameplay perspective, forcing people to play the game in story mode first before giving them the option to play classic mode (a mode more akin to old games where you just go from stage to stage without cutscenes or anything) is a step back from FP1, it reeks of writers throwing a hissy fit at the though that someone might not care about their work, and forcing them to it as an act of rebelion.Now, if the story was at least on par with the first game, where it was not good, but did things interestingly enough, i think it would be ok to suffer through it once, but ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ FP2 story drops the ball way too many times to be passable.The main villain is a walking cliché of rebel without a cause and the writers trying to much at making you want to like her, most actions of Merga in the game comes off as a child throwing a tantrum, and basically boils down to "bad people did bad things so i will destroy the world, even tho the bad people don't even exist anymore".Then you have the plot points that only serve to futher themselves instead of fleshing up the world, and to be honest, just feels like the writers are spending way too much time on twitter.At no point in the first or second game we see any sign of slavery, yet somehow the story talk about it as if it was the most important part of the entire history of the world, the first game makes no distinction between dragon races, but now they have to because they need to push the story forward.In the first game we had a completely ruthless warlord that would get things done and had no time for ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, here we have a child-like snowflake taking her problems on the rest of the world because it hurt her feefees.And again, the story would have zero importance... IF they didn't held classic mode hostage so people would be forced to play through it.Galaxy Trail dropped the ball HARD here, there are some funny conversations and cool secondary characters in it, so it's not all lost, but still a 4/10.So yeah, gameplay, amazing, sound/music, amazing, graphics also amazing, if you can suffer through the garbage story, go for it, i hope they just give us the option to start on classic mode from the get go.all in all, i will still give the game a 8/10, would be a 9/10 if it didn't had any story/if you're playing through classic mode.

_childDocuments_.review: It's been almost two years now since I played the first one and if you remember my review to FP1, you may remember that I really loved this game. Meanwhile, the awesome team at GalaxyTrail was cooking the second game of this young franchise. And after years of waiting (like, the game was announced in 2015), September 13, 2022 rolled around and the floodgates opened. Ladies and gentlemen - Freedom Planet 2.And...with the nearly 11 hours (by the time I write this) invested and the Lilac story finished (complete with all time capsules. Trust me, you want to collect them!), I came to my conclusion rather quickly. FP2 is not just a sequel, no, it feels like an entire revival of the series. While the first game was more on the lines of a 2D quick paced Sonic like game, FP2 feels unique. There is right now no other indie game with that feeling. There's so much you can do - you can do challenges, you can just talk to NPCs, unlock neat Easter Eggs, on top of the core gameplay that remained mostly the same. And yet, it feels refined. You can fight the way you want, you can cyclone into enemies (which no longer uses energy), you can dragon boost into them - or just combine these to deal massive amounts of damage. And that is just Lilac's gameplay, as you can also play with series staples Carol and Milla, as well as the fourth playable character, Neera.Story wise...oh boy. I don't want to spoiler anything, but Merga and the Bakunawa situation were perfectly set up and after the story is done, you are satisfied. There are even some questions you may have from FP1 that are answered in FP2. If you would force me to choose between FP1 and FP2's story, it'd be latter anytime. And Merga is a fantastic and understandable villain. But that, explore for yourselves. Even the length is perfect - with Lilac, I took around 9 hours to finish the game. If you want to go for all characters, expect around 35+ hours. Not even counting the challenges.Ultimately, Freedom Planet 2 takes what made FP1 so cool and does it much better. I don't regret my Day One buy at all, as for me personally, this is the one of the best indie games that ever graced this platform. Absolute recommendation if you are a fan of 2D high speed adventures in the vein of the older Sonic games. And fans of the first game can get this one without doubt. Trust me, you will not be disappointed.Freedom Planet 3, whenever it comes out, will also be a Day One buy. Because if I learned one thing with Freedom Planet 1 and 2, it's that GalaxyTrail know their stuff.

_childDocuments_.review: After playing and loving the first Freedom Planet back in 2015, I've waited years for this sequel to release, and I can happily say this game was WELL worth both the wait and the price. Many improvements and QoL changes have been made to gameplay, art, and presentation compared to its predecessor; the whole experience feels very streamlined and engaging the whole way through, every character feels very action-packed and fun to play (not to mention REALLY entertaining to watch in cutscenes as well), there are a whole bunch of levels with great variety to both explore and speed through, and it runs fast and smooth on my piece of junk laptop which is a miracle in and of itself!I'm nearly 40 hours in and still have 1 and a half campaigns left to finish, and that's not even including completionist tasks and additional challenge playthroughs. _childDocuments_.review: It's taken me quite some time to find how I want to say the praise I want to say, as It's easy to gush so much your feelings come off as insincere.This game.... is so freaking good it  It took 7 years to make, and it shows in just about every aspect of the game. Every. Single. Aspect. Sometimes, such a long dev cycle is a death sentence for a project, and this is THE POLAR OPPOSITE of the case here. I have 11 hours in and I'm not even 2/3 of the way through the first campaign, and have only done a few sidequests and battlesphere missions. THAT is how much content we have here. We have collectibles, a minigame zone in the battlesphere, the achievments.... $25 is a freaking steal for how much there is to do here.I have not tried the new character Neera as of writing, but the three other characters are an absolute delight, not just in fun gameplay and mechanics, and character design, but in POLISH. The game feels as snappy and fluid as something like Rayman Legends.  While the game is fully its own thing, I've noticed several other elements that feel born from criticisms of the same sonic series it's inspired by as well as a bunch of other things. Too many reused levels? Each level is vibrantly crafted to a T and visually distinct; the pixel art feeling less like pixel art and more like the effort Studio MDHR put into Cuphead. Can't see where you're going when you go fast? The screen has an adjustable zoom. "Souls" -like difficulty getting jack.d off to no end? The Game has a casual mode to get you adjusted, as well as a slew of items and settings to truly make your play experience your own, with really the only penalty being fewer rewards at the end of a stage. Story too long, inconsistent and not engaging? The game is much more well-paced, with a MUCH stronger narrative which was confirmed to be inspired by Zootopia and Black Panther. In other words, it explores some darker themes but does not have something like the torture scene from the first game. Some Dialogue still feels off, but that is a nitpick. Even the hub worlds are small, compact, and .Even if you are not a fan of 2D action platformers, I'm willing to bet you know someone who does, and I'll say it once I'll say it again - This game is a worthy inclusion to your library. To list negatives, sometimes the difficulty does not feel balanced, and the aforementioned dialogue feeling off, but really, THAT'S IT. There is no other way to say it. To Miss Diduro, the Galaxytrail team, and contributors like Christian Whitehead, Chris Sabat, and anyone else not mentioned, your game absolutely ROCKS.EDIT: Also behaves quite nicely on steam deck!

_childDocuments_.review: I've played a good amount of 2D platformers, so I'd confidently say that this game is great. If you liked the first Freedom Planet you'll probably love this one. It's a fast-paced, momentum based action-platformer with excellent music, visuals, and level design. There's some really fun boss fights, a surprising amount of fully-voiced cutscenes, and a good amount of replay value.First playthrough took about 9 hours, but I redid a few levels, finished the Battlesphere mode and just generally screwed around a bit. If you're just gunning it the entire time I would say a decent player would finish in 5-6 hours. I'll probably come back and rewrite this after I finish a playthrough with all 4 characters to see what's in store. You can also get a lot of replay value redoing levels to improve your time or get a better ranking if you're into that. Stages are typically under 10 minutes, so you can run through them multiple times pretty fast.So yeah, if you're a fan of action-platformers, or if you're not and just looking for a good game to try out, definitely worth your time.

_childDocuments_.review: I was a Sonic fan for nearly twenty years, almost from the very beginning. The first Freedom Planet managed to impress the hell out of me by out-Sonic-ing Sonic (not that that was hard at the time) and throwing in a perfect blend of elements from classic Treasure games like Gunstar Heroes, and even a bit from my beloved Rocket Knight games.Now, eight years later, here's the sequel... and not only does it out-Sonic Sonic again, I'd go so far as to say it out-Treasures Treasure. This is hands down one of the most impressive platformers I've played in years. It looks and sounds gorgeous, it plays like a dream, its story is wonderfully deep, its mechanics are brilliant, its boss fights are spectacular, and its setpieces keep getting more and more hype, topping themselves with every new level. Everything done well in the first game isn't just done better here, it's given a shot of pure adrenaline and turned up to eleven.If you are or were a fan of classic Sonic or if you like 2D, sprite-based platformers at all, buy this game right now. It's a blast from start to finish.
_childDocuments_.name: Freedom Planet 2

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of people are going to compare the Freedom Planet games to just Sonic, but at this point it's more doing its own thing with an eclectic mix of inspirations from all across Sonic, Treasure's game library and more classic retro platformers besides that. Which is absolutely a good thing.This game is a huge work of passion and you can feel the effort coming from every little detail, to the gorgeous sprite work, the remarkably expansive level design and the great story told through the games main adventure mode.I did definitely get my face beat in by several of the bosses on my first playthrough, and each time I got better- only to get floored by another tougher key boss fight later on in the game (before improving again), which if anything is a sign of a good difficulty curve considering I was constantly improving. But if the difficulty every gets too much at a particular point, there are good assist options in the menus such as infinite revivals (the ability to get up for free after losing a life) and more. To make sure you don't get stuck and unable to continue if platformers aren't your usual game genre.Overall, really, this rules. Loved almost every moment of it, currently on my third playthrough. Sometimes video games can be good it turns out.
