_childDocuments_.review: There's more than enough content in this game to keep your sonic itch scratched, and if you were a fan of the first game I would wholly recommend this sequel as it improves much of what has been done before. The story itself will build on a lot of the same characters you've seen before and introduce new ones who are equally intriguing and have a lot of personality. It answers a few questions while still keeping and introducing more.And there's an emphasis on either plunging the levels' depths to get the most possible out of your run or going as fast as you can, to reach the end and to beat the bosses quickly. And hoo boy, they have a LOT of boss fights in this one, there's at least one per stage and the toughest encounters have their own stages so you won't have to worry about getting sent too far back for dying too much.If it's the only few critiques I can give it's that changing the lives into "stocks" and not providing much opportunity to gain more outside of crystals, potions, and items can put a lot of pressure on the player to avoid restarting the stage once encountering the boss. There is an easy mode, but if that's for new players then they'll have to treat this game as a self-contained adventure rather than a continuation in the world of the previous one.Speaking of the story, for as much as I like the foreshadowing and buildup to the reveal of Merga's plans, I do admit she feels like she gets left on the backburner of the first act a bit long.But these aren't to any detriment of the game itself. If you want the challenge, it's there for you and it's welcomed with open arms.All in all, 11/10 this is a Must-Buy for those that enjoy 2D Sonic and Freedom Planet 1 or other skill and speed-based platformer games as well as people who enjoy the art and style of many genesis classics, fantasy and space sci fi mixed together, and pretty pixel art.

_childDocuments_.review: I have been waiting for this game a long time.As an enthusiastic fan of platformers, given my gaming career began with Sonic 1, I have played many from various different subgenres in my time - all of the Sonics, more technical/precision based ones like The End is Nigh and Wings of Vi, and then I found a little game named Freedom Planet many years ago... and fell in love.The first Freedom Planet was easily one of, if not the best platformer I've played. Out of so many. I adored that game, and couldn't wait for a sequel. Now, after many years, avidly looking for news of it, it finally emerged.Is it a worthy sequel?I would say that while Freedom Planet 1 felt like a new team finding its feet, Freedom Planet 2 is handled with a lot more confidence - storytelling is more streamlined and well-paced, with no very long cutscenes breaking the pacing, while simultaneously telling a surprisingly good story. It feels much wider in scale than the previous game, and makes you think of aspects to the world of Avalice that are not solely related to the current conflict (in comparison, in the first game, everything was against Brevon).The music, unfortunately, I must say is not as good as the first - there are some standout tracks (first Dragon Valley is incredible), but overall I'd say they feel a bit more generic than before. The power of the first game was that each stage had separate music tracks, where the first part would establish some musical theme and the second would develop it - things like Aqua Tunnel, Relic Maze, and Jade Creek from the first game were incredibly beautiful and exciting tracks, and I still listen to them on a regular basis.The game's level structure in the second one no longer has "split acts", and thus the music mostly remains constant throughout - still good to listen to, but I feel that levels generally don't have a distinct theme to them.Gameplay-wise, it's like a smoother and more varied version of the first game. I've only played as Lilac so far, but the change they made to her Cyclone means she's considerably smoother to play. There was no level that frustrated me or that I felt was unfair, and all of the bosses felt good (even if there are some significant difficulty spikes, but only on really climactic bosses, so I thought this was fine - the first game also had big spikes on key bosses, and I think it elevates the moment). I've seen some people complain about the boss design, but I thought they were all fine on Lilac - the true final boss required me to exploit the invincibility of her Dragon Dash, but again - this is a design feature, and in the previous game using it was also baked into my strategy.Overall, if you have any interest in platformers whatsoever, you should buy this game without a shadow of a doubt. It's a more mature story, with very likeable characters and fantastic platforming gameplay. The second-to-last boss (as in, non-True ending boss) may be one of the best fights I've seen in a platformer, period.My only problem with this game is that there will likely be a very long time to wait until the third!
_childDocuments_.name: Freedom Planet 2

_childDocuments_.review: This game is way superior to the first game, and I think the first game is already a masterpiece!The level design has improved so much... there was no stage that I didn't like...On the other side, I think the bosses are great but not as great as they were in the first game... same for some boss themes...Overall, I think this game is way better than the first one!
_childDocuments_.name: Freedom Planet 2

_childDocuments_.review: Freedom Planet 2 is a big improvement over the original game.  Better graphics, more mechanics, more stages, and a new playable character.  Also has a fantastic soundtrack.The biggest change of them all is adding items and assist options to make the game easier for those who struggle with the game's difficulty, especially the later bosses.  This is certainly easier than the first game but still has some challenging bosses later on so these features allow more casual players to still experience the whole game.Overall, if you enjoy fast paced platformers then you will almost certainly enjoy this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Freedom Planet 2

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely astoundingly good platformer from start to finish. The music, art, animation, gameplay mechanics and level design are all top notch. This game's predecessor was already one of the best games i'd ever played, and this improves on it so much - and in every possible regard - that it isn't even funny. _childDocuments_.name: Freedom Planet 2

_childDocuments_.review: Just like the first game, but even more of it. Fast paced gameplay, varied levels, great visuals+music, and a ridiculous amount of content.The level design is still top-tier, with huge sprawling levels full of fun stage gimmicks. Levels are fun whether you're exploring for gems and secrets, trying to beat the par times, or just trying to survive at all. There's around twice as many levels as the first game but they're substantially shorter, but that's fine since the first game's levels all felt like they should have been split in two.The returning characters each got a rework to their moveset, for the better. Lilac only got minor additions, but Carol and Milla got substantial reworks which make them much more fun (Milla is a lot more aggressive, Carol has a more interesting special attack which also provides more moevment). There's also a new fourth character, with her own extremely varied moveset.There's more bosses this time, and more variety to the bosses (lots of 1-on-1 duels with other human-sized characters, in addition to the giant robots with obvious weakpoints). An unfortunate number of them tend to spend most of the fight offscreen in the large arenas, but otherwise their design is quite good. Regular enemy design is good too.Overall, there's lots to love. If you liked the first game, you'll like the sequel.
_childDocuments_.name: Freedom Planet 2

_childDocuments_.review: Hecking great time! _childDocuments_.review: It may have taken seven years since this game was announced, but the payoff's pretty damn great.It's a lot of what a sequel should be, bigger and bolder.Featuring a new playable character, larger skill set for all cast members, more stages, a good chunk of side content.Rankings, par times, accessories, potions, tons of good additions.Only major complaints I have is that the physics are still kind of jank, best way I can describe it is unnecessarily sticky and could benefit from a bigger focus on momentum, but what we have isn't bad, shame the rail sections ain't faster though.Bosses aswell have some camera issues I find, they're fun but some of them could really benefit from having the camera zoomed out way more.Besides that, it is just a joy to go as fast as possible, finding new ways to cut off seconds and get better and better at mastering each stage, it's exactly why I loved the original and why I loved this game.Really hoping we get DLC or a third entry.Game's great, well worth your money, easy recommendation.

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't beaten the game yet, but feel the need to leave something after getting halfway through the game, since I already know what lies ahead of me. I'm a huge fan of the original Freedom Planet, I might not have a ton of hours logged into it on Steam, but on Switch I've played it more. I truly believe this was worth the wait, granted the wait was agonizing, I can't remember the last time I waited almost 10 years for a game and walked away satisfied after playing it. It is clear that there was effort here to make Freedom Planet something other than a Sonic homage; in fact I learned the hard way that you shouldn't be rushing through these stages, take your time and explore. What I truly think gives this game replay value is the stage gimmicks, I say gimmicks in the best way possible since most levels bring some platforming twist to the table, I won't spoil them, but it is satisfying to memorize a level layout and flawlessly reach the end of the stage. Lives are contained to their level and acquiring an extra life isn't as easy like the first game, lives only exist so you can chase those perfect rankings.In the original game if you timed your dragon boost, you could cheese the game; I'm happy to say those moments aren't in this game as much, bosses screen filling attack patterns punishes reckless play. I know I might be made fun of for saying this, I find some of these bosses harder than Hollow Knight's Galaxy Trail really went above and beyond with the challenging boss fights. If there are some negatives I can list, I'm adjusting to navigating the map, I would have preferred a linear point A to point B like the original; but then you wouldn't see these amazing hub worlds that are do detailed I end up hanging out in them anyways( preference I guess). I find healing items a little unnecessary, I believe you should fail to master the game; I welcome the items that handicap the player for extra bonus points. Lastly the pixel work is breathtaking, I would say the 8 year development cycle has paid off. I've been tired of indie pixel games for a long time, I can make an exception in this case since this might be the best sprite work I've seen in a side scroller; it really shows the jump from the original game which used multimedia fusion and this game uses Unity. What really impresses me more than character animations are the background HD sprites, it truly feels like Avalice is a living breathing world. I'm currently on my default Lilac run, I'm itching to get to Milla since she is my favorite character and it looks like she's received the most improvements as a fighter.I would highly recommend this game, it is currently in my game of the year list alongside Bayonetta 3.
_childDocuments_.name: Freedom Planet 2

_childDocuments_.review: Freedom Planet 2 expands on everything in the original game and mostly upgrades it, gameplay is even smoother, abilities chain into each other or have new capabilities. The music is fantastic like the first game, but with some added variety. The storyline was probably the biggest surprise, considering how some people didn't like the darker tone of aspects with the original, they doubled down here but balanced the darker stuff and comedy in a much better way than the original. Aspects from the first game play a big role here, and i'm all there for that. This game also has room for a sequel which I hope happens now.There's a massive amount of stages and collectables here, it's overall just a really magical experience. My only negatives are I feel some of the bosses are a little too awkward, the fact you have to unlock Classic Mode this time, not that I didn't like the story, but I feel some folks aren't going to care and gating Classic Mode behind a first run feels kind of strange. Also where's my mahjong? Full thumbs up though, fantastic followup.

_childDocuments_.review: At the time of writing this review before, I had not finished the game. I am updating it now to show that I have finished it on at least one character. I will say this: It isn't a perfect game, but the passion OOZES out of it. It plays incredibly smoothly and really pushes the player to get good. It does well to recapture the feel of the SNES and SEGA Genesis days, and some of their difficulty. I played it on the hardest difficulty to start with, and it was a painful journey, but it was worthwhile, as it really helped me improve my play. The Normal difficulty will be accessible to people starting the game off or just picking up the genre. The bosses are far more lenient without Hard Mode's doubled damage.The Character designs are even better than they were in the first one, and it really feels like the voice-actors not only enjoyed voicing the characters but had genuine passion for the project. I can only really remark on playstyles I'm proficient with, and I have to say that I am bad at Lilac and Milla, though players good with them in the previous game will have an easy time using them in this one. Carol is a titanic step up from what she was in Freedom Planet 1. Her DPS is much higher, and her gameplay is more streamlined and intuitive. I cannot speak for fans of Carol with the Motorcycle, as I barely used it. To me, it feels and plays worse than without the Motorcycle, but I grew up playing Megaman X and Zero. Since Carol reminds me so much of Zero (Zero series on GBA) in gameplay, I really meshed well with it and it felt amazing to play as. Her kit is excellent, and, once an opening is found, she can eviscerate Boss' health bars with stunning ease. She really plays like a cat.Neera is more sluggish, but she is a precision powerhouse. She is less agile but still quick, more relying on careful positioning than merely blasting through a stage with invincibility (though she is still capable in that regard). Players that like being close to enemies will like her, especially once they really get good with her slower attacks and utilizing her "Focus" self-buff.The Guard System can be thought of as more of a Street Fighter Parry with massively lenient timing. It is required for some Boss fights, and makes some stages much easier, and it is very easy to use (I'm bad at parrying in Street Fighter but I got pretty good with it in this game. It's not hard).The stage design is imperfect but pretty smooth for the most part. There were times where I got lost and questioned which way I was supposed to go, but a little exploration and a lot of going this way and that sorted it out. The terrain is a little frustrating in some places, as surfaces meant to be walked up vertically will throw the character at a sharp angle if a jump is done while running on the wall. Since some terrain behaves in such a way in Boss fights, it makes them unnecessarily difficult, and makes the losses inflicted by them feel unfair. That said, It's all very smooth barring that one hiccup and it will not stop me from recommending the game because it can be played around with even the barest amount of experience. Some enemy placement is annoying, though. On-screening an enemy and then feeling like there is no time to react as one takes damage from something one couldn't have possibly seen feels bad, though, again, it's not game-breaking and these instances don't occur often. The warning markers are a bit large, and, at one time, prevented me from seeing something I was supposed to be avoiding. Not perfect, but still able to be played around and still tons of fun.The story is actually pretty decent for what this game is. The team respected the characters. They expanded on them and leaned into their personalities pretty hard. Carol was already my favorite, and, as a Carol fan, I was exceedingly well-pleased. I'd heard the same for Milla. I'm sure Lilac and Neera's characters are just as well-represented. As a bonus, Neera is actually likable in this game. Hints are dropped of developments in the other parts of the stories, so it really encourages the player to play through with all characters.Merga is a villain that was done well with the narrative and "show, don't tell" techniques used. She was done far better than Brevon, but still, somehow, lacks his innate menace. That said, I really have very few complaints, if any, about the direction the story took. This is how a sequel should be done.The music is excellent, by the way. Maybe not as punchy as some of the first Freedom Planet's tracks in some spots but definitely, DEFINITELY amazing. This OST is a whole lot better than the first Freedom Planet's. I only found a few of the themes not hitting as hard, and that was rare. I also was concentrating on tough boss patterns and trying not to die so I will have time now to appreciate the OST more since I'm not trying to survive something that will delete my health bar.Games like this don't come along too often. Makers rarely have this kind of passion anymore and they rarely execute it even half as well. This is a sequel done right. This is what the Triple A industry can't seem to get right, and yet this little team of developers with gobs of passion and a fraction of the budget did amazingly well. This game is worth every penny and I am glad I could support it.
_childDocuments_.name: Freedom Planet 2

_childDocuments_.review: I am utterly speechless. After just finishing this game completely, I only can say one thing: Thank you, Galaxytrail. Sabrina, you and your team gave us a work of art that I'm going to remember for a long time, and one I'm DEFINITELY going to replay and recommend to others. Worth the 6 year wait by a long shot, even if it is a little buggy still.
_childDocuments_.name: Freedom Planet 2

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic sequel. Takes the first game, makes it bigger, and INJECTS IT WITH DRAGON STEROIDS!The new:- World map- Hub levels (First game was supposed to have them, but were cut, and I see why, because they are HILARIOUSLY glitchy)- Equippable accessories and passive potion charges that alter various stats/effects (but appear to degrade your rank, because REAL MEN DON'T EQUIP RPG TRINKETS TO MAKE THE GAME EASIER (I am not a real man apparently)- 1 new playable character (Neera)- Generally improved combat, as well as a new Dodge/dash function. It works pretty well. I am now going to go back to the first game and try pressing the nonexistent dodge button in vain.- And a bunch more.I'd say the difficulty of bosses are overall a bit harder than the first game's (minus pre-nerf steroido Brevon of FP1), but the ability to dodge-dash makes bosses more tight. Most bosses are fought in the middle or end of a stage, but every now and then it pulls a Klonoa 2, and puts a boss only stage on the map, which is neat, more games like that should do this, at least at times. Speaking of Klonoa 2, just like FP1, some levels do indeed drag on for quite a bit, which I'm fine with, but some people like their bite sized levels. Good old Klonoa 2/Freedom Planet level syndrome.In the hub levels, there's tons of charming characters to talk to for lots of optional dialogue. Soooo many npcs. Some of the characters are designed by Tyson Tan, which I somewhat know from DA eons ago, his artstyle is cool and all, but sometimes its "Hyper cute", whereas I prefer the more consistent artstyle of the first game (Although, I'd say the artstyle of this game is generally better, and certainly more detailed). Whenever I saw something that looked overly Tyson-Tan-y, it kind of took me out of it (both in a good and bad way). Especially that one mech fight. I'm like "Oh no, it's The Tyson Tan Mech" weirdly enough, it's the boss I had the most trouble with, needed like 2-3 continues, didn't think I needed even 1 continue for every other boss. I feel kinda funny now for getting my ass handed to me by something so cute. Speaking of lives, you can't horde them like you could in the first game, but on the flip side, you always start with a few every level (can be increased with a potion effect), as well as having the choice of using a life to start from last checkpoint with full health, or start off exactly where you died, but with low hp (hp recovery can also be increased with a potion effect).How the potions work is that they are passive, you do not actively drink them. There are 5 slots to put whatever potion effect you want, you could have 1 charge of 5 different effects, or 2/3 charges of 2 different effects, or 5 charges with 1 effect, if you want to focus on your favored effect. Makes me feel like a Witcher mixing these potion charges into the bottle. Milla is a Witcher confirmed.You can buy potions/accessories/music from various shops in various towns, by spending either gems, as found in the first game, or enemy cores, dropped by most enemies, or gold pieces, which can be bought with gems/cores, and sometimes found in chests. Several accessories can also be found in chests, but most of them make the game harder in exchange for a bigger gem bonus (reminds me of Supergiant difficulty gimmicks)The music is superb as usual, the levels are fairly similar to FP1's in structure, you have your normal/action stages, puzzle stages, some key item hunty stages, and sometimes a mix of the above. As well as a few SCHMUP stages, just like the first game. That one mech schut stage was pretty ridiculous/chaotic and kind of glitchy. Loved it.The voiceacting is as good as the first's, there's a good lot more of it, and the main villain is likeable and sympathetic . Unlike the first game's villain which was just SCUMSCUMSCUM that you love to hate. I like me a good hateable villain (Brevon), but I usually prefer the more likeable ones that you can sympathize with.There's also some neat twists in the story. Such as the Magister revealing his face

_childDocuments_.review: A modern masterpiece. This game should set the standard for all other games in its devotion to just  in whatever ways they want to.There is an insane amount of quality and polish to the game, even on day 1 of release. It is obviously a labor of love and that is felt through the way its design meets players at whatever level they want to engage with it. Do you just like platforming? Here's ~30 stages for you to run through with unique set pieces like low gravity, air bubbles, boosters, darkness, etc. Quick-reflex combat? Got tons of that with a huge variety of bosses. Story? Dive in or just skip it if you want. Achievements and challenge modes? Go wild. Favor different play styles? There's 4 unique characters you can be. Find the game too easy or difficult? There's assist options and items which augment the difficulty. Speedrunning? Plenty of in-game timers and record trackers available. It's just.... overwhelming. There's  here. There's a museum of collectibles to fill up. There's a photo mode that I don't know who asked for but it's in here! There's hidden collectibles that unlock multiple endings. There's a jukebox. There's dozens of unique fully animated NPCs with distinct character. Basically every single thing from the previous game has been refined and improved to make gameplay more fun and dynamic: cancelable dragon boosts, instant Milla cubes, a guard / instashield button, a broader moveset in general like Lilac's up-slash, Carol's Jump Disc and bike stashing... and also she's actually fun to play as now ( :-P ). Neera adds yet another playstyle to the mix. Bosses do that thing I love where they're actually involved in the course of the whole level and not just showing up out of nowhere at the end. For the most part their fights are fun (maybe just a bit pattern-heavy) but there are a few stinkers (pretty much any water-based boss...) Those are balanced out by the few that had really unique mechanics or were just eye-popping WOWZA the whole way through.There's a lot more I can say about specific things but I want to keep this somewhat brief. Freedom Planet 2 is an easy Game of the Year 2022 for me, and if you ask me in a few months I will probably agree it is one of the finest games I have played in my life.
_childDocuments_.name: Freedom Planet 2

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished it as Lilac. The game absolutely blew me away on multiple occasions. The levels are many but are fun, unique, and varied. Combat mechanics are refined, so many bosses and yet they're all unique and fun to fight. There were so many times where I truly felt like "now I can see why this game took so long!" I really think GalaxyTrail went above and beyond with this game!My biggest gripe would have to be the last two levels. Just like FP1, the last couple of levels feel unfairly difficult. It throws so many enemies your way and traps (like spikes on grind rails while you're going super fast so barely any time to avoid them). These levels did have unique mechanics just like the rest of the game which is very impressive considering the high level count in this game but yeah I think the last two could've been a bit more polished.There were also a few levels where I couldn't figure out how to progress for some time due to unclear objective/path so I think that could've been made a bit more clear.The story won't blow your socks off but as someone who isn't crazily obsessed with finding the best writing ever in video games (like so many gamers tend to be...) I very much enjoyed it. Lots of high stakes and emotional moments. The dialogue is heavily refined from the first game and there are lots of really neat reveals about the characters we know and love from the first game. The music was, as usual, really good but unfortunately nothing really stuck out to me as much as FP1's soundtrack. Still the composer did an excellent job.I hear lots of people have ran into bugs and personally I haven't experienced anything too bad or annoying. I did have trouble setting up my PS3 controller using the Playstation button icons. Lots of the buttons displayed in the game did not match what I pressed on my controller. However, setting the icons back to the default "numbers" made everything a non-issue. I think its worth bringing up to people reading this that, for now as of writing this review on 9/16/2022, you shouldn't bother trying to change icons. Just stick to the numbers!All in all, I think the game was very much worth the wait. Definitely one of my favorite 2D platformers of all time now. I replayed FP1 many times because it's just really fun to play but now I don't think I ever see myself going back to it and instead probably going to replay this game a whole bunch from now on! Thanks GalaxyTrail!
_childDocuments_.name: Freedom Planet 2

_childDocuments_.review: An amazing masterpiece of a sequel to one of my favorite speedy action platformers of all time. I played the original Freedom Planet, and waited 7 long years for Freedom Planet 2. I appreciate the transition from linear classic story progression to branching adventure quests that meet back together into a main path after completion, while exploring various maps with town hubs in between...There are also plenty of items that you can alter gameplay with as you unlock more shops, whether to aid you or to make the game much more challenging which is sometimes required to get the highest ranks.Boss battles are notably memorable and numerous as well in Freedom Planet 2. Many bosses follow a changing pattern, however the boss 'characters' that you can battle are surprisingly responsive and certainly provide that spike in difficulty when a change of pace is needed. Not only that, you can fight the bosses again later after a certain amount of progression.All four main characters are unique and dynamic from everything I've tested. The only things I can say I find lacking, is that I want more playable characters if there aren't any or some kind of online or local PVP character fighting arena...Regardless, the swath of gameplay additions and improvements to Freedom Planet 2 enrich the experience enough as is. The upgrade in graphics certainly has done wonders in the sprites and artwork too. 10/10 I will be taking my time playing this game, that way I can enjoy it for long as I can.

_childDocuments_.review: There's a lot to this game, There's 4 characters with their own skills that completely change how you play the game. Lilac can pull a Rocket Knight and shoot in any of 8 directions with Dragon Boost and she has a double jump that has a slight hover with Cyclone. Carol has a variety of martial arts with a Wild claw for extra damage, wall jump like Mega Man X she can roll to damage enemies and gain speed, can get  a motorcycle to change her moveset entirely where she can backflip, boost and such. Neera has a wand to shoot ice projectiles from, she can cover enemies with ice and bounce off of them or shatter them and even skates at top speed.Milla can build up murder cubes to either spam light attacks or shoot a big shot. She can flutter her limbs for a Yoshi style jump.All characters also have basic attacks and this is my BIGGEST TIP when playing either Freedom Planet 1 or 2:When attacking if you hit up or down will give you different attacks- and different attacks in the air. They're very, VERY useful and most people I've seen play ignore them and these are some of the more damaging attacks.Lilac's up+attack is an uppercut that not only goes a bit higher than her jump, it does far more damage than her cyclone attack- and you can go right into a down+attack that is a stomp that also does a lot of damage.Neera's attacks in the air are vital to her gaining speed, you can really, really make her go super fast and stay in the air a long while.  Carol's down attack is great for her gaining speed and her disc will help you get around the map or double team an enemy since you can attack while it's doing damage on it's own. I haven't played Mila but I know her changes are pretty big vs her in the first game. She can be more aggressive with more attacks for one and I think has more HP than she did previously. So the characters themselves have a ton to offer in terms of variety and replayabilty. The game itself (So far I'm only 4.6 hours in) is crazy just how much they packed in. Huge levels with tons of routes and spots for characters to use their skills to get around with. The game has much improved writing and  voice work over the first. That's not to knock what the VAs did in 1, I felt a lot of it was their equipment being so different - which isn't the case here. I wish I could explain that better, just know if you thought the story and dialog was a bit lacking in 1- 2 is does it all so much better. The game also has items to help or hinder your gameplay.Hindering items are there to 1- challenge yourself and 2- get your bonus up for a higher rank. Potions & positive items will lower your bonus and your rank.So if you have a item with a negative that boosts your bonus by 75% and you fill a potion to a full 5 you lose 25%. Tie that in with a no-hit bonus and you too can get the fancy rainbow S-Rank.Or you can ignore all that because ranks don't really effect anything from what I can tell. The game feels, so good to play. I can tell I'm going to put a lot of time into this one over the years. The one gripe I think someone could leverage against the game is you have to play through the adventure mode once before unlocking classic mode. Classic mode being you just get the stages. But seeing how much work they put into this and how good it is? It's worth it. This is a heck of a game, they really upped everything in this, the art design and visuals are a big leap over the first game, the stages aren't cut into parts anymore and it's just one large stage with SO many routes to go through. They leave it up to you to explore or blitz through. The music is, so, good. Performance: What I really like is the game can run at over 60fps, I don't know all the numbers off hand but I know it can do over 144hz. Other good news the game can run on a potato, my laptop sporting a 5 year old i5 and a HD620 runs the game at 1080p/60fps just fine. Just make sure you have a good set of speakers, the music is worth it. Edit: The bugs I had in the review have been addressed & I beat the game as Lilac (I'm aware there's a 'true ending' but haven't done that. I think Freedom Planet 1 had better bosses & boss music  & FP2 has a level I'd equate to Sonic CD's Wacky Work Bench in terms of "Really bad level design" as it has teleporter walls that send you all over in a disorienting way. But that is just one bad level out of a ton of them and as a whole FP2 is a really great game with a lot of fun levels, great music & fun levels (except the 1). Tons of replayability and I'm sure in a few months I'll have a bunch of hours racked up & will be revisiting this like Sonic 3 & Knuckles since I first got that.

_childDocuments_.review: An awesome sequel with great improvements all around! Highly recommended buy to fans of action platformers.Compared to the sequel it has a ton of new features, modes and content. There are many challenges and the achievements are really fun to complete. The engine is different from the original and thus more robust and stable, I had only very minor technical issues with setting my controller and nearly getting stuck in an area but these are easy fixes and to be expected from a project of this size on release day. I had no major technical or gameplay related issues otherwise which is a lot more than you can say from some AAA titles.There is a ton of character variety and replayability, tons of music that all sounds great. The artwork is beatiful and if it interests you there's many cutscenes and hubworlds with NPC's that are almost entirely voice acted. If that's not your thing it can be skipped more or less in its entirety.I'm singing the game's praises here because it's really just that good and I think there's something here to enjoy for everyone as long as they enjoy platformers at least. The game also has a very good difficulty curve but if you find it too hard there are items you can use and game settings you can enable.If I had to give it a score I'd give it a 9/10 so far. It's engaging, challenging and just plain fun. Definitely a must-buy from me.EDIT: I have now finished the game and it definitely changed character in the end-game. The quality of the level design fell sharply after the first 2/3rds of the levels and even with 7 years of work the later levels feel like they are padded and they lose their sense of direction in a few places. The first game had much better end game both in design and story and the last boss left me feeling quite unfulfilled. The game as a whole is still a definite recommend from me and there are plenty of great parts to enjoy in the mix but I'd probably drop my score to a 7/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, this time I won’t write the review as a joke.This game not only means a lot to me and some of my friends, but I would be certain enough to say it is even a contestant to my favourite game of all time. So of course, to express al the love I feel for this game, I shall prioritize my negative criticism first!Wait-- Some sounds are, like, LOUD, REALLY FREAKING LOUD, LIKE HOLY F**K, more specifically some bosses’ screams but also with stuff like several bombs exploding together, I could lower the volume, sure, but then the game would be too quiet for most of the time.- Music does not loop in some areas. This is a more major gripe, it can kill the mood in some areas, I feel. Sometimes it is not too bad, but there are many areas (usually Lobbies) were music just stopped for no reason and it made me have a poker face for a couple of seconds.- The items. Oh, dear… The items. Like, I find cool that you can “choose your own difficulty”, but why does hard mode have to be linked to two items? It kinda ruined experimentation for my first play-through because I wanted to play it in hard mode right off the bat. I honestly wouldn’t be complaining about this if the taking double damage and no revives mechanics were separated from the item system, or if we had 2 negative item slots separate from positive item slots.- The potions. Great addition to the game, except I didn’t get to use them until late game because I seriously thought that those were 1-use only. I am unsure if there’s some kind of explanation somewhere in the game about how potions work, but I would have appreciated if I got told from the start about this system.- Vsync is on by default. According to my Bible this is a sin.Okay so now for the praises.*Holy Cungadero is this game good*. This is a huge glow up from the first Freedom Planet: the playable characters have a much more unique and diverse moveset than before, there’s a lot of lore and story  to enjoy that explains a lot about this game world’s culture and past, music is fantastic (just like the first game), and even the main antagonist has a much deeper personality. And oh boy, don’t get me freaking started about the artstyle and pixel art… First of all, the entire game’s sprites has “Tyson Tan” written all over them (not literally), and when I got told that this guy was helping in the art department of this FP2, I knew it was gonna look good, but even then, it surpassed my expectations, making my jaw drop a couple of times. What the art and graphics department of Galaxy Trail has achieved is pure freaking magic, I tell you, hahahaha.I could keep praising each individual part of this game, and every single thing I loved about this journey, but I think I already wrote a long enough review. Thanks, Galaxy Trail team, for making not only what should be considered as a perfect sequel, but also the continuation of the game that made me meet what I can consider today as my best friends.

_childDocuments_.review: The fast paced platforming of Freedom Planet returns! Become a full-time cartoon heroine and use abilities and items suited to your play style to explore the world of Avalice and defend its animal citizens.

name: The Shattering
detailed_description: You can’t remember anything. All you see is white around you. You hear a voice. You see a watch, swinging slowly in front of your eyes: “I know you think everything is alright, but tell me, how come you can’t even remember her name?” The Shattering places you in the mind of John Evans, where you struggle to piece together the fragments of your past and present. Not remembering is one thing, but what will happen when your mind leads you down the twisted path of fake memories in order to shelter you from the truth? Follow the voice of the Doctor as it guides you deeper into your mind, and experience the key moments of John’s life that had defined and shaped him. Discover the truth, shatter the lies, find out what happened to John… and remember her name. The Shattering is a first-person, story-driven, psychological thriller. Its defining features are the dynamic environments, beautiful aesthetics and intriguing story. There are no failure conditions in The Shattering, nor complicated puzzles. The gameplay is meant to submerge you in the mind of John, as you take each step forward into the twisted mystery of what had happened. A serene and emotionally charged soundtrack gives life to every single moment, while the visuals delight at every corner. A rich and constantly evolving world taking place in the mind of John, where there are no limits or rules. Beautiful and rich realistic environments painted with a pristine white aesthetic provide a original scenery that stands apart. An intriguing story split into 4 acts that pieces together knowledge of the past and understanding of the present as you progress. A sublime, gripping and intense original score composed for the story of The Shattering breathes live into each moment. The Shattering is a work of passion coming from a small group of 5 close friends lead by Marta Szymanska. Super Sexy Software started in spirit in 2013, when the first echoes of The Shattering started to take form. The project began from studying the contrast of white and black in horror and culture. The core theme draws on the premise that horrors and fear can be achieved through embracing white and the absence of information, rather than darkness and the obvious, though unseen, enemy. Over various iterations, the game took shape and the decision was made to work on it in every spare moment that could be found. With members of the team residing in Poland, France and Switzerland, they grew in experience and efficiency as the true spirit of the studio was born. As the game progressed, the developers and Deck13 met at a networking event and the synergy between the companies resonated immediately. A publisher was found, and all the ingredients to finish The Shattering were ready. With the full development spanning multiple years, births and deaths, tears and laughter, the only joy greater than that of the journey together as one team and family, is the joy of seeing The Shattering take shape and be played by people around the world. We’d like to thank you, the player, for taking interest in our passion. We hope our story can echo out and reach gamers around the world.

_childDocuments_.review: The Shattering is a walking simulator with a slow-paced plot that slowly unravels, focusing and submerging players into its psychological and thriller elements. This narrative is definitely quite abstract in its method of storytelling, with a bleak white aesthetic and  blur between true and fabricated memories. If you enjoy games similar to Layers of Fear, this title is worth both your time and attention.+ A thought-provoking, disjointed story that slowly unravels.+ Striking white aesthetic.+ Authentic, emotional story that truly felt like I was scouring through John's mind, trying to make sense of every detail. + Excellent voice acting, dialogue and graphics that allowed players to become immersed in the surroundings.+ Conveys sensitive mental health topics and confrontational imagery through an educational and pragmatic approach.+ Optional items to collect.+ Steam achievements.- I became rather nauseous after playing for long periods, most likely due to the strobe and motion blur effects. Without any settings to alter this, I had to play in small increments at a time. I have only seen a handful of comments mentioning this and it will obviously only impact certain people, but if you find yourself usually being a victim of sickness in games, it is good to be aware that unfortunately this may be another troublesome title.Players begin as John Evans, a man who has no recollection of past events, or how he came to be sitting in an office, staring at a watch swinging back and forth, being told to 'remember'. This establishes the premise for the game, as we delve deeper into John's mind, trying to put together a jumbled mess of incoherent memories, scrolling all the way through John's childhood, to his adult life. What traumatic event occurred to cause the brain to completely block out reality? How does it all make sense and fit together? Players will find themselves asking these types of questions throughout their time in John's subconscious. However, as the fog begins to clear, we are instead confronted with the dark roots of human psychology and thrown into a poignant narrative.Everything about The Shattering is designed to submerge players into the mind of John. Gameplay is somewhat minimal and can be best compared to walking simulators with heavy, emotional stories. There are 4 acts, and each begins in a room with what appears to be a medical psychologist, encouraging us to remember details by stimulating our memories. John is asked to focus solely on his voice and slowly a scene will unfold with remnants of his past. Majority of the game is spent interacting with objects to gain further insight into the past and reading the resulting dialogue. There are no puzzles or complex, hidden items (discounting the optional extras for achievement hunters) and this results in smooth progression. Despite the gameplay being more involved than traditional walking simulators and there are a few dialogue choices, it is important to note that the game is solely based on immersion and player assiduity.One look at the screenshots on the store page had caught my interest, with Its eye-catching and unique black and white environments, I was interested to see how effective this would be in storytelling.  Despite my slight sickness caused by the colour scheme and motion blur, especially in early acts, the graphics are definitely the defining feature of the game. The smatterings of colour immediately demand attention when entering a scene and the use of blue undertones are beautifully done, bringing life to what is otherwise, a gloomy and melancholic world. As John navigates his world, walls begin to fall into place, objects become clear and the environment slowly begins to take its form. I understood this to be a visual interpretation of the concept of remembering. This created immersive, abstract gameplay and it invoked the idea that I was exploring John's mind, slowly discovering the essence of his character.Although the main protagonist is voiceless, the doctor's articulate, yet soft speech resonated in my head and was the only sense of reality from the beginning. The silence in early Acts made the smallest of noises purposefully unbearable, such as blinds thrashing in the wind or static from a TV. This gave a glimpse into the psychological nature of the protagonist and hinted at his suffering. It was interesting that these scenes are included early on, yet with no context, the full extent of their meaning is only revealed towards completion, which encourages player reflection.The Shattering is an emotionally heavy, story-driven narrative with minimalistic gameplay that delves into the memories of a troubled man's life. Its stark, white aesthetic and focus on human psychology make it stand out from similar titles, with the developers unafraid of focusing on more nefarious topics.  Whilst only averaging around 4 hours, I recommend it for those who enjoy slow-burn thrillers, or players looking for a more meaningful and serious game.This review copy was provided to the OCG-Curations curator.

_childDocuments_.review: I was excited for this game after seeing the trailer and seeing it be compared to 'Edith Finch' which is a game I enjoyed, but it just gets less interesting and more frustrating as the game goes on.You play a guy who had an accident and is remembering his past via his dreams/visions with the help of a shrink. The game is one big dream sequence. It consists of walking from place to place, clicking on stuff and seeing objects float into or out of place with voice overs narrating what they are supposed to represent. It quickly turns into a 'find the hidden object game' which worked so well to break my immersion as I'm just desperately clicking on everything in the room trying to get the game to progress. There are some parts where you choose what to say but it's really just another thing you need to click on.John is a voice-less protagonist who has been through a lot of cliche trauma in his life, being bullied and bashed in school, was inconvenienced in having to find a job, which he found but it was still a 'shattering' experience as the job interview for it was scary, being told by his boss he needs to work a Saturday shift, not being able to work without constantly drinking wine, being mad at 'room service' coming to your door because of the noise, including what is implied at the end.The games way of telling the story is intriguing at first, the game presents a nice creepy atmosphere in certain parts, the visuals and the world do well to articulate what John is trying so desperately to remember, and maybe finding the hidden object is supposed to play into that, but the amount of interest generated initially is nullified by the dullness of the latter parts of the game. I opened all those boxes and I understand that was supposed to be a positive memory sequence, but everything spontaneously goes dark and starts breaking, the dinner turns into a live beating heart and I guess it's still realistic because John's a trauma patient and can't remember everything right now, right? I'm not spoiling anything but the revelation in the end is supposed to be motivated by something else which is not addressed in the game. There's a newspaper article you find that tells you what witnesses in the area theorise what happened, but John is the only one who can know for sure and by the end he still doesn't remember it. The game teases a sequel at the end without providing a complete narrative. John being a trauma patient (and dare I say, this being an indie game) is supposed to be a good enough excuse for that I guess, but for me it still makes for a boring game. The acts of the game could have taken place over days or weeks where John finally remembers why he is there, how he got there and whatever other details that make the shrink just so interested in him. I'm usually quite tolerant when stories in media fall short in some way, but for this I feel it was a major event that took place before the ending, and is a main motivator for the ending. It's too much to leave that for a sequel."If you've played such and such games you'll like this" yeah, but you've also played better games than this. This game might be unique with the trauma patient premise, and while that is done well it still makes for an experience where you'd rather be listening to your Spotify collection again, or checking out what's new on youtube instead of clicking on this next blue-highlighted thing. I wish I could advise my past self to skip this one.

_childDocuments_.review: Walking simulator with interesting gameplay surrounded by a sad story and almost no soundtrack. Very slow start but after the prologue everything becomes faster. The full price is really too high, the work and commitment in this game are there but in this price range you can find better. My rating 7/10 to take at discount
_childDocuments_.name: The Shattering

_childDocuments_.review: The Shattering is an approximately 3 hours long narrative driven walking simulator about John Evans, his life drama and his memory issues. With a help of the Doctor we will experience the key moments of John’s life during our journey through his shattered memories. Gameplay is very minimalistic like in almost any walking simulator - just move and interact with objects, there's even no real puzzles except for 19+6=x² (and it seems like half of the players failed to find "x" for this one, oh well).The story in The Shattering is good enough to catch your attention, however it's uneven at times - mixing really strong and well stages chapters/scenes with relatively filler ones. While game ending was reasonable (not great but good, unlike in many other walking simulators where developers tend to fail it), the mystery unravel process itself wasn't really intriguing (traumatic event is somewhat obvious from the very beginning and the way how the story progresses doesn't make us ask more questions about it).Audio in this game deserves separate praise and it's the main reason why it's much better to experience this game yourself and not to watch streams/letsplays. Excellent voice acting and great soundtrack are also present.Visuals are superb, with nice level design and many scenes are staged really well.All in all, The Shattering is a great narrative driven psychological thriller with engaging story, plenty of memorable scenes and unique setting. A great choice for players who enjoy this kind of games with serious topics and emotional stories. 8/10
_childDocuments_.name: The Shattering

_childDocuments_.review: The Shattering is a unique experience, but it wasn't the game I expected from the steam store page advertising, especially with respect to the horror tag. The game is essentially a first-person walking simulator where you recount the life of John Evans in a greyscale environment. Overall, I just found the game to underwhelming -- all aesthetic, no substance. Oftentimes, I couldn't find the interact-able objects in the environment needed to progress for several minutes. Likewise, the game's narrative was confusing -- several mutually exclusive possibilities are presented as to what is really going on, but, by the end of things, no definitive answers are given.
_childDocuments_.name: The Shattering

_childDocuments_.review: The Shattering is quite a game/experience and turned out to be more compelling than I expected. It is played from the first person perspective of John who is recovering from a severe injury. He is in therapy as he attempts to rebuild memories. The game starts out slowly and then pulls you in as John walks through four key segments from his life and continues to meet with a psychiatrist. Gameplay consists of exploring environments, moving freely, but controlled by doors that lock and unlock as the story progresses. There are no puzzles but there are many items to interact with. The game auto-saves frequently so your progress is never lost.Here's what I thought was so special about The Shattering:1. Artwork is black and white with splashes of accent color (blue butterflies, red wine, yellow candles, etc.). It is just beautifully done.2. Sound track is primarily environmental sounds which, when combined with the art, create a very immersive experience. I was constantly aware of how much the sound track was adding to the atmosphere of the game and playing with headphones is a must.3. Although John interacts with other people who speak to him, there are no faces or bodies shown. The developers did a masterful job of creating the illusion of characters in great detail. They also used mannequins and a teddy bear as placeholders which reflect emotional impact.4. John's mind is shattered and the game builds and destroys objects and scenes in a way that makes you feel his isolation, rage, fear, hope, and desperation.Be advised that there is a single save slot so you have to play from the beginning if you want to try for the alternate ending needed to obtain  100% of the achievements.Overall, I think this is a beautifully done game. At the end, I remain unsure of what was real and what was imagined but perhaps that is all part of the 'shattered mind' experience. I highly recommend it to those who enjoy an exploratory journey that is unique and thought provoking.
_childDocuments_.name: The Shattering

_childDocuments_.review: I want to begin by saying this game is a beautiful, vivid, and artistic abstraction from some very deep underlying morbid tones and i LOVED that about this game and story.  Written and presented with a lot of creativity.  I of course give it a recommendation for the sole reason of its uniqueness and story that had a way of drawing you through until the end.I do however have a couple critiques.  I would say that this game played itself very independently from any input options given to the player and became extremely linear because of this.  I think a title with this much story line potential could really benefit from a few varying opportunities rather than click to play straight through, giving a feel of deeper involvement and really allowing a connection to being John rather than simply watching his memories unfold.  All said and done a very smooth gameplay and riveting story that had me play straight through to finish.
_childDocuments_.name: The Shattering

_childDocuments_.review: This started out spooky  and laden with emotional gravitas, but ultimately devolved into the typical psychological thriller walking-simulator style, quasi-intellectual wank.Positives:-Graphics-  Very nice, and the stark use of colour (or lack there of) for some levels is quite well done.Meh:-Writing, Voice-Acting-  It's not the worst out there (the bar is too low in that regard....) but it meanders far too much, and despite some heavy-duty emotional scenes revolving around abusive peers, loss of family, etc. it ultimately struggles to rise above the hopelessly average.  Oh, and the main voice actors aren't exactly going to set the world on fire.  Not awful, just meh.  It's just a darned shame, because the game starts out so strongly and then just limps lamely to the finish line....-Gameplay-  Meh......it's alright......it's a walking simulator with some minor choice making, so it's not exactly breaking new ground, and with the profoundly, deeply mediocre writing/voice-acting, it starts to get bogged down in repetitive actions.Negatives:  None........but with so much else (beyond the pretty, striking visuals) being lame/nothing new/more of the same/tragically mediocre, there is just so very little to recommend it.Ultimately not recommended, except on a deep, DEEP sale.  Life is too short for games that only rarely rise above the trite and banal.
_childDocuments_.name: The Shattering

_childDocuments_.review: Clearly the team has a lot of good intentions, and there's some really good ideas and art herein. But it's just...boring. I'm sorry to say that. Rarely are games outright boring, but not bad. There's nothing wrong with The Shattering, except it's truly not compelling IMO. It's just a kind-hearted but listless walking sim with basic puzzles. I'd say don't pick it up.

_childDocuments_.review: Walking simulators are a staple of PC gaming thanks to such titles as Gone Home and Firewatch, games that emerged from the indie scene to critical and commercial success. It is a contentious label, but mostly accurate as you spend a lot of your time exploring locations and interacting with the world around you. The Shattering is another example of this genre, that aims to explore the human psyche as well as the wonderfully realised theatre-like scenes presented to you. The Shattering is the debut title from SuperSexySoftware, a small development team based in Gdynia, Poland. It is likely that the first thing you notice about the game is its striking style. The Shattering as a whole is extremely stylised, but its choice of colour palette, or lack thereof, immediately stands out. Everything is a sea of white, black and shades of grey with only the occasional object being doused with a single colour. It’s an interesting choice that at first seems arbitrary, but is later revealed as key to the overall theme.The theme itself is evident from the moment you boot up the game. We are prompted with a warning that the game contains sensitive topics related to mental well-being and health and this is further cemented as the game opens on our character in a psychiatrist’s office. This Doctor acts as our narrator and guide through the game. His notes adorn the loading screens, helping us better understand John, our player character, and his situation. Throughout the three odd hours you explore John’s world the game attempts to address isolation, loneliness, PTSD and suicidal thoughts, amongst others, with varying degrees of success; more on that later.  The Shattering ultimately takes us through different times in John’s life; beginning at childhood and going on to explore his young adult life, leading to the present. The acts are inconsistent in length which makes the game feel uneven, but each segment offers enough in its visual design to push you through its narrative. The narration is supplemented by some good environmental storytelling as gaps in the story are filled using notes within objects you interact with. A patient’s chart will give you hints as to why you are where you are and details hidden in the scenery help flesh out context for your character’s emotions, for example.Visual design is where the game really excels. Environments are well crafted and, as alluded to before, feel like sets from a stage show or play. This is further cemented as the game impressively constructs and deconstructs the scenery around you. This works very well as a representation of John’s memories brought to life; an instance of water slowly flooding into an office and a toy boat appearing, as we start to recall our childhood, stands out as a moment of great game design and visual storytelling. Another section involving your childhood home morphing into something else is another section worth mentioning, but not spoiling. All of this is rendered with the detail it deserves, but not as much can be said for the audio design. Outside of some clever use of audio, telegraphing the story, early on; there’s little to address in regards to sound effects. Voice acting is professionally done,  with performances that try to bring the characters to life, but often characters are barely explored so that this just falls flat.It is also worth mentioning that Al Bowlly’s Guilty of loving you makes an appearance, because of course it does. Guilty of confusing you is perhaps more apt though, as the aforementioned song appears to set the tone early on as a period piece. This is contradicted from the get go though,  given the dates available to you, by exploring the game’s interactive objects. The confusion over the game’s timeline is further compounded by the choice of old television shows and movies that appear on screens. Perhaps this confusion is by design, but it really just served to break the immersion created by the environment. The same can be said for the game’s location as it can seemingly jump between places with little context.The narrative journey as a whole is underwhelming. Whilst it is commendable to broach such subjects as mental health, and the game does convey some aspects of it well, a lot of the message feels shallow and spread thin. It can feel like mental health symptoms are addressed in a list like manner, but never explored and instances of loneliness, depression or trauma feel cliched. Realistically the game doesn’t offer a new or even interesting perspective on such a weighty subject. Again, it is very good to see these subjects tackled in gaming, a media form so often thought of as just guns and explosions, but it lacks a specific story to be told within it. Instead seems to rest on a safe tale of numerous competing mental health issues, that can become difficult to keep track of or interest in.  Mechanically the game is what you would expect, with the main aspects being interacting with objects and/or exploring an area to completion so you can move onto the next. There are no crouching or jumping mechanics, which feels constricting in a game based around exploring, but this isn’t a detraction from the experience particularly. An early instance of using typed sheets to help your progression was interesting but sadly not exploited elsewhere in the game. You’re sometimes given dialogue options, but these only serve to unlock an alternative ending and really have no impact on the game beyond that. The Shattering is a really well made game that excels in its art direction and its visible attention to detail, but falls short in regards to its storytelling and the themes it wishes to embrace. Sequences can feel stitched together without a natural flow, and ultimately the protagonist feels a little empty considering the game’s seemingly devoted attention. In a busy genre The Shattering  doesn’t come close to stalwarts such as Gone Home, Firewatch &  Everybody’s Gone to the Rapture but its intentions are worthy of respect and SuperSexySoftware are a developer to keep an eye on.
_childDocuments_.name: The Shattering

_childDocuments_.review: It's nice to see such a strong first release from a completely unknown Polish team! I cannot recommend it enough for people who love narrative games. Some may say that the plot is not only lacking depth, but also consists of various cliches, and there may be some truth in that, however, all of it can be cast aside by a nearly perfect execution, character development and attention to details. Soundtrack and general sound design are also one of those gems you better not miss. I'm looking forward to see what they will do next, hopefully with bigger budget/team.P.S. I can see where all those comparisons with Edith Finch are coming from, but don't make them fool you, apart from sharing a genre, those are two completely different games.
_childDocuments_.name: The Shattering

_childDocuments_.review: Ugh, what a waste of 7 hours this game turned out to be... First, it literally made me sick - I had to play in several sessions because of fits of dizziness and nausea.  Turning off "motion blur" didn't help at all, by the way.Second, the story was like a collage of cliches badly slapped together.  The only thing that was mildly original was the protagonist's hate of noise, I guess.And last, to add insult to injury, the end was disappointing, at best. I like a lot of stories with the open ending, actually, but this one wasn't one.  It felt like "oi, you think you're so smart, you guess what happened here" ending to me.
_childDocuments_.name: The Shattering

_childDocuments_.review: I do like (or even love) grayscale palette and so I like visual style here.I do like to look on references (and here we do have plenty of them, references to references, a very lot of symbols/symbolism, et cetera)It's not long and this is a plus too.But despite of that during the whole playthrough one, single question keep thumping inside my skull:"I can't understand -- why it is so boring?"
_childDocuments_.name: The Shattering

_childDocuments_.review: is a pretty decent psychological story, though it's by no means groundbreaking with its overall plot. By the time you get to the ending, you'll see that it's a bit more standard than it is when it starts off, but its visual representation is still a big positive.The artistic style is probably its strongest suit. The black and white design allows for interesting vignettes, shadow usage, and it also means colors stand out when they appear, helping to enforce certain scenes.The gameplay is relatively simple as it is a walking simulator with some puzzles. The puzzles are not that complicated, though the game does reach a few points where it's very easy to miss what you're expected to do. At one point, I spent around 10 minutes trying to figure out how to get a certain hallway to show up and it turns out there was a very tiny switch (which did not stand out) in a corner somewhere. The way I found it was by looking up a "Let's Play" and it turned out that they spent around 10 minutes wandering in circles until they found it as well. So there's definitely some problematic situations like that where you might be lucky and immediately find something to interact with, but other people won't.It's hard to talk about the story other than to say that you're delving into the main character's mind in order to see what sort of traumatic situations have led him to his current state. A therapist in the prologue leads you into this and almost the entire game is observing various timelines and emotional situations within John's brain.I'd estimate the general playtime is around 4 to 5 hours, give or take, depending upon your pacing.If this doesn't sound worth its full price, you could always wait for a sale. I think it's worth a try and it has some great production for an indie studio.
_childDocuments_.name: The Shattering

_childDocuments_.review: Sorry, but no! This was a recommendation and supposed to be a game with a deep story telling/atmosphere and an unexpected ending revealing the whole plot......well, it´s not.The story and the way it is represented is good, but anything else is boring and predictable. Half in the game you know in which direction this will end, there is no surprise and no AHA-effect at all. The gameplay is from boring to anoying.Just a big disappointment, at least it was short.

The game could really benefit from being able to replay chapters for this reason, rather than having to start a whole new game on a new save slot just for a wrong turn here or there that was impossible to predict.Also, I don't know if it was a bug or a feature meant to represent the patients state, but at one point when seeing your therapist the prompts for the answers were all over the place rather than connected to the actual words on screen.Anyway.It has it's moments though.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm only about an hour into the game, but the storyline is developing VERY nicely! You are thrown into John's world, except, he doesn't remember a thing - or has blocked out some terrible memories subconsciously (one of my personal favorite ways to start a game!). From there, you seek out to piece together his story. As things progress, it seems John's story might take us down a very, very dark path, but I'm honestly not sure what to expect moving forward (which is great!). I can't wait to find out more!So far, it has been primarily focused on developing the character, John, and the story - which is always important in my opinion. You search around and learn some things about the protagonist. But slowly, some kind of odd things begin to happen. I'm not sure how the gameplay will change moving forward, but there is definitely a progressive feeling present.Marta and her team at Super Sexy Software have done an amazing job in creating a captivating story thus far. For their first official release, this seems to be a great start. I look forward to finishing this game and seeing more in the future!If purchasing this game, my only "tip" would be to keep your head up when interacting with things. Some text displays directly in front of you which can contain important information that could otherwise be missed as it disappears. (I was too busy playing with the chalkboard and other items haha).All in all, the concept of the game is intriguing - and actually kind of reminds me a bit of the movie, Room 1408, - but only because of the fact that it starts off at a hotel (you'll see when you play). Should the story finish as amazing as it started, I'd say its definitely worth the purchase!-MegaMilez

_childDocuments_.review: I wouldn't call this game a "thriller." I found it a little bland and boring. As far as "walking simulators" go, I've seen a lot better, like Gone Home or What Remains of Edith Finch. Those are full of little clues and scraps of information that help you piece together the story. The Shattering is pretty sparse in this respect. There is hardly anything of importance in the environment. Lots of drawers you can open that either contain nothing or are full of objects you can't interact with. No real puzzles to solve. It pretty much consists of finding the next object you have to click to progress the story, which is fed to you by the main action of the story, nothing extra to discover on the side. The  big reveal at the end didn't really shock me. All in all I found this whole game to be just sort of "meh." And only between 3-5 hours long. If you find the positive reviews more convincing than mine, just be sure you get it during a Steam sale, that's all I'm saying.EDIT: Looking at an achievement guide for some of the ones I missed, it turns out there are some secrets to find. The problem was that the game had pretty much trained me in to thinking looking at everything was a waste of time by most of the things I interacted with or examined having no significance at all.

_childDocuments_.review: The Shattering.Expectations? Vastly expected. Enjoyed the motif of blue and shattering. Finding the cigs was hard. But the truth? Harder. The past? Painful. The price? Steep, like a tea bag sitting too long.To build it up just to shatter it to pieces, in an experience that becomes us all. What is love? To me. To you. It's a a truth learned, but a missing piece. A shattered piece.Did we enjoy the Shattering? Yes, with a side of no. We voted on this 3-2, and by split-decision, The Shattering's hand was raised as the victor.Super Sexy Software: I'll be back, and I hope you will be with a better showing.

_childDocuments_.review: I've noticed comments describing everything that was happening throughout the story as weird, illogical, unrealistic, and even senseless. If that's exactly how you feel about it - good for you, I guess, looks like you're mentally stable enough :)John, however, is not.Somehow, I think you kind of need to personally relate to the main character of this game to fully understand it. Dissociative disorder can be a cruel thing, and I genuinely felt sympathy for John. The storytelling is truly remarkable. It's like stepping into the mind of someone dealing with mental health issues, and the way it's depicted makes you feel like you're right there with them, experiencing every emotion. It's a unique experience, and not many games have ever evoked such strong feelings in me.A wonderful tense psychological thriller. I can't believe that this gem has been sitting in my library unplayed for so long. Incredibly immersive, beautifully written, and, well... .

_childDocuments_.review: The Shattering is a walking sim where you travel through the shattered mind and memories of a man named John Evans. With the help of a doctor, he starts piecing things together. It's more of a drama story rather than horror, but at some parts it does get kinda scary. Nothing too scary though, no chase scenes or jumpscares. The most unique thing about this game is the visual style, most of the game are in black-and-white, but there are several colored objects, usually important ones.Length-wise its not that long, but that's probably a good thing. For some reason, this game gave me nausea, which I suspect is because the lack of changeable FOV. It also feels a bit repetitive and confusing, especially during the apartment scene near the end, sometimes we don't know what to interact with next. And some story part just feels not completely told, though it might just be I was unable to read between the lines.Overall, I think The Shattering is still a kinda decent walking sim, especially considering it was made by a small team, and I quite adore the unique artstyle. If you like mystery/horror walking sims, it might be worth trying. Just don't expect a super-good, life-changing walking sim.

_childDocuments_.review: The formula of this game is probably well-known by now: artsy walking sim through visualizations of the protagonist's memories and psyche. This one, however, crafts an engaging story that captures the essence of the psychological thriller, flirts with the love story and loiters in the foyer of Lynchian surrealist horror. No monsters here, save the ones you judge to be such.Graphically the game is impressive, despite the colorless design. Don't be fooled, though. Nothing about it is lazy or accidental. The environment *is* the story - stay sharp, keep your eyes peeled, focus on the symbolic. A lot will make more sense on the second playthrough. You can't get a Game Over, but you sure can fail, by neglecting to gather the pieces to put together.All in all, it's a quality experience for a 4-hour game, especially considering the team's size. Will stay tuned for the studio's next project.
