_childDocuments_.review: As a Civilization veteran, I find many of the concepts in this game refreshing.  I'm enjoying it so much and am concerned by some of the feedback coming from the "20 hour" crowd.  So here is my War and Peace novel on the first 4X game to really suck me in since Civ6.Characters:Its just fun to have to think about your heirs and your spouses and what their attitudes are towards you.  The shock I felt my first game when my daughter assasinated me after several slights was genuine and enjoyable.  I've seen others complain about their characters constantly dying off but I find lifespans to be reasonable and flavorful.  The fact that the attributes of your family and court drive global values is also cool as it gives you a lot of focus and control on what you're doing as your characters level.  Succession planning can actually matter as having high value characters die can have significant impact.  Make sure your heirs are doing something productive, even if they're psychos!Movement/Orders:My workers aren't working because I didn't order them to!  Freaking slackers.  What an adjustment to have a cap on the amount of movement/action (orders) across all your units.  In Civ you could dominate by building a few productive cities and spam units.  Don't try that here.  Having a ♥♥♥♥ ton of warriors doesn't matter if you can only move half of them.  It feels restrictive at first but it really isn't.  It forces you to plan ahead and manage your priorities based on what is happening around you.  As your civilization grows, your legitimacy as a ruler rises and your capacity to multi-task grows as well.  Don't be a zerg.Combat:I've seen some complaints about combat and I think it could be better, but it isn't bad once you understand it.  The ability to move several units across the map quickly means isolated units can get ganged up on and if you don't have sufficient force to punish with a counter attack, you can fall behind very quickly.  This is compounded by the fact that when two melee units clash, the defending unit does relatively little damage compared to the offensive unit.  Because of this, in an offensive war, you can't just sally off attacking the first city you see because the counter-attack can crush you.  On defense, you must balance between barbarian attacks on the edges while still maintaining a sufficient central force that can deploy to a threat.  There is a definite "Battle Brothers" feel to it.  That said, I do wish promotions and generals mattered a bit more.  It definitely feels bad to have the unit you poured resources into get wiped by 3 or 4 scrub archers and a chariot.Winning:4x struggles in the late game.  This is no secret.  Knowing you're going to win but having to complete thousands of meaningless tasks over 2 to 3 hours of game play to get over the finish line can wear you down.  Every Civilization game I've ever played suffers from this.  My general approach is to focus on my win-con, use multi-queuing as much as possible, and try to avoid late game military combat.  So how does this game stack up?  Well, the late game is tedious.  There's a lot to do.  Your court size increases exponentially, worker spam is back, and the more cities you have, the more queues need to be managed.  Multi-queue and automating workers helps a lot once you're comfortably ahead.  But as others have said, waiting for your next turn on larger maps can get pretty tedious as well.  I honestly think that with some optimization and a better balanced set of win conditions, the late game could improve dramatically.  They definitely have some creative ideas in the win condition realm.  Here are my thoughts on where they stand currently:Domination Victory: If you try to do this, good luck.  Even if you manage it, you'll probably trigger another victory condition first.  If you don't, call me in 2 months when you finish.Double Points: This one is actually a bit frustrating on lower levels because it can trigger suddenly.  Basically you earn victory points throughout the game (think Settlers of Catan).  If you double the next highest civ total, the game ends... just when you were starting to have fun.  On higher levels, I doubt this win condition is all that feasible unless you have a God start or do some serious domination.Complete 10 ambitions:  These are random missions that show-up from time-to-time throughout the game.  The AI doesn't have access to this victory condition so its up to you.  There's an element of chance here because Ambitions vary wildly and they're not always compatible with what you're up to.  In addition, if you select one and don't complete it within a certain amount of time, you get a penalty.  I've won this way but its hard to plan it out.  Usually I just happen to get it finished before I reach a points victory that I probably would have gotten anyway.Victory Points: There is a victory point number assigned based on the Map you're on.  First person to get to that total wins.  If 200 years pass and no one reaches the total, highest points win (God help you if you have to go 200 turns).  Most efficient way to do this is typically power as many wonders as possible while pouring culture into your cities.  You get points for cities anyway and as their culture increases, the point values become exponential.  This favors highly expansionist play style.  I've had some fun games carving at AI borders and incorporating enough cities to get over the finish line and I definitely like this win condition as a variety of gameplay can contribute to the total.  In a weird sense, it can almost be THE victory condition as you can use numerous play styles to get to it.Final Thoughts:There are a lot of things going on in this game that are fun and enjoyable to explore.  Not everything is intuitive and it can take some work to figure things out.  But it is very rewarding and the experience is more personal because of the character element.  You also don't have those jarring moments that you have in Civ where you're just starting to enjoy having knights and now you're moving into the industrial era.  You can really relish the experience and flavor of a full game in one era.  I highly recommend it and am hopeful that new features, world events, balancing, and optimization continue coming from the developers.If you made it this far, thanks for reading!

_childDocuments_.review: I love the music in this game.  I love the "undo/ redo" option.  I like how many resources there are in the game. I even like the Orders resource in this game.But the thing that really pulls me away from loving this game is the combat system.  It might be the worst combat in any 4X/ Civ-like game I have ever played.  It actually makes Victoria 3's combat seem reasonably passable.  All they needed to do was allow players to stack units into actual armies (similar to Civ 4 or Humankind or Age of Wonders, etc). Then have characters command ARMIES instead of just single units.  That way you are spending your orders moving entire stacks of units instead of having to micromanage hordes of little units all over the damned place.  It's just... tedious... and also it doesn't make sense because the scale of everything just seems so off.  Slingers throw rocks over the Acropolis and hit people on a hill on the other side.  The Acropolis is ~350m long.  That's quite an arm on those Slingers!  Who needs Trebuchets when Slinger bois can just throw rocks several hundred metres farther!

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent historical grand strategy game. The role playing aspects are really well envisioned and integrated. The devs are supporting the game with various updates, improvements, and additional content. The attention to detail in this game is amazing. The individual characters feel unique. In my first game, Queen Dido married someone with the "Romantic" character trait and with each of the events in the first few years and options for how to respond it felt like a romantic movie playing out in the game between the two (mostly based on the decisions I made for the ruler). There were three back-to-back decisions I had to make for the queen in how she responded. There were lots of options, intentional decisions, and also guesses, but also random events that prompt you to make decisions that sometimes you do not have much control over (which made the game more realistic, to an extent). It's  fun to see how each of the characters interact with each other and you have just enough influence on the ruler's decisions that you can steer things in a certain direction but sometimes things don't turn out the way you hoped (maybe another character starts trouble, for example, you weren't expecting or you lost track of a random minor noble who starting talking with another nation's courtier that then affects your standing in their court) and sometimes they do any number of other things that affect your ruler and nation or individual characters for better or worse. It's detailed, rich content, not always predictable, though characters' opinion of your leader is a good indicator of which characters to keep an eye on and maybe have a courtier send them a gift or intercede on your ruler's behalf to put in a good word. This game is very dynamic and throws in lots of different events that can completely shift your strategy. My second and third games were very different. For one thing, I had different starting characters (I played with a different nation each of my first three games) with a different inheritance law enacted (e.g., seniority primogeniture, or absolute cognatic primogeniture, for example). But even if I didn't, there are so many different ways the games would have been different (leader character traits, for example, random at the start of each game). In one of the games, there was an event that gave me several decisions, one of which was to change the inheritance law (which I decided to do) so this changed things in that game quickly. There are a lot of other examples, but that gets the idea across that no two games are the same.The ruler, their spouse(s), heir(s), the court, appointing ministers, influencing individual characters (the rulers, house leaders, governors, generals, diplomats, chancellor, courtiers, etc., your ruler's children growing up and all the decisions that go into that, who the nobles marry, random events that affect character's traits (there are a lot!), health, wisdom, courage, and on and on the details go. It's got a lot of depth, dynamics, and complexity. The diplomacy feels really well integrated into everything; again, each character is unique and the way they interact is great to interact with in the details. I'm looking forward to seeing what additional DLC there might be from the devs for this game. They do a great job of supporting this game with updates.

_childDocuments_.review: 5/10 so-so.I took the plunge because some reviews raved about it being "better" than Civilisation and that the game was a mix of Civ with Crusader Kings.In reality, it's a fairly narrowly focused 4x game, think of Civilisation but with just the one 'era', and a handful of nations to play with. There are some unique mechanics; Cities can only be settled on pre-defined city sites for example, you also don't benefit from 'tiles' unless you build an economic action (i.e. a farm, mine) on them, and you also can't get luxury resources until you build the economic action PLUS a specialist unit on them.The mechanics make it different, a little flavour to the whole thing, but it's still at its heart a civilisation building game, with the same tricks as always - expand, exploit massively, and carry a bigger stick than your rivals.The other 'unique' spin on the game is a bit of Crusader Kings, you have to settle cities with 'families', who all bring different things to the table; A military family will make a city a military powerhouse, whilst landowners classes make ideal farming cities etc. You get to pick 3 from 4 families, and these families dictate your overall build of cities (ideally), so everytime you find nice farmland areas, out come the landowning classes, and anytime you find a nice seafaring spot, you might pick a family that offers strong naval bonuses.Thrown into this mix, are a fairly watered down family and character setting, with various events to go through ~ you marry people off, have children, educate them for when your leader dies, and so on. Keeping everyone happy is another cog in the machine, but it seldom feels unique and interesting in the grand scheme of things, for me anyway.Overall, it's a decent, average attempt at the genre. Worth the full price? Nope. Worth the sale price? Probably not, unless you get it under £20 personally, unless you're a massive Civ style fan, in which case you probably already own the damn thing.I think it's worth a try, but whether you'll stick to it, is up in the air, it just doesn't really feel that compelling to hang around in tbh.

Old World is a good balance between Economy, War and dynasty RPG.ONE GLARING PROBLEM to fix by Devs:Carthage on generated maps has way way way to small chance to start on the coast. It should be approx 90%!

_childDocuments_.review: I strongly disagree with the combat system.1. Enemy units move over your entire vision range in one turn. I've seen elephants from their capital embark go 7 tiles on boat disembark walk 4 tiles and attack. In a single round. Building fronts is just madness.2. Units that attack take no damage. This is even more absurd. What is this simulating? Game play wise this leads to insane optimal strategies. Since if you are attacked by your western neighbor you should have all you units as far from the front as possible, that you can let them enter deep into your territory and then just kill them with the counterattack taking no damage. What?This also makes combat incredibly one sided. You either just mop the floor with them or vice versa. Edit: After more time i maintain my criticism. The infinite movement is really insane. The enemy is breaking through at the center? Just teleport in 6 units to kill them. Need a unit to finish off an enemy unit? Just teleport a cavalry unit 20 tiles(for three orders over boats btw) and finish off not one but three enemies. On the opponents turn you get to watch this from the other side. Fresh spawned Units just walk from Assur to Babylon(500km in rl) in one round and attack. The effect is that you essentially just trade off units and combat devolves to a drunken bar fight in a chaos dimension. It also devalues a lot of decision making, because mistakes in unit distribution are easily mitigated by just teleporting. There is no possibility to perfectly position your units so you lose nothing in the counterattack because you will be attacked from newly produced units halfway around the world that you obviously could not know about/plan for. Yes if you are inefficient with your orders you pay in the long run. In the context of the war i never ran out of orders for my units (just for everything else at times). If you have a slight advantage you just snowball because defensive positions do not exist. (Not even a city wall(and subsequent defensive buildings)/stronghold/citadel building keeps enemies from entering your urban areas)For me the conclusion is: Tactical combat in old world feels like stepping into a insanity dimension of teleporting bronze-iron age units. If you can accept this it might be worth trying, since it is overall very innovative in every system. I will just mention one and otherwise refer to other reviews: The order mechanic makes alliances incredibly important. If you can get another civ to declare war on a common target and you have 80 orders of your alliance against 40 orders for the target they will loose even if their military would be strong enough to fight both, they just can’t order their troops to fight both. So the setup before the war, the posturing at the border can be genuinely interesting, once the war starts the dice are cast and it gets boring to me. For this reason Multiplayer might be very interesting/stressful. (Though i have not and probably will not try.)

_childDocuments_.review: Has the potential to become my personal favorite 4x **Thoughts on the gameTo me, Old World feels deeper than the Civilization Series. I definitely had to tone down the difficulty for several sessions until I understood the mechanics well enough. The AI overall seems to be pretty competent and doesn't seem to rely on cheating. There were small details that showed that the devs care about their game being polished. I enjoyed the events and the way character attributes provide benefits makes a big difference in the gameplay. It caused a bit of an ebb and flow to strength. For example, you can have a period with a very good leader and good governors where progress and production is quick. Then as that group ages and dies the new leaders aren't as good potentially causing things to worsen. Of course, it is possible that you have a terrible leader, and they die giving way to a much better one. ***Negatives:Couple of crashes/slow downs if I ran the game for a long time. Not too big of an issue for me personally. Small cast of countries; however, they are *very* well balanced.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is excellent! If you've read the reviews out there you might expect it to be clunky or feel like two games crammed together, but it is not - instead you get interesting gameplay with a lot of what I like from other games, sure, but with just the stuff i like from other games. I'd give it a 9.5/10, with the only knock being repeated images for followers and events. My recommend of the year, easy.
_childDocuments_.name: Old World

_childDocuments_.review: Old World is a complex, interdependent game. Everything is related to everything else. The systems all interlock with each other in a deep, satisfying way. The game design is pretty damn incredible in the way that everything works together.That said, because of everything being interrelated, it's going to take some time to learn the game. It is most assuredly not just another version of Civilization. It is its own thing that needs learning on its own terms. Characters in particular add a whole new dimension to the 4x experience that is refreshing, fun, and makes for some epic stories.I still remember some moments from games I've played now months ago -- For example, when I ventured out with some chariots to attack a tribal camp and got surprised by my opponent ambushing with me with a horde of Camel Archers that blocked off my path to retreat. Or when I had my Schemer leader abdicate so his Hero heir could assume the throne and then immediately launch a surprise Launch Offensive against my opponent to beat back their onslaught. Or when I was playing an FFA and, through creative diplomacy, managed to convince a distant Rome to march to my assistance against an aggressive Assyria ... and then 50 turns later, managed to win the game without ever breaking peace with Rome.The developer team has been incredibly responsive to feedback through the early access and post-Epic release period, and I'd expect that same high level of responsiveness to continue now that the game is on Steam. The team clearly loves this game and are dedicated to making it an epic game that will stand the test of time, if you will ;)I've played hundreds of hours of Old World, primarily in multiplayer play-by-cloud games against other human opponents (using the Epic client, before the Steam release).
_childDocuments_.name: Old World

_childDocuments_.review: I thought I'd like this game being as it is Civilization in the classical era. I don't. I don't enjoy this game at all. It's how the units and cities are managed and controlled. The tutorials do a terrible job explaining what their attributes mean and how they are used. The influence and use of characters is terrible. Again, not explained well in the tutorial. This makes the game mechanics more complex. Almost like the designers had to do this so it wouldn't be a Civilization copy. Anyhow, I don't like the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Old World

_childDocuments_.review: Three reasons why this game is amazing:1. Innovation. Old World has a multitude of design decisions which don't follow established conventions of 4X genre. It is also clear that these design decisions weren't just made for the sake of innovation, but following lead designer's overall vision of how to make a 4X game which plays very differently from Civ franchise. You may disagree with certain decisions (and it's clear from browsing the reviews that there are people who do disagree), but they make sense, and are part of what makes the game such a step forward for the genre2. AI. This is the first 4X game I experienced where AI is competent in controlling it units. Of course a human player can still outsmart AI, but it does present a challenge, and a war against AI will never be a walkover. For the first time since Civ5 adopted the 1-unit-per-tile system, we have a game where AI can properly utilise it, and solving tactical puzzles presented by Old World warfare is one of the most satisfying parts of the game3. Multiplayer. Recent Civ titles clearly focusing on single player experience and including abilities which are fun to use in SP but completely break MP. Old World is designed with multiplayer as a cornerstone. In addition to the common online MP, there's play-by-cloud mode, where the save is passed between players by uploading it to the cloud, similarly to how it would be passed by email back in the day. It's a great option for those who like to take their time thinking about a turn, and can't commit several hours to play out an online game
_childDocuments_.name: Old World

_childDocuments_.review: Conquer the Old World in this historical, epic strategy game from Soren Johnson, Lead Designer of Civilization IV and Offworld Trading Company. Every year is a turn, and each leader is a mere mortal, so your lasting legacy will be the dynasty you leave behind.

name: BIOMUTANT
detailed_description: BIOMUTANT® is an open-world, post-apocalyptic Kung-Fu fable RPG, with a unique martial arts styled combat system allowing you to mix melee, shooting and mutant ability action. A plague is ruining the land and the Tree-of-Life is bleeding death from its roots. The Tribes stand divided. Explore a world in turmoil and define its fate – will you be its saviour or lead it to an even darker destiny? Key Features: A NEW TAKE ON 3rd PERSON COMBAT The martial arts style combat system allows you maximum freedom of movement and agility while mixing shooting, melee and powers from your mutations. Learning new Wung-Fu combat forms through progression and learning from masters you’ll meet, will constantly add to your choices and make sure combat never gets old. EVOLVE YOUR GAME-PLAY You’ll be able to re-code your genetic structure to change the way you look and play. This will of course affect your attributes and in addition to this, exposure to bio-contamination in the world will lead to mutations like the Turtleform and Mucus Bubble, while exposure to radioactivity found in bunkers from the old world will affect your mind and unlock psi-mutations like telekinesis, levitation and more. NEXT LEVEL OF CRAFTING You are totally free when crafting weapons. Mix and match parts to create your own unique 1H or 2H slash and crush weapons. Revolvers, rifles and shotguns and add modifications like cork-screws and battery-powered chainsaw modules to bio-contaminated sludge vials adding to your combat arsenal. There are even characters you’ll meet that’ll craft cool stuff for you, like bionic wings, a jump-pack and even let you modify your Automaton - the scrap-toy sidekick! GEAR UP FOR ADVENTURE You are totally free when equipping your character. Not only when it comes to choosing weapons you created, but what type of gear you wear. Equip a gas-mask and an oxygen tank for exploring the Dead Zones, thermos-resistant clothes for venturing into cryonic areas or protective gear for taking on bio-contaminated creatures, the choice is up to you. SURVIVE IN A VIBRANT OPEN WORLD You are free to explore the world and what lies beneath its surface, by foot, mech, jet-ski, air-balloon or area unique mounts. Explore the dying wildland, the tunnels and bunker networks of the underworld, and find your way up the mountains or out in the archipelago. There are lots of discoveries to be made, mysteries to unravel, creatures to confront and weird characters to meet in this vibrant and colorful world. AN UNUSUAL STORY WITH AN UNUSUAL END Your actions play a major part in the unfolding of a story where End is coming to the New World. A plague is ruining the land and the Tree-of-Life is bleeding death from its roots. The Tribes stand divided, in need of someone strong enough to unite them or bring them all down... You are guided through the world by a Storyteller that narrates every step of your journey, but it’s your actions and choices that’ll decide how your story of survival ends.

_childDocuments_.review: I have to admit, I like this game for a few dumb reasons.  I think the creature is cute (a big-eyed, big-eared, blue fuzzy ... trash pandamouse).  The exploration is awesome--always some new, odd add-on for your huge sword or ugly shirt.  I love crafting, especially weapons, as you get to build them from the ground up.  The world is a wonderful to look at, and I like catching animals that sound like raccoons. Apparently you OK, the NPCs need work.  They're stiff little buggers, and you never, ever get to hear directly from them.  The narrator really needs to go.  His little quips and comments get old about ten minutes in.  I have him as turned off as he can be, and he's still a chatterbox.  The fighting is ... well, I'm terrible at it to begin with, so I'm not the person to ask.    It does feel a bit clunky though, even for me.  The stories are cardboard cutouts of one another, flat and just like the last fetch quest.  Only good thing about this is that it eliminates escort quests (sort of).  It needs a lot of help, but it's fun.

_childDocuments_.review: I never kept up on BIOMUTANT but when it got released i thought it would be something fun and new to try, I thought the game started out decent, Went with the commando class beat the tutorial, and sided with the Samurai Meerkats, and started to notice problems. Not Game Breaking problems, just a few little things and a major issue, So: I noticed the game is missing quite Alot of Polish, Almost every weapon that isnt based on or with Psi powers, Mutation powers or Most Combo moves is significantly weak and yet i beat the first major boss, First Major Faction and got to the Mech with just the first and second gun from the start. The dialogue and story is straight up pushy and repetitive; with the plot centered around corporate greed ruined the earth and how much of a good person you still are, with optional dialogue that makes you feel like the conversation only goes one way half of the time, There is also this unshaken feeling that alot of mechanics and events and things were supposed to be in the game but never were, such as the sieges as they feel small and copy pasted, There is a bit more aside from the games LARGEST issue that it is Boring.I will end off my review by saying i went with medium and it felt a bit easy, I have the strong hunch that Hard mode is nothing more than raising Enemy health bars into bullet sponges and Raises Damage to be 2-4 shotting. _childDocuments_.review: This is for Patch 1.5.1 --I finally learned how to use Super-fu which is over powered as you get use to it. There are hidden benefits that exist in ultimate armor sets. Not sure if all of them have these benefits but some do. Some ultimate weapons also have subtle benefits not mentioned as you wear the gear.Critics are correct in technical aspects the game can be improved on small bits and pieces and for the price you would want a AAA game. This needs patches.The developers at Experiment 101 seem to be listening to the game-players and fixed the sound issues, some of the combat aspects, and a few broken quests/items and crafting effects in the game. If they keep this up it truly is a masterpiece but we are likely years away from this.After playing this game quite a while (60+ hours and beaten the game) - I am changing my review to a "not recommend" because the game is getting to where it needs to be and developers are fixing things but are not yet there.It is a 30-40 dollar game but priced at 60 dollars. This is unfortunate. So wait for a sale. They have patched the gear so resistances are correct. They have fixed some items as they were absolutely over powered.There is no trans-mogging which is unfortunate. You often look like a furry covered in various bits of plastic and have metal sticking out like some deranged porcupine that fell into a vat of tar and rolled around in a garbage heap.This matters little as the difficulty level is low in this game. Extreme doesn't make the game harder (hardest setting) it just makes monsters more of a bullet sponge. I've given up the best gear though and gone for a fashion fur look as difficulty is low:Min-maxing strat suggests you focus points in vitality/strength. Charisma is effectively worthless as money is basically worthless at 150 you cap at 75% reduction in price and it does nothing in the way of persuading, Agility is effectively worthless I do not feel faster, and intellect is effectively worthless and often bugged. Intelligence should give you more options in the puzzles (which are very easy) but you often only have 10 choices (the base) no matter what. You don't need to dump a ton into luck just a few points as gear can give you a lot of crit% and other item modifications can give you loot% modifiers. The loot% tables appear to be messed up where you end up getting sawblades for days if you go to heavy in Luck.You don't need too many abilities (nor can you hot key that many) and once you get a few easily acquired ultimate items you can breeze through the game regardless of the difficulty setting. The game itself only takes 3-4 hours to beat so it is very quick.The KlonkFist which is a glove you get early on to break walls need to be a different key than equip-ing as it makes you have to un-equip and re-equip other gear. It is a UI problem that should be fixed. This should be put on a different hot key to select rather than equipping. It has such a niche use it almost seems wasteful on the design side in how it ended up being implemented in the game.Choices do not matter in regard to light and dark. There is only light or dark endings which only seem to matter in picking people for the Arc which also doesn't matter.The combat AI is fairly stale after 10 fights you will know all mobs and how they act. They've patched the controls to a degree. There is a bit of auto-aim now which is good. You can now riposte via canceling your attacking hitting parry button. This is a huge improvement upon the melee concept. The combat against the World Eaters is still bugged as all get out with auto-aim.Most quests are fetch quests - in fact almost all quests are fetch quests. This is unfortunate.There are several locations that hard-blocked by starting quests so unless you reached some other location first or talked to some NPC first you won't be able to go into such-and-such location. This is confusing as you think it is a bug but it is a hard wall and a needless one. There is no narration on this telling you to stop trying to figure out why it is a bug (despite how talkative the narrator normally is) he doesn't actually participate in your game. He just randomly says things. This is not good.Boss fights are often a let down. They're confusing initially, buggy, and generally identical in three phases. You aren't playing your character during these fights though as you would normally for 99% of the game. You're on some mount you acquire for about 1%-2% of total game play and you struggle in the boss fight because you are trying to figure out a pattern, explicit steps, and the mount itself the entire time. This isn't good. For almost all World Boss fights you just need a long range gun with good accuracy and a somewhat fast fire rate. The bosses have 'wave' like attacks that don't allow you to get close.It is okay to do mounted stuff for a little while but intense boss battles is often not the goal.Especially not if you get the mount for literally just that boss fight and never use the mount at any other time. Mounts are the way to travel to get to fast-travel points. I wish these were more clearly marked on the map via a mini-map while going through zones.During Boss fights 90% of the time you are just running around in a circle while shooting at a boss with extremely poor aiming function that fights you all the way through the fight i.e. it constantly targets the boss's face when you're aiming for legs. The one time you get an auto aim it tries to derail your ability to fight. It is weird and poorly implemented.After doing endlessly quests, albeit they encourage you to explore, and the world is very pretty; however, it feels poorly done. The main story is extremely confusing and poorly performed throughout the game. Even if you had no context throughout the game you'd be as confused as if you read the whole set of narration/verbiage from NPCs in storyboard format.Tribes make no sense. Your choices within the game have no real impact on the tribe and the tribe doesn't care what you do even if it is completely counter to what you're doing choosing. This needs a serious fix and the story needs to be re-considered.Items that should be at the start of the game such as the heli-pack are at the very last zone you'd normally go to. Ark decisions such as who gets to go are forced on you right away just as making a 'tribe choice is' and this is a poor implementation of something you'd find in Skyrim but you have no choice here. You must choose. They also are meaningless.Tribe warfare is often identical set ups so you're just repeating the same thing over and over again. This is unfortunate as there isn't a lot of repeat needed here so making it unique shouldn't be that hard.Inside areas are drab and poorly done. Outside areas are beautiful. Effects are often grainy and look bad.Guns are over powered initially because they don't scale. Ultimate weapons are very easy to come by very early on which is not good game design.Audio issues are boundless. Music is mostly not there.They need to add a mini-map with a 'loot radar' in this game because finding the loots to clear an area is sometimes near impossible as the areas are so expansive. I gave up after a while because loot is so common as well and nothing really matters once you get a few ultimate items and relics. This is not good in a game like this. Put a radar in.They have fixed the quick select D-pad that is stays up until you cancel it. This is a huge improvement and actually allows you to heal during fights and select your weapons you want to equip.Regardless...This game is okay.It is reminiscent of fallout New Vegas.I did make a Let's Play of this game. It is complete as well.

_childDocuments_.review: Played difficulty Hard.Class Deadeye.27 hours.Bought for 30€ at a steam sale.TLDR: Cool concept bad execution. Wasted potential.I was very excite for this game, however, it was a bit of a letdown.While it has a cool artstyle and alot of cute mosters (like fuzzy crocodiles wearing pyjamas) its open world was kinda boring. Most quests where simply "Fetch me this" or "Go to place X". The Worldeaters (Big Monsters, that need a beating) where fun.However, it became stale pretty quickly. the are a few weapon styles in this game, that all have the same basic combo inputs, so dual wielding two weapons plays exactly the same as using a two handed one. The only difference is, that it is faster and does less damage. Same goes for the firearms.There are "Magic" abilities, called psionic and mutation. There is only about 10 and you cant level them up. They are bound to the karma systhem, wich lockes some if you are not bad enought or good enought.The crafting is pretty boring. It is about ten or twelve parts, that yo will find over and over again, but with different stats. There are special weapons in the game, that do much more damage, wich makes the crafting kinda useless. I stumbled upon the best two handed slash weapon early in the game and therefore did not need to use it at all.Firearms are kinda unbalanced. I once crafted a machine gun, that did so much dps, that did not even concider using anything else, since I never found anything, that had stats, that where even close.The main story has two branches. Killing the Worldeaters and ending a tribe war.The World eaters where fun creative fights, that all had a similar base designe, but had their own little twist, to how you fight them.The tribe war was abyssmal. It is raiding the same copy and paste camps over and over again. There is about 24 of them. I didnt even bother to complete that questline, since it is so boring.However, to get the ending cutcene and to know how it all ends you need to complete the tripe war.Playing on hard did not make it hard at all. I died about 3 times in fights and about 10 times over all, because I was stupid and jumped into toxic goo.To summon it up I would say, that the idea and creativity would have been cool, if it was not put in a boring repetetive open world. If it was a game, where you had smaller levels, that unlock stuff after avery couple levels it would be much more fun. I do not recommend it, however I keep an eye open, in case, that the devs make a similar game, that is better, since their concept was pretty nice.

_childDocuments_.review: Wanting to like it is about all that keeps me playing this fairly stock-standard RPG. Yet another example of why the words "open world" should instill dread in those that hear them. Biomutant does very little to set itself apart with its color by numbers story, blank open world, and combat that lacks any sense of impact or weight. Multiple story beats right from the get-go that lack any sense of timing, cinematic vision, or even tonal congruity with the rest of the game. While I've yet to run into any debilitating bugs, there is a distinct lack of polish about the game from the way rain falls through enclosed spaces to the way the protagonist slides up ladders and chains hang idle at 90° angles. Every npc interaction is belabored by having to be narrated as well as spoken in an intention to give a storybook feel but that instead comes off as immersion breaking and annoying. Manage your expectations for the character creation as well: I have never seen a circular slider be used to pick something as specific as a pattern before but the character transformations that result from these vague —at best— changes are almost as unpredictable as they are ugly. It must be said that there is an element of fun to be had in one's first few hours exploring the map and making choices along a binary moral choice meter, but how long after play will the "newness" of the world wear off before each scaling enemy encounter, identical grassy hill, and miniboss fight just become boring?

Difficultly setting is Medium. Only time I fire guns is to trigger melee combos.At [3 hours]_________________The game is shaping up to be really good. The weapons, abilities, perks, psionics, etc can be stringed together for some seriously complex gameplay opportunities.In combat, you are only limited by your own imagination(and also whatever you have unlocked so far).If you like Death Stranding, you will probably also like this game considering the world feels just as post apocalyptic and barren with enemies and terrain hazards sprinkled all around.7.5/10 at this time.At [10 hours]_________________This game is giving me serious Witcher 3 vibes, something I totally wasnt expecting. Different monsters in different parts of the map, some similar ones, and a lot more unique ones.  Each having a different combat loop and attack patterns. I get side tracked every other minute while discovering a village(ruins rather), area in the distance, landmark, enemy random quests, all while I originally went out to do something altogether different. I try doing something random, which ends up giving me another quest, while leads to another rabbit hole of activities and bossfights I wasnt expecting and at the end of it all lies a legendary weapon/gear of some kind. _childDocuments_.review: Biomutant : By Triple FIn a world where open-world games often tread familiar paths, "Biomutant" emerges as a breath of fresh air, a colorful tapestry woven with creativity, charm, and adventure. Experiment 101's ambitious debut is an ode to the unconventional, a captivating journey that marries vibrant visuals, a unique combat system, and a plethora of choices that mold the fate of a post-apocalyptic world.Set in a post-apocalyptic universe where mutated animals roam and nature reclaims civilization's ruins, "Biomutant's" standout feature is its unabashed originality. The landscape feels like a painting in motion, a seamless blend of mutated flora, diverse biomes, and stunning day-night cycles that breathe life into the environment. This picturesque world begs to be explored, rewarding intrepid wanderers with hidden stories and awe-inspiring vistas around every corner.Beneath the surface, "Biomutant's" combat system proves to be a double-edged sword. At first glance, the kung-fu-inspired martial arts mixed with firearm skirmishes offer a refreshing take on action game-play. The ability to customize your character's genetic code, leading to mutations that grant both combat and traversal powers, is an exhilarating touch. However, the controls occasionally falter, and the camera angles can become unwieldy, momentarily disrupting the fluidity the game strives to achieve.A symphony of narrator-led storytelling adds a layer of distinctiveness to "Biomutant". The narrator, with a voice that feels like a fireside bard recounting a fantastical epic, guides players through the tale, often interjecting with cheeky remarks and insightful commentary. This storytelling approach is a double-edged sword, as it amplifies the immersion but occasionally clashes with the desire for player agency in shaping the narrative.The true essence of "Biomutant" lies in its moral choices and their palpable consequences. From aligning with various tribes to deciding the fate of rivaling characters, the game presents a web of ethical dilemmas that force players to evaluate the consequences of their actions. Each choice, big or small, becomes a brushstroke on the canvas of the protagonist's journey, leading to multiple endings that beckon replay-ability.Yet, "Biomutant's" beauty is not without blemishes. Some may find the game's pacing a tad inconsistent, with certain segments feeling like a sprint while others a leisurely stroll. Quests, though abundant, occasionally succumb to repetitiveness, dampening the otherwise engrossing experience.In the grand tapestry of gaming, "Biomutant" stands as a testament to the importance of innovation and risk-taking. Its world is a living, breathing work of art, its combat system an amalgamation of styles both fresh and flawed, and its narrative a choose-your-own-adventure with immense consequence. While not devoid of imperfections, Biomutant paints an unforgettable odyssey that rewards those who dare to venture into its vibrant universe.So, is "Biomutant" worth the journey? Absolutely. It might not be flawless, but it's a testament to the magic that can emerge when developers dare to break the mold. With its rich lore, stunning visuals, and a willingness to embrace the unconventional, Biomutant stands tall as an amazing and original gaming experience that deserves a spot in the libraries of adventurers seeking something truly different.

_childDocuments_.review: Biomutant doesn't feel worth the $60 price tag; its content feels shallow and the entire time you're doing quest-related things, you feel like you're being hand held.Wait for the devs to fix the base-line issues with the game before buying it.I played this game for a lot longer than I probably should have. Even after the two-hour long tutorial sequence, I kept playing on, only realizing the longer I played that even after the extra time they took to work on it.. this game just..  feel complete. I've listed the things about it that bother me the most below.The tutorial lasts for two hours, and you're not allowed to go off-rails until you see the first boss in a light cutscene. The  boss, meaning this is the first big bad you'll be fighting in the order of big bads  you opt to take the "good" alignment choice.I beat the first main boss, and it automatically put me on a quest to beat a particular OTHER one. I figured I'd have more agency in its open world to do the bosses in an order of exploration rather than sequence. Even when you're out in the open world, you never shake the feeling that you're out of the tutorial.Once you set your character's appearance, I'm unsure that you can ever change it throughout your playthrough.. even after the time I've spent in it, I've seen no mention of fixing issues I have with my character now that he's moving. It doesn't help that you can't customize your armor aside from stat-increases.. I ended up using less armor on my character because I didn't like the way I looked.The factions are also limited to good and evil, it's not even a gray area or a yin/yang sort of deal, it's just,  versus,  There are no other factions and there are no gray areas. You are good or evil if you choose.The same deal goes for the alignment system.. which feels forced in how it presents itself and only truly has a purpose in the four skills you gain access to if you're good/evil enough. That's four total. Two in each alignment.That said, the skills you can unlock OUTSIDE of the alignment system are limited too. only having 8 mutations and 9 psi powers to unlock. Both types of powers are unlockable through different means, and serve to enhance combat and/or mobility. Those Psi powers include the four (total) alignment-specific skills.. meaning that for the duration of the game, you have access to a whopping 15 total abilities you can use. At 13 hours played, I got through the tutorial, explored an area a bit, and fought a boss. There are four bosses and eight explorable biomes. You'd have to use a combination of 15 abilities for a LONG time.The dialogue drags on due to the little assistant translating every gibberish interaction you have.. wherein you have to wait for it to say what you're trying to read to understand what the person you're talking to is saying.. and there's no option to disable or even turn it down.. it legitimately slows the pace of the game to a crawl if you don't spam through the dialogue.____________________________Biomutant has disappointed on every level except for its graphics and weapon customization.. it's  and you can do some  neat stuff with your guns, but almost everything it offers doesn't have enough depth to sell as a full-priced game.And that's the unfortunate thing about this, because they clearly put a ton of time and effort into making this game what it is.. Until its systems are fleshed out further and the tutorial and dialogue system are overhauled, I'd say anything over $40 is asking for too much.

_childDocuments_.review: I have been gaming for a real long time now and open world rpg is especially my favorite. I am constantly looking for new games in that category to play. But I have grown annoyed over last past few years as the triple A titles starts to become more or less the same boring games made with the same boring recipe: A open world filled with a billion side quest, interest point, treasure, and pointless items to collect. Any interesting loot/skills are locked behind tens and hundreds of gameplay. I shouldn't have to complete the game to obtain a legendary weapon, because at that point I am already done with the game.Here is what Biomutant really excel at. It borrows most of these recipes, but it put a spin on it and kept the distraction at a minimum. In a way, where it felt, doing less is more. The vast open world is a lot more enjoyable to travel and explore when I am not constantly opening my map to check for interest point. Side quests are placed along the way on travel, without needing to go far to hunt them down. The side quests are also kept a minimum, like 2-3 per village I visit. Something to do in-between main mission without the feeling of getting bombarded with task. Like honestly, I really don't need every village to have 14 side quest and 12 wanted side boss kills to feel like the game has content. The quests while not innovative gets the job done. I don't need a 50 page lore to be attached to every quest and I certainly don't need a journal filled with character background info cause I aren't reading that ♥♥♥♥. Sometime there is a Zen to just sit down and burn down a village or punch a raccoon I just saved from the cage.The weapon system and combat is a huge compliant from most of the big reviews, but honestly I don't have a problem with it. Sure there are some balancing issue when it comes to melee, but anyone with an eye can tell the game is made with the intention to be played with a mix of melee, gun, and magic. The mix Kung-fu style along with the comic book text really brings a unique funkyness to the game like no others. The compliant against combat saying you can't go melee/magic only or enemies are too easy are clearly from people walking into the game with selfish intention without consideration of what game is trying to offer. If you want combat focus gameplay with hard enemies, you can go suck at dark souls.Lastly, to touch on NPC and narrations. I went into the game honestly expecting to hate the constant narrations and boy was I wrong. The narration acts more than translation, but as a background storytelling elements. Packed with lores, humors, and snarky judgements on your behaviors. It is like playing a open world rpg with a dungeon master from DnD, which is something I have only really seen in game like Divinity before. This is really refreshing and takes away any need for staring at my journals for 2 hours to figure out why the world has gone to ♥♥♥♥. NPC wise, most of them are fair generic but a few character really stands out. The Elvis Impersonator dude in the 1st memory is an absolute riot and probably one of my favorite.The moral of the story here is don't always trust the reviews because I have played tons of games with great review that made me bored out of my mind within the first 3 hours. Biomutant is definitely not everyone's cup of tea but this has been one of the most engaging game I played in recent years. Sometimes doing less is more, that is ultimately where I felt the game exceed at.If you are interested to watch my first impression of the game and first 4 hours of the game, here is a link to my VoD: Thanks for coming to my TED talk on Biomutant!

_childDocuments_.review: In BIOMUTANT, the combat, graphics, and world are all very compelling. The story and the characters, however, are not compelling at all. In most action games, that's fine, I don't really care. I just keep actioning. But Experiment 101 seems to think that they have written War in Peace, because they want to constantly inundate you with their story and characters, instead of letting you enjoy the combat, crafting, and world design.It's kinda like my 11 year old daughter. She never stops talking. We try to encourage her to only talk when she has something worth saying. But, to no avail. That's BIOMUTANT. It's that 11 year old girl who will talk for hours without really saying anything meaningful. Luckily, if you manage to get past the first 2 hours or so, you'll be let loose to explore and fight and craft, and that's when I started having a lot of fun. At 8 hours in, the story becomes a small part of the experience, and the rest of the game shines.I also GREATLY appreciate playing a game that is almost bug free, looks fantastic and runs like a dream on DAY ONE. That pretty much never happens. While I'm giving this a thumbs up, I would ultimately recommend waiting for a sale and a few patches because I think the game could go from enjoyable to must play with a few teaks concerning narration, difficulty, pacing, and quality of life.

_childDocuments_.review: I've had Biomutant since launch - 25/5/21. I have only just got to it on my backlog of games. I had a bad PC back then so I could hardly run it. I can remember the hype behind it. "OMG, It's and open world fighting game with a martial arts combat system and cool furry creatures!". It looked amazing! But, what we got was an absolute disappointment. Below I will explain why and I'll also give my opinion too! So, let's get to it but first a small disclaimer.  ⚫The "narrator" is clearly a robot. Not only is he DULL and BORING, he just drags everything out and ruins the entire experience. If you removed the Narrator, the game would be a bit better.⚫BIOMUTANT offers you "morality" choices. In reality, you just save or kill everyone. To me, this was very misleading as consequences did not really matter.⚫Loot in this game is in abundance. 90% of the time you will be looting just garbage over and over again with no actual reward.⚫All the puzzles are copy-pasted "mach the colours" and they feel like they are made in 2007.⚫No boss or enemy in the game offered me a challenge which was really disappointing. ⚫The start of the game is so stupidly slow. It takes about 2-3 hours before you can freely explore.⚫It throws about 20 different game mechanics at you within the first 2-3 hours for you to remember rather than teaching you as time goes on.⚫This will be in PROS too - The combat was initially fun at the start of the game but as time went on, it got so stale, boring and repetitive.⚫All the voice acting is done via the narrator. He ruins the immersion and the "creatures" the developers made for this world as they felt FAKE due to this reason. Budget reasons probably. ⚫The character "Creation/picker" is pretty cool. I can make my OWN "BIOMUTANT" look and feel unique to how I tailor It.⚫The world is filled with truly fantastic character designs and many different types of enemies, rival creatures and mutants to battle.⚫The Open-World was gorgeous. Very vibrant and "alive" despite the games setting.⚫The game supports an impressive range of weaponry, skills, abilities that YOU can choose to use/learn to help fight the many dangers in the world. I quote "No 2 friends will have the EXACT same play-style" and it really shows with BIOMUTANT.⚫Another thing about the Open-World was that I felt FREE to explore how I wanted. Go where I wanted to go. It felt fun to just explore, at least for the first half of the game.⚫This will be in CONS too - The combat was initially fun at the start of the game but as time went on, it got so stale, boring and repetitive. If they toned down the narrator, or gave us the option to just TURN HIM OFF COMPLETELY, maybe the game would not be so.... tedious. I mean, the narrators cheap interjections about your character fighting just made me want to mute the entire game... after all... it's basically hamster VS hamster, right? We get the point narrator, just stop talking.If they also made the mechanics more spread out rather than forced upon the player within the first opening hours of the game it would not have been so repetitive, would it? Like, if you learned WUNG-FU after you cleared your first MAJOR boss or you earned your first "powerful" weapon from a morality choice, different being on good or bad. All in all, the fantastic enemy design, gorgeous open-world and being spoiled of choice on how to "build" your character is ruined/spoiled by a NPC like annoying Narrator, who sounds like a cheap David Attenborough,  boring puzzles which are YEARS behind compared to other open-world games and the early repetition on quests leaves a sour taste in your mouth.It's not a bad game, nor is it good. It is VERY, VERY selective. Niche almost. You will either like it or not. Personally... I hated almost every minute of the narrator and every minute of "late game" combat  because of EARLY game.I would not recommend Biomutant full price. You might have more mental stamina than me to be able to put up with the Narrator but honestly, the game is not worth it full price anyway. Grab it on a HEAVY discount.

_childDocuments_.review: is a third-person Action RPG set in a post-apocalyptic future Earth, where mankind has gone extinct due to a massive ecological catastrophe. Sentient life however continues to exist, thanks to a new species of mutated animals that now populates the land. As one of them, the protagonist has to choose his own path across the world, destined to change the balance of things forever.Visually, this game is extraordinary, and not only because of the cutting-edge technologies used. The art direction itself manages to depict an original post-apocalyptic setting that is colorful and vibrant, instead of faded-out and depressing. Rich in detail and nuances for the attentive observer, the vast world is consistent in design and offers solid location variety.Disassembling, reinforcing and mix-matching gear parts is fun and interesting throughout the game. The overall not-so-great diversity of arms types is compensated decently by the possible combinations, which eventually enable creating the perfect weapon roster for any playstyle.Each starting class has several unique passive perks that can define a build. Some of them are more tank-oriented, others best suited for raw DPS. The combination of attributes, passive perks and gear opens up to a good number of play-styles, such as fragile but powerful Psi "mages", agile sharpshooters or durable melee fighters.The overly-used "bad guy killed my family so now I become a warrior" trope is used yet again, to lead a forgettable story that desperately wants to emphasize player choice without succeeding, with a contour of anonymous, bland characters as  cast. The choice of ALWAYS using the same third-person narrator for everything, demolishes any flair characters may have had.Initially, questing and exploring while battling various abominations and fellow (bio)mutants is interesting enough - after some hours however bosses, dungeons, puzzles and quest types start to be always the same, just re-skinned or outright copy-pasted. A wonderful world... filled with utterly repetitive, boring tasks over and over again.The lack of proper enemy-lock on, in favor of a weird "auto-lock" system that in many cases ends up making players attack the wrong enemy, is very frustrating. Unlimited ammo paired with plentiful stamina, mean ANY fight can be won by spamming ranged weapons while dodging in a circle - YES, really! Hitboxes and collisions are floaty, while the general feel of "eurojank" permeates most fights.At around 20 hours in, top-tier gear, weapons and equipment will generally be acquired. Unfortunately, the entirety of the world takes quite a lot more than that to be cleared. This translates into players already having unlocked most abilities and the best gear relatively early, having nothing to look forward to anymore in terms of progression - still huge amounts of filler and quests to clear.Except for the main quest itself, most side-missions have very little to no choice at all in most cases. For example, an evil character cannot choose to kill a secondary character to steal something he needs from him - he will still have to do a "helping quest" just in the same way as if he actually offered to help. On top of that, there can be major inconsistencies between the lore and what actually happens in some situations.Is performed on foot, on mounts when available and also by using several vehicles in specific biomes (such as a jet-ski to traverse watery areas). Fast-travel is available between discovered and "tagged" banners outside of combat, although not while in enclosed spaces. The world is vast, and has many optional areas, secret loot containers and places to discover. Attentively scouting every ruin in search of containers is recommended, to acquire vital consumables and better loot.Plays out in a fast-paced manner, either in melee or using ranged abilities such as various gun types, psi skills or organic mutations, which all need "Ki Energy" (Stamina) to be activated. Melee on the other hand, doesn't consume stamina whatsoever. Depending on character attributes such as strength, intelligence and so on, the damage dealt with a specific offensive means can greatly improve - passive class-specific perks can also greatly help with this, in turn "forcing" specific classes to a certain combat style. Perfect dodges, parries and combos are all present, however none of these mechanics has ulterior depth onto itself, with simplistic combinations and underwhelming risk-reward on most counters. Status effects can be inflicted with elemental weapons or abilities, however their effects are barely noticeable, while the weakness / resistance systems are just an afterthought, never really used in any meaningful way.Is done in a standard inventory menu where one can choose the protagonist's gear loadout. Equipment has a color-coded rarity system, where found loot quality is mainly influenced by the luck statistic, fundamental to get good gear. The mutations panel allows spending three different "currencies" to unlock Wung-Fu combos, mutation-related abilities and perks, other than increase passive elemental resistances. Leveling up and finding specific containers awards such point types. Each level awards 1 (+10) attribute point to spend in one of the six main statistic, and a passive perk point.Is performed in a dedicated menu that allows dismantling, scrapping and creating new weapons. Any melee or ranged arm can be upgraded or changed in type to best suit one's current build and style. The same can't be done with armor, which only can be upgraded with "Addons" but never created from scratch. Eventually the "meta" is taking the best pieces from all the greatest weapons one has, to create the ultimate tool of destruction.

_childDocuments_.review: Treat this review as a maybe rather than a yes or no because I and many others based on the reviews have mixed feelings on Biomutant overall.I'll go over the pros first:The game looks and plays pretty good. Combat is fluid (although I can't speak for the psi powers since I am more of a pew pew and slice kinda player) and feels balanced if not a bit easy.The crafting system lets you make some really nice weapons! Assuming you have the parts... and aren't like me and refuse to make a weapon with good stats because it looks like a rugby bat.The story is ok. Just ok but at least it's there, although predictable (believe me it could've been worse), especially since the game makes you choose your side at the first opportunity. (The story does have issues, we'll get to those later).A narrator, who is occasionally amusing and sometimes annoying. I'm not entirely sure how I feel about him to be honest. I can't help but think they missed out on the opportunity to have the narrator be the voice of reason among the dark and light aspects of your conscience or even be your character internally monologuing to themselves in a voice that definitely does not fit their look. Take it as a mixed bag I guess. You may or may find him a nice addition. I'd rather have him than not so he's going under pros at the very least.The cons: You get railroaded, IMMEDIATELY. Now I don't mind when the game makes me choose how I want the story to end or who I should ally with, but Biomutant forces you to choose a side in the first hour of the game. Not only that but this will have lasting repercussions which forces which ending you will receive at the finale. The only real reason for a story design philosophy such as this is to force the player to replay through the entire game to get the other endings which I could forgive if the story or gameplay for each side was at all different from each other but they just are not.There's no neutral option. You need to either be seen as good or bad, they rebrand it as light and dark but let's face it: light is for all you hero types and dark is for those who want to watch the world burn. It's been so long since I've actually seen a game that didn't offer a neutral path that it feels incredibly strange to me that they would lack the option, especially in a game that focuses so intently on your character's moral decisions. Why do I need to ally with any faction? Can I not save or doom the world by myself without the aid of a fairly useless faction? Or does the game think I'm not dumb enough to try to conquer ALL the tribes for myself? Do the developers think that? Well let me tell you that I AM that dumb and I want the option to express my aggressively stupid neutrality!You can get a cool mech that lasts for all of a fraction of play time. You can only use it in the Deadlands area which is a fairly small area of the game with not much to see or do there apart from the story objective. The only other reason you would be exploring the deadlands is to collect all the mech parts which is redundant since you won't and can't use it outside the area. The story, god the story... I put it under pros, but it's issues also need to be addressed...They had a good premise but too many things are just written in poorly and I can't be sure whether it was the writers' faults or rather lack of implementation in the game's mechanics. Without spoiling too much of the story, if you choose the dark aligned ending then the game will have you still have to fight several bosses that the dark aligned factions don't want to kill so much as tame. The game doesn't do a good job at alerting the character to this fact and they may find themselves wondering why they're going on quests to fight these bosses when you your faction doesn't want to kill them. The gameplay and quests should reflect the change of objective but they don't.The character creation system.It holds the game back. There, I said it. No one wants to customize their character's appearance in a way that gives them terrible stats for the class they want (sure you can customize you appearance separately later if you find the right spots but it's an unnecesary hassle) and no one ever said that they wanted to be locked out of certain perks because of the class they chose. Having classes at all actually limits your character's customization. Instead of being able to build your character's capabilities from scratch the game forces you to choose an archetype that limits you to certain perks which provide the stat bonuses and effects to make your combat style effective. Each class will lock you out a at least one perk which there is no reason for other than limiting character customization. Not to mention you can't get the mercenary class unless you preordered the game or they decided to give it away since I wrote this; the mercenary class is the best melee class given the perks it has access to, so if you wanted to be the best at melee then you'll have to make do with one of the other classes. Despite that, the class system doesn't actually feel like it matters. I focused on guns and still went and melee'd things many times and didn't feel like I was doing any less damage than I would have been doing. It just makes me wonder why bother with the class system at all?That's all I really have to say about the game overall. It's not terrible, but it's not great either. I would say it's painfully average. If you like exploring the world just for the sake of exploring and the combat looks fun then I can't argue but don't play this game expecting a good story or even great replay value.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, it's hard to say if I recommend this game in its current state. $60 is a lot of money and we all want to know we're getting our money's worth. I'm easy to please when it comes to post-apocalyptic animals games, but this review is for people who are thinking of purchasing this game (not for clones of me)...I wanted BIOMUTANT for a while and I'm loving things about it, but sadly, there are some deal-breaking flaws. Please read below for the PROS and CONS that I discovered within the first 1.5 hrs I have played the game (thru the first chapter).PROS: BIOMUTANT has that classic star-quality potential. The game is very wholesome and sweet. It kind of reminds me of Kameo. Anyone remember that adorable game? It was on Xbox in the early 2000s. To me, this is somewhat of a positive because of the whimsical nostaglia; however game quality from the 2000s is nowhere close to what is should be now...so, that is probably a negative for most you who are wondering if you should buy the game. BIOMUTANT has that magical Spyro or RAYMAN quality to it, too, which can be nice for someone who likes pleasant, straightforward  games. They give you an option on your preferred difficulty level, so that's a plus. The first chapter helps you along in gentle way while showing you the ropes (teaching you the controls etc). The story has potential and right out of the gate (pro or con -- you decide) you begin to understand your place in a beautiful plagued World. The first chapter is a great introduction for someone new  to this genre of game. The graphics are insanely gorgeous. Hypnotic almost. You're so charmed by the colors and beauty of the environments that you forget about your computer's mortality. I'm enjoying the game quite a bit, so far, despite the CONS that I will talk about in a minute.  The characters you will meet are presented in an abrupt but pleasant way...even the baddies (meaning the story feels rushed). So, to me, this is a great game for kids to play if you parents are wondering if BIOMUTANT is appropriate for your child. So far, it seems to be the perfect game for kids whose parents are looking for a game option that isn't aggressive and gory. CONS:The developers have really dropped the ball with respect to the game as a product. It sucks to say that because obviously this is someone's baby, ya know? Sadly, even if they are new to the gaming biz they should have a pretty strong grasp on the key components of what makes a game great (as gamers themselves) if they're going to ask for $60. So, this disappoints me, greatly. BIOMUTANT is too expensive in its current state. I think Experiment 101 should have taken maybe 6 more months to a year to develop the game. It feels pretty clunky (character movement/mechanics) and feels moderately unpolished. The story, though passable with potential... is way too rushed. There's no real 'sink your teeth into it' sort of development to the story, so far. It feels forced. The pace makes you worry that your journey in this new World is going to end too quickly. I like to become attached to my own character and develop some empathy for her and wonder, 'What the heck am I doing here?' before I'm forced to become acquainted with a new character. Even if the developers polish up the game, I really see no way to come back from such a fatal flaw. The story is out there. Open-World? Not really. feels very small. Fishbowl small. It almost feels like a platformer and I know that wasn't Experiment 101's intent. Then again, I'm only on the 2nd Chapter so this could change. I hope.It's feels bad to leave a negative because I'm enjoying the game overall. It does feel nice to progress through a game without having to think too much (I'm lookin' at you DARK SOULS), but this could cause some people to become bored pretty quickly, especially for people who are mainly fps. I enjoy wholesome games just as much as I do the less wholesome ones...so again, I'm easy to please. I would say the quality of the game as it stands is probably worth MAYBE $29.99 but during a sale for like $24.99. I hate to say that...I had such high hopes for the game and I still have faith that the developers will take on board the post release reviews and improve the game (if that's possible);  polish it a bit and PLEASE optimize the game so the graphics don't destroy everyone's motherboard.I hope the developers continue to tweak the game because personally, I'm loving it....just a bastard of a game on my computer and I have a decent-ish set up:Alienware Gaming Laptop15.6in Full HDIntel Core i7-7700HQ16GB DDR4 RAM256GB SSD + 1TB HDDGeForce GTX 1070I wish I could recommend this game in its current state but $60 is too much for a game this rushed that was released in 2021. Experiment 101, I'm so sorry for this negative reveiw. PLEASE polish up the game so more people can enjoy the idea and the gem that I know this game can become. Show these folks that the game is worth $60 and that you care about their gaming experience. That said, I will still be playing BIOMUTANT until the end because I like some things about it that matter to me as a player and I have a feeling the developers will fine tune BIOMUTANT for us and it will become a classic. I just hope my adventure doesn't end too quickly. *fingers crossed* I'm only on Chapter 2.Wish I could be of more help to you guys...$60 is a lot of money. I guess it just depends on what a peaceful, yet unpolished gaming experience is worth to you. Good luck! And may the Force be with you, always...

_childDocuments_.review: I saw a trailer for this game and it looked pretty cool. Didn't research the game at all, only found out about it maybe a month ago. I didn't know the game was pushed back and in development hell for so long. So, I went into this game with basically zero expectations other than what I gathered from the trailer I saw. I was expecting a complete game with engaging gameplay that made an overall positive experience. The tribe war seemed cool, with the impending doom of the world tree. So I bought the game day one. And boy, what a terrible mistake that was.As you can see from my time played, I didn't just play this game for a few hours then say it's dog feces and wrote a review about it. I explored the world, sat through 30+ hours of that annoying narrator... narrating things, and dove into the game's mechanics. I grinded XP and leveled up my character into the upgrade system. I chose to take over each enemy tribe instead of opting to quit the game after just TWO TRIBES. I put in the work, I ate up every hour of gameplay this game had to offer. And it sucked. Don't get me wrong, the game looks beautiful. Nobody will argue that. The world is massive and has several different biomes that you have to prepare for with resistance boosts, there are many cool looking structures and broken down buildings due to the apocalypse. But it's just so empty. There are zero enemies out in the wild other than scripted fights of a grand total of 5 NPC's fighting outside outposts. And don't get me STARTED on the outposts. It's basically every Far Cry game in existence. Go to the enemy outpost. Do a mini mission there like blow up a gun, or hack into a door or whatever, or just kill a bunch of people, and then your "faction" takes over that outpost. It's all BS we've seen before, and they did it worse. The devs took a look at that outpost mechanic and made a WHOLE GAME just on that.This game is nothing but literal repetition. Doing the same thing over and over again for hours until eventually you beat the biggest bad guy and beat the game. There's nothing new or special here, and it's clearly unfinished. The world is empty. For a bunch of warring factions, there isn't a whole lot of WAR going on. Do not buy this game. It isn't even CLOSE to being worth $60. Not even $30. Literal free mobile games have more content than this. Rant over.

_childDocuments_.review: So, I completed this game, doing most if not all of the optional side quests, and while fun, it became quite a slog. Other reviews make claims that the crafting is good, combat ~ehh, and story pointless. I agree on all these fronts, maybe not going as far as to call the crafting good... The story: Honestly, I don't know. It seems to harken back to over the top 90's kung fu movies, what with the karma system and quest style of collect five things then go kill god. I didn't really know what was going on the whole time, as the game kept hinting at deeper and deeper lore, but never delivered it. I came, I saw, I kicked ass, then the game was over. The crafting is pretty decent, I guess. At first it can be hard to find the materials necessary to craft, but then they become overabundant with you quickly hitting the cap. The whole system devolves into 1) Find a base item. 2) Find a bunch of accessory items. 3) Bolt those two things together to make the pretty numbers go up. - Not too in depthCombat is... interesting. With general exploration, you should be able to find or make top tier weapons not too far into the game, though it doesn't really matter, as the scaling is generally even. I built a gun maybe 7 hours in that I carried throughout the rest of the game as I couldn't find anything better. Ki-powers and bio-powers are both a joke, as guns do more damage, and have infinite ammo. Circle strafing is your friend/ ex you want to get away from, but keep going back to. Movement is another big issue, basically its ♥♥♥♥. You cant climb beyond specified areas, and while control over your character is generally smooth, there is no freedom of movement like in Breath of the Wild, or other parkour/climbing friendly games. Mounts were also underwhelming. They are only very slightly faster than the player character, and mostly an annoyance I didn't bother with. Special mounts can only be used in certain areas, meaning you're stuck with a goat/horse thing, or a bat glider. The gliding in this game is actually horrendous, as the angle is much too steep, you can't get very far at all, it's better to just drop and run most of the time.The biggest issue I had with this game is the narrator. While good on a professional level, the narrator is the only interaction you will have between yourself and the world around you. Signs, posters, environmental details, are all narrated. AS WELL AS EVERY CONVERSATION IN THE GAME. All spoken dialogue is through the narrator, with NPC's all spouting gibberish, taking turns with the narrator. The only thing you can do to diminish the narrator's role in the story is to turn off his random quotes - a feature I took full advantage of. The narrator became my worst enemy, as well as the fact that every character spouts a bunch of cheesy 'philosophical' crap about the light and dark, what faction you join up with, and what you've done. It's beyond annoying because it makes most if not all of the character dialogue completely pointless, just something to take up more of your time. All your instructions show up on the HUD anyway.I went into this game hoping for an experience similar to Breath of the Wild. I know that its bad to do things like that, but that feel came from all the trailers and info I had seen. This game is like BOTW: Bargain Bin edition, or like off-brand cereal. Not bad, but definitely worse than the inspiration.One other review I read said that most negative reviews didn't blast the game, merely said it had deficiencies. I agree with this. It's honestly a fun little game, best for those prepared for a little slog though repetitive, and I mean repetitive, and I mean repetitive, and I mean repetitive game design. All in all, 6/10, had promise, under delivered. Visuals were great though.
