_childDocuments_.review: Unto the end is overall a really nice game. I find it a lot like Journey in that there's a very simple objective - getting to the top of a mountain in the case of Journey, and getting back home to your family in the case of Unto the End.For both games, you can finish them in just 2-5 hours, and they're both quite visually appealing. I find the sound design of Unto the End very immersive - the crunching of snow under your feet, the echoing of noises in the caverns. So visuals are good, and sound design is good, but what about the combat? The combat in this game completely prevents you from being able to abuse any ability in a fight. You spam your attacks? You're just going to get staggered from being blocked by your enemy too many times. Spam dodge-rolling? After three or so consecutive rolls, you get winded and stop for a second. You can also only carry one throwing dagger at a time, and after you throw it, you have to pick it back up again. The combat system of Unto the End deliberately forces you to develop a cautious fighting style where you're constantly watching for what you're enemy is going to do, and then counter them accordingly. Fighting in this game requires focus and deliberate attacks, rather than just hacking and slashing your way through your foes. I personally really like this about the game, and I haven't seen many other games that have the same combat mechanics as Unto the End. It's very unique and creative - something new.One thing to note is that Unto the End was meant to be played on a controller rather than keyboard. I think it's best if you get this game on a console, but connecting a controller to your pc also works really well. As for the price of the game, I think that's the one drawback; Unto the End is slightly overpriced for its 2-5 hour experience. I do find it quite replayable though, as I enjoy the fun and challenging combat which you don't really get from many other games.And now for the final verdict:Visuals - very goodSound design - very goodCombat - fun, challenging, and very goodPrice - slightly overpriced, but there are not many game experiences like it :)Overall: 9/10Hope you found this review helpful.
_childDocuments_.name: Unto The End

_childDocuments_.review: Though I liked the aesthetics and what this game was attempting to achieve, it was too bogged down by problems to justify the price. The controls are EXTREMELY clunky. The blocking system hinges on being able to read whether an impending attack will be high or low, but these are often poorly telegraphed. The controls don't really feel intuitive, and the fighting never feels good or fluid until you've basically died enough times to memorize all of an enemy's attacks. Even then, all of your moves are stiff and slow. There are items in the game that don't seem to do anything. There are environmental and other puzzles that seem to force trial and error failure. The armor damaging and bleeding system encourages letting yourself die in a fight rather than pushing through, because why waste all those resources that you might not be able to acquire again (you have to rebuild armor from scratch if it completely breaks) when you could just respawn? There are moments when it does seem to hit the mark it set out for, but these are rare, and not worth the price for what this game has to offer. That said, I hope the developers keep at it, and try to get a better handle on gameplay fundamentals for whatever their next project is.
_childDocuments_.name: Unto The End

_childDocuments_.review: A really nice game, I've enjoyed it a lot - it delivers exactly what I was hoping for after playing the demo. The gritty fantasy vibe is really compelling, the pace is close to realistic (no slashing through levels at full speed) and the opponents difficult to beat in a way that makes you respect them. There's no division into powerful bosses and regular minions, which also makes for an interesting gameplay and narrative experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Unto The End

_childDocuments_.review: This game is superb. I loved the fights and they really forgiving if you simply do what you are supposed to do. Not overly hard, but certainly not easy. Don't run expecting to just roll through everything. Enemies will punish you for every error you make. But if I can do it, so can you.My only beef with the game is that much of it takes place in dark caves, some of it obscuring your view. This is only annoying when you're in a fight though. I also think it adds a lot to the atmosphere.Sound design is wonderful, from the music to the breathing of the father.Controls are very responsive, but as I said... Don't mash buttons blindly, because a second roll or wrong parry can spell certain death.Yes the game could be considered short, but I would rather say it's just fine really. I bought it on sale, but I'd say it's worth the full price. Hope to see more from these guys in the future!
_childDocuments_.name: Unto The End

_childDocuments_.review: Short Review: Hunting gone wrong.Long Review: If you looking for a short game that you can beat within an 1-2 hour give this game a shot. The combat in this game can be satisfying. The combat system at first might be complex but you can get used to it over time. The sad truth is that you barely used the system! You can faint but throughout my game play I never fainted. You can duck but you only use it against one troll then you forget about it. The crafting and item management is meh, the only thing you caring about is health brew and armor. Despite the many miss potential the game can work more on, I still enjoy it.
_childDocuments_.name: Unto The End

_childDocuments_.review: Great game, very atmospheric and cinematic: you claw your way through claustrophobic dark caverns, full of dangerous monstrosities, lethal chasms, and echoes of your panting. The fighting system is brutal, the sound design and camerawork are on point, and the animations are surprisingly rich and detailed for the style. Quite a handful of encounters could be bypassed – which is a great way to reinforce the idea that the protagonist wants to get to his family, not slaughter everyone along the way.
_childDocuments_.name: Unto The End

_childDocuments_.review: Okay, I quit this game at the last boss back when it came out in December. I am not a god gamer or anything but I've beaten my fair share of challenging games. The system at that time seemed clunky, there were ways to cheese a lot of fights and the last fight itself felt like a huge gamble with hyper armors and one shots.I am revisiting this game after some time and now I find it much more enjoyable. Some of the gimicky systems got a slight change, the weird one shots are gone and the last fight (while still finger breaking level hard) now feels like a much more fair challenge that can be eased in 3 ways. 1) the devs added a combat speed slider. you may slow down the combat by 25% or even 50% to study your enemies and or just make it easier on your eyes and reflex to keep up. 2) The last boss area (at least for me) contained 2 throw able spears that would do considerable damage to the boss making him much more manageable. I ended up using one after an hour of wipes on him XD. 3) Lastly you can just run away from him LMAOAll in all I can give this game a solid 7.5 maybe even an 8. The concept is really good. The mechanics are interesting but not too overbearing like an actual fighting game. The exploration feels interesting and the interactions with npc's whom you cannot understand verbally but can only guess the intent is quite nice.For its price the game is worth and I also would like to personally thank the devs for the work they've been doing. The steam discussions are being answered daily and the devs even released a new build of the game just because I requested assist with a new ps5 controller support. As expected, the future of gaming is not overpriced tripple A's but small indies like this, looking forward to any future projects
_childDocuments_.name: Unto The End

_childDocuments_.review: Unto the end is an experience. It is a grueling, harsh, gorgeous and mind-shatteringly difficult experience. But it is a game I would highly recommend because it serves a challenge I have yet to see anywhere else. If you want a game where you can be the badass and kill all in your path this is not that game. If you want a game where you feel badass just by beating it, this is the game for it. This game is one of the hardest I've ever played and it does not hold your hand in the slightest but I highly recommend because it is such a fantastic experience. Killing your enemy is rewarding. Hitting a wall happens often and getting over the wall makes you feel amazing.
_childDocuments_.name: Unto The End

_childDocuments_.review: Alas I had to make a decision before reaching a 2 hour play time total if I was going to keep at it and try to master the combat, or refund it.  In the end I decided 'this isn't for me'.  The game is very atmospheric from the very very brief time I played it (didn't even make it to the first boss) and the sound is great.  Torches crackle, the sound of your footfalls in the snow are perfectly done, rocks crack and skitter over the rough cave floors.  Really great stuff. The combat is tricky from my brief experience with it - mostly the sparring, and then a few fights vs the starting enemies.  I can see folks liking it once they became familiar with the combat mechanics.  Alas I became immediately frustrated by several things and decided I'd rather spend time on something else instead.1)- Terrain blocks the camera of your character, preventing you from seeing what the enemies you are fighting are doing at times - so you have to roll, roll, roll away into a place where you can see.  You might take a hit during that time, or have not realized you dropped your torch or sword somewhere in the black screen of the rocks which means roll, roll, rolling back spamming LB hoping you pick them up.2)- There's no way to load from a prior save manually.  All damage you take damages your armor and/or you.  This requires dwindling supplies to repair or heal, which means less for upgrades.  I wanted to just instantly reload from a checkpoint to try things again - as it seemed better to just reload than waste the few starting resources I had.  However this is not possible to do - so you can just stand there and let the creature(s) kill you to get the same effect, but that wastes quite a bit of time.  As a rule I intensely dislike check point save systems.3)- You can't skip cut-scenes and there's no going back to explore things you may have left behind.  That's fine - it's atmospheric and your decisions would matter in such situations.  However if you DO want to go back there's no way to do so other than starting all over.  From the very beginning.  For example - I had realized early on that I went the 'correct' way and might have left some things behind.  I thus started all over to be sure and turns out I missed () and other supplies.  4)- Trying to block enemy combos is extremely tough - I feel like I have to spam 'up' on my game pad given how quick they attack, and these are just the starting enemies. I dread to think about what later ones will do.  EDIT: It turns out there's an 'assist' mode that slows down time slightly to make fighting enemies easier.  I probably should have enabled that.  Alas - I have already refunded the game so it's a no go for me.  Overall I'll come back to this game after a few months and see if it's been improved upon.  I can't recommend it at this point due to the frustrations listed above.  It's a true shame too - this definitely seems like a labor of love.  I wish there was a 'thumb to the side' rating instead I could leave.EDIT: I'm back after a few months to check on the status of the game (today is Feb 3rd 2021).  They've added more options for the combat speed and added numerous other improvements.  The checkpoint system is still in play (not a fan, so the game is not for me) however I don't think I can really keep my thumbs down vote at this point.  I think they've improved  on some of the parts that made it frustrating and have listened to criticism with an open ear and mind.  I'm going to change my thumbs down to a thumbs up.
_childDocuments_.name: Unto The End

_childDocuments_.review: The combat is pretty unique and quite challenging, especially the last few enemies.The game was alright, I'm not a huge fan of caves and sadly at least 50% (if not more) of the game happens underground. It actually shines whenever you are out there in the forest and not finding your way through tiny hallways. I would've liked a tiny bit more context as to what's going on, the races and why did you leave your family in the first place. The ambiance can be quite oppressive at times but it's a cool concept and I hope the couple that made it will continue to explore the combat mechanics they came up with, as well as those cool monsters and world.
_childDocuments_.name: Unto The End

_childDocuments_.review: Pros: Atmosphere, exploration (there are MANY nooks and crannies), minimalist art style for the art snobs, masochistic (for the lovers of difficult games that beat yo ass), possible replayability, puzzles I guess?Cons: Short, dying can sometimes = learning instead of reacting, combat can be so quick you'd think you're fighting the damn Flash (nit pick since I only struggled on the last two enemies and needed combat assist and some cheese), some puzzles are (by the developers own words) obscure af! (I did need to check how to get past one part - after that I understood how the rest could work)Overall: I had fun, I got angri (angri fun) and I enjoyed the exploration and puzzles. Definitely wouldn't recommend to casual players or gamers who want any kind of direction - there is none in this game which is both good and bad (good in that I personally dont ALWAYS want to be treated like a baby - bad in that SOMETIMES I'd like to be treated like a baby and not get shishkebabed a lot)7/10Might die again
_childDocuments_.name: Unto The End

_childDocuments_.review: The Good:It is atmospheric and enjoyable to play (at least in assist mode).It feels like you are playing a real human which is great.I love the world they created.The Bad:I was expecting a story. A game should have some kind of mission. There has to be a reason why I am walking around in this world, like to provide for my family or save my son, or...something, anything. But all I got was gameplay.Verdict:Great world. Would have been a fantastic game if there had been an engaging story somewhere. But still very fun to play, great atmosphere. I am happy I played it. I'll play it again sometime.
_childDocuments_.name: Unto The End

_childDocuments_.review: I'm loving the realistic approach. I can feel the protagonist moving around, breathing, etc. That's cool. The combat felt very promising as well. I love the intention that went into this but... the quality of the enemies attack telegraphing is not good enough compared to the consequence of not avoiding it, (often insta death). That's all. Some enemies arms and weapons seem to teleport from wind up to release. I managed to overcome early basic enemies, because their patterns are somewhat learnable but then I encounter the second yeti which has the most enfuriating set of attacks: Ouch. That's it not fun. I have no issue with hardcore die & retry, as long as the process of retrying is  and as long as I  something from my retries. When the game fails to provide that consistently, it fails to make me wanna retry, which is a shame. I need either more HP (to allow more mistakes per tries) OR better pattern telegraphing so I can learn faster. This is like Punchout but with one hp :D I tried the slow time assist, but it makes things worth, by even widening the gap between windup and release, making it somewhat even more unreadable :sI still recommend the game because it's unique, and cheers to the dev for trying, they are obviously well meaning. But be cautious of what you're stepping in if you buy this game :)
_childDocuments_.name: Unto The End

_childDocuments_.review: Thoroughly enjoyed this game after it stomping on me for the first couple of hours. Played through fully twice with a few restarts. It's a great game, great atmosphere. I only wish it were a bit longer. Some enemies only really appear once. I felt the armour crafting was a bit pointless as it'd constantly degrade. It's a decent idea in practice but the game isn't really long enough to justify it and resource is scarce. Plus near the start of the game there are hidden items that basically negate the need for this. I'd love more of this setting but I doubt we'll get it. Price point is a little high for what it is.The game also seems to have went through significant redesign post announcement. None of the content, other than character sprites, in the trailer from 2017 is present.
_childDocuments_.name: Unto The End

_childDocuments_.review: Unto The End is a challenging combat adventure game in the style of a cinematic platformer. The story is simple: get home to your family. Master read-react combat in intense sword fights. Spot opportunities to trade and use items. An adventure told through your actions, how will you make it home?
_childDocuments_.name: Unto The End

name: Griftlands
detailed_description: Griftlands is a deck-building rogue-like where you fight and negotiate your way through a broken-down sci-fi world. Every decision is important, be it the jobs you take, the friends you make, or the cards you collect. Death comes quickly, but each play offers new situations and strategies to explore. Play as Sal, Rook, or Smith. Three unique character campaigns with their own specialized decks, abilities and maps to explore. Sal is an adventurer out for profit and revenge. Rook is an aging spy working his own agenda. Smith is an idle loafer who might just save the world. Each playable character's story takes place in a unique environment, with different factions and locations to explore and exploit. Battle Challenging Bosses Test your combat decks against powerful foes with unique mechanics and attacks. Build a Team - or Buy One! Hire mercenaries, find pets, or impose upon your friends to accomplish your goals. Master Hundreds of Cards Each character has unique negotiation and combat decks to draft from. Get powerful item cards from fallen foes, or as rewards. Decisions Matter Killing foes may incur the wrath of their friends, but sparing them leaves a dangerous piece on the board. Choose wisely, everyone remembers everything you do! Welcome to Havaria Each playable character's story takes place in a unique environment, with different factions and locations to explore and exploit. Explore A Broken-Down Sci-Fi World The world of Havaria is a harsh place, full of harsher denizens. Explore lush, hand-illustrated environments full of people who want to kill you. Playing Politics For Keeps Each character has a factional allegiance and an opinion of you. Play politics between rivals, and try to capture the most powerful social boons. But watch out -- doublecross the wrong person, and you'll be subject to their bane! Outwit or Overpower Overcome obstacles with the power of your fists - or your words. You'll need to pick your cards and play them right if you're going to survive. Build two decks simultaneously, balancing the tradeoffs of each. Learn from each attempted run through the various stories of the Griftlands. Encounter different combinations of enemies, quests, and events every time you play. Your fate is determined by your choices, and by fate.

short_description: Griftlands is a deck-building roguelite where you negotiate, fight, steal or otherwise persuade others to get your way. Every decision is important, be it the jobs you take, the friends you make, or the cards you collect.

_childDocuments_.review: A very well designed deck-builder that further develops the genre popularized by Slay the Spire. The choices have story and game play elements with lasting consequences that really develop your decks and character. My favorite design choice is that you actually manage multiple decks for different tactics which really breathes life into which encounters to engage in and when to ask for help.Can't wait to see how this game develops and is absolutely worth the purchase during early access.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Griftlands is a game developed and published by Klei EntertainmentThe game offers some nice graphics and environments, although some ugly glitches here and there, it is pleasant all the same and has a really great aestheticAlthough this deckbuilding game isn't my type, and most especially, most deckbuilding games aren't for me, but for what Griftlands offers, I enjoyedGriftlands overall, however, is a fun game to play, and it does get boring if being played for a long time, but is a great roguelite RPG game and to play in short bursts
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: A great roguelike game with nice rpg elements that gives you a story as you go through. There's 3 characters to play through, but the story goes through pretty quickly. Still, this is fundamentally a roguelike deck building game, and it's very fun to play. You can choose to negotiate or fight often, with different decks and strategies for each. You make enemies and allies that give bonuses or penalties, which introduces a really interesting choice to kill your enemies to try to get rid of penalties, or spare them/win them over. Killing them often makes enemies of their friends, so it's a nice strategic touch that mixes well with the story and missions. There's also other modes like playing through 15 fight or negotiate battles with bosses every 5 battles. My only complaint is I wish they either had more characters, or had more story variation, so that even the story felt roguelike. Instead though it's largely fixed (although there are one of two factions to choose in each that change your path accordingly). All said, it's got a great concept, fantastic combat/negotiating combats, the added story is nice and leaves me wanting for more, and it's got a lot of variation that you can add in to change things up. Oh, and let's not forget the persistent talents that give you a little something to carry over on play-throughs. The relationships that give bonuses or penalties was a masterstroke in a genre where items and cards are all that matters, introducing a sort of living item into the mix with all the morality it entails to help someone corrupt or kill an assassin. If you like deck building games or roguelikes, I definitely recommend this game. 9/10
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing game. At first I was skeptical of the combination of inspirations of Slay the Spire and choose-your-own-adventure games: the deckbuilding aspect seemed a bit forced. Moreover, I specifically say Slay the Spire because the first character, Sal, in particular feels like a Frankenstein of various different Slay the Spire mechanics. However, as I continued to play, I adjusted, and I began to feel how natural the swirl of genres could be. The first campaign felt strange, and in many ways it is: 4-5 hours is kinda an odd duration of a story and gameplay, the first character is very cliche as is her surroundings, and I felt like I was stumbling through familiar yet disorienting mechanics but still finished the first campaign with very little challenge, only coming close to failure in the final boss fight. Yet I think this is just because I had not yet adjusted how the game worked, and was still working towards higher difficulties. The thing about Griftlands is that there are a lot of subtle, moving parts. There are a lot of different incentives pulling you different ways. There's a lot of outcomes difficult to predict. There's lots of mechanics you will only learn through repetition. However, I did find that I learned, and it continuously made me excited to keep playing. I felt like I was mastering the game, and yet there was still always more to learn as it got more and more challenging. It felt so rewarding to adapt to a game that feels so odd, and yet still would encourage me to at times abandon "optimal" strategy to help characters and follow plot threads I was more endeared by.The real pull of Griftlands that brings this all together is polish. The game's logic feels consistent and dynamic. The music is fantastic. The art is varied and beautiful. The interface is straight-forward and does well to navigate the many moving parts. The writing is, for the most part, good. Sal and her story is by far the most disappointing: she herself is a stereotypical downtrodden and sarcastic bounty hunter, her setting is classic sci-fi fair of violent insurgent bandits vs corrupt and cruel government police and a plan of vengeance. The other stories are considerably better. Rook is a bit more fun, as both a bit of an old fart but also a genius spy moving through a recognizable spy drama of class warfare and conspiracy, but I felt like it never really payed off because it always feels like you are never in control of the larger conspiracy. Smith's story is by far the best, as Smith is a wonderfully depicted ne'er do well who can be played either as a lovable ruffian with a chaotic heart of gold or as a cruel, selfish, entitled rich kid. His dialogue is consistently hilarious, and his supporting cast is endearing, dynamic, and often perfect straight-mans against Smith's absurdity. The larger story as well feels compelling and driving, and I found his mechanics the most fun to boot, albeit the most complicated. Kind of a bummer it feels like one story got so much more care than the other two.My one real critique is that the meta progression feels a little tacked on. It doesn't feel particularly rewarding or monumental, just small bonuses that eventually add up to greater power/ease. Some of the perks were fun to combine, but for the most part I barely thought about them and didn't really look forward to unlocking new ones much. The huge variety of new unlockable cards and increased difficulty were enough to motivate me.Anyway, great game. Worth many play-throughs. Highly recommend.

_childDocuments_.user: Plump Sweet n Beggin for Cream
_childDocuments_.review: I am SUPER into this game.  It was on my wishlist for a couple of months before I decided to pick it up and it's just amazing. As far as story based content, it kicks ass. Once you've done that and are just playing for the quests and encounters like you'd play any other deck builder, it still holds up really well. Given that it's early access, I'm surprised at how high the quality of everything is. I experienced no bugs in the time I've played so far.The difficulty is pretty low at the time of writing this but there are a number of optional modifiers to runs that can make things more challenging. I'm sure it'll be balanced differently by the  time the next update comes out so the relevance of this part of the review is probably gonna be short lived.Super recommend!
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: After almost 40 hours, this is a really good game.My one gripe is that game play content outstrips the story content. I've probably seen a good chunk of the story, only minor events maybe 5 or so quests I haven't seen. I have pretty much done all the big story choices for two of the three characters. However I am nowhere near the exploring all of the mechanics and using different types of decks.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Slay the Spire, with a story.I really appreciate that negotiation is another type of "battle", meaning being skilled in speech doesn't mean you end up skipping all the gameplay.3 campaigns, each a couple hours of gameplay. Its a roguelite so when you die you start over, with some saved progress. Side jobs and road events are randomized, with some consistent story beats for each campaign. A decent bit of replay value with escalating difficulty and new unlocks.Excellently written, frequently humorous, always engaging.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Griftlands does what it sets out to do, offering a wholly compelling and unique take on its genre influences. It's yet another excellent entry into roguelike deckbuilding experiences and is immediately memorable thanks to its reliance on world-building and character depth. Even better, the story of Griftlands is a fun jaunt through a sci-fi world that is buoyed by an even more exciting card game. Those who loved Hades, Slay the Spire, or similar games will find just as much to love in Griftlands.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Cool game. Interesting characters. Not generally a fan of pre-determined characters, but Sal is pretty amusing. Would be nice if I could get passed Day 3, but I'm sure I'll eventually overcome my own incompetence... or get irritated/bored and never play ever again. Either way, good 4 hours spent so far.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Nice story, great art, but very lacklustre combat. The card systems (both) are bland and uninteresting. After 7 hours I found no interesting cards to look forward to when drafting, no deep interactions. It feels as though the developers set out with certain archetypes and then threw the needed cards in a pile to draft from. In almost all situations going for one archetype is the answer and then trimming the excess cards so you combo more. And due to the limited decksizes (>15 cards) decks never surprise. It's feels like an unfortunate slog clicking through combat just to get to the story. I'd rather have had it the otherway round. Not recommended
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: This game is very well made but it's simply not for everyone. The cardplay mechanics are decently well rounded, although each deck has a fairly obvious meta.The story-telling part of the game is why I could never really get into it, even after several tries. I find it to be very dry and frankly a little boring. There are some people who will absolutely LOVE this game, but it's not the deck builder for me
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: This might be my favorite game of all time.It's a rogue-like, deck-building game dedicated to running through a character's main campaign multiple times, and the premise is that, no play-through is the same as the last, especially when you unlock more and more cards; and you can solve issues through talking, or beating the living Hesh out of anyone and everyone who gets in your way. (You can run a pacifist route by beating people into surrender, but I had to kill everyone for an achievement. Which are pretty difficult, and really fun, to obtain.)The soundtrack is so good, I actually have Smith's on my phone and listen to it nearly daily. You can get to broken numbers in both damage and defense if you're lucky enough to get that setup. The story is simple, rather quick, but there's three of them with characters I adore as the main spotlight. Please, try this game. It's made my day(s) better with just a *thirty* minute run-through at times. Especially if you enjoy min/maxing and silly deck-building of making those numbers skyrocket. Like throwing all of your bottles with, what, 20x3 damage buff on a move that multiplies off your empty bottles, in which I have 19 of? It gets pretty nutty.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: After playing through and beating all the campaigns at prestige 1, I can safely say that it's worth it for the story possibilities alone! But I think Sal's story is a little lackluster compared to Smith's and especially Rook's. I haven't played brawl mode yet. The achievements are difficult enough that they feel like actual accomplishments. I'd guess ~150 to 200 hours for everything.Runs fantastically on my Arch desktop setup, though my laptop (Ubuntu MATE 20.04) complained a little. I'd like to thank Klei for their efforts in porting their games to Linux. You guys and gals are a class act!
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: It has all the polish, style, and fun game play of the Klei game, even through it is still technically in early access.  A strange hybrid of CCG, RPG, and Rogue-like set in a really unique sci-fi world, and it all just comes together beautifully.  I got it when it was on sale, but if I had paid full price I'd still feel like I got my money's worth.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Very solid deckbuilder, already no-life'd it for almost 30 hours. Characters offer some interesting and unique mechanics not seen in other games/deckbuilders, and each character is varied enough to not force you into looking for specific "good" builds. Wide variety of mechanics, and each some seems usable.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic! I got it a few days ago and haven't stopped playing it since.  definitely worth picking up in early access.  I'm started a run as the second character and while I'm not a huge fan of his negotiation mechanic it does cause me to stretch in interesting ways.  besides I found the game isn't very difficult until you reach level 3 prestige on a run and then it gets a huge spike.My main complaint right now is the negotiations.  They aren't bad by any means but it feels off.  As it stands the longer the negotiation lasts the more powerful the enemy becomes in a way you cannot match. It realies on you ramping up faster than your opponent and ending the negotiation before they become too powerful.  All of this sounds well and good in fact there may be some intent there however it feels off.  like its limiting player expression or like they quickly become unfairly strong.  It could be that I'm just trying to play it wrong still/there aren't enough defense cards atm to defend the number of arguments I'm trying to protect.  combined with the way cards upgrade (which is awesome don't get me wrong) you can end up choosing not to upgrade a defensive card just to keep it in your deck. (some upgrades will make the card strong but only usable once for either the rest of the game or per combat)The game is already great but with a little polish on negotiations and a few things then the game will be a legend.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Awesome rougelite with a story. It's really well done, mechanics are very cool, with having both a battle and negotiation deck. The player will mostly have a choice between battling it out or talking your way out of a sticky situation. There are some other unique mechanics to the game, for example, based on the choices you make, you can make someone love you, or hate you. Based on that you gain positive or negative boons that will affect your entire run. Also the story is not just some generic plot, it's filled with great characters and plot twists and quite a bit of humor. It is also very replayable. Every time you start a new run different npc will give you quests, almost all quests can be done in different ways so there are a looot of combinations that will keep every new run fresh. I am a great fan of Slay the Spire and the one thing I find missing in this game is the capacity to have some ridiculous combos like in StS, but I still haven't unlocked all the cards so that may be because of it. All in all, very cool experience, would recommend to all roguelite fans, especially deckbuilding roguelite fans
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: The premise of diplomatic "combat" in a RPG card game was interesting enough for me to check this game out without knowing too much else. With under 2 hours time played, I can already tell this is an incredibly thoughtful game that I will love and remember for years. Minor encounters and character interactions feel unique and complex rather than simply going through the motions. Despite the density of inspired genres crammed into Griftlands, the mechanics blend together in a way feels incredibly cohesive and original. The strategic range is insane, and I can already tell there's so much room for customization and variation from each run and player to the next. Klei Entertainment has become a powerhouse in this medium-indie size production range, and Griftlands feels like the most visionary direction the studio has taken in years.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: First time I played the game, I was so sucked in I didn't realize that I ended up going for about 5 hours. The two characters so far have different styles of play: Sal is pretty straightforward for her battle and negotiation systems but you can obtain cards that pull more cards out of your deck or cause all sorts of status effects to the enemy while Rook's fighting style is set up to work on how much charge his laser pistols have and his negotiations can be effected by a coin toss, powering them up or causing different effects.The first playthrough is a bit tough, but that's par for the course for these types of games since you have basic cards in the beginning but the game has an interesting system where as you use cards they gain experience and can eventually be upgraded to have new effects or to be stronger.I've been a fan of Klei for a while and I've very happy to have bought this on Early Access launch and looking forward to what they'll add over time.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr: A lovely science fiction deckbuilder that's worth playing if you enjoyed Slaying the Spire. Overall: I play a lot of these and I think this is the second best after StS. The plot is that you're a gun-toting, fast-talking "grifter" who makes money in a slumlike backwater city inhabited by several alien species. There are three grifters to play at time of review, though the third character's story is still unfinished. It's lovely and made me laugh quite a bit.Features:  - hand-drawn art style that's cartoony, not pixelated  - semi-dystopian science fiction world where spaceflight was lost  - win over friends by helping to gain big bonuses... or make enemies to get penalties  - two decks to build instead of one: a negotiation deck for persuasion, and a combat deck when they attack  - sweet characters that speak in an alien language that sounds great, but you need to read the text for the story  - it has a lot of heart and cool world-buildingThings Like Slay the Spire:  - deckbuilding where you pick a card from a random set of three, or take coins instead  - artifacts that help you get a bonus permanently  - randomish encounters  - branching path, though it's not as obvious here as the tree in Slay the Spire
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: A phenomenal, content-rich deck builder that I would recommend to just about anyone.Pros:-Gorgeous art style and animations-Soundtrack is killer-The three playable campaigns all feel unique in both story and gameplay (Smith is my personal favorite)-I adore the two deck system. Being able to dodge a deadly encounter by negotiating is always super satisfying.Cons:-Lack of variety in voice acting. You will hear the same handful of lines of dialogue in alien language throughout the game.-There is a big jump in difficulty around day 3 or 4 of each campaign that will stop you in your tracks if you aren't building your deck smartly. -Each run can clock in at over 5 hours, which is a huge investment for a rogue-lite with permadeath. The standard difficulty does give you one more try if you die, but having to start a run over is pretty defeating when there is such a heavy narrative focus.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a breath of fresh air in a sea of remakes , reskins and just poorly executed ideas.Griftlands is a Card game at its core with rogue lite elements that allow you to save one thing from the previous game or once a day your character which i love. Currently there 3 people you can play and they seem to move in and out of each others stories typically reading text in a game can be boring but this game does a great job of telling each person story THE BEST part is the choices you make actually affect things in the game and can cause negative or positive things to happen within your runs. you can talk your way out of things which is its own card game itself different from the fighting one but similar enough that its not to hard to pick up onGameplay 9music 8quality of life 8atmosphere 9story 8
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Game's just great, that's all. It's easy enough to get into and complex enough to provide many hours of replayability. The more you replay the characters  - the more cards you unlock - the more strategies you have at your disposal the next run. I've caught myself doing specific decks and going for thematic runs already ("this time I'll do an influence negotiation run"; "this time I'll focus on the overcharge mechanic in combat"; etc.). Klei delivered and knowing how they take care of their games longterm - it's just a solid title.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: We're living through a golden age in the singleplayer Card-lite genre. We're getting spoiled by Slay the Spire,  Monster Train, and now this. Coming from the first two, this one feels harder to get into, at the start the talking gets in the way of the fighting, and vice versa. Expect the first run on each character to be a scrub while you figure out the mechanics. Even after that, it can be pretty challenging. But figure out what's going on mechanically, and make SURE to read all the story (don't skip through it!) and this game SHINES in its own way, really looking forward to the third character. Excellent Klei polish, interesting characters and scenario, and a really nice twist with the loved/hated buff system, get this!
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: This is an extremely well-executed experience that kind of sneaks up on you with how much depth it really has. The world is reminiscent of space opera universes like Firefly & Saga with some engaging backstory that's introduced to you through dialogue and keywords in said dialogue that you can hover over. The different card decks depending on how you approach a situation is a stellar idea. Don't sleep on this, very engaging.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: So far so good. The argumentation-battle system is pretty neat and unique, though it has gotten repetitive by now. Everything else resembles a cool cross between Slay The Spire and The Banner Saga.EDIT: I don't really like how every run drags on for 2-4 hours. Slay The Spire and Monster Train runs top out at about an hour normally. Prepare yourself accordingly.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Gave it a chance because so many people ere raving on about it, and they were pretty much right. Plenty of fun desicions for fans of card battler roguelites, cool characters and mechanics, it's a solid game.If anything, it's kind of overwhelming when you start, as almost everything you choose has consequences. It's a game with some feel-bad moments as your choices can be which bad thing to deal with. Not too much, but enough to notice.The hype was right, a great example of the genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Truth be told I logged over 60 hours in the *demo* for this game. (It was because of an agreement I had at the time with my wife to not spend money on new games.) The demo was amazing, and the full version is even more so. I keep coming back to it and it never gets old. A masterpiece, in my opinion.10/10 would recommend!
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: This is an absolutely phenomenal card game. I never thought I would see the day where I actively enjoyed a coin flip mechanic, but Griftlands pulled it off.This game is unique in its design; blending a mix of tactics/brute force in both peaceful and nonpeaceful ways, allowing you to craft your own narrative in a way i dont think ive ever seen handled so well in a game before. The three classes are all fleshed out and play completely unique from each other, have tons to see and try and do, and there is content for days in this title.This game is just a flat home run. Love the art, love the sound, love the mechanics. Buy it, support this team!
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I wish there was a third option to "recommend: yes or no" because I don't feel particularly strongly in either direction. But, I had to choose one, so here we are. I don't think I'm liking this game as much as I thought I would. Despite its very unique (and very cool) look, its game play is anything but unique. It feels very generic. Maybe if there weren't SO many other deck building-type games out there right now it would stand out more. Yes, in addition to fighting you can negotiate. That sounds like a stand-out kind of game mechanic, right? But it's not. It's the battle deck re-skinned. Instead of stabbing with a knife, you might use "the power of reason" to damage your foe instead. They do the same thing, just called other names with different artwork. The two systems just aren't different enough; fighting and negotiating feel the same. It's an illusion of deep game play.But again, it does look very cool. I'm also very early in, so maybe it opens up into crazier stuff that I'd be into. But I really don't see that happening. It's far from being the worst game like this. It's just not anywhere near the best. There are better options out there, so can't recommend this. BTW, I update this review as I play more.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: This game is very charming and the unique mechanics, such as juggling two deck types and using strategy to determine whether to talk or fight your way through situations, offer a lot of interesting and engaging gameplay. Out of all the card battler types of games, I would say this one takes my heart, even over Slay the Spire. The roguelite aspects of the game aren't all that relevant, but it does add a little bit of flavor with each run. If you're a fan of deckbuilding rpgs, don't sleep on this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: If you're looking for a fun game to pass the time while watching tv or something, this is great.  The art style was what drew me in at first, but the story and card aspect is fun.  Sometimes negotiating can get a little tedious but meh, not too bad.Replayability is top notch, with 3 characters having 3 different storylines and 3 different ways to play each storyline.  Lots of reasons to return.  Worth the $20 and if found on sale, buy immediately.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I think many others have said it right, this game is a combination of many different elements that sorta works in a lot of different ways but doesn't hit home particularly hard in any of them. The deck building and combat are kinda just bland, nothing too crazy but not bad either. the negotiation deck is interesting but I didn't find much to enjoy in it simply because the actual mechanics didn't really correlate with what you were doing, it just felt like a different form of combat. I almost beat the game on my first and only run and have left it there. Ultimately I would say if you are interested in the narrative you will enjoy this the most. Probably worth just playing it on the easy difficulty and enjoying the story of each character once or twice. That would probably occupy 10-15 hours and be worth your time. For me though I prefer a game that delves into its mechanics a little more. Not a bad game overall though
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: What if Slay the Spire was a RPG?Cool game, nice design, interesting stories, whatever. The visual art is just PERFECT!!! I love every thing tiny bit of it. Just yess!Also the game is nice indeed, really, but THE AAAART!!!!EDIT: so a bit more about this game: it's really good."What about Monster Train and Slay the Spire?"So, I haven't played monster train but I love Slay the Spire. As everyone has probably written around, this game CAN be a bit less focused on deckbuilding and more on other aspects, if you want it.You can play it murdering the s**t out of every living thing, and face the consequences using your perfect battle deck.Or you can play around it, spending money to make friends and avoiding confrontations, arriving at the boss battles with lesser decks, but plenty of buffs and friends and full stats.So, if you care only about playing cards, the two-deck system is really nice, this will entertain you enough, but in the end you will probably like Monster Train or Slay the Spire more. If you want something else beside that, this may be what you want.Finally, VERY IMPORTANT: there are two game modes. One is the story mode, which can take several hours and where the backlash of a poor deck design can arrive after hours of playing, but which will probably be punishing only at higher prestige levels. The other is the brawl mode, which is just one encounter after the other, and so more similar to a slay the spire approach. So even if you don't love the story mode, there is something for you too!
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Engaging mechanics. This is the first roguelike game I've played with an actual in-depth story I fully engaged in while playing the game. Most games like these are purely in it for the gameplay, and while that clearly works, Klei went above and beyond that.The "negotiation battle" aspect will be a bit intimidating at first since the "tutorial" is barely any help and there doesn't seem to be any glossary. Fortunately, if you stick with it and give it a chance, if you're an experienced deckbuilder, you'll get it within perhaps 30 minutes. The things to note here that I had to painstakingly figure out.- "Resolve" is hitpoints/life.- "Composure" is shield.- "Arguments" are just status effects that appear as "objects" in the screen that can be attacked and destroyed.USE YOUR MOUSE and hover all over the place. Klei did the right thing here where almost everything has tooltips.One last thing. Once the negotiating battle starts, ALWAYS check the main "icon" of the opponent to see what his innate abilities are. That will save you a lot of pain and a lot of moments where you have little idea what's going on.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Man, I hate to do a negative review here. I adore Klei for the most part, and have logged stupid hours on Oxygen Not Included. But... Griftlands just isn't that good. Let's break it down.The Good*Art - Very good, solid artwork that portrays the game world very well.*Sound - Music is decent, but the reactive sound system during combat and negotiation is pretty impressive and very immersive. The simlish spoken by the characters is... okay.*Game Modes - Offering a "brawl" mode where you can skip the story and just play is really nice, and I wish more games of this ilk would do the same.The Meh*Mechanics - Most of the card mechanics are strictly okay, and aren't fully utilized. There are a lot of crappy cards that you really don't want, and the game tries to incentivize picking them with a money bonus.*Combat - Tends to last too long and be extremely punishing. Also, not well balanced. Some characters are noticeably stronger than others and as noted above, some mechanics just aren't very good.*Negotiation - The good/bad dichotomy is interesting, but doesn't work well in execution. There's a constant tug of war between charm and intimidation, and it's easy to end up being crap at both.*Stories - Smith's story is pretty entertaining because of the sheer scum-baggery, but Sal and Rook both have fairly forgettable tales. Rook especially - byzantine plots aren't very satisfying when they're run on the rails like a visual novel. Unfortunately, there is close to zero emergent gameplay... and for a Klei title, that's weird and a little sad.The Bad*Character Appeal - The characters are essentially bad people doing bad things and occasionally playing it for dark humor. I never really felt any connection or investment in them as they ran around murdering people and putting off one-liners.*Progression - Not very satisfying and pretty grindy. The unlocking system for perks and such gets old pretty fast.The last point to address is the gorilla in the room: how does it compare to Slay the Spire? StS may be old now, but it's still basically the gold standard for card roguelikes. And... Griftlands doesn't really measure up. It lacks the fine balance, the replayability, and the challenging progression that makes StS still playable today. Klei is a very experimental studio, and sometimes experiments don't really work out. Unfortunately, Griftlands is one of those times.I can't recommend this game as a purchase for anybody, but I do encourage you to check out Klei's other games. Obviously Don't Starve is their big hit, but Oxygen Not Included is remarkable. Do yourself a favor and keep an eye on them. They'll surprise you.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Not even an hour in and I've already encountered several major bugs that ruined my run. Sent the dev team feedback for each of the problems so maybe these things will eventually be fixed. In the meantime, I've requested a steam refund. Can't recommend this game in its current state. Hopefully it will be worth the purchase when it comes out of early access.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: The price is extremely good for the quality of game you are getting from this. The mettle/flourish system is great. A bit harsh how damaging the hate system can be, difficult to predict the consequences of killing an NPC, as some other NPC in another part of the world can smack you with a permanent debuff.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: To me one of the best turn-based games out there. A unique and hard to learn battle style with actual physical battles and negotiations, that play completely differently. I enjoy the different characters, the story and everything else. Haven't figured out the third character yet, but that is what makes it interesting for me. I love Sly the Spire and although this one is more complicated at first and you need to dive into it a little more its actually has a similar feel to it
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Klei have really made their own game here with unique mechanics (though I think fans of Renowned Explorers: International Society will enjoy this and vice versa), visuals, and lore.The initial learning curve may seem steep but this flattens out very quickly, after your first couple battles you will be familiar enough to begin devising effective strategies. It's a fine line for a roguelike to walk when balancing difficulty and after 7 hours I really think Klei has struck a great balance. Early Access Observations: I encountered nothing game breaking; no dead ends, broken text, crashes or frustrations. With an initial price point of $12.74 you just can't go wrong, Klei delivers again!
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I've haven't even scripted this review, going to give my honest thought. Loved the potential of a deckbuilder from Klei, played through dozens of  runs in Slay the Spire  and loved every single one but how the hell did Griftlands get soo darn noisey to a point where is it unbearable to even to look at. Had to refund after just a couple of minutes. I know its not just for a game of this calibre, however ever since the Oxygen Not Included came out Klei's policy of rendering games more rewarding by making players learn on their own with limited HUD and tutorial, became daunting to say the least. It staled very bad very fast. I'm sorry to say this Klei but I have lost faith in your understanding of game-making. Hope you and I can reenact that spark when the DST came out. Love you but I gotta go...
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: This game sucks.  That is all.  It is boring, slow, and requires way to many clicks per function.  I know "too many clicks" seems like a petty complaint, but there is seriously WAY too much boring dialogue that you have to sit and wait to scroll out, then click past.  And they are planning to RAISE THE PRICE of this garbage?  FOH.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Really great game. If you enjoyed Slay the Spire, you'll find yourself right at home here. I really enjoyed the fact that you have two types of encounters, which leads to two different types of decks and skills, making the runs more varied. That said, I felt my builds were a bit less varied than in StS. If you look at the price tag and feel like you'd pay that for 40h of fun, look no further.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: This game is really fun, there are still some bugs that crash the game, but that is to be expected from early access. The combat and negotiation battles are well balanced and there is some challenge to the game. If you have played slay the spire then this will be up your alley. I recommend this game from anyone who liked deck building rouge likes.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: After playing my first 8 hours and dying for the first time I think I'm hooked. Yet another well conceived and implemented game from Klei Entertainment. This game is intuitive without becoming repetitive with enough content to feel like you're constantly progressing towards something. I'm excited to watch development unfold after being in early access with other Klei titles. 10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Obviously as far as storytelling goes, this game is awesome- amazing lore, gorgeous art, great characters. And as far as deck-building mechanics? Also awesome- two decks? With several unique archetypes to build, mix, and break? And as far as fast-paced game-play? Well a lot of the reviews complain that the story modes are too long to be worth replaying, and while I don't completely agree, I think they would enjoy the Brawl gamemode that has been added since release, which brings the game much closer to StS-esque gameplay loops without sacrificing much of what makes Griftlands unique at all.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Hmm. Its strange for me, loving a game I actually not recommend. I love the art style, the storytelling, the characters, and I was like, this will be great...well...was...for the first 5 playthrough....with the same character.....with the same NPCs....with the same storytelling. Yes. It gets repetitive, and that repetitiveness kills the magic around the game. I know, it supposed to be more of a rouglike card game than a livimng-breathing world, but still, I miss the magic about that. What if new missions every time or new excuses when you start over? What if new conditions?I know, it will take a hell of a lot more art and development, but I guess heres hopeing developers gonna realise that the game after a point kills itself with the repetitiveness right now.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Love Klei games... just not this one.I first played this game when it first came out, because it was a Klei game. Beat the game on my first play-through and thought the game was mediocre. Not a real challenge and the story added nothing for me. Then I heard from a friend that the game has gone under MASSIVE updates and revamps. So, I played again years later... it's the same. Only now instead of one character, you get three. Oh, and you can play the same game over and over to be a completion-ist. What good are perks and new cards if you are just going to use them to beat the same game you beat yesterday?
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Griftlands is a card game with rogue-like and dungeon crawler elemnts. The story is intresting and i was surpised by the amount of cards tha the early-access of the game has. The battle mechanics and the fact that u can talk your way pretty match for the majority of the game and your decisions will affect the behaviour of the NPC's is pretty nice. If you like slay the spire u will love this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Everything I love about Monster Train and Slay The Spire + Story. I did luck into a win my very first run so I'm not certain about the difficulty but I do consider myself competent in deckbuilding games.  I did rescue a puppy early on and my game kind of took a dark turn story wise when I maybe gave up on the idea of not killing people.... since they kept attacking my pup. I'm happy to say the pup did survive to the end of the story and went on to have many puppies afterwards. 10/10 would school John Wick again.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Great deckbuilder game with lots of interesting mechanics, great replayability, funny events and beautiful artstyle. You may need some time to learn the cards and what your enemies can do but after that it's always a real blast to play! One of my favourite games released these past years.It's well worth the price and runs on lower-end computers, if you like this kind of game you should at least give it a try.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I really like it. I like the story and that actions have repercussions later on. Also that even though it's a card battler you can do negations instead of fights and spare your opponents, make friends etc.. it's not as violent as many games are. Also big plus for me is that it's pretty relaxed, you can take your time and it doesn't give me so much adrenalin / stress like a shooter..
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: This takes the rogue-like deckbuilder (RLDB) games to a whole new level! The animation and voices are top-notched! What it adds to the typical RLDBs are the narrative stories and the ability to TALK instead of FIGHT. Talking is essentially the same as fighting, but it adds another cool new way to drive the narrative of the game!Check out this link for my video walkthrough and review -
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: This game is beautiful. Genuinely. I'm a really big fan of the fact that there's a story with NPCs you can win over to help you both passively and in the story. It's so sick. Combat is fun, Negotiations are really neat (don't get the difference in red/green yet) and love the backstories of the character.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: A good deck builder in which you manage two decks in each run and can choose from three classes that have unique cards and tactics. This gives it a lot of mechanical variation and good replayability. The world is well thought out and brought to life by a large number of NPCs. The NPCs all have random relationships so be careful if you leave a trail of bodies and don't forget that you can never have too many friends.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed the story line to begin with, and once you're accustomed to it it's quite easy to skip it all or play one of the faster modes. I can see it being a small annoyance after many hours but I still think overall its a plus and something new (for me) to be involved in the story of one of these type of card games.I also think it's great to have two different type of decks and have to balance yourself between both decks.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: First, Shout out to Hutts on Youtube for playing this to me and others through his channel.This game is a great deck builder with choices to be made and never feels boring. I love this game and I am looking forward to what they decide to do with it in future updates and what not. For anyone wondering if you should spend you money on this I would recommend reading reviews and looking at videos to see if this game is up your alley. But if you are reading my review and you are up for deck builders and just good games in general then let me tell you, this game is for you my dude. Buy it while it's on sale and if not then still get it, you will get more than your moneys worth playing it.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a cool concept but the story lines are ridiculously dumb. If you like random religious mumbo jumbo, then this is your game. Why does this game revolve around all of these fake religions and all the stupid aspects of each one? Don't we have enough of that is this world?It seems like this game is trying to make some sort of social commentary but only the developers get the joke.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: You liked Slay the Spire but missed an interesting Story and more in depth mechanics? Then Griftlands is the game for you! A lot of interesting new Mechanics (for example there are 2 battle types, normal battles and negotiations. Both have their unique cards and resolve mechanics), very nice graphic style and a cool sci fi Scenario. You build up relations with different people to get upgrades for your battles, get pets to aid you in battles an so on. For me this was a hidden gem I just stumbled upon
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: This company only makes great games it seems.  Considering the price and that it is early access, the game gives alot of play time.  I had 30 hours in before the third character came out.  Overall great value.  The gameplay mechanics feel original and fresh and keep you interested.  Late game combos feel great.  10/10 everyone should play
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly a wonderful game, music during fights is climactic and even increases in tension as health drops, each character is incredibly unique and introduces phenomenally interesting mechanics, and every correct move feels great when you synergise and link cards together! Truly one of my favorite games of all time, Hutts brought me here and I don't regret coming!! Overall an easy 9/10 for me!
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: The word that comes to mind is polished. Griftlands' balancing, art, and progression are all fantastic, and watching the story unfold is a great experience. Klei always puts out great things, and now they've made the best roguelike I've seen in a while. Please do yourself the favor of getting it, and enjoy your time in Havaria.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Klei does it again.  A brilliant gem full of depth and character.  The art & sound are incredible and set up a wonderful sci-fi almost Mandalorian like atmosphere.  The core gameplay is fun and engaging, easy to pick up hard to master.  Negotiations, the handling of the battles aggressor, the handling of end of battle choices are just some of the wrinkles I've enjoyed vs. the other big dog (Slay the Spire) and it has a great story!  I look forward to watching this one blossom like Oxygen Not Included and Don't Starve before it.  Fun!

_childDocuments_.review: Klei is very good at making games. I'm stating the obvious, but it's true - between the art, gameplay, branching story (and multiple MCs), and replay value, I can't recommend this game enough. I've played 150+ hours of StS and 25+ hours of Monster Train (probably the closest comparable things), I LOVE rogue-likes and deckbuilders. I love the 2 deck system as a fresh take of needing to balance what type of encounters you choose (spoiler: there will ALWAYS be encounters where you have to fight, so always negotiating, like I did initially, can leave your deck woefully unprepared for certain encounters). I like that USING the card is what gains experience for upgrades, so you don't have to wait for certain events. The "relic" system ("grafts") are interesting and pretty well balanced, and they level up based on encounters like your cards. The art is breathtaking and there's a great deal of environmental storytelling. And speaking of storytelling, yes there are some cliches, but overall it provides two (soon to be three) solid MC characters with backgrounds that are fun to explore and branching paths that allow you to craft multiple permutations on the story. Very satisfying, and so much fun to replay.One thing I will say is that this game is still in development, so expect some bugs from time to time. Balance between certain cards, relics, and abilities can be skewed. I've also noticed some balance issues in the "Brawl" modes (i.e. snowballing can be really easy later on in a brawl run), but story gameplay is rather balanced. Overall, these are small observations that don't lessen my enjoyment.Overall, 9.5/10, and that's as a DEVELOPMENTAL build - I can only imagine it will keep getting better and better all the time.

_childDocuments_.review: Through an interesting combination of style and innovation, Klei has nailed what makes deckbuilder games so damn fun to play. Though there are only three characters compared to other builders having a variety of choices, each one is dramatically unique in both styles of card driven combat. How you play one will not be how you play another. And it's not always obvious until you've given it another run or several. However, whether you experience all the game has to offer you (which is a lot) is entirely based on how deeply this game can grab you for each of its extended sessions. At 20 hours, I feel that I'm about at a point where I'm ready to call it enough.So first off, negotiations. Griftlands is all about risk, reward, and relationships - most of them bitter and hateful to some degree. Negotiations hit this the best by being a straightforward source of conflict. If you succeed, something great will happen for you, but if you fail, then you risk failing an objective, or making the following battle harder, or even creating a battle where there wasn't going to be one. Plus it uses its own unique health pool so you're pushed to use it as your first line of defense compared to your "die if exhausted" health pool. If you do really well with it then you can spend a good chunk of your game with health preserved for the really bitter fights - such as the unavoidable boss fights at the end of every day. Following that you have battles, which play more like a traditional deckbuilder in execution - play cards, defeat enemies. Griftlands personalizes it a little more through its complicated sense of morality. You can kill enemies to get more precious limited money and special powerful items - but risk upsetting their friends whom will hate you and inflict potentially crippling debuffs to you. Or you can let them go - often leading to them hating you and inflicting you with crippling debuffs anyways - not that you're aware of these outcomes, it's all in the game.Where I feel Griftlands stumbles is a weird thing to discuss. Past Prestige 0, running out of health means game over which is a loss of your entire run. In Griftlands, a run is about 3 to 5 hours. A lot happens and the game is generous in how it eases up the difficulty so it's rare to actually die, but it is a constant risk to suddenly find that you're back at the start again. Plus every time you gain a level from post-game exp, you gain more interesting cards that can greatly mix up how you play each character in exciting new ways. But I hesitate to go back in knowing that if I don't take breaks (not something I do often with roguelike games) then I'm dedicating a lot of time to a run. Like, a lot of time. Most games have runs that last around an hour and a half at most. It's hard to imagine Griftlands as being a shorter game in its current state. Some of the excitement is in building a monster deck that shreds through foes, decks you spend a lot of time building and perfecting. Even the streamlined Griftlands experience that is Brawl mode will be three hours, and the deck I build feels like one that I wouldn't want to spend less time working on. All these resources to improve, and it's difficult to say that shortening the game in some way would make it better.Ultimately I feel my time with Griftlands is coming to an end, not due to lack of content, interest, enjoyment, or otherwise - but because other roguelike experiences fit in a cleaner time frame. I feel motivated to do run after run in shorter "popcorn run" games. Failure doesn't hit as hard (though, again, terminal failure thankfully doesn't come often in Griftlands). There's a lot still here to experience and it's all very interesting, but I don't think it's for me. Then again I struggled with Slay the Spire and everyone loves that game, so maybe I just am not a big deckbuilder roguelike person. Griftlands gets an easy recommendation at full price, though as of writing Smith (the third character and a personal favorite for getting into fights with) doesn't have a full campaign yet. That doesn't mark against it in the slightest. Klei knows how to make solid beautiful games and continues to demonstrate it with Griftlands.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm playing in early access and this is already a pretty solid game with plenty to do. Good integration of deck-builder with RPG-lite; you don't get  "flavor" dialog choices, but you do make decisions that affect your game and outcomes, and the characters' stories are interesting and fit the gritty feel. The combat system is pretty well balanced and includes some interesting effects, and I like the way that it's heavily tailored to the character you are playing. They feel very distinctly different in their approach and style, and the same is true for the negotiation decks. Making negotiation its own deck battle is an interesting choice and generally works well, adding depth to encounters where you can choose between battling through an adversary or trying to bluff or bamboozle them. Negotiation was a little confusing the first couple of rounds, but it's not hard to pick up. I also like the mechanics of the kill/accept surrender decisions in physical battles; there are consequences for killing people, especially in areas where it's likely to become known, so it's worth weighing the risk/benefit balance and sometimes even figuring out how to stop allies from killing someone. The post-story-line battles are a little less exciting just because they don't lead to any particular goal, but the daily runs shake things up a bit, and the unlockable perks are good and add significantly to a morphing balance of game dynamics. Overall, I feel like I've already gotten my money's worth, and I'm looking forward to the next update.

_childDocuments_.review: The meta-level game design here is on another level. I don't know how they did it, but the game is perfectly paced between runs; something Griftlands does better than any other roguelike deckbuilder I've played. I never felt like I spend too long in a doomed run, and I always felt that even when I whiffed on a run, I was still making the correct amount of progress. This game has probably my most frustrating run in the genre and also my most satisfying. I like the characters, the writing is decent, and the story differs enough that it didn't feel repetitive.

_childDocuments_.review: There are many games that have borrowed slay the spire's mechanics for various twists or innovations. _childDocuments_.review: I'm confused. And I'm confused about why I am confused.It seems the problem is expectations I had by looking at the steam page prior to purchase.That I expected was Slay-the-Spire-like rogue-lite/-like deck building game. But this is a completely wrong analogy.Yes, this game has deck building in it but thats it. No more similarities between the two. And I don't like what I've got in exchange.Now let's assume I had no expectations. How this game fare by itself? Actually pretty bad gameplay-wise:- overcomplicated. Not a "gradual complication increase" as in other deck builders, e.g. Slay the Spire gives you only Warrior at first with extremly simple attacks and grow on that. Here during first few runs you will be overwhelmed with random affixes, buzzwords and whatnot.- story. It's not Hades. I tried read story for first half an hour and clicked through everything afterwards cause it felt like unnecessary bloat (I should mention again, I was looking for Slay-the-Spire-type game, so there might be a bias, but result is result - constant story interjections made my experience worse)- 2 "different" plays: diplomacy and battle. On paper it sure sounds cool but in actuality it's same ♥♥♥♥ but with different abilities. The problem is you have to do both in the same run. Even if you defeat a boss with diplomacy - it will still force you to fight it. So you actually have no actual choice how to do the run - you have to mingle-mangle both battling types. Otherwise if you skew you abilities to either side - you will lose eventually. I feel like it would be much better to allow to use single fighting style per run altogether.At first I thought about trying to play it more, thinking "maybe I just didn't understand it yet" but after reading some reviews it seems I'm in did-not-enjoyed herd here... how unfortunate...
