_childDocuments_.review: I've paid much more for much worse games. All and all if you like deck building games at all this offers a really fun and challenging system. Theres a rougelike element to it, where you're playing the same story over and over but with subtle differences, especially depending on your choices. The story is fairly interesting, though with only limited voice acting it becomes a chore reading all the dialog that has no bearing on your run, and I find myself skipping through quite a bit of it. But its easy enough to scroll back up and see any important detail you skipped if you're confused about whats happening. As far as I'm concerned the real fun is in the cards and just deciding how to deal with situations as they arise. The rest is just cute sci fi set dressing, but i'm not here for the lore and world building tbh. Though if you're more into just reading a sci-fi graphic novel theres also a story emphasized difficulty where you can immerse yourself in the world and not worry about getting good at the card game. All told, 3 hours in and I see myself playing much much more. I assume it'll get a bit boring and tedious doing at some point, but it seems there'll be enough variation in each run to keep it interesting, albeit with maybe some breaks between runs. Not to mention theres a daily challenge mode I unlocked but haven't touched yet. Griftlands is plenty of fun for the price and its a perfect game to relax and unwind with. Even the challenging parts, and times where I got my ass handed to me didn't feel frustrating or necessarily unfair. This is my new go to for now when I need a break from more competitive online games that sometimes get me a little too worked up. I found this game exactly when I needed it. Wonderful!
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Turns out what Slay the Spire was always missing was a greater story focus! The story generally has one clear end goal for each character but everything that happens in between is random or a choice of 2 opposing factions making it unique each time. Some of the random quests are also great. Like I was going for a prisoner exchange and then on the way my team mate says: hold up there is a criminal we should arrest. So I do that and then when we deliver the half dead woman to the prison they are like: that's no criminal that's the admirals second mate! Combat is pretty much the same as sts but you can also hire mercenaries or pets to fight for you. New is the negotiation which is another card battle but with different mechanics and cards. It's really refreshing. Great card game with heavy story focus.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great rogue-lite deck builder.  Stick with it.  It's a lot different than monster train and slay the spire, in with both of those games and other derivatives  I never had a problem jumping in and beating the game in the first run or two but this game required a certain strategy that i haven't seen in clones.  It really took me by surprise because it didn't seem like there were a lot of resources to manage, but as you get into the nooks and crannies there's quite a few strategies you have to worry about with the cards, and again with your relationships in game. _childDocuments_.review: I have played and beat Slay the Spire extensively, up to level 10 ascension if i remember correctly. And i was quite critical of Griftlands when it was first release in early access. The deckbuilding aspect was not balanced and thus not interesting.Several months later, the game has evolved in the right direction. It is not disapointing anymore to me, i actually love it and i am now wondering if i'll go back to slay.If you loved slay the spire and if you like the art of Griftlands, go for it.One thing i didn't see coming is how the story driven adventure influences your deck building and vice versa. An exemple. As the first character, Sal, if you build an aggressive (Red) negociation deck, you might want to team up with the bandits, because if you team up with the cops, you will be facing bandits in negociation battles. But they have an argument : escalation that becomes uber strong if you play a heavy red deck.So you have all this aspect of chosing your missions depending on what kind of deck you built and your relations with the different factions in the game and all of this mixes up pretty darn well.Klei are just that good...

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed this game for its campaign, but I think there are too many negatives to really recommend it as a roguelite deckbuilder.- The campaigns are fun. The latter ones are well-written.- The dual deck system creates some variety of play within a run and theoretically provides some balance decisions (using a deck more makes it better ... but neglecting one can make you lose)- The negotiation format is unique in my experience of deckbuilders and I think it's a neat conceptualization.- Managing relationships with NPCs is simple, intuitive and additive.- Linking upgrades to card use is satisfying.- Artwork and sound design is great.- Run variety is too limited. - Each character has unique elements, but the majority of the mechanics are functionally similar between them.- The starting decks feel a little too thick. This makes it hard to quickly specialize into a build.- The starting cards have too many upgrade options. It's great that they give you two choices, but 90% of the time you want one of those options to be the option where the card is destroyed after a single use so that you can replace it with specialized cards.- The previous points are mainly a problem because .- Mettle progression is super slow relative to the other meta-currencies. And apparently the highest difficulty removes this progress anyway.- For the sheer number of potential friends/enemies, there really isn't much variety. In negotiations, you'll only fight ~10 different enemies. In Battles, most characters are indistinguishable.- And run pacing doesn't feel good in Brawl (roguelite) mode. Part of why Slay the Spire works is that individual battles are fast and you get to update your deck rapidly. Monster Train takes the opposite approach -- fewer battles that take longer, but you make big changes between each. Griftlands has lots of medium-length battles with mostly small upgrades in between. Maybe my decision-making would get faster if I played more, but after 50 hours it's still taking me 2.5 hours per brawl. I was attempting 20-minute runs by that point in Slay the Spire.Ultimately, I think the achievement completion rates are telling. The achievements actually reward doing cool things in the game and I wanted to attempt them ... but the lack of replayability means it's not fun enough to stick around for that. Considering the most-completed achievement is 4.3%, it seems like others agree.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: A good card game of the flavor of Slay the Spire (one of my favorites), but adds an engaging story on top that gives some depth to the characters and battles you are playing. Each of the 3 characters has 2 decks (battle and negotiation) which have different feels to them. Within each deck is 2 clear overarching strategies that play very different and of course can be mixed for extra versatility. Lots of variety packed into 3 story lines that makes me want to keep playing. It was extremely satisfying the first time I won a run, much more so than other games in this genre.

_childDocuments_.review: One word: Mind-blowing.Initially, I suspected this would be a replica of Slay the Spire. But I was proven wrong immediately.First impression of the game - insane. I was blown away the moment I launched the game. I'm someone that takes graphics really seriously so the main menu itself was enough to make an impression. It was so well made. Not just the menu, the game graphics and sounds are amazing. The narration of the story wasn't annoying either. It felt like it was supposed to be there. Everything just gel-ed together.Then there's the gameplay. Sure, it's about playing your cards right, like Slay the Spire and any other card battlers. But there's so much more to  this game than just that. There's 2 types of fights that I am aware of thus far - flat out beating your opponent or negotiating. And both of them are 2 different systems. You get to be more adventurous in how you would like to experience your run.NPCs will also react to you differently based on your choice of actions. Kill their friend? They'll hate you. Give them money? They'll love you. You can even bribe them or buy them drinks to improve your relationship. This just adds a whole new level of depth and immersion to the game because it seems like you have control over your character's fate! Also, befriending different NPCs can provide you different perks, which further contributes diversifies the 'blocks' you can use to build your play style.Oh and did I mention you can get PETS? PETS. Sign me the freak up. I'm more than just in love with this game!
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Griftlands borrows the best gameplay mechanics from Slay the Spire (Deck Building) and FTL (Desicion Making) while also adding some unique twists to this genre. You're playing with two decks. One for fighting one for negotiating.At times the dialogues feels lackluster but seeing that this game's still in Early Access there's still room for improvement on that front. Otherwise the game feels really refreshing when you played your share of Slay the Spire and that's due to the story, the setting and it's characters.And it looks nice as well. You can tell it's made by the creators of Shank and Mark of the Ninja.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who has never played virtual card games before, I wasn't expecting much from Griftlands. But man this game provides so much fun replayability. You have three characters with their own unique stories and encounters. Each of them have their own play styles that can be customised to suit your preferred playstyle. My favourite way to play, so far, is having a mix of (over)charge and burn effects for the character Rook. Oh and you get two decks, one for battle and one for diplomacy. Characters also have different playstyles for diplomacy too, which makes every run feel somewhat new. However, battle decks do take precedence as most bosses will end with a battle (diplomacy can weaken them sometimes). The artstyle and writing is solid. NPCs are quite memorable thanks to the great artwork. Overall, this is a great game with a lot of replayability and it is something I can easily recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing game. Great replay value, probably over 1000 different outcomes based on your decisions. _childDocuments_.review: I love the world. I love the art. I love the dry wit writing. I love the music. I love everything EXCEPT the actual game.Griftlands is a roguelite, but very little actually complements that design. Each of the three campaigns takes roughly 5 hours to complete on average, which is too long for the pick-up-and-play appeal of typical roguelites, but also too short for the kind of multi-layered stories this game wants to tell. I think part of the problem is that the card games, both for fighting and negotiations, take a very long time to play out compared to other games of this type.The main draw of the game is the way the world dynamically reacts to your actions. You make a friend? That friend will help you out when they can, but they might also have enemies. Kill someone? Their friends will be out for your head, but their enemies will like what you're doing. And it gets a lot more nuanced than that. But since the campaigns reset either at the end or if you die, nothing ever sticks. So this system never reaches its full potential.Basically, I'm fascinated by the world this game created, but the roguelite format prevents me from exploring it as much as I would like to. If it were up to me, this game would probably have been better as a D&D-type experience, with procedurally-generated characters existing in this world within the various factions, and a player that can interact with and influence everything for a seamless, evolving story.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting take on the roguelite genre where there's a bigger focus on choice and story. Your actions mostly have consequences but unfortunately, it's easy to see a pattern regarding events and such. You know when things will happen and it's easy to plan your runs which will in turn lower the replayability for standard runs. On the positive side, once you've completed a character's story you can play it with mutators and different card packs which affect the run in different ways. There are currently two different characters implemented, both which provides two very different playstyles (as much as possible, at least) and stories. A third character is in development and if it's on par with the other two then it will most likely be great content.I can't say how the development of the game will progress but I can confidently state that the game is well worth the price of €10 during the sale and will no doubt be worth the full price too. I do recommend the game if you're interested in it, and if you're uncertain then  which they've so helpfully provided.TL;DR:Good content. Do recommend. More content to come.

_childDocuments_.review: I just finished my first run with . It took me 7 hours, because I played very slowly, trying to learn all the cards, grafts and mechanics, and making every possible conversation. Having played Slay the Spire for a while now, it was nice to see a game that is so familiar yet so novel at the same time. For reference, my battle deck came out as a Bleed-focused, fast and aggressive deck (which made me skip a ton of Combo-based cards), a bit familiar with Silent's Poison decks in StS, but with more front-loaded (burst) damage.- The fact that you can choose to fight or negotiate in basically 90% of your decisions.- The story, the writing, the diversity and personality of the characters.- The fact that you can make friends or enemies with basically any person you encounter, and the buffs or debuffs they give.- Familiar, mostly straightforward card mechanics and an easily understandable UI.- The card upgrade system.- I am by no means an experienced player of deck-building games, and my first try did seem a bit too easy. I once got close to being defeated in battle, and once get beaten in a negotiation, but that's it. I blazed through the final boss with only a pet on my side, and . Hopefully the Prestige levels (what Ascensions are in StS) will make the game a bit more difficult.- Replayability in vanilla seems a bit iffy, with the story being the same for each character, but there are different paths you can go down on, different decisions to make, characters to befriend or anger. Also with the new mod compatibility, I'm sure that tons of community-made content will be available, including new stories and PCs.Overall I feel like I found a new favorite, and I'm very much looking forward to the final product and all the additions the developers will implement in the game in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: If you’re a fan of deck-building games with a strong narrative twist, Griftlands is a gem you won’t want to miss. Klei Entertainment has crafted a truly engaging experience that combines strategic deck-building with rich storytelling and decision-making.Griftlands places you in a gritty, dystopian world where every decision can have far-reaching consequences. The game’s standout feature is its dual-layered gameplay: a deck-building system that’s as deep as it is satisfying, and a narrative-driven choice system that keeps the story evolving based on your actions. Each playthrough feels fresh, thanks to the multiple characters you can choose from, each with their own unique storylines and abilities.The deck-building aspect is brilliantly executed. You’ll find yourself constantly tweaking your deck, weighing the pros and cons of various cards, and strategizing how to tackle the diverse challenges that come your way. The combat is engaging and requires tactical thinking, and the blend of negotiation and combat adds a unique layer of depth to the gameplay.Visually, the game is a delight with its distinctive art style that perfectly complements its narrative and thematic elements. The character designs and animations are full of personality and bring the world to life.However, the game’s complexity might be a hurdle for newcomers. There’s a learning curve that can be a bit steep at first, and the sheer amount of mechanics and choices can be overwhelming. But once you get past the initial adjustment period, the rewards are well worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Among the most enjoyable of the Slay the Spire-inspired card games.This is a deck building card battler heavily inspired by Slay the Spire. That said, it offers several interesting twists. Runs are story driven campaigns with three different characters each with unique decks and mechanics. The runs are on the longer side, with each one clocking in at between 2 and 3 hours or so.You're forced to balance two different decks, one for battles and one for negotiations. Cards are upgraded by playing them multiple times, a nice idea with the unfortunate side effect of incentivising you to drag out easy fights as long as possible. My favourite innovation is the relationship system, where your actions can make other characters love, like, dislike or hate you. If a character is positive towards you they will be easier to influence and will help out if they are present for a fight or negotiation, if they dislike you they will work against you. If a character loves you you get useful bonuses and if they hate you you get annoying debuffs. It's a fun system that makes you avoid making too many enemies and forcing you to tread carefully before starting fights in rooms full of people who hate you.The card-play is VERY similar to Slay the Spire and if you enjoy that this will make a fun distraction for a while.There are issues with the game that will hurt its staying power for me though. - The enemies are not compelling. The hardest fights in the game are just 'big number' fights against enemies with lots of hit points, who do more damage. There are very fewer unique enemies that force you to plan your deck around or vary your strategies in any way. - The card pool feels off. There are lots of cards that do very little or provide a small bonus with an annoying debuff to balance it out (if you're a Slay the Spire fan - think of Ironclad card Berserk, many cards like that here). I find myself skipping card after card in this game. A lot of the good cards feel like Attack+ kind of cards, that do a little more damage or apply a debuff. The negotiation decks are more interesting, but a lot of winning decks seem to come down to 'pick a few strong cards and hope for the best'. There are a few archetypes for each character, but not the multitude of synergies and interactions that the best deckbuilders have.- The 'create your own adventure' story path is fun the first time through, but suffers from diminishing returns as you return on harder levels.- You seem to 'snowball' hard in this game, by the halfway point I'm either smashing everything in my path or crawling to inevitable defeat. A couple of strong early rewards can lead to crushingly strong runs. This is not terrible in and of itself, but coupled with the long play time for each run there can be a lengthy 'going through the motions phase'.I've had a lot of fun with it. I've put in many hours and will keep going until I've beaten it on all characters at the highest difficulty, but the meat of the card play is not strong enough that I'll persist after that. One of the stronger games in the genre, but well below Monster Train or StS in my estimation.

_childDocuments_.review: Remember when everyone thought  was going to be the new hotness? No? Can’t say I blame you. For just a moment, it looked fantastic! A super cool world, solid art, and  innovative gameplay. Unfortunately, I found replayability to be low, and it’s too short to be very memorable. But if you are just looking for a something that’s good for 15-30 hours,  is a solid choice.Let’s start at the top. Brought to us by ,  shining star is it’s truly innovative gameplay. This is the same studio that made the surprisingly captivating side-scrolling stealth game , the very non-traditional survival game , and of course, the rougelike rhythm game . Good, innovative games is what  does. combines the deckbuilding rougelike genre with solid RPG elements to make you feel like your choices are much deeper than just, “what’s the best card I can pick.” It also adds . You have two completely separate decks/stats to develop. A traditional combat deck, and a deck built around resolving your conflict via negotiation. Sure, in the grand scheme of things, they are both “card-based combat,” but approaching it as a negotiation means you have to think about the cards and the underlying system completely differently. Do you want to be Intimidating? Or Diplomatic? If you do both, your deck could get watered down. If you don’t have some diversity, you might run into someone who counters you hard. How you chose to approach the Negotiation part of the game has a big impact on how the game plays out as well (people may not like you if you are Intimidating).You also have to be careful to work on both your Negotiation and Combat decks. Negotiation can get you past a lot of encounters, or make some things a lot easier. But your deck gets stronger the more you use it…and by the end of a run you will have some very tough negotiations and combats that you cannot avoid.There are three main characters, each with their own unique story. They all play out very differently, with different combat and negotiation specialties. Skills you learned playing the 1st character, do not translate well when playing the 2nd or 3rd. The story is very well written, and helps you stay tuned into the game. Lastly, the world felt a bit like…(if I can exaggerate a bit)…like watching  for the first time. A deep, well thought out world that has immense potential…and you know you are only seeing a tiny piece of what is possible.My biggest problem with the game revolves around the replayability. Each run consists of 4 days. Within each day, there will be a lot of procedurally generated encounters and events. Even when you are given a “story quest,” more than half the time it is picked from a short list of possible quests. The quests are balanced well for the level that you encounter them, but…What isn’t balanced are the rewards. You might get a rare reward that already plays into your strengths (or you get it early so you can build on it)…or you might get trash that works against the deck you are building. Get that awesome rare late in the game…too bad you didn’t know it was coming because you built your deck wrong. I was on a serious struggle-bus with the 3rd character…I was building him so he had a lot of people love him. I had failed probably 4 or 5 runs in a row. Then I landed a rare (that I didn’t know existed) that turned my “loved” stat into a negotiation buff…WHAT?!  I breezed through that run. I want to think that the skills I was learning had something to do with it, but if I’m honest I think the card combined with my build turned the game into easy mode.Now, I enjoy games that let you try to “break the system,” but they can’t be based around what you randomly get. I don’t want to increase the difficulty because RNG might deal me a pile of crap I can’t win with…or it might deal me a hand that I can win with while I’m passed out drunk on the computer room floor.Sadly, the RPG/story elements make the game a lot of fun to play once…but they make it tedious to play after you have won. The story takes a lot of time, and you find your self trying to frantically click away the dialog because you’ve already read through this part of the story 3 times. I find it sad that the really good story turned into something annoying at the end.As a rougelike, you also expect to lose sometimes as you figure out how to win. Runs take a good bit of time (3-4 hours if you read all the dialog, 2 if you don’t), so failing and starting over starts to become a slog. Buy the time I finally completed a run for a character, I was done with the slog.  I had zero interest in replaying the story on a slightly higher difficulty.The game does offer a “combat arena” if you just want to play the card game without re-slogging (did I just make up a word?) the story. But I never tried it…I felt like too much of the magic was in the narrative and story. Plus, I couldn’t wrap my brain around a “Negotiation” combat arena…where you are negotiating for…what, exactly?So, if you only want/need a game to putz around with for 20-30 hours, there is a whole lot of good in . If you want a serious game that you can sink your teeth into for hundreds of hours, you should probably look somewhere else.

Each mode has its own "HP", if you are low on HP in battle mode, you want to try avoiding battle by winning negotiations when possible since the if you lose all your battle hp, your are just dead. - it has rich lore embedded into the game - a ton of replayability even it is still in early access at the of time of writing. - after you completed the your initial run, you can play the game in Brawl mode which is basically a streamlined mode with less lore related interactions - which essentially more linear and deck building focused. - with the story mode, it feels quite different and refreshing as you also needs to kind of manage your relationship with other NPCs to gain a better negotiation advantage.tldr; if you like Slay The Spire or Monster Train, you will like this.

Crisp sounds, lovely aniamted and "drawn" graphics and animations, THREE SEPARATE and engaging storylines with copious amounts of replay value.New characters, locations and art-work for each of the available characters, the ability to unlock costumes, cards and challenging difficulty modes for each character and playthrough. The variety in the playstyle of each character, mutators that tailor your experience to what YOU want to play... challenges to engage in for added fun and difficulty... and one could go on and on and on, about all the lovely feautres at hand.It's enjoyable in short bursts, repeated playthroughs after breaks, AS WELL as long sessions. No hassle, frustrations or micro transaction for cards and cosmetics... this is simply put **the** premier deckbuilding GAME on the market right now.For the INSANELY LOW PRICE this is truly a steal for a timeless and rejuvenating jewel of a title.If you like card games/engine building games - this is for you; Hell even if you just like fun stories in games with decisions that matter - THIS IS FOR YOU.Get it. It's great.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is very well done.  It has good stories, and a fun card playing experience.- There is a small learning curve as you figure out how certain cards benefit you, but once you get the hang of it you'll be playing cards at a glance.- This is a game that you probably won't beat on the first try.  Expect to die, most likely a few times.  You can choose a mode that takes away perma-death, but it also reduces the difficulty which this game doesn't really need to do, and dying is not all bad.  When you restart with that same character you keep a good amount of the bonuses that you've unlocked for them already so your following runs are easier each time.- The missions are somewhat randomized on each play-through as well.  You may do the same mission but for someone else that gives you an entirely different bonus/ reward, or you may do completely different missions altogether.  Giving this game really good replay value!- Each character has a different map and story, with a unique deck and play-style.  You may find one character better at negotiating and another better at battling.  Whether you chose to negotiate or battle, depending on the mission at hand, you will have a unique deck of cards that you can add to, remove cards from, and upgrade.  Each opponent that you fight or negotiate with also comes with a mostly unique set of cards and abilities.  So, you'll have to figure out what works best for each unique situation.- When you defeat an opponent in battle you may have the choice of killing or sparing them.  Each choice will effect you differently.  Killing someone off may cause someone else to dislike or hate you, though sometimes sparing someone leads to trouble further down the road.- Most NPCs start in neutral status as far as your relationship with them goes.  Based on your decisions in game, they may like you, or if you do enough, even love you.  They can also dislike or hate you.  Any time you get someone into the love or hate category you'll gain a permanent bonus or negative effect respectively.  So keeping people on your good side can be very beneficial, though sometimes impossible.  You can also get someone that likes you to help you in battle or negotiation, just be aware that they too can die.- If I had anything negative to say about this game it would be that I wish you could upgrade more cards more often, and the stories felt a little on the short side, though quite entertaining.Overall, I definitely recommend this game! I'd give it an 8.5/10!

_childDocuments_.review: Griftlands is a deckbuilder in the vein of Slay the Spire, with its own twists and quirks that make it pretty easily stand on its own merits. The visuals are nothing short of stunning, with huge, animated sprites and a surprising variety of motions between all the different character types. It also seems to follow the 'rule of cool' in regards to enemy weapon choice: did the acolyte guys need to use a fistful of cyber-kunai? Do the spear-using enemies have to flashily twirl their weapon with every action? No, but that stuff is so cool to look at that the game is definitely better for it. The detail and flourish to the visuals is remarkable. It's like playing a stylish, beautiful cartoon.The three playable characters have very distinct deck themes and a few mechanics unique to each of them, along with their own story mode, which brings me to my next point. This is not Slay the Spire. Griftlands is far more narratively focused, with an abundance of dialogue, a decent sense of humor, and a fairly long story mode for each character, as well as some emphasis on befriending and hiring NPC party members for temporary support. There is still a more traditional 'Brawl' mode, but it feels less developed than the story modes. There are choices to be made in story mode that change the plot and some events, but it only takes 2-3 runs to see the vast majority of alternate outcomes which does hamper the replay value a bit (it also doesn't take long to unlock all the cards for each character). It does allow for a more relaxed and carefully-paced experience though; there is always a shop available and the rewards for each mission and event are clearly displayed. I would say, on average, it's a bit easier than its peers in the genre, although as always if you crank up the ascension/covenant/griftlands equivalent (prestige) it can still be pretty difficult.I personally enjoy the card exp and variety of upgrades, and how it feels like you're building a character rather than just randomly drafting all the cards you use. It also encourages you to use all of your cards even if it's not an optimal play, as they only gain exp when played early enough in a battle. The negotiation system is also intriguing, with it having its own deck and mechanics for each character, along with the potential unique benefits when you win... but since it's almost entirely optional I feel the meta is, unfortunately, to simply focus on your combat deck and forego negotiation, as you can die in combat encounters but not in negotiations, and every boss is primarily a combat encounter. It can still be fun to negotiate for better rewards or an easier combat, at least at lower difficulties, and building the two decks in parallel can be fun in itself.Klei did a great job with Griftlands, and I hope the game gets some more attention from fans. It should go without saying that the 'soft' parts of the game e.g. the UI, the sound design etc, are capably done and facilitate a smooth gameplay experience. It's a bit less hardcore than Slay the Spire while still being chock full of deckbuilding, synergistic comboing goodness... and style! It's my personal favorite of the genre and I would heartily recommend it, but the gentler challenge and lower replay value could turn more die-hard players away.

_childDocuments_.review: This game could be so good...The main issue I have with this game is the lack of engaging stories in the provided campaigns (excluding one, which is still average at best). The deck building provides some unique twists and gameplay loops, even providing additional ways of play outside of combat, but compared to counterparts like Monster Train and Slay the Spire still feels uncharted and lackluster.  One aspect that balances the scales in favor of Griftlands is the art direction (which Klei never seems to miss) and tight, hypnotic sound effects.Although overall there's still a mediocre experience to be had, it's surprisingly and disappointingly cut short with a lack of variety in deck building content, player-driven decisions that warrant additional playthroughs, and un-engaging short stories that made me wanting more, but having nothing left to play with.

_childDocuments_.review: This was my first deck-building game, and it was a pretty good one to introduce me to the concept. You play as one of three mercenary characters known as Grifters: Sal, Rook, and Smith, each of whom is unlocked after playing through the previous one's story. Sal is on a quest for revenge against the debt broker who sold her into slavery as a child; Rook is a former Admiralty spy now working as a freelance spy, navigating a conflict between the technocratic Spark Barons and the rebellious workers' organization known as the Rise; Smith is the black sheep of his family, looking to gain his place back at the family table after being disowned following his parents' death, and is willing to do what it takes, including taking out his own siblings.Each character starts out with two decks: One for negotiations and one for battle, the two ways you interact with other characters during missions as you make your way through your character's story. Negotiation is used to convince them to do what you want or help you out without violence; Battle is used if you don't have the patience of talk. Sometimes you're given a choice between the two, other times you're forced to do one of them. In negotiations your cards are used to attack your opponent's arguments and shore up yours. In battle you fight one or more enemies, with the option of sparing them or killing them when you win. Be careful, if you kill them in public, one of their friends will hate you, which gives you a disadvantage. Do favors for people, buy them drinks, give them gifts, and they may love you, and give you a special advantage. You can also buy special implants called grafts that give you special bonuses and abilities in negotiation and battle.After each encounter, the cards you used gain experience and can be upgraded, and new cards can be added to your deck. Or not. Having a bloated deck can be hard to play with, having to wait for a particular card to enter your hand. Having a well-curated deck can be the key to victory, especially at harder difficulty levels. Each of the three main characters have unique play styles to mix things up a bit. Each time you play their stories, there are randomized encounters, and different characters play different roles: Someone who was a bouncer or a bodyguard in one play through could be doing something completely different in the next.There's a lot I'm leaving out or forgetting to mention. There are different play modes, prestige difficulty levels, and other stuff. Give the game a try (there's a demo you can download).

_childDocuments_.review: This game takes some really great concepts from Slay the Spire and other games in this genre and packages them into a very unique roguelike. Instead of choosing a clearly drawn path and going from point A to B, you spend days building (or destroying) relationships and deciding between various mutually exclusive encounters. _childDocuments_.review: When I first booted up Griftlands, I was slightly anxious about its busy UI and constant decision making. It was extremely reminiscent of old-school CRPGs, games like classic Fallout or Baldur's Gate, where you're given a lot of freedom and a lot of information right from the beginning, and you have to figure things out for yourself. In theory, I really like games with complex systems where 'your choices matter,' but in practice, they tend to exhaust me, and I rarely finish them. As I kept playing, I got a taste for the mechanics and found them enjoyable. Then I died, restarted, and realized the genius of the game.Griftlands is a Roguelite, so it is intended to be replayed many, many times. This means that you get to screw around in the story, experimenting not just with different playstyles but with different versions of your main character. The game always offers you more than one way to progress, and are given a lot of freedom both in a single run and in between runs to choose the playstyle you want. Want to be a silver-tongued slick talker, avoiding conflicts through wits and negotiation? Give it a try, and then whether you win or die, you can start over and try a more combat-focused approach. Either way, the game rewards you after every run with a bit of progress towards unlocking permanent perks and difficulty modifiers to help you hone any chosen playstyle.And there are a lot of playstyles. Griftlands is also not just one but two very well designed deckbuilder card games. Negotiation and combat each have a dedicated deck with its own set of rules and a handful of different approaches available. Choosing to fight or talk through a problem means choosing which of your two decks to use, and using a deck gives both experience to upgrade your cards and a chance to add new cards to the deck. The more you use one strategy, the better you get at it. Building and playing with a well honed deck can feel really satisfying, and figuring out how to make a good deck is made accessible by the game's replayability. Failing doesn't feel punishing, because you're always moving forwards in something, unlocking some new content or learning something that helps you strategize for your next run.The game is also surprisingly well written. Intriguing moral choices pop up naturally throughout the game, and your responses to them aren't tacked on in cutscenes - they're a natural part of the existing mechanics. There's always two sides to a story, and you are always given the chance to choose sides. A lot of quests have little twists in them, where the person hiring you didn't tell you the whole story or where things just get out of hand and you find yourself with more than one valid way of 'completing' the quest, up to and including failing it on purpose, forfeiting the reward and putting you at odds with the person who hired you. There are no throwaway characters - every NPC is unique, with something to offer if you befriend them and a complication they can toss your way if you get on their bad side. Also, all of them can die - any character you beat in combat gives you the choice to kill or spare them, and there are often compelling reasons on both sides of that coin. Killing opponents can give immediate rewards and remove the ability for that character to complicate things for you later. However, gaining a reputation for murder might affect other aspects of the game, making enemies of your victim's allies and changing how other characters see you. It also removes those characters from the run, while sparing them might open up new options and oppurtunities.Replaying the game and finding out all the different ways things can play out is made rewarding both in gameplay and in the story. This makes roleplaying accessible and interesting, but also makes it fun and engaging to actually learn the ins and outs of the game. The game's difficulty is highly modular, with different characters, modes, and builds that all have an oppurtunity to utterly change the experience. It's not a game you get tired of easily. There's just so much content, and all of it is good.

_childDocuments_.review: Story focused rouge light in a very literal way. This game stands as an interesting counterpoint to Hades. Both are rouge lights focused on story, but each approaches that element completely differently. While Hades streamlines the process with the story on the front and back ends of a run allowing for completely free game play in the middle, this game features story as the game play. Oh boy is there a lot to dissect there. This kind of design choice is inherently front loaded. Because the story is the game play, once you've experienced the story the game play becomes stale, meaning the game is front loaded in terms of play quality. Once you've experienced the story, the story choices you make are completely null because you just start taking the paths that give the best outcome. Each of the three classes has three play troughs at most before you reach that point. At it's most simple, that means you're going to have ten to fifteen hours of the highest quality play time before it gets stale. But here's the thing, the story elements are very enjoyable and the front loaded time is very, very fun. By the time you get to standard rouge light fair of just pushing runs through, you've already had your fill. Now here's where I think the game excels past average, once you reach the point of standard rouge light, it's still surprisingly fun. I warmed up to it. The game gives you a wide range of goals to work towards, and there is just enough variety outside of the story for you to mix things up and experiment. There's issues there, but it's pretty good for what it is. In total, this means Griftlands is above average and worth checking out if you're a fan of the genre. It offers something novel with a moderate amount of replayability, and that's pretty cool, especially for someone like me who has played a lot of rouge lights. I'd still recommend playing Hades first, but this one is pretty fun too. 6/10.

_childDocuments_.review: I think that by the time I finish this game, I will probably have more hours in Klei games than all other games combined.Klei does it again. Did you want a nice fresh new card game with a unique take on Story and Dialogue? No? Well you do now! I had only a slight itch to play a single player card game, and despite that Griftlands has stolen the show in my Steam Library.Original, fun, good looking. Great mechanics and storytelling. Very satisfying with an organic mix of scripted and procedural storytelling done right.My only complaint is that it feels like the game is split in two with a fantastic combat card game and a fantastic dialogue card game, but not much to really unite these two. For example, I'm focusing on the Improvise mechanic in Combat and I feel like that should have some impact on my Dialogue deck. Maybe some cards that can be drawn in Combat and Dialogue with slightly different effects? Maybe an Influence based Dialogue deck could be applied in Combat as ally buffs?Definitely 100% recommend to pretty much anyone, even non-gamers.

_childDocuments_.review: Really just a fantastic game. From sound design to art, from worldbuilding to gameplay, I really can't recommend it more. I'm a huge fan of roguelike card battlers and can say this is probably my favorite one. I'll just gush about the things I love. Worldbuilding and the art/sound design- it all just works together. It's like exploring a civilized Dagobah where the swamps are sentient ancient gods. Gameplay- You get choices between fighting or negotiating your way out of situations, sometimes you get no choice at all. You have health and morale as resource bars and two separate decks to manage and maintain. The balance of it all just rocks and the card battles themselves are CRISP. Choices- There are three separate storylines to follow and each one is interesting and full of replay value. There is a love/hate system that provides buffs and debuffs to your character depending on your choices- it may be easier killing someone to get a job done but you might piss off someone who was friends with them by doing so. Story- There are three characters to follow each with their own unique storyline and personality. Sal the mercenary, Rook the spy, and Smith the disappointment. They are all great for different reasons and part of the fun is deciding who they will be this time playing through their story. There is also a surprising amount of humor that has caught me off guard on several occasions. Replay value- Dude, need more of a challenge? Turn up the difficulty by taking on tougher parameters every time you play through a campaign. Unlock new cards and outfits after your runs. Don't want to do campaigns? Have a daily challenge. Or a boss rush. You do you.Also, I really enjoy that the achievements are just that- meant to be achieved through performing specific self-imposed challenges. 70 hours into this game and I haven't unlocked a single one, and that is by no means a complaint. The game is fun enough, interesting enough, and well designed enough to make me want to get better at it over time just so I can get those achievements later.

_childDocuments_.review: In the modern day sea of early access games or fully completed games being unpolished and poorly executed, Griftlands is a game that restores some faith in the gaming community.It is tagged as Early Access, however that's not accurate. There are 3 characters to play through. 2 of them are completed with their stories while the third is about half way done. And even as they continue to work on the 3rd character content is added that affects all of the characters (like no gameplay mechanics and cards).It's a deck builder rogue-like (I think its rogue like. Can never remember difference between like and lite). Cards you choose from throughout a run are randomized. Encounters are randomized, etc. Standard stuff for anyone who's played StS or Monster Train.Yet, I don't play Griftlands for that bit. I play it for the stories and characters. It's an anthology game. You get three characters and their stories take place in the same world. However, each one plays differently, with different gimmicks, and have their tale set in a different locale then the others. There's references and other things that connect the stories in terms of lore, and there's even a chance of bumping into the other playable characters as NPCs. There's a special touch added to the game that doesn't just make it feel like 'Another run, another deck to build', Every run I do I am curious as to what characters and encounters I'll have to work my way through.And for the gameplay. Look at the reviews. There is So Much to this game, so many layers, when it comes to playing it. I do enjoy my runs of Monster Train. Yet at the end of the day, it's just another Monster Train run. With Griftlands, there are so many perks and modifiers you can add to your run before even starting the damn thing. Then while in the middle of a character's story there is so many things to add to them that isn't just another card for your deck (of which there are two for each character).If you are looking for something in depth. Something fresh and new. Something with a captivating story even though you can play through one in a few hours (or 30 min if you want that achievement). Just buy Griftlands. It is a game that will not disappoint.

_childDocuments_.review: So after spending many hours of playing Slay the Spire on my phone, I decided to give this game a try. If you choose to talk things out you, you can usually save relationships between you and NPCs, however if you choose to fight you’re more than likely gonna have to live with them not liking you very much(if you choose to save them). _childDocuments_.review: Griftlands is an excellent game.It is a Rogue-lite, story-based, deck-building game, so certainly targeted towards a fairly specific niche, but it does it's job excellently. The story is fairly short, so casual players could easily get some enjoyment out of it, but they added a lot of replay-ability, with everything from scaling difficulty levels (prestige), mutators (for custom challenges), daily challenges (for global competition), multiple characters, slightly branching story paths, brawl mode (less story more rogue-lite), etc. The best thing I can say about Griftlands is that it makes your deck building feel creative. While some successful run decks end up essentially being every card with the same keyword on it, many feel like an interesting creation/set of synergies that you've come up with (whether or not that's an illusion). I already have a few pet decks after only 20 hours. Because of the replay-ability, I can assure you I will be putting many more hours into this game. The biggest criticism I can give is the amount of similarities it has to Slay the Spire (which speaks to developer originality rather than quality of the game). While the two deck system and individual mechanics are different, the core gameplay loop- seeing enemies' actions ahead of time, having about 3 action points, not healing between battles, discarding your hand at the end of your turn, even mechanics like expend or removing cards from shop keepers are all there. These mechanics suit rogue-like deck builders perfectly- that's why they were in Slay the Spire. That being said, while fans of Slay the Spire will likely love Griftlands (in the same way they would love Slay the Spire 2), I wouldn't call it an original masterpiece. Griftlands has enough to distinguish itself (especially the story and two decks, but individual mechanics being vastly different help as well) and stand firmly on the idea that it built on the ideas of others in the same genre (just like most video games we play), it is still not as original as it could be. Nonetheless, mostly nothing but praise for the game- it is fast becoming one of my favorites from one of my favorite developers.

_childDocuments_.review: WOW. that's all I would this game about this game.No, really. I was used to other Klei games such as shanks and shanks 2 ( which share similar design) but damn, I was completely blown away by Griftlands.Indeed, as you can guess It's not just a card game. It's way more than that. First things first, the main attraction that distances this game from the rest is the campaigns. Damn well thought. It's probably the first game that FINALLY manages to give some story to card games.And what stories. Damn, I have seen some adventure games with less well paced and intriguing stories than Griftlands.Every single character has its own gameplay style ( actually, you can do even multiple builds for each), motivation ( damn, after shank  - which is not a bad game, just a very single minded one- I didn't think they could pull out something like that) and challenges.And now, the second reason why I rate this game so damn High: it's not just about combat, there are a astonishing well designed talk system in which you need to convince, lie or sway the opponent. Always with cards but thought in a completely different manner.There's even a in-game social system, with boons from your allies and a whole network of people and strategies to employ to get your way... bystanders can help in battle if they see you attacked or engaged in a discussion. And if you do not care who you kill.. remember that Npc have friends and close ones, which death they will want to avenge. There is a whole thought process in which you need to carefully choose your allies and enemies. I know that by the sound of this review, this game doesn't seem all that great. _childDocuments_.review: Griftlands is, in its current form, a good game. The early access build is stable and has a lot of content, so I wouldn't be afraid to check it out because of that. Klei has a good track record for early access.The game itself is built on a roguelike deckbuilding formula that has become exceptionally popular the last year or two. It brings with it some unique ideas, a unique and well-done art style, and Klei's track record of solid games.Unlike many of the heavy hitters in the genre (Slay the Spire, Monster Train), the main mode of Griftlands is story based. You lead one of two (eventually three) characters through their story. I've only played with one of the characters thus far, but the writing in her story is good. The dialogue is interesting and often funny, and I like the world they've put together.The thing is, in a game like this, the 'fail forward' formula of a roguelike doesn't mesh super well with a narrative heavy game. As a result, on my Xth run, I'm skipping most of the dialogue because I've seen it all before. It's a bit of a shame, but I suppose if it did start to bug me I could play the newly introduced Brawl mode, which, to my understanding, is a series of escalating challenges without story.Apart from the narrative, it has what you'd expect from a game like this. You get new cards, upgrade your existing cards, have multiple difficulty tiers that you unlock by winning, unlock new cards into the available pool by finishing a run (win or lose), artifacts-but-not, etc. It does have a few unique ideas, namely that you have two decks per character (one for combat and one for negotiation), and the negotiation half of the game plays quite a bit differently than the combat (which would be similar to Slay the Spire and the like). They also recently added Perks you can unlock through gameplay, and you can take a handful with you per run.For now, I'd say Griftlands is good. It doesn't quite have that spark that makes me want to keep going back to it and back to it and back to it, but it's possible that those hooks will come in a later update. Griftlands has a lot going for it, and while I may be done with it for a while, I look forward to checking out the 1.0 release.

_childDocuments_.review: extremely fun deckbuilding roguelite. i'd put it up there with the greats of the genre in terms of entertainment value.pros:- enjoyable, well-balanced card play for all six different card sets (three characters, combat/negotiation deck for each)- interesting balancing act between improving both of your decks to make sure neither of them are too weak, while still making sure to fight/argue at the right times- the faction and friendship system makes you think about what you're doing more than in other roguelites, killing everybody thoughtlessly will usually end badly if you don't prepare for the large consequences- well-written story and frequently fantastically written and humorous dialogue-surprisingly high replay value for a story-oriented game. there are multiple paths on each campaign, multiple choices to make on those paths, and a large variety of random quests that are pulled from for the random quest sections.grey areas:- you're very likely to make big mistakes if you don't pay attention to the story at all and don't know what's going on. however, if you skip a section of dialogue, you do get a short summary of it in its place. i don't know how effective these summaries are, since i always read the dialogue even whenever i play now, but they're there if you don't want to read the dialogue (i recommend reading it at least the first time though).-runs are quite long. i think the game is well-balanced around its runs being as long as they are, but they're quite long. probably looking at around ~3 hours for a first playthrough of each campaign. which can be somewhat painful if you die. cons:- high ascension levels are pretty poorly balanced in my opinion. some story paths become pointless because the bosses you fight on them are too strong, some builds aren't viable, et cetera.highly recommended. it's on sale at the time of this review. if you're considering it, buy it.
