_childDocuments_.review: Easily one of the best roguelikes. I've had my fair share of time playing games similar to this, chiefly Slay the Spire, and for a game to come out that eclipses it like this is just so good! The combat is very similar to any other deck builder but what really draws me in is the Negotiation option. Having the option to solve things with words instead of violence is super cool and engaging for me and for it to have it's own "combat" mechanics is super fun and makes me wanna silver-tongue my way through the entire game! And you ALMOST can but damn those boss fights are tough!
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I was a bit reluctant to buy this game when it came out because I was not a big fan of its art style, though I do like card game and RPG. After watching reviews and recommendations from a couple of Youtubers, I finally decided to give it a try. And Griftlands does not disappoint. It not only has very high quality of production with all the animations and voice acting and beautiful sceneries, they are reinforced by a tons of interesting mechanics such as the negotiation and battle system, character relationship and related unique perks, recruitable companions, quests and random encounters and emergency events, upgrade choices for cards, equipment, etc. etc.In a market filled with Slay the Spire clones, Driftlands stands out as something that looks similar at first but in the end feels quite different and unique to earn a place of its own. My only regret is that I didn't buy the game earlier. 10 out of 10.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: If you like the first two hours, you'll like the rest. If you don't like the first two hours, you won't like the rest. For me this is a swing and a miss from Klei Entertainment. First of all, the gameplay experience feels very "faux" rogue-like. Meaning, while there are obviously randomized events you are also very clearly hand-held through the story. You are given 2-3 choices of what to do next, and about every 1/2 or 1/3 times you pick a choice, you get pushed alongside the main storyline with handcrafted story quests. So instead of choosing between playing the main story line or doing sidequests, you end up in a loop where you HAVE to do 1-2 sidequests before you are permitted to continue the main storyline. The main questgivers will tell you as much - "go do something else until tomorrow or until I trust you more".Second, they've broadened the scope of a deckbuilder game by introducing the concept of two separate types of decks. One is used in combat, one is used in diplomacy or trying to persuade people. As you progress through the game, you can choose which of the two to specialize in - do you want to be the combat expert or the talky guy? This division between the two is actually extremely well implemented, up until the point where it isn't. Because the main storyline always has unskippable combat/persuasion events. And what one chooses to specialize in, and thus depend on, isn't balanced for these events. Meaning - you can focus primarily on being a talky guy and end up in a super difficult fight that you can't complete. The idea is that if you're super-persuasive, you can convince people to fight with you, or make the enemy fight weaker. The balance of that just doesn't work out. You can spend an hour building up a strong team of people to fight with you, and run into a boss fight that wipes them out in two turns because you didn't choose combat skills.Third, the meta progression is atrocious. By meta progression I mean how you improve between different games. The progression is almost universally "+3 health" or "15 coins at start of game". It is extremely boring. It does not unlock new ways to play the game, or new content for the game such as alternate endings or more events. You know how some games feel like they needed to pad the game length by making you depend on meta progression, literally forcing you to play the same game several times over? This game does that.The deckbuilder design is flawless. The animations/graphics are decent. The storylines and immersion feels pretty good.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: While I was not a big fan of Klei's previous games, I knew that they were a quality developer and this game proves it beyond all doubt. They tell you exactly when each new update is going to be, and they give you a way to directly send feedback through the game itself.While being a huge departure from the survival and base-building games they made, it manages to knock it out of the park with an experience that has the depth and complexity of Slay the Spire while also adding an interesting dialogue and story-based experience that makes it a very unique offering in the single-player card game genre.The main strength of the gameplay is the dual dialogue and combat system, which means in most situations you can choose whether to talk or fight your way through a situation (or both, at times -some enemies will fight you either way,  but softening them up with words beforehand can always be useful).The combat and dialogue systems are both card-based, although quite different from each other. The combat part is basically exactly like Slay The Spire (which is fine, if it ain't broke, don't fix it), the dialogue part is, in my opinion, much more interesting and nuanced. It's hard to explain, you basically target either the enemy's resolve (akin to HP) or their arguments and counterpoints while building up your own verbal skillset. Of course eventually it does boil down to numbers, but there's many skill-based decisions you will have to make in both systems, with just the right amount of randomness to keep things interesting.I also have to point out how flavorful the effects are, which is a staple of good card game design. As for the game's overworld, you travel along a map to many different locations and you meet/fight many different characters. There's a lot of randomly generated mini-events and rewards that make each run unique without breaking the main storyline.Everything is well-drawn and appropriately grimy given the game's dystopian sci-fi setting (think Mass Effect+Fallout), the dialogue is good, the music is good and the progression system is definitely enough to keep you interested for a while.It's basically a completed title despite being in Early Access, for 10 euros it's an absolute STEAL.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent game! Gameplay similar to Slay the Spire but with a story attached this time. Fantastic writing, too. While the stories are not world shattering innovations, they are excellently delivered with good characterization and humorous dialogue and events. I do wish, however, that they let you share difficulty levels between the characters. As it stands you have to clear all 7 difficulty levels with each character independently. So if you reach level 5 on one character and want to play another.. back to level 1 with you. Similarly each character has their own meta-progression that you have to grind out. I think they made these choices to give people more "things to do".. but I really would have preferred if they hadn't. I'd be more likely to play the game more if I could at least share the difficulty levels and play whichever character I wanted without having to go spend hours grinding easier content.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Upgrade your cards - you have two separate customizable decks to upgrade.  Do they summon extra cards?  Upgrade those!  Get upgrades to yourself, and upgrade those too!  Finish a game, and you get upgrades to the game!This game ♥♥♥♥♥♥' slaps.  Its dry sense of humour is just a dollop of whipped cream on top of an itch-scratchingly great upgrade-fest.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Oddly enough, I always hated Deckbuilders prior to playing this game.I consider both Hearthstone and Magic The Gathering pay to win as you can pay to have access to more cards. So I never bothered with either of those. I tried Slay the Spire, but it really lacked in depth during combat, choosing which card to play didn't require much thought at all. The only strategy that game required was building your deck then just relying on the RNG to give you the cards you want.Griftlands on the other hand has a lot of strategy involved while also being an RPG. There's permanent buffs/debuffs you can unlock by choosing different outcomes of Quests and becoming friends/enemies with NPCs, you can level up the cards you play most choosing from multiple upgrade paths for each one. The RPG elements really enhance the gameplay as there's even random events that occur while you're on your quests. I'd highly recommend this game to anyone interested in Deck Builders or even just RPGs as this one combines them really well. Sadly, there's not much voice acting just weird noises made by the characters when talking, but honestly you can probably skip most of the dialogue and just choose what you want to do to each person when the options are given to you lol.There's even 2 main modes to the card combat. Negotiation and regular Combat, both having different decks that you build throughout the campaign. Each playing fairly differently. Negotiation focuses on creating buffs and debuffs while trying to destroy the enemy's buffs, where as regular combat is all about creating combo attacks.It also has a lot of replay value as there's different characters to play as with different starting decks and multiple quests you can do during a playthrough as well as multiple outcomes to each quest.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Shortest way I can describe Griftlands is Slay the Spire meets Fallout. Conflicts are resolved with words or weapons (and sometimes both). The upgrade system means cards are improved with XP, gained by playing them, which is probably my personal favorite upgrade system for card battlers. Each character has a distinct negotiation and battle style, often having two or more distinct specializations of each. Grafts grant further bonuses, and a character's opinion of you can modify the game even further. Just don't expect each run to result in success.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Humourous story mode, but you can play Brawl instead for the same gameplay!More game options unfold over repeat plays, but you're not forced to use any of them!No clock.  Casual friendly.I've been finding it very replay-able.  What's particularly cool about the Negotiation / Battle deck split is that you'll want to invest some time in both modes per game, but you can still have one carry you for most of the fights -- especially when it comes to Rook's Negotiation specialty, the Blacklist.  Enjoy that one before it gets nerfed, I suppose.  Oh, also, alternating between the modes is rewarded because healing is applied to the mode you didn't use.  And the basic cards in each deck don't suck!
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I played through Sal's campaign in one sitting, I was glued to my computer. There is an endless mode like other roguelike card games (ex: Slay the Spire) It has a narrative, there are interesting characters and a relationship system that I really enjoy. It feels like a fully fleshed out game and its still in early access.  I have probably put 30 hours into Slay The Spire but this might take the spot because I really enjoy the RPG elements this game has. The card leveling mechanic is also really neat, you level cards by using them, so it is possible to upgrade multiple cards in a fight.8/10Its not perfect, the story mode is on the shorter side and that's what I felt really shined most but this is a roguelike so you can't really have long campaigns.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: This game is incredible. Not one but TWO different card games with really great mechanics. With RPG elements. With Rouge-like mechanics. With great story-telling, world building, art style. Everything about this game is a hit and it's a blend of ideas I've never seen in a game before. Super impressed.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: It's hard to properly describe this game. Sure, it's a deckbuilder but with unique characters that each have their own story and the choose-your-own-adventure aspect of the level progression is very chooser-friendly, assuming you know what the consequences are for killing that guard instead of letting him surrender and you can live with them. Yeah, he drops a sick graft, but is it worth the barkeep's hatred and possible debufs? As you progress around the map and encounter more vendors, victims and villains you'll find the game asks these questions of you frequently, and just as the risk can be high so too can the reward. The fights themselves also vary in style, sometimes you will be playing an argument deck and others a combat one. It not only keeps things interesting, but I find the arguments fights so wholly enjoyable that I would play them as a stand alone mobile game if it was available. The combat fights are also enjoyable, don't get me wrong, but the arguments just have such a cool and unique feel they stand out to me. Instead of writing 300 more words I'll just wrap up by saying that I don't know a single gamer that I wouldn't recommend this game to. It doesn't matter what style of game you're normally into, this one is just universally engaging with a quirky and rich story, is very well done and lets you "play around" with ideas for different builds which is what we love :)
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: It doesn't matter what type of genre Klei develop their games around, you always get the full package that Klei provides on all of their games:- Amazing art style 9/10- Soundtrack all around good with some really good battle tracks 7/10- Gameplay and UI all self explainatory and easy to follow 8/10- Replayability is there and with easy to follow and regular updates 8/10Some nuisances, but not gamebreaking moments would be:- No glossary, would be nice to summarize in each mode what card types are what called and so on- Some overlapping with popups and the window with recent notations on lower left corner- A visual slider for UI scaling would be nice, sometimes the font size can be a bit small on native 1080p- No log for what happened last round, hard to figure out what type of debuff/buff each NPC made- The way the people are displayed with their status towards you is neat, but I would like a list with names + portraits next to them, or portraits on names if they're mentioned in a quest- Overall score 8/10Definitely worth the wait.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Solid Deck builder with major focus on story.  Lots of interesting choices and mechanics.  Each fight is not too bad but each run is a bit longer than most deck builders.  If you like story choices with gritty characters and deck building mechanics then this is a solid pick.  If any of that doesn't sound interesting then the length of the game could become an issue.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: This Rogue-lite RPG has great style and offers two forms of combat, verbal and physical. Both systems are card based but deck progression is not persistent. Runs vary greatly besides the story beats making each run unique. NPCs speak a gibberish language, which is hilarious to make fun of. (Sounds like Huttese.)
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I was hesitant to try out Griftlands, because I had previously tried out Slay the Spire, another Roguelite Card Battler, and I did not like it.In these games, you have a starting deck of cards that you do battle with, and throughout your adventure you can add new, more powerful cards, as well as get rid of some of your old, weaker cards. The new cards can have synergies with one another, and there were dozens of synergies you could build your deck around in Slay the Spire. My problem with that game, is that 90% of these synergies didn't stand a snowball's chance in hell of making it through the game's 3rd and final level; there's only a couple of builds per character that scaled well enough to actually beat the game with, and everything else felt like a trap. Slay the Spire presents you with a wide range of false choices that will inevitably fail, with a couple of real builds hidden in between; I don't find that enjoyable.By contrast, Griftlands offers you a range of synergistic cards that actually work. Mind-blowing, I know. Griftlands has a far superior art style, it offers different locales with their own distinct atmospheres and circumstances as the adventure's stomping grounds, it has two parallel combat systems in its combat and its diplomacy system, and does a good job of portraying how as you gain notoriety, you gain new friends, but also make new enemies. It's a pretty challenging game, I've had runs where I've lost when my build didn't come together, and other runs where I was a hair's breadth away from losing.So, as someone who didn't like Slay the Spire at all, I would describe Griftlands as: "Like Slay the Spire, but good"
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: 28 hours is long enough to complete the campaigns for all 3 characters, there are prestige levels but those aren't really my bag, there are also other modes and dailies too, not my thing either. The game is good, it's a card game verses AI, 3 different stories, the combat and talking games are pretty similar in mechanics but all enjoyable. As a roguelike it will take you a few runs to build up the mettle to make your character better and learn which things are good which are not.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I picked up the game because I liked Slay the Spire and it was suggested. By adding a second deck during your run and more story-driven choices, the game becomes more interesting (and complex). I really enjoy this addition to the game so far, but I'm not sure if it will continue to be interesting after a few runs.I'm glad I bought the game so far, and I plan to play it through, but since the story is such an important part of the experience, I doubt it will be as replayable as other games.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: This game could've been much better than it is.Alright so what exactly is it? It's a quasi adventure RPG game with a wonderful, original setting that feels like Star Wars somehow meets semi low tech and a bunch of political shifting you can choose to engage with as much or as little as you care to. And you engage with them through three characters, two of which are pretty memorable and well written, through three rather short "campaigns".And then there's the main thing you do... which is a CCG card battler. Which is... fine? In two out of the three campaigns. It's balanced and straightforward and fun if not the ABSOLUTE greatest thing ever. And then the... could've been better part.First, the third campaign is boringly easy. Like, once you "get" the strategy with character number 3 it's seriously a snooze, there's no way you can possibly lose the "death is possible" battle card game, and hells it's pretty damned hard to lose the "talking" parallel card game as well. Who thought this was balanced and ready to release?But the biggest part is... the CCG half of the game wants to be a roguelite. Except, remember how I initially gave the impression that the other half is a story heavy adventure RPG game? Yeah, that part isn't set up to be a Roguelite at all. Zero percent. It doesn't work. Getting invested in an already short ish story only to have roguelite death and restart thrown at your face, with the implication that you have to go through the exact same story again without ANY real variation in the story to speak of and no reason to do so feels... weird. Hades, where the story is set up for repeated deaths, this is not.Nor is the CCG good enough for a roguelike. It's fine. It's fun once through. But the world's most depthful and interesting CCG battler this is not. I feel like a game that embraced the most engaging and well done parts of this game, the story heavy adventure RPG, would have been much, much better paired with something that well... worked well with it. Rather than feeling like ti's arbitrarily grafted onto a roguelike deckbuilder.So, that's the game. Good fun for a few nights. But one very good half welded to one pretty decent half, and the problem is the two halves don't really gel together that well.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful package of pure fun. Story full of laugh out loud moments, sprinkled with some somber moments, rich world lore and awesome characters. I was surprised to find out that each of three characters has totally different story line, totally different world maps, totally different card-mechanics and card sets.Plus, the cards and mechanics are tied neatly with the chars themselves. The turncoat spy and his coin flipping mechanic, the arrogant aristocrat with his bravado and drinking mechanic.. it's all pure gold.Highly recommended if you like a good adventure, unique card games and fine writing.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent game as always from Klei. I don't usually play early-access games because, in my perspective, what's the point of playing something that's incomplete? This was worth it.I was invited by a good friend to try it out. The most charming point of the game is that no two playthroughs are exactly the same. I like how each card seems to tell your story as you play along. During my first few playthroughs, I essentially went on a murder-spree against any of the Admirality faction since it seemed like something that Sal, the first character you play as, would do. Because of that, I earned Battle cards that became more and more geared towards psychopathic tendencies, and my Negotiation cards started to build an interesting mix of overaggressive Hostility with "shuffle"-Diplomacy. In my most recent playthrough, I decided to try a "peaceful route" and focused on making everyone love me instead, which made a cool Negotiation deck based on Arguments, and a Battle deck with Combo-Finishers. There's something addicting about one-hundred percenting these decks.I encourage you to try out the Demo, at least, to support Griftlands and Klei's team. There's a lot of potential for growth through community efforts and feedback. I don't think there's going to be a bigger discount than what we have right now because of how new the game is - it seems like there's already a huge pool of players early-gaming it, so I don't expect any bigger discounts on this game until it's done.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: When I last played, thematically and story-wise, this did a very good job of assembling an interesting and coherent narrative, so if you are interested in that, i would check this game out. The actual gameplay is a little weaker - while it's a deck-builder in style, it doesn't mechanically scratch the great itch of putting together a coherent deck. The upgrade system is interesting, but the requirement to have multiple characters can make combats unbalanced, and negotiation can be a little difficult to parse at times. I do hope those improve while the game is in early access, and the price is a little high as is. However, it's at least worth a look.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Awesome deck builder, each character gets their own story, cards, map and overall playstyle, can't wait to get the rest of Smith's story arc. There's even a brawl mode for a quick playthrough without all the dialogue, challenge mode with draft boss rush... this early release is very promising, give it a try if you're the deck builder type.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: It's a really fun deckbuilding, story-heavy roguelike with one of the unique features being that you have two different decks you use depending on what encounters you get in: either your negotiation deck to talk people over to your point of view or the battle deck for when things come to blows. The negotiations and battles follow similar rules but still play very differently from eachother and the differing playstyles even within the same genre help keep the game feeling more fresh than either of these two styles could do on their own. The consequence-heavy approach to storytelling and the varied random elements ensure that no two playthroughs will be the same, especially since there are multiple paths you can take to your goal even before adding those random elements. One word of warning though, while you can take a break and pick up where you left off without losing much (if any) progress, a single run will be SIGNIFICANTLY longer than your average rougelike. If you're looking to finish a run in 30 minutes to an hour, that won't be possible here. I could talk all day about the nuances to both negotiations and combat, but that'd make this review longer than I feel like typing at the moment.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Addictive and innovative, great "just one more time" feeling. Went in with no expectations, purely based on reviews and publisher, and was pleasantly surprised. Still can't believe it's still in "Early", had zero issues and claims to be getting better. Kinda late to the party but, Klei is quickly becoming one of my favourite publishers.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Very challenging and very satisfying. Both the negotiation deck and the combat decks for each character are fun and it's neat to work with each character's gimmickEdit: now that the game's full campaign is out, I can easily say I loved each and every one of them. Each had their own style to them, and building decks around each play style was a satisfying challenge
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: 7/10A Spire-like with enough uniqueness to stand out. Adds a story, RPG elements, parties, and great art to the Spire formula. I had fun and it's challenging in a good way.Pros:The mechanics are very good. The card-specific XP system forces you into interesting decisions constantly. The character and animation design is really beautiful, top notch work. Having two different decks makes the game more interesting and this mechanic is thematically worked in very nicely.Cons:The card design falls a bit flat. Cards lack the personality / flavour you see in Magic, Hearthstone, or even Spire. Everything from the naming, to the art, to the way the cards are laid out, the mechanics... When you upgrade a card it changes the name. Afterward, I would often be unable to recognize the new card at a glance. I think that speaks for itself.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: It's an interesting take on a roguelike deckbuilder game - it has much more of a focus on a story. The combat is more interesting and deep than many similar games, and the split between physical combat and negotiation gives it a very different feel than many games these days. That said, it's still in development and the more "pure" non-story roguelike aspect of the game needs more work.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Griftlands is a charming deckbuilder roguelite where you play as a variety of characters and manage two distinct decks, a combat deck, and a negotiation deck. You play out a story that evolves as you make decisions, allowing you to recruit allies, make enemies, and gain powerful items to help you in your fights or negotiations. It's generally not a good idea to invest heavily into only one of your two decks, but it can work depending on your foreknowledge of how the run works. I've been impressed by the mechanics, but it's not exactly the most thinking-heavy game. All-in-all it's just good fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely YES! I was just waiting for this game to leave EA to start playing it.It has really all what's needed to make it a true masterpiece, and could be played from every kind of player.- Absoltely original and innovative mechanics- Great feeling of progression and challange- Every run new surprises (bad and good)- Unique approach of having both a battle deck and a diplomacy deck, to face situations- Very well written story, sfx, background soundtrack- Every choice got consequences (Characters love/like/dislike/hate) giving you semi-permanent buff or debuff- Very addictive, especially for completionist!- Regular Updates from Devs, new features, daily challanges and much moreJust go for it, worth the full price definitely.This game definitely won a place on the podium together with slay the spyre and monster train, but it adds as well a story and lore, making it even more valuable!Excellent job, devs!
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I have 12 hours in this game and it feels like 2, and I've only beaten 1 of 3 campaigns (I've done a run of the other two once just to check them out but i haven't beaten them yet). I might be a bit biased because i love this genre, but this game is definitely worth your time.If you care about the story the runs can be very slow paced but fortunately there are options to basically ignore that if you don't care. Its like they knew people would mod in speed modifiers into their game so they just did it themselves. If you don't care about story i would highly recommend jacking the speed settings up after your first run or two.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I couldn't care less about the story, and the fact that there IS a story is basically the only thing Griftlands brings to the rouge-like deck builder genre. That and the fact that you can often choose if you want to fight in a more traditional card battle setup  or if you want to have a "negotiation" where you use a second deck that is overall much less fun and with much more convoluted mechanics. The worst part of the game is the relationship system, how the game tracks who loves, like, dislikes, or hates you. Did some random Chewbacca ripoff attack you? Did you kill this thing? Well now two random dudes you've never met hate you, and this means you get a random debuff like losing a certain amount of currency daily or a ton of other stupid things that a persons hate for me couldn't control. I bought this game because I like the genre and I like Klei, but Griftlands is easily the worst game in their catalog.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: It's still in progress, but it's already a fun deck builder. The story modes are enjoyable and it's easy to get into the RPG aspects of it (do I want to play a more ruthless or cunning character this time?) both in deck choices and non-deck choices.The game is based around managing two decks in a run, one for negotiation encounters and one for combat encounters. These decks have different base play styles and each character has a specific different style of play for both, and there are plenty of choices to make for each. In general though, negotiation encounters make you work back and forth because you can 'attack' the opponents core argument or you can attack their various negotiation buffs, while combat works more like straight forward deck builder RPG combat.I'm not sure if this is just something that has changed or not, but the description of the game as being more about non-deck based game play don't ring true to me. The majority of my enjoyment of this game definitely comes from the combat and negotiations.I don't think the combat flow is as smooth as some other games. Making a really focused deck is tougher in this game because there aren't as many opportunities to gain or lose cards, and card upgrades appear to be random options. Because of this, you often have to balance the decisions you're making in any given turn a little more, even into the end of a run. This is a pro and a con, but it's also balanced out a bit by other things in the run which affect your gameplay, such as bonuses from grafts - items which give a boon for the rest of the run - or nerfs given to you cause an NPC to hate you.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: This is probably one of the best deckbuilder games out there. In short you are a grifter who travels throughout the land taking jobs and performing task in pursuit of rewards that will help you achieve the final goal. Throughout your adventures you meet a variety of characters who may grow to like you or hate you which depends on how you play. It has fun gameplay that is easy to get into, great art style, and a lot of interesting stories/characters. It is in early access but still has tons of content and replayabiltity.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very fun game. The story sections can get old after a while but that's why the game gives you brawl mode eventually. This mode simplifies the game down to just the basic gameplay loop, which is almost endlessly fun. Griftlands isn't the absolute best card game I've ever played, nor is it the greatest story ever told, but I'd really struggle to find anything about it to criticize. It's just really solid.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Very polished for early access. Been following this project for a while before I purchased.Does not mislead you on the difficulty- expect to lose quite often at first, as you get a proper handle on things.Story telling work is excellent. At points I laughed, and at points I actually had to sit and debate myself on the best course of action. It's a 3 energy Card System, like almost every other card system. That's not a complaint, the system works.With two kinds of health pools and two separate decks, which can be developed into very different styles, there's a LOT to explore in this.Small qualms- very rarely, text may be misleading (Gold for friendship bribe and not paying off the debt they hold... which is less than the bribe). This is not a savescumming game. The autosave makes you commit to your mistakes. While never intended, visual glitches tend to be rapid flickering. These will eventually be resolved but worth mentioning if you're photosensitive. I love this game. I'm going to pump a dozen more hours into it, and probably fall back into it once a month for a weekend at a time. I hope most of my friends pick this up, because it's a great time sink for solo play.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I remember not giving this game a shot because I thought it was just another deck building kind of game. Much like how Klei knocked it out of the park in the survival game genre with "Don't Starve", they've done it once again with the rouge-lite, deck building genre with Griftlands. This game manages to make each card you have in your desk tell a story with how your character interacts with the world around them. Although the destination for each character arc remains the same throughout very long, possibly multiple-day runs, how you arrive at that situation is up to you and the types of decks you build- if you can even make it to the end. Really good stuff. Excited to see how they end the third character's arc.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Griftlands is a roguelite deckbuilder in the vein of Slay the Spire and Monster Train. The differentiating element is a focus on story and negotiation.Positives:The main draw is the two different decks that every player will have to manage during a run: one for battles and one for negotiations. If you lean too heavily into charming and bullying your way through obstacles, then your battle deck might end up being insufficient when you eventually face an inescapable violent confrontation. If you prefer to make your problems disappear by physically eliminating the people responsible for them, then your negotiation deck could become cluttered with cards that indicate your character's fearsome reputation.I found myself enjoying the negotations more than the battles, since attacking arguments through a mix of diplomacy and intimidation is a fairly novel system.The production value of the game is very high, in line with previous Klei releases. I found the artwork to be particularly excellent, with the characters all possessing expressive faces and detailed clothing that helped to immerse me in the fictional world. The dialogue is well-written, with humor and snark that match the seedy environment. The storylines are adequate, though standard fare for gritty, urban sci-fi. Each of the three main characters are slightly different variations of the rogue archetype, in the manner of Han Solo.Unlockable meta-progression features include:* More cards for each of the 3 characters.* Persistent character ability upgrades using the meta-currency "mettle".* Powerful "perk" cards that can be played infrequently during runs whenever a "flourish" meter is filled.A more subtle manner of meta-progression involves the various NPCs. Each of them has an associated "boon" and "bane" that grant further bonuses or debuffs depending on whether your character has managed to gain their love or hate during a run. While the particular boons and banes are initially hidden, they become revealed in future runs, giving players another way to stack the odds in their favor by befriending NPCs with boons that are synergistic to their deck's builds.Negatives:The runs in story mode tend to be at least 3 hours long, and usually closer to 4+ hours. While story mode is fairly engaging the first time through for each of the characters, I found it to be fatiguing on subsequent runs. Thankfully, there is a brawl mode that gets unlocked after completing a character's story mode, which pares down the playing experience to a minimalist version of the regular mode in order to focus on deckbuilding and card slinging.If you're looking for something with shorter, more "roguelike-y" runs like Slay the Spire or Monster Train, then you may want to either stick with brawl mode or possibly skip the game altogether.------------------Overall, I would highly recommend Griftlands, both to deckbuilding aficionados and also to those people who might have generally avoided deckbuilders in the past due to desiring more storytelling.The story-driven gameplay is well worth $20 USD, and the game frequently goes on sale on Steam for 20% off.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't know. It's an okay deckbuilder with an okay sci-fi plot, where you have to manage two decks (one for combat and one for negotiation). The grabbiest thing about it are the relationship and morale mechanics. Making friends and enemies opens up more events with them, and also has mechanical effects. Also you don't have to kill other characters in fights, just make them run away by reducing their hit points to a certain threshold. And if you do kill them, on purpose or on accident, you've often made an enemy of someone else. But that wasn't neat enough to make the rest of the game feel more interesting.

_childDocuments_.review: I rarely feel like writing a review for a game, even if I loved it, but seeing the recent mixed reviews angered me enough to write one.This is a deep and highly polished deckbuilder with loads of different builds thanks to the two deck system.Comparing it to Slay the Spire or Monster Train is absolutely ridiculous.Sure, these are also deckbuilders, but they are focused solely on gameplay with just enough plot to justify their existence.This is a story driven game with dialogue and branching scenarios while still being a damn solid deck building game.Claiming the game is not replayable is wild - it has two game modes with the option to apply various rule modifiers, daily challenges and mod support with many mods expanding the gameplay readily available.There isn't any less content here than in other big deckbuilders, but even if there was it would easily make up for it with polish.If you're tired of story mode you can play brawl and focus on battling, but I still keep coming back to story mode because of each scenario having two branches, all quests having at least two solutions and the emergent gameplay based on the relationships you have with characters.I've spent thousands of hours playing deckbuilders, be it big names like StS or less known (and less good) ones like Roguebook, and Griftlands is up there with the best of the best.

We want quickies.And who cares about the story / acting etc once you've seen it once, at the most twice.If they make it more snappy, I will deffo give it another whirl as you can get some good combos flowing.Not worthy of the overwhelmingly positive reviews. _childDocuments_.review: I was skeptical of a deckbuilder focused around negotiation. However, I've found that the negotiation and battle mechanics complement each other nicely. There is no pacifist run possible and it ensures even if your negotiation deck is flawless, you have to develop your battle deck.Outside of the gameplay, the characters and setting are unique and fun to explore. I really enjoy the relationship mechanic which can make your game a lot easier or a lot harder depending how many people you help/screw over. This puts some weight to your interactions with the people you meet.Overall, because I was skeptical about the game. So, I feel it's necessary to tell other people the game is certainly worth trying. _childDocuments_.review: Griftlands is another kind of Deckbuilder Roguelike.And that isn't meant negative, not at all.Just after I thought Monster Train was a fresh take on the Deckbuilder genre and would be my go-to Deckbuilder when I felt like playing one, this gem here came out of nowhere and hooked me.In Griftlands you see, you essentially pick a Character at first (There's currently two, out of which I only played one by this point). This Character has a set goal/story which you play out.Gain friends and make enemies along the story, earn weapons, skills and boons to create your own build.When you manage to beat the story, you unlock Prestige 1, and as you might guess from that, when beating the story at Prestige 1, you unlock Prestige 2 and so on. Even if you lose, you get XP and unlock Cosmetic skins and/or new cards for future runs.The two things that really seperate this Deckbuilder from others, in my opinion are;1. The "rounds" are way longer. In Monster Train, my longer rounds take somewhere from 30-45 minutes. In Slay the Spire I'm anywhere from 45-60. In Griftlands my average is inbetween 2.5 and 3.5 hours.That can be a good thing, with more time on your hand, you get more invested into your current situation.And from a developer standpoint, if you make the rounds have a longer time, you can pack more events and different encounters in those, and they'll never feel repetitive.Of course, sometimes I'll also just want a quick round, but that's not much of a problem, I'll get to why it isn't problematic later in the Review.2. You are building actually 2 decks, not only 1 per run.While in any other Deckbuilder you build only your Combat deck, in Griftlands you also create a Negotiation deck, next to your Combat deck. That way you get a lot of freedom in character-building. You can make a character with a silver-tongue, that doesn't really excel at fighting. A character that mows over people, but has the verbal skills of a speech impaired monkey. Or a well balanced out character that can do both pretty good, or neither, the choice (and as with all Deckbuilders, luck) is yours.To get back to the thing with wanting quicker rounds sometimes.For that, I like to have Monster Train, which I then play, but Griftlands also offers another mode aside from regular Story mode, in which you play it more in a linear fashion, as with most Deckbuilders. In that mode the runs are way shorter and allow for a quick run when you just feel like getting that Deckbuilder fix satisfied.Overall, I can just say; The game released only a little while ago, and is already a lot richer on content than most Deckbuilders out there. Can only recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: I think I bought this game for the wrong reason. It's not a bad game. I was intrigued by the idea of a story-driven rogueliite. I enjoy roguelites pick up and play nature, their good for when I am too busy for bigger games. I find deck builders more engaging than traditional turn-based RPGS. And the artstyle is awesome. So I was excited about this game. I tried it once for about 5 hours, and then stopped playing for months without even realizing. I kept looking at it in my library and being like, "Huh, why did I stop playing that game? I thought it was good." I then picked it up again and realized why I stopped played. The story feels like it may as well not even be there. All the bits are chopped up into ways that you end up just feeling like quickly clicking through because nothing anyone says has any consequences, merit, or weight to you or whats happening. It's all flavor text. And the main plot and characters on their own don't offer enough for me to come back.Also there is an imbalance in getting to "choose" to be passive or aggressive ends up being fake as you end up needing both to progress. So yeah, all the elements I was excited for ended up being not quite there. It's not a bad game, clearly as many people have pointed out, but I got bored as I generally need a story to carry me through these types of games.

_childDocuments_.review: There's a lot more to it than any other roguelike I've played from a story perspective (although that's not to say it's story-driven), and difficulty-wise it's not so bad you'll be restarting every ten minutes, which is what turns me off about others in the genre. _childDocuments_.review: Not really great as a deck builder. _childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing deckbuilder game.Basically "Slay the Spire" with a story.Offers all the typical deckbuilder mechanics with a few neat ideas and tweaks, diverse cards that allow for interesting builds and a meta-progression system for both benefits as well as challenges. There are also custom modes, daily challenge runs and a "brawl" mode (basically allows skipping the story elements of the game).You can choose between three characters with completely unique card sets and innate abilities, that offer a somehwat unique playstyle. Each character comes with a small, enjoyable story-line that add some flavor. The setting and atmosphere resembles a postapocalyptic world with a bit of a humoristic take.It also seems extensively moddable, but I haven't really looked into that yet.Absolutely recommended for anybody who likes deckbuilder games.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: The gameplay of Griftlands isn't as tight, original, or replayable as something like Slay the Spire.  But what it lacks in those departments, it makes up for with to-notch writing, art, and lore.   The stories are delightful.  And the negotiation battles are truly inspired.  If you like deckbuilders and  are willing to overlook some mechanical shaginess in exchange for the opportunity to luxuriate in an exquisitely-drawn world inhabited with charming dirtbags, this game is a great option.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Awesome game, for all the reasons.It is a great take(s) on the deck builder genre.There is a LOT of variety in terms of game play (more on in a bit)The main worry I have with deck builder is replayability, yet I clocked 73 hours and I don't plan to put down this game any time soon.The negociation and combat deck are similar enough to transition from one another smoothly in the game, yet still feel and play completely differently.Learning the game is not hard, even with the more complex mechanisms layered on top of the basic ones.The variety of cards is one way that the game replayable but far from the only one here.The different characters with their own window into the world of griftland is really enjoyable, as I really enjoy the lore.The encounters along the story line make every game unique.Even if I were to get the same cards a few run in a raw, I know I will have different choice to make and uncover another part of the story.Having access to more than just the story mode is great to get games with lower stakes too.The "brawl" option with an arcade feeling is really good to just grind and just play your decks.The daily challenge does what it says on the tin: this is the mode where every detail matter. I'm not so good at those, but winning there is really rewarding.Klei didn't disapoint in terms of graphics, UX, story arcs, character development or lore either.Coming from don't starve, this wasn't a surprise either, because they do very well there.The lore is also not something you have to think about too much if you don't want to. it does add a lot of flavor to the game and bring those interaction with the world into perspective, yet it is not some scripted way you have to follow.I am a sucker for good lore and the more I play the more I get to know the different faction and the more I want to know. I can only hope that more characters than the 3 available will be made, so we can explore more facets of this world.The game is pretty much bug free, even if it is not the finished release I am playing.Lots of game are published half ready, this is not the case here, it is a very solid game.In terms of cons:* At times, the effects a card has is a bit obscure.* I don't think a multiplayer will exist for this game.* The pets are cool but maybe underused or usable more with some character than others.* Would love to see NPC using they as pronoun, as I didn't spotted any yet.12/10, would recommend wholeheartedly
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I did not expect a card-based roguelike to inspire me to write an entire setting for the Genesys RPG system, but it did. The world and lore is just that interesting.Also, this is not a Slay the Spire clone like so, so many others. The limited use items you get in your deck, deciding who to befriend for their bonus and who to kill for their equipment (angering their friends for a penalty), and the card EXP system all create something that feels very, very different - more methodical and calculated.It's still in Early Access, so not all of the story content is present quite yet, but the three characters, each with unique and varied mechanics, present more than enough variety to enjoy the endless "brawl" mode over and over again.Quite simply, Klei knocks it out of the park, again.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Very very fun. If you're a fan of Slay the Spire or Monster Train, you HAVE to try Griftlands. Because the RPG-like story of each roguelite run is so satisfying, it really feels deep. Superb design and writing from the people at Klei as well. Plus the prestige system and multiple characters keeps it very replayable. Highly recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, just wow! It has been awhile since I have played a game so polished to the brim. Griftlands is an immersive, extremely well-made, and wondrous deck-building experience — combining the best elements of card game-play, world-building, narrative storytelling, and social-links into a cohesive and awesome deck-building experience.PROS:+A great deck-building engine that makes sense, creating a seamless card-drafting mechanic from choices made within the game via its branching story, card upgrade options, and social-links (NPC's can love and hate you, providing boons or negative side effects).+The game is extremely optimized with beautiful and creative world-building, characters, animations, and special effects.+The User-Interface, icon placements, and description of status effects or card abilities is displayed in a very convenient and helpful manner. Everything is very well thought out and just clicks!+Replay value is extremely high here with Flourish (Limit Break Unlocks), Mettle (Carrying over perks), and Prestige (Difficulty) mechanics. Bonus points for having varied Character Skins when you progress through these unlocks.+The Daily Challenges with unique modifiers is very well made and works as a quick run to the joyous game-play that is Griftlands!CONS:-Griftlands is extremely ambitious and sets out to do a lot of things at once. However, if you are looking for a complex and in-depth card game with meta deck-building, you might find Griftlands wanting. This can of course be improved by adding more builds and content into the game. over time!NEUTRAL:-I would say that the voice over that is being spoken in gibberish might not appeal to some but this method also allows the creation of more scenarios in the game to be created (without the need for narrated voice-over). It is actually pretty ingenious how the overall design of this game offers a captivating semi-sandbox content packed world-building galore that will only get better in time.The Developers did a phenomenal job and I really hope Griftlands will continue to receive the tender love and care it rightfully deserves with DLC content as the fundamentals for this game is amazingly poised to be one of the best and most polished single-player card games out there.

_childDocuments_.review: Early Access review: If you've played Slay the Spire (amazing deck builder if you haven't played it) you'll understand a lot of the underlying concepts straight up. However Griftlands is different. You're not just dealing with combat, negotiating is a completely different beast (still deck based), and while different, honestly no less enjoyable and cool because it mixes things up. Not only is combat and negotiation different, the narrative is a lot more compelling. A Slay the Spire run when it's going well draws me in pretty hard core, but my desire to go back after playing each character is fairly minimal, although done several times. Griftlands gives you the same journey, but with more journey. Making a decision isn't a split path that you can see ahead of time making the most informed decision, it's a path including the unknown. Going from A to B may mean you run into C, and now you must deal with the consequences of encounter C, which was not planned. And that's why I'd really recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I rarely write reviews and when I do, it's normally a negative one. Griftlands is by far one of the best games I've played in a long time. To summarize, it's a card game at it's core but I've never seen one with some much depth to it. The mechanics aside, your choices and actions have positive and negative consequences. Decide to kill someone instead of accept their surrender? You get a new card that gives you a benefit but a character might hate you because of it giving you a negative world status applicable to certain races.This game has more depth and personality than some triple A titles do. I want more from this game!Pros- StoryCard mechanics (Negotiating and fighting)Random eventsDeck buildingcharacter progressionCons-More music neededMore character voice actingNegotiating battle status applications (Sometimes I'm not sure if an enemy status effect is targeting me or themselves. An arrow or indicator would clear some of that up)

_childDocuments_.review: This is just a fantastic game, and well worth buying even though its not a "full release".  You get two complete characters with two copmletely different playstyles and stories.  The only thing you're waiting on is a third character.  The stories for each characters are entirely isolated to themselves, so the only thing you're missing is just one more short story.The art style is fantastic.  The music is perfect for the mood.  The writing is clear, fun, and has great world building.  Humor is just right, not over the top.  It is a deck builder combined with a choose your own adventure.  Even then, dialog is not too long, and easily skipped on repeat playthroughs.  Combat is quick, has depth, but feels very fair on the beginning difficulties.  Like most deck builders, each "complete" playthrough will unlock more abilities, and make the game more difficult the next time around.I can safely say this is an outstanding game, and likely a masterpiece of this genre.  It is rare to see all the moving parts of a game come together like this, and I am honestly shocked and overjoyed at the quality.  If you have even a passing interest in deck builders, choices, and a decent story, you would be remiss to not grab this gem.Get it.  You won't regret it.  And if you actually do? The battles are very punishing, and it's clear just how much your actions have consequence, though for the most part it's really well balanced! My favourite mechanic has to be the relationship system. It's a fun and comical way to see consequence benefit or impair you. _childDocuments_.review: If you want a longer, more in-depth video review you can watch it here: Griftlands is one of the most revolutionary roguelites I have ever played.It takes inspiration from games like Slay the Spire but completely innovates in a huge amount of ways.The first big thing in the game is the fact that instead of just building one deck you actually are building two. You have your combat deck and then you have a negotiation deck which you use when you try to convince someone of something.The next huge thing is that this is an extremely narrative based game where the runs take around 5 hours to complete.  In these campaigns you can work for different sides and you can make friends or enemies with every npc in the game. You can kill some people and completely remove them from the story and it is all really dynamic. It feels like a big choose your own adventure roguelite which is really cool.The last big thing is just the sheer amount of unique cards, passive grafts, and events. Every game really feels different.I would highly recommend this game as it is one of the most innovative and revolutionary roguelites I have ever played.

_childDocuments_.review: So I have put a TON of hours of gameplay into this game already so it's easy to say I really enjoy this game. That being said, I see a ton of reviews saying it is like STS and that's a fairly decent comparison (I've put plenty of time into both games), although not a completely accurate representation. I would say STS is much more straight forward to pick up, but is more difficult to master at higher ascension levels through the interactions of it's game mechanics such as a higher emphasis of artifact implementation for the deck and the broader card "themes" than you would see in GL. For Griftlands, the learning curve is definitely more steep due to a higher integration of rpg elements. Often you will be looking at the game and wondering if the decisions you could make would benefit you and give you an edge in the story, and it may have nothing to do with the actual deckbuilding elements of the game. There is also the fact there are two decks you're actually building at once, a battle and a negotiation, both of which are used in completely different ways. This may seem overwhelming at first, especially for the negotiation portion because there aren't too many battle systems like it, but it comes together quickly with the unique themes each character provides. The cards make it pretty easy to determine what type of deck you can do early on since they can be extremely useful in one archetype and complete garbage in another with a few exceptions (Rook's Headbang Rare Negotiation card for instance works in a wide variety of decks and I've never felt any dissatisfaction picking it up). After you finish the story for each character, you do unlock a brawl mode which definitely has the familiarity to the Rogue-Type game mode you see in STS. My last dictation for the game is the most recent update, which I admit, I need to spend more time checking out. These are just intitial impressions of what I've seen so far. It has changed it's prestige mode dramatically, which is surprising since there really wasn't a problem with it. It's not better or worse, it's just interesting to change. I do like the perk system which rewards the grind even more with your playthroughs. The mutators are not gone but they are utilized differently, but that's no big deal since most people don't use those game modes until they feel they've reached a limit to the standard play and just want to mess around. The last and -if I had to choose- most irritating change is the interface. It's much more cluttered than it was from previous patches, trying to give all the information on one screen. If I hadn't been playing as much as I already have, I would be completely overwhelmed looking at all the icons. I feel the devs were looking for a look somewhat like STS but there are too many mechanics in GL to do that so it seems more simple to stick with menus which can be opened and closed with quick keys. Overall, Griftlands does not seem to take as long to master as STS but the amount of content this game has is frankly astounding and it is a very rewarding experience to grind, especially since it's in early access. Granted, this could change depending on the state of the game in the future, but as long as they stick with the "if it ain't broke, don't fix it" mentality, keep the game's identity, and focus on creating a more playable experience (A more interactive tutorial for both types of combat for instance), then KLEI Entertainment will have a great title on their hands.

_childDocuments_.review: A fairly early assessment but this might become my all time favourite rogue-lite. It manages to pull off an incredible balancing act between making the story fun and interactive while at the same preserving the core gameplay loop of a deck-building rogue-lite. Being the first of your kind and and starting out with such a hit is quite an impressive feat. The soundtrack is phenomenal and I catch myself humming the battle and negotiation theme all the time now.The tutorials could be a bit more extensive and include an optional training match since a few of the concepts introduced are not exactly intuitive to understand and hovering over 15 icons each battle for the first few runs to understand what they do can probably be annoying for some newcomers.I can't recommend it highly enough right now. _childDocuments_.review: Griftlands is difficult to explain. It's a sci-fi deck-building card battle roguelite  with open world RPG elements and a faction/relationship system where taking missions for certain characters will either make them friendly/antagonistic towards you with two battle systems where you can either attempt to fight or talk your way out of encounters. It's an ambitious idea, and I'm happy to say it works.However, the thing that concerns me is that while Griftlands attempts to be a melting pot of all these ambitious things, it spreads itself thin in some points. For my first run I'm attempting to choose to fight instead of talk my way out of encounters, and while combat is fun it lacks the depth something like Slay The Spire has where you can build some crazy and powerful combos that make you feel like a galaxy brain when you execute them. Hopefully Klei will keep adding onto this in the future, but it's something to note.Overall, it's a fantastic game that is IMO very reasonably priced. It's worth picking up if you a fan of deckbuilding/card battlers and worth at least putting on your wishlist and picking up during a sale even if you aren't a fan of card battlers.

_childDocuments_.review: wonderful story-driven deck building roguelikebe prepared for many deaths as the main mode has permadeaththe way you improve is through death - similar to other roguelikesi feel like a lot of the complaints are for people who either havent experienced this genre of game before or werent expecting the difficultythe multiple options for optimising your character makes for different gameplay every time, as well as the procedurally generated quests and storylinesbalancing the political mechanics and social aspects with the battles is an interesting dynamic - do you keep people alive and let them hate you (which affects gameplay giving you debuffs), and possibly face them again, or do you kill them and create more issues with other people hating you or seeing you as a killer which affects relationships down the linewith the choice of negotiation and combat, and within the choice for a more peaceful or violent / threatening approach, i find my character is different every time and there are multiple ways to playoverall enjoyable game for both the story and gameplaynot to mention the soundtrack, sound effects and visual design which are also impressive and engaging as well as creating a unique world

_childDocuments_.review: What a huge breath of fresh air! I haven't played a game quite like Griftlands, though I've played several games that share facets of the game. It takes bits and pieces from titles like Darkest Dungeon and Slay the Spire, along with nearly other roguelike/lite and deckbuilder from the past decade. And yet Griftlands has an aesthetic that feels like a Sci-Fi version of The Banner Saga; a story filled with intrigue, and several characters to play as through various tales.The combat works much like a traditional RPG, attacking and using abilities in a turn based fashion, but all the while you're performing those actions by using cards, and various mechanics included on them. It gives a bit of randomization to combat, but in deck building lies your consistency, as any TCG Player will tell you. This is standard fair for games that utilize cards as the primary engine for combat. Where Griftlands sets itself apart is by having an entirely separate deck used for diplomacy (or the lack there of). Most encounters will allow you to choose between traditional combat and negotiation. Negotiation is essentially a battle, but it's represented on screen differently, and honestly it's difficult to describe with out seeing it, but essentially your intents are arguments fight against each other until someone's core argument is defeated. Just as pets and temporary allies will help you in normal fights, they will also add arguments to your side of the field as dialogue begins. There's a wealth to do here. I've put in runs as all three characters but have yet to complete a run (Sal's end boss has killed me a few times), but you still earn account wide progression some of which is shared between characters, so eventually you'll gain an easier advantage through the game. Since gear and cards are randomized each game, you never know if you'll get the best deck or be forced to build in another direction, so some runs will be easier than others. I could go on and on, but I'll leave you with this. If you enjoyed any of the games I've mentioned in this review, you'll probably like this game. For bite sized RPG goodness with some TCG flavor, you can't go wrong, and it's CHEAP right now. 10/10. Would graft ♥♥♥♥ to my skull again.

_childDocuments_.review: I was intrigued on how there will be two different types of approaches in the game and I love how it was implemented into the game. You can approach things through negotiations or just be a barbarian and kill/fight everyone. I tried to balance both of my decks during my first run and it was a success. I tried improving only one of my deck in the following run and it was hard because there are some scenarios that forced you to follow a certain approach . If you love deckbuilding games, I highly recommend this game.  In terms of art, music and dialogue, I love everything and it shows how much effort they put into Griftlands. Note: I spent around 10-20 hours of gameplay on my epic account. Kudos to klei for giving everyone who bought from epic an option to get a copy on steam.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR This game is hard to comprehend mechanically and doesn't reward understanding itI understand why people like this game, but it doesn't click for me and I think there is good reason for that. Most times people view a game having a lot of content as a great thing but for me there is a meaningful differentiation with this game. This game has a lot more complexity than it has depth. Each character has a dozen different one word keywords on their cards, some of them do pretty much the same thing but have different names, like defense/composure or adrenaline/temporary power; a lot of the fights have unique passive effects that you only understand if you hover over the opponent and read it and all the little things floating around them; Each encounter has convoluted dialogue that gets thrown at you with little impact. It is hard to engage with everything if I have to memorize a paragraph to know the difference between wound/bleed/burn/poison and all the other debuffs you can apply.Compare this to slay the spire you can see a stark difference. Slay the Spire has low complexity and high depth, Griftlands has high complexity and low depth. If you read a card in Slay the Spire you instantly know what it does if you were to play it in any fight, but each decision you make while drafting or playing matters and is interesting. In Griftlands runs are so inundated with information, I just block it out and just try my best to throw things together.I enjoy the game type and appreciate the hard work that obviously was put in but it feels like there so many mechanics that are in the game for their own sake and do not improve the game.
