_childDocuments_.review: Deck-Building Roguelike set in a low-powered sci-fi setting. The main things Griftlands has over others in the genre is aesthetic -- the signature Klei artstyle looks really good here, and while the constant explaining of in-universe jargon is a little off-putting at first, you get more of a feel for the Griftlands world as you play more.Three characters to play as, each offering different playstyles as well as each having different quests and goals. A bounty hunter, a spy, and a disgraced drunkard noble. You take up jobs, which always result in either a negotiation confrontation, a physical fight, or both.The physical combat is the more familiar of the two if you've played any other deckbuilder. Negotiations might seem perplexing at first -- it looks like the game is throwing a lot of different things around each character. Once you read the cards and character abilities a bit, it's a lot less obtuse than it seems to be.Main complaint i have is that once you play through several runs and start turning up the challenge levels, the charm of the setting starts to wear off. You'll start seeing the same quests again, and you'll disregard the dialogues of the NPCs, trying to click through every text bubble and focusing on which NPCs give you relevant boons. It's a game, not a DM so it won't get mad at you for going full munchkin -- in fact, that's quite necessary at higher levels. But it diminishes the Griftlands world just a bit, in my opinion. EDIT: I forgot that Brawl mode is a thing, which is an endless mode that cuts down on that a bit.Currently, the game is still in early access... But there's a LOT here. 2 of the 3 characters are more or less finished in their storyline, and the third, while not there yet, has a lot to experience still. Mod support was implemented a little while back so you can always mix it up with whatever the community comes up with.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I picked this up early-access and it's my first deck-builder game, though I'd heard a lot already about Slay The Spire and it's similarities. Since I started playing I've been recommending this to everyone. The art style, animations, UI is all sleek, beautiful and masterfully polished as expected from Klei. The soundtrack and SFX is a stand out for me - from the atmospheric background hustle of the Griftlands, to the tense beats that pick up as you get low on health which incites a familiar feeling to those who played old school Pokemon!I thoroughly enjoyed the gameplay too; the three characters all had vastly different stories and play styles, whilst the rogue-element was finessed enough to provide lots of replayability. I've played 50 hours so far and feel like I've not scratched the surface. As other reviews have said, the mechanics of the fights & negotiations is easy to pick up but hard to master, but the game does a great job of making you want to master it. Another unique masterpiece from Klei.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I cannot say enough good things about this game. Roguelite deckbuilding RPG where choices matter, with engaging narratives, great writing, relatable characters, awesome worldbuilding, thoughtful card-drafting elements, not one but TWO deck formats (one for combat, one for negotiation) and loads of replayability. Buy this game. Buy it twice. Buy it for all your friends. Sell your organs and donate the money to Klei so they can develop more content for this masterpiece.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: The mechanics and story were occasionally interesting during Early Access, but now that it's been released, it's all pulled together well. The story is excellent, and the choices do matter. I've played several deckbuilders; this is the first one that I've felt emotionally connected to the characters. And not just the main character! It's impressive what they have pulled off with interstitials that would normally be an instant skip.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: GREAT GAME! . Ive been playing Monster Train lately. (Another card game) Then i found Griftlands and WOW! To keep this short and to the point. Its a card game with animated quest zones and  upgradable stats, if you will. Its a great new twist on card style games and its been very fun and even in being early access, ive had ZERO bugs. . I mean damn this is tight for an early access. I got it on sale and its really worth it if you like this type of game. Its truly deserving of the Overwhelming positive reviews. i dont usually follow the crowd but this is a go!
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Griftlands give a refreshing twist on the usual deck building genre. The character stories are entertaining though leave little room for replaying again, though this is a minor setback from the incredibly re-playable gameplay loop that always gives you a different way to approach each situation. Unique gadgets and pets can give you the edge you need in a bad situation and cybernetic enhancements can completely shift how you play.Another must try from Klei, particularly if you are a fan of Slay the Spire or other deck building games.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I like the option to deal with an encounter through negotiation or battle. Nice character options and good tutorials to get you started. If you already know deck based games you'll be fine, if you don't it may take a bit of time to get used to the strategy. Artwork is fun and the environment is a somewhat gritty-post-apocalyptic sci-fi fantasy world. I also very much appreciate the mix of genders and bizarre races.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: These are my thoughts after 8 hours of play. I have fun playing this game, but for some reason the art for the females makes them sort of masculine looking. The females are all portrayed as being man-like. The replayability is very high as each run awards xp and unlockables that can be used in subsequent runs. The game mechanics are solid and the game feels fair and balanced. The story is so-so and not really my favorite aspect of the game. I want to be the good guy, a traditional hero, not an antihero who only has options of being the misunderstood bad guy or a deliberate bad guy. If the writers wanted to offer a path that allows for villainous behavior then that's fine, but only allowing immoral choices makes the story rather dull. The music and sounds are perfect. The cards are interesting and offer a variety of strategies and tactics. The overall production value of the game is top-notch. This is a triple-A game as far as completeness and quality goes.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Okay. First a friend came and told me: It's like Slay the Spire, but better.I'm like: Hell no. Well, guess what. I've got the game for five days and 30hours in it. In a busy week.This game is really good. NPC interactions, choices that matter, good lore (enough dept to keep you interested, but not enough to write a book about it) and the true gemstone: Two decks.Yeah, you heard it right. The battle deck and the negotiation deck. The battle is like any other game, but the negotiation is a really good system. Fresh and complicated, but easy to learn if you don't mind reading and thinking a bit.This game has lots of potential, a brawl system that works like a endless game mode for those like me who like to do "runs", and even has an 'update counter' telling you when they are goona update it. Worth every second in it.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I love the option to befriend or kill almost everyone I meet. The upgrade system for cards was rewarding and the story satisfyingly thematic. I also appreciate the game saying I can or should kill someone, but giving me the option to spare them even if its not strictly beneficial in the short/long term. (because I'm a good boy) Great visuals, walked the line between difficult and satisfying.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Story focused RPG roguelike? Deck builder dating sim? Griftlands is an innovative fusion of game mechanics with a strong branching story. Each of the characters have stories with multiple decision points allowing you to choose allies and enemies. The game systems echo this choice by giving you options between battles and negotiations. But it doesn't stop there, a negotiation can either be hostile or diplomatic; battles can be aggressive or defensive. All together the game is a fractal, nested set of interesting choices. The Roguelike permadeath style gives you lots of chances to try out different choices.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Griftlands is a great deckbuilder roguelite that is very fun, addictive, brutal, and also rewarding. It offers extreme flexibility in how you approach conflict and achieve your goals, and pulls no punches. Each of the three different characters are very different in a good way, with unique styles and approaches that are very distinctive. Negotiation is a little tricky intially but once you get the hang out of it I found it very rewarding, and combat is a treat. Plus, each successful run allows you to go the next Renown level which is even harder, and so it is never "too easy" from my experience. This is Klei after all. I only wish we had more campaigns then just the three, but hopefully we'll get a sequel. If not, what's here is a lot of fun, and almost every playthrough is different. There's also modding to build on the amazing system here of course.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: too slow for me, way to much story and faffing about between battles. That said it looks and sounds great and works well, just not really what i'm looking for in a deck roguelike builder, others may get more out of it.  I prefer these sort of games where i can complete a run in 30-60 mins e.g. Slay the Spire & Monster Train, which are still the 2 benchmarks for this genre.  If you like Hand of Gilgamesh you will probably like this though, they are similar in that they are more story driven and a bit less"roguey"
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Installed game to just check it out ... 4 hours later it was way past bed time.This game is everything I have been looking for in a Deckbuilder and then some. Great gameplay, great art style,  the games feels fair I learn what works and what does not.If you liked Slay the Spire this is the game you need to be playing. I bought it during the summer sale but it is worth full price for sure.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Like others have mentioned, thumbs sideways(?) would be my rating. I enjoyed the humor, characters, and story, but as a deck builder it never reaches the satisfaction and payoffs like Slay the Spire. And, because of the story length, it feels like much more of a slog to go back through after a run. Still going to recommend for those who are curious and want to go through the scenarios a few times. Thumbs up at a discount.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: This game takes the best of what Slay the Spire has, and add a healthy dose of personality. Your runs don't just feel like an attempt to reach the end of a dungeon. Your character has a past, relationships, bonds, and choices to make. Once your done with a run, you get one of those fun little "where are they now" cutscenes. I've only spent 23 hours on it so far. but there will be many more.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: its a very good game with tons of replaability per each charecter just due to the diferent story choices and murder options available per each run. Its fun its exciting and it does a good job at adding new and interesting mechanics into the deckbuilder roguelike genre. The only real problem ive found with this game is deck building isint super rewarding. Like if you want to make a certain deck architype like bleed for example your only option is to just take bleed cards and ignore the rest I wish there was more room for creativity in deck building possibilitites cause in all honestly it feels like the deck im playing is just premade and this is one of a select few deck options i can viable use. all in all though a very good game soli 8-10 caint wait for 1.0
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: It's not the worst deckbuilder in the world, but now that I finished 2 campaigns out of three, I can say that it didn't provide a lot of enjoyment. It has a lot of qualities (Art, world building, some gameplay ideas), but I will only remember how disappointing and how draining the whole experience was.The runs are so long, at least 4 hours if you make the effort to read half of the dialogues. The difficulty curve is strange. Everything will seem relatively easy for hours and hours, then you'll enter a fight with surprise mechanics and suddenly lose. This feels bad. What's also funny about it is that they implemented a star system to indicate the mission's difficulty but it's totally useless because you have no real alternative (contrary to most RPGs). During a run, you can only make a choice between two missions of the same difficulty (3-star, for instance). Every single time. And that's when you're not doing a main quest on the rails.The deckbuilding is weirdly implemented. There is quite a decent amount of cards, but it's hard to build synergies and make those decks feel personal. They become bloated very quickly, more than in any other deckbuilder, and there are really not enough opportunities to strim them.The story is ultimately uninteresting. The characters can be interesting, the very short relationships are nice (but they are way too short to have an impact), but the overall plot plays with the classic scheme of the rich/dominant class vs the rebels/proletarians, with some good and bad persons in each camp to create few moral dilemmas. The endings are anticlimatic in my opinion. I sadly didn't care, because it's too short as a story, because is too long as a deckbuilder, because it's way too cliché to my taste.It could have been a better game if it wasn't a scripted story. It could have been a true roguelike. They could have kept the world building, the factions, but all the dialogues and relationships, outcomes, would have been influenced by your choices and generated by a complex algorithm. Because right now I have no desire to replay the same characters and the same stories barely modified by the fact that this time I sided with the bad guy... Wow... I'm already bored to death just by thinking about it.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: A very unique and enticing way to look at a deck builder and Klei did a great job with this one. I must say, I found it a bit tiring to play through the story and dialogues over and over again but still doesn't take the fun and thrill of a great story driven deck builder away specially with the mutations and prestige. Definitely up there with Slay the Spire and has a lot of potential!
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: A roguelike RPG & Card battler. It's well made and I didn't encounter any bugs, but for me the pace just doesn't work - roguelike games are fun because you lose fast without investing a lot of time, but here a run can take 6h+. There's also some design issues where choosing some grafts (personal upgrades) make it impossible to complete quests.On the plus side, the card upgrade mechanics are fun (upgrade what you use, multiple upgrade options for each card), and the split between negotiation and combat decks is interesting. But for me it's just not fun enough that I would recommend it to anyone.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Fun deck-builder even in Early access.  Fun stories, with randomly generated encounters.  The encounters do get a bit repetitive after 20 hours of play, but still enjoyable.  The interactions with characters and factions are an interesting element to game-play that might require a bit of pre-planning.  This game is a bit more forgiving than other deck builders out there to start, but prestige modes can be unlocked to ramp up the difficulty.  I'd give this game an 8/10 and it kicks ass!
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I spent a ton of time on this game and have really enjoyed it, but I've disliked nearly every EA change in the last several updates. Their attempt to add rogue-lite meta-progression systems, of which there are now three, have all been increasingly unsatisfying. Compressing the prestige tiers was a good idea, except now they're drastically unbalanced because of card and NPC changes made in light of the meta-progression systems, causing the difficulty to arbitrarily spike because you rolled into a promoted NPC rather than a normal one, for example. Their idea of a daily challenge is one of the least fun of its type I've seen, focusing on an aggressive challenge and score-based model but basically forcing you to play the run twice if you actually want to be competitive- once to see the seed, and then again to actually play your run- otherwise you run into situations like where you intend to use no status ailments, but the card draft hands you nothing but, and your early draft choices are useless because you never found the other pieces. The Mettle and Flourish update also seem to come from a really strange place, offering some of the similar bonuses from the Perks engine, but incremental, and I just don't understand the point of aiming to complete Grifts but also push money into Mettle at the same time, and I definitely have no interest in more grinding. I love Klei's games and their design sensibility is great, and I've recommended Griftlands in the past, but I have no faith in it going forward, since I no longer understand what their design aims are. I don't know if I'll install 1.0 to see the rest of Smith but for the time being, I'm out.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Klei delivers once again.Theres 2 different forms of battle: combat and negotiation.Both have distinct differences and both are fun to play.I also like that on every playthrough you play different missions and interact with different people.Klei did a great job to make every run feel unique and keep you invested and seeing how the story unfolds this time around.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: The worst thing about this game is that it (or should I say "I") suffer from the classic "One More Turn Syndrome".The game is great. The combat/arguments are fun.Really the only reasons I would not suggest this game is either a) you don't like card based games b) you have something you should be doing because this game will suck up all your time.

The stories differ for every character but still feel loosely connected and the game really understands to build an immersive universe around you. The Deck-Building aspect functions a little differently then most other games, which adds another interesting bit. _childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished my first run, that took me around 5 hours - and boy, i enjoyed it much! Alot of mechanics ( like really alot), great visual style (at least for my taste), and even entertaining story with quite alot (at least for a genre) dialogs, wich i even read without skipin'. _childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: This game has taken a lot of good lessons from successful deck builders, and added story elements usually lacking from those games. I was sceptical of the dual conflict systems, but they pull it off well. Don't expect something as single-minded and fine-tuned as Slay the Spire. Griftlands is every bit as fun, and a very different type of experience!
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: sincerely loving this game. i and my friends have put a significant amount of time into slay the spire but between watching my friends play and playing it myself i wanted something new. i am so beyond happy about this game. it's very engaging. i love the way cards upgrade in this game, they gain xp every time you play them until eventually they can upgrade into one of a few choices. i love that you have multiple decks to suit your needs in the story, a deck for combat and a deck for negotiation. so while you can have an amazing negotiation deck you can still kinda get dunked on by combat so it's important to balance out both. i honestly cannot believe this is early access; it's that good.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I was getting burnt out of Slay the Spire and wanted to find a game within the same genre to breathe some life back into it for me, and then I was recommended Griftlands. The game has 2 different "combat" systems, fighting and negotiating, with most scenarios letting you pick which to use. You follow a main storyline for each character, but the game has slightly different paths and choices you can do that's really helpful in keeping you hooked. There is also random encounters and little pop up events you can choose to do, which I also really like. I did mention the branching pathing, and while it did help hold my attention, I do wish there was more choices you made that actually influenced the story. Each of the character's stories only really has 2 endings it can have, along with a couple other minor things that get tacked on along the way. For being mainly a story-driven game, I do feel it needs a bit more juice into it to make it worth the price. I finished all 3 of the storylines within 7 hours.The leveling system is also painfully slow. Similar to StS, the more runs you do on a character (and how well you do) levels them up to unlock new cards. You also earn mettle in-game which can very slightly increase that character's base stats for all future runs. However, the leveling is painfully slow. At 11 hours in with many successful (or good attempt) runs, none of my characters have even reached the halfway mark yet. This just feels like a cheap way to keep players playing, if I'm being honest.That being said, I really enjoyed this game. I look forward to seeing what future content updates they make to it.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Griftlands feels exactly like what all Roguelike Deckbuilders should strive to be, in my opinion. It feels like a classic RPG in that it is story-driven with quests and unique characters to meet and build (or break) relationships with. On top of that, the world feels incredibly alive, with events happening and your character being a part of them, not always being the hero that swoops in to drive the plot entirely. You have to make hard decisions sometimes, even outside of the strategic deckbuilding choices. Maybe it's building one relationship at the expense of tearing another down. Whatever gets you to your desired goal is up to you to decide on each run.Even with all of this, Griftlands doesn't leave out the combat complexity, with 2 independent decks per run to build simultaneously. Both systems (Negotiations and Combat) are deep and rewarding in their own right as well, neither feeling like it completely overshadows the other in importance or depth.I bought it on sale, but I can safely say that this would be worth the purchase at full price if you like anything about the idea of a Story-driven Roguelike Deckbuilder.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: It's a solid game in a lot of ways. The core gameplay is engaging, the artwork is nice, and they clearly put a lot of thought into the world they created. The glaring problem it has in my mind is that they made a rouge-like game with an expectation that the player will fail multiple times before getting a good run, and also included a deeper storyline that gets reset every time the player fails. I found it very annoying to have to click through the same long dialog exchanges between characters every time I started a new run. It prevented me from getting immersed in the storyline and felt like a waste of time. Which is a shame, because it looks like it could have been a good story  if it didn't keep forcing the player to start back at page one over and over again.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Great Indie game with fun world building and pretty good lore. The gameplay is varied and enjoyable the whole way through, the unique battle and negotiation tactics were a cool addition. The stories aren't the best they could be but they are still fun and engaging. Would recommend for people who like card games, if not the game isn't an extremely memorable must play but it is still worth the price.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: An awesome take on deck-building roguelike games with much more engaging story elements than I was expecting. I can see myself plunging dozens of hours into each character, trying different scenarios and plans each time I go through. I love the random encounters and the way that the narrative develops based on the decisions that you make. A 10/10 for me and a no-brainer buy at its price for the amount of good I know I'll get out of it!
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Really great game that can fullfill in an interesting way your thirst for deckbuilder games. You will appreciate it more, tho, if you don't expect a game where you can invest yourself in deep systems (a-la-sts). Griftlands primary focus is the narrative in detriment of the full liberty system in a deckbuilder. So, is that bad? You'll have to think again on your what your standard perspective is. In this day where sts seems to be the norm you'll have to open your mind / lower your expectatives to look how phenomenal Klei has come up with a way to use deckbuilding as a narrative mechanic.This, plus their interaction system (that seams to share it's inspiration with shadows of mordor nemesis system) will give you a truly unique experience that will keep you engaged at least around 20 hours. If i wasnt clear enough, i can explain further my points in the comments.See you around bois!
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I'll add my voice to the chorus: Slay the Spire's bare bones plus Klei's expert fleshing-out leads to this budding masterpiece of a game.Deckbuilder roguelikes are an intensely fun genre for the kind of mind that likes to mini-max on the fly, and in addition to an expert and interesting story and 'persuasion' element that you'll see detailed with many other reviews on here, the deckbuilder framework itself is excellent in Griftlands, not just being a Slay-the-Spire clone but streamlining it.  The most noticeable mechanic is how card upgrades work: instead of relying on special events to upgrade, cards upgrade naturally with use and give you choices in how to upgrade them.  Imagine in Slay the Spire that you were trying to build a card draw deck, and instead of having to lean into card removal the whole game to clear out your strikes and defends, you could choose an upgrade on your strikes and defends that also gave them card draw.Klei games come with sky high expectations for those familiar with the company, and Griftlands delivers.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I feel comfortable recommending Griftlands to literally anyone who is interested in any deck-builder game.Mechanically, Griftlands is exceptionally well put together. The three main scenarios are challenging and varied. The story is well put together and actually has some pretty good writing with some interesting moral dilemmas. Different choices yield different upgrades and challenges, so story choices are impactful and immersing at first, and still engaging when you're playing as a pure psychopath on your hundredth run.The story is also completely unobtrusive for people looking to skip it. We're talking an average of 3-5 seconds between actual decisions when you're skipping stuff. The dialogue/combat battle system is also very compelling. Decisions to fight or talk can have huge impacts for your entire run with the Loved/Hated system that gives you potentially powerful buffs/debuffs.Many simple systems intersect in very complicated ways giving the game an insane amount of depth while still being very approachable. All in all, Griftlands is a great game that you can enjoy in many different ways, making it an easy recommend. I don't really enjoy deck-builders but even I found this game really fun. It's truly under-rated.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Let me start off by saying that I'm a sucker for card-battlers, I probably have over a 1000 hours combined over games like Hearthstone, Slay the Spire, Artifact, Monster Train, etc. I MUST say that this game is deep. I mean seriously deep. There is so much to strategize and plan. It has a great story and slick art. The synergies don't feel forced and the progression system is a straight up dopamine-machine. If you like card games like me, don't skip this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Mixed feelings. Love Klei games. This one did not disappoint either. Deck builder with nice themes and atmosphere. In the game you get to use 2 different types of decks interchangeably (fighting and negotiating), which makes it feel less repetitive. Also, you get to influence relationships with many NPC in the game, which at the end of the spectrum (love or hate) provide buffs or debuffs. Several stories. Each with their own set of cards. Nice. Last time I played was during an early development stage of the 3rd story. Out of the blue a gay marriage is shoved down your throat. I don't mind gay people, but I do mind this shoved down my throat. It's not a part of my life and it is unlikely to become one. Personally, I don't shove down gay people's throat a traditional marriage. So, reverse, I feel, is unjustified. Why can't developers go about it like Deus Ex MD did (if you want to explore, you find it. It's not forced upon you)?
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Too tired to post a proper review, so you probably want to read the next few lines and scroll on.What I can tell you is that this game is amazing. I just did my first run, started some time in the afternoon, looked at the time and it's 1:19 AM. Only other game that's done that to me was Civ 5. Excellent writing really makes the world come to life in all its dark splendor, with just enough humor to keep it in a good spot.The different characters' cards use different mechanics, similarly to Slay The Spire - which on that note, I would absolutely rate this game as well as I would STS which is saying something, seeing how I have hundreds of hours on it (on Switch) and I've never found any other deck builder to come close. The changes are interesting and meaningful (by the looks of it - only done a run with the first character), and there seems to be plenty of variety across the different game facets (cards, interactions, quests, ways to approach just about anything, etc) to warrant multiple runs with each character, providing dozens if not hundreds of hours of gameplay. EDIT: I was too curious and started a new run before heading to bed, and the first 3 quests I could choose from were completely different from the first time, meaning that there's even more variety than I originally thought! This may very well be my new favorite game.Combat is a similar formula to STS, and so is the deck building component, though here cards get upgraded through using them. You can also have a pet or companions which is fun - I think you could also have multiple pets if you worked toward that. There are also prestige levels - 7, at least for the first character, the others may have more / less. The art is unique, and I wasn't sure I'd be into it at first, but it works well with the rest of the game and I found myself enjoying it quite a bit as I explored Murder Bay.A decent amount of unlockables also contribute to the replayability, but because there are so many ways to do things I feel like a lot of them will get unlocked just by playing the game in different ways, making different choices, etc. though there's still something there for those looking for new ways to challenge themselves or something new to aim for. Maybe you just never managed to get that one resident to like you...So anyway, if you're still here, hopefully you'll buy this - it's frankly an amazingly good game. It's extremely immersive in my opinion and they devs built a really interesting world with fitting characters. I hope that we'll be getting either a sequel or some DLC in the years to come, just because I already want to see & know more about this world and its inhabitants!!
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I've only played the first character for 10 hours and I feel like I've only scratched the tip of the iceberg. It's a little complicated unless you're coming from Slay the Spire or some other type of rogue-lite deckbuilder.Runs are pretty long but I don't see it as a downside. Will get a bit faster as you learn the game, of course.There is a story mode and also a 'brawl mode' which is your typical run with almost 0 story for those just tryna play. But the story mode is still a rogue-lite and has its own draw with a few key decisions you can make by befriending certain people or making enemies with them. Yeah, that's a whole system too. Lots of difficulty options. Nothing quite yet feels too strong or underpowered, but all pretty fun. Might come back to this and update it as I play but it's pretty dope so far.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Good deck-building game with solid narration.[+] 3 different characters with their own story, mechanics and musics[+] complex narration with actual choices (for story modes)[+] gameplay and story integration (actions have consequence)[+] music account for dramatic tension (+++ for me, I love this kind of thing)[+] pleasant character designs with cute animations[+] high replayability due to randomized segments and boss mechanics[+] interesting world buildingI enjoyed every moment with this game; 10/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

The cards are not lining up to have some combos, and all the upgrade things are not so helpful. _childDocuments_.review: I've been a fan of card crawlers for a while now (Roguebook, Spire, Monster Train) The bar was set high by these previous games, but I've been totally impressed by this game. It seems to have carved out a very specific, unique niche in this class of game... The visual style is great, and animated constantly, which keeps the relatively still screens feeling 'alive' - Combine that with the choose-your-path adventure story, and this feels like an interactive graphic novel, which kept me engaged in the overall journey.  Fun writing and characters with personality.The negotiation game is a whole different beast from standard-style battles, with its own deck, and is a solidly engaging sequence I never got bored of being in. Negotiation isn't a tack-on minigame, it's a well designed and intricate thing of its own. Almost every single situation allows you to choose Battle or Negociate, so it's totally integrated in the design. So in a nutshell, you're actually getting 2 different card battlers in this one game, and you get to choose how much of each one you spend your time in - beautiful. The way card rewards and upgrades are based on usage, this also builds your character to be strongest in your preferred play-style. All these pieces work together beautifully, I found.I've got very few cons on this one. The biggest 'down' is kind of a compliment too: The character campaigns were too short. When you got me interested in the progress of my character and this world, I was hoping to grow a lot more and see a lot more of my choices ripple forward in time. I was actually kind of stunned when I finished the first run when I thought we were just getting started - This is more of a "one week in a life" tale  rather than the winding RPG adventure I was ready for.So it sits a little uncomfortably for me. The short cycle to complete a run seems to want to be in the "Quick runs" category like Spire. But the heavy emphasis on storytelling, dialog, characters with love/hate meters - All of this seems more about long-term investment in much longer runs. It's too bad, I think this will make it get old faster for me because I'll get sick of going through the same story beats over and over. For a quick run, I'll keep leaning more to Monster Train for its 'disposable' level of attention investment. But maybe Griftlands 2 will see their potential, and lean more towards longer, more complex narratives with rippling choices - to really take advantage of what they got going here. I want to see more games like this one, now that they've set a standard. There's a lot of potential to take this model and push it into something bigger!Overall, if you like the other games referenced at the start, I say you can't go wrong giving this very solid and unique entry a play. It's not just another clone of the genre, and I can feel the care and passion the makers had for this vision.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is exceptional. Tons of branching decision making in the overworld, and a tight slay the spire style deck builder. The idea of having a "negotiation deck" and battling with your words is a novel addition and adds a whole second deck and strategy to manage. _childDocuments_.review: Do you like Roguelikes?If yes: Play itDo you like a story rich campaign with good writing and where your choices matter?If yes: Play it.Did you like the concept of charisma in Fallout, and how it could get you out of trouble if your stat was high enough?This game turns that into a secondary battle system that's just as fleshed out as the normal one and has its own deckDoes that sound interesting? PLAY IT.Do you like deckbuilding and crafting your perfect build?There's tons of cards, and you unlock more as you progress.  You can craft builds for both negotiations AND battles.If you're that kind of person: PLAY IT.Do you actually hate card-based games?If Yes: So did I.  Play it anyway, it'll make you love them.Have you played Slay The Spire?This game is very similar to that, but way deeper, and with a story campaign that slightly changes every time you play, and 3 of them at that, one for each character that's completely unique from the last. _childDocuments_.review: This is definitely my favorite deck-building game since Slay the Spire! I played this since Early Access times, and I'd say it was one of the best EA games out there; there was a lot of content, constant updates, and pretty much no bugs. Now I finally finished the final campaign (there are three different campaigns, one for each character), and I can't recommend it enough. If you liked StS, you'd definitely enjoy this one as well. In addition to pretty addictive gameplay, there are also great stories, characters, and some branching paths. I rarely came back to games after beating them for the first time, but I could already imagine playing this one more time to see some other outcomes and simply try new cards. _childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Wasn't sure if I was going to like this game at first, but I enjoyed it.There's 2 combat systems, negotiation and battling, and you make choices to advance through the story. _childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a complete package. Some games are minimalist, they strive for mechanical perfection, to do one thing really well, the core mechanics. This game takes that fine tuned system from a game like Slay the spire and also build a whole world as setting, a plot, re-occurring cast of characters, introduces multiple ally options and more.While games like Dicey Dungeons can be oppressive with its constant drain of resources, Griftlands gives multiple strategic options on how to cope with that challenge. Lots of tactical considerations at every single step. It's great. And it's in a fuller experience than when it was launched on epic games store. It is the best game in this rogue-like-card-based-tactics subgenre.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I really like this.The way it feels like an RPG, a story game, a card game, a rogue-like--I started it, and thought, "Well, here come's another attempt that will fail somewhere," but I don't think it does. _childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I would very much like to recommend this game, but there is one reason I simply cannot.There are many good things to be said about the wonderful atmosphere, the interesting characters, the great music and a story that's been decent enough so far. However, if there is one thing I simply can't get over is the fact that even if you steamroll all encounters, the final boss will have some overpowered items/abilities at their disposal which provides a massive jump in difficulty that you weren't exactly waiting for. I absolutely hate such unexpected changes when everything else is ridiculously easy. I was very much immersed in the game until that point.Sure, you get a chance to remove one or two of the boss's items if you play well, but there is no reason the first character's final boss should even have those items to begin with and that honestly breaks all immersion for me. Especially since you can't know which items are the worst unless you look it up outside of the game. Not only that, I enjoy the negotiation mechanic but if you want to have a decent enough deck you'll have to do quite a bit of battling and that kinda goes against the way I played this game. Negotiation is useless when you're at the end boss, so just focus on your battle deck throughout the run.Oh, and don't bother asking people on the Steam forums for help. You'll only get to hear 'git gud' and that's about it. I don't play games for their difficulty. I play them to enjoy my free time. This sudden and unnecessary jump to an overpowered end boss that Griftlands did really messed up all enjoyment I had with the game up till that point. I'm not sure if I'll ever come back to the game. The story and choice system was fun, but this boss business looks like a dealbreaker for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: It's Slay the Spire but with way more story, really enjoy going through all the different routes and options and see what happens. Unfortunately the workshop currently is a bit empty, so replayability does end after a while. Also the Brawl mode, at least for me, takes literally everything away that makes the game fun, I don't get it. But the core gameplay is amazing, and the worldbuilding and characters are just fantastic.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Griftlands is just absolutely wonderful. I am usually not really interested in deck-building card games but this one has a really fresh and ambitious take on the genre. The sci-fi world of Griftlands hearkens back strongly to the Gilded Age of the late 1800s (most overtly so in the Bog Job), which presented a unique setting that I really enjoyed seeing in an indirect fashion in this game. The writing is terrific. Not only is the prose striking with many great quips and intriguing world-building, but the information you're told and the decisions you choose to make with them are genuinely meaningful. Even something so little as choosing to ask for clarification from a stranger who's dodgily telling you to quickly do as they say can result in you being caught speaking to a wanted fugitive by a patrolling officer. You have to really think about the options presented to you as they're presented to you. You're not going to have the ludo-narrative dissonance of being told you must act quickly and then you ask numerous questions anyway to receive a lengthy exposition dump before proceeding to successfully act in time as you would in another game. The choices you make can burn you hard enough that sometimes you have to scrutinize the opportunities presented to determine if intervening in a situation and helping either side is even worth the potential trouble. I could gush over how much I love the gameplay of Griftlands all day.Even though I don't have a whole lot of experience with the first character Sal yet (I couldn't get the hang of her in combat). Rook is unbelievably wild in both negotiations and combat. The gamble mechanic allows you to snowball in a super satisfying way if you play your cards right (forgive me), and his pistol charge mechanic gave him good depth in battle, as you're encouraged to flip-flop between low-charge and high-charge for defense and offensive respectively.  Defeating bosses is so unbelievably thrilling in this game, because they're all pretty challenging and I usually only beat them by a hair. All in all, this game is an absolute steal for only 15 USD, and it's only going to get even better as it receives more content.

_childDocuments_.review: Card Rogue-like games have really been extending their boundaries recently. This is one of the newest twist with a large emphasise with story. A risky choice, considering rogue-likes charm is the fast in-and-out replayability. But they really managed to stick the landing. The deck building aspect is simple enough, and if you came here you already know how they work. The interesting part of this game is that you can focus on combat or negotiation and you have two different decks that you build to accommodate that. If you want to be a mass murdering psychopath who everyone hates, you can be that. If you want to be friends and talk your way out of almost every situation you can do that as well. Or maybe somewhere in between is fine as well.Theres a bit of learning you have to go through, but thats part of the fun for starting any new card rogue-like.The only problem I have is that the replayability does seem to get hurt by the huge amount of story it wants you to read. You can skip it, but it just feels odd to do so. Still fun , but its hard to play for long periods of time compared to others in the genre.tldr : A fun new story driven card rogue-like, but is missing the addiction feel that others in the genre have.8.0/10

_childDocuments_.review: Deck builder. Story line. Choices on each run are varied by random one-shot events to choose from.Best art in the genre. Voice acting is appealing. Theme is consistent.UI is elegant though it takes time to get used to (the concentric rings take some time to understand instinctively).and PETS that help in battle and in negotiations.If you enjoy the other titles mentioned in the other reviews, then this is the most polished contender in the field. Is it the best? That's a decision a review can't make for you. But get it. You'll know in less than 2 hours if you dig it.

_childDocuments_.review: Griftlands is a wonderful blend of genres. I had been excited for this game when it was first revealed, and despite the fact the game has been on a strange journey, what the team have produced in the end is a really fun and characterful game. An RPG with card battling and some unique systems, all with a gorgeous art style and that one thing we all love: consequences.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: It seems to me that this game was made by people who really loved Slay the Spire, and wanted to double-down on the elements that that awesome, fun-as-hell deck-builder lacked--and not only did Klei double-down, but they then proceeded nail a hard 21... in spades! (how's that for a strangled metaphor, ey? lol) There's a sly joyfulness to this game--it's a celebration of the genre that will satisfy deck-builder afecionados and entice noobs with its combination of elements. The dialog is witty, the plotlines are engaging, the characters are relatable, and their choices meaningful. As for replicating the things that StS nailed: the combos/synergistic decks you can assemble are pretty much just as addicting, the balance of difficulty and run-length is there, and the additional mechanics (as well as all those other bells and whistles) are integrated perfectly... and, most importantly of all, the sum total is motherheshin' FUN!
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Card games aren't really my thing, but Klei has a knack for taking a genre that I find boring and making it into an amazingly fun experience.Wow. Klei has done it again. The card mechanics are great. They make it easy to understand how the card's affects work. The rogue-like elements allow them to introduce new cards as you play the game. In no time flat, you will understand how the cards are meant to work together, so that you can build decks that capitalize on particular mechanics, and find a strategy that works for you.On top of that, the negotiation game is super interesting. It works out much in the same way that battles do, just with a different set of cards and mechanics. It allows the game to make for diplomatic encounters that are just as fun to play as the combat.In between the card games, you are set loose on a world map that is constantly changing, and giving you fresh options for where you want to go, next. At each story beat, you will encounter a myriad of lovable, charming characters and will have to make the hard choices as to who you want to help, or harm. The dialogue is masterfully written, giving the characters a ton of personality, and describing scenes like an overly dramatic storyteller in a Dungeons & Dragons game.So, satisfying game mechanics that keep me coming back for more. A narrative that makes the context for the gameplay deeply interesting and memorable. Art style/animation that makes me wish it was an animated series. Soundtrack that never gets old. I don't know what else I can say to convince you.Griftlands is a masterwork.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing the game for a couple of hours.For an early access game, it already seems quite polished.The split between negotiation and battle is quite interesting and allows for different solutions to the same quest.I hope the diversity of playstyles is high enough to keep the game interesting for a long time, but so far it's looking good.

Plus the writing and the art are both masterful making this game fun as all hell oh my god.

You are just gonna play this for the characters story.if you want a roguelike deckbuilding game: play Slay the Spire and Monster Trainif you want an RPG deckbuilding: try SteamWorld Questi mean the game's not bad, but its not something that i'd be like 'yo, you gotta play this" either, so yeah... meh...
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible deck-building game, which reminds me of Slay the Spire or Monster Train, but with a lot more diversity in deck-building, and many other fun mechanics which affect the gameplay. The game's relationship system which gives perks, alongside many grafts and card types/deck types, in addition to the negotiation/battle system makes the game very replayable. Lovely Game, 10/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Great game.The design is top notch, and the card play is super fun.My only complaints is the fact that each story is short, and I don't think it's going to have tons of replay value. But, I try to look for at least a dollar an hour in value, and I'm up to 19 hours, and one story to go; so that's pretty good. If you like card games then this is a must have.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: A kickass card building/roguelite game. Has two core mechanics: one is a traditional turn based battle mechanic and a negotiation mechanic which is a bit different but still combat-like. Likable characters, great dialogue, and an accessible story. Honestly, a must buy and an entry fee of $15 is extremely kind. The main menu has a prompt that says when the next update is coming, which is pretty awesome and not something I really have seen before. Also from the creators of Don't Stave, so the quality is certainly there. This really doesn't feel like an early access game, so I cant wait to see what they add.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a very unique experience. The deck-building is similar to 'Slay the Spire', but the world building is more like a tabletop RPG. The cast of characters is quirky, the dialogue is fun and creates an atmosphere of weird late night sci-fi cartoons. The names of the cards is very expressive, building your decks also feels like building your characters attitudes and style. If you like deck-builders and sci-fi, you have to check out GRIFTLANDS!
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: For the asking price this is hours of fun. It´s a deck builder with actual stories and relationships with the characters.Only downside is that if you lose a run to the end boss you might look at hours of gameplay until you can try again, so be prepared for that. Luckily at least the first few times there is a lot of replayability as a lot of events seem to have multiple randomised versions and there are choices to make.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Narrative card collecting rogue-like. Having a narrative plus rogue-like can be a bit tricky, but since there are three characters to switch between, some randomness plus some light choice and consequence you are unlikely to get tired of seeing the same events play out over and over. You can have dialogue battles as well as regular combat, which is a nice touch, though the dialogue combat feels a bit random occasionally. Has that great Klei animation too.After clearing all three campaigns I don't feel the same drive to instantly start over on a higher difficulty level that I had in Slay the Spire or Monster Train, but that's alright, not every game needs to be terribly addictive. I got my money's worth.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Completed one character mission in 5 hours. Its got a casual feel to it which i like. Not as intense as other deck builders like slay the spire. Looks like 2 other characters are available to play. I like how they added some lore and quest behind the cards. Not just a mindless card battler, they make it feel like each duel means something more.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a big fan of card games, I have more than 300 hours in Slay the Spire and finished the game on the hardest difficulty on all characters. but this game, I just can not enjoy.There is just too much in this game, too much that it becomes a negative for me.First there are 2 types of combat, battle and negotiation.Then there is the story, which you have to read line upon lines of dialog to understand, and learn their slang, factions, characters, etc.Then you have to learn all the battle mechanics and keywords, keep track of your deck.Also the negotiation mechanics are quite different, gotta learn it too and the unique keywords.It's just too much for me, I don't have the time nor the energy to spend on this game. Some more things I did not like:RNG (some cards hit from 1 to 4 damage, a very big difference)Game doesn't tell what how your choices help / hurt you. (Seems like you should never kill your opponent because you get a big penalty for that)Deckbuilding and combos don't feel exciting, there aren't any combo like StS which can be fun to execute.I'm not saying this game is bad, the opposite it think it actually good but it just not for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Another one of the card battlers that appeared since Slay the Spire's big success.This one is focused more on a narrative campaign. The design is great, with that classic "Klei" art direction. Gameplay is interesting enough for a few runs but I won't be playing this one nearly as much as Slay the Spire.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Although I don't particularly like roguelite games because of the inherent must-replay-multiple-times-in-order-to-unlock-content mechanic, I did enjoyed playing the three distinct stories through with each character. With no deaths and restarts it'll probably give you around 17 hours of gameplay. The game is not that expensive and Klei is an excellent developer and is worth supporting.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I really like this game for many reasons. I love all three playable character's storylines with all the branching paths. I like the gameplay. I like the pets, and the fact that they're pettable and can be nicknamed (and have some fun random generated nicknames). I like that the alien races seem are portrayed with as much nuance as the humans, being varied in personality and appearance and having some variety in their societal roles. I like how much moral greyness there is in this game's world, and how many characters, even background NPCs, can still be sympathetic despite that. And I like how the NPCs all have different facial expressions, so when I hurt one of them (or think of hurting one), I often feel bad. Because of how upset they look, and the things they say :'D
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: So many games now are "It's a deckbuilder, but with this cool new twist!" and it usually ends up just a worse version of Slay the Spire, where the 'new twist' doesn't actually make the game any more fun.This is NOT the case with Griftlands.Here are the things that make Griftlands special among deckbuilders:    Using a card enough can let you upgrade it (from a random set of upgrades), this brings not only extra customization towards a deck strategy, but can sometimes upgrade it to a 'destroy' option, so sometimes you can get rid of a card that doesn't fit your strategy by playing it enough to upgrade it.    There is a plot, and you can raise or lower your relationship with various NPCs for discounts or even passive bonuses for gameplay.    You have two decks, one for combat encounters, one for social encounters.  They both play VERY differently mechanically, but both feel fully fleshed out as game styles (helps keep things from getting repetitive).Honestly it's a fun, fresh take on deckbuilders with enough depth to play over and over.The one flaw is that the plot gets boring fast, there are currently only 2 characters with 1 plot apiece.  And while there is some variability in their plots, based on who you side with and who you kill, it gets repetitive.  There is a 'brawl' mode that just jumps from battle to battle, but that loses some of its charm.The framework is there though; and if they open this up to modding, where people can customize their own plots and characters, this game could go from clever to HUGE.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I hecking love this game. It's solid gameplay, the deckbuilding is fun and functional, the voice acting of total nonsense fits well with the world and the characters, the music is cool, the writing is GREAT.Fell in love with this pretty much at first glance and spent 4 hours playing it the first day I got it. 7 hours in now, just finished my first run (I died, and will definitely start it all over again, because I'm now invested in getting Sal her REVENGE), and I had a rough-looking puppy help me out in battle, which was amazing.I REPEAT, ROUGH-LOOKING PUPPY. 200% a game worth getting as far as I'm concerned.

_childDocuments_.review: Griftlands is two card battlers rolled into one, with 3 separate sets of rules for them and a great story for each of the 3. You build your deck to discuss with enemies and battle with enemies as you work out what's gone wrong in your character's situation and try to fix it.There's decent RPG decisions to have (so there's replayability) and your usual roguelike unlocks that slowly make your character specialised in different ways. I've not played a game quite like it and I encourage everyone to have a go.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: If Pyre and Pirates Outlaws (or Slay the Spire) had a baby this would be it. It plays a lot longer than most roguelike runs do, which begs the question: are all roguelikes kind of just an rpg with permadeath?To that end, this BARELY feels like a roguelike or a deckbuilder despite those being the pillars on which the gameplay is rested. I wasn't expecting this when I started playing, but I would be surprised if anyone really didn't like it based on how well it blends story and gameplay together. It's refreshing, enticing, and majorly engaging.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Klei! I love Klei. Klei games are the best. Here's another best game; this time a roguelike card battler set out in the backwater badlands of space. You'll meet lots of NPCs who want you to do things for them in exchange for money and favours. Take sides and follow a main quest as one of three playable characters, all with different card decks. Fight battles, but also negotiate; each character has both a battle deck and a negotiation deck, with each type using different mechanics. There's a great number of builds to experiment with, the writing is excellent and it's beautiful to look at. All round super polished and memorable.- Unlike most roguelike card battlers I've played, this actually has a story to follow for each character. It plays as a series of quests and relationships instead of a simple 'walk across the landscape killing things'- Once you've played the main campaign as each character, you can either play at higher prestige levels which make it more difficult (there are perks to unlock), or you can play a sort of "day in the life" where you play as that character just doing normal mercenary jobs.- Gorgeous artwork- It's not just shooty combat. Each character has a deck for combat, and a deck for negotiations. Both of these have different mechanics. In battle you have damage, health and armor. In negotiations you have manipulation, hostility and diplomacy. On top of that, each character not only has their own decks, but their own mechanics. The second character has a coin he flips sometimes, which gives some cards extra effects.- You get a preview of what the enemy is going to do (like Slay the Spire) so you can prepare for it. No randomness.- You can enlist and train pets to fight with you.- One of the first quests had me uncover a theft. I confronted the thief in a bar, but chose to buy them a drink first. Not only did this get them drunk, giving them a disadvantage in combat, but it also made them like me, which reduced their resolve in the following negotiation- Cards gain XP by being used, and you get a choice how to upgrade them. You get a choice between 2 upgrades for each card, with lots of potential different upgrades- In one encounter, I was able to negotiate with them first to demoralise them in the fight afterwards- You earn a permanent currency for every fight, which makes you stronger over time (There are character-specific buffs, character-wide buffs, and perks to unlock)- You have a relationship status with every NPC in the game. Based on that, there are random events. A thug who likes you might share a target for a robbery, or someone who hates you might track you down on the trail and try to murder you when you're in the middle of a job. Relationship statuses also give you passive bonuses or penalties- You can provoke someone who hates you, which causes a negotiation. If you win the negotiation, they'll attack you, which means you're acting in self defense, so you can kill them with no penalty and remove the debuff from having someone hate you- The battle segments are fairly similar to other games; play cards which deal damage to the enemy. The negotiation battles have unique mechanics, and revolve around deploying arguments, manipulating the enemy and protecting yourself with composure- If you play the same story twice but take different sides of the main quests, you can see both sides of each NPC's version of the story- The game says 'progress will be saved at the end of the last conversation', but it seems to be the conversation BEFORE that one because I sometimes had to re-do the latest encounter when loading a game- There's no combat log to see what happened if you didn't understand something or missed it- If you take too long to win a negotiation, the NPC starts getting passive buffs every round called "impatience" which basically makes them do more damage. It's annoying because it stops you from playing a slow build-up/control deck- I feel like I missed something important at the beginning about the story. I know I'm going after Kashio, but everyone keeps talking about an auction that isn't in the introduction video
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: What's so different about yet another deckbuilder? Let me give you a quick run-down:You can play Story Mode or a quicker Brawl (series of 5*5 battles).You've got 2 Characters who each have 2 decks - 1 for Battle (max 4 vs 4, NPCs are AI controlled, play a card on a foe or self) and 1 for Negotiation (you fight against opponent's "core argument", negotiation gets harder the longer it takes). Characters have unique options for both decks, eg Battle focus on Bleed, Discard, or Draw effects. Negotiation on Green Cards (diplomatic) vs Red Cards (aggression).After every conflict you get to pick 1 of 3 cards for the deck you just used.Instead of hoping for an event, you can upgrade your cards when they gain enough XP (1 XP per card play). You can choose between two upgrade versions per card.You have the option to kill or spare an opponent after battle. This influences your relationship with them.Relationships can grant you Boons (eg merchants discount) or Banes (+1 Dmg received).Of course you got also some evergreens like if you beat the story, you can start to modify your game experience with Mutators (eg start with draft decks) or Prestige (more difficulty).

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fantastic. The RPG elements in this deckbuilder are so well done I pretty much consider it a full fletched RPG. The writing is witty, the world is well built, the characters are lively and colorful. Also, the card games that make up the core gameplay loop are extremely well crafted. I finished the first story and am now completely sucked into the second character's story. Even after having played only 10 hours I can already say this title is well worth picking up.

_childDocuments_.review: 1)map feels cramped. Youre not allowed to explore the map you can only go from A to B.  why build a city and fill it with people if you're not allowed to explore it2)love/hate system has no nuance. You kill someone in the middle of a field and suddenly his best friend know you killed them. Kill someone trying to kill you? you're hated. the game is constantly pushing you into situations where you're presented two options of how you want someone to hate you. At one point you will have to choose to support 1 of 2 merchants from the night market. whoever you dont choose will now hate you and will raise their prices by 50%. 3)combat is split between battles and negotiations but battles are magnitudes more important as the game will force you into boss fights that you must fight to survive. impatience mechanic means after 5 or so turns enemies gain +1 damage in negotiations a turn then one more every turn afterwards. a very lazy way to make sure talks more difficult. Enemy resolve is bloated and by the last few days you'll be fighting people with 70 resolve while you're barely over 30. On the final day it is impossible to out to defend and it becomes a dps race4) unless you watch a guide you will not be able to beat the boss your 1st, 2nd, or 3rd try. The final fight its right after you fight for artifacts. You can earn them and they will get the others. They are massively different in how they effect you compared to him. if he wins an item it will give him an automech if you do you get a combat drone. You  get +30 hp they get 80. You get a card that lets you attack once twice, he can summon identical holograms act as rng shields. To make this worse immediately before this fight you have to go through tough fights guarding the entry way to the auction house thats been beefed up by the final day buff. Two enemies can easily deal out 30 damage which is utterly undefendable by anything but a full defense build. the player base is split between people going "wtf is this this" and "lol easy. people think this is hard lul"

_childDocuments_.review: I am 25hrs in and enjoying this game so much that I've stopped playing very many other games in the mean time.  I enjoyed Slay the Spire, but it's lack of story telling made me board, Griftlands has interesting story telling, and a more in depth card system imo.  I would recommend this to anyone that enjoyed Slay the Spire, unless you are a speed runner type player.  This game takes long and has a lot more interesting decision making moments. _childDocuments_.review: Bought because I've played most of the A-tier and B-tier deckbuilders already, enough that I felt willing to take a chance on a developer who I'd normally avoid, since they support Epic/EGS enough to launch a year early there.This is a middling game - there's better places to find a compelling story, and the deckbuilding/resource management balancing is not up to par. Presentation is nice, but that's low on my list of priorities. For example, Dream Quest may have awful presentation, but I'd rate it as having a much higher impact on the genre.If you have any prior card game experience, do yourself a favor and use the developer Unlock mod from the Steam Workshop. Otherwise, you're going to be stuck doing 2-5 hour runs that are excessively easy in order to climb to the true difficulty, which takes 6 runs per character and per mode (36 runs total). After trying each mode once going in blind, I used the mod and queued up a max Prestige run, and even the knowledge gained from two prior runs was enough for me to clear without ever being in serious danger, even coming close to full stunlocking the final boss of that run (they got one move before dying).If you're more casual, and want a timesink where you accrue metaprogression slowly, this game may be a good fit for you. Besides difficulty unlocks, there's a currency for giving your characters permanent stats in all non-max difficulty future runs, another currency that also gives passive effects in all runs, Boons/Banes to discover through each of the many NPCs loving or hating you, card pool unlocks, alternate outfits, and so on. For me this was not respecting the player's time, but a certain type of player will like the grind.Griftlands wants to be the "Hades" of Roguelite Deckbuilders, and in some ways it succeeds. Still, veteran players should look elsewhere (Slay the Spire, Monster Train, Chrono Ark, Nowhere Prophet, Second Second, among many others). Its not an awful game, but there are better alternatives.

_childDocuments_.review: There are a lot of things to like about this game. The whole idea of negotiation vs. actual battle is really cool.Choices actually matter. You can just slaughter everyone you encounter, yes, but there are consequences.Cool art style and worldbuilding in general, although it could use more depth.You can have cute pets.However, I think a big problem is that it lacks complexity. There needs to be more cards and graft options, because currently there's only a few viable deck archetypes for each character. It's also a bit too difficult to get a deck that synergizes well. One of the most fun aspects of a deckbuilder like this is when you manage to make a deck that's just bonkers - something Slay the Spire does well. It's not easy, but that's the point - it rewards good play. Even the best decks I've made in this game don't feel insane, which just isn't very satisfying.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really fun game! It uses strong RPG elements and is more story based than what you usually see in card-rouge games. The world and story is pretty easy to get into and like, and also simple to ignore if you want. It has many elements you'll recognize from card battlers like it, but it's far more unique in a lot of ways. It's not too hard at first but offers increasing difficulty and several strategies and approaches. It also has two systems- fighting and negotiations. The two systems offer more choice in how you interact with people and are equally important, but use different decks/relic items, so it is also a slight balancing act to make sure both decks are in good shape. The negotiation system is quite unique, while the combat is more what you'd expect from combat.The fact this is early access, and recently so, surprises me! It already feels very polished and full, and I'm excited to see what more might be added.
