_childDocuments_.review: I played this game for 8 hours and gave it a good review (read that as fun + minimal bugs).  But after playing for another 15 hours, the mechanics I thought were interesting, I now find as distracting from the experience.Griftlands styles itself as a rogue-like deck-builder, and currently, I consider Slay the Spire to be the Gold Standard for that genre.  Griftlands has some interesting ideas that help it strive for excellence, but in my opinion, it comes up short.  Perhaps Griftlands can close the gap between good and great while it's still in Early Access, but I think some of the core mechanics will prevent it from doing so, but you can decide for yourself:1. Two decks.  Griftlands approaches the idea that if you're buying a deck-builder, then perhaps it can double-the-fun by building 2 decks at the same time.  While this idea has some merit and fits well with the theme of Griftlands and how you approach problems, I think it ultimately detracts from the deck-building experience.  It gives you the illusion of choice that you can focus on negotiations instead of battles, or focus on battles instead of negotiations, but in the end, you focus on both.  And to make matters even less interesting, the decks have nothing to do with each other.  You might as well be playing two different games at the same time bundled together.  The only interaction that I could find between the two was at the end of a battle encounter, if you kept killing people, you would get reputation cards added to your negotiation deck, but even the choice of killing had very little to do with the battle deck itself and was an 'after the battle' decision, and falls more into a choices matter category.2. Actual deck-building.  While there were a lot of cards, I found the actual differences between the cards underwhelming.2a. Battle deck-building.  To understand the problem in the battle cards, you first need to consider these three cards:  Card A is 1 action for 2-5 dmg.  Card B is 1 action for 3 dmg.  Card C is 2 action for 6-12 dmg.  To me, these 3 cards are basically the same card but with slight variations on cost vs output.  Imagine getting +3 minimum dmg, and Card A and B are identical, and imagine getting a +10 received dmg debuff on your target, and Card C is less impressive if action points are scarce.  The cards still have their place, and while I enjoyed the debuff mechanics in Griftlands, each debuff seemed to have the same template of cards to it... such as debuff, dmg+debuff, improvised debuff, discarded debuff, ability related to debuff, etc.  There was nothing that gave each mechanic a life of its own with its own unique cards.  The available battle cards tended to be variations of template vs mechanics to fluff out a large card set.  In a word, disappointing, especially when you consider how varied the lore behind the game is.2b. Negotiation deck-building.  Negotiation cards suffer from the illusion of choice even worse once you realize how negotiations work best.  There are 3 types of cards in negotations: Diplomacy, Hostility, and Manipulation.  Diplomacy cards tend to do lower amounts of damage but synergize with a mechanic called Influence that ensures Diplomacy cards will always do max damage.  Hostility cards synergize with a mechanic call Dominance, which adds +dmg to each hostility card.  What you find quickly is if you focus the deck on one track or the other, it works way better than trying to play both sides of the fence, which means when it comes time to pick a card to add to your deck, there isn't much choice once you've picked the path you want to take.3. Grafts.  This is one part of the game I think Griftlands did really well on.  The variety is a little scarce but unsurprising given the illusion of card choice (imo).  Think of them like relics from Slay the Spire, and they can be leveled up once, like cards.4. Card upgrades.  Cards have an xp bar, and once it's full, the card can be leveled up.  This is an interesting idea, but most my runs ended with 80%-90% of my cards leveled up and I quickly became desensitized to the mechanic, especially when I realized that there were at least 3 options that a card could level up into so even if I got a card leveled up, I might not get the level up I want.  Perhaps if upgraded cards could be merged together or cards could be leveled up multiple times, it might offer some strategic component for leveling cards, but I found this as a noise mechanic that had little impact on my actual deck-building strategy... with one exception.  Any time I could level a card up into something with the Destroy mechanic (to remove the card from the game), it was a guarantee that was the upgrade option I would take to avoid deck-bloat since so few cards had this option.5. Choices matters and NPCs and dialogue.  One of the first impressions I got from Griftlands is the abundance of dialogue it had in the game.  More than you'd expect in a rogue-like, but a great repository for a lot of Griftlands lore.  I was entertained and didn't mind the abundance. In encounter required me to remember a password too, but it was the only time it seemed important that I pay attention  The initial play-thru supported a choices matter feel in the decisions you make when picking encounters and the choices made during the encounter (prior to play the relevant deck).  It also seemed to matter about people liking/disliking you.  Once I started working thru the speed runs (prestige levels) though, I suddenly wondered what game I was playing.  There were no real choices., just encounter after encounter, and I found myself throwing all my money at NPCs to buy them off and get their social boons.  And if I did something that caused an NPC to hate me, resulting in a social bane, odds were that I'd run into that NPC in the tavern and could provoke them so I could kill them too without consequence.  In the end, my choices did not matter during the speed runs, resulting in a drastically different game-style than the initial play-thrus, leaving me wondering which game mode was the intended game-mode and the work that was put into the other game-mode when focusing resources on only one mode may have propelled the game from good to great.6. Allies.  The game offers allies you can take with you on your encounters.  I really like how Griftlands used allies in the negotiation encounters, where allies offer a buff/debuff during the start but leaves the emphasis on the deck once the encounter is running.  Unfortunately in battle encounters, the emphasis shifts away from the battle deck and leans towards a numbers game of dps vs dmg mitigation based on how many allies you have.  The battle deck is still important, but didn't feel as important as the negotiations   Allies is an interesting idea.  I found that battle encounters in the speed run were a lot more balanced than the initial play-thru, but I wish they'd find some other way to balance the battle encounters that contain allies.In conclusion, the game is in Early Access.  While I don't think Griftlands is a great game, it's still a good game, and I don't think it was a waste of money.  However, after 20+ hours in the game, I doubt I'll play it anymore except to explore the Early Access features.

_childDocuments_.review: Griftlands is a nice departure from the deck building rogue-likes we're used to. (Slay the Spire, cough cough) While it maintains many similarities, Griftlands specializes in it's role-playing aspects, but also rewards players who pay attention to the finer detail and patterns.You choose between three Grifters, one of which was just fully released, acting as a sort of sci-fi bounty hunter. Any Boba Fett fans? Cause you can live the dream now. Decide who you're working for, and discover creative ways to tilt odd jobs in your favor or completely muck them up. Will you be a rough and tough street thug, a greedy grifter, or a kind smile in an unforgiving universe? Well you get to decide each job who you're going to be, but remember, actions have consequences.Each character has 5 days to reach their goal. You'll do odd jobs for the most part until scripted story events will further their plot. But each day will be a test of survival, cunning, and luck. Not to mention some subtle influence. ;) But seriously, the card play is familiar if you've played other games like it. You control two decks, one for diplomacy and one for battle. After battles or jobs you'll get to pick a card to add to your deck(s) until you find a synergy that works for you. There is a steep learning curve, even after 80 hours I still find new situations, dialogue, or routes I haven't taken. Try being the good guy, then the bad guy, then bad at being good and good at being bad, pretending to be bad at being good, but really you're good at being bad. That's confusing I bet, but each day gives you options to become something new, or double cross old friends from yesterday, allowing for a LOT of replay value.Each Grifter has unique cards, a unique map, story, and characters, The universe feels very defined and fleshed out, everyone fits in and you have to navigate the faction wars with grace or deception. Another thing worth mentioning are the smaller mechanics, first of all, you can have a cute lil' death trap for a pet! So you never feel alone. Another is that the game will offer you extra gold for picking cards you never pick, rewarding players who step out of their comfort zone. You can also pay a body guard to look the other way, or get people drunk so they love you. Did I mention you can choose 3 perks(or modifiers) each playthrough out of like 20? Again, replay value. Oh and there are prestige modes similar to ascension in StS.So much charm and finesse goes into this great title by Klei. If you're a fan of rogue-likes, deckbuilding, and a bit of roleplay, you'll feel right at home in the Griftlands.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: A card based Rogue rpg game that is far from ordinary. This game has its own style, unique game play, and it charm that really make it stand out in the genre.  The world building, connectable and interesting characters, and great story telling are really where it shines!  The deep customization of your decks, bluff or fight, and its seemingly multitude of play style choices are what keep you playing!
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: While the cardplay will likely not live up to the expectations of a Slay the Spire veteran, this game offers its unique storytelling style, the masterful inclusion of many RPG elements, and dual deck gameplay to make itself stand out against its predecessor. The real highlight of this game is the variety of its gameplay. On top of the inherent variety provided by a typical deckbuilder roguelike, there are 3 different fleshed out campaigns with their own branching stories filled with consequences and variations of stories to tell. And, if for some weird reason you aren't a fan of the storytelling aspect of the game, you can always play the Brawl gamemode, which is more traditional for roguelike veterans. Highly recommended if you are at all interested in the blending of the Roguelike-deckbuilder and RPG genres.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I have dozens of hours on the EGS, as well. This game is basically a story driven card game with hints of roguelike elements. If you liked Slay the Spire, you will very likely love this game. They have made the game substantially easier than previous patches, so I was able to get to the last boss on my first run, but I think it allows for more varied gameplay.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely incredible deckbuilder.  Slay the Spire never clicked with me, but Griftlands hooked me right away.  The writing is hilarious.  I love the art-style.  And I find it pretty intuitive to get some basic deck synergies going.  Can't wait for the final release, but this is already a complete game in terms of value.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: this game is fun due to the 2 types of combat, one for talking it out and the other is also talking it out just with fists instead of words. the main quests give you a choice on who to go with and the style of combat you wish to chose but after completing a main quest you then can do a side quest to get items, improve relationships (or damage some) or flat out trying to get money, also i am fond of the chance to have a random encounter event when moving from place to place because it allow you to get a small bonus.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoy playing Slay the Spire.  This takes everything from StS's combat system and then adds in RP elements and some additional complexity while removing the ability to see the path forward to the end of the chapter clearly.  I wish there was more of a mechanical difference between combat and negotiation, as I find them pretty same-y, aside from theme, but that's a minor issue.  Overall, the game is very enjoyable and I'm very happy I picked it up on the recommendation of a friend who also enjoyed Slay the Spire.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I've experienced nothing bad about this game. It was satisfying every single moment I played it. So many games nowadays have some bad side that you just have to suck up, but this game was just a complete delight the whole way through. Finished my Smith run on the first try and I feel like Hesh itself. This game is incredible and just all around fun fun fun and satisfying with no drawbacks.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Fun deck building rogue-lite. Its nice that it has a story and characters compared to Slay the Spire. One downside so far is that card variety felt a little slim on my first few runs of each character, because it seems more cards become available/unlocked as you gain experience which only consolidates it seems when your run ends. Overall great game.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: My early impressions: This is a cool game that was pretty addictive like slay the spire but better in the fact it meshed a story with your progress. More from my original review. I have done numerous runs, Klei has done an awesome job of making the game feel fresh with each play through. Without spoiling too much, I unlocked  parts of the game that make it even more addictive! Like Slay the Spire you can play and take a break or play long sessions. The game makes me wanna come back for more! Well done Klei.Update: Fast forward to 70+ hours of playtime. When I first played, I had really enjoyed the character Sal. Cool music card battles flowed. I was hooked! I waited for the new characters to try. Although the other chapters are interesting, I still prefer the first character and sadly I lost some of the original pull from Sal's campaign and free form runs. This game is still good but mileage might vary on your play style preferences with each character. Now I am kinda near Neutral for this game. Still not a bad purchase if you like Slay the Spire style games.Early adopters you shouldn't be disappointed!
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a level of polish that most finished games don't have. The final character hasn't even been added yet, but I can't stop exploring the different options in the characters stories and the different mutators you unlock once you beat both characters stories. The most fun aspect of Griftlands in my opinon is how you have the option to solve your problems with your fists or your words. The negotiation aspect of this game is downright amazing, and I have never seen another game which implements this dual deck structure as well as Griftlands. On the cons side, The runs are very long, and this type of deck building rougelike isn't for everyone, but at the very least this is a game to keep on your watch list. Klei knocked it out of the park with this game, and for people who enjoy deck builders like Slay the Spire and Monster Train, I could not recommend picking this game up more. 10/10 game, Ecstatic for what's to come.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: 15 hours in the alpha version. Looking forward to getting back to it now that there is another character and some other updates. Lots of cool things going on in this game. The story mechanics remind me a bit of Banner Saga and I love how every character can impact your game based on how you treat them or their allies. The combat is really good and building two simultaneously decks adds a bit of challenge and I really enjoy the negotiation combat a lot. As a big fan of Slay the Spire it's nice playing a game with solid deck-building and combat that also has a consequential story with decisions that go beyond your deck.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a great evolution of the deck-building roguelite archetype into a full-fledged story driven experience. The writing and world-building is interesting, it doesn't send too much down your throat at any given time, and the mechanics are great. My biggest problem is the UI, it's a little busy at times. But once you get used to it, it's not unmanageable.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Propably Best rogue-card battler.Why ?There is a lots of stuff. Stuff to unlock, to beat. Don't have to kill, just make them surrender.Story is earthly and modern . Reminds me Mandalorian plus Firefly.I actualy have choices, kill or not to kill - sell your soul or not - brake an agreements, that turned crazy. Reputation mechanic.Overall Griftlands is more than DESERVE to be played, and it is constantly updated, adding more to its already rich core.Perfect investment. Klei keep up the good work!
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Easily one of the most underrated games I've played in a long time. Deckbuilder that has a narrative - replayability in terms of gameplay but also because the characters/events/story beats can play out differently on repeat runs, in addition to modes where you just do the combat. This game really has a super high level of polish and quality content.Not sure if this game didn't make a big splash because of early access or what... but it came out around the same time as Wildermyth and while not the exact same concept it does a similar enough thing that it makes me curious as to why this game didn't experience the same level of hype on release.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Great deckbuilding, amazing world building. Managing two decks - combat and negotiation - brings interesting choices to how you approach the story and makes you inhabit the character more fully. Every aspect of the game feels polished and satisfying, from the excellent interface to the interesting writing.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun Unique card game with slay the spire like gameplay but upgraded to feel a whole new dimension of gameplay others cant compare to. The unique twist of negotiation and battle decks makes for unique differences between runs.  I did find the game incredibly easy though. If you have an upgraded pet and mercenary and an ally you can basically destroy anyone with minimal effort, and obtaining those allies isnt hard. I also find theres not enough consquences for letting someone live instead of executing them and recieving negative attributes
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Griftlands is a fantastic deackbuilder with some really unique takes on the genre like the relationship based relics and the second deck and health pool for conversations.My only real gripe with the game is that as a roguelite each individual run is fairly long leading it to not quite give me that "Just one more run" games like Slay The Spire give me when I end up losing. The game's story focus also makes each run feel a bit slow out of the gate as you mash through text to get to the missions. Potentially having a mode where you can save after every day would be really interesting and a welcome addition. As it is now it's deck building and battle, conversation and relationship mechanics are amazing where the roguelite elements feel a bit at odds with the rest of it. Though over all a very solid package.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I've seen and read a lot of great criticism and a lot of great praise for this game. If you liked deck builders like Inscryption or Slay the Spire this game will very likely scratch that itch for you. The text can get very TLDR at times, but I think the negotiation battles puts a fresh and clever spin on the gameplay loop. Some people say there are only two branching paths per story, but there's a multitude of ways those two paths vary from run to run so it doesn't feel stale to me. Overall this is a game that really has something special and clearly had a lot of passion put into it. Just like in film, you can tell when the people don't want to make the piece of media they're creating. This is not the case here.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: One of the funnest rogue-like deck builders I've ever played. It has a great depth of content as at the time of posting I've only unlocked about 30% of all the cards and beaten one of the three characters' campaign. Its story and world are awesome to explore over the multitude of runs you'll inevitably play.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: The game is good, and getting greater with each update, the challenges are amazing, and the mechanics are great.Ignore this review, I lost train of thought, I may edit it later when I remember what I was saying, but I usually mainly do only negotiation, and can deal 50ish damage a turn semi consistently
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Loved Hearthstone back in the day but slowly started to grow sick of how far behind I would get which led to losing game after game. Single player deck games are a godsend for people like me. I also love the rogue like style gameplay with a surprising rich story and lore. Incredible for an early access game too.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I immediately fell in love with this game's art style, but after getting into it I soon realised it wasn't my cup of tea. I was expecting more of a Battle Chasers, even Darkest dungeon experience, which it isn't. It's a damn shame, but the beautiful art style is not enough of a drive for me when I don't enjoy the core gameplay. I'll still leave a positive rating 'cause I can see the game is well done (although I would get rid of the "Sims" talk, just my personal preference), and games with interesting art styles need as much attention as they can get. We need more of 'em!
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Takes the surprisingly prolific Deckbuilding Roguelike genre to the next level, and while I'll always have nothing but respect for the classics like Slay the Spire; I do think that Griftlands improves upon the formula in almost every way.It introduces in depth storytelling (completely optional in case you're just there for the gameplay), two different approaches to most situations using two different decks, branching narratives so that future runs have more value even beyond trying out new synergies and decks.Aside from that the presentation is incredible, with most attacks having unique and beautiful animations, fitting well with a quality sound track that always fits the mood.If you're at all a fan of the genre, or think you might want to get into it, I highly recommend Griftlands.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: If you like other card building games you will for sure love this one. The easiest way I can describe it to compare it to slay the spire. Where as one could describe slay the spire as a hack and slash card builder, Griftlands is more of a story based RPG card builder. _childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Consider this game Baby's First Roguelike.Recommended if you've never played a Deck Builder, don't actually wan't a deck building experience & just want to see 5mins of random procedurally generated NPCS give you randomly procedurally generated fetch quests to do a 2minute braindead combat sequence where you're not actually trying to win and instead just trying to level your cards so they can feel half as impactful as a card from a real deck builder.Difficulty is non existent, normally in games you get through the pointless dialogue so you can go into combat encounters.Not this game, you click through 5minutes of Dialogue you can't automatically skip and then have to click out of the map to click on the only destination you're able to visit where you're presented with two amazing options.1. Watch more dialogue boxes slam into each other for 2 mins, so you can make an already joke difficult battle easier or get money that you can't even spend on anything meaningful 90%2. Waste 5mins using the pretty drawings as sandbags until you have the desired level ups on your cards to make them barely functional.Items are a complete joke, 90% of the items you get in the game are consumable and therefore completely worthless if you're know how to count to 3 to spend your mana each turn, gameplay decisions disgusting favour you to play the worst cards in your deck to level them up because the game is so easy you pretty much never get punished for wasting all your turns to level up your cards.Recommended if you:Like reading dialogueSomehow like the hideous character design of the "main" characters. You're a white haired androgynous human edgelord with a couple of kitchen knives, or a human black dude in a brown trench coat so forgettable I don't even remember if he has a hat.Meanwhile you're fighting cool ass looking, fully fleshed out steam punk cyborgs and angry looking alien dudes slamming massive hammers on your tiny human skull.I really tried to enjoy this game and bought it way too quickily, they're trying so hard to push the "story" and the "negotiation" when every encounter in the game can be won by by literally face rolling your keyboard until you play all your cards.The only "challenge" in the game was the first hour when I had to waste time to read all the new "innovative" card mechanics they added.SPOILERS:Composure is literally just armourInfluence is literally just extra damageResolve is literally just healthThe "innovation" is you have some spells that have their own health bar that the game does an awful job of explaining.You start off with a negotiation seeing all these different colour cards and all these keywords, turns out they all work exactly the same. The only point of having red / green cards they pretend to give you a "choice" by showing you cards that give your red cards extra damage or cards that give your green cards extra damage.... why??Let's just pretend for a minute that I'm not biased because I hate this carebear crap of "wee make sure you protect your enemies from dying so their friends don't get mad and put a magical permanent voodoo curse on you"Art is great, except your main character because f youMusic existsSome of the cards do thingsHigh reviews because art pretty, and everyone's a winner.I think boss fights exist?? they were honestly such a push over and an absolute joke and there is no announcement whatsoever that you're fighting a boss I'm pretty sure for 3/5 of the "boss" encounters i thought it was just another fetch quest NPC and used them as a card training sand bag like every other encounter in the game.Do not buy unless you like pretty colours and drawings and dialogue boxes, in which case you'll have a great time looking at the £10 prefilled colouring book.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Such an easy game to recommend. _childDocuments_.review: An all-around excellent and thematic game, which isn't surprising given that it's from Klei. I do have some concerns regarding card descriptions and the difference between creating argument stacks vs. argument copies, as it's likely to be confusing to new players.Particular props to the writing - given the roguelike nature, it's impressive how much can be characterized in what may sometimes be just a few sentences.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: This game is awesome. For an early access game it is incredibly polished. From the artstyle to the gameplay to the setting, everything is phenomenally done. This game takes an ingenious move with making a card based dialogue system AND combat system. I've loved my time with the game. My only gripe would be asking what the point of the rogue like element is to the game. It's such a dialogue and story based game that making it a rogue like seems out of place. I would love for a developer to explain what the purpose of the rogue like mechanics are of multiple runs so I could better understand. Overall, as a person who is slowly losing hope for new games in the industry, this game is a shining example of a game that was made with passion and skill. A+ Would strongly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Damn Klei, you never let me down.  First off, it's beautiful.  I think Don't Starve's setting is really superb, and I like this better. I love the structure. _childDocuments_.review: Great game, though I find it a bit slow. And I don't just mean the story - that can be skipped - but the fights.Late fights can be longer, when you have some scaling and you can plan some card synergies, but in the first fights you have not much options as your deck is still very basic but you are still forced to do many turns of defending and dealing a small amount of damage and that is very boring.And roguelike/lites cannot be boring. _childDocuments_.review: 9/10 - A colorful ride - pure joy to play yet another entry in the rogue-like, lite card battler+ Perfected mechanics with engaging gameplay+ Lush, shiny enthralling characters set among inspiring locales+ Remarkable music and 'language'+ Great polished writing with memorable wit+ Extensive variation to combos and SUPER combos+ Charismatic cast and confident presentation+ Slay the Spire & Monster Train fans will find much to like here- More content please!
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: If you're a fan of Slay the Spire, but find that the overall story side of the game is lacking then this is the game for you. Griftlands takes a genre, and makes it a work of art. Each mechanic in the game is well thought out and integrated making nothing feel clunky. I'm shocked that this is still in early access with how polished the game is right now. Yes, we're still missing days of campaigns on the third character, but with a nicely detailed roadmap and how well executed this game is so far, I'm confident that it will be delivered... and even if it isn't there's already more than enough of a game here to put away a hell of a lot of hours.Mechanics that i personally enjoyed:Decisions feels like they matter - Everything you do has some form of consequence. You can make friends and enemies, the people you help (or backstab) respond to the actions you take; these give you boons or nerfs when it comes to negotiations and combat, you may also find situations are easier / harder if those people are around. Go on a murderous rampage, friends of the people you kill will start to hate you and make your game harder, and you'll start to get a reputation that inserts cards into your deck.Brawl mode; sometimes i just can't be bothered with the story side of the game and i just want to play a more linear playstyle. Brawl mode allows you to ditch all the fluff and play a game more similar to Slay the Spire. Changing the game - the use of perks and game modes allows you to play in different ways; want to own a pack of dogs to fight at your side, you can do it. want to instead draft your entire starting negotiation deck rather than use the base deck, thats an option. THERE. IS. SO. MUCH. HERE.This game honestly has it all when it comes to this genre of game. I'm trying to think of a negative; you have the ability to change the appearance of your character, this is purely aesthetic, which is fine, and im nitpicking, but if this had some kind of passive depending on the outfit you choose (pick a certain type for a change of picking cards of a certain type, or something) then it would make the game more interesting and give you a reason to try on the different outfits.its safe to say i love this game and its quickly become one of my favourite games of this year.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Griftlands is a deck building rogue-like that borrows its core elements from Slay the Spire wholesale. However, Klei has added several enjoyable twists:-World-building and role-playing elements added to quests-Separate "battle" and "negotiation" decks, which increase strategic options in addition to adding role-playing flavor-A relationship system which offers minor or major buffs/debuffs; also lethal/non-lethal playstyles are supported and tie strategically into these systemsThe game in this state feels essentially like a complete experience, though a new character + campaign is yet to be released. Right now it's much easier to complete a run than in Slay the Spire, but thankfully prestige difficulty and mutator options for campaigns increase replayability. Right now the game is easily worth the full purchase price, even without a sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: IMO a more fun version of slay the spire or at least has the potential to be with a few more updates (although I havent played STS in a while so maybe that game has improved over time). Rougelike card builder with two decks, one for negotiations and one for physical combat. Story mode is much more interesting than more linear rougelikes. On the other hand, I'm about 26 hours in and don't feel like starting up another run. This game just got released for early access, so I think I'll be coming back later down the road once more cards have been released.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: This game, and all the other games from this developer, are a great example for how early access should be used. The game offers a lower price in early access because it wants to reward people that trust the developer. They make clear progress and they keep you up to date. But now, the game itself...It is just a piece of art, the art style is so well done and it really gives the right atmosphere to the game. If you are a person that hates losing / starting over again, don't buy this game. It is a rogue game which means you will start over multiple times and you will have to repeat certain dialogues again. When you die you will receive some perks which will increase your chances of winning for when you try again so that will keep you going for sure.The story is very well done with a nice lore to it. Skipping through dialogues you already had in a previous run is fairly quick so you are not stuck being bored. The music could be better for sure though, it is a little bit annoying at times and very repetitive.The game is not hard on new players, everything is explained thoroughly but it will take you some time to figure out the combat and negotiation system but there is a lot of fun in doing so!There are also no lies told on the store page so if you like what you read on there you should buy it because you'll most certainly like the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun game. Obvious comparison is to Slay the Spire which I think is fair enough to entice people - though after playing for a few hours its quick to see they're far apart beyond genre. Griftlands' strongest point is the story telling for me. I appreciate when games make morality choices just that. You might make an enemy murdering this person, you might have to deal with the consequences of showing mercy if not. While I'm sure you can find ways to min-max the rogue like aspect you at least get a great introduction to the world, story, and characters before the full rogue like side takes over. My only complain is I wish Rook was the starting character. Even though you unlock all characters very quickly he would have been a better first impression in my opinion.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Although I've tried, I've never managed to get into computer deck-builders, which is odd because I love them IRL. This is the single exception. While it says 32 hours of play on Steam, I generally play this on my offline laptop on public transport, and would have clocked up several times that.The difference for me between this game and other digital deckbuilders is that Griftlands works overtime to give context to the gameplay. The game is played on several levels, which includes an overmap and dialogue level between battles. This can be surprisingly fun as you interact with other characters, making friends and enemies, and contributing to an emergent sense of story. How you interact with characters can have surprising effects later on in a campaign.The card component of the game itself is quite engaging, and includes elements that would be extremely difficult to incorporate in a physical card game, such as cards having 'experience'. Each campaign features slightly different mechanics, and there are multiple potential build pathways for each character which allow you to both minmax your deck AND roleplay simultaneously.On top of this, the art style is beautiful, the world is intriguing and feels well-realised, and while the stories are straightforward enough, the writing is quite good.Altogether, a highly recommended game.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr It's fantastic and you should buy itI really love this game! It goes beyond the simple ladder climb of Slay the Spire or Monster Train and fleshes out the deck building experience with an interesting campaign story, which includes some player choices that add variety. I love that there are two different types of combat as that means you're not playing the same deck every single encounter. The characters are fun and the writing is great! I've had a lot of laughs both from onscreen writing and from details I've imagined because of the scenarios the game creates!There's just one slight draw back in my opinion. The cards themselves feel like they lack the depth of some other games, and I've found my decks end up kinda similar each run. The story building is where most of the replayability comes from in this game. This has meant I got bored of it quicker than other, similar games. It doesn't help that games in this take me a lot longer to complete so it feels like more of a commitment to start up. That said, I still put 50 hours on it very quickly, while having a lot of fun, and feel like my money was well spent!I really hope a modding community pops up around this game because that could keep me interested for a very long time!
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: The variety in the cards and characters is just plain refreshing.  As you unlock more, you learn more. Rewarding whether you win or lose a run.  Then you push your limits, and then you learn More. Fun loop. The descriptions on the keywords of each card are also Very useful. Consequences exist in each decision. Just a Great card game all around. Lookin forward to maxing out each character. Easily worth $ per hour.

_childDocuments_.review: Griftlands is an amazingly fun deckbuilder, don't let the Early Access state worry you, its got *plenty of content* to offer already!Its an RPG/Deckbuilder game with rougelike elements where you select a character and play through their story, if you fail you get to keep some of what you earned and try again, gaining experience for how well you did. Experience unlocks more cards and even neat outfits to wear.The game can be challenging but never really feels unfair and its easy to learn after a couple of matches, the two characters are both pretty different, and each one can even have several kinds of builds for even more variation. Rook, for example, can build up charges, each one granting more damage (and overcharges which can be spent by certain cards) or the charges can be spent to gain defense. This allows him to build decks around managing his charge/overcharge, but he also has the option of having a deck built around Burn status ailments and doing damage over time.The story is neat, there's a lot of lore and vibrant characters.As well as fun system that rewards you for befriending or infuriating the various character with boons/banes which are like passives.I can see myself putting well over 100 hours, if not more into this game with its charming artstyle, lovely characters and above all fun deck building gameplay!

_childDocuments_.review: A cleverly done deckbuilder-RPG-roguelike in the spirit of Slay the Spire. Very well executed with a lot of pretty Klei polish on it. It has a lot more flavour and charm for those interested in more than just the challenge of Spire but does not lose sight of presenting a fair and balanced challenge.I'd very much recommend Griftlands, well worth the price.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: It's Klei, so I bought it. They've never disappointed me.This one is different than your usual Klei game though. It doesn't feel yet like much of a sandbox experience, but it's also not a railroaded RPG either. It's ... different. I've never played anything like it.Is it fun? Oh yeah. Absolutely. Different dialogue trees, a lot of different missions and randomness makes for fun on multiple playthroughs. It's hard and you can't restore a saved game so it's very rogue. But it's not frustratingly difficult and I don't feel like the game cheats. All the numbers are there and displayed. I'm going to recommend this one, even so early in early access. Klei sticks to good release schedules and certainly improves things along the way. And the price is good right now too.

_childDocuments_.review: Griftlands is a deckbuilding roguelike game which has been a running trend for quite some time. However, this games stands out in many aspects among a plethora of its competitors. A lot of interesting mechanics and different ways to play for each of the characters, and just the right amount of randomness adds a nice kick to its taste and give it a ton of replayability. It also has outstanding art style and animations which is always nice.

_childDocuments_.review: Griftlands provides an expanded view of what a "Deckbuilder" Card game can be all while looking sleek, polished and unique. With variable card abilities as they gain exp when played from your base deck, two styles of deck and interesting diplomacy versus fighting methodology. The variance on how you can play this game really is astounding and is the closest I've seen to blending the Deckbuilder style games that have become so popular lately with being able to Roleplay a character.

_childDocuments_.review: GRIFTLANDS Mini Review:Deckbuilding Roguelike by the creators of Don't Starve, that tries to push the Deckbuilding genre forward in similar ways Hades did the same for roguelikes overall last year. And for the most part, Griftlands succeeds.Balancing 2 decks, one for battle (think Slay the Spire) and one for Negotiation (pretty unique gameplay) is great. Constructing it all around a narrative with a sprawling cast of interconneted characters and factions, with a TON of options for customizing your playstyle is too.One run takes way more time than in most roguelikes (my first full clear took me around 5 hours, but can definitely be done way faster), but is even more engaging for that reason and rarely ever feels "unfair". You are allowed to play it very safe at all times if you choose to do so, yet run risk of running out of ressources fast if you never take risks.There are 3 different characters with unique decks and a unique storyline. There is a LOT bang for your buck in here. The only issue I've had so far comes with the narrative aspect, which while great, can repeat itself a bit too much after multiple runs with the same character.For: Fans of Deckbuilders and RoguelikesFans of Narrative-Driven games with a lot of personal choices that matterNot For:People who just wanna do "one quick run"People who don't wanna think about narrative consequences in their deckbuilder gameOverall: Great game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a masterpiece of this Genre. It has HANDSDOWN the best art concept of any cardbuilding game for me. The story is phenomenal. Character development too.The concept of Argumentative duels, is ridicolously good, and innovative.The game has great replayability for those who are into that. Myself, I prefer to move on.The soundtrack is a majestic synth that will make you feel chilled, and at the same time connected to the story.The whole setting concept is great, the world building is so interesting. You want to know more about this fiction world. Finally, I would say that this game is a Hidden Gem that most don't know. Buy it, and buy it now. There's now way you'll regret.

_childDocuments_.review: Genuinely thought I hated this game in the first two hours, I wanted a fun fast Slay the Spire clone but instead I got some weird pseudo-RPG with two types of decks and waaaay too much dialogue. Just give it a little time and everything will suddenly start to come together and you've got a game that's just as fun as the best of them out there.

The stories become a pleasant and familiar backdrop to your run and the mechanics of the game sing.The roleplaying elements of this game are stellar. Would recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Did you know that Klei Entertainment makes good games? After 12 hours, there's some criticism to be made here, but it's surface level to the point of it not really needing to be brought up in full. It's got three characters, each with an assortment of styles to play with. It one-ups the likes of Slay the Spire and Monster Train by having actual worldbuilding, and there's a branching story for each character that you can just straight up ignore if you want -- or soak it in with a "story mode" difficulty. Griftlands is really great.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Really fun deck builder.  Just finished the first character's storyline.  Took about 5.5 hours, taking my time and then I started the second character's.  There is a lot of meta progression in the form of upgrades, flourishes (ultimate moves kind of), perks, and card unlocks that definitely has me excited to keep playing and then replaying.  You go through a day and night cycle and each day seems to end with a boss fight.  You get branching choices throughout the day on a map that also has random events sprinkled in so it is like slay the spire's branching choices except you don't see the entirety of what is available before the boss and it just feels really dynamic and fun.  The split between battle and interrogation card battles is just another great way that it builds upon slay the spire's legacy and sets itself above being just a clone.  The story aspect is nice to have, well animated, with nice voiced gibberish and a decent amount of branching decisions.  The card mechanics are excellent.  I haven't played and unlocked enough to know if there are any bad imbalances but all of the build possibilities are enticing and make you want to give them a shot.  You can also get grafts (relics I think they were called in spire) that can define a run and a pet that will fight alongside you.  I bought this full price because I like the developer and I am not disappointed.  This is a nicely polished game well worth the full price and a definite buy if it goes on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: I love, love, love the direction of this game. The art style, the music, the worldbuilding. Unfortunately, as someone who has gotten a bit bored of Slay the Spire, this doesn't replace it for me. This suffers from having too much stuff stuffed into it. Your deck starts with a lot of variety to begin with, and then the amount of choices you are constantly presented with is daunting. The sheer amount of things in your deck(s) you have to keep track of, and all of the various battle/negotiation effects, complete with flashy animations make this game fairly hard to grock. To counter this, the game itself is fairly easy. I never felt like I had to understand much about the various combos, but I could still win regardless. It was on my second or third playthrough that I finally understood every faction has their own traits.It would be nice if this game had a stronger "vanilla" flavor - a more boring starter deck? Make the concepts introduce themselves slower? Make me do multiple playthroughs to unlock factions/card abilities, etc?Obviously, the game may reveal itself on more playthroughs, and maybe I can up the difficulty in turn. But it's hard to pick this up over something that's a truer roguelike. The "runs" are pretty long, maybe a few hours? Definitely feels too long to be a roguelike, but too short for an adventure game. The story mode loses it's replayability a few times through. The game gives some other play modes, like an onslaught mode that just slams random encounters together, which loses a lot of the charm of the story.All that to say, I certainly enjoyed the game! And I will find it easy to get my money's worth! But it's hard to say I needed this game in my collection. And it's really close to something great.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic story line and plot! The game throws you into a completely new sci-fi world but does such a good job of subtly explaining everything, it becomes incredibly immersive and really fun to play. Lots of content, the battles and the deck building are really fun. Also really love the negotiation battles. Once again, a stellar effort from Klei. Cannot wait to see what they bring out next!
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: The combination of all these story and quest elements in a roguelike deckbuilder might seem like a nice idea, but it doesn't work. All those extra elements just add too much length to runs.Giving each character 2 decks means that you only really have enough stuff in a run to customize each deck half as much or less as in Slay the Spire. This makes each run very similar to other runs.The difficulty is weird in this game. I got to the final boss in my first game easily, then it totally crushed me. I thought this was cool, essentially this would have meant the first part of the game is more about setting up that final fight, rather than actually being difficult to survive (similar to FTL). But, that didn't turn out to be the case. I aborted my second run early on because I was unhappy with my choices. My third run I crushed everything in my path including the final boss without any feeling of difficulty. For my fourth run I played the second character for the first time (Rook) and it was the same thing, way too easy.Not sure how the higher prestige levels are, but I don't want to grind for hours just to get to a difficulty I actually enjoy. Compared to Inscryption, the story and atmosphere are dull and repetitive and overstay their welcome.The music is forgettable. The art style is too busy, annoying, and nonsensical. I guess it looks nicer than Slay the Spire, but that's a very low bar.Compared with Slay the Spire, there is a lot more breadth (doing a lot of things at the same time) but this does not make the game better. Slay the Spire has more depth of strategy and is a lot more focused on the most important thing: gameplay. TL;DR: Fun for a bit, but got too repetitive for me after only 4 games.
_childDocuments_.name: Griftlands

_childDocuments_.review: It's basically Spire with a face lift. I was a little disappointed by that. But that's only because I've played a ton of Spire. It's kind of the same card system, and even the same mechanics for the first two characters I've seen so far. The map screen, though it doesn't look like it, is still a progression based over 5 days. It's a clever way of rejigging the mechanic of Spiral but that's what I mean, it is the same mechanics. It does look a ton better though.The characters are better, the story is better, the art is great, the argument system is a nice touch. There is a lot of depth here. If I was going to play this type of game, I'd probably play this over spire now. Having team mates is cool.

name: Empire of Sin
detailed_description: Pick Your Empire of Sin Edition Empire of Sin - Deluxe Edition Upgrade to the Deluxe Edition and receive access to the Mobster Pack which includes four recruitable and playable gangsters, the Golden Weapon Set that comes with three exclusive weapon skins plus “Romero” gun sound effects, and unique execution animation for your boss character - the Curb Stomp Execution. Empire of Sin - Premium Edition The Premium Edition grants access to all Deluxe Edition content - the mobster pack, Golden Weapon set and Curb Stomp Execution kill - plus two post-launch expansions and the stylish Al Capone’s Fur Coat costume. About the Game Empire of Sin is a new strategy game brought to you by Romero Games and Paradox Interactive that puts you at the heart of the ruthless criminal underworld of 1920s Prohibition-era Chicago. Slip into the shoes of one of the fourteen real and historically inspired mob bosses such as Al Capone, Stephanie St. Clair, or Goldie Garneau and assemble a rag-tag gang, build and manage your criminal empire, and defend your turf from rival gangs. It’s up to you to hustle, charm, and intimidate your way to the top and do whatever it takes to stay there - break a leg! Roleplay: Choose one of fourteen unique bosses based on fictional and real-world gangsters, then set out to build and manage your criminal empire in Chicago’s infamous Prohibition era. Empire Management: Build your Empire of Sin and run Chicago’s underworld economy with business savvy, brutality or city-wide notoriety. Strategically manage your establishments such as speakeasies, supply chains, casinos and more. Turn-Based Combat: Assemble your gang and slug it out in turn-based combat to defend and expand your territory – or send a message to opposing gangs.

_childDocuments_.review: I waited for the update/DLC to play this, but it still ended up in disappointment. The premise of the game is great and there's so much historical source material to pull from, so it's really confusing how this was botched this badly. All you had to do was copy the Crusader Kings diplomacy/relationship formula, throw some X-COM in there, and put it in a Prohibition era. I agree with most of the reviews on here: visually, the game is decent, but the gameplay is a an absolute slog. Your territorial expansions and combat wins don't feel rewarding so there's no incentive to keep pushing forward. All the rackets feel the same and the upgrades are still pretty worthless after the update. There's no customization options for anything so everything looks bland as hell. Not to mention the atrocious UI and character movement jankiness. Albeit, there are a ton of different systems and game mechanics scattered throughout the game. However, they either 1) barely have any impact on the gameplay, like the police system and character backstories, or 2) the different systems don't work well together, like the relationship mechanics with the hiring system. Also, this game lacks some serious quality of life upgrades. I cannot believe there's still no way to speed up and/or skip time, which makes the game feel like some weird FTP-mobile-Clash-of-Clans nonsense. TL;DR: great concept, terrible execution.

_childDocuments_.review: Ok, so for anyone who is a sucker for Mafia themed games in any format, its just downright sort of a dream come true. You manage a specific crew with an amazing wide range of bosses to choose at starting point. I wasnt sure about the turn based combat (never played a game with this system before) and dang, its just strategy at its finest. It most def needs many many tweaks, including Diplomacy (useless at this moment), upgrades in rackets again useless, I cannot make money even with a maxed out racket, and also feels like no different to buy a hotel, a brewery or a brothel, they need to implement specific bonuses and stuff to make it more immersive, the need to tweak this asap, relations with the police need be more rewarding specially at higher levels of notoriety, gang relations make no sense, like I am gang A and gang B offers me to join forces to repel gang C, however when I accept I am marked as enemv of gang B but neutral with gang C. Also, in a game being Al Capone, all of the sudden 2 gangs were wiped out, out of the blue by say gang B, which is impossible cause they were controlling several turfs, but the main let down is the sit down with gang leaders, makes no sense as you get to make a deal, and like 2 or 3 mins later your rating decreases and you are in the brink of war. _childDocuments_.review: I don't think I have ever written a review for a game, but this game was so terrible that I felt it necessary.I regret my purchase and I am actually disappointed in Paradox Games, a company that I trust, because this game was not ready to be released. I completed it just because I kept hoping that it was going to get interesting...but when it was over I felt completely underwhelmed.Also, what is up with all of the female gang members? This is the 1920s and women weren't getting involved in organized crime at the level that this game portrays. Also, every "romance" that sprung up for my gangsters was homosexual. That wouldn't have happened openly back in that area. It honestly was just really cringey seeing the lengths that were made to have this game be inclusive or whatever they were going for. _childDocuments_.review: (UPDATED)"Tropico" + "X-Com" + "Mafia". Developed by John Romero (Doom, Quake) and Brenda Romero (Wizardry) Pretty addicting Turn Based Strategy Game with RPG elements. No idea what all the negative reviews are about. The game is much better than expected. The first Empire Builder I've played where I didn't immediately crash the economy. You run around, take over peoples rackets and replace them with your own. You can build breweries, speakeasies, brothels, casinos or hotels. If you have enough gang members, you can build a safehouse and assign a lieutenant to it. There are 14 gang leaders to choose from. Some are real like Dean O'Bannon, Stephanie St Clair and Al Capone, but others are fictional characters created for the game. There is a pretty even mix of male and female bosses, which doesn't seem too forced as there were plenty of real women bootleggers in real life. Some of the gangs are themed around particular rackets and will excel best with that kind of business. Alot of the negative reviews come from people who don't understand how the economy works. You are bootleggers. That means, you have to bootleg. Build breweries and sell top grade liquor to minor factions and rival gangs. Use the funds you earn to crush them. This is what Al Capone did. This is what Arnold Rothstein did. I don't understand how people could get this wrong. If you just keep buying rackets, you'll tank the economy. The best way to expand is to kill the boss of a rival gang. You earn all of their rackets for the cost of one safehouse. There are some issues that I have, but nothing major. When you attack a building, your guys just scramble to their nearest "cover", even if it puts them in a worse position than if they did nothing. This is very annoying sometimes. There's no diplomatic way to play the game. You can't really absorb other gangs.  I also wish you could run legitimate businesses too, like Butcher shops or pizza parlours. Could use more customisation for the gang members (What clothes they can wear, ect). I would like to see these things added in the expansion. UPDATE:The Precinct Update and the Make It Count DLC greatly expand the gameplay and improve many of the features of the game. Gang Turfs now have supply lines that must exist in order for you to invade. Diplomacy is now a valid option with the ability to peacefully buy out a rival's empire. Police response and presence is greatly improved. This update is free and includes mod support. Make It Count adds "Not Meyer Lensky" due to some legal issues with Hollywood and Loansharking. Easily the best boss in the game, Maxim Zelnick, as he is called, has the ability to spawn 2 random expendable henchmen and sic them onto his enemies. He also makes for a good diplomatic playthrough.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played about forty hours so far of Empire of Sin and have finished the game six times.  It's not a perfect game, but I have a lot of fun when I am playing it and it does keep me coming back.The setting is great, and I love the different feels to each of the neighborhoods in Chicago.  I really like the dynamic zoom mechanic that the developers made for this game, where you can smooth-scroll from inside a building to outside the building, to a view of the street, to a tactical view of the neighborhood, to a tactical view of all neighborhoods, all in real-time.  This feature is great and is not getting nearly enough credit in the reviews.The game has quite a bit going on with it.  You've got a light economic management thing going on, which mostly consists of producing and setting the correct types of booze, and buying or taking over buildings.   You can also upgrade establishments, but with the current build of the game (Dec 2020), upgrades are usually not worth it, as they are expensive and take a long time to build after you pay for them.  The game rewards going as wide as possible as quickly as possible, so my go-to strategy is basically to start to clear out and take over the neutral casinos and speakeasies as soon as a new game starts.Meanwhile, you've got a bunch of other mob bosses running around setting up their own empires.  When you meet one, you can either tell them to go pound sand or you can sit down with them to cut a deal.  The deals that you cut with the mob bosses are so incremental that they are barely noticeable, but I think the sit-downs themselves are quite fun, if a tad repetitive.  After your initial meeting, there are a range of diplomacy options available.  These are generally pretty useless, except for the trading, which is currently rigged in the player's favor.  It does not take much to convince bosses to sell your their unique weapons in exchange for some garbage ones and have them walk away thinking they got the better of you.While it is currently very easy to complete the game without diplomacy at all, diplomacy can be used to win, in a manner of speaking.  I did play a game where I quietly took over unoccupied neighborhoods and made nice with all mob bosses and stepped on no toes.  Then, I sold them all weapons for peanuts, and they all trusted me.  Then, I kept calling in favors and repeatedly called in a hit on every boss with every other boss, and watched them wipe each other out.  Then, when there was one left, I just went in with a small team and took that person out.You've also got an RPG-like quest system in this game.  There's a few generic quests available to every mob boss; these were fun in my first playthrough but the rewards were pretty crappy so I have more or less ignored most of them since.  Each boss also has a main questline, this can be a nice diversion.Finally, you've got the gangster system and the tactical battles.The gangster system is a neat idea and does a lot of things right, but needs a bit of work.  There is a roster of henchmen that both you and the CPU opponents can hire.  While theoretically you can assign your henchmen as neighborhood managers or as protectors of one of your buildings, in reality you and your henchmen will all fight together as a roving squad of death, as that is by far the most effective use for them.  Gangsters have different classes, but the doctor and demolitionist classes are far superior to any of the other three, as doctors get free healing and can also use rifles, the best weapon in the game, and demolitionists get a free grenade that does massive AOE damage and causes bleeding. As you increase in notoriety, you can hire more expensive and more skilled henchmen.  Currently, there is not much difference between the cheapest goons and the most elite killers; I would love to see the lower tiers of henchmen nerfed quite a bit, and the higher tiers buffed.The tactical battles are the best part of the game and are the reason I keep coming back.  The difficulty is generally pretty easy, except when you are up against a group of enemies who all decide to lob grenades on the same turn.  The safehouse raids are so much fun!  (they need to be harder, though, and a greater variety of safehouses would be sweet).Empire of Sin also has a great score by Crimson Diamond composer Dan Policar and team; I would pay extra for a soundtrack if Paradox decides to sell one (please, Paradox!).All in all, this game is a lot of fun right now, but also has a lot of room for improvement.  I am optimistic about the future of Empire of Sin.

_childDocuments_.review: Empire of Sin is a mildly-RPG, pauseable RTS of the Prohibition era beginning in 1920--it covers a range of activities and a timeframe that is hard to find anywhere else. The tactical combat is early Xcom style, designed well, top down, with a small range of actions available to each actor. The real joy of this game, IMHO, is the wonderful variety of quirky bad guys--first, a wonderfully broad variety of bosses you can start with, and then dozens of widely differing henchmen which you can select as your tools. The henchmen are categorized by how much they cost you on the regular vis a vis their level of skills, and sometimes, special weaponry. It is important to pay careful attention to your selections for a couple of reasons. First, if you take more than one or two from the top two categories, you will end up spending so much on them you can hardly make your rackets profitable--they run 20% and 16% of your overall take respectively. Second, the relationship between cost and skill lever is less than perfect. One of my most consistent performers is a bottom row doctor named Nora who shoots like a Marine Corps sniper and can heal guys on the fly without meds in the middle of a firefight. Also, some characters are listed as "Giants" with special bonuses in melee, but for some reason their supposed prowess is not reflected either in Hit Points or in melee skill. So pay attention to what you're getting.The music does a wonderful job setting the mood. The dynamics of the social relating with other bosses is great for setting power balances. But, eventually, the game does begin to drag. As you grow in power, and you manage to eliminate a boss or two, the game seems to automatically queue some other organization to declare war on you. Funny thing is, if you take a squad of 4-8 guys with you into a few of their rackets in a row, they will quickly come begging for a truce and may give you 200 barrels of swill or rack to accept. The fights are fun, but they are endless, and even someone who enjoys it as much as I do can tire of the constant need for small skirmishes. There's no targeted assassinations, no blowing up of supply chains, no exploding of rackets. The "missions" available along the way are primarily a means to thrust some additional $$$ at you--this isn't Cyberpunk. Finally, the core management aspect of the game has to do with spending your hard-earned capital on improving your businesses, adding much-needed security, ambiance, protection from the police, and word of mouth reputation. For your breweries, you can raise the quality of your alcohol. For casinos, the quality of your games. But, eventually, it feels like mass tweaking of minor elements of your fortune, repetitive, and without enough engagement of the immersion aspect of those businesses.So, in the final analysis, I give this game a thumbs up. I will start a new boss soon and enjoy a different atmosphere of play... for a while. But from what I can see so far, I will eventually wear the newness and immersion of this one off, and may not go back to it again. It is a slightly better than average implementation of a very rare game focus. I love, love, lover the characters. But it would be nice if you could do more with them.

_childDocuments_.review: Empire of Sin is a turn-based tactical/empire building “gabagool” simulator developed by Romero Games, a studio created by DOOM creator John Romero. Originally coming from the mind of John Romero’s wife Brenda Romero, whose hobbies included creating her own historical board games. This desire to create the game had lasted for around twenty years, and after the studio was formed the two then decided to approach Paradox Interactive, whose history of publishing strategy titles led to a partnership formed for the development of this game. It’s debut started I believe in 2019 E3 during the Nintendo Showcase (according to sources, as though I probably watched this showcase I don’t remember this moment) and was later released December of 2020. My personal history with this game is limited, I honestly don’t remember if I watched the Nintendo Showcase but I do remember hearing “Mafia strategy game” and wishlisting it immediately. I was cautiously excited for the game, hoping that it would be an updated version of Gangsters: Organized Crime. It was not, and debuted with Mixed reviews (almost negative on Steam). However, I picked it up after waiting for it to go on sale I believe at some point and gave it a playthrough (with cheats activated of course, thanks WeMod) to just relax, having replayed it twice or so over the past two years. My opinion on the game is that the mixed reviews are correct, but here’s how I specifically feel.As the most important part of any tactical empire builder game, it’s important to note that the strategy aspect of the game has to be both fun and technically competent. I’ll start with the technically competent one: ehhhh kinda. Sometimes it runs perfectly fine and I can’t complain! Other times, like when I was playing Al Capone’s game, I would be told to, for example, go find Frankie Yale inside of some bar. However, I can’t do that because “the guards” won’t let me do that. I try to talk to the guards, sometimes the guards will attack and sometimes I’ll be able to talk to the guards, who will say “sure come in” and then I still won’t be able to go in. I kill them, still won’t be able to come in. The only way I’ve been able to move past this was if I were to view the inside of the building and then right click to move my guys inside but that’s kind of a hit or miss depending on the objective. Another time I would do a protection treaty with another group, and if another group was bought out but had bad relations and had declared war then the group you’re protecting would ask for your help. Click on the notification and not only does it say that this group is still alive and needs your help, but you won’t be able to close this pop up which requires a full game reset. Stuff like this didn’t occur too much but occurred enough to where after a while of playing it that I need to take a break after a bit. As for if the gameplay is fun, I’ll go through a general description of what the game is like. First when you start up, you start as your boss and go through the tutorials of hiring specific goons (the limit is 16), from there you go to certain buildings which have random thugs and wipe them out in X-COM styled combat in order to take over the building and turn it into a racket. From there you choose between your four (or five depending on if you have DLC) rackets which vary in price depending on district conditions, and from there you grow your money in order to upgrade your rackets. Once you upgrade your main district hideout enough, you can choose between multiple different buildings for bonuses to those districts (ex. Boxing Gloves for an extra guard in that district only, a Mob Lawyer to lower police presence, etc). You can gain more of these by obtaining certain quest awards or using certain bosses (like Malting will boost your booze but can only be unlocked from a side quest outcome, or Al Capone’s Suit Shop which will boost the chances of police bribes being successful that’s unique to him only). You’ll get quests which offer semi open ended pathways which lead to different rewards sometimes (mostly money) while also dealing with a giant contention of other rival gangsters. Your specific gangsters (as well as your boss) form their own relationships with each other (off-screen) and can get perks and traits. For example, one thing I didn’t notice is that when I went AFK one time, I left all my people inside of a pub, where a whole bunch of them became alcoholics and gained negative traits. You can also gain traits and perks due to combat actions, and using perk points can upgrade their skill tree when you level them up.In between dealing with rival gangsters, you’ll also have to deal with the game’s most important currency other than money: booze. Being the Prohibition Era and all, it’s important to establish a consistent stream of booze and supply. Different types of booze lead to different payouts and outcomes, but also lead to rival bosses trying to ride your s h i t. What I’ll say about the bosses aspect is that the way the game limits you, while it may be realistic can also be really annoying. At one point I found out the location of a rival boss's hideout, and I wanted to send a bunch of goons to go in and kill them, but I couldn’t because none of my territory surrounds them and “supply lines are cut off”. Like that hasn’t stopped people from sending in hitmen to kill  bosses, and truth is I’d rather have the option to fail then get restricted like that because it’s really annoying. The only other things I can think of for the gameplay is that you’ll get certain weapons either as loot or through the black market/police contacts. It’s important to get the best hardware that you can possibly get as not only does it help with combat but also rival named goons could have really heavy firepower and could wipe you out quickly. Being a strategy game, there’s so much stuff involved with this game, between police attention/bureau raids as well as balancing diplomacy, random world events, there’s a lot of stuff in there that I know I’m probably missing.The gameplay itself for the most part is fine, and I’ve gotten myself lost in the game’s mechanics multiple times. I personally had fun with the game, though I also messed about using WeMod Dev cheats because I wanted to have a game to chill and vibe too. However, even with the cheat codes, I can still sit there and respect certain aspects and vibes even if I’m not experiencing them due to my mod use. This game feels like a strange mix of complex and painfully simple, which depending on the type of player can be really frustrating or okay. Overall, it’s a decent time as well as a time sink, just have patience with how buggy it can be on the gameplay front at times. Also there's a very small Steam Workshop community that I Hope eventually gets expanded one day because that could add for some variation! _childDocuments_.review: I paid £41.99 for the Deluxe Edition of the game and so far I have 31hrs on the clock, so the question is, do I recommend the game? I have to say YES.That said the game for me currently sits at a sold 6/10, which does not seem to be high after spending £41.99, but there is enough to take away from this game that is good. Having read some of the negative reviews, I can't say that I totally agree with their points of view, although there are one or two things that do ring true.The good bits.1: The game feels authentic to the period, the environment feels authentic to the period, so yea well done to the devs in bringing the 1920s to life. Graphics are good and sound too.2: The story starts at the beginning of the notorious lives of the characters such as Al Capone. Some have argued that its boring all the running around and does not feel authentic. well what people fail to realise is that in the 1920s (just watch Boardwalk Empire) people like Al Capone were nobodies, it took years for them to build up their reputations and power. People like Capone did a lot of the grunt work until such time he could get people to do the work for him.3: The game at the moment provide an average challenge and there is some reasonable character development.The bad bits:1: The game is fun, but very repetitive. There does not seem to be a right or wrong way to play the game and as such if you bypass some of the set missions, all you seem to do is go from A to B, raid a building, and then develop the establishment. And that's it. That's £41.99 right there.2: There are annoying quirks in the game that really serve no purpose, like when gangsters in your team fall out over who they fall in love with. Its a distraction that's not required, but I can probably get into it more if the Devs developed it a bit better such as being able to create multiple teams and you have to choose carefully who to put in that group.3: I have yet to come across any game killing bugs but I have found some annoying mechanics that need to be fixed, such as anomolies of enemy henchmen stuck in walls, or were their movement matrix fails so they can't exit a room. With the first issue I left the area and re-entered, the problem seemed to fix itself. The second issue fixed itself but I had to wait a few mins, I went to make myself a brew, when I came back it was fixed.Although I have ticked yes to recommending the game, in its current state, its not good value for money. I would suggest waiting till it goes on sale and getting it, hopefully by that point we might see a DLC and some mechanics improvements.

I obviously didn't see much of it in 70smthg minutes I played but it didn't promise much.-No campaign; although it seems like all the bosses have their own stories the game doesn't play like a campaign but a sandbox. No one would want to pass hours controlling basic characters defending a speakeasy. -Although I didn't experience it fully, the business side seemed a bit light.-And the biggest no no no THE AI; I have been in fight a few times after the tutorial, and to tell it gently, the AI is bad. On most of the fights the computer chose to move between 2 positions back and forth, without attacking. I was playing on normal difficulty and was expecting a minimum of challenge from the beginning. This game is marketed as a turn-based strategy game, if you failed the AI sorry but you failed the game.These are good though;-Music; sounded good.-City/Neighborhood/Map Graphics; looks pretty although it feels like char animations requires a little more work.-Item and char speciality mechanics seemed good, shame that the negatives are so strong.Notes;I didn't get to meet the game destroying bugs but people who played it longer seems to suffer from them.Although the game is maybe 4/10 I wouldn't have try to refund it if you had put one feature in the game; multiplayer.
