_childDocuments_.review: Finding good games with well-developed LGBTQ+ characters can be challenging. While there are certainly games that have included those characters, and even developed them well, those games are sadly few and far between. It’s even rarer to find an LGBTQ+ character represented as a main rather than a supporting character.  is one of those rare quality finds. follows Bo and Ao, two students just graduating from university in London. While both Bo and Ao are non-binary and use they/them pronouns, in many other respects they are very different from each other. Bo is a native Londoner, while Ao is from Japan; Bo is funding their education with student loans, while Ao’s schooling is being paid for by their parents. The game takes an introspective tone as the characters navigate the major life event of transitioning from university to post-university life. While they pack up their flat to move out, the game explores themes surrounding adulthood, such as student loan debt, job applications, taxes, and affording rent, as well as gender identity, such as dysphoria. Hints of magical realism are also incorporated. is semi-autobiographical, based on the lives of the two main developers Cel Davison and Hana Lee, also both they/them pronouns. The story may resonate differently depending on the age of the player. Players who are more similar to Bo and Ao in age (early 20s) or stage of life (university or recent graduate) may find the game more personally relatable and immediately relevant, while someone who is in their 30s or older and several years past that part of their life may find the game more reminiscent of their past experience.Included in the game is a 10-minute prelude called , which takes place a couple of years before the start of  and before Bo and Ao move in together. There is an option to skip the prelude if desired, but Friary Road is mentioned by several of the characters throughout .Since  is interactive fiction, the mechanics are fairly simple, but still more robust than many visual novels I’ve played. The player alternates between playing as Bo or Ao and can make dialogue choices for them as well as other characters in the story. The playable character can be moved around the environment, which can be fully rotated in 90 degree increments in order to get a different perspective of the space and open up different options for interactions. Icons pop up for looking, talking, or touching depending on which part of the room or place is being viewed.The game has an interesting way of giving instructions regarding how to play, such as saying that the function of your actions may seem abstract and try not to worry about it, or saying that going through doors will help you gather a sense of place. The game autosaves, although players can also choose to manually save. However, there is only one save slot per playthrough (although you can have three playthroughs on file total).The art style for  is minimalist, with characters having no eyes or mouths, yet each character is still visually distinct. The environment is represented in a visually interesting way, with a two-point perspective that can be rotated 360 degrees to, for example, see all four walls of the room and the spatial relationships. Since the game is taking place over a span of time where the characters are moving out of their flat, as the game progresses you can see the effects of slowly packing as objects disappear from walls and boxes appear instead. The animation style is also distinctive, showing the walls floating or sliding in and out from the sides, top, and bottom of the screen to construct or deconstruct the rooms or yard of the flat or widen the view when entering a more mental space.The music for  uses piano and other instruments with synth in the musical tradition of video game composer greats such as Nobuo Uemastu of  fame. The main composer and sound artist, Eli Rainsberry, is also non-binary, and they have crafted tracks that dovetail perfectly with the story. The included ambient sounds also enhance the overall experience, both the sounds that are evident to the characters (such as ambulance sirens or the cat purring) as well as the sounds that are for the player only (such as the apt sounds that play while rotating the environment or while the dialogue text is being typed on screen). While the sounds and music are excellent in and of themselves, I also really enjoyed that the game provided audio descriptions - text describing the music and sounds. I found this text added an interesting extra component in interpreting the game. I imagine that the audio experience would be even further augmented by the recommended use of headphones, but I was able to fully enjoy and immerse myself in the experience with my speaker setup.  has 12 possible Steam achievements. It may be possible to unlock them all in one playthrough, but I at least will have to do a second playthrough to pick them all up. is a brilliant example of LGBTQ+ characters and stories done right. At $14.99 at the time of review and approximately 2-2.5 hours for first playthrough, the game is technically a little expensive in terms of time/content for price when compared to a movie ticket, but I think it’s still worth buying at full price for its treatment of subject matter that is so often handled poorly.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: No Longer Home is a simple game about letting go of the life you've built due to circumstances beyond your control. You get a close look at the lives of Bo and Ao and you learn about their dreams, frustrations and fears. This is an Interactive Story, point-and-click, where you wander through the home shared by the main protagonists and their flatmates.No Longer Home is fine for what it is, but feels like it could have been so much more. The writing is really well done and the characters feel real and well thought out, and the game really hits that "life in your early 20s" vibe that's a crossroads of frustration and uncertainty, but at most times it feels like its dragging on in conversations that are not interesting and not contributing to the story at all.Overall, I did really find the characters and storyline interesting. I genuinely wanted to know more about them and where their story would lead. You know, how the situation between them would change or if it would stay the same, how would the characters evolve and improve themselves, but then the game was over, without any further progress on the story or characters. No finalization of anything. I also find it sad that all those metaphorical symbolisms remained unexplained and vague.In the end, No Longer Home is a decent story based interactive game with LGBTQ+ main characters and relatable story, but it falls short with the storytelling and the story progression finding it's end. I would recommend the game, if you find it on a really good sale, but at full price, the game is not worth it, therefore I will not recommend this game. I wish there was a neutral option for steam, but sadly no.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: Mixed feelings about this one. I say I recommend it just to push up the avg review score, but honestly, I wouldn't recommend it to most people. I enjoyed my time here. It is less of a game and more of a time capsule, both specific to the protagonists and yet relatable to most. 20-somethings who have experienced the sudden thrust into society and been a bit lost. Pressure from family or society pushes against your own desire to do something different. Frustration at yourself and the world for going through the whole academic system and still coming out rather unprepared on the other side. And some rather newer struggles many younger people feel these days about sexuality and gender norms.I never finished uni myself but still had a lot of the same feelings and worries depicted in this. To be honest, I had mostly forgotten them. Having sort've relived them through this game, through the lens of a 30 something year old, I realise that it was a bubble that seemed like a mountain at the time.Any piece of media that can remind me of feelings and times long forgotten, and allow me to reflect on it with a different perspective, is something quite special.I will refrain from giving this a mark out of 10 as it just doesn't feel right for this particular game, but I will recommend this game to anyone going through any of the struggles I have mentioned, or anyone who did years ago and wants to relive it a little.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: No Longer Home had a great deal of inspiration from Kentucky Route Zero, it is a short game which can be completed first time round in under two hours. The game itself is an enjoyable point and click narrative if you are prepared for reading dialogue and the mundane reality of university, figuring out what to do next, I empathised with this aspect as I went through this myself after graduating. It can be hard to figure out a path in life when you are unsure of what career you want. The developers did state it was semi-autobiographical game and I could relate to the themes portrayed.The game itself does not have the eloquence of KRZ in terms of its writing or the length. I do think the price point should be cheaper because of its length and factoring in its price point, however, I did enjoy my time with this game so I will recommend it and suggest buying when it is cheaper.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: €15,- for an incredibly slow, short game?? Definitely overpriced, and I'm glad I got it as part of a Humble bundle with games I'm actually interested in. I can see why this game has mixed reviews. There are some good points (soundtrack, art style, LGBT+ representation), but overall... the experience was just a snore fest. The animations are slow, the camera motions are slow, EVERYTHING is just... so slow... Personally, I cannot recommend this game, but if it feels like something you would enjoy, you can be your own judge and decide for yourself
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: I finished this game in less than 90 minutes my first playthrough, and that was even taking time to explore the environment and reading all the dialogue. I played the first 1/3 of it a second time to get a couple of achievements I'd missed in my first run. About a quarter of that time wasn't time that I could spend interacting with the game - it was time that the game locked my character in place and made the camera zoom in, or out, or pan around, really slowly. It was frustrating at times.I was excited for this game, which is why I was a little let down that I didn't really find it enjoyable. It feels less like a narrative, which goes somewhere and includes some growth or at least change, and more like somebody venting for an hour and a half. The characters begin the story facing both emotional and real-world problems and by the end they've made progress on...none of them. The problems they're facing also don't take place during the game. It's just a little snapshot of life as two twenty-somethings who are unhappy and don't ever do anything to change that. I'm currently somebody who is in their age range and is facing the same uncertainty of graduating from a university soon, and I found both the story and the characters unrelatable and difficult to want to spend time with.This game is also obviously hugely inspired by Kentucky Route Zero, taking a lot of design elements straight from it and even having an easter egg reference KRZ directly in one instance. I've now played both games, and if you're looking for a narrative based game in the magical realism genre and are torn between these two games, I cannot recommend KRZ enough. If you're dead set on this game, pick it up while it's on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: *no spoilers contained* At first I really enjoyed the game, even though the screen rotation system, which won't work until the previous turn is over, and the interaction icons not appearing unless I approach close enough were kinda disturbing. I really found it interesting about the characters and storyline. I genuinely wanted to know more about them. You know, curiosity of where this would lead to and how everything would change or stay. But then the game was over, without any further progress to solve my desire as a player. I'd say I'm very disappointed to not have the opportunity unless they give this game a sequel. I also find it sad that all those metaphorical symbolisms remained unexplained. I kinda get a grip of how it is standing for the situation and mental status of the protagonists, but I wish it could be more clear as the story continues.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: After reading the review that this game is about LGBTQ+ characters and after watching the trailer where you can see some mystical creatures you definitely be curious and after a while buy this game.So, you get a story about two students who live together in a big house. Ao and Bo are not in the relationship but they respect each other and as a player you learn about their problems (adulthood, society acceptance of their gender, etc.) and after a while they are going to move out...The main problem is how could you write a story about student's life SO BORING? It's says that it's a semi-autobiographical story but the story is... just plain.The graphics is not the strong point in indie game though the visual idea where the environment is represented with a two-point perspective that can be rotated 360 degrees looks fascinating. Autosave here is quite annoying. You need to replay the whole game just to know what leads after choosing the second/third reply and you can't skip the dialogues.The game wouldn't be unmemorable if developers had written more lore about Ao, Bo, their friends and neighbours.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: This a really moving story of two non-binary final year students where one is having to move back to Japan forcing the couple to go long distance. Some really emotional scenes about not feeling like you belong and some mental health discussions as it is clear both characters are struggling mentally. Perfect game to try out this pride month!
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: Although the art style and narrative focus are unique, it feels like paying for someone's prototype student project. It doesn't really have any concept of pacing, and although the story is relatable for many, relatability isn't enough to carry a story - it needs to be impactful.It could also do with a clearer description of the length of the game and what the gameplay is like.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: No Longer Home takes you on a journey of finding stability and navigating life post-education. The good: - the game boasts a truly unique art style with beautiful visuals that reflect a clear and well-executed vision. - the audio work is impressive, immersing you in the ambiance of terraced houses on the outskirts of London's first zone (was kind of waiting for the sound of screaming foxes in the background, ngl).The bad: - gameplay tends to be on the dull side, mainly involves walking around the house, pointing, clicking. - the writing feels like a direct transcription of real-life conversations, but unfortunately, it falls short in creating a meaningful connection with the characters... it leaves you feeling more like a spectator at a puppet show. It's not a bad game per se, but grabbing it on sale makes more sense, imo the full price does not justify the ~2-4 hour experience it offers. Despite my hopes for an emotional pull and connection, it unfortunately fell short. There are a lot of similar games that do this better, e.g. Unpacking or Night in the Woods.Overall rating: 2.5/5.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: I liked and disliked this game... but I'll lean towards liking it because I liked what it aspired to do.  How the game went about achieving it though, I disliked.  I'm a big fan of emotional games like this, but this one was rather boring to me.  There's so many different dialogue choices and none of them really feel like they matter.  There's hardly any cutscenes or events that make  you feel like something important and should be remembered is happening.  it's kind of like a dull... end of time kind of feeling, but I suppose that's what you're supposed to feel.  An end is coming, and you're supposed to take everything in and brace for what's coming.  The art style is interesting, reminds me of Untitled Goose Game and Donut County.  I suppose this can be a great experience if you're really trying to take a break from other traditional games, but it just didn't quite hit any marks for me that would make me remember it or even really want to mention it to others.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: Games like these all come down to how well the story is told, and how you as a player connect with the narrative and characters. I didn't mind the slow pace (at first), I thought the minimalist graphics were fine, and I quite enjoyed the music. However the way in which this story was told did not grab me. Everything felt a bit too... hazy? Like all the dialogue was written to evoke an emotional response of nostalgia, but for me it did not, so it just felt meandering for meandering's sake. I did actually enjoy the characters and sympathised with their plight, but the slow pace of the game wore me down over time and I stopped caring after the main point of the story had been reiterated for the hundredth time.The main mechanic of flipping the world around also felt a bit superfluous. It just served to slow the pace down further, for me it didn't enhance my experience at all. I'd also agree that it's overpriced for its runtime of <2hrs. All that said, I admire the developers for making the game that best represented this period of their life, and commend them on being vulnerable enough to make it.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: Having been a long time follower of Humble Grove's work, it's been a delight to finally get to play , which is a project that I know went through many iterations before crystallising into the game it is today. It was well worth the wait.If you’re into weird, deeply human, slow-paced point and click games that will haunt you forever and probably make you cry a bit, then you’re in for a real treat. is a game that wears its heart on its sleeves. It’s extremely confident in its writing, and its ability to convey emotions and small fleeting moments, and the game doesn’t shy away from its influences either. It’s always nice to see such earnest work out in the world.The art style is gorgeous. Every detail in the environment is lovingly rendered, making the small flat feel lived-in and all the more heartbreaking to leave. The soundtrack is also incredible, there’s a moment in the game that pretty much brought me to tears and the music is what really brought it all together. Magical experience.I can see myself coming back to the game whenever I feel a bit lost and need to ground myself and be reminded that in time, things will be OK.Yes the game is short. Yes it costs money to play it. Personally, I think it’s worth it, but I’m also a short games goblin so... *shrugs*
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: Playing this game was an interesting experience, but it had its ups and downs.One of the first things I noticed was the camera movement. Turning around and moving back and forth through the rooms could get pretty dizzying at times, mostly at the start. On the other side, I really liked the animation and art style, it wasn't the kind you are use to which gave the game a distinct look, although it could be improved. However, the game is very slow-paced. The characters walk slowly, and changing rooms takes a while, when talking with other characters there is always this silence waiting to be able to continue playing, so don't expect any fast-paced action here. Another thing that was kinda annoying were the dialogue options. The choices you make don't really affect the conversation, which feels pointless except for getting certain achievements.It was interesting to dive into the characters' lives and choose answers for different characters tho, which I haven't see in many games. A problem i noticed is that, sometimes, if you interact with a specific object, you might lose the chance to interact with another one later, which was frustrating.Personally, I didn't feel very connected to the characters. Even though we get an idea of their thoughts and worries, it wasn't enough to make me want to explore the different dialogue options deeply and therefore get to know them more.Overall, it's not a bad game, but it's not amazing either. It's nice to chill with if you are looking for something low-key.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: This game felt like a chore to play. Writing is good, dialogue feels very authentic, story is interesting if a bit mundane (but it's not really about the plot, it's about the characters, so that's fine). But overall, the game isn't engaging. This would have been far better as a graphic novel than as a game. It's barely interactive, and the interactivity feels like work.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: no longer home captures the hazy, ethereal nature of lying around with your friends hopping from topic to topic of discussion, losing track of time, having your poignant thoughts tumble out unexpectedly. the backgrounds drift in and out of focus along with your own. one second you're talking about a painting in the hallway and the next you're interrogating the nature of yourself.i've written before about how i think games that get in and get out within two hours are the Exact Right length for narrative games, and this is no exception. i love the pacing and length of the game, but somehow i almost wish that there was just liiiittle bit more to sink into.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: No Longer Home is an authentic and often unsettling story about the process of moving out and moving on. Of course, every player will take something different away from their experience playing, but it is an experience that I highly recommend. With beautiful designs, excellent characters, and a great soundtrack, No Longer Home is well worth picking up.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: I had a tough time getting through this game and pretty much just ended up barely registering all of the dialogue early on and only completed it to get it off of my list. It was hard to connect with or care about Ao/Bo even when I had faced similar feelings of apprehension, lost, trying to self-identify, and the like. A lot of the dialogue seemed disingenuous or sort of faux deep especially when trying to touch on depression. The way they communicated with each other and their friends felt like just acquaintances and I was being put through minutes of empty small talk. Aside from that, it was difficult to get actions to register and many times I'd end up across the room because I somehow clicked the action of something across the room even though I was trying to click on a microwave in front of me. It started feeling slow and tedious with the panning in and out that you could not skip and the character movement somehow felt how I felt dealing with how much panning in/out there was. The dialogue choices were inconsequential and some of the choices seem kind of silly to be saying. This game just was not it for me.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: Thankfully I got this game on sale through a certain website, and if I had gotten this game at full price I would've been beyond disappointed. There just isn't enough content to justify a 15$ price tag. The game is incredibly SLOW paced- it took me 2 and a half hours to complete something that should have been an hour tops.  It is so slow that i found myself disengaged during the last chapter and just clicking trying to get the game to finish. Oh and there's no way to skip dialogue that you've already read, so if you're trying to 100% the game, you'll have to sit and click (slowly) through it all again.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed this game a lot. The art is impeccable, the music is a masterpiece (it's my favourite kind of music), and the way the level 'pieces' float and construct themselves is truly astonishing (it really adds this element of atmosphere and reality breaking down). Thoroughly enjoyed the games minimalist, soft art-style and the camera movements are delicious too.I think there is something to be said with just telling a story. Having a story be told is enough (imo). I really connected with subject parts of the narrative, specially Bo (me being from England and being LGBTQ too did help - thats not to say non Brits, or non-LGBTQ's wont, there is something here for you). It is a lovely and thought provoking snippet of two people's lives and their emotions at that time. I think it does handle the subjects discussed goodly, however while in the game, I did find myself needing a minute or two, to process and understand what was being said - which was absolutely fine, since I could take a minute by not progressing the dialogue to reread and grasp the subjects being discussed. I found myself wanting to know more about Ao's and Bo's flatmates Controls are simple and easy to grasp. They worked perfectly fine for me, when I clicked on icons and the ground to move the game did just that. I enjoyed exploring the home, which being so small, enabled the game to be more intimate.I enjoy short, emotional, art games - of course everyone wants more (who doesn't). I would love to see how this story progressed, to see how they both ended up emotionally (but perhaps again, that was too painful or too personal), but hey, short game-play time is not a downside to me :) extending from this, the dev team is fairly small and creating a game like this was no easy task. Adding or extending game-play would have added huge amounts of time onto the dev process - so congrats devs, i see you!To summarise, for me, the art and music of No Longer Home is the best thing about this game. I do hope there is a sequel, if not, I'm excited for the next game!8/10
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: A lovely short story about change, uncertainty and all the feelings that come with it. No Longer Home tells its story through a mixture of writing and exploration with a beautiful use of audio and visuals. Its story focuses on the very grounded idea of graduating and moving out of your house but sprinkles in elements of the surreal to reflect the various emotions of the characters.While the game may be too short, or lack enough interaction for some players, it’s overall aesthetic and presentation is worth checking out for anyone with a love for narrative.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: I got No Longer Home in the Story-Rich Megabundle. The liked the art style of the game, but found the story rather boring. Unfortunately I wasn't able to immerse myself in the world because the characters felt flat and a bit cliche; especially for this genre of game. The game did, however, run well on the Steam Deck.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: The game was kinda boring at first and I can't quite say why but I had the impression the creators want me to care about the characters too fast...? Like, I only just started the game and there's already this disturbing sounding music and disturbing looking shapes floating in the bedroom but I don't really know why I'm supposed to be disturbed, and I don't care. But I liked the deep conversations that happen afterwards, the minigame was a cool distraction, and oh you can pet cats. The cats saved it for me.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful, chill game. There isn't much of a plot beyond what the synopsis already tells you. This game is rather about reminiscing, regrets, anxieties about the future... It's quite introspective, despite there being a lot of dialogue. Gameplay-wise, you explore the flat and make choices during conversations, where you'll reply for either of the characters at times. It is minimalistic in that sense, while the presentation is rather "artsy". I guess it has to be your cup of tea in order for you to enjoy it. I truly did.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: Beautifully crafted game that explores themes of transition, friendship, and the bittersweet nature of moving on. The heartfelt dialogue and relatable characters resonate deeply with anyone who has faced significant life changes.The game's vibrant visuals create a warm atmosphere, while the soothing soundtrack enhances the emotional experience. However, the character movement can feel a bit unpolished, as they sometimes continue walking when obstructed by game objects, disrupting the flow of exploration.Overall, No Longer Home is a touching and introspective journey that captures the complexities of change. I highly recommend it for those seeking a narrative-driven adventure that lingers in your thoughts.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: TL:DR - Only tentatively recommend- Interesting art style- Great soundtrack that sets the tone well - Potentially relatable content for post-uni city dwellers- Love the representation from the protagonists- Not a lot of player agency in enacting change in the world; feels like a long, drawn-out conversation- Choosing responses in a conversation from different characters feels a little unsatisfyingIn all honesty I felt like the game's dialogue went on too long in places, and became tedious to go through as the key concepts were rattled out. While the themes came through clearly, I didn't feel comforted or empowered by the journey of the characters throughout the game. Felt like I was witnessing my generation experiencing a crisis, with little in the way of resolution. Feels like it could have been covered in a graphic novel, rather than a game, as the interactivity with the world itself is so minimal, taking away player agency. I also became a little frustrated by being able to just choose responses from different characters throughout, rather than pick a response for the protagonist I was playing as, and receive one in return based on my choice. Additionally, the relationship between Bo and Ao could have been explored more deeply;Overall interesting concept, but I don't immediately want to replay it. Tentatively recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: This Game just wasn't for me.I'm someone that plays a lot of Visual Novels, but this one just couldn't catch me. After the first half of the Game I didn't even care anymore because the dialoug was as flat as the screen I played it on. I think the problem is, I don't care for either Bo or Ao since all we see is that one evening befor they move out. There maybe people who can relate to them regardless but I wasn't one of them.Still the game isn't bad and just because I couldn't enjoy it doesn't mean someone else can't. Why do I give it a Thumbs down then? Simply because I think the asking Price for nearly 15€ is way to much for what you recieve, even if you are someone who can relate to the Story. If you are able to grab in on sale it is worth a shot but not for the full Price.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: The game has surreal interpretation of scenes and elements and the surrounding ambient music coupled with chill guitar tunes to set the mood, text adventure game within a game, simple polygonic graphics with UI that is from primitive early age of computer graphics, straight lifted from the Kentucky Route Zero from 2013. When you borrow things from creation of others you must draw a line. It's one thing to say that they were 'inspired' by KRZ but this level of copying is shameless in my book.But how is this game really? Dialogues are boring and have a repetitive theme of what they could've done and how it was in the good times. In short, self pitying. I am often referred as a very pessimistic person by the others but even to me reading through all that was pretty exhausting and depressing. As a result, whole game feels like eavesdropping your not-so-special neighbors over a fence or a wall, which might be interesting for a while, but gets annoying after some time. The game's length is also very short, some talking, one BBQ party and following gaming session, some more talking and you're done.A very shallow experience, especially for the price. Hard to recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: this game is exceptional. it filled the KRZ shaped hole in my heart in a beautiful way that was still fresh and something of its own. the characters and their feelings are so real and there is just something cathartic about the experience as someone who is going through a similar transitional period in their life. the visuals are really cinematic and vibrant, and in many cases took my breath away.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: This is definitly not a game for everyone so the mixed reviews are probably warented. It's a lot of slow walking around a flat and having introspective thoughts about dreams, feers, hope and regrets as you look at stuff. While i don't think you have to be lgbtq+ to get something meaningful out of the game, there's also a lot of the chaos of beeing thrown out in adult life with no direction as you graduate, but the nonbinary experience is definitly a huge part of the game. I liked it for that, but it's also very short. I got it from Humble Bundle so I didn't really pay that much.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: I don't usually buy narrative games but I saw this nominated for the game awards and gave it a shot. The game is short and details the time a lot of young people go through at the end of university/college where you have no job and have to reluctantly go back home to live with your parents for a bit. The prospects you thought you were getting in university haven't materialised yet. You thought you were an adult but you are going back to being a kid again. The city around you won't stop changing. You lived in a dump. You love your friends but know that you might not see them again for a long time ...or ever. Everything is changing but it hasn't sunk in yet. The place you lived wasn't perfect but it was home. Your hobbies are incredibly dorky. Narrative wise, the game is good. You get a sense of two people orbiting each other and then having some final goodbyes with friends. Meeting their anxieties manifested as spirits. Having a final talk where the two realise this might be the end for them and blaming circumstance, their identity, themselves, etc. The ending is slightly more hopeful. Gameplay wise, it's slow. Moving around the apartment is a bit of a chore. A few of the superfluous details that you can look at could have been removed (e.g. saying the building is falling apart too much). It does the job but little else. The game art is simple and effective. Music is full of spacey drones and noodling. It fits the setting.All in all it was good and relatable. You get a real sense of the two people who made it had/have a deep affection for each other. I wasn't surprised that the in the credits was a message from one wishing that they could live together again one day (and good luck to them!) I guess the game wants to say something akin to 'change is a lot like loss' or 'we can't control the things that control us'.  It's a bit sad but that is how these things go.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: I know it currently has mixed reviews. But it truly was an amazing game. I really connected with both Bo and Ao and the struggles they were facing. A lot of the dialogue both inner thoughts and with people around them really hit me in such a real and relatable game. I wish that the game was longer. I wanted to see what happens, how their lives change, and if they had a happy ending. Short but really beautiful. Definitely something a person should play.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: is an artistic masterpiece in a style reminiscent of . Explore the difficulty of change and how we often stumble along the strange paths life sets out for us. Sprinkle in a little surreal/abstract design, and focus on the mundane magic that surrounds us, and you've got the recipe for a tremendous experience (and not to mention, a  soundtrack).
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: No Longer Home is a deep audio-visual experience, with a bonus of maybe petting cats. And the beautiful narrative content and themes that follow along with it. The visuals are stunning, the story is great. And damn it. As much as I love deep dialogue, the content here really resonated with me. Being queer, and a just graduated art student. And down to the details of owning a borrowed record player from my parents, and wanting to quit school foundation year. I love how the game builds up simple choices and a sense of direction. Being able to influence how the narrative is told, and feeling like my choices really followed through on the next sentence. That's not always a given in games, that the dialogue resonates as well as it did in No Longer Home!I have to say the most impressive feature- is being able to rotate the room. The simple 3D environment and shading works great, with a sort of abstract feel. Which further emphasizes the characters' feelings. The interactions and accompaning audio really drew my focus into the game. Music, audio design and simple effects works great as a part of the experience, and playing with headphones (as said in the game) is a must-have.Subtle environmental animations are great, with lighting and shading doing most of the work- Good move! And the objects of the environment perfectly conveys the lived in space, down to details of crooked cabinet. The london townhouse seems perfectly sized for this 2h little adventure. Best enjoyed in one sitting (I really stretched it out to 3h + a little break). My advice would be- don't rush through it. If you play this game, I invite you to stand still for a minute. sometime you're a bit into the game. When the audio-landscape is a bit bigger. And just notice the details in the environment. Close your eye for a second. And maybe you hear the neighburs, a cat purring, or city traffic.And a bit of nitpicking- simple ui, symbols and fonts fit nicely to the otherwise minimalistic and abstract styled game. During dialogue option it would however be nice to have a bit more visual difference between the selected text choice. As for animations, character walking isn't completely smoothless and was noticeable a couple of time, but with interesting dialogue I didn't focus too much on it. Also after seemingly stealing the mop and bucket- and putting it in the kitchen. It was still visible on the stairs the day after sleeping? Confused. And my last question I was left with- what happens to the cats when they move out?Thank you developers- for making this game. And delivering a great narrative.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: This game is deeply personal to its creators, but it also turned out to be personal to me. I, too, spent several months in London uncertain about my and my family future, trying to figure out life. Thus, the imagery, the struggle, and the themes felt familiar, dear, and nostalgic. This is not as much as a puzzle or an adventure game as it is a story that you somewhat control or rather follow. Don't expect much of a challenge, just flow with it and feel it. I am, certainly, biased, but I think that the authors achieved their goal with this game, even if none of us, or especially because none of us, knows what the goal was.
_childDocuments_.name: No Longer Home

_childDocuments_.review: No Longer Home is fine for what it is, but feels like it could have been so much more. The writing is really well done and the characters feel real and well thought out, and the game really hits that "life in your early 20s" vibe that's a crossroads of frustration and uncertainty. However, I really feel like it cuts itself off in its first act. What's here is great, but I was really interested to see how the relationships of these people developed or didn't develop post leaving the place they considered home. I don't think it's bad to leave your audience wanting more, but you have to balance it correctly so that people can fill in the gaps themselves or have been with the characters long enough to mentally piece together the next steps in their own head.If a year or two down the line the game received an update and there was even just another hour added as a sort of epilogue to what's presented, I'd say the game is definitely worth trying out, but in its current state it just leaves me wanting more.

_childDocuments_.review: I really liked the game, it left a bittersweet feeling in my heart. I enjoyed the experience to switch between the perspectives of Bo and Ao. It added depth to the story, as you see the shared apartment and their life together, as well as their own individual story and struggles through both sets of eyes. The whole atmosphere of the game was subtle but effective in the way of emphasizing themes of disorientation, belonging, and change or...well the end of something. One of the aspects I like most about the game is how the environment constantly shifts, almost like a dynamic theater stage. The transitions between locations and perspectives might be disorienting (maybe even unpleasant) for some, but I found it perfectly suited to the story's tone.The music/sound complements the atmosphere perfectly. It adds to the overall experience without overpowering the narrative. In this case less really is more. My first impulse was to write that this is a "cozy" game, but I would describe No Longer Home as more melancholic and contemplative. It’s a quiet, very slow and short reflective experience that might not be for everyone, but if you’re in the mood for something that speaks to the quieter, more introspective parts of life, this game is definitely worth your time.

_childDocuments_.review: My recommendation comes with some caveats. If you don't like slow games that are all about walking around and reading a bunch of text, this isn't for you. If you aren't nonbinary, depressed, anxious, poor, or a part of some minority, this isn't for you. That being said, I think this game does well at what it sets out to do, which is tell a deeply personal story and be relatable to certain kinds of people. As a nonbinary, depressed, anxious, poor person myself, I certainly related to Ao and Bo's struggles.

_childDocuments_.review: It made my breath falter and my heart wail. The game is way, way too pricey for what they have got to offer. The scene transition was smooth enough, yet the character movement animation was sloppy. There wasn't much to do. It's more of an interactive fiction than a game, and it's not that interactive, if you ask me.But, yes... the game made my breath falter and my heart wail. Perhaps the feelings the two protagonists went through were universal, or a cliché, you choose. Their doubt, uncertainty, and fear expressed through their dialogues were mutual among people of common experience in life transition. If you are a freshly graduated who are lost, then perhaps this game might give you a pause. Or a reflection. It won't guide you in any way. Yet, all in all, this game is a great reminder to you all who are lost that you are not lost alone, and in the right time, for some people, something like this is most needed. Please note that this alone outweighs my decision to rate this game down. Purchase with caution. P.S. personally, the ending was inexplicably impactful and perfectly encapsulated--or concluded, or accentuated?... words elude me--the whole  of the two. But I really wouldn't want to recommend a game just because of some favorite ending. So, really, purchase (or not) with caution.

_childDocuments_.review: is a semi-autobiographical narrative point-and-click adventure game features an incredibly compelling story about the process of letting go of the past and moving on.The game follows two non-binary roommates named Bo and Ao, who share a flat in London. They are both preparing to leave university after graduation and are struggling to find a job and find meaning in post-education life. The setting perfectly illustrates what life is like at the age of university, with the mess and clutter that kept me extremely nostalgic.The low poly art style is a wise fitting style for . Each character feels distinct, even if all of the people are faceless. The way colors and lighting are used is perfect, and each location feels incredibly unique. The way the rooms change when you rotate them is also a fascinating design choice to watch in action.Overall‚  is an authentic and offer unsettling story about the process of moving out and moving on. Of course, every player will take something different away from their experience playing, but it is an experience that I highly recommend. With beautiful designs, excellent characters, and a great soundtrack,  is well worth picking up.

_childDocuments_.review: NLH is a game made with a great deal of care by very talented people. There’s a lot to explore in it but that’s really on you, the player, to engage with. I’ve played through it three times now (only once on steam) and every time I discover something different I never noticed before, or find a different path to go down. I do think it trusts the player to want to engage with it and think about it and do the legwork. I think it’s probably easy to rush through and that’s where people get short playtimes but it’s a game worth relaxing into and making the effort to explore,For people that have struggled with depression or mental health issues NLH feels very familiar, it’s a story, snapshot, of these characters lives, in a small isolated area. It takes place mainly in one small flat and even when the setting changes during the ‘Between the Leaves’ section it’s not going outwards, it’s shifting inwards. Deeper. During the BBQ you can see the shadows of the clouds shift across the garden and you know that there must be a sun to cast them, but you can’t see it. The way you, the player, see the world is very fixed. Ths isometric view makes me feel like I'm observing the characters in a studious, detached way. For some reason that makes me feel closer to them though, we’re all our own voyeurs, and the sections where the camera sweeps in and gets really close feels all the more intimate for it. Almost frighteningly so. It happens when characters are talking about their feelings and fears and they feel vulnerable at that point. They were safer in that isometric view.Ultimately though, for all the things it makes me feel it’s a game about hope. A good one at that. The mental health issues hit closest to home for me but there’s a lot tied up in there about the violence of capitalism and borders, it’s not navel gazing. It’s in fact a very special journey, one that’s worth engaging with.

_childDocuments_.review: No Longer Home is an absolute amazement!It's a deeply melancholic exploration of loss and uncertainty. The game follows Ao and Bo for a day or two at a turning point in their lives, right after uni, before they know what is coming next. Set in South-West London, Ao is being forced to go back to Japan due to visa regulations, and Bo also needs to leave the apartment and thus their other flatmates due to rising cost of living and not having transitioned into the job world, yet. The game takes place in their flat and the backyard, as they reminisce about the time they have spent there, about the lives they have led, about their perceived failings; personally and as part of a demanding society with very unclear guidelines on how to successfully navigate one's life. Both are at an impasse, without any directions for their future, and struggling with their identity.If you've been in any kind of similar situation, this game hits home way too close. It plays out as a point-and-click exploration with lengthy choice-based conversations, leaving a lot of things unsaid and lingering as unspoken truths and ways the characters see themselves and the world around them. There are many other things that make this game excellent and hauntingly beautiful. The conversations and repeated exploration of the space of the flat itself are dispersed with stage-theatre and dream-like scene transitions that make this game truly shine. The immediate surrounding walls of their flat-and, one can imagine, their everyday boxed-in mindspaces-often fall away and dissociate to give way to their lingering and hauntingly beautiful melancholic imaginary worlds.Dissolvement of boundaries of identity is also a core part of the game in another way: instead of following and "playing" as one character throughout the game, the narrative dialogue choices and perspectives are frequently transgressed from one character to the next. You can often choose not what is said next, but who says it, which enables a symphonic arrangement of voices, but also let's you silence out entire characters if you choose to not engage with what they have to say. This multi-perspective narration reaches one of its heights when we're given the voice and perspective of a neighboring couple that the main characters only ever surmise about. This is also one of the moments where the stage-theatre qualities of the game are executed so flawlessly, literally shining the spotlight on these side characters, giving them their own moment in time and space to be filled with life, instead of just being an idea in the main characters's heads. These kind of techniques are rarely found in video games but are a testament to the maturity of the medium and art form that they are today.Last, but not least-at all-is the music and sound design. The game suggests upfront to use headphones while playing, and I absolutely have to agree with that. The meandering conversations, the exploration of space, the scene transitions are heightened to an immersive experience I had not expected with a point-and-click exploration game. Getting into these characters's heads and imaginary spaces is an experience you want to shut out your own surroundings for. The intimacy and imaginary worlds that are opened up through that are just astounding.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a strange case. I moved multiple times, watched flat shares break apart, said goodbye to people I lived with for years, experienced anxiety about what to become in life, uncertainty about choices I had made, felt the pressure of parental expectations, had periods of existential doubt, consider Kentucky Route Zero one of the best games of all time, in short, I've made many experiences that should make me resonate with this game.But I didn't resonate with it. Not at all.I played it through one evening and found nothing: No memorable characters, no relatable writing, no emotions that mirrored my own. It's just puppets rambling that passes by, with you a spectator watching from outside and finding nothing to latch onto. Normally I'd be the first to defend this kind of game against people demanding conflict, involving gameplay, pacing and character arcs, but I won't do so, because I feel like the game simply failed at what it set out to do: Make a phase of growing-up with all its turmoil and uncertainty relatable.

_childDocuments_.review: No Longer Home is a semi-autobiographical game by the Humble grove team. The game is about two recent graduates Ao and Bo saying goodbye to the home they shared throughout their studies.Felt I could relate to a lot of the themes explored from being a recent graduate myself and also nonbinary, having difficulty finding a place in the world. It’s one of those stories that you need to hear, to be reminded that you are not alone in your experiences or situation. The art style uses a lot of geometric shapes, scenes tend to unravel then disperse with many shapes to make up the building blocks of the world. We are given an aerial view of the house, as if it were a doll house and we the player are moving the characters around, looking through the house from different perspectives. Despite there being a lot of motion in the way the player can rotate the house, move the two characters and interact with objects or other characters. There is a stillness to the game, this sensation that time stops when you are alone as the character, moving through each room and discovering secrets in the house. And time only starts moving again when you interact with other characters or move onto the next sequence. It reminds me of what it is like to dissociate and to lose perception of time. You get so caught up in your own isolation that you forget about your environment and the world around you. We don’t really see the world outside of the house apart from a brief section of the street. The only instance is the sequence where the characters are playing a choose-your-own-adventure game and it takes them through a forest. I guess to create this impression that this place is the most familiar to them and what feels like home out of the rest of this world. It feels more like a memory in a sense to capture that autobiographical image, that this location is the scope of the memory and we are unable to leave it as we will be met with an endless void that exists outside the house.The music as recommended goes in par with the game, it is very dreamy and suits the atmosphere created. It can feel both soothing and isolating, lurking in the background while you explore. Instead of voice acting, there is a sort of “du-du” sound, to mimic the typing sound when pressing keys on a keyboard. As if someone is typing up a journal entry while reflecting back on these memories, you can notice this in how the text in the speech bubbles gradually appears with “du-du” sound for every section of text. Also there is a click sound every time the player clicks on a particular object to continue this effect. Every time the player rotates the room there is a sort of “sifting through boxes” sound, as if the narrator (or us) is trying to remember specific details in the room. I really enjoyed this game, I played through it in the one sitting after I came back from holiday. It was a nice change of pace from the fast-paced action heavy games I was playing at the time. Definitely would recommend to anyone going through similar experiences with their identity or currently dealing with burnout. It was nice to have nonbinary protagonists for a change, I feel it has been long overdue. I hope to see more games of this genre, you don’t really see too many semi-autobiographical games on the market.

_childDocuments_.review: No Longer Home is a small-scale indie point-and-click game, where you switch roles between two students who will soon be graduating from university and are faced with employment and relocation issues, as well as relationship struggles.It's also grossly overpriced for the quality and length of the game.Additionally, it's loaded with insufferable, angst-ridden twaddle masquerading as deep, meaningful dialogue.Positives: It didn't take too long to complete it....but given how generally slow the game felt and how irritated I became with the navel gazing, head-up-arse dialogue, it felt twice as long.  Oh and the graphics are moderately decent to look at in a low-poly way.Meh:  The controls are clunky and the camera doesn't always let you see what you want, resulting in some obscured environments and difficulty getting the right view of clickable objects.  The movement of the characters is also glacially slow.....almost as slow as the pace of the game/dialogue.Negatives:  Did you ever find the character of Holden Caulfield a bit of an annoying, whinging prat?  Did you think that maybe, just maybe, the play Hamlet should have been shortened by at least an act and two or three soliloquies because of how the character just constantly goes on and on about the futility of his existence and whether he should end it all (over and over and over)?  Well, then don't even dream of getting this “game” which is filled to the miserable brim with two characters who do nothing but bemoan their academic existence, and whether they've made the right choices at university, and what they'll do afterwards, and whether they've wasted their time and their parents' time by taking these courses, and on and on and on and on, and NONE of it is interesting or compelling, it's just wank!Totally not recommended, and at 15 USD for this boring, glacially paced excuse for woe-is-me existential ennui, it is not reasonably priced (I got it in a bundle for about three or four bucks, and at that price, if you are someone with a stronger stomach for characters with no emotional spine whatsoever, then it might, MIGHT be worth it).

_childDocuments_.review: It's simple: this is Cultural Marxism disguised as a video game. For reference, I gave this a chance, and finished the game with several achievements. Let's start with the good, because credit is due where credit is due:- the moving geometry designs are really well executed.- the music and sound effect are spot on. Little details here and there give the game its charm.- the game won't make use of it, but supports ultra wide screen (ie, it will boot and run at 21:9 on a 32:9 screen).Now for the bad.- None of the characters in the game are engaging if you are the kind of person who works for a living. You know, if you're part of the working class, or god forbid, if you are 'priviledged like a doctor or a nurse' (both of whom receive scathing commentary from the protagonists). Literally hunchbacked, walking as if they were 80, they spend their time whining about how their (actually privileged) life of drinking and playing video games is boring, aimless. They have no dreams whatsoever. Going to uni in Japan (I wish I ever had the money to do that) paid by mum and dad feels to them like a death sentence. - You can control their dialog but nothing can exit the themes of 'gentrification', 'capitalism' and noting that 'there was a marxist era (??) but that led to "some bickering". Let me help you out honey,  has a list of the millions dead as what you describe as 'bickering'. - Everyone in the game is 'non binary' and visually represented as such. Pronouns are strictly VERBOTEN. In fact, one of the characters laments 'how their Korean parents don't know how to use their pronouns'. Yeah the same Korean parents who paid for your fancy Japanese university and travels to the UK so you can pursue education in 'music' and 'arts' ??? Oh boy do I pitty the parents to have created such offspring.- Finally, as an ultimate affront to common sense, the very same characters benefiting from open borders and lax visa policies forewarn the players of seemingly dreadful immigration laws. Thing is, I AM a first generation immigrant to the UK. My kids are brown and 2nd generation immigrants. I did research if at the time of the game release there were any rumors of such laws. There was none. There are none today, in fact, immigration to the UK is at an all time high, and my family benefited from this directly, complete with a life saving intervention from the NHS to my (foreign) grandfather which cost him nothing. That's the system they hate. Finally, and quite hilariously, the way the character speak in this game is as if it had been written by Americans - no slang such as 'quid' instead of 'pound' is used. I never said this about a video game but it's utterly tone deaf, self pitying, self-loathing, divisive and probably the only video game sanctioned by ANTIFA. The only 'good guys' in the game are the workers briefly depicted building crossrail from under these lazy pseudo-intellectuals too busy to enjoy the smell of each other farts to have ONE decent idea of what to do with their miserable lifes. Absolutely pathetic. And if you hate capitalism so much, please tell me why you charge for this game? I'd like my 7.51 pound back please, I guess I can't, can't I? Also, why release it on STEAM? Surely by your standards STEAM is evil. Funny how that works hey? Pathetic - 0/10.

_childDocuments_.review: The same day I played through most of this I also played through another short narrative game about being a twenty something insecure about the future and nostalgic about the recent past-and this was a much smoother and better designed experience.  Obviously influenced by Kentucky Route Zero, no bad thing thing since that is a great game, you play as two protagonists as they have conversations, get lost in their own thoughts, have surreal encounters, and wander through their apartment that they will be forced to vacate soon. The only downside to the game is that in two hours it did get repetitive (when you aren't having longer conversations with someone, you basically trudge through the same six rooms looking for flavor text).  The upside is that I did feel like I knew the characters as distinct people by the end of the game, not just generic genderqueer narcissistic art students which they could have easily come off as if the writing wasn't as good. I don't know how often this particular moment of life needs to be gamified, but I am glad these developers used their life experiences as inspiration for this game.

_childDocuments_.review: No Longer Home wears its inspiration on its sleeve, having a scene from the opening of Kentucky Route Zero on its protagonist's computer screen at one point. It bears some resemblance to KRZ in its dialogue system and set design, but taking place over a much shorter time-span and much smaller space. This is a nice little slice of life game about a couple of recent college grads about to move onto the next stage of their lives. Taking place the day before the big move, it deals with a lot of the stresses and anxieties that come with not knowing what comes next in life, how your relationships might change, what personal and societal expectations there are for your future, and how the market forces of capitalism muddy the waters even further. While the visual elements are steeped in magical realism, the semi-auto-biographical nature of its writing gives the story a very personal feeling that lets you really linger in this moment of the characters lives. It would have been nice if it had more time to really delve deeper into some of the topics it brings up, but for an exploration of a small moment in life, I enjoyed the brief time I spent here.

_childDocuments_.review: Playing out like a stage play amid a floating, cosmic backdrop, No Longer Home elegantly wrestles with one’s place in the world, or indeed the universe, asking to what extent any of it might matter at all. From Cel Davison and Hana Lee, No Longer Home is a semi-autobiographical point and click story title that charts the anxiety of stepping out of university and into the uncertain wildland beyond where many of us are doomed to be lost. Their character surrogates, Ao and Bo, are in the very last days of university life with the past 4 years of their life seeming a fleeting breeze gone by, and leaving them now directionless and without opportunity. You take partial control over their story, choosing their conversation pieces, but ultimately this story is one that is doomed to slide away from you as it does the characters. With wonderful art direction and deft writing No Longer Home manages to pack itself full with questions and ideas in a little over 2 hours. On the face of it this point and click game in the vein of Kentucky Route Zero might seem straightforward, but there is plenty to be gleaned from this uncomfortable, often otherworldly, journey. _childDocuments_.review: "It feels like it's all rigged against us."Quarter life crises, post-graduation ennui, being non-binary, art students, the melancholy of moving out, expectations, depression, guilt, self-doubt, South London, and a pinch of magical realism are bundled in just 2 hours by Humble Grove (Cel Davison, Hana Lee, Adrienne Lombardo), backed by a nostalgic bittersweet score by Eli Rainsberry and Derek Daley. The game starts with a prelude at Friary Road in Peckham, before they move to Camberwell. Two characters sitting in chairs, silhouetted, then are lit up (much like a stage play) as the camera descends from the stars to the ground. The camera then rotates and objects materialise into existence, which is a cool visual trick that never stops getting old and fits with the magical realism. Ao and Bo, sitting in chairs reflecting on university, describing non-binary identity, parental expectations, debt, and figuring out what things you want to do. The camera pans up to the stars as they discuss extraterrestrial life and parallel universes. Then we come back down and the building comes into view, with an effect much like when stagehands assemble a set in real-time. You as the player can choose Ao and Bo's dialogue in a similar manner to Kentucky Route Zero, along with all the aesthetic choices that pay homage to it (and the developers openly acknowledge and reference throughout). This freewheeling, longshot conversation goes for ten minutes until the second game-length No Longer Home chapter starts.No Longer Home plays like a traditional point-and-click adventure with an isometric perspective where you point to somewhere and your character moves. There are no puzzles here other than the mental puzzle of how to deal with moving on and drifting apart. You can rotate the environment around and much like Fez, some things become more visible and can be interacted with. One neat little quality-of-life addition for this genre is the game automatically knows if you click an area of the screen close enough to the playable character, they will walk (the pointer becomes a plant sprouting up which is very cute) and if you click further away they will automatically know to jog. Before in games like these, you’d have to double click to make them run or press another button. Like mentioned before, there is branching dialogue but it’s not to give you different endings, it’s just to add flavour to the characters and give players some agency in how they define the protagonists (again much like KR0). Unlike other adventure games where you’re travelling to different locations, the story is specifically based in and outside the apartment up to a backyard, so these are intimate spaces being explored. Nonetheless, things and layouts change even in the same rooms such as one tiny room opposite the bedrooms, which lends to the magical realism. There is even a game within a game when all the protagonists’ friends hang out one last time to sit down and play Among The Leaves, a text adventure game where the branching dialogue options are the different characters’ dialogues you can choose from. There are some missable scenes here based on the choices, like I visited a weird underground school but I didn’t come across a Japanese style temple with a lanky creature hanging around. The relationship between Bo and Ao is quite deep and relevant, especially to anyone who’s been through moving house, not sure what they want to do after education, career and financial anxiety, or how to deal with their gender expression (“existing as praxis”) and things in their head. They started off as hesitant to talk to each other, making assumptions one was cooler than the other or not knowing how to be social, but then eventually developed to be able to talk about their own issues. The discussions are often socially relevant and regularly humorous, such as gentrification in London, but never didactic and the dialogue feels authentic to two progressive characters trying to make it out in a capitalist reality. Bo is the more pragmatic of the two but there’s a lot of self-doubt there, and Ao is the more depressed one who can’t handle the expectations of being from a creative family and themselves not amounting to be a very productive artist. There is an initial blame towards others, such as them talking about how parental expectations and the traditional life model messing them up (study->work->family), but they are later able to take responsibility for their own lack of motivation and career aimlessness. However, they both are able to pick each other up when the other one is down on themselves, which goes to show it’s easier to support others more than ourselves. Just as both characters had a long conversation at the start of the game, so does the game beautifully bookend with a 15-minute vulnerable and emotional conversation in bed, and it’s the first time we get to see Ao with their hair down literally and figuratively. For Humble Grove’s first game, the storytelling on display is exceptional. There is an existential, dreamlike mundanity to the game’s atmosphere where these real-life worries about saying goodbye to others and moving out are made extraordinary. The length of scenes being quite short and divergents with other characters goes along with the theme of transient moments, much like in a Richard Linklater film. Self-doubt and self-loathing can manifest as supernatural creatures that you confront in the tiny room. In general, there is an empathic air to the mental health issues explored even with magical realist aspects on top, and that’s quite hard to pull off especially in a videogame without feeling like it’s trivialising. Neglect of the house is represented by the dying plants everywhere and the regret the protagonists have for not taking care of them enough, but as mentioned before, there is hope with the pointer becoming a growing plant animation wherever you click on the screen and Ao and Bo wanting to do better. The cinematography is excellent. A friend leaving the party early helps drift the camera from the BBQ party conversation to the underground train and discussions happen about a possible underground society. There are some cool quirks to the sound design, which is phenomenal overall, such as one scene where Bo talks to a goat-like creature, Lu, about past jam sessions and music (Lu refers to Bo as Edith which confuses them) whose dialogue sound effects are of a bass guitar and if the environment is rotated, it’s a record scratch. The magical and social realism in particular, calls to my mind the work of Apichatpong Weeresethakul. Easily one of my 2021 GOTY contenders for its reflective, dreamlike, and punk quality and depth of storytelling with quite resonant themes and contemporary concerns. For any fans of Kentucky Route Zero, arthouse filmmakers, or just people who appreciate art about mental health issues and quarter life crises in a post-recession world of uncertainty, this is a must play.

_childDocuments_.review: Gentle, sad, and deeply introspective. This is a bittersweet piece of semi-autobiography, and honestly if that doesn't sound your bag then it almost certainly won't be for you. For me, though, spending 90 minutes exploring the relationship and inner thoughts of two people (Ao and Bo) as they come to the end of sharing a home was an affecting experience. A simple, sweet look into the minds of two people going through an everyday, but life-impacting upheaval, No Longer Home offers a rare approach to interactive fiction: no bombast, no excitement, just quiet drama and emotion. It helped me reflect on myself and my own life; seeing aspects of my personality brought to the surface in both Ao and Bo was actually a little startling; it's relatively rare to see myself — particularly the more 'internal' aspects of my personality — reflected in any media, let alone interactive fiction. All in all, this was a moving experience, and I'm glad to have played it.PS - a shout out to the game's aesthetic, as well. The simple, affecting writing is amply supported by a beautiful art style and perfectly matched minimalist soundtrack; the whole thing is just a pleasure to experience.

name: Star Renegades
detailed_description: RESIST. RECLAIM. REVIVE. REPEAT. A service robot named J5T-1N has arrived in your dimension to warn of impending doom from an overwhelming force known as the Imperium. Fight for survival across a procedurally generated and emergent mission-based campaign through reactive, tactical turn-based battle system that emphasizes interrupts and counters. Standing in your way is an intelligent Adversary system with enemy officers that evolve and move up in the ranks. As your band of heroes fall in the fight against invading Imperium and hope is all but lost, J5T-1N must be sent to the next dimension with everything you’ve learned to give the next group of heroes a chance to prevail. Each dimension, and each playthrough is unique, challenging, and never the same. Outwit your foes with interrupts, counters, and combos in our fast-paced Reactive Time Battle System Survive the relentless onslaught of an Intelligent Adversary system that generates unique enemies and bosses that evolve as you play Unlock dozens of alternate characters as your surviving squad members form bonds and create progeny Battle your way into the heart of the Empire as our Rebellion Engine creates a unique experience with each playthrough via emergent gameplay and events, procedurally generated missions, shifting priorities, evolving enemies, and tons of equipment/upgrades for your squad

_childDocuments_.review: Basically, this game starts off feeling like a kinda mean RPG that will kill you, and eventually evolves into its true form as a rpg-inspired puzzle game.  The basic puzzle is to combine all your characters moves to stagger enemies off the timeline and/or kill them before they do damage beyond your shields and start taking chunks out of your much harder to heal health pools.  There are a large number of different characters, and every single one of them is capable of contributing a meaningful way - the balance is great.  There are different strategies that work - tanking/redirecting, healing, and pure stagger, as long as you have enough damage on top of the rest of the build to actually finish off the enemies before you run out of shields.there's a little exploration game, where you decide your specific encounters, and a camping minigame to heal/buff/bond, but the vast majority of the time you are fighting very challenging combats.  The reason the game feels so mean when you just start playing is that there aren't trash mobs.  There's no grinding.  Every enemy has the capability of doing some real damage or even defeating your entire team, ending that run.  The common roguelike expectation of endless trash then some randomly generated elite that 1-shots you is not enforced here.  Every fight feels like you have a chance and if you're careful enough, you could win (well, maaybe not the final boss sometimes if it gets the extra round of summons off.  ugh).  Take the fights slowly and carefully, and never dismiss a fight just because it doesn't seem like that big of a deal, and you can get some real fun out of it.  I did have to use a wiki for the progeny unlocks, though.Anyway, thumbs up.  Great puzzley/tactical gameplay that gives a good thoughtful challenge.  Just dig in and have some fun!

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game as a turn based RPG Rouge Lite is exactly the type of game I've been wanting to play. The time line mechanic is cool, I like the games loot system, item slots etc, and the camp fire mechanic is cool. The Art is fine, becomes an issue later in the game when you are fighting a lot of enemies everything starts to blend together, and that brings us to the biggest issue with the game, the UI and controls. Navigating menus is a chore it's a pain to find the information you're looking for when you want it. The tool tips when they exist aren't great. It can be difficult to click on the enemy you want to attack sometimes, and if you miss click with your final hero it's locked in... feels pretty bad.All in all the game just isn't enjoyable to play due to the UI and controls
