_childDocuments_.review: First, I must disclose I was given this game for free with the purpose of reviewing Undermine.This is a first impressions review.TLDR: If you like roguelikes/roguelites and want something that can be equally (and sometimes more) unforgiving as it can be generous with a sprinkle of humour then this game is for you.Now the first thing I have to mention is the art style, it's great! I love it, it looks a bit dated at first but once you play then you really start to notice how it definitely isn't. They type of art style matches the game perfectly, and is very reminiscent of Neon Abyss! The game starts off relatively slow and progression is also quite slow, however this picks up quite quickly. I did find that for new players this was more unforgiving than most, there isn't much in the way of tutorials to explain how to get through specific blockades or where to find specific items for quests, essentially it does not hold your hand. You also lose gold you find to pilfers quite frequently and whilst this can be annoying you will get used to stopping them. A lot of gold is also lost when you die, and the more gold you have the more you lose. With the gold you do return with there are vendors that allow you to upgrade your health, damage, throw range and upgrades to reduce the amount of gold lost upon death. There are also relics that you can craft however I've noticed even these can be pilfered! Something I massively disagree with, why would there be slimes above the dungeons that steal items you've just crafted after saving up your thorium?! Only for that blueprint to also disappear after crafting. Nonetheless the game keeps slowly unlocking things and you keep getting further and further through the levels whilst sometimes not realising you're getting further and further each time, whether this is due to skill increasing or upgrades, I'm unsure of at this point.This game is not for the faint-hearted, it is difficult and it is unforgiving, but that's what roguelikes are all about right?

_childDocuments_.review: I thought I had found a gem, but I'm really disappointed...When I read about random relics I thought Binding of Isaac, Risk of Rain 1&2, Slay the Spire, Dead Cells, so it was obviously going to be SUPER fun, but no...I'm still rating it positively cause I know it will get better and I just don't want to be negative, but I really wish devs would go in a different design direction.Some of the problems, imo:- You get 4 relics maximum until the first boss (never beat him so don't know after) and they are almost ALL super bad:"Modifying bombs"? Useless. We can't afford to use them for anything else than walls. "More damage at high health"? Almost insignificant. I read damage boosts calculations have been changed, but in terms of relics it doesn't feel impactful."More gold"? We lose so much when dying that it's decent (even after buying the "lose less gold when dying") but still doesn't give my character anything."When gold falls it burns"? What even in the world is that?? How is it going to help me once in front of the boss?? I wanted something like "throw 2 pickaxes", "every swing attacks 2 times", "attacks poison enemies" or some other things that change the gameplay and make a real effect on the player! I read devs talking about "builds" when 1) we don't have ANY control over it, so not really a build and 2) I've NEVER had any relics synergize together. The videos show relics interacting together but it must be in endgame or something cause it never happened to me. I always get stuff like "more gold", "more damage per key", "bombs make fire", "more life"...The best one I found so far was "sometimes creates electricity when hitting", and it doesn't even proc consistently enough for me to feel good about it...Entire runs feel bad and relics are not engaging. We need way more, and way better ones! Devs may want to avoid the "Risk of Rain 2" effect where you get so many relics that you get completely OP (and even like that, it's so well made that it feels super powerful and fun, but you can still die easily) but they should find a middle ground between this and what we have atm...- The consistent freaking slimes appearing when you pop gold are completely useless and having to rush every single time to get my gold ISN'T fun! It simply isn't. The "mini game" doesn't even bring anything to the table. Why? I hate them. SO MUCH.- The controls are SUPER clunky...How am I not able to swing at every direction? Wanting a difficult game is okay, adding false difficulty isn't. Like when you're walking a liiiiiittle bit on the side of a bridge you fall?? Having to always turn around to hit instead of just hitting behind the character and having him turn around?? I play with a controller, and I tried M&K to see if it was better but even the "mouse aim" wasn't good either.- Everything in the hub is way too expensive, and doesn't improve the character enough. I get the point of having to do multiple runs, and I LOVE games like that, but it's just infuriating when I come back from a run and get "more swing damage" but it almost doesn't change anything...Devs should take a look at "Heroes of Hammerwatch" and its hub. When you come back you're so happy cause you buy meaningful improvements for your next runs. Every character empowers the next one so you always want to do another run to go further.- Curses? When you don't even have enough relics and meaningful ones enough too?? Really?! "I lost max health, yaaaaay"...- The first boss is stupidly strong. Can't tell for the others cause I can't beat him...Having to learn patterns is perfectly fine, but having such a clunky character AND having no useful relics AND having to deal with so much damage with a simple pickaxe doing 30 damage a swing isn't, and it's not fun either...I read about the update, and really wanted to check it out, but it appears I'd still need like 10-20 runs to be able to beat the first boss (unless I get good relics...) and it's just not fun anymore. I'll try another time maybe, and hope others may still have fun with the game! I'm having less fun than frustration, and it's the perfect sign to know when you need to stop.

_childDocuments_.name: UnderMine

_childDocuments_.review: Sure, it's probably worth 15 bucks.  It's basically a competent binding of isaac style roguelike.Things that are different from BoI:-melee focus, and you can throw your melee weapon like a boomerang, instead of always ranged attacks.-Progression is not just unlocked options (which are unlocked by crafting them, not just by discovery), but base stat increases between runs-expanded use of environmental effects (more than just those jumping things changing to fire - Undermine also has slimes that can become tar, then fire, or whatever, or throwing your pick through a brazier lights the pick on fire or lights the brazier if the pick is already on fire and the brazier is not)There are a few areas that it could improve, so if you are concerned about these, either wait or skip this one - there are a ton of great options in this genre:-has random relics, but they aren't even a little bit close to the level of crazy combos that you'd see in Isaac, at least so far as I've seen in the first 2 hours.  They're all pretty equivalent, and none make you feel powerful, just very minorly buffed (e.g. do 30 damage instead of 28).  There are a few slightly more interesting ones that offer utility (duplicating money or food, ignoring oil and leaving oil drops when you jump, bouncing ranged attack - which only works with launching, not when returning, making it feel mediocre), but even at their best, relics feel supplemental, not game defining.  And in any given run, I've never found more than 1 interesting utility relic.   But maybe I just haven't seen the Brimstone or Dr. Fetus style uber-relics yet.  But more likely, if crazy relics exist at all, they're blueprints that you'll need to complete tons of the game before they become available.-Mouse aiming support seems pretty bad at launch.  I'd recommend playing with a controller or keyboard only for now at least.  It seems like the mouse aiming might only work if you aren't moving or something?  I dunno, but I clicked enemies, but swung in completely different directions, so I ditched the mouse after like 2 rooms.-bosses feel.. grindy.  I only faced the first one so far, but I never felt like "oh, I can probably do this!"... It was "oh, I guess I need to go get more upgrades, because I can't get this thing below half HP, even if I stay alive for 5 minutes".  It felt like I needed to do like 30+ runs of the first 5 levels before I would even have a chance at defeating the first boss (I'm bad at games).  So yeah, if you're bad at games like me, this game could get to be a serious grindfest, and you might never see the later content, depending on when the upgrades cap.Still, that said, the 2 hours I've played so far have been fun enough to make me want to play it some more, so it's probably worth the asking price if you like the genre.
_childDocuments_.name: UnderMine

_childDocuments_.review: Heigh-ho! Heigh-ho! It's off to die we go!Check out my video if you want to see gameplay. UnderMine is what would happen if The Legend of Zelda - Link's Awakening was a roguelike with simplified puzzles and a boomerang that could deal damage. You play as a revolving door of miners collecting gold and treasure until they die, at which point the door turns, another walks in, and only you and the game counter are aware of how many miners have already died. Each new miner takes half of the previous miner's gold and moves on with any upgrades unlocked, but each will discover new relics as they dive into the mine. The combination makes for a good variety of what you've paid to unlock along with what you stumble across. You'll also rescue townspeople as you dive deeper, so the sense of progression is ever-present.Normally I would include some negatives in my review, but really my only complaint is that it didn't capture me as much as it's captured others. Which is a shame, because having a boomerang that deals damage felt amazing, especially when I found a relic that splits it into three boomerangs. Er, thrown boomerang pickaxes. Same thing, really. So pick up UnderMine. Odds are either you or someone you know will enjoy it.

_childDocuments_.review: Tldr: Good Rogue Lite with great quality of life fixes for common problems with the genre with meh to memorable characters throughout. 10/10Full review: Undermine is a Rogue Lite similar to enter the gungeon (Imo). Where you delve into a mineshaft to earn a profit, when you are forceably recruited by a wizard. And told to solve some problems and bring him back stuff. Each run you'll encounter various things that will hinder or help you in ways you might not think about normally. There is often more than one solution to a problem. And the game is very generous with items. Most of them very useful. And even the ones that aren't as great there's very little reason NOT to have them.Each time you die you're simply the next peasant in line to earn a small fortune. Who you were is gone. But your permeate upgrades carry over. (And a portion of your gold) These can be bought from people you rescue in the mines. Things like increased max health, throw range. And much more. (Also if you don't like your Peasant there's a mirror in the wizard's room you can use to change. It's free so use till you get someone you like it's cosmetic only though)The gameplay is challenging and the jumping can feel way to floaty at times but you'll get the hang of it. For attacks you have a pickaxe you can throw for minor damage and it will always come back to you regardless of what's in between. But it can't go through certain obstacles. But it can catch things like fire which can be used to light other torches to solve puzzles. Or a short ranged swing that does much more damage but can't be used for puzzle solving and is generally a lot riskier. Also if an explosion goes off in a room and doesn't open a secret entrance. There will be yellow sparkles revealing where one IS if you have a spare bomb.Pros: Fun challenging gameplay that rewards exploration and trying random things. Lots of replayability with every run being different and with so many items you're bound to find something that works for you.Cons: Rooms can be just a little bit of a pain at times. Some have minefields that can trigger chain reactions that can be difficult to avoid. Picking up healing foods is automatic even if you're at full health by default so make sure you turn this off otherwise just be careful not to waste them. Pilfers these little slime creatures spawn whenever there's piece of gold on the ground. And they will try to steal it if you don't bat them away. (They are adorable though so it's not so bad) Highly advise taking care of enemies and traps BEFORE mining any gold But some drop bombs which if you're lucky can bust open a secret wall or rock and reveal useful things. _childDocuments_.review: Though I currently have 13 hours logged, probably about 6 of those are actually idle time.The game starts off fun enough, but it doesn't hold up as you progress. The overall premise is somewhat dark, as every character you play inevitably dies — there's no returning from the dungeon. The familiar carries back some portion of your gold, which you can then use to unlock upgrades. However, this can become a slog in certain areas; since you can't control what powers you go into the dungeon with (everything is randomized), you can't plan a strategy until you're already in the room, making it difficult to judge preparations. Even when unlocking items, you can't select them on future runs -- you have to run into them randomly. This can lead to a cycle of entering the dungeon, mining gold as much as possible, then dying without actually progressing in the game, sometimes without even getting a chance to use the item you just invested in.There are a lot of neat environmental variables, but that's not enough for me to recommend this particular game.

I wasn't expecting the difficulty to ramp up so quickly before you have a chance to get upgrades. The minions running around the first few levels are very easy to defeat, and then the first boss is such a jump up in difficulty that I can't get past it. I'm assuming I'm not the target market for this game. But if you are like me and interested in it because of the cute art and mining premise, just know going in that this is a very skill-based game with absolutely no learning curve or difficulty setting. _childDocuments_.review: There's not a "mixed review" option, but the game is fun, it's well polished, it's not bad, it's just another game rogue-like following this tired formula where at the end of a run the items might make you 10-30% stronger and can be ignored for the most part. And for that reason, it will get the brunt of my complaints on where this genre has been heading in general.The developer intends for you to find fun in your motor skills subconsciously adapting to the boss's attack patterns, knowing if they introduced an item that gave you any real advantage at all it would let you bypass this  game-play mechanic. As a result the developers keep a tight lock-down on how "fun" an item is allowed to be. This is all by design, no mistakes.Common red flag for these games: if there's a "level skip" option, it means it's viable to skip floors, and power-ups. But you shouldn't  to skip power-ups, ideally the later floors should be  on the power-ups you get. Otherwise, there's no weight to the items. I find myself skipping shops and power-up rooms because I just didn't care, with virtually no impact on how far I got in the dungeon before dying to an enemy who's attack patterns are unknown, leaving behind a game that is "just OK". No dopamine hits from finding that insanely broken item, just a slow grind in a pretty linear basic game.

_childDocuments_.review: After playing for a while and giving this game chance after chance after chance, I just can't recommend it.But before I get into the review, I will mention that I am a completitionist. Always looking for secrets, always looking to complete the loogbook/Bestiary/unlock every item. Always trying to get all of the achievements, or at least as many as I can. So that said, I'm gonna get into it.It's a long review, so TL;DR at the endCONS:1.) First of all, game can be a grindy to get into. You can have quite a slow start. You are very underpowered, and everything is very crazy and damaging. From a tiny little fly that hits you with one projectile that deals 20 damage, or a bat that flies erratically and has decent range with the attack that does 30 damage, it can get overwhelming. Considering you basically never get health drops naturally, and the usual health item you get heals you for 20, it can get difficult.It wouldn't be so bad however, if the rooms weren't literally filled to the brim with these enemies that are never in sync. You can enter one room and your run is just done. I do not find the enemies -that- difficult anymore, but there are rooms that still end my runs if I'm playing with various challenges enabled (which I will get into later)You also need to collect gold. Which I really liked at the start. But your gold can get taken away if it's on the ground. After a while it gets annoying.You also need that gold for the items you want to buy in the shop during your run, but you also need the gold to buy permanent upgrades in the lobby area. And it makes the game EXTREMELY grindy at the start. You will never have a good run in the beginning because you will probably be saving up for the perma upgrade, where you wont even be able to afford 2 keyes that you need for two rooms that are locked.Now, I don't have issue with grinding. I love grinding. But even for me it was a bit on a tedious side at the start, so I'm putting it into negative, just because I know grinding isn't something people look forward to on average.2.) The enemy design and the enemy "interaction" is quite badAttacks are poorly telegraphed, with basically instant attack as well. Some enemies can be very hard to read and very unpredictable. And the attack/movement pattern and enemy ability just feels cheap at times. The hitboxes are absolutely horrendous though. There are some enemies that begin their attack and damage you before they actually finish their previous attack or start the new one. There is a berserking enemy "Bobo" who runs, then slams into the wall and slams his fist into the ground 3 times. You can be above him hitting him with your pickaxe, but he will suddenly hit you even if he didn't start his charge animation yet and is still in the animation of slamming his fists into the ground3.) Secrets are very convoluted. There are a lot that you can figure out on your own, but there are a lot of them where you just have to go look it up on the wiki. Which is not a big deal if you don't care, but this game is about exploring, unlocking new stuff, getting new items and all that, so having very confusing secrets with specific things you need to do, without having any hints in the game, really takes away from it4.) Meta game is too strong. Basically, if you don't make a ranged build, you will have 10x harder time getting through the game. Melee does more damage, but it's risky. especially early in your save file. Because it doesn't do enough to kill the enemies fast, so you just put yourself in danger of stupid enemies and wonky hitboxes. Later on in your save file you can destroy enemies with melee, but you can do so with range as well, from safety.And basically, whenever I had a melee build, I saw no reason not to use range, or not to go for range. I never see a benefit, although I use melee build to make the game a bit more engaging. There are also very good ranged items you can get, while melee items are "okay" in general, not really comparable with the items for the ranged build.So there is literally no reason for you to go melee if you have even a slightest choice5.) Bosses are BAD.There are 2 alright bosses (just looking at the base design), but most are just... no. I am used to them now so I don't really struggle, but I still think the design from the gameplay point is horrendous. And there is one boss I still despise and struggle with at times and it gets the spot on top 3 of the worst bosses in games I have played. They can be so tedious to fight. They can chunk your health but tank your damage, some spawning ads constantly, some having overlapping attacks, some just having undodgeable attacks. Oh, did I mention BROKEN HITBOXES??6.) The "challenge" I previously mentioned. Now, these are mostly optional. But with a game like this, you want to get your unlocks. And you might be a completitionist like me as well.The extra challenges are unbalanced and even grindierLets start from a normal game progression. Each time you defeat all 5 bosses in ONE RUN you get a new difficulty modifier, whilst before you could skip bosses and come back to them later. Now you need to kill all 5 bosses in one run (there are 6 bosses in total), which makes the game even more repetitive. If you want to get the difficulty modifier, you are forced to kill every boss in one run now. But okay, whatever! Game gets easy after a while so having a natural difficulty modifier is good, even though you're forced to get it one way now. But it gets insane after a while. The bosses get even tankier and can now 2 hit kill you, with their attacks being even faster and overlapping even more than before.-----OthermineOthermine is the game's completely roguelike mode. No perma upgrades. You start fresh, you die, and you repeat. it's very slow, it's very grindy, it's uninspired. The game forces you to take curses as well (negative modifiers) which I just hate. There is also a challenge in Othermine where you need to take the item that gives you a major curse every single floor that you can't remove. And those major curses can be very bad on their own. But now, by the end, you'll have 12 of them- There are also hexes you can take. Yet another way to add challenge and modify your game. And honestly, 90% of them are nonsense and I don't even see why anyone would play with them when not trying to get the related achievementsPROS:1.) I said that the game can be very grindy at the start, but it can be rewarding at times if you get a good run and progress. And maybe you like the grind as wellAfter you start unlocking more stuff and progressing a bit further, that's when the game is most fun. The enemies are still bad, but you are decently equiped to not feel it as much, but you're also not overpowered yet to breeze through everything. There is still challenge, but the bad things are mitigated2.) The curse/blessing system is a nice way to have risk versus reward in the game and I think it's done nicely overall (except in the scenarios I mentioned previously)3.) Pixel art and sound design are greatI don't know how to describe it, but the pixel art is very crispy, and the sound is very addictive. The clinks of the items dropping after you clear a room, gold plopping on the ground. That part is very nicely doneAlthough the rooms can get very cluttered at times, the art is still niceTL;DR:Very grindy at the beginning Bad enemy design, bad hitboxes, bad rooms filled with enemies and traps that do surprising amount of damage for early game. Bosses are bad as well; poorly telegraphed attacks, overlapping attacks, spammy attacks tanky health. "Challenge" and challenge modes, although optional, are cheaply made. Game can be rewarding though after the beginning and before later difficulty, and the pixel art and sound design are wonderful. But it's not enough to outweigh the negatives

_childDocuments_.review: Well, if you're reading these reviews, you've probably already vetted this game half-way decently enough to know its worth trying. THIS IS NOT REALLY TRUE WITH THIS GAME, I am HAPPY to confirm.The randomness actually adds to the diversity of the game, and has kept me playing for a good 30+ hours so far with only 80% of the dungeon explored, so I'd say that is $15 WELL SPENT!  (Found an early release copy still available, which others may be able to as well with a little effort...)  If you like any of the aforementioned games, or any of my ramblings, I'd say give it a shot.  Even at the base $20 price, its probably better than 3/4 of the Indie crap out there right now, and from me, that's sayin something!  GL/HF/GG

_childDocuments_.review: A solid rogue like pixel grinder, Undermine is often fun and pretty much bug free for my complete playthrough of the game. I quite enjoyed how the game has fun with all the characters who keep dying off. While there is a lot of loot there really isn't much that changes your attacks beyond increasing damage, unlike say the Gungeon series or other such games. Its RNG and the loot is not balanced so some times you feel its too easy and sometimes it just feels like you are being punished. My big complaint however is the grinding almost seems like you are being punished especially with the way gold carries over between runs. You want an upgrade for your pickaxe or health or whatever and finally grind out enough gold, but you can only buy items on your next run and you will lose over half the gold when you die. WTF? You can upgrade your character so eventually you only lose a small amount, but that will take a very long time. Also, why does your pet get reset after time? _childDocuments_.review: Would you like a roguelike where, as you descend down the dungeon, you get weaker and weaker as the run goes on? Then this game is for you. You can get such curses as plants, torches, and rocks firing poison, fire and missiles so that every room you enter is a tedium to clear out. You can get curses that cause the artifact that you were about to pick up to be destroyed before you get there. Or if that's not your speed, you can get a curse that makes you lose max health every enemy you kill for the entire run. How about a curse that makes it so the healing items you get poison you? There's even curses that eventually build up to the point where you have to hit the enemies 4 times as much just to kill it. This might not be so bad if it weren't for the fact that curses are EVERYWHERE. Last run I accumulated around 40 curses in about an hour and a half of play. The artifacts you pick up tend to be unimpressive, not fun, and don't even come close to offsetting all these negatives.The worst part is the combat isn't even fun, and everything feels slow and awkward. _childDocuments_.review: If you're like me, you're bored with the 100+ other games in your steam library and are looking for a new game to sink some time into. You're looking for a game that offers an RPG element with lots of ways to upgrade your character/equipment and will keep you hooked for hours. Well, my friend, your search is over.I've really enjoyed the limited time I've spent on this game. It's very similar to Rogue Legacy; spawn, gather as much gold as you can before your inevitable death, purchase upgrades that help you get farther and repeat. That may sound boring but this game also has other elements that make you want to keep hurling the seemingly endless population of peasants down that mine. There's a main "hub" that you spawn in at the beginning of each run. As you delve further and further in the mine, you will come across NPCs that, when rescued, will set up in the hub and offer upgrades. One of those NPCs is blacksmith who will craft various Relics when you find the blueprints for them. To me, the Relics really make each run more fun. Want to add lightning, fire and poison damage to your melee attacks while stealing life with every hit and causing enemies to drop food on death? There's a Relic for that. You also end up with an Alchemist and a Priestess once you get far enough.It's tough to explain, but even after I make it so far with 15+ Relics under my belt only to die, I just want to keep going. Maybe it's the completionist in me that wants to unlock ALL the upgrades. Maybe it's wanting to find out what's at the bottom of the mine (still haven't made it that far). Maybe it's the fact that this game is still Early Access and I'm excited to see the future content. Not bad for $13If you enjoy games like Hero Siege, Rogue Legacy and Hammerwatch, smash that "Add to Cart" button. You won't be disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: UnderMine is a great game! It reminds me of Spelunky + Binding of Isaac + Hero Siege (an indie game on steam that used to be amazing until they changed the core physics.) If you like dungeon crawlers, getting money to upgrade better equipment and fighting/exploration with lots of RNG - this game is for you!The devs of this game seem like they're wonderful, and take feedback from players seriously. I love devs that are inspired by other games because that's how you know that it's going to be cared for (WELL.. most of the time.) That is another reason I bought this game. Being in early access, I haven't ran into ANY issues with the game ... at all.However, the game lacks some content. There are lots of things you can do in this game, so don't let me scare you saying that. Again, the lack of content is only a minor flaw and the devs just released a roadmap for this game that plans to add a lot more before 2020 comes. See Link. At times the game is a bit frustrating and grindy, due to how much gold you  earn, and how you lose a lot of gold when you die (you can upgrade the amount of gold you lose on death, the problem is it gets very expensive - very quickly.) I loooove grinding for things, but sometimes when you die in a very cheap way it can really offset your mood.Another problem with the game that actually really annoys me is the fact that you aren't sure what's permanent and what isn't until the item is in your journal. Relics that are used on your run look the same as items that are permanent inside of the journal. Sometimes I'm not sure if something is worth wasting gold on if it's a one time use. The blacksmith is a bit confusing to use too, because you have to craft the item, and then you get to use it for a one time free charge on your run that you buy it on. I feel like there needs to be more clarification here. I guess you get to buy the item in shops after crafting it?One more problem with the game that I could find is that the relics you pick up can sometimes be very underwhelming. Maybe it's just because they need to add more, which they will. And every time you die your character is carried over by a relation with the same upgrades and things. BUT, it would be fun to be able to choose a random stat every time you die (which shouldn't be permanent if that is added to the game.)Don't get me wrong though, I love this game. And if you love something you have to sometimes critique it. But all in all, you should pick up this game. The price point is very fair and it's a great quality game with great pixel graphics and mostly fun mechanics. I've been waiting for another type of Spelunky game!I have to stop here, as I have some grinding to do!

_childDocuments_.review: Incredibly stale, shallow, slow and cumbersome roguelike.  Probably one of the most mind-numbingly uninspired and clunky roguelikes I've ever played.  There's also performance issues.  After running into "Missing Loc!" errors (which required 4 reinstalls of the game for it to go away), there were the "bog-down" slo-motion moments.  There's no reason this game, with these graphics, should get any kind of slowdown on any machine made in the last ten years.  Basically, on any map zones with more than 5 moving sprites at a time, it would drop to almost half gameplay speed.  There is no reason this should happen on an 5th gen i5 & 8GB RAM.To those who said this is anything like Wizard of Legend, you need to get your head examined.  Wizard of Legend is a fast, dynamic roguelike with responsive and precise controls and plenty of depth to its gameplay.  With WoL, I always felt like I could change my styles depending on the type of run I was trying to do. _childDocuments_.review: So, overall, if you enjoy games like Enter the Gungeon or the Binding of Isaac, then you'll likely enjoy this game as well. That being said, this game has it's fair share of problems, and I'll elaborate on that below. Don't let the feedback below stop you from buying this game. It's very solid. However, the balancing issues and lack of depth are reasonably frustrating in this game, so be ready for that.(New biggest issue is item unlocks. I have had 999 thorium for 10+ hours, and I have dozens of items I've yet to find blueprints for. Blueprints give you the option to spend your special currency to see new items. Despite maxing out my special currency long ago, I still don't have these items unlocked. The developers NEED to let players find more blueprints to spend their hard earned thorium.A simple fix would be that each time you beat a boss again, the chest gives you a guaranteed blueprint. As is, it takes literally hundreds of hours to get lucky for the thorium chests. The devs have a lot of their gameplay locked away, and for no good reason imo. This would give incentives for getting the ascension stone high ranked, and it would let the new items come in at the same rate as you can spend your thorium. I'm not a gamedev, but this seems like an easy solution to implement.)First, certain items will kill you(Since the time of my review, most of these kinds of issues have been fixed. However, certain relics are still detrimental and not worth taking, EG, Karmic Scale.)This isn't the only item that gets you killed, but it's the most pressing example that comes to mind. Several of the upgrades offer so little benefit and so much visual clutter that they actually hamper the player rather than helping them. The synergies between items are multiplicative in nature only; they don't actually synergize. It's simple compounding bonuses like attack speed and damage.Yes, they synergize, but that doesn't really effect gameplay. It just allows you to maintain the core pickaxe swinging and throwing against stronger enemies.(This complaint has sort of been tackled. Some items have been added that do change gameplay a good bit. I simply haven't seen or obtained them yet after beating all three bosses 10+ times.)This isn't the only set of issues with the game either. The grinding between the floors is draining after a while. You can skip floors, but it's purely to your detriment. You are putting yourself at a massive disadvantage, and you need those items to compete with the enemies on later floors. Otherwise, you'll run into a particularly nasty combination of traps, hazards, and baddies before getting blended up like a meat smoothie.(Still not fixed, but they've worked on a few of the other issues. More variety in the floors has helped a bit here, but this is still a problem.)There's another issue. Some rooms are instant death if you don't have the right items. I know what you're thinking. "Dude, just get good! XD." Trust me when I say I'm not the kind of guy to blame the game for my own mistakes. Most of the dark souls series is hard yet fair. Same with Enter the Gungeon or the Binding of Isasc. The issue here comes with how the enemies and traps interact.In some floors, you'll face these very fat, tanky gargoyles. If you don't finish them off, they turn to stone and heal. They also shoot out walls of fire in the same pattern that a rook is allowed to move in chess. I faced two of them along with a few other enemies. The field was pure oil. Nearly 100% of it. On oil, you're slowed and you can't jump. To give you a frame of reference, this is like robbing you of the ability to roll in Dark Souls. Just like rolling in Dark Souls, most of Undermine's skill and depth is from jumping. Without it, you're dead in the water....Or oil in this case.Terrible puns aside, the gargoyles set the entire oil pit on fire, restricting me to a tiny piece not covered by oil. They then used their AOE attacks to force me from safety. Boom. I'm running through fire, swinging for my life, and my life bar is rapidly depleting. I'm attacking as quickly as I can with the range attack, yet it's just not enough DPS. These fat bastards are soooooo tanky, it takes about 10 seconds of dpsing them to take them down.Then they start to heal once the turn to stone.I think you get the idea. I had an amazing build that run. Full health. High deeps. Massive sustain. It was all made irrelevant because I didn't have...wait for it...the goloshes I mentioned earlier. It was so ironic because I found some and didn't pick them up because they killed me the run before. Hah. Hah. HAH.Maddening laughter aside, I gotta say, this game's addicting, but these issues are debilitating. Go into this expecting persistent frustration with the balancing.(This is not as much the case as before due to the better ability to get a LOT of damage. Getting that damage takes quite a bit of a grind though.)♥♥♥♥ it, I'll keep going.The blue-purple chests are NEVER worth picking up. They give you curse and items. It's rare they give you something useful, and the curses in this game act as negative modifiers. They tend to outweigh the equilivent positive blessings, and these chests in particular rarely give you a permanent buff. A permanent debuff for some generic items is just...so bad.(This has been fixed for the most part. The devs added rebalancing for curse mechanics in general. This has made the game some more replayability simply because it has given each run more variability. Nice one devs.)The story robs you of agency as well. It's designed around the concept of you being a pathetic, idiotic, easily manipulated peasant. You're sent down into a mine with the poorest possible equipment, and they expect you to kill elemental golems with a rusty pickaxe. When you do, guess what? They STILL mock you. There's no enhancement of your reputation, or perhaps a building up of your esteem. They game goes out of its way to make it crystal clear that you're a pitiful scumbucket that's being sent to his death.Even this many hours into the game, there's been no shift in that narrative feel. My character is still scrounging for scraps, and these rich ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ are lording over me. Over and over and over again. Come on man, give the poor peasants a break. He killed a shadow demon, an insect queen, and an overcharged lightning golem with a pickaxe. That's badass. Let me, as the guy playing the game, feel badass over doing that. But no,as the player, you're not given that satisfaction. Instead, it's made abundantly clear that you're still a peasant. I get it. I'm at the bottom, that's never going to change, and there's nothing I can do about it. I get enough of that from real life. I don't understand why I would want anymore of that from a video game.So to sum it up, yeah, the game had pretty solid game play. It has some pretty bad balancing issues(Mostly fixed, though a few sore spots here or there), itemization is pretty bland(Getting better), and the story beats you down instead of building you up(Could be fixed later, but hasn't been at all). You wanna feel like a peasant being sent to his death, yet overcoming the odds and prevailing? This isn't the game for you. In this game, you're a peasant. You will be addressed as such.Sit down, be quiet, and do as you're told. To the pits and to death, that's all that awaits you. And a bit of fun I suppose.

_childDocuments_.review: Undermine is a genuinely fantastic roguelike that deserves a lot more attention.It feels like a really neat halfway point between Spelunky and Binding of Isaac, with some of the best perma-progression mechanics I've seen in the genre. I'll elaborate on that.First of all, the world of the game feels dynamic. The reason for that is that there's potential for CHAOS. Slime enemies can change properties based on where they fall. Water slimes can jump into an oil puddle and turn into oil slimes. Oil slimes can spread further oil puddles. Oil puddles can catch fire. Slimes caught on fire turn into fire slimes. There's more examples of these kinds of dynamics in the game, and they're great. They can make deaths feel hilarious sometimes, just like Spelunky.There's also really nice item synergies. Nothing as visually distinct and crazy as in BoI, but mechanically there's absolutely some items that will combine in very exciting and interesting ways.As for the perma-progression, one of the stand-out features is that once you beat certain bosses, new enemy types will pop up in early levels. It's a nice way to keep things feeling fresh without going the more resource-intensive option of offering alternate level paths (like Dead Cells, BoI or Spelunky 2). Another really interesting thing is that bosses don't need to be beat more than once. You can just skip them after the first time (or even before the first time, if you'd like!). There's also little quests that unlock more upgrade options, and all their appearances feel organic. There's no quest tracker or progress log. The upgrades feel like they're less about making things easier and more about helping you progress through early levels faster and giving you more choices of how to do so. It's a smart way of opening up options to players as they become more experienced with the game, while also not making it feel like you're just grinding until you actually have a chance at beating the game.Speaking of, I haven't beaten the game yet, and I might update the review after that.But Undermine is already one of my favorite examples of the genre, and you should absolutely play it.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a top down Rogue-lite game. A fair comparison is The Binding of Isaac or Enter the Gungeon, though with a bigger focus on melee combat and persistent upgrades. It's in early access, but there are already a few dozen hours of content. If you enjoyed those games, I recommend giving this a try.You play as a peasant who is summoned to rid a dungeon of its monsters, collect treasures you find, and complete quests from a variety of interesting NPC hub-folk. When you die, you play a new peasant while keeping most of the upgrades you attained before.The primary challenge of the game is combat. You have a short range melee attack and a thrown attack. Unlike many games in the genre, you also have the ability to jump. This is useful for dodging attacks and traps, an interesting alternative to a dodge roll or a dash.The monsters are of enough variety to keep the combat interesting. There are several bosses already in the game. They feel moderately difficult but pretty well balanced. Nothing stands out as cheesy or unfair.Exploration consists of finding Relics, potions and basic items that help you find go deeper into the dungeon. Relics are comparable to items in Isaac, mostly passively changing your attacks or the economy. The potions have a wide variety of uses, from healing you to shooting fireballs. The basic items are keys, bombs and food. All of these help you earn gold and thorium which can be used to buy persistent upgrades and unlocks which help your future runs.Like all Rogue-lites, death is part of the game. You aren't meant to take it in one go. Nor are you even able to. The satisfying part of this kind of loop is when your abilities begin to snowball. After a few hours in, I feel like my character is making a lot of progress. The first floors feel much easier and faster. The runs at the beginning took me about 20 minutes to a half hour. Short enough that I don't feel too frustrated when I die to a boss (or die walking into spikes.)All in all I'm satisfied with this purchase and I'm eager to see where they take it. I've had really good luck with early access games of this type. I feel like player feedback leads to a lot of positive changes, especially regarding QoL improvements.

_childDocuments_.review: It’s very rare that I play rogue-like or rogue-lite games, simply because I tend to not enjoy the idea of randomly generated infinitely replayable titles, vastly preferring the hand-crafted games with a definitive end to them (that I can simply replay if I liked them a lot). However, there have been a few titles that despite all odds got me invested. And somehow Undermine joined their ranks. I’ll try to understand why.Undermine is a rogue-lite with room-by-room exploration in a layered dungeon, isometric view, permanent upgrades and jumping as means of dodging attacks and also exploring. It’s biggest influence seems to be The Binding of Isaac (which in turn has been influenced by the original The Legend of Zelda dungeons) and most of the basic ideas are the same. Each dungeon zone has several floors (4 to be precise). Each floor is divided into rooms that take up the entire screen and are connected to other rooms, sometimes directly, sometimes via a door requiring a key and sometimes via wall that must be bombed or destroyed by an enemy. Additional secret rooms and items might be hidden under/inside rocks that can be bombed or also destroyed by enemies. Rooms often include enemies, in which case the doors to other rooms get locked until you kill all of them, sometimes additional hazards, sometimes only hazards, and there’s almost always a shop somewhere in the level. Oh and also every floor has a Relic, which is a special upgrade item that stays with you until the end of the run, while in very few exceptional cases you might also find permanent items called Artifacts, or upgrades. Also, there’s lots of gold everywhere which you should mine to get upgrades in the starting hub.Most of what I’ve described is almost exactly the same as it was in Isaac, except now focusing more on melee attacks and almost entirely devoid of bullet-hell-like sections. Additionally, you can avoid all damage if you’re jumping as whatever is dealing damage passes under you. You will still take damage if you land on the damage dealing enemy or hazard, but, interestingly, vast majority of enemies in the game don’t deal contact damage and have attacks with clearly defined tells. Oh and, of course, the permanent upgrades are also a thing that clearly differentiates this from Isaac, as your starting area contains several kinds of shops that provide either upgrades, or new kinds of relics, potions, blessings and other kinds of things that you will encounter during the run.None of this is specifically fantastic, I must stress. The combat is pretty simple, though you do get to learn some tricks as you play, as you realize how to better use the melee and throwing attacks and how and when to jump or use bombs. Or get better at using the relics you find, blessings you get or even detrimental curses to your advantage. But it remains quite simple, as do the levels, bosses, enemies, hazards, “puzzles” and other things you encounter. You get more of everything as you play, but most of it doesn’t become much deeper. Yet… something about this simplicity clicks. At least it did with me. And the permanent upgrades and unlocks are often a good enough hook to keep you invested even in a run where you’re clearly going to die very soon.It also helps that both the visual style and the soundtrack are very nice. Also the story, as simple as it is, is doing what it needs to do. And the characters are cute. All of this is also not specifically fantastic, but simply very very good. And for those who like rogue-lites more than I do, there are even more additional things and run modes and unlocks that you get after you complete the game once, that I didn’t particularly care about, but you might.So, despite the fact that some of the enemies in the game are more annoying that anything. Despite the really visually inconsistent way you can fall into holes. Despite the fact that some rooms are poorly thought out and some are super easy to accidentally exit from before you collect everything you want. I really-really liked playing this game. And might even play it again in the future. And some of the music tracks are definitely going into my main playlist, even though at first I found them really silly. Undermine isn’t a game that’s really great, or striking, or memorable, or anything deserving an extreme kind of praise. But it’s really good and it’s very fun to play. And sometimes that's exactly what you need.

_childDocuments_.review: Being a big roguelike/roguelite fan, i picked this game up on a whim. I'm happy to say it is a pretty solid game. **Graphics** - This game is beautifully animated. The art style definitely sticks out among a vast sea of other games of this genre. Great colors, great character designs, and gorgeous animations. 9/10 **Audio** - The sound effects are pretty good, hitting enemies, using your pickaxe to mine gold, all sounds very solid. The music is good. Not anything to write home about, but definitely not bad. 6/10 **Gameplay** - With this game being a roguelike, you know for the most part what you are getting. You kill enemies, collect items to power up and try to progress further. After every run you have an opportunity to purchase upgrades to make your next run better. There are 2 main methods of attacking, swing your pickaxe, and throwing your pickaxe. Compared to other roguelikes the melee attack definitely feels clunky and awkward at first, while the ranged attack is far easier to use more effectively. But as you get more comfortable with using it, the melee attack is very good. There are a very good amount of items/unlockables. The difficulty between floors can spike at times, which can be frustrating, but practice makes perfect. 7.5/10 **Other Notes** - The game is very fun currently, but the devs have updated this game very frequently, with very sizeable additions, with more and more coming out all the time. The devs are doing a great job of supporting it.Final Score: 8.25/10 **Final Words** - A must buy for roguelike fans, and definitely a recommendation for anyone who is on the fence about it. Good Luck and Have Fun!

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not normally a huge fan of roguelites, but UnderMine caught my eye (thanks to DangerouslyFunny's videos). I've played about 16 hours of it so far (version 0.3.3.8), and I must say that it shows amazing promise. The game already feels like a fully released title, despite still being in early access.The aim of the game is simple - progress through (currently) 12 levels of the mines, fighting creatures and hoarding gold. Along the way you'll find NPCs who return to your hub and offer their services, secret areas that reward you, artifacts to power you up, and curses which have various negative effects, but offer some reward in return.The permanent unlocks are one of the things that caught my eye. Once you have enough gold and have the correct NPCs unlocked, you can upgrade your character for every subsequent run. This can be more health or damage, the ability to carry more potions, or even an upgraded sack to lose less gold on death. This means that no matter how poorly a run goes, you still feel like you've achieved something.The runs themselves can last up to about 30 minutes - so they're well suited to shorter play sessions. There always seems to be something new to find, and in 16 hours, I definitely haven't seen all the game has to offer.The graphics and audio are also well polished, and I haven't noticed any bugs so far. Once you've finished the current content, you get an item which respawns the bosses and ups the difficulty slightly (while improving the rewards). In the recent update, you also have the ability to toggle the level of this item, so you can return to non-NG+ if you prefer.UnderMine is an excellent game, and the developer deserves to sell a lot of copies. It's definitely worth the current asking price of €12.50, and I hope the community around the game grows. I can't wait to see what's in store for future updates as well.

_childDocuments_.review: Rating: 4.7/5"UnderMine" offers an exhilarating journey into the depths of its labyrinthine world, combining the thrill of action-adventure with the strategic elements of a roguelike. This game expertly weaves together combat, exploration, and RPG-like progression to create an experience that is as challenging as it is rewarding.Gameplay:The core gameplay loop of "UnderMine" is incredibly engaging. Players delve deep into the ever-changing dungeon, fighting their way through hordes of enemies and gathering valuable resources. Each run is unique, thanks to the game's procedural generation, which keeps the experience fresh and unpredictable. The combat is fluid and satisfying, requiring both skill and strategy to overcome the various challenges that lie within.Roguelike Elements:As a roguelike, "UnderMine" embraces the concept of incremental progression. Each death is not the end, but rather an opportunity to upgrade and strengthen your character. Mining gold, collecting relics, and discovering powerful potions and blessings allow for significant customization and experimentation. The variety of items and their potential combinations ensure that no two runs feel the same, providing a rich and varied experience.Upgrades and Progression:The game's RPG-like progression system is one of its standout features. Players can rescue characters within the dungeon who then offer new upgrades and abilities, enhancing the player's chances in subsequent runs. This progression system is deeply satisfying, as each upgrade feels impactful and brings you closer to uncovering the dungeon’s many secrets.Story and Atmosphere:"UnderMine" also excels in its storytelling and atmosphere. The cryptic messages from the dungeon’s residents add a layer of mystery and intrigue, encouraging players to delve deeper and piece together the narrative. The game's art style and sound design further immerse players in its dark, underground world, creating a sense of tension and excitement as they explore its depths.Boss Battles:Challenging boss battles punctuate the experience, providing intense and memorable encounters. These fights require players to utilize all their skills and upgrades, testing their abilities and offering a great sense of accomplishment upon victory.Conclusion:Overall, "UnderMine" is a masterfully crafted game that delivers a captivating blend of action, exploration, and strategic progression. Its roguelike elements and RPG-like upgrades create a highly addictive gameplay loop that keeps players coming back for more. With its unique items, engaging combat, and mysterious narrative, "UnderMine" stands out as a must-play for fans of the genre. Whether you’re mining for gold or battling formidable bosses, the adventure that awaits in the depths of "UnderMine" is one that should not be missed.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros: - New NPCs / Game mechanics get introduced at a good pace and unlocking them feels satisfying- Polished graphics- Bosses have interesting mechanicsCons:- Gameplay is not very interesting and feels repetitive. Almost all relics and blessings are just stat buffs, so the runs feel all the same- Jump mechanic feels very awkward. It is very hard to estimate where you are going to land and hard to steer mid-air. Platforming feels terrible. A dash-mechanic (which most other roguelikes go for) would probably have been better.- Bosses don't respawn. This is especially disappointing since the bosses are the main strength of this game. Not being able to replay them feels like a poor design decision.- Difficulty of rooms varies widely. Sometimes your run will just end because of a room full of mines with moving sawblades, several holes in the ground and a ton of enemies shooting at you. This kind of rng would not really be a problem if not for the next point.- I don't like that the in-run and out-of-run currencies are identical. This leads to me never buying any expensive items in-run since the run may be over anytime because of a very difficult room and i would rather save the gold for permanent upgrades. I understand that this is a deliberate design decision but i personally don't like it.Conclusion:I am especially disappointed in this game because the core idea is really good (of course a lot is copied from Binding of Isaac), boss design is really cool and the game feels very polished (except the wonky jump mechanic). But the main point of a roguelike is having great replayability through different playstiles in different runs. Unfortunately, Undermine does not deliver this at all. If you are new to roguelikes, this game may be for you. Otherwise, i would rather play Hades, Dead Cells or Binding of Isaac.

_childDocuments_.review: If i could put a review as "meh", i'd put it as so. If you haven't played any roguelikes (which this game isn't, more below), or really few roguelites (which the game isn't... either), you might find this enjoyable. If, like me, you have, you quickly notice it has zero originality. You know that time you forgot to name your game in that game dev sim and it came out as "Game #27"? This is that game.If you don't want to read the detailed description, there is a summary at the end.Gameplay - General: It's a slog. Enemy attack patterns either aren't a thing at all (rats), only exist to slow you down (slimes, yetis), or just get random free hits on you when they shouldn't (any enemy that fires projectiles). Your hitbox is gigantic, and you often fall down pits for the sole reason that your pinky toe happened to brush the edge. Bosses are nothing but gigantic health bars with mechanics that often have zero windup, so either you spend an absurd amount of time playing it safe and getting 1 hit in every minute, or you grind for money. There are no other options.Gameplay - Character: I don't know if the peasant class is intentionally garbage, or is it even the only class in the game. However, it feels like it is intentionally garbage. Your attack has extremely short range, and stops you dead in your tracks. Your melee attack is entirely worthless except for disposing of enemies that can't hit you when hitting them in melee (smaller rats), every other enemy is better fought with the weaker ranged attack that doesn't completely stop you. You have a jump, which makes you seemingly completely immune to damage, but it doesn't work as a dodging mechanic when they're trying to pull off attack patterns like ones seen in Enter the Gungeon and Binding of Isaac, both games you should be playing instead of this.Gameplay - Items: There's 2 kinds of items in this game, most of them in the latter category: useful, and useless. Most treasures/relics/whatever you have are completely worthless. Gold explodes as it drops? Wow, it could deal a tiny amount of damage to an enemy if you hit a rock twice instead of hitting an enemy. Gold arcs lightning to an enemy when picked up? You could just hit the enemy instead for the same reason as above. There are no items that stand out, and the only even slightly useful relic i found throughout the entire gameplay (and i found more than 20) was one that let the thrown weapon ricochet to 3 enemies. On that note, the descriptions of the relics are awful. There's boots that state "they allow walking and jumping in oil", what do they actually do? While they do allow you to jump in oil, they also drop a splatter of oil at your feet after any jump. There are a lot of items that say "increases damage", but none of them say how much. Details. They're important.Graphic Design: Here lie more or less the only good parts of the game at its current stage. The pause menu fade is genius, the enemies are well animated and have a lot of love poured on them. While the maps themselves are pretty bland, the graphic design still feels tight and unique.Sound Design: I already forgot how anything in the game sounds, and i shut it down 10 minutes ago. "Generic" is literally the only thing that comes to mind.Polish levels: Really, really low amount of gameplay testing, the core gameplay loop is not only really slow, but it gets repetitive within 2 hours. The bosses as mentioned before are just giant slabs of meat that take hundreds of hits. It is not fun to play at this stage and it was put out on early access far too early.Game Design: Ctrl+C, Ctrl+V. There is nothing even close to original here, and despite that, the level of quality is as if they're trodding on completely uncharted territory and making it up as they go along. There exists countless of examples of exact replicas of what this game has in other games, all of them doing it better. Binding of Isaac and Enter the Gungeon are the obvious comparisons, but it even muddles down those so much that it only becomes an action RPG with kind-of-but-not-really permadeath mechanics. And even that "RPG" part of action RPG is missing. There are so many examples they could've drawn and iterated from and try to do better."Roguelike": No. Not even close. Nethack is a roguelike. Dungeon Crawl: Stone soup is a roguelike. Dwarf Fortress (adventure mode) is a roguelike. The genre's name already explains itself "a game that is like Rogue". There is nothing comparable to Rogue here. For that matter, it isn't Roguelite either. The items you get in the dungeon itself are so powerless, and the bosses have such absurd levels of health, the entire game hinges on you spending thousands and thousands of gold after you've died so you can have at least feasible chance of taking the bosses on.Difficulty: Healing is expensive gold-wise, and heal-item drops are very rare. While the average character dies in 10-15 hits, there are a lot of cases where there is legitimately unavoidable damage in the game, particularly with bosses if you ever wish to damage them even slightly. Unavoidable damage should only really appear as a dilemma in these types of games, but here it's rampant. As previously stated, the bosses are the worst offendee in the difficulty department. They don't have difficult attack patterns or complex, varied mechanics, so they just have an absolute assload of health, and guaranteed hits on you.Summary: As stated in the prologue, meh. It's original only in how unoriginal it is. The graphics design is great and lively, but apart from that it seems to fail at every single hurdle there is. It copies mechanics from already existing (and in some cases cheaper) games that have come before it and instead of trying to do better, it does worse and makes things clumsy. Its lack of difficulty is compensated by bosses having unavoidable attacks and absurdly high amount of health that practically forces you to grind if you don't wish to spend the better part of an hour on the first "real" boss even if you happen to chance a good item drop. The item drops in most cases are not even worth picking up, and they aren't inventive or clever. It's not a roguelike or a roguelite, and calling it even an action RPG would be an insult to games like Secret of Mana that did this style of combat well nearly 3 decades ago.

_childDocuments_.review: Undermine is an incredibly fun roguelike that I think anyone who enjoys there genre will enjoy, there's a few reason for this. At its core the roguelike mechanics work well with randomly generated floor that follow a theme and death is sometimes more of an opportunity than that of a hassle. Personally I am a big fan of seeing where even though death is permanent, you can still see yourself getting stronger and improving one way or another. Not to mention the different cute familiars you can get that can fit whatever playstyle you prefer.But whats great is that while the base game of undermine is a bit easier than many other roguelike, the game provides plenty of ways to give more of a challenge should you request it. There's the summoning stones the can make subsequent runs harder, the hexes from the crone that can give you permanent difficult curses, and of course, the Othermine which lets truly has no progress and you have a random start to challenge the Othermine. The gameplay mechanics and the sound absolutely slaps, and there's plenty of variety in types of rooms, enemies, relics, and curses that its takes a while for it to feel repetitive.Speaking of those things, Undermine also has does something that I think all great roguelike (e.g. binding of Isaac) should do. The relics and blessings that you receive can inadvertently combine into incredible combinations that are powerful and fun. Probably the most infamous example would be getting the right relics to essentially drop a nuke whenver you place a bomb that can wipe out the entire room (and maybe you in the process). Another thing in that regard which I consider a plus is that curses you receive can also combine in such terrible ways that you feel like you're getting screwed other and wonder which god you anger to deserve such karma.Lastly, the more QoL things, the different interactions and the story you see unfolding with the characters in the nexus is rather charming. It doesn't have the detail of games like Hades by any means but its nice to see you slowly bringing more and more people and as a result life to the nexus by saving people or completing quests in the mines that make you feel like you've truly contributed to the mines. However, no game is without flaw and I think undermines biggest flaw is the pacing of unlocking things. There are many different relics, potions, and familiars to unlock in Undermine and many of them require finding the blueprints for them. This isn't too bad because you can get a lot of recipes from the Othermine but the thorium needed to unlock all of these recipes can feel rather slow. Sometimes it can feel like it takes a while to unlock all of the upgrades but this is mostly post endgame content.Overall, Undermine is a great game that is definitely worth the price. I would recommend this game to anyone who enjoys roguelikes or has an interest in them. Its a fantastic game for beginners and veterans alike to play and I'm sure you'll enjoy it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has 3 problems I can see after playing for a few hours.1. Basic combat is not that enjoyable, no variety of attacks available.2. Gold pickup. It's a chore to have to run around and pick up 4-6 gold pieces every time you hit a rock. That alone is a waste of time. On top of that, you have their mascot (Pilfers) coming to steal the gold if you're not fast enough. How is this an enjoyable gameplay loop? It's like if you bought french fries at the beach, someone knocked it out of your hands, and said "Better go pick it up before the seagulls get it." In Wizard of Legend you just have gold magnet to you if you're close at all.3. Gold integrity. It's fine to lose a percentage of your gold before the next run. But consider Rogue Legacy. In that game, you get to spend from your total earned gold, then you lose a percentage of the unspent gold right before the run starts. In this game, you lose a percentage of all earned gold right when you die. You know for a fact that 50% (starting value) of your gold is going to waste.So my experience was farming for increased gold integrity (50%->70%) since I don't want any gold to go to waste. When farming for gold I have to rush to pick it up or lose it to the Pilfers. Then even when I get it, it's reduced no matter what. Also the whole game is brown apart from the dungeon, which is grey. Maybe different floors could have different themes.It's not a terrible game, but it is tedious. You have to question what the devs are thinking with some of these decisions. They could learn from previously released roguelikes.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game. The music, art style, and setting are really well done. Let highlight a few things the developer(s) absolutely need to spend some time on.1. Losing gold mechanic - Starting with a blanket 50% loss of gold when you die is really bad mechanic. This isn't a problem starting out as the upgrades are relatively cheap and you can quickly reduce this to 65-70%. HOWEVER, little monsters in the dungeon ALSO steal gold if you don't get to it quick enough, making it probably closer to an extra -5-10% per run loss depending on your skill and luck. Please, for the love of god, implement a floor with the sack upgrades, ie (Level 1, 500 minimum, then 50% loss) or something. The way it works currently makes saving for upgrades extremely risky, even just with two separate runs.  If you happen to be unlucky with your 20 grand starting off, welp, sucks that you now have 14 grand. Also, for please re-evaluate the monsters stealing gold - either in intensity or in having them literally be worth SOMETHING for killing. 2. Unavoidable Damage - what I mean by this is it's entirely possible to get hit by a monster that deals damage, which then pushes you into spikes dealing more damage, which then knocks you into a hole, for some more damage. For god sake, implement a small invulnerability timer. This exemplifies point #1 for some real deep frustration on gold loss, taking 50-60% of your heath in damage in one go.3. Power Loss - It might be because of #1 again but skipping dungeon floors seems extremely hard to do because getting upgrades is also really hard to do. You need the relics you get in order to actually progress.4. Relic Tooltips - Some of the artifact tooltips almost seem intentionally vague. Kurtz' Statche for example (description: "A mysterious box that invites calamity"). Look, the secret rooms in the game are already obscured, and some rooms themselves having puzzles are sometimes impossible to figure out what to do from the environment - the last thing you need to do is make the items the players' have already EARNED puzzles too. Also, some of the relics are just really bad by themselves (Catalyst) unless paired with another relic. Make the relics be able to stand alone by themselves at least. The chances of getting the correct combo with ~100 relics is mathematically unlikely, especially when skipping dungeon rooms.

_childDocuments_.review: In short: After playing 8 hours into the game I cannot recommend it. It is too repetative with too little progression.Spoilers ahead:The good part: -I've seen no bugs, It runs smoothly.-The absensce of an (interesting) story is in this case actually a good thing. I don't miss anything, If I have to do the stuff over and over again.The bad ones:I've compared with lets play and goodled, if I simply was mistaken. But there is barely some progression. You will fight the same areas and the same enimies with barely rising stats over and over. Only to -maybe- buy a new item that barely changes anything.On top of feeling no progress the death penalty of loosing gold is another downer. It is somewhat the designing boni and mali. because what if instead of losing gold just pick up less gold in the first place? to me this was mostly a "awww ♥♥♥♥ again" moment I didn't need.On top I really don't like, that the game forces you to 1: enter a room 2: kill everything 3: loot everything 4: enter next room. The enemies never give you anything. the only reason to kill them is to open the doors the the adjacent screens. There is no "nope , I'll come back later' and no 'nope I just loot and run past the bad guys'. It's like the devs force you to aproach a room in this manner.The mechanics of fighting almost never change. You're stuck with Axe swing/ throw and jump. Most upgrades consist of +x to some stat. Sometimes you find a temporary relic for a run, that makes you perhaps use the throw more often than just hitting the thing. In my 8 hours I just got better with using the basic moveset. On that note I even wondered why there are 3 saveslots. Because doing different builds is unlikely to happen.After the first exitements of purple chests I started to avoid everything of that color. They give you a small benefit, most likely not relevant, and a curse, most likely to increase the chances of death. In a game all about avoiding death as long as possible it is reasonable to ignore the shiny violet chests(and flames). I know that the curses can be lifted, but this is a rare happening. So actively ignoring content is the strategy.When I discovered a NPC that can teleport me, I was not convinced as well. This "Hoodie" guy just teleports you down in the mines. First: Why do you want to teleport into dangerous levels, when you need the items of the lower and easy levels?Second: I asked myself several times, If he can teleport you again up to the village. This is of cours only motivated by the Idea of avoiding the death money loss. So in the end I ignored him.

_childDocuments_.review: It's not a bad game, exactly. It's kind of fun. But it's not great. It's like dollar slice pizza. I've played a lot of Binding of Isaac so the comparisons are easy to make, and this game isn't quite as good as it. Some key points:- The items you find don't spice up the gameplay that much.  There doesn't seem to be anything like Brimstone or Ipecac like you'd find in Isaac that really change things up. There don't seem to be (m)any interactions, either.- Running the early levels repeatedly gets boring. That's tied to the above, I think. In Isaac you can find some weird ♥♥♥♥ in the basement and it gets fun right away.  Also each area in Isaac is two floors, and there's four here.  Twice as long, but not twice as fun. Isaac also gives you at least two items per floor (room + boss), but you only get one here. This game seems to only have you fight bosses once instead of every run. Boss fights can be more interesting than just trash. - Metagame progression feels like a grind. I had the same problem with Rogue Legacy and to a lesser extent Dead Cells. You can upgrade your stats for gold. You always get gold for a run. If I spent a day grinding gold runs while watching youtube, I could max out my stats. Knowing that is irritating to me. I prefer how in Isaac all the unlocks are tied to accomplishments (win with this character, take no damage, do this thing, etc) or even just luck. You can't really grind to change your stats there.  Here, you can, and it kind of feels like a time gate for some of the later levels. I'm sure someone has beat the whole thing without any upgrades, but I'm not that good. I don't like the grinding the difficulty down like this, though.I could also compare it to Dead Cells. Dead Cells has some of the same problems (namely, the metagame grind). But Dead Cells is also a much *faster* game, and encourages you to go fast. By comparison, replaying undermine's early levels feels glacial.Overall it's not *bad*, it's just not as good as the nearest competitors.

_childDocuments_.review: UnderMine is an action-adventure roguelike where you play as miners who should delve deeper in the mine/dungeon to farm gold and occasionally discover secrets. A roguelite progression system is also available - you spend gold on permanent upgrades for your gear/shops/vendors/blessings etc.There's a lot of aspects that would be familiar for The Binding of Isaac players but at the same time UnderMine succeeds at delivering its own unique experience. I totally enjoyed my first 6-7 hours in the game:+ A really good first Early Access build. A lot of content, no bugs (at least from my experience).+ The game is actually fun to play.+ There's some characters you can interact with and each of them has some cool dialogues/jokes.+ Nice visuals and music.+ Decently balanced progression via unlocks/upgrades. It's not perfect but it's good enough to entertain you while providing challenging gameplay.+- When playing this game I compare it mostly to Isaac and some of UnderMine aspects (jumps and combat mechanics in general) are just not my cup of tea. Maybe I'd like those more at later stages of the game. Variety of axe attacks/improvements (and character development in general in terms of combat) is quite poor.- You can attack only in 4 directions with melee attacks (up, down, left, right) and this could and will lead to stupid misses. Why not to make it possible to attack diagonally?- Falling down is not really fun and player hitbox makes it even worse. "Airwalking shoes" is the best item in the game by far. is one of the best roguelikes in a long time with a good potential to enhance during Early Access period. Highly recommended for fans of the genre. 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: It has been a long time since a game captured my heart enough to write a review. Its been a long time since a game devastated my sleep, but oh did I welcome this endlessly sweet sin with Undermine. Roguelike's comprise a massive part of my steam library, they are most likely my favorite genre of game. As of late, I haven't found one that's captured that "ONE MORE RUN" feeling they used to. I've been in pursuit of something desperately fresh from the genre, but I was wrong. Undermine takes all that you know about Roguelites and roguelikes and packages them in an incredibly smooth and delicious game. So far, I've experienced what is seemingly ENDLESS progression. IN ALL ASPECTS. BOSS PROGRESSION. DEEP STORY PROGRESSION. GLORIOUS ITEM PROGRESSION. NPC CHARACTER DEVELOPMENT. DELVING INTO A MULTI LEVEL UNDERMINE FULL OF SECRETS AND BEAUTY ( and plenty of horrors). IT JUST KEEPS GOING. And I'm talking directly to a scope that feels nearly unobtainable at the moment, and I LOVE IT.But if that wasn't enough, it boasts possibly the most aesthetically pleasing art in the genre, a soundtrack of BANGERS, a cast of varied characters you actually want to learn more about...
