_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: 8/10 will recommend.Pro’s:- Not that hard, but slightly unforgiving as well.- Funny at times, especially in dialog with NPCs.- Surprising sometimes.- It contains hidden things, like entrances to extra rooms, but also in what you (accidentally) can do.- The developers did listen to the players and made the game way better during early access.Con’s:- A bit of a grind at start (for upgrades).- A bit repetitive, but not really boring due to random generated maps. And when you get better and upgraded, you can access more difficult areas with more ease.Tips: - Play with controller, but mouse also works. You can switch anytime you like.- Use the mirror in the room left of the starting hub to change your gender.I enjoy this game as an easy way to set off my mind after a hard day's work or something else that I need to calm down after. It is definitely not frustrating. Defeat is not that big of an impact, but it does come with a minor setback (losing some gold to buy upgrades mostly). Just enough to keep me going without stress. I love that idea!It is a bit of a grind at start though, especially when you lack the skills of mastering a controller like I do/did. It may take a while you get enough gold to get good upgrades (gear, bag, abilities) and enough currency to get potions and gear crafted by the NPCs, but for me just when it started to get repetitive and boring, I finally managed to kill the first real boss and it opened up a way to skip the starting zone (Goldmine) to the next part where the scenery does change enough to keep my interest again. Explanation: when you die, your pet tries to bring your gold back to the starting hub, but it does not contain all your gold anymore. Upgraded bags loose (slightly) less gold on death.Also the hidden things keeps me interested. Not only for entrances to hidden side rooms, but also for things you can do. Throwing your pickaxe on fire through a brazier and cooking some food while doing that, as for an example.And the way you do your “quests” (no quest list, just something asked by an NPC) for unlocking the NPCs and meeting some other NPCs in the dungeons was also nicely done.The game is quite not a graphical masterpiece, but still appealing to the eye. Also goes for the sound.I played since the end of early access and I can confirm the developers really did listen to the players and improved the game with their feedback. Bonus points for that!

_childDocuments_.review: If you like games with permanent upgrades, roguelike runs through randomly generated dungeons and items, and unlocking stuff as you play I highly suggest trying this. I think this game is at a good place for where it is in development.The game is ultimately unfinished as stated when you "finish" the content that they have, which took me roughly 12 hours to complete.  The game makes a statement that there is further content on the way.I definitely would like to see a bit more content for the game.  It felt like a full game, but I think it would thrive with a couple major updates.The devs also sound super exicted and passionate about the game from posts they've made in game and on the update logs, so I get a good feeling that they're not going to abandon the game.The concept is similar to The Binding of Isaac- each level is a floor where you can find a treasure room items, shops, bombs, keys, health ups, secret rooms, and you jump down a shaft to get to the next level. However, it does not feel like Isaac, to me at least.  I feel like it's a neutral aspect. I really liked:-The game felt overall fun.  I have a positive experience with the game and looked forward to coming back to it to play more.-The upgrade system.  You go dig for gold and use it for permanent upgrades and unlocking things around the base.-The game felt decently challenging.  Some of the rooms felt a little unfair, but I feel like it had the correct difficulty when it comes to an item dependent type of run.-The bosses were unique enough for me-While there are a few bugs I encountered, none of them were anywhere near game breaking, the game felt decently polished.  I saw a lot of people complaining about the movements and combat but I never had any issues with it.There are a few things I would like to see improved.-A lot of the items feel a bit under powered.-The blessing/curse system is a bit unbalanced as the curses are way more detrimental than the blessings are helpful.  Every time you get a blessing you receive a curse as well, while it's not too hard to get rid of the curses, some of them are just brutal.  I eventually just started ignoring the entire system and played without it as it felt too unbalanced towards failure.-The progress is a little bit slow, even for me.  It starts off decent but noticeably tapers off.  The higher upgrades get really expensive but the money is hard to gather as you lose a decent percentage of it when you die, and the only option is in the run is to die... as you find out after the first run or two.  There are upgrades to reduce the percent loss but it becomes expensive to upgrade it.-The prices of the shop start to scale up and become pretty pricey as the game goes on.-The game in its current state does not seem like it has much replayability once you "finish" the content they have.None of those were major killers for me,  just something I would like to see improved on.I'd say the price should be more around $10, but I'm glad I got it, and I feel like future update will justify its cost.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: Game improved enough for me to recommend. More variety, combat is..better, and now has enough content to make it enjoyable. (Old review)It's not quite there, but with a few tweaks it certainly can be.My main issues lie with the combat: Your throwing attack needs to be painfully precise. Hit boxes on smaller mobs are, not surprisingly, small, and your pickaxe never feels like it's covering enough area to hit what you're aiming for.The speed in which some enemies move doesn't really dance well with your attacks either. You are often clunky, while enemies are much more agile (and abundant. I'll get to that). Put it all together, and it makes you feel like you're threading a needle that's moving around like a hummingbird. Enemies: Their movements are okay in theory, but I don't know if they thought about all the different variables when packing these rooms full of different enemies. Some enemy attacks require you to move and do things a certain way, while others require you to do something wildly different. That's okay on paper, I mean, it's a game.. but if you get a variety of these mobs in a room, and they do wildly different things, you end up with a conflict. One mob will make you suffer for doing whatever it is you did to dodge the other, with no solution but to take a hit. So..what do you do if you have many things coming in at every direction, beating on you? Well, you jump around in circles like a madman, dodging everything you can! That's where the holes and spikes come in. Again, too many variables, and not enough thought as to how they work with one another. I shouldn't have to jump around in circles. There should be options and a way to "dodge" this, while I "attack" that. Before I go on, I have to say I'm a huge Isaac fan. I have over 2k hours in the game. Since the games are so similar, I have to be honest and say that it also suffers from the above conflict. The difference here is that Isaac has a multitude of options and choices that takes the edge off. Sometimes the game is unfair to you, but sometimes you are unfair to the game..if that makes any sense. Undermine either feels fair enough, or not fair at all.Bosses: Boss difficulty is controversial in games, but I find it really hard to believe that anyone thinks the final boss (for now) is harder than Selt (the first boss not counting that rock guy you fight literally once and never see again). It actually feels like the difficulty decreases boss-wise. I beat the final boss the first time, and every time after that, and I'm still dying to Selt. I think a lot of it has to do with the small area you have to hit on him, so it suffers from the combat issues I explained above.Build variety: There isn't any. Well, not much. You either A: Go for a gold-seeker build, getting relics, blessings, and potions that maximize your gold collecting. B: Increase your throw stats with speed and damage or  C: Increase stats for the regular swing attackEven those build don't end up different from one another. You'll find yourself mostly mixing because, to make your gold collecting worth it, you'll need to be strong to get through it all. So all variety in builds end up narrowing down to about the same thing every time.There are very few item combinations that do anything together uniquely. But I'm not gonna hold it against the game too much. It is still early days. I feel like the game needs a musket or something. I dunno. All that said, I do think the game can be really great instead of mostly frustrating with just a few changes. They really did put a lot of work into it, and it shows. Hopefully they take feedback well, and if they do, I see this being a solid entry into the rouge-lite genre once it comes out of EA.

_childDocuments_.review: The developers mention Rogue Legacy as part of the description - and I think with very good reason.  This is a souped up version of Rogue Legacy.You send your miner down to explore rooms, beat up enemies, find random relics (buffs) and decide whether you want to risk taking random curses (debuffs) in order to get some known or unknown relics.  The relics have a very similar graphical and gameplay impact as in Slay the Spire.  In a similar way you can get lucky on a run and have several relics that work very nicely together.Combat is quite simple.  You choose between swinging your axe and throwing it.  If you have extra bombs you might even drop those as you fight the enemies - but for me I have enough on my plate with using a single attack (throwing axe for me).There are nasty boss monsters like in Dead Cells, but they can be mostly skipped apparently.  I didn't figure out how to skip them myself, but from achievement statistics I can see that 15% of players that got down to a particular level haven't managed to kill the boss guardian for that level yet.Each run doesn't take too long, and once you have beaten a room it is safe to hang around in it.  This means that casual players can easily take breaks (such as us dads who get interruptions) - and easy to dip in and out on shorter gameplay sessions.  You can rush through the rooms at top speed, or you can take your time smashing every barrel and plant for the chance to find a key or bit of meat.There are secret rooms to keep an eye out for, and quite a few rooms hold secret bonuses, such as finding a way to light up bowls of oil.  At the same time some rooms are a bit baffling, such as a secret room I often come across with 3 floating platforms and spikes on the bottom half, but no matter letting myself be spiked, bombing things etc. I've not managed to figure out how to trigger it.The core Rogue Legacy part is the ability to upgrade permanent things using money you picked up in your run.  Max health, hit power, throw power, % of gold kept, throw length, bomb strength, potion duration, number of potions, effects of food etc.The only disappointment in this area is that you can't really focus a strength and push a character down a particular path.  For example I increase my axe throw a few times, now it costs 3000 for next upgrade vs 1000 for my axe hit - so you end up increasing more or less everything without a character build strategy apart from improving certain areas slightly faster.  I would have liked better to be able to take my character down a unique path, and perhaps also influence the skew of relics by paying to have certain genres of relics have a greater or lesser chance to appear each time.There is an additional development area of crafting relics and potions using blueprints founds.  Currently I'm bring a bit picky on the ones I actually build so that I don't have less useful ones appearing in my runs.I'm currently 13 hours in at the time of writing - and there seems plenty more still to do.  There will be some limiting factor around the permanent developments that will eventually limit my gameplay - but for now there is plenty of variety in each run to keep things fresh each time I play - and I assume more variety of relics and potions will be gradually added to the game.My final suggestion to the developers for extending total gameplay is to consider a "prestige" system as you have in idle games - where you reset your character back to zero in order to get a certain number of prestige points to spend on a different type of upgrade tree.  This could help triple the average total gameplay hours of casual players.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a great introduction to the rogue-like genre, with charm and great art to boot, but also offers plenty to keep veterans coming back for more. Undermine walks that fine line between "sense of progression" and "just one more try". I'm someone who's generally wary of rogue-likes. While I almost always love the aesthetic and those 'OMG-long-runs' that happen every once in awhile, I often find the lack of progression and/or the constant restarting to be highly frustrating.That said, I've spent my fair share of time in the genre. Of course like anyone else, I praise instant classics like Dead Cells and Binding of Isaac; I was a fan of Hero Siege and Rogue Legacy. In that same vein, Undermine might just be another standard for the rogue-like genre; Undermine deserves to be held in that same regard.There's plenty to enjoy here as well. Beyond the great art and music, it has a nice collection of tile sets (five+ iirc) and a spectacular risk/reward item system. Like most rogue-likes, there are trinkets to collect that give the standard benefits you've expect. Where the game gets really interesting is in its "blessing"/"curse" system. There are blessings that bestow incremental buffs (e.g. swing damage, throw distance, max hp, etc.), but they are almost always combined with a curse. A curse can decrease your stats (e.g. swing damage, throw distance, max hp. etc.). The end result is a sort of min/max system whereby if you really want to push your character to the highest strength levels and delve into the mine as deep as possible you will have to give something up to get something in return. The net result is the ability to craft your character for that run. Have you gotten two throw buffs and a swing debuff? I guess it's a throw run. Did you get a really interesting bomb trinket? Time to play with bombs. Etc.And it's in that trinket and blessing/curse system that the game begins to shine. Granted it's not necessarily as deep or varied as Binding of Isaac for example, but considering how much more Undermine has to offer beyond just those two systems, it's not noticeable.I'd rather not explain more about how the game works or what you'll discover, because that's part of the joy of Undermine. Rest assured, the game has a lot to offer and for those seeking more replayability and harder/longer challenges, you will be very satisfied.

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of people will tell you how great roguelikes like Binding of Isaac, Dead Cells or Hades are and while I agree that those are great games, the one I always liked the most was Undermine. I think the reason I liked this game the most was because it wasn't overly complicated and had the core concept nailed down perfectly.Undermine is inspired by The Legend of Zelda and it shows in its gameplay. You play as a poor peasant who was forced along with many of his colleagues to get down a mine, investigate what is going on there and retrieve seal stones to deal with an evil god. A lot of stuff to handle for a poor overworked peasant. The gameplay of Undermine is easy to understand and never gets too crazy. You have a pickaxe which is your main weapon. You can swing it around like a sword or you can throw it like a boomerang. That way you have both a melee attack and a ranged attack which you can use however you want. You also can place bombs if you have any and those deal a lot of damage, unfortunately to you too. Bombs can also break stones and reveal secrets rooms if you bomb the right wall. You will also carry a small familiar with you, you start with a canary bird that collects gold for you but you can get other pets later. Each pet has three levels and on each level it gets a useful effect for you. You level up those pets during your run, each pet has a different method to get XP and some take very long to level up but have very powerful effects.Everywhere in the mine you can find gold embedded inside walls and rocks, hitting it a few times with your pickaxe will release it across the floor. But be fast to collect it because a neutral enemy type, called the pilfer, will appear if any gold is on the ground. Thiose little slime bastards will grab any free gold they find and escape with it, but a single hit will send them flying away. There are also different pilfer variants, like a bomb variant that drops a bomb if hit and a beefy one that takes more hits and pushes you away on contact. There is even a golden pilfer who will run aimlessy around and try to get away from you but drops a lot of gold if hit.Gold is your currency in the game buy items in shops, each floor has a shop but often the shop is locked behind a door. You can open locked doors and also locked chests with a key but those are rare drops. The shop usually has a selection of keys, bombs, food (which heals you), potions and even relics. The last one are items that give you a passive effect for your run. Relics can have all kinds of effects and can give you buffs for your attacks, your character, your bombs or even duplicate gold and items you find during the run. Some relics can be even combined for better effects. Besides relics, there are also blessings that you can unlock. Those are more simple buffs for your run. They usually affect your stats directly like attack damage, HP, how much gold you find and so on. You get blessings from shrines but using a shrine for a blessing will always give you a curse. Curses are the opposite of blessings and give you a small or big debuff depending on how unlucky you are, those are almost always simple stat reductions and having the mirrored versions of a curse and a blessing will simply negate each other. You can also use shrines to purge a curse but this will damage you and with each purge you take more damage from it.There are also potions which provide a tempory buff or can simply heal you. YOu can carry potions with you and use them at any point but you have a limited amount of slots for them.The general goal of the game is to reach the lowest floor and beat every enemy and every boss that is in your way. Each floor has multiple rooms that are connected together just like in The Legend of Zelda. If there are any enemies inside a room, the doors will close and you can only get out once you have defeated them all. Unlike The Binding of Isaac you cannot bomb open doors. On each floor you will always find a shop and a relic room but there are also secret rooms with additional rewards. You don't have to visit every room but it is advised because that way you get the most gold out of it, even if you take more damage on the way. There is usually plenty of healing, the game is overall more forgiving for a roguelike. The game is divided into multiple zones and each zone is made of four floors. The last floor on a zone will contain a powerful boss that, if you beat him, will give you one of the seals that you need to unlock the final boss. But, surprisingly, you don't have to beat the bosses to win a run. Each floor with a boss has a way to skip the boss entirely. And, if you have beaten the boss for the first time, you never have to beat him on any other runs. YOu can still do it for a gold bonus but once you have beaten him you can just bypass him completely. If you die or beat a run, you return back to the first floor of the mine which acts as your base of operations. Leftover gold you had can e used to buy permanent upgrades but if you died you will loose a god portion of it. You can also find Thorium inside the mine which can be used to unlock more relics, potions and blessings for your runs. There is also a small shop which sells you small items for your next run so you don't start emptyhanded. Investing in all those things will make the game easier over time which makes the game more of a roguelite. But fear not, for those who want a more challenging experience, there is also the Othermine. This part ofg the gameplay is unlocked once you have reached the end of the mine for the first time and offers a more traditional roguelike experience. All your permanent upgrades are deactivated here, only your unlocked items count. The Othermine also has some other rules to make the gameplay more unpredictble and give the player a good challenge. There is no big reward for beating the Othermine, it is simply meant for players who want a more traditional roguelike mode.And, if you want to play daily challenges, this is here too. The game offers "WHIP", a challenge mode flor the main game that adds different muttators to the usual gameplay. Getting high scores on those will also unlock alternative skins for your familiars. It does not affect gameplay in any way and is just meant to entertain the player. I like that about the game, they don't lock any gameplay elements behind harder difficulties and you either get nothing or simply cosmetics.Overall the reason why I love this game so much is because it is easy to understand, easy to get into but still has many good items and synergies that give you interesting runs. This is the type of game that I like to play after a hard day at work to relax, a game where I don't have to think too hard or need all my concentration for.

_childDocuments_.review: Another fun dungeon crawler but nothing very special.If you're into this genre like me, you'll probably like this solidly executed roguelite. I think it's also something for people who enjoy the visual style and want to try it, as it's a fairly forgiving roguelike - even if you die early, there are a lot of abilities you can upgrade or unlock using the ressources you found. Additionally, once you beat a boss, you don't have to fight it in subsequent runs until you choose to reset it and increase the difficulty.There's a lot of variety in all mechanics of the game: You can find a lot of items with vastly different effects, that force you to make spontaneous decisions about your build and playstyle in a run. You can take risks by taking on curses which grant you in turn more benefits in a different area, allowing you to boost specific abilities that are useful to your current loadout. There are a lot of different enemies to fight, including good boss-design. Overall, the game gives you a bunch of fun and very different mechanics to experiment with and well designed enemies to test them against.On one hand I don't think Undermine stands out a ton compared to other games in the genre - it has the same formula of repeating randomized runs, always pushing a bit further until a final goal and a progression system to unlock new gameplay possibilities throughout. If this interests you and you haven't played games like Hades or Dead Cells yet, I recommend starting there. However, if you're still looking for more of the same formula with slightly different spin, theme and mechanics, you might enjoy this like I did.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: They've fixed a lot of the issues I've had. Risky gameplay isn't punished so harshly now and most of the curses are fair, ie, they do the exact same thing as the blessings but in reverse. Curses are also easier to get rid of now. There are still plenty of relics that don't do much, but many were buffed up a bit so that you can feel an impact. The spider room was actually fixed (the spiders are more spread around the room and they don't aggro you all at once) but I've not had a chance to face the boss again since one match and you're done. All in all, they did a good job and I'm glad to see the active development.Pros-Good sprites, good animations.-fun gameplay loop of slowly powering up your characterCons-punishes risky gameplay, rewards boring tactics. If the game offers you a cursed chest, 9 times out of 10 the curse is going to be way more debilitating than whatever treasure might be inside. By which I mean, it will reward you with something like 50g and maybe a key, but punish you with buffing all enemies with poison attacks that double their effective damage or empty out every chest you find for the rest of that run or make you lose max health every time you kill an enemy...even though killing every enemy in a room is mandatory to progress.-It's not just that you should ignore cursed chests either. You'll also come across levers which you can pay 15 health to pull with a chance of a reward. Testing them out, I pulled them as much as I could in three separate runs, knocking my health all the way to 0. In that time, 80% of the time they dropped worthless skulls, and the other 17% of the time they dropped 5 gold, and 3% of the time they dropped a food item to heal me for 20 health. Basically ever RNG mechanic in the game is rigged against the player, making the optimal play to IGNORE ALL NOVEL ENCOUNTERS.-The curses are super debilitating, but the vast majority of the relics you can find in a run are almost always mediocre at best. There's a lot of variance, with the best one I've encountered being "your ranged attack autohits two extra times after a successful hit", but most are middling like "you don't take damage from spike traps" or "gold does a tiny bit of damage when you mine and throw it around the room uncontrollably", down to incredibly useless stuff like "increased defense at critical health, ie you might be able to take an one extra hit at low health, unless that attack killed you outright" or "the shop stocks an extra item, feel free to buy it, though that will gimp your longterm progress"-some of the rooms can be unfair. In particular, sometimes you'll be put in a room filled with spiders that all immediately jump on you and hit you with a ton of poison damage, and since they stagger their jumps, avoiding all of them while fighting back is nearly impossible.-the 2nd boss is a giant headache. I'm not much of an expert at gaming, but I can at least handle the final boss of Dead Cells with 2 boss cells activated, the final boss of Hades with 50 skulls active, and cleared some runs of binding of isaac. The second boss is more difficult than most of those because it's constantly spawning minions, it's invincible everywhere aside from its butt, it moves around unpredictably with only a few chances for you to land attacks, and when you do attack it, it has a ton of health, all the while hoping it doesn't change direction to immediately hit you and lop off a fifth of your health twice in a row because the cooldown on taking damage from enemy attacks is basically nonexistent. The game has potential, but it's very Early Access and rough right now.

I feel like I'm hit with projectiles I dodge, and occasionally not hit with projectiles I don't. 2. Sometimes gold can appear in walls in the corridors between rooms, if you accidentally enter the room while trying to pick up gold, any you've left behind will be gone.3. Cursed chests/torches are usually not worth whatever is inside of them. Some curses are basically benign (shop cost inflation), and others make boss fights impossible (swing speed -). There may be some tweaking there for these to feel balanced.4. The pilfers are really annoying. I get that they add some urgency to grabbing gold, but they just annoy me since they make clearing an empty room more tedious.Quick tip: Play with a controller, or at least try it. This game was made for it. KB+M controls work (I played my first 6 hours or so on them) but I found controller play to be much easier.

_childDocuments_.review: Updating my December 2019 review to reflect my views now the game has been further updated.The Othermine update truly makes this a solid Roguelite, and is truly the mode the game should be played. It addresses my previous gripes of the game - runs are now shorted, relics are fewer and transmuting/rerolling them is much harder to do, and your gold actually matters. By limiting the choice you have, it makes your decisions more impactful and your run play out in its own isolated way - no more is the game "transmute until you get Key Blade or a similarly broken item" and instead you play each run through the Undermine in a unique way. My first Othermine victory was a throwing build, a build I never used in regular ascensions 1-15 because why would I bother? But my Othermine run strengthened that area of my play and limited what other options were available. It was fun, it was unique and it made me appreciate more of the items in the game and regularly made my decisions more impactful.Previously, I'd have given this a 6/10, now this is easily an 8/10 with more room for improvements if they lean into Othermine as the "true" mode of the game with further updates.

_childDocuments_.review: As a huge roguelite fan, I've gotta say UnderMine has been a blast so far. _childDocuments_.review: Skip. This is inherently a frustrating classic isometric roguelike.Play Binding of Isaac, Risk of Rain, Dead Cells, or FTL if you like Roguelikes.Play Rogue Legacy or Hades if you like Rogue-RPGs.If you like difficult games, this is more just frustrating.Play anything else if these are not your thing.The bombs are highly limited but key to gameplay. Bombs are used for both damage (see trite 'RPG upgrades') and for finding secret rooms, often on accident as there's no indicator except sparkles, which don't always appear. The special abilities don't make you feel special and are often either a plain stat increase, side-grade, or self-harming playstyle. You'll get bounced around by enemies and bombs and control taken from you, fall down a hole, take damage, and bounced again; the only means of dodging is to jump, which takes away control. Controls aren't very responsive. There's no just-in-time response to pits or dodging. Art is good but animation feels repetitive and unfeeling (get hit, bounce, anything, same walking animation). The addition of upgrades bought with gold is just a crap unlocking schema which feels more like an added reason to grind. I wanted to like this. I love Rogue Legacy and Hades. I'm not big into arcade games (which is what a roguelike is after finishing grindy item unlocks), but I know a good one when I see it, and this isn't.

_childDocuments_.review: Feels like an isaac clone but more annoying. Rooms are just designed not to be hard but to deliberately be annoying.For example, there is rooms where you gotta go across while dodging spinning blades and holes. But the damage debuffs are as obnoxious as they were in the final stage of Hades where fire, poison, electricity, ect just MELT your HP at an insanely fast rate.Chests are fun unless you get ones that give you said debuff, unlike the bomb ones in isaac where you have a chance to avoid them, if you open a chest you have a chance to just be screwed out of a lot of HP. _childDocuments_.review: For me, Undermine was one of those games that I sucked super hard for at least the first handful of runs, but the Roguelite elements of freeing NPCs to unlock purchasable items next run, steadily buying upgrades to beef up my "peasant", while learning all the lore, easter eggs, and ridiculous mechanic possibilities I could do with the right relics and potions unlocked, quickly made this game approach a concerning level of addictive for me. Brings the completionist out of me like the other great Roguelite/like games of this style like none other. Highly recommend to any who relate to my description. Great value for the price and potential time sink.
_childDocuments_.name: UnderMine

_childDocuments_.review: After some playtime I decided to give this game a negative review. It started out promising with a beautiful art style, a fun combat system (with a mix of melee and range attacks) and much stuff to discover (items, NPCs, new levels).Unfortunately, the game becomes one thing after said playtime: tedious. Mining for gold becomes a boring grind, and the upgrades you get for it don't feel powerful or effective at all. The game offers a variety of items - buffs, companions, potions and such - but you won't see 80 percent of them. Because they never appear (nor their recipes). Some buffs offer synergies, so they evolve into a more powerful version - I've only managed to get one of those...Another thing is the control of your runs. Or the lack thereof. You can't really influence, which buffs you get, some of them are utterly useless, some of them have the same effect as another buff. Your success is greatly depending on luck. Which adds to the grind factor.There are 5 bosses, after that the game is supposed to offer new challenge modes and a new dungeon. I never got that far. I think I could handle boss no. 4, but after some fruitless attempts with nearly the same useless buffs/items I asked myself: Why continue playing?

_childDocuments_.name: UnderMine

_childDocuments_.review: If you are in it for the grind, this game is for you. It's a great game to pick up and play after a long day of work. It doesn't require a lot of thought, and the room gen is just entertaining enough to keep it interesting, but boring enough to be low stress. Not a great gamer? No problem. This game is all about slow and incremental progression that gives you enough time to learn how to git gud. I think playing this actually made me better at playing other rogue-like games. Plus it's cute, it has a lot of easy and satisfying achievements on Steam, and can be played with a controller or keyboard+mouse. It's probably not the game for everyone, but I am enjoying it for what it is!

_childDocuments_.review: !CONTAINS SPOILERS! Overall the game is really, really good and has a lot of moments and items that made me go "nice!" or "wow!"Polished graphic style,good non-invasive bg music,variation of attacks even on enemies with the same base model,lots of different rooms and secrets to find,many different levels of selectable difficulty between Classic and Othermine + Hexes,Also being able to chose between two independent types of basic attack and relative upgrades gives a nice tactic choice in order to approach enemies, even if it's the first time you see them.The Curse system adds a good amount of decision making in order to balance between benefits and maluses you get from smashing/opening/buying certain things.Now to the things that, for me, might need some tweaking:Your character is absolutely anonymous and will remain like that through the whole game even in overpowered, items-rich runs; apart from orbital items, I suffer not seeing SOME change in it. Like wearing one of the 4 pairs of boots i dropped, or armor pieces, or the Indiana hat.Also related to this, weapons have very very few unique attack effects that clearly distinc them from one another; most of the times, finding a melee weapon translates in "you swing harder, bigger, faster" and a thrown weapon reads "you throw your pickaxe harder, bigger, faster". I wish that, at least graphicly, something other than numbers would give away that I'm wielding a "freaking cursed sword of oneshotting foes".Finally: combined relics, not enough of them; right now the game has 12 and I wish it had a hundred times more, this has to be improved.

_childDocuments_.review: I've really enjoyed my time with this game, and I'm still looking forward to new content and release. Runs are long enough to feel satisfying, and you start to get attached to your build/character before dying or finishing the bottom level. This game is much like Isaac but with a lot of progression overarching each run. Initially, the runs feel pretty varied based on the items and upgrades that are found in randomized levels. Eventually, after buying a good amount of upgrades and finding a lot of the items (and there are a lot), it starts to feel much more consistent, making it easier to put together certain types of builds. Some rooms continue to feel challenging in late game (of current content). The latest update adding familiars adds another layer of gameplay as well. Highly recommended for an early access buy, and it's well worth the purchase price.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun gold-grind roguelite with RPG elements. Interesting curse/blessing system for buffs and debuffs that can be managed throughout a run. It's kinda like gambling on your run every time you come across an alter or a cursed chest/room, seeing if you can come out ahead by potentially removing really bad curses along the way and reaping the benefits of the extra blessings and relics you get by potentially nuking your run with a nasty amount of curses. Challenging in the short term with big payoffs and rewards for those willing to put their nose to the grindstone and dig into this thing. Cool cast of characters for the small amount of lore available right now. Would love to see it keep expanding somehow and get a little deeper (pun intended) on that aspect of the game. Overall a solid game and it's still Early Access.
_childDocuments_.name: UnderMine

_childDocuments_.review: Most times, nostalgia is a mistake.Most of the difficulty in this game is due to poor control and annoying/clumsy design choices. Besides an unfortunate desire of the designers to restrict you to old school zelda controls, you get a wonky jump with no air control. They'd likely try to pawn this off as "plan your inputs carefully," but that's a mentality better reserved for games that have tight player interaction like enter the gungeon, where your tools are useful and varied, not so loose that you can get shoved into pits by hard to see bottles dropped with gold. Most fights involve running around, swinging and then mashing jump to avoid incoming armored punish from your spongy foes. Unlike other roguelikes, it's rather difficult to find relics and blessings that fit together, and those that you do generally fall under three camps. 1. Generally good, flat bonuses that are useful but don't really affect your playstyle for a run. 2. Mediocre build changing items that force you to play suboptimally and can't be removed. 3. Useless chaff. There are maybe 2-3 relics that are great and unfortunately game breaking - having them means I'm beating the next boss, until then grind gold again to get past the next gear check, but they're also boring (like the soul aegis).There's a misvaluation of opportunity costs everywhere because most choices you have terrible returns for the risk. Everything costs too much, and gold is unreliable so the cost of a run is prohibitive - this leads to runs where you get as much gold as you can and die, and then true runs where you try to beat content. That's inherently boring game design.Blessings are trash due to the lack of predictability of curses, and are so weak that it's almost always a waste of time to get them even if you can double back for an omori to cleanse them. The other trade you'll often find yourself making is whether to carry keys or bombs, but besides a few relics, keys = gold and meat, and bombs = gold  meat and damage. The bomb relics are all "bombastic" and unfortunately risky and stupid. In most cases you don't want to upgrade your bombs because the bomb upgrades hurt you and are less predictable. 1-2 of them are better for bossing but destroy items you want. Also, there are several "dead" rooms that spawn with nothing in them, or rooms that take lots of resources to provide you with a trapped box. The latter is par for the course with Roguelikes, but Roguelikes also rarely give you rooms that have immense rewards to counteract this. I have pretty much never found a room or item in this game that made me feel a sense of satisfaction.You're better off with Enter the Gungeon, Hades, Dead Cells, hell even Rogue Legacy is more entertaining.

_childDocuments_.review: I gave my best shot but I cannot find enjoyment playing this game. Combat is barebones yet it is also slow & repetitive at the same time. Floors are filled with traps and pitfalls to the point you have to actively focus at looking around the room while multitasking fighting enemies, which gets tiring & annoying very fast. Jumping is clunky and you have no air control. You aren't even allowed to relax and feel rewarded for collecting Gold, because Pilfers constantly try to steal it as soon as it drops on the ground. Most relics (at least during my playtime) fail at making a major impact or making runs feel different from each other. Upgrading/progression also feels like it moves at a glacial pace, you spend something like 20 minutes on a decent run and after losing half of your gold on death you spend the rest of it on only being slightly (if not barely) stronger, making the game feel unrewarding for how much time you're spending on it. If anything, I feel WEAKER because it seemed like as I kept doing runs, the game would spawn stronger new enemies on the first floors, so instead of doing better & progressing, I'd die at around the same points and get stuck. Making the player feel like they are becoming weaker in a game about upgrading & strengthening the character, is bizarre. That was when I ran out of patience with the game.
_childDocuments_.name: UnderMine

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Overall the music and the graphics of this game is great and i had a whole lot of fun.  However there are stuff that separate this from an amazing roguelite game like hades. Played for a solid 13 hours and it is quite fun.  it draws on a lot of mechanics from old school zelda games which i love,  however there are a few issues i find which separates this game from an amazing rouguelite.1) I still recommend it as i had some fun but this is not hades.  it takes a while to build up the equivalence of a boon in hades and there are a lot more trashy ones which makes you feel like you wasted your time.  2) unlike hades, you know when you stumble upon an amazing build and the game really makes you feel satisfied.  you feel powerful and it makes you want to keep playing.  Undermine just lacked that little rewarding feeling.  I got 5x relics (boon equivalence) that boosted my throw damage but i didn't feel strong, the relics didn't have amazing visual/audio effects to feel different.  Overall you just feel like you're stacking numbers. 3) hit boxes doesn't feel very clean, sometimes you miss a mob even though it feels like you hit them.4) quite similarly there is a few times i walked near a hole, totally still on the edge and my guy just fell in.5) progression seems a bit unbalance.  I get that they want to make gold easily obtainable so that it reduces the grind.  however i feel like those upgrades makes it so that you are very strong which makes the game easier (make you tankier, do more damage, more range).  In comparison to hades (again, i am using this example cos that was a rouguelite that just blew my mind) which the permanent unlocks are a completely different playstyle, something that is more challenging/higher learning curve with higher potential to get you further each run. So i feel like the permanent progression mechanic of undermine just shortens the re-playability of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: UnderMine

_childDocuments_.review: I will give this a thumbs up with a big BUT. Undermine is a fun rogue-lite with cute pixel-art graphics and a satisfying meta-progression where you permanently upgrade your character and hub base. At least for the first 10-15 hours. The game gets pretty grindy later when enemies deal out massive amounts of damage and also take dozens of hits before dying so that you have to upgrade your equipment to stand a chance. And upgrading equipment gets expensive ... very expensive. Later stages also feel overwhelming with how many enemies and traps there can be in cramped places. Sometimes there is hardly any room to properly react and you can get caught up in chain reactions that are out of your control.It doesn't help that the risk/reward mechanics in this game feel very unrewarding. 90% of any risk you take will be bad for you. The positive effects rarely seem worth the potential negatives. Or you will just straight out lose copious amounts of gold and health whenever engaging in one of the slot machines like the mechanics of the game. Which ultimately led me to just not engage in any risk/reward stuff and just go with what I get guaranteed. Another problem is that you can't really create awesome builds in this game. The temporary upgrades and potions you get feel like they hardly make a difference. Sure, some upgrades are really good, but the chances to get them in a run are small and most of the time you will clear rooms with a cumbersome mix of jumping around and throwing and swinging your axe, trying to not get hit. And yeah, those jumping mechanics suck. Instead of just having a button to dodge enemy attacks like in other rouge-likes you have to awkwardly jump around with your character often leading to landing in traps or chasms.Still, I enjoy playing this for "just another" run to get more gold, to work towards the next upgrading hoping to finally clear the next floor. It helps that runs can be quick and that there are shortcuts and unlocks to quickly get where you left.
_childDocuments_.name: UnderMine

_childDocuments_.review: Movement feels sluggish. Combat is pretty simplistic. You have two attacks: swinging your pickax, or tossing it to have it return like a boomerang. The former animation locks you until you finish the swing - which hampers combat flow imo. Enemies get really annoying late game - doesn't help that healing is somewhat sparse. Most relics - items that give you abilities during each run - are pretty anemic. The ones I encountered hardly altered my current run, although I did run into a flat "Increase Damage" relic a few times. But yet, the game requires you to use keys to unlock relic rooms after a certain floor. Ugh.Oh, but I forgot the STUPIDEST thing about UnderMine: .In UnderMine, gold is a very important resource. It's used for purchasing items from shops during a run, AND is used to permanently upgrade your character's stats (max health, ranged/melee damage, etc.) from the game's hubworld. When you die, a portion of your current gold is kept - and you use this to buy upgrades to your health, swing damage, throw range, etc. gold is dropped in a room, a bunch of NPCs called pilfers spawn and try to snag it. If they grab a gold piece and get to the edge of the room's screen, they get away with your hard-earned gold. You have to hit them with your clunky swing attack, or aim just right and throw your pickax. Either way, you can end up missing a few pilfers because of the clunky attack animations, and be short of whatever gold dropped in a room.Now, making a resource/"XP" for a character a time-limited pick-up is not a new mechanic at all; Nuclear Throne's rads (XP) disappear in a few seconds, and Voidigo's shards (currency) de-value over time the moment they drop.But UnderMine's pilfers are non-damaging enemies that sometimes move faster than your character, and can swarm over gold easily if a room contains active hazards like sawblades or fire-orb firing turrets. One time I walked over a pit to reach a treasure chest, on a spindly-pair of minecart tracks that had a sawblade running on them. I got to a chest that spewed a bunch of gold on the tracks. At least half of the gold was either snagged by pilfers or knocked off into the pit by the moving sawblade - lost forever. Real fun.  I believe you can purchase a pass to prevent pilfers from spawning during a run, but it costs a ludicrous amount of gold. Wow!Did I mention sometimes, a pilfer that drops an active bomb upon death spawns when gold drops? Who even thought this was a good mechanic?
_childDocuments_.name: UnderMine

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun, well-priced, and addicting roguelite with a Zelda Link to the Past aesthetic where you battle your way through floors/bosses/etc collecting randomized artefacts and power-ups making some insane OP builds and building around drops. There's a huge plethora of metaprogression upgrades into unlockable familiars, upgrading your pickaxe damage/throws/armors/potion slots/etc etc. If you liked games like Spelunky, Dead Cells, Enter the Gungeon, Nuclear Throne, Immortal Redneck, Rogue Legacy, etc, you'll like this. It may not be super innovative on the roguelite-metaprogression formula itself, but it's gorgeous, very well polished, and very slick.And so, so, so many  moments of "OH FOR F--- SAKE THAT WAS A BS DEATH ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥! ok ok ok chill out... one more run... this is my last one i promise I've got this down I'm gunna do it this time" *6 hours laters its 3AM* "ok just one more run i really gotta sleep since i have work tomorrow.... totally got it this time i swear....."
_childDocuments_.name: UnderMine

_childDocuments_.review: Full of awful design choices, bad game flow and bad progression that other games in the genre that came before it fixed.- 4 direction swing? Why? Just feels like a lazy choice trying to ape 'retro' games when it's unecessary- Hefty animation lock and unresponsive controls- 'Feast or famine' RNG drops - no keys? no bombs? Guess you're not getting any items this run!- Needlessly starved progression, as the gold you gather and spend in dungeon is also used on permanent upgrades- Gold is stolen from you on death! Why? What's the point of taking a hefty percentage of it except to soak up money on the upgrade to lose less? If that upgrade is a necessity, it should just be baseline, or not exist at all! Taking more gold into the next dungeon run doesn't help anyway as you're reliant on a shop showing up.- 'Pilfers' show up and steal your gold if you don't pick it up quick enough - why? What does this add to gameplay except that you have to run around grabbing gold in an empty, or that you leave all the gold piles until a room is clear of enemies?- Hitboxes on attacks way larger than their animation- 'Vacuum' pits that suck you in despite not being close enough to fall in them - I assume this is because the game is lazily designed on a grid- Over reliance on spikes and traps- The majority of items aren't impactful, some are even completely useless, there's no feeling of growing stronger- No normalisation on curses - some are merely bad, some are utterly crippling, double costs means doors now take two keys? You barely get enough keys to begin with! That's an absurd 'design choice'- Bosses are just damage sponges with one or two attacks rather than having an interesting mechanics- Currency to unlock new relics is needlessly rare and far too much is requiredAny developer in this genre just needs to look at Enter the Gungeon and the patches they applied over time to learn how to actually make and balance their game. Changing key mechanics to make items accessible, improving gameplay flow and function, just overall polish!This game isn't it. Don't buy, not even on sale.

If being relentlessly ground under the bootheel of a sadist dev appeals to you, then by all means enjoy Undermine; otherwise get Rogue Legacy for a much better take on a generational rogue-lite.

The upgrades each have their own dynamics and synergies are varied and relevant, this is great!Visuals are not very stylized, they are just genuinely very pretty in a comfortable way.The curses add a dimension to the game that keeps things interesting, I love that!If you like action rogue-lites and are ok with keeping the same attacks/movement scheme throughout the game, this is one of the best there is!

_childDocuments_.review: You ever heard of Binding Of Isaac? Think that, but instead of unlocking new characters, items, challenges, and bosses as you play, you get money and blueprints. Spend this money to get higher base stats, and unlock new items, and keep trying and trying and trying again to beat a run. Of course dying does set you back a bit of gold, but there's items and upgrades that prevent too big a loss. In addition, the combat is more than just ranged. You have a melee attack as well, which leaves you vulnerable in a way but has higher damaged than the ranged attack. There's also a curse/blessing system which can add a lot of variety to a run outside of the items you get. All in all, a great game if you've played the heck out of Binding of Isaac and are looking for a new distinct flavour in the genre. Just be ready to sacrifice a few peasants along the way.

It's even better now with the addition of faster movement between the rooms, more items/synergies, more levels  and other QOL-changes. Cool graphics and variated combat. _childDocuments_.review: I played this game back in early access quite a while ago and loaded it up a few times throughout. Now that it's been released, I gave it another shot. This isn't a bad game, but I don't like it, and therefore do not recommend it. The problem for me is that it just isn't fun. I love rogue-lites/likes and dungeon crawlers but there are a few gameplay elements here that add up to a final product that mostly just annoys me. A few things such as: 1) healing is very sparse and you take a lot of damage easily. This in itself wouldn't be so bad except that there are certain things that contribute to you losing health too easily such as:   -- getting any kind of "homing" or "duplicating" relics and hitting a lightning mite shocks you beyond your control (for a whopping 30hp)  -- it's very easy to get pinballed around the screen and knocked into holes  -- certain curses damage your health (I'm thinking of one that just changed all locks to require 50hp instead of a key)  -- potions feel almost worthless; they don't heal for much hp and/or they feel gimmicky (I'm thinking of the one potion I find fairly often that causes the next damage you take to heal you instead ... one time)- this all leads to a situation that constantly feels tense ... but not in a good way. Healing foods feel common enough but they heal a pitiful amount. 2) Curses! Want some blessings? Have some curses! Want to remove a curse at the prayer altar? Gonna cost you some hp ... and you don't get to choose which curse to remove! - some curses suck more than others (dropping one bomb uses 2; no more picking up potions; etc.)- I can't stress this enough -- it sucks that you can't choose which curse to remove but it does so seemingly randomly- you can't really avoid curses as they are packed in with positive thingsNot only does this mechanic feel unfun, it mentally feels bad because a curse is a "negative" thing and they just pile on. It becomes an annoyance. I think it is supposed to be a "challenging" mutator to runs, but I really dislike it. 3) Relics & blessings- They just don't feel as fun as they should. There are some that have cool effects, but lots of them are just "do more swing damage" -- which is often negated by the increasing number of curses you pick up. 4) Fast travelYou eventually get the option to skip ahead in the dungeon when you enter.  However, doing so leaves you woefully under-powered and unprepared. They tried to address this by giving you a "care package" with some relics ... but it doesn't include bombs or keys, so good luck navigating the floor you just arrived on. Overall, this game looks good and it's obvious work went into it. It's technically a good game and I know there are people who love it. However, I just don't enjoy it and find it more an exercise in frustration. It's not that it's even particularly difficult, just really annoying and dissatisfying.

_childDocuments_.review: Disappointed with how the game progresses. At first Undermine comes off as bright and fun with lots of potential to discover while definitely hitting that "just one more run" mentality that steals hours from you before you realize the sun's gone down, but the further you get into the game, the more bafflingly empty and repetitive it feels.This is because of a decision that takes a lot of life out of future runs being that bosses do not respawn. So if you defeated the first floor's boss, it will never come back (until you complete the entire game) and since a lot of your progression will be tied to losing runs and using the gold you've gathered during lost runs to upgrade your stats, you will end up doing many runs that feel like slow methodical grinds for gold and not exciting unique romps into a fun randomized world with exciting battles and payoffs at the end of each floor. The further you get into Undermine, the worse this problem becomes.There is a system that lets you skip floors entirely, but using it feels like you're setting yourself up for failure. Not only will you miss out on all the gold you could've collected during a full normal run, but you'll lose out on tons of upgrade relics, blessings, familiar XP, and consumables along the way leaving you feeling completely underpowered (The game tries to compensate you by handing you 2 free relics per floor you skipped, but on average you'd get 4-5 relics per floor + many other minor upgrades if you played normally) Thus, if you wanna give yourself the best shot at overall progression, you have to slowly grind through the entire game sans its bosses every single time. This becomes incredibly boring when you're in the end game and have to go through 20 levels that take upwards to an hour to complete before having a chance at fighting its 5th boss.The bread and butter of a proper rouguelite, imo, is having enough variety to keep the many runs you're going to do feeling different and unique. Undermine is rather restrictive with its weapon which does not change or get altered in any significant ways from its items so the game never feels different at any point. At most, maybe you'll have a run where your melee has slightly more range, or you prefer using your ranged attack because you got several damage buffs to it. You'll also be seeing the same items all the time, many of them feeling rather unhelpful.Undermine has a lot of charm to it, great graphics, fun characters, and it controls very nicely. And at first, it feels very fun and fresh as you have plenty of mysteries to uncover from its mines and powerful foes to defeat, but the further you get, the more boring it all becomes, and a rougelite shouldn't feel like a sluggish grind before you've even fully beaten it once. After beating Undermine, I had very little reason to want to replay it or do more runs because all I could remember is the taste in my mouth of grinding gold for hours on end and the disappointment of runs feeling too identical to each other to at least add some excitement to the mix.If you're looking for something that'll kill a good 5-10 hours while retaining its charm or if you're someone who loves grinding up stats to better tackle future runs, you might like this game a lot! But if you're hoping for a rouguelite that'll let you replay it over and over always promising something fun, silly, or unique, this won't be your next Isaac.
_childDocuments_.name: UnderMine

_childDocuments_.review: It surprises me that this is sitting at "overwhelmingly positive". I... guess I would attribute that to Binding of Isaac players being starved for something new.  It's certainly not bad, and since it's still got "Early Access" status, maybe it will get somewhere interesting, but--currently--I'm done after an hour or so. Wish it weren't too late to get a refund.Why do I feel this way? How does it fall short? The art style is pretty good. The basic mechanics are... serviceable, if not exciting. The biggest problem with this game is that it feels samey almost immediately. The character sprites are compelling enough, but the elements used in the procedural generation are so few, and so consistent, that it never feels like exploration. It feels like what it is: a small network of rooms that will disappear forever as soon as I find a trapdoor. I can hardly tell one run from another. And the absolutely-never-fail nature of the creatures that steal my gold? Makes them groan-worthy. They always arrive, and they always arrive at exactly the same pace, and they almost always beat you to something. It makes me not want to mine gold. And I LIKE mining gold!Three things would thrill me, if achieved before the end of EA:1) Much more variety to the tiles and other elements that make up the procedural generation.2) Punchier sound / haptic feedback design. Make me feel the combat, viscerally.3) Here's a thought: folks emulate Binding of Isaac, but they never seem to go after what I personally think is the most intriguing element of that game: complex synergies between items. Novel combinations. Transformations (in the case of this game, maybe this could manifest itself as class-style equipment variations. And--hey--even though there's not technically much story to Isaac, the very NAMES chosen for the elements are colorful, evocative, and make each fresh run feel like it's got its own story to tell.I give this game a 6/10, and I will try to remember to check back to see where you've taken it.

_childDocuments_.review: UnderMine has good music/art/characters and it feels polished. But the core gameplay loop is just repetitive and tedious. Randomization (maps, artifacts, potions) barely changes anything. Combat is roughly limited to two attacks (close & long-range) which never change. And combat movement isn't precise. There is also a horribly slow 2 seconds transition between combat zones and monsters that try to steal your gold as if you had too much of it. So you're left with repeating the same levels over and over again with almost no differences in gameplay to come back fighting whatever you died on until you learn the mechanic. With enough grind, you might get enough upgrades to see a noticeable impact. It's lightyears away from titles like Hades or Dead Cells.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR; Worth it for <$8, could be a $20 game if the devs keep with it and sort out the issues. If you've played a handful of other rogue-likes, keep this one on the watchlist and wait for some updates before committing.I'm aware that this game is currently in development, but this has been my experience thus far:The game is fun enough, but at this point in does not offer much fresh material to the ever-expanding list of rogue-likes. The combat is stiff, your character is slower than many enemies, and relies on jumping as the only means of avoiding attacks. Armed with a boomerang-pickaxe, you must delve down through the levels to uncover the mystery of what's causing underground tremors. The art style is cute and light, but the systems in place for risky investments into your character are quite unbalanced. Ordinarily, such trade-offs are handled in the form of minor setbacks like max HP loss or minor curses. On two different occasions I accepted a curse, which caused my character to receive double damage, and in return I got one measly bomb, which there are usually plenty of lying around. The curse system does not ever seem  to make the investments worth the setback, and so far I have been completely put-off from accepting the risk, because no matter how far ahead I am on supplies, money, and health, the curses will inevitably end my current run short. Healing your character is no easy feat, as you rely solely on the RNG of food drops as you explore, or buying potions from the merchant. Even then, only so much healing can be done, and even if you are loaded with gold, you will have a hard time keeping healthy if you can't dodge all attacks headed your way.Also, jumping is clunky, as you have no control over your momentum in mid-air, and there are numerous traps and pitfalls that are rather punishing to the player. With jumping being the only means of dodging attacks, this lack of control requires extra precision and awareness of your surroundings. I think I end up taking more fall damage and trap damage than anything else usually. At the current price this isn't a bad game to add to the collection, nor is it unfriendly to those new to the type of game. However, compared to other games, there are many that are significantly better balanced, and just as affordable. This game needs time and care to reach its potential, but from what I've seen, dedication from the devs will result in a new favorite rogue-like for me.However, this level of unpolished code can't get a recommendation from me, but I will continue coming back from time to time, hoping to see some real innovation.
_childDocuments_.name: UnderMine

_childDocuments_.review: A twinstick shooter roguelike reminiscent of Binding of Isaac while also including some of the puzzle elements from Zelda. All of the pieces of this game create an atmosphere of exploration and mystery that provided a ton of excitement. The first time the player starts the game, they will be dropped into an empty hub world that doesn’t have much in it besides the wizard who is the one who wanted someone to check out the mines due to earthquakes and something he has lost. While initially devoid of life, the hub world soon becomes lively as soon as the player begins to rescue the NPCs trapped in the mines; often due to the wizard as well. All of the NPCs, except for the pets, have a purpose and are designed to help make the player more powerful with every subsequent run. It is fun to watch a former ghost town become full of life ready to assist the player, though for a price.Combat is the main gameplay loot for Undermine. The player has a few ways to attack. The first way is by performing a melee swing with the pickaxe which has decently high damage while also providing minor knockback against enemies which is perfect when defending against melee focused opponents. The second way to attack is by throwing the pickaxe like a boomerang. This attack is ranged, but does less damage and leaves the player vulnerable as they can’t attack without their weapon. Bombs are a last resort tool for attacking as they have a lot of utility, but they are also devastating forces of destruction with proper placement. Their main issue is that they are limited in uses and are not always easy to find. Combat stays interesting due to the large variety of enemies. Even ten hours into the game I found that I would find an enemy that wasn’t previously seen in one of my runs. Early enemies are focused on melee attacks, but more powerful enemies often focus on ranged attacks with multiple bullets creating a bullet hell style of gameplay. There are some enemies that are reskins of enemies found early on, but the new enemies have new attack patterns so I didn’t mind as much. They are also much more the exception than the rule. Finally, the player is able to dodge similar to the one found in souls-like games. The main issue is that it is instead a jump which doesn’t fit well with the two-dimensional play space. The shadow isn’t noticeable enough and can make it difficult to know exactly where the player is going to land. The best way to improve the player’s randomized character each run is by picking up the relics available every level. The items, known as relics, provide passive abilities to the player in a variety of ways. One such example would be the glaive relic which makes the pickaxe huge when thrown which makes it very easy to hit whichever target is closest to the player. These effects can be combined though, which creates some very fun combinations that can absolutely destroy enemies. An example of a combo would be the glaive along with the triple throw. This will allow the player to throw three giant pickaxes in a cone formation. Some relics are unique and don’t play well with other unique relics. This is usually due to the fact that they are quite powerful. Two examples that I liked would be the aforementioned triple throw which has the potential to triple to player’s thrown damage and makes the ranged attack more effective as a shotgun and the golden bomb, which turns rocks that are bombed out into useful gold.Secret rooms are easy to find as the wall has a small sparkle effect on it. Secret rooms will sometimes be treasure rooms, but it can also be a small puzzle that is solved using visual clues. It keeps the secret rooms interesting, but they are a bit annoying when the puzzle requires bombs or keys that the player doesn't have. There are also secret rooms hidden under rocks. A great way to  find these secrets is by using a rock breaking enemy to open them up for free. Every set of levels has an end boss which is a difficult test of skill that has a powerful gimmick. Once the bosses are defeated, the player gets a boss key and they can continue to the next set of levels. Once a boss key is used, the player doesn’t have to get another,  the doors to the next set of levels will simply be open. I also like how the player obtains the blueprint to a relic that allows the player to use the boss’ gimmick for themselves.Progression is cumulative and every upgrade bought is inherited by the future peasant after death. The upgrades are necessary to beat stronger levels and the player is able to gain some upgrades besides damage once the appropriate NPC is unlocked in the hub world. The main aspect of the progression I dislike would be that when the player forges a new relic from a blueprint, they are given the relic. Subsequently crafted relics are taken away by a pilfer, so the player is only able to have the first one. This is only a one time thing though, which makes it feel  like one might be gimping a future run by unlocking a cool new relic early game.Not much story in this roguelike. The player is one of an army of peasants that make a contract with a wizard to mine for riches.  The music is quite good and doesn't get in the way of the gameplay. It instead adds a layer of ambiance that can be tuned out when in an intense battle. The sound design is great an provides a lot of auditory feedback to the player. This is done through hit sounds and unique sound effects for certain enemy abilities. The game uses a pixel art style that has a lot of pixels that provides a smooth look with jagged edges. The graphics do a great job at relaying that there may be secrets or what a monster may do. One such example is the purple braziers will provide items if blown up, but also curse the player. This purple is consistent with curses which allows players to know when they should avoid things. The aspect of this game that is frustrating is that some enemies will jump which uses higher z-levels. Considering this game is two-dimensional, it can be very hard to judge where they are going to land.The controls work quite well using a controller. All of the buttons were easy to reach and were well laid out. The twinstick controls are easy to access while not taking away from the melee aspect of the game.: I didn’t experience any bugs.I had seen a decent amount of the content, especially the items and enemies, but there were always new secrets that would appear and would surprise me.  👍  👍Beautiful graphicsLots of secretsCrazy item combos👎  👎Annoying dodge ability

_childDocuments_.review: I've been looking for games comparable to Zelda A Link to the Past for a long time now.  That game holds a high place in my pantheon of favorite games and this game strongly reminds me of it which for me equates to glowing praise.  Understand that this is a game that stands on it's own merits and does things differently but I often find myself reviewing games by drawing comparisons because I don't have time to write an in depth review.The dungeons of Undermine are randomized but in such a way that I could see someone having actually having designed them so however the algorithm puts them together it's doing it's job properly. _childDocuments_.review: Undermine, a simple game that was made with love.This is simply my opinion and feelings about Undermine, so please try it out for yourself before you decide!At first I didn't expect anything other than a simple rouge-like/lite that was randomly generated as you played. What I ended up experiencing was so much more than that. Regardless of whether you enjoy rouge-like games or not, everyone should give Undermine a go.Gameplay: You have three basic movements. Close-up melee with your pickaxe, throwing your pickaxe and jumping. You will be jumping around a lot! I found the jumping mechanic to be so interesting in a top down pixel based dungeon crawler and it makes for learning some really fun quick reflexes as you learn the game. You will also use your pickaxe for the act of mining for gold, which you will buy items with or simply hoard all of your gold if you must. I mostly play throwing my pickaxe everywhere but swinging it as a close ranged weapon is also fun. I understand for some people this may sound a little boring, but the Relic system is really where the combat shines in this game.Every level offers a Relic, which grants you a special ability or buff. Some are better than others, and I love that I never know what I'll end up getting. You may get shoes that allow you to float over holes in the dungeon, or a relic that makes all gold explode on impact. There are also Curses in the game, which are a bit self explanatory but really kick up the notch in difficulty. Your healing items may be less effective, your potions may break, or all of the enemies turn into tiny spiders when they explode and die!All rooms are randomly generated and some offer puzzles that you can complete to get a chest full of items, or a relic. There are many secret rooms and levels in each play-through and some wonderful characters and situations to find. You can find recipes for crafting items and potions, as well as eggs for pets to help you in your journey.There is an amazing end game that steps up the difficulty quite a lot, and without spoiling anything, I really love what is offered in the endgame and I am still working on quite a bit of that. It's challenging, but also very rewarding.I'm so happy they included pets that you can collect that really can save you from some dire situations and help out a lot with combat, or doing very specific tasks that are immensely helpful. They are also adorable.Art: The pixel art is incredible, so much love has gone into the visual aesthetic and design of this game. From the peasants that you play that go down into the mine, to the small details like wiggling mushrooms as you stand on them, to the fun designs of each boss you will encounter at the end of each dungeon. The animation of the pixel art is also done so well, and I wish other games achieved it to this level of quality.Music: The music is great and really sets the tone for the game, it can get a little repetitive when you've played quite a lot but I still really enjoy it. The sound design is well done, I love the sound effects of jumping, using the axe, killing enemies and all abilities that are used. I especially love the sound that plays when you discover a secret.Story: This was something unexpected. I really did not expect much of a story, but as I played through the game I actually really enjoyed the characters that you begin to find throughout playing. They are wonderfully designed and are full of character. The only downside to the story is that I would love to have a DLC that offers some more story content. I enjoy that there is a bit of a mystery as to why this king is sending peasants into the mine and how that is just acceptable in this universe! The pilfer characters that look like little slimes are great, and if you play it enough there's some fantastic secrets about them that you will discover over time. There is also a great sense of humour all throughout the game that I really appreciated.Overall I just really love this game and continue to play through end game content. It has wonderful replay value and I hope to get all of the achievements at one point.The only negative about this game, for me, is that there isn't any DLC. There is also no co-op, which is a real shame as I think this game could be fantastic for either couch co-op or online co-op. I hope the developers work on some DLC, but I will also be very curious about any upcoming games they may be working on.I rate this a 99/100 gold nuggets. I very much recommend you play this game and I hope you enjoy it as much as I have.A big thank you to the developers who worked so hard on this game, you have given me so many hours of joy.
_childDocuments_.name: UnderMine

_childDocuments_.review: I'll keep this short. Roguelikes come in two varities usually: slow and tactical or fast and reactionary. Undermine does a clunky job at trying to have both. The axe throw is borderline useless, and this game commits a cardinal sin of action games of having some enemies that stagger on hit like rats, and others that do not like the jelly and bat. Why would you do this?Combat is really not fun especially versus bosses because the boss attack comes out so fast that you barely have enough time to do damage before you have to jump away. The hitbox is kind of ridiculous, such as when fighting the blue yeti monster the moment he finishes his claw attack you have like 10 frames to attack and jump away because the moment he is done, his body turns into a hitbox while he runs. Just silly. I killed the first boss in 10 seconds by spamming the Rook bomb (I somehow got 8 before floor 3). Without this, it would have taken minutes to kill this guy despite having a braindead attack pattern.I finally quit when I saw a room with a pit, and across the pit there was gold in the walls. "How do I get that gold?" I thought. I threw my axe, nothing. Maybe that sliver of space is enough to stand? Nope. Fell into the pit and took damage. Why design rooms like that? No QA?

_childDocuments_.review: Very few items (About 150) and even fewer synergies between them. There are only like 10 or less item combinations and they are not even interesting. Most of the items are just stat sticks or gimmicks. Unlike The Binding of Isaac this game lacks a lot of depth. Unlocking every item is counterproductive since it hinders your future runs. You will most likely be aiming for only a few select items each run and employing the same strategy again and again. This strategy will most likely be blessing stacking with Sylph familiar. There are quite a few familiars (around 10) that level up but most of them suck compared to Sylph.All in all a shallow and mediocre roguelike with identity problems. Quite honestly The Binding of Isaac started out like this but it got better and better every update. Sadly I don't think this will be the case with this game.
