_childDocuments_.review: Bugsnax is by far one of the most fun creature collector games I ever played. The setting is nice: a (possibly) uninhabited island full of oddly food-shaped and flavored living insect-like, googly-eyed looking treats. These delicious representatives of real food are ripe for the catching, all while being challenging enough to find and capture. The other characters in here are a real riot. I find it hilarious that, except for certain pairs, most of nobody else can stand each other. Being sent to an island filled with horrible people in an almost entirely kid-friendly game yields many comedic opportunities.There are bosses to fight, many, MANY sidequests to complete, everybody and your hut can be decorated, and so much more. It's also cool that the DLC is built into this game. Overall, this game is a solid 8.5/10. It's not too long of a game, the puzzles and characters are really entertaining, and I really like how it makes usage of each tool every Grumpus gives you. Worth the price, 100% the game in less than 40 hours, and while it wasn't some life-changing godlike philosophical experience of a game, it's more than worth picking up.Seriously, give this game a try. It's really damn good.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is funny and addictive. I was able to wiggle and jump my way out of it, fast traveling with the map is another solution.After defeating Mothza Supreme for the first time I was capturing Bombinos and threw one at a group of three. One of those four fell through the map, I could see the stun timer moving with no Bombino in sight for it.The worst glitch I was when interviewing Eggabell for the second time. When asking about the player character's Bugsnax allergy there is a dialogue option after Eggabell asks what you've been eating. After choosing one I was curious about the other and clicked the allergy question again. The dialogue option appeared again, but trying to choose the other one activated the interview quesion 'Why did you leave town?' Trying it again soft locked me at the dialogue option. The game didn't freeze, but I couldn't click on anything. I got out of that with Task Manager(press CTRL, SHIFT and ESC at the same time).9.5/10 Will play again.

_childDocuments_.review: Finished but not completed.Bugsnax is an all-around good game, it offers a blend of adventure and puzzle-solving gameplay mechanics. The vibrant, cartoonish graphics and entertaining characters immediately draw you in. The gameplay mechanics are simple, centered around using the various tools you are provided with to capture Bugsnax, each with their own unique behaviours, capture methods, and interactions with each other.The mail challenges, though engaging at first, became quite tedious near the end. I completed about 85% of them before I felt myself no longer enjoying the game as much.The story of Bugsnax is fairly good. It doesn’t try to be anything more than it is – a funny and enjoyable game to spend about 12 hours in with a satisfying ending. The writing is straightforward yet engaging, filled with humour and emotion. The characters are well-developed, each with their quirks and backstories that add depth to the game.The sound design and music are also notable, with catchy tunes and fitting sound effects that enhance the overall experience. The voice acting is particularly strong, especially Bunger, love that silly little Bugsnax.I got this game when it was on sale for CDN$8.69 which for the 12 hours of gameplay I got was well worth the price.In summary, Bugsnax is a great little game with a charming aesthetic, creative gameplay, and a lighthearted story. While the mail challenges get repetitive, the overall experience is fun and worth the play through. It’s a great choice for anyone looking for a humorous and engaging adventure. I would recommend getting this game if you like casual adventure puzzle solving, and you are okay with spending CDN$28.99 on a 21-hour experience, if not, then maybe wait until it is on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Interested and intrigued to play Bugsnax? GOOD.Bugsnax is a seemingly cozy and fun creature collector but it is secretly a psychological horror LGBTQ+ story title. I felt so cool catching the harder bugsnax like the Scoopy Banoopy. All the bugsnax have such cute and playful names such as Sandopede which is a kind of 4-part centipede made out of sandwiches. My favorite bugsnak, Rootle is a carrot worm that burrows itself into the ground if you scare it. I love the sound it makes when you catch it, the sound it makes sounds so cute and I can't stop petting it in the barn, YES, YOU CAN CATCH BUGSNAX AND DONATE THEM TO GRAMBLE'S BARN AND PET THEM!!! (and eventually dress them with hats!!!). ROoOoOotle...Don't be fooled by the bugsnak's cute nature, the story behind Snaktooth Island and Bugsnax as a whole is terrifying and DEFINITELY not fit for a children's game. Eating bugsnax has a severe side effect of body disfigurement which turns body parts into the thus eaten bugsnax. The bugsnax have been on Snaktooth Island for years and years, who knows where they came from. THEY AREN'T WHAT YOU THINK THEY ARE.I recommend!

_childDocuments_.review: You can view my VR Beta gameplay here: Yes, Bugsnax is getting official VR support soon as a FREE UPDATE!! It's also currently at a big discount at 72% off (I already owned on the Evil Game Store, but decided to buy on Steam as well to show the dev support for bringing this free VR update!!) The game is rated overwhelmingly positive so it's an easy recommend from me.However, I'm here to rate the current VR experience, should you decide to try out the VR Beta that just released today. The VR port is pretty good, but not exactly great currently. The reason being because most of the interactions are point and click instead of being more immersive VR motion based interactions. For example, you press a button to spawn a scanner / camera instead of pulling out the tool with your hands and holding it with your motion controllers. Game is running on a custom engine. On my RTX 3080, on medium graphical settings (default for me), I was getting anywhere from 45-90 FPS, although usually closer to 90 fps. The variable frame rates did not bother me, but I could see it making it difficult for some to play in VR. You have full locomotion, along with smooth or snap turning available. You can play comfortably seated or standing. I did not experience any serious issues or bugs (well, yes the character bugs, but not bugs as in errors). Lastly, I just want to give a huge thank you to the dev for bringing free VR support to Bugsnax. I highly recommend this game to all my fellow VR veterans. We don't get too many free VR ports these days, so please show this dev team some love from the PCVR community.

_childDocuments_.review: Bugsnax is... surprising. What it is. is a game about catching bugs that look like snacks. But what it really is, is a mystery game about a missing person (sorry, Grumpus). But ACTUALLY, what it really is, is a game with a deep historical mystery. But really, though, what it truly is, is a game about goofy muppet people who all have goals and relationships being challenged by negative core beliefs about themselves, and your journey to help them overcome the obstacles within and achieve self actualization. But for real, though, what it really really is, is a game about Sandopedes and putting launchers under them so they break into little bits of sandwich that fly everywhere.This is a bafflingly captivating game with great characters, clever writing, and excellent voice actors all under the guise of a silly children's game. The story is engaging, there's several fun mysteries to be solved, there are tons of Bugsnax to catch (each requiring cleverly using your tools in different combinations to get them), and it's just straight-up fun. While the tag labeled "psychological horror" is not exactly lying, you will not be frightened by this game. There are no jumpscares or outright horror elements here, though if you have a good, hard think about some of the secrets you'll uncover in your time on the island, it will definitely provoke some creepy ideas and there are a few underlying mysteries with some surprisingly dark connotation--WITH THAT SAID, this is a peaceful, chill game. It's not very difficult (it's more about puzzling things out than having quick reflexes), it's got a really relaxing atmosphere, it is played all at your own pace, you're free to explore anywhere you go, and there are plenty of funny and wholesome moments to even things out. I found myself laughing often with the dialogue.I'm not yet fully through my first playthrough, but nearing the end at around 13 hours of playtime. I do plan to 100% this game, though, as it's such a great way to unwind in the evenings. Overall, I was really surprised by the emotional spectrum that this game explores and just how much authenticity is buried under such an absurd and silly concept. I was also surprised at just how much fun this game ended up being. It even runs beautifully on Linux. This is an easy recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Literally unplayable. This game is full of bugs, but also snacks, so I feel like that balances out the bugs.BUNGER? BUNGER BUNGER BUNGER BUNGER BUNGER BUNGERThis is the game that caused the infamous Cyberpunk delay. CD Projekt Red really didn't want the smoke, and tbh I don't blame them.Bugsnax is amazing. I fell in love with it so fast. The characters are so well written. And I still quote 'I'ma lift your crib, dawg' weekly. It has this weird dark vibe under all the cuteness that is just unsettling. It’s like the child friendly version of the film Annihilation. Bugsnax is not what it looks like on the surface. Going into this game I expected a kids Pokemon like game. I got that, but a s**t ton more. I got to meet super memorable characters all with their own personality and relationships with one another. The game has some of the most brutally honest dialogue, its amazing writing and delivery. Cute, silly, great voice acting and a surprisingly kid-friendly introduction to the wholesome world of body horror. I tried it out for its premise, but I stayed for the surprisingly deep characters.Once the characters start getting into their discussions, you learn it is in fact a decently mature story with elements of mental health problems, relationship dynamics and complications, as well as introspective analysis of the main characters and how they behave/respond to those around them.The whole vibe is also just amazing. Super eerie which I was very surprised about with the whole mystery feel going on which I loved. From the very beginning of the game you start to speculate and realize things are not what they seem and you start to understand there’s a lot more depth to it. There’s just such a sense of mystery and a slight unease that I hadn't felt from a game in a very long time. Amazing soundtrack as well.The game may look very simple, but they did a lot with it, from fully physics-based creature states to fire and ice gameplay mechanics as well as top-tier quest-tracking/management UI.  Each bugsnax is such a treat to discover and learn about and every single one is voice-acted, and though they can only say their name, they didn't just settle on 1 recording of it, all Bugsnax have 3 or so variations of saying their name so it never really gets monotonous or annoying, and each actor is bringing something unique to their performance which keeps it fun and adds a lot of personality to each creature.Also, the ending may be on of the biggest reveals and best endings in recent memory. I’m not spoiling but it is definitely something I believe everyone should experience for themselves. I seriously was moved to tears when it ended. You just can't even imagine how well the game gets to its end. Seeing how some your actions have consequences for the ending is great and offers some replayability to see how characters change and react differently depending on your choices. Game is literally the definition of not judging a book by its cover.People laugh at it but I would recommend it to anyone. 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: What a brilliant game. I'm still unsure over what surprised me more about this game - the fact that the gameplay continuously remained fresh and fantastic or the elusively compact story and character writing. And yes seriously, even though the characters in this game look like Sesame Street stand-ins, each and every one of them present such compelling arcs that urge you to interact with them as much as possible. The entire game is a surprise in the best possible sense. Catching each and every uniquely designed Bugsnax is a treat within itself - that core gameplay loop never becomes stale thanks to the large variety of methods and strategies the game allows you to experiment with when it comes to snagging one. Mixing and matching the tools in your arsenal to fashion more effective methods of capture never gets old - and the game pushes you to even utilise Bugsnax themselves in your experimentation, which leads to even more fun and super satisfying outcomes when it all comes together. Can't stress enough how much I enjoyed the gameplay, real surprise it never got stale at any point. As with the gameplay loop, the game also provides you a surprising amount of customization when it comes to your home or even the characters around you, freely being able to transform each of them into any of the 112 Bugsnax present in the game. In short, every playable facet of the game gives the player tons of room to experiment - so it never gets old.The story, as many of those interested in this game may have heard, does indeed have a darker side to it. One of my fears going into this is that it would just be a random dark twist towards the end of the game - and while events towards the end are certainly more darker in tone compared to everything prior, there is a subtle dark tone of mystery that pervades the entire game, portrayed through ancient murals or elusive figures hiding in the dark... there are certainly secrets to be found that give the game a really compelling depth. The story never slowed for me personally, as its driven largely by a central mystery - one that really tickles your curiosity and keeps you going to discover more. The darker tones in particular are an awesome contrast against the generally light-natured surface of the game. I would write further about the characters, but this review is already so long and I'm tired - but I urge you to play it for yourself to find out. At the beginning, many of them aren't particularly likeable - at least I felt so - but the fact that I came to genuinely care for each and every one of them, even the ones that irritated me the most at first, is a testament to the progression they all go through, depending on whether you choose to interact with them or not. And the game actively pushes you to do so - the main story is essentially about uniting a town broken by strife and fighting, so even if some characters irk you at first, caring for one of them will eventually encourage you to try reaching out to the others more. Its great. My personal favourites are probably Snorpy, Floofty, Wambus and surprisingly Beffica. Chandlo deserves a shout-out too. My only complaint - and this isn't neccessarily a fault of the game - is that I personally placed too much stock in the "Psychological Horror" tag. Having been meaning to buy this game long before I finally did, my expectations of Bugsnax was morphed by continuously seeing people call it a horror and parade its darker tones - which made me expect far too much of that. So yes, personally I would say that the psychological horror tag on the game isn't warranted, but maybe that's cause my expectations for it in that regard were far too high. On the other hand, if you went into this game really just expecting a fun child-like game, then I can definitely see why you'd come away and slap a horror tag on it! TLDR: Play this game, you won't regret it. Pure fun.Edit: Even though this came out in 2020, I'm voting it as Steam GOTY. Because it is.

_childDocuments_.review: 10/10 I have this game on Playstation, PC, and Steam because this game has easily became a top 5 fav!Bugsnax is such a simple clever concept its remarkable beautiful yet cutesy Graphics is pleasing and comforting. The Unique and Puzzling ways to catch and find Bugnax can range from Easy to Tricky and sometimes you unnecessarily make it more difficult then it is. being able to change Grumpuses into Snax is a fun yet creepy form of Customisation you can make all sorts of Variants and combinations.Now the Story is the most amazing thing about this game with a wide range of characters with unique personalities and backstories. while sometimes border lining on Psychological Horror you will most likely relate to one of the characters struggles and the fact Lgbtq+ Representation is just in the game without the need to be Announced or Explained should be the new Norm for game titles and how the story tackles Mental Issues is serious and self aware without making fun on these communities.I could not recommend this game more what a unique experience I had in this game and not only do i look forward to a Bugnax 2 Im also excited to see what Young Horses will do next even if your not a fan of Creature Collectathon Bugsnax is definitely my go to recommendation for friends!

_childDocuments_.review: Bugsnax is an adventure game released back in 2020 on Playstation 4 & 5 and Epic Games Store. It takes place on a mysterious island called Snaktooth which is a home for these interesting creatures called “Bugsnax'' which as you have guessed are half bug and half snack.You play as a journalist who writes articles about mysterious incidents and unknown anomalies. In the beginning you receive a video message from Lizbert Megafig the fame explorer essentially inviting YOU, the journalist, to the said island so you could investigate the Bugsnax being the best person to tell the world about them by making a huge article about it saving your career along the way. With her associates, Lizbert built a settlement called Snaxburg in order to better study the Bugsnax. Half bugs, half snacks - no one has ever seen anything like it and what awaits the protagonist on this journey is up to YOU, the player, to discover.I discovered this game on the Nintendo Switch over a year ago, and I was deeply invested in it until I caught every single snack on the island, completed every single quest, and unlocked every available achievement. This is truly one of my greatest achievements because not only did I really enjoy doing so, but it was also very rewarding. The game captivated me with its charm, uniquely designed characters and creatures, engaging gameplay that requires you to think outside the box from time to time, the catchy soundtrack, and the intriguing story that kept me engaged until the very end. I almost completed it in one go the first time. Later on, I purchased the game on the Epic Games Store so I could play it on my newly acquired Steam Deck, and I enjoyed it even more in high definition, with an increased field of view and smoother frame rates. This was indeed a dream game for me after a long while.Recently, after the announcement that the VR version of Bugsnax was in development and the public beta was available for virtually anyone with a VR headset, I reached out to the Young Horses Games Discord to ask if the beta would ever be coming to the Epic Games Store. Eventually, I was DM'd by one of the devs with a Bugsnax Steam key, a gesture I will definitely remember for a long while. P.S. The VR version is also great, although it's still far from being finished.The gameplay can be described as a miniature BOTW or, for comparison, "Journey to the Savage Planet." You are set in an open world filled with different types of "Pokemon-like" creatures. You are equipped with an arsenal of different traps to catch them, and all of them unlock progressively during the story in a sort of Metroidvania way. Each Bugsnack requires a different approach to catch them, and that's what makes it so fun - figuring out exactly how to do it. Whether you experiment or use unconventional methods because you lack a certain trap at the moment, it all works, and that's what I like about this game - the open approach and sandbox nature of being able to catch Bugsnax in different ways.During the story, you visit all sorts of biomes, each one very different from another, and they all feature their own Bugsnax adapted to live in these conditions. Some of them only appear during certain times of the day or under specific weather conditions, and this ecosystem truly makes the world feel alive. Some snacks appear more dangerous than others and require a special approach, but the game doesn't have a health bar or any sort of fail state, so you can try to catch them as many times as you need.The game doesn't consist solely of gameplay. Sometimes, the action settles down into narrative cutscenes, showing relationships between the Grumpuses, their daily life on the island, or sometimes their deepest secrets. The writing is genuinely good, even if it's overwhelming at times, but I still like it. The game also features bosses, but this is more in spoiler territory; it's best that you see them for yourself. Overall, it's very satisfying, has great controls, engaging puzzles, and a variety of different environments and characters you can love, hate, or Snackify to the point they're unrecognizable.The soundtrack is written by Seth Parker. The same guy who also wrote the Octodad OST and I noticed that they were pretty similar. The songs vary in genre from track to track, sometimes they give out a chill vibe, sometimes they are electronic or dramatic. Doesn’t matter what situation you're in, the soundtrack always accompanies the whole experience too well. If nobody’s got me I know that the Bugsnax OST does.10/10 - Hey, we're making this funny game about sentient food with googly eyes don’t go too hard on the OST. Seth Parker: hold my Sodie.Overall, Bugsnax is a fantastic treat for all indie game enthusiasts and those who are open to experimenting with new titles. It has the potential to carve out a special place in your heart, but it can also be enjoyable in any case. It's worth noting, however, that this game may not appeal to everyone. For instance, individuals who are arachnophobic, sensitive to themes of body dysmorphia, or uncomfortable with queer representation in media might not find it to their liking.But otherwise, The creators of Octodad did not reinvent the wheel and come up with another game with awkward controls and funny physics. This is a fun adventure for a couple of evenings that can be stretched out if you enjoy catching adorable creatures. The game is available on all modern platforms even on the iOS and SteamVR so you can enjoy the thrilling Snaxcatching action on anything, anywhere, anytime.

_childDocuments_.review: There's a lot I want to say on Bugsnax. First and foremost, it's a phenomenal game. Young Horses is a very talented team of developers that know how to create engaging characters in unique settings. That being said, I was biased and had high hopes for the game, and I think those hopes were definitely met, but there's a few key things that bothered me just a little bit that are a blemish on an otherwise incredible enjoyable experience.The gameplay cycle is very simple and satisfying. Anyone that enjoys creature collection, from Animal Crossing to Pokémon, will find that the way it works in Bugsnax is more akin to a puzzle than anything. Every time you discover a new region, it's exciting to see all the different Bugsnax, and I immediately found myself brainstorming "okay, how do I catch this one"? Each Bugsnax is a thought exercise on how to potentially catch them, and the variety in ways to catch them, including multiple ways to achieve doing so, are quite nice and it feels good. The small nitpick I have here is that the number of variant Bugsnax is quite high, and it feels like about 50% of them is just a copy of the same Bugsnax, but in a different color and a slightly different method of catching. This isn't a big deal, but it is less fun.The characters are fantastic and lovable, they mimic real people and are quite believable in a lot of ways. The dynamics and interactions feel really smooth and natural and it's a big reason of why the game doesn't feel like a chore. Many games struggle coming up with characters that are fun or funny which then lowers your investment. Even the inclusion of gay couples don't feel forced, in fact, I'd point to this being one the best game examples for how to do LGBT+ writing properly.Now, the story. It's... a mess. The setting and lore are great, but the way the story progresses is very hamfisted, without spoiling anything, the reason you're even beginning your adventure in the first place does not make sense once you see the full ending. There's also a lack of critical thinking among everyone; the game really does not stop for one second to make it's plot twist any more obvious. From the beginning it's painfully clear what's going to happen and the truth behind Bugsnax, and I don't even need to tell you what it is for you to already know. This is a shame, because I feel like more could have been done with it, and a subversion of a subversion may have been more enjoyable.The OST is quite nice actually, it hits a fantastic sweet spot between cute and adventurous, they're mostly light-hearted tracks that make you want to go out and explore, which I think is a great tone for the majority of the game that just works with the setting. But the soundtrack doesn't struggle to become more heavy when necessary either. Seth Parker did a good job on it.In summary, minus a few shortcomings, Bugsnax is really a great game anyone who enjoys this genre owes themselves to try. The environments are neat and the semi-metroidvania aspects of the way the progression works make it fun to come back to older areas, too. If you don't read too much into the plot the game is trying to weave, and you're just having fun with the gameplay and enjoy the character banter, you're in for a thoroughly enjoyable time.

_childDocuments_.review: I won't talk a lot about what you'll be doing, but most of the time you'll be capturing bugsnax and feeding them to the npcs. Basically speaking, the majority of them are captured by setting a trap and waiting for them to come near it without having to do a lot of work. Throughout the game you'll find new tools to help you capture some bugsnax, some of them will need patience and strategies to get.There is a day/night cycle which is really nice it makes you feel more immersed in the game. There is also a mechanic that changes the moon phases which is important because some bugsnax only appears in certain ones. You can also skip the time by sleeping.There are a lot of quests, most of them are side quests and "requests". Completing requests will get you  rewarded with a decoration for your house.And yes, you can have a house and customize it in some ways. There are some areas available for you to change the furniture to another one, you can also change the painting of the walls etc. It's pleasant and satisfying to get a nice decoration to put in your home. are really unique, each one of them has their own personality, which is reflected by their colors, expressions, thoughts and actions. They really show that to the player and to the other npcs. For example, you'll often see them talking to each other about themselves/ sharing their own thoughts. This is also really good because it makes the Snaxburg (Camp - the place where they live) alive, which also contributes to immersion. The bugsnax are the peak of creativity in this game. they often represent food. You are going to find a lot of food types in each one of them and It's really interesting, they also make funny and cute sounds, It's hard not to like them and hard to describe them. Beautiful! Very pleasant views with nice colors that represents the biomes in a very charming way. On top of that we also have an amazing soundtrack which consists in electronic music, synthesizers in a very ethereal sounding while representing the biome in which the player is located. Very relaxing and memorable songs. Really gooood. I love the island itself (Broken tooth). I didn't feel tired to be there, and spoilers ahead . I won't talk a lot about this dlc (you really should discover it by yourself), but It's very worth it. It introduces a new mechanic to get the bugsnax in there, and there is some secrets there too + it also has a nice plot and dialogues between the characters. I really recommend playing the dlc before finishing the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I've waited for exclusivity deals to expire and dodged spoilers for two years to play this game.Was it worth it?Yes. Yes it was.Young Horses delivers again with a wildly creative and engaging monster collecting game featuring an expertly written cast of characters I grew fond for over the course of my playthrough. While I was drawn in by the cute bugsnax designs and the planning process behind catching them, learning about the residents of Snaktooth Island and breaking down their personalities, strengths, weaknesses, and so on while unraveling the mystery behind Lizbert's disappearance kept me hooked right up to the end.Besides the story, Bugsnax is a game that encourages creative use of your tools and the environment when going about catching snax, and I was often finding very creative methods for using what i had on hand. While the game isn't incredibly punishing (you cannot get hurt or die in any way) it can still provide a unique challenge to new and seasoned players alike.Overall, I found Bugsnax a wonderfully charming and engaging experience and would encourage giving it a try if it seems even remotely interesting to you.

_childDocuments_.review: Goofy, sweet, and fun.Most of the game is about collecting adorable and hilarious—and weird—critters. They start easy, but as the game progresses you'll have to use your tools, and wits, and patience creatively. It's not very hard but it's not a casual game either. I was challenged.There's actually a story and characters and they're fairly fleshed out and elaborated, at least within the ridiculous logic of 's ridiculous world. Do you gay? Yes. There is gay. The kind of gay that is just taken for granted: portrayals of same-sex love and non-gender conforming folk. And those are just inconsequential details in the story, as they should be in real life. Do you therapy? It normalizes that, too.Most surprising is how many hours of fun you will have. Or will you? Beyond the main quest there are a few optional quests and also a great many optional challenges. My one criticism of the game is that there are just too many of them. More than 100! Optional does mean optional, but the game unfortunately doesn't warn you or tell you how many you have left. Once you start going down that road you might stubbornly decide to see it through, and ... well, there are really too many. As much as I enjoyed the game, it felt very repetitive and tedious getting to that "100% achievements" finish line. I don't regret it, but, yeah, 50 instead of 100 would also have been great.But don't you worry your fruity, chocolatey, crispy little head over a minor flaw.  is not just a surprisingly good game, it's a good game, period. I had fun, laughed, and learned a valuable lesson about getting along with people with difficult personalities. Oh, and to avoid eating foods that turn you into themselves.Bugsnax!

_childDocuments_.review: Great story, amazing voice actors, fantastic gameBugsnax is a fun game where you collect bugs that look like snacks. You play as a journalist reporter who was invited to Snaktooth island by world renown explorer, Elizabert Megafig, to come interview and report on Snaktooth island. Making it to the island you find out that Snaxburg, the settlement Lizabert set up, is abandoned and Elizabert is nowhere to be found. The last remaining resident and only mayor, Filbo, asks for your help to bring everyone back to town and help find Elizabert, while collecting bugsnax for the hungry townsfolk.The game at first glance is very silly and childlike. The game is very bright and vibrant, you have walking food creatures with googly eyes saying their names like Pokemon do and with names like Filbo Fiddlepie, Wambus Troubleham, and Gramble Gigglefunny, you'd probably assume this is a baby game made for small babies. Well you aren't entirely wrong... but you are still wrong. Bugsnax is a game that can be enjoyed by all ages where you collect and and document bugsnax. Yes there are silly names with silly food bugs running around, but the characters are incredibly well written with amazing voice actors that brush over mature themes that even us big kids are more than familiar with. I can't emphasize enough how fantastic the voice work is for this game. The contrast of what the characters are talking and the vibrant carefree world they live in makes it even funnier. The further along in the story you get the more serious the tone of the game is, with an intense and horrifying twist near the end.If you have the money, buy this game. It's fun to play and is easy to pick back up again after a long break. The story good, the characters are endearing, it scratches the completionist itch, and it's just a fun game to sit down and unwind to.

_childDocuments_.review: Where to even begin with this one. Yes, it's fun. Yes, it's well-designed. Yes, it has a nice amount of variety. It has good writing, proper pacing, fantastic sound design... and yes, it very much is psychological horror. I won't elaborate on that because of spoilers, but let me just ask you this: don't you think catching and eating cute little googly eyed creatures who clearly feel things like fear or anger is a little messed up? Well, let's just leave it at that.It definitely doesn't fit any common genre descriptions. My best attempt would be... story-driven open-world puzzle creature collectathon? For the most part, you'll be walking around one of the areas trying to catch some Bugsnax - either to fill that compendium, or to complete a quest. See, most quests are pretty much "catch X of Snak Y and put them in my mouth". But no worries - these things are anything but fetch quests! Catching Bugsnax is both non-trivial and fun, and there's lots of different ways to catch them. Let me explain, if you'd like.Every Bugsnak is a little puzzle. How do I catch it? Some are completely trivial - just use tool X - but as the game progresses, you'll find that many Snax have multiple layers of protection to them, and figuring out how to take them all down at once is where the fun really is. Let's take a Snak I'll call "B". B is quite aggressive and will charge at you when you get close. If you manage to stun him somehow, you'll find that you still can't catch him, because he's covered in ice - trying will simply freeze you and your traps. So the puzzle becomes "how to unfreeze B?". But then when you do unfreeze him, he breaks into two smaller Snax... so what am I supposed to do? What indeed!Some Snax are essentially versions of Snax you've already seen, but with one additional problem. You've seen Snak C? Get ready for Snak C... but on fire! It might sound lazy at first, but the added complexity keeps things fresh at all times.And then of course there are Boss Bugsnax... these are multi-part encounters that are completely unique and have their own set of mechanics. They also often are at the end of one of many storylines. Oh yeah, the story!Busgnax has the aesthetic of a kid's game, but it is anything but. The story is surprisingly deep and touches upon some dark elements of the human condition. I won't write what they are, find out yourself.What I will write about are the characters. At first they appear as pretty stereotypical stock characters - a loser who thinks he's got power, a hostile farmer, a dumb jock bro... but then it turns out they're all quite interesting subversions of those tropes. For example, the dumb jock bro? He's anything but dumb, and when you ask him what's his job, he responds with "I lift". Weights? Yeah, that too, but generally anything that needs lifting. Weights, spirits, people when they're down... you know, it's a philosophy, bro. Oh and that horror thing I mentioned earlier? Depending on how you play the game it can be mostly simply as an implication of certain things, but also it can get a little more... graphic. What I'm saying is I wouldn't recommend this to kids.The game's good. Fun, pleasant, thought-provoking, all that stuff. And while I definitely enjoyed it a lot, I wouldn't call Bugsnax great. I'm not sure why that is. Something is missing. All elements of the game are top-notch, but they just kind of... refuse to come together. For me, at least.Still, I definitely recommend it. If nothing else, it's a good time and the Bugsnax are cute.

_childDocuments_.review: Everyone's talking about bugsnax! Bugsnax, the indie hit that came out last year to widespread acclaim for its art design, music, and characters. I want to eat several of the adorable creatures, and that is a true testament to the art department. This is an indie game, so there is some jank, but nothing that stops you from enjoying the creatures on display and the story unfolding before you. Without going into spoilers, there is a ton to discover on this little island, and the puzzles are fun to figure out. The DLC adds another two to three hours onto this adventure, and adds a new area for you to explore, along with new puzzles and bugsnax to catch. _childDocuments_.review: Bugsnax has always been a comfort game to me. You play as a journalist grump (yep, grump) who has set off to find the missing explorer Elizabert Batternugget who tells us to meet her at Snaktooth Island, the location of the illusive "bugsnax". Once you arrive, or rather, crash land, you meet all the grumps who traveled to Snaktooth Island with Lizbert and help them find out what happened to their mysterious leader.The overall premise of the game being catching bugs that are shaped and taste like snacks and bringing them to your new friends to consume is such a goofy and unique concept. I love how colorful each snak is and how vibrant the surrounding areas are - the island shares a beach, a desert, a lucious forrest, and a frozen mountainous terrain. Each of the grumps have their own personalities and insecurities that you learn about and they can feel pretty heavy at times. Perhaps being on an island that defies reality doesn't mean you left all your emotional baggage at home. Bugsnax takes a wonderful approach of how to deal with your past, emotions, and insecurities to better yourself as a person (grump?).While searching and finding unique ways to catch bugsnax can be fun, that's basically... all you're really doing in order to advance the story. It can feel pretty repetitive at times and some of the ways you capture bugsnax are not very intuitive (I'm looking at YOU Flamin' Cheepoof!!). I wish they had integrated other elements into the story missions, but honestly, I really love running around and catching all the bugsnax and supporting my new friends with everything going on in their intertwined lives. It's very heartwarming to see everyone come together over time and rekindle relationships.Obviously every game will have at least one flaw, even the best of the best have at least unlikable trait to them - but I have such an easy time looking past these small issues that it's an easy 10/10 for me. It's such a colorful and beautiful game with a very interesting premise that no sane person would have come up with on their own, and I completely mean that. Part of me really hopes to see a sequel at some point because I just can't get enough of these wonderful Bugsnax!

_childDocuments_.review: Never have I ever been so compelled to give a thorough review for such a game. The last review I made was nothing more than a half-assed attempt to be "funny" 3 years ago. On the surface level, Bugsnax is not an entirely complex game - the description follows suit.Just as the description seems simple, so is the game at it's core. What ended up being an impulse buy to play a casual game, ended up becoming a (perhaps) unhealthy obsession over the world, the characters, the environment, the setting. Everything was wonderful, and wonderfully goofy. The Bunger and it's glory is but one of the many Bugsnax that can be seen in game. It's a game that runs with it's concept, utilizing simple concepts to solve different puzzles, and though I can't tell you that this game offers an extremely varied way to solve everything, I can tell you that it gets close enough.The development of characters - both physically and mentally - create a solid foundation of characters that you can love, and grow to love (or ultimately just hate). Those same characters are not as they first appear, nor are they static. They change as you help them change, offering to solve their problems - and by extension, help them grow through it. My addiction to side quests, whether attributed to my ADHD or not, was enhanced by the characters offering them, those likable and real people that are vibrant and exuberant, just like the scenery itself.Speaking of which, this world isn't that huge once you've explored everything. Quite honestly, this isn't a particularly big game, taking around 10 hours to really push through the story. I find that it's the side characters and the missions you can do for them that makes this game much more huger. Though I have 100% on the achievements in Bugsnax, it doesn't mean that I've unlocked everything in the game. There isn't much merit for it other than personal, and I already feel achieved enough throughout this game.A wonderful story, setting, character cast, and charming premise for a game that I assumed would be something I'd put down after an hour or 2. I can't believe that I spent so long on this game, but I know it was worth the time spent. Hell, a majority of the time was me streaming this game to my girlfriend, even the side-quests and letters that are arguably much better spent playing than watching. She played Bunger voice clips while a very dramatic scene was playing towards the end, so that was pretty lit.Buy the game if you at least want something entertaining for a couple hours. It'll be worth the money, I guarantee it.

_childDocuments_.review: Bugsnax is the most mid game in existence. In a world of so many more interesting and worthwhile games, like ULTRAKILL, TUNIC, and Elden Ring, a mediocre game like Bugsnax is not worth your time.It has:* A generic, cliche story* Mediocre, uninspired art style, with little visual flare* Boring ass dialogue* Mid voice acting by the grumpuses* Generic gameplay* Simple, flat, boring level designThe most interesting thing about the game is the namesake bug-catching mechanics, which, while having gotten the most focus out of any aspect of the game, still manage to be barely on par with Ape Escape Academy in terms of fun factor, player expression, and overall game feel. Also, the funny voice acting for the bugsnax is entertaining for a couple seconds every time you hear "Bunger!" or "Bopsicle!".Much of the quests involve - you guessed it - catching bugsnax, and it doesn't vary much from that. Unless you reeealy like catchin' those snax and listening to cringy, cliche dialogue, you're gonna have a rough time pushing through this game, much like I did.Maybe I'd recommend it to a young kid, who might be a more appropriate audience for this game, but even then there are plenty of much better alternative games I'd let a child play before touching Bugsnax. (Think Kirby, Mario Kart, etc.)All in all, you dont get much beyond what you see in the trailer, and if that doesn't absolutely captivate you from the first 5 seconds, i'd say skip this one.

_childDocuments_.review: Bugsnax was cute, amazingly voice acted, funny and oddly addicting in a calming way. The gameplay was basically about capturing ridiculous food themed creatures with a variety of silly traps in semi-creative ways to accomplish little goals in your quest to discover what happened to expedition exploring the island. The relaxing music is catchy and the characters are fun to listen to, going from fuzzy puppet-like beings to becoming more complex as the story moves on. The story isn’t too complex in itself, in fact the “twist” ending is very easy to guess if you are paying any sort of attention and the “psychological horror” tag featured in the description doesn’t really hold up for older audiences, but the characters keep you invested. The characters are amazingly voice acted and you do begin to care about what happens to them. Understanding them and watching them try to sort out their personal issues is the heart of the story.All told it was a cheery and relaxing experience from the gameplay itself. Much like a fishing or trapper game, except you listen to cheery music while gently puzzling out how to catch the adorable hamburger creature using ketchup as a lure instead of some fish. There are a large variety of bugsnax, some more complex than others to capture, all of them cute…until the last one, anyway. The only ping of stress occurs at the final act and that only occurs because it’s a contrast to the game being pretty much stress free until that point.I enjoyed it to the point where I got all the achievements and ended the game with a smile. Thumbs up, Bugsnax.
_childDocuments_.name: Bugsnax

_childDocuments_.review: This game is amazingly fun and very addicting to play. Ten minutes after putting it down I just want to pick it up again! I've been streaming it to my friends so we can all enjoy the adventure together, however that being said... Now all it takes is one person to dare utter "Bunger" and the entire call erupts in parroting of Bugsnax names."Bunger, Bunger, Bunger!""Nooooodler. NooOOdler! NOODLER!""ScoOOoopy BanoOOpy." _childDocuments_.review: Trying to be as objective as I possibly can; Bugsnax is a fun, quirky, charming, extremely charismatic experience. It's style is well defined, the gameplay is massively entertaining, the silly-yet-real dialogue is backed up by a surprisingly strong voice acting cast, and there's a clearly good staff putting it all together seamlessly. In short words: Bugsnax good, play Bugsnax.However, I will allow myself to embrace a bigger level of subjectivity here. Bugsnax is downright one of the best games I've ever played, and it has consumed me whole like a Bunger in the maw of a hungry Grumpus. This is the only game in Steam I have all achievements on. I've actually 100%'ed my first playthrough, not just all the snax and junk, I mean ACTUAL 100%, as in: Literally ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ everything. I scanned everything that's scannable, got all mail, discovered the secret area, caught all snax, did all the sidequests, got all 112 Snax on Gramble's farm and got all the tapes. I ain't an achievement hunter or a completionist type, it was all out of genuine, raw, unadulterated love for the game. Charm is definitely the word I would use to TLDR the experience. Is easy to get hooked when everything is clearly filled with an astonishing level of love and care. The tiny additions of dark humor and messed up subjects played completely straight in spite of it stark contrast with the colorful, bubblegum pop of the visuals and designs is handled wonderfully; None of the elements fight between each other, they hold hands and dance around, creating a perfect balance between honesty and self awareess.Its utterly ridiculous, it knows its ridiculous and yet it is so emotionally earnest it loops around and becomes endearing.

_childDocuments_.review: This game surprised me. It's a fun premise populated with strongly-characterized characters that have believable relationships and conflicts between them. Even the abrasive characters had sides to them that made me appreciate them. The central mystery was genuinely interesting to me, and while not top-tier stuff, used my care for the characters well.On the note of characters, voice-acting, so far as I can tell these things, is excellent.The designs of the Bugsnax themselves are wonderful, with their dorky, pun-ny, creative designs and Pokemon-esque vocalizations. Catching them was a simple, but engaging puzzle using different or different combinations of tools, environment features, or interactions with other Bugsnax to catch them.I found the simplicity of the gameplay loop to border on tiring as I neared the end of the game, but the mystery itself held my interest, and they mixed up the gameplay enough to keep me going.Visually, it's incredibly charming and strongly stylized and designed. But... taking too long to find the right wording here, but I'll be blunt: it's not a very technically good looking game. I know one comparison I found myself making was to Viva Piñata on the Xbox 360, and that game looks better than this. Not that I'm a stickler for visuals, I understand the limitations of smaller teams, and you need to prioritize resources (and I'd say whatever compromise was made here was worth it, the game excels in so much). It just drew my attention how barren the landscapes could feel at times.

_childDocuments_.review: Bugsnax, from the small amount of time I played it, was fun, if a tad quirky (like one of those B movies that you can't help but enjoy anyway). The gameplay is alright, though I found myself getting a bit bored. The voice acting is very nice. The Grumpus models... are wacky. But none of those reasons are why I am returning this game.This game portrays itself as a game for kids.. at least, that's what you would think upon seeing the colorful characters. However.. not even 15 minutes into the game, and it pushes a (flirtatious) lesbian relationship into my face. Okay, fine, whatever. I keep playing, and there's a whopping total of THREE romantic relationships in this game that I have seen thus far. I find that odd in and of itself. *But the real reason why I am returning this game is because of the inappropriate joke this game contains.* We already established earlier that this game looks like it would be for kids. Well, one of the aforementioned lesbian characters (who is actually pivotal to the plot), is being tended to by her partner, who is a doctor. The doctor stresses that she needs to stop moving, or she will be forced to restrain her. The one who is being tended to shockingly states along the lines of, "Not on camera!" Again, this relationship was conveyed as very flirtatious, and taking into consideration the context and perceived intended audience, I found myself repulsed by this. Fun game, horrible writing.

_childDocuments_.review: "Bugsnax," a seemingly innocent foray into whimsy, unfolds into a harrowing nightmare, a psychological abyss that transcends conventional horror. Snaktooth Island, bathed in an eerie glow, devolves into a sinister labyrinth where reality warps with each flutter of a Bugsnak's wings. The once-charming creatures, now grotesque amalgamations of flesh and limbs, stalk your every move. Shadows whisper unsettling secrets, and the island's serene facade masks a malevolent force that preys on your deepest fears.The protagonist's descent into madness is palpable, their sanity unraveling with each elusive Bugsnak. The ethereal soundtrack, once a playful melody, distorts into dissonant chords that echo through the haunted landscape. Inexplicable occurrences and spectral visions blur the line between reality and nightmare, forcing players to question their own sanity.As you delve into the darkness, Bugsnax cease to be mere creatures; they morph into manifestations of your deepest anxieties. The once comforting crunch of a snack now induces terror, and the island's lush flora transforms into a twisted, sentient maze that distorts perception. The narrative, a web of psychological horror, leaves players grappling with existential dread, questioning the very fabric of their reality.In this macabre odyssey, Bugsnax transcends its façade, leaving players with an enduring sense of dread. The horror is not confined to jump scares; it seeps into the subconscious, lingering like a malevolent specter. Bugsnax is not a game; it's a phantasmagoric descent into the abyss of the mind, an experience that will haunt your dreams and redefine your perception of horror in the gaming realm.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the most unexpected games I've ever played. Went in not anticipating whatever I went through, however this is a good thing. The game is very cute and is a fantastic example of collection games with a unique twist. All the Bugsnax have great designs and are a delight to figure out how to catch properly. Also the fact the Bugsnax say their names in classic Pokemon style makes me crack up especially when the voice over is bizarre and stupid in the best of ways. Scoopy Banoopy is my favorite Bugsnax, he is the best ever, I love him. This is also baby's first introduction to body horror, yes I mean it, it gets weird. All the Grumpus are really cute and they have a wide range of personalities as well as being really inclusive without it being a distraction to the story overall. I'd recommend this to anyone who likes silly games but also to anyone really, I've never played a game quite like this one. Pacing is good, the ending is wacky, Love it... 9 out of 10 Bungers

_childDocuments_.review: Behind the game's basic premise of catching the titular creatures lies a brilliantly-paced story with plenty of intrigue and phenomenal character development. As the protagonist looks for Lizbert, the explorer that led the expedition to the island, they meet the other members of her team and work on reassembling their community, while piecing together clues to her wheareabouts.Figuring out how to best use the traps to catch each of the 100+ species of Bugsnax is a rather rewarding experience, and the process of discovering their effects on fellow grumps is also amusing — mixing and matching different 'Snax allows for the creation of unique looks. As for the creatures themselves, their design is very creative and their Pokémon-like cries, although goofy in nature, are inherently fun.All in all, I had a very enjoyable time playing Bugsnax, and I guarantee it's among the best games I've played this year so far. By taking your time tinkering with the game mechanics, running every single quest and errand, and solving every mystery, the game can be finished in around 20hs.

The added customizable house and "mail quests" system are less of a hit for me: these quests put a little bit of bloat on an otherwise pretty tight experience; you wouldn't miss too much skipping these and sticking to the original story and sidequests you get from speaking to characters.

_childDocuments_.review: I picked up Bugsnax on sale because I had seen marketing for it a while ago, and being a fan of Pokemon and other creature collectors, I figured this would be fun. The story is a little off-kilter, but given the design of the game's monsters, it really works with the setting and other characters you interact with. The creature designs and names are cute and creative, and it was always fun seeing what new Bugsnax would appear in every new locale I visited.My first takeaway was the visuals. Overall I just wish it was sharper or cleaner. Considering this was a PS5 launch title, I'm surprised the PC port doesn't give the user options to increase the resolution scaling or other graphical options to improve the visuals. Secondly, it was a bit short; my playthrough clocked in at just under 6 hours, although I didn't engage much with the post game side quests and other content. In my opinion, the mechanics and runtime meshed together well, as I wouldn't have wanted to keep playing much longer to finish the game as is.The rest of the game was fine. Really, that's about all I have to say about it. By the end, I was more interested in just finishing the game than doing all the side objectives because I wasn't really having a lot of fun. I think that if there was more to the Bugsnax mechanic (like a cooking minigame, or maybe creating fusions of Snax) other than just catching them, I would be incentivized to explore the game's mechanics and catch rare Bugsnax. If a sequel is ever made, I'd love to see them add more depth to the Snax themselves. Overall I'd recommend Bugsnax, but only if it's on sale.

I'm not including spoilers in this review because I really want to encourage people to buy it for themselves but I loveloveLOVE the "twist," it includes alot of my favorite things in very unexpected ways. _childDocuments_.review: So tempting to just write a review about bungers...This game is way better than I expected. I found it in a kind of weird way. We were listening to a Kero Kero Bonito song (flamingo), and the one they wrote for Bugsnax came on after. Later on I saw it on steam on sale and bought it out of curiosity (and begging from my kids). The reviews about this game are super confusing so I'll help out. It's not a horror or any kind of deeply disturbing thing that people act like it is. It's a bit silly, and very bizarre, and there is a very small (but extremely predictable) twist ending. It's family appropriate depending on your views on LGBTQ as there are same-sex relationships and non binary characters. I will say that it is very natural and does not feel forced for "check boxes" like some media. It just makes sense for the characters. I was rooting for them. Characters are great! Voice acting and their personalities and stories are really well done. The game is fun, the puzzles are fun, the story is interesting, the snax are cute. Had a lot of fun doing a 100% run but it took under 30 hours. I bought it on sale and it's VERY worth it on sale but honestly I'd probably pay full price for it because I really did enjoy it and my kids are obsessed.Bonus, the Kero Kero Bonito Bugsnax song is pretty good too.

_childDocuments_.review: I give this game a rank D+ (50-55%)Forgettable game - sadly nothing really good here..See my profile for more details about my reviews.I should have refunded this game, then I would not have felt bad to give it a thumbs down. Thank you no thank you Steam for your stupid system I disapprove with (I still believe a rating like on BGG is better). I give Bugsnax about 52% in rating, and in my notation, it means that no, I would not particularly recommend it. I should have stopped before the 2 hours mark and refunded it, then I would not have had to review it negatively. At least I am just glad it won't hurt its standing on Steam at all (what is one little negative review with 94% positive reviews!). And who knows, maybe my kids will enjoy this game?I wanted meaningful depth and emotional sense from this game, and I got neither. As soon as the game started, the cartooney art, the funny voices (an hilarious spider squeaking and running away from you) and the quirky mechanisms of the game made me think "could it be an Outer Wilds-ish game?!". Which meant HIGH level for me. And that is what I kept hoping all throughout the game. But after 10 hours, I finished it, and NEVER got what I expected. My bad! I am not the target for this.The silly outlook of it felt like a pretend to me, some kind of appearance to hide something more meaningful, and so I was waiting for the depth at every corner... but in the end it was silly and non-sensical all the way through. Despite a very interesting take on some recent genres such as Outer Wilds, Subnautica, Slime Rancher or even Stardew Valley and a Short Hike (very, very light influence for some, mind you), this game was just silly, awkward and cringey all the way. And if it was just for the bad style that I did not like... but the problem is, I also disapprove with the content: this is NOT a good, worthy of narrative fictional content in my opinion. The bugsnax (pokemon-ish creatures) and story (stranded on a weird island) are quirky but secondary in content, the primary content here seems to be relationships? emotional feelings of awkward people towards others, as awkward, in a broken society? Practically all the characters work as a couple (either of friends, hetero, gay, enemies, bromance, what have you), and they all try to live with that. And all the dialogues and story revolve around that.And that might be why the game is not for me: I don't care! I don't give a damn about that. Some people will wrongly use the tag LGBT to promote this game, while some others will dumbly use it to condemn the game: who cares! I don't like to be shoved in the face with relational stuff, private stuff, emotional-baggage-issue-stuff ("I am worthless!" "no you aren't!" "yes I am!" "no you are beautiful as you are!" "oh thank you come here let's kiss" "smoochie smoochie"), I never enjoyed that in any piece of art whether it is a movie, a painting, a video game, maybe it is my autism and lack of empathy, but I just can't relate and get into it. It has NOTHING to do with emotions, as I can definitely cry in a game like Outer Wilds. It is just private stuff RUBBED in your face, and I could not care less. AND it is shown here in a quirky, silly, nickelodeon style, which I truthfully abhor.Also, half a joke but let me give an additional thumbs down to the bugsnax representation: I don't mind Pokemon (who cares) but what a WEIRD look on food, what a broken, sick relationship to gastronomy, what a weird depiction of ingredients and meals... only a US studio could imagine such a thing I guess.Is it a generation thing? Maybe if you are 15 and love this content? I am a simple man who doesn't like intellectualism from Jonathan Blow, but I also am a grumpy old man who can't suffer this silly non sense. Note however that I don't give this game a 20 or 30% in rating: I do not think it is BADLY made. I just think there is nothing worth people's time here, there are better things out there. Sad, because the voice over is remarkable, the dialogues are very well written despite all the characters being insufferable, and the mechanisms of catching bugs are clever. Oh well! is  on  on  on

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, I don't have enough words to expound just how much of an enjoyable experience it was to play this game and earn all possible achievements. Bugsnax is a masterpiece; from the Grumpuses and their interactions/relationships to the bugsnax designs, their characteristics, and their environments ..... I couldn't stop looking around in AWE, just taking it all in. Every single biome felt lived in and so well crafted. I had a blast just exploring and learning more about this well-crafted world as the game progressed. The game also did a great job of requiring different strategies needed to catch all bugsnax, prompting the player to continue thinking outside the box and paying attention to patterns/timing. The natural and expected trials and errors during the gameplay made the achievements feel as though they were truly earned and there was the added bonus that the achievements could be challenging, at times, but never cruel. In this, any many other regards, Bugsnax struck a delicate balance and scratched an itch I didn't even know that I had. I am more than willing to recommend this game to others as a lot of love and consideration clearly went into its making.

_childDocuments_.review: Bugsnax is a beautiful game for everyone. The Psychological horror tag on steam is not a joke, this game has body horror "for children" but Bugsnax with its wonderful story, amazing characters and absolutely wonderful voice acting it transforms the horrors that it presents into resolutions about our bodies, our relationship with food and accepting ourselves and the other people that surrounds us. For the gameplay its comparable to pokemon "gotta catch em all", but its mechanics specially at the end make for satisfying solutions and challenging puzzles. This is all thanks to its very "Alive" gameplay with a lot of elements (fire, water, ice, etc) working with each other making plenty of correct solutions. You can really be creative with all the tools that the game gives you, But at some points specially in the middle the game for a moment feels like just fetch quests for others, thankfully these are quick and are just at the very satisfying end. in conclusion this game is a great narrative experience even do sometimes it can be a bit overwhelming the overall story is amazing and its worth experiencing.

Bugsnax are cool finding and such find out how each work, but I often found the gadgets you were given pretty ridiculous, catching a specific bugsnax never seemed very intuative,  you always had to do some weird mix of gadgets that were very weird, sometimes it would work and others times it wouldn't and then other bugsnax would come in your way, idk it was almost always pretty annoying, and going for 100% completing all quests some of these bugsnax became very annoying on already 2nd and 3rd catch. _childDocuments_.review: You know how in Animal Crossing there's the whole collecting critters thing? What if thats the whole game, with some body horror and NPCs suffering from personal issues?Well, thats Bugsnax. And it works suprisingly well.The game revolves around catching them, most of the time because some NPC wanted one. This is most of the time because they either want to eat, or, in the more interesting case, because they want to fix something or other about themselves. I don't really want to get into what, just that the meaning behind it is often quite human problems, making for a very engaging story. If you plan on buying the game, definitely play the sidequests as they are integral for this (Not the mail requests, those are pretty much just busywork).But what about catching the Bugsnax? Well, its essentially a mini puzzle game each time, with all of them having specific attributes that change how you need to approach catching them. It's fun trying to think of optimal ways, and also fun finding ridiculous ways that still work. After finishing my playthrough I watched someone else play, who solved many things differently; some more optimal, some less.All in all the game took me 14h to complete to 100%, except for the mail assignments where i did about 80% before getting tired of them. Can definitely recommend, especially since the game got a free DLC after release. Who does that today?

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting game for all ages. The "overwhelmingly positive" is a bit of a misleading (I'd say it's a solid 8/10 game, without question) take on it. despite having a whole collection of tools and biomes to explore, it seemed like every bugsnax was essentially caught in 1 of 4 possible ways: put it in an opposing element, use 2-3 tools in a row, make one bugsnax attack another, or just toss a basic trap down and catch it easily. Since this is the ONLY gameplay in the entire game, I was a bit let down...but the short length is a blessing for this game! Beatable in 8-10 hours easily, so I have a feeling the devs knew their gameplay was a little weak. The narrative is alright, but its strength is in the characters and their development, not the actual story arc, which is reminiscent if every Resident Evil plot ever, but presented in a Muppet style, and to be honest not very satisfying. If it wasn't for the character development, I don't think I'd be recommending this game because the main arc and the gameplay really aren't that interesting once you get over the whole "they eat bugsnax and it changes their bodies" concept. If anything at all looks interesting in this game to you, 100% play it. But if you watch the trailers and you don't think it looks like your cup of tea, just move on to the next game. Bugsnax is a great game with a lot of love put into it, but its not a "must play" for everyone.

_childDocuments_.review: Bugsnax is a monster catching game where you catch... food. The games allows you to explore an island full of creatures to capture and characters to befriend. With  compelling story and characters, a lot of tasks to complete, and cosy graphics and music Bugsnax is quite an amazing game to experience. If some aspects of the gameplay can be a bit repetitive or frustrating, the game still manage to offer an Amazing experience. When Bugsnax was revealed years ago I was a bit sceptic about what it could offer as it seemed to be a monster catching game with a simple twist, the monsters are food-like creatures. Still a bit curious about it, I booted the game only to discover that this twist was more than it first seemed. The game has a cartoonish and colourful look that only gives more reason to explore each of the map the game offers. Although simple, the game has a cosy vibe, and the design of the game is definitely a strong point. If anything, they contribute to reenforce the serious moments of the story by contrasting so much with them. The music goes quite well with the cute graphics as it showcases fun synth music but also some other elements such as acoustic guitar played by one of the game’s characters.  Some notable tracks are:  If you’re going to spend that much time hunting creatures, their designs have to be good to keep you interested. In Bugsnax you can find 112 Bugsnax. They are typically a mix of a bug and a snack (hence the name). Of course like in many of those games, some of the Bugsnax you will encounter are recoloured versions of previous ones but overall they are quite inventive and interesting. Each creature has a different label like “spicy” or “cholate filled” which allow them to be notable during side quests where you have to collect snacks with particular tastes. A lot of them are simply a pair of googly eye on top of a fruit and although it could seem bad, it is enough. None of the creature look bad and they fit well in the environment they are found in.  Another nice touch is that the names of the creatures are often puns like Tacroach or Crapple.You’re exploring an island divided into 8 zones and a resting area. Each zone is filled with different types of Bugsnax that you’ll have to catch to complete various quests. The nice thing about it is that each snax asks you to use a different method to get them. You start with two tools but then unlock more throughout the game. It can feel like each zone is a tutorial for each tool at times, but it’s never totally the case. Some tools are definitely better than others and some can be a bit frustrating until you discover some hidden usage by experimenting (or going through the game but I was taking my time to do everything before moving on). I mentioned the completion of quests which are almost entirely fetch quests. You have story quests, secondary quests and also mail quests which are little challenges such as “catch three snax with one trap” etc. A particularity of Snax is that they transform the body of the person eating it, meaning that some quests ask you to transform characters in particular ways too. Something I appreciate a lot was that the game gives you a house in the village and that you receive furniture by completing the mail quests. It’s simple but it such a nice thing to have in a game and they do it less and less. You play as a journalist that goes to the Island to investigate the discovery of Bugsnax by a famous explorer. When they were there, they build a whole community and a village and each of them contributed to the life on the island. However, something happened before you arrived, and the leader of the community disappeared and consequently all the inhabitants scattered around the island and abandoned the community. You will have to bring them back but also discover the mystery of the island and the disappearance of the community leader.A good thing is that the characters are very likeable and although they are often representing one stereotypical type of character (jock, scientist...) they have still nice back stories and elements that make them compelling. The game also present different couples and even place two gay couples in the centre of its storyline which is quite nice! Well, to be fair once you discovered the end of the story and catch all the bugsnax, there isn’t much else to do. Maybe if you got stuck with a bad ending then you can retry and have the right one but I got the best ending directly and did everything the games had to offer in about 20 hours.  Bugsnax has 30 achievements and none of them are missable. A lot of them are story related but you also unlock some of them by trying new things within the game. Quite easy to get all of them too.

_childDocuments_.review: A solid thumbs up.Why? The graphics aren't the best. The music seems a bit out of place. The gameplay loop can get old after a while. It was a novelty launch title for a console. etc etcAnd yet it stays good. It's hard to really compress why it's good into a review without spoilers, but let's just say that the flavour hits you in waves. Initially you have this cutesy game with muppety creatures called Grumpus that are searching for their two lost friends, and you're there to help them because you want to get a career-saving interview. You have the mysterious Bugsnax that are like food-based pokemon in that they can only vocalise their own names, and have weaknesses you have to exploit to catch them, with each zone being a little playground of sorts where you learn how to exploit their interactions to be able to catch them to tick off your roster and meet one of the many fetch-quests.But just as that gets old, the next layer kicks in. These happy-go-lucky Grumpus muppets and their soft cartoon peril start to reveal that actually they have a bit of depth, and that they aren't purely one-tone tropes even if they stay true to the parts they play. Sub-themes start to appear. Before you know it, you're not playing because you just want to catch that one adorably dumb flying tree-banana creature, but because you want to see what happens next, or how the interactions will develop.It sounds odd, but go into this game as blind as you can, and try not to google anything. If you get really stuck then maybe ask a buddy who has played it before. Also don't sweat the small stuff, because while there is a "point of no return", you can load the game and go back to tie up any sidequests or extra missions you didn't do later on.Also, those dumb little Bungers are stupidly adorable. I bought a friend a plush one for christmas. :)

_childDocuments_.review: - Honestly, the game looks incredible. I was consistently surprised by the quality of the textures and lighting. Pretty unexpected for a game about catching edible bugs for muppets- Speaking of The Muppets, I grew up watching them, so the design of the Grumpuses (Grumpi?) felt oddly familiar and nostalgic- The music and voice acting are both top notch. Really, the overall presentation of the game, from the character animations to the menus, is very well done- Plot-wise, you play as a journalist trying to find out what's happening on a mysterious island after receiving a strange invitation from a famous explorer named Elizabert Batternugget. Over your boss's objections, you depart for the island to figure out what's become of Elizabert and the group of Grumpuses who followed her there- Although the bright colors and Henson-esque characters definitely play into the game's robust sense of humor, there's some surprising emotional depth to the game. As you help out the Grumpuses on the island, you learn more about them, their insecurities, their personal tragedies, and their hopes and dreams. These puppets have some surprisingly heavy backstories. I was also pleased to find that the game took a tasteful approach to the topic of mental health- The vibes are hard to pin down. Sure, everything is colorful and reminiscent of a children's morning show, but Bugsnax manages to leverage that silliness to enhance the tongue-in-cheek humor while additionally going on to pull off moments of touching sincerity. The quality of the coordination between the artists and writers is really evident- The presentation isn't the only thing that's good. The gameplay is also pretty fun if you're looking to chill out. Bugsnax is part 1st-person adventure game, part creature collector, and part platformer, and all of those gameplay components work cohesively together- Movement feels snappy, quick, and responsive, so playing in the first person perspective feels better than what many FPS games try to pull off. Movement factors heavily into the creature collection and platforming components (which often go hand-in-hand), so getting the "feel" of it right really enhances the experience- The equipment you accumulate over the course of the game add further interesting wrinkles to the bug catching and platforming, and most of it is fun to use- Unfortunately, I was a little disappointed by some of the adventure parts of the game. Most (but not all, thankfully) of the side quests boil down to a bunch of fetch quests. This is especially annoying when you run out of places to store bugsnax or accidentally feed/donate a big right before a Grumpus requests it for them- I also kinda hated the overuse of invisible walls. There are some parts of the game that look traversable but aren't for arbitrary reasons. I understand if they exist to prevent a player from leaving an area, but it feels silly to not let me jump onto a moderately sized rock to get a better view of an area- I'm glad I finally pulled this game off my backlog. I just wanted a colorful, silly game to play for 12ish hours. That desire was definitely fulfilled, but all the additional depth and snappy gameplay added so much more to the experience- Even the performance was good. My hardware is all stuff that came out in 2019, and I was surprised with how much I was able to up the visuals with virtually no impact on framerate- . While not a perfect experience, Bugsnax exceeded my expectations in virtually every respect. I thought it was going to be shiny and colorful but lacking in substance, but the writing and presentation were top notch

Each character and their flaws had a very realistic and well understood approach and presentation, and I truly felt the gravity of their unique situations.  NGThe gameplay is similar to pokemon, with more elaborate mechanics for catching different bugsnax. as you progress to new areas you unlock new tools that make the process gradually more complex until in some cases catching a snak feels like solving a puzzle. Catch bugsnax, complete quests, learn about your fellow villagers, and learn about what bugsnax are. ERAn unforgettable experience. 9/10

At some point, you can customise every single body part, and also decide what food appears there. You like customising? You like playing dollhouse with your Barbies?
